tool_diagnostics.message: apply_patch verification failed: invalid patch: The last line of the patch must be '*** End Patch'

row.note: Paul makes the omitted verb explicit: every word and deed is done in the Lord Jesus' name with thanksgiving. This is the commentary's portable opening formula applied to any act.
James corrects merchants' unqualified tomorrow plan with "if the Lord wills"; this closely parallels the commentary's extension of divine naming to future acts.
The Lord's Prayer first asks that the Father's name be hallowed before its petitions, comparable to Fatiha's unnamed act becoming praise, service, and request after the divine name.

row.basis: service and oath in God's name
row.note: The verse joins fearing and serving YHWH with swearing by his name, combining the commentary's worshiped owner, invocation, and oath functions of Allah's name.
The proclamation starts with YHWH's name and immediately names him compassionate and gracious; it is a close Biblical companion to "in the name of Allah, the Rahman, the Rahim."
Hebrew raḥum, used here for YHWH, is a Semitic cognate of the commentary's r-h-m mercy words; its setting makes mercy a named divine quality, not a free-standing sentiment.
The same name-proclamation preserves steadfast love and forgiveness yet does not clear guilt; it directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that expansive mercy does not abolish reckoning.

row.basis: meat and blood do not feed God
row.note: The psalm asks whether God eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood, a pointed parallel to the commentary's claim that sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God.
The sacrifice is praise, the verbal fruit that acknowledges God's name; it closely matches the commentary's movement from animal material to piety and named praise.
The text calls doing good and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God, giving a Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that the moral disposition of offerers, not animal flesh, reaches God.
At the authorized altar God makes his name remembered, receives offerings, and blesses; this joins the commentary's name-over-sacrifice with its claim that the name changes the ritual relation.

Israel is warned that joining a neighboring people's sacrifice and eating it draws one into their gods; this closely parallels food's altered status through a name, though the Torah narrates covenantal entanglement rather than the Qur'anic slaughter formula.
Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons and not to God, making the recipient decisive for communion just as the commentary makes the name over meat decisive for its ritual status.

Genesis commands Noah and all his household into the ark because of Noah's righteousness; beside the commentary's 11:45-46, its inclusion of the household sharpens the Qur'anic denial that descent alone secures Noah's son.
God remembers Noah, every beast, and the livestock in the ark and begins to subdue the flood; this is the Biblical rescue scene beside the commentary's journey enclosed by divine mercy.
First Peter identifies the few preserved through the floodwaters, keeping the ark's protected passage central to its retelling of Noah.
The author makes the floodwater correspond to baptism; this Christian rereading changes the commentary's ark-as-mercy enclosure into a rite that saves through Christ's resurrection.
Wisdom depicts Wisdom saving the righteous man by steering him on a small piece of wood when the earth flooded, a Jewish retelling of the voyage whose movement the commentary places under God's name.
Moses comes down, sees the calf and dancing, burns with anger, and throws the tablets; the scene directly accompanies the commentary's Musa, Harun, calf, anger, and later mercy sequence.
YHWH relents from the announced disaster after Moses' intercession. It gives the Biblical side of the commentary's movement from anger at the calf toward mercy.

The psalm uses the Hebrew r-ḥ-m verb for a father's compassion to children and then YHWH's compassion to those who fear him, closely matching the commentary's Rahim as mercy directed toward particular recipients.
YHWH's goodness is said to reach all and his compassion all he has made, a close textual partner for the commentary's Rahman as overflowing mercy that encompasses everything.

Jonah invokes God's gracious, compassionate, slow-to-anger character as the reason Nineveh may be spared; it makes the scope and scandal of divine mercy concrete alongside the commentary's universal Rahman.
The verse uses Hebrew reḥem, cognate with the commentary's rahim, while God describes bearing Israel from the womb onward; it tightly joins womb imagery to sustaining divine care.

Isaiah asks whether a mother can fail to have compassion for her womb-born child, then contrasts that possibility with God's unfailing remembrance. It gives a direct Biblical analogue for mercy's maternal, protective image.
The psalm credits God with forming the speaker's inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, matching the commentary's claim that the one named in 1:1 forms persons in wombs.
True worship includes feeding the hungry, housing the homeless, clothing the naked, and not hiding from one's own flesh; it joins the commentary's kinship-from-one-womb and mercy-as-concrete-good.
The Samaritan is moved with compassion and immediately tends the vulnerable stranger. This gives narrative form to the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that entails beneficent action.
Jesus commands disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful, an explicit movement from divine mercy to directed human practice like the commentary's Rahim.
Boaz blesses Ruth for seeking refuge beneath YHWH's wings; it offers a concrete Biblical image for the commentary's mercy as a place one enters for protection.
Jesus likens his desired gathering of Jerusalem to a hen gathering chicks under wings. The protective enclosure closely meets the commentary's womb-house image, while the refusal adds its boundary.
Approaching the divine throne yields mercy and grace for timely help, directly meeting the commentary's final pairing of Rahman with the one from whom help is sought.
The psalmist's help comes from YHWH, maker of heaven and earth; it is a concise Biblical partner for the commentary's musta'an and nasta'in connection.
YHWH declares "that is my name" and refuses his glory to another, a direct companion to the commentary's no-namesake claim and its empty rival names.
The prophet asks to whom God can be compared or likened. Its question closely meets the commentary's rhetorical question whether any being can carry God's name as an equal.
God identifies the divine name as the name to be remembered through generations; this provides a Biblical scene where divine self-naming makes invocation and memory possible.
The commentary's ilah/Allah explanation meets Hebrew elohenu, a Semitic cognate in Israel's confession that YHWH is one; the verse links cognate divine terminology to exclusive worship.

row.basis: no utterance of other gods' names
row.note: The command forbids mentioning other gods' names. It supplies a Torah counterpart to the commentary's contrast between Allah's name and names that lack divine warrant.
Paul says an idol has no real existence and that there is no God but one; it is a close Christian articulation of the commentary's empty names and single object of worship.

row.basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism, exalted name
row.note: Babel's builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower; Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, and the verse makes name, height, reputation, and self-exaltation a single scene.
God promises Abram a great name, a close narrative counterpart to the commentary's raising of remembrance as a divine gift rather than self-made reputation.

row.basis: God grants David a great name
row.note: God says he has made David's name great among the great ones of the earth. This supplies another named person whose elevated remembrance is bestowed rather than merely claimed.
The psalm calls YHWH's name majestic in all the earth and sets his splendor above the heavens, directly pairing exalted name with the commentary's horizon-and-sky imagery.
The moon is made for appointed times, a specific Biblical counterpart to the commentary's newly visible crescent as a temporal sign.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars not worshiped
row.note: The Torah forbids being drawn into worshiping the celestial host. It directly sits beside the commentary's images of moon and sun rising and its warning that a celestial body can be treated as a god.
God brings animals to the human to see what he will call them, and their names establish recognition. It is a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that learned names open knowledge.
One person writes "YHWH's" on his hand and takes Israel's name; name and written sign together mark membership, closely paralleling the commentary's name as an owner-identifying brand.
A mark is placed on the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations before judgment. It makes the commentary's visible sign of allegiance an instrument of recognition and protection.
God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before destructive judgment proceeds, a Christian development of the commentary's mark that identifies whose people are protected.
The Lamb's followers bear his name and the Father's name on their foreheads; this is an especially direct Christian image of a name functioning as a public mark of whose people they are.
The beast's mark or name controls buying and selling. It offers a contrary apocalyptic development of the commentary's mark/name motif: a rival name brands allegiance and changes permitted commerce.

Jacob's agreement assigns livestock by visible color markings, so a distinguishable animal becomes identifiable as his wage. This gives a concrete Biblical parallel to the commentary's branded camel known by its owner.
False swearing by YHWH's name profanes it, closely matching the commentary's treatment of the name as both an invoked refuge and a witness in an oath.

row.basis: calling on the name in distress
row.note: The psalmist calls on YHWH's name for deliverance, giving a Biblical prayer-act to place beside the commentary's name that attaches the speaker to its owner.

row.basis: calling on Lord's name for salvation
row.note: Paul makes calling on the Lord's name the stated means of salvation, an explicit Christian use of divine-name invocation as refuge.
The annunciation says Mary's child will be called Son of God. It directly contrasts with the commentary's use of womb-rooted Rahman while denying that Rahman takes a child.

John's soteriological claim that God gives the only Son gives a central Christian form of the proposition the commentary rejects when it says the merciful divine name does not entail divine childbearing.

row.basis: single baptismal name with Father, Son, Spirit
row.note: The baptismal command places Father, Son, and Holy Spirit under the name; beside the commentary's exclusive names of Allah and Rahman and denial of childship, its different name theology is the point.

row.basis: Jesus given the name above every name
row.note: Philippians says God grants Jesus the name above every name. It is a Christian reconfiguration of exalted name that must be read beside the commentary's insistence that no one can bear or rival God's name.

The enthronement psalm calls the king God's son on the day of decree; as royal or adoptive language rather than a birth narrative, it clarifies one Jewish background whose terminology differs from the commentary's categorical denial of divine child-taking.

row.basis: justice and steadfast love over ritual display
row.note: Micah answers sacrificial excess with doing justice, loving steadfast love, and walking humbly with God. It closely parallels the commentary's movement from animal matter to the worshiper's moral posture.
James says judgment without mercy falls on one who did not show mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this gives a focused Christian counterpart to the commentary's mercy and reckoning tension.

row.basis: golden calf reread as church warning
row.note: Paul quotes the calf episode to warn Corinthian believers against idolatry. This Christian reuse makes the commentary's Musa-and-calf scene an ongoing warning about rival worship.

row.basis: Creator forms life in the mother's womb
row.note: The mother tells her sons that God, not she, gave them life and ordered their elements in her womb. This Jewish text closely accompanies the commentary's divine formation and sustenance within rahim.

row.basis: letter written in a ruler's name
row.note: The royal order is written in the king's name and sealed with his signet; like the commentary's Solomon letter, sender, authority, and visible mark frame a document before its command is acted upon.
God stretches out the heavens like a curtain and spreads them as a tent. This is a specific Biblical meeting with the commentary's sky as the roof and shelter above an inhabited house.
A person plans a path, but YHWH directs the step. It is a concise Hebrew Bible analogue to the commentary's claim that an intended future act must remain tied to God's will.
Divine rain gives seed and bread by making earth sprout. It specifically meets the commentary's secondary sky-cloud-water-vegetation image, though it does not make that image a theory of names.
Jesus says the Father gives sun and rain to both righteous and unrighteous. This is a plausible Christian meeting with the commentary's rain as mercy and Rahman's wide reach.

row.basis: blessing before benefit and divine ownership
row.note: The Talmud treats benefit from the world without a blessing as misappropriating what belongs to the Holy One. It gives a Jewish rationale for the commentary's claim that naming God over food changes its relation to the eater.

row.basis: all deeds for the sake of Heaven
row.note: The maxim that all one's deeds should be for the sake of Heaven offers a Jewish ethical analogue to the commentary's ellipsis, where whatever act follows is placed under God's name.

row.basis: fetus in a protected and taught womb
row.note: The passage imagines the fetus within the womb under divine care and instruction before birth. It develops the commentary's rahim as a sustaining interior home, though through rabbinic imagination rather than the Qur'anic wordplay.

row.basis: meal thanksgiving for the holy name
row.note: The post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for the holy name made to dwell in believers' hearts. It provides an early Christian liturgical parallel for placing food and thanksgiving under a divine name.

row.ref: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 6
row.note: Cyprian argues from Noah's ark that salvation is not found outside the Church. This makes an ecclesial boundary out of the commentary's ark-as-protective-mercy image.
David answers Goliath that he comes in the name of YHWH before acting in battle. It is a direct Hebrew Bible instance of a concrete, otherwise ordinary act explicitly placed under the divine name.
Peter commands the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ. This supplies a New Testament instance of the commentary's bi-ism relation functioning as the means or accompaniment of an act.
The name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are protected. It closely joins the commentary's divine name, Noah's protective enclosure, and mercy as a place of refuge.

row.basis: putting the name upon a people
row.note: The priests put YHWH's name upon Israel and God blesses them. This makes the name an identifying, protective inscription on a community, extending the commentary's owner-mark image.
The command not to profane YHWH's holy name but to sanctify it among Israel gives a Torah counterpart to the commentary's raised name and to prayer's opening hallowing of God.

row.basis: name dwelling where offerings are brought
row.note: The sanctuary is the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, and Israel brings its offerings there. This directly joins named divine presence, a house, and the sacrificial animals discussed in the commentary.

The text directs Israel's slaughtered animals to be brought to YHWH as sacrifices rather than left in the open field. It is a concrete Torah companion to the commentary's meat whose ritual character depends on the one named over it.

Food is said to be sanctified through God's word and prayer. This offers a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that the divine reference over food changes its status without changing its substance.

row.basis: food entering a person and defilement
row.note: Jesus says that what enters from outside cannot defile a person. Read beside the commentary's named-slaughter material, it supplies a focused alternative account of how food is or is not religiously altered.

YHWH desires steadfast love and knowledge of God rather than sacrifice. Its contrast closely supports the commentary's claim that moral God-consciousness, not animal material, is what matters in offering.

The makers of the calf name it as the god or gods who brought Israel from Egypt. This is the core Biblical scene behind the commentary's calf episode, where a manufactured object displaces the merciful Lord.

row.basis: who belongs to YHWH after the calf
row.note: Moses' call, "Who is for YHWH?", turns the calf crisis into a test of exclusive allegiance. It sharpens the commentary's link between the divine name, worship, and refusal of rival names.

Job describes the heart being enticed by the shining sun or splendid moon and the hand sent a kiss. It gives a vivid Hebrew Bible parallel to the commentary's celestial images and its warning against treating them as gods.
God places the lights in the sky for signs, appointed times, days, and years. This is a creation account counterpart to the commentary's visible crescent as a calendrical sign.

row.basis: pain in carrying and giving birth
row.note: The woman's pain in childbearing gives a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the womb that bears and nourishes also bears the cost of birth.
A nearest relative is charged to redeem a brother's land when he becomes poor. This gives legal concreteness to the commentary's move from common womb to obligations of kinship.

God's compassion is stirred while anger against Ephraim is held back. It closely accompanies the commentary's Rahman/Rahim and wrath tension, especially its calf scene in which anger turns toward mercy.
Paul says that all have been enclosed in disobedience so that God may have mercy on all. This gives a Christian formulation of mercy's widest scope while retaining an account of disobedience.

row.basis: Son sent and born of a woman
row.note: Paul says God sent his Son, born of a woman. The verse pairs divine sonship with human birth and therefore stands directly beside the commentary's womb-rooted mercy and rejection of divine child-taking.
The name of the God of Jacob protects the petitioner in a day of trouble. This is a separate Biblical instance of the commentary's name as a refuge rather than only an address or oath.
Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name. It gives a specifically Christian development of the commentary's idea that entry under the divine name is a sphere of preservation.

row.basis: teaching as rain that makes growth
row.note: Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on grass and vegetation. It meets the commentary's secondary cloud-water-growth image and its association of divine instruction with life-giving nurture.

row.basis: voyage brought to a desired haven
row.note: After the storm is quieted, God brings sailors to their desired haven. This is a concrete Biblical meeting with the commentary's concern for a ship's movement and its safe coming to rest.

row.basis: sign on hand, memorial, and speech
row.note: The exodus observance is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction is in the mouth. It brings together visible mark, remembrance, and spoken devotion in a way that complements the commentary's name-as-sign.

row.basis: mercy attributes recited as a prayer order
row.note: The Talmud portrays God showing Moses the order for invoking the mercy attributes when Israel sins. This makes the Exodus mercy-name formula a repeated liturgical opening, a close Jewish interpretive companion to the recited Fatiha.

row.basis: mercy toward creatures and mercy from heaven
row.note: The maxim that one who has mercy on creatures receives mercy from Heaven turns divine compassion into a directed human ethic, parallel to the commentary's Rahim as mercy reaching particular vulnerable beings.

row.basis: witnessed appearance of the new moon
row.note: The mishnah's procedure for father-and-son witnesses who saw the new moon makes communal testimony depend on the newly visible lunar form. It is a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's rising crescent becoming a recognized sign.
The source commentary centers Allah’s name with Raḥmān/Raḥīm; Exodus has YHWH self-identify as compassionate and gracious, using the Hebrew RḤM cognate in the same divine-name formula.
The commentary links Raḥīm to the womb as a sheltering home; Isaiah asks whether a mother can withhold compassion from the child of her womb, joining the womb image to the RḤM root.
The commentary treats God’s name as a mark identifying the work or creature as belonging to its bearer; the priestly blessing says God’s name is placed on Israel and blesses them.
The commentary connects invoking God’s name with animal offerings; the psalmist makes a thank offering while calling on YHWH’s name, joining liturgical offering and invocation.
The source commentary’s Arabic bism means beginning an act by God’s name; Abram builds an altar and calls in YHWH’s name, a close Hebrew name-invocation formula.
The source labels Allah as the worshipped one and bismillah as name-invocation; Daniel blesses the name of God in Aramaic, using the cognate Elaha for God and linking name, praise, wisdom, and power.
The commentary says expansive mercy does not erase account or judgment; the continuation of the name formula says God forgives while not simply clearing guilt, holding mercy and consequence together.
Jonah cites YHWH’s compassionate, gracious character to explain his flight from the mission; the same RḤM name formula shows mercy reaching even Nineveh, which Jonah resents.
The commentary joins God’s name to mercy and kinship; Jacob asks El Shaddai to grant compassion as his sons travel into danger, with the Hebrew RḤM word directed toward brothers and family.
The source commentary describes mercy through the womb’s care for a helpless child; the true mother’s compassion rises for the living infant and makes her surrender him rather than see him killed.
The commentary presents Rahīm as compassion directed to particular recipients; God speaks of Ephraim as a dear child and says divine compassion is stirred toward him, using the RḤM root.
The commentary distinguishes mercy’s overflowing source from its particular recipients; God says mercy and grace are shown to whom God chooses, with the Hebrew RḤM cognate.
The commentary describes the womb as sustaining a child who cannot ask or repay; the psalm compares YHWH’s compassion to a father’s compassion for children.

row.basis: The Arabic and Hebrew mercy roots
row.note: The commentary’s source label is Arabic ر ح م; Exodus uses Hebrew רַחוּם for God’s compassion. The cognate shows the attribute in its own covenantal declaration, not merely a similar sound.

row.basis: Sun and moon as objects of worship
row.note: The commentary recalls Abraham testing the rising star, moon, and sun and rejecting them when they set; Job names gazing at sun or moon in splendor as the setup for a forbidden act of worship.
The commentary contrasts Allah’s name with a sun treated as divine; Job specifies the hand-kiss that would follow an inwardly enticed heart, making the bodily act of astral devotion explicit.

row.basis: Worship of celestial bodies as disloyalty
row.note: The commentary’s Abraham scene withdraws divine status from a setting star; Job calls sun or moon worship a denial of the God above, supplying the same reversal in an oath.
The commentary distinguishes Allah’s name from empty names assigned to idols; Elijah makes rival groups call on their gods’ names and lets the answer by fire reveal which is truly God.
The commentary contrasts God’s substantial name with names assigned to powerless gods; Isaiah joins YHWH’s self-declared name to refusal to give divine glory to idols.
The commentary says idols are names assigned by people without divine warrant; Jeremiah says the gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish, contrasting them with the Creator.
The commentary cites Aaron warning Israel that the calf is a test and that their Lord is Rahman; Exodus instead has Aaron take their gold and fashion the calf, a sharp difference in the same episode.
The commentary describes Moses returning angry from the calf and throwing down the tablets; Exodus narrates the same action when Moses sees the calf and the dancing.

The commentary presents Aaron warning the people against the calf while Moses challenges him; Exodus has Aaron explain that he cast the gold into the fire and the calf came out, assigning Aaron a different role.

The commentary stresses that Noah’s son refuses the ark and that safety is not inherited by blood; Genesis lists Noah, his sons, and their wives entering, without an estranged son in the passenger scene.
The commentary places the voyage and its beginning under God’s name and mercy; Genesis says YHWH shut Noah in, making divine protection rather than Noah’s invocation the explicit safeguard.
The commentary unpacks Noah’s phrase for the ark’s movement and anchoring as a whole journey under God’s name; Genesis narrates the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat after the flood.
The commentary pairs Noah’s embarkation formula with praise and a request for a blessed landing; after leaving the ark, Genesis has Noah build an altar and offer burnt offerings.
The commentary begins with God’s name and mercy; the Talmud reads Exodus 34:6–7 as a ritual order of divine attributes that Israel can recite when seeking forgiveness.
The commentary reads the Fātiḥa’s opening name as leading into praise, service, and request for guidance; the Talmud says prayer should begin with praise of God before petition.

The commentary says animal flesh and blood do not reach God, but piety does; the psalm says God’s desired sacrifice is a broken and contrite spirit, distinguishing inward devotion from ritual material.
The commentary treats sacrifice as meaningful only under God’s name and with piety; Hosea says God desires steadfast love rather than sacrifice, giving the ethical quality priority over the offering.
The commentary contrasts the animal’s meat and blood with the worshipper’s piety; Micah begins by asking whether burnt offerings and year-old calves can satisfy God.

row.basis: Thousands of rams do not suffice
row.note: The commentary says sacrificial quantity is not what reaches God; Micah escalates to thousands of rams and rivers of oil, then even a firstborn, exposing the insufficiency of material offering.
The commentary identifies piety rather than meat or blood as what reaches God; Micah answers the sacrifice questions with justice, covenant love, and walking humbly with God.
The commentary makes the worshipper’s God-conscious piety decisive; Samuel says listening to YHWH is better than sacrifice and obedience better than sacrificial fat.
The commentary’s brand image says a mark identifies the animal’s owner; Isaiah says God called Israel by name and that Israel belongs to God.

row.basis: A mark that identifies and protects
row.note: The commentary describes a brand as an identifying trace that distinguishes its bearer; Ezekiel marks the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem’s evils so they are spared in judgment.

row.basis: A divine name on the forehead
row.note: The commentary develops the name as an identifying mark; the high priest wears an engraved plate reading holy to YHWH on his forehead while serving with Israel’s offerings.
The commentary says a name raises the named person’s remembrance; God promises to make Abram’s name great, using name for public standing rather than a mere label.
The commentary joins slaughtered animals, a sign, and protection; Exodus directs Israel to put the Passover lamb’s blood on doorposts as a visible sign for the household.

row.basis: The sign and protection from death
row.note: The commentary connects an identifying mark with refuge; Exodus says the blood-marked houses will be passed over when the plague strikes Egypt.
The commentary develops the crescent’s first appearance as a visible time marker and cites pilgrimage timing; Numbers orders trumpet blasts at new moons and festivals as Israel’s calendar signals.
The commentary links mercy to rain that reaches dead ground and brings forth growth; Isaiah compares rain and snow watering earth and making it sprout to God’s life-giving word.
The commentary connects the name formula with conditional speech about future action; James says plans should be stated as what one will do if the Lord wills and one lives.

row.basis: Every act done in the Lord’s name
row.note: The commentary says the missing verb in bismillah is supplied by whatever the speaker is doing; Paul explicitly extends action in the Lord Jesus’ name to every word and deed, with thanksgiving.
The commentary says invocation changes how food is received and used; the letter says every created thing is good when received with thanksgiving to God.
The commentary links naming God with the status of food; the letter says food is sanctified through God’s word and prayer, a Christian meal practice with a different rule from Qur’anic slaughter.
The commentary says meat is not to be eaten when God’s name was not invoked; Paul tells Christians to eat market meat without raising questions of conscience, showing a different criterion.

The commentary makes the invoked name decisive for meat; Paul tells a believer to abstain when someone identifies meat as sacrificial, because of that person’s conscience rather than absence of God’s name.

row.basis: Eating and drinking for God’s glory
row.note: The commentary describes food as transformed by naming God; Paul says eating and drinking alike should be done for God’s glory, giving an explicit Christian frame for ordinary meals.

row.basis: Prayer begins by hallowing the Name
row.note: The commentary says the opening name leads into the Fātiḥa’s praise, service, and request; Jesus’ prayer begins with the Father’s name being hallowed before petitions for provision and forgiveness.

row.basis: A gift because the recipient bears the Name
row.note: The commentary’s brand image identifies who owns the bearer; Jesus promises that a cup of water given because someone belongs to Christ will not lose its reward.

row.basis: The Name exalted above every name
row.note: The commentary explains the name as raised into prominence and uniqueness; Paul says God exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, a Christian confession with a distinct account of divine naming.
The commentary uses Noah’s ark as the refuge in which mercy protects some while others perish; Peter recalls eight people saved through water in Noah’s ark.

The commentary treats entry into Noah’s ark as rescue under divine mercy; Peter interprets the flood’s water typologically through baptism, adding a Christian account of the ark’s saving significance.

The commentary says all who come under Rahman’s mercy are servants, not children of God; Luke’s annunciation calls the child conceived by divine action the Son of God, marking a real difference in theological language.
The commentary says the worshipper’s piety, not sacrificial meat and blood, reaches God; Jesus quotes the prophetic preference for mercy over sacrifice while calling sinners.
The commentary’s stamp image says a name marks who owns the bearer; Revelation depicts the Lamb’s people with his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.
The commentary presents Raḥmān and Raḥīm as divine mercy’s source and reach; the psalm repeats the Hebrew RḤM adjective with grace, patience, and abundant steadfast love.

The commentary holds mercy together with reckoning; Moses invokes the compassionate-name formula after Israel’s rebellion and asks God to forgive while the verse also names consequences across generations.
The commentary explains a name as elevated remembrance and good public report; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than precious oil, treating the name as reputation.

row.basis: Calling to God during a storm
row.note: The commentary places Noah’s ship under God’s name through its motion and rest; the sailors in the psalm cry to YHWH from a storm-tossed ship.
The commentary stresses both the ark’s journey and its anchoring; the psalm says God brings storm-tossed sailors to their desired harbor, a sea-voyage counterpart without making it Noah’s story.
The commentary describes the womb as the child’s protected home and relates its growth to God’s nurturing; the psalm says God formed the speaker in the womb.
The commentary distinguishes overflowing mercy from its direction to individual recipients; the psalm calls YHWH compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and great in steadfast love.
The commentary reads the divine name as having no namesake or rival; David says there is no God besides YHWH and no one like him.
The commentary develops the question whether God has a namesake or equal; Isaiah says there is no one like God and no other God, a direct theological counterpart.

The commentary connects the unspoken verb of bismillah with whatever work a speaker begins and cites a warning about future plans; James addresses people planning travel, trade, and profit for tomorrow.
The commentary says the work is not self-contained but begins under God’s name; James reminds planners that they do not know what tomorrow brings and that life is brief.

The commentary prohibits meat offered under another god’s name; the Jerusalem decree tells Gentile believers to avoid food sacrificed to idols and blood, preserving a related but differently framed boundary.
The commentary ties the name over an act to its proper religious meaning; Jesus repeats the preference for mercy over sacrifice while defending hungry disciples’ action on the Sabbath.
The commentary pictures mercy as a parent’s active care for a dependent child; the father sees his returning son, is moved with compassion, and runs to embrace him before any repayment.

row.basis: Mercy belongs to God to give
row.note: The commentary distinguishes abundant mercy from its direction to recipients; Paul quotes God’s words to Moses that mercy is shown according to God’s choice, using the same scriptural basis as Exodus 33:19.
The commentary explains a brand as a visible mark identifying the bearer and protecting what is marked; Revelation commands the servants of God to be sealed on their foreheads before judgment.
After declaring the compassionate divine name, Moses asks God to go among Israel, pardon its iniquity, and take it as an inheritance; this makes mercy an active covenantal presence.
Solomon asks God to forgive exiles and grant them compassion before their captors, using the RḤM root; this makes Raḥīm protection concrete for a vulnerable people.
The commentary describes mercy as shelter and as directed care; Moses promises that after exile God will have compassion on Israel and gather the scattered, using the RḤM root.
David chooses to fall into YHWH’s hand because divine mercies are great, rather than into human hands; this links RḤM mercy to the protection and refuge described in the commentary.
The commentary connects Rahman’s name with the Fātiḥa’s request for help; the psalm says Israel’s help is in YHWH’s name, the maker of heaven and earth.

row.basis: The Name as a safe place
row.note: The commentary puts the ark and the womb under the protection of God’s name and mercy; Proverbs says YHWH’s name is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe.

row.basis: The place where God’s Name dwells
row.note: The commentary links animals offered at the House with the name spoken over them; Deuteronomy sends Israel to the place God chooses to make his name dwell.

row.basis: Offerings brought to the named place
row.note: The commentary describes animals separated from the herd and brought to the House under God’s name; Deuteronomy lists sacrifices and firstlings brought to the place chosen for YHWH’s name.

row.basis: A ram offered in place of a son
row.note: The commentary considers the status of sacrificial animals and their relation to God; in the binding of Isaac, Abraham offers a ram instead of his son, making the animal’s offering inseparable from a threatened life.

row.basis: God rejects offerings without right conduct
row.note: The commentary says meat and blood do not reach God while piety does; Isaiah has God reject abundant burnt offerings in a community whose worship is disconnected from justice.
The commentary locates the value of offering in the worshipper’s piety; Isaiah turns from rejected sacrifices to washing, ceasing evil, and cleansing conduct.
The commentary says what reaches God is not sacrificial flesh but the worshipper’s God-consciousness; Isaiah specifies justice for the oppressed, orphan, and widow as the required response.
The commentary subordinates sacrificial material to piety; Amos says God will not accept Israel’s burnt offerings and grain offerings in a community facing judgment.
The commentary makes devotion visible in the worshipper rather than the animal’s flesh and blood; Amos follows rejected offerings with a demand that justice flow like water.

The commentary says invoking God’s name changes the status of food; the Mishnah prescribes a blessing before eating different kinds of food, a Jewish table practice that places ordinary eating under God’s name.
The commentary connects God’s name to whether food may be eaten; the Talmud says one may not benefit from the world without a blessing, directly linking invocation to eating.
The commentary’s Raḥmān and Raḥīm name God’s mercy and forgiveness; Sirach says the Lord is compassionate and merciful, forgives sins, and saves in distress.

The commentary distinguishes overflowing mercy from its direction to recipients; Sirach contrasts human compassion for a neighbor with the Lord’s compassion for all living beings and a shepherd’s care for the flock.
The commentary says divine mercy encompasses everything; Wisdom says God has mercy on all because God can do all things and patiently allows sinners to repent.

row.basis: Creation belongs to its merciful Lord
row.note: The commentary links the name with mercy toward creatures; Wisdom says God spares all because all are God’s, adding belonging to universal mercy.
The commentary holds mercy together with judgment; Nehemiah’s communal confession recalls rebellion and calls God ready to pardon, gracious, and merciful, using the RḤM formula.

The commentary describes expansive mercy that does not erase moral reckoning; Joel uses the compassionate-name formula to call Israel to return, with God’s relenting from calamity as the hoped-for response.
The commentary says Raḥīm turns toward particular people; Hezekiah promises that returning exiles’ kin may find compassion because YHWH is gracious and merciful and will not turn away.
The commentary joins mercy to God’s name and care for those under it; Moses says YHWH is a merciful God who will not abandon Israel or forget the covenant, using the RḤM root.

row.basis: A deed begun in YHWH’s Name
row.note: The commentary says the speaker puts God’s name before the action; David tells Goliath that he comes against him in the name of YHWH, making the name the declared authority for a concrete deed.
The commentary opens with God’s name and leads into praise; Mary’s song says the Mighty One has done great things and his name is holy, placing the Name in a liturgical act of thanksgiving.
The commentary joins God’s name with mercy; Mary’s song immediately describes mercy extending through generations to those who fear God, making the two themes part of one praise sequence.
The commentary treats God’s name as a mark that identifies and claims the bearer; Jesus commands baptism into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian ritual that marks belonging.

row.basis: Communion limited to the baptized in the Name
row.note: The commentary links God’s name to food’s religious status; the Didache says only the baptized into the Lord’s name may eat or drink the Eucharist, making the Name a boundary for a sacred meal.

row.basis: Thanksgiving for the holy Name at the meal
row.note: The commentary places food and praise under God’s name; the Didache’s post-meal thanksgiving blesses God for the holy Name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
The commentary says the divine name accompanies a concrete action; Peter tells the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ, making the Name the stated means of the act.

row.basis: Calling on the Lord’s Name for rescue
row.note: The commentary connects God’s name with seeking help and protection; Peter quotes Joel that everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved, applying the invocation to deliverance.

row.basis: The one who comes in the Lord’s Name
row.note: The commentary describes the Name at the threshold of a journey and cites a letter identified by sender and divine Name; the crowd welcomes Jesus with the scriptural blessing for the one who comes in the Lord’s name.
The commentary distinguishes piety from animal flesh and blood; Peter describes believers as a priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
The commentary reads rain and fruitful earth as signs of mercy that feed life; Paul says God gave rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness as testimony to divine goodness.
The commentary contrasts God’s living name with human-assigned empty divine names; Paul says an idol is nothing and that there is no God but one.
The commentary keeps Rahman’s mercy in view alongside the Day of Judgment; James says mercy triumphs over judgment, making mercy’s role at judgment explicit.

The commentary presents Harun warning Israel rather than endorsing the calf; Rashi reads Aaron’s announcement of a festival “tomorrow” as an attempt to delay the people until Moses returned, mitigating Aaron’s role in the parallel episode.

row.basis: Mercy invoked by an individual petitioner
row.note: The commentary describes Raḥīm as compassion directed toward a recipient; the psalmist calls on the merciful, gracious, patient God while asking for personal mercy and rescue.
The commentary presents Rahman’s mercy as encompassing creation; the psalm says YHWH is good to all and has compassion over all his works.
The commentary says the missing verb in bismillah is supplied by the act being undertaken; Moses tells God he has spoken to Pharaoh in God’s name, a specific speech act placed under the Name.

row.basis: A people publicly identified by the Name
row.note: The commentary’s brand image makes a mark identify its bearer; Deuteronomy says the nations will see that Israel is called by YHWH’s name and fear them.

row.basis: Stars as created signs, not gods
row.note: The commentary recalls Abraham considering the star, moon, and sun as possible lords before rejecting them; Genesis has God point to the stars as a promise of descendants, giving celestial bodies a created sign-function instead of divine status.

The commentary connects Raḥīm with the womb and bodily care; Luke speaks of the tender compassion of God using an inward-organ image, then pictures dawn visiting from on high. The Greek image is a motif, not a cognate.
The commentary connects invocation and food; the Didache begins its Eucharistic thanksgiving over the cup, showing a communal meal opened by blessing and gratitude.

row.basis: The worshipper as a living offering
row.note: The commentary says piety, rather than meat and blood, reaches God; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice, making devotion itself the offering.

row.basis: Praise as a sacrifice of the lips
row.note: The commentary’s opening name leads into praise and service; Hebrews calls continual praise, confessing God’s name, a sacrifice offered through Jesus.

The commentary says sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God, while piety does; Hebrews says animal blood cannot take away sins and directs its argument toward Christ’s offering, a different account of sacrifice’s efficacy.
The commentary says Allah’s name identifies the sole one worthy of worship; Paul confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, while distinguishing the Christian formulation.
The commentary describes compassion as active kindness toward the vulnerable; Jesus blesses the merciful with the promise that they will receive mercy.

row.basis: Mercy not earned by human effort
row.note: The commentary says sacrificial material does not reach God but piety does; Paul’s continuation says mercy does not depend on human willing or running but on God’s mercy, a distinct account of agency and merit.

tool_diagnostics.message: apply_patch verification failed: Failed to find expected lines in /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/sec1/luna/list.tsv:

row.note: Abraham’s servant says YHWH led him by the right road to his master’s kin; this gives the commentary’s pairing of showing a road and its destination a literal travel scene.

row.basis: cloud and fire go before Israel
row.note: YHWH leads the people through the wilderness with a column before them; the route is a community following its guide.

row.basis: God goes ahead to find a camp
row.note: The verse says God went before Israel on the way and sought a place to camp, joining precedence with the destination of rest.
The ark goes ahead for three days to seek a resting place for Israel, closely matching a guide who leads a group toward where the road ends.

row.basis: ark leads on an unfamiliar way
row.note: Israel is told to follow the ark so it can know which way to go, since it has not passed that way before; guidance makes an unknown route traversable.

row.basis: messenger sent ahead on the way
row.note: God sends a messenger before Israel to guard them on the road and bring them to a prepared place, combining the guide’s precedence with a known destination.

row.basis: wanderers cannot find a dwelling city
row.note: The travelers lose their way in the wilderness and find no city to live in; this makes the commentary’s image of failing to find both road and home concrete.

row.basis: God leads to a city by a straight way
row.note: After wandering, the travelers are led on a straight route to an inhabited city; road, guidance, straightness, and home converge in one verse.

row.basis: ancient road and a walkable good way
row.note: At a crossroads the people are told to ask for old paths, find the good way, and walk in it; the inherited road has already been trodden and must be continued.
The returning people are told to set up waymarks and guideposts on the highway home; this is a direct counterpart to signs that help a traveler recover direction.

row.basis: blind travelers led on unknown paths
row.note: God promises to lead the blind by paths they do not know, turn darkness to light, and smooth rough places; the text reverses being lost and unable to proceed.

row.basis: highway where travelers do not stray
row.note: The holy highway leads the redeemed toward Zion, and even a fool will not lose the way; the route supplies the destination and protects against the commentary’s lost traveler.

row.basis: voice identifies the way and forbids turns
row.note: A voice tells the traveler, “This is the way; walk in it,” when turning right or left; it makes guidance an ongoing correction against leaving the route.
The shepherd leads the speaker along paths of righteousness, joining a guide who goes ahead with the communal and ethical road in the commentary.
The speaker asks God to make the divine ways known and teach the paths; this is a direct prayer for the commentary’s first movement, having the route shown.
The speaker asks God to lead him in truth; it adds active guidance to the commentary’s request to be taken along a known route.

row.basis: light leads to the divine dwelling
row.note: The speaker asks for light and truth to lead him to the holy mountain and dwelling; a guiding marker and the road’s destination meet in one prayer.

row.basis: lamp at the feet and light on the path
row.note: The divine word illuminates the traveler’s feet and path, a concrete scriptural image for signs that allow a person to keep direction.
The promise that God will make the paths straight connects acknowledgment of God with a route made traversable and direct.

row.basis: do not turn right or left
row.note: The instruction is to keep one’s foot from evil and not swerve to either side; it gives the commentary’s straight line and refusal to deviate an ethical form.
These people abandon upright paths and walk in dark ways; the contrast supplies a specific scriptural picture of turning away from the straight route.

row.basis: apparently right way ends in death
row.note: A way that seems right leads to death; the destination tests the apparent route, complementing the commentary’s insistence that knowing a way includes knowing where it leads.

row.basis: lost sheep and a search for return
row.note: The speaker calls himself a straying sheep and asks God to seek him; this is a close image of a lost traveler needing the guide to bring him back.

row.basis: each sheep turns to its own way
row.note: All the people have gone astray, each turning to a separate way; the verse links losing the route with communal dispersal.

row.basis: lost sheep, misleading shepherds, forgotten fold
row.note: Israel is pictured as lost sheep whose shepherds turned them aside until they forgot their fold; wrong guidance ends in losing both route and home.

row.basis: scattered sheep on mountains without a shepherd
row.note: The flock wanders over mountains and hills and is scattered because no one searches for it; this supplies a concrete communal counterpart to dispersion and lost direction.

row.basis: two paths and their different ends
row.note: The Lord knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes; the verse makes a community’s road a moral course with distinct outcomes.

row.basis: Hebrew עבד and Arabic ع ب د
row.note: The Arabic root label ع ب د belongs to the commentary, while the Hebrew verb עבד here means serving God; the cognate appears in a verse that also commands walking in God’s ways.

row.basis: serving God joined to walking in his ways
row.note: The verse places wholehearted service beside walking in all God’s ways, giving the commentary’s worship-as-a-walked path a direct ethical counterpart.

row.basis: Aramaic דִּינָא in the judgment scene
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن; Daniel’s Aramaic cognate appears as the court sits for judgment and the books open, grounding the judgment sense associated with the Day of Reckoning.

row.basis: nations taught divine paths and walking together
row.note: Many peoples come to learn God’s ways and walk in them; the route is explicitly a shared path of a gathered community.

row.basis: leading the people to a holy abode
row.note: The song says God led the redeemed people toward the dwelling-place of holiness, joining guidance to arrival at a home.

row.basis: Raphael knows the road and guides Tobias
row.note: Tobias seeks a companion who knows the route, and Raphael offers to go because he knows the roads; this is a literal guide-and-traveler scene.

row.basis: cloud seen over the mountain as a sign
row.note: The midrash reads Abraham’s distant sight of Moriah as a cloud attached to the mountain; it makes the destination visible as a waymark during the journey.

row.basis: star goes ahead and stops at the destination
row.note: The star leads the travelers in front of them and stops over the place of the child; it joins a celestial sign, a guide’s precedence, and arrival.

row.basis: shepherd walks ahead of the sheep
row.note: The shepherd goes before the flock and the sheep follow his voice, matching the commentary’s guide defined by leading from the front.

row.basis: the Father’s house as the destination
row.note: Jesus speaks of many dwelling places in his Father’s house and says he goes to prepare a place; this makes the destination part of knowing the way.

row.basis: Thomas does not know the way to the destination
row.note: Thomas says they do not know where Jesus is going and therefore cannot know the way; the exchange dramatizes the commentary’s link between route knowledge and knowing the house.

row.basis: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
row.note: The destination is the Father, while Jesus calls himself the way to it; this is a Christian formulation in which the guide and route are one.

row.basis: guiding feet into the way of peace
row.note: The hymn says the dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, directly joining a guide, bodily walking, and a named route.

row.basis: a broad road leads to destruction
row.note: The broad entrance and road lead to destruction; it gives the commentary’s contrast between a single right path and ways that end elsewhere a specific image.

row.basis: a narrow way leads to life
row.note: The narrow way leads to life and few find it, pairing a difficult route with its destination and the people who find it.

row.basis: following the light prevents walking in darkness
row.note: Jesus says the follower will not walk in darkness but have the light of life; this ties following a guide to avoiding the lost traveler’s darkness.

row.basis: shepherd searches for a sheep that strayed
row.note: The shepherd goes after the one lost sheep until he finds it; this is a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s person who has lost the way.

row.basis: straying sheep return to their shepherd
row.note: The readers were straying like sheep and have now returned to the shepherd and guardian; the route from loss to restored guidance is explicit.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way for error
row.note: The false teachers leave the straight way and go astray after Balaam; it directly depicts abandoning the route and its ethical course.

row.basis: a wanderer is turned back from error
row.note: A person who wanders from the truth is brought back by another; the passage gives the commentary’s companions calling the lost traveler a communal form.

row.basis: the followers are called people of the Way
row.note: Saul seeks those who belong to the Way; the path is the name of a community, not merely an individual direction.

row.basis: a traveler asks for someone to guide him
row.note: On the road, the Ethiopian says he cannot understand without a guide, and Philip joins him to interpret the text; this makes guidance both travel and instruction.

row.basis: Jesus enters ahead as a forerunner
row.note: Jesus goes into the sanctuary as a forerunner on behalf of others; the text directly connects precedence with leading people toward a destination.
At the Son of Man’s judgment, people are separated as a shepherd divides sheep from goats; this adds the day’s sorting of communities to the commentary’s divided paths.

row.basis: judgment accounts for deeds done in life
row.note: All appear before the judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, connecting the commentary’s Day of Reckoning with a person’s lived course.

row.basis: Abraham obeys without knowing the destination
row.note: Hebrews says Abraham set out without knowing where he was going; this counterpoint qualifies the commentary’s image of guidance that includes knowing the road’s destination, since faithful following can precede that knowledge.

row.basis: prepare a straight road in the wilderness
row.note: Mark applies the call to prepare the Lord’s way and make paths straight; the route is cleared for the Lord’s arrival, adding a preparatory road to the commentary’s walkable path.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The teaching opens by distinguishing a way of life from a way of death; it places the commentary’s contrast between the guided path and its opposite in early Christian moral instruction.

row.basis: two ways of light and darkness
row.note: Barnabas describes two ways, light and darkness, under different authorities; this makes the competing routes a community’s ethical and spiritual allegiance.
The Community Rule assigns people to opposing spirits and ways of righteousness or perversity; it gives the commentary’s favored community versus those led astray a sectarian map of competing routes.

row.basis: one perilous passage to the inherited city
row.note: Ezra’s angel explains that reaching the city requires passing through a narrow way between dangers; the destination is accessible only by the difficult route.

row.basis: God chooses a longer route to avoid return
row.note: God does not lead Israel by the nearest road because danger might make them turn back to Egypt; the chosen path is a concrete route shaped to keep travelers on course.

row.basis: walking God’s way as sustained practice
row.note: Israel is told to keep God’s commandments and walk in his ways; this gives the commentary’s secondary image of a route maintained through repeated conduct a covenant setting.

row.basis: walking in God’s ways leads to life
row.note: The command to love God and walk in his ways is joined to living and flourishing; it makes the moral route a practiced choice with consequences.

row.basis: walking, standing, and sitting as a settled pattern
row.note: The verse traces a person’s association with wicked counsel from walking to standing to sitting; it gives the commentary’s secondary sense of a route as a gradually settled pattern.

row.basis: path of life and its destination
row.note: God makes known the path of life, whose endpoint is joy in God’s presence; this is a specific path-and-destination image without a guide walking ahead.

row.basis: walking in the midst of paths of justice
row.note: Wisdom says she walks in the way of righteousness, in the midst of paths of justice; the wording offers a concrete counterpart to the commentary’s road-center image.

row.basis: keeping to the way without turning aside
row.note: Job says his foot has held to God’s steps and he has kept the way without turning aside; it links following a track with continued fidelity.

row.basis: teach me your way so I can walk in truth
row.note: The prayer asks God to teach the way and unite the speaker’s heart to serve God; it joins route instruction to worshipful commitment.
The song says the Lord alone led Israel, with no foreign god beside him; it gives the favored community a single guide for its journey.

row.basis: the household must keep the way of the Lord
row.note: Abraham is chosen to direct his descendants to keep the Lord’s way by doing justice and righteousness; the road is transmitted through a community and its practice.

row.basis: straight highway prepared through the wilderness
row.note: A voice calls for a way to be prepared and a highway made straight in the desert; the relation is the route-clearing image, though this verse emphasizes preparation for God’s coming.

row.basis: Isaiah’s straight-way call applied to the Lord’s arrival
row.note: Mark uses the wilderness highway text to frame John’s preparation of the Lord’s way; it makes the route a communal expectation of arrival.

row.basis: sheep distressed and scattered without a shepherd
row.note: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image links a scattered people with the need for a guide, though it does not itself describe their road.
The wilderness generation is described as always going astray in heart and not knowing God’s ways; the passage links lost direction with failure to know the divine route.

row.basis: Christ as the way to the Father
row.note: Augustine reads Jesus’s “I am the way” as Christ himself mediating access to the Father; this interprets the route-and-destination relation as a person rather than a road.
The testament contrasts good and evil ways and the dispositions that choose them; it is a specific Jewish two-route parallel, though its verse divisions vary between editions.

row.basis: he heavenly lights serve as signs
row.note: Genesis assigns the lights signs for seasons and days, not route guidance; this is a limited counterpart to the commentary’s stars as travelers’ markers and keeps the two uses distinct.

row.basis: staff carried through a dangerous valley
row.note: The speaker’s rod and staff comfort him while walking through the valley, a concrete staff-on-the-road image; the verse does not say the staff goes ahead as the commentary’s gloss does.

row.basis: guarded way to the tree of life
row.note: After expulsion from Eden, cherubim guard the way to the tree of life; this turns loss of the home into a blocked route that cannot simply be found again.

row.basis: prepared roads to cities of refuge
row.note: The Torah orders roads prepared so a manslayer can flee to a refuge city; a safe destination depends on a deliberately marked, usable route.

The Talmud expands the command to prepare refuge roads with clear routes and signs at junctions directing fugitives to refuge; it makes the road markers a practical answer to someone who could otherwise lose the way.

row.basis: Moses asks God to show the way
row.note: Moses asks to know God by being shown God’s ways; this is a direct communal prayer for the route to be disclosed.

row.basis: God’s presence goes with the people and gives rest
row.note: The answer promises that God’s presence will go with Moses and give rest; guidance is a presence that accompanies the travelers to a resting place.

row.basis: God finds Israel in wilderness and leads them
row.note: The song says God found Israel in a wilderness waste and led and guarded them; it joins a lost, exposed community with the guide who brings it through.

row.basis: Israel returns by a straight way without stumbling
row.note: God leads the returning people by streams on a straight road where they will not stumble; this combines communal return, guidance, straightness, and a safe destination.

row.basis: teaching and leading on a level path
row.note: The speaker asks God to teach the way and lead him on a level path; the prayer unites instruction with continued movement on course.

row.basis: instruction in the way with a guiding eye
row.note: God promises to instruct and teach the way and guide the learner with an eye; this makes guidance personal and ongoing rather than a bare direction.

row.basis: highways held in the heart toward Zion
row.note: The pilgrims have highways in their hearts as they go toward God in Zion; the road is the inwardly held route of a worshiping community.
The travelers pass through a dry valley that becomes springs; it supplies a concrete terrain on the community’s road to worship.

row.basis: the pilgrims arrive before God in Zion
row.note: The group goes from strength to strength until each appears before God in Zion; this completes the journey’s destination rather than leaving the path abstract.

row.basis: feet arrive at the gates of the Lord’s house
row.note: The speaker says their feet are standing inside Jerusalem’s gates after the call to go to the Lord’s house; it gives the route-to-home image a communal pilgrimage and worship setting.

row.basis: Wisdom calls from heights beside a crossroads
row.note: Wisdom stations herself at high places beside the road and where paths meet; this joins a visible landmark, a guide, and the place where a traveler chooses a way.
The righteous person’s path shines like dawn until full day; the image connects a straight moral course with light that makes direction visible.

row.basis: the wicked path is dark and causes stumbling
row.note: The wicked way is darkness, and its travelers do not know what makes them stumble; this gives the commentary’s lost traveler a specific dark-road counterpart.

row.basis: make a level path for the feet
row.note: The instruction is to make the footpath level and keep the feet steady; it adds the practical shaping of a walkable route to the commentary’s straight road.

row.basis: steps made firm by the divine word
row.note: The speaker asks that his steps be established by God’s word so sin will not rule him; the path is held steady through instruction.

row.basis: the prayer asks to know which way to go
row.note: The speaker asks God to make him know the way he should go; this is nearly the same act of petition as the commentary’s opening request for guidance.

row.basis: God teaches and leads on level ground
row.note: The prayer asks God to teach the divine will and lead the speaker on level ground; it joins teaching, guidance, and a straight route.

row.basis: the Lord establishes a person’s steps
row.note: The Lord establishes the steps of the one whose way pleases him; the path is shaped and sustained by divine guidance.

row.basis: the Lord holds the traveler when he stumbles
row.note: Even if the righteous person stumbles, the Lord holds his hand and keeps him from falling; this adds support on the path when the walk falters.

row.basis: God continually guides through dry country
row.note: God promises to guide continually and satisfy the person in scorched places; it is a specific image of guidance when the terrain offers no easy direction.

row.basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and holds him
row.note: God says he taught Ephraim to walk and took the child in his arms; the guide is a caregiver enabling the community to move.
The Lord’s ways are straight, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble; this closely joins the straight communal route with its opposite.

row.basis: blind groping and failure in one’s ways
row.note: The afflicted person gropes at noon as a blind person in darkness and does not prosper in his ways; this concretizes loss of direction on land.

row.basis: the way of peace is unknown
row.note: The people do not know the way of peace; it gives a specific scriptural statement of failing to know the right route.

row.basis: leaders wander in a trackless waste
row.note: God makes the leaders of the earth wander in a wasteland where there is no way; this is a concrete landscape of disorientation.

The commentary labels Arabic ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ with the source root ق و م; Hebrew קום here means to stand, not to be straight. Its use when the wicked cannot stand in judgment makes the cognate’s judgment setting a secondary echo, not an equivalent meaning.

row.basis: standing in the righteous congregation at judgment
row.note: The wicked cannot stand in judgment or remain in the congregation of the righteous; this adds the separation of communities at judgment to the contrast of their ways in the neighboring verse.

row.basis: Hebrew נעם in the name of a shepherd’s staff
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic أَنْعَمْتَ with source root ن ع م; Hebrew נֹעַם names a staff and belongs to the related Semitic n-ʿ-m family, though its sense here is pleasantness rather than the verb of bestowing favor.

row.basis: staff named Favor in a shepherding scene
row.note: The shepherd tends the flock with two staffs, one named Noam and one named Bonds; this brings a favor-named staff, guidance, and a gathered flock into one concrete scene.
Hagar leaves into the wilderness with her child and wanders there; this is a specific human scene of displacement and lost direction.

row.basis: opened eyes reveal water in the wilderness
row.note: God opens Hagar’s eyes and she sees a well; the lost traveler is helped by a new sightline that reveals the needed destination.

row.basis: Qumran reads the wilderness road as Torah study
row.note: The Community Rule applies the call to prepare the Lord’s way in the wilderness to its separation in the desert and study of Torah; this turns the road into the community’s disciplined religious practice.

row.basis: the speaker says they strayed from truth’s way
row.note: The speakers confess that they left the way of truth and lacked the light of righteousness; the passage connects wrong direction with moral failure and lost illumination.
The speakers say they traveled through trackless deserts without knowing the Lord’s way; this brings astray, pathlessness, and ignorance of the right route together.

row.basis: walking God’s way and living in peace
row.note: Baruch says Israel would live in peace if it had walked in God’s way; the community’s route is a sustained choice with a collective outcome.

row.basis: holding to the law means life, forsaking it means death
row.note: Baruch identifies the enduring law as the way that gives life and says those who forsake it die; this makes the chosen route an ongoing communal practice with an endpoint.

row.basis: this world as a vestibule before the banquet hall
row.note: The Mishnah calls this world a vestibule and urges preparation to enter the world to come; life is framed as a passage whose destination lies beyond it.

row.basis: run the course set before the community
row.note: The hearers are told to run with endurance the race set before them; the path becomes a shared course that must be followed to its finish.

row.basis: Jesus as pioneer and perfecter of the course
row.note: Jesus is named the pioneer and perfecter of faith; this gives the community a forerunner who goes ahead and completes the way.

row.basis: make straight paths so the lame can be healed
row.note: The hearers must make straight paths for their feet so the lame will not be put out of joint but healed; straightening the route protects struggling travelers.

row.basis: the guide joins travelers from beside them
row.note: On the road to Emmaus, Jesus draws near and walks with the disciples rather than going ahead; this offers a specific counter-image to the commentary’s guide defined by precedence.

row.basis: scriptural explanation changes how the travelers see the road
row.note: The disciples recall how their hearts burned while Jesus explained the Scriptures on the road; guidance includes interpreting the text during travel.

row.basis: the travelers turn back toward the community
row.note: After recognizing Jesus, the disciples immediately return to Jerusalem; the road that had led away from the group is reversed toward reunion.

row.basis: Elymas perverts the straight ways of the Lord
row.note: Paul accuses Elymas of trying to make the Lord’s straight ways crooked; this is a direct Christian image of an adversary obstructing the right route.
Paul says he worships God according to the Way; this uniquely joins the commentary’s worship and path images in one statement.

row.basis: walking in darkness means not knowing where one goes
row.note: Jesus warns that the person who walks in darkness does not know where he is going; it directly links lost orientation with darkness.

row.basis: blind guides lead others into a pit
row.note: Jesus calls the teachers blind guides whose followers fall with them; it adds the danger of a guide who cannot see the right way.

row.basis: the way of peace is unknown
row.note: Paul cites the claim that people have not known the way of peace; this carries the Hebrew Bible’s lost-route image into his account of human wrongdoing.

row.basis: the serpent leads minds away from devotion
row.note: Paul fears that, as the serpent deceived Eve, the community’s minds may be led astray from devotion to Christ; this gives the commentary’s ambushing adversary a specific Christian counterpart.

row.basis: Apollos is instructed in the Lord’s way but incompletely
row.note: Apollos knows and teaches the way of the Lord but knows only John’s baptism; his case makes clear that a guide can have real direction while still lacking part of the route.

row.basis: Priscilla and Aquila explain the way more accurately
row.note: The couple takes Apollos aside and explains the way of God more accurately; a community helps its guide correct and complete his direction.

row.basis: a vision calls the travelers toward Macedonia
row.note: Paul sees a Macedonian asking him to come and help; the call gives a specific divine direction for a traveling group.

row.basis: the group infers its destination from the call
row.note: The travelers conclude that God has called them to preach in Macedonia and set out; guidance becomes a shared decision about where to go.

row.basis: people walk in works prepared by God
row.note: The community is created for good works God prepared beforehand for them to walk in; the path is a sustained practice laid out by God.

row.basis: following Jesus is taken up daily
row.note: Jesus says a follower must take up the cross daily and follow him; the route is maintained through repeated, embodied commitment.

row.basis: the travelers seek a homeland and a prepared city
row.note: The faithful desire a better country and a city God has prepared; this develops the commentary’s claim that a route is oriented toward a home.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds the people to springs of water
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the gathered people and guides them to springs of living water; guidance ends in rest and relief for the community.

row.basis: the firstfruits follow the Lamb wherever he goes
row.note: The faithful are defined as those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes; the path is the shared movement of a favored group after its guide.
The judgment scene ends with one group entering eternal life and the other punishment; this adds the destination split to the commentary’s distinction between the guided and rejected.

row.basis: Joseph serves Potiphar and is set over his household
row.note: The commentary uses Yusuf's human rabb as an owner who gives him a good home; Genesis places Joseph as servant in Potiphar's house and then makes him its manager, supplying the matching household relation in the shared Joseph story.

row.basis: Joseph's master leaves his house and possessions in Joseph's hand
row.note: The commentary describes rabb as owner of a house and malik as what a hand possesses; Genesis gives Joseph authority over his master's house while Potiphar retains ownership, sharpening the distinction between a human master's trust and ownership.

The commentary's Moses scene contrasts being raised in Pharaoh's house with Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; Exodus describes the same people forced into labor, giving the human domination behind that contrast.

row.basis: Harsh labor and servitude in Egypt
row.note: The commentary's account of Pharaoh enslaving Israel is matched by Exodus's description of bitter labor under Egyptian taskmasters; the narrative adds the grinding work through which human rule humbles its subjects.

The commentary contrasts human enslavement with worship due to God; here God demands that Pharaoh release Israel so the people can serve God, recasting the exodus as a transfer from Pharaoh's forced labor to divine service.

row.basis: Hebrew עבד for service to God
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for both worship and human enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד for Israel's service to God, showing the cultic use of the same Semitic service word in the story of release from forced labor.

row.basis: A slave chooses to remain with his master
row.note: The commentary says human servitude to God begins through creation rather than a slave's choice; this law has a Hebrew slave declare love for his master and refuse release, a concrete human bond chosen after the term of service.

row.basis: Israelites are God's servants and not human property
row.note: The commentary says all people belong to God whether free or enslaved; Leviticus grounds Israel's status as God's servants in the exodus and bars their sale as slaves, limiting human ownership by God's prior claim.

The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for worship and service and reads 1:5 as service to God alone; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד in its command to serve the Lord alone, giving a direct lexical and ethical counterpart.

row.basis: Collective pledge to serve and obey the Lord
row.note: The commentary hears the owned servant speak directly to the owner in the first-person plural; Israel here answers in a collective pledge to serve the Lord and obey his voice, adding a covenantal setting for that spoken allegiance.

row.basis: The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary's malik image includes everything held in the owner's hand; this psalm assigns the earth and all within it to the Lord, extending the property image from household goods to the world.

row.basis: Bowing and kneeling before the maker
row.note: The commentary calls worship the utmost humbling of the servant; the psalm invites worshippers to bow and kneel before their maker, giving bodily posture to its account of submission.

row.basis: People as sheep of God's hand
row.note: The commentary makes the servant God's owned person and places him in the master's house; the psalm calls the worshippers God's people and the sheep of his hand, combining belonging with a shepherd's care.

row.basis: Every knee bends and every tongue swears
row.note: The commentary says every human is already God's servant by creation and that the servant addresses God directly; Isaiah pictures universal bodily submission and confession before God, adding a public, eschatological form of that allegiance.

The commentary labels Arabic م ل ك for malik as owner and sovereign; Zechariah uses the cognate Hebrew מלך for the Lord's kingship over the whole earth, showing the sovereign sense without importing the commentary's separate property sense.

The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن and links it to humbling, enslavement, possession, and the Day of Judgment; Daniel's Aramaic cognate root names the court's judgment, directly matching the judgment sense while not supporting those other senses.

row.basis: Dominion and service of the humanlike figure
row.note: The commentary joins malik sovereignty to the servant's worship; Daniel gives everlasting dominion to one like a son of man and says peoples and languages will serve him, a close image of universal service under a ruler with a distinct figure in the vision.

row.basis: Donkey's burden and the slave's work
row.note: The commentary moves from a camel subdued by tar to a humbled human slave; Sirach places fodder, stick, and burden for a donkey beside bread, discipline, and work for a slave, explicitly bringing animal control and human servitude together.

row.basis: A master assigns a servant work and finds rest
row.note: The commentary describes a human owner using a slave's labor and calls the servant humbled by work; Sirach says setting the servant to work gives the master rest, making the labor relation explicit.

row.basis: Yoke and harness bend a servant's neck
row.note: The commentary's common image is one who has been subdued; Sirach describes yoke and harness bending the neck and punishment for a bad servant, offering a concrete Jewish parallel for bodily subjection.

row.basis: Reciting Shema as accepting heaven's yoke
