The commentary ties mercy to household care and provision; the Samaritan binds the wounded man, puts him on his animal, and takes him to an inn, supplying a temporary home for the vulnerable.

row.basis: a father receives his child with compassion
row.note: The commentary places mercy around the image of a child growing under parental care; the father sees his returning son, is moved with compassion, runs to him, embraces and kisses him, restoring a broken household bond.

The commentary says mercy bends toward the weak and recounts a mother’s separation from Moses; Jesus is moved with compassion for a widow whose only son is being carried out, a distinct mother-and-son scene.

row.basis: the son returned to his mother
row.note: The commentary recounts Moses being returned to his mother; Jesus restores the widow’s son to life and gives him back to her, so the shared detail is reunion, though Luke’s son is grown and the event is a resurrection.
The commentary’s rahma is tenderness expressed as care and its Rab image is nurturing; Paul says he was gentle among the Thessalonians like a nursing mother cherishing her own children.

The commentary describes care as more than a feeling, extending to an actual good for the cared-for; Paul says he shared not only the gospel but his own life with the community because they had become dear to him.
The commentary calls a teacher one who feeds people small portions of knowledge; Paul says he fed the Corinthians milk rather than solid food because they were not ready for it.

row.basis: milk and solid food mark learning stages
row.note: The commentary defines upbringing as moving from state to state toward completion; Hebrews rebukes hearers who still need milk rather than solid food when they should be teachers.
The commentary’s education image moves toward completion; Hebrews says solid food belongs to the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil.
The commentary’s child grows through successive stages under nurture; Peter urges newborn infants to long for pure spiritual milk so they may grow into salvation.
The commentary defines Rab as raising a child toward completion; Ephesians tells fathers to bring children up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction, placing education inside parental care.

row.basis: Jesus grows in wisdom and favor
row.note: The commentary describes upbringing as carrying a child from one state to completion; Luke reports Jesus growing in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and people.
The commentary’s womb image and staged raising meet Paul’s labor metaphor: he is again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in his converts.
The commentary joins the household’s protection to the image of a vulnerable child; Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, but they are unwilling.
The commentary explains “rahim” as kin related because they came from one womb; Jesus calls those who do God’s will his brother, sister, and mother, extending family relation beyond biological birth.
The commentary pairs worship of God with doing good to parents who raised the child; Ephesians repeats the command to honor father and mother, grounding filial duty in the commandment.
The commentary says children owe good and mercy to the parents who raised them; Jesus condemns a dedication formula that lets a person withhold material support from father or mother.
The commentary links mercy toward parents to their raising the child while small; Paul says descendants should learn to show piety at home and make some return to their parents and grandparents.
The commentary’s household upholder supplies and protects the family; Paul says providing for one’s own household is a concrete family duty and failure repudiates the faith.

row.basis: food and clothing for the fatherless and widow
row.note: The commentary defines mercy as doing good to the weak and mentions household provision; Deuteronomy says God upholds the orphan and widow and gives the resident alien food and clothing.
The commentary frames care as beginning in the womb and continuing through growth; Isaiah says God has carried Israel from the womb, extending the image from birth into a people’s long life.
The commentary depicts nurture continuing toward completion; Isaiah promises to carry Israel even to old age and gray hairs, extending womb care across the whole life course.
The commentary describes rahma as tenderness that becomes care; Isaiah compares God’s comfort of Jerusalem to a mother comforting her child, making maternal affection the measure of divine care.
The commentary links the merciful Lord with the teacher who raises people gradually; Wisdom says God’s imperishable spirit is in all things, directly joining divine presence with sustained life.
The commentary says children should respond with mercy to parents who raised them when they were small; Sirach instructs a child to help the father in old age and not grieve him.
The commentary’s filial image includes lowering oneself in mercy before parents; Sirach tells the child to be patient if the father’s mind fails and not to despise him in the child’s own strength.
The commentary grounds care of parents in their earlier nurturing; Sirach says kindness to a father will not be forgotten and will count against sins.

The commentary’s image of the foster parent is explicitly about taking charge of a child one did not give birth to; Moses uses the nurse carrying a suckling to describe being made responsible for a people he did not conceive.

row.basis: new family formed at the cross
row.note: The commentary describes kinship through a shared womb and care within a household; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, forming a caregiving family relation not based on common birth.

The commentary labels Arabic ر ب ب as the root behind “Rab” and associates it with raising and teaching; Mary addresses Jesus as Rabbouni, “my teacher,” in the scene where she recognizes him after the resurrection.

The commentary calls Pharaoh’s “we raised you” only a partial claim; Stephen says Moses was instructed in all Egyptian wisdom and was powerful in words and deeds, preserving palace education alongside the commentary’s emphasis on his mother and God.

The commentary recounts Moses’ exposure and return to his mother; Stephen recalls Pharaoh’s daughter taking and raising him as her own son, a Christian retelling that foregrounds the adoptive household.

The commentary calls Pharaoh’s claim to have raised Moses only partial; Hebrews says Moses, when grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, making royal upbringing distinct from the identity he chose.
The commentary’s parent-child frame moves from receiving nurture to responding to parents; Ephesians addresses children directly and commands obedience in the Lord.
The commentary presents raising a child as beneficial formation toward completion; Colossians warns fathers not to embitter children lest they lose heart, marking a limit on parental authority.
The commentary joins the merciful Lord with formation; Titus says God’s saving grace has appeared for all people, setting the context for grace’s ethical training in the next verse.

row.basis: grace trains people to live well
row.note: The commentary describes nurture as gradual formation toward completion; Titus says grace trains people to renounce ungodliness and live with self-control, righteousness, and devotion.
The commentary defines Rab as raising a child through successive stages; Hosea says God taught Ephraim to walk and took the child by the arms, presenting divine care as hands-on early nurture.

The commentary links mercy with beneficence and raising a child toward completion; Hosea says God led Israel with loving bonds, bent down, and fed them. The middle image is rendered either as lifting an infant to the cheek or lifting a yoke from the jaws, so both readings remain visible.

row.basis: God carries Israel as a father carries a son
row.note: The commentary moves from the womb to a child raised by a household; Moses recalls God carrying Israel through the wilderness as a man carries his son, a direct parental-care image.

row.basis: God who gave birth is forgotten
row.note: The commentary surrounds nurture with womb and parental care; Moses’ song accuses Israel of forgetting the Rock who gave birth to them, reversing the expected child’s response to the one who formed and raised them.
The commentary calls the womb a child’s first home and describes subsequent nurture; the psalmist says God took him from the womb and made him secure at his mother’s breasts.

row.basis: cast from the womb toward God
row.note: The commentary’s womb image is a home for the child; the psalm says the speaker was cast upon God from birth and relied on God from his mother’s womb, extending the image from maternal shelter to divine care.
The commentary pictures mercy as care that begins in the womb and continues through a child’s growth; the psalmist says he has leaned on God from birth and was taken from the womb by God.

row.basis: children as fruit of the womb
row.note: The commentary begins its frame with the womb as the child’s home; the psalm calls children an inheritance from God and the fruit of the womb a reward, assigning value to the life that grows there.

row.basis: a weaned child with its mother
row.note: The commentary describes a child’s growth inside a home and the transition toward completion; the psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child beside its mother, where dependence has changed but maternal closeness remains.
The commentary makes the womb a place where a child grows and is formed; the psalm says God knit the speaker together in his mother’s womb, locating divine making within that home.

The commentary labels Arabic ن ع م and glosses it with raising children in comfort; Hebrew naʿim is a cognate meaning pleasant, used here of brothers dwelling together, so the source’s comfort image meets a concrete kin household.

row.basis: q-w-m / children rise in the household
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ق و م for the one who keeps household affairs standing; Hebrew qûm is a cognate used when the woman’s children rise to call her blessed, placing the root in a household where her care is recognized.

row.basis: Israel loved as a child and called out of Egypt
row.note: The commentary recounts Moses’ threatened infancy and return to his mother; Hosea depicts Israel collectively as God’s child, loved and called out of Egypt, turning the Exodus setting into a parent-child relation.

row.basis: shepherd carries lambs and leads nursing ewes
row.note: The commentary describes the home as a place of protection and sustenance; Isaiah pictures God gathering lambs in his arms, carrying them close, and gently leading nursing mothers.

The commentary links the womb to a child’s home and later nurture; Isaiah depicts Jerusalem’s children nursing, being carried on her hip, and bounced on her knees, giving several concrete stages of maternal care.

row.basis: Hannah continues to provide after weaning
row.note: The commentary treats nurturing as continuing beyond birth and recognizes care by someone outside the child’s daily home; although Samuel serves at Shiloh, his mother brings him a small robe each year.

row.basis: Elijah returns a son to his mother
row.note: The commentary recounts Moses being restored to his mother after separation; Elijah brings the widow’s revived son down and gives him to her, a distinct Hebrew Bible reunion scene.
The commentary describes raising a child from state to state; Abraham’s feast on the day Isaac is weaned marks the end of nursing and a public transition in the child’s life.

row.basis: a mother and child expelled from home
row.note: The commentary presents the home as the child’s place of nurture and protection; Sarah demands Hagar and her son be sent away, showing the contrary case of a household withdrawing that shelter.

row.basis: Moses hidden before being sent onto the river
row.note: The commentary’s Qur’anic account begins with God directing Moses’ mother to nurse him and then place him in the water; Exodus first says she hides the newborn for three months, a distinct step before the basket episode.

The commentary says the Pharaoh household takes Moses but emphasizes the sister’s proposal and his return to his mother; Exodus identifies Pharaoh’s daughter as the one who finds the basket and sends her servant to fetch it.

The commentary explains “rahim” kinship as relatives who came from one womb; Genesis gives a different foundation for family relation, saying husband and wife become one flesh, adding a bond formed through shared life rather than birth.

row.basis: train a child in a way
row.note: The commentary defines tarbiya as bringing a thing through stages toward completion; Proverbs tells an adult to train a child in the way he should go, relating instruction to the child’s later life.
The commentary portrays raising a child as purposeful formation; Proverbs connects a parent’s love with diligent correction, a sharper form of nurture than the commentary’s gentler household image.

row.basis: q-w-m is not the link; parental discipline is
row.note: The commentary defines Rab as raising a child toward completion; Proverbs says the Lord corrects the one he loves as a father corrects a son, supplying a direct Hebrew parental-formation motif.

row.basis: Christian reading of Proverbs’ fatherly discipline
row.note: The commentary describes nurture as formation toward completion; Hebrews quotes the father-son discipline saying from Proverbs and interprets hardship as the Lord’s treatment of children he receives, giving correction a filial meaning.

row.basis: parents give good gifts to children
row.note: The commentary joins mercy with doing good and the Lord with a child’s nurturer; Jesus argues from human parents giving good gifts to their children toward the heavenly Father’s greater generosity.

The commentary describes a home that nurtures and protects its members; Ephesians says no one hates his own body but nourishes and cherishes it, then uses that care to explain Christ’s care for the church.
The commentary pairs the mother’s womb and a father’s role in raising a child; Paul recalls exhorting and encouraging each Thessalonian as a father addresses his own children.

row.basis: parental guidance toward a worthy life
row.note: The commentary says upbringing leads step by step toward completion; Paul says he urged the community to live worthily of God, like a father guiding children toward their calling.

row.basis: womb and breasts named as maternal blessing
row.note: The commentary explicitly develops the womb, the child’s home, and the nurturing relation; a woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts that nursed him.

row.basis: Jesus redirects blessing to hearing the word
row.note: The commentary connects maternal nurture with the teacher who feeds learners; Jesus answers the womb-and-breast blessing by calling blessed those who hear God’s word and keep it, shifting the measure toward instruction and response.

row.basis: the disciple takes Mary into his home
row.note: The commentary describes kinship through a shared womb and care within a household; after entrusting his mother to the disciple, Jesus’ words lead the disciple to take her into his own home, making protection concrete.

row.basis: Jesus takes children in his arms
row.note: The commentary says mercy especially bends toward the weak; Jesus takes little children in his arms, lays hands on them, and blesses them after the disciples tried to keep them away.

row.basis: a child moves in the womb
row.note: The commentary’s central image is the womb as the child’s home; Elizabeth says the child in her womb leapt when Mary’s greeting reached her, a specific intrauterine scene.

row.basis: labor pain and joy after birth
row.note: The commentary recalls pain in the womb after delivery; Jesus compares grief followed by joy to a woman distressed in labor who rejoices after her child is born, preserving the passage’s focus on labor and birth rather than postpartum illness.

The commentary notes a spouse raising a child who is not biologically theirs; Paul says Christ redeems those under the law so they may receive adoption as children, applying household adoption to believers.

row.basis: father’s concrete duties to a son
row.note: The commentary’s Rab raises and teaches a child; Kiddushin lists a father’s obligations to his son, including teaching Torah and a trade, making nurture a set of practical responsibilities.

row.basis: Musa's mother, nursing child, water separation
row.note: When Moses' mother can no longer conceal him, she puts him in a waterproof basket among the Nile reeds. It is the concrete biblical water-separation scene beside the commentary's mother who nurses Musa and sends him into the yamm; Exodus supplies concealment as the immediate motive.
Moses' sister stations herself to learn what will happen to him. This is the narrative counterpart to the sister who identifies a household able to foster Musa in the commentary.

row.basis: mercy for the crying, exposed child
row.note: Pharaoh's daughter opens the basket, sees the crying child, and has compassion. Her response makes the commentary's claim that mercy turns toward the weak into the act that begins Moses' rescue.

The sister offers to call a Hebrew woman to nurse the child. The same child-sister-household nexus underlies Qur'an 28:12's offer of an ahl bayt who will care for him, though Exodus specifies a wet nurse.

row.basis: mother is returned as paid nurse
row.note: Pharaoh's daughter entrusts the child to his own mother to nurse and pays her. It is the close biblical counterpart to Musa's return to his mother, joining maternal breast, a nonmaternal household, and providential restoration.

After he grows, Moses becomes Pharaoh's daughter's son. This makes Qur'an 26:18's collective claim that Pharaoh's household raised Musa a pointedly different household claim: the biblical named foster parent is the daughter, not Pharaoh as speaker.

row.basis: Moses nurtured in his father's house
row.note: Stephen says Moses was brought up for three months in his father's house. The retelling explicitly foregrounds the protected natal home before exposure, which the commentary contrasts with later palace claims.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter raises Moses as son
row.note: Acts says that Pharaoh's daughter took up the exposed Moses and raised him as her own son. It preserves the foster-child transition central to the commentary's distinction between birth, nursing, and a later household's nurture.

The Bavli expands Exodus 2 by making Moses refuse Egyptian nurses until his own mother feeds him, because his mouth is destined for divine speech. That interpretation intensifies the commentary's claim that his true nurture occurs at his mother's breast under God's care.

row.basis: source ر ح م: Hebrew רחם/רחמים, nursing mother
row.note: The Hebrew r-ḥ-m root supplies the verb for a mother's compassion while the verse speaks of her nursing child and the son of her belly. It is a close Semitic witness to the commentary's womb-to-mercy movement, then extends it to God's unfailing remembrance.

row.basis: God forms within the mother's womb
row.note: The psalm credits God with forming the inward parts and weaving the speaker in the mother's womb. It directly accompanies the commentary's Qur'an 3:6 image of God shaping a person in the rahim as a place of formation.

row.basis: gestation figured as milk being poured and curdled
row.note: Job describes his bodily beginning through liquid and milk-curdling imagery before the later clothing of flesh. Its deliberately domestic, embodied account of gestation belongs beside the commentary's womb as vessel and its lactating-animal image.

row.basis: God forms and knows the prophet before birth
row.note: God says that he formed Jeremiah in the womb and knew him before he came out of it. This gives a biblical instance of prenatal divine formation that develops the commentary's claim that the womb is God's workshop.

row.basis: God brings the speaker from womb to mother's breasts
row.note: The speaker credits God with drawing him from the womb and making him trust at his mother's breasts. It holds together God's hidden guardianship and maternal nourishment, the two agents the commentary distinguishes in Musa's infancy.

row.basis: God carries people from belly and womb
row.note: God addresses those borne from the belly and carried from the womb. The parent-like divine carrying extends the commentary's home-to-maturity image beyond gestation into sustained care.

The verse makes painful childbearing part of Eve's condition. It is the direct biblical analogue for the commentary's insistence that the womb-house has a bodily cost after birth, even though its narrative frame is different.

row.basis: one Maker fashions persons in the womb
row.note: Job grounds his refusal to oppress servants in the fact that the same Maker formed both parties in the womb. It turns shared prenatal origin into an ethical relation, illuminating the commentary's move from one womb to kinship and mercy for the vulnerable.

row.basis: source ر ح م: maternal רחמים acts to save a son
row.note: The true mother's compassion, Hebrew rahamim, is stirred for her son and she yields him rather than see him killed. This is not merely emotion: it performs the commentary's definition of rahma as tenderness that entails beneficent action toward the weak.

row.basis: source ر ح م: fatherly compassion for children
row.note: The psalm compares YHWH's compassion for those who fear him to a father's compassion for children, using the r-ḥ-m root. It gives a paternal rendering of the commentary's Rahman/Rahim frame around nurturing lordship.

row.basis: source ر ح م: divine compassion for a remembered son
row.note: Ephraim is called God's dear child; divine inward yearning culminates in the emphatic r-ḥ-m promise of mercy. The verse joins father-son relation and womb-derived compassion, sharpening the commentary's family account of rahma.

Hosea's daughter is named Lo-Ruhamah because God announces a withdrawal of r-ḥ-m compassion. Its negative naming makes the repeated Qur'anic merciful names more consequential: mercy can be represented as a relation to a child that is withheld as well as bestowed.

The restoration oracle says that God will show r-ḥ-m compassion to Lo-Ruhamah and restore a belonging relation. Read after Hos. 1:6, it gives a narrative reversal of estrangement into parental mercy relevant to the commentary's merciful enclosing frame.

row.basis: shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads mothers
row.note: The shepherd gathers lambs in his arms, carries them at his breast, and gently leads ewes with young. This joins weak young, maternal animals, and a caregiver's measured pace, supplying a pastoral analogue to the commentary's child and lactating-sheep images.

Moses protests that he did not conceive or bear Israel and so cannot carry them as a nurse carries a suckling child. The verse is a precise nonbiological-caregiver analogy for the commentary's rabb/rabba and nurse who undertake a child's nurture.

Kings are promised as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers. This explicit pairing of adoptive authority and lactation provides a biblical counterpart to the commentary's nonbirth parent and child-minder senses of the r-b-b family.

row.basis: Mordecai brings up an orphan as his daughter
row.note: Mordecai raises Hadassah after the death of her parents and takes her as his own daughter. It is a concrete household instance of the commentary's claim that raising a child can belong to someone other than the one who gave birth.

row.basis: Naomi holds the child and becomes his nurse
row.note: Naomi takes the newborn to her bosom and becomes his nurse. The scene makes kinship, bodily closeness, and an elder woman's nonmaternal nurture converge in the way the commentary's womb-derived family language invites.

row.basis: God carries Israel as a parent carries a child
row.note: Moses recalls YHWH carrying Israel in the wilderness as a man carries his son. It makes the divine Lord a sustaining parent across a journey, not simply a begetter, matching the commentary's transition from womb to ongoing rabbi-like cultivation.

row.basis: divine discipline as a father disciplines a son
row.note: Israel is to recognize that YHWH disciplines it as a man disciplines his son. This gives a biblical parent-child account of formative correction, a necessary complication and parallel to terbiye as gradual movement toward completion.

All of Zion's children are described as taught by YHWH. The verse directly accompanies the commentary's Rahman who teaches and its extension of rabb into the teacher who feeds learners with small portions of knowledge.

row.basis: God instructs with an eye upon the learner
row.note: God promises to instruct and teach the way to go, counsel the speaker, and keep an eye upon him. It closely matches the commentary's conjunction of teaching and Musa being raised under God's eye.

row.basis: Abraham directs children and household in God's way
row.note: God's election of Abraham is tied to his commanding his children and household after him to keep YHWH's way. It puts religious formation inside the house, as the commentary puts nurture and teaching inside a family setting.

row.basis: teach the words diligently to children at home
row.note: Israel is commanded to teach the words to children while sitting at home, walking, lying down, and rising. This supplies a concrete domestic rhythm for the commentary's claim that upbringing extends into instruction.

row.basis: Samuel grows in stature and favor
row.note: The child Samuel continues to grow in stature and in favor with YHWH and people. It is a concise biblical sequence from protected childhood toward mature, socially and divinely recognized formation.

row.basis: a household official becomes a father to inhabitants
row.note: Eliakim receives office and is called a father to Jerusalem's inhabitants and Judah's house. It translates the commentary's qawwam image of one who upholds a household into public stewardship with explicitly parental language.

The capable woman rises at night to give food to her household and portions to her servants. It realizes the commentary's secondary image of provisions brought into a home as an act that keeps its members alive.

row.basis: fetus taught Torah in the womb
row.note: The Bavli imagines an angel teaching the fetus the whole Torah in the womb before birth. This is an interpretive, not narrative, parallel that fuses the commentary's womb-house with its later claim that nurture reaches teaching.

row.basis: father, mother, and God as partners in a child's formation
row.note: The Bavli divides a child's making among father, mother, and the Holy One. Its three-agent account offers a Jewish interpretive framework for the commentary's distinction between maternal body, human caregivers, and the divine shaper.

row.basis: common formation in a mother's womb
row.note: The speaker says that he was molded in flesh in a mother's womb and had the same entrance into life as all others. This Jewish reflection turns prenatal formation into common human kinship, echoing the commentary's one-womb logic.

row.basis: mother credits the Creator with her children's life
row.note: The martyred brothers' mother says she does not know how they came to be in her womb and attributes life, breath, and bodily formation to the Creator. It directly combines maternal gestation with divine formative agency.

row.basis: remember the dangers endured in the womb
row.note: Tobit tells his son to remember the many dangers his mother underwent for him in her womb. It is a close Jewish counterpart to the commentary's refusal to sentimentalize the womb-house or detach filial duty from maternal cost.

row.basis: honor and help a father in old age
row.note: Ben Sira tells a child to help rather than grieve a father in old age. This places the grown child's mercy and practical care toward parents beside the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal of the earlier raising relationship.

row.basis: ordered ages for Scripture, Mishnah, commandments, and maturity
row.note: Avot's age sequence makes learning and responsibility unfold in stages. It supplies a rabbinic analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as bringing a thing state by state to completion.

row.basis: source ر ب ب: ῥαββί glossed as Teacher
row.note: John preserves the Semitic address ῥαββί and immediately glosses it as Teacher. As an actual r-b-b cognate, it substantiates the commentary's carefully developed extension from Rabb to a teacher rather than relying on the root label alone.

row.basis: all will be taught by God
row.note: Jesus cites the promise that all will be taught by God. The direct divine-teacher formulation is a New Testament companion to the commentary's Rahman who teaches the Qur'an and teaches human expression.

row.basis: Jesus grows, becomes strong, and is filled with wisdom
row.note: The infancy narrative describes Jesus' growth, strengthening, wisdom, and divine favor. It gives a canonical Christian rendering of child development in stages rather than a single moment of birth.

row.basis: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor
row.note: Jesus continues to advance in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and people. Its triadic maturation closely fits the commentary's movement from a child's home through cultivation toward completion.

row.basis: merciful as the Father is merciful
row.note: Jesus grounds merciful action in the Father's mercy. This provides a father-child divine frame for the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that becomes beneficence toward others.

row.basis: father gives good things to children
row.note: Human parents' giving of good gifts becomes the measure for the heavenly Father's generosity. It joins parental provision and divine goodness, illuminating the commentary's en'amte image of children being reared in ease.

row.basis: mother bird gathers young under her wings
row.note: Jesus compares his desired protection of Jerusalem's children to a hen gathering her brood under her wings. The maternal protective figure supplies a New Testament meeting with the commentary's mercy, weak young, and guarded household.

row.basis: child placed under guardians and household managers
row.note: The heir, while a child, is under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time. This is a particularly exact legal and domestic analogue for the commentary's nonbirth caregiver and the person who maintains a household's affairs.

row.basis: maternal labor until Christ is formed in learners
row.note: Paul likens his pastoral work to being in labor until Christ is formed in his children. It turns the commentary's womb, labor, and gradual formation into an explicitly pedagogical Christian metaphor.

row.basis: birth pain gives way to joy at the child's arrival
row.note: Jesus uses a woman in labor whose anguish turns to joy when a human being is born. It directly meets the commentary's emphasis on the bodily cost of birth, while assigning that image an eschatological meaning.

row.basis: teacher gives milk before solid food
row.note: Paul says he gave the Corinthians milk rather than solid food because they were not ready. It is the clearest New Testament analogue to the commentary's teacher who nourishes people first with small portions of knowledge.

row.basis: nursing mother cherishes her own children
row.note: Paul depicts his gentle pastoral care as a nursing mother cherishing her children. The image links bodily nurture and nonbiological teaching care in precisely the double register developed by the commentary.

row.basis: father exhorts, encourages, and comforts children
row.note: Paul also compares his work to a father dealing with each child through exhortation, encouragement, and consolation. Together with maternal nursing in the preceding image, it makes cultivation a patient parental practice.
The community is to reach mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's full stature. This provides an explicit Christian endpoint for the commentary's halden hale movement to the limit of completion.

row.basis: bring children up in instruction of the Lord
row.note: Fathers are told to bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord rather than embitter them. It directly connects household upbringing, moral formation, and teaching.

row.basis: newborns crave milk in order to grow
row.note: Newborn infants are urged to desire pure spiritual milk so that they may grow toward salvation. The verse makes milk, infancy, teaching, and purposeful maturation one integrated image.

row.basis: solid food belongs to the mature
row.note: Maturity is marked by solid food and trained powers of discernment. It completes the milk-to-maturity progression that the commentary's small portions of knowledge and final completion invite readers to trace.

Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it. Its temporal account of costly formation is a close conceptual partner to terbiye as gradual maturation.

row.basis: faithful manager supplies food at the proper time
row.note: Jesus' faithful household manager gives the servants their food allowance at the proper time. This joins the commentary's qawwam-like keeper of household affairs with its secondary image of food provision and measured nurture.

row.basis: managing one's household and caring for God's assembly
row.note: The argument reasons from managing one's own household to caring for God's church. It is a direct Christian development of the commentary's claim that standing up a household's affairs is a genuine form of care.

One who sees a sibling in need and closes the inward organs of compassion is challenged to show God's love. The verse makes compassion concrete through goods and need, matching the commentary's insistence that mercy entails beneficent action.

row.basis: source ر ح م: brotherly compassion, רחמים
row.note: Joseph's compassion for his brother is stirred so strongly that he must withdraw and weep. The Hebrew r-ḥ-m vocabulary lets the commentary's womb-derived kinship become a specific fraternal affect, without claiming that the two narratives are the same.

row.basis: source ق و م: Hebrew הקים, raising and establishing a descendant
row.note: God promises David that he will raise up his offspring after him and establish his kingdom. Hebrew q-w-m is a real cognate field for the commentary's qawwam, but this verse shifts from daily household support to securing a child and dynasty.

row.basis: source ن ع م: Hebrew נעם, pleasant paths
row.note: Wisdom's ways are called ways of pleasantness and her paths peace. Hebrew n-ʿ-m is cognate with the source en'amte family, but the biblical verse applies pleasantness to wisdom's path rather than importing the commentary's child-rearing sense.

A husband's spirit of jealousy arises in the ordeal for a wife suspected of infidelity. It is a concrete biblical household setting for the commentary's secondary gayrah image of guarding family, but its suspicion and legal ordeal complicate any simple protective reading.

row.basis: returning to the mother's womb questioned
row.note: Nicodemus asks whether an adult can enter a mother's womb a second time and be born. The question makes physical womb-life explicit, while the ensuing Johannine discourse redirects birth to a different, Spirit-centered register rather than the commentary's original womb-house.

row.basis: a chosen disciple takes Jesus' mother into his home
row.note: Jesus establishes a new mother-son relation, and the disciple takes her into his own household. This is a concrete Christian scene of nonbiological family care that belongs beside the commentary's step-parent and child-minder images.

row.basis: God supplies an infant through the mother's breasts
row.note: Augustine thanks God for providing infant food through the mother's breasts rather than treating maternal nursing as self-sufficient. This Christian reading closely parallels the commentary's distinction between the visible mother and the true divine guardian of a child's nurture.

In the usual chapter division, the priests assign the older Joseph to keep Mary when she can no longer remain in the temple. This infancy tradition extends the commentary's nonbirth-caregiver question into a Christian guardianship narrative; details and chapter subdivision vary by translation.

row.basis: virgin's womb holds the Provider as an infant
row.note: Ephrem's Nativity hymn dwells on the paradox that the Provider enters the Virgin's womb and accepts infant need. It is a Syriac Christian theological rereading of womb as dwelling and nurture; stanza numbering varies across editions.

row.basis: painless virginal delivery in a Christian hymn
row.note: The ode's birth image is commonly read as portraying the Virgin's delivery without pain. Against the commentary's laboring maternal body, it offers a specifically Christian theological reversal rather than a shared account; the ode's transmission and verse division warrant caution.

row.basis: Pharaoh orders sons cast into the Nile
row.note: Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile. This supplies the lethal political setting that makes Moses' mother's water placement in the commentary a protective counter-use of the same water.

row.basis: mother bears, sees, and hides Moses
row.note: Moses' mother gives birth, sees that he is good, and hides him for three months. This verse supplies the maternal fear and prior home-care that precede the basket scene and the commentary's nursing mother.

row.basis: tender children and nursing flocks require a slow pace
row.note: Jacob refuses to drive on too hard because the children are tender and the flocks and herds are nursing. The verse unusually joins vulnerable children, lactating animals, and measured care, meeting the commentary's child and milk-sheep imagery.
Jacob's blessing names the breasts and womb among God's life-giving blessings. It is a concentrated biblical counterpart to the commentary's paired attention to womb, birth, and milk-giving nurture.

row.basis: Joseph provides for kin and their little ones
row.note: Joseph promises to provide for his brothers and their little ones, then comforts them. It makes familial mercy material through food and reassurance, closely fitting the commentary's provisions-in-the-house and mercy-as-beneficence claims.
God calls Israel his firstborn son in the message to Pharaoh. This makes divine lordship a parental relation and gives political force to the commentary's account of the Rabb who nurtures children.

row.basis: God feeds and clothes the vulnerable outsider
row.note: God executes justice for orphan and widow and loves the resident alien by giving food and clothing. It offers a concrete biblical form of the commentary's mercy that bends toward the weak and becomes provision.

row.basis: God guards Israel as the apple of his eye
row.note: The wilderness song says that God found, encircled, cared for, and guarded Israel as the apple of his eye. This is a close biblical companion to Musa being brought up under God's eye rather than merely under Pharaoh's claim.

row.basis: a parent bird trains and carries its young
row.note: The eagle stirs its nest, hovers over its young, spreads wings, takes them, and bears them. Its patient sequence of urging, sheltering, and carrying gives a vivid animal analogue to terbiye as growth through successive states.

row.basis: God as father who disciplines a son
row.note: God promises of David's heir, "I will be his father and he will be my son," and speaks of correction when he errs. This is a direct biblical parent-child account of lordly formation that includes discipline as well as care.

row.basis: lamb grows inside the household as a daughter
row.note: Nathan's poor man's lamb grows up with him and his children, shares food and drink, lies in his bosom, and is like a daughter. It makes the commentary's domestic sheep image into a striking household scene of nurtured dependence.

row.basis: child and nurse hidden from royal violence
row.note: Jehosheba takes the infant Joash with his nurse and hides them in a bedroom from those killing royal children. This is a separate biblical child-preservation scene joining danger, a nurse, concealment, and a substitute household.

row.basis: God receives the one abandoned by parents
row.note: Even if father and mother forsake the speaker, YHWH receives him. It provides a compact divine-foster-parent image beside the commentary's insistence that the one who truly raises a child may be other than the visible household.

row.basis: quieted soul like a weaned child with its mother
row.note: The psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child with its mother. It adds the post-nursing stage of peaceful attachment to the commentary's womb, breast, and gradual completion sequence.

row.basis: train a child in the way to go
row.note: The proverb explicitly speaks of training a child for his way so that age will not make him depart from it. It is a concise Hebrew Bible formulation of the commentary's terbiye as directed, enduring formation.

row.basis: God's work hidden in a pregnant womb
row.note: Qoheleth compares the unknowable work of God with not knowing how bones develop in a pregnant woman's womb. The comparison makes prenatal formation an arena of divine hiddenness, complementing the commentary's more affirmative image of God shaping there.

row.basis: God brings to birth and does not shut the womb
row.note: God asks whether the one who brings to birth would fail to cause delivery or shut the womb. It gives a prophetic divine-birth image that directly accompanies the commentary's womb as a place governed by God.

row.basis: an abandoned newborn lacks ordinary care
row.note: Jerusalem is figured as a newborn whose cord is not cut and who is not washed, salted, or swaddled. This negative picture makes bodily care of a weak infant the test case for the mercy and household nurture developed in the commentary.

row.basis: God sees the exposed infant and commands life
row.note: God passes the infant abandoned in blood and says, "Live." The rescue turns compassion toward a helpless child into decisive action, directly illuminating the commentary's definition of mercy as beneficence toward the weak.

row.basis: rescued infant grows to mature bodily fullness
row.note: In the continuing infant allegory, God causes the child to grow and arrive at maturity. The verse supplies a disturbing but precise prophetic instance of growth from exposure toward fullness, making the commentary's state-by-state completion image less sentimental.

row.basis: two opposed peoples issue from one womb
row.note: God tells Rebekah that two nations and divided peoples are in her womb. It qualifies the commentary's association of one womb with kinship by showing a biblical womb that contains rivalry and eventual separation.

In siege, women called compassionate cook their own children for food. This horrific reversal makes maternal compassion and household nourishment collapse into their opposites, a counter-image to the commentary's merciful womb-home.

row.basis: God retains the key of childbirth
row.note: The Bavli lists childbirth among the keys that God does not entrust to an intermediary, grounding it in Rachel's opened womb. This is a direct Jewish interpretive assertion of the divine agency behind the commentary's womb and birth images.

row.basis: parental duties of bodily, Torah, and vocational formation
row.note: The Bavli enumerates a father's obligations toward a son, including circumcision, redemption, Torah instruction, marriage, and a trade. It gives a concrete rabbinic map of upbringing that moves beyond birth toward a child's completed social and religious formation.

The account of Joshua ben Gamla's school reform makes accessible teachers for children a communal duty. It develops the commentary's teacher-nurturer image into an institutional form of care for learners who cannot yet sustain themselves.

row.basis: an infant responds within the mother's womb
row.note: At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb and she is filled with the Holy Spirit. The scene gives the womb a responsive sacred interior, alongside the commentary's womb as a divinely active place of formation.

row.basis: compassion for a bereaved mother and her only son
row.note: Jesus sees the bereaved widow and is moved with compassion before addressing her loss. The scene places mercy beside a mother's emptied household and anticipates restoration of her child, close to the commentary's maternal grief and return motif.

row.basis: womb and breasts praised for bearing and nursing Jesus
row.note: A woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts he nursed. This is an unusually explicit New Testament meeting with the commentary's womb-as-home and maternal-nourishment language.

row.basis: blessedness redirected to hearing and keeping God's word
row.note: Jesus answers the blessing of womb and breasts by pronouncing blessed those who hear and keep God's word. The response does not erase the preceding maternal image, but redirects its privileged meaning toward received teaching, a contrast central to the commentary's womb-to-learning movement.

row.basis: the Father's will that no little one perish
row.note: Jesus states that the heavenly Father does not will the loss of even one little one. It is a precise divine-parental articulation of mercy toward the weak child.

row.basis: birth from God rather than blood or human will
row.note: The prologue describes those born not from blood, fleshly will, or a man's will, but from God. It offers a Johannine redescription of descent that stands in productive tension with the commentary's bodily womb and kinship account.

Stephen says Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and became powerful in words and deeds. It supplies the educational continuation of the foster-household narrative, relevant to the commentary's move from being raised to being taught.

row.basis: adoption and the cry Abba, Father
row.note: The Spirit of adoption enables believers to cry, "Abba, Father." This makes nonbiological incorporation into a parental divine household an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's birth-parent and foster-parent distinctions.

Paul contrasts many guardians in Christ with his singular fatherhood through the gospel. It gives a particularly close Christian distinction between a supervising caregiver and a formative parent, matching the commentary's careful nonbirth-parent vocabulary.

Paul uses the passage from child to adult as the figure for a completed mode of knowing. It is a brief but exact New Testament staging of maturation that belongs beside terbiye's movement toward completion.

Paul invokes the household norm that parents should save for children, not children for parents. It directly connects parenthood with provision, complementing the commentary's domestic food and child-rearing images.

row.basis: God's son born of a woman
row.note: God sends his Son, born of a woman and under the law. The verse keeps incarnation within a concrete maternal birth while the surrounding argument moves toward adoption, furnishing both sides of the commentary's womb and foster-family frame.

row.basis: nourishing and cherishing as embodied care
row.note: A person nourishes and cherishes his own body, as Christ does the church. The verb for nourishing extends the commentary's rearing imagery into a Christian account of sustained, intimate care.

row.basis: children repay parents through care for their household
row.note: Children and grandchildren must first practice piety toward their own household and make return to their parents. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal from parental raising to a child's merciful responsibility.
Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy, which can make him wise for salvation. It is a direct image of instruction beginning in childhood and reaching mature discernment.

row.basis: milk and elementary instruction before mature teaching
row.note: The readers, who should be teachers, need the elementary words again and have become people needing milk. It adds the pedagogical problem behind the commentary's image of feeding learners small pieces of knowledge.

row.basis: fatherly discipline addressed to a son
row.note: The exhortation cites the address, "My son," and tells the child not to reject the Lord's discipline. This supplies the explicit father-son language whose later training result appears in Heb. 12:11.

row.basis: straight paths heal what is weak
row.note: After the discipline argument, hearers are told to make straight paths for their feet so that what is lame may be healed. It links the commentary's straight path to formative care for the weak rather than to direction alone.

row.basis: compassion fails without food and clothing
row.note: James rejects telling an inadequately clothed and hungry sibling to depart in peace without giving what the body needs. It makes the commentary's mercy-to-beneficence claim a sharply practical test involving household necessities.

row.basis: Mary's childhood nourishment in the temple
row.note: In the common chapter division, three-year-old Mary is placed at the temple and receives food from an angel. This infancy tradition adds a distinctly Christian scene of a child reared outside her parents' home; chapter and verse divisions vary by translation.

row.basis: God creates humans to grow toward perfection
row.note: Irenaeus argues that created humanity must grow gradually toward perfection rather than receive its final capacity all at once. This patristic account gives a theological analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as movement through states to completion.
The commentary labels ar-Raḥmān and ar-Raḥīm with Arabic root r-ḥ-m; YHWH names himself raḥum and gracious here, giving the mercy cognate a divine self-description.
The commentary's mercy words share a Semitic root with Moses' raḥum; Deuteronomy grounds that compassion in God's refusal to abandon the covenant people.
The commentary repeats mercy in 1:1 and 1:3; Lamentations uses the cognate raḥamim for compassion that has not ended, renewed each morning.
The commentary makes mercy the source of bestowed good; the psalm describes YHWH as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.

The commentary labels anʿamta with Arabic n-ʿ-m and glosses the gift as a good state; the cognate Hebrew pleasantness word describes the allotted inheritance as pleasant places, though it does not mean a bestowed favor here.
The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the cognate Hebrew noʿam describes Wisdom's ways as pleasant and her paths as peace, a limited lexical bridge to the commentary's path image.

The commentary identifies Rabb as the giver who completes beneficence; Daniel's Aramaic cognate rav means chief or superior for Daniel's appointment, showing related lordly rank language without the commentary's beneficence sense.
The commentary pictures niʿma as a hand extending good; Israel's creed says God brought them out with a strong hand and outstretched arm, naming the rescue behind their received good.
The commentary says the gift becomes a community's path; Israel recounts being brought into a land flowing with milk and honey before presenting its first fruits.
The commentary says the recipient answers a gift with hamd; the offerer sets the first fruits before God and bows, turning received land into a grateful act.
The commentary makes a bestowed favor belong to a community; Israel rejoices in every good received with Levite and resident alien, extending the response to fellow recipients.
The commentary says praise answers received favor; Moses commands Israel to eat, be satisfied, and bless YHWH for the good land.
The commentary contrasts praise of the giver with forgetting the gift; Moses warns that fullness can lead Israel to forget YHWH.
The commentary warns against claiming one's own spending as a favor; Moses anticipates Israel saying its own power made its wealth.
The commentary locates the gift in its giver; Moses tells Israel to remember YHWH, who gives the power to make wealth and confirms the covenant.
The commentary's hamd includes telling another person the giver's good acts; Moses recounts to Jethro what YHWH did for Israel and the hardships from which he rescued them.
The commentary pictures praise of the benefactor in another's presence; Jethro rejoices at the good YHWH has done for Israel after hearing Moses' account.
The commentary links reporting God's favor with praise; Jethro blesses YHWH before naming the rescue from Egypt and Pharaoh.

row.basis: praise and thanks for received gifts
row.note: The commentary places hamd before the named favor; David's assembly blesses God's glorious name and gives thanks for all that comes from him.
The commentary treats the recipient's praise as an answer to favor; David says that all things come from God and that the offering is given from what is already God's.

row.basis: giving from what belongs to God
row.note: The commentary depicts the giver's good passing to a recipient; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says to give God what is God's, since the person and possessions are God's, interpreting David's words in 1 Chronicles 29:14.

row.basis: blessing before benefiting from the world
row.note: The commentary says hamd answers a received favor; the rabbis rule that one may not enjoy worldly benefit without a blessing, making praise a recognition of God's ownership and gift.
The commentary says the recipient recounts the benefactor's goodness before others; the rescued speaker promises to tell God's name to his brothers and praise him in the congregation.

row.basis: poor eat, are satisfied, and praise
row.note: The commentary joins received provision to praise; in the same psalm's assembly the poor eat and are satisfied, and those seeking God praise him.
The commentary distinguishes recounting God's favors from boasting in one's own giving; the psalmist's soul boasts in YHWH, so the humble hear and rejoice.
The commentary makes praise the recipient's response; the psalmist magnifies YHWH and reports that God answered and delivered him from fear.
The commentary's hamd includes telling others about the giver's favors; the psalmist invites God-fearers to hear what God did for him.

row.basis: making God's deeds known among peoples
row.note: The commentary says the benefactor's kindnesses are recounted to others; the psalm commands thanks to YHWH and making his deeds known among the peoples.
The commentary's praise names the giver's good before others; the psalm calls for singing and telling all God's wondrous works.
The commentary says praise answers received good; worshippers enter with thanksgiving and praise, naming God as their benefactor.
The commentary roots good in mercy; the psalm grounds praise in God's goodness and enduring steadfast love.
The commentary says recipients recount the giver's favors; the psalmist tells his own soul not to forget all God's benefits.
The commentary describes nimah as good bestowed on a recipient; the psalm names forgiveness and healing among God's benefits.
The commentary pictures favor as a gift reaching its recipient; the psalm says God redeems life and crowns the speaker with steadfast love and compassion.
The commentary's secondary gloss says giving can mean adding beyond enough; the psalm says God satisfies life with good and renews youth.
The commentary labels its repeated ar-Raḥmān/ar-Raḥīm with Arabic r-ḥ-m; this psalm uses the cognate compassion language alongside grace and abundant steadfast love.

row.basis: thanks for steadfast love and wonders
row.note: The commentary says beneficiaries recount good received; the psalm repeatedly calls the redeemed to thank YHWH for his steadfast love and wonderful works.
The commentary says the giver's favor reaches a needy recipient; the psalm says God satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's answer to favor; the psalmist asks what he can return to YHWH for all his benefits.
The commentary includes telling God's favors before others; the psalmist fulfills his vows to YHWH in the presence of all God's people.
The commentary makes divine mercy the source of good; the psalm praises YHWH as gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and great in steadfast love.
The commentary visualizes a hand extending a gift; the psalm says God opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing.
The commentary says the recipient's praise names the benefactor; the psalm ends by calling all flesh to bless God's holy name forever.

row.basis: asking to be shown God's ways
row.note: The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the psalmist asks God to make his ways known.
The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the path; the psalm asks God to lead and teach the speaker because God is his salvation.

row.basis: all paths are love and faithfulness
row.note: The commentary joins divine favor to the path; the psalm says all YHWH's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant.
The commentary names Rabb as the one completing good and making the recipient's way possible; the psalm calls YHWH shepherd and says the speaker lacks nothing.
The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the shepherd psalm says God restores the soul and leads the speaker in right paths.
The commentary asks for the path of those favored and distinguishes them from the other groups; the psalm contrasts the way YHWH knows with the way of the wicked that perishes.
The commentary calls the gift a path on which one walks; Proverbs depicts the righteous person's way as a light growing brighter toward day.
The commentary sets the favored path against those who stray; Proverbs contrasts the dark way of the wicked, who stumble without knowing what made them fall.
The commentary asks for the path of the favored rather than the opposing path; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life.

row.basis: loving and holding fast to God
row.note: The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the path; Moses identifies life with loving, obeying, and holding fast to YHWH.

row.basis: hearts that stray and do not know God's ways
row.note: The commentary distinguishes those who receive guidance from those who stray; the psalm identifies the wilderness generation by their wandering hearts and failure to know God's ways.

row.basis: divine anger and exclusion from rest
row.note: The commentary names those under anger as the contrary group; the psalm's wilderness oracle ends with God's oath that they will not enter his rest.

row.basis: we strayed from the way of truth
row.note: The commentary contrasts the sought path with those who stray; the wicked in Wisdom confess that they left the way of truth and righteousness.
The commentary excludes those who lose the way; the same confession says the wicked wearied themselves on paths of lawlessness, giving the wandering a moral setting.

row.basis: the broad way leading to destruction
row.note: The commentary asks for one path and distinguishes its recipients from those astray; Jesus says the wide gate and broad way lead to destruction.

row.basis: the narrow way leading to life
row.note: The commentary asks for the path of the favored; Jesus contrasts the narrow gate and hard way that lead to life.
The commentary makes hamd the answer to received favor; Zechariah begins by blessing Israel's God for visiting and redeeming his people.
The commentary connects the path of the favored to divine mercy; Zechariah says the redemption enacts mercy promised to the ancestors and remembrance of the covenant.
The commentary says mercy is the source of beneficence; Zechariah attributes the coming dawn to the tender mercy of God.

row.basis: guiding feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary joins received favor to a path; Zechariah says the dawn will guide feet into the way of peace.
The commentary says the path is a favor received from God; Paul describes salvation as grace through faith and God's gift.

row.basis: no boasting in one's own works
row.note: The commentary rejects claiming one's own expenditure as a favor; Paul excludes boasting because salvation is not from works.
The commentary says the favor is completed by walking the path; Paul says God made believers for good works prepared for them to walk in.
The commentary's B002 gloss on Rabb is completion of beneficence and its path ends in walking; Paul trusts God to complete the good work begun in the believers until Christ's day.
The commentary says praise answers a gift and its B010 gloss includes giving more; Jesus gives thanks, distributes the loaves, and feeds the crowd.
The commentary says anʿama can mean adding beyond enough; after the crowd is filled, Jesus orders the surplus fragments gathered so none is lost.

row.basis: fullness received as grace upon grace
row.note: The commentary's secondary gloss says a gift may be increased beyond measure; John says all received from Christ's fullness, grace upon grace.

row.basis: thanks for grace given in Christ
row.note: The commentary makes praise the response to a received gift; Paul thanks God for grace given to the Corinthian believers in Christ.

row.basis: God sustains believers to the end
row.note: The commentary links a completed favor to a walked path; Paul says Christ will strengthen the community to the end, blameless at his day.

row.basis: what was received leaves no ground to boast
row.note: The commentary warns against advertising what one spent as one's own merit; Paul asks what anyone has that was not received and rejects boasting as though it were not received.

row.basis: failure to glorify or give thanks
row.note: The commentary presents praise as the due answer to received good; Paul describes people who knew God yet neither glorified him nor gave thanks.
The commentary says mercy is the source of the favor that guides a person; Paul says God's kindness, forbearance, and patience lead toward repentance.
The commentary warns against self-praise for a favor received; Paul tells grafted-in Gentiles not to boast over the natural branches because the root supports them.

The commentary distinguishes those receiving favor from those under anger; Paul sets God's kindness toward believers beside severity toward those who fell, and warns the former to continue in kindness.

row.basis: the healed man glorifies God aloud
row.note: The commentary says the recipient recounts the giver's favor; one healed leper returns, loudly glorifying God.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's answer to a gift; the Samaritan falls at Jesus' feet and thanks him after healing.

row.basis: the foreigner returns to praise God
row.note: The commentary says praise of the benefactor should be voiced; Jesus asks whether only the foreigner returned to give glory to God.

row.basis: food, gladness, and witness to God's goodness
row.note: The commentary connects divine favor to the provision of good; Paul says God gave rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness, leaving witness among the nations.

row.basis: grace multiplying thanksgiving to God's glory
row.note: The commentary says the recipient's praise follows God's favor; Paul says grace reaching more people multiplies thanksgiving to God's glory.
The commentary's B010 branch says giving may exceed what is sufficient; Paul says God can make grace abound so believers have sufficiency for every good work.
The commentary says the giver's good reaches a recipient who praises; Paul says generosity enriches the giver and produces thanksgiving to God through the recipients.
The commentary links conveyed good with praise of its source; Paul says the service supplies the saints' needs and overflows in many thanksgivings to God.
The commentary depicts beneficiaries recounting the giver's good; Paul says recipients glorify God for the donors' confession and generous sharing.
The commentary says praise answers a gift; Paul closes the account of giving by thanking God for his inexpressible gift.

row.basis: called from darkness to proclaim praises
row.note: The commentary asks for the path of people favored by God; Peter describes a people called from darkness into marvelous light to proclaim God's excellencies.

row.basis: once not a people, now recipients of mercy
row.note: The commentary identifies a community by the favor it received; Peter says those once outside the people have become God's people and have received mercy.

row.basis: blessing God for new birth and hope
row.note: The commentary makes hamd the answer to a favor; Peter blesses God for new birth to a living hope through Jesus' resurrection.
The commentary says the favor belongs to a community and its path; Peter names an imperishable inheritance kept in heaven for believers.

row.basis: faith tested toward praise and honor
row.note: The commentary makes the path end in a completed favor; Peter says tested faith will result in praise, glory, and honor at Jesus' revelation.

row.basis: thanksgiving and praise before the throne
row.note: The commentary places hamd as the fitting answer to God's favor; the heavenly assembly ascribes blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might to God.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds and guides to water
row.note: The commentary joins divine favor with a path; the Lamb shepherds the multitude and guides them to springs of living water.
The commentary distinguishes recounting God's favors from holding one's own generosity over people; Jesus warns that public almsgiving for recognition receives its reward from people.

row.basis: the giver does not advertise the gift
row.note: The commentary condemns self-credit for one's spending; Jesus says the giver's left hand should not know what the right hand gives.
The commentary contrasts service with self-praise; Jesus says secret giving is seen and rewarded by the Father.
The commentary distinguishes praise of the giver from claiming one's own merit; the Pharisee thanks God while boasting that he is unlike other people.

row.basis: the self-exalting and humble are reversed
row.note: The commentary contrasts benefactor-praise with self-praise; Jesus says the self-exalting Pharisee is not justified, while the humble tax collector is.

row.basis: do not add reproach to a gift
row.note: The commentary describes hamd's reverse as rubbing one's favor in another's face; Ben Sira directly says not to add reproach or hurtful words when doing good or giving.
The commentary warns that the recipient can be humiliated by a favor held over them; Ben Sira says a gift from a grudging person dims the eyes, showing how manner changes the gift.
The commentary pictures good passing from one hand to another; the king has compassion and cancels a servant's debt, a received favor that sets up the servant's obligation toward another.

row.basis: failure to pass received mercy onward
row.note: The commentary says an act of kindness is carried to another; the king condemns the forgiven servant for failing to show his fellow servant the mercy he received.
The commentary says mercy is the source of beneficence; Jesus describes God as kind even to the ungrateful and evil, then commands love of enemies.
The commentary presents receiving God's mercy as the ground of a favored way; Jesus tells disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful.

row.basis: love as a response to prior love
row.note: The commentary makes the recipient's response follow the giver's favor; John says believers love because God first loved them.

row.basis: received goods shared with a brother
row.note: The commentary's hand-to-hand image traces good from giver to recipient; John asks how God's love can remain in someone who sees a needy brother and closes the heart despite possessing the world's goods.

row.basis: love enacted rather than merely spoken
row.note: The commentary contrasts genuine praise and giving with words that claim merit; John requires love in deed and truth, giving the response a practical form.

row.basis: bless God for all his works
row.note: The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to God's favor; Ben Sira blesses the God who does great things everywhere and asks that God grant joy of heart.

row.basis: declare God's greatness among the nations
row.note: The commentary says God's favor should be told to others; Tobit calls Israel to declare God's greatness before the nations and praise him in Jerusalem.
The commentary joins received mercy with a public response; Tobit says those who turn to God with their whole heart will bless him in truth.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's response to a gift; the community's meal prayer gives thanks over the cup and broken bread as gifts from God through Jesus.

row.basis: gathering the Church as one people
row.note: The commentary says favor belongs to a community and its path; the Eucharistic prayer asks that the scattered Church be gathered into God's kingdom, like bread once scattered and made one.

row.basis: thanksgiving for gifts of knowledge and life
row.note: The commentary says praise follows what God gives; after the meal the community thanks the holy Father for his name, knowledge, faith, and immortality given through Jesus.

row.basis: the prayer ends in glory to God
row.note: The commentary says the opening hamd returns at the end of the path; the Didache's thanksgiving closes by ascribing glory to God forever.

row.basis: praise as the creature's response to its maker
row.note: The commentary places hamd before naming the specific gift; Augustine opens by praising God as creator and says human beings are made for God, so praise is the fitting response to dependence itself.
The commentary says recipients answer good with praise; after Israel is rescued from Egypt, Moses and Israel sing to YHWH about the victory.
The commentary's praise names the giver and his good; the song calls YHWH strength, song, and salvation, joining worship to received deliverance.

row.basis: anger turns and comfort is received
row.note: The commentary distinguishes those under anger from those given favor; Isaiah's rescued speaker says God's anger has turned away and he has comforted him.
The commentary says one should recount the giver's favor; Isaiah calls the people to thank YHWH and make his deeds known among the peoples.
The commentary's hamd is voiced before others; Isaiah calls the people to sing because God has done gloriously and make it known throughout the earth.

row.basis: rejoicing in the Holy One among the people
row.note: The commentary links divine favor to a community's road; Isaiah calls Zion to shout and sing because the Holy One is great in Israel's midst.
The commentary says the recipient's answer is praise; Isaiah says the people God formed are to recount God's praise.

row.basis: God teaches the way to walk
row.note: The commentary says the favor is a path-gift; Isaiah names YHWH as teacher who leads Israel in the way it should go.

row.basis: being led out in joy and peace
row.note: The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the way; Isaiah depicts the redeemed going out with joy and being led in peace.
The commentary says praise can tell others the giver's favors; Isaiah's speaker publicly recounts YHWH's acts of steadfast love and praise for Israel.
The commentary makes mercy the source of good bestowed on a people; Isaiah says God saved them in love and pity and carried them through their days.

row.basis: boasting in strength or wealth is rejected
row.note: The commentary rejects making one's own expenditure a public merit; Jeremiah says the wise, mighty, and rich must not boast in their own wisdom, power, or riches.

row.basis: boast only in knowing the God who does kindness
row.note: The commentary says praise should name the benefactor's goodness; Jeremiah permits boasting only in understanding and knowing YHWH, who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.
The commentary says hamd reaches beyond thanking for a particular material gift; Habakkuk imagines the loss of figs, grapes, olives, fields, and flock.
The commentary's praise is directed to the giver rather than only to goods; Habakkuk rejoices in YHWH and exults in the God of salvation despite the failed harvest.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter, rather than Pharaoh, adopts Moses
row.note: The commentary recalls Pharaoh claiming Moses' upbringing as a favor; Exodus says Pharaoh's daughter draws the child from the water and adopts him, shifting the rescuer from the king to his daughter.
The commentary's Pharaoh reproaches Moses with a personal favor while Moses answers with Israel's oppression; Exodus presents Pharaoh as the ruler who sets taskmasters over Israel.
The commentary says Moses answers the favor-reproach by naming Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; Exodus narrates the Egyptians' ruthless forced labor as the background that reverses the king's claim.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses as her son
row.note: The commentary places the claim of raising Moses in Pharaoh's mouth; Stephen's retelling attributes his rescue and adoption to Pharaoh's daughter, preserving the household upbringing but changing the agent.

row.basis: Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son
row.note: The commentary presents a royal upbringing invoked as a favor; Hebrews says Moses later refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, emphasizing his break with that household identity.

row.basis: compassion shown beyond the expected group
row.note: The commentary asks for the path of those favored; Jonah resents God's graciousness and compassion toward Nineveh, exposing the tension over who receives mercy.

row.basis: Jeshurun grows full and forgets the giver
row.note: The commentary warns that good must be answered with praise rather than taken for granted; Moses says Jeshurun grew fat, then forsook the God who made him.

row.basis: he people receive provision from heaven
row.note: The commentary describes favor as good conveyed to a recipient; the psalm says God opened heaven and rained manna to feed Israel.

row.basis: the people remain ungrateful after wonders
row.note: The commentary makes praise the fitting response to received benefits; despite God's wonders, the people continue to sin and fail to trust.
The commentary distinguishes divine mercy from anger; the psalm says God is compassionate, forgives, and often turns away his anger from the people.

row.basis: merciful and gracious remembrance of wonders
row.note: The commentary links mercy with the praise-worthy giver; the psalm says God made his wonders remembered and is gracious and compassionate.

row.basis: thanks for God's goodness and enduring love
row.note: The commentary says praise answers received good; the litany begins by thanking God for goodness and repeats enduring love through its account of creation and deliverance.
The commentary's ar-Raḥmān/ar-Raḥīm share the Semitic mercy root with the psalm's raḥum; the verse describes God's compassion, patience, and great love.

row.basis: Moses' mercy attributes become a repeated prayer form
row.note: The commentary repeats the mercy formula in 1:1 and 1:3; the rabbis read Exodus 34:6 as the order of divine attributes Moses was taught to invoke whenever Israel sins and seeks forgiveness.

row.basis: bowing and worship after the mercy formula
row.note: The commentary presents mercy as the source of good and hamd as the response; after YHWH proclaims compassion, Moses bows to the ground and worships.

row.basis: mercy requested for a people on the way
row.note: The commentary links the favor of a people to their path; Moses asks God to go among them, pardon their sin, and take them as his inheritance.
The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to favor; after Samuel's birth Hannah rejoices in YHWH and his salvation, telling of God's reversal of her condition.
The commentary describes hamd as response to a gift; David asks who he is and what his house is that God has brought him this far, receiving the promised future as undeserved good.
The commentary says praise names the benefactor; David declares that there is no one like YHWH and no God besides him after hearing the promise to his house.
The commentary says the recipient recognizes the giver's good; David calls God's words true and recalls that God has promised this good to his servant.

row.basis: land received without the people's labor
row.note: The commentary describes favor as good conveyed to a community; Joshua recalls that God gave Israel land, cities, vineyards, and olive groves they had not made or planted.
The commentary makes worship an answer to benefit; Joshua therefore tells Israel to fear and serve YHWH sincerely, remembering God's prior acts.
The commentary asks for the way of those favored; Joshua puts rival forms of service before Israel and calls the people to choose whom they will serve.

row.basis: remembering great deeds as a reason to serve
row.note: The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to good; Samuel tells Israel to fear and serve YHWH faithfully and consider the great things he has done for them.

The commentary says the recipient's praise returns at the journey's end; after God turns mourning into dancing, the psalmist says his soul will sing praise and give thanks forever. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)
The commentary says God's favors are recounted before others; the psalmist does not hide God's deliverance, faithfulness, and love from the great congregation. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

row.basis: blessing that makes God's way known
row.note: The commentary joins a bestowed favor to a path; the psalm asks God to bless the people so that God's way and saving power become known on earth. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

row.basis: nations rejoice under God's just guidance
row.note: The commentary asks for a path of divine favor; the psalm calls the nations to rejoice because God judges peoples with equity and guides the nations on earth. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

row.basis: blessing that reaches the ends of the earth
row.note: The commentary describes a community receiving favor; the psalm asks God to bless Israel so that all the ends of the earth fear him. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

The commentary's account of hamd includes telling another person the giver's goodness; this verse says the speaker has not concealed God's steadfast love and faithfulness from the assembly. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)
The commentary calls the received favor a path-gift; pilgrims crossing the Valley of Baca make it a spring, and the early rain covers it with blessings. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

row.basis: God's love and faithfulness told for generations
row.note: The commentary says the benefactor's good is told aloud; the psalmist says he will sing of YHWH's steadfast love and make his faithfulness known through every generation. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

row.basis: compassion pictured as a father's care
