row.note: The commentary grounds good in mercy; the psalm compares YHWH's compassion for those who fear him to a father's compassion for his children.
The commentary includes recounting a giver's favor before others; the psalm tells the redeemed to offer thanksgiving sacrifices and tell God's works with songs of joy.

row.basis: thanksgiving as a public act of worship
row.note: The commentary makes hamd the response to a received benefit; the psalmist offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name after asking how to repay God's benefits.
The commentary says recipients tell the benefactor's kindnesses; the psalm says they pour out the memory of God's abundant goodness and sing of his righteousness.
The commentary presents mercy as the source of bestowed good; the psalm says YHWH is good to all and his compassion extends to all he has made.

row.basis: happiness grounded in God as helper
row.note: The commentary identifies the favored as a people whose good comes from God; the psalm calls blessed the person whose help is the God of Jacob and whose hope rests in YHWH.
The commentary's image is good reaching a recipient; the psalm praises God who executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry.
The commentary calls favor a path on which one walks; Isaiah says the way of the righteous is level and God makes it smooth.

row.basis: the Holy Way for the redeemed
row.note: The commentary asks for the path of those given favor; Isaiah depicts a holy highway on which the redeemed walk and from which the unclean are excluded.

row.basis: the redeemed return with praise and joy
row.note: The commentary says the path ends in completed favor; Isaiah says YHWH's ransomed return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy.
The commentary links mercy, provision, and a path; Isaiah says the compassionate one guides the redeemed and leads them beside springs of water so they do not hunger or thirst.
The commentary makes mercy the source of favor; YHWH says he has loved Israel with an everlasting love and drawn the people with steadfast love.

row.basis: leading the people on a straight path
row.note: The commentary says the favor is completed by walking a way; YHWH leads the returning people by streams of water on a straight path where they will not stumble.

row.basis: mercy despite a people's refusal to follow
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the favored path from those who stray; Nehemiah's prayer recounts Israel's rebellion yet calls God gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.
The commentary links a bestowed good to guidance along the way; Nehemiah's prayer says God gave his good spirit to instruct the people and supplied manna and water.

row.basis: fullness and delight in great goodness
row.note: The commentary says recipients should answer favor with praise; Nehemiah recalls that Israel ate, was filled, and delighted in God's great goodness.

The commentary contrasts the guided community with those who reject the way; Nehemiah says Israel became disobedient and killed the prophets who warned them after God had given them rest and abundance.
The commentary presents mercy as a source of continuing favor; Nehemiah says God did not make a complete end of Israel or abandon them because of his great mercies.

row.basis: God delights in mercy and forgives
row.note: The commentary connects divine mercy to the favored community; Micah praises the God who pardons iniquity and does not retain anger forever because he delights in steadfast love.
The commentary describes mercy as good reaching its recipients; Micah says God again has compassion and casts the people's sins away.

row.basis: steadfast love kept to the ancestors
row.note: The commentary treats favor as a communal inheritance; Micah says God keeps faith and steadfast love promised to Abraham and Jacob.

row.basis: Mary magnifies God in response to favor
row.note: The commentary says the receiver answers a gift with praise; Mary publicly magnifies the Lord and rejoices in God her savior.

row.basis: God has done great things for Mary
row.note: The commentary's hamd recounts the giver's good; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and names his holiness.
The commentary presents mercy as the source of blessing; Mary says God's mercy extends from generation to generation to those who fear him.

row.basis: God raises the lowly and brings down rulers
row.note: The commentary distinguishes those given favor from the contrary way; Mary's song describes God reversing status by bringing rulers down and exalting the lowly.
The commentary says favor is a gift delivered to recipients; Mary sings that God fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty.

row.basis: sun and rain given to just and unjust
row.note: The commentary identifies mercy as the source of good; Jesus says the Father gives sun and rain to both evil and good, extending divine beneficence beyond a single favored group.

row.basis: freely received good freely passed on
row.note: The commentary pictures favor passing from hand to hand; Jesus tells disciples that what they received freely they should give freely as they heal and proclaim.

row.basis: the healed man walks and praises God
row.note: The commentary joins a received favor to its path and response; the healed man enters the temple walking and leaping while praising God.

row.basis: the public sees the recipient praising
row.note: The commentary says the beneficiary can voice praise before others; everyone sees the formerly lame man walking and praising God.

row.basis: God gives life and breath to all
row.note: The commentary describes the giver as the source of good; Paul says God is not served as though needy, since he himself gives all people life, breath, and everything.

row.basis: no one first gives to God
row.note: The commentary says the beneficiary answers a gift with praise rather than claiming merit; Paul asks who has ever given God something first so that God must repay.

row.basis: all things come from God and return to him
row.note: The commentary makes the giver's favor the source and goal of the recipient's path; Paul says all things are from, through, and for God, to whom glory belongs.

row.basis: work attributed to grace rather than self
row.note: The commentary warns against presenting one's own effort as a merit; Paul says he worked hard, yet attributes what he is and his work to God's grace.
The commentary names mercy as the source of good; Paul blesses the Father of mercies and God of all comfort.

row.basis: comfort received and passed to others
row.note: The commentary pictures beneficence moving from giver to recipient; Paul says God comforts believers so they can comfort others in the trouble they themselves have received comfort through.

row.basis: thanks for a share in the inheritance
row.note: The commentary says a community receives a path and a gift; Paul gives thanks to the Father who qualified believers to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.

row.basis: transfer from darkness into a kingdom
row.note: The commentary contrasts the favored path with those astray; Paul says God rescued believers from the authority of darkness and transferred them into the Son's kingdom.
The commentary says favor is completed by walking its path; Paul tells believers to walk in Christ Jesus, whom they received.
The commentary joins the path of favor to praise; Paul describes believers as rooted and built up in Christ, abounding in thanksgiving.
The commentary says a gift can be ruined by holding it over its recipient; James says God gives wisdom generously to all and does not reproach the one who asks.

row.basis: every good gift comes from above
row.note: The commentary says all good reaches the recipient from its giver; James says every good giving and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights.

row.basis: divine power grants what leads to life
row.note: The commentary joins bestowed favor with a path to walk; Peter says God's power has granted everything needed for life and godliness, calling believers by glory and excellence.

row.basis: riches are gifts, not grounds for pride
row.note: The commentary rejects self-credit for what one has received; Paul tells the rich not to be arrogant but to hope in God, who richly provides all things to enjoy.

row.basis: received wealth used generously for others
row.note: The commentary depicts good passing from hand to hand; Paul tells the wealthy to do good, be generous, and ready to share.

row.basis: stewarding a gift for one another
row.note: The commentary pictures favor as good delivered to another; Peter tells each person to use the gift received to serve others as a steward of God's varied grace.

row.basis: salvation from mercy rather than deeds
row.note: The commentary makes divine mercy the source of favor; Titus says God saved people through mercy, not righteous works they had done.

row.basis: grace makes recipients heirs in hope
row.note: The commentary says favor is a gift that carries a community toward its end; Titus says believers justified by grace become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

row.basis: praise voiced as the fruit of lips
row.note: The commentary says the recipient should recount the benefactor's good; Hebrews calls believers to offer continual praise to God, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
The commentary asks for a path that does not stray; Jude praises God who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless.

row.basis: glory to the only God at the journey's end
row.note: The commentary says the opening praise returns at the end of the path; Jude's closing doxology gives glory, majesty, power, and authority to God through Jesus Christ.

row.basis: creatures acknowledge the giver of all things
row.note: The commentary makes praise the response to God's favor; the heavenly elders worship the creator because all things exist by his will.

row.basis: salvation belongs to God and the Lamb
row.note: The commentary names a community by the favor it received; the multitude cries that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb before the elders' full doxology.

row.basis: blessing God for adversity as well as good
row.note: The commentary says hamd is broader than thanks for a discrete favor; the Mishnah requires a blessing for bad events as for good, extending praise beyond a favorable outcome.

row.basis: food blessings traced to manna and land
row.note: The commentary places praise after a received benefit; the rabbis attribute the blessings after meals to Moses at the manna, Joshua on entering the land, and David and Solomon at Jerusalem, reading Israel's liturgy through successive gifts.

row.basis: command to declare God's deeds to the living
row.note: The commentary says the recipient should tell others about the giver's favor; Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias to bless God, give thanks, and declare God's works before all the living.

row.basis: a victory hymn directed to God
row.note: The commentary says a beneficiary answers good with public praise; after Israel's deliverance Judith begins a song to her God with instruments.

row.basis: singing a new song for God's strength
row.note: The commentary describes praise that tells the giver's deeds; Judith sings a new song to God and praises his greatness and invincible power.

row.basis: the delivered people bless God's holy name
row.note: The commentary makes praise follow received deliverance; Wisdom says the righteous sang praise and blessed God's holy name after their rescue.
The commentary says God's favor includes the capacity to praise; Wisdom says the divine Wisdom opened the mouths of the mute and made the tongues of infants clear.

row.basis: food given so people may thank the creator
row.note: The commentary says recipients answer God's provision with hamd; the post-meal prayer says God gave food and drink to humanity so that people might thank him, then names the community's spiritual food and drink.

row.basis: celestial lights mark seasons and years
row.note: The commentary cites crescents as time markers and lunar stations for calculation; Genesis assigns the heavenly lights to seasons, days, and years, placing calendrical order in the created sky.

row.basis: moon for appointed times; sun's setting
row.note: The commentary defines yawm by sunrise and sunset and adds lunar stations; this verse assigns the moon to appointed times and says the sun knows its setting, joining both clocks in one creation hymn.
The commentary's yawm runs from sunrise to sunset; Ecclesiastes depicts the sun rising, setting, and returning to its place, making the repeated daytime circuit explicit.
The commentary pictures the sky turning through the day; the psalm's sun runs across the heavens from one end to the other, adding a full-circuit image to the sunrise-to-sunset gloss.
The commentary's Arabic root gloss pictures the sun standing at noon; Joshua says the sun stood in mid-heaven and did not hurry to set, presenting a miraculous extension of daylight.
The commentary's gloss places the sun upright at noon with almost no shadow; Amos reverses that image by making the sun set at noon and darkening the day as a judgment sign.

The commentary says the cave's sun shifts aside from the sleepers; the psalm promises that sun will not strike by day nor moon by night under God's keeping, a close image of shelter from celestial exposure.
The commentary cites the crescent as a time marker for people and pilgrimage; the psalm sounds a trumpet at the new moon and full moon for a feast, showing lunar phases setting communal worship time.

The commentary's source gloss describes a crescent just risen above the horizon; the Mishnah has Rabban Gamliel use moon-shaped images to question witnesses, showing how visible lunar form could govern the calendar.

row.basis: moon phases mark seasons and festivals
row.note: The commentary names lunar stations as aids to reckoning and crescents as time signs; Sirach describes the moon's phases as markers of seasons and feast days, an explicit Jewish calendrical parallel.

row.basis: sun shining and moon in splendor
row.note: The commentary's Abraham says he does not love the setting luminaries; Job describes seeing the bright sun or moon walking in splendor, then tests whether that sight entices him to worship.
The commentary contrasts worship of the sun with worship of God alone; Job names a secretly enticed heart and a hand kissing the mouth as the gesture of astral devotion.
The commentary's Abraham turns from setting lights to the Creator of heaven and earth; Job says worship of the sun or moon would deny the God above, making the theological judgment explicit.

row.basis: sun, moon, and host of heaven
row.note: The commentary distinguishes worship of the rising and setting lights from worship of their Creator; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, stars, or heavenly host.
The commentary cites the prohibition on prostrating to sun and moon; Deuteronomy treats serving either luminary or the host of heaven as covenantal apostasy, giving the prohibition a legal setting.

row.basis: men bowing to the eastern sun
row.note: The commentary describes people prostrating to the sun instead of God; Ezekiel sees men with their backs to the temple and faces east, bowing to the sun, making the bodily reversal concrete.
The commentary's sun-worshippers have a public cult; Kings reports priests burning incense to the sun, moon, constellations, and all the host of heaven, supplying an Israelite institutional example.

row.basis: star carried as a god's image
row.note: The commentary's Abraham sees a star and rejects a setting object as lord; WLC Amos names a star of a god among Israel's cult objects, showing the same kind of celestial body made an object of worship.
The commentary says sun-worship kept a people from the path; Stephen says God turned away and gave Israel over to worship the host of heaven, linking astral worship with divine abandonment.

The commentary's Abraham refuses a celestial body as lord; Stephen revoices the star-god tradition of Amos as the star of Rephan and connects the cult to exile, showing a Christian reception of Israel's astral-idolatry text.

The commentary rejects worship of sun and moon and turns to their Creator; Wisdom says people may take sun, moon, and stars for gods because of their beauty, but should recognize their Lord as greater because he made them.

The commentary ends Abraham's sky scene with his face turned to the Creator of heaven and earth; in Genesis Abraham swears by the Most High, maker of heaven and earth, giving a close Abrahamic statement of allegiance.

row.ref: Jacob of Serugh, Homily on the Young Men of Ephesus
row.note: The commentary describes young sleepers sheltered in a cave; Jacob's Syriac homily recounts the Christian youths of Ephesus sleeping in a cave, a close narrative parallel, while the Qur'anic commentary singles out the sun's path around them.
The commentary's root gloss evokes a high, unobscured midday sun; Mark places darkness over the land from the sixth hour, a contrary noon image in a distinct scene.

The commentary links the straight-path image to the sun at its noon height; Proverbs pictures the righteous path as dawn light growing brighter until full day, joining ethical direction to the day's light.
The commentary's source gloss describes the sky as what is above and shades a person; this psalm calls the LORD one's shade at the right hand, transferring the shelter image to divine protection.

The commentary evokes a crescent and a station of the moon; 1 Enoch lays out the moon's recurring phases and course, giving a Jewish astronomical account of the ordered lunar cycle without equating its system with the commentary's term.

The commentary cites lunar stations for counting years and crescents for marking times; Jubilees prescribes a 364-day year and warns against lunar reckoning that disrupts the seasons, a specific Jewish calendar counter-position.

row.basis: horses and chariots for the sun
row.note: The commentary names the sun as an object people worship; Kings reports solar horses and chariots at the temple entrance, a distinct royal rite removed by Josiah.

The commentary's Abraham tests a star, moon, and sun and turns to their Creator; Jubilees presents Abram studying celestial signs before recognizing sun, moon, and stars as subject to the Lord, a related Abraham tradition whose concern is prognostication rather than a sequence of rival lords.

row.basis: stars as a promise, not lords
row.note: The commentary's Abraham treats a star's setting as grounds not to love it; Genesis directs Abraham to count the stars as a sign of promised descendants, giving the same celestial gaze a promise-bearing rather than devotional role.

The commentary's Abraham seeks guidance after the moon sets and turns to the Creator; Genesis says Abraham believes the LORD in the star-promise scene, placing trust in God rather than in the lights themselves.
The commentary mentions a woman ruling the sun-worshipping people; Kings introduces the Queen of Sheba coming to Solomon, a matching royal setting for the Qur'anic report.

The commentary places a female ruler over a sun-worshipping people; in Kings the Queen of Sheba blesses the LORD for establishing Solomon, so the parallel foregrounds different religious emphases in the two Sheba accounts.

The commentary's command rejects prostration to sun and moon in favor of their Creator; Paul names the same creator-creature reversal in describing people who worship and serve what was made, though he does not specify the luminaries.

The commentary treats the crescent and lunar stations as useful measures of time; Paul places observance of days, months, seasons, and years within the Galatians' return to bondage, a contrasting Christian evaluation, though he does not name the crescent.

row.basis: Father of lights without turning's shadow
row.note: The commentary's image makes the sun, moon, and sky change position and cast or lose shadows; James calls God the Father of lights with no variation or shadow from turning, a specific image-level contrast between changing lights and God.

row.basis: greater and lesser lights govern day and night
row.note: The commentary's command rejects prostration to sun and moon because they are created; Genesis says God made the greater and lesser lights to govern day and night, supplying the creation order behind their demotion from gods.

row.basis: sunrise and the creatures' daily cycle
row.note: The commentary defines yawm by the sun's course from sunrise to sunset; this verse says the sun rises and nocturnal animals return to their dens, showing the daily transition.
The commentary's yawm spans sunrise to sunset; the next verse places human labor between sunrise and evening, giving that span a human daily rhythm.
The commentary joins the turning daylight to Fatiha's praise of God; this psalm says the LORD's name is praised from the sun's rising to its setting, making worship fill the same solar interval.

row.basis: God's name great from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary separates worship of the sun from worship of God; Malachi says God's name is great among the nations from the sun's rising to its setting and that incense is offered to him everywhere.

row.basis: sun and moon praise the LORD
row.note: The commentary says people must worship the Creator rather than the sun and moon; the psalm calls those same luminaries to praise the LORD, reversing the direction of worship.
The commentary's solar prohibition directs worship to the one who made the luminaries; Nehemiah's prayer says the host of heaven worships the God who made heaven and all its host.

row.basis: divine light and truth lead the speaker
row.note: The commentary's Abraham fears becoming astray without the Lord's guidance and turns from transient lights; the psalm asks God's light and truth to lead the speaker to God's altar, making divine illumination a guide rather than an object of worship.

row.basis: God appoints sun, moon, and stars
row.note: The commentary presents the sky's daily and lunar motions as a created order; Jeremiah names God as the one who gives the sun for daytime light and appoints the moon and stars by night.

row.basis: sun's rising and heat at noon
row.note: The commentary's source gloss describes the sun standing at noon with little shadow; Sirach praises the sun at its rising and its powerful heat at noon, giving a Jewish description of the same daily solar arc.

The commentary pictures the sky turning through the day from sunrise to sunset; the Astronomical Book describes the sun's ordered rising and setting through heavenly gates, an expanded Jewish account of the solar course.

row.basis: straying from the way as light and sun fail
row.note: The commentary joins Abraham's fear of being astray with the setting of celestial lights; Wisdom's condemned speakers say they strayed from the way of truth, that righteousness's light did not shine, and that the sun did not rise for them.

row.basis: YHWH replaces sun and moon as light
row.note: The commentary calls sun and moon created lights that must not receive worship; Isaiah says restored Zion will no longer need the sun by day or moon by night because YHWH will be its everlasting light.

The commentary directs worship from sun and moon to their Creator; Revelation's city needs neither because God's glory illuminates it and the Lamb is its lamp, carrying Isaiah's contrast into a Christian vision.

row.basis: light guides feet to the way of peace
row.note: The commentary's Abraham asks for guidance away from error and the Fatiha asks for the straight path; Zechariah's song has dawn-light reach those in darkness and guide their feet to peace.

The commentary's Abraham watches star, moon, and sun before turning to the Creator; Genesis Rabbah reads God's instruction to look at the stars as answering Abram's astrological forecast that he would have no child, a Jewish interpretation that subordinates celestial fate to divine guidance.

row.basis: sun darkened before the day of the LORD
row.note: The commentary defines the day under the sun's ordinary rise and setting; in WLC numbering Joel places the sun's darkening and moon's change before the great day of the LORD, joining celestial reversal to a day of judgment.

The commentary presents the crescent as a marker for communal time and pilgrimage; Colossians names festivals and new moons among observances over which Christians should not be judged, a different religious framing of lunar time.
The commentary's image follows celestial lights rising over the horizon; Zechariah's song names a dawn from on high visiting the people, using sunrise as an image of divine arrival.

row.basis: star leads the travelers and stands over the child
row.note: The commentary's Abraham sees a star and rejects it as lord when it sets; Matthew's star serves as a sign that leads the travelers to the child, giving the celestial object a guiding rather than divine role.

row.basis: worship directed to the child, not the star
row.note: The commentary distinguishes worship of God from worship of celestial lights; after the star guides them, the Magi fall down before the child, so the narrative directs prostration away from the star.

row.basis: sun and moon darkened at the coming of the Son of Man
row.note: The commentary places the day of judgment alongside the ordinary solar day; Matthew describes sun and moon losing their light and stars falling before the Son of Man, giving a Christian apocalyptic meeting of judgment and celestial signs.

row.basis: the sun's light fails at the sixth hour
row.note: The commentary's root gloss pictures the sun standing high at noon; Luke says the sun's light failed during the darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour, a distinct Christian noon reversal.

row.basis: shadow moves backward as a solar sign
row.note: The commentary's source gloss pictures noon with the shadow nearly absent; Hezekiah asks for the shadow to move backward on the steps, using the sun-shadow relation as a miraculous sign rather than a stable midday balance.

The commentary's source glossary calls al-na'im one lunar mansion; Job names Mazzaroth in its season among celestial groups, a possible parallel in ordered sky stations, though the identity of Mazzaroth and its relation to lunar mansions are uncertain.

row.basis: Ox knows owner; donkey knows manger
row.note: The commentary says a stray camel has an unknown owner but livestock recognize their master; Isaiah turns ox and donkey's recognition into a rebuke because Israel does not know its Lord.
The commentary contrasts animals that know their owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah says migratory birds know their times while God's people do not know his ordinance.

row.basis: Donkey sees the angel and leaves the road
row.note: The commentary makes guidance a question of following a lead animal; here Balaam's donkey detects the blocked path that the human seer misses, reversing human and animal discernment.

row.basis: Straying ox or sheep must be returned
row.note: The commentary's dālle camel has escaped its owner; Torah treats a neighbor's stray livestock as recoverable property and forbids ignoring it.

row.basis: Keep the animal until its absent owner seeks it
row.note: The commentary defines the stray camel as remaining where its owner is unknown; this law makes the finder temporarily responsible when the owner is not nearby.

row.basis: Return an enemy's straying ox or donkey
row.note: The commentary's ownerless camel prompts the question of the finder's relation to its owner; Exodus extends recovery duty even to an enemy's animal.

row.basis: The Lord as shepherd; the speaker as sheep
row.note: The commentary links Rabb to an animal's owner; the psalm names God as shepherd and makes the human speaker part of his flock.

row.basis: Shepherd settles sheep in green pasture
row.note: The commentary develops a herd remaining at its pasture and land pleasing for grazing; this verse joins the shepherd's care to settled, nourishing pasture.
The commentary turns ihdinā into a flock's following its foreleader; the shepherd leads the speaker on right paths, joining guidance to the animal image.

row.basis: Forest beasts and cattle belong to God
row.note: The commentary glosses its source form rabb (رَبّ) as owner and begins with an owned camel herd; this verse explicitly places wild beasts and cattle under divine ownership.

row.basis: The world and all in it belong to God
row.note: The commentary's source gloss says the Rabb of each thing is its owner; the psalm applies ownership universally, beyond a single herd.

row.basis: Wanderers lost in an empty desert without a town
row.note: The commentary describes a camel escaping and remaining in a desolate place; this psalm opens with people wandering in waste without an inhabited settlement.

row.basis: The lost cry to the Lord for help
row.note: The commentary pairs an ownerless animal's lost state with the surah's request for help; here the wilderness wanderers cry out and receive divine rescue.

row.basis: God leads them by a straight way
row.note: The commentary makes the camel's foreleader an image for asking to be guided on the straight path; this verse explicitly joins divine leading to a straight way.

row.basis: God leads his people like a flock through the wilderness
row.note: The commentary's flock follows its leading animal; the psalm depicts God leading his people as sheep through a wilderness journey.

row.basis: People are God's pasture flock and hear his voice
row.note: The commentary joins herd ownership to following a leader; the psalm calls the people sheep of God's hand and immediately calls them to hear his voice.

row.basis: A lost sheep asks its owner to seek it
row.note: The commentary's dālle camel is lost from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek his servant.

row.basis: Israel must not be left like sheep without a shepherd
row.note: The commentary says the request for guidance entails a foreleader whom the rest follow; Moses asks for a successor so the congregation will not be leaderless like sheep.

row.basis: Lost sheep are led astray by their shepherds
row.note: The commentary contrasts a herd's leader with the danger of losing the way; Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose own shepherds mislead them, making the guide itself culpable.

row.basis: Scattered sheep have no shepherd to seek them
row.note: The commentary's stray camel remains in a wasteland with no known owner; Ezekiel pictures scattered sheep with no shepherd and no one searching for them.

row.basis: God himself searches for his sheep
row.note: The commentary's lost camel has an unknown owner; Ezekiel answers with God personally seeking and rescuing his scattered flock.

row.basis: A shepherd gathers a scattered flock
row.note: The commentary's animal is lost in a desolate place; this verse compares God's search to a shepherd inspecting his flock and rescuing sheep dispersed on a cloudy day.
The commentary links an animal's owner with its herd; Ezekiel closes by identifying Israel as God's human flock and God as their God.

row.basis: The wild donkey is released from its bonds
row.note: The commentary distinguishes an owned, tamed camel from ownerless wild herds; Job asks who freed the wild donkey, marking its opposite relation to human ownership.

row.basis: The wilderness is the wild donkey's home
row.note: The commentary's camel is stranded in a desolate place while wild asses live outside owned herds; Job makes the wilderness the wild donkey's dwelling.

row.basis: The wild donkey searches the mountains for pasture
row.note: The commentary develops pasture as the place a herd stays and names wild-ass herds; Job gives the untamed animal a mountain range to roam for grazing.

row.basis: The wild ox will not serve a human master
row.note: The commentary's dictionary form al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad is a tarred/tamed camel; Job sets against it a wild ox that will not submit to service.

row.basis: The wild ox cannot be harnessed to plow
row.note: The commentary describes a subdued camel within an owned herd; Job specifies the practical limit of human control over the wild ox.

row.basis: God teaches and points out the way
row.note: The commentary makes ihdinā a request for the leader of a following herd; the psalm has God promise to instruct and guide the person in the way.

row.basis: Horse and mule need bit and bridle to be guided
row.note: The commentary treats the flock's voluntarily followed foreleader as an image for guidance; the psalm contrasts an instructed person with animals that must be restrained to come near.

row.basis: The king goes out before the people
row.note: The commentary cites the dictionary form milk (مَلِك) for the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is its Semitic cognate, and Israel asks for a king who will go before them in battle.

row.basis: David is taken from ewes to shepherd Israel
row.note: The commentary's malik is the animal ahead of a herd; this verse makes a former shepherd the ruler appointed over God's people.

row.basis: David shepherds and guides with integrity
row.note: The commentary joins a lead animal to guidance of those following; this verse presents Israel's ruler as one who shepherds and guides the people.

row.basis: Pleasant boundary lines and a good inheritance
row.note: The commentary labels root ن ع م and says camels are called en-naʿam for the good and blessing they bring; Hebrew nʿm in this verse describes pleasant boundaries beside a good inheritance, a cognate semantic field rather than an animal term.

row.basis: Blessing includes cattle and flock offspring
row.note: The commentary explains its source form en-naʿam as livestock that brings good and blessing; Deuteronomy lists the increase of cattle and flock among God's covenant blessings.

row.basis: A faithful ruler shepherds the Lord's flock in pasture
row.note: The commentary's malik is the herd's foreleader and its hadī guides followers; this Jewish royal hope joins a shepherd-ruler to faithful care and a pasture where sheep do not stumble.

row.basis: God turns people back like a shepherd his flock
row.note: The commentary's camel is lost from its owner; Sirach compares God's correction and teaching to a shepherd bringing back his flock.
The commentary's source gloss calls the Rabb of everything its owner; Wisdom grounds God's sparing care in the claim that all things belong to him.

row.basis: A shepherd searches for one sheep that strayed
row.note: The commentary defines a dālle camel as escaped and ownerless; Jesus' parable gives the lost animal an owner who searches until he finds it.

row.basis: The found sheep is brought back and celebrated
row.note: The commentary leaves the lost camel separated from its owner; Luke's shepherd returns with the found sheep and gathers friends to celebrate, supplying a recovery scene.

row.basis: Heaven rejoices over a sinner who repents
row.note: The commentary compares human misguidance with a camel that is lost from its owner; Luke interprets the recovered sheep as the sinner who turns back, connecting return to repentance.

row.basis: A shepherd seeks a wandering sheep
row.note: The commentary's lost camel has no known owner; Matthew's parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to seek the one that wandered.

row.basis: The shepherd rejoices when the sheep is found
row.note: The commentary describes the camel only while lost; Matthew emphasizes the owner's joy at recovery.

row.basis: The Father wills that none of the little ones perish
row.note: The commentary contrasts a lost animal with humans more lost than cattle; Matthew uses the shepherd image to say the Father seeks the vulnerable rather than letting one perish.

row.basis: People are harassed like sheep without a shepherd
row.note: The commentary says the request for guidance needs a leader ahead of the flock; Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, making the human need for guidance explicit.
The commentary makes a leading animal the image behind the request to be guided; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins teaching them, acting as guide.

row.basis: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name
row.note: The commentary says a brand identifies whose camel it is and that the stray camel's owner is unknown; John's shepherd knows and summons each animal as his own.

row.basis: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow
row.note: The commentary's malik is the animal at the head of the herd and its hadī leads the others; Jesus describes the shepherd walking ahead and his sheep following.

row.basis: Sheep do not follow a stranger
row.note: The commentary says the herd follows its foreleader; John adds recognition as the criterion, since sheep flee from an unfamiliar voice.

row.basis: The shepherd knows his sheep and they follow him
row.note: The commentary joins owner, animal, and following leader; Jesus says he knows his sheep and they follow his voice.

The commentary's dictionary form rabb (رَبّ) is glossed 'owner'; John's Greek preserves the Aramaic rbb title 'my teacher,' a related Semitic master-title used for a teacher rather than a livestock owner.

row.basis: Straying sheep return to the shepherd and overseer
row.note: The commentary calls the camel dālle when lost from its owner; Peter says his readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd who watches them.

row.basis: The Lamb shepherds people to springs of water
row.note: The commentary combines a leading animal with pasture and the request for guidance; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and guides people to springs.

row.basis: Followers go wherever the Lamb goes
row.note: The commentary says a herd follows the lead animal and makes this the force of asking for guidance; Revelation describes people following the Lamb wherever he goes.

row.basis: Spotted and speckled animals distinguish Jacob's flock
row.note: The commentary says a brand shows whose camel it is; Jacob proposes coat patterns as a visible way to distinguish which animals are his, though these are natural markings, not brands.

row.basis: A mark distinguishes those spared from judgment
row.note: The commentary's camel brand identifies the animal's owner; Ezekiel's mark distinguishes people to be spared, shifting identification from property to protection.

row.basis: The wise are put to shame and reject the Lord's word
row.note: The commentary contrasts animals that recognize an owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah's immediate context extends the bird comparison to the people's rejection of divine instruction.

row.basis: People are God's flock and pasture sheep
row.note: The commentary connects an animal to its owner; this liturgical line identifies worshippers as God's people and sheep, adding communal belonging to the flock image.

row.basis: Earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary glosses rabb as the owner of each thing; the psalm states the same universal ownership in a creation hymn.

row.basis: Hebrew ʿābad means to work or serve
row.note: The commentary labels root ع ب د in naʿbudu and quotes al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad, a tamed/tarred camel; Genesis uses the cognate Hebrew root for the human's work in Eden, preserving a service/work sense without making the garden animal imagery.
The commentary labels source root ن ع م and explains en-naʿam through good and blessing; Hebrew nʿm describes pleasantness here, a cognate sense-family rather than a reference to livestock.

row.basis: A bit directs a horse's whole body
row.note: The commentary says the horse's hādī may be its neck or the foremost group; James supplies a different concrete steering image, the bit by which a human turns a horse.

row.basis: God's servants receive a seal on their foreheads
row.note: The commentary's brand identifies the camel's owner; Revelation's seal marks those who belong to God and are protected, transferring ownership-identification to people.

row.basis: The beast's mark identifies its adherents
row.note: The commentary's camel brand indicates whose herd an animal belongs to; Revelation's imposed mark signals allegiance to the beast, a hostile counterpart rather than the same kind of ownership.

row.basis: A shepherd searches for his one lost sheep
row.note: The commentary's dālle camel escapes and remains away from its owner; Thomas preserves a lost-sheep parable in which the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the stray.

row.basis: Hebrew melek is a ruler who goes before the people
row.note: The commentary's dictionary form milk (مَلِك) names the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is a cognate ruler-title, and this verse gives the king the specific role of going before Israel.

row.basis: Shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads the flock
row.note: The commentary's lead animal and the request for guidance meet Isaiah's shepherd, who gathers lambs, carries them, and gently leads the nursing ewes.

row.basis: All people wander like sheep, each to a separate way
row.note: The commentary says a camel can stray from its owner and that some people are more astray than animals; Isaiah makes human wandering itself a sheep-going-astray image.

row.basis: A gathered flock crowds its fold
row.note: The commentary pictures a herd remaining together at its place; Micah portrays the restored remnant gathered like sheep in a fold and pasture.

row.basis: The king and the Lord go before the gathered people
row.note: The commentary's malik and hādī are foreleaders followed by the herd; Micah's gate-breaking leader, king, and Lord pass ahead of the flock.

row.basis: Israel is scattered like sheep without a master
row.note: The commentary connects losing a camel's owner with the need for a leader; Micaiah sees Israel dispersed on the hills like sheep without a shepherd, then sent home because they have no master.

row.basis: When the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter
row.note: The commentary says a herd follows its foreleader; Zechariah gives the contrary scene in which losing that leader disperses the flock.

row.basis: People wander like sheep because there is no shepherd
row.note: The commentary makes the request for guidance a need for a foreleader; Zechariah explains the people's wandering by the absence of a shepherd.

row.basis: God settles his sheep in good pasture
row.note: The commentary develops merabb as the place camels stay and a pasture the land's inhabitant likes; Ezekiel's shepherd puts the recovered flock on good grazing land.

row.basis: God feeds his flock and gives it rest
row.note: The commentary links owner, herd, and the place where animals remain; God promises both to feed his sheep and to make them lie down.

row.basis: The ark goes ahead to find the people a resting place
row.note: The commentary's leader walks before a following herd and its pasture is where it stays; Israel's ark travels ahead to seek a place of rest.

row.basis: Sheep, oxen, and wild beasts are under human rule
row.note: The commentary distinguishes owned livestock from wild herds; the psalm specifies domestic flock and oxen alongside beasts of the field under human dominion.

row.basis: Ants work without a chief or ruler
row.note: The commentary names the bee's leader with the source dictionary form melīku; Proverbs supplies a useful contrast in a social insect whose ordered work needs no ruler.

row.basis: Locusts march in ranks without a king
row.note: The commentary extends malik to a bee's leader; Proverbs says locusts move together despite having no king, contrasting organized animal following with leaderless coordination.

row.basis: Stubborn Israel is compared to a heifer and a lamb in pasture
row.note: The commentary contrasts a tamed camel with straying animals and develops pasture; Hosea calls Israel a stubborn heifer and then invokes a lamb in broad pasture, applying animal behavior to Israel's relation to God.

row.basis: People do not know the way of peace and make crooked paths
row.note: The commentary pairs the requested straight path with roads that turn aside; Isaiah describes people whose paths are crooked and who therefore do not know peace.

row.basis: Lost property is returned by identifying signs
row.note: The commentary says a camel's brand reveals its owner, while a stray camel has an unknown owner; the Bavli's reading of Deuteronomy's return law uses identifying signs to establish who may reclaim a found object.

row.basis: The shepherd-king leads the flock in holiness
row.note: The commentary joins the foreleading malik to the guide who takes a herd along a path; this Jewish royal psalm continues its shepherd image by saying the king will lead the people in holiness.

row.basis: The broad road leads to destruction
row.note: The commentary develops the straight path alongside deviation; Jesus contrasts a broad road that many enter with the path of life, giving the wrong way a destination.

row.basis: Few find the narrow way that leads to life
row.note: The commentary's request for guidance asks for a leader and a straight route; Jesus describes the difficult path to life that few find.

row.basis: Jesus applies the struck-shepherd saying to his disciples' flight
row.note: The commentary says followers depend on their herd's foreleader; Mark quotes Zechariah's struck shepherd and interprets the scattered sheep as the disciples who will fall away at Jesus' arrest.

row.basis: The king separates people as a shepherd separates sheep and goats
row.note: The commentary places the herd-leader image beside Malik, owner of Judgment Day; Jesus' judgment scene joins royal authority with a shepherd sorting livestock.

row.basis: Sheep stand at the king's right and goats at his left
row.note: The commentary presents a herd under a leader and names the owner of Judgment Day; Matthew makes the judgment division visible by assigning the sheep and goats opposite sides.

row.basis: The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the known owner from the camel left without one; Jesus defines the true shepherd by risking his life for the flock that belongs to him.

row.basis: A hired worker abandons sheep when a wolf comes
row.note: The commentary ties the camel to its owner and herd; John's contrast distinguishes a genuine keeper from a hired hand who does not own the sheep and flees danger.

row.basis: The hired hand flees because the sheep are not his
row.note: The commentary's mark identifies whose camel it is; John makes ownership the reason the hired worker fails to care for the flock.

row.basis: Other sheep are brought into one flock under one shepherd
row.note: The commentary contrasts owned herds with wild flocks outside a known owner; Jesus speaks of gathering other sheep so that they become one flock with one shepherd.

row.basis: Peter is charged to shepherd Jesus' sheep
row.note: The commentary's herd follows a foreleader; the risen Jesus delegates care of his own sheep to Peter, distinguishing the flock's owner from its appointed shepherd.

row.basis: Elders must shepherd and oversee God's flock
row.note: The commentary develops a leading animal whose herd follows it; Peter assigns human leaders a shepherd's oversight of God's flock, making the guide's duty explicit.
The commentary uses malik for the animal at the head of the herd; Peter calls Christ the chief shepherd who appears above the delegated flock leaders.

The verse anticipates finding a straying animal when its owner is not near or is not known, keeping it until the owner seeks it, and restoring it; this is a close legal counterpart to the dālla camel whose rab/mālik is unknown.
The command to return a brother’s ox or sheep that has gone astray gives the commentary’s escaped animal a concrete action and owner relation rather than treating “straying” as an abstraction.
Even an enemy’s wandering ox or donkey must be returned; the scene joins a loose pack animal to the obligation created by its known owner.

row.basis: when a roadside animal counts as lost
row.note: The mishnah distinguishes an animal merely grazing on a road from one whose state shows genuine loss, then requires return; it gives a legal test for the commentary’s concrete dālla rather than equating every free animal with a lost one.

The discussion of simanim in the law of lost property makes an identifying sign the means by which an item can be restored; it is a direct legal analogue to the camel’s wasm/sīmah by which it is recognized.

row.basis: speckled and spotted flock as wages
row.note: Jacob sets visibly marked sheep and goats apart as his wages, so an animal’s visible feature allocates it within a flock to a particular claimant.

row.basis: visible color proving ownership or theft
row.note: Jacob says the flock’s visible coloring will demonstrate his innocence and expose a stolen animal; this makes an animal mark an evidentiary sign of whose it is.

row.basis: ox knows owner; donkey master’s manger
row.note: Isaiah says an ox knows its owner and a donkey its master’s manger while Israel does not know; it directly parallels the commentary’s claim that livestock recognize owner and place while humans can be more lost.

row.basis: lost sheep; misleading shepherds; resting place
row.note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep, says their shepherds led them astray, and says they forgot their resting place; it combines the commentary’s stray animal, failed leader, path, and merabb-like place of remaining.

row.basis: lost sheep asks to be sought
row.note: The speaker says that he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asks the Lord to seek his servant, turning the lost-animal image into a prayer for recovery by the rightful master.

row.basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
row.note: God’s shepherding promise explicitly seeks the lost and returns the strayed, supplying the caring owner-side of the commentary’s camel left in an unowned place.

row.basis: Moses follows a runaway lamb to water
row.note: The midrash has Moses pursue a lamb that has run from Jethro’s flock, find it drinking, and carry it back; God makes that care the reason he can shepherd Israel, joining the stray animal, water/pasture, and qualified leader.

row.basis: one lost sheep sought by its owner
row.note: The man who loses one of a hundred sheep goes after the lost one, a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s animal separated from its owner and herd.

row.basis: one strayed sheep valued above the ninety-nine
row.note: This lost-sheep version has the shepherd seek the one that strayed and value it above the ninety-nine, a distinct Christian apocryphal intensification of the individual animal’s recovery.

row.basis: straying sheep return to Shepherd and Overseer
row.note: The addressees were sheep going astray but have returned to a Shepherd and Overseer; it connects wandering from the way with restoration to a guiding, responsible figure.

row.basis: own sheep called by name and led out
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining recognized belonging with a leader who initiates the flock’s movement.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
row.note: The shepherd goes in front and the sheep follow his voice, the closest New Testament rendering of the commentary’s front animal/hādī followed by the rest of the herd.

row.basis: owner and flock know one another
row.note: The reciprocal knowledge of shepherd and sheep gives a direct positive counterpart to the dālla whose rab and mālik cannot be identified.
Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image makes the lack of a leading, responsible figure the cause of a dispersed and distressed flock.

row.basis: leader goes out before the people
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before and bring the people in, so that they will not be sheep without a shepherd; it applies the commentary’s front-leading herd image to communal guidance.

row.basis: God goes before to lead by the way
row.note: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar to lead them on the way, giving the request for guidance a concrete leading-before movement like the commentary’s hādī.

row.basis: what goes ahead seeks a resting place
row.note: The ark goes before the people to seek out a resting place for them; it binds the front guide to finding the place where the moving community may remain.

row.basis: people led like sheep through wilderness
row.note: God leads the people out like sheep and guides them like a flock in the wilderness, directly joining flock, guidance, and a journey through exposed country.
The declaration that the Lord is the speaker’s shepherd gives the commentary’s rab/mālik relation its classic pastoral form: a flock has a guiding provider.
The shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them to resting waters, closely matching the herd’s fixed place and the pasture it finds pleasing.
The shepherd restores life and leads in right tracks, providing a pastoral analogue to ihdinā and the straight path rather than guidance as a disembodied instruction.

row.basis: shepherd feeds, gathers, and gently leads
row.note: The divine shepherd feeds the flock, gathers lambs, and gently leads nursing ewes; it develops both pasture-care and differentiated leadership within a herd.

row.basis: good pasture and secure lying down
row.note: God promises good pasture where the flock will lie down, a precise counterpart to the merabb where camels stay and the land whose grazing is approved.
Wisdom guides the righteous person on straight paths in its account of divine guidance; it supplies a Jewish Second Temple formulation for the commentary’s moving sense of the straight path.
God leads the blind on an unknown way and makes crooked ground straight, directly pairing guidance with the contrast between a right path and a deviating one.

row.basis: perverting the straight paths of the Lord
row.note: The rebuke names the straight paths of the Lord and accuses its target of making them crooked, a concrete New Testament counterpart to the commentary’s path that turns aside from the qasd.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
row.note: The text says its opponents abandoned the straight way and went astray, retaining both sides of the commentary’s road vocabulary rather than merely a general moral failure.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
row.note: The Lamb becomes the flock’s shepherd and guides them to springs of water; this striking reversal makes an animal the leader while retaining the commentary’s guide-and-pasture movement.

row.basis: followers go wherever the Lamb goes
row.note: The redeemed follow the Lamb wherever he goes, an explicit following relation that gives the commentary’s herd behind its leading animal a Christian eschatological form.
God declares every forest beast and the cattle on a thousand hills to be his, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary’s claim that every creature has its rab/mālik.

row.basis: divine blessing includes six thousand camels
row.note: The verse calls Job’s latter state blessed and immediately counts his camels among its abundance, closely matching the commentary’s association of camels with niʿma, benefit, and blessing.

row.basis: camels bear precious cargo over distance
row.note: A multitude of camels carries gold and frankincense and brings proclamation of the Lord’s praises; it closely matches the commentary’s load-bearing animals and its hamd/benefit frame.
God causes grass to grow for cattle, giving the good pasture in the commentary a providential source rather than treating it as only a herd preference.
The command to help an enemy’s donkey collapsed under its load gives an ethical counterpart to the commentary’s carrying mount: its legs bear burdens, so the human associated with it must assist.

Humanity is told to rule the moving creatures, a creation-account counterpart to the commentary’s Qur’anic picture of livestock made subject to human possession; the biblical verse frames that relation as a commission.

row.basis: the righteous know an animal’s needs
row.note: The righteous person knows the life or needs of his animal, adding responsibility and attention to the commentary’s owner-and-herd relation.
God’s stated pity for Nineveh explicitly includes its many cattle, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary’s move from useful animals to the Lord’s compassion.

row.basis: wild ass sent free and unbound
row.note: Job asks who released the wild ass and loosed its bonds; it gives the commentary’s wild-ass herd a theological counterweight to the tame, owner-marked animal.

row.basis: wild ass given wilderness as home
row.note: God gives the wild ass the steppe and salt land as its dwelling, making the wilderness place in the commentary’s lost-animal definition a positive habitat for a creature not domesticated by humans.

row.basis: horse and mule need bit and bridle
row.note: The psalm contrasts a human who should understand with horse and mule controlled by bridle; its training image usefully complicates the commentary’s tame camel and animal-led guidance without making the two moral claims identical.
The Lamb’s followers visibly bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads, a personal and covenantal analogue to the commentary’s visible brand that makes an animal’s belonging recognizable.

Basil’s bee discussion presents the hive as an ordered community under a king; it supplies a Christian natural-theological analogue to the commentary’s malik of the bees, though section divisions vary by edition.

row.basis: unmuzzled ox re-read for human workers
row.note: Paul invokes the rule against muzzling a grain-treading ox in an argument about the support of human workers; this Christian reading turns a working animal’s claim into a claim about labor, relevant to the commentary’s tamed, load-bearing animal.

row.basis: Hebrew melek goes before the people
row.note: Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary’s m-l-k label, and this verse asks for a king who will go before Israel; its own context thus pairs the cognate title with the front-leading function the commentary gives to milk.

Hebrew ʿbd is cognate with the commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d label; Joshua’s choice to serve the Lord supplies the worship-side use of that family, without transferring the camel-treatment sense into the verse.
Hebrew noʿam is cognate with the commentary’s n-ʿ-m label, and Wisdom’s ways are called ways of pleasantness; the verse joins the source’s blessing/pleasant-pasture association to a path.

row.basis: Aramaic Rabbi as an authority title
row.note: The source labels rabb as an owner-title; John retains the Semitic title Rabbi and glosses it as Teacher. The likely cognate relation supplies only a title comparison here, not evidence that John’s teacher image is a flock-owner image.

row.basis: Lord’s mercy trains and turns back like a shepherd
row.note: Sirach describes the Lord’s compassion as rebuking, training, teaching, and turning creatures back as a shepherd turns his flock; it gathers the commentary’s merciful rab, tamed animal, straying, and restoration into one Jewish formulation.

row.basis: donkey turns aside because it sees the angel
row.note: Balaam’s donkey leaves the road after seeing the divine messenger while its human rider cannot see and beats it. The scene reverses the surface value of an animal’s turning aside: the animal is the one properly guided, sharpening the commentary’s animal-and-human contrast.
Hosea calls Ephraim a trained heifer and describes placing a yoke on its fair neck for work; this is a close prophetic animal image for the commentary’s muʿabbad camel and its guiding neck.

row.basis: cords of love; yoke lifted; feeding
row.note: God leads Israel with cords of kindness and love, lifts the yoke from its jaws, and bends down to feed it. The verse combines animal training, gentle leading, pasture-like provision, and divine compassion.

row.basis: wild ox will not serve or stay at the manger
row.note: The divine questions ask whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or spend the night at the manger, directly contrasting a human-owned, tamed herd with a wild bovine beyond ordinary possession.

row.basis: wild ox bound to furrow and harrow
row.note: The next question tests whether the wild ox can be bound with a cord to plow and harrow; it supplies the laboring, guided-animal side of the commentary’s mount carried and directed by its body.

row.basis: camel humps carrying treasure through hard country
row.note: The oracle pictures wealth carried on camels’ humps through a land of distress, a specific Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary’s animals carrying burdens to distant places.

row.basis: where the shepherd pastures and lets flock rest
row.note: The beloved asks where the shepherd pastures his flock and makes it lie down at noon, directly matching the commentary’s owner, grazing place, and place of remaining.

row.basis: follow flock tracks and pasture kids near shepherd tents
row.note: The reply directs the seeker to go out by the tracks of the flock and pasture her kids beside shepherds’ tents; it gives an unusually exact literary image of following a herd’s route toward a shepherded grazing place.

row.basis: led by water on a straight path without stumbling
row.note: God promises to lead the returning people by streams of water on a straight way where they will not stumble, binding the commentary’s guidance request, straight path, and animal-water/pasture scene.

row.basis: compassionate guide leads to water springs
row.note: The compassionate one leads the hungry and thirsty and guides them by springs of water, a direct guide-and-pasture counterpart to the hādī leading a herd.

row.basis: flock wanders for lack of shepherd
row.note: The people wander like sheep and suffer because there is no shepherd, making the absence of the commentary’s front-leading, responsible figure the stated cause of dispersion.

row.basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
row.note: The proverb requires careful knowledge of the state of one’s flock and attention to herds, adding the sustained ownerly care absent from the unknown-owner definition of the dālla.

row.basis: a sheep fallen into a pit is lifted out
row.note: Jesus assumes that an owner will take hold of and lift out a sheep fallen into a pit even on the Sabbath, a concrete recovery scene for the commentary’s animal left in an exposed place.
After finding the lost sheep, the shepherd lays it on his shoulders with joy; this supplies the bodily return of the escaped animal that the preceding search scene alone does not state.

row.basis: owner unties ox or donkey and leads it to water
row.note: Jesus describes each person untying an ox or donkey from the stall and leading it to water, joining a known owner, a restrained domestic animal, purposeful leading, and animal provision.

The elders must shepherd God’s flock, which God acquired, while serving as overseers. It distinguishes the true owner from delegated guides in a way that closely illuminates the commentary’s rab/mālik and leading-animal relation.

row.basis: shepherd the flock of God under oversight
row.note: The elders are told to shepherd the flock of God and exercise oversight, a specific Christian instruction about the responsibility attached to leading another’s flock.

row.basis: untrained calf asks to be turned back
row.note: Ephraim compares itself to an untrained calf and asks God to turn it back. The image gives the commentary’s tamed animal and its loss of direction a penitential human counterpart.

row.basis: shepherd moderates pace for tender flock
row.note: Jacob says tender children and nursing flocks cannot be driven hard without losing the herd. It adds a concrete criterion for a leader’s guidance: the front-moving party must accommodate the flock it leads.
Job invites the sufferer to ask the animals, which will teach him. This develops the commentary’s secondary reversal in which animal life may disclose what a human who has lost the way fails to know.

row.basis: wild asses drink from God’s waters
row.note: God’s waters give drink to beasts of the field and quench the thirst of wild asses, giving the commentary’s ownerless wild-ass image a providential water-and-habitat setting.
Hosea compares political wandering to a wild donkey going alone; it supplies a biblical use of the wild-ass figure for self-directed separation rather than the secure movement of a herd.

row.basis: called by name and declared God’s own
row.note: The creator calls Israel by name and says “you are mine,” a human counterpart to the commentary’s brand that makes an animal’s belonging and owner recognizable.

row.basis: working ox must not be muzzled
row.note: The law preserves the feeding claim of an ox while it works, adding an ethical limit to treating the commentary’s tamed, useful animal solely as a bearer of human benefit.

row.basis: flock-tender receives milk from the flock
row.note: Paul’s labor argument asks who tends a flock without drinking its milk. Alongside his ox citation, this turns the material benefit of a tended flock into an analogy for the guide’s rightful support.

row.basis: seal says the Lord knows those who are his
row.note: God’s firm foundation bears a seal declaring that the Lord knows those who are his, a textual counterpart to the commentary’s visible mark and the lost camel whose owner cannot be known.

row.basis: take my yoke and learn from me
row.note: Jesus’ invitation to take his yoke and learn makes animal harness a figure for guided discipleship, offering a Christian transformation of the commentary’s subdued, neck-directed animal.
