row.basis: straight way to an inhabited city
row.note: After wilderness wandering, God leads the travellers by a straight way to a city where they can dwell; it gives the road the arrived-at end that the commentary says distinguishes sirat from disappearance.
The travellers wander in a desert route and find no inhabited city, a concrete itinerary whose missing destination illuminates the commentary's person who goes away with no known arrival.

row.basis: highway where travellers do not err
row.note: Isaiah's holy highway is specifically a way on which even wayfarers do not go astray, closely joining a directed road to the commentary's contrast between sirat and dalal.
In the return-from-exile procession God leads people beside water on a straight path where they will not stumble; its physical homeward route gives a destination to divinely guided movement.

row.basis: guard on the way, brought to a place
row.note: The angel is sent ahead both to guard Israel on the way and to bring it to the prepared place, the same two-part image of guidance and arrival developed for the sirat.

row.basis: make a straight highway for God
row.note: The wilderness proclamation makes a straight highway for God's coming; it supplies the road-and-arrival imagery behind a straight way without reducing the Qur'anic prayer to a lexical match.

row.basis: Isaiah's straight paths applied to John's mission
row.note: Luke reuses the wilderness voice and straight paths for John the Baptist's preparation of the Lord's advent, a Christian framing of the same directed-road image.
God leads blind people on ways they have not known and turns darkness to light before them; this is the salvific reversal of the commentary's sightless people unable to find the path.

row.basis: wicked way as darkness and unknown stumbling
row.note: The wicked walk in deep darkness and do not know over what they stumble, directly pairing loss of sight and loss of bearing as in the commentary's blind rush toward a road.
Proverbs makes the outcome explicit: the path of righteousness is life and its track has no death, sharpening the commentary's claim that the difference between two goings lies in where they lead.

row.basis: a seemingly right way ending in death
row.note: The proverb warns that a way which appears right can end in death, making destination rather than outward direction the test of a road.

row.basis: water vanishes from its place in heat
row.note: Job's seasonal streams are scorched and disappear from their place; this is a textual water-loss image beside the commentary's example of something consumed and lost in water.

row.basis: caravans leave their course and perish
row.note: The same wadi scene has caravan routes turn aside into waste and perish, bringing the commentary's linked images of vanishing water and travellers without a destination into one scene.
God makes leaders wander in a trackless waste; its stated absence of a road concretizes dalal as a going whose direction cannot be found.
Those made to grope without light stagger like the drunk, supplying a close bodily counterpart to the commentary's blind people who cannot see a path.
The people grope like the blind and stumble at midday as in twilight, a direct image of vision failing to orient movement.
Jesus' saying has a blind guide and blind follower both fall into a pit, making the commentary's sightless route-seeking and its well/pit image meet in one contrary destination.

row.basis: walking in darkness without knowing where one goes
row.note: Jesus says that the person walking in darkness does not know where he is going, an exact formulation of movement whose destination has vanished from knowledge.

row.basis: lost sheep led astray by shepherds
row.note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray across mountains; its failed guides give the commentary's dalal a communal and directional scene.

row.basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
row.note: God promises to seek the lost and bring back the strayed sheep, turning unknown disappearance into known recovery and return.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to their shepherd
row.note: The readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd, a concise Christian movement from lost wandering to a responsible destination.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
row.note: The false teachers abandon the straight way and go astray, directly setting a right route against wandering in the terms the commentary contrasts.
The restricted way leads to life and is found by few; it makes the endpoint of a path, rather than mere motion, decisive.
The broad road leads to destruction, furnishing the adverse route and end alongside Matthew's life-leading way.
Thomas explicitly links not knowing Jesus' destination with not knowing the way, the very relation between route and arrival made central in the commentary.

row.basis: Jesus as way to the Father
row.note: Jesus identifies himself as the way by which one comes to the Father; it is a Christian construal of a road whose point is arrival before God.

row.basis: Joseph cast into a wilderness pit
row.note: Reuben directs that Joseph be put into a pit in the wilderness rather than killed, giving the older narrative's concrete counterpart to Joseph's removal into the hidden bottom of a well.

row.basis: traders draw Joseph from the pit and take him to Egypt
row.note: Passing traders draw Joseph out and carry him toward Egypt, so the pit disappearance becomes a transit with an unforeseen destination, as the commentary emphasizes.

row.basis: Joseph sold into Egypt, yet God with him
row.note: Stephen's retelling retains the brothers' sale of Joseph but adds that God was with him, explicitly reading the apparent loss as a providentially accompanied passage.

row.basis: graves opened and people brought to their land
row.note: God opens graves, brings the dead up, and brings them into Israel's land; earth's enclosure is therefore a stage on a directed restoration, not their final disappearance.
The dead live and the dwellers in dust awake, a direct answer to the image of bodies hidden in earth and then newly created.
Many sleeping in the dust of the earth awake for divergent final outcomes, closely matching burial in earth followed by new life and judgment.

row.basis: earth and Sheol return what was entrusted
row.note: The earth and Sheol give back what was entrusted to them; this treats apparent disappearance into the underworld as custody before eschatological return.

row.basis: earth and dust give up their sleepers
row.note: At judgment the earth gives up those asleep in it and dust those dwelling silently, an unusually close Jewish apocalyptic answer to people thought lost in earth.

row.basis: earth preserves and restores the dead
row.note: The earth receives the dead to preserve them and restores them as received, making burial a guarded holding rather than annihilation.

row.basis: all in tombs hear the summons
row.note: All who are in tombs hear the Son's voice; the verse denies that hidden burial places can make the dead unavailable to resurrection.
Those in tombs come out for life or judgment, supplying both the new emergence and the accountable end that the commentary joins to earth-loss.

row.basis: sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead
row.note: The sea, Death, and Hades yield their dead for judgment, a precise final-assize counter-image to persons or things apparently lost in earth or water.
God raises believers with Jesus and presents them together; resurrection is explicitly a movement into God's presence rather than a terminal vanishing.
A book of remembrance is written before God for those who fear him, closely paralleling the commentary's divine book in which past generations are neither lost nor forgotten.
Even a mother's possible forgetting is contrasted with God's refusal to forget Zion, giving a precise divine answer to human memory's loss.

row.basis: every deed written in a book
row.note: The maxim's seeing eye, hearing ear, and book recording all deeds make the commentary's claim that the Lord neither loses nor forgets a concrete ethical-accounting image.

row.basis: God is not unjust to forget work
row.note: Hebrews explicitly denies that God forgets the readers' work and love, a direct theological counterpart to the commentary's negation of divine loss and forgetting.
Not one of five sparrows is forgotten before God; the small-scale saying gives a vivid instance of divine attention that does not lose what creatures lose from sight.

row.basis: books opened for the dead's judgment
row.note: The dead stand before the throne and are judged from opened books, joining the commentary's book, non-forgetting, and no-one-absent motifs in one judgment scene.

row.basis: no escape through Sheol or heaven
row.note: Even descent to Sheol or ascent to heaven cannot evade God's hand; it is a close prophetic analogue to the claim that none can disappear from the day of reckoning.
No creature is unseen before God and all are exposed to him, supplying the divine-sight side of the commentary's assertion that nobody can be absent from judgment.
In Isaiah's day-of-the-Lord scene idols utterly pass away, closely matching the commentary's judgment image of fabricated objects vanishing from their makers.
The Aramaic denunciation says gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish, a specific biblical counterpart to invented divine partners disappearing at judgment.

row.basis: an idol has no real being
row.note: Paul's claim that an idol has no real existence supplies a Christian conceptual counterpart to the commentary's false, fabricated objects proving absent rather than dependable.

row.basis: from a drop to dust, then account before the King
row.note: The maxim makes a person consider both the destination of the body in dust and the coming account before God; it places earth-bound mortality and divine encounter side by side.

row.basis: God takes and will restore the soul
row.note: The morning prayer says God will take the soul and restore it in the time to come, a liturgical Jewish expression of temporary loss followed by restoration.

row.basis: two ways, of life and death
row.note: The Didache's opening contrast of the Way of Life and the Way of Death makes the commentary's two kinds of going into an early Christian ethical map.

row.basis: Joseph's waterless pit contains snakes and scorpions
row.note: The rabbinic reading of Genesis 37:24 says the pit lacked water but held snakes and scorpions, making the hidden descent more perilous and sharpening the preservation implicit in Joseph's later emergence.

Genesis' mortality judgment sends the human back to dust without adding a resurrection in this utterance; the commentary begins with comparable earth-loss but answers sceptical finality with new creation and meeting God.
Qoheleth says the dead's remembrance is forgotten, a bounded human-memory counterpoint that makes the commentary's stronger claim about God's unfailing book and knowledge more pointed.

row.basis: lamp for feet and light for path
row.note: The psalm supplies light specifically for feet and a path, directly reversing the commentary's scene of people unable to see where the road lies.

row.basis: lost sheep sought by its master
row.note: The speaker confesses, "I have gone astray like a lost sheep," and asks to be sought; this turns dalal as unknown departure into a personal petition for recovery.

row.basis: "This is the way; walk in it"
row.note: A voice guides those turning right or left by naming the way they must walk, a particularly close divine answer to the request to be guided on a path.

row.basis: blind groping and failure in one's ways
row.note: The curse imagines groping at noon as a blind person in darkness and not succeeding in one's ways, combining impaired sight with failed direction.

row.basis: upward path of life versus Sheol below
row.note: For the wise, the path of life rises upward in order to turn away from Sheol below; its vertical destinations sharpen the commentary's distinction between a journey that arrives and one that is lost.

row.basis: wandering from understanding to the assembly of the dead
row.note: Proverbs gives wandering from the way of understanding an explicit resting place among the dead, a grave outcome for directionless movement.

row.basis: earth opens its mouth and swallows Korah's company
row.note: The earth literally opens and swallows the rebels and their households, a forceful Torah scene for the commentary's paired images of swallowing and disappearance into ground.

row.basis: earth closes over the living as they descend to Sheol
row.note: The swallowed group goes down alive to Sheol, the earth closes over them, and they perish from the assembly; it gives the earth-loss image its punitive, destinationless extreme.
Isaiah reverses the commentary's swallowing image by making God consume death itself, then remove tears; the shared bodily image serves an opposite eschatological result without claiming cognacy.

row.basis: sea depths made into a way for the redeemed
row.note: God makes a way through the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross, a vivid counter-image in which water becomes a directed road rather than a place where things disappear.

row.basis: God sees every human way and step
row.note: God's eyes are upon a person's ways and see every step, directly answering the commentary's difference between a traveller leaving human sight and nothing being lost to divine knowledge.

row.basis: waters over the head and the cry "I am cut off"
row.note: The lamenter describes water closing over his head and concludes that he is cut off, a close scriptural scene of disappearance in water.

row.basis: calling God's name from the lowest pit
row.note: From the lowest pit the speaker calls on God by name, making the concealed pit a place from which relationship and appeal remain possible.

row.basis: God comes near to the pit-bound caller
row.note: God draws near when the speaker calls and says not to fear; this supplies the response that turns the preceding pit-disappearance into an encounter rather than abandonment.

row.basis: the King of the world raises the dead
row.note: The martyred brother says that the King of the world will raise those who die for the law to everlasting life, a direct Jewish rebuttal to death as final loss.

row.basis: hearts go astray and do not know God's ways
row.note: Hebrews applies the wilderness generation's persistent going astray to its failure to know God's ways, directly coupling dalal-like error with an unrecognized divine route.
The divine oath that the straying generation will not enter God's rest supplies the destination denied to those who have not known God's ways.

row.basis: confidence to enter the holy places
row.note: The verse names entry into God's holy presence as the believers' goal, the arrival required to read the next verse's new and living way as more than a road metaphor.

row.basis: new and living way through the veil
row.note: Jesus inaugurates a new and living way through the veil; the Christian image joins a specifically living route to access before God.

row.basis: Red Sea crossed as dry land, Egyptians swallowed by it
row.note: Israel crosses the sea as dry ground while the Egyptians are swallowed when they attempt it, sharply contrasting water as a way of arrival with water as consuming loss.

row.basis: make straight paths for your feet
row.note: The exhortation to make straight paths for the feet seeks restoration rather than dislocation for the lame, a pastoral Christian use of straight-path imagery.

row.basis: God will no longer remember sins
row.note: Hebrews uses divine non-remembrance as covenantal forgiveness of sins, not as failed recall; that deliberate sense of "not remember" usefully distinguishes it from the commentary's claim that God never loses knowledge or forgets.

row.note: The commentary sends Musa on a road to Midian and then to its water; Exodus 2:15 sends fleeing Moses to Midian, where he sits by a well, supplying the same journey-to-well opening.
The commentary identifies two women unable to water their herds; Exodus 2:16 has seven daughters come to draw water and fill the troughs, giving the shared well scene its Israelite form.
The commentary says Musa waters the women’s flocks; Exodus 2:17 has Moses rise, defend the daughters from shepherds, and water their flock.

row.basis: who makes room at the well
row.note: The commentary says the women wait for shepherds to leave and Musa then waters them; Exodus has Moses drive the shepherds off himself, shifting the aid from waiting and serving to direct intervention.
The commentary’s scene ends with Musa watering two women’s flocks; Exodus 2:19 has the daughters report that an Egyptian rescued them and drew water for them and their flock.

row.basis: traveler and camels at a well
row.note: The commentary makes a road traveler’s water and a well central; Abraham’s servant reaches a town well with camels and waits there as women come to draw water.

row.basis: prayer for success at the well
row.note: After Musa waters the women, the commentary quotes his prayer for whatever good God sends; Abraham’s servant prays at the well for success, making a water encounter the setting for a request for divine direction.

row.basis: women draw water at the spring
row.note: The commentary centers women who come to a water source with flocks; the servant in Genesis stands by the spring as the city’s daughters come out to draw water.

row.basis: water for a stranger and his animals
row.note: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks; Rebekah gives Abraham’s servant a drink and then draws for his camels, closely joining stranger, well, and animal water.

row.basis: water runs out in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary asks who can bring running water when a person’s supply sinks away; Hagar’s water skin is empty in the wilderness, making thirst on a journey concrete.
The commentary asks who supplies water when it disappears; God opens Hagar’s eyes to a well, and she draws water for the child, a direct scene of provision after water runs out.

The commentary says Yusuf’s brothers propose the pit so a passing traveler may take him; Reuben instead proposes the pit to keep the brothers from killing Joseph, a shared rescue-through-the-pit plan with a changed rationale.

The commentary describes Yusuf thrown into the dark bottom of a well before travelers arrive; Genesis has Joseph put into an empty cistern, matching the pit while withholding the Qur’anic water-drawing detail.
The commentary’s next Yusuf scene has a bucket lowered to draw water and a boy discovered; Genesis explicitly says Joseph’s cistern was empty, making the means of discovery differ.

row.basis: caravan and the boy in the pit
row.note: The commentary says a caravan arrives and its water drawer finds Yusuf; Genesis has traders pass and Joseph brought up from the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites, sharing the pit-and-caravan turn.

The commentary makes the lowered water bucket the way the passing caravan finds Yusuf; Genesis has traders pull Joseph from the pit and sell him, replacing a chance discovery during water-drawing with deliberate removal and sale.

row.basis: water from the ground sustains land
row.note: The commentary distinguishes rain from above and well water drawn from below; Genesis 2:6 pictures mist rising from the ground to water the soil before cultivated growth.
The commentary links water to vegetation and livelihood; Genesis 2:10 describes a river flowing from Eden to water the garden, locating plant life beside a sustaining source.
The commentary follows rain into soil and plants; Deuteronomy contrasts a land that drinks rain from heaven with Egypt’s irrigation, making rainfall the land’s source of fertility.
The commentary traces rain to vegetation and provision; Deuteronomy promises rain at its proper season so grain, wine, and oil can grow.
The commentary’s cloud and rain enlarge the earth with plant growth; Leviticus promises seasonal rain followed by a land that yields produce and trees that bear fruit.

row.basis: springs and streams in good land
row.note: The commentary pairs the traveler’s road with water and treats water as the support of livelihood; Deuteronomy describes a land of brooks, springs, and deep waters that sustains its inhabitants.
The commentary moves from rain to green land and food; Isaac’s blessing asks for dew from heaven, fatness of earth, and abundant grain and wine.

row.basis: tree beside streams, leaf does not wither
row.note: The commentary’s ribba is a tender plant said not to wither in summer; Psalm 1’s tree by streams bears fruit and keeps its leaf, joining steady water to enduring growth.

The commentary pairs the straight path with the Day of Judgment and distinguishes graced people from those under wrath; Psalm 1 says the wicked will not stand in judgment or in the righteous assembly.

row.basis: the righteous way and the perishing way
row.note: The commentary asks for the path of the favored rather than those who stray; Psalm 1 says the LORD knows the way of the righteous while the wicked way perishes.
The commentary distinguishes those given favor from those under wrath or astray; Jeremiah sets the blessed person who trusts the LORD against the dry shrub of the preceding verse.
The commentary’s tender plant does not wither in summer; Jeremiah’s tree beside water is unafraid of heat, keeps green leaves, and does not stop bearing fruit.
The commentary’s straight road includes water for the traveler; Isaiah says the compassionate guide leads the redeemed beside springs, where they do not hunger or thirst.
The commentary joins a request for the straight path to water that sustains life; Isaiah says the LORD will guide continually and make the faithful like a watered garden and an unfailing spring.
The commentary places road travel, thirst, and water together; Isaiah says waters break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert, turning the barren route into a place of life.

The commentary’s sirat is a path the traveler walks with water at hand; Isaiah 35:8 describes a highway called the Holy Way for the redeemed, pairing a marked route with the wilderness water of the same restoration scene.
The commentary asks God to guide people on a straight road; Isaiah promises a voice behind the listener saying “this is the way, walk in it,” an explicit divine direction for the traveler.
The commentary joins the straight road to rain-fed growth and food; immediately after Isaiah’s way instruction, God sends rain for the seed sown in the ground and makes the harvest abundant.
The commentary’s well scene moves from watering to shade, and its rain grows plants; the shepherd leads the speaker to green pasture and still water, portraying care as food and water on a journey.
The commentary asks for the straight path and says water keeps the traveler’s affairs upright; the shepherd restores the soul and leads by paths of righteousness.
The commentary places Musa in shade after watering the women; the psalm describes walking through the shadowed valley under the shepherd’s protection.
The commentary extends rain and water into food for people and animals; the shepherd prepares a table and provides an overflowing cup, completing its picture of provision along the way.
The commentary cites rain, mercy, and hamd together in Qur’an 42:28; Psalm 65 opens with praise to God and then describes God watering the earth and making it fruitful.
The commentary links rain with mercy and the revival of soil; Psalm 65 says God visits and waters the earth, filling the divine river and preparing grain.

row.basis: showers soften furrows and bless growth
row.note: The commentary traces the first rain into green plants and provision; Psalm 65 pictures showers softening the furrows and blessing the growth of the earth.
The commentary says rain leaves a green mark on the soil and pairs water with the straight path; Psalm 65 says God’s tracks drip with abundance as the year is crowned with goodness.
The commentary takes rain through soil to plants and food; Psalm 65 ends with pastures, hills, and valleys clothed in flocks and grain.
The commentary connects hamd with rain and the earth’s fertility; Psalm 104 begins in praise and then describes God’s care of clouds, mountains, plants, and food.
The commentary describes layered clouds and rain that grows plants; Psalm 104 says God waters the mountains from the upper chambers and satisfies the earth with fruit.
The commentary follows rain into tender plants and fields; Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for people to cultivate.

row.basis: food and drink from the earth
row.note: The commentary links water to livelihood and food; Psalm 104 names wine, oil, and bread as gifts that gladden, nourish, and strengthen human life.

row.basis: cloud, rain, and grass in one verse
row.note: The commentary links clouds and moisture to plant growth; Psalm 147 says God covers the heavens with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the hills.
The commentary follows rain into pasture and names water as the support of affairs; Psalm 147 says God gives food to beasts and to the young ravens that cry.
The commentary places hamd beside rain and mercy; Psalm 147’s call to sing with thanksgiving leads directly into its account of clouds, rain, grass, and animal food.
The commentary’s first rain marks soil with vegetation and then becomes food; Isaiah says rain and snow water the earth, make it bud, and provide seed and bread.

row.basis: rain’s work and the effective word
row.note: The commentary describes rain as a mark written into the earth and asks for guidance; Isaiah compares the word from God’s mouth to rain that does not return before accomplishing its purpose.
The commentary’s rain repairs people’s condition and benefits them; Isaiah promises water for thirsty land and streams on dry ground, followed by God’s spirit on the people.
The commentary says the first rain marks earth with plants; Isaiah pictures descendants springing up like grass and willows beside flowing water.
The commentary says rain writes its mark in green growth and asks for guidance; Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew that fall on tender grass, making the same image a vehicle for instruction.
The commentary describes clouds that carry water and grow plants; Job says God draws up drops of water and distills rain from the mist.
The commentary develops the cloud as a layered bearer of rain; Job says clouds pour down water upon humankind.

row.basis: wind, clouds, and rain in sequence
row.note: The commentary says winds move and spread clouds before rain; Jeremiah says God makes clouds rise, flashes lightning for rain, and brings wind from storehouses.

row.basis: wind and rain from God’s storehouses
row.note: The commentary pairs wind, heavy cloud, and rainfall; Psalm 135 gives the same cluster as God’s work, bringing clouds, lightning for rain, and winds from storehouses.
The commentary follows wind-borne clouds until they become heavy with rain; Elijah’s servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea as the sign of coming rain.
The commentary makes wind and cloud the forerunners of rain; in Elijah’s scene the sky darkens with clouds and wind before a great rain falls.
The commentary’s ribba is a plant that does not wither in summer; Ezekiel’s trees beside the river bear fruit every month and keep leaves that do not wither.
The commentary asks who can bring running water when it sinks away; Jeremiah calls God the fountain of living waters and condemns people who abandon it for cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.
The commentary says water is the support by which affairs stand; Psalm 46’s river gladdens God’s city, where God’s presence keeps it from being moved.
The commentary presents rain as what restores soil and makes it useful; Job asks who sends rain on land where no person lives, watering the wilderness for growth.
The commentary asks for the straight path and excludes the astray; Jesus contrasts the narrow gate and hard way leading to life with the broad way leading to destruction.
The commentary asks to be guided on the straight road; Jesus says the way to life is narrow and difficult and few find it.
The commentary names the Owner of the Day of Judgment and separates the favored from the rejected; Jesus depicts the Son of Man enthroned and gathering the nations for judgment.
The commentary asks for the path of those granted favor rather than those under wrath; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.
The commentary distinguishes the favored from those under anger; the same judgment scene sends the cursed away, giving a concrete Christian counterpart to its divided outcome.

row.basis: guide to springs of living water
row.note: The commentary joins guidance on a road to water for the traveler; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water.
The commentary calls water the support and “king” of human affairs; Revelation’s river of life flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, joining rule to life-giving water.
The commentary links gathered water to persistent vegetation; Revelation places the tree of life beside the river, bearing fruit and leaves for healing.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Revelation depicts the dead standing before the throne and being judged from the opened books according to their deeds.

The commentary brings cloud, travel, and water together; Paul recalls Israel’s ancestors under the cloud and on their wilderness passage, supplying the Christian pilgrimage setting for his water reference.

The commentary treats water as the literal support of the traveler; Paul rereads Israel’s wilderness drink from the rock as spiritual drink from Christ, adding a Christian interpretation to water on the journey.

row.basis: weary traveler rests at a well
row.note: The commentary’s Musa reaches a well after travel and later withdraws to shade; Jesus, tired from his journey, sits beside Jacob’s well, a close Christian well-side travel scene.

row.basis: request for water at the well
row.note: The commentary has Musa water women at Midian; Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink at Jacob’s well, making the well encounter turn on who gives water.

row.basis: ordinary well water becomes living water
row.note: The commentary insists that a traveler’s water sustains his affairs; Jesus interprets the well encounter through the gift of living water, adding a spiritual reading to literal thirst.
The commentary follows rain and well water into enduring life; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring within the recipient, a Christian expansion from provision to lasting life.

row.basis: thirsty people are invited to come
row.note: The commentary says water keeps the traveler from thirst and supports life; Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, turning thirst into a direct spiritual appeal.
The commentary traces water from source to soil and growth; Jesus describes rivers of living water flowing from the believer, extending the image from provision to inward abundance.

row.basis: seasonal mention of rain in prayer
row.note: The commentary develops rain and wind as divine provision; the Mishnah debates when the rain petition enters the daily prayer cycle, showing rain as a recurring Jewish liturgical request.

row.basis: prayer formula for wind and rain
row.note: The commentary joins wind, clouds, and rain; the Talmud explains the seasonal prayer formula that asks God to make wind blow and rain fall.

row.basis: rain and resurrection as divine acts
row.note: The commentary cites a Qur’anic scene where rain-bearing clouds lead into the raising of the dead; the Talmud groups rain and resurrection among powers God has not delegated, giving the same pair a Jewish theological frame.

row.basis: sheep gone astray from their way
row.note: The commentary asks not to follow those who stray and elsewhere describes flocks at the well; Isaiah says all sheep have gone astray, each turning to its own way, joining animal wandering to the path language.
The commentary makes rain a sign of divine benefit and renewal; Hosea compares God’s coming to dawn and to rain that waters the earth, giving the rain a covenantal and restorative meaning.
The commentary follows rain into green growth and provision; Joel promises early and late rains as part of restoration, tying weather to renewed harvest.
The commentary traces water toward food; Joel’s restoration scene has threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after the rains.

row.basis: ask for rain in its season
row.note: The commentary’s imagery treats rain as provision from God; Zechariah explicitly tells people to ask the LORD for rain at the time of spring rain.
The commentary says rain improves people’s state and benefits them; Ezekiel promises showers of blessing, making rain a direct sign of restored divine care.

row.basis: prayer to be led in God’s truth
row.note: The commentary’s central petition is “guide us” on a straight path; David asks God to lead him in truth and teach him, a close prayer-form parallel.
The commentary grounds guidance in divine favor and benefit; the psalm asks God to remember compassion and steadfast love, linking direction to mercy.
The commentary asks for the straight way; the psalm asks God’s good Spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, a specific guidance formula.

row.basis: rain falls on just and unjust
row.note: The commentary says rain corrects people’s condition and benefits them while the surah distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Jesus says God gives rain to both just and unjust, making rain’s reach broader than the moral division.
The commentary opens with bism and develops its name/mark association; the Lord’s Prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, a parallel invocation before petitions.
The commentary calls God master of the Judgment Day; the Lord’s Prayer petitions for God’s kingdom and will, placing divine rule before requests for provision and guidance.
The commentary moves from rain and water to food for people and animals; the Lord’s Prayer asks for daily bread, making sustenance part of the prayer’s petition.

row.basis: lead away from trial and evil
row.note: The commentary asks for the right path and exclusion from straying; the Lord’s Prayer asks not to be led into trial and to be delivered from evil, a neighboring petition for safe direction.
The commentary moves from invoking God’s name to divine rule and guidance; Luke’s Lord’s Prayer likewise begins with the Father’s name and kingdom before its requests.
The commentary follows rainwater into food and livelihood; Luke’s prayer asks for daily bread, placing provision within the same petitionary form.
The commentary asks to be guided away from a mistaken path; Luke’s prayer asks not to be brought into trial, a specific prayer for protection from a wrong course.
The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored by God from the paths of wrath and straying; the Didache opens its instruction with two ways, one of life and one of death.

row.basis: water from the rock on the way
row.note: The commentary says water keeps a traveler’s work standing; Paul recalls Israel drinking from a spiritual rock in the wilderness, making provision on a journey the basis for a Christian reading.
The commentary calls water the support of affairs and traces it into food; Sirach lists water among the necessities of human life beside bread, fire, salt, and other provisions.

row.basis: Hebrew shem, name placed on people
row.note: The commentary labels bism with a name-related source and then links it to wasm, a mark made by first rain; Numbers says the priests put God’s name upon Israel and God blesses them, joining name, marking, and benefit.

The commentary labels Qur’anic mālik from M-L-K and calls water “our kings”; Psalm 47 uses the cognate Hebrew melek for God as king over all earth, showing the sovereignty sense beyond the water metaphor.

The commentary labels mustaqim from Q-W-M and says water is what makes affairs stand; Psalm 1 uses Hebrew yaqumu for sinners who will not stand in judgment, connecting uprightness with the judgment scene.
The commentary’s N-ʿ-M family describes life’s beauty and freshness; Psalm 133 calls shared life good and pleasant with Hebrew na'im, a cognate use centered on what is delightful.

The commentary labels al-ʿālamīn from ʿ-L-M and also develops a deep, water-filled well from that family; the Peshitta uses cognate ʿālmā for “world,” showing the word’s spatial world sense in a Christian text.

The commentary calls the plant-growing cloud by the Qur’anic title Rabb; John preserves the Aramaic address rabbi and glosses it as teacher, showing a related Semitic master-title in a human teaching relation.

The commentary labels its cloud and tender-plant forms from R-B-B; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew revivim for showers falling on tender grass, a plausible cognate cluster whose exact lexical relationship should be checked in the Hebrew text.

The commentary labels hamd from Ḥ-M-D and says the earth is pleasing to inhabit or pasture; Psalm 19 calls the teaching desirable, a possible cognate that preserves a pleasing/desirable sense without equating it with praise.

row.basis: shade and rest in the day’s heat
row.note: The commentary has Musa withdraw to shade after watering the women; Genesis places Abraham at his tent entrance under the oaks in the heat of the day, a parallel of shelter after exertion.
The commentary joins water at the well with Musa’s retreat to shade; Abraham offers water to wash his visitors’ feet and rest under a tree, bringing water and shade together in hospitality.
The commentary follows water into food and livelihood; Abraham’s visitors are offered bread after water and rest, extending the same hospitality sequence from drink to food.

The commentary describes the mouth of a well and its beam, pulley, and bucket; Jacob’s scene identifies a large stone laid over the well’s mouth, giving a distinct biblical mechanism for controlling access to well water.

The commentary says the women wait to water until shepherds depart; Genesis has shepherds wait until all flocks gather before moving the stone and watering them, making control of access to a well part of the scene.

row.basis: Jacob opens the well and waters a flock
row.note: The commentary’s Musa waters women’s flocks at a well; Jacob moves the stone from the well’s mouth and waters Rachel’s flock, another well-side meeting involving a woman and animal water.
The commentary links the road with the traveler’s need for water; Exodus says Israel travels through the wilderness and has no water to drink, making thirst an immediate danger of the route.
The commentary treats water as what keeps a traveler’s affairs standing; in the wilderness God brings water from the rock at Horeb for the people to drink.

row.basis: water gushes from the rock again
row.note: The commentary presents water as life-sustaining provision; in a second wilderness account Moses strikes the rock and water gushes out for the congregation and their animals.
The commentary joins journey, well, and water for people and flocks; at Beer God tells Moses to gather the people and promises to give them water.
The commentary carefully develops the well’s mouth and the apparatus for drawing water; Israel sings to the well, “Spring up,” making a well itself the focus of a public water song.
The commentary says water is the support and “king” of communal affairs; Numbers says princes and nobles dug this well with their staffs, tying water access to leaders’ work.

row.basis: water from the deep in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary explains that water holds up the traveler’s affairs; Psalm 78 recalls God splitting rocks in the wilderness and giving drink as from the deep.
The commentary moves between the deep well and water that sustains life; Psalm 78 says streams came from the rock and ran like rivers.

row.basis: water and food on the journey
row.note: The commentary traces water toward food and livelihood; Psalm 78 recalls water gushing from the rock and immediately asks whether God can also provide bread and meat.
The commentary describes tender growth that survives summer and rain that revives the earth; Job says a felled tree still has hope of sprouting again.

row.basis: scent of water renews the tree
row.note: The commentary says rain marks soil with green growth; Job’s tree buds and puts forth branches at the scent of water, making renewed vegetation a sign of life after apparent death.

row.basis: tree renewal beside the question of human life
row.note: The commentary connects revived earth with the raising of the dead; Job asks whether a human who dies will live again after describing a tree renewed by water.
The commentary cites rain as a sign of the earth’s revival and connects rain to raising the dead; Hosea promises that God will revive Israel and raise it up on the third day.
The commentary’s rain revives dead earth and points toward resurrection; Ezekiel is told to promise breath to dry bones so that they will live.
The commentary links rain, renewed earth, and raising the dead; Ezekiel’s breath enters the bones, they live, and stand on their feet as a vast assembly.

row.basis: blessing or curse set before the people
row.note: The commentary distinguishes those granted favor from those under wrath or astray; Deuteronomy explicitly sets blessing and curse before Israel in the same chapter that ties rain to obedience and harvest.
The commentary asks for the path of those given favor; Deuteronomy says blessing follows listening to the LORD’s commandments.
The commentary asks not to follow the straying path; Deuteronomy names a curse for disobeying and turning aside to other gods.

row.basis: life and good set against death and evil
row.note: The commentary asks for the straight path and distinguishes its people from those who stray; Moses places life and good before Israel alongside death and evil.
The commentary seeks the way of those granted favor, not the way of wrath; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and sets life and death, blessing and curse before the people.

row.basis: hold fast to God, who is life
row.note: The commentary asks to be guided on a path that sustains life; Deuteronomy says to love the LORD, listen to his voice, and hold fast to him because he is the people’s life.
The commentary’s central request is guidance on the straight path; Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one’s ways results in God making the paths straight.
The commentary pairs the straight path with travel and water in the wilderness; Isaiah calls for a highway to be made straight in the desert for God.
The commentary asks for the straight path; Matthew applies Isaiah’s wilderness voice to John, who prepares the Lord’s way and makes his paths straight.
The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Mark opens John’s wilderness preaching with Isaiah’s call to prepare the Lord’s way.
The commentary’s sirat is a road to be made straight; Luke quotes Isaiah’s command to prepare the Lord’s way and make his paths straight.
The commentary asks to be guided on the straight path; John the Baptist identifies himself with Isaiah’s voice calling for the Lord’s way to be made straight.

row.basis: wind shelter, dry-land stream, and shade
row.note: The commentary brings wind, water, and Musa’s shade together; Isaiah describes a refuge from wind and storm, streams in dry land, and shade from a great rock in a weary land.
The commentary says rain restores soil and makes it fruitful; Psalm 107 says God turns wilderness into a pool and parched land into springs.
The commentary moves from water to livelihood; Psalm 107 says God settles hungry people there and they establish a city to live in.
The commentary follows rain into plants and food; Psalm 107 describes sowing fields, planting vineyards, and obtaining a fruitful yield.
The commentary says rain improves people’s condition and feeds animals; Psalm 107 says God blesses the people so they multiply and their livestock increase.
The commentary calls God mālik on the Day of Judgment and says water is “our king”; Psalm 72 asks that the king judge the people with righteousness and the poor with justice.

row.basis: rain on cut grass under the king
row.note: The commentary joins the kingly water image to rain-fed growth; Psalm 72 compares the king’s reign to rain falling on mown grass and showers watering the earth.

row.basis: grace and blessing for the people
row.note: The commentary connects hamd with rain and mercy; Psalm 67 asks God to be gracious and bless the people before describing the earth’s yield and the nations’ praise.
The commentary traces rain to plants and food; Psalm 67 says the earth has yielded its increase and asks God to bless the people.
The commentary names the Lord of all worlds and invokes praise; Psalm 67 ends with all the ends of the earth fearing God after the earth’s harvest.
The commentary names God as ruler of the Day of Judgment and Lord of the worlds; Psalm 96 says the LORD reigns and judges the peoples with equity.

row.basis: God comes to judge the earth
row.note: The commentary calls God the Owner of the Day of Judgment; Psalm 96 says God comes to judge the earth with righteousness and the peoples with faithfulness.
The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Daniel sees the court sit and books open, giving an apocalyptic court scene for divine judgment.

row.basis: a human-like figure approaches the Ancient of Days
row.note: The commentary calls God the sovereign of the judgment day; Daniel sees one like a son of man come before the Ancient of Days in the heavenly court.
The commentary calls God mālik and Lord of all worlds; Daniel’s human-like figure receives dominion and a kingdom served by all peoples and nations.

row.basis: a fixed day to judge the world
row.note: The commentary names the Day of Judgment; Paul says God appointed a day to judge the inhabited world in righteousness and gave assurance by raising the appointed man.

row.basis: feet guided into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary asks God to guide “us” on a straight path; Zechariah’s hymn says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: a king longs for well water
row.note: The commentary says a tribe calls its waters “our kings” because water holds affairs together; David, himself king, longs for a drink from the well of Bethlehem.

row.basis: men risk their lives to draw water
row.note: The commentary says the traveler’s water lets him hold his affairs in hand; David’s men break through enemy lines to draw the well water he longs for.
The commentary treats water as the support of life and rule; David refuses to drink the water because it represents the blood of men who risked their lives to fetch it.
The commentary places rain, harvest, and the Day of Judgment together; the Mishnah says the world is judged at Sukkot concerning water, joining seasonal rain to a global judgment calendar.

row.basis: water drawing as a temple rite
row.note: The commentary describes water drawn from a well and rain as divine provision; the Mishnah describes drawing water from Siloam for the Temple’s water libation, making water-drawing a liturgical act.

The commentary labels bism with S-M-W and develops Arabic sama for cloud, rain, and plant; Genesis uses the related Hebrew shamayim for the heavens, retaining the sky sense while the commentary’s Arabic examples extend it to what falls and grows.

The commentary distinguishes the path of those favored from the paths of wrath and straying; the Community Rule contrasts the spirits of truth and perversity and their opposed ways, giving a Jewish sectarian account of moral paths.

row.basis: way of light and way of darkness
row.note: The commentary asks for the straight path rather than the paths of wrath and straying; Barnabas sets out a way of light against a way of darkness, a Christian ethical expansion of the two-way contrast.
The commentary connects rain-soaked soil, plant growth, and the raising of the dead; Paul says the seed is not made alive unless it dies, using planted growth to explain resurrection.

row.basis: a bare kernel becomes a plant
row.note: The commentary says rain leaves a green trace on earth; Paul distinguishes the bare kernel sown from the body that will grow, making plant emergence a model for resurrection.
The commentary links renewed earth to the resurrection of the dead; Paul explicitly compares a perishable seed sown in the ground with the imperishable body raised.

The commentary says the first rain marks soil with green growth and distinguishes favored from rejected paths; Ezekiel orders a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve, so they are distinguished when judgment falls.
The commentary develops rain as a mark on the earth and distinguishes people on the final path; Revelation seals God’s servants before harm comes to earth, sea, and trees.

The commentary's Qārūn and his house are swallowed after his treasure claim; Numbers likewise has the earth open and swallow Korah, his household, and possessions, a close narrative meeting without deciding the figures' identity.
The shared destruction sharpens a real difference: Numbers makes Korah's fate part of a revolt against Moses and Aaron, while the commentary makes Qārūn's self-credit for wealth the decisive issue.
Pharaoh's claim to have raised Moses in the commentary has its Pentateuchal scene here: after the child grows, Pharaoh's daughter takes him as her son.
The commentary lets Moses answer Pharaoh's fosterage claim by naming Israel's enslavement; Exodus describes Egypt making Israel's life bitter through forced labor.

row.basis: Moses nourished as Pharaoh's daughter's son
row.note: Stephen's retelling says Pharaoh's daughter took the exposed Moses and reared him as her own son, supplying a New Testament version of the upbringing at issue in the commentary.

row.basis: wealth credited to one's own power
row.note: Qārūn says his riches came through knowledge possessed by himself; Deuteronomy anticipates the same self-attribution when a heart says, “my power” produced this wealth.

row.basis: God gives power to acquire wealth
row.note: The next verse redirects the ability behind wealth to God, closely matching the commentary's insistence that praise return to the actual giver rather than the recipient's supposed knowledge.

row.basis: riches and power come from God
row.note: David's blessing names riches, honor, strength, and rule as coming from God; it is a concrete biblical counterpoint to Qārūn's private claim over the source of his riches.

Paul asks what anyone has that was not received and rejects boasting as though it were self-produced, directly illuminating the commentary's contrast between received benefit and self-directed praise.
Herod is struck after accepting a crowd's divine acclamation because he did not give glory to God; this supplies a narrative judgment on praise being drawn to the wrong recipient.
Jesus' warning about giving in order to be praised by people closely meets the commentary's discussion of benefaction turned into a claim on others' praise.

row.basis: seeking human glory rather than God's
row.note: The verse contrasts receiving glory from one another with seeking the glory of the one God, making explicit the misdirection of praise that the commentary traces in self-congratulation.

row.basis: God's glory and praise withheld from idols
row.note: Isaiah assigns glory and praise exclusively to YHWH rather than idols, a precise biblical form of the commentary's claim that praise cannot be divided among rival claimants.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars not worshiped
row.note: The commentary calls the lights signs and refuses prostration to them; Deuteronomy warns against being drawn to worship precisely the sun, moon, and heavenly host.
Wisdom lists fire, wind, stars, and the heavenly lights among things people may take as gods, preserving the same sign-versus-object-of-worship tension developed in the commentary.

row.basis: luminaries made for signs and seasons
row.note: Genesis gives the heavenly lights the created work of marking signs, seasons, days, and years, supplying a concrete counterpart to the commentary's lights as indicators rather than Lords.
Wisdom says the Maker is perceived from the greatness and beauty of creatures, closely matching the commentary's claim that the worlds are signs through which their Lord is recognized.
Paul describes God's invisible reality as perceived in creation; this gives a New Testament formulation for the commentary's movement from visible worlds and signs to recognition of their Lord.

row.basis: knowing God without glorifying or thanking him
row.note: Romans joins failed knowledge of God to failure to glorify or give thanks, directly relating the commentary's hamd-as-recognition to its opposite.
The passage contrasts serving the creature with the Creator, exactly the distinction the commentary stages through sun, moon, and star as signs that cannot be Rabb.

row.basis: turning from idols to heaven-and-earth's maker
row.note: Paul and Barnabas tell worshipers to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven, earth, sea, and all within them; its anti-idolatrous Creator claim closely parallels the commentary's argument.

row.basis: rain, food, and joy as divine witness
row.note: The speaker calls rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness God's witness, providing a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's cloud, rain, vegetation, and provision as signs.

row.basis: creation answers that it was made
row.note: Augustine questions earth, sea, air, sky, and luminaries; their answer directs him beyond themselves to their Maker. This is a concentrated Christian reading of the commentary's created signs that cannot be worshiped as God.
The commentary makes the worlds signs that make their Lord known; this verse gives the heavens an active declaration of God's glory.
The commentary says every thing praises in a mode humans may not understand; this verse depicts the heavens' witness as lacking ordinary speech and audible words.

row.basis: sole creator, sustainer, and worshiped Lord
row.note: Nehemiah calls God alone maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all in them, giver of life to all, while heaven's host worships him; it closely gathers the commentary's Lord-of-worlds and cosmic-praise claims.

row.basis: every creature gives blessing and honor
row.note: Revelation hears every creature in heaven, earth, under earth, and sea bless the enthroned God and the Lamb, an unusually exact counterpart to the commentary's all-encompassing praise.

row.basis: creation makes God worthy of glory
row.note: The heavenly elders declare God worthy because all things exist and were created by his will, matching the commentary's attribution of praise to the doer of the praiseworthy work.

row.basis: all things from, through, and for God
row.note: Paul's doxology returns all things to God and gives him glory, a compact New Testament analogue to the commentary's totalizing li that returns praise to its source.

row.basis: all in heaven and earth belongs to God
row.note: David's blessing joins God's greatness and glory to the claim that everything in heaven and earth is his, closely paralleling praise of the Lord of all worlds.

row.basis: heaven, earth, and all belong to God
row.note: The verse assigns the highest heavens, earth, and all within them to YHWH, supplying an ownership formulation for the commentary's expansive rabbi'l-ʿālamīn.

row.basis: Lord of heaven and earth made the world
row.note: Paul calls the maker of the world and everything in it Lord of heaven and earth, an especially close Greek-scriptural counterpart to “Lord of the worlds.”

row.basis: God gives all life, breath, and everything
row.note: The God who needs nothing from human hands gives life, breath, and all things, directly supporting the commentary's claim that praise does not arise from God's need and provision does not originate in the recipient.

row.basis: all things upheld by divine word
row.note: The Son sustains all things by his powerful word; this specifically parallels the commentary's image of the Lord holding the potentially scattered worlds in being.
The statement that all things cohere in him offers a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's reading of the Lord as one who keeps a diverse creation from falling apart.

row.basis: no servant can serve two masters
row.note: Jesus' two-master saying gives a concrete counterpart to the commentary's competing owners and its contrast between divided servitude and belonging to one lord.

row.basis: one God as source of all and one Lord
row.note: Against “many gods and many lords,” Paul identifies one God from whom all things are and one Lord, directly illuminating the commentary's single Lord versus many rival masters.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars summoned to praise
row.note: The commentary's sun, moon, and stars are created signs; this psalm turns those very luminaries into praise-givers rather than recipients of worship.

row.basis: animals and birds summoned to praise
row.note: The commentary includes every creaturely kind among the worlds; Psalm 148 explicitly brings beasts, livestock, creeping things, and birds into the praise.

row.basis: God's name alone exalted by creation
row.note: After calling the creatures to praise, the psalm says YHWH's name alone is exalted, clarifying the commentary's claim that universal praise has one proper destination.
The final imperative extends praise to all that has breath, a concise biblical analogue to the commentary's premise that praise exceeds a single human speaker.
Jesus says that if the disciples fall silent, stones will cry out, a pointed New Testament image for the commentary's subjectless, nonhuman praise.

A great heavenly multitude gives praise immediately after the destructive judgment of Babylon, closely matching the commentary's insistence that praise can follow a judged end rather than a private benefit.

row.basis: praise grounded in true and just judgment
row.note: The next verse makes the ground of the heavenly acclamation God's true and just judgment, directly illuminating hamd in the commentary as a verdict on what has been rightly done.
The altar's response calls God's judgments true and just; it supplies a close Christian formulation for the commentary's praise as confirmation of a righteous judicial outcome.
Moses and Israel sing to YHWH after the defeat of Pharaoh's army, a concrete Pentateuchal instance of praise after deliverance and judgment that belongs beside the commentary's ending scenes.
At the Lord's coming hidden things are disclosed and each receives praise from God, directly joining evaluative judgment to praise as the commentary does.

row.basis: rain waters the earth and yields food
row.note: God waters the mountains from his chambers and the earth is satisfied with his work's fruit, closely matching the commentary's cloud-to-soil nurture scene.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human food
row.note: The verse connects divine cultivation to both herds and human sustenance, fitting the commentary's joined images of pasture, animals, and the nurturing Lord.

row.basis: all creatures await food from God
row.note: The creatures look to God to give their food in season, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that the Lord of worlds feeds even at the intimate scale.

row.basis: life of every creature in God's hand
row.note: Job places every living being's life and every human breath in God's hand, a specific parallel to the commentary's world-wide yet bodily account of divine sustaining.
Jesus points to birds fed by the heavenly Father; this gives a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Rab who provides food across the creaturely world.

row.basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and heals
row.note: Hosea depicts God taking Israel by the arms, teaching it to walk, and healing it, closely matching the commentary's Rab as one who carries a child through stages toward maturity.
Deuteronomy compares God's wilderness care to a man carrying his son, a precise parental image for the commentary's account of nurturing rather than mere possession.

row.basis: shepherd gathers lambs and leads nursing ewes
row.note: Isaiah combines flock care, carrying lambs, and gentle guidance of nursing mothers, bringing together the commentary's herd, home, and gradual nurture imagery.

row.basis: God personally pastures and rests sheep
row.note: God promises to feed and make his flock lie down himself, a direct theological counterpart to the commentary's rab as owner, leader, and provider of pasture.

row.basis: Father of lights without turning shadow
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the enduring Lord from setting lights; James calls God the Father of lights in whom there is no variation or shadow caused by turning.
Isaiah names YHWH the everlasting creator of the earth's ends, providing a direct contrast to the commentary's transitory star, moon, and sun.
Israel answers the covenant book with a corporate assent to do and heed all God has spoken, a concrete scriptural comparison for the commentary's collective “yes, we witness” to the Lord.
Joshua calls the people witnesses against themselves and they answer that they are witnesses, closely echoing the commentary's covenantal self-witness before their Rab.
Hebrews makes the grown Moses refuse the title “son of Pharaoh's daughter,” an interpretive development that highlights the identity question behind Pharaoh's remembered fosterage in the commentary.

The tractate associates one of Joseph's hidden Egyptian treasures with Korah. If Qārūn is read beside Korah, this later Jewish wealth tradition is a specific, though non-identifying, backdrop to the commentary's treasure scene.

row.basis: Abraham infers one Creator from celestial changes
row.note: Josephus portrays Abraham reasoning from the changes of land, sea, sun, and moon to one Creator and rejecting their divinity, an extra-biblical Jewish counterpart to the commentary's anti-astral Abraham scene.

row.basis: Mary's temple upbringing and angelic food
row.note: The commentary's Mary is beautifully grown by God, entrusted to Zechariah, and found with provision; this Christian infancy gospel likewise places Mary in the temple and gives her angelic provision.

row.basis: blessing for adversity as for prosperity
row.note: The Mishnah requires blessing God for bad as for good, an interpretive parallel to the commentary's refusal to reduce hamd to relief or gratitude for a favorable outcome.

row.basis: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed
row.note: Isaiah follows rain and snow from heaven into watering, sprouting, seed, and bread, furnishing a focused biblical analogue for the commentary's rain-cloud-to-plant nurture.

row.basis: rain satisfies waste land and makes grass sprout
row.note: God's rain makes grass grow even in desolate land, sharpening the commentary's claim that divine nurture of earth does not depend on a human beneficiary or speaker.

row.basis: God keeps and continually waters the vineyard
row.note: In its vineyard metaphor God guards and waters what he tends, a particular biblical image for the commentary's Rab who does not create and abandon what he cultivates.
The verse compares God's discipline to a man's discipline of his son, supplying a parental formation analogue to the commentary's step-by-step tarbiya.
Hebrews describes God's fatherly discipline as ordered toward shared holiness, a Christian development of the commentary's nurture as movement toward completion.

row.basis: the one who began good work completes it
row.note: Paul's confidence that God completes the good work he began specifically parallels the commentary's Rab as one who brings an initially given benefit through to its completion.

row.basis: one God rather than many lords
row.note: The confession of YHWH's oneness provides the Hebrew Bible's concise counterpart to the commentary's contrast between competing rabb and the single Lord of all worlds.

row.basis: covenant: God and his people belong to each other
row.note: The new-covenant citation makes God say, “I will be their God, and they will be my people,” offering a Christian covenantal counterpart to the commentary's primal Rab-and-witness relation.

row.basis: star leads travelers to their destination
row.note: The commentary treats stars as directional signs for a traveler; Matthew narrates a star going before the magi until it reaches the child, a concrete but secondary navigation parallel.

row.basis: Creator counts and calls the stars by name
row.note: Isaiah presents the stars as a numbered host summoned by their Creator, strengthening the commentary's claim that celestial signs belong under, rather than compete with, the Lord.

row.basis: animals and birds teach God's handiwork
row.note: Job invites the reader to learn from beasts and birds about God's hand, a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's creatures as signs from which their Lord is known.

row.basis: rich fool's goods meet sudden divine verdict
row.note: The rich man's self-secure plan is interrupted by God's demand for his life, an indirect but concrete comparison to the commentary's Qārūn, whose wealth cannot preserve him from a sudden end.

The commentary's rabbānī teaches by feeding learners small portions of knowledge; Hebrews uses milk rather than solid food for elementary teaching, an apt pedagogical parallel rather than a lexical equation.

row.basis: a shepherd seeks a lost animal
row.note: The commentary's secondary herd image reaches the ownerless, wandering animal of 1:7; Jesus' shepherd goes after a lost sheep. The species and setting differ, so the link is only an image-level comparison.

row.basis: God sees creation as very good
row.note: The commentary treats hamd as a judgment reached after something is found worthy; Genesis closes creation with God's own evaluative verdict that all he made is very good.

Paul says the approved person is not the one who commends himself but the one commended by the Lord, a precise New Testament analogue to the commentary's tested praise rather than self-attributed praise.

row.basis: praise from God rather than people
row.note: Paul locates a person's praise in God rather than human beings, directly sharpening the commentary's contrast between praise's rightful source and the human craving to receive it.
The tested genuineness of faith is said to result in praise, glory, and honor at revelation, closely matching the commentary's account of praise as an approval following trial.

row.basis: God awesome in praises and doing wonders
row.note: In the Exodus victory song, God's incomparable holiness is described as awesome in praises and as doing wonders, joining praiseworthy action to praise after deliverance.

row.basis: Judge of all the earth does justice
row.note: Abraham's question presumes that the judge of all the earth acts justly, a concentrated Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's praise after an objectively righteous judgment.

row.basis: worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs
row.note: The angel commands glory and worship for the Creator of heaven, earth, sea, and water sources at the hour of judgment, gathering the commentary's exclusive worship, worlds, water, and verdict motifs.

row.basis: song of Moses praises true and just ways
row.note: The heavenly song calls the Lord's works great and marvelous and his ways righteous and true, a direct praise-formula counterpart to hamd as a judgment on divine action.

row.basis: nations worship after God's judgments are manifest
row.note: The verse grounds universal worship and glorification of God's name in the manifestation of his righteous judgments, closely matching the commentary's final judgment-and-praise scenes.

row.basis: rivers clap and hills sing together
row.note: Rivers and hills are imagined as applauding and singing, a distinct Hebrew Bible instance of nonhuman creation voicing the praise that the commentary extends beyond human speech.

row.basis: God comes to judge the inhabited world
row.note: The psalm's cosmic celebration is oriented to God's coming judgment of the world with righteousness and equity, providing the necessary verdict side of its nonhuman praise scene.

row.basis: heavens, earth, mountains, forest, and trees celebrate redemption
row.note: Isaiah commands the whole created landscape to shout because God has redeemed Jacob, an especially concrete counterpart to the commentary's cosmic praise that follows a decisive saving act.
God names Israel his witnesses so that they may know and understand him, and denies any god before or after him; this sharply joins the commentary's sign, recognition, witness, and one-Lord themes.
The Exodus song ends by declaring YHWH's eternal reign, a close counterpoint to the commentary's enduring Rab set against celestial bodies that appear and vanish.

row.basis: God alone exalted when human pride is brought low
row.note: Isaiah's day of judgment lowers human haughtiness so that YHWH alone is exalted, giving a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's critique of self-praise and divided praise.

row.basis: God knows and weighs human actions
row.note: Hannah's song rejects arrogant speech because YHWH knows and weighs deeds, an evaluative setting that illuminates the commentary's hamd as a verdict after appraisal.

row.basis: God weighs the spirit behind apparently clean ways
row.note: Proverbs contrasts human self-assessment with YHWH's weighing of motives, a focused analogue to the commentary's distinction between an act's appearance and its proper judgment.

row.basis: clouds, rain, and grass on mountains
row.note: The psalm gives God the work of covering heaven with clouds, preparing rain, and making grass grow, closely meeting the commentary's cloud-to-soil-to-plant nurturing scene.
The desert's flowering is said to reveal YHWH's glory and majesty, a specific biblical bridge from cultivated growth to recognition of the Lord.
Job pictures God stretching the north over emptiness and hanging the earth on nothing, a concrete cosmological parallel to the commentary's Lord who keeps the worlds from slipping away.
The passage gives eternal honor and dominion to the one who alone has immortality, a Christian formulation that clarifies the commentary's contrast between transient luminaries and the abiding Lord.

row.basis: covenant made beyond those immediately present
row.note: Moses says the covenant is not made with the assembled hearers alone, providing a specific communal-and-transgenerational comparison for the commentary's primal covenantal witness to the Rab.

row.basis: heaven and earth summoned as covenant witnesses
row.note: Moses calls heaven and earth to witness the life-and-death covenant choice, a distinct scriptural use of the worlds as witnesses alongside the commentary's “we witness” scene.

row.basis: one Father and one Creator bind a people
row.note: Malachi asks whether all have one Father and one Creator before naming covenantal betrayal, combining parental creation and binding relation in a way that advances the commentary's Rab imagery.

row.basis: a people formed to recount divine praise
row.note: Unlike the deliberately subjectless praise sentence the commentary identifies in Fātiḥa, Isaiah explicitly gives a formed people the vocation of recounting God's praise; the contrast clarifies two distinct speech acts.
The Spirit's cry of filial address gives a New Testament expression of the intimate child-to-God relation that the commentary develops through nurture, care, and the name Rab.

row.basis: the sun moves at its Maker's command
row.note: Sirach presents the sun's course as obedience to the great Lord who made it, a Jewish sapiential counterpart to the commentary's sun as a created sign rather than a god.

row.basis: human praise cannot exhaust the Creator
row.note: Sirach asks where strength sufficient to praise God can be found because he exceeds all his works; this interpretive reflection helps preserve the commentary's total hamd beyond any individual speaker's act.

row.basis: honor belongs to one who honors creatures
row.note: Ben Zoma defines the honored person by honoring others and anchors the claim in God's honoring those who honor him, a Jewish ethical interpretation relevant to the commentary's refusal of self-seeking praise.

Valid hunk headers: '*** Add File: {path}', '*** Delete File: {path}', '*** Update File: {path}'

row.note: Musa'nın önünde YHWH adını ilan ederken Tanrı kendisini bağışlayıcı ve merhametli diye niteler; açılıştaki Rahman-Rahim ile adın birlikte söylenmesine doğrudan bir karşılık verir.
Bu sugyada Tanrı'nın Musa'ya merhamet sıfatlarının düzenini bir dua önderi gibi öğrettiği okunur; adın ilanını çağrı ve bağışlanma pratiği haline getirir.
YHWH bu adı nesiller boyunca anılacak adı olarak verir; yorumdaki en büyük adın çağrıda söylenmesi ve tanınmayı taşımasıyla buluşur.
Mezmur, YHWH'nin adını bütün yeryüzünde görkemli ve ihtişamını göklerin üstüne konmuş diye över; ad-yükseklik birleşimini açıkça kurar.
Zafer sevincini Tanrı'nın adıyla sancak dikmekle birleştirir; yorumdaki adın ve savaş nişanının aynı tanıtıcı iş oluşuna en yakın birleşik örnektir.
Kâhinlerin İsrail'in üzerine YHWH adını koyması, adın kişilerin üstüne yerleştirilen ve onları belirleyen bir işaret oluşunu somutlaştırır.
Diğer halklar İsrail'in YHWH adıyla çağrıldığını görür; adın bir topluluğu dışarıdan tanınır kılan nişan olmasıyla birleşir.
Musa YHWH adını ilan edeceğini ve Tanrı'ya büyüklük atfedilmesini ister; yorumdaki adın yükseltilmesi ile çağrının birleştiği litürjik biçimdir.
Buyruk, Tanrı adının boş ya da yalancı amaçla taşınmasını veya kaldırılmasını yasaklar; yorumdaki yükseltilmiş ad ile altında gerçek bulunmayan ad ayrımına etik bir sınır çizer.
Yüksek ve yüce Olan kendisini adı Kutsal olan diye tanımlar; yükseklik ile ilâhî adın yan yana gelişi yorumun ilk imgesine yakındır.
YHWH'nin adı uluslar arasında büyük, her yerde sunuyla onurlandırılan bir addır; iyi adın insanlar arasında yayılması imgesini ilâhî ölçekte işler.
YHWH'nin adı güçlü kule diye nitelenir ve doğru kişi ona koşar; ad burada yalnız bir etiket değil, kendisiyle eyleme girilen tanınmış kudrettir.
Enoş günlerinde YHWH adını çağırmaya başlanır; yorumdaki Ya Allah diye seslenme ve adla başlangıç için eski bir çağrı örneğidir.
Davud silaha karşı YHWH'nin adıyla geldiğini söyler; adın savaşçının taşıdığı nişanla aynı sahada yetki ve aidiyet göstermesine karşılık gelir.
Eschatolojik tabloda YHWH bir ve adı bir olacaktır; yorumdaki O'nun adını taşıyacak dengin bulunmamasıyla somut bir tek-ad iddiasında buluşur.
İsrail başka tanrıların adını ağza almamakla yükümlüdür; Yusuf'un gerçekliği olmayan adları eleştirmesine, adın söyleyişinin de kullukla ilgili olduğunu gösteren bir eşliktir.
Kenan ibadet yerlerinde put adlarının silinmesi emredilir; sahipsiz ya da rakip adların kaldırılması, yorumdaki adın altında tanıtacak bir şey bulunmaması eleştirisini somutlaştırır.
YHWH kendi adını söyler ve yüceliğini başkasına vermeyeceğini bildirir; en büyük ad ile eşsiz kulluk arasındaki ilişkiyi işler.
Karmel'de hangi tanrının ateşle cevap vereceği, onun Tanrı olduğunu gösterecektir; çağrılan adın gerçek sahibi tanıtıp tanıtmadığını sahneleştirir.
Baal'ın adı uzun süre çağrılır ama ses ve cevap gelmez; Yusuf'un ataların taktığı boş adlar sözüne anlatı biçiminde bir karşılık verir.
Yorumdaki Âdem'e bütün adların öğretilmesiyle aynı sahnede Tanrı hayvanları Âdem'e getirip onları ne adlandıracağını görür; burada ad veren insan, öğreten Tanrı değildir.
Âdem evcil hayvanlara, kuşlara ve kır hayvanlarına ad verir; Kur'an yorumunun ilâhî ad öğretisi vurgusuna karşı insanın ayırt edip ad verme görevini öne çıkarır.
Midraş, meleklerin söyleyemediği hayvan adlarını Âdem'in söylemesini Tanrı'nın sınaması olarak anlatır; isim verme olayını tanıma ve ayırt etme bilgeliği diye açar.
İsrail oymakları kendi sancakları ve ata evlerinin işaretleri yanında konaklar; yorumdaki savaşta süvarinin nişanı ve bayrağın ayırt edici işleviyle örtüşür.
Yesse'nin kökü halklar için bir işaret olarak durur ve uluslar onu arar; yükseltilen görünür işaretin tanınma ve toplanma sağlamasıdır.
YHWH uluslara bir sancak kaldırır ve dağılmışları toplar; yorumdaki alem ve sancak imgesinin işaret etme işini doğrudan paylaşır.
Yılanın direğe konması ve ısırılanın ona bakarak yaşaması, yukarı konmuş görünür bir nesnenin tanınma ve hayatla ilişkisini kurar.

Mişna, yılanın kendi başına öldürüp diriltmediğini; İsrail gözünü yukarı kaldırıp yüreğini Tanrı'ya bağladığında iyileştiğini açıklar. Yükseltilmiş işaretin bilgiyi Tanrı'ya yöneltmesi yorumuna yorum geleneği ekler.
Şeria'dan alınan taşlar çocukların anlamını soracağı bir işaret olur; işaretin bir olayı kendisiyle bilinir ve anlatılır kılması yorumdaki tanıma işlevini somutlaştırır.
Şabatlar, YHWH'nin onları kutsadığını bilmeleri için İsrail ile Tanrı arasındaki işaret olarak verilir; nişanın varlık sebebinin bilmek olduğu cümleye çok yakındır.
Gök ışıkları zamanlar ve mevsimler için işaret olarak yaratılır; yorumun bütün yaratılışı Rabbin tanıtıcı işaretleri olarak okumasının kozmik bir örneğidir.
Gökler Tanrı'nın yüceliğini anlatır ve gökkubbe el işini bildirir; yaratılmış âlemin kendisiyle yaratanın bilindiği görüşünü şiirsel olarak kurar.
Eyüp, hayvanlara ve kuşlara sorulursa öğreteceklerini söyler; her canlı türünün kendi başına öğretici işaret olması fikrine belirli bir hayvanlar sahnesi verir.
Bu canlılar arasında YHWH'nin elinin bunu yaptığını bilmeyen kimdir diye sorar; izden yaratanı tanıma sonucunu açıkça söyler.
Yaratılmışların büyüklüğü ve güzelliğinden yapıcının kıyasla kavrandığını söyler; âlemlerin birer tanıtıcı nişan olması için yakın Yahudi hikmet paralelidir.
Tanrı'nın görünmeyen niteliklerinin yaratılmış şeyler aracılığıyla görülüp anlaşıldığını söyler; yaratılışı bilgiyi taşıyan işaret olarak okur.
Tanrı Kayin'i bulanların onu öldürmemesi için üzerine işaret koyar; Kur'an'daki buruna vurulacak cezalandırıcı damgaya karşı, tanınabilir işaret burada koruyucudur.
Sünnet, bedende İbrahim antlaşmasının işareti olarak verilir; yorumdaki dağlanmış tanıma izine karşı bedensel işaretin aidiyet ve antlaşma işlevini gösterir.
Kan, evleri tanıtan ve felaketten esirgeyen işarettir; Kur'an'daki cezaya ait damga ile aynı ayırt etme biçiminin ters sonucunu verir.
Çıkış anması elde işaret ve gözler arasında anı olarak konur, böylece YHWH'nin öğretisi ağızda kalır; beden izi, bellek ve tanımanın birlikte işlemesidir.
Yeruşalim'in günahına yas tutanların alınlarına işaret konur; burada görünür damga seçilmişleri korurken Kur'an'daki burun damgası mahkûmiyet bildirir.

row.basis: Ezekiel'deki tavın mürekkep ve kanla okunması
row.note: Talmud, Ezekiel'in alnındaki işareti doğrular için mürekkep, kötüler için kan diye ayrıntılandırır; işaretin hayır ve şerri okuyup ayırması yorumdaki tevesseme temasını keskinleştirir.

row.basis: elde yazı ve YHWH'ye ait ad
row.note: Kişi eline YHWH'ye ait olduğunu yazar ve kendini İsrail adıyla adlandırır; ad ile bedensel işaretin aynı aidiyet bildiriminde birleşmesidir.
Şölen sırasında insan eli duvarın sıvasına yazı yazar; görülen ama ilk anda okunmayan işaret, yorumdaki iz okuma imgesine yargı sahnesi ekler.
