Daniel duvardaki Mene, Tekel ve Parsin yazısını bildirir; bir izin okunması doğrudan krallığın ahlâkî hükmünü tanımaya dönüşür.
YHWH Sodom ve Gomora üzerine kükürt ve ateş yağdırır; Lut kentinin altüst edilmesinden sonra işaretler okunmasıyla ilgili Kur'an sahnesinin doğrudan anlatı eşidir.
Sodom ve Gomora'nın kül edilmesi tanrısızlara gelecek şeylerin örneği olarak sunulur; yok edilmiş şehrin okunabilir bir uyarı işareti haline gelmesini açıklar.

row.basis: kral adıyla yazılmış ve mühürlenmiş mektup
row.note: Kraliyet mektupları Ahaşveroş'un adıyla yazılıp yüzüğüyle mühürlenir; Süleyman'ın mektubundaki başlığın kimden ve hangi yetkiyle geldiğini bildirmesiyle birleşir.
Pavlus kendi eliyle selamının her mektuptaki işaret olduğunu söyler; yazının başındaki ya da sonundaki iz aracılığıyla göndericinin tanınmasını sağlar.
Seba kraliçesi Süleyman'ın ününü duyup onu sınamaya gelir; Kur'an'ın aynı hükümdarlar arasında kraliçeye gönderilmiş mektup anlatması, ortak kişileri farklı diplomatik sahnelerde kurar.
YHWH Nuh'a bütün eviyle gemiye girmesini buyurur; yorumdaki Nuh'un gemiye binme çağrısının aynı tufan eşiğini, fakat ilâhî ad formülü olmadan, verir.
Sular çekilince Tanrı Nuh'a gemiden çıkmasını söyler; Kur'an'daki geminin yürüyüşü ve duruşunun adla anılması yanında varış ve duruş anını tamamlar.
İyi adın büyük servetten daha çok seçilmeye değer olduğu söylenir; yorumdaki iyilikle insanlar arasında yayılan ad için özlü bir ahlâkî paraleldir.
İyi adın güzel yağdan iyi olması, adın kişinin görünür şöhret ve ayırt edici izi olarak değerlendirilmesini sağlar.
Bilgelik metni iyi adın büyük hazinelerden daha uzun kaldığını söyler; yorumun insanlar arasında dolaşan hayırlı adını zaman içindeki kalıcılığa taşır.
Mişna üç tacı sayıp iyi adın tacını onların üstünde tutar; iyi adın yükselmesi imgesini yorum geleneğinde açık bir değer hükmüne çevirir.
İsa'nın dua öğretisi Baba'nın adının kutsanmasıyla başlar; ibadet başlangıcında adın yüceltilmesi, bismillahın açılış işleviyle karşılaşır.
İsa Baba'nın adını kendisine verilen insanlara açığa çıkardığını söyler; adın adlandırılanı bilinir kılan işaret olması düşüncesini doğrudan teolojik biçimde kullanır.
Çocuğa İsa adı verilmesi, halkını günahlarından kurtaracağı gerekçesiyle açıklanır; adın yalnız ses değil, taşıdığı kişiyi ve işini tanıtan işaret oluşudur.

row.basis: bir eylemin hangi adla yapıldığını sormak
row.note: Yetkililer iyileştirmenin hangi güç veya hangi adla yapıldığını sorar; yorumdaki işe bir adla başlama ve adın yetkiyi göstermesiyle doğrudan buluşur.
Petrus, topalın Nasıralı İsa Mesih'in adıyla iyileştiğini bildirir; eylemin kaynağını ilan eden ad, mektup başlığındaki yetki işareti gibi çalışır.
Kurtuluşun gök altında insanlara verilmiş başka hiçbir adda bulunmadığı İsa adına bağlanır; yorumun eşsiz ilâhî adını Allah'a ayırmasıyla belirgin bir Hristiyan karşı-anlatısıdır.
Rabbin adını çağıran herkesin kurtulacağı söylenir; yorumdaki bağışlanma için ilâhî ada seslenme ile aynı çağrı eylemini taşır.
Korint'teki kutsallar, her yerde Rab İsa Mesih'in adını çağıranlar diye tanımlanır; ortak ibadeti adı taşıyan ve çağıran topluluğun nişanı yapar.

row.basis: her işi Rab İsa adıyla yapmak
row.note: Sözde ve işte her şeyin Rab İsa'nın adıyla yapılması öğretilir; yorumdaki bir işe tanınmış adın altına koyarak başlama düşüncesine çok yakındır.
Efes'teki olaylardan sonra Rab İsa'nın adı büyütülür; yorumun iyilikle insanlar arasında yayılan ve yükselen ad imgesine kamusal bir anlatı verir.

row.basis: adı konmuş çok sayıda tanrı ve rab
row.note: Metin, gökte ve yerde tanrı ve rab diye adlandırılan çok şey bulunduğunu kabul eder; Yusuf'un insanların koyduğu adlar ile gerçek ilâhlık arasındaki ayrım için yakın bir tartışma bağlamıdır.

row.basis: Baba ve Rab İsa'nın birlikte anıldığı itiraf
row.note: Tek Tanrı Baba ile tek Rab İsa Mesih'i birlikte itiraf eder; yorumdaki Allah'a hiçbir adaş veya dengi bulunmadığı açıklaması yanında Hristiyan iki-terimli itirafın farkını görünür kılar.
Tanrı'nın İsa'yı yükseltip ona her adın üstünde adı verdiği söylenir; ad-yükseklik dilini İsa'ya yönelten güçlü Hristiyan karşı-anlatısıdır.
Öğrenciler Baba, Oğul ve Kutsal Ruh adına vaftiz etmeye gönderilir; ad, yeni aidiyetin ritüelle kişiye konan tanıtıcı çerçevesi olur.
Pavlus'a vaftiz olup İsa'nın adını çağırarak günahlarını yıkaması söylenir; çağrı, bedensel ritüel ve yeni aidiyet aynı eylemde birleşir.
Korintliler herkesin bildiği ve okuduğu mektup diye nitelenir; yorumdaki okunabilen iz ile mektubun sahibini tanıtan işaret arasında belirli bir yazı metaforu kurar.
Topluluğun mürekkeple değil Ruh'la yazılmış Mesih mektubu olduğu söylenir; görünür ya da yazılı nişanın kimin adına konuştuğunu bildirmesi düşüncesini dönüştürür.
İsa, Musa'nın çölde yılanı yükseltmesini kendi yükseltilmesi için yorumlar; Sayılar'daki dikili işareti Hristiyan yorumunda tanınma ve hayat veren bir figüre çevirir.
Yıkım melekleri, Tanrı kulları alınlarından mühürleninceye dek bekler; Kur'an'daki cezalandırıcı yüz damgasına karşı burada işaret koruyucu aidiyet taşır.

row.basis: sağ el ve alına zorunlu işaret
row.note: Canavar herkese sağ eline ya da alnına işaret aldırır; beden üzerindeki tanıtıcı damgayı ibadet ve zorlayıcı bağlılık anlatısına çevirir.

row.basis: canavarın adı veya sayısı olan işaret
row.note: Alım satım, canavarın adı ya da adının sayısı olan işarete bağlanır; ad ile damganın sahipsiz işaret değil rakip iktidarın talebi oluşunu gösterir.
Kuzu ile duranların alınlarında onun ve Babasının adı yazılıdır; ilâhî adın insan üzerinde okunabilir aidiyet nişanı olmasıdır.
Son görümde Tanrı'nın kullarının alınlarında onun adı bulunur; adın kalıcı, görünür ve kişiyi tanıtan iz olarak tamamlanmış biçimini verir.
Yorumdaki bismi'deki ism ile ayetteki İbranice şēm, aynı Sami ad sözünün biçimleridir; ayet bu sözü kalıcı biçimde anılan Tanrı adı için kullanır.
Targum, Yesse soyundan gelen kişiyi halklar için sancak olarak okur; Yeşaya'nın kaldırılmış işaretini mesihî tanınma ve toplanma yönünde belirginleştirir.

row.basis: kâhinlerin ad koyması ve Tanrı'nın bereketi
row.note: Sifre, kâhinlerin adı koyduğu berekette nihai bereketin Tanrı'dan geldiğini vurgular; Sayılar 6'daki adın bir sihir sözü değil ilâhî yetki işareti oluşunu açıklar.
Yağmur, verimli mevsimler ve rızık Tanrı'nın kendisini tanıksız bırakmadığının kanıtları diye anlatılır; yaratılışı Rabbe işaret eden izler olarak okur.
Kana'daki ilk işaret İsa'nın yüceliğini gösterip öğrencilerde iman doğurur; işaretin kendisinden öte bir kişiyi tanıttığı anlatı biçimidir.
Seçilmiş işaretlerin okuyucunun İsa'yı Mesih ve Tanrı'nın Oğlu bilip inanması için yazıldığı söylenir; okunmuş nişan ile tanıma arasındaki bağı kurar.
İsa Baba'nın adıyla geldiğini, başkasının kendi adıyla gelebileceğini karşılaştırır; mektubun başındaki ad gibi, gönderenin kimliğinin temsilcinin yetkisini belirlemesiyle birleşir.
Dağ üzerine kurulmuş kentin gizlenemeyeceğini söyler; yorumdaki ufukta yükseldikçe seçilen şekil benzetmesi için belirli bir görünürlük paralelidir.
Fatihin üstüne Tanrı'nın, yeni Yeruşalim'in ve İsa'nın yeni adının yazılması vaat edilir; adların kişiyi tanıtan çoklu aidiyet işaretleri olarak işlenmesidir.
Pavlus bedeninde İsa'nın stigmata'sını taşıdığını söyler; yorumdaki dağlama iziyle aynı bedensel işaret sözlüğünü, acı çekmiş bağlılık anlamında kullanır.
Bu benzetme, Tanrı Oğlunun adını taşımayı su mührüyle ilişkilendirir; adın kişiye konmuş, krallığa girişte tanınan bir işaret olması yorumunu geliştirir.

row.ref: Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh 8
row.note: Tertullian bedenin ruh güçlensin diye imzalandığını ya da mühürlendiğini söyler; Hristiyan ritüel yorumunda beden işaretinin koruma ve aidiyet anlamı kazanmasına tanıklık eder.
Peshitta'da kutsansın diye dua edilen şmā, yorumdaki bismi'deki ism ile aynı Sami ad sözüdür; Süryanice dua da adın yüceltilmesiyle açılır.
Musa Tanrı'nın adını sorunca Ehyeh cevabını alır; adın adlandırılanı tanınır kılan işaret olması düşüncesini ilâhî özdeşlik sorusunun içinde kurar.
Metin, atalara El-Şadday olarak görünmesi ile YHWH adının tanınmasını ayırır; Allah ve Rahman gibi farklı ilâhî adların çağrıda yan yana durduğu yorum için belirli bir ad-açıklama paralelidir.
Tanrı yayını buluta koyup onu kendisi ile yeryüzü arasındaki antlaşmanın işareti kılar; bütün göğe asılmış tanınabilir iz, yorumdaki yükseltilmiş alamet imgesini kozmik ölçekte işler.
Lavan taş yığınının iki taraf arasında tanık olduğunu söyleyip ona Galed adını verir; yükseltilmiş nesne, ad ve ilişkinin tanınmasını aynı anda taşır.
Baş kâhinin altın levhasına mühür kazısı gibi YHWH'ye Kutsal yazılır; yorumdaki yakılmış ya da yükseltilmiş iz yerine, adı görünür kılan kutsal bir yazı işareti sunar.
Kutsal levha Harun'un alnında durur ve kutsal sunuların suçunu taşır; alın üzerindeki adla bağlı işaretin aidiyet ve hüküm işlevini birleştirir.
İsrailliler giysilerinin uçlarına püskül ve mavi ip koyar; taşınan görünür işaretin kişiyi ayırt etmesi ile yorumdaki nişan fikri buluşur.
Püskül görülür, YHWH'nin buyrukları hatırlanır ve uygulanır; iz okununca bilgi ve davranış doğması, tevesseme ile anlatılan işleyişe yakındır.
Bir peygamber YHWH adıyla konuştuğunda söz gerçekleşmezse onun Tanrı'dan olmadığının bilineceği söylenir; adın altında gerçek bir yetkinin bulunup bulunmadığını sonuçtan tanımayı öğretir.
Rahav'ın evini tanınır kılan kırmızı ip, ailesini yıkımdan koruyacaktır; Kur'an'daki cezaya ait damganın tersine, görünür işaret burada kurtarır.
Gidyon, kendisiyle konuşanın gerçekten Tanrı olduğunu bilebilmek için işaret ister; işaretin asıl işinin bir faili tanınır kılmak olduğunu açıkça söyler.
Süleyman, Tanrı'nın adı burada olacak dediği eve gözlerinin açık kalmasını diler; ad, bir yazının ya da yapının hangi ilâhî yetkiyle ilişkili olduğunu belirler.
Çocuğun doğumu bir işaret olarak verilir ve adı İmmanuel olur; ad, kişiyi tanıtan ses ile tarihsel/teolojik işaretin aynı olayda birleşmesidir.
Yeşaya büyük bir levhaya halkın okuyacağı yazıyla Maher-Şalal-Haş-Baz adını yazar; adın kamuya açık yazı izi olarak yaklaşan olayı tanıtmasıdır.
Yeşaya kendisi ve YHWH'nin verdiği çocukları İsrail'de işaretler ve alametler diye niteler; kişi adlarının bütün bir peygamberlik nişanı haline gelmesidir.
Ev ve surlar içinde oğul ve kızlardan iyi, kesilmeyecek ebedî bir ad verilir; yorumdaki tanınmayı taşıyan adın kalıcılık ve şeref boyutunu açar.

row.basis: lanet için bırakılan ad ve yeni ad
row.note: Yargılananların adı seçilmişler için lanet sözü olarak kalır, Tanrı ise kullarını başka bir adla çağırır; iyi ve kötü adın kamu önünde okunur iz oluşunu ters yüzleriyle işler.
Tanrı uluslar arasında kirletilmiş büyük adını kutsayacak ve uluslar onu tanıyacaktır; adın kamusal tanınma, yücelik ve ahlâkî itibar taşımasıyla doğrudan buluşur.

row.basis: kalbe ve sunak boynuzlarına kazınmış günah
row.note: Yahuda'nın günahı demir kalemle kalbine ve sunakların boynuzlarına kazınmış diye tasvir edilir; hayır ya da şerri bedendeki ve nesnedeki izden okumak temasına sert bir karşılıktır.
Görüm levhalara açıkça yazılır ki okuyan onu okuyabilsin; okunabilir iz ile bir hakikatin tanınması arasındaki ilişkiyi doğrudan kurar.
Hoşea'nın kızına Merhamet Edilmeyen adı verilir ve Tanrı artık merhamet etmeyeceğini açıklar; açılıştaki Rahman-Rahim adlarının ters yönünde, adın hüküm bildiren işaret oluşunu sahneler.
Halkların hepsinin YHWH adını çağırması ve omuz omuza hizmet etmesi için dillerinin arıtılacağı söylenir; ad, çağrı ve kulluğun tek formülde birleşmesidir.

row.basis: İsa adıyla yapılmış ama reddedilen eylemler
row.note: Bazıları İsa'nın adıyla peygamberlik ve kudretli işler yaptıklarını söyler, fakat İsa onları tanımaz; yalnızca adı kullanmanın altında gerçek bir bağlılık bulunmayabileceğini gösterir.
Melek, beze sarılı ve yemlikte yatan bebeğin çobanlar için işaret olacağını söyler; işaretin tanınacak kişiyi belirlemesi yorumun temel tanımına yakındır.
Topal adamın İsa'nın adıyla güç kazandığı ve bunun ada imanla olduğu söylenir; okunur bir iyileşme, adın failini tanıtıcı kudret olarak işleyişidir.
Tanrı adının uluslar arasında İsrail'in davranışı yüzünden kötülenmesi, yorumdaki iyi adın insanlar arasında yayılması düşüncesinin olumsuz toplumsal yüzüdür.
İsa'nın adıyla gökte, yerde ve yer altında her dizin çökeceği söylenir; yükseltilmiş adın kulluk doğurması imgesini İsa'ya bağlayan önceki ayetin gerekli Hristiyan devamıdır.
İnanlılar Tanrı'ya İsa aracılığıyla sürekli övgü kurbanı, yani adı ikrar eden dudakların ürünü sunar; adın çağrı ve ibadette sesli işaret oluşudur.
Topluluk ihtiyarları hastaya Rabbin adıyla yağ sürüp dua eder; somut bir eylemin ad altında yapılması, bismillahın fiile verdiği çerçeveyle birleşir.
Tanrı Oğlunun adına iman edenlerin ebedî hayata sahip olduklarını bilmeleri için yazıldığını söyler; ad, bilme ve yaşama ulaştıran belirleyici tanım olur.
Büyük Babil'in alnında gizemli bir ad yazılıdır; ad ve alın damgası burada putperest şehir kimliğini açığa çıkarır ve ilâhî ada ait işaretleri tersine çevirir.
Atlı savaşçının kaftanı ve uyluğu üzerinde Kralların Kralı ve Rablerin Rabbi adı yazılıdır; savaş sahnesinde ad, taşınan nişan ve egemenlik bildirisi olur.
Talmud, Tanrı adı ve krallığı anılmayan bereketin bereket olmadığını öğretir; ilâhî adın dua formülünde gerekli tanıtıcı unsur oluşunu açıklar.
Talmud mavi püsküle bakışı deniz, gök ve ilâhî taht üzerinden hatırlamaya bağlar; giysideki izden anlam okuyuşunu ayrıntılandırır.
Baş kâhin kefaret itirafında ilâhî adı söylediğinde dinleyenlerin yere kapanması anlatılır; en büyük adın sesli çağrıda kulluk doğurması için litürjik bir örnektir.

row.basis: adı uluslara ve krallara taşıyan kişi
row.note: Pavlus, İsa'nın adını uluslar, krallar ve İsrailliler önünde taşımak için seçilmiş araç diye tanımlanır; adın insanlar arasında dolaşan kamusal tanıtım oluşuna anlatısal karşılık verir.
İman edenler vaat edilen Kutsal Ruh'la mühürlenir; bedensel damga yerine görünmez ama tanıyıcı bir aidiyet mührünün Hristiyan yorumudur.

row.basis: Rabbin adını anmak ve kötülükten ayrılmak
row.note: Rabbin adını anan herkesin haksızlıktan uzaklaşması emredilir; yorumdaki ad, bilgi ve kulluk bağını ahlâkî davranışa bağlar.
Çocukların günahlarının İsa'nın adı uğruna bağışlandığı söylenir; açılıştaki merhamet adının çağrıyla bağışlanma ilişkisine Hristiyan bir karşılık verir.
Fatih kişiye yalnız kendisinin bildiği yeni ad yazılı beyaz taş verilir; adın herkese açık tanıtıcı iz oluşuna karşı gizli ve kişisel bir tanınma biçimi kurar.
Kyrillos haç işaretinin alna ve gündelik eylemlere cesaretle konmasını öğütler; Hristiyan uygulamasında görünür işaretin beden, ibadet ve aidiyeti birleştirmesidir.
The Hebrew verb yādîn, “he will judge,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic d-y-n; here YHWH judges his people and vindicates them against their oppressors.
The Aramaic court term dînâ is cognate with Arabic dīn; in the same verse the court sits and books are opened, so the cognate occurs in a concrete judgment scene.
Hebrew melekh, “king,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k; Isaiah uses it for the Lord beside “judge” and “lawgiver.”
Hebrew yôm is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic y-w-m; this verse says day and night belong to God and names the appointed light and sun.
The commentary lets mālik carry both possession and rule; Isaiah places the Lord’s judicial, legislative, royal, and saving roles in one verse.

row.basis: All things and kingship belong to God
row.note: David’s prayer assigns everything in heaven and earth, and the kingdom itself, to God; this makes human ownership provisional beside the Day’s sole owner.
Abraham asks whether the judge of all the earth will do what is just; the universal jurisdiction gives the commentary’s judgment day a concrete biblical counterpart.
Within Moses’ song, God reserves vengeance and repayment for the appointed time; this links the day’s closing account with a reckoning that no human claimant controls.
The law says parents and children die for their own offenses, not one another’s; it parallels the commentary’s day when no person can own or pay another’s account.
At the close of Ecclesiastes, God brings every deed to judgment, even what is concealed; this matches the commentary’s expansion from public evidence to inward acts.
Elihu says God repays a person according to what that person has done; the direct correspondence is the commentary’s account settled in full on the owned day.
The Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to conduct; this connects the commentary’s private intention and heart-accounting with an explicit biblical judgment formula.
Hannah says the Lord weighs actions; this gives the commentary’s image of an unbending scale a moral use, not merely a lexical association with measure.

row.basis: Just scales belong to the Lord
row.note: Proverbs says honest balances and weights are the Lord’s; the commentary likewise makes the final account a measure whose standard belongs to the day’s owner.
Daniel interprets the king’s writing as a verdict that he was weighed and found deficient; it turns the commentary’s balance image into a royal judgment scene.
Daniel sees the court seated and books opened before the Ancient of Days; this closely matches the commentary’s tribunal, record, witnesses, and full payment of deeds.
Malachi records the words of those who fear the Lord in a book before him; the written record parallels the commentary’s books that preserve what people did.
WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; in English numbering this is Psalm 49:7. The singer says no person can ransom a brother from death, matching the day when no one can pay another’s due.
Job says he came naked from the womb and will return naked; this sharpens the commentary’s image of property and servants left behind when a person comes alone.

row.basis: The dead awake to opposed destinies
row.note: Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening to everlasting life or disgrace; it supplies resurrection and final outcome for the commentary’s day of reckoning.
Zephaniah calls the Lord’s day near and bitter, a day of battle cries; the day is an approaching event that overtakes people, as the commentary emphasizes.
Isaiah pictures the heavens rolled up like a scroll as the host falls; this matches the commentary’s cosmic unmaking, in which the sky can no longer serve as a clock.
Joel’s day of the Lord darkens the sun and moon and shakes the heavens; the signs make the commentary’s judgment day exceed ordinary solar measurement.
Amos announces darkness at midday as judgment on Israel; unlike the final day in the commentary, this is a historical oracle, but it makes the solar clock fail at the moment of reckoning.
WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 90:4. A thousand years are like yesterday before God, matching the commentary’s day whose measure is not the sun’s daily course.
The vision waits for its appointed time and will not fail to arrive; this connects the commentary’s “falling/coming event” sense of the day with an event whose date is delayed but certain.
The prophet says the day of the watchmen and punishment has come amid social collapse; Micah’s next verses name betrayal within households, echoing the commentary’s day when ties fail.
Son, daughter, and daughter-in-law turn against close kin; in Micah this follows the announced day of punishment, a concrete social image for the commentary’s fleeing family bonds.
Zechariah commands true justice and mercy, then forbids oppressing widow, orphan, stranger, and poor; this joins the commentary’s judgment day to its contrast between mercy and punishment.
The same verse also works as a motif: day, night, sun, and light are under God’s ordering, making time itself part of the sovereignty the commentary assigns to the Day.

row.basis: Judge who feeds and clothes the vulnerable
row.note: God executes justice for orphan and widow and gives food and clothing to the stranger; this connects the commentary’s merciful owner with concrete care for those who lack worldly power.
Sirach says God judges without favoritism and hears the wronged, orphan, and widow; this puts mercy toward the vulnerable inside the same final-account framework as the commentary.

row.basis: All are God’s and spared by mercy
row.note: Wisdom says God loves what exists and spares it because it is his; this joins the commentary’s ownership language to the mercy that precedes its judgment title.
The midrash says creation could not stand by strict justice alone, so mercy was placed first and justice joined to it; this illuminates Fatiha’s sequence of Rahman/Rahim before the Day of judgment.
Akavya tells each person to consider where they came from, where they go, and before whom they will give account; it gives the commentary’s solitary arrival a Jewish ethical formulation.
The shopkeeper gives credit, the ledger is open, and collectors regularly collect; the image makes the commentary’s debt, record, due date, and final repayment unusually concrete.

row.basis: Judgment before the King of Kings
row.note: The saying pairs unavoidable death with judgment before the King of Kings, matching the commentary’s sovereign who owns the day and the account due then.
The Talmud pictures three books opened on Rosh Hashanah for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate; it develops the commentary’s book-and-verdict image into a graded inscription tradition.

The Talmud’s questions at judgment include whether one dealt faithfully in business and pursued wisdom; this makes ordinary habits part of the account, as the commentary says sustained conduct is judged.

row.basis: Throne and books of the living
row.note: Enoch sees the Head of Days on his throne as the books of the living are opened; this is a close Jewish apocalyptic court scene for the commentary’s records and final accounting.
At the world’s end the Most High appears on the judgment seat and recompense follows; this parallels the commentary’s day when the account is complete and no earthly claim can alter it.
The prayer addresses God as “Our Father, our King” and asks for inscription in the book of life; it holds royal sovereignty and hoped-for mercy together in a judgment-season setting.

row.basis: The Son of Man enthroned as King
row.note: Jesus’ discourse places the glorious Son of Man on a throne before the nations are judged; it gives the commentary’s “owner of the day” a concrete royal court scene.
The king separates people as a shepherd sorts sheep from goats; this joins the commentary’s day of division to its image of a leader whose destination determines the followers’ fate.

At judgment, giving drink to a thirsty person is evidence of mercy; the commentary instead shows condemned people asking for water and being refused, so the shared water scene exposes opposite outcomes.
The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus with water for his burning tongue; this closely matches the commentary’s damned who call across the divide for water.
Abraham says a great chasm prevents passage between the two sides; it explains why the water plea in Luke cannot be met and parallels the commentary’s closed access to the saved community’s water.
The king has compassion and releases a servant by cancelling his enormous debt; this is a specific Christian image for the commentary’s owner who can forgive what is owed on the day of settlement.
The Son of Man comes in glory and repays each person according to conduct; it directly matches the commentary’s account fully paid to every person.
Paul says God judges people’s secrets through Christ; this is a precise bridge to the commentary’s claim that hidden intentions enter the final account.
Paul says all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat to receive for what was done in the body; it joins individual embodiment and deeds to the commentary’s personal reckoning.
The author says no creature is concealed and all are exposed before the one to whom account must be given; this matches the commentary’s turn from public records to the heart’s hidden contents.

row.basis: Books opened and the dead judged
row.note: John sees the dead judged by what is written in opened books, each according to deeds; this is a close Christian counterpart to the commentary’s court, records, and full recompense.
After Babylon’s fall, the heavenly crowd praises God because his judgments are true and just; this parallels the commentary’s praise formula voiced after judgment is completed.

row.basis: Sun and moon lose their light
row.note: The sun turns dark and the moon like blood as the day of wrath unfolds; this matches the commentary’s judgment scene in which the sun ceases to measure the day.

row.basis: Sky rolls up like a scroll
row.note: John sees the sky vanish like a rolled scroll; this is a close image for the commentary’s cosmic collapse and the end of ordinary celestial order.
Peter compares a day before the Lord to a thousand years; this makes explicit the commentary’s contrast between solar days and divine time.

row.basis: An appointed day and righteous judgment
row.note: Paul says God fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness, with resurrection as assurance; the verse directly links day, divine judgment, and resurrection.
James says judgment is without mercy for one who has shown no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this holds the commentary’s mercy and wrath together as an ethical test.

John says the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son; this differs from the commentary’s emphasis on God as sole owner and final judge by assigning the court’s execution to a distinct divine figure.

row.basis: Christ intercedes at God’s right hand
row.note: Paul identifies the risen Christ as intercessor; beside the commentary’s speech and intercession available only by the Rahman’s leave, this gives that permitted role a specific Christian mediator.
The doxology calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords; it complements the commentary’s distinction between possession and rule by declaring ultimate royal authority.

row.basis: Stored wealth cannot accompany the dead
row.note: God tells the rich fool that his life is demanded that night and asks who will own his stores; this dramatizes the commentary’s claim that worldly property stays behind when a person comes alone.
Paul says the trumpet sounds and the dead are raised imperishable; this supplies the resurrection event behind the commentary’s final-day accounting.
The author links death once with judgment afterward; this brings the commentary’s deathbed scene and the day of account into one sequence.

row.basis: Patristic reading of the last judgment
row.note: Augustine’s discussion of the final judgment around Revelation 20 treats it as a public reckoning of the dead; it gives the commentary’s opened court and day-as-event a major Christian interpretive frame.

row.basis: The King’s judgment measured by mercy
row.note: Chrysostom’s homily on Matthew 25 reads feeding and giving drink to the needy as the King’s criterion at judgment; it clarifies the ethical weight of the commentary’s denied water and neglected poor.

The hymn imagines the judge arriving, the trumpet summoning the dead, and a written record disclosing deeds; it gathers the commentary’s day, resurrection, and account into Christian liturgical language.

The next verse names widow, orphan, stranger, and poor and forbids plotting harm against one another; it makes Zechariah’s justice-and-mercy command concrete, as the commentary links final belief to how the weak are treated.

row.basis: Kings and times given or removed
row.note: Daniel’s prayer says God changes times, removes kings, and raises kings; this directly supports the commentary’s point that worldly possession and rule are granted and withdrawn by the day’s true sovereign.

Isaiah asks who measured the waters in the hollow of a hand, marked the heavens, and weighed mountains; this gathers the commentary’s strong grasp, water, cosmic ownership, and scale into one biblical image.

WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 23:2. The Lord leads the speaker to waters of rest, matching the commentary’s meeting of guide, path, and water that sustains a traveler.

Jesus contrasts the broad road to destruction with the narrow way to life; this gives a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary’s path-center, guidance, and danger of following a misleading route.

row.basis: The Lamb guides to living water
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water; this brings the commentary’s leading guide and life-sustaining water together in an eschatological scene.
Jesus’ parable says neither debtor can pay, so the creditor cancels both debts; this illuminates the commentary’s image of the Day’s owner as a creditor able to forgive what is owed.
The Lord’s Prayer asks God to forgive debts as worshippers forgive their debtors; it links the commentary’s debt-account sense of dīn with the ethical practice of releasing another’s claim.
The verse says each believer will give an account of himself to God; it is a direct New Testament parallel to the commentary’s day when no one can answer or pay for another.

row.basis: Hidden purposes of the heart revealed
row.note: Paul says the Lord will expose what is hidden in darkness and disclose the heart’s purposes; this closely matches the commentary’s inner account that public records cannot exhaust.

row.basis: Trumpet and raising of the dead
row.note: At the last trumpet the dead are raised imperishable; this supplies a Christian resurrection scene for the commentary’s final day and the transition from death to account.
Daniel’s Aramaic malkû names the enduring kingdom given to the humanlike figure; it is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k and appears in a scene where all peoples serve the ruler.

God names himself compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in covenant love; this is a close biblical pairing for the commentary’s Rahman/Rahim immediately before the title “owner of the Day.”
The same self-revelation says God forgives wrongdoing yet does not simply clear the guilty; this preserves both mercy and accountability in the sequence the commentary develops.
The proverb asks whether the one who weighs hearts will not know, then says he repays each according to work; it joins hidden motives to exact recompense in one passage.

row.basis: The Lord comes to judge the world
row.note: The psalm says the Lord comes to judge earth and peoples with righteousness; creation’s response makes this a compact scene of universal judgment, not just a shared “day” word.
The next verse after Zephaniah’s approaching day names distress, darkness, and a trumpet blast; it adds the day’s sensory and cosmic disturbance to the commentary’s non-solar event.

WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 103:10. The psalm says God has not treated people according to their sins, a concrete counterweight to the commentary’s full repayment and merciful creditor.
Abraham’s vision shows a soul assessed by its deeds on a balance; this is a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary’s upright scale and final account.

row.basis: Prayer and offering for the dead
row.note: Judas arranges atonement for fallen soldiers in hope that they may be freed from sin; this gives a different account of aid across death from the commentary’s claim that no one can pay another’s due.

row.ref: Unetanneh Tokef, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur liturgy
row.basis: Creatures pass before the King and records seal fate
row.note: The prayer pictures all creatures passing before God, with life and death written and sealed; it extends the commentary’s sovereign day, personal account, and written verdict in a Jewish liturgical setting.

The kings and mighty see the Son of Man on the throne and are overcome with fear while the righteous stand before him; this adds the commentary’s royal sovereignty and the collapse of worldly rank to Enoch’s court scene.
Jesus says people will give account on the day of judgment for careless words; this gives a concrete relation between the commentary’s loss of speech-rights and the court’s accounting.

row.basis: The day’s date is not disclosed
row.note: Jesus says no one knows the day or hour; alongside the commentary’s answer to “when?” by describing what happens rather than naming a date, it keeps the reader’s attention on the event and readiness.

Peter says all will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead; this gathers the commentary’s death scene, universal judgment, and personal accounting in a concise Christian formulation.

row.basis: Death and Hades release their dead
row.note: The next verse after John’s opened books says sea, Death, and Hades give up the dead for judgment; it adds the gathering of every person from death’s custody to the commentary’s tribunal scene.

The commentary's day makes every act answerable through a written record; Daniel's Aramaic vision seats the court before the Ancient of Days and opens books. It supplies the same concentrated scene of final judicial authority and record.

The commentary develops Arabic dîn as judgment, account, and recompense; Daniel calls the seated court dîn in Biblical Aramaic. The actual cognate is used there precisely for the court that opens the books.

The commentary says the deferred account arrives with a written book and exact repayment; Revelation has the dead stand before a throne, books open, and judgment proceed from what is written and done.
The commentary makes the day one on which no person's work escapes payment; Paul says all must appear before Christ's tribunal to receive for the things done in the body.
The commentary distinguishes a human court's limit from God's accounting for what is hidden within; Paul locates God's judgment specifically in the hidden things of people.
The commentary says the day exposes what written contracts and outward witnesses cannot reach; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the purposes of hearts.
The commentary joins the heart's concealed gain to final recompense; Jeremiah depicts YHWH as searching heart and mind in order to give each person according to conduct.
The commentary's final ledger includes what a person concealed; Qohelet says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment.

row.basis: seeing eye; hearing ear; written book
row.note: The commentary's record is not merely a human document but an exhaustive divine account; Avot turns that claim into an ethical warning through God's seeing, hearing, and the book in which all deeds are written.

row.basis: open ledger; credit; collectors; true judgment
row.note: The commentary reads dîn through debt, a due date, writing, and full settlement; Akiva's saying imagines life as credit entered in an open ledger, collected without exception, ending in a true judgment.

row.basis: account and reckoning before King of kings
row.note: The commentary calls the owner of the day the sole ruler before whom people stand; Avot frames mortal life as preparation to give account and reckoning before the King of kings.
The commentary emphasizes differentiated repayment from a preserved record; this talmudic discussion opens books for the wholly righteous, wholly wicked, and intermediates on the day of judgment.
The commentary's owner of the day presides over a universal judicial scene; Enoch presents the Head of Days seated on a throne while the books of the living are opened before the heavenly host.
The commentary links remembered deeds, a book, and the approaching day; Malachi records a book of remembrance before YHWH for those who fear him as it moves toward the day when he acts.

row.basis: book and deliverance at final time
row.note: The commentary has people individually counted and brought to the day; Daniel's time of unparalleled trouble delivers those found written in the book.
The commentary treats the day as the event in which final recompense arrives; Daniel's sleepers awake to two sharply different enduring outcomes.
The commentary's day brings people out for a decisive accounting; John describes those in the tombs coming out into resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment.
The commentary places the day amid the trumpet and an altered created order; Paul makes the last trumpet the moment when the dead are raised and the living changed.

row.basis: time to judge dead and reward servants
row.note: The commentary's single day pays every person and exposes rival rule; Revelation's trumpet vision calls it the time to judge the dead, reward God's servants, and destroy destroyers of the earth.

The commentary presents the day as the direct exercise of its one owner's judgment; Paul also says God fixed a day for world judgment, but specifies that he will judge through a man appointed and validated by resurrection.

row.basis: all judgment given to the Son
row.note: The commentary's claim that all lesser possession and authority fall away leaves one owner of judgment; John assigns all judgment from the Father to the Son, a specifically Christological distribution of that role.

row.basis: YHWH alone exalted in that day
row.note: The commentary says the day leaves one answer to the question of rule; Isaiah's day humbles every human height so that YHWH alone is exalted.
The commentary insists that worldly possession and dominion are lent and can be withdrawn; Daniel's king is made to confess that the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them to whom he wills.

row.basis: source m-l-k; Hebrew melek; judge and king
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the Arabic m-l-k words for owner and king while joining authority and judgment; Isaiah names YHWH both judge and king, using Hebrew melek, a cognate of the commentary's malik/melik family.

row.basis: YHWH one king over all earth
row.note: The commentary's day reduces contested dominion to one owner; Zechariah's eschatological vision makes YHWH king over all earth and stresses his oneness.

The commentary develops possession as a relation of master and servant, then makes all people arrive as servants; Leviticus grounds Israel's release from human bondage in their belonging as servants to YHWH.

row.basis: all lives belong to God; individual liability
row.note: The commentary joins belonging to God with personal accounting; Ezekiel says every life belongs to God and immediately makes the sinner, rather than a relative, answer for sin.
The commentary says death cannot remove a person from the owner's claim; Paul says Christ died and lived again in order to be Lord of both the dead and the living.

row.basis: body not one's own; bought at a price
row.note: The commentary's owner-servant language denies autonomous human possession; Paul tells believers that they are not their own because they were bought at a price.

row.basis: Noah, Daniel, Job save only themselves
row.note: The commentary says neither a parent, child, friend, nor other human can pay for another on that day; Ezekiel says even three exemplary righteous figures would deliver only themselves amid judgment.
The commentary renders the collapse of family and patronage as each person's individual reckoning; Paul states that each of us will give an account of himself to God.

row.basis: silver and gold cannot deliver in YHWH's day
row.note: The commentary contrasts what hands possess with what can actually save on the day; Zephaniah says neither silver nor gold can deliver its owner on YHWH's day of wrath.

row.basis: riches fail on day of wrath
row.note: The commentary's mal and children lose their usefulness when the account comes due; Proverbs directly says riches do not profit in a day of wrath.
The commentary says a person cannot offer another person or any possession as final payment; Jesus asks what anyone could give in exchange for the life or soul.

The commentary portrays death as the moment human ownership proves powerless and the person comes alone; the rich fool hears that his life is demanded that night and his accumulated things will belong to someone else.

row.basis: source yawm; Hebrew yom; solar days
row.note: The commentary first defines yawm by sunrise and sunset before showing that the judgment day breaks that measure; Genesis uses cognate Hebrew yom for days and years marked by the heavenly lights, establishing the ordinary solar frame.

row.basis: unique day, neither day nor night
row.note: The commentary calls the judgment day a duration no longer measured by the sun; Zechariah describes a unique day known to YHWH that is neither ordinary day nor night.
The commentary deliberately detaches the final day from human solar duration; 2 Peter likewise measures a day and a thousand years differently before describing the day of the Lord.
The commentary's day outlasts the solar clock because the heavenly lights themselves are undone; Isaiah's day of wrath darkens the stars, sun, and moon.
The commentary imagines the day after the sun's ordinary measuring work has ceased; Jesus' eschatological discourse darkens sun and moon after tribulation.
The commentary speaks of the heavens being folded in the day of God's grasp; Isaiah depicts the host of heaven decaying and the skies rolling up like a scroll.
The commentary's cosmic day folds the sky in the owner's hand; Revelation's sixth-seal vision has the sky recede as a scroll being rolled up.

row.basis: day of the Lord; heavens and elements dissolved
row.note: The commentary names the day an arriving event that overturns the normal heavens and earth; 2 Peter's day of the Lord comes unexpectedly and dissolves the cosmic order while exposing earthly works.

row.basis: moon and sun ashamed when YHWH reigns
row.note: The commentary binds the undoing of solar measure to the owner's unshared rule; Isaiah makes moon and sun pale before YHWH's royal reign on Zion.

row.basis: source dîn; Hebrew dîn; judgment after Egypt
row.note: The commentary connects dîn as recompense with God's days of rescue from Pharaoh; in the promise to Abram, Hebrew dîn names God's judgment of the enslaving nation before its victims leave.
The commentary calls a remembered divine day both rescue and judgment, using Moses' deliverance as its model; Exodus explicitly marks the sea deliverance from Pharaoh as the day YHWH saved Israel.
The commentary's praise continues into the day that establishes sole rule; Israel's song after Pharaoh's defeat acclaims YHWH's kingship forever.

row.basis: praise after true and just judgments
row.note: The commentary hears praise of the Lord of all worlds after judgment has been completed; Revelation's heavenly multitude praises God because his judgments are true and just after Babylon's fall.
The commentary pictures angels encircling the throne in praise; Revelation explicitly sets angels around the throne, elders, and living creatures as they fall and worship.

row.basis: YHWH goes ahead to lead on the way
row.note: The commentary's owner is also the one who walks in front and gives the route; Exodus portrays YHWH going before Israel in cloud and fire to lead the way.
The commentary's flock image makes the leader's direction decisive; Jesus' shepherd goes out ahead, and the sheep follow because they know his voice.
The commentary joins herd imagery to the day on which direction and destination are disclosed; Matthew gathers all nations before the enthroned judge for a shepherd's separation of sheep from goats.

row.basis: all pass before him like sheep
row.note: The commentary's day combines flock, an owner, and universal standing to account; the Mishnah says all inhabitants of the world pass before God like a flock on Rosh Hashanah.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds to springs of life-water
row.note: The commentary contrasts a true leader's water with those driven toward fire and denied water; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and leads the thirsty saved to springs of living water.

row.basis: water from rock for wilderness people
row.note: The commentary calls water the thing by which a traveler can keep going; in Israel's wilderness journey, God provides water from the rock for the people at their stopping place.

row.basis: water begged for amid postmortem fire
row.note: The commentary's condemned ask the blessed for water and cannot obtain it; the rich man in Hades asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue while in tormenting fire.

row.basis: debt release and the poor person's claim
row.note: The commentary links a debtor's due date with the poor person's real claim on wealth; Deuteronomy forbids withholding from a poor kin because the remission year is near and treats that refusal as guilt.

row.basis: generosity to poor as loan repaid by YHWH
row.note: The commentary imagines the day owner as a creditor who can forgive and repay; Proverbs calls generosity to the poor a loan to YHWH, who repays the giver.

row.basis: king begins to settle servants' accounts
row.note: The commentary's dîn is a sovereign's final settlement of deferred debt; Jesus' parable opens with a king who wishes to settle accounts with his servants.
The commentary makes forgiving a debtor an earthly image of hoping for divine forgiveness; the king rebukes his servant for refusing the mercy he himself had received.
The commentary refuses to separate the just account from the merciful owner; James makes lack of mercy meet merciless judgment while saying mercy triumphs over judgment.
The commentary argues that relinquishing another's debt belongs with hope for one's own forgiveness; this talmudic maxim says that Heaven overlooks the transgressions of one who overlooks injuries.

The commentary treats forgiving a hard-pressed debtor as an image of the merciful day owner; Jesus commands lending without hope of return and connects its reward with resemblance to the merciful Father.

row.basis: care for the least as judgment criterion
row.note: The commentary says denial of the poor's share accompanies denial of the day of recompense; the judge in Matthew identifies concrete care for the least with service rendered to himself.

row.basis: YHWH judges people and has compassion on servants
row.note: The commentary places Rahman's mercy immediately beside his ownership of the day; Deuteronomy holds judgment and compassion together when YHWH judges his people and has compassion on his servants.

row.basis: no intercessor; God's own arm acts
row.note: The commentary says no human can possess aid or speech on another's behalf unless the owner permits it; Isaiah sees that there is no intercessor and portrays God's own arm as bringing salvation.

The commentary allows intercession only as a prerogative of the day's owner; Hebrews gives the Christian account a continuing named intercessor, Christ, who appears to save those approaching God through him.
The commentary says even the right to speak falls under the owner on that day; Paul depicts every mouth stopped so that the whole world becomes accountable to God.

row.basis: account for every idle word on judgment day
row.note: The commentary extends final accounting beyond outward property to words and hidden responsibility; Jesus says people will render an account for every careless word on the day of judgment.
The commentary's day has an unbending scale that judges even rulers who claim possession; Daniel's royal verdict says Belshazzar has been weighed in balances and found lacking.

row.basis: wealth testifies in the last days
row.note: The commentary lets the hand's accumulated wealth become evidence against its owner; James says corroded gold and silver will testify against the rich and consume them like fire in the last days.

The commentary makes the merciful name immediately govern the day of judgment and leaves room for forgiveness; 4 Ezra depicts the judgment seat as the point where compassion and patience withdraw and uncompromised recompense remains.

row.basis: books, weighing, and adjudication of souls
row.note: The commentary's book, exact reckoning, and balance form one final-account scene; the Testament of Abraham gives those elements a visionary judicial tableau in which souls are weighed and their deeds examined.

The commentary's arriving day begins with trumpet and overturns ordinary life; the Didache's closing apocalypse likewise names the trumpet and resurrection among the signs before the Lord's appearing.
The commentary's guide and path images culminate in a destination revealed at the day; the Didache opens by setting a way of life beside a way of death.

row.basis: way without turning right or left
row.note: The commentary develops the road's middle as the route that must not be abandoned; Deuteronomy makes not turning right or left the concrete form of walking in the commanded way.
The commentary turns the owner's firm grasp into earth held and sky folded on the final day; Isaiah's creation hymn measures waters in God's hand and the heavens by his span.

row.basis: built objects cry out against injustice
row.note: The commentary gives the final account witnesses beyond a person's self, including what hands have done; Habakkuk makes a stone from an unjust house cry out and its timber answer it.
The commentary's day removes ungranted speech before sovereign authority; Jesus' royal wedding parable renders the improperly clothed guest speechless when the king questions him.

row.basis: marriage of the Lamb after judgment praise
row.note: The commentary uses marriage as one human binding that cannot secure a person on the day; Revelation follows its judgment praise with an eschatological marriage in which the bride is made ready for the Lamb.

row.basis: silence in heaven before trumpet judgments
row.note: The commentary's scene of unowned speech includes silence before the day owner's action; Revelation places a half-hour of heavenly silence immediately before the trumpet judgments begin.

row.basis: all flesh silent before YHWH rises
row.note: The commentary says speech and intercession are not human possessions in the day; Zechariah commands all flesh to be silent before YHWH as he rises from his holy dwelling.

row.basis: treasured possession; mercy on the day
row.note: The commentary calls the day owner both merciful and the one to whom all finally belong; Malachi says that on the day he acts, YHWH will make those who fear him his treasured possession and spare them as a father spares a serving son.

row.basis: Day of YHWH; wrath against sinners
row.note: The commentary calls the day an arriving event rather than a calendar date; Isaiah announces the coming Day of YHWH as a day of wrath that makes the land desolate and destroys its sinners.

row.basis: source yawm; Hebrew yom; approaching bitter day
row.note: The commentary gives yawm the force of an approaching overwhelming event; cognate Hebrew yom in Zephaniah's Day of YHWH is near, bitter, and marked by the warrior's cry rather than ordinary solar routine.
The commentary's day makes those who have died arrive for final accounting; Isaiah speaks of the dead living, corpses rising, and those in the dust awakening.
The commentary makes leading a flock a form of responsible possession; Ezekiel has God oppose the self-feeding shepherds, require his sheep from their hand, and reclaim the flock.

row.basis: judgment between sheep, rams, and goats
row.note: The commentary turns flock imagery into a day of differentiation and account; Ezekiel explicitly says God judges between sheep and sheep, rams and goats.
The commentary contrasts the true caller who leads straight with Pharaoh's fatal leadership; Isaiah says a people's leaders make them err and those led by them are swallowed up.

row.basis: YHWH at the head of a people going out
row.note: The commentary's guide is the one who goes before and determines the route; Micah's restoration procession has its king pass before the people with YHWH at their head.
The commentary's false front-runner brings followers to fire instead of water; Jesus calls false leaders blind guides and says guide and follower alike fall into a pit.

row.basis: hour of judgment; worship of Creator
row.note: The commentary joins sole ownership, the coming day, and worship; Revelation's angel announces that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls all to worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs.

row.basis: coming with recompense for each work
row.note: The commentary defines dîn as exact return for what each person has done; the coming speaker in Revelation brings recompense to repay each according to work.

row.basis: repayment to each according to works
row.note: The commentary makes final repayment individual and proportionate; Paul states the same judicial rule in saying that God renders to each person according to works.

row.basis: all exposed before the one to whom account is due
row.note: The commentary says the hidden interior reaches the account after human witnesses stop; Hebrews says no creature is hidden and all are naked and exposed before the one to whom account must be given.
The commentary uses the deathbed to show that a person cannot recover the life already claimed; Hebrews sets death once for humans and judgment afterward.

row.basis: bring nothing in; take nothing out
row.note: The commentary says possessions, servants, and status are left behind when the person comes alone; Paul states the compact formula that nothing was brought into the world and nothing can be taken out.

The commentary moves from naming the owner to direct address and treats debt forgiveness as the measure of hoped-for mercy; the Lord's Prayer asks the Father to forgive debts as petitioners forgive their debtors.

row.basis: postmortem reversal of comfort and anguish
row.note: The commentary's denied water scene is a recompense in which prior possession no longer helps; Abraham explains the rich man's torment and Lazarus's comfort as a reversal of their former received portions.

row.basis: withheld wages cry to the Lord
row.note: The commentary binds denial of the poor's due to the day of account; James says unpaid wages cry out and the cries of harvesters reach the Lord of hosts.

row.basis: Christ titled King of kings and Lord of lords
row.note: The commentary concentrates final kingship in the one divine owner of the day; Revelation gives the victorious Christ the title King of kings and Lord of lords, a specifically Christian royal identification.
The commentary links debt's due date to ownership and servitude; Proverbs states the social analogy directly by making the borrower servant to the lender.

row.basis: God weighs heart and repays work
row.note: The commentary's unbending scale reaches the heart as well as outward deeds; Proverbs asks whether the one who weighs the heart does not know and then says he repays each according to work.
The commentary turns the day into a balance that cannot bend for wealth or status; Job asks to be weighed in just scales so that God may know his integrity.
The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives with fire and judgment; Isaiah presents YHWH entering judgment with fire and sword against all flesh.

row.basis: Lord Jesus revealed in flaming fire
row.note: The commentary names the single owner as the judge of the fire-bound day; 2 Thessalonians presents the revealed Lord Jesus in flaming fire as the one inflicting retribution, a Christian specification of the judging figure.

The commentary treats death, return, and accounting as one continuous claim of the day owner; Avot's maxim makes those born die, the dead live, and the living stand for judgment before the King of kings.

The commentary uses debt writing and commercial honesty to show that ordinary accounts continue before God; this talmudic judgment scene begins by asking whether a person conducted business faithfully.

row.basis: one mediator between God and humans
row.note: The commentary limits effective intercession to the owner's authorization; 1 Timothy states a Christian mediatorial formula that names one God and one mediator, the human Christ Jesus.

row.basis: throne before which earth and sky flee
row.note: The commentary's day has the earth grasped and the heavens folded beneath sovereign rule; at Revelation's great white throne, earth and sky flee from the judge's presence.

The commentary uses spouse and family bonds to show relations that cannot carry another person through the day; Jesus recasts the resurrection state as one in which people neither marry nor are given in marriage.
The commentary calls the owned day the time when all accounts close; Qohelet says God judges righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.
The commentary describes dîn as a counterweight that returns what a person has done; Jesus says the measure used for others will be measured back to the user.
The commentary sees final recompense as the completion of habitual conduct rather than an isolated act; Paul says no one mocks God because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
The commentary labels naʿbudu with Arabic ʿ-b-d; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew ʿābad for serving YHWH alone, showing the same service and worship range.
The commentary stresses that the foregrounded “you” excludes every other object of worship; Deut 6:13 commands Israel to fear and serve YHWH alone.
The commentary makes exclusive address the point of “you alone”; the Shema confesses YHWH as Israel’s one God, grounding that exclusivity in Israel’s central creed.
The commentary labels naʿbudu from Arabic ʿ-b-d; Psalm 100 uses Hebrew ʿābad for the community’s joyful service of YHWH as it comes before him with song.
The commentary treats “we” as a community that knows its owner; the psalm names worshippers as God’s people and sheep of his pasture, giving communal service a shepherd-and-flock image.
The commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d is cognate with the Hebrew root in “you shall serve God”; Exodus makes service to God the destination of Israel’s release from Egypt.
The commentary recalls Pharaoh’s enslavement of Israel and its reversal in exclusive service to God; Moses is told that the people will serve God on this mountain after leaving Egypt.
The commentary links ʿabd to both belonging and enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew service word for Israel’s bitter forced labor under Egypt.
The commentary’s Pharaoh scene treats human mastery as the corrupt form of servitude; Exodus describes the Egyptians making Israel’s life bitter with hard labor.
The commentary calls the worshipper God’s owned servant; Leviticus calls Israelites God’s servants, brought out of Egypt, and forbids selling them as slaves.
The commentary links service with a trodden, guided way; Deut 10:12 puts walking in God’s ways beside serving him with all one’s heart and soul.
The commentary hears a path within service and then asks for guidance; Moses joins walking in God’s ways to loving and serving him wholeheartedly.
The commentary describes worship as an all-encompassing allegiance; Deut 11:13 uses the cognate Hebrew service root in a command to love and serve YHWH with all heart and soul.
The commentary’s naʿbudu and Joshua’s “we will serve YHWH” use cognate Arabic and Hebrew roots for service.
The commentary reads “we” as a worshipping community; Joshua sets rival gods before Israel and declares that he and his household will serve YHWH.
The commentary makes the worshipper’s exclusive choice rule out other masters; Jacob tells his whole household to put away foreign gods before going to Bethel.
The commentary joins service and asking help in one first-person plural prayer; Jacob calls the household to make an altar to the God who answered him in distress and stayed with him on the way.
The commentary contrasts one owner with competing masters; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and calls for a decision between YHWH and Baal.
The commentary’s fronted “you” excludes all other recipients of worship; the psalmist addresses God as great and says that he alone is God.
The commentary distinguishes asking God for aid from the means used to endure; Psalm 50 joins calling on God in trouble, his deliverance, and the worshipper’s honoring him.
The commentary says God is not a servant or a needy recipient of help; Psalm 50 says God would not need to tell Israel if he were hungry because the world is his.
The commentary leaves the requested aid open to every need; the pilgrim psalm names YHWH, maker of heaven and earth, as the speaker’s help.
The commentary explains service as obedience reaching humility; the psalm calls the community to bow and kneel before its maker.
The commentary’s “we” is a community belonging to one owner; the psalm calls Israel God’s people and the sheep of his hand.
The commentary speaks for a plural worshipping community that asks only God for aid; the psalm tells Israel to trust YHWH, its help and shield.
The commentary moves from praise of God to direct address and exclusive service; Nehemiah’s communal prayer says “you alone” are YHWH, maker of all, while heaven’s host worships you.
The commentary has a praying “we” address God directly for aid; Nehemiah’s communal confession turns to “our God” and asks him to attend to the people’s hardship.
The commentary’s aid includes support for the worn traveler; Isaiah contrasts idols that must be carried with God’s promise to carry and rescue Israel from birth to old age.
The commentary asks why help should be sought from what cannot benefit or save; Isaiah says an idol cannot answer its worshippers or rescue them from trouble.
The commentary says false objects of worship cannot provide aid; in Elijah’s contest Baal’s prophets call and dance, but no voice answers them.
The commentary develops the worked, passable road as an image beside service and guidance; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared for the Lord’s coming.
The commentary describes a road made easy by being flattened; Isaiah pictures valleys raised and rough ground leveled to make the Lord’s highway passable.
The commentary says the first-person plural community is open to people from different paths; Isaiah includes foreigners who join themselves to YHWH, serve him, and love his name.
The commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from human agents who can assist; Aaron and Hur physically support Moses’ hands when he grows tired.
The commentary emphasizes that “you alone” excludes every rival recipient; Jesus answers the tempter by commanding worship and service of the Lord God alone.
The commentary stresses the turn from speaking about God to speaking to him, and the plural “we”; Jesus teaches disciples to begin prayer with “Our Father.”
The commentary says the second “you” separately directs the request for aid to God; the Lord’s Prayer asks the Father for daily bread in the first-person plural.
The commentary joins worship with dependence on God for help; the Lord’s Prayer asks God to deliver the praying community from evil.
The commentary’s ownership section contrasts a person shared by quarrelling owners with one belonging to a single master; Jesus says a slave cannot serve two masters.
The commentary explains worship as belonging and obedience, while also recalling human enslavement; Paul says people become slaves of the one they obey, whether sin or righteousness.
The commentary contrasts belonging to God with being enslaved by human masters; Paul tells believers bought with a price not to become slaves of people.
The commentary’s opening praise calls God Lord of the worlds; Paul proclaims the maker of the world as Lord of heaven and earth.

row.basis: God does not need human service
row.note: The commentary says God has no need of a helper; Paul says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he gives life and breath to all.
The commentary says service is a state of belonging, not merely a scheduled rite; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and their life as worship.
The commentary treats aid as an open request addressed to God; Hebrews invites people to approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find help in need.
The commentary reads both verbs as an ongoing state rather than a past act or future promise; Paul’s instruction to pray continually gives that persistence a Christian practice.
The commentary’s “we” speaks directly to God; the gathered believers pray together to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them.
The commentary says aid is separately directed to God; the gathered church asks God to enable his servants to speak boldly amid threats.
The commentary notes that aid among humans can be real while God remains the one finally sought; Paul tells believers to bear one another’s burdens.
The commentary cites Jesus refusing divine status; when Cornelius falls before Peter, Peter raises him and says he too is only a man.
The commentary describes angels rejecting worship directed to them; John falls before an angel, who refuses it and says to worship God.
The commentary’s cited Qur’anic scene has angels deny being objects of worship; Hebrews instead says all God’s angels are to worship the Son, a direct difference over the recipient.

row.basis: worship of God and the Lamb
row.note: The commentary insists on address to God alone and cites Jesus’ rejection of being made divine; Revelation depicts every creature giving blessing and honor to the one on the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary’s exclusive “you” is addressed to God and notes Jesus rejecting divine status; Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as “my Lord and my God,” making the Christological difference explicit.
The commentary says those who belong to God are protected from the adversary; Jesus describes his sheep as his own and says no one will snatch them from his hand.
The commentary understands “we” as a community of God’s servants; Peter calls believers God’s own people, set apart to proclaim his acts.
The commentary notes that Fatiha is recited in every prayer, so even an individual says “we”; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily.
The commentary distinguishes worship from asking aid while placing both inside prayer; the rabbis interpret “serve him with all your heart” as prayer, treating petition itself as service.
The commentary says worship exceeds scheduled rites but is spoken within ritual prayer; the Talmud relates the fixed prayers to the daily offerings, preserving a sacrificial dimension of prayer.
The commentary’s communal “we” includes earlier generations; the Mishnah teaches each generation to see itself as having come out of Egypt, making inherited history a present first-person identity.
The commentary evokes a traveler whose mount fails and who needs support; Qoheleth says a companion can lift someone who falls, making human aid concrete beneath reliance on God.
The commentary warns that backing someone can aid wrongdoing; Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked and loving those who hate YHWH.
The commentary presents a community whose “we” can include people of distinct backgrounds; Isaiah says the foreigners who join YHWH will be brought to his house of prayer.
The commentary connects belonging to God’s servants with protection from Satan; Jesus gives his disciples authority over the enemy’s power and danger.
The commentary links service with the straight path and contrasts it with roads that scatter people; Jesus describes the narrow way that leads to life.
The commentary explains service as reaching bodily humility; Paul pictures every knee bending at Jesus’ name, adding a Christian account of universal homage.
The commentary emphasizes the worshipper’s direct turn toward God; the Mishnah says prayer should begin in solemn focus, with the pious waiting before they pray to direct their hearts.

The commentary says the prayer’s first direct word places God before the speaker’s own action; Augustine opens by addressing God in praise and describes the human heart as restless until it rests in God.
The commentary develops the owner, leading animal, pasture, and vulnerable wanderer within its herd imagery; the psalm names YHWH as shepherd and the speaker as a sheep who lacks nothing.
The commentary joins the service-path image to a later request for guidance; the shepherd psalm leads the sheep on right paths for his name’s sake.
The commentary pictures a worn traveler needing support and asks God for help; the psalmist walks through a deadly valley with the shepherd’s rod and staff as comfort.
The commentary contrasts a community that knows its owner with strays who lose the way; Ezekiel pictures YHWH searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from where they have wandered.
The commentary’s root imagery includes the lost traveler and the herd animal gone astray; YHWH promises to seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind the injured, and strengthen the weak.
The commentary’s augment links direct address to God’s answer to those who call; the psalm says YHWH hears those who call on him and saves them.

row.basis: our eyes on you for help
row.note: The commentary makes the aid request a separate act addressed to God; Jehoshaphat prays for the whole people, “we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
The commentary leaves the need for help open while making God its sole source; after the communal plea, Judah is told to stand and see the salvation YHWH will give.
The commentary describes the human speaker as belonging to the Lord of all creation; the psalm says the earth and all who dwell in it belong to YHWH.
The commentary says worship is addressed to God alone; Isaiah’s oracle has every knee bow to YHWH and every tongue swear allegiance to him.
The commentary recalls Moses asking God for Aaron’s help in the mission to Pharaoh; in Exodus God appoints Aaron to meet Moses and assist him as spokesman.

row.basis: God helps through a human agent
row.note: The commentary distinguishes asking God for help from receiving human assistance; God tells Moses to speak with Aaron and promises to help both of them speak.

row.basis: life and death belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary says a person belongs to God beyond scheduled acts of worship; Paul says that whether believers live or die, they belong to the Lord.
The commentary puts worship and asking aid side by side; Paul tells the community to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, joining petition to praise.
The commentary says worship is a continuing state and can be spoken in prayer; Hebrews calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through their lips.
The commentary moves from “we ask you for aid” to the next verse’s request for guidance; James tells anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
The commentary leaves the aid requested open to every need; Peter tells believers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them.
The commentary reads “we” as a community that reaches beyond a solitary worshipper; Revelation gathers a multitude from every nation before the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary notes that the soul is first welcomed among God’s servants before entering the garden; Revelation depicts the gathered multitude serving God before his throne day and night.
The commentary develops the lost traveler, the herd, and the need for guidance and help; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherd leading the people to springs of living water.
The commentary places the community among God’s servants before naming the garden; Revelation’s final city is where God’s servants worship him and see his face.
The commentary says people or other means may assist while God remains the one ultimately asked for help; Hebrews describes angels as spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation.
The commentary joins aid to worship and prayer; Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray.
The commentary evokes the strayed herd animal and the traveler who cannot find the way; Jesus’ parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep.
The commentary’s image of a vulnerable traveler needing support is made concrete when the shepherd finds the lost sheep, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it home.
The commentary describes asking God for aid across all needs; Revelation says the gathered servants will hunger and thirst no more under the Lamb’s care.
The commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from those who can serve as instruments; Hebrews presents angels as agents sent to aid the heirs of salvation.

The commentary reads naʿbudu as belonging and obedient service rather than a confined rite. After release from Egypt, this verse promises that the people will serve God on the mountain; Hebrew עבד is cognate with the Arabic root in naʿbudu, and the scene redirects an ex-slave community to God.

row.basis: naʿbudu: God owns the liberated servant
row.note: The commentary contrasts belonging to God with Pharaoh's claim over Israel. This verse calls the Israelites God's servants precisely because he brought them out of Egypt, making divine ownership the reason no human master may finally possess them.
The commentary's first iyyāka binds worship to one addressee. Moses likewise binds Israel's fear, service, and sworn speech to YHWH in a single covenantal command.
The commentary says the fronted object closes every other possible object of worship. This verse states the corresponding prohibition: Israel must not follow other gods.

The commentary joins the root-image of a path to worship understood as obedience. This verse gathers walking after God, fearing him, keeping his commands, obeying his voice, serving him, and clinging to him into one sustained allegiance.

The commentary makes the plural naʿbudu a communal declaration that divides one allegiance from rival masters. Joshua's household answer is the same kind of public collective choice: “we will serve YHWH.”

row.basis: remove foreign gods; serve him alone
row.note: The commentary treats exclusive worship as a break with competing objects of service. Samuel makes that sequence explicit: return wholeheartedly, remove foreign gods, direct the heart to YHWH, and serve him alone.
The commentary sets belonging to God against a ruler's power to demand service. The three Judeans tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his image, even under a death threat.

The commentary emphasizes the abrupt collective turn from speaking about God to directly saying “you alone.” Nehemiah's communal prayer begins by directly naming YHWH alone as creator and says that the host of heaven worships him.

row.basis: come, bow, kneel before our maker
row.note: The commentary explains naʿbudu as embodied humility and full submission. This communal summons joins bowing and kneeling to worship before the God who made the worshippers.

row.basis: not to us, but to your name
row.note: The commentary makes the addressee precede the speaker's own act: “you” comes before “we worship.” This plural prayer similarly removes glory from “us” and places God's name first.

row.basis: servants' eyes on a master's hand
row.note: The commentary's owned-servant image does not reduce worship to servility; the servant looks to the one able to give help. The psalm compares the community's eyes toward YHWH with servants watching a master's hand until he shows mercy.
The commentary connects being God's servant with release from other masters. The psalmist directly says “I am your servant” and credits YHWH with loosening his bonds.
The commentary reads “we worship you and ask you for help” as a voiced acknowledgment of belonging. This verse places possession and petition together in the first person: “I am yours; save me.”

row.basis: our help in the creator's name
row.note: The commentary's second iyyāka directs communal help-seeking to God alone. This concluding plural confession locates “our help” in the name of YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.

row.basis: our soul waits; he is our help
row.note: The commentary insists that worship and asking for aid remain distinct acts addressed to the same one. The psalm's corporate voice waits for YHWH and names him both “our help” and shield.

row.basis: help from maker of heaven and earth
row.note: The commentary says the requested avn is not merely an instrument but is sought from God. This pilgrim confession identifies the source of help as YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.

The commentary connects direct address with the God who answers those who call. In a named crisis, the psalmist calls to YHWH and cries to his God; the verse answers the plea with God's hearing from his temple.

row.basis: help us because we rely on you
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a concrete need from the one ultimately asked for help. Asa's public prayer names YHWH as uniquely able to help the weak against the strong and asks “help us” because the people rely on him.

row.basis: stand before you and cry for salvation
row.note: The commentary places help-seeking within worship rather than outside it. Jehoshaphat's community says that in disaster it will stand before God at his house, cry to him in distress, and expect him to hear and save.

row.basis: we have no power; our eyes are on you
row.note: The commentary's plural speaker admits dependence without specifying every possible distress. Facing a particular army, this communal prayer confesses that it has no power and turns its eyes only toward God.

row.basis: seeking Egypt for help instead of YHWH
row.note: The commentary contrasts tools and human allies with the one from whom help is to be sought. Isaiah rebukes those who look to Egypt's horses and chariots for aid while not looking to or seeking YHWH.

row.basis: I hold your hand; I will help you
row.note: The commentary's exhausted-traveler image joins a request for help to support that makes walking possible. Here God takes Israel by the hand and explicitly says, “I will help you.”

row.basis: creator who spread out earth alone
row.note: The commentary says God receives worship and help-seeking but needs no helper himself. This creator declaration stresses that YHWH stretched out the heavens alone and spread out the earth by himself.

row.basis: cry to chosen gods; let them save
row.note: The commentary exposes the contradiction of asking powerless objects for aid. Israel is told to cry to the gods it chose and let them save it in trouble, a deliberately negative counterpart to asking God for help.

row.basis: an idol cannot answer or save
row.note: The commentary says a worshipped other cannot remove distress or supply help. Isaiah's carried image remains fixed; when one cries to it, it cannot answer or save from trouble.

The commentary develops the root's secondary image of a ship sealed with pitch so that it can endure water. This verse commands Noah to coat the ark inside and out with pitch, the same concrete act of making a wooden vessel water-resistant.

row.basis: bitumen and pitch on a basket-ark
row.note: The commentary's tarred-ship image is about a vulnerable vessel made able to withstand the water. Moses' mother coats the basket-ark with bitumen and pitch before setting it on the Nile.

row.basis: worship after being led on the way
row.note: The commentary lets the support-seeking traveler and the coming request for the road resonate within 1:5. Abraham's servant bows in worship because YHWH led him on the right way to his destination.

row.basis: show me the way I should walk
