row.note: The commentary says help asked in 1:5 immediately opens toward the next request for guidance. This direct prayer lifts the self to God and asks to be shown the way in which to walk.

row.basis: bless at all times; ask for straight paths
row.note: The commentary treats worship and help as continuing present acts and connects aid to the road. Tobit's instruction tells a traveler to bless God at all times and ask him to make one's ways straight and one's paths successful.

row.basis: no caller on the Lord is overlooked
row.note: The commentary's direct address presupposes that God hears a caller seeking help. Ben Sira asks readers to recall whether anyone who called on the Lord was ever overlooked, making remembered answered prayer the ground of trust.

The commentary describes avn as support for one who cannot bear the burden alone. Judith's prayer calls God helper of the oppressed, supporter of the weak, protector of the forsaken, and savior of the hopeless.

The commentary distinguishes human capacity from the divine help asked for in a threatened task. Judas tells his outnumbered force that victory is not determined by army size because strength comes from heaven.
The commentary expands naʿbudu beyond timed ritual into obedient belonging. Samuel contrasts sacrifice with obeying YHWH's voice, so the text tests worship by submission in action.
The commentary reads the fronted iyyāka as an exclusion of every rival object of worship. Jesus answers the tempter with the same double claim: worship the Lord God and serve him alone.

row.basis: God to whom I belong and whom I serve
row.note: The commentary makes naʿbudu a declaration of both ownership and worship. In a crisis at sea, Paul describes God with the paired relation “whose I am” and “whom I serve.”

row.basis: freed from sin, enslaved to God
row.note: The commentary opposes belonging to God to service under other enslaving powers. Paul describes release from sin as becoming enslaved to God, with sanctification and life as the result.

row.basis: bought at a price; not human slaves
row.note: The commentary sets divine ownership against becoming another person's possessed servant. Paul tells the community that it was bought at a price and therefore must not become slaves of human beings.

row.basis: obey God rather than human beings
row.note: The commentary glosses worship as obedient submission and contrasts it with a human authority's demand. Peter and the apostles answer a governing prohibition by saying that obedience belongs to God rather than humans.

row.basis: turn from idols to serve the living God
row.note: The commentary makes exclusive worship both a turning from other objects and a turn toward God. Paul recounts the Thessalonians' conversion from idols to serve a living and true God.
The commentary treats worship wrongly directed to another as allegiance with real consequences. Paul warns that pagan sacrifice makes participants sharers with demons rather than with God.
The commentary rejects a reduction of worship to bounded ritual times. Paul calls for the presenting of whole bodies as a living sacrifice and names that all-of-life offering as worship.

row.basis: serve the Lord Christ in ordinary work
row.note: The commentary says one master changes the meaning of every act, not just formal devotion. In instructions to workers, Paul identifies the ultimate recipient of service as the Lord Christ rather than the human workplace.

The commentary holds worship and the help needed to carry it out together without confusing them. This verse directs the one who serves to do so from the strength that God supplies, so that God is glorified.

row.basis: God equips people to do his will
row.note: The commentary presents help-seeking as internal to sustained obedience. This benediction asks God to equip the hearers with every good thing for doing his will and to work in them what pleases him.
The commentary's nesteʿīnu names God as the one asked for help. The Christian speaker can therefore confess, in the words of the verse, that the Lord is “my helper” and need not fear people.

The commentary depicts direct address as a request made within worship. This verse invites believers to draw near confidently to God's throne in order to receive mercy and find grace for help at the needed time.

row.basis: one voice directly addresses the creator
row.note: The commentary gives theological weight to a plural community speaking directly to God. The gathered church raises one voice and addresses the Sovereign Lord as maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all within them.

row.basis: collective prayer for strength to speak
row.note: The commentary's “we ask you for help” joins a common task to a direct petition. Under threat, the church asks the Lord to notice the threats and grant his servants boldness for their speech.
The commentary emphasizes that even a lone reciter says “we” while addressing God as “you.” Jesus' model prayer begins with the communal direct address “Our Father,” before its petitions.
The commentary separates worship from help-seeking while binding each to the same addressee. This petition keeps the plural voice and directly asks God for the day's needed provision.

The commentary's angel scene rejects the transfer of worship from God to a creature. The angel in this scene refuses John’s prostration, calls himself a fellow servant, and directs him to worship God.

row.basis: submit to God; resist the devil
row.note: The commentary links exclusive divine allegiance with protection from Satan's authority. James places those acts together: submit to God, resist the devil, and the devil will flee.

row.basis: the evil one does not touch God's-born
row.note: The commentary says belonging to God limits Satan's power over the devoted. This verse states that the evil one does not touch the one born from God, grounding protection in divine keeping.

row.basis: the Lord strengthens and guards from evil
row.note: The commentary combines reliance on the Lord with freedom from the adversary's authority. Paul calls the Lord faithful and says he will strengthen the community and guard it from the evil one.

row.basis: God is not served as one needing help
row.note: The commentary sharply distinguishes the worshipper who needs aid from God, who needs no helper. Paul's Areopagus speech says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, because he gives life, breath, and all things.

row.basis: direct divine confession to the risen Jesus
row.note: The commentary reserves the first direct “you” and exclusive worship-address for God. In this Christian resurrection scene Thomas addresses Jesus himself as “my Lord and my God,” making the different object of direct confession a material comparison.

The commentary treats asking help as speech directed only to God. While dying, Stephen invokes the Lord Jesus and asks him to receive his spirit; the Christian scene therefore relocates a direct final petition to Jesus.

row.basis: angels called to worship the Son
row.note: The commentary's heavenly scene has angels refuse worship and turn it back to God. This verse, in its Christian enthronement argument, commands God's angels to worship the Son, so the angelic relation becomes a pointed contrary reading.

row.basis: highway where the traveler does not stray
row.note: The commentary treats the trodden-path image in naʿbudu as preparation for the surah's next request for a straight way. Isaiah's holy highway is a specific travel image in which even the wayfarer does not go astray.

row.basis: a journey too great for the exhausted traveler
row.note: The commentary develops the root's stranded traveler as one who needs support before the next request for guidance. An angel tells exhausted Elijah to rise and eat because the journey is too great for him, making provision the condition of continuing the way.

row.basis: walk without fainting through hope in YHWH
row.note: The commentary's image of help under a burden includes endurance rather than escape from every task. Isaiah says those who wait for YHWH receive renewed strength and can walk without fainting.

row.basis: Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' heavy hands
row.note: The commentary distinguishes human assistance from the divine source to whom help is asked. This battle scene gives the physical image of two companions supporting Moses' failing hands, a concrete human form of shared avn-like help.

row.basis: Jonathan strengthens David's hand in God
row.note: The commentary allows people to assist one another while locating ultimate reliance in God. Jonathan's help is specifically to strengthen David's hand “in God,” rather than to replace God as the ground of security.

row.basis: one lifts a companion who falls
row.note: The commentary explicitly says help can occur among people as well as being asked of God. Qoheleth gives the simple travel-like image of one companion raising the other when one falls.

row.basis: foreigners join themselves to serve YHWH
row.note: The commentary says the “we” of worship is not closed to those arriving from elsewhere. Isaiah names foreigners who join themselves to YHWH in order to serve him and love his name.

row.basis: house of prayer for all peoples
row.note: The commentary's plural worshipper belongs to a community whose address can gather others. This verse calls God's house a house of prayer for all peoples, extending communal direct prayer beyond one ethnic group.

row.basis: servants of YHWH protected from attack
row.note: The commentary says belonging to the sole master protects against a hostile power. Isaiah calls the defeat of weapons and accusations the heritage of YHWH's servants, a parallel protection image without making the adversary Satan in this verse.

The commentary says Satan has no unconstrained authority over God's servants. Job's trial gives a qualified analogue: God permits the adversary access to Job's goods but explicitly sets a limit, so it clarifies protection as bounded testing rather than effortless immunity.

row.basis: travelers' prayer for straight steps and deliverance
row.note: The commentary's support-seeking traveler makes the road a place of dependence. The Babylonian Talmud's travelers' prayer asks God to lead and direct one's steps in peace and to deliver the traveler from danger.

row.basis: God works willing and acting within believers
row.note: The commentary says the servant's ongoing acts need divine help without ceasing to be the servant's acts. Paul says God is at work in believers both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

The commentary separates the human help that can be offered from the God to whom aid is ultimately directed. Paul says the Corinthians help him through prayer, so their shared action participates in God's deliverance rather than displacing it.
The commentary calls avn support that stands behind another's burden and also permits mutual help. This instruction makes that image ethical: the community is to carry one another's burdens.

The commentary hears the imperfect verbs “we worship” and “we ask help” as ongoing rather than completed acts. Paul's compact command to pray without ceasing supplies a Christian formulation of that continuing posture.

row.basis: Lord's Prayer recited three times daily
row.note: The commentary reflects on a communal direct address repeated within regular worship without becoming merely a one-time formula. The Didache directs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, an early Christian practice that makes a plural address and petitions habitual.

row.basis: angels as ministering servants sent to aid heirs
row.note: The commentary distinguishes angels from the one to be worshipped and allows creaturely assistance under God. This verse defines angels as ministering spirits sent for the benefit of those inheriting salvation, supplying a Christian hierarchy of worship above angelic service.

row.basis: bowing to images and serving them
row.note: The commentary's object-first iyyāka excludes every alternate object of worship. This command joins the two forbidden acts in one verse: bowing to carved images and serving them.
The commentary treats exclusive worship as a decisive separation from competing masters. Elijah forces the same choice before Israel: if YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him.

row.basis: fearing YHWH while serving other gods
row.note: The commentary insists that a single confession cannot leave competing objects in place. This verse names the divided arrangement directly: the people fear YHWH while continuing to serve their own gods.

row.basis: God's glory given to no other
row.note: The commentary understands “you alone” as a refusal to transfer divine honor elsewhere. YHWH's self-declaration likewise withholds his glory from another and his praise from images.
The commentary says that help finally comes from the one addressed in worship. This verse makes the exclusion explicit in saving language: apart from YHWH there is no savior.

row.basis: turn to me and be saved; no other God
row.note: The commentary's direct address makes the worshipper turn to the sole source of aid. Isaiah summons the ends of the earth to turn to God and be saved because he is God and there is no other.

row.basis: created by God and called his
row.note: The commentary grounds belonging to God in creation before it becomes a spoken act of worship. This direct divine address joins creation, redemption, naming, and possession: “you are mine.”

row.basis: all gifts come from God first
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper seeks help from God while God needs no supporting power. David's corporate prayer admits that people can offer only what already comes from God: “from your own hand we have given you.”

row.basis: God does not need creatures' offerings
row.note: The commentary denies that God has the weakness or need for a helper. In a sacrifice-focused speech, God says that even if he were hungry he would not tell the worshipper, because the world and all within it are his.

The commentary distinguishes the worshipper who asks help from the God who does not require it. This verse says that when God found no helper, his own arm brought salvation and his own wrath sustained him.

row.basis: arm of flesh versus God who helps
row.note: The commentary allows human means but refuses to make them the final ground of aid. Hezekiah contrasts the enemy's “arm of flesh” with YHWH, who is with Judah to help it and fight its battles.

row.basis: God supports the hand of one who falls
row.note: The commentary's traveler image includes help that keeps a person from collapsing under the way's burden. This verse says that though the faithful person falls, YHWH upholds that person's hand.

row.basis: God's hand leads and holds the traveler
row.note: The commentary connects help with guidance on the way. The psalmist says that even at the farthest place God's hand will lead and his right hand will hold him fast.

row.basis: God guides the redeemed people to his dwelling
row.note: The commentary makes the plural worshipper a community whose help opens toward a journey and destination. The song after the sea says that God's steadfast love led the people he redeemed and guided them toward his holy habitation.

row.basis: teach your way; unite my heart to fear your name
row.note: The commentary joins a single object of worship to the road imagery and to a heart not divided among masters. This prayer asks God to teach his way and to make the speaker's heart one in fearing God's name.

row.basis: worship God in spirit and truth
row.note: The commentary extends worship beyond a narrow set of ritual acts into a whole posture of submission. Jesus' saying defines fitting worship by its relation to God's Spirit and truth rather than to an external location or rite.

row.basis: bowing before Jesus and saying “Lord, help me”
row.note: The commentary directs both worship and the explicit request for help to Allah alone. In this healing scene, the woman bows before Jesus and addresses to him the direct plea, “Lord, help me,” forming a particularly close Christian counter-narrative.

row.basis: one God, the Father; one Lord, Jesus Christ
row.note: The commentary's exclusive divine address has one undivided addressee. Paul preserves “one God, the Father” while placing “one Lord, Jesus Christ” within the same creational confession, a distinctively Christian reconfiguration of exclusive devotion.

row.basis: every knee bends at Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary treats bodily submission in worship as due only to God. This eschatological Christian scene says that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bend at Jesus' name.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord
row.note: The commentary's direct confession separates the one worshipped from all rivals. This verse gives universal confession of Jesus Christ as Lord while directing the resulting glory to God the Father, a two-term Christian formulation absent from the commentary's formula.

row.basis: shared heavenly praise of God and the Lamb
row.note: The commentary's heavenly worship returns praise away from creatures to God alone. Revelation's universal hymn offers blessing, honor, glory, and might together to the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb, an explicit alternative heavenly distribution of praise.

row.basis: asking the Father in Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary makes direct petition itself part of exclusive worship. Jesus instructs disciples to ask the Father in his name, providing a Christian pattern of petition mediated through Jesus.

row.basis: one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus
row.note: The commentary's worshipper addresses God without a named mediating figure. This confession likewise says “one God” but adds one mediator between God and humanity, the human Christ Jesus.

row.basis: the Spirit helps weakness in prayer
row.note: The commentary makes asking for help an act inside worship and acknowledges that the burden exceeds the worshipper's strength. Paul says the Spirit helps human weakness precisely where people do not know how to pray as they ought.

row.basis: Jesus asks the Father to keep disciples from the evil one
row.note: The commentary links belonging and reliance on God to protection from Satan's authority. Jesus' prayer asks the Father not to remove the disciples from the world but to keep them from the evil one.
The commentary presents help as what enables a servant to stand under a task rather than as an escape from all burden. The divine reply to Paul calls grace sufficient and power perfected in weakness.

row.basis: make every request known to God
row.note: The commentary leaves the object of aid in 1:5 deliberately open to every need while fixing its addressee. Paul likewise tells believers to bring requests about everything to God by prayer, petition, and thanksgiving.

The commentary's help supports endurance beneath worship's weight and protects the devoted. This promise says that after suffering, the God of all grace will restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish the believers.

row.basis: in life and death, we belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary stretches worship beyond a momentary rite into a declaration of who owns one's whole life. Paul says that whether believers live or die, they are the Lord's.

row.basis: bought at a price; glorify God in the body
row.note: The commentary makes belonging to God encompass more than a discrete ritual act. This verse joins being bought at a price to the command to glorify God in the body.

row.basis: offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe
row.note: The commentary glosses worship as humility carried to its limit. Hebrews calls the community to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe in response to the kingdom it receives.

row.basis: servants worship day and night and are sheltered
row.note: The commentary's “we” is a protected community whose worship is ongoing. Revelation pictures the multitude before God's throne serving him day and night, while the enthroned one shelters them.

row.basis: the church prays earnestly to God for Peter
row.note: The commentary uses a plural voice for direct aid-seeking within a community. During Peter's imprisonment, the church's response is persistent prayer to God on his behalf.

row.basis: the Lord stands by and strengthens the servant
row.note: The commentary's avn is support that stands behind a burdened person. Paul reports that the Lord stood by him and strengthened him for the proclamation entrusted to him.

row.basis: acknowledge God in all ways; paths made straight
row.note: The commentary lets 1:5's help-seeking reach forward to the straight path while keeping God before the worshipper's own action. Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one's ways results in God making one's paths straight.

row.basis: send wisdom to labor alongside the petitioner
row.note: The commentary says aid can be an enabling companion while its ultimate source remains God. Solomon's prayer asks God to send Wisdom from the holy heavens so that she may be with him and labor with him.

row.basis: make God's will one's own will
row.note: The commentary explains worship as obedient belonging, not a merely timed ceremony. This rabbinic maxim tells the disciple to make God's will like one's own will and to set aside one's own will before God's.
The commentary treats guidance as both knowing a route and being led along it; the psalm asks God to make his ways known and teach his paths.
The commentary's “lead us on the straight path” is a prayer for continuing direction; this verse asks God to lead the speaker in truth and teach him.

row.basis: teach me your way; unite my heart
row.note: The commentary links walking God's way with exclusive worship; this prayer asks to be taught God's way in order to walk in truth with an undivided heart.
The commentary asks God to guide a dependent traveler and stresses a level, sustained walk; the psalm asks God to teach his will and have his good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground.
The commentary hears the straight path as a route that must be followed and protected; the psalm asks God to teach his way and lead the speaker on a level path despite hostile witnesses.
The commentary asks for guidance along a lived route; the psalm's shepherd leads the speaker on tracks of righteousness, joining direction with sustained care.

The commentary's collective petition asks God to keep worshipers on the way; Jeremiah pictures a weeping returning people led by God, with supplication, along a straight path to water where they will not stumble.

row.basis: blind led on an unknown way
row.note: The commentary describes people who cannot find the route without a guide; God promises here to lead the blind by a way they do not know, turning darkness to light and rough ground level.

row.basis: the voice says, “this is the way”
row.note: The commentary presents guidance as an ongoing walk rather than a one-time conversion; this verse gives travelers a voice directing them to keep walking the way when they veer right or left.
The commentary asks God to lead a community already devoted to him; Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one's ways brings his making the paths straight.
The commentary makes God the source of guidance and its ongoing teacher; here God says he teaches what is beneficial and leads Israel in the way it should go.

row.basis: the path of the righteous made level
row.note: The commentary connects the straight path with an even, unbent course; Isaiah says the path of the righteous is level because God makes it smooth.
The commentary identifies the requested route with the company of those favored by God; Isaiah's highway is called the holy way and is reserved for the redeemed returning to Zion.

row.basis: straight road to an inhabited city
row.note: The commentary says the road ends in a home that receives the traveler; after the lost and hungry wanderers cry for help, God leads them by a straight way to a city where they can dwell.

row.basis: travelers cry to God for help
row.note: The commentary connects the request to be guided with the preceding plea for help; this verse depicts travelers crying to God in distress and being delivered before the straight road and city of the next verse.

row.basis: God leads the redeemed to his holy abode
row.note: The commentary's journey ends in a place of welcome; the Song of the Sea says God leads the people he redeemed toward his holy dwelling by steadfast love.

row.basis: bring and plant at the sanctuary
row.note: The commentary hears guidance as arrival at a home or refuge; Moses' song asks God to bring the people to his mountain and plant them at the sanctuary he established.
The commentary names Moses and Aaron as people led on the straight way; in the Exodus narrative God goes before Israel as cloud and fire to guide their day-and-night wilderness journey.

row.basis: God goes ahead to find a camp
row.note: The commentary's guide goes in front and shows where to walk; Moses recalls God going ahead of Israel to find camping places and show the route.
The commentary says the request is directed only to the one who can truly guide; Moses' song says the Lord alone led Jacob, with no foreign god beside him.

row.basis: the ark goes before, seeking a resting place
row.note: The commentary's guide goes ahead of the travelers and leads toward a place of rest; the ark precedes Israel in the wilderness to seek a resting place for them.
The commentary connects guidance with reaching a place of shelter and sustaining water; Isaiah says the compassionate guide leads the returning people to springs of water.

row.basis: continual guidance like a watered garden
row.note: The commentary insists that guidance continues along the road and mentions water that sustains life; Isaiah promises that God will guide continually and make the people like a watered garden.

row.basis: the highways to Zion in the heart
row.note: The commentary's path is walked toward a welcomed destination; the pilgrim psalm blesses those whose hearts are set on the highways to God's house.
The commentary associates the road with sustaining water and support for the traveler; this pilgrimage verse describes a dry valley becoming a place of springs on the way to Zion.

row.basis: from strength to strength, appearing before God
row.note: The commentary says the route is a walk that continues until arrival; the pilgrim psalm describes travelers gaining strength as they go until each appears before God in Zion.

row.basis: make a level path for your feet
row.note: The commentary develops uprightness as a bodily walk that must remain straight; Proverbs tells the hearer to make a level path for the feet and have all ways be firm.

row.basis: do not swerve right or left
row.note: The commentary places the straight path between deviations and asks for help to stay on it; Proverbs commands the traveler not to turn right or left but to keep the foot from evil.

row.basis: ask for the good ancient way and walk in it
row.note: The commentary treats guidance as something to be requested repeatedly and then walked; Jeremiah tells the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, though they refuse.

row.basis: the Lord knows the righteous way; the wicked way perishes
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the favored people's path from ways that end in loss; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous, known by the Lord, with the way of the wicked, which perishes.
The commentary names a straight path between opposed outcomes; Moses sets life and death before Israel and calls them to choose life by loving and obeying God.

row.basis: the Lord's way is justice and righteousness
row.note: The commentary says the path is a lived course shaped by worship; God says Abraham's household is to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice.
The commentary depicts the traveler as wavering and asks for an unwavering path; Elijah challenges Israel for limping between the Lord and Baal and demands a clear choice of whom to serve.

row.basis: the right way leads to a bride's home
row.note: The commentary develops guidance as escorting a bride to the home where she will be received; Abraham's servant says the Lord led him on the right way to find Rebekah as a wife for Isaac.

row.basis: offerings brought to the chosen place
row.note: The commentary's h-d-y word family includes an offering animal brought to its appointed sanctuary; Deuteronomy directs Israel to bring sacrifices and firstborn offerings to the place God chooses.

row.basis: trust; help; make your ways straight
row.note: The commentary presents the request for guidance as trustful dependence on God, not self-direction; Sirach tells the faithful to trust God for help, make their ways straight, and hope in him.

row.basis: ask God to make your ways straight
row.note: The commentary frames guidance as a direct request to God along life's journey; Tobit advises blessing God and asking him to make one's ways and plans straight.

row.basis: paths set right by divine wisdom
row.note: The commentary asks God to lead a community into the right way; Wisdom says that by divine wisdom the paths of people on earth were set right and they learned what pleases God.
The commentary's petition asks God to lead the worshipers along the way; the travelers' prayer asks God to lead and direct the traveler safely on the road.

row.basis: prayers on entering and leaving a city
row.note: The commentary hears guidance as a journey toward a place that will receive the traveler; this passage gives prayers asking God to lead a traveler into and out of a city in peace.

row.basis: the two spirits and their ways
row.note: The commentary places the straight way between the ways of those favored and those who go astray; the Community Rule develops a moral choice between the paths of truth and perversity, light and darkness.

row.basis: the straight path a person should choose
row.note: The commentary asks God to lead a worshiping community on the straight way; this rabbinic teaching asks which straight path a person should choose and defines it by ethical conduct and its effects on others.

row.basis: the perilous afterlife path between fire and water
row.note: The commentary explicitly corrects the popular image of ṣirāṭ as an afterlife bridge, saying the Qur'anic word is a road walked in this life; 4 Ezra pictures the narrow, dangerous path to the future city between fire and deep water.
The commentary names the straight way against the ways of anger and straying; the Didache opens its moral instruction by setting the way of life against the way of death.
The commentary hears mustaqīm's straightness as a scale that does not tip to either side; Leviticus commands honest weights and measures, making uprightness a practice of fair judgment.
The commentary links straightness with keeping the balance from leaning; Proverbs says dishonest scales are an abomination to the Lord, while a just weight pleases him.

row.basis: the scales belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary treats balance as part of the requested upright path; Proverbs says accurate scales and weights belong to the Lord, grounding fair measure in divine order.

row.basis: Arabic q-w-m; Hebrew q-w-m in “walk upright”
row.note: The commentary labels al-mustaqīm with Arabic root q-w-m and develops upright bodily walking; Leviticus uses the cognate Hebrew root in saying God made Israel walk erect after breaking the yoke.

row.basis: Arabic q-w-m; Hebrew q-w-m, rise and stand
row.note: The commentary labels al-mustaqīm with Arabic q-w-m and associates it with an upright walk; this verse uses the cognate Hebrew root for rising and standing upright, in contrast to enemies who fall.

row.basis: God upholds the falling and raises the bowed
row.note: The commentary describes a traveler who sways and needs support before walking steadily; the psalm says God supports those who are falling and raises those bowed down.

row.basis: the Lord holds the hand of one who falls
row.note: The commentary's route includes a dependent walker who needs support to continue; the psalm says even if the righteous person falls, the Lord holds his hand.

row.basis: humans cannot direct their own steps
row.note: The commentary asks God to guide the collective because the traveler needs an outside guide; Jeremiah says a person's way is not in his own control and he cannot direct his steps.

row.basis: a way that seems right ends in death
row.note: The commentary warns that a path's goodness depends on where it leads and who walks it; Proverbs warns that a way may seem right yet end in death.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary asks for guidance on a path that leads to a welcomed end; Zechariah's hymn says God's mercy will guide “our feet” into the way of peace, from darkness toward light.

The commentary notes a communal “us” speaking directly to God in a pleading imperative; the Lord's Prayer likewise addresses God as “you” and asks collectively not to be led into trial but to be delivered from evil.

row.basis: belief that still asks for help
row.note: The commentary says people already on the way still ask to be guided at every step; the father who says “I believe” immediately asks Jesus to help his unbelief.

row.basis: the shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow
row.note: The commentary hears the guide as a leader who walks in front so others can follow; Jesus' shepherd calls his own sheep and goes ahead of them, and they follow.
The commentary reserves guidance to God and connects the path with truth; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth.
The commentary describes a traveler unable to find the route alone; the Ethiopian reader asks how he can understand Isaiah unless someone guides him, and Philip joins him as an interpreter.
The commentary stresses a path that is walked and followed, not a one-time threshold; Acts calls the community Saul seeks to arrest “the Way,” naming the movement as a lived route.

row.basis: the way that leads to life
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the straight way from roads ending in loss; Jesus describes a narrow way leading to life, found by few, against the broad way leading to destruction.
The commentary hears the road as leading to a home where the traveler is received; Jesus speaks of many dwelling places in his Father's house and going to prepare a place for his followers.

row.basis: Jesus as the way to the Father
row.note: The commentary asks God to guide the collective on God's straight path; John identifies Jesus himself as the way through whom people come to the Father, giving the shared journey-to-God image a distinct Christian mediation.

row.basis: a new and living way into the sanctuary
row.note: The commentary's path leads to a place of divine welcome; Hebrews describes access to the holy place through a new and living way opened through the veil, identified with Jesus' flesh.

row.basis: straight paths for the feet; healing the lame
row.note: The commentary develops upright walking and the support needed by a wavering traveler; Hebrews applies the “straight paths” image to a community so the lame may be healed rather than disabled.
The commentary says guidance must be sought again because a person can leave the path after finding it; Peter describes false teachers who have left the straight way and gone astray.

row.basis: grace as a gift, not earned payment
row.note: The commentary says the requested guidance is a loving gift rather than a wage; Ephesians says salvation is by grace as God's gift, not the result of works.
The commentary joins the gift of guidance to a path that must actually be walked; Ephesians says God prepared good works beforehand for people to walk in.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds to springs of water
row.note: The commentary combines a leading guide with the road's life-giving destination; Revelation says the Lamb will shepherd the multitude and guide them to springs of living water.
The commentary pictures guidance as following an advance leader; Peter says Christ left an example so believers may follow in his steps.

row.basis: John applies Isaiah's straight-way prophecy to his own mission
row.note: The commentary hears a requested path as the route along which a community must walk; John the Baptist identifies himself as the wilderness voice of Isaiah 40:3, interpreting preparation of the Lord's way as his prophetic task.

row.basis: lead and guide for your name's sake
row.note: The commentary asks God to guide the worshipers along the way; this psalm asks God, as refuge, to lead and guide the speaker for his name's sake.

row.basis: instruction and counsel on the way
row.note: The commentary presents guidance as ongoing accompaniment; God promises here to instruct and teach the way, keeping watch and giving counsel.

row.basis: light and truth lead to the holy hill
row.note: The commentary's route ends in God's welcoming presence; the psalm asks God to send light and truth to lead the speaker to the holy mountain and dwelling.
The commentary's “us” asks God for guidance as a community; this psalm says of God, “this is our God,” who guides us forever.

row.basis: make me walk the path of your commands
row.note: The commentary asks for a route that is actually walked; this prayer asks God to make the speaker walk the path of the commandments and says that he delights in it.

row.basis: a lamp to the feet and light to the path
row.note: The commentary develops guidance through signs and landmarks; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and a light on the path.

row.basis: make my steps firm; do not let sin rule
row.note: The commentary asks for continuing guidance and protection from leaving the way; this prayer asks God to make the speaker's steps firm and keep wrongdoing from ruling him.

row.basis: feet set on rock; steps made firm
row.note: The commentary's traveler needs support to move steadily after losing the way; the psalm describes being lifted from a pit, set on rock, and given firm steps.

row.basis: God led Israel like a flock
row.note: The commentary develops the guide who goes ahead of dependent travelers; this poetic retelling says God led Israel safely like a flock through the wilderness.

row.basis: God guards the paths of justice
row.note: The commentary joins the straight path to just balance and right conduct; Proverbs says God guards the paths of justice and preserves the way of his faithful ones.

row.basis: the righteous path brightens as daybreak
row.note: The commentary stresses that guidance is a continuing walk, not a single arrival; Proverbs pictures the righteous path growing brighter until full day.
The commentary says even worshipers already on the way need God to lead them at each step; Proverbs distinguishes a person's plans from the Lord's direction of the steps.

row.basis: road markers for the returning traveler
row.note: The commentary develops signs and landmarks that help a traveler find the route; Jeremiah tells the returning people to set up road markers and guideposts and remember the highway they traveled.

The commentary's “straight path” is a divinely chosen route, not merely the shortest line; God deliberately does not lead Israel by the Philistine road because seeing war might make them return to Egypt.

row.basis: the detour protects Israel from turning back
row.note: The commentary treats guidance as God's care for travelers; the Mekhilta reads the longer Exodus route as protective pedagogy, since the newly freed people might turn back when faced with war.

row.basis: a messenger goes ahead and brings Israel to the prepared place
row.note: The commentary's guide leads from the front and brings travelers to their destination; God promises to send a messenger ahead of Israel to guard them and bring them to the prepared place.

row.basis: prepare a straight highway for God
row.note: The commentary hears a path that must be made straight and walked; Isaiah calls for a straight highway in the wilderness as the Lord comes to his people.

row.basis: the shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads
row.note: The commentary describes both a guide who goes ahead and a dependent traveler who needs support; Isaiah pictures God carrying lambs close and gently leading the nursing sheep.

row.basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and takes him by the arms
row.note: The commentary portrays a traveler who sways and needs support; God recalls teaching Ephraim to walk and taking him by the arms, though Ephraim did not recognize the healing.
The commentary connects guidance with gentle, loving care rather than payment; Hosea describes God leading Israel with human kindness and cords of love.

row.basis: God shepherds and gives the flock rest
row.note: The commentary asks for a guide who leads dependent travelers to a place of welcome; God promises to shepherd his own flock and make them lie down in safety.

row.basis: wilderness turned into pools and dry ground into springs
row.note: The commentary connects the route with sustaining water and the land's life-giving support; this verse pictures God transforming the wilderness into pools and dry ground into springs.

row.basis: a blind guide and a blind follower both fall
row.note: The commentary says a guide who cannot see the route cannot lead others; Jesus asks whether a blind person can guide another blind person without both falling into a pit.

row.basis: the Father draws people to the Son
row.note: The commentary insists that ultimate guidance belongs to God; Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws that person.

row.basis: walk in the light before darkness overtakes you
row.note: The commentary warns that the traveler can lose the way after having found it; Jesus tells his hearers to walk while they have the light, lest darkness overtake them and leave them unable to know where they are going.

row.basis: God makes a way out of temptation
row.note: The commentary pictures an ambush on the straight path and asks for continued guidance; Paul says God will not let testing exceed what can be borne and will provide a way of escape.

row.basis: a generation that strays in heart and does not know God's ways
row.note: The commentary says guidance must be renewed because people can turn aside after being led; Hebrews recalls the wilderness generation as continually straying in heart and not knowing God's ways.

row.basis: those led by God's Spirit are God's children
row.note: The commentary makes divine guidance the continuing mark of those who worship God; Paul identifies those led by God's Spirit as children of God.

row.basis: two ways, light and darkness, under opposed powers
row.note: The commentary sets the straight path against straying and describes an adversary lying in wait on it; Barnabas develops two moral ways, light and darkness, under God's angels and Satan's angels.

consolidation_error: invalid TSV: ['line 11: unknown verse in specified edition: WLC:Ps.139.25']

row.note: The commentary says the requested road is recognized by its travelers; Psalm 1:6 says YHWH knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes, making the walkers and their endpoint distinguish the two paths.

The commentary reads the straight road as a lived route shaped by its company; Psalm 23:3 has the shepherd restore the speaker and lead him on paths of righteousness, so guidance is personal and ongoing.

The commentary says the blessed path is practiced, not inherited automatically; Genesis 18:19 says Abraham is chosen so his household and descendants keep YHWH's way by doing righteousness and justice.

row.basis: choose life or death, blessing or curse
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the blessed from wrath-struck and straying groups without making status hereditary; Deuteronomy sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and urges a choice, tying destination to response.

The commentary says the road belongs to those who walk it, not to a blessed person's descendants by birth; Ezekiel says neither son nor father bears the other's guilt, locating judgment in each person's own conduct.

row.basis: the wicked can turn and live
row.note: The commentary treats straying as a state from which a person may return; Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns from sin and keeps justice will live, making the path recoverable.

The commentary refuses to make the blessed road an inherited, permanent label; Ezekiel also says a formerly righteous person who turns to wrongdoing will die, so past standing does not replace present walking.

row.basis: God leads Israel through the wilderness
row.note: The commentary calls the requested road an everyday route with a guide and fellow travelers; Exodus depicts YHWH going before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on their journey, grounding the image in a people led together.

The commentary treats guidance as a path actually walked and tested; Deuteronomy asks Israel to remember the whole way YHWH led them for forty years, adding that the road forms the travelers as it brings them onward.

row.basis: nations learn and walk God's paths
row.note: The commentary says the path is identified by the people who walk it; Isaiah has many peoples invite one another to learn God's ways and walk in his paths, turning guidance into a shared, imitable course.

row.basis: voice says which way to walk
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a guided route from wandering; Isaiah 30:21 pictures a voice behind the hearer directing, “This is the way; walk in it,” when the hearer turns right or left.

row.basis: wanderers led on a straight way
row.note: The commentary contrasts lost wandering with a road that reaches its destination; Psalm 107:7 says God led the wanderers on a straight way to an inhabited city, joining guidance to arrival and shelter.

The commentary distinguishes the straight path from straying by how its travelers proceed; Proverbs 4:18 compares the righteous path to dawn light growing brighter, giving the good road a visible direction.
The commentary says straying is a journey without a clear way; Proverbs 4:19 says the wicked way is darkness and its travelers do not know what makes them stumble.

The commentary insists that a road is defined by its destination and travelers; Isaiah describes a highway called holy on which the redeemed walk, with the unclean excluded, making holiness a quality of the company and course.

row.basis: God leads the blind on an unknown road
row.note: The commentary's straying image includes not knowing where one goes; Isaiah promises to lead the blind by an unfamiliar way, turn darkness to light, and not forsake them, so lostness can be met by divine guidance.

row.basis: each sheep turns to its own way
row.note: The commentary contrasts a shared road with paths lost by following the wrong company; Isaiah says all have gone astray like sheep, each turning to his own way, giving the collective image of dispersed travelers a moral edge.

The commentary describes a route inherited through the footprints of earlier walkers; Jeremiah calls the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, while the verse records their refusal.

row.basis: prayer to be led on level ground
row.note: The commentary reads the ayah as a direct request for guidance into the path of God's favored people; the psalmist asks God to teach his will and have the good spirit lead him on level ground, making the route itself a prayer.

row.basis: lost sheep asks to be sought
row.note: The commentary keeps the lost traveler distinct from the guide and the destination; Psalm 119:176 calls the speaker a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, adding that straying need not be the final identity.

row.basis: Ruth chooses Naomi's people and God
row.note: The commentary says the road's companions are joined by faithful walking rather than automatic descent; Ruth, a foreign widow, binds herself to Naomi's people and God, showing chosen belonging through shared life.

row.basis: choice between following YHWH and Baal
row.note: The commentary separates two opposed paths with a renewed negation; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and tells them to follow whichever god is truly God, making divided allegiance a concrete fork in the road.

row.basis: confession of having left truth's way
row.note: The commentary contrasts a road that reaches its goal with straying into loss; the condemned in Wisdom 5 confess that they left the way of truth, missed righteousness's light, and traveled trackless paths, turning the image into a retrospective confession.

row.basis: narrow route between fire and deep water
row.note: The commentary explicitly treats the straight path as lived conduct rather than a hair-thin bridge; 4 Ezra pictures the desired city as an inheritance reached by one path between fire and deep water, a distinct Jewish afterlife image that contrasts with the daily road described here.

The commentary says descendants do not inherit the blessed path without walking it; Avot tells the learner to prepare for Torah because it is not an inheritance, making study and practice rather than ancestry the condition of belonging.

row.basis: Noah walks with God, Abraham before God
row.note: The commentary makes following earlier walkers the way into the path; Genesis Rabbah interprets “walked with God” of Noah as needing support, but “walk before me” of Abraham as strength, changing the parallel into two forms of guided walking.

row.basis: feet guided into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary asks for guidance into a road walked by people; Luke's song says the dawn from on high will guide our feet into the way of peace and shine on those in darkness, joining guided steps to rescue from lostness.

row.basis: followers walk in light, not darkness
row.note: The commentary contrasts the guided road with wandering; Jesus says the one who follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life, explicitly tying a person's path to whom they follow.

The commentary says the path is known by its walkers and their guide; John depicts the shepherd going ahead and the sheep following because they know his voice, making guidance a relationship shared by a flock.

The commentary says the Qur'anic road is ordinary lived conduct, not a trial bridge; Matthew's narrow road leads to life and is found by few, a close two-path comparison that also preserves a different emphasis on entry and destination.

row.basis: blessed inherit the kingdom at judgment
row.note: The commentary names those receiving God's favor and sets them apart from the wrath-struck and straying; at judgment the Son of Man calls the sheep blessed by his Father and invites them to inherit the kingdom, linking blessing to an eschatological company.
The commentary distinguishes the blessed from those under wrath; Matthew has the King send the goats away as cursed, supplying a judgment scene with a sharply separated opposite company.

The commentary says the path does not pass automatically from blessed ancestors to descendants; John warns his hearers not to rely on “We have Abraham as father,” since God can raise Abraham's children from stones, shifting status to repentance and fruit.

The commentary says the blessed road belongs to those who walk as earlier figures walked; Jesus says Abraham's true children would do Abraham's works, making kinship a matter of imitation rather than ancestry alone.

row.basis: Abraham's children walk in his faith's footsteps
row.note: The commentary describes a road as the trace left by its earlier travelers; Paul identifies Abraham's family with those who walk in the footsteps of the faith Abraham had, an unusually close formulation of the path's companions.

The commentary's last group can be anyone who loses the way, and its camel image is a separated animal; Jesus' shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek one lost sheep, showing that the straying traveler remains sought and valued.

row.basis: straying sheep return to their shepherd
row.note: The commentary holds straying and return together rather than treating the lost as a fixed people; Peter says his hearers were like sheep going astray but have returned to the shepherd and guardian of their souls.

The commentary separates the guided road from straying and asks the reader to recognize their travelers; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, then distinguishes them by concrete conduct.

row.basis: two ways of light and darkness
row.note: The commentary sets the blessed path against distinct forms of ruin; Barnabas introduces two ways, light and darkness, and says their governing powers and travelers differ, offering an early Christian ethical map alongside the Qur'anic prayer.

row.basis: God finds and guards Israel in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary's image of lostness includes a traveler without a known route; Deuteronomy says God found Israel in a desert waste, guarded him, and cared for him, supplying a scriptural scene of the lost being gathered into God's care.

The commentary labels anʿamta with Arabic root n-ʿ-m and develops softness, ease, and favor as nearby resonances; Hebrew no'am in Psalm 90:17 asks that the Lord's pleasant favor rest on his servants and establish their work, a cognate echo without equating the senses.

The commentary identifies the road by the character of its travelers; Avot distinguishes Abraham's disciples from Balaam's by their eye, spirit, and soul, so following a patriarch is ethical imitation rather than mere descent.

row.basis: repentant can rise beyond the righteous
row.note: The commentary says a straying person may return to the guided path; Berakhot teaches that penitents stand where the completely righteous cannot, giving rabbinic weight to movement between the categories.

The commentary says the path's company is not inherited by blood; Jesus says people will come from east and west, north and south to dine in God's kingdom, while others claiming place are excluded, unsettling inherited privilege.

row.basis: people of faith are Abraham's children
row.note: The commentary makes the way of the blessed a path that can be joined by walking it; Paul calls those of faith Abraham's children, extending kinship by allegiance rather than genealogy.
The commentary says the road is recognized by the people who walk it; Acts describes the Damascus believers as belonging to “the Way,” showing a Christian community named by its shared route.

The commentary says a road is recognized by its travelers; Hosea closes by saying YHWH's ways are right, the righteous walk in them, and rebels stumble, a particularly compact formulation of the ayah's contrast.

The commentary frames the ayah as a plea for guidance to the road of God's favored people; Psalm 25:8 says the good and upright Lord therefore teaches sinners his way, pairing divine character with instruction for the errant.

row.basis: God's paths are covenant love and faithfulness
row.note: The commentary identifies the good road by its walkers and destination; Psalm 25:10 says all the Lord's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant, specifying what the path offers its companions.
The commentary places the bestowed favor beside those under wrath; Habakkuk asks God to revive his work and, in wrath, remember mercy, a prayer that holds judgment and favor together.

The commentary notes that the same people may move from received favor to feared wrath; after the calf, Moses asks God to turn from fierce anger against Israel, making intercession a response to that transition.
The commentary leaves return open after wrath; following Moses' plea in the calf episode, this verse says the Lord relented from the threatened disaster, showing the people's condition can change.

row.basis: anger is brief, favor lasts a lifetime
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes those who receive favor and those under wrath; the psalm says God's anger lasts a moment while his favor lasts a lifetime, giving the contrast a temporal shape.

row.basis: Abraham blessed to become a blessing
row.note: The commentary names a people by God's act of favor; God tells Abraham he will bless him and make him a blessing, so bestowed favor turns its recipient into a source of good for others.

row.basis: a new generation does not know YHWH
row.note: The commentary says the favored generations do not pass the path automatically to their heirs; Judges says the generation after Joshua arose without knowing YHWH or his deeds, explaining how descendants can lose the inherited way.

row.basis: descendants warned against their fathers' path
row.note: The commentary says descendants must walk as the favored did rather than inherit their standing; Psalm 78:8 urges the next generation not to be like their stubborn, faithless fathers, making faithful transmission a learned response.

row.basis: forgetting the giver leads to ruin
row.note: The commentary says favor can be lost when its recipients change their conduct; Deuteronomy warns that forgetting YHWH and following other gods will lead to destruction, a concrete reversal from gift to judgment.

The commentary allows people who have strayed to return to the guided path; Deuteronomy pictures exiles returning to YHWH and obeying him with heart and soul, after the preceding blessings and curses have come upon them.

row.basis: repentance can turn sins into merits
row.note: The commentary treats guidance and straying as states that can change; Yoma interprets repentance from love as making prior deliberate sins count as merits, extending the possibility of reversal beyond simple pardon.

row.basis: mercy shown on the road defines the neighbor
row.note: The commentary says the way is known by the people who walk it; after the wounded traveler is passed by a priest and Levite, Jesus identifies the neighbor as the one who showed mercy and commands the hearer to do likewise.

row.basis: the foreigner returns to give God glory
row.note: The commentary links favor received from God with joining the company of the righteous; after ten are healed, Jesus asks why only the foreigner returned to give glory to God, distinguishing gratitude and return from merely receiving a gift.

The commentary describes the requested path as the trace left by earlier walkers; Peter says Christ suffered leaving an example so others might follow in his steps, making the guide's life a traversable pattern.

The commentary distinguishes the straight route from being led astray; Paul rebukes Elymas for trying to make the Lord's straight paths crooked, a concrete image of a person redirecting others from the way.

row.basis: leaving the straight way to follow Balaam
row.note: The commentary says the path can be lost by following earlier strayers; Peter says false teachers abandoned the straight way and went astray, following Balaam's path, linking a changed route to the company one imitates.

row.basis: make straight paths for the feet
row.note: The commentary emphasizes a road walked by actual feet and the form of walking; Hebrews commands readers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame limb may be healed rather than put out of joint.

row.basis: walk in good works prepared by God
row.note: The commentary holds divine favor and human walking together; Ephesians says people are God's workmanship, created for good works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in, joining gift to practiced conduct.

row.basis: darkness leaves a traveler unsure where he goes
row.note: The commentary describes straying as a journey whose direction and destination disappear; Jesus warns that one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, giving that lostness a precise image.

The commentary says the path is not guaranteed by descent from blessed ancestors; Jesus pictures some seeing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in God's kingdom while they themselves are thrown out, reversing inherited confidence.

row.basis: Jesus joins disciples on the road
row.note: The commentary describes the path as a shared walk whose travelers can guide one another; on the Emmaus road Jesus draws near and walks with two disciples, then interprets the scriptures to them, making companionship part of how the route is understood.

row.basis: wrath falls on those obeying unrighteousness
row.note: The commentary distinguishes wrath-struck people from active wanderers while allowing their conditions to meet; Paul says those who disobey truth and obey unrighteousness receive wrath, explicitly connecting a chosen course with judgment.

row.basis: walking, standing, sitting as a progression
row.note: The commentary identifies a person's path by the company and actions along it; Augustine reads Psalm 1's movement from walking in wicked counsel to standing in sin's way and sitting among scoffers as increasing entrenchment, sharpening the way's moral development.

The commentary contrasts aimless disappearance with a road that reaches a known end; Ps 107 first portrays desert wanderers unable to find a road to an inhabited city, a concrete scene of the former condition.
After the city-less wandering of Ps 107, God leads the travelers by a straight way to a settled city; this gives the commentary's purposeful, destination-bearing sirat a close journey scene.
The commentary's road is recognized through a guide and a flock rather than as a bare line; Ps 23 has the divine shepherd restore the traveler and lead him in right paths.

row.basis: lost sheep sought by its master
row.note: The final word dalin is heard beside an animal separated from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, joining straying to a continuing master-servant relation.

Jeremiah calls Israel lost sheep whose shepherds made them wander from mountain to hill and forget their resting place; it directly joins the commentary's bad leader, lost flock, and missed destination.

The ownerless camel image is answered by Ezekiel's sheep scattered over mountains and hills while no one searches for them; the verse makes abandonment by responsible guides part of the straying scene.
Where the commentary leaves open that the stray can cease being lost, God promises to seek the lost sheep and bring back the one driven away; the owner actively reverses dispersion.

Moses asks for a leader who goes out before and comes in before the community so that Israel will not be sheep without a shepherd; this closely matches the commentary's forward guide and people identified by the road they follow.
The commentary treats sirat as an ordinary journey with signs rather than a postmortem bridge; the pillar of cloud and fire goes before Israel to lead its actual day-and-night route.

row.basis: guardian on the road to a prepared place
row.note: God's messenger guards Israel on the way and brings it to a prepared destination, furnishing a precise counterpart to the commentary's guided road whose goodness comes from where it leads.
The commentary resists treating favor as an inherited status; Deuteronomy recalls that God led Israel through the wilderness in order to humble and test what was in its heart.

The text's provision of manna is said to humble, test, and finally do Israel good; it supplies a close scriptural instance of a bestowed benefit that neither ends moral testing nor guarantees a fixed condition.

row.basis: walking as the condition of blessing
row.note: The commentary makes the way belong to those who actually walk it; Deuteronomy couples loving God, walking in his ways, and keeping commands with life, increase, and divine blessing.

row.basis: Abraham's household keeps the Lord's way
row.note: The commentary distinguishes descent from walking as earlier recipients walked; Abraham's descendants receive the promised outcome through being instructed to keep the Lord's way by righteousness and justice.

row.basis: a later generation does not know the deeds
row.note: The commentary's procession of guided prophets is followed by descendants who can abandon their way; Judges explicitly introduces a subsequent generation that did not know the Lord or the work done for Israel.
The commentary says the road is not inherited merely through descent. Ezekiel states that child and parent do not bear one another's guilt, making moral standing personal rather than genealogical.
Jeremiah tells the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, but records their refusal; it closely matches the commentary's prior walkers as a real but uncoercive guide.
The commentary makes good and bad fellow-travelers decisive. Proverbs says one who walks with the wise becomes wise, while a companion of fools suffers harm.

row.basis: lamp for feet and light for a path
row.note: The commentary develops road signs and walking feet; the psalm gives God's word the specific job of a lamp for the foot and a light for the path.

row.basis: a voice identifies the road at each turn
row.note: The commentary's straight road is a route that must be recognized while walking. Isaiah pictures a word heard behind the traveler saying, "This is the way; walk in it," when turning right or left.

row.basis: water and a level road for the returning community
row.note: The commentary joins guided travel, water, and a destination. Jeremiah's restoration oracle leads the weeping returnees by streams of water on an even path where they will not stumble.

row.basis: compassion guiding a flock to springs
row.note: The page's shade, water, and flock imagery converges in Isaiah: the compassionate one leads the returned people and guides them by springs of water.

row.basis: people who err and do not know God's ways
row.note: The commentary separates active straying from an externally received condition. Ps 95 describes a people who go astray in their heart and do not know God's ways, locating the deviation in their own stance.

row.basis: wrath and failure to enter rest
row.note: The commentary makes wrath and being lost related yet distinct dangers with different ends. Ps 95 has divine wrath bar this erring people from God's rest, making the destination of the negative path explicit.

row.basis: turning aside from the commanded way for the calf
row.note: The commentary itself uses the calf episode to show a favored community turning aside. Exodus describes the same community as quickly turning from the commanded way in making the calf.

The passive maghdub formula is illuminated by the narrative in which divine anger burns against the calf-making people; the source makes the wrath's historical trigger explicit without collapsing it into mere ethnic identity.

row.basis: intercession and relenting from announced disaster
row.note: The commentary calls wrath an threshold rather than a sealed door. In the calf narrative God relents from the disaster announced against the people after Moses's intercession.

row.basis: a people turns and the announced judgment changes
row.note: The commentary connects the gayr/change language to a condition that can move from favor to wrath and back. Jeremiah explicitly says that if the warned nation turns from evil, God relents from the disaster planned for it.

row.basis: the wicked person turns and lives
row.note: The page's repentance sequence after anger is not merely communal: Ezekiel says that a wicked person who turns from sins and keeps the statutes will live, giving the stray a concrete route of return.

row.basis: stone heart replaced by flesh heart
row.note: The commentary contrasts the hard, shield-like texture beside wrath with softening beside favor. Ezekiel's replacement of a heart of stone by a heart of flesh makes that material contrast an explicit transformation.

row.basis: inner renewal causes walking in statutes
row.note: The commentary links softened interior life to a traversed way. Ezekiel follows the new heart with God's Spirit causing the people to walk in God's statutes, tying transformation directly to a manner of walking.
The commentary's dalin carries a stray camel separated from its owner. Deuteronomy legislates the opposite response: do not ignore a brother's ox or sheep that has gone astray, but return it.

row.basis: caring for an animal when its owner is unknown
row.note: The definition of the lost camel stresses that its owner is not known. Deuteronomy imagines precisely that case and requires keeping the animal until its owner seeks it, so apparent ownerlessness is not final abandonment.

row.basis: religious guides cause many to stumble
row.note: The commentary warns that the track one follows may belong to a misguiding companion. Malachi accuses priests of departing from the way and causing many to stumble by their instruction.

row.basis: sheep each turning to its own way
row.note: The text hears dalin as both loss of a route and a dispersed flock. Isaiah describes all as sheep gone astray, each turning to its own way, giving the self-directed aspect of straying a flock image.

row.basis: graves opened and bodies brought up
row.note: The commentary pairs a body disappearing into earth with the claim that disappearance need not be annihilation. Ezekiel's vision has God open graves and bring the buried people up from them.

row.basis: dust sleepers awakened to divergent ends
row.note: The page distinguishes vanishing into earth from a journey with an end. Daniel says that sleepers in the dust awake, with opposed eschatological outcomes, providing a Hebrew Bible answer to the question of the body lost in soil.

The commentary follows a community from blessing to wrath when its inner condition changes. Isaiah recalls that the people rebelled and grieved God's spirit, so that their former helper turned to be their enemy.

row.basis: election is not proof of the recipient's righteousness
row.note: The commentary refuses to make the recipients of favor a permanently righteous lineage. Deuteronomy warns Israel not to explain its gift of land by saying it receives it because of its own righteousness.

The commentary defines the requested route through people already on it. Paul tells readers to imitate him and to observe those who walk according to the example they have received, an unusually close formulation of a path recognized by walkers.

The trace left by earlier guided people is central to the commentary. First Peter says that Christ left an example so that believers should follow in his footsteps, making the image literal and ethical.

row.basis: Abrahamic descent defined by walking in faith
row.note: The commentary says Abrahamic relation comes through walking as the earlier recipient walked. Paul calls Abraham father of those who do not merely possess a mark of descent but walk in the footsteps of his faith.
The commentary calls a road by the people who traverse it. Acts uses "the Way" as the name for a body of men and women, making route and communal identity inseparable in its own context.

row.basis: shepherd goes before and sheep follow his voice
row.note: The page's herd scene requires an owner, a forward guide, and animals that do not remain ownerless. Jesus's shepherd goes ahead of his sheep, who follow because they know his voice.

row.basis: straying sheep return to shepherd and guardian
row.note: The commentary closes the flock image with a creature separated from its rab/owner. First Peter says its readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

row.basis: owner searches until the lost sheep is found
row.note: The commentary's stray animal can be unrecognizable in the wilderness. Jesus's parable supplies a counter-movement: the owner leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the lost sheep until he finds it.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life
row.note: The commentary joins flock, guidance, and water found on the journey. Revelation makes the Lamb shepherd the worshipers and guide them to springs of the water of life.

row.basis: privileged wilderness generation still displeases God
row.note: The commentary insists that bestowed favor does not become an inherited guarantee. Paul recalls the exodus generation's shared sacred passage and provision, then says that with most of them God was not pleased and they fell in the wilderness.

row.basis: present hearers must watch against falling
row.note: Paul turns Israel's wilderness failure into a warning for the church: one who thinks he stands must watch lest he fall. This Christian reading sharpens the commentary's claim that later members cannot rely on former recipients' path.

row.basis: hearts that wander and do not know God's ways
row.note: Hebrews cites the Ps 95 generation as people who always go astray in heart and do not know God's ways; it carries the commentary's heart-level dalal into an address to present believers.

row.basis: mutual exhortation against a hardened heart
row.note: The commentary puts companionship beside both guidance and hardening. Hebrews commands daily mutual encouragement so that no member is hardened by sin's deceit, making the community a remedy rather than a source of straying.

row.basis: kindness intended to lead to repentance
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a gift from a permanent certificate of favor. Paul says God's kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead the recipient to repentance, giving the benefit a directional purpose.

The page sets divine favor's soft texture against anger's hardening. Paul pairs an unrepentant hardened heart with the accumulation of wrath, closely joining the commentary's inner texture and its wrath scene.

The commentary's same alayhim can move from favor to wrath as a community changes. Paul tells his readers to consider God's kindness and severity, with kindness continuing only if they remain in it and otherwise being cut off.

row.basis: one member turns back a wanderer
row.note: The commentary's lost traveler is called by companions toward guidance. James addresses a member who wanders from the truth and another person who turns that wanderer back, giving the image a communal act of restoration.

row.basis: body sown in corruption and raised transformed
row.note: The commentary's milk-in-water and body-in-earth images distinguish loss of visible form from annihilation. Paul uses sowing and rising to describe a body that is transformed rather than simply lost in burial.

row.basis: wilderness water reread as accompanying rock
row.note: The page's water found along a guided route recalls wilderness provision. Paul rereads Israel's drink from the rock as spiritual drink from a rock that accompanied them, extending the journey-and-water scene into Christian interpretation.

row.basis: a person named the way to the Father
row.note: The commentary says the requested road is clarified by its prior walkers. John goes further in a distinct Christological direction, placing the way in Jesus's own person as the route to the Father; the contrast helps specify what it means to name a path through a person.

row.basis: Abrahamic ancestry does not secure standing
row.note: The commentary denies that a favorable path is automatically inherited. John the Baptist warns his hearers not to claim Abraham as father as a guarantee, making the same anti-genealogical pressure explicit.

row.basis: Hebrew noam and paths of peace
row.note: Hebrew נֹעַם (noam, N-ʿ-M, a cognate of the source commentary's Arabic n-ʿ-m label) describes Wisdom's ways as ways of pleasantness and her paths as peace. It gives the commentary's secondary softness and goodness of ni'met a specific Hebrew path-setting without equating the two lexemes' full ranges.

row.basis: divine noam resting upon a people
row.note: The same Hebrew N-ʿ-M cognate appears when the psalm asks that God's noam, favor or pleasantness, be upon the community. Its "upon us" formulation provides a focused lexical and syntactic bridge to en'amte alayhim.

row.basis: divine anger qualified as unlike human anger
row.note: The commentary explicitly refuses to carry bodily boiling into its account of divine wrath. Hosea declares that God will not execute burning anger because God is not a human, offering a nearby Hebrew Bible qualification of wrath-language.

row.basis: witnesses surround a race to be run
row.note: The commentary sees an earlier company leaving a trace for later travelers. Hebrews imagines a cloud of witnesses surrounding present runners, joining predecessors, endurance, and an appointed course without making ancestry itself salvific.

The commentary's hard and soft surfaces become an inner moral contrast. Paul describes Christ's letter as written by the Spirit on tablets of human hearts rather than stone tablets, an interpretive bridge to Ezekiel-like softening.

row.basis: good giving comes from the Father
row.note: The active second-person en'amte foregrounds a giver of every benefit. James identifies every good giving and perfect gift as coming down from the Father, a close grammatical-theological counterpart to favor as gift rather than possession.

row.basis: one's own desire lures the person away
row.note: The commentary's dalin is an active condition rather than simply an anger imposed from above. James locates temptation in each person's being drawn out and lured by that person's own desire, a concrete account of self-involving deviation.

row.basis: a constricted way leading to life
row.note: The commentary expressly says that sirat here is not a razor-thin ordeal bridge but an ordinary traveled road. Matthew uses a deliberately constricted gate and hard way leading to life, so its different road image is a useful counter-narrative rather than an equation of the two terms.

row.basis: narrow access path between fire and water
row.note: The commentary rejects a narrow bridge reading of sirat. 4 Ezra's vision of a city reached only through a perilously narrow path between fire and deep water supplies a Jewish apocalyptic road image whose contrast clarifies that rejection.

row.basis: life and death set before human choice
row.note: The commentary's two negative possibilities and active straying belong to a moral choice rather than a hereditary identity. Sirach sets life and death before a person and says the chosen option will be given, a concise Jewish two-way formulation.

row.basis: departure with a knowledgeable companion and divine accompaniment
row.note: The commentary's path needs both a human guide and God's guidance. In Tobit's journey narrative, Tobias departs with the apparently human guide Azariah after his father entrusts the journey to God and the accompanying angel.

row.basis: hope of bodily resurrection from God
row.note: The commentary hears dalal as burial and loss into earth but then asks about renewed creation. The fourth martyr expects God to raise the body again, making non-annihilation after death an explicit Jewish answer.

The commentary makes anger an opening to forgiveness rather than an irrevocable end. Wisdom says God overlooks human sins so that people may repent, giving that transition a Hellenistic Jewish formulation.

row.basis: acquire a teacher and a friend
row.note: The commentary's right road is known through those who have traveled it, and companionship can guide or mislead. Avot's instruction to make for oneself a teacher and acquire a friend gives a compact rabbinic discipline for forming such company.

row.basis: do not separate from the community or trust oneself permanently
