row.note: The commentary denies that one is safely placed by family descent or a past state. Avot warns against separating from the community and against trusting oneself until death, an ethical reading of the path as ongoing rather than inherited security.

row.basis: walking after God by imitating divine deeds
row.note: The commentary describes following guided predecessors as entering the road itself. Sotah interprets walking after God as imitating God's merciful and caring acts, turning the way into practices learned from the divine exemplar.

row.basis: repentance changes the moral force of past sin
row.note: The commentary's wrath scene is followed by forgiveness and renewed guidance. Yoma's discussion of teshuvah treats return as able to alter how intentional sins are reckoned, a rabbinic intensification of that open path back.

row.basis: two spirits and the ways of light and darkness
row.note: The commentary carefully keeps distinct adverse paths rather than assigning every failure to one group. The Rule of the Community says humanity walks under spirits of truth and perversity and speaks of ways of light and darkness, a Second Temple two-path framework.

row.basis: the way of life and the way of death
row.note: The commentary contrasts a guided road with divergent forms of loss. The Didache opens its instruction with two ways, one of life and one of death, a concise early Christian reception of route language as communal ethics.

row.basis: two communities formed by two loves
row.note: The commentary treats the three groups as conditions of walking and receiving rather than permanent ethnic boxes. Augustine's two cities arise from opposed loves, an interpretive tradition that likewise grounds divergent communal destinies in an orientation of desire.

row.basis: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: The earlier part of the Ps 95 sequence calls the worshiping community God's pasture-people and sheep of God's hand. It supplies the flock-and-owner setting that precedes the later verses on erring hearts, unknown ways, and wrath.

row.basis: prayer to be taught God's ways
row.note: The commentary is itself a plea to be led along a defined road. Ps 25 asks God to make known God's ways and teach the psalmist God's paths, a direct Hebrew prayer parallel to the request for guidance.

row.basis: level path amid those lying in wait
row.note: The commentary includes a road vulnerable to an ambush and distinguishes upright travel from being made to stray. Ps 27 asks to be taught God's way and led on a level path specifically because of hostile watchers.

row.basis: blind travelers led on unknown paths
row.note: The prose treats a route as something found by marks and a traveler as liable to lose it. Isaiah promises to lead blind people by paths they do not know and to turn darkness to light and crooked ground straight before them.

row.basis: forsaking a way and returning for mercy
row.note: The commentary makes the lost condition recoverable through a change of walking and repentance. Isaiah commands the wicked to forsake their way and return to the Lord, whose mercy and pardon answer that turn.

row.basis: walking in stubborn counsel and going backward
row.note: The commentary contrasts the forward trace of guided people with following one's own desire or misleading predecessors. Jeremiah says the people walked in the counsels of their stubborn evil heart and went backward rather than forward.

The commentary sets a united company on one route against dispersal from it. Deuteronomy describes God restoring the fortunes of a returning people and gathering them from the peoples among whom they have been scattered.

row.basis: water for a congregation and its livestock
row.note: The commentary's journey imagery joins a guide, water, and a flock or herd. At Meribah Moses is told that water will come from the rock for the assembled community and its animals, a wilderness provision scene with both elements.

The commentary warns that a track may be defined by the wrong companions and ancestors. Ps 1 locates the blessed person's first refusal in not walking in the counsel of the wicked, before its standing and sitting images of belonging.

row.basis: guiding feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary repeatedly locates guidance in actual feet and a road rather than an abstract orientation. Zechariah's hymn asks for light that will guide human feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: walking in darkness without knowing one's destination
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a traveler carried toward a destination from one who has lost direction. Jesus warns that the person who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, a sharply corresponding formulation.

row.basis: blind guides and a shared fall
row.note: The commentary makes the identity of the guide decisive and notices sight as necessary for finding the route. Jesus calls the Pharisees blind guides; when blind lead blind, both fall into a pit.

The page's flock is safe only when it knows its guide rather than following every track. In the continuation of the shepherd image, sheep flee rather than follow a stranger because they do not know that voice.

row.basis: former branches broken off and present standing by faith
row.note: The commentary argues that a community can pass from favor into judgment rather than carrying favor as descent. Paul says that some branches were broken off through unbelief and that the present reader stands only by faith.

row.basis: former branches can be grafted in again
row.note: The commentary's movement from wrath through repentance to renewed guidance has a structural counterpart in Paul's claim that excluded branches can be grafted in again if they do not persist in unbelief.

row.basis: seed must die before it comes to life
row.note: The commentary's two forms of disappearance ask whether entry into earth means extinction or a directed transformation. Paul's seed image says what is sown does not come to life unless it dies, giving burial-like loss a generative end.
The commentary's bad companion can divert a traveler after guidance has been received. Paul makes the same social mechanism explicit by warning that bad associations corrupt good character.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and following Balaam
row.note: The commentary joins departure from a straight track to imitation of a misleading predecessor. Second Peter says false teachers have forsaken the straight way, gone astray, and followed Balaam's way.

row.basis: straight paths for feet that heal the lame
row.note: The commentary's road is not merely a verdict but a route that can steady or lose a walker. Hebrews asks the community to make straight paths for its feet so that what is lame is healed rather than dislocated.

row.basis: cling to a good way and avoid an evil one
row.note: The commentary examines right paths, false companions, and distinct negative routes. Avot records a debate over the good way to which a person should cleave and the evil way from which one should keep distance, including good and evil friends among the answers.

row.basis: distance from a bad neighbor and the wicked
row.note: The commentary's companion may either sustain the route or lead one away from it. Avot instructs its reader to keep far from a bad neighbor and not join the wicked, a rabbinic social safeguard for the path.

row.basis: one is led in the way one chooses
row.note: The commentary differentiates God's bestowal of guidance from the traveler's active straying. Makkot crystallizes that tension in its maxim that a person is led along the way that person wants to go.

row.basis: prayer that ways be made straight
row.note: Tobit's fatherly instruction combines fidelity, wise counsel, and a prayer that the son's ways be made straight and his paths prosper. It is a Jewish family-to-traveler counterpart to the commentary's route that must be walked rather than merely inherited.

row.basis: Father who made and acquired you
row.note: The song calls God the Father who made, acquired, and established Israel, closely matching the commentary's claim that createdness establishes a prior divine belonging.
The creator-former addresses Israel by name and says “you are mine,” an unusually direct biblical formulation of created persons as belonging to God.
Israel is told, “you are my servant; I formed you,” joining servanthood to divine formation in the same sequence the commentary makes explicit.

row.basis: made by God, his people and flock
row.note: WLC's ketiv reads that God made us “and not we [ourselves],” while its qere reads “and we are his”; the verse then calls the people his and the flock of his pasture, so both streams need to be kept distinct in this creation-and-belonging parallel.
God declares that every life, parent and child alike, is God's; the assertion broadens the commentary's ownership image from a household slave to all human persons.

row.basis: servant honors master, God as master
row.note: Malachi argues from a servant's honor for a master to God's claim on Israel's honor, directly using household hierarchy to define proper reverence for God.
The psalm compares Israel's eyes toward God to servants' eyes toward a master's hand and a maid's toward her mistress; it is an exact prayer-image of dependent, direct address.
The liturgical command to serve YHWH joyfully gives a cultic form of service that is more than inward feeling, while changing the commentary's stress on extreme abasement.

row.basis: Arabic إله/الله (source label ء ل ه B001), Hebrew אלהיך
row.note: The command to fear and serve “YHWH your God” uses Hebrew אלהיך from the same ʾ-l-h family as the commentary's ilāh/Allah label and directs exclusive service toward that God.

row.basis: Arabic ع ب د (source labels B001-B006), Hebrew עבד
row.note: The prohibition against bowing to or serving other gods uses Hebrew עבד; it gives the cognate root an explicit exclusive-worship setting rather than merely a lexical resemblance.

row.basis: choose whom to serve; household service
row.note: Joshua makes service a confessed choice—“as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH”—which closely parallels the commentary's movement from an existing status to the servant's own voiced assent.
God's oath that every knee will bend before him gives a universal biblical scene of bodily submission corresponding to the commentary's claim that all creatures finally come as servants.
The wilderness voice commands a way to be prepared and a highway made straight for God, the nearest biblical counterpart to the commentary's trodden, made-level road.

row.basis: valleys raised, mountains lowered, rough ground level
row.note: The next verse specifies the leveling and smoothing of the road, adding the physical process of subduing terrain rather than only the abstract image of a path.

row.basis: level ground for Israel's safe walking
row.note: Baruch says God commands mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel may walk safely on level ground, a Jewish expansion of Isaiah's road image into divinely prepared passage.
Luke's Isaian quotation retains valleys filled, mountains lowered, and rough places made smooth; it carries the commentary's rendered-road image into the Gospel's preparation for God's coming.

row.basis: prepare the Lord's way, make paths straight
row.note: Mark applies the wilderness-road summons to John's proclamation, making the straightened path a concrete Gospel preparation for the Lord rather than a bare travel image.

Rabbi Joshua ben Korha explains the order of the Shema as first accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven and then the yoke of commandments; this gives a Jewish liturgical reading of willingly assumed divine obedience.
Antigonus instructs disciples to serve the master without serving for reward and to keep the fear of heaven; it probes how divine service can be freely offered rather than merely compelled.

row.basis: ear piercing and servants of God
row.note: The Talmud explains the permanently pierced Hebrew servant through the Sinai claim that Israel belongs to God, criticizing one who acquires a human master; it is a direct Jewish limit on human lordship.
James says every kind of beast, bird, reptile, and sea creature is tamed by humanity, a precise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's language of animal domestication.
The immediately following contrast says no human can tame the tongue; it gives the tamed-animal figure a moral reversal in which the human speaker remains resistant to mastery.
Jesus answers temptation with worship of and service to God alone, a direct Gospel formulation of the exclusive “you we worship” relation.

row.basis: no one can serve two masters
row.note: The maxim about serving God or Mammon makes divided mastership impossible, a close counterpart to the commentary's restriction on treating people or possessions as rival lords.
Jesus asks why people call him “Lord, Lord” but do not do what he says; the verse explicitly joins the master's title to obedience, not to verbal address alone.

row.basis: servant returns from plowing or shepherding
row.note: Jesus' household example assumes a servant who comes in from field work and still prepares the master's meal, preserving the literal labor-and-master scene that underlies the commentary's slave image.

row.basis: servants have done only their duty
row.note: After doing all commanded, disciples are to call themselves servants who have only done their duty; it supplies a Christian idiom of obedience and lowly self-description.

The returning master dresses for service, seats his servants, and serves them; this deliberately reverses the commentary's one-way household hierarchy and its claim that the master does not lower himself.
Jesus accepts the disciples' titles “Teacher” and “Lord,” giving the human speech of lordship in the commentary an explicit Gospel parallel before the following reversal.
The one called Lord and Teacher washes disciples' feet and makes it exemplary; the action directly counters the commentary's asymmetry in which humiliation belongs only to the servant.

row.basis: Gentile rulers lord it over others
row.note: Jesus names dominating rule as the practice of Gentile rulers, making human lordship a social pattern that his teaching will explicitly reject.
The next verse reverses status: whoever wants greatness must become the others' servant, changing the master-slave scale from ownership to service.

row.basis: Son of Man serves and gives ransom
row.note: The Son of Man comes not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom, a concentrated counter-scene to a master who only receives service.
The hymn begins with Christ in God's form, establishing the high status whose subsequent self-emptying makes its relation to the commentary's unlowered owner deliberate rather than generic humility.
Christ takes the form of a slave; the verse turns the commentary's owned and humbled slave role into the role voluntarily assumed by the exalted figure.
The hymn explicitly says he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, matching the commentary's association of worship/service with abasement while reversing who undergoes it.

row.basis: God highly exalts the humbled one
row.note: God's exaltation follows the slave-form and humbling, giving the commentary's secondary movement from lowliness to honor a markedly different Christian sequence.

row.basis: every knee bends at Jesus' name
row.note: The universal bending of knees echoes the commentary's eschatological servanthood, but directs it in the hymn's Christological pattern.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
row.note: The final confession calls Jesus “Lord” to the Father's glory, pairing the master's title, universal confession, and worship after the servant-form reversal.

Paul states that a person becomes a slave of the one obeyed, whether sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness; it closely binds slavery to obedience as the commentary's dīn discussion does.

row.basis: freed from sin, enslaved to God
row.note: Paul calls believers both freed from sin and enslaved to God, a consciously paradoxical account of divine belonging and moral freedom.

row.basis: slave as Lord's freedperson, free as Christ's slave
row.note: Paul reverses ordinary social labels: the enslaved called in the Lord is free, while the free person is Christ's slave; it sharply reframes the commentary's fixed owner-slave status.

row.basis: bought at a price; do not become human slaves
row.note: Because believers were bought at a price, Paul warns them not to become slaves of humans; divine purchase becomes an argument against human mastery.

row.basis: no longer slave but child and heir
row.note: The believer is no longer a slave but a child and heir through God, changing the household relation from permanent servitude to filial inheritance.

row.basis: not slavery to fear but adoption
row.note: Paul contrasts a spirit of slavery leading to fear with adoption that cries “Abba, Father,” offering a different mode of direct address and belonging from the commentary's servile abasement.

row.basis: earthly masters share a Master in heaven
row.note: Christian masters must stop threatening because their own and their slaves' Master is in heaven and shows no partiality; the verse limits human ownership from above.

row.basis: God made the world and is Lord of heaven and earth
row.note: Paul calls the creator Lord of heaven and earth, a New Testament statement of comprehensive divine sovereignty over the worlds named in the commentary.

row.basis: God is not served as needing anything
row.note: God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, because he gives life and breath to all; it closely supports the commentary's insistence that the true owner lacks no helper and is not reduced by need.

row.basis: bought with a price and glorify God
row.note: Believers are said to have been bought at a price and therefore to glorify God bodily, joining ownership language to a lived act of worship.
A believer is called another's household servant who stands or falls before his own Lord; the verse makes mastership a reason not to usurp judgment over someone else's servant.
The parable begins with a man entrusting his own property to his servants, preserving the master-property-servant relation that the commentary treats as a single image.
The servants' master returns after a long time and settles accounts with them, a literal parabolic meeting of ownership, service, and the reckoning associated with the Day of dīn.

row.basis: father restores the returning son with honor
row.note: The father answers the returning son's household shame with robe, ring, and sandals, making the master's house a place of restorative honor rather than the fixed abasement expected in the commentary.

row.basis: fear, glory, judgment, worship the creator
row.note: The angel announces judgment and commands worship of the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs, bringing creator-ownership and Day-of-judgment worship together.
A heavenly voice calls all God's servants, great and small, to praise him; it provides a direct apocalyptic equivalent to praise voiced by those who belong to God.
The angel refuses John's prostration, identifies as a fellow servant, and commands worship of God; it sharply distinguishes servanthood from receiving worship.

row.basis: God's servants serve in the final city
row.note: In the city of God's throne and the Lamb's throne, the servants will serve him; the final setting gives an eschatological counterpart to universal divine service.

row.basis: Moses as servant in God's whole house
row.note: Moses is faithful as a servant in all God's house, preserving the commentary's house/master/servant relation in an explicitly theological household.

row.basis: Christ as Son over God's house
row.note: The contrast makes Christ Son over God's house and the believers that house, distinguishing sonship and household membership from slave status.

Psalm 23 moves from “he” as the shepherd who leads in verses 1-3 to direct “you” in verse 4; its exact pronoun turn offers a literary analogue to the commentary's movement from third-person praise to second-person address, though its figure is shepherd and flock.

row.basis: Arabic د ي ن (source labels B001, B004), Aramaic דינא
row.note: Daniel's Aramaic heavenly court says that the dīn sat and books were opened; the cognate juridical word keeps the judgment sense of “Day of dīn” beside the commentary's developed obedience and ownership senses.

row.basis: Arabic م ل ك (source label B002), Hebrew מלך
row.note: Isaiah sees YHWH as “the King”; Hebrew מלך shares the m-l-k root with the commentary's Mālik label, while the verse contributes royal sovereignty rather than treating the Hebrew word as a property term.

row.basis: prepare the way through Torah study
row.note: The Community Rule applies Isaiah's wilderness-way language to a separated group preparing God's way by studying and doing Torah, an interpretive conversion of road-making into disciplined obedience.

row.basis: yoke of Torah releases other yokes
row.note: The mishnah says accepting the yoke of Torah removes the yoke of government and worldly burdens; it develops divine submission as release from rival subjections.
After its donkey-and-slave discipline imagery, Sirach tells the owner to treat a servant as a brother; the nearby ethical reversal complicates a reading of the owned person as only property.

row.basis: slave and son in the household
row.note: Jesus says a slave does not remain in the household forever but the son does; it uses the house image to contrast slave impermanence with filial permanence.
Jesus no longer calls disciples servants because a servant does not know the master's affairs, but friends; intimate disclosure revises the distance assumed by the master-property model.

row.basis: no longer a slave but a beloved brother
row.note: Paul asks that Onesimus be received no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother in the Lord, an explicit Christian re-description of an owned person's relation.

row.basis: master and slave hope in the same God
row.note: The Didache forbids bitter commands to male or female slaves because both slave and master hope in the same God; it applies common divine lordship to household conduct.

row.basis: creation, animal rule, slavery after sin
row.note: Augustine argues that the created order gives humans rule over irrational creatures, while human slavery is bound to sin; this Christian reading separates animal dominion from a natural right to own persons.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4
row.basis: buying humans made in God's image
row.note: Gregory's homily on Ecclesiastes 2:7 attacks the purchase of human beings by appealing to their divine image and created freedom, a pointed patristic challenge to calling a person property.

row.basis: returning son asks to be a hired servant
row.note: The returning son proposes admission to his father's house as a hired servant; paired with the father's response in verse 22, it makes the commentary's servant-at-the-master's-house image a precise Gospel encounter.

row.basis: house, servants, ox, donkey, every possession
row.note: The anti-coveting command gathers a neighbor's house, male and female servants, ox, donkey, and other possessions into one household inventory, closely matching the commentary's owner-house-animal-slave tableau.

row.basis: servant chooses master, wife, children, household
row.note: The Hebrew servant says that he loves his master, wife, and children and will not go free; this gives a legal counter-case in which continued belonging is explicitly voiced as a choice.
The master brings the willing servant to the doorpost and pierces his ear for lifelong service, a concrete ritualization of ownership and enduring service in the master's house.

row.basis: Sabbath rest for ox, donkey, servant
row.note: The Sabbath command joins the ox and donkey to the child of the slave woman and resident alien in receiving rest, placing a divine limit on the labor imposed upon both working animals and dependent people.
The Decalogue's Sabbath law requires the male and female servant to rest as the owner rests; it turns the master-slave relation into an equality of rest before God.
When Israel has gone, Egypt describes the loss as letting them go “from serving us”; the phrasing gives the Pharaoh-Israel bondage in the commentary a direct narrative counterpart.

row.basis: human master bounded by sin against God
row.note: Joseph says his master has withheld nothing but his wife, yet refuses because the act would be a sin against God; the human householder's wide control is subordinated to a higher Lord.

row.basis: direct “I am your servant”; bonds loosed
row.note: The psalmist directly calls himself God's servant and son of God's maidservant, then says God has loosed his bonds; it keeps divine servanthood and liberation together in one prayer.
The congregation is summoned to bow down and kneel before YHWH its maker, a close liturgical image of embodied abasement before the creator.

row.basis: people of pasture, flock of God's hand
row.note: The worshippers are God's people and the flock of his hand; it combines animal dependence, the owner's hand, and collective divine belonging.

row.basis: life of animals and humans in God's hand
row.note: Job places the life of every living creature and the breath of all humanity in God's hand, extending the commentary's hand-held possession figure beyond livestock to all life.

row.basis: everything under heaven belongs to God
row.note: God asks who could give first so that God owed repayment, because all under heaven is God's; it joins universal possession to divine non-dependence.

row.basis: earth and inhabitants belong to YHWH
row.note: The psalm's opening ownership formula gives YHWH the earth, its fullness, the world, and its inhabitants, an explicit scriptural horizon for “Lord of the worlds.”

row.basis: all comes from God; gifts returned
row.note: David's praise says all things come from God and that Israel gives only what is already God's; it makes praise an acknowledgment that human possessions remain received goods.

row.basis: wise servant shares a son's inheritance
row.note: A prudent servant rules over a shameful son and shares the inheritance with the brothers, overturning a fixed hierarchy of owner, household, and slave.

row.basis: one guarding a master is honored
row.note: Proverbs says the one who keeps or attends to a master will be honored, a compact wisdom parallel to the commentary's secondary possibility that service and honor meet.
God's servant is described as raised, lifted up, and greatly exalted, supplying a scriptural servant-and-honor trajectory beside the commentary's muʿabbad sense.
The fast God chooses loosens bonds, frees the oppressed, and breaks every yoke; it makes worship answer human subjugation by liberation rather than by extending it.

row.basis: Father, potter, clay, work of hands
row.note: The prayer calls God Father and potter and the people clay made by God's hand, a creation-and-forming image for dependence that does not reduce them to household property.

row.basis: clay in potter's hand, house of Israel
row.note: God compares the house of Israel to clay in a potter's hand, a particularly close biblical image for formed material held under a maker's authority.

row.basis: refusal to serve gods or worship the image
row.note: The Judean servants tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his golden image, a concrete refusal of a ruler's imposed cultic mastery.
YHWH is named Israel's judge, lawgiver, and king; the verse gathers the judicial and sovereign dimensions that meet in the commentary's Mālik of the Day of dīn.

row.basis: God brings every deed into judgment
row.note: The closing maxim says God will bring every deed, hidden or open, into judgment, providing an explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the reckoning implied by Day of dīn.

Zion's king comes righteous and victorious yet humble, mounted on a donkey; the royal figure unites authority, lowliness, and a domesticated animal in a configuration that reverses the commentary's unlowered master.
Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than put out of joint, turning the made-level road into a communal moral action.
Matthew presents the king as gentle and mounted on a donkey, carrying Zechariah's master-humility-and-domesticated-animal figure into the Gospel entry scene.

row.basis: servant falls before master over debt
row.note: The servant falls down before his master and begs for patience over the debt, giving a literal scene of servile prostration, ownership, and reckoning.

row.basis: master releases servant and forgives debt
row.note: The master is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and cancels the debt; this masterly authority is expressed through liberation rather than permanent subjection.

row.basis: direct prayer to creator as Sovereign Master
row.note: The community addresses God as despota, the Sovereign Master who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; it joins direct address, mastery, and creation in one prayer.

row.basis: Cornelius falls at a human's feet
row.note: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet and prostrates before him, staging the very transfer of honor to a human figure that the commentary's limit on human lords excludes.
Peter raises Cornelius and says that he too is human, turning the preceding act into an explicit rejection of worshipful elevation of a person.

row.basis: bodies offered as living sacrifice and worship
row.note: Paul calls the presentation of embodied life to God a living sacrifice and rational worship, giving worship a concrete, whole-person form beyond a merely verbal confession.
In an instruction to household slaves, Paul says that the service ultimately rendered is to the Lord Christ and promises an inheritance, placing earthly service under a different master and reward.

row.basis: free people as slaves of God
row.note: Believers are to live as free people while also as God's slaves; the deliberate pairing gives a Christian reversal of the commentary's ordinary contrast between freedom and owned status.

row.basis: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
row.note: The community is to offer acceptable worship to God with reverence and awe because it receives an unshakable kingdom, a liturgical form of humble service before sovereignty.

row.basis: all appear before Christ's judgment seat
row.note: All people must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds, an individual accounting scene for the Day of dīn dimension.

row.basis: a fixed day for judging the world
row.note: Paul says God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, making the day-and-judgment element explicit in the same speech that calls God creator and Lord.

row.basis: only Sovereign, King of kings, Lord of lords
row.note: The doxology calls God the only Sovereign and the King of kings and Lord of lords, a compact New Testament royal-master formulation beside Mālik.
The heavenly elders say directly, “You are worthy,” because God created all things by his will; it closely joins praise, direct address, and creation-based sovereignty.
The martyrs address God as Sovereign Lord and ask when God will judge, bringing master-language and the delayed final judgment into a single direct prayer.

row.basis: acquiring a Hebrew servant acquires a master
row.note: The Talmud's maxim that one who acquires a Hebrew servant acquires a master develops Torah's service law into a reversal: the owner must meet the servant's needs so fully that mastery is ethically displaced.

row.basis: slaves serve for God's glory and better freedom
row.note: Ignatius tells enslaved Christians to serve more diligently for God's glory so that they may receive a better freedom from God, preserving the tension between social servitude and divine freedom.
The commentary joins a name to a distinguishing mark; Exodus has Israel's names engraved on shoulder stones like a signet, memorializing who the bearer represents.

row.basis: the Name placed on a people
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies its bearer; here the priests put YHWH's name on Israel and YHWH blesses them, making the name a communal identity.
The commentary's burned mark identifies its bearer; circumcision is explicitly a covenant sign in the flesh, marking Abraham's descendants as belonging to the covenant.
The commentary describes a mark that makes its bearer recognizable; blood on the houses is a sign that YHWH sees and that protects those inside.
The commentary's brand makes a bearer distinguishable; Ezekiel orders a mark on the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations, identifying them within the city.
The commentary's identifying brand can be read as a mark of belonging; Ezekiel's executioners must spare everyone bearing the mark, giving it an explicit protective function.

row.basis: writing YHWH's name on a hand
row.note: The commentary says a name is an identifying sign; Isaiah pictures a person writing “I am YHWH's” on the hand and taking Israel's name, making affiliation bodily visible.

row.basis: sign on hand and between the eyes
row.note: The commentary's brand is a bodily sign; Deuteronomy makes God's words a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes, a visible and remembered mark of allegiance.

row.basis: Sabbath sign that makes God known
row.note: The commentary connects a distinguishing mark with knowing; Sabbath is explicitly a sign between YHWH and Israel “that you may know” who sanctifies them.
The commentary treats a burned brand as a mark that identifies; Leviticus forbids incisions and tattoo marks on the body for the dead, adding a distinct Israelite boundary around bodily marking.

row.basis: the Lamb's and Father's names on foreheads
row.note: The commentary treats a mark as a sign that identifies its bearer; Revelation names the Lamb's followers by the names written on their foreheads.
The commentary's brand distinguishes a bearer; Revelation seals God's servants on the forehead before harm reaches the earth.

row.basis: the beast's mark on hand or forehead
row.note: The commentary's mark identifies whose a bearer is; Revelation gives the beast's followers a contrary mark on hand or forehead, signaling a rival allegiance.

row.basis: mark, name, and number control buying
row.note: The commentary links a mark to recognition; Revelation connects the beast's mark with its name or number and access to trade, showing identity enforced publicly.

The commentary's wasm image is a visible bodily trace; Paul says he bears Jesus' marks on his body. Here the marks are scars of suffering, so the connection is bodily identification, not a claim of literal branding.

row.basis: seal, God's knowledge, and naming the Lord
row.note: The commentary joins sign, name, and knowing; this verse says God's seal declares “the Lord knows those who are his” and addresses everyone who names the Lord.

row.basis: the good name invoked over believers
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies the one named; James calls Jesus' name the good name invoked over the community, making the name a mark of affiliation.
The commentary says beginning under a name places an act beneath that identity; Jesus commissions baptism into the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, marking discipleship.
The commentary describes a rising shape becoming recognizable; the shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they recognize his voice, making naming a concrete act of recognition.
The commentary calls the world and each species a distinguishing sign; Israel camps by its tribal standard, which marks each group within the larger people.
The commentary brings a raised name together with a standard; Moses names the altar “YHWH is my banner,” explicitly joining divine name and battle sign.

row.basis: a sign whose child bears a revealing name
row.note: The commentary makes a name an elevated sign; Isaiah's promised sign is a child named Immanuel, “God with us,” whose name interprets the sign.

row.basis: the majestic name over earth and heavens
row.note: The commentary reads the opening Name as raised for recognition; the psalm calls YHWH's name majestic in all the earth and places glory above the heavens.
The commentary cites a name praised as exalted; this verse blesses YHWH's name from now and forever, giving the name an enduring liturgical praise.
The commentary joins name and height; the psalm says YHWH is high above all nations and his glory above the heavens.

row.basis: the Name alone exalted over creation
row.note: The commentary makes every created kind a sign of its Lord; the psalm calls all creation to praise the name, which alone is exalted over earth and heaven.
The commentary says each created kind is itself a sign; Job tells the hearer to ask beasts, birds, and the earth, which teach what humans should recognize.
The commentary reads the world as a mark by which its Lord is known; Job concludes that the hand of YHWH made these things.

row.basis: the creator calls stars by name
row.note: The commentary joins creation, distinction, and knowing; Isaiah says God brings out the starry host by number and calls each by name, with none missing.
The commentary says the world is a sign that makes its Lord known; the heavens declare God's glory and the firmament announces his handiwork.
The commentary calls every created kind a sign; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of created things let observers recognize their maker.

row.basis: creation makes the creator's qualities perceptible
row.note: The commentary reads the created world as a sign of its Lord; Romans says God's invisible attributes are understood through the things made.

row.basis: the divine name hallowed in prayer
row.note: The commentary opens with Allah's name and gives a spoken invocation; Jesus teaches prayer by asking that the Father's name be hallowed.

row.basis: every deed done in the Lord's name
row.note: The commentary says to begin an act in God's name is to place it under that recognized sign; Paul extends this to every word and deed done in Jesus' name.
The commentary calls Allah the greatest name and develops the image of a name raised high; Paul says God gave Jesus the name above every name.

row.basis: glory due the Name and an offering
row.note: The commentary links the divine name with worship and placing work under that name; the psalm asks worshipers to ascribe glory due his name and bring an offering.

row.basis: proclaiming the Name and ascribing greatness
row.note: The commentary says Allah's name is the greatest and raised for recognition; Moses proclaims YHWH's name and calls the hearers to ascribe greatness to God.
The commentary includes the invocation “O Allah, forgive me”; Acts promises salvation to everyone who calls on the Lord's name.

The commentary warns that a raised name can lack what it is supposed to identify; Paul takes an altar's label for an unknown god and announces the creator as the referent, while Luke preserves the Athenians' admission of ignorance.
The commentary says humanly assigned deity names may be only names; Paul says an idol is nothing and there is one God, a close polemical counterpart.

row.basis: a deity is not a human-made image
row.note: The commentary says humanly assigned names can have nothing beneath them; Acts says the divine being is not like gold, silver, or stone shaped by human art and imagination.

row.basis: Adam and the naming of creatures
row.note: The commentary recalls Adam being taught names; Genesis has God bring the animals to Adam to see what he will call them, a shared naming scene.

row.basis: who teaches or gives the names
row.note: The commentary cites Qur'an 2:31, where God teaches Adam all the names; Genesis instead has God bring animals for Adam to name, shifting agency and the scope of the naming scene.
The commentary cites Noah addressing those boarding the ark; Genesis has YHWH command Noah and his household to enter it, preserving the shared boarding scene but assigning the speech to God.
The commentary says Noah places the ark's sailing and mooring under God's name; Genesis reports that the ark came to rest on Ararat without naming that action as an invocation.
The commentary cites Lot's overturned city as a sign for discerning readers; Genesis has Abraham look toward Sodom and see smoke rising like a furnace, a visible trace left by the same destruction.

row.basis: the Queen of Sheba hears Solomon's fame
row.note: The commentary's letter scene names Solomon and the Queen of Sheba; Kings says she came after hearing Solomon's fame concerning YHWH's name, linking the same queen and the divine name.
The commentary's Sheba letter begins in Allah's name; after testing Solomon, the biblical queen blesses YHWH, his God, giving the shared encounter a spoken praise of the sender's deity.
The commentary includes calling Allah by name; Genesis says people began to call on the name of YHWH, an early narrative use of invocation.

row.basis: a great name given by God
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises and spreads among people; God promises Abram that he will make his name great, making reputation a bestowed sign.
The commentary contrasts the highest divine name with empty names assigned by humans; Babel's builders explicitly seek to make a name for themselves, a human project of self-exaltation.
The commentary treats a name as what makes its bearer known; Exodus gives YHWH's name as a memorial for all generations.

row.basis: the Name remembered at an altar
row.note: The commentary connects God's name with invocation and beginning an act under it; Exodus says YHWH will come and bless at every place where he causes his name to be remembered.

row.basis: the name must not be borne falsely
row.note: The commentary presents the name as a mark placed over an action; the command against bearing YHWH's name in vain gives that practice an ethical limit.

row.basis: an action begun in YHWH's name
row.note: The commentary says beginning work in God's name places the deed under that sign; David enters battle saying he comes against Goliath in the name of YHWH.
The commentary presents Allah as the greatest name and as a name spoken in invocation; here YHWH descends and proclaims the divine name to Moses.

row.basis: the proclaimed name described as merciful
row.note: The opening formula names Allah with al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus follows the proclamation of YHWH's name with “merciful and gracious,” connecting divine naming with mercy.
The commentary's 1:1 includes the names al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus places YHWH's name beside the description “merciful and gracious,” a close formula-level bridge.

The commentary's Qur'an 12:40 places Joseph's religious speech among prison companions; in Genesis 40:8 he tells two inmates that interpretations belong to God. Genesis does not discuss their idols, so the shared prison speech makes the difference in subject clear.

row.basis: sailors invoke YHWH in danger at sea
row.note: The commentary has Noah invoke God's name over the ark's movement and rest; Jonah's sailors cry to YHWH during a life-threatening voyage, joining divine invocation to a vessel at sea.
The commentary says an act begun in God's name is placed under that sign; Proverbs says YHWH's name is a strong tower into which the righteous run, making the name protective.
The commentary treats a name as what distinguishes and makes a bearer known; Malachi describes a book of remembrance written before YHWH for those who fear him and esteem his name.
The commentary makes a name an identifying mark; Jesus tells his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, a written record of belonging.
The commentary says a name lets its bearer be known; Jesus says he has manifested the Father's name to the disciples, connecting revelation of the name with recognition.

row.basis: letters written and sealed in a king's name
row.note: The commentary says a letter's opening name identifies its sender and authority; Jezebel writes in Ahab's name and seals the letters with his seal, showing the name and mark authorizing a document.

row.basis: a decree in the king's name, sealed
row.note: The commentary reads the basmala at the head of Solomon's letter as an authority marker; Esther's officials write a decree in the king's name and seal it with his ring.
Isaiah's sign child is named Immanuel; Matthew applies the name “God with us” to Jesus, making the name a Christian reading of the sign's referent.

row.basis: a name interprets the child's role
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies what is named; Matthew says Jesus is to be named for he will save his people, making the name a sign of his action.
The commentary links a visible sign with knowing and recognition; Exodus says the deliverance from Egypt is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes.

row.basis: righteous and wicked names remembered differently
row.note: The commentary says a good name circulates for good, not evil; Proverbs contrasts the blessed memory of the righteous with the rotting name of the wicked.

row.basis: a good name valued above good oil
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises among people; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than good oil, treating reputation as a lasting public distinction.

The Arabic word ism in 1:1 and Hebrew shem are Semitic cognates; Ecclesiastes uses shem for a good reputation, matching the commentary's account of a name circulating as honor. Its s-m-w and w-s-m source labels are not the basis for this comparison.
The Arabic word ism in 1:1 and Aramaic shema are cognates; Daniel blesses God's name forever, showing the cognate in a liturgical use of the divine name.
The commentary names Allah in 1:1; Arabic Allah and Hebrew El/Eloah are related Semitic divine terms, while Jacob names an altar El-Elohe-Israel. The terms are cognate, not identical titles.

The 1:1 formula includes al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus calls YHWH rahum, “merciful.” These forms share the Semitic R-Ḥ-M root, while the commentary's listed root labels do not establish that relationship.

row.basis: the crown of a good name
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises among people; Avot says the crown of a good name surpasses Torah, priesthood, and kingship, turning reputation into the highest social distinction.

row.basis: the Name as written and its liturgical substitute
row.note: The commentary emphasizes calling Allah and naming him; the Mishnah distinguishes pronouncing the divine Name as written in the Temple from using a substitute elsewhere, showing that recognition and utterance are context-bound.

row.basis: the congregation answers the divine Name
row.note: The commentary pairs God's name with invocation; in the High Priest's confession, the congregation responds with the blessing of God's glorious kingdom, making the Name part of communal liturgy.

row.basis: the mark on Ezekiel's foreheads interpreted as a letter
row.note: The commentary's brand is a sign read on a body; the Talmud debates what Ezekiel's tav-mark signifies, turning the mark into a letter whose reading distinguishes life from death.

row.basis: the attributes of mercy as a prayer order
row.note: The commentary gives an invocation asking Allah for forgiveness and names Allah with mercy epithets; this tradition reads Exodus 34's proclaimed attributes as a prayer pattern by which Israel seeks forgiveness.

row.basis: tribal banners as detailed identity signs
row.note: The commentary treats a standard as a distinguishing mark; the midrash elaborates the tribal banners by colors and stones, making the standards a visual code for each tribe.

row.basis: regard for a name that outlasts wealth
row.note: The commentary says a name spreads as a person's public honor; Sirach urges regard for one's name because it remains longer than great stores of gold.

row.basis: the Temple response blesses the Name
row.note: The commentary says Allah's name is called in prayer; this Mishnah preserves the Temple response “Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever,” an explicit liturgical elevation of the Name.
The commentary's camel brand lets observers recognize its bearer; Genesis says God gives Cain a sign so that anyone finding him will not kill him, though it does not say the sign is a bodily brand.

row.basis: a changed name as a promise-sign
row.note: The commentary treats a name as an identifying sign; God changes Abram's name to Abraham because he will be father of many nations, so the name points to a promised identity.
The commentary contrasts the highest divine name with names assigned by humans; Babel's builders seek to make their own name through a tower, a specific reversal of placing a deed under God's name.
The commentary defines an identifying trace; God sets the bow in the cloud as a sign of the covenant between God and earth, adding a visible sign that recalls a relation.

row.basis: tribal names borne over the heart
row.note: The commentary says a name makes its bearer known; the high priest carries Israel's names over his heart as a memorial before YHWH, so the names identify the people in worship.

row.basis: engraved Name on the high priest's forehead
row.note: The commentary joins a distinguishing sign with a name; Aaron wears a gold plate engraved “Holy to YHWH” on his forehead, a literal inscribed name-mark.
The commentary says reading a mark means seeing a trace; Israelites are to see the fringes, remember the commandments, and do them, making a worn sign a prompt to recognize and obey.
The commentary links names with identifying marks; the tribal leaders' names are written on their staffs, and Aaron's name is written on Levi's staff.

row.basis: a blossoming staff identifies God's choice
row.note: The commentary says a mark distinguishes one bearer from others; the staff that blossoms identifies the person YHWH chooses and is to end the people's complaints.
The commentary's brand marks a bearer so it can be recognized; Zechariah says even horses' bells will bear an inscription of holiness to YHWH, extending the Name-mark to animal equipment.

row.basis: the prophet and his children as signs
row.note: The commentary calls each created kind a sign; Isaiah says he and the children YHWH gave him are signs and portents in Israel, making human lives and names part of the message.

row.basis: called by name and claimed as God's own
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies its bearer; YHWH says he has called Israel by name and that Israel is his, directly joining recognition with belonging.
The commentary defines a name as what makes a being known; YHWH tells Moses, “I know you by name,” giving that definition a direct biblical use.
The commentary says a name is a mark by which its bearer is known; God promises deliverance to the one who knows his name, linking recognition with protection.

row.basis: pardon requested for the sake of God's name
row.note: The commentary gives the invocation “O Allah, forgive me”; the psalmist asks YHWH to pardon his iniquity for the sake of YHWH's name. This is Hebrew WLC numbering; the petition is commonly numbered Psalm 25:11 in English.

row.basis: service and oath in the divine name
row.note: The commentary joins the name with worship and calling; Deuteronomy commands Israel to fear and serve YHWH and swear by his name.

row.basis: call on the Name and tell its deeds among nations
row.note: The commentary says a good name circulates among people; this hymn joins calling on YHWH's name with making his deeds known among the peoples.

row.basis: creation praises the Name because it was created
row.note: The commentary joins the divine name to all created kinds as signs; the psalm says creation praises YHWH's name because he commanded and it was created.

row.basis: people fail to read creation's sign
row.note: The commentary says created things make their Lord knowable; Wisdom says some observe the works but fail to recognize their maker, a specific failure to read the sign.

row.basis: stars answer when their maker calls
row.note: The commentary says each created kind is a sign and names make things recognizable; Baruch pictures stars answering their maker's call and shining for him, giving creation a responsive voice.

row.basis: God as maker and Lord of the whole world
row.note: The commentary reads al-ʿālamīn as the created realm belonging to its Lord; Paul identifies the unknown God as maker of the world and Lord of heaven and earth.
The commentary says creation bears signs of its Lord; Paul says God did not leave himself without witness, giving rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness.
The commentary says gods named by people may be only names; Paul distinguishes so-called gods from the one God acknowledged by believers.
The commentary calls Allah the greatest name and asks whether any equal deserves God's name; Peter says no other name under heaven is given by which people must be saved.

row.basis: every knee bows at Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary joins the highest name with worship; Paul says every knee bows at the name of Jesus, showing what exaltation of the Name entails.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
row.note: The commentary connects divine naming with worship and calling; Paul adds that every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord, the verbal response to the name's exaltation.
The commentary treats a name as the mark that identifies a bearer; Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name, giving the name a protective and communal role.

row.basis: forgiveness proclaimed in Jesus' name to all nations
row.note: The commentary includes calling Allah for forgiveness and names Allah with mercy; Jesus commissions repentance and forgiveness to be proclaimed in his name to all nations.

row.basis: all who call on YHWH's name are saved
row.note: The commentary includes invocation of Allah's name; Joel promises deliverance to everyone who calls on YHWH's name. Hebrew WLC numbering places this at Joel 3:5, often Joel 2:32 in English.
The commentary explains “semiyy” as an equal worthy of God's name; the song asks who among the gods is like YHWH, giving a direct biblical formulation of divine incomparability.

row.basis: none like YHWH, whose name is great
row.note: The commentary says Allah is the greatest name and has no equal namesake; Jeremiah says none is like YHWH and that his name is great in might.

row.basis: signs and wonders make a name
row.note: The commentary joins the name as a sign with creation as signs of the Lord; Jeremiah says God performed signs and wonders and made a name for himself, explicitly bringing the two images together.

row.basis: the people bear YHWH's called name before nations
row.note: The commentary treats a name as a sign identifying its bearer; the nations see that YHWH's name is called over Israel and fear them.

row.basis: midrash on Adam naming the animals
row.note: The commentary recalls Adam receiving names; the midrash expands Genesis's naming scene by treating Adam's naming of the creatures as an act of discernment, making the name's relation to what is named explicit.

row.basis: the divine name as a promise of presence
row.note: The commentary says a name is more than an arbitrary label and is spoken in invocation; this midrash reads God's answer to Moses as a pledge of presence with Israel in its affliction.
The commentary pairs God's name with mercy; the continuation says YHWH forgives iniquity yet does not simply clear guilt, preserving the judgment side of the name-and-mercy formula.

The Qur'anic word al-ʿālamīn and Syriac ʿālmā (“world”) appear to be related forms, though the commentary's ʿ-l-m labels do not prove cognacy. The Peshitta says the world was made through the Word yet did not know him, a specific counterpoint to the commentary's world as a sign by which its Lord is known.

row.basis: visible religious signs used for public honor
row.note: The commentary says a sign makes a bearer recognizable and notes that a good name can spread among people; Jesus criticizes enlarging phylacteries to be seen by others, showing how a visible religious mark can become a bid for reputation.

row.basis: a public name written on the forehead
row.note: The commentary treats a mark or name as a readable identity; Revelation places the name “Babylon the Great” on the woman's forehead, using inscription to expose a rival allegiance.

row.basis: a title written on robe and thigh
row.note: The commentary develops names as visible marks of identity; the rider's garment bears “King of kings and Lord of lords,” a public inscription of authority.

row.basis: a written name no one knows
row.note: The commentary says a name makes its bearer recognizable; Revelation's rider bears a written name known only to himself, preserving a counter-reading in which the sign marks identity without making it public.
The commentary defines a name as what lets one know its bearer; Jacob asks the divine wrestler's name but receives the reply “Why do you ask my name?”, setting a limit on that knowledge.

row.basis: a place named after seeing God
row.note: The commentary says a name is a sign by which a reality is recognized; Jacob names the place Peniel after seeing God face to face, turning an encounter into a place-name.

row.basis: gök cisimleri; vakitler, günler ve yıllar
row.note: Yorum Ay'ın konaklarını yılların sayısı ve hesap için kurulmuş vakit işaretleri sayar; Yaratılış'ta ışıklar gök kubbeye mevsimler, günler ve yıllar için işaret olsun diye yerleştirilir. Ayet, bu takvim işlevini yaratılış düzenine bağlar.

row.basis: büyük ve küçük ışık; gündüz-gece yönetimi
row.note: Yorum gündüzü güneşin doğuşundan batışına, Ay'ı da ayrı bir göksel zaman işaretine bağlar; Yaratılış büyük ışığın gündüze, küçük ışığın geceye hükmetmesiyle bu iki görevi ayırır.

row.basis: Ay mevsimler için; güneş batışını bilir
row.note: Yorumdaki Ay'ın menzilleriyle hesap ve doğup batan güneş aynı ayette yan yana gelir; Mezmur Ay'ı belirlenmiş vakitler için, güneşi de kendi batış vaktini bilen bir gök cismi olarak anlatır.

row.basis: Ay; bayram vakitleri ve ayın azalması
row.note: Yorum hilalleri ve Ay'ın konaklarını insan vakitlerinin hesabı sayar; Sirak Ay'ı bayram vakitlerini belirleyen ve devrinde eksilen bir işaret olarak niteler.
Yorumdaki hilal ile Ay menzili, Ay'ın ölçülü görünüşüne dayanır; Sirak ayın adını Aydan türetir ve onun evreler boyunca büyüyüp küçülmesini anlatır.

row.basis: güneşin doğu-batı kapıları ve gün uzunluğu
row.note: Yorum güneşin doğuşu ile batışı arasını gün diye tarif eder; 1 Enoch'un gökbilim kitabı güneşin doğudaki kapılardan çıkıp batıdakilerden girmesini ve buna göre değişen günleri düzenler.

Yorumda Ay'ın menzilleri, yükselen hilal ve hesap birlikte işlenir; 1 Enoch Ay'ı kendi göksel yolu, doğuşu ve batışı olan küçük ışık olarak ele alır. Bu, menzillerin astronomik bir tasavvur içinde okunmasını sağlar.
Yorum hilalleri halk için vakit işaretleri sayar; Mişna'da yeni Ay'ı gören tanıkların haber vermesi, görünen hilalin kamusal takvimi başlatan işlevini somutlaştırır.
Yorum ufuktan biraz yükselmiş hilalin görünen biçimini özellikle açar; Mişna, Rabban Gamliel'in tanıklara gördükleri Ay'ın biçimini sorabilmek için Ay tasvirleri kullandığını anlatır.
Yorum hilalleri insanlara vakit ölçüsü yapar; Sayılar'da bayramlar ve yeni aylarda boru çalınması, bu göksel zamanın toplu ibadette kullanılan işaret oluşunu gösterir.
Yorumun hilal-vakit bağına karşılık Mezmur, yeni Ayda ve bayram dolunayında boru çalınmasını emreder. Bu, Ay devrinin yalnız gözlem değil litürjik düzen kurduğunu ekler.

row.basis: güneş, Ay, işaretler, günler ve yıllar
row.note: Yorum Ay'ın hesabını ve güneşin gündüzünü yaratılmış düzen sayar; Jubileler güneş, Ay ve yıldızların gündüz-geceyi ayırmak, işaretleri, günleri ve yılları göstermek üzere yaratıldığını söyler.

Yorum Ay menzillerini yılların sayısı ve hesap için olumlu bir düzen diye sunar; Jubileler'in bu kısmı Ay gözleminin bayram ve mevsim hesabını saptıracağını savunur. Aynı göksel hesap konusunda farklı bir takvim öğretisi verir.
Yorum güneş ve Aya secde etmeyip onları yaratana kulluk etmeyi öne çıkarır; Tesniye göğe bakanın güneş, Ay ve gök ordusuna kapılıp onlara tapınmasını açıkça yasaklar.

row.basis: güneşe, Aya veya gök ordusuna kulluk
row.note: Yorum güneşe tapmayı doğru yoldan alıkonma ile bağlar; Tesniye bu kulluğu İsrail için yasaklanmış bir ihlal ve yargı konusu olarak tarif eder.
Yorum İbrahim'in yıldız, Ay ve güneşe yönelip onların batışını sınamasıyla göksel tapınmayı tartışır; Eyüp, parlayan güneşe ya da görkemle ilerleyen Aya bakmayı olası bir sapma olarak sorgular.
Yorumdaki secde yasağı, gök cismine yönelen bedensel kulluğu dışlar; Eyüp'te güneş ve Aya bakışın ardından kalbin gizlice ayartılması ve ele öpücük gönderilmesi, bu tür bir kült jestini adlandırır.
Yorum göksel ışıklara kulluğu onların yaratıcısına kulluktan ayırır; Eyüp, böyle bir güneş-Ay kültünü yukarıdaki Tanrı'ya sadakatsizlik sayar.

row.basis: güneşe, Aya ve gök ordusuna tütsü
row.note: Yorum Hüdhüd'ün haberindeki halkın güneşe secdesini aktarır; Yoşiya'nın reformunda görevden alınan kâhinler güneşe, Aya ve gök ordusuna tütsü sunmaktadır.
Yorumdaki güneşe tapınma soyut bir hata değil kamusal bir kulluk biçimidir; Yoşiya'nın tapınak girişindeki güneş atlarını ve arabalarını kaldırması, ayrı bir somut güneş kültü pratiğini gösterir.
Yorum güneşe secde eden halktan söz eder; Hezekiel tapınak avlusunda yüzleri doğuya dönük erkeklerin güneşe eğildiğini görür. Yön, beden ve ibadet eylemi iki sahneyi özellikle yakınlaştırır.
Yorumda göksel ışıklara kulluk yol kaybıyla sonuçlanır; Yeremya'nın yargı tasvirinde ölülerin kemikleri, sevdikleri, hizmet ettikleri ve önünde eğildikleri güneş, Ay ve gök ordusunun önüne serilir.
Yorumdaki güneş kültü Allah'a kullukla çatışır; Sefanya damlarda gök ordusuna secde eden ve aynı anda YHWH adına ant içen senkretik ibadeti mahkûm eder.
Yorum güneş ve Aya secdeyi yaratıcıya kulluktan ayırır; Bilgelik, göğün ışıklarını ve yıldız çevrimini dünyayı yöneten tanrılar sayanları doğrudan eleştirir.
Yorum İbrahim'in yüzünü göklerin ve yerin yaratıcısına çevirmesiyle gök cisimlerini aşar; Bilgelik, yaratılmışların güzelliğinden onların Yaratıcısının anlaşılması gerektiğini savunur.

row.basis: güneş, Ay ve yıldızların buyrukla seyri
row.note: Yorum Ay menzillerini hesap için kurulmuş, güneş ve Ayı yaratılmış işaretler sayar; Mektup güneş, Ay ve yıldızların parlak ama gönderildikleri görevde itaatkâr varlıklar olduğunu söyler.
Yorum secdeyi güneş ve Aydan onların yaratıcısına çevirir; Nehemya'da göklerin ve bütün ordusunun yaratıcısı YHWH'dir ve gök ordusu ona secde eder.
Yorumda güneş ve Aya kul olunmaz; Mezmur güneş ile Aya kendilerinin YHWH'yi övmesi emrini verir. Böylece ışıklar ibadet alan değil, öven yaratıklar olur.

row.ref: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men 62
row.note: Yorum göksel ışıkları secde edilecek varlıklar olmaktan çıkarır; Üç Gencin İlahisi güneş ve Aya Rab'bi kutsama çağrısı yapar ve onları litürjik özne olarak konumlandırır.
Yorum 41:37'nin çizgisinde güneş ve Aya değil yaratana secde eder; Vahiy yargı saatinde göğü, yeri, denizi ve pınarları yaratana tapınma çağrısı yapar.
Yorum göksel varlıklara kulluğu bırakıp yaratana yönelmeyi ister; Pavlus ile Barnaba kendilerine yönelen kültü reddedip göğü, yeri, denizi ve içindekileri yapan diri Tanrı'ya dönmeyi buyurur.
Yorum günü güneşin doğuşundan batışına kadar sürdürür ve kulluğu güneşten Allah'a çevirir; Mezmur aynı iki ufuk arasını YHWH adının övülme zamanı yapar.
Yorum güneşe kulluğu reddeder; İşaya güneşin doğduğu yerden batıya kadar YHWH'den başka olmadığını ilan eder. Güneşin günlük yayı burada tektanrıcılık iddiasını taşır.
Yorum güneşin gündüzünü ve Ay'ın belirlenmiş menzillerini bir gök düzeni içinde anlatır; Yeremya güneşi gündüz ışığına, Ay ve yıldızları gece düzenine verenin YHWH olduğunu söyler.

row.basis: güneşin doğup batması ve yerine dönmesi
row.note: Yorum günün süresini güneşin doğuşu ve batışıyla çizer; Vaiz güneşin doğup battığını ve yeniden doğacağı yere yöneldiğini söyler. Bu, aynı günlük devri yaratıcı-kult karşıtlığı olmadan kaydeder.

row.basis: güneşin gök altında devri ve ısısı
row.note: Yorum gök küresini güneşin günlük hareketiyle doldurur; Mezmur güneşin bir uçtan çıkıp göklerin öbür ucuna devrini ve ısısından saklı hiçbir şey kalmamasını söyler.
Yorum göksel ışıkları yaratıcıya bağımlı sayar; Eyüp Tanrı'nın güneşe buyurup onu doğmaz kılabildiğini ve yıldızları mühürlediğini söyler.

Yorumda öğle, güneşin dikildiği ve gölgenin neredeyse kaybolduğu andır; Yeşu anlatısında güneş göğün ortasında durur, Ay da duraklar. Bu, güneş hareketinin olağanüstü biçimde askıya alınmış bir anlatısıdır.
Yorum öğle güneşinin dikilmesini göksel bir an olarak işler; Habakkuk'un ilahisinde ilahî savaşın ışığı karşısında güneş ve Ay kendi konutlarında durur.
Yorum öğleyi gölgenin neredeyse düşmediği güneş anıyla açıklar; Hezekiya kıssasında YHWH'nin işaretiyle güneş saatindeki gölge on basamak geri gider. Gölge, göksel zamanın görünen ölçüsü olur.
Yorum semayı üstte durup gölge eden şey diye açıklar; Mezmur koruyan YHWH'yi kişinin sağında gölge olarak adlandırır. Göksel örtü imgesi koruma ilişkisine dönüşür.

row.basis: gündüz güneşi ve gece Ayı zarar vermez
row.note: Yorumda güneş ve Ay yaratılmış gök işaretleridir; Mezmur güneşin gündüz, Ayın gece kişiye vurmayacağını söyler. Bu, ikisini ilahî korumaya tâbi güçler olarak çizer.
Yorum güneş tepede iken gölgenin kaybolmasını ve göğün gölge etmesini yan yana koyar; İşaya öğlenin ortasında gece gibi gölge yapılmasını, sığınmacıların korunması için ister.

row.basis: öğle vakti güneşten parlak göksel ışık
row.note: Yorum öğle güneşi, yol ve hidayeti bir araya getirir; Pavlus, yolda öğlen vakti güneşten daha parlak bir ışığın çevresini sardığını anlatır. Işık burada yön değiştiren çağrının aracı olur.

row.ref: Jacob of Serugh, Homily on the Youths of Ephesus
row.note: Yorumun mağara sahnesinde gençler, üzerlerinden kayan güneş ve Allah'ın hidayeti birlikte anılır; Yakup'un Homilisi Efesli Gençlerin mağaraya sığınmasını ve ilahî korumayı anlatan Süryanice Hristiyan paralelidir.

Yorum Hüdhüd'ün güneşe secde eden halka kadın hükümdar bulduğunu bildirir; Krallar'da Seba kraliçesi Süleyman'ın, YHWH adıyla bağlantılı hikmetini sınamak için gelir. Ortak hükümdar karşılaşması, göksel kült ayrıntısı olmadan anlatılır.

Yorumdaki kadın hükümdar ve halkı güneşe secde eder; Krallar'da Seba kraliçesi Süleyman'ı kral yapan YHWH'yi kutsar. Bu, ortak figür çevresinde ibadetin yönünü tersine çeviren belirgin bir anlatı farkıdır.

Yorum B004'te السماء'yı üstte duran gök diye açıklar; Yaratılış gök kubbeye שָׁמַיִם adını verir. Arapça samāʾ ile İbranice šāmayim akraba gök terimleridir; bu satır yalnız ortak gök adlandırmasını taşır.

Yorum B001'de Allah adının yanında güneş için ilāha denilen ikincil kullanımı kaydeder; Tesniye'nin güneş-Ay tapınma yasağı YHWH ʾĕlōheḵā adına bağlanır. Arapça ilāh ile İbranice ʾĕlōah/ʾĕlōhîm akrabadır; İbranice bağlam güneş anlamı vermez.

row.basis: İbrahim; güneş, Ay ve düzenli gök
row.note: Yorumdaki İbrahim batan yıldız, Ay ve güneşi Rabb saymaktan vazgeçer; Josephus İbrahim'in güneş, Ay ve gök cisimlerinin kendi güçleriyle değil tek Yaratıcı'nın buyruğuyla hareket ettiğini ilan ettiğini söyler. Bu, İbrahim'e atfedilen farklı bir astral putperestlik reddidir.

Yorum İbrahim'in göksel ışıkları sınayıp yaratıcısına yönelmesini işler; Maimonides İbrahim'in sürekli dönen gök küresinin kendi kendine tanrı olamayacağını düşünerek tek yöneticiyi kavradığını anlatır.

Yorum B001 yevmi güneşin doğuşu-batışı arasındaki süre olarak tarif eder; Yaratılış ışığa yôm adını verir ve akşamla sabahı bir günün çerçevesine koyar. Arapça yawm ile İbranice yôm akraba zaman adlarıdır, fakat ayetin gün sınırı yoruma göre farklıdır.
Yorum günü güneş doğuşundan batışına kadar tarif eder; Levililer Şabat'ı akşamdan akşama tutmayı buyurur. Aynı gün hesabında farklı bir sınır koyar.

row.basis: B017 q-w-m; İbranice qûmî ve ışık
row.note: Yorum B017 q-w-m ailesini öğle güneşinin dikilişiyle ve dosdoğru yolla yan yana getirir; İşaya'da qûmî, ışığın gelişiyle birlikte "kalk" çağrısıdır. Arapça qāma ile İbranice qûm akrabadır, fakat ayet öğle etimolojisi kurmaz.

Yorum B007'de enʿamta kökünün Ay menzili anlamını da kaydeder; Mezmur YHWH'nin nōʿamını, yani hoşluğu/lütfunu halkın üzerinde ister. İbranice nōʿam Arapça niʿma ile akrabadır; Mezmurda Ay menzili anlamı yoktur.
Yorum semayı üstte durup gölge eden şey, âlemi de gök küresi diye anlatır; Mezmur Tanrı'nın gökleri bir çadır gibi yaydığını söyler. Bu, göğün kapsayan örtü imgesini verir.

row.basis: gökleri perde ve çadır gibi yayma
row.note: Yorumdaki gök küresi her şeyi içine alan üst örtüdür; İşaya Tanrı'nın gökleri perde gibi gerip oturulacak çadır gibi yaydığını söyler. Metin, küre tanımı değil kapsayan gök tasviridir.
Yorum öğleyi gündüzün terazisinin dengesi olarak anlatır; Mezmur doğruluğun ışık, hakkın da öğle parlaklığı gibi ortaya çıkacağını söyler. Öğle, doğruluğu görünür kılan ölçü olur.

row.basis: doğruların yolu ve tam gün ışığı
row.note: Yorum dosdoğru yol ile öğle güneşinin dengesini yan yana getirir; Özdeyişler doğruların yolunu gün tamamlanıncaya dek artan şafak ışığına benzetir. Yol ile gündüz ışığını birleştirir, fakat gölge etimolojisi ileri sürmez.

Yorumda hidayet ve yol, güneşin en dik anıyla karşılaştırılır; İşaya'da halk duvar arar ve öğlen alacakaranlıktaymış gibi sendeleyerek yolunu bulamaz. Gündüz ışığı ile yön bulma arasındaki ters imgeyi sağlar.
Yorum öğleyi güneşin tepede, gölgenin en az olduğu düzenli an sayar; Amos yargı gününde güneşi öğlen batırıp yeryüzünü gündüz karartacağını bildirir. Olağan göksel ölçüyü tersine çevirir.
Yorum göğü gölge eden üst varlık olarak tarif eder ve mağarada güneşten korunma sahnesini anar; İşaya'da gündüz sıcağına karşı gölge veren bir sığınak tasarlanır.
Yorum günün göksel devrini Fâtiha'nın kulluk dili yanında işler; Mezmur akşam, sabah ve öğlen yakarıp sesini yükselten kişiyi anlatır. Öğleyi günlük yönelişin belirli vakti yapar.
Yorum güneşin dikildiği öğle anını belirler; Mişna sabah duasının öğleye kadar söylenebileceği vakit sınırını verir. Güneşin gün içindeki ortası burada litürjik bir sınırdır.
Yorum hilalleri insanların vakitleri için işaret sayar; Babil Talmudu yeni Ay görüldüğünde söylenen kutsamayı düzenler. Hilalin gözlemini rabbanî ibadet pratiğine taşır.

row.basis: İbrahim, göğe bakış ve yıldızlarla soy vaadi
row.note: Yorum İbrahim'in yıldızı Rab sayıp batışıyla ondan yüz çevirdiğini anlatır; Yaratılış'ta aynı kişi göğe bakar, yıldızları sayması istenir ve onlar soyunun vaadi olur. Yıldız, ilahlık sınaması yerine vaat işareti olur.

Yorum İbrahim'i gök cisimlerinin doğuş-batışı üzerinden yaratıcıya yöneltir; Philo, Keldani gök gözleminden hareket eden İbrahim'in duyulur göğü aşarak nedenine yöneldiğini yorumlar. Aynı geçişi felsefî bir dilde kurar.

Yorum İbrahim'in göksel Rab adaylarını reddetmesini putperestlikten ayrılış olarak verir; Midraş, İbrahim'in babasının putlarını kırıp onların güçsüzlüğünü açığa çıkardığı ayrı bir reddediş hikâyesi anlatır.

row.basis: yanan saray ve sahibini arayan İbrahim
row.note: Yorum İbrahim'in yüzünü göklerin ve yerin yaratıcısına çevirmesiyle biter; Midraş, dünyayı yanan bir saraya benzetip İbrahim'in onun sahibini sormasını anlatır. Kozmostan sahibine geçişi yorumlar.
Yorum İbrahim'in göksel kulluğu bırakıp Rabbinden hidayet istemesini anlatır; Jubileler'de genç Abram yeryüzünün putperestlik hatasını kavrar, putlardan ayrılır ve her şeyin Yaratıcısına dua eder.

Yorumdaki kadın hükümdar Süleyman'ın hüküm sürdüğü güneşe tapan halka bağlıdır; İsa'nın sözü Güney kraliçesini Süleyman'ın hikmetini dinlemek için gelen ve yargıda tanıklık edecek bir figür olarak yeniden kullanır.

row.basis: Babanın güneşi iyi ve kötü üzerine doğurtması
row.note: Yorum güneşi tapınılacak değil yaratılmış ışık sayar; İsa gökteki Baba'nın güneşini iyi ile kötü üzerine doğurttuğunu söyler. Güneşin kendi iradesi değil Tanrı'nın bağışı olduğu vurgulanır.

Yorumda yolunu bulma, güneşe secdeden ayrılma ve hidayetle karşıtlanır; İsa ışık varken yürümeyi, karanlıkta yürüyenin nereye gittiğini bilmemesini söyler. Fiziksel ışık-yol imgesi ahlâkî yön bulmaya taşınır.

row.basis: yüksekten doğuş ve barış yoluna yöneltme
row.note: Yorum gündoğumu, gök ve hidayet kelimelerini birlikte tutar; Zekeriya'nın ilahisi yüksekten doğacak ışığın karanlıktakileri aydınlatıp ayakları barış yoluna yönelteceğini söyler.
Yorum gök örtüsünü, güneşin sağa-sola kaydığı mağara korumasını hatırlatır; Vahiy'de kurtulmuşlara güneşin ya da kavurucu sıcağın artık vurmayacağı vaat edilir.

Yorum güneş ve Aya değil onları yaratana secde edilmesini söyler; Romalılar, insanların Yaratıcı yerine yaratılmışa kulluk etmesini yanlış yöneliş olarak niteler. Ayet göksel örnekleri saymaz, ama yaratıcı-yaratık ayrımını açıklar.

Yorum güneş kültünü gerçek kulluktan ayırır; Tertullian, doğuya yönelen dua yüzünden Hristiyanların güneşe taptığı yolundaki suçlamayı ele alıp reddeder. Geç antik dönemde aynı ayrımın polemiksel bir okumasını verir.
Yorum gündüzü güneşin doğuşundan batışına kadar açıklar; Mezmur, güneşi gündüze hükmetsin diye yapanı litürjik olarak över. Güneşin devri, yaratılmış bir görev olarak ifade edilir.
Yorum Ay'ı insan vakitleri için menzillere ayrılmış ışık sayar; Mezmur Ay ve yıldızların geceye hükmetmesini aynı yaratıcıya hamdın gerekçesi yapar.
Yorum güneşin doğuşuyla günü başlatır ve gök ışığını kulluk nesnesinden ayırır; Sirak, güneşin doğuşunda görünen ihtişamını En Yüce'nin yapılmış aracı olarak niteler.
Yorum öğleyi güneşin tepede dikildiği, gölgenin en azaldığı an sayar; Sirak doğrudan öğle vaktinde güneşin ülkeyi kavurduğunu ve sıcağına kimin dayanabileceğini sorar.
Yorum güneşin günlük hareketini göksel düzenin parçası sayar; Sirak güneşi yapan Rabbin buyruğuyla onun kendi seyrinde hızlandığını söyler. Işığın yaratıcıya bağlılığı belirgindir.

Yorum gök cisimlerine değil yaratana yönelmeyi ister; Baruk'ta Tanrı ışığı gönderir, yıldızları çağırır, onlar sevinçle karşılık verir ve onu yapan için parlar. Bu, göksel ışıkları itaat eden yaratıklar olarak gösterir.

row.basis: güneş ve Ay tasvirlerinin put sayılması
row.note: Yorum güneşe ve Aya secdeyi reddeder; Mişna, üzerinde güneş ya da Ay biçimi bulunan kapların putperestlikle ilişkisi yüzünden ortadan kaldırılmasını buyurur. Rabbanî hukuk, gök cismi imgesinin kült nesnesine dönüşmesi sorununu somutlaştırır.
Yorum güneşe tapmayı sapma olarak anlatır; Krallar'da İsrail'in YHWH buyruklarını bırakıp bütün gök ordusuna tapması ve Baal'e kulluk etmesi, bu sapmayı tarihsel bir topluluk pratiği olarak sunar.
Yorumda göksel ışıklara kulluk gerçek Rabbe kulluğun karşıtıdır; Manasse, gök ordusuna tapıp hizmet eder ve onlar için altarlar kurar.
Yorum güneşe tapmanın yoldan alıkoyduğunu söyler; İstefanos, İsrail'in gök ordusuna kulluk etmesine Tanrı'nın onları teslim ettiğini aktarır. Gök kültünü ilahî terk ediliş diliyle değerlendirir.
Yorumdaki yıldız-Ay-güneş Rab adaylarının reddi yanında, İstefanos'un aktardığı gelenek Moloch çadırı ile Rephan adlı tanrının yıldızını taşınan tapınma imgeleri arasında sayar.

row.basis: kentin güneşe ve Aya ihtiyaç duymaması
row.note: Yorum güneş ve Ayın yaratılmış ışıklar, tapınmanın ise yaratana ait olduğunu vurgular; Vahiy'in yeni kentinde Tanrı'nın görkemi ve Kuzu ışık verdiği için güneşe ya da Aya ihtiyaç kalmaz. Göksel ışıkların son kaynak olmadığını eskatolojik biçimde söyler.

Yorum mağaradaki gençlerin üstünden güneşin kaymasını hidayetle bitirir; İşaya'da halkı ne güneş ne yakıcı rüzgâr vurur ve merhamet eden onları su kaynaklarına yönlendirir. Koruyan gölge ile yol gösterme aynı vaatte birleşir.
Yorum güneşe ve Aya secdeyi onların yaratıcısına yönelişle değiştirir; İşaya'nın eskatolojik kenti için gündüz güneşinin ve Ay ışığının yerini YHWH'nin kalıcı ışığı alır.
Yorum günün başlangıcını güneşin doğuşuyla kurar; Tanrı Eyüp'e sabaha buyurup ona yerini bildirip bildirmediğini sorar. Gün doğumunun insan değil yaratıcı buyruğunda olduğunu vurgular.
Yorum gündüzün iki ufkunu güneşe değil Allah'a kullukla birleştirir; Malaki Rabbin adının güneş doğuşundan batışına uluslar arasında yüce olduğunu ve her yerde ona sunu getirildiğini bildirir.

row.basis: sabahı karanlıktan çıkaran, gündüzü gece yapan Yaratıcı
row.note: Yorum göksel düzeni ve hidayeti yaratana bağlar; Amos Ülker ve Orion'u yapanın derin karanlığı sabaha çevirdiğini, gündüzü de geceye kararttığını ilan eder. Gün ışığı üzerindeki kudreti yıldızların yaratıcısına verir.

row.basis: bilinmeyen yolda körleri yönetmek; karanlığı ışık yapmak
row.note: Yorum yol, hidayet ve göksel ışığı aynı sahnede tutar; İşaya Tanrı'nın körleri bilmedikleri yolda götürüp önlerindeki karanlığı ışığa ve eğri yerleri düzlüğe çevireceğini söyler. Yol bulmanın ışıkla ilişkisini açıklaştırır.

Yorum İbrahim'in Rab hidayet etmezse sapmış kavimden olacağını, Fâtiha'nın da dosdoğru yol istediğini hatırlatır; İşaya'da bir şose "Kutsallık Yolu" adını alır ve o yolda yürüyenlerin sapmayacağı söylenir.

Yorum öğleyi güneşin en dik ve gündüzün dengeli anı sayar; Markos İsa'nın çarmıha gerilişinde altıncı saatten dokuzuncu saate kadar bütün ülkeye karanlık çöktüğünü anlatır. Öğle ışığını tersine çeviren bir anlatı imgesidir.

row.basis: yeni Ay ve Şabat günü ziyaret
row.note: Yorum hilalleri insanlara vakit işareti yapar; Şunemli kadının hikâyesinde kocası, peygambere gitmek için neden "bugün" denildiğini sorar ve günün ne yeni Ay ne de Şabat olduğunu belirtir. Yeni Ayın düzenli dinî ziyaret vakti olduğunu gösterir.

row.basis: Ay ışığının güneş ışığı gibi olması
row.note: Yorum güneşin öğle parlaklığını Ayın ayrı ışığıyla karşılaştırır; İşaya'nın iyileşme tasvirinde Ayın ışığı güneşinki gibi, güneşin ışığı da kat kat parlak olur. İki ışığı ilahî onarımın kozmik işareti yapar.

row.basis: güneş doğmadan şükür ve sabah duası
row.note: Yorum günün güneş doğuşuyla başlayan devrini kulluk dili yanında verir; Bilgelik, Tanrı'ya şükretmek için güneşten önce kalkmak ve sabah ışığında yardım istemek gerektiğini söyler.
Yorum semayı üstte gölge eden şey diye açıklar ve mağara gençlerinin güneşten korunmasını anar; Mezmur En Yüce'nin sığınağında oturanın Her Şeye Gücü Yeten'in gölgesinde konakladığını söyler.

row.basis: bayram, yeni Ay ve Şabat üzerindeki hüküm
row.note: Yorum Ayı toplumsal vakit işareti sayar; Pavlus'un mektubu yiyecek, bayram, yeni Ay ve Şabat uygulamaları hakkında kimsenin hüküm vermemesini ister. Yeni Ayın erken Hristiyan tartışmasında tanınan takvim terimi oluşunu gösterir.

Yorum Ay menzillerini yılların hesabı için olumlu bir işaret sayar; Pavlus muhataplarının günleri, ayları, mevsimleri ve yılları gözetmesinden kaygı duyar. Buradaki uygulamaların tam referenti tartışmalıdır; satır yalnız farklı bir takvimsel kaygıyı işaret eder.
Moses' hands become heavy, and Aaron and Hur hold them up from opposite sides; this is the commentary's concrete image of a failing body steadied by people on both sides.
The wilderness wanderers cry to the LORD in distress and are delivered; it supplies a narrative form for the move from a stranded traveler to nasta'inu, asking for aid.
After their cry, God leads the wanderers by a straight way to a settled place; it closely joins requested help to ihdina and the straight route.

row.basis: q-w-m B002; arise and hold a hand
