row.note: Genesis tells Hagar to arise (Hebrew qumi) and to hold the boy's hand in the wilderness; the genuine q-w-m cognate joins the source's uprightness to hand-held aid.
The angel tells exhausted Elijah to arise and eat because the journey is too much for him; Hebrew qum gives the source's q-w-m standing image a traveler-specific setting of divine provision.
Strengthened by the food, Elijah travels forty days to Horeb; this realizes the commentary's sequence in which help restores a body for the road.
God gives power to the faint and strength to the powerless, directly matching the source's weak traveler who cannot proceed unaided.
Those who wait for the LORD receive renewed strength and walk without fainting; it gives the commentary's aided and composed walking an explicit divine outcome.
The speaker's words uphold one who stumbles and make weak knees firm; this supplies a verbal and social analogue to the bodily support in the commentary.
Job says he was feet to the lame; the figure makes another person capable of movement, as the source's helpers make a weak walker mobile.

row.basis: holding the right hand; divine help
row.note: God takes Israel's right hand and says, I help you; it fuses the commentary's hand-supported traveler with its explicit request for help.
God promises to strengthen, help, and uphold with the righteous right hand; the three actions closely mirror aid becoming upright stability.
The LORD supports all who fall and raises those bowed down; it gives a divine counterpart to the source's movement from collapse toward an upright body.
Though the righteous fall, they are not cast down because the LORD holds their hand; the text makes support at the moment of failed footing the reason for recovery.
Angels bear the faithful person on their hands lest a foot strike a stone; it is a particularly close scriptural image for support that protects a traveler's gait.
The pilgrim identifies the LORD as the source of help; beside nasta'inu it makes aid a prayerful reliance rather than merely an abstract resource.
The helper will not let the pilgrim's foot slip; it makes the aid of the preceding verse legible in the commentary's terms of stable walking.
God's everlasting arms are beneath Israel; this gives the source's image of being borne from the sides a protective, sustaining underside.
The prophetic command to strengthen weak hands and make feeble knees firm directly shares the commentary's debilitated body before it can walk well.

row.basis: highway; walkers do not go astray
row.note: The Way of Holiness is a highway on which even inexperienced walkers do not go astray; it brings bodily frailty and a protected route into one prophetic scene.

row.basis: this is the way; right or left
row.note: A voice tells the traveler, This is the way, walk in it, when turning right or left; it answers the commentary's swaying walker with directional guidance.
God leads the returning people by watercourses on a straight path where they will not stumble; this is an unusually close pairing of divine leading, straightness, and safe feet.

row.basis: leading the blind; rough ground level
row.note: God leads blind people on an unknown way and makes rough places level; it extends the source's guide beyond a front-runner to aid for those unable to navigate alone.
The LORD continually guides, satisfies need in parched places, and makes the bones strong; this joins the commentary's need, support, and restored movement.
Acknowledging God results in paths made straight; it is a concise wisdom analogue to the communal petition for the straight path.
The teacher leads the pupil in the way of wisdom and paths of uprightness; it joins route-guidance to the moral and bodily verticality heard in mustaqim.

row.basis: unhampered steps; no stumble in running
row.note: The instructed walker has unhampered steps and does not stumble even when running; it gives a contrast to the source's impaired gait and its recovery.

row.basis: do not turn right or left
row.note: The command not to swerve right or left and to keep the foot from evil makes the commentary's literal side-to-side wavering an ethical path image.
The proverb says that one who hastens with the feet misses the way; it supplies a wisdom contrast to the source's calm, non-panicked good walking.
The LORD goes before Israel in a pillar to lead the way; it brings together the commentary's guide, road, and qiyam-as-pillar imagery.
The shepherd seeks the lost, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak; it converts the source's individual supporting act into pastoral responsibility.
The source labels na'budu with the 'ayn-b-d root; Isaiah calls the chosen eved God's servant and says God upholds him, a cognate service-and-support pairing.
The source labels malik with m-l-k; Isaiah's melek is the cognate king term and names the LORD as king who saves us, tying sovereignty to needed deliverance.

row.basis: help the weak against the mighty
row.note: Asa asks God to help the powerless against the mighty because none is like God in helping; this makes the source's request for aid an explicit prayer from weakness.

row.basis: servants' eyes toward a master's hand
row.note: The psalm likens its dependence on the LORD's mercy to servants watching their master's hand; it gives the juxtaposition of na'budu and nasta'inu a relational image.
When one person falls, the other lifts the companion; it supplies the social logic behind the source's weak traveler being held rather than left alone.

row.basis: traveler seeks someone who knows the road
row.note: Raphael says he knows the roads to Media and has traveled them often; Tobias's journey turns the request for guidance into finding a competent companion.
Wisdom guides the fleeing righteous person on straight paths; this is a Jewish-scriptural personification of the guidance sought in ihdina.

row.basis: level ground so Israel walks safely
row.note: God levels mountains and fills valleys so Israel may walk safely; it develops the source's straightened route as a bodily safe passage.

row.basis: traveler's prayer for leading and safe arrival
row.note: The Tefillat ha-Derekh asks God to lead, guide, sustain, and bring the traveler to the destination in peace; it is a direct Jewish liturgical analogue to asking aid and a way.

row.basis: rider on a donkey directs the heart
row.note: The mishnah treats a rider on a donkey who cannot dismount for prayer and directs the heart toward the sanctuary; it keeps the source's mount-bound traveler inside a disciplined prayer practice.
The exhortation to lift drooping hands and strengthen weak knees takes up the same weakened limbs that the commentary imagines before aid.

row.basis: straight paths for feet; lame healed
row.note: Straight paths are to be made for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than dislocated; it is one of the closest Christian fusions of straight path, gait, and restoration.
Peter takes the lame man by the right hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles become strong; it gives the source's hand-held help a concrete upright result.
The healed man leaps up, stands, and walks; this provides the full bodily sequence that the commentary reads into aid followed by upright movement.
The woman's disabling spirit leaves her bent and unable to straighten; it supplies an exact counter-image to the upright mustaqim walker.
After Jesus lays hands on her, the woman is immediately made straight; the touch makes aid visibly become upright posture.

row.basis: no one to help the disabled man
row.note: The disabled man says he has no person to put him into the pool; this sharpens the commentary's premise that a weak traveler cannot manage alone.
Jesus commands the man to rise, carry his bed, and walk; it gives the source's requested help its compact standing-and-road outcome.
Four people carry the paralytic to Jesus; the scene makes communal bodily assistance the condition of bringing an immobilized person forward.
The paralytic is told to rise, take up his mat, and go home; it turns the carried body's recovery into independent walking.
Paul commands a man disabled in his feet to stand upright, and he leaps and walks; its wording explicitly joins uprightness to restored motion.

row.basis: injured traveler placed on an animal
row.note: The Samaritan binds an injured traveler's wounds, puts him on his own animal, and brings him to care; it reverses the source's failed mount into a means of carrying the weak.

row.basis: weary and burdened invited to rest
row.note: Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest; it gives the commentary's exhausted traveler a direct address and relief.

row.basis: gentle yoke and rest for souls
row.note: Taking Jesus' gentle yoke brings rest; it supplies a Christian image of a burden that supports rather than overwhelms the weak walker.
Peter begins to sink while walking and cries, Lord, save me; the scene makes the commentary's helpless request arise at a literal failure of footing.
Jesus immediately reaches out and takes the sinking man's hand; it is a direct one-handed counterpart to the source's supported traveler.
The Spirit helps human weakness when people do not know how to pray; it applies requested divine aid to the very act of supplication.
Approaching the throne yields mercy and grace for timely help; it sets the source's plea for aid before a sovereign, as malik frames the petition.
The strong are obliged to bear the frailties of the weak; it states the communal duty implicit in the commentary's two supporting companions.
Bearing one another's burdens makes bodily support an ethic of communal walking rather than an isolated rescue.
The community is told to help the weak and be patient with all; it pairs the source's assistance with the unhurried disposition of good walking.
The elders are reminded that one must help the weak; this concise imperative provides a communal form of the source's avn, help.

row.basis: guide feet into the way of peace
row.note: The dawn from on high guides feet into the way of peace; it closely matches ihdina as guidance enacted at the feet.
John's proclamation uses Isaiah's command to make the Lord's paths straight; it gives the straight-path language a preparatory and eschatological Christian setting.

row.basis: How can I unless someone guides me?
row.note: The Ethiopian traveler asks how he can understand unless someone guides him and invites Philip into the chariot; it turns guidance into companioned instruction on a journey.
The prayer of faith saves the sick and the Lord raises the person up; it joins prayer for aid to physical recovery and rising.

row.basis: the Lord stood by and strengthened me
row.note: The Lord stands by Paul and strengthens him in abandonment; it gives the commentary's needed support a personal divine companion.
Believers are rooted, built up, and established in faith; it brings together the commentary's tree-on-roots and stable-wall images.

row.basis: body held together by supporting joints
row.note: The whole body is joined and held together through every supporting joint; it translates the commentary's body-support image into reciprocal communal cohesion.

row.basis: house does not fall because founded on rock
row.note: The house withstands storm because it has a rock foundation; it gives the source's wall and structural support imagery an ethical architectural counterpart.

row.basis: kept from stumbling and made to stand
row.note: God is able to keep believers from stumbling and make them stand; it compresses the source's protected gait and upright result into doxology.

row.basis: tree with many roots resists wind
row.note: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah compares deeds exceeding wisdom to a tree with many roots that storms cannot uproot; it interprets rootedness as the moral stability behind the source's standing tree.

row.basis: sons of righteousness walk in paths of light
row.note: The Community Rule places the sons of righteousness under the Prince of Lights and says they walk in paths of light; it gives the requested right way an angelic and communal Second Temple framing.

row.basis: walking after God means acts of care
row.note: The talmudic reading of walking after God turns the command into clothing, visiting, comforting, and burying the vulnerable; it makes walking with God inseparable from supporting the weak.
The tempter cites angelic foot-protection to urge Jesus to leap; beside the source's needy petition, it raises the distinct question of asking for aid versus demanding a proof of it.
Jesus answers the appeal to protection by forbidding the testing of God; it supplies the interpretive boundary for the preceding scene's use of divine support.

row.basis: Jesus identifies himself as the way
row.note: Where the source has a community ask God to guide it on a straight path, John identifies Jesus himself as the way to the Father; the contrast is a substantive Christological recasting of path language.
The Spirit of truth guides disciples into all truth; it extends the source's request for a guide from physical route-finding to discernment.

row.basis: Jesus joins travelers on the road
row.note: Jesus draws near and travels with the disoriented disciples to Emmaus; it makes guidance take the form of a companion sharing the road.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to waters
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the afflicted and guides them to springs of life-giving water; it combines leadership, relief, and a destination for the needy traveler.
The church is called the pillar and foundation of truth; it gives the commentary's qiyam-as-pillar image an ecclesial structural use.
Christ's power is made perfect in weakness; it supplies a theological reading in which the source's weakness remains the place where enabling aid is displayed.

row.basis: apart from me you can do nothing
row.note: Branches can bear fruit only by remaining in the vine, and apart from Christ disciples can do nothing; it gives the source's inability to proceed alone an organic image of dependence.

row.basis: the Way of Life and the Way of Death
row.note: The Didache opens with the Way of Life and the Way of Death; it supplies an early Christian ethical development of the path metaphor, though its two-way scheme goes beyond this section's single petition.

row.basis: we seek from God a straight way
row.note: Ezra proclaims a fast so the traveling community may seek from God a straight way for themselves, their children, and their goods; it closely joins communal petition, dependence, and the requested road.

row.basis: God's hand helps travelers on the road
row.note: Ezra contrasts royal military help with God's favorable hand on those who seek him while facing enemies on the way; it gives nasta'inu a travel-specific account of divine aid.

row.basis: fasting and entreating God for the journey
row.note: The community fasts and entreats God for the safe journey, and God answers; it supplies a concrete liturgical continuation of asking help before setting out.
The law requires helping even an enemy's donkey when it lies under its load; it gives the commentary's exhausted mount an ethical command not to leave it stranded.

row.basis: fallen donkey on the road; lift it up
row.note: The law forbids ignoring a fellow Israelite's fallen donkey on the road and requires raising it with the owner; it directly answers the source's stopped mount with shared assistance.

row.basis: traveler asks guarding, food, and clothing
row.note: Jacob asks that God be with him, guard him on the way, and provide bread and clothing; it gives the vulnerable traveler a prayer for both protection and material support.

row.basis: guide on a way not traveled before
row.note: The ark goes ahead so Israel will know the way to go because it has not passed that way before; it is a precise narrative of a guide for people unable to orient themselves alone.
Deuteronomy couples walking in all God's ways with serving God from the whole heart; Hebrew avad is cognate with the source label for na'budu and preserves its worship-and-way sequence.
Israel is to serve God, who blesses bread and water and removes sickness; the Hebrew avad cognate places service beside the bodily strengthening the commentary associates with aid.

row.basis: mercy leads and guides to water
row.note: The hungry and thirsty are protected from scorching because the merciful one leads and guides them to springs; it gives the source's needy traveler both relief and a destination.

row.basis: build up the way; remove obstruction
row.note: God commands that a road be built and every obstruction removed from the people's way; it turns the commentary's support and wall imagery into preparation for safe passage.

row.basis: carry, bear, and save through frailty
row.note: God promises to carry and bear people even into old age and gray hair; it supplies a sustained divine counterpart to the source's body that needs to be held up.
God will gather the lame, the outcast, and those afflicted; it makes the physically impaired people in the source an object of restoration rather than abandonment.

row.basis: lame remnant made a strong nation
row.note: The lame are made a remnant and the outcast a strong nation; this gives the commentary's movement from weakness to solidity a collective prophetic form.

row.basis: save the lame and gather the outcast
row.note: God promises to save the lame and gather the outcast; it gives direct prophetic content to aid for those whose movement and social standing are impaired.

row.basis: spirit sets the hearer on his feet
row.note: The spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet while God speaks; it is a direct scene in which enabling presence produces upright posture.

row.basis: touch that strengthens a weakened body
row.note: A humanlike figure touches the overwhelmed Daniel and strengthens him; this supplies a bodily counterpart to the source's aid turning weakness into steadiness.

row.basis: peace and strength received after speech
row.note: The messenger says peace and be strong, and Daniel reports being strengthened; it adds spoken reassurance to the commentary's supported, non-panicked recovery.

row.basis: feet made like a deer's; secure heights
row.note: God gives the speaker agile feet and sets him securely on heights; it reframes restored walking as divinely given bodily surety.
God's right hand supports the speaker; it is a close biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that aid is a support under a vulnerable person.

row.basis: broad footing; ankles do not slip
row.note: God makes room for the speaker's steps so the ankles do not give way; it specifies secure footing as the result of help.

row.basis: God gives strength and sure feet
row.note: God is the speaker's strength, makes the feet like a deer's, and enables walking on heights; it closely combines strength, gait, and difficult terrain.
The path of the righteous is level because God makes it level; it supplies a Hebrew formulation in which moral rightness and an even route converge.

row.basis: God leads in the way one should go
row.note: God teaches what is beneficial and leads the people in the way they should go; it is a direct prophetic response to the plea ihdina.

row.basis: walk securely; foot does not stumble
row.note: The wise person walks securely and does not stumble; it gives the commentary's restored gait a wisdom counterpart.

row.basis: lead me in the path of commandments
row.note: The psalmist asks to be led in the path of God's commandments; this is a direct first-person prayer for guidance alongside ihdina.

row.basis: establish my steps in your word
row.note: The psalmist asks God to establish the steps in the divine word; it joins the source's standing and walking imagery to a petition for firm footing.

row.basis: Wisdom helps those who seek her
row.note: Wisdom instructs her children and gives help to those who seek her; it explicitly joins sought assistance to instruction and guidance.

row.basis: pray that the Most High direct your way
row.note: The sage tells the reader to pray that the Most High direct the way in truth; it is a close Jewish wisdom analogue to asking for the straight path.

row.basis: Moses' raised hands interpreted as dependence
row.note: The talmudic reading of Exodus 17 says Moses' hands did not themselves win the battle; Israel prevailed when they turned their hearts upward, turning bodily support into worshipful dependence.

row.basis: supports used to undergird a ship
row.note: In a storm the sailors use supports to undergird their ship; this gives the commentary's avn as what one relies on a literal structural and travel-related enactment.

row.basis: worship while leaning on a staff
row.note: Jacob worships while leaning on the top of his staff; it brings worship, bodily support, and the vulnerable traveler's staff into a single Christian-scriptural image.

row.basis: taken by hand, raised, then serves
row.note: Jesus takes the fevered woman by the hand and raises her, after which she serves; the scene sequences aid, upright recovery, and service like the source's linked worship and help.

row.basis: Jesus takes a hand, raises, and the boy stands
row.note: Jesus takes the boy's hand, raises him, and he stands; it closely parallels the source's hand-supported body becoming upright.

row.basis: traveler left half dead on the road
row.note: The traveler falls among robbers and is left half dead; this supplies the vulnerable roadside condition to which the Samaritan's assistance in the existing scene responds.
The shepherd places the found sheep on his shoulders; it offers a pastoral image of carrying one unable to return by its own strength.
A Macedonian man asks Paul to cross over and help them; the request makes aid both communal and tied to a journey across a boundary.

row.basis: servant made to stand by the Lord
row.note: The servant stands or falls before the master, yet the Lord is able to make the servant stand; it brings service, dependence, and uprightness into one statement.

row.basis: do not place a stumbling block before the blind
row.note: The law prohibits placing a stumbling block before the blind; it gives the source's guided weak traveler a negative ethical counterpart, removing what causes a fall.

row.basis: curse on making a blind person stray
row.note: The curse falls on one who makes a blind person wander off the road; it casts the source's needed guidance as a communal obligation not to misdirect the vulnerable.

row.basis: communal petition for protection from testing
row.note: The plural prayer asks not to be brought into testing and to be delivered from evil; it forms a Christian liturgical companion to the communal request for guided protection.

row.basis: do not put obstacle in a brother's way
row.note: Believers are told not to put a stumbling block or obstacle in another's way; it turns the source's safe path into a responsibility toward a fellow walker.

row.basis: weaker members of the body are indispensable
row.note: The body's apparently weaker members are indispensable; it deepens the commentary's body-and-support image by making weakness a condition for mutual care.

row.basis: able to help those being tested
row.note: Because Jesus suffered when tested, he is able to help those tested; it offers a Christological account of help arising from shared vulnerability.
God restores, strengthens, establishes, and founds believers after suffering; the cluster gives the source's wall, pillar, and uprightness images a Christian form.

row.basis: lordly service enacted by washing feet
row.note: Jesus the Lord washes disciples' feet and commands reciprocal service; it joins the source's worship-and-help pair to a concrete care for the body's walking members.
Believers are strengthened with power for endurance and patience; it gives the source's aided, unhurried walking an inward ethical correlate.

row.basis: ask God to give what God commands
row.note: Augustine asks God to give what God commands before commanding what God wills; it is a classic Christian interpretation of obedience as requiring the very aid the worshiper petitions for.

row.basis: an angel strengthens Jesus in prayer
row.note: The angel strengthens Jesus during prayer, closely joining supplication and enabling aid; the verses are absent from some early witnesses, so this candidate requires textual verification.
Exodus says God led the redeemed people by strength to his holy abode; it supplies a scriptural journey whose end is a dwelling, the completion the commentary hears in ihdinā.
The psalm asks that God's light and truth lead the speaker and bring him to God's holy hill and dwellings, closely joining guidance with arrival at a sacred home.
God leads wilderness wanderers by a straight way until they reach a city to inhabit; the verse makes a straight road culminate in a place of belonging.
God sends an angel to guard Israel on the way and bring them to a prepared place, combining escort, safety, and a divinely assigned destination.
Nations go up to the house of Jacob's God so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk his paths; house and guided way are one scene.
Abraham is told to go to Moriah and offer on a mountain God will show him, a sacrifice directed toward a disclosed destination rather than offered anywhere.
The ram caught at Moriah is offered in Isaac's place, giving the selected mountain an actual animal offering within the Akedah scene.
Chronicles places Solomon's Temple on Mount Moriah, canonically joining the shown sacrificial mountain to the later house of worship.
God calls the chosen Temple site a house of sacrifice, an unusually direct biblical pairing of house and sacrificial destination.
An ox, lamb, or goat slaughtered for sacrifice must be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting before YHWH; the animal's holy use depends on reaching the appointed place.
Israel must bring its offerings to the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, directly linking name, sacred house, and transported sacrifices.
The Passover sacrifice is taken from flock or herd and offered at the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, closely matching animal, house, and named worship.
God brings foreign adherents to his holy mountain; their offerings are accepted on his altar in a house of prayer, bringing outsider reception and sacrifice together.
Camels carry gold and frankincense to Zion while proclaiming YHWH's praise, a caravan image that joins the commentary's camels, carried gift, and exalted name.

row.basis: flocks on altar and glorified house
row.note: Flocks are accepted on God's altar and he glorifies his house; this makes herd animals reach the sanctuary for worship.
A gift or tribute is brought to the place of the name of YHWH on Zion, giving a biblical destination for a carried offering.

row.basis: male from flock and great Name
row.note: Malachi contrasts a vowed male animal withheld from sacrifice with YHWH's great name among nations, directly coupling flock, offering, and name.
The worshiper offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name, an explicit analogue to sacrifice accompanied by divine naming.
The prophetic vision of incense and a pure offering for YHWH's great name gives the name-and-offering conjunction developed in the commentary.
The Passover sacrifice belongs to YHWH who passed over Israelite houses; sacrifice, named worship, household, and protection meet in one rite.
Rebekah and her attendants mount camels and follow Abraham's servant, beginning a bridal journey with the animal explicitly named in the commentary.
Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah's tent and takes her as wife; the bridal journey ends in incorporation into the husband's household.
God forms the woman and brings her to the man, a concise biblical scene of a bride being led to her husband.
Laban brings Leah to Jacob at night; the same transfer scene appears here within a deceptive marriage narrative, which keeps the relation from being idealized.
Esther is taken to the king in his royal palace, a courtly version of a woman being conveyed into a husband's household.
Boaz says that he has acquired Ruth as wife; it is a biblical legal idiom in which marriage is expressed through acquisition, relevant to the commentary's imlāk image.
God covers Jerusalem, swears an oath, enters covenant, and says she became his; the prophetic marriage image makes covenant the act that establishes belonging.
The servant gives Rebekah ornaments and gives precious things to her kin, a gift-bearing scene embedded in the transfer of a bride.
The Queen of Sheba herself comes to Solomon with a camel caravan and wealth, whereas the Qur'anic scene developed in the commentary has the queen send a gift before meeting him.
The queen gives Solomon gold, spices, and precious stones; Kings narrates the transfer without Solomon's Qur'anic rebuff of the gift.
Kings has Solomon give the queen all she desired in addition to royal gifts, making reciprocal exchange rather than rejection the outcome of the parallel royal encounter.
God says he will not accept an offering from the speakers' hand; it supplies a different reason for an offered gift to fail to reach its intended acceptance.
At the three annual appearances before God, no one is to appear empty-handed; seasonal gathering, journey to the chosen place, and carried gift form one obligation.
Each pilgrim gives according to the blessing YHWH has given, a concrete biblical joining of gift, pilgrimage, and received benefit.
The mo'adim are YHWH's appointed times and holy convocations, a calendrical gathering marked out in a way comparable to the commentary's season-sign.
God appoints a place to which an accidental killer may flee, a foundational legal scene of flight toward secured space.
Israel designates cities of refuge so that a manslayer may flee there; refuge is reached by travel to a named communal place.
The refuge cities are for Israelites, resident aliens, and sojourners, making protected arrival available across communal status.

row.basis: admission and a place to dwell
row.note: A fugitive reaches the city gate, states his case to elders, is admitted, and receives a place to live among them; this is especially close to the commentary's seeker of protection.
The community may not hand an escaped slave back to his master, a direct rule against returning a person who has sought safety.
The escaped slave may live among the community in the place he chooses and must not be oppressed; protection is completed by a chosen home.
The appeal asks Judah to provide shade like night and hide the outcasts, a vivid shelter image for endangered arrivals.
The speaker asks that Moab's outcasts live with Judah and that Judah be a shelter from the destroyer, closely matching asylum in another community.
Adonijah fears Solomon and takes hold of the altar's horns, using sacred space and its object as a claim to protection.

row.basis: altar refuge has a legal limit
row.note: Exodus orders a presumptuous murderer taken even from God's altar; against the commentary's inviolable protected person, this marks the Torah's stated limit on sanctuary asylum.
Joshua makes peace with the Gibeonites, makes a covenant, and leaders swear to them; a community's word creates their protected status.
The leaders say the sworn oath prevents the congregation from striking the Gibeonites, showing the protective force of a covenantal promise.

row.basis: protective sign on a vulnerable person
row.note: God puts a sign on Cain so that no one who finds him will kill him; it is a marked person's inviolability, though not an asylum treaty.
Blood serves as a sign on Israelite houses and causes the plague to pass over; a mark makes a dwelling and those inside it inviolable.
God brings scattered people to dwell in Jerusalem, and they become his people while he becomes their God in faithfulness; arrival and covenantal belonging are inseparable.
Midrash on the Akedah identifies Moriah with the later sanctuary, reading Abraham's sacrificial journey as oriented toward the place that becomes God's house.
Pesahim contrasts Abraham's mountain and Isaac's field with Jacob's name for the future sanctuary as a house, sharpening the commentary's claim that sacred approach ends at a home.
The Mishnah makes appearance at the pilgrimage festivals an obligation with an offering, preserving the gathered-season and carried-sacrifice pattern as law.
The first-fruit towns assemble and ascend toward Zion in procession; it is a Jewish ritual realization of a marked gathering traveling with gifts to God's place.
The Mishnah describes first fruits borne in baskets and handed to priests, a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's carried gift and its tray.
The Mishnah says that after Jerusalem was chosen, high places were forbidden permanently; it interprets sacrifice as bound to its final house.
The midrash depicts God as acting as Adam's bridal attendant when he brings Eve to him, explicitly elaborating Genesis's bride-transfer scene.
The Mishnah opens by saying that a woman is acquired in three ways; it gives a Jewish legal frame for the commentary's marriage language in the malik family.
High priests' mothers supply food and clothing to accidental killers in refuge cities, treating arrival at refuge as an ongoing protected residence.
The Mishnah describes roads marked 'refuge, refuge' toward the cities of refuge; it makes the road itself visibly direct a fleeing person toward safety.
The star goes ahead of the magi until it stands over the place of the child, a guided journey that has a precise domestic destination.
The magi enter a house, worship the child, and open their treasures; destination, reverence, and a carried gift converge without requiring the gift to be a sacrifice.
Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, a New Testament movement of a person toward the holy place for cultic presentation.
The couple offers the prescribed birds at the Temple; this supplies the animal-offering side of the Jerusalem presentation scene.
Those judged righteous say they gathered in a stranger; the concrete act of receiving an outsider gives a Christian household analogue to the protected arrival.
The Samaritan puts the wounded man on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and cares for him, a notably close scene of transport into safety.
Jesus describes his Father's house as having many dwelling places, giving the prayer for guidance an explicitly eschatological house as destination.
Jesus promises to come again and take his followers to himself so that they may be where he is, turning destination into belonging with a person.
Jesus calls himself the way to the Father; the Christian text personalizes the path whose end is the Father's house in the same discourse.

row.basis: betrothed and presented to one husband
row.note: Paul says he betrothed the community to one husband in order to present it as a pure virgin to Christ, directly recasting bride-transfer in ecclesial terms.
Ephesians names Gentiles as aliens from Israel and strangers to the covenants; it gives the exclusion from which the commentary's asylum-and-covenant image moves.
Those once strangers and aliens become fellow citizens and members of God's household, an unusually direct Christian counterpart to secure communal belonging.
Christ presents the church to himself in splendor; the marital image supplies the end-point of a bride brought to her husband.
Believers present their bodies as a living sacrifice, which Paul calls worship; it explicitly joins sacrifice with the service dimension the commentary draws from عبادت.
God highly exalts Jesus and grants the name above every name after the obedient self-giving of the preceding verse, a close Christian analogue to raised name and obedient service.
Paul calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant, acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God, combining an affectional gift with sacrificial language.

row.basis: entry into holy place through sacrifice
row.note: Believers have confidence to enter the holy places by Jesus' blood; sacrifice here grants access to the sacred destination.
The access of the preceding verse is described as a new and living way, explicitly making sacrificial approach a path.

row.basis: sacrifice of praise and confession of Name
row.note: Through Jesus believers offer continual praise to God, identified as lips confessing his name; name and sacrifice are made verbal rather than animal.
Believers are built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices, fusing house, communal belonging, and worship.
Revelation's Lamb shepherds and guides people to springs of living water; it reverses the commentary's guided sacrificial animal into an animal figure that guides others.
The marriage of the Lamb comes and his bride has made herself ready, a final wedding scene that gives the bridal route an eschatological destination.
New Jerusalem descends prepared as a bride adorned for her husband; city-home and bride are deliberately merged in one arrival image.
The divine dwelling is among human beings and they are God's people, providing the final communal home sought in the commentary's road image.

row.basis: glory and honor brought into the city
row.note: The glory and honor of nations are brought into New Jerusalem, an eschatological analogue to gifts conveyed into the sacred home.
The victor becomes a permanent pillar in God's temple and bears God's name and the name of the new Jerusalem, combining inviolability, house, and name.
The Didache directs the community to gather, give thanks, and make its sacrifice pure; it is an early Christian liturgical continuation of gathered worship and offering.
Justin identifies Malachi's pure offering with Christian Eucharistic bread and cup, changing the prophetic name-and-offering text into a communal Christian rite.

row.basis: Arabic ع ب د and Hebrew עבד
row.note: The commentary's ع ب د label and Hebrew עבד are cognate service terms; Exodus has Israel serve God on the mountain after deliverance, without importing the commentary's camel sense into Hebrew.
Joshua's 'my house will serve YHWH' uses Hebrew עבד, cognate with the commentary's عبادت family, and locates worshipful service within a household declaration.

The commentary's explicit Beyt or house image corresponds formally to Hebrew bêt in 'house of the God of Jacob'; the verse's actual context supplies ascent and taught paths, not a lexical claim alone.

Arabic ism in بِسْمِ and Hebrew shem are cognate name terms; Deuteronomy uses shem for the divine name dwelling where offerings are brought, while the commentary's listed س م و label is not being treated as proof.

row.basis: Arabic م ل ك and Hebrew מלך
row.note: Hebrew melek, cognate with the source's مٰلِك family, means king here; Esther's actual transfer to the king's palace gives a concrete royal-marital setting without equating the two traditions' marriage vocabulary.
The lights serve for signs and appointed seasons; this is a specific biblical pairing for the commentary's marked season, though it is cosmic rather than pilgrimage law.
Israel camps by standards and signs of ancestral houses around the Tent; marked communal gathering around a dwelling gives a concrete analogue to the season-as-sign image.
The ark goes before Israel to seek out a resting place, a covenantal guide moving the people toward a place where they may settle.
God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble; it gives a prophetic form of safe guidance, though the verse names no house.
Boaz says Ruth has come to seek refuge under YHWH's wings after leaving her own people; it is a personal migration into protected covenantal belonging.
The Targum renders Ruth's refuge as taking shelter under the wings of the Shekinah, making her foreign arrival an explicitly Jewish covenantal shelter image.
Abigail loads food gifts onto donkeys and takes them to David during a dangerous encounter; it is a carried gift aimed at a potentially hostile recipient.
Abigail calls the gift she has brought David a blessing, supplying a biblical way in which a conveyed present is spoken of as benefit.
Jacob asks Esau to accept his blessing, meaning the present sent ahead; a gift between estranged kin is thus expressed through blessing language.

row.basis: gift opens access to the great
row.note: A person's gift makes room for him and brings him before great people, a concise wisdom-text account of a gift as mediated access to a recipient.

row.basis: gift at altar and reconciled relation
row.note: Jesus' altar saying makes the acceptability of a gift depend on repairing a broken relation first, a relevant contrast to the commentary's distinction between gift to friend and to rival.
The prepared virgins go with the bridegroom into the wedding feast and the door is shut, portraying a completed movement into a wedding household.

row.basis: shepherd calls by name and leads sheep
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; animal, name, and guidance are joined, though the sheep are not sacrificial offerings.
Whoever enters through Jesus is saved and finds pasture; the doorway turns guidance into safety and sustenance rather than a Temple destination.
Zacharias says God's dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, a focused New Testament articulation of the prayer for guidance without the house image.
The shepherd comes home with the recovered sheep and calls friends and neighbors to rejoice; return, animal, home, and friendship meet in the parable.
The faithful seek a better, heavenly country, and God has prepared a city for them; pilgrimage toward a divinely prepared home is explicit.
Believers have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, expressing the destination as an already approached heavenly sanctuary.
Christians have no lasting city here but seek the city that is coming, a compact formulation of road-like yearning for final belonging.
Paul calls Christ the sacrificed Passover; read beside Exodus 12, it recasts the household-protecting sacrificial pattern through Christ rather than a Temple-bound animal.
Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus in a house, a concrete gift of devotion whose domestic setting and beloved recipient recall the commentary's gift image.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 67.2
row.basis: many dwellings in the Father's house
row.note: Augustine reads John 14's many dwellings as the differing places of blessedness in God's one house, making the destination more than a passing lodging.

row.basis: house of God and gate of heaven
row.note: Jacob calls Bethel the house of God and the gate of heaven; it gives the commentary's final home a threshold where earthly travel meets divine presence.
Jacob's vow asks God to be with him and guard him on the way he travels, a direct individual counterpart to a request for guidance with protection.

row.basis: return in peace to father's house
row.note: Jacob seeks to return safely to his father's house; the goal of the guarded road is explicitly a home and restored belonging.
The Bethel stone is to become God's house, and Jacob vows a tithe from what God gives him; sacred dwelling and conveyed gift are conjoined.

row.basis: go to Bethel, dwell, and build altar
row.note: God tells Jacob to arise, go to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar; route, settlement, and sacrificial worship are inseparable instructions.
Jacob says God answered him in distress and was with him on the way, then calls his household to go build an altar at Bethel.
Jacob builds an altar at Bethel and names the place El-Bethel, making arrival at God's house culminate in sacrificial action.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on the way, an explicit wilderness model for divine direction.
Following the holy-dwelling line, the song says God will bring and plant his people at the mountain of his inheritance, the place made for his dwelling and sanctuary.
God says he bore Israel on eagles' wings and brought them to himself; divine conveyance creates the covenantal nearness sought in the commentary.
God permits an altar for animal offerings and promises to come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this directly joins sacrifice, name, and divine approach.
God promises that no one will covet Israel's land while its males go up for the three pilgrimage festivals; travel to worship is placed under explicit protection.

row.basis: first fruits brought to God's house
row.note: The first of the land's produce must be brought into the house of YHWH, a compact Torah model for a gift physically conveyed to the sacred home.
A voluntary herd burnt offering is brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for acceptance before YHWH, giving a more formal sacrificial arrival scene.

row.basis: seeking the place of the Name
row.note: Israel is commanded to seek the place YHWH chooses for his name and dwelling; the verb of seeking makes pilgrimage toward the house explicit.

row.basis: journey too long to carry the gift
row.note: Deuteronomy considers the practical case in which the chosen place is too far for someone to carry the tithe, a precise biblical reflection on a religious gift in transit.
Firstborn animals from herd and flock are eaten before YHWH year by year at the chosen place, combining animal, pilgrimage, and household celebration.
The household rejoices at the place where YHWH causes his name to dwell together with Levite, resident alien, orphan, and widow; seasonal gathering includes vulnerable outsiders.

row.basis: basket of first fruits to chosen place
row.note: The worshiper takes first fruits in a basket and goes to the place YHWH chooses for his name; this is unusually close to the commentary's tray-borne gift.

row.basis: gift set before God and worshiped
row.note: The first fruits are brought and set before YHWH, followed by worship; gift delivery becomes an act of devotion at the sacred destination.
God promises to gather Israel even from the ends of heaven, a return movement for people who are dispersed and outside their secure place.
God brings the gathered people back into the land of their ancestors and makes them possess it, making return culminate in a home and inheritance.
Rahab and her family are spared and she dwells in Israel because of the oath-bound protection she gave the spies; asylum, covenant, and communal incorporation coincide.

row.basis: foreigner comes from afar for the Name
row.note: Solomon imagines a foreigner hearing of YHWH's great name and coming from a distant country, a pilgrimage of an outsider toward the named house.
God is asked to hear the foreigner who prays toward the Temple so all peoples know his name; house, name, and outsider access are explicitly related.
The congregation is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come before him; elevated name and conveyed offering share one command.

row.basis: house and altar of burnt offering
row.note: David identifies the future site as both God's house and the altar of burnt offering for Israel, an exact house-and-sacrifice formulation.
God's choice of Jerusalem for his name makes the temple city a named destination, supplementing the commentary's stress on a house reached through worship.

row.basis: right way for people and possessions
row.note: Ezra proclaims a fast to seek from God a right way for the returning people, their children, and their property, a concrete prayer for safeguarded travel.
God's hand delivers the returning caravan from enemy and ambush on the way, giving the safe-route element a historical narrative form.
The transported silver, gold, and vessels are weighed in the house of God at Jerusalem; a carried offering demonstrably reaches its sacred recipient.
Job says no stranger had to lodge in the street because he opened his doors to the traveler, a domestic counterpart to sheltering the one who arrives.

row.basis: homeless poor brought into one's house
row.note: Isaiah defines righteous care in part as bringing the homeless poor into one's house, an exact home-making act for a vulnerable outsider.
On God's holy mountain Israel will serve him and bring offerings, first fruits, and holy gifts; destination, service, and conveyed gift all appear in one verse.
God makes an everlasting covenant of peace, multiplies the people, and sets his sanctuary among them; covenant becomes enduring protected proximity.
God's dwelling is with the people, and he is their God while they are his people; the final home is reciprocal belonging.
Resident aliens who live among Israel and have children there receive inheritance among the tribes; protection reaches the level of a permanent home.
The prophet calls prisoners of hope to return to their stronghold, a compact return-to-safety image for threatened people.
Abel brings firstborn animals from his flock and their fat portions, and YHWH regards him and his offering; animal gift and acceptance are explicit.
Cain's offering is not regarded, providing another scriptural instance in which the relation between giver and recipient, rather than conveyance alone, determines an offering's reception.
Samuel says obedience and listening are better than sacrifice and rams' fat; this directly challenges any reading in which the guided animal itself exhausts worship.

row.basis: rejected offerings at a hated festival
row.note: God says he will not accept offerings or regard peace offerings in a prophetic critique of cult; it counterbalances the commentary's festival sacrifice with the ethical conditions of acceptance.
The worshiper is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come into his courts, a close formulaic counterpart to the commentary's named animal and house.
The speaker says the king has brought her into his chambers, a concise bridal arrival image in which the groom's dwelling is the destination.
The woman says she would lead her beloved into her mother's house; its reversed direction and household make it a useful contrary bride-and-home image.
Malachi calls the wife a partner and wife of covenant, giving a concise biblical equation of marriage with a binding protective relationship.

row.basis: blessing expressed in herds and camels
row.note: Abraham's blessing is narrated as flocks, herds, wealth, servants, camels, and donkeys; it illuminates the commentary's association of received benefit with herd animals and the bridal camel journey.
Jacob selects a gift for Esau before their feared meeting, an actual gift sent ahead to repair a dangerous relationship.

row.basis: gifts carried to a powerful unknown recipient
row.note: Jacob sends his sons with choice products as a present to the Egyptian ruler, a carried gift aimed at a recipient whose disposition is uncertain.
God says the priests place his name on Israel and he blesses them; the name functions as a bearer of benefit rather than merely an utterance over an animal.
Israel is to fear and serve YHWH and swear by his name; Hebrew עבד supplies a cognate service context alongside the commentary's name-and-worship connection.

row.basis: nations bring gifts to God's Name
row.note: Tobit's hymn foresees nations coming from afar with gifts in hand for the heavenly king because of the Lord's name, combining pilgrimage, gift, and exalted name.
An angel directs Joseph to take the child and mother and flee to Egypt from lethal danger, a New Testament journey of protected asylum.
Joseph takes the child and mother by night and withdraws to Egypt, giving the refugee movement itself its own narrative verse.
The angel tells Joseph to take the child and mother back to Israel because the threat has died; refuge ends in a guided return home.

row.basis: going out to meet the bridegroom
row.note: The virgins take lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom, supplying the journey-to-wedding aspect whose arrival is described later in the parable.
John calls the bride the bridegroom's and identifies the listening friend who rejoices at his voice; bride, husband, and friend are explicitly differentiated.
Jesus says he guarded his followers in the Father's name and none was lost except the designated exception; the name is presented as protective custody.

row.basis: relief gift for a distant community
row.note: The disciples determine to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, an actual communal gift conveyed to people in need.
The relief is sent to the elders through Barnabas and Saul, preserving the physical mediation of a gift's journey to its recipients.

row.basis: alms and offerings brought after travel
row.note: Paul says that after years away he came to bring alms for his nation and offerings, directly joining travel, gift, and cultic act.
Macedonia and Achaia make a contribution for poor saints in Jerusalem, a Christian gift carried toward a named communal home.
The author speaks of people who have fled for refuge to hold fast hope; an asylum image is used directly, even though its meaning is theological.
Hope enters the inner place behind the curtain, carrying the refuge image into access to God's sanctuary rather than a secular shelter.
The author praises faithful service to brothers who are strangers, a concrete Christian mandate to receive travelling outsiders.
The travelling brothers go out for the sake of the Name while taking nothing from outsiders, relating hospitality to named religious mission.
Angels are told not to harm land or sea until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads; a visible divine mark creates temporary inviolability.

row.basis: only the unsealed may be harmed
row.note: The destructive creatures may harm only those lacking God's seal on their foreheads, continuing the marked-protection pattern with an explicit exclusion.
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with people bearing his and his Father's name on their foreheads, binding Name, mark, and sacred destination.

row.basis: invited to the Lamb's marriage supper
row.note: The blessed are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, giving the bridal arrival a communal table and final welcome.

row.basis: servants worship in the final city
row.note: In the renewed city God's servants worship him; permanent dwelling and service meet after the removal of the curse.
The servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads, completing the New Testament line of name as identity and protection.
After shipwreck, the islanders show unusual kindness and kindle a fire for all the survivors, a narrative of emergency welcome.

row.basis: shipwrecked travelers received into a house
row.note: Publius receives Paul and the shipwrecked party and entertains them for three days, an explicit house-based shelter for travellers.

This Mekhilta discussion is commonly cited as reading Exodus 15's holy dwelling and sanctuary in Temple terms; the exact wording and subdivision should be verified, but its interpretive bridge is sacrifice's destination as God's house.

row.basis: pilgrims form a common sacred homeland
row.note: Philo describes festival pilgrims leaving their local places for the Temple and recovering a common kinship there; the cited section should be checked, but it is a specific Hellenistic-Jewish expansion of travel into sacred home.

row.basis: God leads the restored people with joy
row.note: Baruch says God will lead Israel in joy by the light of his glory with mercy and righteousness; its restoration context supplies a later Jewish guided-homecoming image.
After finding the sheep, the shepherd puts it on his shoulders rejoicing; this is the carrying action that culminates in the homecoming already represented by the next verse.

row.basis: prisoners welcomed into the jailer's house
row.note: The jailer brings Paul and Silas into his house and sets food before them after their release, converting a scene of custody and fear into domestic welcome.

row.basis: receive a contested person as oneself
row.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul; without assuming Onesimus's legal status, the verse makes personal welcome the requested resolution.
Christ's death mediates a new covenant so those called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, relating sacrifice to secure belonging rather than an animal's arrival.

row.basis: na'budu; Hebrew la'avod; walk all his ways
row.note: Joshua joins serving YHWH with walking all his ways; Hebrew avad is cognate with the commentary's na'budu, making its service-and-road equation concrete.

row.basis: obey, be my people, walk the commanded way
row.note: Jeremiah makes obedience and walking the commanded way the condition of belonging to God, clarifying the commentary's owned servant who addresses the true master.
Abraham's worship is expressed as a journey with a promised return, a precise counterpart to the commentary's claim that worship and the traversed way are one action.
Proverbs tells the walker to level the track under his feet, directly supplying the commentary's image of feet making a road surface straight and firm.

row.basis: prepare YHWH's way; make a highway straight
row.note: Isaiah's prepared, straight desert highway gives a scriptural form to the requested sirat as a route made ready for the divine encounter.

row.basis: Way of Holiness; walkers do not go astray
row.note: The highway is explicitly contrasted with going astray, matching the commentary's straight communal road and its lost alternative.

row.basis: this is the way; walk in it; right or left
row.note: A guiding voice gives the traveller the exact formula and directional correction developed in the commentary's guide who goes before the wayfarer.

row.basis: led by streams on a straight, non-stumbling path
row.note: Jeremiah combines a gathered people, water, divine leading, a straight path, and freedom from stumbling in one verse.

row.basis: continual guidance, thirst satisfied, watered garden
row.note: Isaiah binds guidance to provision in dry ground, closely meeting the commentary's route, water, need, and nurturing Lord.

row.basis: make me know your ways; teach me your paths
row.note: This direct prayer for taught paths is a close liturgical companion to ihdina al-sirat.

row.basis: instruct and teach the way to go
row.note: The speaker promises personal instruction and counsel about a particular way, giving a biblical analogue to the hadi who guides a traveller.

row.basis: hand leads and right hand holds
row.note: The psalm makes being led and physically held together, illuminating the commentary's traveller supported while he walks.

row.basis: I hold your right hand; I help you
row.note: YHWH's direct promise to hold the hand and help gives concrete form to the worshipper's request for assistance.

row.basis: teach me to do your will; lead me on level ground
row.note: Prayer for obedience and for the good Spirit to lead on level ground links voluntary service, help, and an upright route.

row.basis: for your name's sake lead and guide me
row.note: The psalm joins the divine name to being led and guided, sharpening the commentary's movement from a naming sign to a requested way.

row.basis: build up the highway; lift a signal for peoples
row.note: Isaiah places a raised signal and a cleared communal road in the same command, matching the commentary's opening sign and constructed path.

row.basis: YHWH's house, taught ways, walked paths
row.note: The nations go to a house so that they may learn and walk God's paths, giving the commentary's road both a community and a destination.

row.basis: level ground so Israel may walk safely
row.note: Baruch makes the leveling of mountains and valleys serve Israel's safe walking, a close late-Jewish parallel to the straight road's communal movement.

row.basis: trees shade Israel at God's command
row.note: The commanded shade gives a direct textual companion to the commentary's road, water, and shade cluster.

row.basis: God leads Israel with mercy and righteousness
row.note: The closing promise combines divine leading, a people on the move, mercy, and righteousness in the terms developed around rahim and guidance.

row.basis: trust, help, make your ways straight
row.note: Sirach joins reliance on God, promised help, and straightened ways in a compact form that closely mirrors the fifth and sixth ayat's prayer.

row.basis: bless God and ask that your ways be made straight
row.note: Tobit's instruction makes blessing the Lord and asking for straight paths one devotional practice, matching the commentary's praise-to-guidance movement.

row.basis: ways of truth and perversity; peace or wrath
row.note: The Rule of the Community develops two opposed ways whose outcomes are peace or divine wrath, supplying a precise Second Temple counterpart to the two faces of losing the path.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The opening Two Ways instruction gives a Christian communal formulation for the commentary's straight route and its opposed lost route.

row.basis: YHWH goes before to lead them by the way
row.note: The pillar goes before Israel specifically in order to lead them on the journey, a direct analogue for the guide preceding the traveller.

row.basis: God goes before to find a place to camp
row.note: Deuteronomy depicts God travelling ahead to locate the people's resting place, adding a destination to the commentary's forward-leading guide.

row.basis: take my yoke; learn from me; find rest
row.note: Jesus turns the animal yoke into willing discipleship and rest, directly meeting the commentary's tamed servant and weary traveller.

row.basis: my yoke is easy and my burden light
row.note: The easy yoke and light burden give a concrete Christian counterpart to submissive service that does not crush the one who seeks help.

row.basis: make straight paths for your feet; the lame be healed
row.note: The command retains both the physical track made by feet and the contrast of injury with restored upright movement.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: Zechariah's hymn gives the guide the precise task of directing feet into a saving way.
The contrast of a life-giving way with another route gives an explicit Christian form to the commentary's road with two divergent endings.

row.basis: forsook the straight way and went astray
row.note: Second Peter uses the paired language of a straight way and straying, directly matching the commentary's upright walker and dallin.
Jesus describes the Father's house as the destination prepared for his people, illuminating the commentary's road that has a final home.

row.basis: I am the way to the Father
row.note: The way is identified with the mediator who brings people to the Father, a direct Christian meeting of route, guide, and home.

row.basis: kept from stumbling and made to stand
row.note: Jude pairs divine preservation from falling with standing before glory, exactly reversing the commentary's falling under wrath.

row.basis: serve not for the sake of reward
row.note: Avot distinguishes service for reward from service freely given to the master, clarifying the commentary's contrast between coerced slavery and chosen worship.

row.basis: freed from sin and enslaved to God
row.note: Paul's paradox of liberation into God's service gives a sharp Christian analogue to voluntary servitude under the true owner.

row.basis: free people, yet servants of God
row.note: The verse expressly holds freedom and God's service together, directly illuminating the commentary's freely chosen kul.

row.basis: Israelites are my servants, brought from Egypt
row.note: Leviticus opposes Egyptian bondage to belonging as God's servants; Hebrew avadim is cognate with Arabic abd and makes the true-owner contrast explicit.
Exodus supplies the forced enslavement that the commentary sets against Moses's willing service to the real Rabb.
Calling enslaved Israel God's son places divine parenthood over Pharaoh's claimed control, sharpening the false-nurturer and true-Rabb contrast.

row.basis: Moses's mother nurses him for Pharaoh's daughter
row.note: Where the Qur'anic Pharaoh presents upbringing as a claim upon Moses, Exodus makes his own mother the nurse and Pharaoh's daughter the payer.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter takes and names Moses
row.note: Exodus assigns adoption and naming to Pharaoh's daughter, a significant alternative to Pharaoh himself claiming to have reared Moses in his household.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses and raises him
row.note: Stephen retells the royal adoption in the same terms that frame the commentary's Pharaoh-and-Moses dispute.

row.basis: Moses refuses to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son
row.note: Hebrews interprets Moses's adult choice as rejection of the royal identity, reinforcing the commentary's contrast of imposed palace status and chosen allegiance.

row.basis: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well
row.note: The verse fixes the journey and the well that the commentary gathers into Moses's guided road-and-water scene.

row.basis: Midian's daughters draw water and fill troughs
row.note: The source scene explicitly joins the well, women drawing water, and troughs for a flock.

row.basis: Moses helps the women and waters their flock
row.note: Moses's intervention at the well culminates in watering another's flock, the direct biblical parallel to the commentary's scene.

row.basis: the women return to their father's house
row.note: The return home after the well episode adds the household destination that the commentary gives to the road and sacrificial herd.

row.basis: camels kneel by a well as women come to draw water
row.note: The servant's journey joins camel, well, water, and a household-seeking mission in a single scene.

row.basis: Rebekah draws water for the camels
row.note: Water is given to the traveller's animals as well as the traveller, a close counterpart to herd, need, and guidance meeting at the well.

row.basis: YHWH led me on the way to my master's kin
row.note: The servant explicitly credits God with leading him on a route to a household, closely matching guide, owner, way, and home.

row.basis: Jacob rolls the stone and waters Laban's flock
row.note: Jacob's well scene conjoins a journeying relative, water, a flock, and movement into a household as Moses's Midian scene does.

row.basis: water for feet and rest under a tree
row.note: Abraham's hospitality gives travelling visitors water and shade, an exact meeting of two images developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Abraham takes a tender calf from the herd
row.note: The animal from the herd is selected for a household offering of hospitality, paralleling the commentary's separated herd-animal brought to a home.

row.basis: Abraham serves food under the tree
row.note: Serving guests under shade joins willing service, food, and shelter in the Abrahamic setting beside the commentary's route-and-need imagery.

row.basis: Judge of all the earth does justice
row.note: Abraham's appeal to the Judge of all the earth gives a biblical analogue to Rabb al-alamin and the day when justice is rendered.

row.basis: I am dust and ashes before the Lord
row.note: Abraham's self-description before judgment supplies a concrete biblical face-to-dust counterpart to the commentary's humiliated, fallen side of the day.

row.basis: God will provide the lamb for the offering
row.note: Abraham's answer makes the sacrificial animal God's provision, linking herd, divine name, and the journey to worship.

row.basis: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well
row.note: The scene makes a tired traveller, a road, and a well coincide, closely matching the commentary's Moses cluster.

row.basis: YHWH is my shepherd; I lack nothing
row.note: The shepherd relation gives the herd a known owner whose care answers the commentary's ownerless animal and needy traveller.

row.basis: green pasture and waters of rest
row.note: The shepherd's grazing place and waters give a close biblical form to the flock's going out and returning around water.

row.basis: he leads me in right paths
row.note: The same shepherd restores and guides on right paths, fusing herd leadership and the straight road.

row.basis: shepherd gathers, carries, and gently leads the flock
row.note: The tender leader of the flock gives a strong counterpart to hadi as both guide and herd-leader.

row.basis: no hunger or thirst; guide them to springs
row.note: The promised guide supplies water and relief from need, directly meeting the commentary's travel, thirst, and leading.

row.basis: unknown owner, animal kept at home until restored
row.note: The law expressly imagines not knowing an animal's owner and bringing it home until it can be returned, a close legal counterpart to the ownerless camel.
The speaker is simultaneously a strayed sheep and God's servant who asks to be sought, tightly joining dallin, herd, and worship.

row.basis: lost sheep led astray by their shepherds
row.note: Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose leaders turned them from their resting place, directly meeting wrong guidance, herd, and home.

row.basis: seek lost, bring back strayed, bind injured
row.note: The divine shepherd's actions reverse loss, falling, and weakness in the terms developed across the commentary's way and herd images.

row.basis: shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out
row.note: The sheep's known name, owner, and being led out directly counter the commentary's animal whose master is unknown.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow his voice
row.note: The shepherd's going before the flock is a precise Christian analogue to the guide ahead of both traveller and herd.

row.basis: I know my own and my own know me
row.note: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep intensifies the commentary's final contrast between known ownership and the animal cut off from its owner.

row.basis: seek the one lost sheep until he finds it
row.note: The search for the strayed sheep gives the commentary's lost animal a returning shepherd and a deliberate homeward movement.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to Shepherd and Overseer
row.note: First Peter explicitly turns straying into return to a shepherd, a direct Christian parallel to dallin and guided recovery.
Jesus reads an unguided crowd through the exact herd-and-leader image the commentary develops for hadi.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
row.note: The Lamb who is also shepherd fuses sacrificial animal, herd leader, and water-guidance in an eschatological form.

row.basis: all who enter the world pass before God for judgment
row.note: The Mishnah makes universal judgment resemble a passing flock, closely joining the commentary's herd image to the day of reckoning.

row.basis: horse or mule restrained by bit and bridle
row.note: The psalm's undisciplined animal needing restraint provides a direct counter-image to the commentary's tamed camel and willing servant.

row.basis: YHWH is shade at your right hand
row.note: The divine keeper as shade on the traveller's side gives a compact biblical counterpart to the commentary's shade and sustaining help.

row.basis: clouds, rain, and grass on the hills
row.note: The psalm explicitly has God nourish vegetation through cloud and rain, matching the commentary's nourishing Rabb.

row.basis: rain, fruitful seasons, food from heaven
row.note: Paul's speech identifies the Creator through rain, crops, and food, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's clouds and plants nourished by the Rabb.
Isaiah joins a nursing child, a mother's womb, and rachem; that Hebrew root is cognate with the commentary's rahim and supplies its maternal-mercy image.

row.basis: my name forever; my memorial for generations
row.note: God's self-naming gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's beginning with a name that identifies the owner.

row.basis: called by name; you are mine
row.note: Being called by name and declared God's own directly answers the commentary's contrast between recognized ownership and the masterless animal.

row.basis: put my name on Israel and bless them
row.note: The priestly formula treats the divine name as a mark of belonging and blessing, illuminating name, sign, and completed favor.

row.basis: bring offerings to the place where YHWH's name dwells
row.note: The verse brings sacrifice, divine name, and a chosen dwelling together, closely matching the commentary's herd-animal, spoken name, and home.

row.basis: lamb taken according to each household
row.note: The Passover instruction joins a selected flock-animal to a household, offering a concrete biblical counterpart to sacrifice brought home.
Genesis calls the heavenly lights signs rather than gods, directly serving the commentary's distinction between a sign and what it signifies.

row.basis: Abraham looks at counted stars as promised descendants
row.note: Genesis gives Abraham's star-gazing a covenantal meaning rather than a test of a celestial lord, a meaningful alternative to the commentary's night scene.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars must not be bowed to or served
row.note: The warning against serving the host of heaven is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's sun-worshippers who mistake sign for Rabb.

row.basis: sun shining and moon moving in splendor
row.note: Job names the very visual appeal of sun and moon that makes the commentary's ascending celestial signs a test of discernment.

row.basis: heart secretly enticed; hand kissed in worship
row.note: The next verse identifies the move from seeing luminaries to idolatrous devotion, making explicit the error the commentary assigns to sun-worship.

row.basis: sun, moon, stars, and heavenly lights treated as gods
row.note: Wisdom lists the celestial bodies people mistake for rulers of the world, an unusually close Jewish parallel to the commentary's Abrahamic scene.

row.basis: creator perceived from the greatness of created things
row.note: The argument from visible beauty to the Maker directly articulates the commentary's rule that a sign is not the thing it signals.

row.basis: host of heaven worships its maker
row.note: Nehemiah reverses astral worship: the heavenly host itself worships YHWH, so celestial things become servants rather than lords.

row.basis: people worship the sun toward the east
row.note: Ezekiel supplies a concrete scene of sun worship, the precise failure the commentary describes when rising things are treated as Rabb.
The heavens function as proclamation of God rather than as God, giving a concise biblical form to the sign-and-signified distinction.

row.basis: served the creature rather than the Creator
row.note: Paul makes the inversion of worship explicit, directly matching the commentary's warning against taking a created heavenly sign for its Lord.

row.basis: earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, and stars say they are not God
row.note: Augustine stages the commentary's distinction in first-person form: visible creatures direct the seeker beyond themselves to their maker.

row.basis: YHWH our judge, lawgiver, king, and savior
row.note: Isaiah gathers judge and king in one confession; Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary's Malik, while the verse joins ownership to deliverance.

row.basis: wicked will not stand in the judgment
row.note: Hebrew qum, to stand, is cognate with the commentary's qama, and the verse places that standing exactly in the judgment scene.

row.basis: Aramaic dina, court seated, books opened
row.note: Daniel's Aramaic dina is cognate with the commentary's din; court, books, and the assembled host make its day-of-reckoning image especially close.

row.basis: Hebrew yadin judges the world in righteousness
row.note: The Hebrew d-y-n verb gives the dīn root a judicial use while its object is the whole world, matching din and alamin.

row.basis: weighed in balances and found lacking
row.note: Daniel turns the balance into a verdict on a king, directly meeting the commentary's scale and judgment-day imagery.
The Torah's command makes an unbent balance an ethical demand, supplying the legal ground for the commentary's warning about deficient measure.
The proverb sets deceitful scale against the weight God delights in, sharpening the commentary's moral reading of the mizan.

row.basis: make the ephah small and the shekel great; falsify scales
row.note: Amos supplies the concrete market fraud behind the commentary's scene of those who cheat in measure before the Lord of worlds.

row.basis: let God weigh me in just balances
row.note: Job asks for divine weighing that will disclose integrity, directly pairing balance with the final moral account.

row.basis: measured waters and heavens; weighed mountains in scales
row.note: Isaiah places sky, waters, and scales in one divine act, a close counterpart to the commentary's meeting of heaven and balance.

row.basis: all things arranged by measure, number, and weight
row.note: Wisdom makes cosmic order a matter of measure and weight, directly enlarging the commentary's scale from commerce to the worlds.

row.basis: deed written, sealed, witnessed, and weighed out
row.note: Jeremiah's purchase preserves writing, seal, witnesses, money, and duration together, closely paralleling the commentary's debt-document scene.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: The law's witnesses make a legal matter stand, directly illuminating the commentary's witness, forgetting, and uprightly established writing.

row.basis: credit, open ledger, writing hand, collectors, true judgment
row.note: Avot's shop-and-ledger parable unites debt, recorded accounts, payment, and a true judgment in the exact cluster developed in the commentary.

row.basis: three books opened at the new-year judgment
row.note: The Talmud's books for righteous, wicked, and intermediate persons make the judgment day an explicit written accounting.

row.basis: some awaken to life and some to shame
row.note: Daniel's resurrection divides the outcome of the final scene into honor and shame, matching the commentary's contrasting faces on the day.

row.basis: wise shine like the brightness of the sky
row.note: The shining righteous after judgment supplies a biblical counterpart to the softened or radiant face set against dust and disgrace.
The righteous standing before their former oppressors closely matches the commentary's upright figure set against those who fall under wrath.

row.basis: they go astray in heart and do not know my ways
row.note: The psalm explicitly combines straying, ignorance of God's ways, and the divine response later called wrath.

row.basis: in my wrath they shall not enter my rest
row.note: The oath of wrath gives the opposite destination to the guided flock's place of rest.

row.basis: way of wicked is darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble
row.note: Proverbs makes lost direction visible as a walker who stumbles without knowing why, closely matching the commentary's fallen wayfarer.

row.basis: crooked paths; walkers do not know peace
row.note: Isaiah's crooked paths and absence of peace provide a direct Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's route that bends away from guidance.

row.basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
row.note: Paul's phrase directly joins wrath to an appointed judicial day, the pair the commentary gathers around din.

row.basis: God fixed a day to judge the inhabited world
row.note: Paul's Areopagus speech gives the judgment day a universal scope, closely corresponding to the Lord of the worlds.

row.basis: all appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due
row.note: The verse treats final judgment as recompense owed, a precise Christian counterpart to din as a day of settled debt.
