row.basis: dead stand, books open, judged by recorded deeds
row.note: Revelation combines standing persons, opened books, and individual judgment, the central visual cluster of the commentary's day.

row.basis: hide from the face of the enthroned one and the Lamb's wrath
row.note: The terrified call for mountains to fall over them gives an exact Christian image of wrath, faces, and falling.

row.basis: the great day of wrath has come; who can stand
row.note: The verse explicitly sets wrath's day against the ability to stand, matching the commentary's fall-versus-upright contrast.

row.basis: all nations gathered and separated as sheep from goats
row.note: The final judgment is staged as a shepherd's sorting of animals, directly meeting herd imagery and the day of account.

row.basis: sheep on the right and goats on the left
row.note: The bodily arrangement of the flock makes the judgment's two outcomes spatial, complementing the commentary's two ways of being lost.
The king's adverse verdict supplies an explicit Christian judgement-and-wrath counterpart to the angry path's end.

row.basis: stand upright and lift your heads at redemption
row.note: Jesus's command gives the positive posture opposed to the commentary's face-down falling under wrath.

row.basis: they always go astray and have not known my ways
row.note: Hebrews carries the Psalm's language of straying and unknown ways into a Christian warning.

row.basis: they shall not enter my rest in my wrath
row.note: The next verse retains wrath and denied rest, sharpening the commentary's opposed destinations.

row.basis: the measure used is measured back
row.note: The same measure becomes judicial reciprocity, a compact Christian counterpart to balance and account.

row.basis: give account on the day of judgment
row.note: Jesus explicitly uses the language of rendering an account on the final day, closely meeting the commentary's debt-and-record imagery.

row.basis: a king settles accounts with his servants
row.note: The parable puts king, servants, debt, and reckoning in one scene, directly paralleling Malik, abd, and the day debt is closed.

row.basis: settle with an accuser while on the way to the magistrate
row.note: Luke makes the road itself the place to resolve a debt before judgment, an unusually close meeting of path, debt, and day.

row.basis: record of debt with legal demands erased
row.note: Paul's cancelled written debt gives a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's written obligation and its final settlement.

row.basis: each gives an account of himself to God
row.note: The individual account to God directly maps the commentary's day when every person stands before the Lord of worlds.

row.basis: black horse holds a balance scale
row.note: The apocalyptic balance makes measure part of a judgment sequence, extending the commentary's mizan into a Christian final-day image.

row.basis: our Father; hallowed be your name
row.note: The Lord's Prayer opens with a named, direct address to God, closely accompanying the commentary's movement from divine name to second-person devotion.

row.basis: give us today our daily bread
row.note: The shared prayer moves from address to requested provision, matching the commentary's needy traveller and nurturing Lord.
The petition uses debt to name what requires divine resolution, directly accompanying the commentary's din-and-borrowing imagery.

row.basis: do not lead us into trial; deliver us from evil
row.note: The final petition asks not to be led into a destructive course and for rescue, closely paralleling help and the requested right way.

row.basis: God's servants worship before the throne
row.note: The final city presents uncoerced service before the true ruler, a culminating Christian counterpart to na'budu.

row.basis: they see his face and bear his name
row.note: The named servants see God's face in the final home, reversing the commentary's faceless loss, wrath, and unknown ownership.

row.basis: distinguish one who serves God from one who does not
row.note: Malachi makes service to God the criterion separating two destinies as judgment approaches, closely matching the commentary's willing servant and two outcomes.
Nehemiah joins debt to forced enslavement in a concrete social scene, illuminating the commentary's juxtaposition of debt and coerced servitude.

row.basis: I will lead slowly according to the livestock's pace
row.note: Jacob's journey places a leader ahead of children and nursing flocks, supplying a specific pastoral bridge to the commentary's guide, herd, and tired traveller.

row.basis: living water given at the well
row.note: At the traveller's well, water becomes a divine gift; this extends the commentary's physical water-and-need scene into John's symbolic register.
Acts turns a communal allegiance into the name of a way, a specific but non-narrative counterpart to the commentary's path joined to a people.

row.basis: benei maron read through sheep or a narrow pass
row.note: The Talmud's interpretations of the Mishnah's procession make individual passage before the judge resemble either a flock or a constricted route, joining herd, path, and judgment.

row.basis: Abraham's anti-idol argument in Terah's workshop
row.note: The midrash recasts Abraham's discernment of false gods as a contest with made images, extending the commentary's sign-versus-Lord distinction.

row.basis: Abraham teaches one creator rather than celestial powers
row.note: Josephus interprets Abraham as arguing from the ordered cosmos to one creator, a close historical reception of the commentary's astral scene.

row.basis: Moses refuses Egyptian nurses and is nursed by his mother
row.note: The tradition makes Pharaoh's household dependent on Moses's own mother for his nurture, intensifying the commentary's challenge to Pharaoh's claim of upbringing.

row.basis: Moses thought his brothers would understand his deliverance
row.note: Stephen supplies a positive intention for Moses's intervention among the oppressed, an interpretive counterpoint to the commentary's self-description as among the lost.

row.basis: Wisdom enters the servant of the Lord against dread kings
row.note: Wisdom portrays Moses as God's servant confronting royal power, giving a late-Jewish bridge between the commentary's true Rabb and Pharaoh's coercion.

row.basis: records, weighing, and judgment of souls
row.note: The apocalypse's judgment tableau gathers written records, scales, and verdicts, a close later-Jewish expansion of the commentary's balance-and-account scene.

row.basis: look to him, become radiant, faces not ashamed
row.note: The psalm's radiant, unashamed faces give a specific positive counterpart to the commentary's contrasting faces, though outside its final-judgment setting.

row.basis: no one can serve two masters
row.note: Jesus's master-servant saying supplies a focused Christian bridge between worship, ownership, and the commentary's contrast of true and false masters.

row.basis: offering drawn from cattle or flock
row.note: Leviticus supplies the sacrificial category of herd and flock behind the commentary's animal separated for an offering, without its full homeward scene.

row.basis: root of Jesse as a signal sought by nations
row.note: The raised signal draws a people toward a resting place, a secondary biblical bridge to the commentary's sign, path, and communal destination.
YHWH proclaims himself compassionate and slow to anger; Hebrew rahum shares the r-h-m root with the commentary's rahim and directly sets mercy beside wrath.
Psalm 103 uses the r-h-m root for a father's compassion toward children, adding a paternal form to the commentary's nurturing Rabb and rahim.

row.basis: wandered without a way to an inhabited city
row.note: The psalm begins with people lost on a desert route and unable to find a city to dwell in, closely matching the commentary's road without its final home.

row.basis: hungry, thirsty, and fainting on the way
row.note: The travellers' thirst and failing strength give a direct biblical counterpart to the weary wayfarer who asks the Rabb for help.

row.basis: led by a straight way to a city to dwell in
row.note: YHWH leads the lost travellers on a straight way to habitation, combining guidance, road, and house in the commentary's exact sequence.

row.basis: lead the blind by an unknown way and make crooked places straight
row.note: Isaiah's guide leads those who do not know the route and straightens its crooked parts, directly reversing the commentary's dallin.

row.basis: an angel guards the way and brings Israel to a prepared place
row.note: The messenger goes before Israel to protect the road and bring them to a destination, giving a close biblical form to the helper-guide and final home.

row.basis: leader goes out before the people so they are not sheep without a shepherd
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who goes before and leads the congregation, explicitly joining the traveller-guide and herd-leader images.

row.basis: the breaker and king go before the people
row.note: Micah imagines a path opened and a king going at the people's head, a strong counterpart to the commentary's guide who precedes the community.

row.basis: YHWH goes before and is Israel's rear guard
row.note: The divine escort ahead and behind gives a precise scriptural counterpart to the commentary's traveller held from both sides.

row.basis: lamp for my feet and light for my path
row.note: The word gives a walker light exactly at the feet and on the path, sharpening the commentary's concrete imagery of movement and guidance.

row.basis: the path of the righteous is level
row.note: The upright God makes the righteous person's path level, directly echoing the commentary's uprightness and smoothed road.

row.basis: led his people like sheep and guided them like a flock
row.note: The exodus is described as divine guidance of sheep through the wilderness, fusing route, herd, and true shepherd.

row.basis: livestock led down to rest by YHWH's Spirit
row.note: Isaiah compares the Spirit-led people to livestock brought to rest and connects the leading with God's name, meeting herd, guide, destination, and sign.

row.basis: gathered flock brought to its land and fed
row.note: Ezekiel's shepherd brings scattered sheep home and feeds them on their own land, supplying the return-to-home side of the commentary's herd route.

row.basis: people wander like sheep for lack of a shepherd
row.note: Zechariah states the inverse of the commentary's hadi: sheep wander and suffer when no shepherd leads them.

row.basis: come, worship, bow down, and kneel before the maker
row.note: The psalm gives worship a bodily posture of bending before the creator, a close counterpart to willing, tamed service.

row.basis: people of his pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: The worshipping people are simultaneously a flock possessed and tended by God, directly answering the commentary's ownerless animal.
The psalm's raising of the bent gives a direct positive counterpart to the commentary's fallen person and its upright walker.

row.basis: God opens Hagar's eyes to a well and gives the child water
row.note: Guidance to a well supplies water in a wilderness crisis, a close parallel to the commentary's path, water, need, and divine provision.

row.basis: Moses brings water from the rock for the thirsty people
row.note: The Exodus water scene gives Moses a second, communal road-and-water episode beside the Midian well developed in the commentary.

row.basis: God leads through dry wilderness and brings water from rock
row.note: Deuteronomy explicitly binds wilderness leading to water for a thirsty people, closely matching the commentary's guided journey and well.

row.basis: a way in wilderness and rivers in desert
row.note: Isaiah places road-making and water-making together in an otherwise impassable land, a direct counterpart to the commentary's path and water.

row.basis: water in wilderness to give drink to God's people
row.note: The water is expressly given for the chosen people's drinking, adding communal provision to the commentary's individual thirsty traveller.

row.basis: waters break out in wilderness and streams in desert
row.note: The water imagery supplies the necessary environmental counterpart to Isaiah's Way of Holiness already relevant to the commentary's straight route.

row.basis: springs sent into valleys to run among mountains
row.note: The creator directs springs through the land, a strong biblical image for water set into a traversable landscape.

row.basis: wild animals drink from the springs
row.note: The springs meet the thirst of animals, directly extending the commentary's convergence of water and herd.

row.basis: grass for livestock and food from the earth
row.note: God's vegetation feeds both livestock and humans, closely matching the commentary's Rabb who nourishes creatures through plant growth.

row.basis: rain waters earth and gives seed and bread
row.note: Rain's passage into growth and food supplies a precise scriptural counterpart to clouds, plants, and completed provision.

row.basis: taught Ephraim to walk and carried him in arms
row.note: Hosea makes God the one who teaches a child to walk and carries him, an especially close true-Rabb counterpart to Pharaoh's claimed upbringing.

row.basis: children raised and brought up, yet rebellious
row.note: Isaiah's parental complaint gives a biblical counterpoint to nurture received as a claim and to the servant who must choose allegiance.

row.basis: a mother comforts her child; God comforts Jerusalem
row.note: The maternal comparison gives rahim's nurturing register a concrete biblical counterpart in divine comfort.

row.basis: ram offered in place of Abraham's son
row.note: The caught ram realizes the sacrificial animal that Abraham said God would provide, adding the herd-animal's actual offering to the journey scene.

row.basis: seek the place where God puts his name to dwell
row.note: The chosen dwelling and its resident name provide the house-and-name side of the sacrificial movement developed in the commentary.

row.basis: words bound as a sign on hand and forehead
row.note: The covenantal sign worn on the body gives a Jewish scriptural counterpart to the commentary's image of name and stamp.

row.basis: a mark set on foreheads before punishment
row.note: Ezekiel joins a distinguishing mark on faces with the approach of judgment, closely meeting the commentary's sign, face, and wrath cluster.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars loved, served, followed, and worshipped
row.note: Jeremiah explicitly combines astral worship with service and following, a very close counterpart to the commentary's celestial false lords and path imagery.

row.basis: do not fear the signs of heaven as the nations do
row.note: Jeremiah joins the heavenly signs to the nations' mistaken way, directly extending the commentary's distinction between sign and Lord.

row.basis: God appoints the sun, moon, and stars for their courses
row.note: The luminaries are governed creations under God's ordinance, a direct counter-narrative to calling them Rabb.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars praise YHWH
row.note: The celestial bodies are themselves worshippers, reversing the commentary's scene of humans worshipping them.

row.basis: every knee bows and every tongue swears to YHWH
row.note: The universal bodily confession gives a direct biblical form to worship before the sole sovereign.

row.basis: day God rises to gather nations and pour wrath
row.note: Zephaniah combines divine rising, gathered peoples, and poured wrath in a final-day scene beside the commentary's standing and anger imagery.

row.basis: recompense, a slipping foot, and the near day of calamity
row.note: The Song of Moses connects repayment and an imminent day with a foot that slips, closely matching debt, judgment, and falling from the path.

row.basis: though fallen, I rise; darkness becomes light
row.note: Micah gives the commentary's fallen and upright walker an explicit scriptural reversal.

row.basis: first judgment question asks whether business was conducted faithfully
row.note: The Talmud makes honest commercial dealing the first question at judgment, a precise rabbinic bridge between false measure and final account.

row.basis: formed, born, die, and give account before the King of kings
row.note: Avot places unavoidable life and death under a final accounting before the King, tightly joining Malik, din, and personal debt.

row.basis: narrow path to a city between fire and water
row.note: The vision's perilous single route toward an inheritable city makes road, water, danger, and destination a striking Second Temple counterpart to the commentary's way.

row.basis: Moses's generation drinks from the spiritual rock, identified as Christ
row.note: Paul explicitly rereads the wilderness water episode, extending the commentary's Moses-water meeting through a Christian interpretive claim.

row.basis: water becomes a spring to eternal life
row.note: John turns water received at the well into a spring within the receiver, a distinct continuation of the commentary's water-and-need image.

row.basis: the thirsty are invited to come and drink
row.note: Jesus's public invitation makes thirst a route toward divinely given water, closely accompanying the commentary's needy traveller.

row.basis: the thirsty may take the water of life freely
row.note: The final invitation joins thirst, gift, and the completed eschatological home developed at the commentary's road's end.

row.basis: the king receives food and drink given to the needy
row.note: In the judgment scene, service to the hungry and thirsty is received by the king himself, linking need, willing service, and din.

row.basis: present bodies as a living sacrifice in worship
row.note: Paul turns voluntary embodied worship into sacrifice, a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's chosen servant and offered animal.

row.basis: sacrifice of praise and lips confessing God's name
row.note: The verse makes praise of the divine name a sacrifice, closely joining the commentary's name, praise, and ritual offering.

row.basis: spiritual house, priesthood, and spiritual sacrifices
row.note: First Peter unites house and sacrifice in a worshipping community, providing a Christian counterpart to the commentary's destination-house and sacrificial herd.

row.basis: new and living way opened through the curtain
row.note: The sanctuary is entered by a named living way, a precise Christian meeting of route and the divine house.

row.basis: God brings up the great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: Hebrews names the eschatological shepherd in a covenant setting, directly meeting herd, sacrifice, and true guidance.

row.basis: God equips people to do God's will
row.note: The prayer for divine equipping gives a Christian form to the commentary's servant who asks for help in willing obedience.

row.basis: seal God's servants on their foreheads before harm
row.note: The seal marks divine servants before approaching catastrophe, closely corresponding to the commentary's stamp, ownership, and wrath.

row.basis: the Lord knows those who are his; the foundation bears a seal
row.note: The seal combines known ownership and moral departure from evil, directly reversing the commentary's animal with no known master.

row.basis: one God and one Lord through whom all things are
row.note: In the context of many so-called heavenly gods and lords, Paul names one God and one Lord, closely matching the commentary's rejection of celestial rivals.

row.basis: turn from idols to serve a living and true God
row.note: The conversion formula explicitly combines leaving false objects of service with serving the living true God.

row.basis: creator is Lord of heaven and earth
row.note: Paul names the maker of the world and all it contains as Lord of heaven and earth, a direct Christian counterpart to Rabb al-alamin.

row.basis: fear God, give glory, judgment hour, worship the creator
row.note: This angelic proclamation joins praise, judgment, worship, creation, and springs of water in one unusually close parallel to the commentary's whole movement.

row.basis: righteous shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom
row.note: The final shining of the righteous gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's contrasting judgment-day faces.

row.basis: Hallelujah: salvation, glory, and power belong to God
row.note: The heavenly acclamation places praise before the declaration of judgment that follows, paralleling the commentary's hamd before the narrated gift.

row.basis: God's judgments are true and just
row.note: Revelation answers the praise with true and just judgment, directly joining hamd, din, and the correction of corrupt judgment.
The source commentary joins worship with walking a road; Hebrew ʿābad, cognate with the source's Arabic ʿ-b-d form, is placed beside walking in YHWH's ways.

row.basis: Serving and walking in God's ways
row.note: Moses' appeal puts serving YHWH beside loving him and walking in his ways, matching the commentary's fusion of the Fatiha's worshipper with the straight path.
Jesus refuses Satan's offer by saying worship belongs to God and service to God alone; this gives the commentary's freely chosen service a precise scriptural formulation.
The Lord's Prayer addresses the heavenly Father and asks that his name be hallowed, a close liturgical meeting with the Fatiha's opening invocation of God's name.
The prayer asks that God's kingdom come and his will be done, placing divine rule before the ensuing human petitions as the Fatiha places praise and lordship before its request for guidance.
The petition for daily bread gives a concrete counterpart to the commentary's picture of the needy traveler asking the Lord for help and provision.
The prayer asks God to forgive debts as worshippers forgive debtors, bringing the commentary's day of repayment and its debt imagery into a prayer of dependence on mercy.

row.basis: Guidance away from trial and evil
row.note: The prayer asks not to be led into trial and to be rescued from evil, a specific negative counterpart to the Fatiha's request to be led on the straight path and kept from its failed routes.
The psalmist asks God to make his ways known, matching the Fatiha's direct request for guidance and the commentary's road imagery.
The speaker asks God to lead him and teach him, grounding the commentary's image of a traveler who needs a guide in a first-person prayer.
The psalm asks God to remember his mercy, linking the commentary's joining of mercy with the request for a way under divine care.
The speaker asks that God's mercy, rather than remembered youthful sins, govern his answer; this joins guidance with mercy as in the commentary's favored and lost paths.
God's goodness and uprightness lead him to teach sinners the way, a specific meeting of mercy, moral direction, and the path requested in the Fatiha.

row.basis: The humble are taught the way
row.note: God guides the humble in justice and teaches them his way, matching the commentary's dependent traveler and a road learned from a guide.

row.basis: Paths marked by mercy and truth
row.note: The psalm calls all YHWH's paths steadfast love and faithfulness for covenant keepers, joining a path to divine favor rather than treating it as mere geography.

row.basis: Teach me your way; unite my heart
row.note: The speaker asks to walk in God's truth and fear his name with an undivided heart, combining the commentary's path, God's name, and exclusive worship.
The pilgrim looks to the hills and asks where help will come from, closely echoing the Fatiha's tired traveler's request for help.
The answer locates help in YHWH, maker of heaven and earth, joining the commentary's help petition to its praise of the Lord of all realms.
The psalm says YHWH made the people and that they are his people and flock; this closely meets the commentary's move from Lordship to owned worshippers and a guided herd.
The worshippers enter God's gates with thanksgiving and praise, a liturgical path toward the divine house that complements the commentary's praise and destination-house imagery.
YHWH proclaims himself compassionate, gracious, and abundant in steadfast love; the paired mercy language is a close scriptural counterpart to the Fatiha's repeated merciful names.
The continuation specifies forgiveness alongside accountability for wrongdoing, joining the commentary's mercy with its account of judgment and repayment.
The psalmist commands his soul to bless YHWH's holy name, matching the commentary's opening movement from the named Lord to praise.
The speaker says not to forget God's benefits immediately after praising him, echoing the commentary's observation that praise comes before the gifts are named.
The benefits named are forgiveness and healing, giving content to the commentary's claim that divine mercy completes the good received from the Lord.
God crowns the worshipper with steadfast love and compassion, connecting the commentary's blessing-completed-by-mercy image to a concrete praise text.
The psalm says God satisfies the worshipper with good and renews life, a specific image of divine nurture after praise.
This reprise of YHWH's merciful attributes closely matches the Fatiha's mercy names and the commentary's emphasis on God's completed care.
YHWH establishes his throne in heaven and rules over all, directly complementing the commentary's Lord of all worlds and master of the judgment day.
The psalm calls powerful heavenly servants to obey God's word and bless him, extending praise beyond the human petitioner to the created order.
The closing call to all God's works to bless him matches the commentary's universal Lordship and praise before any specific benefit is named.

row.basis: Arabic raḥīm; Hebrew reḥem and raḥam
row.note: The source commentary links raḥīm with the womb; Hebrew uses the cognate r-ḥ-m family in this verse for both a mother's womb and compassion for its child, making the image of mercy bodily and relational.
The commentary reads the surah's opening name as an identifying sign; this verse says God's name is placed upon Israel in blessing, a concrete use of the cognate name-word as belonging and blessing.
The source calls God master of the judgment day; the Hebrew m-l-k root here says YHWH reigns and judges peoples with equity, joining kingship to judgment in its own setting.
The source commentary connects yawm al-dīn with settlement and judgment; Daniel's Aramaic cognate dīnā names the court session in which books are opened.
The commentary joins a standing balance to people standing on judgment day; the Hebrew cognate q-w-m says the wicked will not stand in the judgment assembly.
The source's malik names rule over the day; Daniel uses the Aramaic cognate malkā for the dominion given to the humanlike figure, whose rule includes peoples and nations.
The source's “worlds” and the Syriac cognate ʿālmā meet in the Peshitta's statement that God loved the world, linking divine lordship to the world as the object of God's care.
Sirach treats keeping accounts with a partner as a matter of honest conduct, directly meeting the commentary's debt record and witness imagery.
Sirach names exact scales and weights, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's balance, upright measure, and final judgment.
Sirach instructs that stored goods and transactions be counted, joining the commentary's written debt, due date, and fear of an error in the record.
Jeremiah writes and seals the deed of purchase and obtains witnesses, matching the commentary's concern with a debt or transaction made stable through proper writing.
The purchase deed exists in both sealed and open forms, a specific legal record parallel to the commentary's account of writing and witnesses.
The deed is handed to Baruch in the presence of witnesses, echoing the commentary's emphasis on a witness in a recorded obligation.

row.basis: Preserve the record for later proof
row.note: The deeds are stored so they may last many days, giving a concrete scriptural purpose for accurate records beyond the immediate transaction.
The steward summons debtors and asks the amount owed, a direct scene of accounts being settled that clarifies the commentary's debt imagery.

row.basis: A debt is reduced in writing
row.note: The manager tells a debtor to alter the written amount, turning the commentary's upright, witnessed debt record into a deliberate manipulation within Jesus' parable.
A second written obligation is reduced as well; the parable's manager uses debt documents for advantage, a concrete counter-scene to the commentary's just record and balance.
The proverb says false scales are detestable to YHWH but accurate weights please him, directly joining the commentary's balance image to divine judgment.

row.basis: The poor are crushed by merchants
row.note: Amos condemns sellers who trample the needy, giving the commentary's fraudulent-weigher scene its concrete victims.
The merchants make the measure small and the shekel large, a direct account of the crooked balance image developed by the commentary.

row.basis: The poor are bought for debt
row.note: Amos says the poor are bought for silver and the needy for the price of sandals, tying dishonest trade to debt and coerced servitude.
YHWH swears not to forget the merchants' deeds, making the cheating in measures answerable to divine judgment.
Daniel depicts a heavenly court with books opened, a close image for the commentary's day of repayment, scales, and people called to account.
Daniel says the dead awaken to everlasting life or shame, a specific judgment-day division that adds consequence to the Fatiha's contrasting destinations.

row.basis: The wise shine like the sky
row.note: The wise shine like the brightness of the firmament after the resurrection, matching the commentary's radiant face on one side of the judgment scene.
The sun and moon darken before the great day of YHWH, a concrete “day of God” judgment image for the commentary's days of punishment.

row.basis: Rescue for those who call on YHWH
row.note: The same oracle promises deliverance to those who call on YHWH, giving the day both judgment and rescue as in the commentary's paired punishment and forgiveness.

row.basis: People pass before God like a flock
row.note: The Mishnah says all humanity passes before God on the New Year like sheep, uniting the commentary's judgment day and herd imagery in a single Jewish liturgical account.

row.basis: The Son of Man comes to judge
row.note: The Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, making this a direct scene of the judgment day named in the Fatiha.

row.basis: The nations are separated like a flock
row.note: The judge separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, matching the commentary's meeting of judgment, herd, and divided outcomes.

row.basis: Sheep on the right, goats on the left
row.note: The placement of two groups on opposite sides gives a concrete parallel to the commentary's blessed, wrathful, and lost groups.

row.basis: The king blesses and invites inheritance
row.note: The king calls the blessed to inherit what was prepared for them, joining divine kingship, favor, and final recompense.

row.basis: Mercy toward the needy is service to the king
row.note: The king identifies care for the least with care for himself, giving a specific ethical meaning to the commentary's freely offered service.

row.basis: The other group departs under a curse
row.note: The condemned are sent away from the king, a counter-destination to the blessed path and welcome described in the commentary.
The passage ends with punishment for one group and life for the other, a direct counterpart to the commentary's divided outcomes on the judgment day.
The covenant blessing reaches the people in their city and field, giving a concrete communal form to the Fatiha's request for the path of those favored.

row.basis: Refusing to heed brings a curse
row.note: The counterpart covenant warning makes disobedience lead to a curse, a specific relation between a community's conduct and the commentary's images of favor and wrath.
The just person's path is dawn light growing brighter, closely matching the commentary's upright walking on a straight path.
The wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble, a precise parallel to the commentary's lost traveler and fallen person under wrath.

row.basis: The broad way ends in destruction
row.note: Jesus contrasts a broad road and gate leading to destruction with the narrow entrance, giving a concrete two-way choice for the commentary's path and its failures.

row.basis: The narrow way leads to life
row.note: The difficult road leads to life and is found by few, joining path, guidance, and destination in Jesus' own teaching.

row.basis: A voice identifies the road to walk
row.note: The hearer is told “this is the way, walk in it” when turning aside, directly matching the commentary's traveler who asks for a guide and straight route.
YHWH leads Israel by cloud and fire on the way, a specific counterpart to the guide walking ahead of a traveler and the leader of a herd.
The psalm calls YHWH the shepherd of the speaker and says he lacks nothing, matching the commentary's move from Lordship to the cared-for flock.

row.basis: The shepherd gives rest by water
row.note: The flock is made to lie down in green pastures and led beside waters, combining the commentary's herd, water, and traveler's rest.

row.basis: The shepherd leads on right paths
row.note: God restores the soul and leads it on right paths, directly joining the commentary's guide, herd leader, and straight way.

row.basis: The path crosses a threatening valley
row.note: The speaker walks through a dark valley without fear because God is with him, a concrete image of the dependent traveler who needs help along the road.
God provides a table in the presence of enemies, a specific image of nurture and favor amid threat.

row.basis: The road ends in the Lord's house
row.note: The speaker expects to dwell in YHWH's house, joining the commentary's path to a destination home under the owner's care.
God brings his people out like a flock and leads them through the wilderness, directly matching the commentary's guide at the head of the herd.
The people are led securely while their enemies are overwhelmed, adding safety on the road to the commentary's request for guidance.

row.basis: The Lord gathers and leads his flock
row.note: The shepherd gathers lambs, carries them, and gently leads nursing ewes, a precise image of divine guidance shaped as care for a herd.
God says he will search for and seek his sheep, directly answering the commentary's final image of an animal separated from its owner.
YHWH rescues his flock from the places where it was scattered, giving a specific counterpart to the lost animal whose trace has vanished.

row.basis: The shepherd makes the flock lie down
row.note: YHWH says he will feed his sheep and make them lie down, bringing herd, nourishment, and rest together.

row.basis: The lost and strayed are brought back
row.note: God seeks the lost and brings back the strayed, a direct reversal of the commentary's animal that does not know its owner or route home.

row.basis: The shepherd calls sheep by name
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, linking the commentary's name, ownership, and guide images.

row.basis: The flock follows the known shepherd
row.note: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow because they know his voice, closely matching the commentary's leader at the front of a guided herd.
Jesus says he knows his own sheep and they know him, reversing the commentary's final picture of an animal whose owner is unknown.

row.basis: The owner searches for one lost sheep
row.note: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost one, making the lost animal's relation to its owner the center of Jesus' parable.

row.basis: The lost sheep is carried home
row.note: The shepherd puts the found sheep on his shoulders, a concrete rescue and return that reverses the commentary's animal wandering without a known owner.
The shepherd calls friends to rejoice over the found sheep, giving the lost animal a known owner and restored community.
Jesus interprets the sheep as a sinner who repents, making the recovery a moral return to God rather than a mere animal story.

row.basis: A shepherd seeks the strayed one
row.note: Jesus asks whether a shepherd would not seek a sheep that strayed, echoing the commentary's last image of an animal lost from its owner.

row.basis: Joy when the strayed sheep is found
row.note: The shepherd rejoices over the recovered sheep, emphasizing the owner's active care that contrasts with the commentary's unrecognized master.

row.basis: The Lamb shepherds to living water
row.note: The Lamb leads the multitude to springs of living water and God wipes away tears, uniting the commentary's herd, guide, water, and final relief in an eschatological scene.

row.basis: Pilgrims set their hearts on highways to Zion
row.note: The blessed traveler has highways in the heart and goes toward God, a close image for the commentary's community traveling toward a house.

row.basis: The valley becomes a place of springs
row.note: Pilgrims pass through a dry valley that becomes a spring, joining road and water as in the commentary's well scene.
The travelers go from strength to strength until each appears before God in Zion, giving the commentary's path a worshipful destination.

row.basis: Moses is raised in Pharaoh's house
row.note: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses as her son after rescuing him, the narrative behind the later claim of royal rearing that the commentary sets against the true Lord's gift.

row.basis: The princess, not Pharaoh, raises Moses
row.note: The Torah names Pharaoh's daughter as the one who adopts and raises Moses; the Qur'anic exchange instead gives Pharaoh the claim “we raised you,” then answers it with the real Lord's gifts, making attribution of nurture the difference.
The threatened Moses escapes Pharaoh and reaches Midian, matching the commentary's transition from royal upbringing and forced power to the Midian journey.
Jethro's daughters come to draw water for their father's flock, placing the well, water, and herd at the center of Moses' Midian scene.

row.basis: Moses helps the women water the flock
row.note: Moses stands up for the women and waters their flock, closely matching the commentary's Moses helping others at the well before resting.

row.basis: The women return to their father
row.note: The daughters report their encounter to Reuel, carrying the well scene into a household that receives Moses.

row.basis: Moses is remembered as a rescuer and water-drawer
row.note: The women describe an Egyptian who rescued them and drew water, matching the commentary's specific action of helping at the well.
Reuel asks why the daughters left the man behind and invites him to eat, linking the journey and water scene to welcome at a house.
Moses consents to dwell with Reuel, an arrival and household destination after the road and well.

row.basis: God sends Moses back to Pharaoh
row.note: The God who sees Israel's oppression sends Moses to bring the people out, matching the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's coercive claim and the true Lord's commission.

row.basis: Freedom's purpose is service to God
row.note: God promises that after the exodus the people will serve him at this mountain, a direct answer to the commentary's contrast between forced slavery and freely chosen worship.

row.basis: The enslaved son is released to serve YHWH
row.note: Moses must tell Pharaoh to let God's son go so that he may serve God, joining coerced enslavement, divine parenthood, and worship in one claim.

row.basis: Moses is adopted as Pharaoh's daughter’s son
row.note: Stephen retells the adoption by Pharaoh's daughter, confirming the Torah's detail while the Qur'anic retelling shifts Pharaoh himself into the speaker who claims to have raised Moses.

Stephen says Moses was educated in Egyptian wisdom and became powerful in words and deeds, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's claim that the true Lord gives Moses judgment and messenger authority.

row.basis: Moses turns toward his oppressed kin
row.note: At forty Moses visits his Israelite brothers, matching the commentary's movement from palace upbringing to the enslaved people he identifies with.

row.basis: Moses sees an Israelite being wronged
row.note: Moses defends the oppressed man, giving the royal-raised Moses' first decisive action for his enslaved people.
Stephen says Moses fled and became a resident alien in Midian, matching the commentary's move from Pharaoh's palace to the well journey.

row.basis: God sees the people's oppression and sends Moses
row.note: The Lord says he has seen Israel's suffering and sends Moses to deliver them, matching the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's boast and the real Lord's action.

row.basis: The rejected Moses becomes ruler and deliverer
row.note: Stephen says God sent as ruler and deliverer the very Moses whom Israel rejected, a precise reversal of Pharaoh's claimed benefaction and a strong instance of the commentary's true-Rab contrast.
Moses refuses to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son, directly meeting the commentary's contrast between palace upbringing and voluntary belonging to God's people.

row.basis: He chooses hardship with God's people
row.note: Moses chooses mistreatment with the people of God over temporary pleasure, a specific counterpart to the commentary's enslaved people and willing servant.

row.basis: He values reproach above Egypt's wealth
row.note: Moses regards disgrace for God's anointed one as greater wealth than Egypt's treasure, clarifying why royal nurture does not define his allegiance.

row.basis: Moses is tested as a shepherd
row.note: The midrash says Moses' care for a lamb at the well proves his fitness to shepherd Israel; it turns the Midian watering episode into the qualification of the future guide of a people.

row.basis: A traveler asks God to guide his journey
row.note: Abraham's servant asks the Lord to grant success and steadfast love during his search, closely matching the commentary's dependent traveler asking for a guided road.

row.basis: A sign at the well identifies the right encounter
row.note: The servant asks for a sign involving water for himself and the camels, meeting the commentary's connection of guidance, a sign, and a herd at a well.
The servant asks Rebekah for a drink at the well, continuing the journey's concrete need for water.

row.basis: Rebekah offers water to the camels
row.note: She draws water until the camels have finished drinking, joining the well to care for the traveler's herd.

row.basis: The Lord has led the servant to the household
row.note: The servant blesses YHWH for leading him on the way to his master's kin, explicitly joining guidance, route, and arrival at a household.

row.basis: The servant blesses God for the right way
row.note: He says YHWH led him on the right way to find the daughter for Isaac, a close narrative counterpart to asking for the straight path.

row.basis: Jacob arrives at a well with flocks
row.note: Jacob sees a well with three flocks beside it, joining a traveler, water source, and herd as in the commentary's Midian scene.

row.basis: Rachel approaches with her father's flock
row.note: The traveler learns that Rachel is coming with the sheep, a specific meeting of person, herd, and well.

row.basis: Rachel brings the flock to the well
row.note: Rachel is a shepherdess arriving as Jacob speaks, making the well scene a meeting place for a journey and a herd.
Jacob rolls away the stone and waters the flock, closely matching Moses' action of watering women’s animals at Midian.

row.basis: God promises to guard Jacob on the journey
row.note: God promises to be with Jacob, guard him wherever he goes, and bring him back, a specific promise to a traveler asking for a safe route and return.

row.basis: The destination is called God's house
row.note: Jacob calls the place the house of God and heaven's gate, giving the commentary's path-to-house image a concrete patriarchal setting.

row.basis: A traveler asks for food, clothing, and safe return
row.note: Jacob's vow asks for divine presence and provision until he returns to his father's house, joining guidance, sustenance, and destination.

row.basis: The house becomes a place of worship
row.note: Jacob vows that the stone will be God's house and that he will give a tenth, turning arrival into service and worship.

row.basis: God Most High is creator of heaven and earth
row.note: Melchizedek blesses Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth, giving concrete language for the commentary's Lord of all worlds.
Abram blesses God Most High after rescue, meeting the Fatiha's praise of the Lord in a scene where God's help is named.

row.basis: Abram identifies YHWH as creator of heaven and earth
row.note: Abram calls YHWH God Most High and maker of heaven and earth, a direct creator-and-owner claim in his own speech.

row.basis: Stars mark a promise, not a deity
row.note: God brings Abram outside to count the stars as a sign of his descendants; unlike the commentary's astral worshippers, the stars here point beyond themselves to the promise-giver.

row.basis: Luminaries are not to be worshipped
row.note: Deuteronomy names sun, moon, and stars as created lights allotted to peoples and forbids worshipping them, matching the commentary's distinction between a sign and what it signifies.

row.basis: People fail to recognize the creator
row.note: Wisdom says people who observe the world did not recognize its maker, the same error the commentary assigns to worshippers who take a rising sign for the Lord.

row.basis: They treat created lights as gods
row.note: The text names fire, wind, stars, and lights of heaven as things mistakenly taken for gods, closely matching the commentary's star, moon, and sun scene.

row.basis: Creation's greatness points to its maker
row.note: Wisdom argues that the beauty and power of created things should lead observers to their maker, exactly the sign-versus-signified distinction in the commentary.

row.basis: Searching creation should lead to its Lord
row.note: The people investigate created things but are captivated by their appearance; this explains the commentary's claim that the worshippers stop at the sign.
Wisdom says such people remain blameworthy, giving moral force to the commentary's contrast between a sign and worship of the created object.

row.basis: They should have found the Lord sooner
row.note: Those who can investigate the world should have been able to find its Lord, closely matching the commentary's lostness when a sign is mistaken for its owner.

row.basis: Knowing God but failing to honor him
row.note: Paul says people knew God yet did not glorify or thank him, matching the commentary's astral worshippers who encounter signs but fail to direct praise to their source.
Paul says those who claim wisdom became fools, a pointed counterpart to the commentary's people who misread the heavens and lose the way.

row.basis: The creator's glory is exchanged for images
row.note: Paul describes exchanging God's glory for images of created beings, directly matching the commentary's distinction between a sign and the divine reality it points toward.

row.basis: The creature is worshipped instead of the creator
row.note: Paul's explicit contrast between creator and creature matches the commentary's claim that sun-worshippers confuse the sign with the one signified.

row.basis: The world is a palace with an owner
row.note: The midrash pictures Abraham seeing a palace on fire and asking whether it can lack an owner; God reveals himself as the master. It interprets creation as a sign that directs the seeker to its owner, close to the commentary's night-sky lesson.

row.basis: God's name rests on the people as blessing
row.note: The priests place YHWH's name upon Israel and bless them, giving the commentary's opening name-as-identifying-sign a liturgical and communal form.

row.basis: Offerings go to the chosen dwelling
row.note: Israel must seek the place YHWH chooses for his name and bring offerings there, joining the commentary's named sacrificial herd to the destination house.

row.basis: The offering is brought to God's place
row.note: Burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, and vowed gifts are brought to the chosen place, a concrete connection between herd, worship, and house.

row.basis: The household eats and rejoices before God
row.note: The worshippers eat before YHWH and rejoice in their work, connecting offering, household, and divine provision.

row.basis: Thanksgiving offering and invocation of the name
row.note: The speaker offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving and calls on YHWH's name, matching the commentary's named offering and worship.

row.basis: The vow is paid before the people
row.note: The speaker fulfills vows in the presence of God's people, giving a public setting to the act of offering and praise.

row.basis: The offering reaches the Lord's house
row.note: The vow is fulfilled in Jerusalem, in the courts of YHWH's house, directly joining sacrifice, name, worship, and the destination house.

row.basis: A ram is offered in place of the son
row.note: Abraham offers the ram caught in the thicket instead of Isaac, a specific sacrificial animal separated from the flock and presented at the place of testing.

row.basis: The place is named for YHWH's provision
row.note: Abraham names the site for YHWH's provision, joining an offering with the naming of God at its destination.

row.basis: The cloud's movement sets the community on the road
row.note: Israel travels when the cloud lifts and camps when it settles, giving the community a guide who determines the path and its timing.
The people move and remain according to YHWH's word, a specific expression of collective dependence on guidance.

row.basis: God gives life and breath to all
row.note: Paul says God gives everyone life, breath, and everything, matching the commentary's Lord of all worlds who gives nourishment and help.
Paul says God made all nations and set their times and boundaries, linking universal lordship to the ordered movement of peoples.

row.basis: People seek God and may find him
row.note: The nations are placed so they might seek God, a direct meeting with the commentary's lost seeker, guidance, and discovery of the true owner.

row.basis: Prayer begins with Father and holy name
row.note: Jesus' prayer addresses the Father and asks that his name be hallowed, adding Luke's distinct liturgical form to the Fatiha's named invocation and direct address.
The prayer asks for daily bread, giving a concrete petition for provision within the same short prayer that asks for God's reign.
The prayer asks forgiveness and not to be brought into trial, a distinct compact counterpart to the Fatiha's dependence, guidance, and avoidance of failed paths.

row.basis: Wanderers cannot find a way to an inhabited city
row.note: The psalm describes hungry and thirsty travelers lost in a wilderness with no city in reach, closely meeting the commentary's lost traveler and destination-home imagery.

row.basis: The lost cry to YHWH for help
row.note: The wanderers cry to God in distress and he rescues them, matching the commentary's needy traveler who asks the Lord for aid.

row.basis: God leads them by a straight way to a city
row.note: YHWH guides the travelers on a straight road to an inhabited city, joining the commentary's requested guidance, straight path, and arrival place in one scene.

row.basis: Thanks for steadfast love after rescue
row.note: The rescued are urged to thank YHWH for his steadfast love, linking praise to the help received along the road.

row.basis: God satisfies the thirsty and hungry
row.note: God fills the hungry and satisfies the thirsty, adding provision to the lost traveler's rescue and the commentary's water imagery.

row.basis: A highway called the holy way
row.note: Isaiah describes a raised road for the redeemed, called the Way of Holiness, giving a communal and sacred version of the straight path requested in the Fatiha.

row.basis: No danger on the redeemed road
row.note: No lion or dangerous beast is found on this highway, a concrete promise of safe travel for the people whom God guides.

row.basis: The redeemed return to Zion with joy
row.note: The travelers arrive in Zion singing, with lasting joy, giving the commentary's road a communal destination in God's house.

row.basis: God leads exiles by streams of water on a straight path
row.note: Jeremiah pictures God guiding returning Israel beside streams and on a straight road, while calling Israel God's firstborn; this joins the commentary's water, way, and belonging-to-the-Lord images.

row.basis: Prepare a road for YHWH in the wilderness
row.note: The voice calls for a road to be made straight in the wilderness, matching the commentary's image of a path prepared by others for the guided traveler.

row.basis: The road is leveled for the coming Lord
row.note: Valleys rise and rough ground is leveled, making straightness physical and communal as in the commentary's trodden, smoothed road.

row.basis: Mark applies Isaiah's road to John's preparation
row.note: Mark identifies Isaiah's wilderness voice with John the Baptist preparing the Lord's way; this Christian reading makes the straight road a call to prepare for God's arrival.

row.basis: Show me the way I should walk
row.note: The speaker asks God to let him hear steadfast love and show the way to go, closely joining the Fatiha's request for guidance with its reliance on mercy.

row.basis: God's good spirit leads on level ground
row.note: The psalm asks God's spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, a direct image of the upright path and guide developed in the commentary.

row.basis: The Lord is gracious, compassionate, and slow to anger
row.note: This praise formula names the same divine qualities as the Fatiha's mercy names and places them within a hymn of praise.

row.basis: The Lord's compassion extends to all he made
row.note: God's compassion reaches all his works, concretely joining mercy to the commentary's Lord of all worlds.

row.basis: God's kingdom is everlasting and faithful
row.note: The psalm's account of God's enduring kingdom joins praise of divine sovereignty to the commentary's master of the judgment day.

row.basis: All creatures look to God for food
row.note: Every living thing looks to God for sustenance, matching the commentary's picture of the needy traveler and its Lord who provides.

row.basis: God opens his hand and satisfies living things
row.note: The open hand that satisfies all living things gives a specific image for completed divine favor and care.

row.basis: The blessed person meditates on Torah day and night
row.note: The psalm defines the blessed person's way through delight in God's instruction, adding a Torah-centered Jewish account of how the favored path is walked.

row.basis: The righteous are planted beside water
row.note: The person on the good way is like a tree planted beside streams, bearing fruit in season; this links the blessed path to the commentary's water and nourishment imagery.

row.basis: Walking God's way is imitation of God's traits
row.note: The midrash reads “walk in all his ways” as imitating God's compassion and other attributes; it turns the commentary's literal path joined to worship into an ethical practice of mercy.

row.basis: The Father's house has many dwellings
row.note: Jesus speaks of dwelling places in his Father's house, giving a specific Christian destination-house image for the commentary's road toward a home.

row.basis: The guide brings his followers to the house
row.note: Jesus promises to return and take his followers to himself, connecting a trusted guide with arrival at the Father's house.

row.basis: The disciples are shown the way to the destination
row.note: Jesus says the disciples know the way to where he is going, a direct meeting of guide, road, and destination.

row.basis: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
row.note: Jesus calls himself the way and says access to the Father is through him, a Christian interpretation that makes the requested path personal and relational.

row.basis: God's mercy brings dawn to those in darkness
row.note: Zechariah's song says God's tender mercy brings light to those sitting in darkness, joining mercy with the commentary's lostness and its contrast between radiant and dark outcomes.

row.basis: God guides feet into the way of peace
row.note: The song says the dawn will guide people's feet into the way of peace, closely matching the Fatiha's request for a straight path and the commentary's walking image.

row.basis: The fallen opponents contrast with those who rise and stand
row.note: The psalm says others collapse and fall while the worshippers rise and stand, closely matching the commentary's contrast between falling under wrath and upright walking.

row.basis: The day is wrath, distress, and devastation
row.note: Zephaniah calls YHWH's day a day of wrath and distress, giving the commentary's judgment day a sharply adverse side.

row.basis: The day brings alarm against fortified cities
row.note: The trumpet and alarm on that day give a specific public scene of judgment rather than a generic reference to divine anger.

row.basis: The day consumes the earth in divine anger
row.note: The oracle says neither silver nor gold can rescue people from YHWH's wrath, adding a concrete reckoning to the commentary's account of judgment.

row.basis: A creditor must respect the debtor's household
row.note: The creditor may not enter the borrower's house to seize a pledge, a concrete legal limit on the debt relation behind the commentary's debt and witness imagery.

row.basis: The borrower brings the pledge out
row.note: The lender must remain outside while the debtor brings the pledge, preserving the debtor's agency within the written obligation.

row.basis: A poor debtor's cloak cannot be kept overnight
row.note: The creditor must not retain a poor person's pledge, directly connecting debt law with care for a vulnerable person.

row.basis: Returning the cloak is righteousness before God
row.note: The pledge must be returned before sunset so the debtor can sleep in it; God hears the debtor's cry, joining debt, timely repayment, and divine judgment of conduct.

row.basis: A king settles accounts with his servants
row.note: Jesus begins a parable with a king who calls servants to settle their debts, bringing the commentary's king, day of repayment, and debt together in one scene.

row.basis: A servant owes an unpayable sum
row.note: The first servant's vast debt makes the account concrete and sets up the king's decision about repayment and mercy.
The servant falls down and asks the king for patience, matching the commentary's dependent petitioner before a sovereign.

row.basis: The king releases the debt out of compassion
row.note: The king has compassion and cancels the debt, combining sovereignty, repayment, and mercy in a direct parallel to the commentary's divine attributes.

row.basis: The forgiven servant demands payment from another
row.note: The servant then seizes a fellow servant over a smaller debt, turning received mercy into a test of how the forgiven person treats others.

row.basis: The king recalls the canceled debt
row.note: The king confronts the servant with the debt he had canceled, making remembered mercy and account-keeping central to judgment.

row.basis: The servant should have shown compassion
row.note: The king asks whether the servant should have shown the same mercy he received, connecting compassion to the ethical use of favor.

row.basis: The king hands the unmerciful debtor over
row.note: The angry king delivers the servant to punishment until the debt is paid, directly joining unpaid debt, wrath, and reckoning.

row.basis: The parable applies the account to forgiveness
row.note: Jesus says the heavenly Father will treat those who refuse forgiveness similarly, making mercy the decisive conduct at the final account.

row.basis: Forgive a neighbor and one's own sins are forgiven
row.note: Sirach directly joins forgiving another's wrong with forgiveness when one prays, adding a Jewish ethical interpretation to the commentary's pairing of mercy and judgment.

row.basis: The written debt record is erased
row.note: Paul says the record of debt against people is canceled and removed, a Christian theological reading that turns the commentary's written account into an image of forgiven guilt.

row.basis: The weary are invited to come for rest
row.note: Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest, matching the commentary's tired traveler who asks for help.

row.basis: A gentle teacher gives a yoke
row.note: Jesus calls disciples to take his yoke and learn from him because he is gentle and humble; as a discipleship metaphor, it connects the commentary's voluntarily tamed servant with rest under a trusted guide.
Jesus says his yoke is easy and burden light, giving a concrete contrast to coercive enslavement in the commentary's Moses scene.

row.basis: God leads the blind by an unknown road
row.note: YHWH promises to lead the blind on an unfamiliar path and turn darkness to light, directly joining lostness, guidance, and divine care.

row.basis: The guide does not abandon those he leads
row.note: The same promise says God will not forsake them, contrasting the commentary's unrecognized owner with a Lord who remains responsible for the lost.

row.basis: The traveler bows after God guides him
row.note: Abraham's servant bows and worships YHWH at the well after seeing the sign, adding an explicit worship response to the commentary's meeting of guidance, water, and travel.

row.basis: Two people go to the temple to pray
row.note: Jesus frames the contrast as a temple encounter, giving a concrete communal setting to the commentary's worshipper speaking directly to God.

row.basis: The tax collector asks God for mercy without lifting his eyes
row.note: The petitioner stands at a distance and asks for mercy, a specific posture of dependence that echoes the commentary's needy servant asking the Lord for help.

row.basis: The humble petitioner goes home justified
row.note: Jesus says the humble petitioner, rather than the self-exalting one, is justified; this joins prayer, moral standing, and the final verdict.
