row.note: The commentary places manna and quail after Israel's rescue from an enemy; this song says YHWH redeemed and led that people, supplying the narrative transition into the wilderness provision.
The commentary's gift that comes down upon the rescued Israelites meets YHWH's promise to rain bread from heaven for them; the verse makes the descent and divine giver explicit.
The commentary names quail among Israel's bestowed food; Exodus reports quail covering the camp in the evening, the same wilderness provision scene.
The commentary joins quail with a warning that wrath may descend; Numbers has YHWH bring quail to the camp immediately before its punitive outcome, preserving both food and danger in one scene.
The commentary's warning that transgression after provision brings wrath closely meets the account in which YHWH's anger flares against the people while the quail is still in their mouths.
The commentary treats manna as divine provision joined to moral direction; Deuteronomy says God fed Israel manna in order to teach dependence on the divine word.
The commentary couples food, forgiveness, and finding the way; Nehemiah's retrospective prayer says God gave a good spirit to instruct Israel and did not withhold manna or water.

row.basis: heavenly manna suited to every taste
row.note: The commentary draws the ni'ma family's softness and delight out of the manna scene; Wisdom retells that manna as heavenly food containing every pleasure and fitted to each taste.

row.basis: calf and turning aside from the way
row.note: The commentary makes the calf episode a junction of wrath and losing the way; Exodus says Israel quickly turned aside from the commanded way and made a calf.

row.basis: YHWH's burning anger at the calf
row.note: The commentary says calf worship incurs wrath from the Lord; YHWH tells Moses that his anger burns and proposes consuming the calf-making people.

row.basis: wrath against the people brought from Egypt
row.note: The commentary recalls a people rescued from an enemy who then risk wrath; Moses explicitly asks why YHWH's anger burns against the people brought out of Egypt.
The commentary juxtaposes descending wrath with abundant forgiveness; the calf narrative itself reports that YHWH relented from the disaster announced for the people.

row.basis: Moses angry on seeing the calf
row.note: The commentary says Moses returned to his people angry and grieving after the calf; Exodus narrates his anger blazing when he saw the calf and dancing.
The commentary's calf scene holds wrath and a way back together; Moses says he feared the anger and wrath that would destroy Israel, yet YHWH listened to him.
The commentary contrasts divine wrath with a forgiving end for those who return; Nehemiah interprets Israel's rebellion through God's readiness to forgive, grace, mercy, and slowness to anger.
The commentary names the calf as the concrete offense beneath the wrath; Nehemiah's liturgical retelling specifies Israel's making of the calf and its attribution of the exodus to it.

row.basis: merciful and gracious, slow to anger
row.note: The commentary opposes rida and ghadaab while retaining forgiveness after the calf; YHWH's self-proclamation names mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love in that same aftermath.
The commentary holds mercy beside real wrath rather than treating them as interchangeable; the continuation both forgives iniquity and says guilt is not simply cleared.
The commentary's favorable group receives grace and travels together; Moses asks that, if he has found favor, God pardon the people and take them as an inheritance.
The commentary needs the relation of calf-wrath to forgiveness; this rabbinic reading makes Exodus 34's attributes a liturgical pattern by which Israel seeks pardon after sin.
The commentary's calf episode is retold here with Israel making the calf, offering sacrifice to it, and rejoicing in what their hands made.
The commentary's wilderness food is recalled by Paul as the spiritual food shared by the whole exodus generation, a Christian rereading of the manna gift.

row.basis: God not pleased in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary makes divine pleasure the opposite of wrath; Paul says God was not pleased with most of the manna-fed generation and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness.
The commentary uses the calf to connect provision, idolatry, and wrath; Paul invokes the calf tradition to warn his readers not to be idolaters.
The commentary binds divine anger to losing the right path; this wilderness interpretation says God was angry because the generation went astray in heart and did not know his ways.

row.basis: angry forty years and fallen bodies
row.note: The commentary calls wrath a fall; Hebrews explicitly asks whether God was angry with those whose bodies fell in the wilderness.

row.basis: Jesus as exodus deliverer and judge
row.note: The commentary recalls God delivering Israel and then judging rebellion; Jude's text names Jesus as the one who saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed unbelievers, a Christological retelling of the scene.
The commentary dwells on wrath descending upon alayhim; Zephaniah has YHWH say he will pour his indignation and burning anger upon them, making the agent and collective onset explicit.

row.basis: anger, perishing in the way, and blessing
row.note: The commentary makes wrath a loss of the way while the other group is favored; this verse joins divine anger, perishing in the way, and blessing for those who take refuge.
The commentary explicitly sets rida against ghadaab; the psalm compresses the same polarity into God's momentary anger and lifelong favor.
The commentary's n-' -m family joins bestowed favor to softness; Hebrew no'am, a cognate form, asks that God's pleasantness or favor be upon us, closely matching the favor-upon-a-group construction.
The commentary says anger leaves a visible face; after Cain's offering is not regarded, he becomes very angry and his face falls.
The commentary gives favor a softened face and cooled eye; Ezra calls the remnant's reprieve divine favor and says it brightens their eyes and gives reviving.
The commentary's blessed side is visibly softened and bright; the priestly blessing asks that YHWH's face shine upon the people and be gracious to them.
The commentary contrasts a burdened face with a favored one; the blessing asks YHWH to lift his face toward the people and give them peace.
The commentary makes favor legible in a brightened face; Moses' face radiates after speaking with YHWH, supplying a concrete biblical face-of-divine-encounter image.
The commentary describes the final day as two visibly different destinies; Daniel's resurrection vision divides the sleepers between everlasting life and everlasting contempt.
The commentary's favored faces are luminous; Daniel says the wise, including those who turn many to righteousness, will shine like the expanse and stars.

row.basis: anger and a person following his own way
row.note: The commentary links anger to straying from the path; Isaiah says God was angry at iniquity, yet the person went on in the way of his own heart.
The commentary's alternative to wrath is forgiveness followed by finding the way; immediately after the angry-wandering image, God says he will heal, lead, and restore comfort.
The commentary places repentance and forgiveness against wrath; the summons to faithless Israel to return grounds mercy in God's refusal to keep anger forever.

row.basis: return, mercy, and relenting from disaster
row.note: The commentary's forgiving end asks for turning back after wrongdoing; Joel calls for a return of heart because God is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and relents from calamity.
The commentary sets divine anger against rida or merciful approval; Micah says God does not retain anger forever because he delights in steadfast love.

row.basis: turn from a way and live
row.note: The commentary says the forgiven turn toward the right way; God asks whether he delights in the wicked person's death rather than in that person's turning from the way and living.

row.basis: leave a wicked way and receive pardon
row.note: The commentary gives forgiveness a turn toward guidance; Isaiah calls the wicked to leave their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon.

row.basis: blind led from darkness into a way
row.note: The commentary's opposing outcomes are found or lost way; YHWH promises to lead blind people by an unknown way and make darkness light before them.

row.basis: guided on a straight path without stumbling
row.note: The commentary's favorable group is a company on a road; Jeremiah's restored people are led by streams on a straight path where they do not stumble.
The commentary combines a favorable face with a rightly found path; Proverbs compares the righteous path to growing daylight.
The commentary connects loss of the way with the darkened other side; Proverbs says the wicked path is darkness and its walkers do not know what makes them stumble.

row.basis: known righteous way and perishing wicked way
row.note: The commentary's two groups are distinguished by the road they inhabit; the psalm contrasts YHWH's knowing of the righteous way with the wicked way's perishing.

row.basis: good eye, good companion, good way
row.note: The commentary reads the favored path as one walked with good companions and a settled eye; this mishnah deliberately pairs a good eye and good companion with a good way, then supplies their evil counterparts.
The commentary's wrath side is a lost way and a fall; Jesus describes a broad way that leads to destruction and has many travelers.
The commentary's favored side is a found path; Jesus contrasts it with a narrow way that leads to life and is found by few.
The commentary says anger and error lose the road; Jesus says one walking in darkness does not know where one is going.

row.basis: darkness blinds the eyes and obscures the way
row.note: The commentary's hostile face includes disturbed eyes and its theological result is waylessness; this verse says hatred leaves a person in darkness, blinded in the eyes, ignorant of where to go.

row.basis: eyes opened, darkness turned to light, forgiveness
row.note: The commentary joins seeing, guidance, repentance, and favor; Paul's commission is to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light, and give forgiveness and an inheritance.

row.basis: light and feet guided into peace
row.note: The commentary puts the favorable face and the right road together; Zechariah's hymn says divine dawn shines on those in darkness and guides their feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: light of God's glory in Christ's face
row.note: The commentary makes divine favor visible on the face; Paul says God has shone in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ.
The commentary's final-day favored faces shine; Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom.
The commentary's bright face is set in a Moses-and-wrath complex; Paul rereads Moses' radiant face as the visible glory of the old covenant.
The commentary turns divine favor into a face's condition; Paul extends the Moses image to believers whose unveiled faces are being transformed into the same image.

row.basis: the Lord's eyes on righteous and face against evil
row.note: The commentary contrasts a favored group with those under divine disfavor and makes face and eye central; Peter juxtaposes the Lord's eyes upon the righteous with the Lord's face against evildoers.
The commentary emphasizes wrath as something that comes upon a group without naming its agent in the Arabic passive; Paul uses the closely parallel image that wrath has come upon them.

row.basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
row.note: The commentary calls yawm the days carrying punishment and forgiveness; Paul speaks of a day of wrath and revelation of God's righteous judgment.
The commentary's favor side includes faithful action and an ultimate outcome; Paul names eternal life for those persevering in good work and seeking glory, honor, and incorruptibility.
The commentary makes wrath the adverse outcome of rebellion; Paul sets wrath and anger on those who reject truth and obey unrighteousness.
The commentary ends with a collective named by wrath; Paul describes a former corporate condition as being children of wrath.
The commentary does not end at wrath but gives forgiveness a path onward; Paul immediately counters the prior wrath condition with God's rich mercy and great love.

row.basis: appointed for salvation rather than wrath
row.note: The commentary divides humanity between a gift-bearing and a wrath-bearing outcome; Paul explicitly says God has not appointed believers for wrath but for obtaining salvation.
The commentary's favored group receives a divine gift and shares a destination; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.
The commentary's second group bears divine wrath and abasement; the king's opposite verdict sends the cursed away to the prepared fire.

row.basis: company with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
row.note: The commentary says the favored road is shared with exemplary companions; Jesus depicts many joining the patriarchs at the kingdom meal.
The commentary gives the adverse group a dark, humiliated bodily condition; Jesus contrasts the kingdom meal with expulsion into outer darkness, weeping, and gnashing.

row.basis: hiding from the enthroned face and the Lamb's wrath
row.note: The commentary makes wrath and a face inseparable images; those facing judgment seek to hide from the face of the enthroned one and from the Lamb's wrath.
The commentary's yawm carries the two outcomes; Revelation calls the crisis the great day of their wrath and asks who can stand.
The commentary's favorable final side has a transformed face; Revelation's servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads.

row.basis: God's light on the final servants
row.note: The commentary's bright face belongs to a final favored community; Revelation says the Lord God will give light to his servants, with no more night.
The commentary presents manna as a remembered divine favor; Jesus contrasts that wilderness manna with death, so the Christian discourse assigns the old gift a deliberately limited result.

row.basis: living bread from heaven gives life
row.note: The commentary's descending provision is manna; Jesus identifies himself as the living bread come down from heaven, turning the exodus image toward his life-giving claim.

row.basis: all stray, iniquity laid on one
row.note: The commentary says a straying collective bears wrath upon itself; Isaiah describes all as going astray yet makes YHWH lay the iniquity of all upon a single servant, reversing the placement of consequence.

row.basis: Christ becoming a curse for others
row.note: The commentary contrasts a group under anger with a group granted favor; Paul presents Christ as becoming a curse in order to redeem others from the law's curse, a different distributive account of adverse judgment.

row.basis: servants fed and rejoicing while others hunger and are ashamed
row.note: The commentary's two groups receive contrary bodily conditions; Isaiah contrasts God's servants eating, drinking, and rejoicing with others' hunger, thirst, and shame.

row.basis: joyful heart versus pain and broken spirit
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is softened while the adverse face is afflicted; Isaiah continues the division with joyful song from the heart versus cry of pain and a broken spirit.

row.basis: faces to the ground in praise
row.note: The commentary depicts the favored, guided people prostrating and praises God; Israel sees divine glory and fire, bows with faces to the ground, worships, and gives thanks.
The commentary's selected group falls in prostration; at Ezra's blessing the people answer Amen, lift hands, and bow with faces to the ground.

row.basis: all heavenly attendants fall on their faces
row.note: The commentary joins the favored assembly to prostration; angels, elders, and living creatures fall before the throne on their faces and worship God.

row.basis: walking in light, fellowship, and cleansing
row.note: The commentary says the favored path is traveled with companions and ends in forgiveness; John links walking in light to fellowship with one another and cleansing from sin.

The commentary divides recipients of divine provision from those exposed to wrath; this rabbinic manna tradition differentiates where the righteous, intermediate, and wicked find the food, making provision a visible moral index.
The commentary treats rida and anger as opposed divine dispositions; the high-priest tradition has God speak of mercy overcoming anger, an interpretive attempt to hold the opposition together.
The commentary's grammar turns Arabic alayhim into the site of descending wrath; Hebrew alehem is its cognate prepositional form in Zephaniah's statement that indignation is poured upon them.
The commentary calls rida the opposite of anger; Hebrew ratsah, a likely cognate of Arabic rida, says the offering will be accepted for the worshiper to make atonement.

row.basis: no'am joined to ways of peace
row.note: The commentary associates the n-' -m family with a softened favorable condition and a path; Proverbs calls wisdom's ways ways of no'am, pleasantness, and all her paths peace.

row.basis: royal favor versus wrath toward shame
row.note: The commentary opposes favor and wrath and reads abasement in the adverse side; Proverbs gives the same pair in a king's favor for a prudent servant and wrath toward a shameful one.

row.basis: wrath like lion and favor like dew
row.note: The commentary contrasts an overwhelming anger with a gentle blessing that comes upon people; Proverbs compares a king's wrath to a lion's roar and his favor to dew on grass.

row.basis: light of a king's face and rainlike favor
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is soft and bright, and its blessing descends; Proverbs says life is in the light of a king's face and his favor is like a latter-rain cloud.

row.basis: faces as flames on the day of YHWH
row.note: The commentary describes anger in a reddened face and attaches outcomes to a day; Isaiah's day-of-YHWH terror says people's faces are flames, though the verse depicts fear rather than anger.

row.basis: Hebrew yom in a wrathful divine day
row.note: The commentary's yawm denotes days when punishment or mercy comes down; Hebrew yom is its clear cognate, and Isaiah calls the day of YHWH a day of wrath and fierce anger.

row.basis: dust on heads and faces lowered
row.note: The commentary has dust descend over adverse faces; Jerusalem's mourners put dust on their heads and lower their heads to the ground under judgment, a concrete adjacent image of abasement.
The commentary contrasts luminous favored faces with a darkened other side; Lamentations says the sufferers' faces are blacker than soot.

row.basis: no more shame or pale face
row.note: The commentary's blessed outcome reverses the shame of adverse faces; the restoration promise says Jacob will no longer be ashamed and his face will no longer grow pale.
The commentary's favorable face becomes visibly bright; Isaiah says Zion will see and be radiant in the context of restored divine abundance.

row.basis: wisdom lighting and changing a hard face
row.note: The commentary says favor makes the face soft rather than frowning; Ecclesiastes says wisdom lights a person's face and changes its hardness.

row.basis: joyful heart making a face good
row.note: The commentary reads inner favor or anger through the face; Proverbs similarly says a joyful heart makes the face good while sorrow crushes the spirit.

row.basis: light of the eyes gladdening the heart
row.note: The commentary's ni'ma image is an eye made calm and refreshed; Proverbs links the light of the eyes with a glad heart and bodily renewal.

row.basis: favor sought and a no-longer-sad face
row.note: The commentary makes favor visible in a changed face; after Hannah asks to find favor and receives Eli's word of peace, she eats and her face is no longer as before.

row.basis: shame of face under sin and judgment
row.note: The commentary's adverse group bears a humiliated face; Daniel assigns shame of face to Israel and its rulers because of unfaithfulness before God's righteousness.
The commentary's final favorable face is relieved of its burden; Isaiah's salvation oracle promises to wipe tears from all faces and remove reproach.

row.basis: praise replacing a faint spirit and ashes
row.note: The commentary makes hamd the opposite of blame and favors a softened countenance; Isaiah's restoration gives a garland instead of ashes and a garment of praise instead of a faint spirit.

row.basis: curse for turning aside from the way
row.note: The commentary places divine disfavor upon those who lose the way; Deuteronomy defines the curse through disobedience and turning aside from the commanded way.

row.basis: life and good against death and evil
row.note: The commentary divides recipients into contrary divine outcomes; Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and urges the choice of life.

row.basis: a holy way on which the unclean do not stray
row.note: The commentary's goal is a road not lost after forgiveness; Isaiah's holy way excludes the unclean and says even fools will not go astray on it.

row.basis: God teaching and leading in the way
row.note: The commentary describes hidaya as the counterpart to falling under wrath; YHWH identifies himself as the one who teaches for profit and leads in the way to go.

row.basis: walking all God's ways after the calf intercession
row.note: The commentary's mercy sequence ends in a rightly lived way; after the calf-and-intercession complex, Moses states the requirement to fear, love, serve, and walk in all God's ways.

row.basis: walking with God and turning many from iniquity
row.note: The commentary's gifted people travel a way together and turn toward guidance; Levi is said to have walked with God in peace and uprightness and to have turned many from iniquity.

row.basis: walking God's ways among those standing before him
row.note: The commentary calls the righteous a company on the favored road; the high priest is promised access among those standing before God if he walks in God's ways.

row.basis: falling on the face before covenant blessing
row.note: The commentary's chosen and blessed figures fall in prostration; Abram falls on his face immediately before God gives covenantal promises of fruitfulness and nations.

row.basis: faces down and confession after divine fire
row.note: The commentary associates prostration and praise with a divinely favored manifestation; after the fire, the people fall on their faces and confess that YHWH is God.

row.basis: tender mercy and dawn from on high
row.note: The commentary joins divine favor to the image of a day and light; Zechariah grounds the rising dawn in the tender mercy of God before its guidance imagery in the next verse.

row.basis: eyes of the heart enlightened for hope
row.note: The commentary makes the eye's condition carry guidance and favor; Paul prays for enlightened heart-eyes so believers know the hope of calling and inheritance.

row.basis: Jesus' face shining like the sun
row.note: The commentary gives the blessed face a luminous aspect; the transfiguration states that Jesus' face shone like the sun, within a scene of divine approval.
The commentary treats the face as a bearer of a person's spiritual condition; Stephen's opponents see his face as that of an angel while he testifies before judgment.

row.basis: the healthy eye filling the body with light
row.note: The commentary's favorable eye is calm and bright; Jesus uses a healthy eye as the condition by which the whole body is full of light.
The commentary's adverse face includes an afflicted eye and dark covering; Jesus's paired image makes the bad eye produce darkness throughout the body.
The commentary turns favor into an eye's state; Jesus calls the eyes blessed that see what prophets and kings desired to see.

row.basis: rescue from darkness into a kingdom
row.note: The commentary's divine deliverance moves people away from the lost side; Paul says the Father rescues people from the domain of darkness and transfers them to the Son's kingdom.

row.basis: praise from God at final judgment
row.note: The commentary opens its contrast with hamd, praise and approval, and names a day of reckoning; Paul locates each person's praise from God at the Lord's coming judgment.

row.basis: well-done approval and entry into joy
row.note: The commentary glosses hamd as approval or being pleased; the master praises the faithful servant and admits that servant into the master's joy.

row.basis: glory, honor, and peace for doing good
row.note: The commentary's favorable side receives an approving divine outcome; Paul promises glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, against the wrath named in the same argument.

row.basis: lost and found at a father's welcome
row.note: The commentary contrasts being lost with a forgiven return to the way; the father identifies the returned son as formerly lost and now found and celebrates him.
The commentary makes repentance and a turn toward right guidance the way out of wrath; Peter calls hearers to repent and turn so that sins may be wiped out.

row.basis: confession followed by forgiveness and cleansing
row.note: The commentary's grace side includes forgiveness after wrongdoing; John says confession is met by God's faithful forgiveness and cleansing from unrighteousness.

row.basis: no hunger, thirst, scorching, or heat
row.note: The commentary begins with wilderness food and ends with bodily marked destinies; Revelation's favorable multitude will neither hunger nor thirst and will not be struck by scorching heat.

row.basis: guided to living water and tears wiped
row.note: The commentary couples a gifted community with guidance and a relaxed face; the Lamb shepherds the multitude to springs of living water and God wipes every tear from their eyes.

row.basis: cloud of witnesses and a race to run
row.note: The commentary's favored way is a shared route with exemplary companions; Hebrews places believers within a cloud of witnesses and tells them to run the course set before them.

row.basis: glory's Spirit resting upon the reviled
row.note: The commentary's favor is something that descends upon a group; Peter calls reviled believers blessed because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon them.
The commentary's en'amte alayhim has an explicit giver and a group upon whom favor rests; Acts says great grace was upon all the witness-bearing community.
The commentary turns the calf's idolatry into a wrath-bearing fate visible on the face; Revelation marks beast-worshipers on forehead or hand before announcing their judgment.
The commentary's golden-calf warning culminates in divine anger; Revelation gives beast worshipers wine of God's wrath, a later apocalyptic pairing of idolatry and wrath.
The commentary's two faces foreshadow differing final bodily states; Paul contrasts a body sown in dishonor and weakness with one raised in glory and power.
The commentary makes final grace visible in bodily appearance; Paul expects Christ to transform the lowly body into conformity with his glorious body.

row.basis: elders fall and worship in praise
row.note: The commentary's chosen company prostrates in praise; the elders fall before the enthroned one, worship, and cast down their crowns.
The commentary recalls manna as an indicator of divine favor; Revelation promises hidden manna specifically to the one who conquers, relocating wilderness provision into an eschatological reward.

The commentary glosses hamd as approving or finding something good; Hebrew h-m-d is plausibly cognate but in this verse calls the forbidden tree desirable to the eyes, so the semantic divergence rather than a direct parallel is the point.

row.basis: red face and shadowed eyelids in suffering
row.note: The commentary describes redness and the eye-area as outward marks of anger; Job instead describes his own face reddened by weeping and shadow on his eyelids, a specific but affectively different bodily image.
The commentary's descent of ni'ma after rescue is named here by the Israelites as bread that YHWH has given them to eat; it supplies the explicit attribution absent from the passive wrath phrase.
The commentary combines wilderness provision with moral testing and a beneficial end; Deuteronomy says YHWH fed Israel manna to humble and test them, in order to do them good in the end.

row.basis: cloud and fire leading the people
row.note: The commentary's favorable alternative to wrath is a guided road; Nehemiah's retelling says God's mercies did not forsake Israel and that cloud and fire continued to lead them on the way.
The commentary glosses hamd through approval and turns ni'ma into favor bestowed on people; YHWH tells Moses that he has found favor in his eyes and is known by name.

row.basis: Moses bows in response to mercy
row.note: The commentary joins the favored, guided community with prostration; directly after the mercy-and-forgiveness proclamation Moses hurriedly bows his head to the earth and worships.
The commentary's calf-makers receive divine anger and abasement; Exodus closes the narrative with YHWH striking the people with a plague because of the calf.

row.basis: anger, hidden face, and people consumed
row.note: The commentary makes wrath a condition borne by a group and visualizes face; Moses says YHWH's anger will burn, his face will be hidden, and the people will be consumed by evils.

row.basis: lifted countenance versus sin at the door
row.note: The commentary's angry face is the inverse of divine approval; God's reply to Cain contrasts the lifting granted for doing well with sin crouching at the door if he does not.

row.basis: God's face set against the disobedient
row.note: The commentary pairs adverse divine judgment with face imagery; YHWH says he will set his face against Israel, after which they are defeated and flee.
The commentary's central contrast is wrath against a merciful favorable state; this thanksgiving says God's anger was directed at the speaker but turned away, and God became comfort.

row.basis: face hidden in wrath, everlasting compassion after it
row.note: The commentary treats anger as a visible, descending judgment and favor as its contrary; Isaiah says God hid his face in overflowing wrath for a moment but has everlasting compassion.

row.basis: looking to God, radiant faces, no shame
row.note: The commentary's favorable final face is luminous rather than humiliated; the psalm says those who look to YHWH are radiant and their faces are not ashamed.
The commentary connects divine favor, a shining face, and deliverance; the refrain asks God to restore the people, make his face shine, and save them.

row.basis: no shame and a consequent fall
row.note: The commentary makes the adverse face abased and says wrath is a fall; Jeremiah says the wicked neither feel shame nor know how to blush, therefore they will fall.

row.basis: shame on every face in judgment
row.note: The commentary's final adverse side bears a darkened or humiliated face; Ezekiel's judgment scene says shame will be on every face as people put on sackcloth and tremble.

row.basis: joy for the faithful and shame for opponents
row.note: The commentary separates a favored community from an abased one; Isaiah tells those who tremble at God's word that God will appear to their joy while their hostile brethren are put to shame.

row.basis: rejoicing heart and flourishing body versus indignation
row.note: The commentary makes the two divine outcomes bodily visible; Isaiah promises servants a rejoicing heart and flourishing bones while God's indignation is known against enemies.

row.basis: good person obtains favor, schemer condemned
row.note: The commentary relates approval and praise to the contrary of wrath; Proverbs says a good person obtains favor from YHWH while a person of schemes is condemned.

row.basis: confessing and forsaking sins obtains mercy
row.note: The commentary's route out of wrath includes repentance and changed conduct; Proverbs contrasts hiding transgressions with confessing and forsaking them in order to receive mercy.

row.basis: grace and mercy upon the elect
row.note: The commentary's en'amte alayhim makes grace a gift resting upon a chosen group; Wisdom says grace and mercy are upon God's holy ones and care attends the elect.
The commentary's two groups have opposed paths, visual states, and ends; the Community Rule's two-spirits instruction systematically assigns light and darkness, conduct, and judgment to opposed lots.

row.basis: Way of Life and Way of Death
row.note: The commentary's road splits between a favored and a ruined group; this early Christian teaching opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.

row.basis: way of light and way of darkness
row.note: The commentary's found path is associated with brightness and its lost path with dark affliction; Barnabas frames its ethical teaching as the two ways of light and darkness.
The commentary joins correct guidance to light and an unfallen walk; Jesus says that a person walking in the day does not stumble because that person sees the world's light.
The commentary's wrath-side loses the way and falls; Jesus's paired saying makes the night-walker stumble because light is not in that person.

row.basis: darkness falling on a judgment-blinded eye
row.note: The commentary gives anger a bodily eye-image and says something comes upon its recipient; Paul announces the Lord's hand against Elymas, after which mist and darkness immediately fall on him and he seeks a guide.
The commentary juxtaposes wrath with a saving, favorable end; Paul describes Jesus as the one who rescues believers from the wrath that is coming.

row.basis: chosen people called from darkness to light
row.note: The commentary's favored community is both chosen and visibly luminous; Peter calls a chosen people out of darkness into God's marvelous light.

row.basis: formerly without mercy, now receiving mercy
row.note: The commentary's two groups are distinguished by bestowed ni'ma versus divine disfavor; Peter contrasts being not a people and without mercy with becoming God's people and receiving mercy.

row.basis: conqueror inherits and belongs to God
row.note: The commentary's favorable side receives a gift and shares a divine companionship; Revelation promises inheritance and a God-child relation to the one who conquers.

row.basis: lake of fire for the unfaithful
row.note: The commentary's adverse group has an eschatological judgment distinct from the favored group; Revelation supplies the opposed fate for the cowardly, faithless, and idolaters.
The commentary develops ni'ma as softness, delicacy, and a restful sensory condition; Exodus describes manna as white and tasting like wafers made with honey.

The commentary gives ni'ma an eye-image while recalling manna; the dissatisfied wilderness people say that nothing is before their eyes except manna, an intentionally contrary eye-and-provision scene.

row.basis: God does not destroy after Moses' intercession
row.note: The commentary's wrath sequence is countered by forgiveness and a continued path; Deuteronomy's retrospective account says YHWH listened to Moses and was unwilling to destroy Israel after the calf.

row.basis: Moses offers himself for the people's sin
row.note: The commentary describes wrath as falling on the culpable group; Moses instead offers to be blotted from God's book if Israel cannot be forgiven, a different placement of the consequence within the same calf scene.
The commentary's ni'ma is an enduring divine favor rather than a single meal; Nehemiah says Israel lacked nothing for forty years, with garments and feet preserved in the wilderness.
The commentary's adverse outcome is a humiliated face under sin; Ezra confesses being ashamed and unable to lift his face to God because Israel's iniquities have risen high.
The commentary's guided, forgiven figures prostrate themselves; Ezra's confession is made while weeping and lying face down before God's house, gathering a repentant community.

row.basis: faces growing pale before the divine day
row.note: The commentary describes an anger-marked red face and a final day; Joel's approaching day makes the nations writhe and all faces gather pallor, a related but distinct facial response.

row.basis: judgment changing a king's facial color
row.note: The commentary reads judgment in the body's face; after the divine writing appears, Belshazzar's facial color changes and his body is visibly shaken.

row.basis: life and favor for finding wisdom
row.note: The commentary's blessing is joined to finding the right way; Proverbs says whoever finds wisdom finds life and obtains favor from YHWH.

row.basis: good understanding gives favor, treacherous way is hard
row.note: The commentary sets favor against the condition of the lost way; Proverbs joins good understanding that gives favor to the hard way of the treacherous.

row.basis: blessing God for evil as for good
row.note: The commentary begins with hamd and its opposition to blame while contrasting ni'ma and wrath; this mishnah requires blessing God for adverse events as for good, changing how praise relates to an unwelcome divine event.
The commentary treats anger and rida as opposed dispositions; this temperament teaching distinguishes people by being easy or hard to anger and easy or hard to appease.
The commentary enumerates prophets and martyrs among the favored companions; Jesus tells the persecuted to rejoice because their reward is great and the prophets were persecuted before them.

row.basis: judgment as loving darkness rather than light
row.note: The commentary's two groups end in luminous or darkened conditions; Jesus explains judgment through the light's arrival and evildoers' love of darkness.

row.basis: doing truth and coming to light
row.note: The commentary's favorable side joins right action to a found way; the one doing truth comes to the light so deeds can be seen as done in God.

The commentary makes a face show an inward religious condition and begins with praise; Jesus criticizes fasters who disfigure their faces to be seen by people, distinguishing their received human reward from divine regard.

row.basis: anointed head and washed face before the Father
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is not merely a legal verdict; Jesus tells secret fasters to anoint the head and wash the face so the Father, rather than observers, sees and rewards.
The commentary calls wrath something that descends upon people; Paul describes God's wrath as being revealed from heaven against ungodliness and unrighteousness.

row.basis: justification and rescue from wrath through Christ
row.note: The commentary describes repentance, faith, good action, and guidance as the route beyond wrath; Paul frames rescue from wrath through Christ's blood, a distinct Christian account of the saving transition.
The commentary's rida-ghadaab contrast is expressed as two divine dispositions; Paul asks readers to consider God's kindness and severity, with continuance in kindness opposed to being cut off.

row.basis: formerly darkness, now light, therefore walk
row.note: The commentary's contrast joins identity, light, and a road; Paul says believers were darkness but are now light in the Lord and commands them to walk as children of light.

row.basis: Christ shining on one who rises
row.note: The commentary's eschatological face is lit after a fall or deathlike state; the cited hymn commands the sleeper to rise from the dead so Christ will shine upon that person.

row.basis: patience seeking repentance rather than perishing
row.note: The commentary contrasts a wrathful fall with repentance and a found way; Peter explains divine patience as not wishing people to perish but to come to repentance.

row.basis: eye salve, white garments, and exposed shame
row.note: The commentary's two faces include afflicted eyes and visible favor; the risen Christ counsels the blind, naked church to obtain eye salve for sight and white garments to cover shame.

row.basis: God's glory as the city's light
row.note: The commentary's blessed final side is luminous; Revelation says the eschatological city needs neither sun nor moon because God's glory gives it light.

row.note: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well, the direct narrative setting behind the commentary's Musa who reaches the water of Midian while seeking a way on his journey.

The verse gives the precise well-side tableau developed beside Qur'an 28:23: Midian's priest has daughters who draw water and fill troughs to water their flock; Exodus says seven where the Qur'anic scene has two.

row.basis: Moses aids women and waters flock
row.note: Exodus makes Moses drive off the hostile shepherds and personally water the flock. It is the close counterpart to the commentary's two women who cannot water until the shepherds leave and are then helped by Musa.
Genesis explicitly calls Joseph's pit empty and waterless. That sharpens the commentary's contrasting Qur'anic well scene, where a caravan's water-drawer lowers a bucket and finds the boy.

Midianite traders draw and lift Joseph from the pit and carry him away. The commentary's Qur'anic caravan likewise removes Joseph from a well, but gives the discovery to a water-carrier lowering his bucket.
When Hagar's water is gone in the wilderness, God opens her eyes to a well. It is a concrete companion to the commentary's traveller whose survival and affairs depend on water being found or brought.
Isaac's servants dig in a valley and find a well described as living water. Its fresh, discovered source closely meets the commentary's deep, full well and its concern for sweet, abundant water.

The verse places three flocks at a well whose mouth is covered by a large stone, because the flocks are watered there. It supplies a biblical well-mouth structure for the commentary's beam, pulley, and watering work.

row.basis: traveller rolls well stone and waters flock
row.note: The travelling Jacob rolls the covering stone from the well's mouth and waters Laban's flock. It joins road, well mechanism, and life-giving water in the way the commentary joins the straight path to the water that sustains a traveller.
Water comes from the struck rock so that the people may drink. This gives a wilderness counterpart to the commentary's claim that water is what keeps communal and travelling life standing.

At Beer, God commands that the people be gathered so that he may give them water. The collective provisioning clarifies why the commentary treats a well as the support of an affair rather than a private possession.

Israel answers the provision of water with the command to the well to spring up and with a song. The liturgical address makes the well itself a source of communal life, matching the commentary's concentrated water imagery.
Seasonal rain makes the land yield produce and trees bear fruit. It directly supplies the rain-to-growing-earth sequence through which the commentary hears the growing Rab and the rain-marked ground.
The promised land drinks water from rain of the heavens, directly holding together sky, rain, ground, and dependence that the commentary develops under the Arabic sky/cloud naming.

The rain in its season yields grain, wine, oil, and grass for livestock. This is a close biblical analogue to the commentary's sequence from poured water to human food, animal provision, and livelihood.
Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rise from the sea before the rain. It is a focused companion to the commentary's cloud that forms above and becomes the bearer of growing water.
The sky turns dark with clouds and wind before a great rain. Its linked weather actors answer the commentary's prolonged cloud and moist south-wind scene without requiring the same wind direction.
Job describes God drawing up drops of water and distilling them as rain. It offers a precise account of the water-to-cloud-to-rain process behind the commentary's layered, plant-growing cloud.
The skies pour water down abundantly on humankind. This gives a direct counterpart to the commentary's gathering of abundant water and rain as public benefit.
The thick cloud is loaded with moisture and then spread abroad. Its particular image of a moisture-bearing cloud parallels the commentary's layered cloud and the wet wind associated with it.

row.basis: tree by water, leaf does not wither
row.note: The tree planted by channels of water bears fruit and does not wither. It is the closest biblical image for the commentary's tender plant that remains fresh even through summer.

row.basis: green pasture and waters of rest
row.note: The shepherd makes the speaker rest in green pastures and leads beside waters of rest. It combines the commentary's growing ground, water, guidance, and wayfarer in one pastoral line.
God waters furrows, softens earth with showers, and blesses its growth. This particularly matches the commentary's first rain writing vegetation into the ground and the cloud that grows plants.
God waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his work. It is a close scriptural formulation of heavenly water sustaining terrestrial growth.

row.basis: grass and plants grow from water
row.note: The same hymn says God causes grass to grow for cattle and plants for human cultivation. It supplies the food-and-livestock outcome that the commentary connects to rain and provision.

row.basis: desert turned to pools and springs
row.note: God turns desert into a pool and parched ground into water springs. The reversal makes a concrete companion to rain repairing a people's condition and to water being drawn from otherwise dry ground.
God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on hills. Its exact three-part image is especially close to the commentary's cloud, rain, and plant meeting.

row.basis: rain for seed, rich bread, livestock
row.note: Rain is given for the seed sown in the ground, producing abundant bread and pasture for livestock. This directly meets the commentary's water, food, animals, and sustaining livelihood.

row.basis: waters in wilderness, streams in desert
row.note: Waters break out in the wilderness and streams in the desert. The verse makes the life-restoring turn from dryness to water that the commentary associates with rain, mercy, and fresh life.

row.basis: rivers, fountains, pools on dry land
row.note: God opens rivers and fountains and turns wilderness into pools and dry ground into springs. This is a direct biblical counterpart to both the commentary's well-water and its fear that water may sink out of reach.

Water is poured on thirsty land and streams on dry ground. It directly parallels the commentary's rain sent to barren earth, while its following spiritual application makes the literal image more than a weather report.

The compassionate guide leads the hungry and thirsty to springs of water. Its explicit joining of guidance, a way, and water is a strong companion to the commentary's straight path beside the sustaining well.

God continually guides, satisfies the parched person, and makes that person like a watered garden and an unfailing spring. It closely joins the commentary's guidance, fresh life, and never-failing water.

row.basis: tree by water stays green in drought
row.note: The water-side tree has green leaves and does not cease bearing fruit in drought. Its drought-resistant freshness is a particularly close counterpart to the commentary's summer-unwithered ribbe plant.

God leads the returning people to watercourses on a straight path where they do not stumble. This is an unusually exact meeting of the commentary's dosdoğru yol with water that makes the journey possible.

Where the temple river goes, every living creature lives and the water becomes fresh. It supplies a concentrated account of water's restorative, life-making work behind the commentary's full, sweet, beneficial water.

Trees beside the river bear fruit continually and their leaves do not wither because their water comes from the sanctuary. It directly amplifies the commentary's enduring green plant and abundant sustaining water.
The rain is given in its proper season, including the early and latter rains. It provides a biblical seasonal setting for the commentary's first rain that marks the earth with vegetation.

row.basis: spring rain, storm clouds, field plants
row.note: God makes storm clouds, gives rain showers, and provides vegetation in every field. The verse has the same cloud-rain-plant sequence developed in the commentary.

row.basis: living waters in summer and winter
row.note: Living waters flow in both summer and winter. Its year-round flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's fresh plant that does not fade in summer and its well of plentiful water.
The Father sends rain on both just and unjust. It gives a New Testament articulation of rain as unearned divine beneficence, relevant to the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit.

row.basis: weary traveller seated at Jacob's well
row.note: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well. This makes a close well-side counterpart to the commentary's traveller who reaches water and whose journey depends on it.
A woman arrives to draw water, turning the well into a meeting between a traveller and a woman obtaining water. It closely accompanies the commentary's Musa, the two women, and the Midian water.

row.basis: gift of God and living water
row.note: Jesus offers living water at the well. It moves the commentary's full, beneficial well from physical support to a divine gift without erasing the scene of drawing water.
The water Jesus gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Its self-renewing spring is a concentrated Christian analogue to the commentary's water that keeps life and affairs standing.

The believer is described as the source from whom streams of living water flow. It extends the living-water image from the well to an overflowing source, a useful counterpart to the commentary's abundant gathered water.
God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. It exactly connects divine rain with the food and livelihood results developed in the commentary.
Paul plants, Apollos waters, and God gives the growth. Its agricultural distinction makes explicit the commentary's basic figure: water serves growth, yet the giver of growth remains God.
Israel's wilderness journey takes place under the cloud. Together with the water in verse 4, this creates a Christian rereading in which cloud and water accompany a people on the way.

row.basis: water from the rock for the journey
row.note: The wilderness people drink from the spiritual rock that follows them. It is a strong counterpart to the commentary's claim that water beside the traveller sustains the journey and its affairs.

row.basis: land drinks rain and yields plants
row.note: Land that drinks repeatedly falling rain and produces useful vegetation receives blessing. It directly restates the commentary's heavenly water making the earth grow.

row.basis: farmer waits for early and late rain
row.note: The farmer waits for the earth's precious fruit through the early and late rains. It offers a New Testament seasonal analogue to the commentary's first rain and rain-grown vegetation.

Jude's false teachers are waterless clouds carried by winds. This is a deliberate negative inversion of the commentary's moist, rain-bearing cloud that grows plants: a cloud that promises but gives no life.

row.basis: springs without water and driven mist
row.note: The false teachers are compared to waterless springs and mists driven by storm. Its paired failures of well and cloud form a precise inverse to the commentary's full well and productive cloud.
The Lamb shepherds and guides the thirsty to springs of the water of life. It closely meets the commentary's way, guidance, shepherding provision, and water that removes want.
The thirsty receive water of life freely from the spring. It gives an eschatological form to the commentary's water as indispensable gift and remedy for need.

A bright river of water of life proceeds from God's throne. The throne-source relationship gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's unusual claim that water is a kingdom's or traveller's holding power.

The trees beside the life-river bear fruit continually and their leaves serve healing. Its flourishing trees supply a Christian counterpart to the commentary's plant nourished into unfading freshness.

A water source rising from the earth waters the whole ground before rain is mentioned. Because the Hebrew term's exact physical sense is debated, it is a cautious companion to the commentary's two routes of water: sky-rain and water drawn from below.

row.basis: camels at well at drawing time
row.note: Abraham's servant stops with camels at a well at the time women come to draw water. It supplies the practical journey-and-well setting behind the commentary's water carried by a traveller.
Rebekah draws until the camels have drunk. Her labour at the well gives another concrete biblical instance of water as the support of travellers and animals.

The waters at Marah are made sweet so the people can drink. It offers a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's distinction of abundant water that can be called sweet and water that repairs a people's condition.

The good land is defined by brooks, fountains, and depths issuing in valley and hill. It complements the commentary's deep water-filled well and its concern that a water source might withdraw underground.
Joyful drawing from wells becomes the image of salvation. The verse gives a scriptural way in which the literal action central to the commentary's pulley and well bears a second, saving sense.

row.basis: needy seek water and find none
row.note: The poor and needy seek water with their tongues parched, and God answers them. It is a direct companion to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's water has gone down.

The heavens rain and the earth opens to sprout salvation and righteousness. It recasts the commentary's rain-and-growing-earth image as an ethical and saving figure rather than a purely agricultural one.
The thirsty are invited to come to water without payment. Its invitation turns the commentary's traveller's necessary water into a public gift available to those in need.

The people abandon a fountain of living water for cracked cisterns that cannot retain water. It offers a negative well-and-storage counterpart to the commentary's gathered water and the structural devices at a well's mouth.

The commentary's source label س م و develops sky, cloud, rain, and plant under samāʾ. Hebrew šāmayim in this verse is a cognate sky term, but the verse keeps heaven and its rain distinct while making the land drink the rain; that difference is informative rather than evidence for identical usage.

The commentary explicitly ties أَنْعَمْتَ and n-ʿ-m to freshness and beneficent support. Hebrew neʿimot, a cognate form here, accompanies the path of life and enduring delight; it gives a linguistic and contextual companion to the commentary's path plus life-giving blessing.

row.basis: Arabic q-w-m and Hebrew qwm restore
row.note: The commentary's ق و م label names the pulley and what makes an affair stand. Hebrew qwm in this verse describes raising up and restoring enduring foundations; beside the watered-garden guidance of verse 11, it supplies a cognate support-and-restoration sense without claiming a well in Isaiah 58:12.

The Mishnah lists Miriam's well among things prepared at creation's twilight. This later Jewish tradition makes a well a providential provision for Israel, clarifying the commentary's water as what sustains a travelling community.

row.basis: clouds of glory and Miriam's well
row.note: The Talmud associates Israel's wilderness gifts with the cloud and Miriam's well. Its deliberate pairing is an especially close Jewish counterpart to this section's meeting of growing cloud and well.

On Genesis 37:24, the Talmud reads "no water" as leaving room for snakes and scorpions. The interpretation sharpens the commentary's Joseph contrast: the biblical pit is not a usable water source even when it is not simply empty space.

The common division of Genesis Rabbah says that the water rose to meet Jacob at Haran. That interpretive expansion transforms the covered well of Genesis 29 into a responsive source, useful beside the commentary's well apparatus and abundant water.

The tradition commonly cited at this place has the well water rise for Rebekah as she draws for the camels. It re-reads the traveller-and-well service of Genesis 24 as a sign of blessing, adding a Jewish interpretive layer to the commentary's water as benefit.

The Mishnah fixes when a community begins mentioning and requesting rain. Its concrete liturgical ordering of rain gives a Jewish communal counterpart to the commentary's rain as mercy and repair rather than merely weather.

The Talmud develops the scriptural comparison of Torah with water. This changes water from material provision into descending and sought instruction, a useful interpretive bridge to the commentary's pairing of guidance with sustaining water.
On a wilderness road the Ethiopian traveller sees water and asks for baptism. The scene is a Christian travel-and-water meeting that gives the commentary's road beside water a ritual extension.
Human flesh is compared to grass that withers and a flower that falls. As an explicit inverse, it helps define the significance of the commentary's exceptional plant that does not wither in summer.

The Didache prefers baptism in living water. Its ritual preference turns running or fresh water into a sign of new life, extending the commentary's literal contrast between a life-giving source and lost water.

In the usual chapter division, Mary goes out with a water jar and hears the annunciatory greeting. This Christian apocryphal well-side encounter belongs beside the commentary's women at water, where drawing water becomes a setting for divine gift.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 15
row.note: Augustine's treatment of the Samaritan-woman scene reads Christ's living water as spiritual grace rather than ordinary well water alone. It shows how a Christian interpreter changes the literal traveller-and-well meeting that parallels the commentary.

Origen's homily on Isaac's reopened wells treats digging wells as recovering the deep waters of Scripture. The reading gives a Christian interpretive afterlife to the commentary's well as a source that must be reached and kept open.

The waters below the sky are gathered into one place so that dry ground appears. It is a foundational counterpart to the commentary's claim that abundant water is named for its gathering and to its distinction between water above and water held below.

Israel reaches Elim, with twelve water springs and seventy palms, and camps by the water. This joins a travelling people, a water source, and flourishing vegetation in the concrete way the commentary joins road, well, and growing ground.

Israel asks to travel on the king's highway while promising not to drink from field, vineyard, or well. The verse unusually binds road, traveller, well water, and king in one practical scene, directly meeting the commentary's straight path and water-as-royal-support imagery.

row.basis: well dug by nobles with staffs
row.note: The well is dug by princes and hollowed by nobles with their staffs. As the necessary continuation of the well-song, it makes rulership and a constructed water source meet, closely accompanying the commentary's waters called rulers and its beam-and-pulley well mouth.

David longs for water from the well by Bethlehem's gate. The king's desire for a particular well makes water a royal concern, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary's phrase that a community's waters are its kings.

row.basis: men draw and carry well water to David
row.note: David's warriors break through, draw water from the Bethlehem well, and bring it to him. The verse supplies the physical act of drawing and carrying water for a ruler, beside the commentary's pulley, traveller's water, and royal-water wordplay.

Elisha throws salt into a spring and declares its waters healed, so that death and barrenness will no longer come from it. It gives a sharp biblical counterpart to rain or water improving a people's condition and to the commentary's fresh, beneficial water.

The valley will be filled with water even though neither wind nor rain is seen. Its explicit separation of water provision from visible wind and rain is a useful contrary configuration beside the commentary's wind moving cloud toward rain.

The verse calls YHWH melekh, a cognate of the commentary's م ل ك / mālik label, while placing him over the flood. It gives a substantive Hebrew king-and-water meeting, not merely a shared root, beside the commentary's water as what holds an affair together.

row.basis: Baca valley made a spring by rain
row.note: Those crossing the Valley of Baca make it a place of springs, and early rain covers it with blessings. The transforming rain-and-spring image supplies a pilgrimage-scale companion to the commentary's path that cannot be separated from water.

row.basis: full clouds empty rain on earth
row.note: When clouds are full, they pour rain on the earth. The compact image answers the commentary's layered cloud, its accumulated moisture, and the eventual transfer of gathered water to the ground.

By divine knowledge the depths break open and the skies drip dew. It is a compact biblical pairing of water from below with moisture from above, closely matching the commentary's well-water and heaven-rain as two routes of water.

A person who boasts of a false gift is like clouds and wind with no rain. This negative weather image precisely defines the loss implicit in the commentary's productive cloud: visible cloud and wind do not suffice unless water reaches the earth.

row.basis: garden fountain and well of living water
row.note: The beloved is called a garden fountain, a well of living waters, and streams flowing from Lebanon. Its gathered garden, well, freshness, and flow make it a particularly close biblical companion to the commentary's full well and unfading vegetation.
YHWH guards the vineyard and waters it continually. It supplies the direct divine-cultivator sense that the commentary hears in Rab as the one associated with plant growth.

row.basis: sowing by waters with ox and donkey
row.note: The blessed sow beside all waters and let ox and donkey range out. It joins water, cultivation, and working animals, the same practical provision sequence that the commentary traces from rain to food and livestock.

The nobles send servants for water, but cisterns have none and the vessels return empty. Its social consequence of missing water is a direct counterpart to the commentary's question of who can bring water when a community's source has withdrawn.

Jeremiah asks whether foreign gods or the heavens can give showers, and confesses that YHWH made all these things. This makes rain a dependent gift of the creator, closely matching the commentary's rain as mercy and benefit rather than autonomous weather.

The restored people receive grain, wine, oil, flock, and herd, and their life becomes like a watered garden. This is the necessary agricultural continuation of the watercourse-and-straight-way image in Jeremiah 31:9 already relevant to the commentary.
God's coming is compared to rain and to the latter rain watering the earth. It directly supplies the rain-as-divine-mercy reading that the commentary develops around rahmet and revived ground.
God will be like dew to Israel, and Israel will blossom like the lily. This adds the secondary, non-rain moisture route by which divine beneficence makes a plant fresh and flourishing.

row.basis: shut sky so rain does not fall
row.note: The witnesses have authority to shut the sky so that rain does not fall during their prophecy. Its withheld-rain image is a specific inverse to the commentary's cloud and rain as mercy that restores life.

The earth is commanded to sprout grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees. Read after the gathered-water scene of Genesis 1:9, its own contribution is the created vegetation that corresponds to the commentary's ground marked and grown green.

row.basis: cistern and own well as ethical figure
row.note: The proverb commands drinking from one's own cistern and well. It takes the literal infrastructure central to the commentary and makes its contained water an ethical image of faithful, rightly bounded household life.

row.basis: Adam recognizes need of rain and prays
row.note: In the usual division, the midrash explains the delayed rain of Genesis 2 by saying that rain came after Adam recognized its need and prayed. It adds a Jewish reading in which rain, vegetation, human need, and prayer are deliberately joined.

row.basis: well enclosures for pilgrims and animals
row.note: The Mishnah permits a distinctive post-and-enclosure arrangement around wells so that festival travellers' animals can be watered. Its legal concern with well-side construction, travellers, and animal water is unusually close to the commentary's detailed well-mouth apparatus.

The Honi story treats drought-ending rain as a communal need and distinguishes an unhelpful rain from the desired beneficial rain. It gives a Jewish narrative counterpart to the commentary's rain that repairs a people's condition.

The sick man says that when the pool's water is stirred, he has no one to put him in it before another enters. It supplies a Christian scene where need, water, and the absence of a helper meet, a useful counterpart to the women who cannot water without aid.

row.basis: leading ox or donkey to water
row.note: Jesus invokes the ordinary act of untying an ox or donkey and leading it to water. The concrete animal-watering practice complements the commentary's water as livelihood and its well scene of flocks needing to be watered.

The waters become bitter and people die from them. This is a specific negative counterpart to the commentary's sweet, abundant, life-sustaining water and to its image of water repairing rather than harming a community.

Hermas's vision of the Church as a tower built on water explains water as the means through which life is saved. This early Christian interpretation turns water into an actual foundation, closely echoing the commentary's qiwām and milāk language for what keeps a matter standing.

row.basis: storm-cloud, rain, grass in each field
row.note: The commentary traces cloud, lightning, rain, and pasture as one descent; Zechariah tells people to ask YHWH, who makes storm clouds, gives showers, and gives vegetation to each field, making that full sequence explicit.

The commentary’s vertical column runs from an overhead covering through cloud and rain to grass; this psalm says God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains.
The commentary treats hurūj as the cloud’s first appearance; Elijah’s servant sees a cloud only “like a man’s hand” rising from the sea, a sharply drawn first emergence before the rain.

row.basis: black sky, cloud, wind, heavy rain
row.note: The commentary joins a lingering cloud and the south wind to the coming rain; the sequel makes the sky black with clouds and wind before a great rain, adding a narrated weather sequence.

row.basis: lightning for rain, wind from storehouses
row.note: The commentary’s weak edge-lightning and wind-driven cloud are not separate images here: the psalm has God make lightning for rain and bring wind from storehouses.
The commentary’s cloud first flashes and then rains under divine agency; Jeremiah’s storm formula raises clouds, makes lightning with rain, and sends out wind, supplying the same linked elements.

row.basis: path for rain torrent and lightning
row.note: The commentary supplies an unspoken rain between pasture’s emergence and decay and notices lightning at the cloud’s edge; Job asks who cut a channel for the rain-torrent and a path for the thunderbolt.
The commentary calls rain the life of earth and the cause of the pasture’s emergence; Job says rain satisfies desolate ground and causes the grass to sprout.

row.basis: no rain, no field plant, no cultivation
row.note: The commentary deliberately infers the unnamed rain needed for pasture; Genesis explicitly says that no field shrub or plant had yet grown because YHWH had not sent rain and there was no human to cultivate the ground.

row.basis: rain on one plot, another withering
row.note: The commentary notes first green appearing patchily, “in one place and not another”; Amos describes rain sent on one field while the field without rain withers.

row.basis: clear light after rain, grass from earth
row.note: The commentary’s first green follows rain after a cloud-and-lightning scene; David’s last words compare righteous rule to clear morning light after rain that makes grass spring from earth.

row.basis: early and latter rain for the land
row.note: The commentary calls the first rain vesmī and makes seasonal rain the source of vegetation; Deuteronomy promises early and latter rain so the land’s grain, wine, and oil can be gathered.
The commentary focuses on the first rain’s visible mark on the earth; Joel summons Zion to rejoice because God sends the seasonal former and latter rains.

row.basis: farmer, precious fruit, early and latter rain
row.note: The commentary’s first rain begins the plant’s whole life; James uses a farmer waiting for earth’s precious fruit through the early and latter rains as the ethical analogue.

row.basis: rain from heaven makes earth sprout
row.note: The commentary’s sky-to-ground chain makes rain bring out vegetation; Isaiah’s rain and snow descend from heaven, water the earth, and make it bring forth and sprout before the word comparison begins.

row.basis: water on thirsty ground, life-giving outpouring
row.note: The commentary calls rain ḥayāʾ because it gives life to earth; Isaiah pairs water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land with God’s life-giving outpouring on descendants.
The commentary’s rain leaves green growth on the ground; the next verse says the recipients will spring up among grass like willows beside watercourses.

row.basis: land drinking rain and producing a crop
row.note: The commentary turns rain into the cause of a pasture’s emergence; Hebrews describes land drinking repeated rain and bearing a useful crop, with divine blessing on that fertility.

row.basis: rain-fed land yielding thorns, ending in burning
row.note: The commentary follows grass from rain to blackened refuse; Hebrews deliberately reverses the fruitful field, where land that drinks rain but produces thorns is rejected and ends in burning.
The commentary connects rain-made emergence to the surah’s later reminder and names Moses at its close; Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech distil like dew on grass.
The commentary begins with the imperative to glorify the Lord’s name; in the immediately following line Moses says he will proclaim YHWH’s name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God.

row.basis: cloud for covering, fire for night light
row.note: The commentary defines sky as what stands overhead and shades, then hears faint night lightning at the cloud’s edge; this psalm says God spread a cloud for covering and fire to give light by night.

row.basis: cloud by day, flaming brightness by night
row.note: The commentary’s overhead shade and cloud-edge light are joined in Isaiah’s Zion vision, where a cloud and smoke appear by day and flaming brightness by night over the whole site.

row.basis: shade and refuge from storm and rain
row.note: The commentary glosses samāʾ as what rises above and casts shade; Isaiah calls the canopy a shade by day and a refuge from storm and rain.

row.basis: cloud covering, fire-like appearance at night
row.note: The commentary associates cloud duration with night-watched lightning; at the tabernacle the cloud covers the dwelling and appears as fire from evening until morning.
The commentary’s Arabic branch hears a cloud that stays rather than passing on; Numbers specifies that when the cloud remained many days over the dwelling, Israel remained camped beneath it.
The commentary connects what is hidden with a faint light in cloud; Job says God exposes deep things from darkness and brings deep gloom into light.

row.basis: God knows hidden things and light dwells with him
row.note: The commentary reads S87:7’s divine knowledge of what is open and hidden beside cloud-light; Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and that light dwells with him.

The commentary keeps the Qur’anic claim that God knows what is manifest and concealed even while expanding the weather image; Hebrews states that no creature is hidden from God and all are exposed to his sight.

The commentary’s hiddenness root is heard in weak lightning and rain drawing animals from their holes; Jesus’ saying that nothing hidden remains undisclosed provides the same movement from concealment into appearing.

row.basis: praise of the exalted divine name
row.note: The commentary begins “glorify the name of your Most High Lord”; the psalm calls all creation to praise YHWH’s name because that name alone is exalted.

row.basis: YHWH Most High over all earth
row.note: The commentary’s opening title is “the Most High”; this psalm explicitly calls YHWH Most High over all the earth, placing exalted lordship over the created field and sky.
The commentary makes praise of the divine name the entry into its heaven-to-earth image; Jesus’ prayer begins by hallowing the Father’s name and locating the addressee in the heavens.

row.basis: good pasture under the divine shepherd
row.note: The commentary insists that marʿā carries grass, pasture-place, and grazing together; Ezekiel’s divine shepherd feeds the flock in a good pasture and lets them lie down there.

row.basis: Arabic ر ع ي source label and Hebrew רעה/מרעה
row.note: The source commentary labels المرعى with Arabic R-ʿ-Y; Ezekiel’s feeding in מרעה and use of the Hebrew pastoral root רעה furnish a genuine cognate setting where pasture is both place and act of tending.

The commentary treats ahrāja as real extraction of vegetation from soil; Jesus’ seed parable says the earth produces first stalk, then head, then full grain, making the staged emergence itself the figure.
The commentary supplies rain as the agency behind pasture’s emergence; Paul distinguishes his planting and Apollos’ watering from God’s giving the growth.

The commentary calls the rain-grounded growth God’s act rather than a self-contained natural cycle; Paul’s conclusion likewise makes neither planter nor waterer decisive, but God who makes things grow.

row.basis: watered tree whose leaf does not wither
row.note: The commentary sets the ordinary pasture’s drying fate against plants that do not perish in summer; the righteous person is a water-planted tree whose leaf does not wither.
The commentary calls the pasture’s end dry, tasteless debris moved by flood; the psalm turns the contrasting human fate into chaff that wind drives away.
The commentary compresses the plant’s whole lifetime from emergence to decay; this psalm compares human generations to grass that changes in the morning.

row.basis: grass flourishing then withering by evening
row.note: The commentary’s green pasture becomes dried residue; the next line says the grass flourishes and changes in the morning but fades and withers in the evening.
The commentary later lets the plant’s fate interpret human mortality; this psalm explicitly compares human days to grass and a field flower.

row.basis: wind passing and the grass gone
row.note: The commentary’s dead grass is moved away by the elements; the psalm says wind passes over the flower and it is gone, so even its place no longer knows it.

row.basis: grass withering under the divine breath
row.note: The commentary develops fresh green becoming dry and blackened; Isaiah says grass withers and flower fades when YHWH’s breath blows on it.
The commentary moves from the pasture’s passing life to what is better and more enduring; Isaiah counters fading grass with the word of God that stands forever.

row.basis: green tree dried and dry tree made to flourish
row.note: The commentary’s creator both brings out pasture and turns it into dark refuse; Ezekiel makes the reversal explicit when God dries the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish.

row.basis: green leaf and fruit in drought
row.note: The commentary contrasts the pasture’s summer death with a named plant that does not dry; Jeremiah’s water-rooted tree stays green in heat and does not cease bearing fruit in drought.

row.basis: leaves not withering beside life-giving water
row.note: The commentary places the darkening pasture beside an imagined undrying plant; Ezekiel’s river trees bear continual fruit and their leaves do not wither because their water flows from the sanctuary.

row.basis: world-empires like chaff carried by wind
row.note: The commentary notes that the Qur’an can make human communities, not only grass, into flood-debris; Daniel makes shattered kingdoms into chaff carried off by the wind.

row.basis: kingdom that will not be destroyed
row.note: The commentary balances grass’s disappearance with the better, lasting hereafter; Daniel contrasts the wind-carried debris of prior kingdoms with God’s kingdom that will never be destroyed.
The commentary’s pasture is briefly green before its terminal transformation, while S87 later speaks of great fire; Jesus calls field grass present today and cast into an oven tomorrow.

row.basis: scorching heat, grass withering, flower falling
row.note: The commentary observes both green fullness and its darkened, dried end; James gives the sequence of sun’s scorching heat, grass withering, flower falling, and beauty perishing.

row.basis: all flesh as grass that withers
row.note: The commentary extends pasture’s life-cycle toward the human condition; Peter directly applies the grass-and-flower image to all flesh and says the grass withers.
The commentary asks what remains after earthly vegetation and life have passed; Peter contrasts the withering grass with the Lord’s word that remains forever.

row.basis: perishing food and food abiding to eternal life
row.note: The commentary contrasts worldly life with what is better and more lasting; Jesus distinguishes food that perishes from food that endures to eternal life.
The commentary makes the pasture’s vanishing a bridge to S87:17’s enduring hereafter; Paul explicitly calls visible things temporary and unseen things eternal.
The commentary’s moving debris figures the passing world before the lasting good; this verse says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God’s will remains forever.

row.basis: no lasting city here, one to come
row.note: The commentary’s final contrast is between the transient present and a better enduring future; Hebrews says believers have no enduring city here but seek the one to come.
The commentary’s grass becomes dry debris and its later ayat reach the great fire; John’s harvest image gathers chaff and burns it with unquenchable fire.
