row.basis: old stump budding at the scent of water
row.note: The commentary calls rain the earth’s life and hears fresh, trembling vegetation in the life-root; Job says even an old stump buds at the scent of water and produces branches again.

row.basis: man dying unlike the reviving tree
row.note: The commentary uses the pasture’s life and death to frame the human neither-living-nor-dying state; Job sharply distinguishes the tree’s renewal from a human who dies and is no longer found.
The commentary links ground-made life to the later horizon of death and life; Isaiah commands those dwelling in dust to awake because the dead will live and corpses rise.

row.basis: breath entering dry bones so they live
row.note: The commentary moves from dead ground to living vegetation and then to S87:13’s life/death problem; Ezekiel’s vision has God promise dry bones breath so that they will live.

row.basis: Arabic ح ي ي source label and Hebrew חיה
row.note: The source commentary explicitly labels S87:13’s “live” with Arabic Ḥ-Y-Y; Ezekiel’s חיה, “you shall live,” is its clear Hebrew cognate and applies life to dry, death-marked matter.

row.basis: graves opened and people brought up
row.note: The commentary calls ahrāja concrete bringing-out and then recalls resurrection through rain; Ezekiel’s God opens graves and brings the people up from them, giving a human analogue to emergence from ground.

row.basis: dust sleepers to everlasting life or abhorrence
row.note: The commentary’s final contrast includes durable afterlife and the terrible non-life of fire; Daniel’s dust sleepers awaken either to everlasting life or to everlasting contempt.

row.basis: Arabic م و ت source label and Hebrew מות
row.note: The source commentary labels S87:13’s “die” with Arabic M-W-T; Isaiah uses the cognate Hebrew מות when God swallows death forever, turning the shared death-word toward eschatological victory.
The commentary’s great fire holds its inhabitant in neither ordinary death nor life; Isaiah’s final vision likewise depicts rebels under fire that is not quenched and a worm that does not die.

row.basis: worm not dying and fire not quenched
row.note: The commentary’s wording at S87:13 makes unending fire a state outside normal dying and living; Jesus cites Isaiah’s paired image of the worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched.

The commentary presents a fire in which one neither dies nor lives; Jesus identifies himself as resurrection and life and says the believer will live even if he dies, an explicit opposing resolution of death and life.

row.basis: resurrection to life and resurrection to judgment
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the vegetative life-cycle from an ultimate human fate; Jesus speaks of those in tombs coming out either to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment.

row.basis: grain dying in earth and bearing much fruit
row.note: The commentary’s pasture emerges from soil and its life/death vocabulary opens onto human destiny; Jesus makes a grain falling into earth and dying the condition of much fruit.

row.basis: what is sown does not come alive unless it dies
row.note: The commentary refuses to collapse plant life into the person in fire but sets them in one frame; Paul makes the seed’s dying-and-coming-alive sequence an argument for resurrection.
The commentary moves from perishable grass to “better and more enduring”; Paul’s resurrection contrast says what is sown perishable is raised imperishable.

row.basis: smoke rising forever and no rest
row.note: The commentary’s fire leaves no ordinary death or life; Revelation describes the smoke of torment rising forever and its worshippers having no rest day or night.

row.basis: lake of fire called the second death
row.note: The commentary calls the fire-state neither death nor life; Revelation instead names the lake of fire “the second death,” a close but deliberately different way of construing final punishment.

row.basis: corpses read as sinners’ souls in Gehenna
row.note: The commentary’s question is how a person can remain in fire without ordinary death or life; the Targum’s rendering of Isaiah shifts the visible corpses to sinners’ souls and explicitly situates their punishment in Gehenna.

row.basis: rain named with resurrection in rabbinic prayer
row.note: The commentary makes rain the life of earth and uses it as a bridge toward resurrection; this discussion places the mention of rain in the blessing for revival of the dead and argues from that liturgical pairing.

row.basis: day of rain compared with resurrection of the dead
row.note: The commentary’s rain-to-life-to-resurrection chain receives an explicit rabbinic comparison here, where the day of rain is measured against the resurrection of the dead.
The commentary’s “bringing out” of life from earth is extended to the dead; 4 Ezra says the earth will give back those asleep in it and the dust those dwelling silently there.
The commentary’s ground moves from lifelessness to living growth and then resurrection; 2 Baruch says the earth will surely restore the dead it now receives.

row.basis: earth and Sheol returning their deposits
row.note: The commentary’s extracted pasture becomes a model for “bringing out” the dead; 1 Enoch says the earth and Sheol will give back what was entrusted to them.

row.basis: King of the world raising to everlasting life
row.note: The commentary’s final scale is a better, enduring afterlife beyond mortal destruction; the second brother expects the King of the world to raise him to an everlasting renewal of life.
The commentary contrasts the world’s drying life with what abides; Wisdom says that, though the righteous seem to have died, their hope is full of immortality.

row.basis: seed decaying in earth and rising to fruit
row.note: The commentary’s living pasture and dead ground become a resurrection bridge; 1 Clement develops the sown seed’s decay in earth and providential rise into much fruit as evidence for resurrection.

The commentary’s great-fire figure is neither normally dead nor alive; Augustine argues that bodies of the damned can suffer eternal fire without being consumed, a later Christian account of that paradoxical endurance.

row.basis: green vegetation as food for living creatures
row.note: The commentary says المرعى contains grass, its place, and grazing; Genesis gives every green plant to the animals as food, supplying the feeding relation embedded in pasture.
The commentary hears pasture as both site and act of grazing; Jesus says that the one entering through him will go in and out and find pasture, preserving that concrete pastoral sense.

row.basis: grass made to grow for cattle
row.note: The commentary calls rain the earth’s life and pasture’s source; this creation psalm says God causes grass to grow for cattle, keeping the animal-feeding end of the image visible.

row.basis: south wind blowing on a garden
row.note: The commentary makes the south wind a secondary branch of the word for turning aside and lets it drive the cloud; the Song directly summons the south wind to blow upon a garden so its scents flow.

row.basis: watered growth beside inscription of the divine name
row.note: The commentary’s alternate derivation of “name” from a mark makes first rain stamp the earth with vegetation; after Isaiah’s water-and-grass image, this verse has people write the Lord’s name as an identifying inscription.

row.basis: sanctification and magnification of the Name
row.note: The commentary opens with glorifying the Lord’s name; the Jewish doxology asks that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified, offering a liturgical counterpart to that act.

row.basis: this world and the world to come compared
row.note: The commentary reads the pasture’s passing cycle into S87:16–17’s world-to-come contrast; Avot weighs a moment of repentance and good deeds here against a moment of bliss in the world to come, preserving the tension rather than simply equating the two.

row.basis: conscious speech and thirst in postmortem flame
row.note: The commentary’s fire-state is described as neither living nor dying; in Jesus’ rich-man story the dead man speaks from flame and asks for water, an explicitly conscious alternative picture of fiery postmortem punishment.

The commentary singles out weak lightning at the cloud’s edges before rain; Job describes God loading the cloud with moisture and scattering the cloud of his light, keeping those two features together.

row.basis: drops drawn up and rain distilled from mist
row.note: The commentary fills the unspoken interval from cloud to rain; Job describes the water cycle as God drawing up drops and distilling rain from mist.

row.basis: God visiting and richly watering earth
row.note: The commentary calls rain the life of earth that produces pasture; this psalm says God visits the earth, waters it, and greatly enriches it in preparation for grain.

row.basis: furrows softened by showers and growth blessed
row.note: The commentary’s first rain leaves a visible green mark in the soil; the psalm describes water in furrows, showers softening ridges, and God blessing the earth’s growth.
The commentary treats marʿā as grass and pasture-place, not an abstract crop; after the rain imagery this psalm says the wilderness pastures overflow with abundance.

row.basis: rains in season, land yield, tree fruit
row.note: The commentary makes seasonal rain the cause of pasture’s first appearance; the covenant blessing promises rains in their season, land produce, and fruit from field trees.

row.basis: rain for seed and broad pasture for cattle
row.note: The commentary joins rain, ground-emergence, and the feeding sense of pasture; Isaiah promises rain for sown seed, rich produce, and cattle grazing in a broad pasture.

row.basis: showers of blessing on fields and trees
row.note: The commentary’s nurturing Lord is heard in a cloud that feeds plants; Ezekiel calls the timely rain “showers of blessing” and immediately has field trees yield their fruit.
The commentary tracks the pasture from first green emergence onward; Joel tells the animals not to fear because the wilderness pastures have sprouted and the trees bear fruit.

row.basis: cloud rising and a coming shower
row.note: The commentary dwells on the cloud’s first appearance as a sign that rain will come; Jesus describes observers seeing a cloud rise in the west and correctly expecting a shower.
The commentary gives the south wind a secondary role beside the cloud; Jesus likewise uses the south wind as a recognized weather sign, here for scorching heat.
The commentary notes first green appearing only in some patches of earth; in the sower parable seed on shallow rocky soil springs up immediately because the soil has no depth.
The commentary follows fresh green into dried refuse; the parable’s quickly sprouted plant is scorched by the sun and withers because it has no root.
The commentary makes aḥwā hold lush green darkness beside the blackened end of vegetation; Job’s plant is still green and uncut when it withers before other plants.
The commentary stresses that the same creator who brings out pasture turns it into a later state; Jonah’s God appoints a worm to strike the sheltering plant, and it withers.

row.basis: east wind making a growing vine wither
row.note: The commentary assigns wind a role in the cloud-and-grass sequence and ends with dried vegetation; Ezekiel’s vine is flourishing until an east wind strikes it and makes it wither where it grew.

row.basis: morning mist, dew, wind-driven chaff, smoke
row.note: The commentary moves from cloud and first moisture to plant-debris, then notes that such debris can figure people; Hosea describes the guilty as morning mist, vanishing dew, whirlwind-driven chaff, and smoke.

row.basis: full clouds emptying rain on earth
row.note: The commentary infers rain as the causal middle between cloud and pasture; Qoheleth states the connection plainly: clouds full of rain empty it on the earth.

row.basis: watching wind and clouds instead of sowing and reaping
row.note: The commentary imagines someone spending the night watching lightning to learn where it will flash; Qoheleth turns weather-observation into an agricultural warning, since one who watches wind will not sow and one who looks at clouds will not reap.
The commentary calls the Lord “Most High” and defines the sky by its overarching shade; this psalm places the one dwelling in the shelter of the Most High in the shadow of the Almighty.

row.basis: high exaltation and name above every name
row.note: The commentary’s first command joins the divine name to highestness; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and granted him the name above every name.
The commentary contrasts ordinary grass that dries with plants that escape summer death; Isaiah promises a well-watered garden and a spring whose water does not fail.

row.basis: tree of life with unceasing fruit and healing leaves
row.note: The commentary sets darkened, dried pasture beside the Qur’anic image of enduring lush gardens; Revelation’s final garden has the tree of life yielding fruit each month and leaves for healing.

row.basis: hidden face, death, and return to dust
row.note: The commentary pairs S87:7’s hiddenness with S87:13’s death and life; this psalm says that when God hides his face creatures are dismayed, lose breath, die, and return to dust.

row.basis: sent breath creating and renewing the ground
row.note: The commentary makes earth’s rain-borne life a bridge to restoration; the answering verse has God send breath, create living beings, and renew the face of the ground.
The commentary defines dead land as land not yet made alive by sowing or repair; Ezekiel says the desolate land will be cultivated instead of lying desolate.

row.basis: desolate land becoming the garden of Eden
row.note: The commentary’s green-to-black scene also holds the possibility of a contrary garden; Ezekiel’s restored land is compared to Eden after its devastated places are rebuilt.

row.basis: perishing heaven and earth, everlasting salvation
row.note: The commentary begins with sky and ends by weighing the passing world against what endures; Isaiah says heaven vanishes and earth wears out, while God’s salvation is forever.
The commentary highlights S87:17’s claim that the future is both better and more lasting; Hebrews uses the same paired valuation when it speaks of a better and abiding possession.

row.basis: weeds gathered and burned at the end of the age
row.note: The commentary notes that the Qur’an can transfer vegetative debris to human communities and then reaches the great fire; Jesus’ interpretation transfers weeds into people gathered for burning at the age’s end.
The commentary’s fire-state is a human fate after the plant image; Jesus’ sequel says the evildoers are thrown into a fiery furnace, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

row.basis: branch not abiding, withering, gathered for fire
row.note: The commentary contrasts the pasture’s fleeting life with what remains and then turns to fire; Jesus says a branch that does not abide is thrown out, withers, is gathered, and burned.
The commentary’s “neither dies nor lives” in great fire is set against a better enduring hereafter; Jesus’ final judgment explicitly divides people between eternal punishment and eternal life.

row.basis: leaves falling and new leaves growing
row.note: The commentary makes the complete plant life-cycle interpret human mortality; Sirach compares generations of flesh and blood to a tree whose leaves fall while others grow.

row.basis: sowing to corruption or eternal life
row.note: The commentary’s pasture becomes a moral contrast between passing life and what endures; Paul’s sowing image makes flesh reap corruption and Spirit reap eternal life.
The commentary calls unseeded, unrepaired soil “dead land”; Hosea turns breaking fallow ground, sowing, and reaping into an ethical summons to seek YHWH.

row.basis: water becoming a spring of eternal life
row.note: The commentary calls rain life because it brings life to earth; Jesus recasts given water as a spring welling up to eternal life, shifting the image to a person’s lasting life.

row.basis: hidden things of darkness brought to light
row.note: The commentary combines God’s knowledge of hidden things with faint light in cloud; Paul says the Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the heart’s purposes.

row.basis: soul like a watered garden, no longer languishing
row.note: The commentary opposes dried pasture to an undying green state; Jeremiah describes restored Israel’s life as a watered garden that will languish no more.

row.basis: seasonal mention of the power of rain
row.note: The commentary names the first rain and treats rain as a bridge toward the life/death horizon; the Mishnah debates when the “power of rain” begins to be mentioned in communal seasonal prayer.

row.basis: ungodly hope swept like light chaff or froth
row.note: The commentary’s ghuthā is dry debris carried away and can figure people; Wisdom similarly compares the ungodly’s hope to light material driven off by wind and storm, though English renderings vary in the precise plant term.

The commentary sets rain held in rock hollows against vegetation that dries into residue; Psalm 1's tree by irrigation channels bears fruit and does not wither, making lasting nourishment the counterpart to passing debris.

The commentary's Arabic غثاء is flood-borne plant residue that surfaces and disperses; Psalm 1 says the wicked are like chaff the wind drives away, making the discarded plant matter a moral image of what does not endure.
The commentary identifies غثاء as dried vegetation carried off by a flood; Isaiah's grass and flower wither, portraying created vitality as transient and preparing the contrast with what endures.

The commentary pairs a reminder that benefits with the hereafter as more abiding; Isaiah says the grass fades but God's word stands forever, giving divine speech the permanence absent from the residue.
The commentary says a reminder may benefit and defines benefit as help toward good; Moses describes his teaching as rain and dew, making instruction itself life-giving water.

The commentary joins stored water to a reminder that may help people reach good; Isaiah compares God's effective word to rain, saying it does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, an explicit scriptural bridge from water to beneficial speech.

The commentary includes foam on molten metal among the residue that separates from useful substance; Proverbs says removing dross from silver leaves material for the silversmith's vessel, a refining counterpart to foam departing while value remains.

The commentary's flood carries surface debris that disperses; Isaiah's restless sea casts up mire and mud and cannot rest, using the water's refuse as an image of the wicked, while the surah's foam is what the current leaves behind.

The commentary links its measured wadis to created rock hollows that collect rain; Isaiah asks who measured the waters and marked off the heavens, placing water's bounded order under the Creator's measure.

row.basis: rock becomes pool and flint spring
row.note: The commentary describes God-created hollows in rock that collect rainwater; Psalm 114 says God turns rock into a pool and flint into a spring, adding the reversal in which rock itself becomes a source of provision.

The commentary defines benefit as what helps attain good and sets retained water against useless residue; Hebrews pictures ground drinking repeated rain and producing a useful crop, explicitly joining water with benefit.

The commentary's dried plant matter becomes flood refuse that goes away; Hebrews contrasts useful crop with land bearing thorns and thistles, rejected and ending in fire, giving the unproductive growth an ethical and judgmental outcome.

The commentary moves from God creating and ordering water-holding rock to the hereafter being more abiding; Ecclesiastes says whatever God does endures forever, directly joining divine action and permanence.

The commentary says God knows what is public and what is hidden; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment, adding the ethical consequence of divine knowledge.

The commentary calls the hereafter better and more abiding than worldly life; Daniel's resurrection scene distinguishes everlasting life from disgrace, giving a concrete scriptural account of the lasting afterlife.
The commentary calls the hereafter more abiding; Wisdom says the righteous may seem to die but their hope is full of immortality, explaining how apparent loss can conceal a lasting good.

The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; the martyr in 2 Maccabees expects the King of the world to raise the dead to renewed life, placing endurance in bodily resurrection rather than present survival.

The commentary's rock hollows and its explanation of abundant water as water gathered both stress collected water; Genesis makes gathering the waters an act of creation, showing such pools within a larger scriptural ordering of water.

The commentary describes sky-water collected in hollows and links water's benefit to good; Isaiah's rain waters the earth and makes it bring forth seed and bread, supplying the agricultural effect behind its water-and-benefit comparison.

The commentary's dried plant residue belongs to the cycle of pasture becoming waste; Isaiah begins its grass-and-flower comparison by declaring all flesh grass, extending that transience from vegetation to human life.

The commentary distinguishes flood foam that disperses from water that remains; in the psalm's tumultuous scene the waters roar and foam as mountains shake, making foam part of threatening upheaval rather than a sign of useful water.
The commentary says God knows the public and the hidden; the psalm says even darkness is not dark to God, making concealment itself no barrier to divine knowledge.

The commentary makes the benefit of a reminder depend on its helping people reach good and imagines water gathered in hollows; Ta'anit 7a compares Torah to water that descends from high places to low and says Torah endures in the humble, giving receptivity a rabbinic interpretation.

row.basis: water drops wear stone; Torah study
row.note: The commentary imagines rain held in a rock hollow and a beneficial reminder as retained water; Rabbi Akiva's story has drops wear a stone and prompt him to begin Torah study, turning the rock-water meeting into an image of instruction's effect rather than storage.

The commentary compares a beneficial reminder to water held in created rock hollows; Jesus says the one who hears and does his words is like a house built on rock, joining received teaching to stability.

row.basis: rain and flood test the rock house
row.note: The commentary sets water that stays against foam and debris that wash away; Matthew's rain, floods, and winds batter the rock-founded house without bringing it down, making endurance under water the result of doing the teaching.

row.basis: rain and flood collapse the sand house
row.note: The commentary contrasts water retained with transient residue; Matthew's rain and floods collapse the house built on sand, the contrary outcome when the teaching is heard but not done.

The commentary's غثاء is plant residue that disperses and counts for nothing; John gathers wheat into the barn and burns the chaff, making agricultural separation a judgment image of what is kept and what is discarded.

row.basis: water springing up to eternal life
row.note: The commentary connects water held in rock hollows with the hereafter's greater permanence; Jesus says the water he gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, joining water's benefit to enduring life.

The commentary describes the hereafter as better and more abiding; Hebrews says its addressees know they possess a better and abiding possession, a close formulation of the same contrast in a persecution context.

The commentary contrasts vanishing foam with the more abiding hereafter; 1 John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, giving the contrast an ethical criterion.

row.basis: seen is transient; unseen is eternal
row.note: The commentary pairs God's knowledge of what is public and hidden with a more abiding hereafter; Paul contrasts visible transient things with unseen eternal things, bringing hiddenness and permanence together.
The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding; 1 Peter describes an inheritance kept in heaven as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, specifying what such permanence means.

row.basis: river of the water of life
row.note: The commentary links water gathered and retained with the lasting hereafter; Revelation's final-city vision has the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, making life-giving water an eschatological provision.

The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and sets it beside the abiding hereafter; Revelation's tree by the river bears fruit and leaves for the healing of nations, giving the final water scene a concrete benefit.

row.basis: word of the Lord remains forever
row.note: The commentary pairs beneficial reminder with an abiding hereafter; Peter quotes the grass that withers and then says the Lord's word remains forever, applying Isaiah's transience contrast to the proclaimed good news.
The commentary's dried pasture becomes residue that disperses; Peter quotes Isaiah's grass and flower image for all flesh and human glory, extending the fading-vegetation picture to human life.

row.basis: treasure in heaven does not decay
row.note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding than the transient; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that moth and rust cannot consume, making durability a reason to value the future.

row.basis: earthly treasure is destroyed or stolen
row.note: The commentary's foam is what goes while beneficial value remains; Jesus names moth, rust, and thieves as agents that remove earthly treasure, supplying concrete forms of worldly loss against the heavenly treasure in the next verse.

row.basis: the Father sees what is done secretly
row.note: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden; Jesus says the Father who sees what is done in secret will reward, adding a moral consequence to divine knowledge of concealed acts.
The commentary says God knows what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose heart's purposes, specifying hidden human motives as the object of that knowledge.

row.basis: word held fast and bearing fruit
row.note: The commentary makes reminder beneficial only where it helps toward good and compares it to water held in hollows; Luke's good soil hears the word, holds it fast, and bears fruit with patience, giving reception and retention an ethical outcome.

The commentary asks whether a reminder benefits and defines benefit by help toward good; Paul describes Scripture as useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, a direct Christian account of beneficial instruction.

The commentary links benefit to reaching good and the hereafter to what is better; Paul says Scripture equips the person of God for every good work, identifying the practical result of useful instruction.

row.basis: flower fades and rich man withers
row.note: The commentary calls the plant residue dried and passing; James likens the rich person to a flower that withers under scorching heat, applying the fading-plant image to worldly prosperity.

The commentary's created rock hollows retain sky-water while flood foam disperses; Jeremiah contrasts the fountain of living water with cisterns unable to hold water, making failed retention an explicit counter-image.

The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a mud-covered well until clear water appears; Proverbs makes a muddied spring the image of a righteous person yielding to wickedness, giving the same water-clarity image an ethical force.

The commentary joins flood-borne residue to water that remains; Isaiah depicts roaring nations rebuked and chased like chaff before wind, bringing the water-and-disappearing-residue images together in a judgment scene.

The commentary defines benefit as help toward good and describes rain held in rock pools; Ezekiel's river nourishes trees whose fruit feeds and leaves heal, making the water's benefit concrete in an eschatological landscape.
The commentary's well is cleared of mud until its water appears clean; Zechariah's opened fountain cleanses sin and impurity, turning clear water into a specific image of moral purification.

The commentary cites cleaning a well until clear water appears; Elisha goes to Jericho's source and heals its water, so the unusable source becomes sound, a narrative counterpart to water cleared for use.
The commentary's muddy well is cleaned until clear water appears; Ezekiel promises clean water that cleanses Israel from uncleanness, extending the well-clearing image to covenant restoration.

The commentary sets dried pasture against water gathered in hollows; Jeremiah's tree sends roots to water, keeps green leaves through heat and drought, and continues bearing fruit, giving rooted endurance a distinct trust-and-drought setting.

The commentary calls flood-borne plant matter residue that goes away; Hosea compares idolatrous Ephraim to dew that vanishes and chaff swept from the threshing floor, adding transient moisture to the disappearing residue image.

row.basis: water wears stone and washes soil
row.note: The commentary describes rock hollows holding rain and flood matter dispersing; Job reverses the relation as water erodes stone and torrents sweep soil away, setting retained water against destructive runoff.
The commentary includes foam separating from molten metal while useful metal remains; Isaiah's refiner removes Zion's dross and alloy, applying metal separation to the city's moral purification.
The commentary's molten-metal foam separates from what can be used; Malachi depicts a refiner purifying silver and the Levites, giving separation of dross a priestly and ethical interpretation.

The commentary explicitly labels its Arabic branch ر ب ب and glosses it as abundant water named for gathering; Numbers uses Hebrew מַיִם רַבִּים for abundant water gushing from the rock. The matching r-b-b form and water context suggest a cognate, though the source label alone does not establish it.

The commentary distinguishes useless metal foam from the useful metal that remains; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel silver dross in a furnace, reversing the comparison so the community itself is the refuse to be judged.

The commentary's metal image separates passing foam from enduring value; Wisdom says God tests the righteous like gold in a furnace and accepts them, interpreting hardship as refinement rather than waste.

The commentary's metal foam separates from useful material, and its later image distinguishes what vanishes from what remains; Paul says fire tests the quality of each person's work, giving that separation an explicit judgment setting.
The commentary says the hereafter is more abiding and that foam goes while what benefits remains; Paul says the builder whose work remains receives a reward, linking endurance to evaluated work.
The commentary casts the residue as what goes and is not counted; Paul says burned work brings loss, the contrary outcome to work that survives the fire.

row.basis: faith tested as gold by fire
row.note: The commentary invokes metal melted for useful things and contrasts transient residue with lasting good; Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire and locates its result at Jesus' appearing.

row.basis: shaken things removed; unshaken things remain
row.note: The commentary's foam goes while water remains and calls the hereafter more abiding; Hebrews says what can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken remains, making permanence the outcome of divine judgment.

row.basis: one spring cannot yield fresh and bitter water
row.note: The commentary's source gloss describes cleaning a well until clear water appears, and it presents reminder as speech that may benefit; James uses spring-water quality to test speech, asking whether one opening can yield both fresh and bitter water.

row.basis: withered grass and the word that stands
row.note: Isaiah places fading grass and flower beside God's word that stands forever, joining this commentary's dry pasture and vanishing refuse to its useful reminder and abiding side.
Peter applies the grass-and-flower image to mortal flesh; it gives a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's pasture becoming transient debris.
The verse makes the preached word enduring after the preceding grass has withered, a direct analogue for the reminder whose benefit outlasts what goes away.
The one formed by instruction is a tree planted by water that continually yields fruit; it supplies the productive, life-giving side of water kept for benefit.
The wicked are like chaff the wind drives away, a precise land-based counterpart to the flood or pot refuse that is scattered, lost, and not retained.

Jeremiah contrasts God as a source of living water with human-cut cisterns that cannot retain water. Its failure of retention reverses the commentary's God-created rock hollows that hold sky water, making the contrast instructive.

row.basis: rock turned into a pool and flint into a spring
row.note: God makes hard rock a water pool and flint a fountain, directly matching the commentary's unusual attention to water gathered or appearing in rock.

row.basis: rain watering earth for seed and bread
row.note: Rain descends and makes the earth produce food; this is the productive-water half of the commentary's comparison between retained water and a reminder that benefits.

Isaiah's following word-image says God's utterance does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, supplying a textual model for speech evaluated by its benefit rather than its surface appearance.

row.basis: teaching as rain and speech as dew
row.note: Moses explicitly casts teaching and speech as rain and dew on vegetation, a direct bridge between beneficial admonition and the commentary's water imagery.

row.basis: teaching of the wise as a fountain of life
row.note: The wise person's instruction is a life-giving fountain, joining the commentary's useful reminder to its well of plentiful, clear water.

row.basis: deep waters and a bubbling fountain of wisdom
row.note: The proverb calls human words deep waters and wisdom's fountain a flowing brook; it makes the word-water connection explicit without reducing the commentary's wells to a mere lexical cognate.

row.basis: remove dross so a usable vessel emerges
row.note: Removing silver's dross produces a vessel for the refiner. This closely meets the commentary's furnace scene, where a surface waste separates from metal meant for useful objects.

row.basis: wicked removed like dross; statutes loved
row.note: The psalmist describes the wicked as dross removed from earth and responds by loving God's statutes, pairing discarded matter with enduring, valued instruction.
The command to fill a wadi with excavated ditches is a close scene-parallel to the commentary's winding low-lying hollows prepared to receive water.

row.basis: water filling the wadi and its pits
row.note: Water fills the excavated valley despite the absence of visible rain or wind, extending the preceding ditch scene into an image of water retained in depressions.

row.basis: reservoir for old-pool water and its maker
row.note: Isaiah names a built reservoir holding former-pool water but rebukes those who do not look to its Maker. It sets human water engineering beside the commentary's created rock cavities and keeps the Creator relation in view.
Divine guidance yields a watered garden and a spring whose waters do not fail, a concentrated counterpart to water that stays, aids people, and is more lasting.

row.basis: desert made pool and dry ground springs
row.note: The psalm reverses barrenness by making pools and springs from dry land, a direct water-gathering image alongside the commentary's flood-filled hollows.

row.basis: hungry people settle by the water
row.note: The next verse gives the human result of the new water: hungry people establish a habitation. It sharpens the commentary's phrase about what benefits people and remains.

row.basis: garden fountain, living-water well, Lebanon streams
row.note: The Song joins a well of living water to abundant running streams and a garden, furnishing a rich biblical counterpart for the commentary's plentiful well and water-fed ground.

row.basis: springs in valleys and pools in dry land
row.note: God opens fountains in valleys and makes pools and springs in dry country; the verse directly gathers the commentary's hollows, low places, and life-preserving water.

row.basis: rooted tree remains green and fruitful by water
row.note: A tree stretching roots to a stream does not fear heat or cease bearing fruit. It provides the durable, useful counterpoint to vegetation that becomes scattered and gone.

row.basis: water wherever the river goes gives life
row.note: Ezekiel's river makes living creatures live wherever it reaches, an expansive counterpart to water as the useful residue rather than the discarded surface matter.

row.basis: perennial fruit and healing leaves by the river
row.note: River-fed trees bear new fruit continually and have healing leaves, developing the lasting-benefit side that the commentary distributes between water, usefulness, and endurance.
A fountain is opened to cleanse impurity; this provides a ritual analogue to the commentary's muddy well being cleared until its water appears and is clean.
Ezekiel's sprinkling of clean water makes cleansing the point of the water image, an explicit interpretive bridge to the commentary's purified, visible well-water.

row.basis: restless sea casting up mire and dirt
row.note: Isaiah's restless sea throws mire and dirt onto its surface, the negative inverse of the commentary's well cleared of mud so that water can appear clear.
The powerful sheep foul the water left for others. This ethical inversion of clean, beneficial water adds a social consequence to the commentary's insistence that what remains should benefit people.

row.basis: wadi streams dry up and vanish in heat
row.note: Job's unreliable watercourses disappear when heat comes, a close negative counterpart to the commentary's water held in pits and wells rather than lost with passing refuse.

row.basis: dew, chaff, and smoke driven away
row.note: Hosea layers quickly disappearing dew with wind-driven chaff and smoke, an unusually close biblical cluster for the commentary's floatable debris that is scattered and gone.

row.basis: wind-driven chaff, frost, smoke, and forgotten guest
row.note: The Wisdom writer depicts the impious hope as material blown or dispersed and as a guest's vanished memory. It closely illuminates the commentary's proverbial sense of refuse that disappears and is not reckoned with.
Ecclesiastes says that what God does endures and cannot be altered, a compact counterpart to the commentary's definition of remaining in one's original state against annihilation.
Daniel's resurrection scene distinguishes everlasting life from everlasting contempt, giving a Hebrew Bible eschatological analogue for the more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: resurrection to everlasting renewal of life
row.note: The martyr contrasts present death with the world's King's everlasting renewal. It supplies a Second Temple Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that the final life is better and more lasting.

row.basis: inexhaustible fountain of righteousness and springs of wisdom
row.note: The thirsty drink from an inexhaustible fountain and are filled with wisdom; it makes abundant water a specific image for wisdom that benefits and does not run out.

row.basis: plastered cistern that loses not a drop
row.note: The saying praises Rabbi Eliezer's retention of teaching as a cistern that loses no water. It turns the commentary's held water into a precise Jewish image of durable remembrance.
Study for its own sake makes a person like an ever-strengthening spring and a river that does not cease, an interpretive expansion of beneficial instruction into enduring water.

row.basis: water interpreted as Torah and recurring public reading
row.note: The Bavli reads Israel's three waterless days as three days without Torah and grounds regular Torah reading in that image. It gives the commentary's beneficial reminder a concrete water-and-remembrance practice.

row.basis: Torah likened to water that descends to low places
row.note: The Bavli's water-Torah comparison adds humility to the commentary's teaching-as-water connection: water leaves high places for low ones, as Torah is received by the humble.

row.basis: land drinks rain and yields useful vegetation
row.note: Land that drinks repeated rain and bears a crop useful to its cultivators receives blessing. Its exact useful-water logic closely mirrors the commentary's water that remains and benefits people.

row.basis: thorns prove worthless and end in burning
row.note: The same field image sets useful rain-fed growth against worthless thorns whose end is burning, adding a Christian antithesis to the commentary's residue versus what is discarded.

row.basis: digging deep to rock; flood cannot shake the house
row.note: The hearer who acts digs deep, founds on rock, and withstands a flood. This is a particularly close meeting of useful admonition, a worked depth in rock, and endurance under rushing water.

row.basis: water becomes a spring into eternal life
row.note: Jesus' water becomes an inner spring that wells into eternal life, bringing together well water, benefit, and the enduring final life named in the commentary.
The believer is promised flowing living water; it develops the commentary's life-bearing abundance beyond water merely trapped in a well or hollow.

row.basis: living-water image explained as the Spirit
row.note: The narrator identifies the preceding rivers of living water with the Spirit, giving an internal Christian interpretation that prevents the water image from being read as only physical supply.

row.basis: washing of water with the word
row.note: Ephesians explicitly joins cleansing water to the word, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's clear well and reminder that does good.

row.basis: passing heaven and earth; imperishable words
row.note: Jesus contrasts the passing of heaven and earth with words that will not pass, a direct word-level counterpart to the commentary's contrast between what goes away and what is more lasting.

row.basis: world passes away; God-doer remains forever
row.note: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever. It gives a concise ethical form to the commentary's passing-versus-abiding contrast.

row.basis: shaken things removed so unshakable things remain
row.note: Hebrews reads cosmic shaking as removal of what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain, an eschatological counterpart to separating passing surface matter from what stays.

row.basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
row.note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food enduring to eternal life, directly joining utility, perishing, and the permanent life foregrounded by the commentary.
Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary seen realm with the eternal unseen one, a close Pauline formulation of the commentary's final better-and-more-enduring horizon.
The resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable, placing the commentary's language of permanence in a bodily Christian eschatological setting.

row.basis: treasure immune to decay and theft
row.note: Treasure in heaven avoids moth, corrosion, and theft, a concrete Jesus tradition for valuing what lasts over what is consumed or lost.

row.basis: work burned and its maker suffers loss
row.note: In the fire-test of works, what burns is lost. Alongside the commentary's metal-smelting foam, it supplies a Christian judgment image where material does not endure the furnace.

row.basis: perishable gold tested by fire and proven faith
row.note: Peter calls even fire-tested gold perishable while faith is proved through trial, a carefully different but relevant interpretation of the commentary's molten-metal image and its question of what endures.
James describes sun-scorched grass, a fallen flower, and fading beauty; it closely echoes the commentary's pasture that becomes dry, transient matter.

row.basis: waterless springs and storm-driven mists as false teachers
row.note: False teachers are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. The deliberately unhelpful water image gives a sharp inverse to the commentary's reminder that must benefit and water that truly remains.

row.basis: waterless clouds carried by winds and fruitless uprooted trees
row.note: Jude's false teachers promise water but carry none and are wind-driven, fruitless trees. This combines empty water, dispersal, and failed vegetation against the commentary's useful retained water.

row.basis: one spring cannot issue fresh and bitter water
row.note: James uses a spring's water quality to test speech, giving the commentary's clear well an ethical and verbal extension rather than a merely physical one.

row.basis: wave driven and tossed by wind
row.note: The doubter is a sea-wave driven by wind, a specific instability image that helps mark why the commentary values what settles, remains, and can benefit.

row.basis: river of water of life from God's throne
row.note: The final vision's pure river of life flowing from God's throne gives an eschatological culmination to the commentary's contrast between passing surface matter and life-bearing water.

row.basis: perpetual fruit and healing leaves by life-water
row.note: The tree beside the life-river bears fruit continually and heals nations, developing the water's durable public benefit beyond the commentary's immediate flood scene.

row.basis: silver become dross and wine diluted with water
row.note: Isaiah puts debased silver and weakened water in one moral image. Its deliberate dross-and-water pairing is a close biblical companion to the commentary's two-sided flood-and-metal surface waste.

row.basis: God smelts away dross and removes alloy
row.note: God's restorative judgment removes dross from Jerusalem. It gives the commentary's furnace residue a moral purification setting in which what corrupts is taken away so that a renewed community remains.

row.basis: refining and purifying silver for righteous offering
row.note: The refiner purifies the Levites like gold and silver so that their offering is righteous. This develops the commentary's molten-metal scene into a distinction between discarded impurity and enduring service.

row.basis: refining goes on in vain because wickedness is not removed
row.note: Jeremiah describes a failed furnace process: the fire works but the evil is not separated. It is a pointed inverse to the commentary's clean division in which the useless surface matter actually goes away.

row.basis: waters wear stone and wash away earth
row.note: Job makes flowing water an agent that erodes stone and carries soil away, a somber counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying scattered material off its surface.

row.basis: roaring waters answered by wind-driven chaff
row.note: Nations roar like many waters yet flee at rebuke like chaff before the wind. The verse unusually joins a water figure to dispersed chaff, close to the commentary's flood and unreckoned debris.

Creation begins with waters being gathered so dry land can appear. This is a direct counterpart to the commentary's note that abundant water is named for its gathering, while retaining the creation setting.

row.basis: wells stopped and filled with earth
row.note: The Philistines block Abraham's wells with earth, the physical inverse of the commentary's well cleared of covering mud so its water can be seen and used.
Isaac digs again the wells that had been stopped. The recovery of usable water supplies a narrative continuation for the commentary's action of clearing a well until its water reappears.

row.basis: well of living water found in a valley
row.note: Isaac's servants find living water while digging in a valley, closely bringing together the commentary's low-lying hollows, plentiful well, and water that can be retained for life.

row.basis: water from rock for a thirsty people
row.note: Water comes from a rock and the people drink. Unlike a lexical comparison, the shared scene joins rock, abundant water, and direct human benefit that the commentary develops across its word-families.

row.basis: singing to a well that springs up
row.note: Israel sings for a well to rise. The liturgical address to a spring offers a communal counterpart to the commentary's gathering water and its opening exhortation to praise the Lord.

row.basis: streams, fountains, and depths in valleys and hills
row.note: The promised land is characterized by plentiful water emerging through valleys and hills. It gives a land-scale counterpart to the commentary's wells, hollows, and flood-filled low places.

row.basis: bad water healed so death and barrenness cease
row.note: Elisha heals a city's bad water, ending its deadly effect. This gives a narrative extension to the commentary's water made clear and useful rather than left covered or corrupt.

row.basis: drawing water from wells of salvation
row.note: The joyful drawing of water from salvation's wells turns stored well-water into a salvation image, complementing the commentary's claim that retained water helps one reach the good.

row.basis: precepts remembered because they give life
row.note: The psalmist vows never to forget God's precepts because through them God gives life. It directly joins the commentary's remembrance condition to demonstrable benefit.

row.basis: Wisdom as a canal from a river into a garden
row.note: Personified Wisdom describes herself as a canal from a river entering a garden. The scene makes instruction's water a deliberately directed supply rather than passing flood debris.

row.basis: teaching poured out for future generations
row.note: In the same water-and-Wisdom sequence, teaching is poured out and left for generations to come. It adds explicit transmission and duration to the commentary's useful reminder and what remains.

row.basis: spiritual drink from the rock interpreted as Christ
row.note: Paul identifies Israel's water-giving rock with Christ. This Christian reading brings the commentary's rock-and-water image into a specific typological tradition rather than treating it as a generic well motif.

row.basis: message heard but not benefiting its hearers
row.note: Hebrews says that a proclaimed message did not benefit some hearers because it was not joined to faith. It is an unusually exact Christian counterpoint to the commentary's conditional, benefit-bearing reminder.

row.basis: piety useful now and for the coming life
row.note: Piety is called beneficial and is said to promise life both now and in the future. The verse tightly pairs the commentary's benefit vocabulary with its final-life horizon.

row.basis: Scripture useful for teaching, correction, and training
row.note: Scripture is explicitly useful for teaching and correction, a precise Christian formulation of admonition whose value lies in actually helping its recipient.

row.basis: destroyed earthly dwelling and eternal heavenly dwelling
row.note: Paul contrasts the destructible earthly tent with an eternal dwelling from God. It gives the commentary's better, more enduring hereafter a concrete dwelling-place form.

row.basis: no lasting city here and a future city sought
row.note: Hebrews explicitly denies a lasting city in the present and directs attention to the one to come, closely matching the commentary's contrast between what goes and the more abiding final reality.

row.basis: sowing to decay or to eternal life
row.note: Paul contrasts a harvest of corruption from flesh with eternal life from the Spirit. The agricultural separation adds a Christian ethical form to the commentary's perishing residue and abiding good.

row.basis: Lamb guides to springs of life-water
row.note: The Lamb guides the afflicted to springs of life-water and removes tears. This eschatological pastoral use of water sharpens the commentary's claim that the final state is better and enduring.

row.basis: water of life freely given to the thirsty
row.note: The enthroned speaker gives life-water freely to the thirsty in the new creation, an explicit final-state counterpart to water as what truly benefits and remains.

Peter's flood reference makes water the medium through which a few are preserved rather than merely a current that carries refuse away. That reversal gives the commentary's flood image a distinct Christian eschatological reading.

row.basis: flood water interpreted through baptism and a good conscience
row.note: The next verse interprets the flood-water figure as baptism, expressly denying a merely bodily washing and locating its benefit in an appeal to God through resurrection.
The commentary develops Rab as owner and the flock’s protector; Jacob blesses his descendants through the God who shepherded him all his life, making the personal shepherd relation explicit.
The commentary’s owner and guardian of the herd meets Jacob’s naming of Israel’s God as Shepherd and Rock; the image adds steadfast protection amid Joseph’s affliction.

The commentary’s wild leaders guiding those behind them meets Moses’ request for a leader who goes out and comes in before Israel, lest the congregation be sheep without a shepherd; it connects guidance with accountable rule.
The commentary says Rab is owner and later notes one who names “his Lord”; David calls YHWH “my shepherd,” making ownership a personal relation of trust.
The commentary joins the one who guides a flock to protected pasture; YHWH makes the speaker lie down in green pastures and leads him beside waters, furnishing the same pastoral sequence.
The commentary’s Rab can mean one who sets things right and its guidance image leads the herd; here the shepherd restores the soul and leads in right paths, linking care with moral direction.
The commentary glosses the shepherd as surrounding and protecting livestock; the speaker fears no evil in the dark valley because YHWH is with him and uses rod and staff to comfort him.
The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and evokes a herd; God says every forest animal and cattle on a thousand hills are his, giving the ownership claim concrete scope.

The commentary includes a wild-cattle herd under the r-b-b word family; God says he knows every bird of the mountains and the creatures of the field are his, extending divine ownership to wild creatures.
The commentary’s Rab means owner of everything; God says the world and all it contains are his, grounding the pasture scene in universal possession.
The commentary presents a pasture brought forth for a herd; the psalm depicts pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, adding an image of abundance to divine provision.

The commentary makes the owner, the ones leading ahead, and pasture parts of one scene; God brings Israel out like sheep and leads them through the wilderness, joining divine guidance to flock imagery.
The commentary says the shepherd protects the animals he guides; Israel is led safely here, with the sea overwhelming its enemies, pairing guidance with protection.
The commentary’s owner-guiding-a-flock scene is directly named in the address to the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; the prayer turns the image into a plea for divine attention.
The commentary joins ownership, care, and pasture; the psalm calls worshippers the people of God’s pasture and sheep of his hand, adding belonging to the grazing image.
The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and presents a protected pasture; the psalm says Israel is God’s people and sheep of his pasture, explicitly uniting ownership and flock.
The commentary says the Lord brings forth pasture and that its root-family includes grazing animals; YHWH causes grass to grow for cattle, closely matching divine provision of fodder.
The commentary’s owner produces pasture for dependent herds; all creatures here look to God for food in its season, adding ongoing dependence to the created pasture scene.
The commentary links God’s act of bringing forth pasture with a shepherd’s provision; YHWH covers the sky with clouds and makes grass grow on the mountains, naming the growth as God’s work.
The commentary connects pasture with guarded livestock; God gives animals their food, even young ravens when they cry, extending the provision beyond a human flock.
The commentary’s shepherd surrounds and protects the animals; God gathers lambs in his arms and carries them close, making tender protection part of divine rule.
The commentary says a ruler shepherds and guards his people; Jeremiah condemns shepherds who destroy and scatter God’s pasture-sheep, showing that political care can fail the pastoral duty.
The commentary extends animal care to a ruler’s care of subjects; Jeremiah holds Israel’s shepherds responsible for not attending the flock, sharpening the ethical burden of that analogy.
The commentary’s owner shepherds a flock to its pasture; God promises to gather the remnant from the lands where he scattered them and bring them back, connecting divine ownership with restoration.
The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who protects the herd; the promised shepherds will tend the people so they need not fear or be dismayed, spelling out the result of care.

The commentary says the ruler tends his subjects like a shepherd tends livestock; Ezekiel indicts Israel’s shepherds for feeding themselves rather than the flock, making rule answerable to those cared for.
The commentary defines the shepherd as one who surrounds and protects livestock; Ezekiel’s bad shepherds do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or seek the lost, specifying failures of that care.
The commentary fuses owner and shepherd in one scene; God says he himself will search for and seek his sheep, making divine ownership active rather than merely possessive.
The commentary’s shepherd guards the flock; God rescues his sheep from the cloudy, dark day on which they were scattered, adding rescue at the moment of peril.
The commentary’s owner guides a herd to pasture; God brings the sheep out from the peoples and feeds them on Israel’s mountains, joining gathering, guidance, and grazing.
The commentary calls the pasture protected and supplied; God feeds his sheep in good grazing land and on rich pasture, giving a direct counterpart to the image of pasture provided by its owner.
The commentary’s Lord is the flock’s owner and the shepherd who guards it; God says he will shepherd his sheep and make them lie down, uniting those roles in the same figure.

The commentary’s shepherd protects the herd and watches where affairs will end; God seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak, while judging the fat and strong sheep.

The commentary records Arabic رَعَى (source lexeme in its r-ʿ-y branches) for grazing and tending; Jacob uses Hebrew רעה while offering to pasture Laban’s flock, giving the pastoral sense a specific Semitic lexical counterpart.

row.basis: Grass in the fields for cattle
row.note: The commentary says God brings forth pasture and animals graze it; the promise of rain includes grass in the fields for cattle, making pasture provision part of the land’s gift.
The commentary moves from pasture becoming debris to the temporary life of this world; this psalm compares people to grass swept away, connecting vegetation’s short life to human transience.
The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; the psalm’s grass sprouts in the morning and withers by evening, giving a daily image of swift change.
The commentary reads the pasture’s decay toward the temporary world; human days are compared to grass here, and flourishing to a field flower, carrying the vegetation image into mortality.

row.basis: The place no longer knows it
row.note: The commentary makes the pasture’s transformation a sign of transience; after wind passes over the field-flower, its place knows it no more, sharpening the image of disappearance.
The commentary links pasture turning to debris with the transient worldly life; Isaiah compares all flesh to grass, making human fragility the point of the plant image.
The commentary notes the pasture’s change into waste; Isaiah says grass withers when the breath of YHWH blows on it, adding divine sovereignty over its disappearance.

row.basis: The enduring word contrasts with grass
row.note: The commentary’s pasture decays while its owner knows its end; Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the word of God that stands forever, making permanence the counterpoint to decay.

row.basis: People as sheep without a shepherd
row.note: The commentary extends shepherding from livestock to a ruler’s subjects; Jesus sees the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, making the image a diagnosis of neglected people.
The commentary connects a shepherd’s guidance with care for a community; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins to teach them, showing guidance as an answer to that lack.

row.basis: The shepherd calls his own sheep
row.note: The commentary calls Rab the herd’s owner and describes the one who guides it; the shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining ownership to personal guidance.
The commentary’s leaders among wild animals go ahead and guide the rest; Jesus’ shepherd goes ahead of his sheep and they follow, a close image of leading from the front.
The commentary’s owner guides the herd to pasture; Jesus says those entering through him will go in and out and find pasture, placing access to grazing within the shepherd image.

row.basis: The good shepherd protects the sheep
row.note: The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who surrounds and preserves the animals; Jesus says the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, making protection costly and deliberate.

row.basis: A failed guardian abandons the flock
row.note: The commentary’s shepherd protects livestock; the hired hand sees the wolf, abandons the sheep, and flees, dramatizing the difference between a true guardian and mere employment.
The commentary describes a single owner’s care of a flock; Jesus knows his own sheep and is known by them, adding reciprocal recognition to ownership and tending.
The commentary says the shepherd guards the flock and watches where matters lead; a shepherd searches for one lost sheep until he finds it, showing care as sustained attention to an outcome.

The commentary explicitly says a governor tends his subjects as a shepherd tends livestock; elders are told to shepherd God’s flock and oversee it willingly, applying the pastoral relation to community leadership.
The commentary’s human ruler is a shepherd under the owner’s care; Peter calls Christ the chief Shepherd whose appearing brings a crown, making human oversight subordinate to divine shepherding.
The commentary’s scene brings a flock to pasture under its owner’s guidance; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water, joining shepherding with final provision.

The commentary moves from pasture made waste to the temporary life of this world; Jesus contrasts grass in the field today with its being thrown into the oven tomorrow, using the plant’s short course to teach about trust in God’s provision.
The commentary reads pasture’s decay as a path toward worldly transience; Peter applies Isaiah’s grass-withering image to all flesh and human glory, making mortality explicit.
The commentary presents the Lord as the one who brings forth pasture for herds; creation assigns every beast the green plant for food, placing animal grazing within God’s original provision.

row.basis: Moses as a shepherd before his mission
row.note: The commentary points to Moses’ answer to Pharaoh as its explicit grazing scene; Exodus first shows Moses shepherding Jethro’s flock and bringing it to Horeb, giving that speaker a prior pastoral setting without retelling the Pharaoh encounter.

row.basis: Moses’ compassion for a stray lamb
row.note: The commentary says a shepherd surrounds and protects animals and compares this to a ruler’s care of subjects; this midrash says Moses was chosen after he carried a tired lamb to water, interpreting leadership as attentive care for the vulnerable.

row.basis: A shepherd protects his flock from predators
row.note: The commentary defines the shepherd as protecting livestock; David recounts pursuing a lion or bear that took a lamb from the flock, giving a concrete human example of pastoral guardianship.

row.basis: Rescuing the lamb from the predator
row.note: The commentary’s shepherd preserves the herd; David says he struck the predator and rescued the lamb from its mouth, specifying protection as active recovery.

row.basis: Shepherd and ruler are one role
row.note: The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Israel’s elders tell David that he will shepherd Israel and be its leader, explicitly joining pastoral care and political rule.

row.basis: Moses leads Israel like a flock
row.note: The commentary points to Moses’ pastoral reply to Pharaoh and develops guidance of a herd; the psalm recalls God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, placing the image in the Exodus story.

The commentary links the shepherd of animals to the ruler of people; God takes David from following nursing ewes to shepherd Jacob, making the transition from literal flock care to leadership explicit.
The commentary’s flock leaders guide those behind them and its ruler tends subjects; David shepherds Israel with an upright heart and guides them with skillful hands, uniting care and guidance.

row.basis: Know the state of the flock
row.note: The commentary describes a shepherd who watches where matters will lead and a ruler who tends subjects; this proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flocks and attend to his herds, turning oversight into concrete attention.

row.basis: Stars counted and called by God
row.note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch includes watching the stars and connects oversight with knowing an outcome; Isaiah asks the reader to look at the created host, which God brings out by number and calls by name, relocating cosmic knowledge in the Creator.
The commentary extends shepherding to rulers over people; Isaiah calls Cyrus God’s shepherd, who will carry out the rebuilding of Jerusalem, giving the political metaphor a foreign royal instance.

row.basis: Moses leads God’s flock through the sea
row.note: The commentary invokes Moses speaking of grazing to Pharaoh; Isaiah recalls the one who brought Moses and God’s flock up from the sea, connecting the named speaker with God’s shepherding in the Exodus deliverance.

The commentary says rulers shepherd their subjects and the herd’s leaders guide others; God promises shepherds who will feed the people with knowledge and understanding, specifying instruction as a form of guidance.

The commentary’s herd leaders are those who guide others; Jeremiah describes lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray in the mountains, showing the same leadership relation reversed into misguidance.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and watches over the herd; Ezekiel’s sheep wander across mountains and hills with no one searching for them, portraying the result when pastoral oversight fails.
The commentary pairs a protected pasture with a shepherd who guards it; Ezekiel asks why well-fed sheep trample the rest of the pasture, making care for shared grazing land part of the pastoral duty.
The commentary’s pasture is a provision belonging to the flock; Ezekiel says God’s sheep must eat what the strong sheep have trampled, adding harm within the flock to the image.
The commentary makes the owner, the flock, and its guide parts of one scene; God promises one shepherd, his servant David, over the sheep, linking divine ownership with a human ruler’s care.

The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Micah’s ruler stands and shepherds his flock in YHWH’s strength, after which the people dwell securely, joining leadership, divine backing, and protection.

row.basis: Stars as a sign of future outcome
row.note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch connects watching stars with seeing where an affair will end; God brings Abram outside to look at the stars as a sign of his future descendants, a related but distinct use of the heavens to frame what is to come.

row.basis: Watching stars and refusing their worship
row.note: The commentary mentions star-watching as a secondary r-ʿ-y sense while assigning the ultimate oversight to the Lord; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, and stars, adding a caution about confusing observation with divine rule.

The commentary connects pasture brought forth by God with grazing animals; Isaiah promises rain for seed and fodder for livestock, then says the land’s produce will be rich, joining animal provision to the land’s yield.

The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; Joel depicts cattle groaning and herds wandering because there is no pasture, showing the consequence for dependent animals when grazing land is lost.

row.basis: Peter told to shepherd Jesus’ sheep
row.note: The commentary extends the shepherd’s care to a ruler’s subjects; the risen Jesus tells Peter to shepherd his sheep, transferring pastoral responsibility to a human leader.
The commentary’s shepherd protects and tends livestock; Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep, specifying practical provision as part of the leadership charge.
The commentary says a governor shepherds his subjects; Paul charges overseers to shepherd God’s church, which God acquired, making pastoral leadership both delegated and accountable.

The commentary describes the shepherd as one who watches over and protects a flock; Peter says the addressees returned from straying like sheep to the shepherd and guardian of their souls, applying the image to spiritual oversight.

The commentary compares a ruler’s care for subjects with a shepherd’s care for livestock; Peter tells elders not to dominate those entrusted to them but to be examples, adding an ethical limit to pastoral authority.

row.basis: The great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: The commentary’s Rab is owner and shepherd of the flock; Hebrews calls Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep, grounding pastoral leadership in God’s covenant and the raising of Jesus from the dead.

The commentary says a ruler shepherds his subjects; Revelation depicts the child destined to shepherd all nations with an iron rod, preserving the political shepherd image while giving it a forceful judgment register.

The commentary makes the second and third ayat sound like a shaped, straight arrow whose point leads, and separately notes a bag for arrows; Isaiah's servant is made as a polished arrow and hidden in YHWH's quiver, adding a scriptural image of divine preparation and readiness.
The commentary reads creation through measuring before shaping; Job says God assigned weight to wind and measure to waters, making measure itself part of divine ordering.

The commentary's craft scene joins creating with sizing and straightening; Isaiah portrays the creator measuring waters, spanning heavens, and weighing mountains, giving that workmanship a cosmic scale.

The commentary links خلق and قدر as making and setting a measure; Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight, an unusually exact Jewish formulation of creation as measured order.

The commentary treats the game arrows as assigning shares by chance and contrasts them with the share set by God; Proverbs says a lot is cast but its decision belongs to YHWH, so the lot is not an independent force.

row.basis: teaching for benefit and leading in a way
row.note: The commentary joins the ayat's guiding verb with its reminder's benefit; Isaiah's Redeemer says he teaches what is profitable and leads in the way one should go, bringing those two actions together without implying a cognate.

The commentary's artisan first thinks through how to prepare and straighten an object, then turns to guidance; Proverbs says a person plans a way but YHWH establishes the steps, a close sequence of planning followed by direction.

The commentary links the staff straightened over fire to the same fire entered by the condemned in 87:12; Malachi's refiner-fire purifies the Levites, giving fire a restorative craft function rather than a punitive end.

The commentary says the game arrows distribute portions and that this chance share is forbidden; Joshua has Israel receive its territorial inheritance by lot before YHWH, a concrete sacred allotment with a different function.

The commentary's arrows determine a game's shares, while Ezekiel's Babylonian king shakes arrows among other divinations to choose his military route; the shared arrow practice illuminates how a chance sign could direct action, though here it selects a route rather than a portion.

The commentary reads 87:16–17 as preferring one share over another and calls the Hereafter better and more enduring; Jesus says Mary chose the good portion that will not be taken away, a close image of a selected, lasting share.

The commentary contrasts preference for present life with the better, more lasting Hereafter; Hebrews says believers accept loss of possessions because they know they have a better and abiding possession, spelling out that temporal-versus-enduring choice.

The commentary's 87:7 says God knows what is aloud and what is hidden; Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God's sight and all is exposed before him, a direct counterpart to the hidden side of that claim.

The commentary describes a camel cut into pieces and shares assigned by arrows; John says the soldiers cast lots for Jesus' seamless tunic rather than tear it, an adjacent but distinct use of lots to allocate a possession.

The commentary gives قدر the secondary sense of a thing's amount and term; Job says a person's days are fixed, months numbered, and limit set, making the finite term a specific instance of divinely measured life.
The commentary says every thing has an amount and term; the psalmist says his unformed substance and all his days were seen and written before they arrived, joining formation to a measured lifespan.

row.basis: God teaches Ephraim to walk and heals him
row.note: The commentary glosses Rab as bringing something through stages toward completion; Hosea pictures God teaching Ephraim to walk, holding him, and healing him, giving a relational image of gradual nurture.

row.basis: restored and led on right paths
row.note: The commentary links the Lord's completing care with guidance and describes a staff that goes ahead of its bearer; the psalm's shepherd restores the speaker and leads him on right paths, combining care and direction.

The commentary's arrow-making scene joins straightening what is bent to directing its point; Proverbs says YHWH makes a person's paths straight, bringing straightness and guidance together in a path image.

The commentary connects creation with measuring and assigning each thing its share; the psalm says God counts the stars and calls them by name, a concrete image of creation known and ordered individually.

row.basis: the Lord as portion, cup, and lot
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the game's allotted share from the share given by the measure-setter; the psalmist calls YHWH his portion, cup, and lot, recasting allotment as trust in God rather than a game.

row.basis: measured boundary lines and secure inheritance
row.note: The commentary says an arrow-game share is measured out and contrasts it with the enduring Hereafter; the psalmist's boundary lines fall in pleasant places and his inheritance is secure, a fixed inheritance rather than a chance stake.

row.basis: lots assign the goats' ritual roles
row.note: The commentary rejects the meysir arrows used to assign shares; Leviticus uses lots to distinguish the goat for YHWH from the one for Azazel, showing a ritual allocation rather than gambling.

The commentary calls 87:16–17 a choice of share between present life and the better Hereafter; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life, turning choice into an ethical decision with consequences.

row.basis: garments divided and clothing allotted by lot
row.note: The commentary's game divides a slaughtered camel into portions chosen by arrows; the psalm describes people dividing garments and casting lots for clothing, a specific allocation scene without the game's animal shares.

row.basis: God sees the heart rather than appearance
row.note: The commentary says God knows what is public and what is hidden; Samuel contrasts what humans see outwardly with YHWH's regard for the heart, specifying inward knowledge against visible appearance.

row.basis: God knows a word before it is spoken
row.note: The commentary names both what is aloud and what is hidden as known to God; the psalmist says God knows his word before it reaches his tongue, extending the claim to speech not yet made public.

The commentary's waterbag is measured, fitted with side pieces, treated, and eventually worn smooth; Joshua's travelers carry old wineskins that are worn, torn, and patched, a concrete scriptural witness to the used leather vessel.

row.basis: a wineskin in smoke and remembrance
row.note: The commentary separately describes a waterbag becoming smooth with use and a reminder that may benefit; the psalmist likens himself to a wineskin in smoke yet says he has not forgotten God's statutes, joining a worn vessel image to remembering, though the psalm's image is distress rather than ordinary use.

The commentary identifies the forbidden game as arrow-drawn allocation of shares; Acts describes the gathered disciples praying and casting lots to select Matthias, a communal appointment rather than a distribution game.

The commentary says God makes the way easy for the addressed messenger and then describes avoidance of the reminder and the great fire; Matthew calls the broad, easy way destruction-bound. The link is limited because the easy way has a different referent, but the contrast makes ease point toward opposite outcomes.

The commentary associates divine facilitation with ease and sets successful guidance against the fire; Matthew says the narrow, hard way leads to life, an explicit reversal of the easy/destructive route in the neighboring verse, though the addressees and settings differ.

row.basis: measured carpenter's work makes an idol
row.note: The commentary's opening craft scene has measuring before cutting and shaping; Isaiah describes a carpenter stretching a line, marking, planing, and using a compass to form an idol, making a pointed contrast between measured human manufacture and the Lord who creates in 87:2–3.

The commentary links creation to an artisan's measured preparation; Job's creation challenge asks who fixed earth's measurements and stretched a line upon it, giving the image of measurement a concrete construction tool.
