row.basis: God leads the blind and levels rough places
row.note: The commentary joins straightening what is bent to the arrow point's guidance; Isaiah says YHWH leads the blind on an unknown road, makes darkness light, and levels rough places, combining the same two actions in a divine-guidance promise.

row.basis: YHWH goes before Israel to lead them
row.note: The commentary says a staff is named as a guide because it precedes its bearer; Exodus pictures YHWH going before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to lead them, making the leading-ahead image a narrative act.

row.basis: Hebrew צלה and Arabic ṣ-l-y, roasting over fire
row.note: The source commentary labels the Qur'anic word يَصْلَى with root ṣ-l-y and also gives a fire-working sense for straightening a stick; Exodus uses the related Hebrew roast verb for Passover meat cooked over fire, showing a cognate fire-use in its own ritual context.

row.basis: Hebrew עליון and Arabic al-aʿlā, the Most High
row.note: The commentary's ayah calls God al-Aʿlā and notes that the same Arabic root names the highest game arrow; the psalm calls YHWH Most High over all the earth, so a related Semitic height term belongs to divine supremacy here, not a gaming share.

row.basis: every deed, including the hidden, brought to judgment
row.note: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden before describing the condemned person's fire; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including the hidden one, into judgment, joining hidden knowledge to accountability.

row.basis: Torah as plan consulted before creation
row.note: The commentary reads creation as craft with planning before shaping; Genesis Rabbah compares a king consulting an architect's plan before building a palace with God consulting Torah before creating the world, supplying a Jewish interpretation of creation as planned workmanship.

The commentary's measure-and-shape sequence evokes preparing an object toward its finished form; Jeremiah watches a potter reshape a spoiled clay vessel as seemed good to him, a concrete craft scene that makes re-forming part of the maker's work.

row.basis: lots identify the cause of a calamity
row.note: The commentary describes arrows drawing shares in a game; the sailors cast lots to discover whose account brought the storm, and the lot falls on Jonah, a distinct use of chance to identify responsibility rather than divide goods.

row.basis: Pur selects the date for Haman's plan
row.note: The commentary's arrows distribute shares by a lottery; Haman casts Pur to select a date for destroying the Jews, showing a lot used to schedule a fateful act rather than allot portions.

The commentary says God knows what is aloud and what is hidden; Jesus says what was spoken in the dark and whispered in inner rooms will be heard and proclaimed publicly, a specific speech-level counterpart that turns secrecy into disclosure.

row.basis: gaining the world at the cost of life
row.note: The commentary says people prefer present life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life, making the cost of that preference explicit.

The commentary contrasts preference for present life with the better lasting Hereafter; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are reversed after death, a narrative counterpart to the choice's final share.

row.basis: measure of faith allotted to each
row.note: The commentary's source gloss gives قدر the sense of setting a measure and each person's share; Paul says God has allotted each a measure of faith, a direct Christian example of individualized measure without claiming identical doctrine.

The commentary moves from craft preparation and fire used to straighten a staff to the condemned entering fire; Paul says the Day reveals each person's building work and fire tests it, shifting fire from the final punishment to an assay of workmanship.

The commentary describes turning a stick over fire to straighten it and uses the same source-labeled Arabic root in 87:12's fire; Isaiah's smith works iron over coals and hammers it into shape, adding a concrete forge scene where fire serves manufacture.

row.basis: sons compared to arrows in a warrior's hand
row.note: The commentary develops a shaped arrow and a quiver-like container; the psalm compares sons of youth to arrows in a warrior's hand, adding a family image in which the prepared arrow represents offspring ready for action.

row.basis: Hagar carries a skin of water into the wilderness
row.note: The commentary develops how a leather waterbag is measured, fitted, treated, shaken, and worn; Genesis gives a concrete narrative use of a water skin carried with a child into the wilderness, where its capacity becomes life-critical.

row.basis: Israel as clay in the potter's hand
row.note: The commentary's creation verbs are framed as a maker forming and ordering material; Jeremiah explicitly applies the potter-and-clay scene to YHWH and Israel, turning craft into a claim about the maker's authority over a people.

row.basis: fixed animal portions for the priest
row.note: The commentary describes slaughtering a camel and sharing its pieces by game arrows, then contrasts that with a measured share from God; Deuteronomy assigns the priest the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach from an ox or sheep, a specific animal share fixed by law rather than chance.

row.basis: God gives growth after planting and watering
row.note: The commentary glosses the Rab family as bringing something through stages toward completion; Paul distinguishes planting and watering from God's giving the growth, a compact image of development that culminates through divine action.

The commentary's condemned person enters the great fire, while its craft scene uses fire to correct a stick; Paul says a builder's work may burn while the builder himself is saved, even as through fire, distinguishing tested work from final destruction.

The commentary presents the reminder conditionally in terms of benefit; Timothy says scripture is useful for teaching, correction, and training, making the ethical usefulness of instruction explicit in a Christian context.

The commentary's 87:11–12 moves from avoiding the reminder to entering the great fire; Matthew's judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire, a direct eschatological fire counterpart with its own judgment setting.

row.basis: this world as a vestibule before the world to come
row.note: The commentary says people prefer this life although the Hereafter is better and more enduring; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for the latter, giving the preference a Jewish ethical formulation.

row.basis: two ways, one of life and one of death
row.note: The commentary contrasts the share chosen in present life with the better Hereafter and the fire awaiting the worst; the Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death, framing the moral choice as a path with opposed outcomes.

row.basis: Aramaic rabbi, teacher, and Arabic rabb
row.note: The source commentary labels the ayah's رَبّ with root r-b-b and glosses a family of nurturing and completing senses; John's Greek text preserves the Aramaic address Rabbi and explains it as Teacher, a related Semitic authority term with a narrower use here.

row.basis: Hebrew שוה, making equal, and Arabic s-w-y
row.note: The source commentary labels سوّى with root s-w-y and explains it as straightening what is crooked; Isaiah uses the related Hebrew verb in asking whom an idol can be made equal to, adding the sense of leveling or equality in a polemic against rival images.

Genesis forms the human from ground and then gives life by divine breath. It provides a close biblical sequence for the commentary's ordered body and its cited Q 32:9 breath, while retaining an earthly material origin.

Job says God's hands fashioned him all around, then protests that the same maker turns to destroy him. The shared embodied formation is set in a lament, a deliberate tension with the praise of creating and proportioning in Q 87:2.
Job figures his prenatal making as liquid poured like milk and curdled like cheese. That material, staged image belongs beside the commentary's formed and unformed embryonic body.

Job describes being clothed with skin and flesh and woven with bones and sinews. It is a concrete bodily counterpart to the commentary's claim that creation and setting right can be heard as bodily formation.

After the anatomical images, Job says God granted life and guarded his spirit. It joins formed flesh to a divinely sustained life, as the commentary joins proportioning to breath and eventual revivification.
Job says a person's days and months are determined and bounded by God. This directly supplies the temporal side of the commentary's particular measure (qaddara) across a human life.
Job grounds equal human standing in one maker who made both people in the womb and fashioned them there. The shared point is divine womb-formation, not merely a general creator title.
The psalmist places dependence on God from the mother's belly onward. Together with its old-age plea, it gives the lifespan arc that the commentary hears in child-rearing and senescence.
The same speaker asks not to be abandoned in old age when strength fails. This is a specific biblical counterpart to the commentary's move from fetal formation through maturity toward old age.

The psalm explicitly compares a human's days to grass and a flowering field. It closely matches the commentary's pairing of the ordered body with the pasture that dries up as one warning about mortal life.
The following verse makes the grass vanish when the wind passes over it. It supplies the disappearance that gives the body-and-pasture comparison its warning force.
When God takes away breath, living creatures die and return to dust. This links breath, bodily mortality, and earth in the same sequence the commentary connects to creation and resurrection.

God sends breath, creatures are created, and the ground is renewed. The verse places animate creation and revived earth together, paralleling the commentary's juxtaposition of body and watered pasture.
The psalm attributes the inward parts and covering in the mother's womb to God. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's womb enclosure and fetal bodily formation.
The speaker's frame is made in secret and woven in hidden depths. Its hidden craftsmanship gives a biblical form to the commentary's transition from unformed to fully shaped body.

God sees the speaker's unformed substance, and the days are written before they arrive. The verse combines embryo imagery with a measured lifespan, the two strands of the commentary's reading of created and apportioned life.

Ecclesiastes invokes the formation of bones in a pregnant woman as something humans do not know, then extends that ignorance to God's work. It checks any attempt to turn the commentary's lexical fetal images into a claimed account of fetal mechanics.

row.basis: earth gives birth to the dead
row.note: Isaiah calls sleepers in dust to awake and portrays earth as giving birth to the dead. The birth image makes an especially close counterpart to the commentary's inference from prenatal formation to resurrection.
Isaiah names the Lord as both maker and one who forms the addressee from the womb. This directly joins the two creation verbs that the commentary develops as fetal formation.

The speaker again identifies himself as maker of all and former of the addressee from the womb. Its cosmic and prenatal scopes together illuminate the commentary's claim that a measured human body belongs to a larger created order.
God addresses those carried from the belly and borne from the womb. It begins a divine care sequence at prenatal and birth stages, matching the commentary's life-course reading.

row.basis: until old age and gray hair
row.note: The same divine bearer remains present until old age and gray hair. This is a particularly exact lifespan counterpart to the commentary's movement from the womb through maturity to senescence.
The servant says the Lord formed him from the womb for service. It joins bodily formation to calling, a useful counterpart both to Q 87:2's formation and to the recited commission in Q 87:6.

row.basis: formed, known, and appointed before birth
row.note: Jeremiah is known before womb-formation and appointed before emergence. The verse makes divine formation part of a life directed toward a purpose, sharpening the commentary's measure-and-guidance claim.

In Ezekiel's vision God promises breath to dry bones so that they will live. It supplies an explicit bodily-revival analogue for the commentary's citation of embryonic creation as evidence for raising the dead.

God orders sinews, flesh, skin, and breath onto bones. The ordered rebuilding of a body is a close counterpart to formed flesh, bodily proportion, and later life; Ezekiel's own vision then identifies this with Israel's restoration.

row.basis: breath gives life to assembled bodies
row.note: Once breath enters, the assembled bodies live and stand. The verse completes the formation-to-life sequence that the commentary traces from fetal body to resurrection.
God promises to put his spirit within the people so that they live. Its own national-restoration setting makes the bodily image an interpretive rather than a simple individual-resurrection equation.
Daniel depicts many sleeping in earth's dust awakening to divergent lasting destinies. It gives the eschatological endpoint of the commentary's earth-to-body-to-resurrection arc.
Isaiah's voice calls all flesh grass and human constancy a field flower. The explicit flesh-and-grass equation strongly parallels the commentary's body and drying pasture as two faces of one warning.
Grass withers and the flower fades when the Lord's breath blows on it. It adds the agency of divine breath to the commentary's life-and-pasture contrast.

row.basis: molded into flesh in mother's womb
row.note: Wisdom's speaker says he was molded into flesh in a mother's womb. It is a late Jewish, explicitly prenatal formulation of the bodily shaping developed in the commentary.
The next verse describes gestation in a fixed period and bodily material from seed and blood. Its timed, material account closely meets the commentary's womb gathering and measured formation.
The speaker moves from womb formation to birth and breathing the common air. That transition is useful beside the commentary's formed body followed by divine breath and life.

Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. This is an unusually exact Jewish formulation of the commentary's account of qaddara as placing each thing in a particular measure and form.

row.basis: from mother's womb to return to earth
row.note: Sirach frames the human burden from leaving the mother's womb until returning to the mother of all. It explicitly spans the bodily life course from birth to death that the commentary assembles from its roots.

The mother of the martyrs says she does not know how her children came to be in her womb and denies that she gave them life or set their elements in order. It closely mirrors the commentary's created, ordered fetus while locating agency in the Creator.

The mother says the Creator will return life and breath to her sons. The verse directly makes prenatal formation an argument for resurrection, exactly the inferential move foregrounded by the commentary.
The mother points to heaven, earth, and the human race as made by God. In her martyrdom context this supports hope beyond death, extending the commentary's creation-to-resurrection reasoning.

row.basis: formed in wisdom; openings and cavities
row.note: The Asher Yatzar blessing praises the one who formed the human in wisdom with openings and cavities whose proper functioning sustains life. It offers a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's well-proportioned, disease-free body ordered by wisdom.

row.basis: parents' material and God's life-giving share
row.note: The Talmud distinguishes parental contributions to bones, flesh, and other features from God's gift of spirit, soul, senses, and understanding. It is a detailed Jewish account of an ordered body joined to life and capacity.

row.basis: fetus in womb taught Torah then made to forget
row.note: Niddah says the fetus is taught Torah in the womb and an angel causes it to forget at birth. The combination of womb, instruction, and forgetting is a specific meeting with Q 87:6's recitation and not-forgetting beside the commentary's womb sense for its root.

row.basis: grain buried and clothed in rising
row.note: Rabbi Meir answers a resurrection question with wheat that is buried bare and emerges clothed. The rabbinic analogy joins vegetal renewal to bodily resurrection, like the commentary's body-and-pasture pairing.
Paul says God gives all people life, breath, and everything. It is a concise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's sequence from shaped body to enlivening breath.

Paul says God determined allotted times and the bounds of peoples' habitation. This gives a concrete New Testament use of divine determination as ordered measure, rather than an imported lexical equation.

row.basis: Spirit gives life to mortal bodies
row.note: The Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to mortal bodies. It directly joins divine indwelling spirit, bodily mortality, and resurrection in the way the commentary connects formation, breath, and revivification.
Paul explicitly asks how the dead are raised and with what sort of body they come. This names the bodily-resurrection question that the commentary raises through Q 75:40.
Paul's seed image says death precedes new life. It provides a vegetal pattern for the commentary's move from a dying pasture and mortal body toward life beyond death.

row.basis: bare grain and body to come
row.note: The sower does not sow the body that will come, but a bare grain. This distinguishes initial material from its later formed body, a strong analogue to the commentary's unformed and completed stages.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body
row.note: God gives the seed a body as he chooses, to each seed its own body. The sentence makes divine assignment of bodily form an explicit resurrection counterpart to creating and proportioning.
Paul contrasts a perishable sown body with an imperishable raised one. It makes the commentary's mortality-and-afterlife warning bodily and eschatological.
The body is sown in weakness and raised in power. This supplies an eschatological reversal of the frailty and declining strength that the commentary associates with old age.
Paul distinguishes a natural body from a raised spiritual body, without discarding bodiliness. It is a useful Christian development of the commentary's body-plus-breath sequence.
Christ will transform the body of lowliness to conform to his glorious body. The verse gives a specifically Christian answer to the commentary's movement from mortal formed body to life after death.

row.basis: rich person and fading grass flower
row.note: James tells the rich to boast in lowliness because they pass away like a flower of grass. It closely matches the commentary's confident garden owner and the warning conveyed by worldly life and withering pasture.

row.basis: sun scorches grass and beauty perishes
row.note: James completes the image: sun scorches the grass, its flower falls, and the rich fade in their pursuits. This gives the image an ethical warning about transient prosperity, as in the commentary's ruined garden.

First Peter quotes the formula that all flesh is like grass and its glory like a grass flower. It is the New Testament's closest verbal and conceptual counterpart to the commentary's juxtaposition of human body and withering pasture.
The human formed from ground is told to return to dust. It supplies the deathward side of the commentary's earth, body, and resurrection sequence, though it does not itself promise revival.

row.basis: hands made and fashioned; request for understanding
row.note: The psalmist says divine hands made and fashioned him, then asks for understanding of commandments. It brings formed person and divinely directed understanding together, bridging Q 87:2-3's creation and guidance.

row.basis: breath to people and spirit to walkers
row.note: Isaiah's creator gives breath to the people on earth and spirit to those who walk on it. This is a compact creation-and-life formulation alongside the commentary's Q 32:9 comparison.

Sirach describes the Lord assigning created works their portions and arranging them in order. It is a Jewish development of the commentary's claim that each thing is put in a particular measure and mode.

row.basis: human from earth and returned to it
row.note: Sirach says the Lord created humans from earth and lets them return to it. It adds a sapiential version of the soil-to-body-to-death arc underlying the commentary's resurrection reflection.

Onkelos renders the human made living in Genesis as a speaking spirit. That interpretive rendering links the formed and breathed body to speech, which helps place Q 87:6's recitation beside the commentary's bodily reading of its root.

row.basis: origin in a drop; return to dust
row.note: Avot asks a person to remember the bodily origin in a drop and the destination of dust and decay. Its ethical memento turns the life-course images of the commentary into a warning against worldly self-assurance.

Jesus asks which anxious person can add a span to life. This is a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's measured human lifespan, with a warning against investing trust in present life.

Jesus describes grass alive today and thrown into an oven tomorrow while arguing for divine care. The image links bodily concern and transient grass, though its immediate point is anxiety rather than resurrection.

John is said to be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb. It makes the womb a site of divine life and vocation, a specific New Testament counterpart to the commentary's prenatal life imagery.
At Mary's greeting, the child leaps in Elizabeth's womb. The narrative gives a concrete fetal bodily response to divine visitation, rather than an abstract use of womb language.

row.basis: growth in wisdom, stature, and favor
row.note: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor. It is a concise New Testament life-stage counterpart to the commentary's sense of reaching full youth and ordered maturation.

row.basis: life required from the storing rich man
row.note: God tells the rich planner that his life is demanded that night. The sudden end to stored abundance is a close ethical meeting with the commentary's garden owner who trusts worldly security before it vanishes.

Nicodemus hears new birth in literal bodily terms and asks about entering a mother's womb a second time. The question exposes the bodily reading that the following saying redirects, creating a useful contrast with the commentary's literal fetal imagery.

Jesus answers the womb question with birth from water and Spirit. It reworks birth imagery toward eschatological renewal, a Christian counter-reading to place beside the commentary's body-and-breath account.

Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him through grace. Like Isaiah's womb-formed servant, it joins prenatal life to a directed vocation and the commentary's creation-guidance sequence.

Paul figures the whole creation as groaning together in childbirth. The verse applies labor imagery to creation's movement toward redemption, an interpretive extension of the commentary's body, earth, and resurrection linkage.
Paul contrasts outward decay with inward renewal day by day. It makes the commentary's old-age and enduring-afterlife contrast a present bodily and spiritual discipline.

row.basis: mature person and measure of fullness
row.note: The church's goal is mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's fullness. It takes maturity and measure into an ecclesial-ethical register, rather than describing fetal anatomy.

row.basis: spirit, soul, and body preserved whole
row.note: Paul prays that spirit, soul, and body be kept whole for the Lord's coming. It is a Christian holistic counterpart to the commentary's fully ordered body and its final-life horizon.

First Peter describes a new birth through imperishable seed and enduring word. It offers a Christian extension from bodily birth to lasting life, anticipating the flesh-and-grass contrast in the next verse.

row.basis: Christ's clay healing and primal formation
row.note: Irenaeus reads Jesus' clay healing of the man born blind as the Creator's original art of forming humanity from earth being displayed and restored. This patristic reading makes bodily formation and repair central to resurrection faith.

row.basis: Hebrew qara, calling names after formation
row.note: Hebrew qara, to call or name, belongs to the Semitic q-r-ʾ family also heard in Q 87:6's recitation verb. Here Adam names creatures after their formation, so it supports speech after creation but does not carry the commentary's Arabic womb-closure sense.

Hebrew rabah, to become many, is a cognate family relevant to the commentary's source label r-b-b. Genesis uses it for human fruitfulness and multiplication, not for the Arabic sense of rearing a child stage by stage.

Job calls God kabbir, great or mighty, a cognate family of Arabic kabir. The Hebrew context keeps greatness rather than age in view, which helps distinguish the commentary's age-related Arabic root note from the actual 'great' fire of Q 87:12.

row.basis: from mother's womb to naked return
row.note: Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked. The saying compresses bodily origin and mortality into the life-course arc that the commentary traces from womb formation to its end.

row.basis: Spirit made me; breath gives life
row.note: Job's interlocutor says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a particularly direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's formed body followed by enlivening breath.
Elihu imagines God gathering back to himself a creature's spirit and breath. This supplies the withdrawal side of the commentary's body-and-breath sequence.

row.basis: all flesh perishes and returns to dust
row.note: The consequence of withdrawn breath is that all flesh dies and humanity returns to dust. It makes the body, breath, and earth sequence explicit before any resurrection answer is supplied.

row.basis: God knows the frame and remembers dust
row.note: The psalm says God knows the human frame and remembers that humans are dust. It ties bodily construction to earthly frailty, supplementing the commentary's formed body and its eventual decline.

row.basis: dust returns; spirit returns to God
row.note: Ecclesiastes separates the body's return to earth from the spirit's return to God. It gives a sharply stated deathward counterpart to the commentary's body-and-breath account and its afterlife horizon.
Isaiah calls a mortal human being like grass. This directly joins the human body and fading vegetation that the commentary treats as one warning about temporary worldly life.

Wisdom says God created humanity for incorruption and made it in the likeness of divine eternity. It gives a Jewish counterweight to bodily decay that closely matches the commentary's contrast of worldly life with what endures.

row.basis: power over life, death, and return
row.note: Wisdom attributes authority over life and death to God, including bringing people down to Hades and back. It is a direct Jewish formulation of the creation-to-resurrection inference developed in the commentary.

row.basis: dust-made body and breath of life
row.note: Fourth Ezra says God commanded dust to give Adam, a lifeless body formed by divine hands, then breathed life into him. The retelling explicitly combines the commentary's earth, fashioned body, and breath sequence.

row.basis: formed, born, lives, dies, and gives account
row.note: Avot presents human formation, birth, life, death, and judgment as an involuntary ordered sequence. It is a rabbinic whole-life formulation for the stages the commentary assembles from womb to old age and final reckoning.

row.basis: those in tombs hear the voice
row.note: Jesus says all who are in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a New Testament voice-to-bodily-resurrection counterpart to the commentary's move from divine speech and formation to the raising of the dead.
Those who hear come out, to life or judgment according to their deeds. The bodily emergence and divided final outcome develop the resurrection horizon invoked by the commentary.

row.basis: gives life to dead and calls what is not
row.note: Paul characterizes God as giving life to the dead and calling into being things that are not. The paired creation-and-revival formula closely matches the commentary's use of fetal creation as evidence for resurrection.

Paul rereads Adam's becoming a living soul against the last Adam as life-giving Spirit. This Christian interpretation directly develops the formed-and-breathed human of Genesis into an eschatological body-and-life contrast.

At the Lord's commanding call, the dead in Christ rise first. It gives a concrete Christian scene of divine sound followed by resurrection, alongside the commentary's recitation and revivification themes.
The psalmist asks to know the measure and extent of his days. This gives a personal, prayerful analogue to the commentary's understanding of qaddara as a life set to a measure.

row.basis: remember Creator in days of youth
row.note: Ecclesiastes calls for remembering the Creator during youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes youth and later decline an ethical frame, matching the commentary's use of completed youth and old age as life stages.

row.basis: spirit and breath made by God
row.note: Isaiah says that the spirit would fail before God, along with the breaths God has made. The verse joins creaturely frailty with divine authorship of breath, though its immediate context is divine restraint from wrath.

Sirach attributes human tongue, eyes, ears, mind, knowledge, and understanding to God. It offers a sapiential expansion of the commentary's properly ordered body into its sensory and cognitive capacities.
Paul says believers will bear the image of the heavenly one. It continues his bodily-resurrection argument by moving from an earthly formed humanity toward a transformed eschatological embodiment.

row.basis: new birth through resurrection to living hope
row.note: First Peter blesses God for giving a new birth into living hope through Jesus' resurrection. It extends the commentary's birth-and-revival nexus into a Christian account of renewed life.

row.basis: earthly tent and enduring divine dwelling
row.note: Paul contrasts the destruction of the earthly tent with an enduring dwelling from God. Its body-as-dwelling image makes the commentary's perishable worldly life and lasting future into an explicit Christian contrast.

row.basis: life as a briefly appearing vapor
row.note: James describes present life as vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. It provides a compact ethical analogue to the commentary's warning that worldly life and its flourishing are transient.

row.basis: praising the name; the name exalted
row.note: The opening command to glorify the Lord's name meets the psalm's call to praise YHWH's name because his name alone is exalted; the psalm joins the act of praise to the name's height.
The commentary reads the Lord's name as a sign of ownership and distinction; here YHWH calls Jacob by name and declares Israel his, making naming an explicit claim of belonging.
The commentary's “name as an identifying mark” is literalized when a person writes YHWH on his hand and claims the name Israel; the verse presents the mark as chosen allegiance.

row.basis: engraved holiness on the priest's forehead
row.note: A gold plate engraved “Holy to YHWH” is worn on Aaron's forehead; the bodily inscription identifies sacred service and makes concrete the commentary's hearing of the Lord's name as a distinguishing mark.
The priests “put” YHWH's name upon Israel and God blesses them; this is a direct name-as-belonging-sign parallel to the commentary's gloss of the Lord as owner and the name as his mark.
Circumcision is explicitly called a covenant sign “in your flesh”; this gives the commentary's skin-mark scene a concrete covenantal counterpart that distinguishes a community through a bodily sign.

row.basis: Sabbath as a sign between YHWH and Israel
row.note: The Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel, by which they know that YHWH sanctifies them; it connects a religious act with a visible community identity and holiness, as the commentary connects remembrance and prayer with the Lord's mark.

The blood on the doorways is a sign by which YHWH distinguishes Israelite houses and spares them; it shows a mark identifying whose household is under protection, while the commentary also gives marks opposite fates.

row.basis: sign on hand; memorial of deliverance
row.note: The exodus instruction makes the remembered law a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes; it brings bodily marking together with remembering the Lord's deliverance, a specific ritual counterpart to the commentary's name-and-remembrance reading.

When a servant chooses to remain with his master, his ear is pierced and he stays for life; a chosen attachment leaves a bodily trace that identifies an enduring relation, matching the commentary's claim that preference leaves a mark.

Before Jerusalem's slaughter, a mark is placed on the foreheads of those grieving its abominations so they are passed over; this is a precise counter-role to the stigmatizing brand in the commentary's Q 68 scene: a mark can distinguish and spare.

The frozen commentary labels Q 87:1's word “name” under a disputed w-s-m branch. Hebrew shem here is YHWH's enduring self-designation and memorial across generations; the name-word correspondence is a possible Semitic cognate, without validating the commentary's debated branding etymology.

row.basis: hidden things and good or evil judged
row.note: The verse says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment, whether good or evil; it closely joins the commentary's “knows the hidden” clause to its reading of traces that reveal good and evil.

row.basis: word known before it is spoken
row.note: The psalm says YHWH knows a word before it reaches the speaker's tongue; this specifies divine knowledge of what is concealed behind public speech, as in the commentary's open/hidden pairing.

Humans see outward appearance, but YHWH sees the heart; beside the commentary's readable marks on faces and its claim that God knows what is hidden, this warns that an exterior sign and inward state are not identical.
YHWH puts a sign on Cain so that anyone who finds him will not kill him; unlike the humiliating brand in the commentary's Q 68 example, this bodily sign protects a marked offender.
The lover asks to be set as a seal on heart and arm, a durable bodily claim of love; it offers a distinct intimate use of the commentary's seal-like mark, binding the marked person to another.
Genesis tells the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah by fire and sulfur; it is the Torah narrative behind the commentary's appeal to the ruined Lot-city as a readable sign.

The cities and surrounding plain are overthrown in the Lot narrative, directly matching the commentary's scene of the settlements turned upside down and supplying the story's own account of the ruin later read as a sign.

row.basis: smoke rising from the destroyed land
row.note: Abraham looks toward Sodom and sees smoke rising like smoke from a furnace; the visible aftermath is a trace by which a witness can recognize what happened, close to the commentary's readers of ruined places.

row.basis: smoking wasteland; pillar of salt as memorial
row.note: Wisdom retells Lot's escape and describes the cities' smoking waste and the salt pillar as a monument to an unbelieving soul; it makes the remains themselves evidence of the event, illuminating the commentary's “signs for those who read” the ruined site.

row.basis: failure left as a reminder that cannot be hidden
row.note: Wisdom says those who rejected wisdom failed to recognize good and left a memorial of folly so their failures could not remain hidden; this interprets the surviving ruin as a trace that teaches later observers, closely matching the commentary's reading of signs in a destroyed place.

Ptolemy's decree brands Jews with Dionysus's ivy symbol and reduces them to a subjected status; this makes a bodily mark an imposed religious-identity sign, unlike the individual punitive nose brand in the commentary. Verse wording and numbering can vary by edition.

row.basis: Ezekiel's forehead marks; ink and blood
row.note: The rabbis read Ezekiel's mark as different signs for righteous and wicked, then debate the hidden failure of the righteous to protest; this connects bodily signs with God's knowledge of concealed moral responsibility, complicating the mark's simple protective role.

row.basis: tattoo as writing; Rabbi Shimon's name condition
row.note: The Mishnah discusses Lev 19:28's tattoo ban and Rabbi Shimon's view that liability requires writing a name; it makes the content of a skin mark, specifically a name, matter alongside the commentary's name/brand association.

Leviticus forbids gashing the flesh for the dead and tattoo marks; against the commentary's pious trace of prostration and punitive brand, it supplies a distinct Israelite boundary on inscribing the body.

row.basis: Biblical Aramaic nûr, “fire”; furnace for image-refusal
row.note: The commentary labels the source root of Qur'anic al-nār as n-w-r and develops fire as a camel brand; Biblical Aramaic nûr in Daniel names the furnace imposed on those who refuse the king's image. The cognate fire-word appears in a scene where worship allegiance carries a fiery penalty, though Daniel's furnace is not a brand.

YHWH writes the covenant instruction on the people's hearts; this gives an inward, lasting inscription alongside the commentary's bodily mark and its claim that a person's chosen relation leaves a trace.

row.basis: shepherd calls his own sheep by name
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; the passage joins naming with ownership and recognition, directly clarifying the commentary's interpretation of the Lord's name as a sign of whose something is.

row.basis: bought with a price; glorify God in the body
row.note: Paul says believers were bought and therefore must glorify God in their bodies; this brings the commentary's owner-mark reading of glorifying the Lord's name onto the body itself, while using ethical language rather than a brand.

row.basis: God's seal; the Lord knows his own
row.note: The verse describes God's foundation as bearing a seal: the Lord knows those who are his, and those who name the Lord must turn from wrongdoing. It unites name, ownership, distinguishing knowledge, and keeping the sign morally clean, closely matching the commentary's developed reading.

row.basis: Father's and Lamb's names on foreheads
row.note: The Lamb's followers bear the names of the Father and Lamb on their foreheads; this is a direct image of divine names as visible belonging marks, corresponding to the commentary's name-as-owner-sign and its facial traces of worship.

The angel warns against worshiping the beast and receiving its mark on forehead or hand; like the commentary's contrast between the Lord's name and a hostile mark, this sign identifies a rival allegiance, though the source's punitive brand is aimed at a denier rather than a worshiping community.

row.basis: fire for those marked and worshiping
row.note: The next verse makes the marked beast-worshiper's fate torment in fire and sulfur; Revelation thus explicitly joins the mark and fire that the commentary sets as opposed traces, with a different allegiance determining the outcome.
The mark, beast's name, or number is required to buy or sell; this adds the mark's public social function as a way to identify and separate people, beyond its bodily placement.

row.basis: marks of Jesus on Paul's body
row.note: Paul says he bears Jesus's marks on his body; these scars identify the allegiance and service that have left a trace, offering a Christian bodily-mark counterpart distinct from a branded animal or punitive stigma.

Thomas demands to see the mark of the nails and the wound in Jesus's side; the wounds are bodily traces used to recognize the crucified person, paralleling the commentary's claim that a mark on a body can be read.

Jesus tells the fasting person to wash and anoint the face so the fast is not displayed to others, while the Father sees in secret; this offers a contrary reading to the commentary's visible prostration mark by locating devotional recognition in concealed practice.

Jesus says people are recognized by their fruits; the produced result functions as a readable trace of the source, matching the commentary's explanation of athar as what remains and its claim that good and evil can be discerned from a mark.
The bad tree that fails to make good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this uniquely joins the commentary's readable good/bad trace with its other image of fire as the fate of the rejected.

Jesus says hidden things are destined to be disclosed; the verse concerns eventual revelation rather than God's present omniscience, but it connects the commentary's hidden trace with its public/hidden distinction.

row.basis: nothing hidden; all laid bare before God
row.note: No creature is hidden from God's sight and all is exposed before the one to whom account is given; this develops the commentary's statement that God knows the open and hidden and that traces can disclose a person's condition.

row.basis: circumcision of heart by the Spirit
row.note: Paul interprets true circumcision as inward, of the heart and Spirit rather than letter; this re-reads the fleshly covenant sign of Genesis 17 and brings an invisible moral trace beside the commentary's literal brand and outward prayer mark.

Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; this meets both the commentary's visible/invisible trace and its contrast between preferred worldly life and the more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: world passing; God's will remains forever
row.note: The world and its desires pass away, while the one doing God's will remains forever; this directly answers the commentary's “you prefer worldly life” beside “the hereafter is better and more lasting.”

Jesus warns that earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth and decay; this gives a concrete instance of the worldly life that does not endure, setting up the commentary's contrast with the lasting hereafter.
Heavenly treasure cannot be destroyed or stolen; this is a concrete counterpart to the commentary's claim that the hereafter is better and more enduring than worldly life.
Jesus says the heart is where one's treasure is; it links preference to an inward mark or orientation, specifying how what one values identifies the person.

row.basis: Moses chooses hardship over sin's fleeting pleasure
row.note: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over temporary enjoyment in sin; the passage gives a concrete reversal of preferring present worldly life and shows a chosen allegiance that shapes a life.

Moses considers disgrace for the anointed greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it explicitly links choosing what is lasting with what is better, echoing the commentary's contrast of worldly preference and the enduring hereafter.

row.basis: work disclosed and tested by fire
row.note: Each one's work becomes manifest at the Day and is tested by fire; this joins the commentary's residue that distinguishes a person with its fire image, as actions are exposed and their quality shown.

row.basis: Sodom reduced to ashes as an example
row.note: Peter says God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and made them an example of what awaits the ungodly; it interprets the Lot-city's destruction as a readable warning, complementing the commentary's signs in the ruined site.

row.basis: Sodom as example of punishment by eternal fire
row.note: Jude presents Sodom and neighboring cities as an example by undergoing punishment of eternal fire; the Christian interpretation makes the destroyed place a sign of the future fiery fate, joining the commentary's readable ruins and Great Fire.

The command forbids bearing YHWH's name falsely and says the guilty will not be acquitted; it gives a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's secondary hearing of glorifying the name as keeping the Lord's identifying mark free from fault.

The narrative identifies a man who blasphemes and curses the Name; this directly intersects the commentary's concern for the Lord's name and its account of a denier whose contemptuous speech earns a bodily stigma.
The same law sentences the blasphemer of YHWH's name to death; it adds a concrete sanction for dishonoring the name beside the commentary's punitive mark for dismissing revelation.

YHWH says he will sanctify his great name, which Israel profaned among the nations; this directly develops the commentary's secondary sense of keeping the Lord's name-mark free of blemish, and makes public reputation part of the issue.

row.basis: nose and ears cut; survivors consumed by fire
row.note: In the allegory of Jerusalem and Samaria's infidelity, enemies mutilate the women's faces and the remnant is consumed by fire; it supplies a concrete judgment-image of facial stigma joined to fire, while the context and instrument differ from the commentary's brand.

row.basis: Abel's blood cries from the ground
row.note: Cain's hidden murder is disclosed when Abel's blood cries to God from the ground; this is a specific trace left on earth that reveals an act and its agent, enriching the commentary's claim that an effect can remain visible or unseen.

YHWH says Zion is engraved on his palms and continually before him; this reverses the commentary's owner-mark image, showing the marked person preserved in the owner's memory, and adds permanence to the trace.

row.basis: forehead plate and acceptance of offerings
row.note: Aaron bears the guilt attached to the sacred gifts on the forehead plate so the offerings may be accepted; this continuation gives the inscribed holiness a cleansing and acceptance function beside the commentary's call to keep the Lord's mark pure.

YHWH asks whether anyone can hide where he cannot see and says he fills heaven and earth; it directly specifies that concealed conduct remains within divine sight, as in the commentary's public/hidden pair.

row.basis: God reveals hidden things and knows darkness
row.note: Daniel's prayer says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness; this supplies a close biblical-Aramaic formulation of divine knowledge of the concealed alongside the commentary's explicit open/hidden clause.

row.basis: book of remembrance for those who esteem YHWH's name
row.note: A book of remembrance is written for those who fear YHWH and esteem his name; it makes devotion leave a durable written trace and connects remembrance of the name with later recognition.

row.basis: distinction between the righteous and the wicked
row.note: The audience will again see a distinction between the righteous and wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not; this specifies the commentary's claim that a mark distinguishes one person from another by the allegiance it records.

row.basis: book of the covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses reads the book of the covenant to Israel, who answer to its words; this gives a concrete scriptural witness for the commentary's contrast between dismissing ancient accounts as tales and receiving the earliest writings as revelation.

row.basis: Moses' scroll kept as a witness
row.note: Moses orders the written law to be placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel; this directly illuminates the surah's appeal to the scrolls of Moses after the commentary's denier labels the stories of the ancients fables.

row.basis: Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt
row.note: During the escape from Sodom, Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt; this is an individual bodily remnant within the same destruction story, later read in Wisdom 10:7 as a memorial, adding a concrete trace beside the commentary's ruined-city signs.

Wisdom says every utterance is heard and no secret whisper escapes; this gives a Jewish formulation of concealed speech remaining knowable, particularly apt beside the commentary's open/hidden knowledge and its judged denier's words.

row.basis: people inscribed and sealed for life or death
row.note: The rabbinic judgment tradition pictures books opened and the wholly righteous sealed for life, the wholly wicked for death; it interprets a written mark as distinguishing moral status and fate, extending the commentary's identity-mark contrast into an eschatological register.

row.basis: Christ's letter written on hearts and read by all
row.note: Paul calls the community a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit on human hearts and known and read by everyone; this is an inward trace that identifies its source and can be read, directly developing the commentary's mark-and-recognition relation.

row.basis: God's seal and Spirit in hearts
row.note: Paul says God set his seal on believers and gave the Spirit in their hearts as a pledge; this specifies an inward divine mark of belonging and a lasting guarantee, distinct from the name-inscription in the commentary.

row.basis: circumcision interpreted as a seal of faith
row.note: Paul calls Abraham's circumcision a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith he already had; this Christian reading interprets the fleshly sign in Genesis 17 as certifying an inward allegiance, adding a distinct meaning to the commentary's mark of ownership.

row.basis: God's servants sealed on their foreheads before harm
row.note: The servants of God receive a seal on their foreheads before the earth is harmed; besides Revelation 14's names of belonging, this mark specifically distinguishes and protects a community before destruction, like Ezekiel's spared mourners.

row.basis: account for every careless word at judgment
row.note: Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this connects the commentary's denier's spoken dismissal and God's knowledge of the open and hidden with a verbal trace that carries consequences.

Jesus says a person is justified or condemned by their words; this adds the words' role as evidence that distinguishes a person's standing, alongside the commentary's punishment of one who calls revelation ancient fables.

row.basis: hidden heart-counsels disclosed; praise from God
row.note: At the Lord's coming, hidden things of darkness and heart-counsels are brought to light, and each receives praise from God; this joins concealed traces, divine recognition, and moral evaluation in a way close to the commentary's open/hidden knowledge.

row.basis: one tongue blesses God and curses people
row.note: James says the tongue blesses the Lord and Father yet curses people made in God's likeness; it gives a specific ethical test for honoring God's name, relevant to the commentary's contrast between glorifying the Lord and contemptuous speech.

row.basis: gain the world and forfeit oneself
row.note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while losing or forfeiting oneself; this sharply reverses preference for worldly life and specifies its cost beside the commentary's better, lasting hereafter.

row.basis: sowing to flesh or Spirit yields corruption or eternal life
row.note: Paul says sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; the harvested result is a trace of one's chosen orientation, directly linking preference, remainder, and lasting fate.

row.basis: fruit of former conduct ends in death
row.note: Paul asks what fruit came from former shameful practices and says their end is death; the fruit is a readable remainder of chosen conduct, tied to the fate that contrasts with the commentary's lasting hereafter.

row.basis: fruit of holiness and end of eternal life
row.note: Freed from sin and enslaved to God, believers bear fruit for holiness whose end is eternal life; this combines the commentary's owner relation, trace of action, and lasting destiny in one passage.

row.basis: acts toward the least counted as acts toward the king
row.note: In the judgment scene, care for the least is counted as service to the king; deeds become the trace by which allegiance is recognized, giving a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that preference leaves an identifying mark.

The judgment ends with the two groups sent to eternal punishment or eternal life; this supplies a specific Christian formulation of the commentary's contrast between the fire-bound and the better, enduring hereafter.

row.basis: books opened; the dead judged by their deeds
row.note: The dead are judged according to their deeds recorded in opened books; this turns the commentary's trace into an eschatological record that exposes and distinguishes each person's conduct.

row.basis: name absent from the book of life; lake of fire
row.note: Anyone not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire; this explicitly makes a written name the mark distinguishing the saved from those assigned to fire, uniting the commentary's owner-sign and fire images.
The commentary has Moses spot a fire and go toward it before the divine address; Exodus places the angel of YHWH in a flame within a bush, making the fire the setting of a call.
The commentary says Moses reaches the fire and is addressed; at the bush God calls “Moses, Moses” and Moses answers, giving the same encounter its direct biblical scene.
The commentary links the fire scene with blessing and glorification; Exodus names the ground around the bush holy and commands Moses to approach reverently, locating sanctity at the fire.

The commentary recalls fires lit as waymarks so people could find and follow a route; Exodus says YHWH led Israel by a pillar of fire at night, an explicit divine fire that lights and guides a journey.

The commentary distinguishes ordinary fire used for warmth from the great punitive fire; Isaiah describes a person using part of his wood fire to warm himself and bake bread, then turns to the religious meaning of the remainder.
The commentary cites roasting meat as one sense of ṣ-l-y; Isaiah's man uses the same fire to roast meat and eat, grounding that sense in an ordinary domestic scene.

The commentary calls the kindled small fire a reminder and contrasts it with turning away from admonition; Isaiah makes the remainder of the cooking fire into an idol that the man bows to, a pointed reversal of fire's proper reminder.

The commentary explicitly reports Arabic nūr and nār together through illumination, while biblical Aramaic uses nūrā for the furnace fire; this supplies a concrete fire-word cognate without proving the commentary's etymology.

The commentary identifies the wretched person as entering the great fire; Isaiah asks who can dwell with consuming fire and everlasting burnings, then answers with the righteous, shifting the question from doomed entry to who can endure God's presence.

The commentary connects Saqar's “does not leave or spare” with the warning that the damned neither die nor live; Isaiah's final image is corpses of rebels with a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched.

The commentary presents entry into the great fire as punishment for the wretched; Daniel sees the three faithful men walking unharmed inside the furnace with a fourth figure, reversing the expected result of fire-entry.

The Qur'anic Moses scene has blessing and glorification spoken at the fire; after the furnace rescue, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of the three men, connecting fire, deliverance, and praise in a different scene.

row.ref: Song of the Three Young Men 3:52-56
row.note: The commentary places glorification at Moses' fire and contrasts prayer with damnation; the youths' song blesses and praises God amid the furnace, adding a liturgical voice from inside a fire.
The commentary locates Moses' sighting at the side of Tur; Exodus first brings Moses' flock to Horeb, the mountain of God, grounding the shared fire encounter in its mountain setting.

The commentary quotes the Qur'anic command at the fire to worship and establish prayer; Exodus says Israel will serve God on this mountain after the bush call, linking the encounter to worship while leaving prayer-for-remembrance distinctive to the Qur'anic wording.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name and prays; at the bush God gives the name by which generations will remember him, making divine name and remembrance part of the same Mosaic scene.

The commentary invokes Moses seeing fire before hearing a call; Stephen recounts the angel appearing in a flame from a bush and introduces Moses' commission, preserving the scene in an early Christian retelling.

The commentary distinguishes the fire verb ṣ-l-y from the prayer verb ṣ-l-w; Daniel's Aramaic verb for his three daily prayers is from the prayer sense, a close Semitic cognate that supports the prayer-side echo without merging the Qur'anic roots.

The commentary contrasts the one who prays with those who say they were not among the prayerful; Daniel keeps praying and thanking God three times daily despite the royal decree, giving a concrete scene of persevering prayer.

The commentary includes roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus names the Passover lamb as roasted with fire, a plausible weak-consonant Semitic cognate for that cooking sense, not for the distinct prayer root.
The commentary's person remembers the Lord's name and then prays; the psalm summons the worshipper to bless YHWH and not forget his benefits, joining remembrance to liturgical praise.
The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Jesus' prayer begins by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, a concrete prayer-formula parallel while the verbs differ.
The commentary identifies the wretched one as entering the great fire; the judgment scene assigns the condemned to eternal fire, sharpening the relation between moral fate and fire.

The commentary connects non-ending punishment with fire that does not spare; Jesus applies Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire language to Gehenna, making the prophetic image an explicit warning about final judgment.

The commentary's damned neither die nor live and the Saqar fire does not relent; Revelation says the smoke of the beast-worshippers' torment rises forever and they have no rest, an analogous account of unending punishment with a distinct image.
The commentary moves from fire at Moses' call to worship and prayer; Hebrews calls God a consuming fire in a passage urging reverent worship, holding judgment-fire and devotion together.

The commentary makes Moses' fire a route to divine address; the midrash reads the thornbush's burning without destruction as God's presence with Israel in affliction, turning the fire into a sign of solidarity and survival.
The commentary joins fire with guidance on a path; Wisdom's retelling says Wisdom guided the holy people and became a starry flame at night, interpreting Israel's fire-guidance as Wisdom's work.
The commentary calls the punishment fire “the great” one; Isaiah describes Topheth's pyre as deep and broad with abundant fire, supplying a concrete biblical scale image for punitive fire.

row.basis: righteousness as the answer to fire
row.note: The commentary contrasts one person entering fire with another remembering God and praying; Isaiah's next verse answers who can dwell by naming the one who acts righteously, offering a specific ethical counterpart to the doomed entrant.

row.basis: self-kindled fire as light, then torment
row.note: The commentary recalls fire used to find a path and contrasts useful fire with the great punishment; Isaiah addresses people who kindle a fire, walk by its light, and end by lying down in torment.

The commentary's Moses hears the divine address at a fire; at Horeb Elijah sees wind, earthquake, and fire, but this verse says YHWH is not in the fire and is encountered in the quiet sound, a distinct counter-scene about revelation.
The commentary treats entry into fire as punishment; after Israel's complaint, YHWH's fire burns at the edge of the camp, giving a concrete wilderness scene of punitive fire.
The commentary contrasts the condemned entrant with the one who remembers God and prays; Moses cries to YHWH and the fire subsides, making prayer an intervention that ends a punitive fire.

row.basis: Elijah's prayer names God before fire
row.note: The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Elijah invokes the God of the ancestors and asks that Israel know YHWH is God before fire answers, joining prayer, divine identity, and fire.

row.basis: fire descends in answer to prayer
row.note: The commentary contrasts going toward a guiding fire with entering a punitive one; after Elijah's prayer, fire falls from YHWH and consumes the offering, reversing the human direction toward fire into a divine response.
The commentary's Moses scene ends in worship and prayer at a fire; after the fire on Carmel, the people fall on their faces and confess YHWH as God, giving a distinct fire-to-worship sequence.

The commentary contrasts the wretched who enter the great fire with the pious kept from it; in Hebrew-numbered Malachi, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like an oven, leaving no root or branch.

row.basis: he name-fearing spared from the burning day
row.note: The commentary pairs remembering the Lord's name and prayer with safety from fire; the next Hebrew-numbered verse promises healing to those who fear God's name, setting their fate against the wicked burned in 3:19.
The commentary glosses al-kubrā through Arabic k-b-r as greatness; Job calls God kabîr, “mighty,” a possible same-root cognate that applies the scale-word to God rather than to a punitive fire.

The commentary develops a fire as a road-marker and links it to being guided; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and light for the path, pairing illumination with guidance without requiring a shared fire scene.

row.basis: fire recalled in communal prayer as guidance
row.note: The commentary joins fire as a way-sign to remembrance and prayer; Nehemiah's communal confession addresses God while recalling the pillar of fire that lit Israel's path, bringing the same guidance image into a liturgical act.
The commentary stresses the great fire's heat and severity; Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace heated seven times more than usual, intensifying the furnace image beyond an ordinary flame.

row.basis: fire kills those who cast the men in
row.note: The commentary describes the damned as enduring the fire's heat; Daniel says the furnace's flame kills the men who throw the faithful into it, while the next scene preserves those inside, distinguishing the fire's effects.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name before prayer; at Moses' fire encounter God gives the self-designation “I am who I am,” adding the name's own explanation to the memorial naming in 3:15.

row.basis: a sign shown in Moses' call
row.note: The commentary cites God's promise to show Moses the greatest signs at the fire; in the continuing bush-call episode Moses' staff becomes a serpent as a sign, giving a concrete counterpart to the signs promised in Qur'an 20:23.

The commentary says the condemned neither die nor live and endure the fire's severity; Luke depicts a dead rich man conscious in flame and asking for relief, adding a specific afterlife image of felt torment.

The commentary presents the great fire as the wretched person's punishment; Hebrews recalls faithful people who quenched the power of fire, giving a Christian counter-example in which fidelity protects from its force.

row.basis: flaming fire for those who reject the message
row.note: The commentary says the wretched turns away from admonition and enters the great fire; Paul describes judgment in flaming fire against those who do not know God or obey the gospel, making the rejection-to-fire sequence explicit.

The commentary records roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus uses the Hebrew roasting form for the Passover lamb, a possible cognate for that culinary sense, though the weak final consonants make the relationship uncertain.

The commentary calls the Satanic offer a tree of immortality and an imperishable realm; Genesis says the human might eat from the tree of life and live forever, giving the Eden scene its own guarded version of the desired permanence.

The commentary treats Satan's promise of the tree of immortality as counterfeit permanence; in Genesis the serpent directly contradicts the death warning, so the promised escape from death is itself suspect.

The serpent's denial uses the Hebrew root מות for dying, a concrete cognate of the ayah's يَمُوتُ; here the word is a denied consequence of eating, sharpening the contrast with the condemned person who cannot die.

Genesis uses the Hebrew life root in its statement that eating from the tree could make the human live forever; this is a direct cognate to يَحْيَىٰ in the commentary's contrast between life and death.

Pharaoh orders that every daughter be kept alive (תְּחַיּוּן); the Hebrew life verb matches the commentary's cited Arabic gloss of “let live” as “keep them alive,” including the survival sense rather than mere vitality.

Isaiah addresses the dead as rising and waking from dust, whereas the commentary's damned person has neither death's release nor life's benefit; this is a specific prophetic reversal of that suspended fate.

Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake to divergent outcomes, including everlasting life; this supplies the afterlife distinction that the commentary uses to contrast worldly life with the hereafter and its condemned endpoint.

The commentary adds the Paradise water that revives whatever it touches; Ezekiel's temple river heals its waters and makes living creatures live wherever the stream goes, a concrete life-giving-water image.

The commentary closes by citing Abraham's claim that God kills and then gives life; Deuteronomy puts that same power in God's own speech, making life and death dependent on God rather than on a ruler's threat.

The commentary describes people in fire who neither die nor live; Isaiah's closing image has the rebels' corpses exposed to a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched, a related but carefully different image of unending judgment.

The commentary distinguishes life as benefit and good from mere biological existence; the Talmud reads “the living know they will die” so the righteous are called living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive, turning the life/death terms into moral evaluations.

The Mishnah explicitly says one hour of bliss in the world to come is better than all the life of this world; this is the closest Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that the hereafter is better and more enduring than preferred worldly life.

The commentary rejects both death and beneficial life for the condemned; Wisdom says the righteous seemed dead to observers but are at peace and have hope full of immortality, preserving an important alternative reading of death's appearance.

A tortured brother accepts death while trusting that the King of the universe will raise him to renewed life; the scene concretely shows why the better lasting life can be preferred over survival now.

row.basis: No resurrection to life for the tyrant
row.note: The martyr says that for the persecuting king there will be no resurrection to life; this gives the commentary's contrast between the condemned state and lasting life a specific judgment scene.

Jesus says the one who seeks to save life will lose it, while the one who loses it for his sake will find it; this reverses the commentary's condemned preference for immediate worldly life over the life that lasts.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the commentary likewise condemns preferring the near worldly life over the better, enduring hereafter.
The rich fool plans many years of ease from his stored goods, but his life is demanded that night; this concretely exposes the false permanence behind investment in worldly life.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin; this is a specific counter-choice to the commentary's charge that people prefer the near life.
Hebrews explains Moses' choice by his regard for a greater future reward; the commentary likewise ranks the hereafter above the present life and calls it more enduring.
Jesus says the believer who dies will live; this is a direct reversal of the commentary's “neither dies nor lives,” though it concerns the faithful and resurrection rather than punishment.
Jesus adds that whoever lives and believes will never die; this supplies an affirmative, promised form of permanence in contrast to the commentary's barren non-life.
Paul sets sin's wage, death, against God's gift of eternal life; the opposed outcomes make explicit the moral choice between death and lasting life that frames the commentary's contrast.

Paul's resurrection scene says the mortal must put on immortality and death is swallowed up in victory; it gives the hereafter's enduring life a concrete bodily endpoint unlike the fire's suspended condition.
John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever; this closely specifies the commentary's near worldly life versus the more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: Death abolished in the renewed world
row.note: Revelation promises that death will be no more, alongside the end of mourning and pain; unlike the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief, this is death's removal within restored life.

row.basis: River of the water of life
row.note: The commentary cites a Paradise water that revives what it touches; Revelation's river of the water of life flows from God's throne through the holy city, giving a precise Christian paradise-water counterpart.
Jesus describes water becoming a spring that wells up to eternal life; this connects the commentary's life-giving Paradise water with an image of water whose effect is enduring life.

row.basis: Living and dead as distinct states
row.note: Qohelet contrasts the living, who know they will die, with the dead, who know nothing; against that clean division, the commentary stresses the disturbing condition that is neither death nor beneficial life.

row.basis: מות and חיה in one reversal
row.note: Isaiah uses cognates for “your dead” and “will live” in a single resurrection claim; the same death/life vocabulary in the ayah is here joined affirmatively rather than negated.

The Mishnah pictures this world as a vestibule from which one prepares to enter the world to come; this interprets present life as provisional, clarifying why the commentary calls the hereafter the better lasting choice.

row.basis: God leads to Hades and raises
row.note: Wisdom says God has power over life and death, leads down to Hades and brings up again; this expands the commentary's final claim that God both causes death and gives life.

At resurrection the righteous are changed into splendor and live in an enduring order while the wicked wither; this gives apocalyptic detail to the commentary's contrast between the hereafter and the fate of those who reject it.

Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac even from the dead; this is a Christian interpretation of the Abraham story that makes concrete the commentary's closing claim that God kills and then gives life.

row.basis: Departing to be with Christ is better
row.note: Paul says departure to be with Christ is far better than remaining alive; this states a specific preference for the life beyond the present one, matching the commentary's ranking of hereafter over worldly life.

Mark places Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire in Jesus' warning about Gehenna; the Christian reuse shifts Isaiah's corpse image into a warning about final judgment, while still not saying the condemned themselves are alive.

After warning against trust in uncertain riches, Paul urges the rich to lay hold of “the life that is truly life”; this gives a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's distinction between mere worldly life and life as real benefit.
Paul says Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light; this offers a Christian counter-image to the condemned person's unrelieved suspension between death and life.

The Paradise river's tree bears leaves for healing the nations; beside the commentary's water that revives anything it touches, Revelation depicts life-giving restoration extending through the whole blessed scene.

row.basis: Paradise trees and no taste of death
row.note: The saying describes unchanging trees in Paradise and promises that those who know them will not taste death; this is a concrete apocryphal image of the immortality sought in the commentary's false tree offer, recast as a blessed promise.

Moses urges Israel to choose life so that they and their offspring may live; the Hebrew life cognate matches the ayah's life vocabulary, though its immediate setting is covenantal survival in the land rather than the commentary's hereafter.

Revelation calls those who die in the Lord blessed and says they rest from their labors; this complicates the commentary's negated death/life condition by presenting death as a blessed rest for a different group.

row.basis: Death warning before the serpent's claim
row.note: The commentary recalls Satan's offer of a tree of immortality; God first warns that eating brings death, the particular claim the serpent then denies, making this neighboring verse necessary to read the promise as counterfeit.

row.basis: The way to the life tree barred
row.note: After the promise of living forever, Genesis stations guardians at the way to the tree of life; this adds the scene's denial of humanly seized permanence beside the commentary's false offer of an imperishable kingdom.

Isaiah promises that God will swallow death forever and wipe away tears; this is an affirmative restoration in which death ends and life remains, a sharp contrast to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life brings relief.

The psalm asks whether anyone can be ransomed so as to live forever without seeing the pit; against the commentary's counterfeit promise of an imperishable kingdom, it says wealth cannot secure permanence against death.

Ezekiel's temple river nourishes trees whose leaves heal; alongside the commentary's Paradise water that revives whatever it touches, this supplies the complementary healing effect of the life-giving waterscape.
Jesus warns that moth, rust, and thieves undo treasure stored on earth; this gives concrete form to the commentary's near worldly life as a poor choice beside what endures.
Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven where it is not destroyed or stolen; the contrast makes explicit the commentary's preference for the better, more enduring hereafter.
Jesus' judgment scene ends with two enduring outcomes, punishment and life; this closely joins the commentary's fire-bound non-life to its claim that the hereafter is lasting and better.
Jesus contrasts entering life with being thrown into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; this connects the commentary's fire and negated life to an explicit choice between life and punishment.

Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in his lifetime while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and the rich man suffers; this is a specific reversal of preferring present worldly ease over the afterlife.

Paul quotes the death-and-Sheol taunt associated with Hosea to celebrate resurrection's victory; this Christian reading turns the Hebrew prophet's ambiguous challenge into an assured defeat of death, unlike the commentary's unrelieved punishment.

row.basis: Tree of life in God's Paradise
row.note: The victor is promised fruit from the tree of life in God's Paradise; this is the positive, divinely granted counterpart to the commentary's Satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

row.basis: No rest in the judgment fire
row.note: The worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night under smoke of torment; this gives a specific Christian judgment image comparable to the commentary's fire without death's release, while the verse itself does not say they neither live nor die.

Hezekiah says the living, unlike those descended to the pit, give thanks to God; this concretely illustrates the commentary's gloss of life as benefit and good, though its setting is recovery from illness rather than final judgment.

Hosea voices Death and Sheol as powers from which Israel may be ransomed, echoing the commentary's claim that God alone gives life after death; the Hebrew can be read as a threat as well as a promise, so the connection should retain that uncertainty.

Jesus says the believer has passed from death into life and will not come into judgment; this is distinct from the future resurrection promise in John 11, presenting life as a present changed status rather than the commentary's condemned suspension.

row.basis: Visible things pass, unseen things are eternal
row.note: Paul contrasts visible, temporary things with unseen, eternal things; this makes a concrete temporal-versus-enduring contrast for the commentary's worldly life and better hereafter.
Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here and seek the city to come; this gives a concrete formulation of present life as provisional beside the commentary's more enduring hereafter.
Peter describes an inheritance in heaven that cannot perish, spoil, or fade; this specifies what enduring future good means beside the commentary's contrast with the near world.

James compares human life to a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; this makes the present life transitory beside the commentary's enduring hereafter, though it does not itself describe resurrection.

row.basis: death sought but cannot be found
row.note: Under locust torment people seek death and cannot find it; like the fire-dweller of 87:13, torment continues while the normal exit of death is withheld.
Isaiah calls the rebels corpses, while the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; that allocation differs from the commentary's conscious fire-inhabitant who is neither dead nor alive.
The Targum turns Isaiah's corpse-and-fire scene into punishment in Gehinnom in which the sinners' souls do not die, an interpretive move that closely approaches the commentary's deathless fire.
Augustine argues that the damned can endure punitive death without being annihilated; this gives a Christian account of the continuing, non-living condition the commentary marks in 87:13.
