The beast-worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur, a concrete New Testament fire-punishment scene beside the commentary's fire where death does not end suffering.

row.basis: no rest day or night, smoke forever
row.note: The people under judgment have no rest day or night and their torment's smoke rises forever; this specifically parallels the commentary's exclusion of sleep or a recoverable lapse in the fire.
The devil, beast, and false prophet are tormented day and night for ever and ever, supplying an explicit Christian image of punitive remaining rather than release through death.

row.basis: source label م و ت B012; sleep of death
row.note: The psalm asks not to sleep the sleep of death; Hebrew מָוֶת is a genuine cognate of the source label م و ت, and the verse supplies the sleep-as-death figure that the commentary says is unavailable in the fire.

row.basis: sleepers in dust awaken to enduring fates
row.note: Those sleeping in dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to disgrace; it makes the commentary's sleep, life, and lasting afterlife distinctions into two final outcomes rather than the suspended state of 87:13.
Jesus calls Lazarus asleep and says that he will awaken him, a recoverable sleep-state set against the commentary's insistence that the fire offers neither sleep nor waking.

row.basis: death when divine breath is withdrawn
row.note: When God takes away creatures' breath, they die and return to dust; this concretizes the commentary's source definition of death as strength or life-force withdrawn from a thing.

row.basis: source label ح ي ي B013; life and good versus death and evil
row.note: Moses places life and good over against death and evil; Hebrew חַיִּים is cognate with the source label ح ي ي, and the explicit life/good pairing closely supports the commentary's secondary definition of life as benefit and goodness.

row.basis: source label ح ي ي B013; desiring life and seeing good
row.note: The psalm joins desiring life with loving days in order to see good; its Hebrew life-word is cognate with ح ي ي and gives a precise biblical analogue to the commentary's life/good connection.

row.basis: future treasure and the life that is truly life
row.note: Generous use of wealth lays a foundation for the future so that one may grasp "the life that is truly life"; it is a pointed counterpart to choosing near worldly life over the enduring real life.

row.basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
row.note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that endures to eternal life, directly framing a present material pursuit against an abiding life as the commentary does in 87:16-17.

row.basis: world passes away, God-doer abides forever
row.note: The world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will abides forever; this is a close formulation of transient worldly life against lasting life.

row.basis: no enduring city here, one to come
row.note: Believers have no lasting city here but seek the city to come, making the commentary's near-life and abiding-hereafter contrast spatial and communal.
The seen is temporary and the unseen eternal; its explicit temporal-eternal contrast supplies the evaluative frame of "better and more enduring" in 87:17.

row.basis: one hour in this world and one hour in the world to come
row.note: Avot says both that repentance and good deeds in this world outweigh all life in the world to come and that one hour of bliss there outweighs all life here; its two-sided valuation complicates a simple worldly-life versus afterlife ranking.

row.basis: good things in lifetime, anguish after death
row.note: Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things in his lifetime with his present anguish and Lazarus's comfort; the story concretely tests the commentary's claim that preferring the near life ends in a radically different final condition.

row.basis: tyrant's torture and everlasting renewal of life
row.note: A tortured brother tells the king that the King of the universe will raise the faithful to an everlasting renewal of life; like the commentary's Pharaoh-and-magicians scene, a ruler's bodily threat is answered by appeal to durable divine life.

row.basis: resurrection to life denied to the persecutor
row.note: The martyr tells the king that he will have no resurrection to life, a direct two-fate response to tyrannical violence that sharpens the commentary's contrast between punishment and the purified person's recompense.

row.basis: faithful people before a king's fiery threat
row.note: The three Judeans tell the king that their God can rescue them from the blazing furnace and from his hand; this supplies a scriptural tyrant, fire, and faithful confession beside Pharaoh's threatened believers.

row.basis: Egyptian magicians name God's finger while Pharaoh hardens
row.note: Moses' Egyptian magicians identify the plague as God's finger, but Pharaoh remains hard; the shared Moses-magicians-Pharaoh scene differs from the commentary's magicians who openly believe and receive Pharaoh's threat.

The letter names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses and compares false teachers to them; this Christian memory of the magicians reverses the commentary's scene of Pharaoh's magicians becoming faithful.

row.basis: source label ح ي ي B006; daughters are to be kept alive
row.note: Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill a Hebrew son but let a daughter live; it is the biblical Pharaoh setting that makes the commentary's "leave your women alive" formula a concrete survival claim.

row.basis: source label ح ي ي B006; keep every female alive
row.note: Moses asks whether the women have all been kept alive; Hebrew הַחִיִּיתֶם uses the cognate life root and gives a sharply specific biblical use of the source commentary's "leaving women alive" sense.

row.basis: source label ب ق ي B003; preserve a remnant and keep alive
row.note: Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep the family alive; this joins remaining after threatened extinction to living, precisely the relation developed under the commentary's remaining/sparing branch.
God declares, "I kill and I make alive"; this is a direct Hebrew Bible formulation for the commentary's claim that Abraham assigns both death and life to the Lord.

row.basis: God kills, makes alive, lowers and raises
row.note: Hannah's hymn says that the Lord kills and makes alive and brings down to Sheol and raises; it gives a fuller scriptural pattern of divine control over the two poles named in the commentary.

row.basis: Father raises the dead and gives life
row.note: As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wishes; this is a direct Christian articulation of death and life as divine acts.

row.basis: Abraham expects God to raise the dead
row.note: Hebrews reads Abraham's offering of Isaac through resurrection: he considers God able to raise even from the dead. That interpretation makes the commentary's Abrahamic death-and-life confession into a specific remembered test.
The serpent tells the woman that she will not surely die; this is the Torah's direct temptation by a denial of death beside the commentary's satanic offer of a tree of immortality.

row.basis: tree of life and living forever
row.note: God bars the human from eating the tree of life and living forever; its actual tree-and-everlasting-life scene provides the closest biblical counterpart to the commentary's deceptive tree of immortality.

Wisdom says God created humans for incorruption and made them in the image of divine eternity; it supplies a late Jewish account of true enduring life against the commentary's false promise of permanence.

row.basis: death enters through the devil's envy
row.note: Wisdom attributes death's entrance into the world to the devil's envy, a direct Jewish development of the Adam-and-tempter relation that illuminates the commentary's satanic lure of immortality.

The devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms shown to him if Jesus will worship him; this is a Christian temptation scene in which the tempter offers dominion, alongside the commentary's offer of an imperishable kingdom to Adam.

row.basis: everlasting dominion that will not pass away
row.note: The Son of Man receives a dominion that is everlasting and will not pass away; it supplies a divinely granted, genuinely imperishable rule in contrast to the commentary's satanic promise of a kingdom that does not wear out.

row.basis: water makes everything live where the river goes
row.note: Every living creature lives wherever Ezekiel's eschatological river goes; this is a close prophetic counterpart to the commentary's paradise water that vivifies whatever it reaches.

row.basis: river of water of life in the final paradise
row.note: John's final city contains a river of the water of life flowing from God's throne, a directly corresponding paradise-water image for the commentary's life-giving water.

row.basis: tree of life and leaves for healing
row.note: Beside the river stands the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations; it brings the commentary's life-water and immortality-tree images together in the final garden.

row.basis: living water wells up to eternal life
row.note: Jesus promises water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, making life-giving water an interior and enduring reality rather than merely a garden image.
Isaiah calls the dead to live and the dust-dwellers to awake and sing; this eschatological reversal is the positive opposite of the commentary's fire where neither death concludes nor life begins.

Jesus identifies himself as resurrection and life and promises life to the believer who dies; it supplies a concise Christian answer to the commentary's contrast between ordinary death and true enduring life.
The final judgment divides people between eternal punishment and eternal life; its paired lasting destinies are a direct comparison for the commentary's fire and enduring afterlife.

row.basis: fading grass and the word standing forever
row.note: Grass withers and the flower fades, but God's word stands forever; this concrete transient/enduring contrast supports the commentary's evaluation of the near life against what remains.

row.basis: people longing for death do not find it
row.note: Job describes sufferers who long for death but cannot find it; although it is not a fire judgment, it gives a specific suffering-and-unavailable-death analogue to the commentary's secondary Qur'anic comparison.

row.basis: profit from the world and forfeiting one's life
row.note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; the profit/life juxtaposition closely engages the commentary's claim that life includes benefit and its warning about choosing the worldly life.

row.basis: temporary enjoyment versus suffering with God's people
row.note: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a Pharaoh-linked Christian reading of a choice between passing advantage and a more durable divine horizon.
The rich man in flame asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue; it sets a denied water-image inside punitive fire against the commentary's paradise water that confers life.

row.basis: ordinary Gehinnom judgment limited to twelve months
row.note: Mishnah Eduyot limits the ordinary judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom to twelve months; that rabbinic duration qualifies the commentary's image of remaining in fire without death.

row.basis: righteous called living in death, wicked dead in life
row.note: The rabbinic maxim calls the righteous living even in death and the wicked dead even while alive; it makes life and death moral-spiritual categories, a useful interpretive comparison for the commentary's non-biological definition of life as good and benefit.
In the final renewed creation death is no more; this is the eschatological antithesis to the commentary's punitive place where death is indefinitely withheld.

row.basis: life as a vapor that appears briefly
row.note: James calls present life a vapor appearing for a little while and vanishing, a concrete Christian account of the brevity implied by the commentary's name for the near life.

Jesus directs disciples to treasure in heaven where decay and theft do not destroy; it translates the commentary's contrast between perishable present possession and what remains into a practice of investment.

The disobedient suffer "eternal destruction" away from the Lord; the wording gives a Christian punitive alternative to 87:13's unusual condition in which the condemned do not die, while leaving the meaning of destruction to be read in its own context.

row.basis: reputation of life but actual death
row.note: The Sardis church has a name of being alive but is dead; this non-biological use of life and death concretely parallels the commentary's definition of life by active goodness rather than mere survival.

row.basis: not leaving any breathing thing alive
row.note: The ban commands that no breathing thing be left alive, using survival as the opposite of total extirpation; this gives a concrete Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's remaining/sparing sense of life.

row.basis: believers who sleep and hope beyond grief
row.note: Paul calls the deceased "those who sleep" and contrasts believers' grief with those without hope; this Christian death-as-sleep idiom supplies the recoverable horizon that the commentary denies to the fire-dweller.

row.basis: entering life versus Gehenna's unquenchable fire
row.note: Jesus contrasts entering life, even maimed, with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; it directly joins the commentary's two outcomes of real life and fire rather than merely naming punishment.

row.basis: worm does not die and fire is not quenched
row.note: Mark reapplies the Isaiah image within Jesus' Gehenna teaching: the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. It supplies a Christian continuation of the deathless, unextinguished fire imagery, while the undying subject remains the worm rather than the punished person.

row.basis: body and soul destroyed in Gehenna
row.note: Jesus distinguishes human killing of the body from God's ability to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna; this provides a concrete Christian counter-formula to the commentary's fire in which the condemned do not die.

row.basis: lake of fire identified as the second death
row.note: The lake burning with fire and sulfur is called the second death. The identification gives the Christian fire a death-name, in pointed contrast to 87:13's non-dying condition.

A human being lies down and does not rise, not waking or being roused from sleep until the heavens are no more; Job supplies the unrecovered sleep/death image whose absence is developed in the commentary.

row.basis: death swallowed forever and tears wiped away
row.note: God swallows up death forever and wipes tears from faces; this is a prophetic final reversal of the commentary's place where death does not provide release and true life is absent.

row.basis: torture refused for a better resurrection
row.note: Some are tortured and refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection; this is a direct martyr-and-tyrant counterpart to the commentary's believing magicians facing Pharaoh's violence for a more lasting outcome.

row.basis: departure to be with Christ is far better
row.note: Paul calls departing to be with Christ "far better," an unusually explicit Christian comparative for the commentary's assertion that the afterlife is better than the near life.

row.basis: earthly tent and eternal heavenly house
row.note: The earthly tent is contrasted with an eternal house in the heavens not made by hands; the image maps present bodily life and a durable future dwelling onto the commentary's transient/enduring division.
Paul says that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, a concise Christian expression of life overcoming mortality that illuminates the commentary's definition of true life as permanence.
Resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable; it gives a bodily account of the enduring life set over against death in the commentary.
The believer has passed from death into life and does not come into judgment, a compact Johannine two-destiny formulation beside 87:13's denied life in punishment.

row.basis: tree of life in God's paradise
row.note: The conqueror is granted food from the tree of life in God's paradise; this is a final Christian counterpart to the commentary's tree of immortality and its distinction between deceptive and true permanence.

row.basis: waters of life and tears removed
row.note: The Lamb guides the redeemed to springs of waters of life and God wipes every tear; it combines the commentary's paradise water that gives life with an eschatological relief opposite fire-torment.

row.basis: water of life given freely to the thirsty
row.note: God gives the thirsty person water from the spring of life without payment; it is a direct final-life-water analogue to the commentary's revivifying water in paradise.
The psalm calls God's presence the fountain of life; it offers a Hebrew poetic precursor for the commentary's link between life, a divine source, and life-giving water.

row.basis: living waters flow in every season
row.note: Living waters flow from Jerusalem both in summer and winter, an eschatological water image whose ongoing flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's paradise water and abiding life.

row.basis: God's Spirit put within the dead so they live
row.note: God promises to put his spirit within the restored people so that they live; this specifies divine reanimation by a life-giving force, the positive opposite of the fire's absence of life.

row.basis: hope full of immortality despite apparent punishment
row.note: Though the righteous seem punished in human sight, their hope is full of immortality; this late Jewish reversal of apparent death and suffering closely complements the commentary's true, enduring life.

row.basis: furnace of Gehenna opposite paradise of delight
row.note: 4 Ezra displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite the place of rest and paradise of delight, a Jewish apocalyptic pairing that makes the commentary's fire and true-life alternatives into adjacent final scenes.

row.basis: this world as corridor before the world to come
row.note: Avot calls this world a corridor before the world to come and urges preparation here; its spatial-temporal image closely frames the commentary's near worldly life as preparatory rather than abiding.

row.basis: world to come without bodily needs, righteous enjoy divine splendor
row.note: The rabbinic description removes eating, drinking, and other bodily satisfactions from the world to come while the righteous enjoy divine splendor; it offers a specific Jewish construal of the commentary's true life as more than ordinary worldly vitality.

row.basis: eternal fire that punishes without consuming
row.note: Tertullian's final-judgment account treats eternal fire as ongoing punishment rather than a fire that simply consumes its victims, a patristic counterpart to the commentary's persistent fire; the precise translation should be verified.

The great chasm between the tormented rich man and Lazarus is fixed so that no one can cross; this continuation of the water-and-fire scene adds the commentary's concern with remaining in a condition without an exit.

row.basis: Egyptian riches set against a future reward
row.note: Moses considers reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it separately supplies the Egypt-specific valuation of durable reward over near advantage developed in 87:16-17.

row.basis: sin's wage death, God's gift eternal life
row.note: Paul pairs sin's wage of death with God's gift of eternal life, a moral and eschatological life/death contrast that extends the commentary's link between life, goodness, and final outcome.

row.basis: sowing to flesh yields corruption, Spirit yields eternal life
row.note: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; its present choice and later harvest closely match the commentary's worldly preference and enduring consequence.

row.basis: earthly-minded people have destruction as their end
row.note: Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end; this makes the commentary's choice of near life into a concrete moral orientation and eschatological consequence.
Believers' citizenship is in heaven, giving the alternative to the preceding earthly-minded end a communal home that resonates with the commentary's enduring hereafter.

row.basis: the dead know nothing and have no further reward
row.note: Qohelet says the dead know nothing and no longer have reward; within its under-the-sun argument, this is a sharp Hebrew Bible counterpoint to the commentary's afterlife as the locus of true life.

Hezekiah says that the living, the living give thanks to God; it makes active grateful goodness a mark of life, supporting the commentary's claim that bare survival without benefit or good is not life in the full sense.

row.basis: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
row.note: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; the proverb joins the commentary's benefit-language to a final reckoning that defeats merely worldly acquisition.

row.basis: righteous path is life and has no death
row.note: The path of righteousness is life and its way has no death; this ethical use of life gives a precise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's definition of life through good.

row.basis: fear of God as a fountain of life
row.note: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life that turns one from death's snares; it gives an ethical-metaphorical use of life-water, distinct from the commentary's paradise-water image.

row.basis: shares and exclusions in the world to come
row.note: The mishnah grants all Israel a share in the world to come while listing exclusions; it gives a Jewish interpretive map of who receives enduring future life, relevant to the commentary's final division without claiming the same criteria.

row.basis: Sheol and death in a disputed redemption formula
row.note: Hosea speaks of ransoming from Sheol and redeeming from death, but the grammar and immediate judgment context make its force disputed; its later life-over-death reception remains a cautious counterpart to the commentary's final death/life contrast.

row.note: 87:1 commands glorification of the Lord's name; Moses says that he will proclaim YHWH's name and calls his hearers to ascribe greatness to God, joining the two acts in one formula.
Melchizedek blesses God Most High after deliverance; the explicit divine title and blessing give a close Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's Lord Most High whose name is glorified.

row.basis: glory due the Name; offering and worship
row.note: The verse moves from giving YHWH the glory due his name to bringing an offering and worshipping, closely matching the commentary's treatment of praise of the Name and formal worship as one practice.

row.basis: Name, sunrise and sunset, pure offering
row.note: Malachi makes YHWH's name great from sunrise to sunset and connects it with incense and a pure offering; it gathers the commentary's daily praise, Name, ritual action, and 14–15 purification link.

row.basis: Name praised from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary invokes praise before sunrise and before sunset; this verse explicitly makes the praise of YHWH's name extend from the sun's rising to its setting.

row.basis: blessing the great God; bowing and face-to-ground worship
row.note: Ezra blesses YHWH the great God, and the assembly answers, raises hands, bows, and worships with faces to the ground; it is a compact public analogue to praise, utterance, and bodily prayer together.
The people stand to read Torah and then confess and worship; this concretely parallels the commentary's claim that recitation, admonitory remembrance, and prayer belong to the same devotional work.

row.basis: kneeling, prayer, thanksgiving, three daily times
row.note: Daniel kneels three times a day, prays, and gives thanks before his God, furnishing a specific counterpart to prayer as bodily movement, supplication, praise, and a recurring practice.

row.basis: lips moving; voice unheard; inward prayer
row.note: Hannah speaks in her heart while her lips move and her voice is not heard; the contrast supplies a precise counterpart to the commentary's open vocal prayer or recitation and God's knowledge of what is hidden.

row.basis: bowing and kneeling before the Maker
row.note: The psalm's invitation to worship, bow down, and kneel gives named bodily acts corresponding to the commentary's standing, bowing, prostration, and supplication as prayer.

row.basis: falling on faces; spoken confession of God
row.note: The people fall on their faces and voice a confession of YHWH; the verse joins the physical prostration and verbal God-remembrance that the commentary treats as a single act.
The verse forbids profaning the holy Name and calls God the one who sanctifies Israel, sharpening the commentary's 14–15 linkage between a worshipper's prayer and God's purifying action.

row.basis: purified speech; calling on the Name; united service
row.note: God gives peoples a purified lip so that they may call on YHWH's name and serve together; it links the commentary's tongue-bound dhikr, purification, and obedient worship without reducing them to mere speech.

row.basis: book in the mouth; meditation; doing
row.note: Joshua is to keep the Torah-book in his mouth, meditate on it day and night, and do it; this closely parallels the commentary's inclusion of recitation, tongue, intention, and obedient action within remembrance.

row.basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The covenant song is to remain unforgotten from Israel's mouths; it supplies a concrete scriptural analogue to the commentary's movement from being made to recite to not forgetting and then reminding.

row.basis: lips honoring God; heart far away
row.note: Isaiah distinguishes lip-honor from a distant heart; it illuminates the commentary's insistence that tesbih involves word, action, and intention, and its warning about heedless prayer.
God refuses many prayers while the worshippers' hands are full of blood; this gives a pointed ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that prayer turns people away from indecency and wrong.

row.basis: forced prostration to an image; fiery punishment
row.note: The verse orders bodily falling and worship under threat of a burning furnace. Alongside the commentary's prostration as Lord-directed prayer and its fire imagery, it makes the object and moral character of bodily worship decisive.

row.basis: falling face-down before God Most High
row.note: The assembled people fall on their faces to worship the Almighty, God Most High; it brings together the commentary's epithet, public liturgy, and prostrating body.

On hearing the explicit Name from the high priest, priests and people kneel, prostrate, fall on their faces, and bless the Name; this rabbinic liturgy tightly combines the Name and the bodily acts named in the commentary.

Rabbi Eliezer's dictum that a prayer made fixed is not supplication gives a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the commentary's explicit gloss that salat is du'a, while resisting prayer as empty routine.

row.basis: Hannah's moving lips and unraised voice
row.note: The Talmud reads Hannah's silent, lip-moving prayer as a source for how the Amidah is voiced. That interpretation makes the commentary's audible prayer or recitation and its hidden dimension a concrete liturgical question.

row.basis: blessing the Name at light and darkness
row.note: The Rule of the Community schedules blessing God's name at the turning points of light and darkness, a close sectarian-Jewish analogue to the commentary's praise before sunrise and sunset.

row.basis: magnifying and sanctifying the great Name
row.note: Kaddish begins by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified; its congregational formula directly stands beside 87:1's command to glorify the Lord's name.

row.basis: hallowing the Father's name in prayer
row.note: Jesus' model prayer makes the hallowing of God's name its first petition, directly pairing prayer with the treatment of the divine name central to 87:1 and 87:15.

row.basis: sacrifice of praise; fruit of lips confessing the Name
row.note: Hebrews calls continual praise the fruit of lips that confess God's name; it closely matches the commentary's dhikr as the Name on the tongue and tesbih as worship.

row.basis: praying and singing praise with spirit and mind
row.note: Paul deliberately pairs prayer and praise in both spirit and mind, providing a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's unified tesbih, remembrance, and prayer with intentional participation.
Paul joins prayer and supplication with thanksgiving in one act of address to God, closely echoing the commentary's salat as du'a and dhikr as praise and thanks.

row.basis: praying and hymn-singing heard by others
row.note: Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight, with prisoners listening; this is a specific scene of the vocal, audible devotional practice developed from jahr in the commentary.

row.basis: word dwelling, teaching and admonition, psalms and gratitude
row.note: The verse puts instruction and admonition together with psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and gratitude; it closely resembles the commentary's intervening recitation, reminder, and worship as one practice.

Paul describes offering bodies as a living sacrifice and worship; it gives a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that worship includes bodily action as well as verbal and intentional devotion.

row.basis: falling on the face and praying
row.note: Jesus falls on his face and prays in Gethsemane, an explicit conjunction of prostrating posture and supplication comparable to the prayer movements named in the commentary.

row.basis: bodily humility and a plea for mercy
row.note: The tax collector stands at a distance, lowers his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy; it supplies a concrete Christian scene in which bodily prayer and du'a-like petition are inseparable.

row.basis: bowing every knee at a name
row.note: In its Christological setting, the verse makes the response to Jesus' name a universal bending of knees; it is a precise Christian meeting of named confession and the bodily prayer emphasized in the commentary.

row.basis: prayer in secret; the Father seeing the hidden
row.note: Jesus directs prayer to the hidden place and grounds it in the Father's seeing what is hidden; this complements 87:7 as read in the commentary, where God knows both vocalized and concealed devotion.

Jesus applies Isaiah's lips-and-heart critique to a dispute about worship and tradition. It provides a Christian interpretive development of the commentary's contrast between tongue-level mention and wholehearted, attentive worship.

row.basis: calling on the Lord's name and salvation
row.note: Paul's citation makes calling on the Lord's name the path to salvation; it gives a specific New Testament meeting with the commentary's sequence of remembering the Name, praying, and flourishing.

row.basis: threefold holy acclamation; glory filling earth
row.note: The seraphim's antiphonal holy acclamation is a heavenly praise formula for YHWH. It offers a liturgical setting for the commentary's tesbih of the transcendent Lord, though it does not reproduce its prayer sequence.

row.basis: the high and lifted One; holy Name; reviving the lowly
row.note: Isaiah calls God high and lifted up, whose name is Holy, and says that he revives the contrite. This joins the Most High epithet to a divine restoring action relevant to the commentary's praise and purification pairing.

row.basis: Arabic س ب ح (B001); Hebrew שׁבח
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic س ب ح as B001. Psalm 117 uses the Hebrew Piel imperative שַׁבְּחוּהוּ, “praise him,” a likely Semitic cognate in a summons for all peoples to praise YHWH.

row.basis: Arabic ذ ك ر (B004/B005); Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels ذ ك ر as B004/B005 and develops remembering the Lord. Deuteronomy's זכר, “remember,” directs Israel to remember YHWH as the giver of power, a cognate used for faithful recollection rather than merely saying a word.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل و (B002/B003); Biblical Aramaic מְצַלֵּא
row.note: The commentary labels ص ل و as B002/B003. Daniel's Aramaic מְצַלֵּא, “praying,” is a close Aramaic-Syriac cognate form; its repeated kneeling and thanksgiving make the linguistic meeting concrete.

row.basis: Torah reading, Shema, directing the heart
row.note: The Mishnah asks whether someone already reading Torah fulfils the Shema when its time comes, and makes the answer turn on directing the heart. It clarifies the commentary's claim that recitation can be remembrance and worship only with intention.

The early pietists pause before prayer in order to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; this gives a concrete rabbinic practice for the commentary's inclusion of intention within tesbih and salat.

row.basis: patriarchal derivation of fixed prayer times
row.note: The Talmud derives the three daily prayer services from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Its interpretive fixing of prayer in the day supplies a Jewish liturgical bridge to the commentary's praise at the sun's turning points.
Peter and John go up together to the temple at the appointed hour of prayer. The scene offers a specific communal, timed counterpart to the commentary's recurring prayer and praise.

Jesus identifies true worship with spirit and truth. It gives an interpretive complement to the commentary's refusal to reduce worship to bodily movement or spoken formula, while retaining worship as an enacted practice.

row.basis: psalms and hymns spoken and sung in the heart
row.note: The exhortation joins speaking psalms and hymns with singing in the heart to the Lord; it reflects the commentary's double focus on vocal remembrance and inward devotion.
The command to pray without ceasing provides a Christian analogue to the commentary's repeated, abundant tesbih and remembrance, although it does not prescribe the same ritual form.

row.basis: doing good and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God
row.note: This verse calls concrete beneficence and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God. It extends the commentary's word-action-intention account of worship to an explicitly ethical Christian practice.
God forgives and cleanses those who confess; it provides a specific Christian pairing of spoken penitential address and divine purification relevant to the commentary's 14–15 relation.

row.basis: reciting the Lord's Prayer three times daily
row.note: The Didache turns the Lord's Prayer into a thrice-daily discipline. This early Christian rule offers a concrete liturgical counterpart to the commentary's repeated prayer and remembrance around the day.

row.basis: singing to YHWH; blessing the Name day by day
row.note: The psalm commands singing to YHWH, blessing his name, and proclaiming salvation from day to day; it supplies a distinct psalmic formulation of the commentary's vocal praise, Name, recitation, and recurring practice.

Entering God's courts entails thanksgiving and praise, then giving thanks to him and blessing his name. The verse closely joins the commentary's dhikr as praise and thanks with public worship of the Name.
The psalmist vows not to forget God's word; this is a direct, text-specific counterpart to the commentary's recitation, non-forgetting, and later reminder within the surah's devotional sequence.

row.basis: lips pouring out praise after instruction
row.note: The psalmist's lips pour out praise because God teaches statutes. It specifically joins a tongue-level act of praise to received teaching, as the commentary joins Qur'an recitation and dhikr.
The psalmist's tongue sings God's word; this is a precise oral-scriptural parallel to the commentary's statement that reading the Qur'an belongs to remembrance.

row.basis: prayer as incense; lifted hands as evening offering
row.note: Prayer is likened to incense and raised hands to the evening offering. It supplies a concrete bodily and time-marked analogue to the commentary's prayer as supplication and enacted worship.

God's house is called a house of prayer for all peoples, where offerings are accepted. This directly pairs prayer with formal communal worship, an important aspect of the commentary's unified tesbih, dhikr, and salat.

row.basis: lifting heart with hands to God
row.note: Lamentations calls for lifting both heart and hands to God. The explicit union of inward disposition and visible bodily action sharpens the commentary's word-action-intention account of prayer.

row.basis: standing before the altar; spreading hands toward heaven
row.note: Solomon stands before the altar in the assembled people's presence and spreads his hands heavenward. It supplies a specific biblical prayer posture alongside the commentary's standing and supplicatory movements.

Solomon asks God to hear prayer and supplication and to forgive. The verse gives a direct biblical meeting between human du'a-like appeal and the divine cleansing or forgiveness side of the commentary's 14–15 linkage.
At the evening offering Ezra rises from his self-affliction, falls to his knees, and spreads his hands to God. Its timed and bodily prayer scene closely meets the commentary's descriptions of salat.

row.basis: voice of thanksgiving; sacrifice; vowed act
row.note: Jonah promises sacrifice with a voice of thanksgiving and the fulfilment of vows. This compactly combines vocal praise, gratitude, ritual action, and obedience, all senses the commentary assigns to dhikr and tesbih.

row.basis: God sprinkling clean water and cleansing
row.note: Ezekiel depicts God cleansing the people from impurity. It does not itself define prayer, but it supplies the divine purification pole required by the commentary's linking of 87:14 to God's purifying salat.

row.basis: whole heart and voice; blessing the Lord's Name
row.note: Ben Sira tells hearers to give thanks with all heart and voice and bless the Lord's name. It is an unusually close Jewish synthesis of inward intent, vocal praise, and the Name.

row.basis: service of the heart interpreted as prayer
row.note: The Talmud asks what service is performed with the heart and answers, prayer. This interpretation directly illuminates the commentary's claim that worship includes intention as well as its audible and bodily forms.

row.basis: a blessing requires God's Name and kingship
row.note: The rule that a blessing without the Name and kingship is no blessing makes formal invocation of the divine Name a defining liturgical act, a useful rabbinic counterpart to 87:1 and 87:15.

row.basis: public Torah and Shema recitation in temple liturgy
row.note: The daily temple order combines blessings with recitation of Torah passages and the Shema. It gives a concrete Jewish liturgical setting for the commentary's claim that scriptural reading is part of remembrance and worship.

row.basis: public prayer performed to be seen
row.note: Jesus criticizes prayer offered for public display. In conjunction with the commentary's treatment of jahr as audible prayer, it makes intention rather than volume the relevant ethical distinction.

The continuation of Jesus' Isaiah citation calls worship vain when it teaches merely human precepts. It gives the explicit Christian continuation needed for the commentary's concern with heedless or merely external worship.
Jesus rises while it is still dark and prays in a solitary place. This is a specific Christian scene for the commentary's praise and prayer before the sun's rising.

row.basis: the people praying at the hour of incense
row.note: The whole assembled multitude prays outside during the incense hour. It offers a precise communal and timed liturgical counterpart to the commentary's formal prayer practice.

row.basis: night-and-day service with fasting and prayers
row.note: Anna serves God night and day through fasting and prayers. Her recurring discipline meets the commentary's abundant remembrance and continuing worship without reducing it to one isolated prayer.

row.basis: prayers and alms as a memorial before God
row.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms ascend as a memorial before God. The passage gives a striking New Testament link between remembrance, prayer, and obedient action, matching the commentary's broad account of dhikr.

row.basis: washing away sins while calling on the Name
row.note: Paul is told to be washed from sins while calling on the Lord's name. It specifically joins name-invocation to cleansing, a close Christian meeting of the commentary's remembrance and divine purification relation.

row.basis: secrets of the heart; falling face-down; worship and confession
row.note: When hidden heart-secrets are disclosed, the hearer falls on his face, worships God, and declares God truly present. This unusually combines the commentary's hidden/open axis, prostration, and voiced God-remembrance.

row.basis: every tongue confessing to God's glory
row.note: The verse completes the preceding knee-bending with every tongue's confession to the glory of God the Father. It gives the verbal side of the name-and-body meeting already present in the commentary.

row.basis: word and deed in the Name; thanksgiving
row.note: Whatever is done in word or deed is to be done in the Lord's name with thanks. This directly mirrors the commentary's integration of utterance, deed, Name, and gratitude under worship.

The verse deliberately lists supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings. It supplies a close Christian comparison to the commentary's semantic expansion of salat and dhikr into du'a, praise, and thanks.

row.basis: prayer everywhere; lifted holy hands; moral restraint
row.note: The instruction to pray everywhere with lifted holy hands is joined to rejection of anger and disputing. It connects the commentary's bodily prayer with its ethical claim that prayer opposes wrongdoing.

row.basis: drawing near; hearts sprinkled clean; bodies washed
row.note: Hebrews couples approach to God with a true heart and imagery of cleansed hearts and washed bodies. It provides a Christian purification-and-worship analogue to the commentary's 87:14–15 association.

row.basis: falling in worship; harps; bowls identified as prayers
row.note: The elders fall before the Lamb while holding harps and bowls of incense identified as the saints' prayers. This heavenly liturgy joins body, praise music, and prayer in a form especially relevant to the commentary's single devotional practice.

row.basis: glorifying the Name and worship by all nations
row.note: The hymn asks who would not glorify the Lord's name and says all nations will come and worship. It directly pairs name-glorification with worship in a Christian doxological formula.

row.basis: Lord's Prayer formula; hallowing the Name
row.note: The Didache transmits the Lord's Prayer as the form believers are to pray, including the hallowing of the Father's name. It supplies the early Christian liturgical text that its following thrice-daily rule presupposes.

The commentary makes dhikr both preservation and remembrance; Malachi uses the cognate in a book written for those who fear the Lord and honor his name, joining remembered devotion to a written record.

row.basis: fearers, the Lord's name, book of remembrance
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember and that remembrance of the Lord's name leads to prayer; Malachi's fearers honor the name and are recorded in a book of remembrance.
The commentary's dhikr family includes remembrance; here the cognate names a written memorial, giving the word-family a concrete inscriptional use.

row.basis: write as memorial; recite in Joshua's hearing
row.note: The commentary links reminder to written pages and collected recitation; Exodus commands both a written memorial and oral telling, preserving a past event in two forms.
The commentary's q-r-ء family begins with joining words in recitation; Exodus uses the cognate when Moses reads the written covenant aloud to the people.

row.basis: Book of the Covenant read to the people
row.note: The commentary joins recitation to pages; Moses reads a written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer that they will do its words.

row.basis: guard memory; teach children and grandchildren
row.note: The commentary contrasts preservation with forgetting and commands reminder; Moses warns Israel not to forget what it saw and to pass it to descendants.

row.basis: written song taught to Israel as witness
row.note: The commentary moves from recited revelation to written pages; God tells Moses to write and teach a song so it remains in Israel's mouth as a witness.

row.basis: Book of the Law placed beside the Ark
row.note: The commentary calls Moses' pages a preserved source for the message; Deuteronomy orders the written Law kept beside the Ark as a standing witness.
The commentary's reading-to-pages sequence is enacted when Jeremiah speaks God's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll.

row.basis: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the scroll
row.note: The commentary describes deliberate forgetting and a promise that recited words will not be lost; the king deliberately destroys the written words, a sharp counter-scene to that assurance.

After the scroll is burned, Jeremiah dictates again and Baruch writes a replacement with more words; this gives the commentary's movement from loss to recollection and pages a concrete recovery narrative.

row.basis: never forgetting precepts that preserve life
row.note: The commentary says remembrance is the opposite of forgetting and that remembered teaching is kept; the psalmist says God's precepts preserve life and therefore will not be forgotten.

row.basis: lost sheep; seek your servant; I have not forgotten
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has gone missing; the psalmist asks God to seek him as a lost sheep while affirming that he remembers God's commandments.

row.basis: one person's guilt is not borne by another
row.note: The commentary cites the principle that no burden-bearer carries another's burden; Ezekiel says children do not bear parents' guilt or parents children's, grounding the same individual accountability in a different legal setting.

row.basis: gather leftover fragments so none is lost
row.note: The commentary pictures forgotten matter as dropped remnants and traces a movement toward gathering; Jesus orders the leftover fragments gathered so that none is lost.

row.basis: searching for a lost coin until it is found
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; the woman searches carefully for a lost coin, making recovery an active search rather than passive recall.

row.basis: Spirit teaches and reminds disciples of Jesus' words
row.note: The commentary joins divine teaching to the promise of not forgetting; Jesus says the Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of what he said.
The commentary connects reminder with retrieving what has passed and pages that preserve teaching; Peter writes so his readers can recall these things after his death.

row.basis: Scripture announces good news beforehand to Abraham
row.note: The commentary says its message is already in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Paul reads Abraham's promise as Scripture's prior announcement of the gospel to the nations.
The commentary places its present message in Moses' pages; Jesus interprets Moses' writing as testimony about him, a distinct Christian claim about what those pages contain.

row.basis: treasure stored on earth is vulnerable to loss
row.note: The commentary condemns preferring worldly life to what lasts; Jesus warns against storing treasure where moth and rust consume and thieves break in.
The commentary calls the afterlife better and more lasting than worldly life; Jesus contrasts earthly loss with treasure in heaven that is not consumed or stolen.

row.basis: gain the whole world yet forfeit one's life
row.note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life in light of the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world at the cost of one's life.

row.basis: world passes; the one doing God's will remains
row.note: The commentary contrasts the preferred worldly life with an afterlife that lasts; John says the world and its desire are passing, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

row.basis: Moses values reward above Egypt's treasure
row.note: The commentary names Moses after rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews says Moses counted reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward.

row.basis: each person carries their own load
row.note: The commentary cites the rule that no bearer carries another's burden; Paul says each person will carry their own load, though his surrounding discussion distinguishes this from helping others in trouble.

row.basis: the speakers urge enjoyment of present goods
row.note: The commentary says people prefer present worldly life although the afterlife is more lasting; Wisdom's speakers instead propose enjoying the good things available now, voicing the contrary valuation.

row.basis: forgetting one point of Torah is treated as grave culpability
row.note: The commentary treats forgetting entrusted teaching as loss; this rabbinic reading of Deuteronomy 4:9 makes forgetting a single learned point a serious covenantal offense.

row.basis: Moses is given a written record amid predicted Israelite forgetfulness
row.note: The commentary links revelation, memory and Moses' pages; Jubilees frames a written account given to Moses as a safeguard in a story that anticipates Israel's disobedience and forgetting.

row.basis: forgetting the God who brought Israel out of Egypt
row.note: The commentary explicitly gives forgetting the secondary sense of abandoning God; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord after receiving his commands, making that sense a covenant warning.

row.basis: distinction between those serving God and those not
row.note: The commentary separates the one who fears and remembers from the one who avoids reminder; Malachi says a coming distinction will be made between the righteous and the wicked.

row.basis: God promises not to forget Zion
row.note: The commentary's promise is that the Prophet will not forget the recited message; Isaiah reverses the direction, portraying God as the one who will not forget Zion even if a mother could forget her child.

row.basis: reading the Law with explanation so people understand
row.note: The commentary treats reminder as an aid to recover needed knowledge; Nehemiah describes public reading of the book with explanation that makes its meaning clear to listeners.

row.basis: stirring readers by way of reminder
row.note: The commentary says reminder brings a needed matter back to mind; Peter explicitly describes his writing as stirring readers up by reminding them while he is still alive.

The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name immediately before prayer; Jesus tells disciples to repeat a meal in remembrance of him, a distinct Christian liturgical act built around remembrance.

row.basis: hold teaching received by spoken word or letter
row.note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages and notes a root sense of transmitted report; Paul tells the community to hold traditions delivered either orally or by letter.

row.basis: command to bear one another's burdens
row.note: The commentary quotes a rule against one person carrying another's burden; Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, a real ethical counterpoint whose context is helping someone caught in transgression.

row.basis: each person gives an account to God
row.note: The commentary links individual effort with its outcome; Paul says each person will give an account of themselves to God, adding a judgment setting to personal responsibility.

row.basis: visible things are temporary, unseen things eternal
row.note: The commentary contrasts the chosen present life with what endures; Paul distinguishes what is seen and temporary from what is unseen and eternal.

row.basis: the speakers deny return after death
row.note: The commentary affirms an afterlife better and more lasting than present life; Wisdom's speakers argue that death has no return, directly opposing that horizon.

row.basis: Enoch reads heavenly tablets recording human deeds
row.note: The commentary connects prophetic teaching with preserved pages; Enoch is shown written heavenly tablets and reads a record of human deeds, extending the page motif to a celestial archive.

row.basis: Ezra dictates books after the Law has been lost
row.note: The commentary moves from received recitation to gathered pages; 4 Ezra depicts inspired dictation that restores public books after the earlier Law's loss, making preservation through writing central.

row.basis: memory as capacious halls and treasuries
row.note: The commentary pictures memory as a sequence of containers holding what is entrusted; Augustine describes memory as immense halls containing innumerable images, a close account of memory as a storehouse.

row.basis: searching memory for what has been lost
row.note: The commentary defines recollection as seeking what has slipped away; Augustine describes searching memory for a lost item, giving that definition an introspective account.

row.basis: repeating words to children in ordinary daily life
row.note: The commentary moves from received recitation to remembrance; Moses commands repeated teaching at home, on the road, at bedtime and on rising, embedding words in daily memory.

row.basis: words written on doorposts and gates
row.note: The commentary describes written pages as a way to preserve recited teaching; Deuteronomy places the words visibly on household entrances, a distinct public inscriptional form.

row.basis: king writes a copy of the Law from the priests' book
row.note: The commentary connects Moses' pages with a collected written scripture; this law makes the king produce his own copy from the priestly source.

row.basis: king reads the book all his days to learn fear and obey
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears will remember; Deuteronomy ties daily reading of the written Law to fear of God and keeping its words.

row.basis: ancestral deliverance recited in the first-fruits rite
row.note: The commentary links reminder to scripture and worship; the offerer recites a fixed account of Israel's descent to Egypt and deliverance while presenting first fruits.

row.basis: first fruits placed before God with worship
row.note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord's name before prayer; this liturgy moves from the ancestral recital to presenting the gift and bowing before God.

row.basis: song will not be forgotten by descendants
row.note: The commentary contrasts retained revelation with forgetting; Moses says the taught song will remain in descendants' mouths and testify when later troubles come.

row.basis: Moses finishes writing the whole Law in a book
row.note: The commentary says Moses' pages preserve the message across generations; this verse specifically marks completion of the written book, distinct from its later placement beside the Ark.

row.basis: remember God's works and keep commandments
row.note: The commentary says remembrance preserves teaching; the psalm's intergenerational instruction aims to make children hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.

row.basis: word stored in the heart to prevent sin
row.note: The commentary depicts teaching retained rather than lost; the psalmist says he has stored God's word in his heart so he will not sin.

row.basis: do not forget teaching; let the heart keep commands
row.note: The commentary opposes forgetting to keeping entrusted teaching; Proverbs pairs an explicit command not to forget with the heart's custody of instruction.
The commentary moves between memory and physical pages; Proverbs says to bind fidelity around the neck and write it on the heart, relocating inscription inside the learner.

row.basis: write the oracle on a tablet and in a book as lasting witness
row.note: The commentary carries recited teaching into preserved pages; Isaiah orders a written record for future time, explicitly making inscription a witness that endures.

row.basis: Daniel reads the books and understands Jeremiah's years
row.note: The commentary says the present admonition is already in earlier scriptures; Daniel reads Jeremiah's written prophecy to understand the allotted years, a concrete act of consulting prior pages.

row.basis: prophet eats a scroll, then must speak its words to Israel
row.note: The commentary links divine recitation with a prophet's retention; Ezekiel internalizes a written scroll before being sent to transmit its words to the people.

row.basis: scroll fills the belly and tastes sweet
row.note: The commentary's arc makes written words something received and held; Ezekiel's scroll is taken into his body as nourishment before prophetic speech.

row.basis: prophet finds, eats and delights in God's words
row.note: The commentary connects recitation with remembering the Lord's name; Jeremiah says he found and ate God's words and that God's name was invoked over him, joining reception of words to prophetic identity.

row.basis: word taken from the heart before it is believed
row.note: The commentary contrasts retained reminder with what is lost; in Jesus' explanation of the seed, the devil removes the word from hearers' hearts so they will not believe.

row.basis: cares, riches and pleasures choke the word
row.note: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Jesus says worldly cares, wealth and pleasures choke the heard word before it matures.

row.basis: hearers hold the word fast and bear fruit
row.note: The commentary says the one who fears remembers; Jesus contrasts good soil that holds the heard word fast and bears fruit with the losses in the preceding soils.

row.basis: hearer looks and then forgets what he was like
row.note: The commentary warns that a received thing can be let go; James's forgetful hearer leaves the mirror and immediately forgets, making departure from instruction concrete.

row.basis: persevering doer looks into the law and is blessed
row.note: The commentary links retained remembrance to action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with one who perseveres in the law and acts, who is blessed.

row.basis: guard the good deposit entrusted to you
row.note: The commentary defines forgetting as failing to keep what was entrusted; Paul tells Timothy to guard the entrusted deposit through the Holy Spirit.

row.basis: Paul delivers what he received, according to Scripture
row.note: The commentary notes a secondary sense of transmitting a report from another; Paul says he handed on what he had received and frames the message as occurring according to Scripture.

row.basis: orderly written account compiled from earlier testimony
row.note: The commentary's q-r-ء discussion presents reading as gathering elements together; Luke says he carefully followed the received accounts and writes them in order.

row.basis: written account meant to establish certainty about teaching
row.note: The commentary's pages preserve what was recited; Luke states that his account is written so Theophilus can know the certainty of what he was taught.

row.basis: books opened; the dead judged by recorded deeds
row.note: The commentary connects earlier pages with each person's own effort and outcome; Revelation depicts the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds.
The commentary describes teaching held in memory before it appears on pages; Deuteronomy first places God's words on the heart, the inner counterpart to later visible inscription.

row.basis: God remembers sins no more as an act of forgiveness
row.note: The commentary cites divine forgetting as abandonment of the unfaithful; Jeremiah uses not remembering sins as covenant forgiveness, giving divine non-remembrance an opposite moral valence.

row.basis: Job wishes his words written in a book
row.note: The commentary traces recitation into written pages; Job asks for his own words to be recorded in a book, a lament's appeal for durable preservation.

row.basis: words engraved in rock with iron and lead
row.note: The commentary says the written pages preserve what memory might lose; Job intensifies the wish by asking for words cut permanently into rock.

row.basis: read the Lord's book; none of the creatures is missing
row.note: The commentary says collection prevents the recited word from being dropped; Isaiah directs readers to the Lord's book and claims that none of the listed creatures is absent from its account.

row.basis: those written in the book are delivered in the time of distress
row.note: The commentary joins Moses' pages to the surah's outcomes; Daniel's book records those who will be delivered in a final crisis, linking writing with ultimate fate.

row.basis: joyful reception without roots ends in falling away
row.note: The commentary says a reminder benefits the one who retains it; Jesus describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tested because it has no root.

row.basis: Timothy has known sacred writings since childhood
row.note: The commentary identifies Moses' pages as a source of teaching; Paul points to Timothy's childhood familiarity with sacred writings and their power to make him wise for salvation.

row.basis: law placed in minds and written on hearts
row.note: The commentary moves between retained memory and pages; Hebrews quotes a covenant promise that God's laws will be placed in minds and written on hearts.

row.basis: community is a letter written by the Spirit on hearts
row.note: The commentary joins human retention to written pages; Paul calls the community a letter of Christ written not in ink but by the Spirit on human hearts.

row.basis: Jesus reads Isaiah's scroll in the synagogue
row.note: The commentary connects recited revelation with prophetic pages; Luke depicts Jesus opening Isaiah's scroll and reading it aloud in a public worship setting.

row.basis: Jesus says the read scripture is fulfilled that day
row.note: The commentary says its message was already present in earlier pages; after reading Isaiah, Jesus interprets the passage as fulfilled in the hearers' present.

row.basis: Law, Prophets and Psalms written about Jesus' suffering and rising
row.note: The commentary asserts that its message is found in Abraham's and Moses' pages; Jesus gives a distinct Christian reading in which the wider scriptural corpus points to his passion and resurrection.

row.basis: John eats a little scroll before receiving a prophetic task
row.note: The commentary's recitation begins with revelation received by a prophet; John takes a written scroll into himself, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, before being told to prophesy.

row.basis: John is told to prophesy again to many peoples
row.note: The commentary moves received words toward public reminder; after the scroll is eaten, John is commissioned to speak again to many peoples and nations.

row.basis: learning compared to writing on fresh or erased paper
row.note: The commentary connects remembrance with written pages; this rabbinic saying uses the durability of writing on a clean sheet to explain why learning in youth is more firmly retained.

row.basis: Hebrew נשה (nashah, forget), a likely cognate of Arabic نسي
row.note: The commentary develops Arabic n-s-y as forgetting; Joseph names Manasseh because God made him forget hardship, likely sharing the Semitic root, though this is positive relief from suffering rather than forgetting revelation.
God promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to speak, a direct Mosaic counterpart to 87:6's God-caused recitation.

row.basis: words put in a prophet's mouth
row.note: YHWH puts words in the coming prophet's mouth and requires him to speak them, closely matching the commentary's active causative sense of making a messenger recite.

row.basis: YHWH puts words in Jeremiah's mouth
row.note: The mouth-touching call scene makes prophetic speech a deposited divine word, illuminating 87:6 before the commentary turns to retention.
The covenant promises that God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or his descendants' mouths, a generational form of the no-forgetting promise.

row.basis: write, teach, put the song in mouths
row.note: Moses must write the song, teach it, and place it in Israel's mouths; it joins written preservation with learned recitation as the commentary does.

row.basis: the song will not be forgotten
row.note: The song's continuing presence in descendants' mouths is explicitly said not to be forgotten, an unusually close scriptural analogue to 87:6.

row.basis: seek and read YHWH's book; none missing
row.note: In the oracle's announced animal assembly, the reader is sent to YHWH's book and told none will be missing because his Spirit has gathered them; that concrete book-and-gathering image sharpens the commentary's claim that what God collects is not dropped.

Hebrew q-r-ʾ is used for public reading of God's written Torah with explanation; its formal cognacy with the commentary's قرأ makes 87:6's recitation a textual and communal act, not only private memory.

row.basis: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
row.note: Joshua is told that the Torah book must not depart from his mouth and must be meditated on continually, combining a book, oral repetition, and obedient retention.
Moses' writing of all the spoken words supplies a Mosaic instance of divine speech becoming a durable written collection.

row.basis: Moses reads the covenant book aloud
row.note: The written covenant is then read in the people's hearing, giving the read-and-hear sequence behind the commentary's movement from gathered words to pages.

row.basis: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
row.note: The verse explicitly marks completion of Moses' written Torah, a close biblical comparator for 87:19's named Mosaic sheets.

row.basis: place the Torah book beside the ark
row.note: The finished book is placed beside the ark as a witness, making physical custody part of preserving the words rather than leaving them only to memory.

row.basis: lost law book found and read
row.note: Hilkiah finds the book of the Torah in the temple and gives it to Shaphan to read, a narrative reversal of scripture left out of use and then recovered.

row.basis: write spoken prophecies on a scroll
row.note: YHWH orders Jeremiah to put all the words spoken against Israel and Judah on a scroll, directly joining oral revelation and a written surface.
Baruch writes the divine words from Jeremiah's mouth on a scroll, a particularly close scene of mediated recital becoming pages.
Jehoiakim cuts and burns the written columns; its deliberate loss gives a concrete contrary case to the commentary's claim that divine collection is not dropped.

row.basis: rewrite the burned scroll's former words
row.note: After the scroll is burned, YHWH commands another scroll containing the former words, making restoration after textual loss part of the parallel.
Ezekiel is commanded to consume the scroll before speaking to Israel, an embodied image of written revelation being internalized and reissued.

row.basis: write the vision so a reader can run
row.note: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader, an explicit practical reason for fixing revelation in readable written form.

row.basis: bind testimony and seal Torah among disciples
row.note: The prophet binds and seals testimony among disciples, coupling guarded writing to a community that carries it forward.

row.basis: I will not forget your word
row.note: The psalmist's pledge not to forget God's word is the direct devotional counterpart to the commentary's contrast between forgetting and preserving.

row.basis: do not forget teaching; heart keeps commands
row.note: Forgetting Torah is opposed to the heart's keeping commandments, closely matching the commentary's definition of forgetting as failure to hold what was entrusted.

row.basis: visible fringe as a reminder to obey
row.note: The tassel is to be seen so Israel remembers and performs the commands; it gives a material tadhkira-like aid to recall.
The Sabbath command uses Hebrew z-k-r, formally cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر, for a liturgical remembering that issues in sanctification.

row.basis: Israel forgets God despite the bride comparison
row.note: Jeremiah contrasts a bride who remembers her adornments with Israel that has forgotten God for countless days, making forgetfulness concrete as covenantal abandonment.

row.basis: forgotten Torah answered by divine forgetting
row.note: Because the priests have forgotten God's Torah, God says he will forget their children; this directly parallels the commentary's reciprocal forgetting and judgment.
The maternal comparison culminates in God's refusal to forget Zion, a personal counterpart to the unforgetting Lord and his record in the commentary.

row.basis: book of remembrance for those who fear the Name
row.note: Those who fear YHWH are recorded in a book of remembrance before him, bringing together fear, the divine Name, remembering, and a written record as in 87:9-10 and 15-19.
The closing command to remember Moses' Torah makes remembrance itself the mode by which a Mosaic written legacy remains operative.

row.basis: court sits and books are opened
row.note: The heavenly court's opened books give a biblical image for the commentary's Lord whose knowledge of former generations is securely recorded.
Daniel's resurrection contrast gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to 87:16-17's preference for the present life over the enduring future.

row.basis: grass withers but God's word stands forever
row.note: The contrast between perishing grass and the enduring divine word relates the commentary's passing worldly life to retained and lasting revelation.

row.basis: each person dies for his own sin
row.note: The legal rule rejects transferring a parent's or child's guilt, directly paralleling the commentary's cited content of Abrahamic and Mosaic sheets that no bearer carries another's burden.

row.basis: the sinner bears his own iniquity
row.note: Ezekiel's sustained individual-accountability claim is a close theological counterpart to the commentary's 53:38 reading of the earlier sheets.

row.basis: spirit returns to God who gave it
row.note: The return of the spirit to its giver gives a Hebrew Bible formulation beside the commentary's statement that the final endpoint is the Lord.

row.basis: plastered cistern that loses not a drop
row.note: The rabbinic praise of learned retention as a cistern that loses no drop closely realizes the commentary's memory-as-container and dropped-object imagery.
The mishnah treats losing even one learned word as grave, making the commentary's forgetting of an entrusted teaching a concrete Torah-study ethic.
Its chain from Moses through successive teachers supplies a Jewish model for the commentary's source label on transmitting a report received from another.

row.basis: Torah given scroll by scroll or as one whole
row.note: The rabbinic dispute over separate scrolls versus a completed Torah directly frames the commentary's progression from written sheets to a gathered codex as a question about revelation's material form.
By reading Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's observance of the whole Torah before its giving to Moses, the tradition supplies a Jewish bridge to 87:19's Abraham-and-Moses pairing.
Ezra laments that the law has been burned and therefore the past and future cannot be known, a direct apocalypse-era opposite to a protected, retained scripture.
After drinking the fiery cup, Ezra's wisdom increases and his spirit retains memory, closely matching divine enablement to remember revelation.

row.basis: Ezra dictates while five scribes write
row.note: Five men write what Ezra dictates over forty days, a detailed Jewish scene of inspired speech being gathered into text.
The completed production of ninety-four books makes collected written revelation, rather than a single remembered saying, the explicit outcome.

row.basis: Nehemiah founds a library and collects books
row.note: The account of Nehemiah gathering books about kings, prophets, David, and royal letters gives a rare explicit Jewish image of assembling scattered scriptural materials.

row.basis: Judas collects books scattered by war
row.note: Judas' recovery of books dispersed through war closely matches the commentary's path from loss and dispersal to gathered pages.

row.basis: books of the law torn and burned
row.note: The persecution's tearing and burning of Torah books provides a historical contrary case to the durable custody imagined by 87:18-19.

row.basis: book of commandments held fast for life
row.note: The text calls the law an enduring book and contrasts holding it fast with forsaking it, directly echoing the commentary's held versus lost revelation.

row.basis: Mosaic law called the covenant book
row.note: Ben Sira identifies the law commanded by Moses as the book of the Most High's covenant, a Second Temple way of naming a Mosaic written corpus.

row.basis: this world as corridor before the world to come
row.note: The corridor-and-banquet-hall contrast gives a compact rabbinic analogue to preferring the nearer worldly life over the lasting life to come.

row.basis: the Father's Spirit speaks through disciples
row.note: Jesus assures messengers that the Spirit of their Father speaks through them, a New Testament form of divinely enabled prophetic speech.
The Paraclete will teach all things and bring Jesus' words back to memory, directly pairing instruction with divinely secured recollection.
The entrusted teaching is to be guarded through the Holy Spirit, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's definition of forgetting as failing to hold an entrusted thing.

row.basis: God does not forget faithful work
row.note: God's refusal to forget service makes divine non-forgetting an ethical and judicial claim beside the commentary's Lord who neither strays nor forgets.

row.basis: remember what was received and heard; keep it
row.note: The church is commanded to remember received and heard teaching and to keep it, closely mapping receipt, recall, and retention onto 87:6 and 87:9.
James' hearer immediately forgets after seeing himself, a specific Christian image of received perception that is not retained or acted on.

row.basis: remember prophets' words and apostolic command
row.note: The letter explicitly asks readers to recall former prophetic speech and the apostolic command, joining old writings and present exhortation.

row.basis: provision for recall after the speaker's departure
row.note: The author seeks to ensure that readers can recall the teaching after his death, making durable remembrance a stated literary purpose.

row.basis: do this in remembrance of me
row.note: The meal command turns remembrance into a repeated communal act, a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's reminder as an instrument of recall.

row.basis: what was received is delivered onward
row.note: Paul's received-and-delivered formula is a precise early Christian transmission chain for the commentary's sense of passing on a report from another.

row.basis: heard teaching entrusted through further teachers
row.note: What Timothy heard is entrusted to reliable people who will teach others, making preservation a multi-generation oral chain.

row.basis: hold traditions taught by word or letter
row.note: The command explicitly joins oral teaching and written letter as forms of retained tradition, directly comparable to recitation becoming pages.
Luke begins from traditions delivered by eyewitnesses and servants of the word, a narrative account of report transmission before the written Gospel.

row.basis: word dwelling richly through teaching and admonition
row.note: The indwelling word produces reciprocal teaching and admonition, a communal version of 87:9's beneficial reminder.
The triad makes public reading serve exhortation and teaching, placing Christian practice beside the commentary's joined recitation and reminder.

row.basis: reader, hearers, and keepers of written prophecy
row.note: Blessing attaches to the reader, hearers, and those who keep a written prophecy's words, tightly joining book, recitation, hearing, and retention.

row.basis: taking away words from prophecy's book
row.note: The warning against taking away words from the prophetic book gives a Christian textual counterpart to the commentary's insistence that what God gathers is not lost.
Paul contrasts ink and stone with the Spirit's writing on human hearts, a Christian reworking of the commentary's relation between held memory and written sheets.

row.basis: laws put in minds and written on hearts
row.note: The new-covenant citation makes divine law both mentally placed and internally written, closely paralleling the commentary's movement from memory to inscription.

row.basis: take and eat the little scroll
row.note: John consumes the revealed scroll, a New Testament image of a written message entering the prophet before further speech.

row.basis: must prophesy again after the scroll
row.note: After the consumed scroll, John is told to prophesy again to peoples and kings; the sequence echoes internalized text becoming renewed proclamation.
Paul's request for books and parchments gives a concrete Christian reference for the commentary's material sheets of skin or parchment.

row.basis: each person bears his own load
row.note: Paul's individual load supplies a direct New Testament comparator to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet claim that no bearer bears another's burden.

row.basis: each receives wages according to personal labor
row.note: Paul's reward according to one's own labor closely parallels the commentary's cited content that a person has only what he has striven for.

row.basis: each receives what was done in the body
row.note: Universal appearance before Christ's judgment seat gives the individual recompense setting behind the commentary's sheets-of-Moses-and-Abraham ethics.

row.basis: gain the world and forfeit one's life
row.note: Jesus' question about gaining the whole world at the cost of life is a pointed Christian analogue to preferring worldly life over what lasts.

row.basis: seen things temporary; unseen things eternal
row.note: The visible-temporary versus invisible-eternal contrast states the same valuation pattern developed around 87:16-17.

row.basis: Moses values future reward above Egypt's wealth
row.note: Moses judges reproach for the Messiah greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to reward, a particularly apt Mosaic comparison for 87:16-19.

row.basis: the world passes; God's doer abides forever
row.note: The world and its desire pass away while the doer of God's will remains forever, directly matching the contrast of worldly preference and endurance.
The opened books of judgment make a Christian image of divine record-keeping beside the commentary's unforgetting Lord and the earlier sheets.
