The rabbinic derivation of Sabbath remembrance over wine interprets the Hebrew cognate z-k-r as enacted recall, sharpening the liturgical side of the commentary's ذ ك ر.

row.basis: letters read and exchanged between churches
row.note: A letter is read in one church and exchanged for reading in another, a concrete case of written teaching being circulated rather than left as an isolated page.

row.basis: former writings written for present instruction
row.note: Paul presents earlier written scripture as instruction for later readers, a Christian account of how first writings remain active in a new community.

row.basis: Scripture proclaims good news beforehand to Abraham
row.note: Paul reads the Abrahamic promise as Scripture's advance proclamation of the gospel; it supplies a Christian interpretive analogue, rather than literal Abrahamic pages, for ancient Abrahamic revelation.

row.basis: Abrahamic covenant temporally distinguished from later law
row.note: Paul's argument separates the Abrahamic promise from the law arriving 430 years later, a different ordering of Abraham and Moses that must remain visible beside 87:18-19's paired sheets.
Jesus' claim that Moses wrote about him is a Christian rereading of Mosaic writing that changes what a reader finds in the pages named in 87:19.
Isaiah's learned reader cannot read the sealed book, a precise inverse scene to 87:6's divine promise to make the messenger recite and retain.

row.basis: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws
row.note: Genesis presents Abraham as obedient to divine laws but does not narrate a written Abrahamic corpus; the distinction cautions against simply identifying 87:19's sheets with a Genesis document.
Augustine's image of memory as a vast interior storehouse gives a Christian interpretive companion to the commentary's container imagery for what is held, retrieved, or dropped.

row.basis: Adam takes and eats the forbidden fruit
row.note: Genesis depicts Adam's first transgression as eating fruit in the woman's temptation scene rather than naming forgetfulness; it is the necessary biblical counter-narrative to the commentary's Adam of Q 20:115 who forgets and lacks resolve.

row.basis: written Torah read continually to learn fear
row.note: The king keeps a written Torah with him and reads it all his days in order to fear YHWH and keep its words, concentrating the commentary's book, recitation, retention, and fear motifs in one scene.

row.basis: word near in mouth and heart
row.note: The word's nearness in Israel's mouth and heart for doing it gives a compact Torah formulation for revelation that is both recited and inwardly held.

row.basis: write on tablet and book for a future day
row.note: Isaiah is told to inscribe the testimony so it endures as a witness for the future, a specific biblical reason to preserve prophetic speech in writing.

row.basis: former scroll restored with additional words
row.note: After the burning, Baruch writes the former words from Jeremiah's mouth and many similar words are added; this distinct final step makes remembered speech both recoverable and expandable in a new scroll.

row.basis: God gives each according to ways and deeds
row.note: YHWH's searching judgment and recompense according to each person's ways supplies a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet ethics of personal effort and return.
The final judgment of every hidden good or evil deed adds the judicial outcome to the commentary's 53:38-42 sequence of individual burden, effort, and return to God.

row.basis: God gives Moses divinely written tablets to teach
row.note: Jubilees opens by having God give Moses tablets of law and commandment already written for teaching Israel, a Second Temple expansion of the Mosaic written-revelation scene.

row.basis: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath from ancient generations
row.note: James describes Moses as publicly read every Sabbath in city synagogues, a New Testament witness to the continuing recitation of an ancient Mosaic written legacy.

row.basis: an orderly written account follows received tradition
row.note: After the eyewitness delivery described in Luke 1:2, the author writes an orderly account; the verse supplies the distinct written outcome of the oral transmission already in view.

row.basis: hearers hold the word fast in a good heart
row.note: In the good-soil explanation, hearers retain the word and bear fruit with endurance, a precise Christian image for held rather than dropped revelation.

row.basis: Jesus' words will not pass away
row.note: The contrast of passing heaven and earth with imperishable words is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's passing worldly life and retained divine speech.

row.basis: the Lord's word endures and is preached
row.note: The Petrine reuse of the enduring-word formula identifies that lasting word with the gospel preached to its readers, combining permanence and proclamation.

row.basis: name not erased from the book of life
row.note: The promise not to erase the conqueror's name gives a Christian book-image for being retained before God, alongside the commentary's contrast between forgetting and divine record.

row.basis: each person gives an account to God
row.note: Paul's formula of each person giving an account of self directly reinforces the individual accountability the commentary attributes to the earlier sheets.

row.basis: Job desires his words inscribed permanently
row.note: Job's wish that his words be written in a book makes durable inscription the response to threatened loss in a non-prophetic setting, extending the commentary's concern with pages that hold what speech might otherwise lose.

row.basis: seal the book until the time of the end
row.note: Daniel is told to keep the words secret and seal the book until the end; its guarded, delayed access provides a qualified inverse to 87:6's enabled recital and 87:18's available earlier sheets.

row.basis: Moses' authorship and the catalog of biblical books
row.note: The rabbinic discussion that attributes Moses' book and other works to named authors is a later Jewish way of organizing the textual corpus behind the commentary's named Mosaic pages.

row.basis: one hundred versus one hundred and one reviews
row.note: The contrast between reviewing a lesson one hundred and one times versus one hundred times supplies a rabbinic practice of repetition aimed at preventing the loss the commentary calls forgetting.

row.basis: Papias prefers the living voice to information from books
row.note: Papias' reported preference for remembered living testimony over books gives a Christian counter-emphasis: the commentary joins memory to sheets, whereas this reception tradition privileges living recall over written repositories.

row.basis: written teaching and unwritten apostolic tradition
row.note: Basil distinguishes church teaching received from writing from teaching transmitted through unwritten apostolic tradition, a later Christian framework that complicates any simple equation of preserved revelation with pages alone.

The commentary says remembrance occurs on the tongue and in the heart; the psalm asks that both its mouth's words and its heart's meditation be acceptable to YHWH, joining voiced utterance and inward devotion.
Hannah speaks in her heart, moves her lips, but has no audible voice; this gives the commentary's inward recitation and remembrance a concrete prayer scene.

row.basis: Hannah as a model for prayer
row.note: The Talmud reads Hannah's moving lips and unheard voice as a rule for prayer: articulate the words without raising the voice, an explicit interpretation of the commentary's inner and audible modes.
The Mishnah disputes whether Shema must be audible to its reciter; this liturgical ruling makes the commentary's distinction between an inward reading and a voiced one consequential.
Moses says the command is near, in Israel's mouth and heart, to be done; the commentary likewise places remembered or recited divine words in both tongue and heart.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy's near word as the message of faith, confessing with the mouth and believing in the heart; this gives the commentary's two modes of receiving sacred speech a Christian interpretive counterpart.
The command's words are to be upon Israel's heart, matching the commentary's claim that remembrance is inward as well as spoken.
Israel is to repeat the words to children and speak them at home, on the road, at lying down and rising; this makes remembered scripture recurrent speech, not only silent possession.
The Torah is not to depart from Joshua's mouth and is to be murmured day and night; this closely joins oral recitation with sustained inward attention, as the commentary does.
The Levites read the Torah from the book and give its sense so the people understand; this is a public, text-in-hand counterpart to the commentary's reading by looking into the text.
The source commentary labels Qur'anic recitation with Arabic q-r-ʾ; here Hebrew q-r-ʾ commands reading the Torah before all Israel, showing the cognate's public scriptural-reading use.

The source commentary labels remembrance with Arabic dh-k-r; the psalm uses the Hebrew cognate for remembering YHWH's name at night, a private act of recollection that sharpens the commentary's tongue-and-heart account.

Jesus promises that the Holy Spirit will teach the disciples and bring to their memory what he said; this parallels the commentary's divine enabling of recitation without forgetting, while giving the promise a different speaker and setting.
After hearing the shepherds' report, Mary keeps and ponders it in her heart; this shows heard speech being retained inwardly, one side of the commentary's oral and internal reading scene.
The message of Christ is to dwell richly among the community, which teaches and sings psalms with gratitude in the heart; this joins remembered sacred words, voiced praise and inward devotion.
The community speaks to one another in psalms and sings to the Lord in its heart; this pairs voiced religious speech with the inward orientation that the commentary assigns to remembrance.

The Hebrew verse assigns hidden things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel and its children; this directly frames the commentary's claim that the Lord knows what is concealed as well as disclosed. WLC numbering is used.
Daniel praises God as the one who reveals deep, hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with him; this closely joins knowing concealment and disclosure, as in the commentary.

In the poem about mining, God-like human searching stops streams and brings hidden things to light; the concrete extraction from earth echoes the commentary's movement from what is covered to what emerges.
Job says God reveals deep things from darkness and brings deep gloom into light; this gives a direct scriptural image for the commentary's concealed becoming manifest.
Wisdom says God witnesses the inmost feelings, observes the heart, and hears the tongue; this closely matches the commentary's pairing of voiced remembrance with what remains inward.
The Spirit of the Lord fills the world and knows what is said; this extends the commentary's claim that speech and its hidden counterpart are known by God.
Wisdom says a jealous ear hears all things and that murmuring does not go unnoticed; this specifically connects quiet, concealed speech with divine knowledge.
Sirach says God searches the abyss and the human heart and sees hidden things; this gives the commentary's divine knowledge of concealed matters a close wisdom-text counterpart.
Sirach adds that no thought escapes God and that he reveals what is hidden; this joins inward thought, concealment and disclosure in the way the commentary does.
The sinner supposes that darkness and walls hide his conduct from notice; this is the mistaken secrecy answered by the commentary's statement that the Lord knows what is hidden.

row.basis: God's eyes brighter than the sun
row.note: Sirach answers that the Lord's eyes are far brighter than the sun and see every human way; the image connects divine knowledge of hidden conduct with the commentary's paradox that excessive light can itself obstruct sight.

YHWH asks whether anyone can hide in a secret place beyond his sight and says he fills heaven and earth; this directly supports the commentary's open/hidden pair as two states within divine knowledge.

row.basis: secret chamber and claimed divine blindness
row.note: The elders act in hidden chambers and say YHWH does not see them; this concrete scene of concealed worship supplies the claim that the commentary's verse rejects by affirming God's knowledge of what is hidden.
Qoheleth says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment; this adds an eventual consequence to the commentary's assertion that concealment is no limit on divine knowledge.
The psalm places secret sins in the light of God's presence; it joins what is concealed to disclosure and divine sight, echoing the commentary's open/hidden pairing.
The psalm says YHWH knows the whole word before it reaches the speaker's tongue; this makes divine knowledge of unvoiced as well as spoken content concrete.
The psalm says darkness is not dark to God and night shines like day; this directly answers the commentary's hidden/light contrast without equating darkness with ignorance for God.

Those who fear YHWH speak to one another and meditate on his name; YHWH listens, hears, and a book of remembrance is written. This uniquely joins speech, divine hearing, the name and remembrance as the commentary's scene does.
Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things of darkness to light and disclose the purposes of hearts; this fuses the commentary's concealed matters with its inward remembrance and divine knowing.

Hebrews describes God's word as discerning thoughts and intentions of the heart; this connects recited divine speech to inward content, a specific bridge to the commentary's reading and knowing scenes.
Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God and all lie exposed before him; this is a close formulation of the commentary's claim that the Lord knows what is disclosed and concealed.
The risen Christ says he searches minds and hearts and repays each according to deeds; this gives the commentary's divine knowledge of hidden inward life a Christian apocalyptic counterpart.
Jesus says nothing covered will not be uncovered and nothing hidden will not be known; this closely matches the commentary's movement from concealment to disclosure.

Jesus contrasts what he tells the disciples in darkness and whispers in the ear with what they must proclaim in the light and from rooftops; this specifically joins the commentary's loud and inward/hidden speech.
Jesus says what is covered will be uncovered and what is hidden will be known; this repeats the commentary's open/hidden claim in a warning about hypocrisy.
Jesus says words spoken in private rooms will be proclaimed from rooftops; this is a particularly close speech-level counterpart to the commentary's high voice and hidden utterance.
In the parable discourse, Jesus says what is hidden is meant to be revealed and what is secret to come to light; this parallels the commentary's concealed thing becoming manifest.

row.basis: hidden revealed in a hearing context
row.note: Luke says nothing hidden will remain unrevealed and nothing secret unknown, in a passage that also warns listeners to take care how they hear; this links the commentary's hiddenness with its recitation and listening scene.
Paul says God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ; this adds judgment to the commentary's claim that hidden matters are known, while locating it in Christian eschatology.

Jesus instructs the disciple to pray in a closed room, assuring that the Father sees in secret; the commentary also affirms divine knowledge of inward prayer, while Jesus makes secrecy a practice rather than merely a known state.

The Mishnah warns that an eye sees, an ear hears, and deeds are recorded; this ethical formulation makes both visible action and audible speech answerable to the all-knowing judge described in the commentary.

Paul interprets Moses' veil as remaining over readers of the old covenant until Christ removes it; this Christian reading makes the commentary's conjunction of recitation, concealment and disclosure a live interpretive question.
Paul says a veil lies over the heart when Moses is read; this explicitly joins textual reading to inward concealment, the two fields the commentary brings together.
Paul says the veil is removed when one turns to the Lord; this gives a Christian interpretive account of concealment as something lifted through turning toward God.

After speaking with Israel, Moses covers his face; the commentary likewise places disclosure beside covering, though Exodus presents a practice of veiling rather than blindness caused by excess light.
Israel sees Moses' face shine and he again covers it; this supplies the concrete pairing of visible radiance and a covering that the commentary's excess-light observation invites readers to notice.
Paul says he could not see because of the glory of the light; this directly matches the commentary's secondary observation that too much light can itself become a veil.

Isaiah depicts Jerusalem speaking low from the ground, with speech whispering from the dust; this is a specific convergence of hushed voice and emergence from a covering/earth, though the prophetic scene is humiliation, not recitation.

The psalm pictures refuge under God's pinions; this is a limited image-parallel to the commentary's hidden feathers beneath the wing's upper feathers, though the psalm speaks of protection rather than feather anatomy.

Jesus' parable turns on a treasure concealed in a field and discovered; this gives a concrete instance of the commentary's secondary sense in which what is hidden can be brought out, without making the parable about divine omniscience.

row.basis: grass springs in a barren land
row.note: God questions Job about satisfying desolate land and causing grass to sprout; this closely matches the commentary's reading of pasture emerging from earth through rain.
The psalm says God prepares rain for the earth and makes grass grow on the mountains; this is a direct creation-motif parallel to the commentary's rain bringing pasture out of soil.
God promises water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land; this supplies the rain/water side of the commentary's emergence scene.
The next verse pictures descendants springing up like grass by streams; this gives the commentary's emerging pasture a close image of growth appearing where water reaches dry land.
The psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle; this is a close claim-level parallel to the commentary's pasture brought forth by the Creator.
The seed sprouts and grows while the sower does not know how; this makes the hidden process behind visible growth explicit, joining the commentary's concealed/emergent pair to its pasture image.
The earth produces first the blade, then the head, then full grain; this is a direct emergence-and-growth sequence beside the commentary's pasture brought out from the ground.

At the meal Jesus gives thanks and commands the bread to be taken in remembrance of him; this is a specific liturgical pairing of remembrance and prayerful thanksgiving alongside the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name followed by prayer.

row.basis: remembering the divine name at night
row.note: The psalmist remembers YHWH's name at night and keeps his Torah; this is a concrete inward/nighttime counterpart to the commentary's remembrance of the Lord and also illustrates its Arabic-Hebrew cognate link.
The psalm summons all that is within the speaker to bless YHWH's holy name; this closely parallels the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name with the heart as well as the tongue.

Joel promises deliverance to everyone who calls on YHWH's name; this gives the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name followed by prayer a specific scriptural invocation formula. WLC numbering is used.

The heavens have no speech or words, yet their voice is heard throughout the earth; this is a specific nonverbal counterpart to the commentary's movement from a voiced reading to meaning that need not be outwardly spoken.

God commands Moses to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths; this joins divinely supplied words, memorization and recitation, adding a communal preservation scene to the commentary's promise of reading without forgetting.

Israel is warned not to forget what its eyes saw or let it depart from the heart, and to teach children; this makes retention of received revelation a concrete counterpart to the commentary's recitation and memory.
The psalmist stores God's word in the heart; this directly connects the commentary's inward reading with its secondary sense of what is hidden.
The speaker says he will never forget God's precepts because they gave him life; this is a direct personal counterpart to the promise that recited revelation will not be forgotten.

The righteous person delights in the Lord's Torah and murmurs on it day and night; this links inward meditation with repeated, potentially subvocal recitation, complementing the commentary's high-voice and inward-reading pair.

row.basis: God teaches Moses what to say
row.note: God promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to speak; this is a specific prophetic counterpart to the commentary's divine enabling of the Prophet's recitation.

row.basis: words put in a prophet's mouth
row.note: God promises to put his words in the coming prophet's mouth, who will speak what God commands; this gives the commentary's divinely enabled recitation a prophetic parallel.
YHWH touches Jeremiah's mouth and says he has placed his words there; this closely parallels the commentary's account of God making the Prophet recite.

row.basis: word remains in the prophet's mouth
row.note: God promises that his words will remain in the mouth of the prophet and his descendants; this adds enduring transmission to the commentary's promise of recitation and retention.

Paul says salvation involves confessing Jesus as Lord with the mouth and believing in the heart; this makes explicit the outward/inward pairing that the commentary develops for recitation and remembrance.
Paul assigns belief to the heart and confession to the mouth; this is a direct formula for two modes of religious response, distinct from verse 8's quoted near-word.
The Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words; this supplies a Christian case of prayer that is inward and unvoiced, a specific extension of the commentary's inner recitation scene.
Paul says the one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's intention; this directly joins unvoiced prayer to divine knowledge of hidden inward content.

Paul says a person speaking in a tongue speaks mysteries to God and not to people; this gives a precise case of utterance hidden from human hearers yet addressed to God, who knows what the commentary says is hidden.
Paul distinguishes and then joins praying and singing with the spirit and with the mind; this is a particularly close Christian formulation alongside the commentary's tongue-and-heart remembrance.
Paul says a visitor's heart secrets become manifest through prophecy, leading to worship; this connects inward hidden matter, public speech and prayer in one scene.
Jesus receives Isaiah's scroll, opens it, and finds the passage to read; this is a concrete text-in-hand scene beside the commentary's account of reading by looking into the book.
Philip hears the Ethiopian reading Isaiah and asks whether he understands; this joins voiced recitation from a written text to inward comprehension, two aspects the commentary holds together.
Paul directs Timothy to devote himself to public reading, exhortation and teaching; this is a specific Christian liturgical counterpart to the commentary's reading aloud and by sight.
Revelation blesses the one who reads its prophecy aloud and those who hear and keep it; this explicitly combines oral reading, listening and inward retention.
Solomon asks God to hear each person's prayer and plea while noting that God alone knows every human heart; this directly joins spoken supplication with inward knowledge, as the commentary does.
Job says no darkness or death-shadow can hide wrongdoers from God; this is a specific statement of the commentary's claim that what is concealed remains known.
The psalm asks whether the maker of the ear cannot hear and the maker of the eye cannot see; this specifically unites audible speech and visible disclosure under God's awareness.
The psalm says YHWH knows that human thoughts are futile; this adds inward thought to the audible and visible dimensions of divine knowing.

row.basis: God's lamp searches the inner self
row.note: Proverbs calls the human spirit the lamp of YHWH, searching the innermost parts; this gives the commentary's hidden inner life a concrete illumination image, while differing from its warning that excess light can obscure sight.
Isaiah condemns people who conceal their plans from YHWH and act in darkness, asking who sees them; this is a concrete human denial of the divine knowledge affirmed by the commentary.

row.basis: a well seen when eyes are opened
row.note: God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well; this is a specific scene of a water source becoming visible, beside the commentary's hidden-water/well example and its movement from concealment to emergence.
Jesus says the Father knows what the disciples need before they ask; this specifically extends the commentary's claim that God knows inward content as well as voiced words.

row.basis: call on and proclaim the name
row.note: The psalm calls Israel to give thanks, call on YHWH's name, and make his deeds known; this supplies a liturgical pairing of invoking the divine name and verbal praise beside the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's name followed by prayer.
The verse names Samuel among those who call on YHWH's name and says they called to him and he answered; this is a concrete prayer scene connecting the divine name with invocation.

The Mishnah says the early pietists waited before prayer in order to direct their hearts to God; this gives a Jewish liturgical interpretation of the inward attention that accompanies the commentary's remembrance and prayer.

The Didache prescribes the Lord's Prayer three times daily, including the petition that God's name be hallowed; this gives a concrete Christian practice joining repeated recitation, the divine name and prayer.

Justin describes the memoirs of the apostles or prophets being read in the Sunday gathering, followed by instruction; this is a specific Christian public-reading practice alongside the commentary's recitation and text-in-hand reading.
Josephus says the law is read and learned on the Sabbath; this gives a Jewish communal setting for the commentary's pairing of recitation, hearing and retained scripture.

The commentary joins remembrance on the tongue and in the heart; Hannah prays in her heart, with moving lips but an unheard voice, making an unusually close scriptural scene of inward yet bodily prayer.

Berakhot derives prayer rules from Hannah's verse: direct the heart, move the lips, and do not make the voice heard. It gives the commentary's loud/quiet prayer contrast a precise rabbinic liturgical reading.

row.basis: quiet prayer; God hears the heart
row.note: Cyprian teaches that prayer should be quiet because God hears the heart rather than the volume of a voice. This directly interprets the commentary's claim that God knows recitation whether it is on the tongue or in the heart.

row.basis: secret prayer; Father sees in secret
row.note: The commentary pairs inward prayer with God's knowledge of what is concealed; Jesus commands prayer in the shut room, where the Father sees in secret, giving that pair a Christian discipline of prayer.

The commentary says the Lord knows worship that remains inside; Romans names God as the searcher of hearts who knows the Spirit's intention, making divine knowledge the ground of unvoiced intercession.
The commentary's God knows what is hidden as well as what is uttered; Mark's Jesus immediately knows the scribes' inward reasoning, a narrative Christian counterpart focused on concealed thought.

The commentary explicitly sets raised speech beside what remains hidden. Psalm 139 says that before a word is on the tongue, YHWH knows it completely, giving the verbal side of that claim its closest Hebrew formulation.

row.basis: God observes heart and hears tongue
row.note: The commentary distinguishes heart and tongue while affirming God's knowledge of both. Wisdom calls God an observer of the heart and a hearer of the tongue, preserving both terms in one ethical warning about speech.
The commentary joins disclosed speech to what stays concealed; Sirach says that no thought escapes God and no word is hidden from him, supplying a compact Jewish formulation of both halves.

The commentary treats hidden and open things as known by God and brought into relation with recited teaching. Deuteronomy assigns secret things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel for doing the Torah, sharpening the disclosure boundary.

row.basis: God reveals deep and hidden things
row.note: The commentary turns concealment into emergence and says God knows the hidden. Daniel's God reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with him, matching both disclosure and light-darkness imagery.

The commentary contrasts what is open with inward reality. In Samuel, humans look at outward appearance while YHWH looks at the heart, a concrete distinction between visible surface and divinely known interior.

row.basis: YHWH searches heart and tests inward self
row.note: The commentary says the hidden interior is known even when no voice exposes it. Jeremiah presents YHWH as searching the heart and testing the inward person, placing that claim in judgment language.

row.basis: deep things from darkness brought to light
row.note: The commentary's second scene makes the concealed come out from its cover. Job says God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings deep shadow into light, a direct divine movement from hiddenness to exposure.

The commentary uses physical emergence and a cleared well to picture disclosure. Job's mining poem says that a hidden thing is brought to light, supplying a terrestrial extraction image without making the human miner identical with God.

row.basis: no creature hidden; all exposed to God
row.note: The commentary's open/hidden pair is made absolute here: Hebrews says no creature is hidden before God and all stand exposed to his eyes, extending the claim beyond speech to every creature.

row.basis: hidden darkness and counsels of hearts disclosed
row.note: The commentary joins concealed things emerging from cover with the knowledge of inner reality. Paul says the Lord will bring hidden darkness to light and disclose the counsels of hearts, uniting both movements in judgment.

row.basis: hidden made manifest; secret made known
row.note: The commentary describes concealment as capable of becoming visible. Jesus states that nothing hidden will fail to become manifest and no secret will fail to become known and come to light, a close disclosure formula.

The commentary frames recited divine speech around what God knows in secret. Amos says the Lord reveals his secret to prophetic servants, adding a biblical account of hidden counsel becoming prophetic proclamation.

row.basis: mystery hidden through ages now manifested
row.note: The commentary makes the hidden something God can bring out. Colossians calls Christ's mystery hidden through ages and generations but now manifested to the saints, a Christian revelation-history form of that movement.

row.basis: written song taught and put in mouths
row.note: The commentary reads 87:6 as recitation from memory or from a text. Deuteronomy orders a song to be written, taught, and put in Israel's mouths, explicitly joining writing, learning, and oral recitation.

row.basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The commentary foregrounds the promise of recitation without forgetting. Deuteronomy says the taught song will not be forgotten from descendants' mouths, a close covenantal counterpart to preserved oral memory.

row.basis: Torah book in mouth and meditation
row.note: The commentary joins an uttered reading to an inward one. Joshua requires the Torah book not to depart from the mouth and commands meditation on it day and night, holding oral and interior engagement together.
The commentary calls recitation possible from the heart. The psalmist says the divine word has been stored or hidden in the heart, turning inward retention into a safeguard for faithful action.
The commentary's central pair is stated almost structurally here: Deuteronomy says the word is very near, in the mouth and in the heart, so that it can be done.

The commentary says the taught word is known whether voiced or held within. Romans reuses the mouth-and-heart formula for the proclaimed word of faith, giving the paired locations a Christ-centered reading.

row.basis: law placed in mind and written on heart
row.note: The commentary's recitation from the heart is not merely silent sound. Hebrews describes God's law placed in minds and written on hearts, a durable inward inscription of revealed teaching.

row.basis: word dwelling richly; songs in hearts
row.note: The commentary connects recitation, remembrance, and worship in tongue and heart. Colossians commands Christ's word to dwell richly and joins teaching with sung worship in hearts, preserving that combined practice.

row.basis: spoken psalms and melody in heart
row.note: The commentary distinguishes audible speech from inward remembrance without separating them. Ephesians pairs speaking psalms and hymns with singing and making melody in the heart to the Lord.

row.basis: one reads aloud and others hear
row.note: The commentary begins with the voice of recitation. Revelation blesses the single reader who reads prophecy aloud together with those who hear it, a specific early Christian scene of voiced scripture.

row.basis: God's words remain in successive mouths
row.note: The commentary treats divine teaching as recited and not forgotten. Isaiah's covenant says God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or the mouths of descendants, extending memorized speech through generations.

row.basis: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' reading
row.note: The commentary labels the 87:6 reading root q-r-'. Deuteronomy uses the Hebrew cognate qara' for reading the Torah before all Israel in their hearing, showing a Semitic root in an explicitly public reading act.

row.basis: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zkr and God's name
row.note: The commentary labels 87:15 with dhikr and has the worshipper remember the Lord's name. Psalm 20 uses Hebrew zkr for Israel's making mention of YHWH's name, a close cognate-and-ritual match.

row.basis: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zikri and divine name
row.note: The commentary's dhikr label joins remembrance to the Lord's name. Exodus calls YHWH's declared name his zikri, "my memorial/remembrance," making name and remembrance inseparable in divine self-disclosure.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr, book of remembrance, and honored name
row.note: The commentary's dhikr of the Lord's name is voiced worship. Malachi has God hear those who speak together and honor his name, then records them in a book of remembrance from Hebrew zkr.

The commentary ends the sequence with remembering the Lord's name and praying. Romans applies the scriptural promise that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, making invocation of the name a Christian prayer act.

row.basis: rain makes earth bring forth and sprout
row.note: The commentary says rain draws pasture from soil. Isaiah compares rain and snow that water the earth and make it bring forth and sprout, a close image of divinely enabled vegetal emergence.

The commentary moves from rain and earth to grass coming out. In God's questions to Job, the desolate ground is satisfied so that grass is caused to sprout, placing pasture-growth under divine agency.

row.basis: God makes grass grow from earth
row.note: The commentary links 87:4's bringing out of pasture to divine action. Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and vegetation for human service, a direct hymn-like counterpart to that pastoral image.

The commentary adds the paradox that excessive sunlight can obstruct sight. Job says people cannot see the bright light in the skies, giving a specific biblical instance where brightness defeats vision.

row.basis: unable to see because of brilliant light
row.note: The commentary's cehra image is an eye unable to see in sun. Paul says he could not see because of the brilliance of the heavenly light, a narrative instance of sight overwhelmed by light.

row.basis: Shema audible to one's own ear
row.note: The commentary places elevated and inward recitation together. This Mishnah debates whether a Shema made audible to the reciter's own ear fulfills the duty, giving low but articulated sound a specific legal significance.

The commentary allows worship to remain within rather than rise as loud speech. Romans describes the Spirit's intercession through groanings too deep for words, an explicit Christian image of prayer beyond utterance.

row.basis: communal silence and speech to self and God
row.note: The commentary balances voiced and internal devotion. Paul tells an uninterpreted speaker to keep silence in the assembly while speaking to himself and to God, distinguishing public sound from God-directed speech.

row.basis: God knows needs before spoken prayer
row.note: The commentary says God knows an inward as well as uttered reading. Augustine explains that prayer-words do not inform God, who already knows human need, but exercise the pray-er’s desire; this is a patristic account of the same premise.

row.basis: seed sprouts and grows without the sower's knowing
row.note: The commentary makes hiddenness a process of emergence, especially grass from earth. Jesus' seed sprouts and grows while the sower does not know how, setting hidden vegetal growth beside the commentary's divine knowing.

row.basis: opened eyes and a seen well of water
row.note: The commentary uses a cleared, visible well as an image of disclosure. God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well of water, making hidden provision visible without claiming that the well itself was newly created.

The commentary's hawafi are feathers hidden below the leading wing-feathers. Psalm 91 pictures protection under God's wings and feathers, offering a concrete feather-cover image while giving it a protective sense.

row.basis: chicks gathered under a bird's wings
row.note: The commentary uses concealed lesser feathers beneath a wing. Jesus' hen image gathers chicks under wings, another bird-cover scene whose protective purpose adds a relational use of the concealed space.

row.basis: shining face covered by a veil
row.note: The commentary says excess light can itself become a covering. Exodus combines Moses' shining face with his putting on a veil, a biblical scene in which radiance and covering are deliberately held together.

row.basis: fire followed by a sound of thin silence
row.note: The commentary connects volume, concealment, and the Qur'anic approach to Moses' fire. After fire, Elijah's Horeb scene contains qol demamah daqqah, a "sound of thin silence," an indirect but unusually apt acoustic counter-image.

row.basis: Moses and fire in the bush
row.note: The commentary locates the Qur'anic loud/hidden saying immediately before Moses sees fire. Exodus likewise gives Moses a fire-theophany, though specifically a bush burning without being consumed, so the shared scene and its differing detail can be compared.

row.basis: God calls Moses from the bush
row.note: The commentary's nearby Qur'anic setting moves from divine knowledge of speech to the Moses-fire encounter. Exodus 3:4 contributes the verbal side within its own verse: God calls Moses by name from the bush.

row.basis: revealed words placed on the heart
row.note: The commentary says the taught word may be held in the heart as well as voiced. Deuteronomy commands that the words given that day be upon Israel's heart, making inward retention the first response to revelation.

row.basis: repeated words spoken through daily life
row.note: The commentary treats recitation as an active oral practice. Deuteronomy tells Israel to repeat the words to children and speak of them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and on rising, giving memorized teaching a daily voice.

row.basis: teaching kept within and ready on lips
row.note: The commentary's tongue-and-heart recitation has a close wisdom counterpart: Proverbs calls it pleasant to keep teachings within oneself when they are all ready upon one's lips.

row.basis: Torah within and written on heart
row.note: The commentary's inward reading is more than quiet sound. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise places the Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, a strong Hebrew Bible image of internalized revelation.

row.basis: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' book-reading
row.note: The commentary labels 87:6 with q-r-'. Nehemiah uses Hebrew qara' for reading aloud from the Torah book and adds interpretation so that listeners understand, linking cognate reading to voiced instruction and comprehension.

The commentary joins recitation with being aware of what is said. Philip hears the Ethiopian reading and asks whether he understands what he reads, a concrete Christian scene of oral scripture and understanding.

The commentary contrasts a text looked at with one retained in the heart. Paul calls the Corinthians Christ's letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than with ink, making inward inscription a reading-image.

row.basis: Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: The commentary reads 87:6 as divinely enabled recitation that does not forget. Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of his words, a direct Christian account of preserved taught speech.

row.basis: speak in hearts and be silent
row.note: The commentary's first scene holds lowered voice beside interior speech. This psalm commands hearers to speak in their hearts upon their beds and be silent, a compact Hebrew pairing of inward utterance and silence.

row.basis: lips honor God while heart is distant
row.note: The commentary permits remembrance with tongue and heart together. Isaiah critiques honor rendered with lips while the heart remains far away, adding the ethical test that exterior speech cannot replace inward attachment.

The commentary's two locations of worship are tested by Jesus' citation: these people honor God with lips while their heart is far from him. Its Christian use makes the tongue-heart relation a question of genuine worship.

row.basis: prayer and song with spirit and mind
row.note: The commentary distinguishes raised sound from an inward mode of worship. Paul resolves a comparable pairing by praying and singing with both spirit and mind, bringing cognition into voiced prayer and song.
The commentary closes with remembering the Lord's name and prayer. Genesis describes people beginning to call on YHWH's name, an early biblical scene in which the divine name is invoked in worship.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr: God causes his name to be remembered
row.note: The commentary's dhikr label links remembrance to the Lord's name. At the altar, YHWH promises to come where he causes his name to be remembered, using Hebrew zkr in a specifically cultic setting.

row.basis: Hebrew zekher, name, and desire of the soul
row.note: The commentary's dhikr is possible in the heart as well as on the tongue. Isaiah joins God's name and zekher, "memorial/remembrance," to the desire of the soul, an inward cognate counterpart.
The commentary says God knows what is not openly voiced. YHWH questions Sarah's private laughter and its inner reasoning, giving a narrative instance in which concealed thought is directly known.

The commentary allows divine address to remain inward. Abraham's servant says he had not finished speaking in his heart when Rebekah appeared, a prayer narrative that makes interior speech consequential before God.

row.basis: God alone knows every human heart
row.note: The commentary joins prayer to divine knowledge of the hidden. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven because God alone knows the heart of every person, making omniscience part of temple prayer.

row.basis: deep counsel in the heart drawn out
row.note: The commentary says a hidden thing can be extracted and illustrates it with water and a well. Proverbs likens purpose in a person's heart to deep water that one of understanding draws out, joining inner concealment and extraction.

row.basis: body made in secret not hidden from God
row.note: The commentary moves from what is hidden to what God knows and brings into view. This psalm says a body made in secret in earth-like depths was not hidden from God, extending the claim to concealed organic formation.

row.basis: mouth uttering things hidden from the foundation
row.note: The commentary connects recited speech with the disclosure of what lies hidden. Matthew presents Jesus' parabolic speech as uttering things hidden from the world's foundation, a Christian form of voiced unveiling.

row.basis: prayer to the Lord as knower of all hearts
row.note: The commentary says inward realities are known to God. Before choosing Matthias, the disciples pray to the Lord specifically as the knower of everyone's heart, making the claim part of communal discernment.

row.basis: word judges thoughts and intentions of heart
row.note: The commentary treats the recited word and hidden interior as joined under divine knowledge. Hebrews says God's word discerns thoughts and intentions of the heart, making spoken or written revelation an examiner of what is concealed.

row.basis: secrets of heart disclosed in worship
row.note: The commentary connects hidden knowledge, audible word, and prayer. Paul says an outsider's heart-secrets are disclosed and that person then worships God and declares God's presence, a tightly related congregational scene.

row.basis: rain prepared for earth and grass made to grow
row.note: The commentary explicitly imagines rain drawing pasture from soil. Psalm 147 says God prepares rain for the earth and makes grass sprout on mountains, matching rain, ground, growth, and divine agency in one verse.

row.basis: planting, watering, and God giving growth
row.note: The commentary makes pasture's emergence God's act despite rain and soil. Paul distinguishes human planting and watering from God who gives the growth, a Christian agricultural image of the same agency distinction.

row.basis: voice heard from fire but no form seen
row.note: The commentary locates loud and hidden speech beside Moses' fire and explores visible versus concealed. Deuteronomy says YHWH spoke from fire, Israel heard a sound of words, but saw no form, uniting auditory revelation with visual withholding.

row.basis: fire, dense darkness, and a great voice
row.note: The commentary places loud speech, concealment, and the Moses-fire setting together. In WLC's Hebrew verse numbering, Deuteronomy recounts YHWH's great voice from fire, cloud, and dense darkness, an unusually close cluster of those images.

row.basis: brightness that Israel could not gaze at
row.note: The commentary's secondary image is sight defeated by excessive light. Paul says Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of its glory, making visual incapacity caused by radiance explicit.

row.basis: unheard voice without speech or words
row.note: The commentary's phonetic scene contrasts audible high speech with what remains unspoken. Psalm 19 says there is no speech or words and no voice is heard, yet its surrounding hymn presents creation as communicating; the parallel is poetic rather than liturgical.

The commentary invokes a measured rather than raised prayer-voice. Ecclesiastes warns against hasty speech before God and says that human words should be few, an explicit wisdom restraint on devotional utterance.

row.basis: Moses read while a veil lies on the heart
row.note: The commentary connects reading, heart, and covering. Paul says that when Moses is read a veil lies on the heart, a Christian interpretive image in which scriptural reading itself can remain interiorly covered.

row.basis: mouth opened in parable and ancient dark sayings
row.note: The commentary makes disclosure possible through a spoken word. The psalmist opens his mouth in a parable to utter ancient riddling sayings, a Hebrew example of voiced transmission of what is not immediately plain.

The commentary joins dhikr to prayer. Paul's Eucharistic command, "do this in remembrance of me," makes remembrance a repeated Christian worship-act, though its object and rite differ from remembering God's name in 87:15.

row.basis: keep a king's secret; reveal God's works
row.note: The commentary turns secret and open into a movement of disclosure. Tobit distinguishes keeping a ruler's secret from honoring God by revealing God's deeds, supplying a Jewish ethical rule about concealment and proclamation.

row.basis: earth produces first blade, then ear and grain
row.note: The commentary's pasture comes out of the earth. Jesus describes the earth producing the crop in ordered stages beginning with the blade, a parabolic vegetal emergence whose setting differs from the commentary's rain image.

row.basis: well-mouth stone rolled away for watering
row.note: The commentary gives a cleared well whose water is made visible as an image of disclosure. Genesis describes shepherds rolling the stone from a well's mouth to water sheep and replacing it, a concrete cover-and-uncover water scene.

The commentary says God may bring the hidden out. Isaiah tells the audience that hidden things they had not known are now announced, a prophetic disclosure formula rather than a physical emergence image.

row.basis: unapproachable light that no human can see
row.note: The commentary says overwhelming light can function like a cover to sight. First Timothy places God in unapproachable light whom no human has seen or can see, a theological extension of visual excess beyond the sun-image.
