row.note: The commentary links Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis makes the ground cursed and toil the consequence of his disobedience in the same story.
The commentary recalls hardship following Adam’s exile; Genesis specifies that he eats bread by the sweat of his face, giving that hardship its daily labor.
The commentary’s Abraham asks to be kept from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s father and ancestors served other gods, locating the danger his prayer names.

row.basis: God took Abraham across the river
row.note: The commentary has Abraham ask God to keep his family from idols; Joshua recounts God taking Abraham from beyond the Euphrates into Canaan, a narrated removal from his idolatrous setting.

row.basis: not in haste or flight; God goes before
row.note: The commentary defines the guide as one who precedes and describes a calm walk rather than a flight; Isaiah joins both details, saying the departing people need not hurry or flee because God goes before them and guards their rear.
The commentary’s mountain ridge is long yet easier to climb and its mount has light legs; the psalm combines hind-like feet with being set on high places, an image of sure-footed ascent.

row.basis: righteous walk the same paths transgressors fall on
row.note: The commentary says the road may be the same while the traveler’s manner differs; Hosea says the just walk in the Lord’s right ways while transgressors fall in those very ways.

row.basis: God teaches the way one should walk
row.note: The commentary develops guidance as someone going ahead to show a road; the psalm has God instruct and teach the way the addressee should walk, making the guide’s instruction explicit.
The commentary says the wretched person keeps the reminder at a distance; personified Wisdom says her hearers rejected her counsel and reproof, a concrete scene of refusing admonition.

row.basis: donkey turns aside from the blocked road
row.note: The commentary’s mount is easy to lead and quick to follow; Balaam’s donkey instead leaves the road when it sees the angel blocking the way, and that refusal protects its rider.

The commentary makes the traveler’s conduct, not the road itself, decisive; the angel tells Balaam that his way is perverse, while the donkey’s apparent deviation is the safer response to the blocked path.

row.basis: two gates and roads with different ends
row.note: The commentary sets a shown route beside a steep climb that is not attempted; Jesus describes a broad road entered by a wide gate that leads to destruction, making the traveler’s chosen way consequential.
The commentary’s two high routes and the unattempted ascent invite comparison with Jesus’ narrow way to life, which few find; this adds a sharply difficult route alongside the easy-way image.

row.basis: one side of the afterlife sees the other
row.note: In the commentary’s cited scene a person in bliss looks down and sees his former companion in Hell; Luke has the tormented rich man lift his eyes and see Lazarus with Abraham at a distance, reversing the direction of the postmortem gaze.

row.basis: horse or mule needs bit and bridle
row.note: The commentary’s animal is pliant and follows readily; the psalm warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be controlled with bit and bridle, a pointed contrast between willing guidance and restraint.
The commentary’s verse turns pasture into debris; Psalm 1 uses chaff for the wicked, adding an ethical judgment to the image of vegetation reduced to residue.

The commentary distinguishes the person who follows guidance from the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving the two responses different ends.

row.basis: a highway on which even a fool will not stray
row.note: The commentary describes being made ready for the easier way; Isaiah’s holy highway is so clearly marked that even a fool will not err on it, a concrete image of an accessible route.

row.basis: the command is not too hard or far away
row.note: The commentary reads the promised easy way as a facilitated course; Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or remote, linking divine instruction with practicable action.
The commentary pairs guidance with the traveler’s response and outcome; Moses sets life and death before Israel and tells them to choose life, a direct choice between destinations.

row.basis: the word is near and doable
row.note: The commentary’s easy way is prepared for its addressee; Deuteronomy places the word in mouth and heart, near enough to do, making accessibility an inward as well as traveled route.

row.basis: the shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
row.note: The commentary pictures a guide leading the way; the psalm’s shepherd restores the speaker and leads him in righteous paths, joining care for the traveler to a directed route.

row.basis: a voice behind says, “This is the way”
row.note: The commentary calls the guide one who goes ahead; Isaiah’s traveler hears a voice behind identifying the way to walk, a concrete reversal of the guide’s position while preserving the path instruction.

The commentary’s lexical note describes a weak person walking while leaning on two others; Ecclesiastes says one companion raises another who falls, a close support image though not a description of walking gait.
The commentary brings together weakness, light legs, and easy travel; Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord walk without fainting, portraying renewed capacity for the journey.

row.basis: riding camels and following the guide
row.note: The commentary’s easy-to-follow animal carries a rider along a route; Rebekah and her attendants ride camels and follow Abraham’s servant, a concrete guided journey on mounts.

row.basis: Rachel sits on the camel saddle
row.note: The commentary describes a wrapped cover placed over a camel’s hump and then ridden; Genesis has Rachel sit on the camel’s saddle, supplying a biblical riding-seat scene, though it uses the saddle to conceal idols.

row.basis: Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods
row.note: The commentary contrasts keeping counsel away with Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons away from idols; Jacob directs his household to remove its foreign gods and purify itself, a family-level act of separation.

row.basis: foreign gods buried beneath the oak
row.note: The commentary’s Abraham asks for protection from idol worship; Jacob’s household hands over its foreign gods, which Jacob buries beneath the oak, showing the concrete removal that follows his command.

The commentary recalls Abraham’s prayer that he and his descendants be kept from idol worship; Genesis Rabbah’s story of the young Abraham breaking the idols in Terah’s shop interprets that separation as an active rejection of his father’s cult.

row.basis: weary and burdened people receive rest
row.note: The commentary reads the promise of ease as relief on a journey; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him and promises rest, giving the ease image a human burden-bearing context.
The commentary’s mount is readily led and takes the way with light steps; Jesus calls his yoke easy and his burden light, applying ease to the discipline of following him.

row.basis: God promises to be with Moses’ mouth
row.note: The commentary cites Moses asking God to make his task easy; when Moses objects to speaking, God promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, a narrative answer that equips him for the mission.

row.basis: possible Arabic s-w-y / Hebrew שוה cognate
row.note: The commentary reports an Arabic family sense of equality alongside “middle”; Isaiah uses the Hebrew root שוה for being equal or compared. The semantic link is specific, but the cognate relationship needs lexical confirmation and does not carry the camel-seat sense.

row.basis: ancient paths, rest, and refusal to walk
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person leaves the reminder beside his route; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not walk there, joining guidance, a way, and its refusal.

row.basis: prepare a way in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary develops a guide who goes ahead and a route made easy; Isaiah’s voice calls for the Lord’s way to be prepared in the wilderness, an explicit road-making image.

row.basis: mountains lowered and rough ground made level
row.note: The commentary describes a long ridge that is nevertheless easier to climb; Isaiah pictures hills lowered and rough places leveled so a route can be traversed.

row.basis: donkey riders, saddle-related sitting, and walkers on the road
row.note: The commentary brings together a riding cover, the mount, and a person’s route; Deborah’s song groups donkey-riders and walkers on the road with people sitting on a term sometimes understood as saddle-cloths, though that wording is uncertain.

row.basis: the Shunammite’s urgent ride on an ass
row.note: The commentary describes a mount that follows readily and takes light steps; the Shunammite rides an ass and tells her servant not to slacken the pace, a concrete scene of directing a mount along a journey.

row.basis: God chooses a longer route because the people might turn back
row.note: The commentary’s promise makes the way easier for its addressee; Exodus says God avoids the nearer Philistine route lest the people see war and return to Egypt, showing guidance adjusted to the travelers’ weakness.

row.basis: Adam sent from Eden to till the ground
row.note: The commentary connects Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis explicitly sends him out of Eden to work the ground, joining exile to the labor that follows.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary develops guidance as showing a road and easing the traveler’s way; Zechariah’s prophecy says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace, directly joining guidance, feet, and route.

row.basis: straight paths for the feet so the lame may be healed
row.note: The commentary pairs a difficult ascent with weak, swaying walking; Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so the lame limb will be healed rather than injured, joining path preparation to bodily weakness.

row.basis: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
row.note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person relying on support; Isaiah tells the hearers to strengthen weak hands and make firm feeble knees, a concrete bodily response to weakness.

row.basis: the lame leap like a deer
row.note: The commentary links a mount’s light legs with a ridge that can be climbed; Isaiah says the lame will leap like a deer, turning impaired gait into agile movement.

row.basis: a lame man is raised by the hand and strengthened
row.note: The commentary recalls a weak person who needs support to walk; Peter takes the man lame from birth by the hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles are strengthened, a concrete healing of unsupported gait.

row.basis: the healed man walks and leaps
row.note: The commentary’s lexical image is a weak, swaying walker; after the healing in Acts, the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, showing the restored movement that support makes possible.

row.basis: make level paths for your feet
row.note: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long but easier to climb and its route is made accessible; Proverbs urges the traveler to consider the path of his feet and make his ways firm, a practical image of preparing one’s course.

row.basis: human plans, the Lord directs the steps
row.note: The commentary says the road can be the same while the traveler’s conduct differs; Proverbs contrasts a person’s plans with the Lord’s direction of his steps, clarifying the relation between human course and divine guidance.

row.basis: turn away from the evil path
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person steps aside from the reminder; Proverbs commands the traveler to avoid the wicked path, turn from it, and pass on, a useful reversal in which one should leave the road rather than the warning.

row.basis: a man lame from birth is carried to the temple gate
row.note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person who relies on support; Acts describes a man lame from birth being carried and placed at the temple gate, a specific scene of dependence before his healing.

row.basis: John identifies himself as Isaiah’s wilderness voice
row.note: The commentary develops the guide and the way that is made ready; John applies Isaiah’s road-preparation oracle to his own role as herald, reading the route as preparation of people for the Lord’s coming.

row.basis: Balaam as one who leaves the straight way
row.note: The commentary says a traveler can take a wrong course while the road remains; 2 Peter interprets Balaam as one who leaves the straight way for wrongdoing, giving the Numbers donkey episode an explicit moral reading of straying for gain.

row.basis: take the yoke, learn, and find rest
row.note: The commentary’s easy mount follows its guide and carries its rider along the way; Jesus invites hearers to take his yoke and learn from him, promising rest for their souls, a distinct image of following under an easy discipline.

row.basis: the shepherd strengthens the sick and binds the injured
row.note: The commentary’s guide imagery includes a weak walker who relies on support; God as shepherd says he will bind the injured, strengthen the sick, and seek the lost, joining direction with care for the weak.

row.basis: be swift as a deer and light as an eagle
row.note: The commentary’s lexicon gives a mount that follows quickly and has light legs; Rabbi Judah ben Tema uses deer-swiftness and eagle-lightness as traits for doing the will of Heaven, turning animal agility into an ethical image.

row.basis: life and death are set before a person to choose
row.note: The commentary links guidance with a traveler’s response and outcome; Sirach says life and death are before a person and the choice is given to him, extending the choice-of-way motif into Jewish wisdom teaching.

The commentary glosses h-d-y as showing someone both the road and the house. Abraham's servant says that God led him on the road to his master's kinsmen's house, giving the journey image a concrete destination.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire expressly to lead them on the road. This closely supplies the commentary's claim that the guide is named for advancing ahead of the travelers.
The promised messenger is sent before Israel to guard the way and bring them to a prepared place. It joins the commentary's forward guide, safe route, and arrival.
God goes ahead on Israel's way to seek a place to camp and shows them which route to take. The text makes the guide's prior movement and knowledge of resting place explicit.
The commentary contrasts an unhurried, composed walk with fleeing. Isaiah says the departing people will neither leave in haste nor flee because YHWH goes before them and guards behind.

The commentary's hadi goes ahead and the animal follows readily. Jesus' shepherd goes before his sheep, and they follow because they know his voice, a close Christian pastoral rendering of both actions.
Zechariah's prophecy says the divine visitation will guide feet into the way of peace. It turns the commentary's road-leading and calm gait into an explicitly salvific destination.

When a traveler turns right or left, Isaiah's voice says, "This is the way; walk in it." That is a precise counterpart to the commentary's guide who identifies a road rather than merely giving advice.
God leads blind people on unfamiliar roads and makes rough places level. This combines the commentary's guided traveler with its concern for a route made passable.
The commentary dwells on a long mountain ridge whose climb is made easier. Isaiah's preparation of the divine way lowers mountains, raises valleys, and smooths rough ground.
Baruch says God orders mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel can walk safely. Its return procession makes the commentary's high route and divinely eased walking a single scene.
Luke applies the leveling of valleys, mountains, crooked places, and rough roads to the coming salvation. It gives a Christian reception of the terrain that the commentary reads as a journey.
God leads Israel through the depths like a horse in the wilderness so that it does not stumble. This directly links the commentary's guided animal and its light, sure movement.
Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and lets him tread on high places. It is a compact analogue to the commentary's light legs and mountain-ridge travel.
Wisdom's path leaves the walker's stride unconfined and prevents stumbling even when running. It concretizes the commentary's easy road and untroubled gait.

The commentary imagines a horse that yields easily and follows quickly. Psalm 32 warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be restrained by bit and bridle, an instructive inverse image of responsive guidance.
James puts bits in horses' mouths so that they obey and their whole bodies are guided. Its explicit horse, obedience, and direction closely illuminate the commentary's easy-to-lead mount.

The commentary gives the secondary image of a weakened person sustained between two people. Aaron and Hur support Moses' heavy hands from either side, supplying a concrete biblical pattern of two-sided aid to weakness.
The commentary's route concerns weak movement and a path made easy. Hebrews orders straight paths for the feet so that what is lame is healed rather than put out of joint.
Moses' work is too heavy alone, and shared judgment will make it easier for him. This provides a narrative analogue to the commentary's ease as the removal of disabling strain.

row.basis: guide who knows the road to Media
row.note: Tobiah seeks a companion who knows the road, and Raphael assures him that he knows it from repeated travel. The scene gives the commentary's forward guide a named journey companion and a known destination.

After the heavenly encounter leaves Saul unable to see, his companions lead him by hand to Damascus. It offers a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's weakened traveler needing bodily guidance.

The commentary turns the promise of ease into a rider-and-mount picture. The Samaritan places the wounded traveler on his own animal and conveys him to care, making the animal an instrument of supported passage.

row.basis: donkey turns aside before the angel
row.note: The commentary reads the wretched person's tajannub as passing the warning by and keeping it at the roadside. Balaam's donkey turns aside from the road because it sees the armed divine messenger that its rider misses; here the sideways movement is the faithful response to warning.

YHWH tells the people to stand at the roads, ask for the good ancient path, walk it, and find rest; they answer that they will not walk in it. This is a close counterpart to the reminder that the wretched person avoids.
Those addressed refuse to heed, turn a rebellious shoulder, and make their ears heavy. The bodily turning away makes unusually concrete the commentary's interpretation of avoiding the reminder.

In Luke's explanation, seed beside the road is the word heard and then removed before belief. It gives the commentary's image of keeping the admonition at one's roadside an explicit parabolic setting.

Hebrews repeats the summons to hear God's voice today and not harden the heart. It places the commentary's contrast between fruitful reminder and wretched avoidance in an exhortatory Christian reception.
Isaiah makes dry grass and stubble burn because the people rejected YHWH's instruction. It binds the commentary's pasture becoming refuse to its adjacent scene of admonition refused and fire.

The commentary's pasture ends as ghutha, expendable dark refuse. Psalm 1 gives the wicked the specific image of chaff driven away, adding an ethical use of agricultural residue without equating the texts.
The pasture in the commentary is brought forth and then becomes dark waste. Isaiah's grass withers and flower fades when the breath of YHWH blows on it, a close vegetation-to-decay image.

James describes the sun's scorching rise: grass withers, its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. This supplies a Christian moral use of the transience visually developed in the commentary's pasture.
The commentary places ghutha beside the wretched person's great fire. Matthew's winnowing scene gathers chaff and burns it, giving an eschatological continuation to that agricultural residue.

The commentary explicitly reads Adam's expulsion from the garden as entry into shaqa, hardship. Genesis curses the ground for Adam and makes his eating depend on toil, the matching narrative consequence.
Genesis sends Adam out of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken. This supplies the expulsion-and-labor scene behind the commentary's Adamic account of hardship.

row.basis: Abraham saddles a donkey for the journey
row.note: The commentary's rider-and-mount imagery ends by invoking Abraham's plea against idols. Genesis shows Abraham rising, saddling his donkey, and setting out, furnishing a literal Abrahamic journey without identifying its purpose with the Qur'anic prayer.

The commentary contrasts the wretched person who keeps the reminder at a distance with Abraham's request to be kept from idols. Isaiah commands defiling and casting away idol-images as something unclean.
Joshua commands Israel to put away the foreign gods among them and incline the heart to YHWH. It makes the commentary's requested separation from idolatry an enacted turn of direction.
The Thessalonians turn to God from idols to serve the living and true God. That conversion gives a New Testament counterpart to Abraham's desire that he and his sons be kept from idol worship.
Paul's direct command to flee idolatry supplies a Christian imperative for the commentary's inverted use of janb: deliberate distance from the false object rather than distance from divine reminder.

This midrash expands Abraham's anti-idolatry into the episode of smashing Terah's images. It gives Jewish narrative force to the commentary's Abrahamic request for separation from idols, while remaining an interpretive tradition rather than a shared biblical scene.

Jubilees portrays Abram burning the house of idols and the resulting crisis in Terah's household. The expansion makes active rupture with idols the narrative counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic prayer for protection from them.

row.basis: creation by measure number and weight
row.note: The commentary begins with the Creator who creates and proportions. Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, a particularly exact Jewish articulation of ordered creation.
God asks who fixed the earth's measures and stretched a line over it. It supplies a biblical cosmic instance of the measuring and proportioning named in the commentary on 87:2–3.

row.basis: weight for wind and measure for waters
row.note: Job describes God assigning weight to wind and measure to waters. This makes the commentary's divine measuring a material ordering of a world through which creatures travel.

The Two Spirits Treatise says that God made humanity and appointed two spirits for people to walk by until visitation. It is an unusually close Second Temple analogue to the commentary's created traveler facing divergent roads.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death. Its explicit road-formulation belongs beside the commentary's one route whose ends become ease or hardship.

row.basis: way of light and way of darkness
row.note: Barnabas introduces two ways of teaching and authority, light and darkness. This Christian two-way schema sharpens the commentary's moral split between following guidance and moving away from warning.
Matthew contrasts the broad way that leads to destruction with the life-giving entrance. It gives a concrete New Testament road division for the commentary's opposed courses of ease and hardship.

The commentary can picture the difficult side as the road of wretchedness, while Matthew calls the life-giving way constricted and hard. The contrary assignment of difficulty makes the comparison interpretively useful rather than a simple equation.

row.basis: narrow path between fire and water
row.note: 4 Ezra imagines the entrance to a city as a single narrow path between fire and deep water. Its perilous route makes the commentary's ridge, choice, and final destination into a vivid Jewish apocalyptic travel scene.

row.basis: life and death set before a person
row.note: Sirach sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what is chosen. It provides a wisdom-text counterpart to the commentary's guided road that divides according to the traveler's response.

row.basis: yoke of Torah and released burdens
row.note: Avot says accepting the yoke of Torah removes other yokes, while throwing it off brings them on. This rabbinic interpretation makes the commentary's ease and hardship consequences of what one willingly follows.
The commentary's yusr is ease, compliant following, and light movement. Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a direct Christian moral use of ease in animal-yoke imagery.

Acts calls a disputed yoke one that neither ancestors nor present hearers could bear. In contrast to the commentary's mount readily yielding to its rider, this verse tests which religious burden is actually bearable.

God promises to put his spirit within Israel and cause them to walk in his statutes. It supplies a biblical model of divine enablement for the commentary's promise to make a person ready for the easy course.

row.basis: highway on which travelers do not stray
row.note: Isaiah's holy highway is a route on which even inexperienced travelers do not go astray. It joins the commentary's explicit guiding with a road made reliable for its walkers.

row.basis: straight way to an inhabited town
row.note: God leads wandering people by a straight way until they reach an inhabited town. Like the commentary's road-and-house gloss, its guidance ends in arrival and habitation.
God promises to make a way in wilderness and rivers in desert. This develops the commentary's divine route-making where the natural terrain itself offers no easy passage.

The Spirit is said to guide the disciples into all truth. It transfers the commentary's guide who shows the road into a Christian account of revelatory direction, rather than treating guidance as mere locomotion.
The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23's shepherd restores life and guides on right tracks, keeping pasture and route together in a single pastoral image.

row.basis: ascending mountain to learn God's paths
row.note: Nations go up YHWH's mountain so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk in his paths. It connects the commentary's mountain ascent with instruction that directs walking.

After the road-to-house guidance of the same narrative, Rebekah and her companions mount camels and follow the servant. It supplies a literal caravan version of the commentary's rider, animal, and following image.

row.basis: idols concealed in a camel saddle
row.note: The commentary links a camel-hump covering for riding with Abraham's plea to be kept from idols. Rachel hides household gods in a camel saddle and sits on it, a concrete inverse scene in which idolatry is carried inside the riding equipment.

row.basis: riding on the heights of the land
row.note: God makes Israel ride on the heights of the land. It is a poetic counterpart to the commentary's mount and elevated ridge, though it does not itself explain the ease of ascent.
Isaiah calls the righteous person's path level and says the Upright One makes it even. This adds a moral use of levelness to the commentary's easier, balanced road.
The commentary's good hedy is not a fleeing rush. Isaiah says the one who trusts will not act in haste, giving calm movement a faith-based interpretation.
Proverbs warns that haste of feet makes a person miss the way. It provides a compact wisdom counterpoint to the commentary's measured, unhurried gait.

row.basis: walking backward after refusing to hear
row.note: Jeremiah says the people did not listen, walked in their own counsels, and went backward rather than forward. It makes the commentary's contrast between a forward guide and avoidance of admonition spatially explicit.

row.basis: the two ways and the wicked's end
row.note: Psalm 1 contrasts the way known by YHWH with the way of the wicked that perishes. It is a foundational but less pictorial parallel to the commentary's road whose result depends on the traveler.
Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and calls for choosing life. It provides covenantal language for the commentary's opposed outcomes of a shown way.

row.basis: wicked path as darkness and stumbling
row.note: The wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble. It complements the commentary's wretched traveler with a path whose very obstacles are unrecognized.
The Testament of Asher describes two ways and corresponding dispositions and outcomes. It is a Jewish para-scriptural development of the moral road division in the commentary.

Sirach urges the learner to put neck and shoulder under Wisdom's yoke, which becomes an ornament. It complicates the commentary's easy animal image by treating willingly borne discipline as the route to a good end.
The commentary's weak walker is sustained by others and its easy route relieves hardship. Paul commands mutual burden-bearing, an ethical counterpart without the travel scene itself.

The commentary treats turning aside from the true reminder as the wretched response. Jesus' sheep flee a stranger precisely because they do not know that voice, showing that withdrawal is right or wrong according to the guide recognized.
Christ leaves an example so believers may follow in his steps. This is a Christian ethical use of the commentary's following-behind-a-guide image, without its animal figure.

row.basis: Lamb shepherding and guiding to waters
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water. It reverses ordinary rider-and-animal roles while retaining the commentary's leading figure and safe destination.

row.basis: tormented man sees the blessed afar
row.note: The commentary's wrong road culminates with a blessed person looking down to a companion in hell's center. Luke reverses the viewpoint: a tormented rich man sees Abraham and Lazarus far away, a related but differently arranged afterlife sightline.

row.basis: Balaam as one leaving the straight way
row.note: Second Peter calls corrupt teachers people who leave the straight way and follow Balaam's way. Read beside Numbers 22:23, it turns the donkey-and-road episode into a Christian moral warning relevant to the commentary's guidance and wrong turning.

row.basis: Hebrew shavah and the source label sawa
row.note: The commentary explicitly gives سوى the sense of equality and a balanced middle. Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה, a likely Semitic cognate, for being equal or comparable to the Holy One; its context checks the equality sense while supplying no camel-saddle image.

The commentary treats guidance as showing a real road and making a journey possible. Isaiah's command to prepare YHWH's way and make a highway straight supplies the route-formula that precedes its leveling in 40:4.
Luke quotes the call to prepare the Lord's way and make his paths straight. It is the Christian continuation that supplies the guide-and-road formula distinct from the terrain changes in Luke 3:5.

row.basis: remove obstacles from my people's way
row.note: A voice orders a way built up and every obstruction removed from the people's path. This directly realizes the commentary's promise of a road made easy for its walker.

The prophet tells people to pass through the gates, build up the highway, and clear its stones. Its public roadwork makes concrete the commentary's eased route rather than a merely inward disposition.
God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble. This closely combines the commentary's guide, light movement, and secure arrival.
God leads his people out like sheep and guides them through the wilderness like a flock. It gives the commentary's guide-before-followers image an explicitly animal-shaped biblical form.

row.basis: word as lamp for feet and path
row.note: The commentary makes divine guidance a journey and its rejected message a reminder. Psalm 119 calls God's word a lamp for feet and light for a path, joining revelation and locomotion.

row.basis: commandment as lamp and reproof as way of life
row.note: Proverbs calls commandment a lamp, teaching light, and corrective reproofs the way of life. This makes the commentary's admonition something that should direct a traveler rather than be passed by.

row.basis: God teaches and leads the profitable way
row.note: YHWH teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go. It directly pairs the commentary's divine huda with yusr as a beneficial course.
The psalm asks that God's good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground. It unites the commentary's leading guide with its balanced, easier terrain.
YHWH promises continual guidance, satisfaction in dry places, and strength for the bones. Its linked guidance and bodily renewal answer the commentary's weak traveler and easy course.

row.basis: green pastures and leading beside waters
row.note: The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23 makes the shepherd cause rest in green pastures and lead beside quiet waters, preserving both landscape and direction.

row.basis: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
row.note: The commentary's secondary h-d-y image is a weakened person needing support. Isaiah commands the strengthening of weak hands and unsteady knees before its highway vision.

row.basis: lame person leaping like a deer
row.note: Isaiah's lame person leaps like a deer. This is a sharply specific transformation of weak legs into the light, high-country movement developed in the commentary.

row.basis: weak hands and feeble knees restored
row.note: Hebrews calls for drooping hands and weak knees to be strengthened. Together with its next verse on straight paths, it supplies the bodily side of the commentary's supported traveler.
God makes the singer's feet like a deer's and sets him on high places. This repeated biblical formulation independently confirms the commentary's light legs and elevated route.

row.basis: sweat of the face after exile
row.note: The commentary relates Adam's leaving the garden to hardship. Genesis specifies that he will eat bread by the sweat of his face until returning to the ground, intensifying the toil already named in 3:17.
Sirach describes great toil and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam. It is a Jewish wisdom expansion of the commentary's Adamic movement from garden ease into hardship.

row.basis: Moses turns aside to see the sign
row.note: The commentary treats turning aside from the reminder as the wretched movement. Moses says he will turn aside to see the burning bush, making the same spatial gesture an attentive response to a divine sign.

row.basis: God calls when Moses has turned aside
row.note: When YHWH sees Moses turn aside to look, God calls him by name. This completes the counter-image: a sideways movement that receives, rather than avoids, divine address.
Jonah physically sets out for Tarshish to flee from YHWH after receiving a commission. The narrative gives the commentary's avoidance of a divine reminder a full journey-shaped enactment.

row.basis: disciples withdraw and stop walking with Jesus
row.note: After Jesus' difficult teaching, many disciples go back and no longer walk with him. It provides a Christian scene of abandoning a guide after hearing his words, close to the commentary's wretched avoidance.
Elijah asks how long Israel will limp between two positions and demands following either YHWH or Baal. It fuses the commentary's uneven walking, forked road, and Abrahamic anti-idolatry concern.

row.basis: put away foreign gods and purify
row.note: Jacob orders his household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change garments. This is a concrete household enactment of the commentary's wish to be kept apart from idols.

row.basis: turn from futile things to the living Creator
row.note: Paul and Barnabas urge idolizing crowds to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth. It directly connects the commentary's creation claim to its movement away from idolatry.
Paul contrasts the temple of the living God with idols. This establishes the Christian side of the commentary's Abrahamic separation between divine worship and false objects.
The command to come out from their midst and be separate gives bodily force to the commentary's janb image of keeping oneself away from a thing; its immediate setting is the idol contrast of 6:16.

row.basis: way of life and way of death
row.note: YHWH sets before Jerusalem the way of life and the way of death. The formula supplies a direct prophetic counterpart to the commentary's one journey resolving into opposed ends.

row.basis: one is led on the path one chooses
row.note: The Talmud states that a person is led on the way the person wishes to go. This rabbinic maxim is especially close to the commentary's claim that the same divine easing works toward ease or hardship according to the traveler's direction.

row.basis: arrogant and evildoers as stubble in fire
row.note: In Hebrew WLC versification, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like stubble. It joins the commentary's vegetal residue, wretchedness, and final fire in one prophetic image.
First Peter repeats that all flesh is grass and that grass withers. It gives the commentary's pasture-to-waste image a Christian scriptural reception centered on mortality.

row.basis: weary and burdened people invited to rest
row.note: Before calling his yoke easy, Jesus invites those laboring and heavily burdened to come for rest. This names the human hardship to which the commentary's promise of ease responds.
First John says love of God keeps his commandments and that those commandments are not burdensome. It provides a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's ease as obedient responsiveness.
Jesus identifies himself as the way leading to the Father. This is a concentrated Christian transformation of the commentary's guide, path, and destination pattern.
On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus goes ahead of the disciples while they follow in awe and fear. The scene realizes the commentary's guide who moves in front of those on the journey.

row.basis: following the light without walking in darkness
row.note: Jesus says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. It makes following the true guide the opposite of the commentary's lost or warning-avoiding traveler.

row.basis: way to the tree of life guarded after Eden
row.note: After expelling Adam, God stations guardians to keep the way to the tree of life. It supplies a route closed by the Edenic fall, a spatial counterpart to the commentary's loss of ease after leaving the garden.

row.basis: riding on the heights of earth
row.note: God promises to make the faithful ride on the heights of the earth. It gives a second prophetic use of riding and high terrain alongside the commentary's mount and mountain ridge.
The psalm asks to be taught YHWH's way and led on a level path because of enemies. It adds a prayerful use of the commentary's guided, balanced road.

row.basis: upward path of life away from Sheol
row.note: For the prudent, the path of life leads upward in order to turn from Sheol below. It aligns the commentary's elevated road with its contrasting endpoint in the fire, though it does not share the animal imagery.
Land bearing thorns and thistles is rejected, near a curse, and ends in burning. This extends the commentary's vegetation-and-fire sequence through a Christian agricultural warning.

People once strayed like sheep but have returned to the shepherd and overseer of their souls. It gives a Christian recovery-from-wrong-route counterpart to the commentary's guide and its animal family.

row.basis: Creator forms and establishes the earth
row.note: The Creator forms, makes, and establishes the earth for habitation rather than emptiness. This enriches the commentary's brief claim that God creates and proportions, though it does not develop the travel imagery.

row.basis: created for works prepared to walk in
row.note: Believers are called God's workmanship, created for works God prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them. It combines the commentary's creation language with a divinely prepared course of action.

row.basis: God gives the horse its strength
row.note: God asks Job whether he gives the horse its strength and clothes its neck. It places the equine capacity behind the commentary's readily led horse within the Creator's ordering of creatures.

row.basis: garments laid on a mount for Jesus to sit
row.note: The commentary develops a cover placed on a camel's hump and a rider settling on the animal. Matthew narrates garments laid on the donkey and colt before Jesus sits, a literal Christian journey image of mount and seat-covering.

row.basis: sun as runner on its course
row.note: The commentary extends 87:1's galloping-horse image to stars swimming in their courses; this psalm depicts the sun rejoicing like a champion to run its course, adding a celestial runner.
The commentary joins 87:3's guidance to the later place in the procession; the psalm says God guides the speaker and afterward receives him to glory, making guidance lead toward a later reward.
The commentary turns 87:3's guidance into vanguard leaders; Exodus says YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire to lead the route, giving guidance a literal front-of-column position.

row.basis: cloud shifts from front to rear
row.note: The commentary tracks leaders and those at the people's rear; as Egypt approaches, Exodus moves the divine messenger and cloud from before Israel to behind them, making the procession's order protective.
The commentary says the group's “after” names those at its end; Numbers assigns Dan's camp the rear guard for Israel's moving camps, a concrete final rank in the column.
The commentary develops a front rank and followers behind; Joshua's Jericho procession places armed men before the priests and a rear guard behind the ark, adding a ritual march with both positions.
The commentary maps first and last onto a moving line; Isaiah describes the departing people going without haste because YHWH goes before them and Israel's God is their rear guard.

The commentary sets a leading rank against those at the rear; Isaiah promises healing with righteousness going before the people and YHWH's glory as their rear guard, giving the order a salvific meaning.

The commentary brings together swimming water and a running horse; Habakkuk's theophany has God tread the sea with horses, a concrete meeting of water and equine movement without equating their actions.

row.basis: people led through depths like a sure-footed horse
row.note: The commentary praises an animal's well-placed steps and recalls swimming; Isaiah describes God leading Israel through depths like a horse in the wilderness that does not stumble, joining deep-water passage to sure-footed motion.
The commentary's yusr gloss depicts an animal transferring its legs well; the psalm says God makes the speaker's feet like a deer and sets him on high places, making sure-footed ascent a divine gift.

The commentary reads 87:8's animal stride as well-placed movement; Habakkuk's prayer gives the speaker hind-like feet on high places amid crop failure and distress, adding sure footing as trust through crisis.

row.basis: running with horses as endurance test
row.note: The commentary says the trailing horse has saved some running for later; Jeremiah's rebuke asks whether the prophet can contend with horses if footmen tire him, making endurance rather than an early lead the test.

The commentary says the first to arrive is not necessarily the winner; Ecclesiastes says the race is not to the swift and outcomes do not reliably follow strength or speed, directly unsettling rank by pace.
The commentary distinguishes the first horse from the one following; Ahimaaz outruns the Cushite in a messenger race, supplying a narrative pair of first and trailing runners.

row.basis: first arrival lacks the decisive answer
row.note: The commentary warns that the first to arrive need not win; after outrunning the Cushite, Ahimaaz reaches David but cannot say what happened to Absalom, so speed does not deliver the needed result.

The commentary says the one behind may matter more than the first; the Cushite arrives after Ahimaaz and answers David about Absalom, completing a messenger race in which the later report is decisive.

row.basis: horses set against invoking God's name
row.note: The commentary pairs 87:15's remembering the Lord's name with horse imagery; this psalm contrasts trust in horses with invoking YHWH's name, adding a counterpoint in which the horse is inadequate as security.
The commentary couples guidance with an animal's ordered stride; the psalmist says he will run the way of God's commandments when his heart is enlarged, turning directed movement into obedience.
The commentary's horse saves part of its run for the later stretch; Isaiah promises that those who hope in YHWH will run without weariness, making sustained movement the result of renewed strength.

row.basis: Arabic source root س ب ح and Aramaic š-b-ḥ, praise
row.note: The commentary labels 87:1's Arabic root س ب ح and develops swimming and galloping associations; Daniel's Aramaic prayer uses the cognate root š-b-ḥ to praise God, grounding the worship sense without importing Daniel's word into the motion gloss.

row.basis: Arabic source root ص ل و and Aramaic ṣ-l-y, pray
row.note: The commentary labels 87:15 فَصَلَّى as prayer, then notes a second-horse sense in its lexical family; Daniel's Aramaic cognate describes his three daily prayers, anchoring the worship sense while leaving the horse image secondary.

row.basis: Arabic source آخرة and Hebrew אחרית, latter end
row.note: The commentary says the Arabic “after/latter” root names those at the rear; Ecclesiastes uses the Hebrew cognate אחרית for a matter's end, and explicitly calls that end better than its beginning.
The commentary says the later runner may be better than the first arrival; Ecclesiastes explicitly values a matter's end over its beginning, giving the temporal reversal a wisdom saying.

row.basis: vestibule before the World to Come
row.note: The commentary makes the nearer life the first part of a sequence and the afterlife the later part; Avot pictures this world as a vestibule before the World to Come, adding a preparatory threshold image.

row.basis: relative worth of the two worlds
row.note: The commentary calls the later life better and more enduring; Avot preserves both valuations: an hour of good deeds here exceeds the future world's whole life, yet an hour of its bliss exceeds all this world's life, complicating a simple ranking.

row.basis: fruit now, principal preserved for the World to Come
row.note: The commentary contrasts the near life with what remains afterward; Peah says some deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the World to Come, adding a specific image of reward held for later.

The commentary says the later life is more enduring than the present; Wisdom says the righteous dead seem destroyed to observers but have hope full of immortality, adding the hidden outcome behind apparent loss.

The commentary criticizes preferring the nearer life over what follows; the second Maccabean martyr refuses the king's offer and expects the King of the universe to raise him, presenting the contrary choice of future life over present survival.
The commentary calls the hereafter better and lasting; a brother facing execution says the dead will be raised to life, adding resurrection as the concrete future that makes present death bearable.

The commentary distinguishes the leading and following horses and says early arrival is not the whole contest; Paul invokes runners in a stadium and urges the Corinthians to run to obtain the prize, making disciplined pursuit—not mere rank—the point.

The commentary calls the later life more enduring and compares it to a horse saving its run; Paul contrasts athletes' perishable wreath with the imperishable one sought by Christians, joining race discipline to lasting reward.

row.basis: run the set race with endurance
row.note: The commentary's final runner preserves strength for the later stretch; Hebrews tells its hearers to run the race set before them with endurance, making perseverance the necessary path to the finish.

row.basis: joy set ahead of present suffering
row.note: The commentary values what comes later over the first arrival; Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him and then sat at God's right hand, giving present suffering a future-directed end.

The commentary's race image turns the two lives into first and later positions; Paul says he forgets what lies behind and reaches toward what lies ahead, making forward orientation the posture of pursuit.
The commentary says the later result is better than the early lead; Paul presses toward the goal for the prize of God's upward call in Christ, specifying a future prize as the runner's measure.
The commentary warns that arriving first is not the final victory; Paul says near death that he has finished the race and kept the faith, making completion rather than an early position decisive.

row.basis: crown laid up for that day
row.note: The commentary says the latter life is better and longer-lasting; Paul expects a crown of righteousness reserved for the Lord's appearing, giving the race a reward kept for the end.
The commentary says people prefer the life of this world; John warns against loving the world and its desires, giving a direct ethical reversal of that preference.

row.basis: world passes, God's will remains forever
row.note: The commentary calls the hereafter better and more enduring; John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, stating transience versus permanence.
The commentary says people prefer the nearer life despite what follows; Jesus warns that earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth and corrosion, adding a concrete form of what does not last.
The commentary calls what follows more enduring than the present; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy, specifying a lasting object of preference.

row.basis: gain the world, lose one's life
row.note: The commentary criticizes preferring worldly life over the better later outcome; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world yet forfeit one's life, making the choice a question of ultimate value.

The commentary sets present life against a better later one; Jesus promises those who leave home or kin for his name a hundredfold and eternal life in the age to come, making present relinquishment point forward.
The commentary says the early arrival is not necessarily the winner; after the promise of eternal life, Jesus says many who are first will be last and last first, explicitly reversing expected order.

row.basis: late workers paid before the first
row.note: The commentary makes the first arrival no guarantee of winning; in the vineyard parable's conclusion the last are first and first last, adding a narrative reversal of rank and reward.

row.basis: rich toward God rather than stored wealth
row.note: The commentary says people prefer the life now at the expense of what follows; Jesus ends the rich fool's story by contrasting treasure for oneself with being rich toward God, adding a sudden-death case of misplaced priority.

The commentary says the first life is not the final winner and the later one is better; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and he is in agony.

row.basis: departing to Christ is far better
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is better than the current life; Paul says he desires to depart and be with Christ because that is far better, while remaining in the flesh benefits others.

row.basis: present suffering outweighed by coming glory
row.note: The commentary compares the present life with a better and more lasting later one; Paul says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, making the future outweigh the present.
The commentary contrasts the near world with what lasts afterward; Paul says visible things are temporary and unseen things eternal, giving the present/later contrast an explicit duration.

row.basis: preferring to be with the Lord
row.note: The commentary says the later life is better than the present one; Paul says he would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord, making the preference explicit while describing his own hope.

row.basis: sun's ordered course through the gates
row.note: The commentary's source gloss pictures stars swimming in their courses; the Astronomical Book lays out the sun's recurring course through the heavenly gates, adding a Jewish account of ordered celestial motion without equating it with swimming.

The commentary gives the stars an ordered orbit; Enoch's vision associates a sinful age with celestial lights departing their appointed order, preserving a contrary image in which the course itself fails.

row.basis: water deep enough to swim in
row.note: The commentary gives س ب ح the literal gloss “swim in water”; Ezekiel's temple river grows until it is deep enough for swimming, adding a sacred, measured current as a concrete water-motion image.
The commentary's yusr gloss praises an animal's well-transferred steps; Proverbs calls several creatures stately in their going, making dignified gait itself the point rather than speed.

row.basis: separated herds in a moving caravan
row.note: The commentary arranges horses and camels by those ahead and behind; Jacob sends successive animal droves ahead with space between them, adding a staged caravan whose order serves a plan.

row.basis: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחרית, latter end
row.note: The commentary labels 87:17's Arabic al-ākhirah with the root ء خ ر and describes what remains behind; Moses recalls wilderness testing intended to do Israel good at its אחרית, its latter end, giving the cognate a delayed-benefit context.

row.basis: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחור, behind
row.note: The commentary uses the Arabic root for both the afterlife and those at the rear; the psalm says God encompasses the speaker “behind and before,” showing the Hebrew cognate's spatial sense alongside the source's temporal one.

row.basis: Arabic source al-ākhirah and Hebrew אחרית, future
row.note: The commentary says the Arabic “after/latter” names those at a group's end; the psalm uses Hebrew אחרית for the peaceful person's future, adding an ethical outcome to the cognate's temporal sense.

The commentary contrasts the near life with what lasts afterward; the final brother says those who endured brief suffering have entered ever-flowing life, making the short/lasting contrast explicit in a martyr's speech.
The commentary says the later life is better and more enduring; Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening, some to everlasting life, supplying an explicit resurrection horizon.

row.basis: rest, then rise at the end of days
row.note: The commentary makes the afterlife the latter stage and calls it lasting; Daniel is told to go to his rest and rise for his allotted inheritance at the end of days, giving that sequence a personal resurrection outcome.
The commentary says the message is in earlier scrolls and names Moses; Deuteronomy says Moses finishes writing the words of the Torah in a book, a concrete Mosaic witness to written scripture.

row.basis: book of the law deposited as witness
row.note: The commentary names Moses among the sources of the earlier scrolls; Moses orders the written book of the law placed beside the covenant ark as a witness, adding its preserved public role.

The commentary extends a race's front and rear positions to the afterlife; Berakhot portrays the World to Come without eating, trade, jealousy, hatred, or competition, with the righteous enjoying God's presence, limiting the race image to this life's sequence.

row.basis: thanksgiving and calling on God's name
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and prays; the psalm joins a thanksgiving offering with calling on YHWH's name, adding a concrete liturgical form of that pairing.

row.basis: the present age and the future age
row.note: The commentary contrasts the near life with the better, lasting life after it; in chapter 7 Uriel compares the hard passage of the present age with the future age's reward. Verse divisions vary by edition, so this is cited at chapter level.
The commentary condemns preferring the near life over what follows; Esau trades his birthright for food and despises it, a concrete choice of immediate satisfaction over a later inheritance.

row.basis: Esau sells inheritance for a meal
row.note: The commentary's 87:16–17 contrast is immediate preference against later good; Hebrews names Esau as one who sold his birthright for a single meal, turning the Genesis episode into an ethical warning about short-term choice.

row.basis: later regret cannot recover the blessing
row.note: The commentary says the early choice may not win the final outcome; Hebrews recalls that Esau later sought the blessing with tears but could not reverse what happened, adding the consequence of a short-sighted exchange.

row.basis: Abraham's company desires a better country
row.note: The commentary names Abraham in the former scrolls and says the later life is better; Hebrews says the patriarchs desired a better, heavenly country, making Abrahamic faith look beyond the present homeland.
The commentary criticizes preferring this world's life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a direct choice against near pleasure.

The commentary says what follows is better than the first gain; Hebrews says Moses valued reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked toward the reward, making future recompense govern present choice.
The commentary says the message is in former scrolls and names Moses; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, a New Testament interpretation that gives Mosaic scripture a forward-looking witness.

row.basis: losing present life to keep eternal life
row.note: The commentary says people prefer worldly life over the better later one; Jesus says one who loves life loses it, while one who gives up life in this world keeps it for eternal life, directly reversing that preference.

row.basis: prayer begins by hallowing the Father's name
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and then prays; Jesus teaches prayer that opens by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, joining divine-name devotion to the prayer itself.

row.basis: last and first at the kingdom's table
row.note: The commentary says the first arrival is not necessarily the winner; after describing entry into God's kingdom, Jesus says some who are last will be first and first last, placing the reversal in an eschatological gathering.
The commentary's horse holds strength for the latter stretch; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making final persistence decisive.

The commentary says an early position does not guarantee the final win; Paul disciplines his body lest, after preaching to others, he himself be disqualified, adding the possibility that even a runner can fail at the end.

row.basis: athlete crowned only under the rules
row.note: The commentary links the race order to a later prize; Paul says an athlete is not crowned unless competing lawfully, adding that position and desire alone do not secure the outcome.

row.basis: rich urged not to hope in uncertain wealth
row.note: The commentary says people prefer worldly life; Paul tells the rich not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God, a specific correction to misplaced present security.

row.basis: treasure stored for the future life
row.note: The commentary calls the later life better and lasting; Paul says the rich should store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life, spelling out present action for future gain.
The commentary says the horse preserves its running for later; James blesses the one who endures trial and promises the crown of life, making the reward follow sustained endurance.
The commentary says the afterlife is more enduring; Peter describes an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven, adding a reserved future possession.

The commentary treats this life as an earlier position before the lasting life; Diognetus describes Christians as dwelling on earth while their citizenship is in heaven, giving the temporal contrast the image of temporary residence versus permanent homeland.

row.basis: fear of YHWH's word and protective action
row.note: In the Moses-and-Pharaoh plague setting explicitly developed in the commentary, officials who fear YHWH's word act on the warning and bring servants and livestock under cover; reverent fear makes a transmitted warning beneficial.

The paired Pharaoh-scene verse describes the person who does not set his heart on YHWH's word and leaves those in his charge exposed, a concrete counterpart to the bedbaht recipient who keeps the reminder at a distance.

row.basis: Pharaoh's not knowing and not listening
row.note: Pharaoh answers Moses that he does not know YHWH and will not listen to his voice; it binds failed knowledge to refusal of the prophetic command, beside the commentary's offer of guidance intended to yield fear.

row.basis: heart that fears and obedience for good
row.note: YHWH wishes Israel had a heart to fear him and keep his commands so that it would go well with them; this joins reverential fear, reception of instruction, and benefit in one appeal.
At Horeb the people are gathered to hear God's words, learn to fear him, and teach their children, giving a communal scriptural form to the commentary's reminder that passes from speaker to hearer.

row.basis: public Torah reading, hearing, fear, observance
row.note: The commanded assembly is to hear, learn, fear YHWH, and observe Torah; its ordered response closely matches instruction received by one who fears.

row.basis: teacher's address and fear of YHWH
row.note: "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of YHWH" makes fear the explicit subject of a directed instruction, rather than an undifferentiated emotion.

row.basis: reproof received by wise, hated by scoffer
row.note: The proverb differentiates the recipient of reproof: the scoffer hates correction while the wise person loves it, a compact analogue to reminder received by one person and avoided by another.

row.basis: fear of YHWH and knowledge of God
row.note: This verse places understanding the fear of YHWH alongside finding knowledge of God, supplying a Wisdom counterpart to the commentary's close account of fear and knowledge.

row.basis: hating knowledge and not choosing fear
row.note: The rejected way is specified as both hatred of knowledge and refusal to choose the fear of YHWH, a precise negative counterpart to the fearful rememberer.
Isaiah identifies the person who trembles at God's word; the bodily image and reverent reception give a close counterpart to the commentary's "içi titreyen" hearer.

row.basis: teaching for benefit and leading in the way
row.note: YHWH describes himself as the one who teaches Israel for its benefit and leads it in the way it should go, joining the commentary's benefit of reminder to its secondary guidance language.
The gentle speech commanded to Moses and Aaron in the commentary has a Wisdom analogue in the soft answer that turns away wrath; both treat the manner of address as consequential.
The command to rebuke one's neighbour makes correction an act directed toward another person, matching the commentary's insistence that reminder is transitive rather than merely inward recollection.

row.basis: hear or refuse a prophetic word
row.note: Ezekiel is told to announce that whoever hears may hear and whoever refuses may refuse; the prophet delivers a word while the hearer divides into the two responses foregrounded here.

row.basis: warning, turning, and the watchman's limit
row.note: If the watchman warns the wicked to turn, the warned person's response determines the outcome while the watchman has discharged his task; this illuminates both beneficial reminder and the commentary's limit on the reminder-giver.

row.basis: turning the shoulder and stopping the ears
row.note: Those addressed refuse attention, turn a stubborn shoulder, and stop their ears from hearing; its physical language of withdrawal closely specifies the commentary's claim that the wretched person keeps admonition away rather than simply arguing with it.

Hebrew zkr is cognate with the source commentary's Arabic dhikr root. Joseph asks the cupbearer both to remember him and to cause Pharaoh to remember him, an especially clear instance of remembrance deliberately carried to another.

The Bavli's maxim that one should say a matter that will be heard and should not say one that will not be heard is a direct Jewish interpretive counterpart to the conditional "if the reminder benefits."

Hebrews says the word heard did not benefit its earlier hearers because it was not joined with faith, an unusually exact New Testament articulation of the commentary's conditional benefit of reminder.
Private reproof is directed to a brother, and hearing the reprover gains that brother; it concretely pairs transitive admonition with a beneficial response.
The community is to exhort one another daily so that none is hardened by sin's deceit; it makes repeated mutual reminder the antidote to the inward condition that refuses a divine word.

row.basis: Scripture profitable for teaching and reproof
row.note: Scripture is called profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training, giving a direct Christian formulation of the reminder's possible usefulness.

The teacher corrects opponents with gentleness in hope that God grants repentance leading to knowledge of truth; this closely accompanies the commentary's gentle address to Pharaoh and its fear-knowledge nexus.
Those described turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to myths, a verbal and spatially shaped counterpart to the recipient who avoids the reminder.
James commands hearers to receive the implanted word, which is able to save them; its reception-versus-rejection logic makes the benefit of a delivered word explicit.

row.basis: blessed hearers and keepers of God's word
row.note: Jesus calls those who hear God's word and keep it blessed, supplying the positive happy pole beside the commentary's fearful receiver and its contrast with the most wretched.
The warning not to refuse the one who speaks preserves the commentary's agency distinction: a divine word is offered, and refusal is the hearer's perilous response.
The good-soil hearers hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this gives a concrete Gospel image for a reminder whose reception has beneficial effect.

The Hiphil azkir, "cause my name to be remembered," belongs to the Hebrew zkr cognate family of Arabic dhikr. Its cultic setting adds an external, name-centred form of caused remembrance, not a claim that the two rituals are identical.

row.basis: fearers and a book of zikkaron
row.note: The verse couples those who fear YHWH with a written zikkaron, "remembrance," from the Hebrew cognate family of dhikr; it is a distinct divine memorial usage alongside the commentary's human-directed reminder.

Proverbs calls fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge, whereas the commentary says its reverential fear commonly arises from knowledge. The differing order is the point of comparison, while both tightly link the two.
God promises to put his fear in the people's hearts so that they will not turn away from him. It reverses the commentary's sequence by making fear the force that keeps a recipient from withdrawal.

A priest affected by seminal emission may not eat holy things until clean. This supplies a Hebrew Bible ritual analogue to the commentary's postcoital distance claim, while the verse concerns holy food rather than mosque prayer.

Before Sinai's divine encounter the people are told not to approach a woman. It makes sexual abstention part of preparation for sacred approach, a related but not identical frame to the commentary's junub explanation.

row.basis: baal qeri and recitation of Shema
row.note: The mishnah limits a man with a seminal emission to inward reflection on the Shema rather than its normal verbal recitation. It provides a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's association of the postcoital state with distance from prayer, without equating their rules.

row.basis: happiness and keeping away from wicked counsel
row.note: Psalm 1 calls happy the person who keeps away from wicked counsel. Its ethical allocation reverses the commentary's image: distance is good when the counsel is wicked, while keeping a beneficial reminder distant marks the wretched person.

row.basis: blindness, ethical care, and fear of God
row.note: The prohibition against putting a stumbling block before the blind concludes with fear of God. It gives a Torah ethical setting for the commentary's blind, fearful visitor, though it is not the same incident.

Paul permits spouses temporary, agreed abstinence in order to devote themselves to prayer. This is a close Christian prayer-and-sexuality parallel, but frames abstention as voluntary and temporary rather than an automatic ritual bar.

row.basis: Jesus stops for a blind petitioner
row.note: Jesus stops and has the blind Bartimaeus called to him. Beside the commentary's rebuke of a prophet who turned from a blind seeker, it offers a controlled comparison of a religious teacher's response to a blind petitioner, not the same story.

The evil-doer hates the light and does not come to it lest deeds be exposed. Its avoidance is more active than verbal contradiction, clarifying the commentary's spatial account of shunning admonition.

row.basis: attention to what was heard and drifting away
row.note: Hebrews calls for closer attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away; the nautical image supplies a concrete Christian counterpart to turning aside from a reminder.

row.basis: harm to persons, animals, and crops in the field
row.note: The hail strikes people, animals, and vegetation left in the field, supplying the explicit harmful outcome beside the commentary's contrast between a warning that benefits and its disregard in the Pharaoh narrative.
The Psalm's urgent "Today, if you hear his voice" casts receptivity to divine speech as a present decision, directly sharpening the commentary's offered reminder and its possible uptake.
The command not to harden the heart gives a specific inner opposite to the fearful hearer: an inward state that converts hearing into resistance.

row.basis: an ear listening to life-giving reproof
row.note: The verse calls reproof "life-giving" and locates its effect in an ear that listens, an exact Wisdom formulation of a beneficial admonition received by its hearer.

row.basis: ignoring instruction versus listening to reproof
row.note: Ignoring discipline is self-despising, while listening to reproof gains understanding; this makes the two possible responses to instruction carry opposed effects.
A rebuke enters more deeply into one with understanding than repeated blows into a fool, distinguishing a receptive, knowing addressee from a resistant one.
The wise reprover is compared to precious adornment for a listening ear, a precise image of admonition whose value depends on a receptive recipient.

row.basis: hearing prophetic words without doing them
row.note: The audience sits before Ezekiel and hears his words but does not do them; it supplies the intermediate case the commentary's spatial account allows, outward proximity without inward reception.
When watchmen call for attention to the trumpet, the people answer that they will not listen. This is a direct prophetic-warning scene of the reminder being refused.

row.basis: a message of rest that hearers will not hear
row.note: The offered word identifies rest and relief for the weary, yet its hearers will not hear it; benefit is explicitly offered and then declined.

row.basis: request for smooth speech instead of what is right
row.note: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, demanding smooth things and illusions. It specifies active evasion of admonition rather than a simple intellectual objection.

row.basis: willing obedience and good of the land
row.note: Willingness and obedience lead to eating the land's good, a concise prophetic rendering of the benefit pole in the commentary's benefit-and-harm contrast.
The following alternative makes refusal and rebellion lead to being devoured by the sword, preserving the contrary harm pole in its own verse.

row.basis: hearing Jesus' words and doing them
row.note: The hearer who acts on Jesus' words is the wise house-builder; this gives an enacted Christian counterpart to beneficial reception of admonition.
The person who hears Jesus' words but does not act is the foolish house-builder, a distinct outcome for external hearing without the response commended in the commentary.

row.basis: hearing or rejecting the commissioned messenger
row.note: Jesus says that hearing his envoys is hearing him, while rejecting them reaches through to the sender. It clarifies the commentary's distinction between the reminder-giver and the addressee responsible for reception.

row.basis: teaching that saves teacher and hearers
row.note: Persistent attention to life and teaching is said to save both the teacher and those who hear, making the possible benefit of instruction explicitly bilateral.
The charge to proclaim the word includes reproof, rebuke, and exhortation with patient teaching, a direct Christian description of the outward act the commentary calls reminder.
The indwelling word leads the community to teach and admonish one another in wisdom, preserving the commentary's specifically interpersonal account of reminder.

row.basis: receiving apostolic speech as God's word
row.note: The Thessalonians receive the word heard from messengers as God's word, which works in believers; it gives a concrete positive response to a delivered message.

row.basis: rejecting God's word and its consequence
row.note: Paul tells his audience that, by thrusting aside God's word, they judge themselves unworthy of eternal life. This is a missionary scene in which refusal of the offered word has a declared result.

row.basis: one person bringing back a wanderer
row.note: James imagines a person wandering from truth and another bringing that person back, an interpersonal counterpart to reminder aimed at someone who has moved away.

row.basis: turning a sinner back from wandering
row.note: The one who turns a sinner from wandering saves a soul from death and covers sins, making the benefit of successful corrective return concrete.

row.basis: intentional reminder to those who already know
row.note: The author intends continually to remind hearers of things they already know and in which they stand established; it directly supports the commentary's definition of reminder as a deliberate act toward others.
Paul sends Timothy to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways in Christ, giving a mediated New Testament instance of a reminder passed from one person to another.

row.basis: fear of the Lord as wisdom
row.note: Job defines fear of the Lord as wisdom and departure from evil as understanding. It is a close Wisdom comparison to the commentary's fear-and-knowledge claim, while ordering the relation differently.

row.basis: turn away and pass on from an evil path
row.note: The sage commands turning away and passing on from the path of the wicked. Its spatial idiom reverses the commentary's moral allocation: avoidance is wise when its object is evil, whereas its wretched recipient avoids beneficial reminder.

The Bavli holds a person accountable for failing to protest wrongdoing within the reach of that person's influence. It is a Jewish extension of the duty to address another, complementing but not collapsing the commentary's limit on the reminder-giver.

row.basis: first and second warning to a divisive person
row.note: After a first and second warning, the community is to decline further association with a divisive person. It gives a concrete Christian boundary for correction after a recipient proves unreceptive.
Where people neither receive the envoy nor hear the words, disciples leave and shake dust from their feet. It supplies a narrative counterpart to the commentary's limited role for the admonisher.

row.basis: one message, perishing and saving hearers
row.note: The word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing and God's power to those being saved. Its divided audience gives a Christian message-and-recipient pattern, though its proclamation is not identical with the Qur'anic reminder.

row.basis: God as giver of growth beyond the teacher
row.note: Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who gives growth. This reframes the commentary's reminder-giver limit through the Christian image of teachers who act without controlling the result.

row.basis: cloud, rain, grass made to grow
row.note: The psalm supplies the causal sequence left unspoken in 87:4: God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow. It places the brought-forth pasture between the cloud's appearance and its nourishment.

row.basis: grass for cattle and food from earth
row.note: God causes grass to grow for cattle and vegetation to yield human food. This makes explicit the commentary's claim that merʿā is grass seen as sustenance for animals and, through them, people.

row.basis: God makes grass sprout in desolation
row.note: In God's speech to Job, rain satisfies the waste land and causes tender grass to sprout. It is a close divine-agent counterpart to bringing pasture out of apparently barren ground.

row.basis: grass for livestock, then human satiety
row.note: God promises grass in the fields for Israel's livestock before saying that Israel will eat and be satisfied. The animal-before-human order directly illuminates the commentary's food chain around pasture.

row.basis: rain for seed and broad pasture
row.note: God gives rain to seed sown in the ground, rich bread from its produce, and broad pasture for livestock. It joins the commentary's rain, growth, food, and grazing scenes in one verse.

row.basis: rain waters earth, sprouting, seed and bread
