row.note: Rain and snow water the earth so that it brings forth and sprouts, supplying seed to the sower and bread to the eater. This gives the full hidden-to-edible growth sequence developed from 87:4.

row.basis: God causes growth out of ground
row.note: The LORD God causes trees to sprout out of the ground. Its divine causation and movement from earth into visible life closely match the commentary's concrete sense of إخراج.
Human life is compared to grass that sprouts in the morning and fades and withers in the evening. It gives a tightly ordered life-and-loss counterpart to 87:4–5's green pasture becoming dark debris.

row.basis: grass withers under the LORD's breath
row.note: Grass withers and flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it. The verse sharpens the commentary's insistence that the pasture's end, like its emergence, remains under divine action.

row.basis: withering grass and enduring divine word
row.note: After grass withers and flowers fade, God's word stands forever. This is a particularly close counterpart to the commentary's contrast between perishable vegetation and the recited word that is not forgotten.
The wicked are likened to chaff driven away by wind. It gives a Hebrew-scriptural use of dry vegetal waste that helps read 87:5's transformed pasture as an image of passing and loss.

row.basis: God opens graves and brings people up
row.note: God promises to open Israel's graves and bring the people up from them. It is a direct second-emergence counterpart to the commentary's move from vegetation coming out of earth to the dead being brought out.
The dead live, those dwelling in dust awake, and the earth gives birth to the dead. The earth-to-life movement directly accompanies the commentary's claim that pasture makes resurrection imaginable.

row.basis: awakening from dust to two outcomes
row.note: Those sleeping in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame. It closely parallels the commentary's second emergence and its insistence that the final state divides into contrasting outcomes.

row.basis: Midianite daughters at the well with their flock
row.note: Exodus places Moses at a Midian well where the priest's daughters arrive to water their father's flock. It is the same narrative setting behind the commentary's two women, livestock, and Moses at Midian.

row.basis: Moses helps and waters the flock
row.note: Moses intervenes for the women and waters their flock. This is the specific action that stands beside the commentary's account of Musa watering the women's animals before his pastoral years.

row.basis: Moses shepherding Jethro's flock at Horeb
row.note: Moses is tending Jethro's flock when he leads it to Horeb. It directly matches the commentary's portrait of Musa as a shepherd before the fire and prophetic call.

row.basis: Hebrew מִרְעֶה and רעה, pasture and shepherding
row.note: Hebrew mirʿeh, “pasture,” and the verb rʿh, “to shepherd/feed,” are cognate with the commentary's merʿā and rāʿā family. Ezekiel's God feeds the flock in good pasture, making explicit the pastoral semantic field that 87:4 evokes without naming God a shepherd.

row.basis: earth gives up those sleeping in it
row.note: The apocalypse says that the earth will give up those who sleep in it and the dust those who rest in silence. It supplies a Jewish articulation of the commentary's earth-to-resurrection inference.

row.basis: earth restores the dead it received
row.note: 2 Baruch imagines the earth returning the dead it has received and preserved. Its soil as temporary keeper of bodies closely corresponds to the commentary's “another bringing out” from ground.

row.basis: rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food
row.note: Paul's speech describes God giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. It is a direct Christian-scriptural analogue for 87:4's providential pasture as nourishment.

Jesus calls the grass of the field present today and thrown into an oven tomorrow, while stressing God's care for it. This matches the commentary's abrupt movement from green pasture to a fire-adjacent perishable end.

In the seed parable, the sower sleeps and rises while the seed sprouts and grows in a way he does not know. It closely reflects the commentary's hidden seed and root becoming visible vegetation beyond human control.

row.basis: earth yields blade, ear, full grain
row.note: The earth produces first a blade, then an ear, then full grain. Its staged growth gives a New Testament counterpart to the commentary's water-to-plant-to-green-to-grain sequence.
Land drinks rain and produces a useful crop, receiving blessing from God. The verse aligns rain, productive soil, and divine blessing with the commentary's pasture as a granted provision.

row.basis: land yielding thorns ends in burning
row.note: The immediately contrasted land yields thorns and thistles and ends in burning. It gives a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's patchy fertile and barren ground, and to vegetation's ominous end.

Paul distinguishes his planting and Apollos's watering from God giving the growth. It directly supports the commentary's pedagogical extension: human teaching may cultivate, but emergence and maturation belong to God.
Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who makes things grow. This is an unusually exact counterpart to the page's focus on who, rather than what mechanism, brings pasture forth.

row.basis: seed dies before coming to life
row.note: Paul answers the resurrection question by saying a sown thing does not come to life unless it dies. It gives the commentary's pasture-to-resurrection reasoning a direct agricultural form.

row.basis: bare grain is sown before its future body
row.note: The passage identifies the sown object as bare grain rather than the body it will become. It makes concrete the commentary's contrast between hidden seed, visible plant, and a later embodied emergence.

row.basis: God gives the seed its body
row.note: God gives the seed a body as he wills. This attributes the transition from grain to formed life to divine choice, like 87:4's attribution of pasture's coming forth.

row.basis: all in tombs hear and come out
row.note: Jesus says all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. It is a direct verbal and conceptual counterpart to the commentary's second خروج from the earth.

row.basis: coming out to life or judgment
row.note: Those who come out do so to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment. This supplies the two final destinations which the commentary sets after vegetation's single temporary course.

row.basis: all flesh as grass that withers
row.note: The epistle quotes the grass-and-flower image for mortal flesh. It is a close Christian reuse of the same vegetal transience that the commentary reads from 87:4 into 87:5.

The Lord's word remains forever after the preceding grass image. Like the commentary's comparison of fading pasture with unforgotten recitation, it contrasts transient vegetation with enduring proclamation.

row.basis: buried seed rises as proof of resurrection
row.note: 1 Clement uses a seed sown dry and naked in earth, then rising into life, as an argument for resurrection. It is a close early Christian interpretation of the natural cycle that the commentary presents as evidence for a second emergence.

row.basis: livestock fed before a person eats
row.note: The Talmud reads Deuteronomy 11:15's order as forbidding a person to eat before feeding an animal. That interpretation develops precisely the commentary's observation that pasture first sustains the herd.

row.basis: Moses's care for a lamb proves him fit to lead Israel
row.note: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate shepherding the test that qualifies him to shepherd Israel. It directly develops the commentary's passage from Musa's flock, staff, and care to the shepherd-leader sense of the root.

row.basis: God commands earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation
row.note: God commands the earth to sprout vegetation, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees according to kinds. It contributes the created order and measured differentiation that surround 87:4 in the commentary.

row.basis: God shepherded Jacob all his life
row.note: Jacob calls God the one who shepherded him throughout his life. It offers a personal divine-shepherd use of the Hebrew cognate field beside the commentary's cautious pastoral associations of merʿā.
David shepherds Israel with integrity and guides them with skillful hands. It realizes the commentary's extension from grazing and guarding a flock to leadership that sees a people toward its end.

row.basis: God reveals hidden things and knows darkness
row.note: God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness. This gives a biblical counterpart to the commentary's linkage of hidden seed, what is brought out, and God's knowledge of concealed things.

The servant's commission includes bringing prisoners out of a dungeon and those sitting in darkness into light. It provides a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's secondary movement from hidden darkness to an instructed, illuminated human life.

row.basis: teaching as rain and dew on grass
row.note: Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on tender grass and vegetation. It joins the page's rain-grown pasture to its later account of instruction that brings people beyond ignorance.

row.basis: harvest's edge left for poor and resident alien
row.note: The harvest owner must leave the field's edge and gleanings for the poor and alien. It is a concrete Torah counterpart to the commentary's claim that what the ground yields carries a due share for others.

row.basis: firstfruits brought before God in worship
row.note: Israel brings the first of the ground's fruit before the LORD and bows in worship. It pairs agricultural yield with praise, echoing the commentary's ordering of divine provision and sanctifying the Lord's name.

row.basis: water and food without money or price
row.note: The thirsty are invited to water, wine, and milk without money or price. Its gratuitous food image gives a close biblical analogue to the commentary's provision and admonition offered without demanded payment.

row.basis: God needs no food from creatures
row.note: God says that if hungry he would not tell humans, since the world and its fullness are his. It clarifies the commentary's claim that the giver of pasture does not need a return payment from those who live on it.

row.basis: being sent out of the garden to the ground
row.note: The LORD sends the human out of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken. It gives a specific biblical instance of the commentary's secondary sense of “bringing out” as removal from an inhabited place rather than plant emergence.

row.basis: brought out in order to be brought in
row.note: God brings Israel out from Egypt in order to bring them into the promised land. The out/in pair closely accompanies the commentary's semantic contrast between departure from a place and entry into one.

row.basis: life made in secret in earth-like depths
row.note: The psalmist's frame is not hidden when made in secret and woven in the depths of the earth. It extends the commentary's unseen earth imagery from seed to the hidden beginning of human life.

row.basis: God renews the face of the ground
row.note: When God sends his spirit, creatures are created and the face of the ground is renewed. It is a natural-renewal analogue for the commentary's annual revivification of dead land.

row.basis: earth's sprouts image righteousness and praise
row.note: As earth brings forth sprouts and a garden makes seed sprout, God causes righteousness and praise to sprout. This is a precise biblical bridge between vegetation emerging from soil and the commentary's cultivation of human understanding.

row.basis: peah and firstfruits among required agricultural gifts
row.note: The Mishnah lists the field-corner gift and firstfruits among practices without a fixed measure. It gives Jewish legal shape to the commentary's harvest-as-yield that is not merely possessed but bears a claim for others.

The Talmud compares the day of rain with the resurrection of the dead. That explicit rabbinic pairing makes visible the inferential bridge from rain-fed revival of land to resurrection that the commentary draws.

row.basis: good soil receives the word and bears fruit
row.note: Jesus interprets the good soil as hearers who receive the word and bear fruit. It changes the commentary's physically uneven soil into a teaching image, making the interpretive bridge explicit rather than assuming it.

row.basis: commission to turn people from darkness to light
row.note: Paul's commission opens eyes and turns people from darkness to light. It closely parallels the commentary's secondary use of bringing out as education and deliverance from darkness.

row.basis: hidden things of darkness brought to light
row.note: At judgment the Lord brings to light what is hidden in darkness and discloses hearts' purposes. It gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's hidden seed and divine disclosure of what lies concealed.
Jesus tells the disciples to give freely because they received freely. It specifically parallels the commentary's extension from freely given pasture to an admonitory ministry that asks no fee.
Paul describes making the gospel free of charge rather than using his right to support. This is the concrete apostolic counterpart to the commentary's unpaid teaching and uncharged provision.
Elders are told to shepherd God's flock while exercising oversight. It closely matches the commentary's semantic account in which grazing, guarding, and watchful responsibility belong together.

row.basis: good shepherd gives life for sheep
row.note: Jesus identifies himself as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. It offers the specifically Christian development of the shepherd image lying at the edge of the commentary's merʿā-root reflection.

The Creator who commanded light from darkness shines in hearts to give knowledge. It joins creation, illumination, and learning in the manner of the commentary's move from soil-darkness to instruction.

row.basis: world passes but God's doer remains
row.note: The world and its desire pass away, but the one who does God's will remains forever. It supplies a Christian ethical form of the commentary's contrast between transient pasture and what is more enduring.

row.basis: sun withers grass and rich person's flower falls
row.note: The sun's heat withers grass and makes its flower fall while the rich person fades in pursuits. It gives another focused New Testament use of vegetal decline for the passing human condition.

row.basis: grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: A grain of wheat falls into earth and dies in order to bear much fruit. It forms a Christological transformation of the seed-death-and-new-life pattern the commentary applies to pasture and later emergence.
Nothing hidden remains without becoming manifest and coming to light. It parallels the commentary's secondary association of bringing forth with making the concealed visible.
The visible is temporary while the unseen is eternal. It gives a concise Christian analogue for the commentary's contrast of what emerges and perishes in this world with the lasting final reality.

row.basis: God feeds birds without their sowing or harvesting
row.note: The heavenly Father feeds birds that neither sow nor reap nor store. It complements the commentary's pasture-as-provision theme by making divine feeding independent of the creatures' own agricultural control.

row.basis: green pastures and waters under the shepherd's lead
row.note: The psalm's shepherd makes the flock lie down in green pasture and leads it beside waters. It supplies the water and shepherd-led grazing scene that the commentary says is compressed into merʿā.

row.basis: Hebrew רֹעִי, “my shepherd,” cognate with رعي
row.note: The Hebrew rōʿî belongs to the rʿh cognate family developed in the commentary for merʿā and rāʿā. The verse gives the compact title “my shepherd,” against which the page's deliberately indirect pastoral language can be assessed.

row.basis: Hebrew רְעוּ, “pasture the flock,” after watering
row.note: Jacob tells the shepherds to water the flock and then pasture it. This nonmetaphorical cognate use joins the commentary's sequence of water, grass, animal mouth, and the act of grazing.

row.basis: shepherding a people with a staff
row.note: The prayer asks God to shepherd his people with his staff and let the flock graze. It brings together the staff, flock, and pastoral rule that the commentary develops from Musa's staff and the merʿā root family.

row.basis: leader who leads out and brings in so sheep have a shepherd
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out and come in before the people, lead them out and bring them in, so they are not sheep without a shepherd. It tightly joins the commentary's secondary out/in sense with its leader-shepherd sense.

row.basis: rain in season and earth yielding produce
row.note: God promises rain in its season, the land's yield, and fruit from the trees. It is a direct covenantal counterpart to the commentary's source-to-pasture sequence of rain, ground, and provision.

row.basis: storm clouds, showers, and field vegetation
row.note: The LORD makes storm clouds, gives showers of rain, and gives vegetation in the field. It closely matches the page's cloud-to-rain-to-plant chain, including the cloud's first visible role.

row.basis: seasonal rain before gathered grain, wine, and oil
row.note: God gives the early and latter rain so Israel gathers the field's produce. This provides the rain-and-annual-yield side of the pasture provision that the next verse extends to livestock.
At the call, God asks Moses what is in his hand and he answers, “a staff.” It is the direct Torah counterpart to the commentary's remembered shepherd's staff at the fire.

row.basis: staff cast down and becoming a serpent
row.note: Moses casts the staff down and it becomes a serpent. This supplies the specific transformation noted when the commentary follows the shepherd's staff into the call narrative.

row.basis: God makes a green tree wither and a dry tree flourish
row.note: God declares that he brings down the high tree, makes the green tree wither, and makes the dry tree flourish. Its divine reversal gives a close prophetic counterpart to 87:4–5's brought-forth green turning dark, while retaining renewal as God's act.

row.basis: command for the dead Lazarus to come out
row.note: Jesus calls the dead Lazarus to come out of the tomb. It is a narrative realization of the commentary's second emergence: a dead human is summoned from the place that held him.

row.basis: sown in decay and raised in incorruption
row.note: Paul describes the body as sown in corruption and raised in incorruption. It gives the page's perishing vegetation and more lasting future a direct resurrection contrast.

row.basis: raised to everlasting life, with a contrary final outcome
row.note: A martyr expects God to raise the faithful to everlasting life while denying the persecutor a resurrection to life. It specifically parallels the commentary's move from earthly death to distinct final destinies.

Job observes that a cut tree still has hope because it can sprout again. The natural recovery image gives a focused Hebrew Bible companion to the commentary's vegetation-based inference that death need not be the final state.

row.basis: deep things out of darkness brought to light
row.note: God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings gloom to light. It makes explicit the hidden-to-visible movement that the commentary hears in pasture emerging from unseen soil.

row.basis: God's word goes out and accomplishes its purpose
row.note: God's word goes out and succeeds in its appointed work. Following the rain-and-sprouting comparison immediately before it, this verse provides a biblical bridge to the commentary's contrast between fading grass and effective instruction.

row.basis: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: In a worship setting, Israel is called the people of God's pasture and the sheep of his hand. It joins praise, divine identity, pasture, and flock in a form particularly close to the commentary's opening “He who” descriptions.

row.basis: field's seventh-year yield for poor and wild animals
row.note: The seventh year's field produce is left so the poor may eat and wild animals take what remains. It gives a concrete Torah form to the commentary's pasture as freely available sustenance rather than a commodity retained by its grower.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf left for vulnerable neighbors
row.note: A forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow. This is a distinct harvest-share counterpart to the commentary's claim that land's yield bears a due for others.

row.basis: seedtime and harvest as an unbroken seasonal rhythm
row.note: Seedtime and harvest are promised to continue while the earth endures. It supplies the annual rhythm behind the commentary's description of pasture as the year's recurring yield.

row.basis: water on dry ground and spirit on descendants
row.note: God promises water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land, then his spirit on descendants. It explicitly makes physical revival of dry earth the vehicle for a human, spiritual enlargement like the commentary's move from growth to education.

row.basis: descendants sprout among grass beside watercourses
row.note: The recipients of the preceding promise are said to sprout among grass like trees by flowing water. It is a specific biblical use of vegetal emergence to depict a human community's growth.
The human returns to the dust from which he was taken. It supplies the first half of the commentary's earth–return–second-emergence pattern, while leaving the later resurrection claim to other texts.

row.basis: Zipporah given after Moses agrees to dwell with her father
row.note: Exodus says Moses agrees to dwell with the Midianite and is then given Zipporah; the commentary's Qur'anic scene makes marriage contingent on a stated term of shepherding labor. The shared Midian sequence is clear, but the terms of the marriage arrangement differ.

row.basis: tree by water, seasonal fruit, unfading leaf
row.note: The Torah-meditating person is like a water-fed tree with seasonal fruit and a leaf that does not wither. It offers a deliberate counter-image to the commentary's temporary pasture and links lasting fruitfulness to received instruction.

row.basis: idols cannot give rain; the LORD made all
row.note: Jeremiah asks whether any false gods can make rain and answers by hoping in the LORD who made all things. It is a precise anti-idolatry-and-provision companion to the commentary's worship question around the one who brings hidden life out.

row.basis: watered tree stays green in heat and drought
row.note: The trusting person is like a tree by water whose leaves stay green and whose fruit does not fail in drought. It gives a biblical counter-pattern to the green pasture that dries, with endurance read through trust.
The restored community's bones flourish like grass as God's hand is made known. This unusually bodily grass image bridges the commentary's vegetal revival with its attention to embodied resurrection.

row.basis: sprouted seed scorched and withered for lack of root
row.note: The sun scorches the sprouted seed and it withers because it has no root. It gives a close specific counterpart to the commentary's green growth that reaches a dry, perishing end.
When the grain permits it, the sickle is sent because harvest has come. It adds the completed crop and reaping stage to the page's account of yearly yield and the plant's full course.

row.basis: farmer waits for precious fruit and seasonal rains
row.note: The farmer patiently waits for the earth's valuable fruit through early and latter rains. In its context of awaiting the Lord, it couples the annual crop cycle with expectant eschatological patience.

row.basis: God supplies seed, bread, and harvest of righteousness
row.note: God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, then increases the harvest of righteousness. It directly joins material produce, gratuitous provision, and the moral growth that the commentary develops from the pasture image.

row.basis: water of life received without price
row.note: The thirsty are invited to take the water of life without cost. It provides an eschatological Christian counterpart to the commentary's theme of life-giving provision and admonition that demand no payment.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life-water
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water. It is a Christian eschatological development of the pasture, care, guidance, and enduring-life complex explored in the commentary.

row.basis: sowing for corruption or eternal life
row.note: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life. The agricultural figure makes the commentary's transient growth and divergent final outcomes into an explicit ethical contrast.

row.basis: harvest as the end of the age
row.note: Jesus identifies the harvest as the end of the age and the reapers as angels. It gives the commentary's annual field imagery an explicitly eschatological culmination without reducing the physical pasture itself to allegory.
The psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, giving the source's Rab who owns and directs the herd a direct divine pastoral frame.
The shepherd brings the dependent flock to nourishing pasture and rest, closely matching the commentary's owner who brings the herd to a protected grazing place.

row.basis: restore and guide in right paths
row.note: The same shepherd restores and leads the person on paths; this makes the source's هدى B003 front-leading image part of pastoral care rather than mere travel.

row.basis: we are his; people and sheep of his pasture
row.note: The verse joins belonging to the creator with being the sheep of his pasture, directly combining the source's Rab-as-owner with its herd and grazing scene.

row.basis: cattle on a thousand hills are mine
row.note: God's claim over cattle supplies a concrete biblical form for the commentary's insistence that Rab is the owner before he is the herd's guide.

row.basis: ox knows owner; donkey its master's manger
row.note: Isaiah makes an animal's recognition of its owner and feeding-place a rebuke to Israel; it adds a reversal to the source's animal scene and its later naming of one's own Rab.

row.basis: green vegetation assigned as animal food
row.note: The creation decree gives green plants to land animals for food, a direct scriptural counterpart to God bringing forth pasture for livestock.

row.basis: grass for livestock and food for people
row.note: The land blessing explicitly moves from grass supplied for cattle to human eating, paralleling the commentary's pasture as provision for both people and their animals.

row.basis: grass for cattle; plants and food for humans
row.note: The psalm treats the sprouting of grass for cattle and human food as God's work, closely matching the source's creator of pasture and its 79:33 and 80:31 provision motif.

row.basis: rain makes grass grow on mountains
row.note: God covers the sky, prepares rain, and sprouts grass on the mountains; this connects divine production of grazing land with the commentary's mountain-and-pasture association.
The creator's provision of food to animals makes explicit the care for livestock that the source reads into pasture.

row.basis: leader goes before the people; sheep without shepherd
row.note: Moses asks for a successor who goes out before and brings in the congregation so it is not sheep without a shepherd; it directly joins the source's Musa setting, B003 leading-from-the-front, and ruler-as-shepherd.

row.basis: Moses and Aaron lead God's people like a flock
row.note: The psalm says God led the people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, giving the commentary's Moses-linked scene a divine owner, human agents, and flock in one verse.
Israel tells David that he will shepherd God's people and be their ruler; its royal formula is a precise analogue to the source's B002 equation of governor and shepherd.

row.basis: God leads people as sheep and guides them as flock
row.note: The wilderness exodus is described with both flock-leading and guidance, closely matching the source's single work of owner, guide, and herd.

row.basis: David shepherds with integrity and skillful guidance
row.note: David's shepherding is defined by inner integrity and skilled leading, developing the source's claim that pastoral language can describe competent public rule.

row.basis: gather, carry, and gently lead the flock
row.note: The divine shepherd gathers vulnerable lambs, carries them, and gently leads nursing ewes; it gives concrete protective actions to the source's guarded pasture and leading owner.

row.basis: God gathers and keeps Israel as a shepherd
row.note: The one who scattered Israel gathers and guards it as a shepherd guards a flock, making protection and restoration integral to divine ownership.

row.basis: shepherd-rulers feed themselves instead of flock
row.note: Ezekiel's indictment turns the source's ruler-as-shepherd image into a negative test: leaders who consume provision themselves fail the flock entrusted to them.

row.basis: God gathers sheep and feeds them on mountains
row.note: God himself brings the scattered flock out, gathers it, and feeds it on the mountains; this is a particularly close scene of owner, leading, and pasture.

row.basis: good pasture and secure grazing land
row.note: The promised sheep receive good pasture and lie down in rich grazing land, supplying the protected-pasture element of the source without reducing it to a word match.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002/B003/B007; Hebrew רעה and מרעה
row.note: The Hebrew verb for tending and noun for pasture are cognate with the source's ر ع ي family; here they describe God feeding sheep in a good pasture, including both the source's shepherd and marʿā senses.

row.basis: God himself pastures and gives rest
row.note: The divine speaker personally shepherds the flock and makes it lie down, the clearest biblical formulation of the commentary's owner who both leads and supplies the grazing place.
God appoints David as the flock's shepherd, preserving the distinction between the ultimate owner and a commissioned human ruler developed in the source.
In the restoration promise, the released people feed along the ways and find pasture even on bare heights; it extends the source's pasture image into guided return and unexpected provision.

row.basis: guide to springs after hunger and thirst
row.note: The compassionate leader guides the redeemed to water after removing hunger and thirst, pairing direction with provision as the commentary does.

row.basis: ruler stands and shepherds in the LORD's strength
row.note: Micah joins rule, secure dwelling, and shepherding in the strength of God, a direct royal form of the source's ruler who tends his people.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002/B007; Hebrew רְעוּ pasture the flock
row.note: Jacob's well scene tells the herdsmen to water the flock and then go pasture it; the Hebrew cognate shows the source's ر ع ي family in an ordinary husbandry setting.

row.basis: grass withers when the LORD's breath blows
row.note: The grass fades under God's breath, furnishing a close biblical image for the source's pasture that is later made into dark debris and for its turn toward the temporary world.

row.basis: grass fades but God's word endures
row.note: The contrast between fading grass and what endures gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's move from temporary worldly provision to the better, lasting life.

row.basis: Moses carries the thirsty straying lamb
row.note: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate attention to a runaway lamb the reason God entrusts Israel to him; it turns the source's Musa-and-shepherd scene into a criterion for protective leadership.

row.basis: leader must go out and come in before Israel
row.note: The exposition of Numbers 27:17 reads Moses's request as one for a leader present with the people rather than distant from them, sharpening the source's image of the animal that leads the others from in front.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002; Aramaic rʿyā for shepherd
row.note: The Aramaic witness retains the congregation-as-sheep-without-a-shepherd image in Moses's succession request; its rʿyā is a cognate of the source's rāʿī and still carries public leadership.

row.basis: calls own sheep and leads them out
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, an unusually exact New Testament counterpart to the source's owner and B003 animal-leader scene.

row.basis: goes before sheep and they follow
row.note: The shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and they follow his known voice, directly realizing the commentary's detail of front animals guiding those behind.

row.basis: go in and out and find pasture
row.note: Within the shepherd discourse, entering through Jesus leads to safety and pasture; it joins protection with access to grazing as in the source's unified scene.

row.basis: good shepherd lays down life for sheep
row.note: The good shepherd's self-giving makes protection of the flock more radical than the source's lexical description of the shepherd who surrounds and preserves livestock.

row.basis: hired hand does not own sheep and abandons them
row.note: The contrast hinges on ownership and guarding: a hireling flees while the true shepherd's sheep are endangered, a negative foil to the source's owner who protects the herd.
Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep develops the source's closing move in which the person names this owner as his own Rab.
Matthew's citation calls the coming figure both ruler and shepherd of Israel, precisely echoing the source's ruler/shepherd equation.

row.basis: crowd as sheep without shepherd; Jesus teaches
row.note: Jesus responds to a shepherdless crowd by teaching it, making guidance of people the action expected from the missing shepherd.
The risen Jesus entrusts his own sheep to Peter's care, distinguishing the flock's owner from the human leader who is commissioned to tend it.
The elders must watch over the whole flock and shepherd God's assembly; it makes pastoral rule explicitly attentive and accountable, resonating with B002 and the source's B003 watchfulness.

row.basis: return to shepherd and overseer of souls
row.note: Straying sheep return to a shepherd who is also an overseer, joining restoration, guidance, and supervisory care in the source's pastoral image.

row.basis: elders shepherd God's flock with oversight
row.note: The elders' charge makes shepherding a form of responsible oversight, giving a Christian communal application to the source's ruler who tends a people.
The title chief shepherd places local shepherd-leaders under a higher shepherd, akin to the source's distinction between the owner and those who lead within the herd scene.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life
row.note: The Lamb becomes the shepherd who guides the flock to living-water springs; it carries the source's pasture-and-guidance image into its own enduring, eschatological setting.

row.basis: ruling nations expressed by the shepherd verb
row.note: The royal judge's rule over nations is stated with the verb to shepherd, preserving the political sense of tending subjects foregrounded in source B002.

row.basis: all flesh like grass; grass withers
row.note: Peter applies fading grass to human mortality, a direct Christian extension of the source's pasture-to-debris and worldly-transience turn.
The verse's enduring word completes the preceding grass image with a lasting contrast, comparable to the source's contrast between worldly life and what remains.

row.basis: source ر ع ي B002; Syriac rʿyā, shepherd
row.note: The Peshitta's Syriac rʿyā for Jesus as the good shepherd is cognate with Arabic rāʿī in the source and uses the shared root for self-giving flock care.

row.basis: Moses pastures Jethro's flock to Horeb
row.note: The biblical Moses first appears at Horeb while tending and leading a flock; alongside the commentary's explicit Musa setting, this gives a concrete narrative pastoral setting without claiming the two accounts are the same scene.

row.basis: Moses protects shepherds and waters their flock
row.note: Moses drives away attackers and waters the flock for Midianite shepherds, a specific earlier portrayal of the protective action the source assigns to a shepherd.

row.basis: land belongs to God; people are temporary residents
row.note: God's ownership of land and the people's temporary tenancy give a land-based counterpart to the source's Rab-as-owner and its explanation of pasture as temporary metāʿ.

row.basis: Lord of sheep and accountable appointed shepherds
row.note: The Animal Apocalypse represents Israel as sheep under the Lord of the sheep and appointed shepherds whose stewardship is judged; it expands the source's owner, flock, and delegated leaders into an apocalyptic history.

row.basis: owner seeks the one lost sheep
row.note: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost sheep, making the source's enclosing and preserving shepherd an active seeker rather than only a keeper of pasture.

row.basis: Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: The title great shepherd binds communal pastoral imagery to the God of peace and resurrection, a Christian theological development of the source's divine owner/shepherd.

row.basis: grass today, cast into an oven tomorrow
row.note: Jesus uses grass's brief life to teach trust in God's provision; the image closely meets the source's created pasture that soon changes, while its argument concerns anxious humans rather than livestock.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 46
row.basis: Christ as good shepherd versus hireling
row.note: Augustine's exposition of John 10 reads the good shepherd's care and self-giving as Christological, giving a major Christian interpretive frame for the owner, flock, and protective contrast in the source.

row.basis: angel of repentance appears as shepherd
row.note: Hermas receives moral commands from a shepherd figure; this later Christian use turns pastoral guidance into corrective formation, a plausible extension of the source's Rab-as-corrector within its herd image.

row.basis: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: The verse makes Israel both God's people and the sheep held in his hand; its call to hear his voice joins ownership, pastoral care, and responsive recognition of the Rab.

row.basis: Shepherd of Israel leads Joseph like a flock
row.note: The invocation directly addresses God as Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph as a flock, concentrating the source's owner and front-leading functions.

row.basis: shepherd and carry God's inheritance forever
row.note: The plea asks God to save, bless, shepherd, and carry his people forever; it makes protective pastoral rule explicitly enduring, relevant to the source's turn from temporary pasture to what lasts.

row.basis: God has shepherded Jacob all his life
row.note: Jacob calls God the one who has been his shepherd throughout life, giving the source's personal naming of one's Rab a concentrated ancestral precedent.

row.basis: flock of God's pasture gives thanks forever
row.note: The flock-of-your-pasture formula culminates in perpetual thanksgiving; it brings the source's opening glorification of the Rab into the pastoral relation itself.

row.basis: David taken from pasture and following sheep to rule Israel
row.note: God recalls taking David from following sheep to be prince over Israel, making the shepherd-to-ruler transition explicit rather than merely metaphorical.

row.basis: David pursues a predator and rescues the lamb
row.note: David's shepherding includes going after the lion or bear and delivering the sheep from its mouth, a concrete protective action for the source's keeper who guards livestock.

row.basis: shepherd bears loss for animals torn or stolen
row.note: Jacob describes accepting liability for flock losses rather than passing them to the owner; this gives a demanding economic form to the source's protective shepherd.

row.basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
row.note: The instruction requires sustained, informed attention to a herd, closely matching the source's B003 extension from shepherding to watching where a matter is going.

row.basis: old grass passes and new growth appears
row.note: The pastoral maxim traces hay's disappearance, fresh growth, and mountain vegetation; it offers a close agrarian counterpart to pasture brought forth and then transformed.

row.basis: rain, abundant bread, and livestock grazing broad pasture
row.note: The promised divine rain produces abundance and broad pasture for cattle, directly matching the commentary's creator who produces grazing provision for people and animals.

row.basis: working oxen and donkeys eat prepared fodder
row.note: Farm animals receive rich fodder while doing agricultural work, a close counterpart to the source's B007 detail of working animals grazing around a settled community.

row.basis: Moses gives water to congregation and livestock
row.note: God instructs Moses to bring water from the rock for both the people and their animals; it is a specific Mosaic scene of shared human-and-livestock provision.

row.basis: just rule in the fear of God
row.note: David's oracle defines the God-fearing ruler whose effect is developed in the next verse; it supplies the governing member of the source's shepherd-ruler image.

row.basis: rain causes grass to sprout from the earth
row.note: The next line compares the just ruler's advent to light and rain that sprouts grass, a striking joining of righteous rule with the growth of the source's pasture.

row.basis: pastures clothed with flocks and fields sing
row.note: Pastures are filled with flocks and the fertile landscape shouts and sings; it lets the source's opening praise encompass the very pasture and herd that God causes to thrive.

row.basis: evil-doers sprout like grass only for destruction
row.note: The psalm uses flourishing grass for a short-lived prosperity that ends in destruction, closely paralleling the source's pasture that becomes debris and its warning about transient life.
The contrast calls YHWH the Most High forever, joining the source's al-Aʿlā title to its contrast between fading grass and enduring reality.

row.basis: wise instruction given by one shepherd
row.note: Ecclesiastes attributes wisdom that prods and steadies its hearers to one shepherd, extending the source's pastoral guide into correction and instruction.

row.basis: failed shepherds do not strengthen, heal, bind, seek, or restore
row.note: The detailed catalogue says what pastoral rule owes the vulnerable flock; it concretizes the source's claim that the shepherd surrounds and preserves those in his care.

row.basis: God seeks lost, restores strayed, binds injured, and strengthens weak
row.note: God's own response reverses failed leadership through specific acts of search, restoration, and healing, deepening the source's owner-protector scene.
The chapter's conclusion explicitly calls the people God's sheep and flock of his pasture, completing the source's owner, people, and grazing-place relation.

row.basis: shepherds after God's heart feed knowledge and understanding
row.note: God promises leaders who feed the people with knowledge and discernment, making pastoral governance an intellectual and moral guidance like the source's leading function.

row.basis: shepherds lead sheep astray from their resting place
row.note: The lost sheep are misdirected by their shepherds through the mountains and forget their resting place; this is a pointed negative reversal of the source's guide who brings a flock to pasture.

row.basis: shepherd rescues remnants from a lion's mouth
row.note: Amos's image of a shepherd recovering only a leg or ear from a predator gives a grim, concrete limit case for the source's protecting shepherd.

row.basis: foolish shepherd neither seeks, heals, nor nourishes
row.note: The false shepherd neglects the lost and injured and consumes the fat flock instead; this negative portrait tests every protective and provisioning element developed in the source.

row.basis: grazing leads to fullness, pride, and forgetting the owner
row.note: Hosea depicts pasture and fullness producing self-exaltation and forgetfulness of God, an ethical counterpoint to the source's pasture as temporary provision under its owner.

row.basis: Davidic king shepherds the Lord's flock faithfully
row.note: The psalm portrays the hoped-for Davidic ruler as faithfully shepherding the Lord's flock, preventing their stumbling in pasture and leading them in holiness; it fuses delegated rule, divine ownership, and guidance.

row.basis: eternal life and no snatching from the shepherd's hand
row.note: Jesus gives the sheep unending life and guarantees that no one will snatch them away, bringing the source's guarded flock and its lasting-life contrast together.

row.basis: fierce wolves will not spare the flock
row.note: Paul's warning supplies the threat that makes pastoral watchfulness necessary, sharpening the source's protective shepherd rather than repeating its generic title.

row.basis: leaders do not dominate but become examples to the flock
row.note: The elders are forbidden to lord it over those entrusted to them and instead model conduct; it qualifies the source's ruler-shepherd relation with a specific non-dominating form of leadership.

row.basis: flock no longer hungers or thirsts
row.note: The eschatological community's freedom from hunger and thirst supplies the provision that the following shepherd-and-springs image brings to completion, echoing the source's pasture and lasting-life movement.

row.basis: pastors joined with teachers in communal leadership
row.note: The risen Christ gives pastors-and-teachers to the community, a concise Christian institutional use of shepherd language for guiding and forming people.

row.basis: Paul rereads the unmuzzled ox command for apostolic support
row.note: Paul cites the Torah's feeding of a working ox and asks how its principle bears on apostolic workers; this is a deliberate interpretive reapplication of animal provision, not simply a duplicate pasture image.

row.basis: the world passes away while the doer of God's will remains
row.note: The verse gives a direct Christian formulation of the source's distinction between the passing worldly life reached through temporary provision and what endures.

row.basis: riches and crown do not endure
row.note: Following the flock-watch instruction, the proverb states that wealth and political standing are not permanent; its own transience claim clarifies why the source calls pasture provision temporary metāʿ.

row.basis: working ox must not be muzzled
row.note: The law protects an animal's access to food while it works, a concrete ethical analogue to the source's working camels and livestock sustained by grazing.

row.basis: camels receive straw and fodder at a household
row.note: The servant's camels are unloaded and supplied with straw and fodder at the house, a specific narrative counterpart to the source's camels grazing around people and dwellings.

row.basis: God makes grass sprout in desolate ground
row.note: God satisfies wasteland and makes grass grow where people do not cultivate it; this extends the source's pasture-maker to nonhuman and wild terrain.

row.basis: God declares the end from the beginning
row.note: The source explicitly makes the pasture's maker one who sees what it will become; Isaiah's divine knowledge of end from beginning is a precise theological bridge for that secondary claim.

row.basis: a child leads reconciled wild and domestic animals
row.note: The future peace scene gives a child the action of leading a mixed animal company, an indirect but specific counterpart to the source's B003 image of a leader before other animals.

row.basis: cow and bear graze; lion eats straw like ox
row.note: The transformed creation is pictured through shared grazing and fodder among animals, a distinct eschatological extension of the source's pasture and livestock scene.

row.basis: the righteous knows an animal's needs
row.note: The proverb makes attentive care for an animal a mark of righteousness, giving an ethical consequence to the source's shepherd who protects livestock.

row.basis: one who tends a flock shares its milk
row.note: Paul's pastoral labor analogy assumes that the flock's keeper receives its produce, linking the source's pasture as provision with the work of tending it.

row.basis: plowman and thresher work in hope of a share
row.note: Paul states the human-worker application of the ox text: laborers should expect a share of the yield. It reframes the source's livestock provision as a principle about those who serve a community.

row.basis: little flock and the Father's gift of the kingdom
row.note: Jesus calls the disciples a little flock while locating their security in the Father's gift of the kingdom, joining pastoral belonging with the source's movement beyond temporary worldly provision.

row.basis: seen things are temporary and unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul's temporal-eternal contrast is a close Christian formulation of the source's conclusion about the worldly life and the more enduring reality, though it does not itself use pasture imagery.

row.basis: shepherd separates sheep from goats at judgment
row.note: The final judgment is pictured through a shepherd sorting a mixed herd; it gives the source's animal scene an eschatological use distinct from provisioning and protection.
The passion prediction reverses the source's secure owner-and-flock scene: when the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter, showing the flock's dependence on its guide.

row.basis: lost largest sheep sought over the ninety-nine
row.note: This Christian apocryphal version makes the wandering sheep the largest and specially loved one; it is a distinctive reception of the owner who actively seeks and values a member of the flock.

row.basis: Creator fixes earth's measurements and stretches a line
row.note: Job's creator asks who set the earth's measures and stretched the measuring line over it. It supplies the same concrete move from creating to proportioning that the commentary hears in خلق followed by قدّر.

God gives the wind a weight and apportions waters by measure. The verse makes cosmic making an act of exact weighting and measurement, matching the commentary's maker sequence rather than a generic creation claim.

row.basis: measured waters, heavens, dust, and mountains
row.note: The maker measures waters, marks off heaven, and weighs earth and mountains. Its successive hand-measurements are a close biblical counterpart to the commentary's picture of creation as skilled measuring and setting straight.
Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. This gives an explicit Jewish formulation of the commentary's claim that created things have a determined measure.
Qohelet assigns a time to every matter under heaven. It closely meets the commentary's secondary claim that every thing has both a measure and an appointed term.

Paul says the creator determined the allotted periods and boundaries of the nations. The text extends measured creation into fixed historical limits, the same measure-and-end dimension developed from قدّر.

row.basis: crooked made straight; rough made level
row.note: The preparation of the Lord's way turns crooked ground straight and rough terrain level. This is the physical road-making counterpart to the commentary's سوّى as correcting crookedness before guidance.

row.basis: God leads blind people and levels rough places
row.note: God leads those who cannot see on an unknown way and makes rough places level before them. The verse joins the two actions that the commentary keeps together: smoothing or straightening, then leading toward a way.

row.basis: goes before and levels the way
row.note: God promises to go before Cyrus and level the elevated ground. Going in front, as the commentary's staff does, is paired here with making a traversable route.

row.basis: pillar goes before Israel to lead the way
row.note: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar in order to lead them on the road. It gives a narrative form to the commentary's explanation that a leading implement receives its name from going ahead of its bearer.

row.basis: teaching what profits and leading the right way
row.note: God identifies himself as the one who teaches Israel for its profit and leads it in the way it should go. The unusual pairing directly brings 87:9's benefit together with 87:3's guidance.

row.basis: teaching Ephraim to walk, carrying him
row.note: God recalls teaching Ephraim to walk and taking him up in his arms. This depicts the Lord's care as gradual formation and direction, close to the commentary's ربّ as bringing something through stages to completion.

row.basis: God's workmanship, created and prepared for a walk
row.note: Believers are God's workmanship, created for works God prepared beforehand so that they would walk in them. The verse makes creation a crafted making with a prepared direction of travel.

row.basis: maturity and the measure of full stature
row.note: The community is brought to a mature person and the measure of Christ's full stature. It offers a Christian development of the commentary's phase-by-phase movement to a completed limit.
The one who began a good work will bring it to completion. Its beginning-to-finish divine workmanship closely parallels the commentary's account of ربّ as completing what is gradually made.

row.basis: servant made a polished arrow and hidden in a quiver
row.note: God makes the servant a polished arrow and conceals him in a quiver. This directly meets the commentary's smoothed arrow shaft and arrow-container, while making the fashioned projectile a figure of a divinely directed mission.

row.basis: God creates the smith who blows the coal fire and makes a weapon
row.note: The creator is said to make the smith, his coal fire, and the weapon fitted for its task. It makes the commentary's fire, straightening craft, and aimed implement part of a single divine-artisan scene.

row.basis: plumb line set against a built wall
row.note: The Lord stands by a wall made with a plumb line and holds the line himself. This supplies an Israelite image of measuring straightness that turns the commentary's artisanal measuring into an evaluative act.

row.basis: measuring reed or rod for temple, altar, and worshipers
row.note: John is given a reed like a rod and commanded to measure the temple, altar, and worshipers. The passage preserves the joined material images of a staff-like implement and exact measurement.

row.basis: wineskin in smoke that does not forget statutes
row.note: The speaker has become like a wineskin in smoke but does not forget God's statutes. It tightly joins the commentary's weathered leather vessel with its later concern for a remembrance that remains effective.

row.basis: God knows hidden things and darkness
row.note: God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness. This is a direct counterpart to 87:7's knowledge of what is openly spoken and what remains concealed.
God will bring every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment. It adds the judicial consequence to the commentary's open-and-hidden knowledge and its ensuing fire.
No creature is hidden from God's sight; all are exposed before the one to whom account is given. This follows the same speaker, hiddenness, and accountability structure as 87:7.

row.basis: hidden darkness and heart-intentions disclosed at judgment
row.note: The Lord brings to light what is hidden in darkness and discloses the purposes of hearts. It gives a specific New Testament development of concealed knowledge becoming morally consequential.

row.basis: reproof helps the wise but provokes the scoffer
row.note: Reproof is hated by a scoffer but loved by the wise. It gives a close sapiential analogue to the commentary's conditional reminder: the same admonition benefits a receptive person and is rejected by another.

row.basis: those who fear God and a book of remembrance
row.note: Those who fear the Lord are heard, and a book of remembrance is written before him. The verse specifically links fear with remembrance, the sequence named in 87:9-10.

row.basis: hearing God's voice rather than hardening the heart
row.note: The exhortation says that when God's voice is heard, hearers must not harden their hearts. It is a close response-pattern counterpart to the wretched person who keeps away from the reminder.

row.basis: Babylonian king shakes arrows for divination
row.note: At a crossroads the Babylonian king shakes arrows, consults household gods, and examines a liver to choose his route. This is the clearest biblical scene of arrow-divination beside the commentary's Qur'anic prohibition of seeking apportioned outcomes through azlam.

row.basis: surveyed land in seven divisions followed by lots
row.note: Joshua orders a written division of the land into seven parts and then casts lots before the Lord. It combines prior measurement and description with the distribution of shares by lot, just as the commentary moves from measure to apportioned portions.

row.basis: lot cast and land apportioned by a measuring line
row.note: God casts the lot for the creatures and apportions their land with a line. This unusually joins the commentary's two main operations: measured boundary-making and assigned lot.

row.basis: lot cast, but its decision from the Lord
row.note: Proverbs says a lot is cast into the lap while every judgment of it comes from the Lord. Against the commentary's ban on divinatory arrows, it supplies a contrasting Israelite maxim that assigns a cast lot's outcome to divine decision.

row.basis: inheritance divided by lot among named tribes
row.note: Israel's land inheritance is divided by lot according to ancestral names. The text gives a non-gambling form of the commentary's measured share: a durable allotted possession.

row.basis: Aaron's two ritual lots for the goats
row.note: Aaron casts lots to distinguish the goat for the Lord from the goat for Azazel. The regulated cultic lot is a useful counterpoint to the commentary's prohibited lot-arrows, because the difference in ritual setting is the point.

row.basis: lots for household portions; prohibition of gambling with others
row.note: The Mishnah permits household members to determine portions by lot but forbids doing so with outsiders as gambling. Its legal distinction directly illuminates the commentary's double sense of maysir as distribution of portions and condemned game.

Zechariah receives the sanctuary task by lot under priestly custom. This is a Christian-scriptural instance of a regulated sacred lot, to be read beside the commentary's sharply negative treatment of divinatory or gambling arrows.

row.basis: Matthias selected when the lot falls to him
row.note: After prayer, the apostles cast lots and Matthias receives the lot for the apostolic vacancy. It is a concrete Christian counterpart for lot as discerned communal selection rather than camel-game distribution.

row.basis: God as the speaker's portion and holder of his lot
row.note: The psalm calls the Lord the speaker's portion and cup and says that God holds his lot. It provides a theological alternative to a self-sought gambling share: the decisive portion is received from God.

row.basis: God apportions a measure of faith to each
row.note: Each person is to think according to the measure of faith God apportioned. The verse turns the commentary's measure-and-share vocabulary into a differentiated divine gift rather than a prize won by chance.

row.basis: inheritance received according to a prior divine purpose
row.note: The community receives an inheritance after being predestined according to God's purpose. It joins an allotted share to prior determination, a close counterpart to the commentary's measured portion.

row.basis: share in the inheritance of the saints in light
row.note: The Father qualifies believers for a share in the inheritance of the saints in light. It supplies the positive eschatological share that the commentary contrasts with having no share in the hereafter.

row.basis: wicked people's allotted portion in the burning lake
row.note: The listed wicked receive their portion in the lake burning with fire and sulfur. It brings together the commentary's two final terms, allotted share and the great fire, in one eschatological sentence.

row.basis: unquenched fire and an undying worm for rebels
row.note: The rebels' worm does not die and their fire is not quenched. It is a close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the surah's fire immediately followed by neither dying nor living.

row.basis: Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire applied to Gehenna
row.note: Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire in teaching about Gehenna. This Christian reuse gives the Isaiah image an explicitly punitive afterlife setting beside the commentary's great fire.

row.basis: Hebrew h-l-q: smooth stones, portion, and lot
row.note: Isaiah plays on smooth valley stones, a person's portion, and lot in one idolatry verse. Hebrew h-l-q is a concrete Semitic cognate meeting for the commentary's Arabic خ ل ق cluster, which likewise develops smoothing and the apportioned خلاق; the cultic setting keeps the comparison specific.

row.basis: God Most High in Abraham's oath
row.note: Abraham names the creator God Most High in his oath. Hebrew Elyon and the commentary's al-A'la belong to the same highness vocabulary, while Abraham's presence answers the section's closing turn to Ibrahim.

row.basis: Isaiah's crooked roads made straight in John the Baptist's preparation
row.note: Luke places the leveling of valleys, straightening of crooked places, and smoothing of rough ways in the preparation for the Lord's coming. It is a specifically Christian reading of the road-making image that the commentary hears in سوّى and هدى.

row.basis: the shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
row.note: The shepherd brings out his own sheep, goes before them, and they follow. This gives a close living analogue to the commentary's leading staff, named for preceding the one it guides.

row.basis: arrow of the Lord's victory shot toward the east
row.note: Elisha orders an eastward shot and calls it the Lord's arrow of victory. It gives the fashioned arrow a prophetic target and direction, like the commentary's hearing of guidance through an arrowhead aimed ahead.

row.basis: an arrow beyond the boy signals David's course
row.note: Jonathan's cry that the arrow is beyond the boy functions as a directional signal to the hidden David. This adds a narrative use in which an arrow tells someone where danger and movement lie.

row.basis: God opens Hagar's eyes and she fills a water-skin at the well
row.note: After God opens Hagar's eyes to a well, she fills the skin and gives the child water. It puts the commentary's prepared water-skin into a scene of guided provision rather than treating the vessel as a mere shared object.

The Gibeonites display wineskins that were new when filled but are now worn out. This is a concrete biblical analogue to the commentary's account of a leather vessel becoming smooth and spent through use.

row.basis: fresh wineskins preserve what they contain
row.note: New wine must be put into fresh wineskins so that both vessel and wine are preserved. Its point depends on the condition and fitness of worked leather containers, an apt counterpart to the commentary's detailed water-skin craftsmanship.

row.basis: potter, clay, and the work of divine hands
row.note: Israel calls God its potter and itself the work of God's hands. It offers another concrete artisan image for the commentary's claim that creation verbs sound like stages in a maker's work.

row.basis: human artisan measures and shapes an idol
row.note: A carpenter stretches a line, marks, planes, and compasses an image for a house. The measured craft resembles the commentary's workshop sequence, but Isaiah uses it to expose a human-made idol whereas the Qur'anic sequence predicates measured making of God.

row.basis: sailors cast lots to identify the cause of disaster
row.note: The sailors cast lots to discover on whose account the storm has come. This is a specific narrative analogue to seeking a hidden judgment through a lot, the sort of divinatory use that makes the Qur'anic ban on arrow-lots intelligible.

The Mishnah lists a player with dice among people disqualified from giving testimony. Its legal suspicion of gaming supplies a Jewish ethical counterpart to the commentary's contrast between apportioned share and maysir.

row.basis: ban on divination and related practices
row.note: The Didache tells its reader not to become a diviner or seek such practices. Though it does not name arrows, it provides an early Christian prohibition of the divinatory aim that the commentary identifies in lot-arrows.

row.basis: traits allotted at conception but not righteousness or wickedness
row.note: The Talmud imagines an angel asking what a conceived drop will become—strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor—while excluding righteous or wicked. It is a precise Jewish qualification of measured human endowment that preserves the moral choice foregrounded by the commentary's final contrast.

row.basis: a heavenly mazal tells each blade of grass to grow
row.note: The midrash says no blade of grass lacks a heavenly mazal that strikes it and says, Grow. It develops divine guidance of created life at the creaturely level, giving a Jewish interpretive analogue to قدر then هدى.

row.basis: two spirits appointed for people to walk in until visitation
row.note: The Community Rule says God appoints two spirits in which humans walk until the time of visitation. Its measured duration and directed paths make a specific Second Temple comparison for the commentary's divine determination, guidance, and consequential choice.
Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light. This is a close Christian use of ease as the character of a divinely given way, beside 87:8's promise of being eased toward ease.

row.basis: not a forgetful hearer, but a doer blessed in action
row.note: James contrasts a forgetful hearer with one who persists in the liberating law and is blessed in doing. It gives the commentary's beneficial reminder a practical outcome rather than mere recollection.

row.basis: avoid, turn away from, and pass beyond the wicked path
row.note: The father repeatedly commands avoidance of the wicked path: do not enter it, turn away, and pass on. Its verbs give a concrete path-image for the commentary's yatajannabuha, even though the object there is the reminder.

The Passover flesh is to be eaten roasted with fire. Hebrew tz-l-h and Arabic s-l-y are a plausible Semitic lexical meeting for the commentary's fire verb, but the Hebrew passage concerns cooking rather than entering or straightening at a fire, so the semantic link should remain qualified.

row.basis: lights appointed for signs, seasons, days, and years
row.note: The created lights are set in the firmament to mark signs, seasons, days, and years. This gives a creation passage in which making also establishes the measured temporal order and term developed from قدر.

row.basis: a boundary inscribed on the waters at light's limit
row.note: God draws a boundary on the face of the waters at the limit between light and darkness. The image is a precise act of measured delimitation within creation, extending the commentary's maker scene beyond tools and objects.

row.basis: the sea's limit and earth's foundations marked out
row.note: Wisdom recalls God assigning the sea a limit so its waters do not transgress and marking the earth's foundations. It specifies measurement as a boundary that guides created elements in their proper course.

row.basis: human planning and the Lord establishing steps
row.note: A person's heart plans a way, but the Lord establishes the steps. This compresses the commentary's pondering of how to prepare a matter and the subsequent divine directing of its course.

row.basis: teaching a way of wisdom and leading in upright tracks
row.note: The parental teacher says, I have taught you the way of wisdom and led you in upright tracks. Its joined teaching, leading, and straight path provide a sapiential counterpart to measured preparation followed by guidance.

row.basis: a voice identifies the way to walk
row.note: When hearers turn right or left, a voice behind them says, This is the way; walk in it. The verse gives guidance a concrete directional utterance, like the commentary's implement aimed ahead.

row.basis: a leader who goes out before and brings the people in
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before the congregation, bring them out and in, so they will not be sheep without a shepherd. It makes the before-going action a responsible form of guidance in the Moses context named at the end of the surah.

row.basis: remembering the whole way God led in the wilderness
row.note: Israel is commanded to remember the whole way the Lord led it for forty years, including the testing that exposed what was in the heart. This joins remembrance, divine leading, and knowledge of the concealed interior.

row.basis: remember the creator before the evil days
row.note: Qohelet commands remembrance of the creator before the days of decline arrive. It gives the commentary's creation and reminder motifs a single temporal exhortation.

row.basis: humans see appearance while the Lord sees the heart
row.note: The Lord distinguishes human sight of outward appearance from his own sight of the heart. It is a particularly concrete counterpart to knowing the public and the concealed.

row.basis: refusal to listen, turned shoulder, and stopped ears
row.note: The ancestors refuse to pay attention, turn a stubborn shoulder, and make their ears too heavy to hear prophetic instruction. This is a close narrative profile of keeping away from a reminder.

row.basis: Scripture profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training
row.note: Scripture is called profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. It gives a direct Christian account of how a reminder can be beneficial rather than merely repeated.

row.basis: person of God made complete and equipped
row.note: The stated result of useful instruction is that God's person becomes complete and equipped for every good work. This translates the commentary's prepared, finished artisan object into moral and communal formation.

row.basis: what the Lord assigned and the path each person walks
row.note: Each person is to walk as the Lord assigned and as God called. The verse closely unites an apportioned share with a directed way of life.

row.basis: Spirit apportions gifts individually as it wills
row.note: The one Spirit distributes gifts to each person individually as it wills. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's measured portion given by a determining giver rather than won in a game.

row.basis: the measure and field God apportioned
row.note: Paul refuses to boast beyond the measure of the field God apportioned to him. The passage uses an assigned measure as a real limit and vocation, preserving both senses in the commentary's قدر.

row.basis: golden measuring rod for city, gates, and wall
row.note: The angel holds a golden measuring rod to measure the city, its gates, and its wall. This provides a second, eschatological scene in which a rod and exact measurement belong together.

row.basis: do not refuse the one who speaks
row.note: The readers are warned not to refuse the one who speaks from heaven. It is a direct continuation of the response contrast in 87:9-11: warning becomes deadly when its speaker is avoided.

row.basis: eternal fire prepared for the cursed
row.note: The cursed are told to depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. This is a distinct Christian judgment scene for the great fire, with preparation language that also recalls the commentary's crafted readiness.

The Lord sits as a refiner and purifier of silver to cleanse the Levites. It gives fire an artisan's transformative function, close to the commentary's fire used to straighten a staff, while retaining its own priestly context.

row.basis: Hagar sent out with bread and a skin of water
row.note: Abraham places bread and a skin of water on Hagar before sending her into the wilderness. As the necessary beginning of the later well scene, it shows the water-skin's carrying function and the vulnerability that makes its refilling significant.

Elihu compares pent-up speech to wine without a vent, like new wineskins ready to burst. This gives the leather vessel a dynamic of internal pressure, a distinct material counterpart to the commentary's shaken and worked skin.

row.basis: Pur cast day by day to select a destructive date
row.note: Haman casts Pur, explicitly a lot, to select the day and month for his plan against the Jews. This is a sharply negative biblical lot scene beside the commentary's concern that a share sought through chance can become morally corrupt.

row.basis: all foreseen, yet freedom of choice given
row.note: Avot holds together divine foreknowledge and granted human choice. This is a concise Jewish formulation for reading the commentary's measured determination without collapsing its final moral choosing into fatalism.

row.basis: everything in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven
row.note: The Talmud's maxim reserves fear of Heaven from what is in Heaven's hands. It places 87:10's fear within a Jewish distinction between divine determination and responsible response.

row.basis: Spirit of truth guides into all truth
row.note: The Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth. It supplies a distinctly Christian form of the commentary's guidance motif, where leading reaches truthful understanding rather than a physical target.

row.basis: discipline for good and a share in holiness
row.note: God's discipline is for the hearers' good so that they may share in holiness. The verse joins staged parental formation, benefit, and received share, three elements the commentary develops separately.

The day reveals each person's work because it is disclosed in fire, which tests its quality. This gives a distinct Christian use of fire as testing crafted work, beside the commentary's staff-shaping fire and punitive fire.

row.basis: the measure used returns to the measurer
row.note: The measure used in judgment is measured back to the judge. It turns the commentary's measuring vocabulary into an ethical rule of reciprocal assessment.

row.basis: Hebrew halaq, smooth rather than hairy
row.note: Jacob calls himself a smooth man in contrast with Esau's hairiness. Hebrew h-l-q is a plausible cognate meeting for the commentary's Arabic خ ل ق in its developed smoothness sense, but the verse concerns bodily texture rather than a smoothed arrow or worn skin.
Psalm 7 joins the two terms that open the commentary's axis: the singer praises YHWH and sings to the name of YHWH Most High.
The Sabbath psalm calls it good to sing to the name of the Most High, a close liturgical counterpart to glorifying the Lord's name in 87:1.
The final petition identifies the one whose name is YHWH as alone Most High over all the earth, opposing a creature's appropriation of that height.

row.basis: El Elyon; creator heaven and earth
row.note: Melchizedek blesses Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; it supplies a biblical divine title whose height belongs to the Creator.
The Hebrew title עֶלְיוֹן (Most High) is a cognate comparison for the commentary's ٱلْأَعْلَى, and Gen 14 uses it of the Creator rather than an exalted ruler.
Nebuchadnezzar calls the rescued men servants of the Most High God at the mouth of the furnace, holding the high divine title and a decisive fire in one scene.
Daniel's Aramaic עִלָּיָא, used for God beside the furnace, is a cognate witness for the high-title language developed around ٱلْأَعْلَى.
God calls YHWH his name forever and his memorial through generations, directly pairing the divine name with remembrance as 87:15 does.
God's זִכְרִי, “memorial,” is a Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ذِكْر; the verse makes it inseparable from the revealed divine name.
The verse's שֵׁם, God's enduring name, provides an actual Hebrew cognate comparison for the commentary's ٱسْم rather than a root-label inference.
At an altar, God promises to come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this is a spatial worship counterpart to remembering the Lord's name and praying.
The psalm sets YHWH's name and memorial across generations, adding durability to the commentary's contrast between divine remembrance and the lower, passing life.
Isaiah says that YHWH's name and memorial are the soul's desire, making remembered divine naming an act of directed longing rather than mere recollection.
Where the commentary contrasts remembering the Lord's name with preferring the near life, the psalm contrasts remembering God's name with trust in chariots and horses.
The Levites bless God's glorious name as exalted above every blessing and praise, a particularly close formulation of name, elevation, and worship.

row.basis: name exalted above earth and heaven
row.note: The hymn says YHWH's name alone is exalted and his majesty is above earth and heaven, extending the commentary's vertical axis to the whole cosmos.
Praise of YHWH's name runs from the sun's rising to its setting; it gives a biblical horizon image to the commentary's rising, visible form.
This verse places YHWH high above nations and his glory above the heavens, matching the commentary's move from the Most High to the high heavens.
Israel must not profane but sanctify God's holy name, specifying the ethical content of glorifying a divine name.
God vindicates and sanctifies his great name after its profanation; this supplies a public, historical dimension to the commentary's divine-name praise.
The seraphic acclamation declares God holy while the whole earth is full of glory, a temple vision that gives concrete content to the commentary's tasbih as divine transcendence.
The one dwelling in the high and holy place says his name is Holy, binding the commentary's two opening poles, height and divine naming, in one prophetic declaration.
God's name is great among the nations and receives pure incense; it relates exaltation of the name to a concrete communal act of worship.

row.basis: make a name; tower to heaven
row.note: Babel's builders say “make a name for ourselves” while raising a tower toward heaven, a deliberate human self-elevation that reverses glorification of the Most High's name.
God, rather than Abram, promises to make Abram's name great; this distinguishes bestowed honorable remembrance from the self-made name of Babel and Pharaoh-like pride.
God grants faithful outsiders an everlasting name better than sons and daughters, making elevated naming a divine gift that outlasts ordinary earthly continuance.
