Exodus portrays Pharaoh answering “Who is YHWH?” and refusing obedience; beside the commentary's Pharaoh who claims the highest lordship, this is a rival account of his rejection of the true Lord.
God charges Pharaoh with still exalting himself against the people, a direct biblical instance of the commentary's warning that earthly height becomes arrogant tyranny.
Jethro confesses YHWH greater than all gods precisely in the affair where Egyptians acted presumptuously, pairing divine greatness with the undoing of proud power.
Isaiah says haughty human eyes will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted, making the commentary's high/low axis a judgment on rival elevation.

row.basis: aspiring to likeness of the Most High
row.note: The taunt's arrogant ruler plans to ascend above clouds and make himself like the Most High; its counter-claim clarifies why a creature's use of supreme height is corrupt.
Nebuchadnezzar's heart is lifted up and he is deposed from royal throne, a royal narrative of self-exaltation turned into abasement.

row.basis: Belshazzar lifts himself against heaven's Lord
row.note: Belshazzar exalts himself against the Lord of heaven and fails to glorify the God who holds his breath, closely matching the commentary's opposition between claimed greatness and divine praise.
The Tyrian ruler's heart becomes proud because of his splendor and he is cast to the ground, a vivid vertical reversal for corrupted height.
The same ruler's profanation brings fire from his midst to consume him; it joins arrogant elevation and punitive fire without treating divine glory itself as evil.
In WLC's Hebrew numbering, the coming day burns like an oven and makes all arrogant evildoers stubble, a close judgmental counterpart to the greatest fire.

row.basis: Hebrew כַּבִּיר; Arabic ك ب ر
row.note: Job calls God כַּבִּיר, mighty/great; this is a contextual Hebrew cognate comparison for the commentary's ك ب ر discussion of divine greatness and takbir.
The command to Moses and the elders, “Come up to YHWH,” realizes the commentary's observation that an invitation to come can be a summons toward a height.
YHWH calls Moses to Sinai's summit and Moses goes up, giving a concrete sacred scene for upward call, divine height, and revelation.
Isaiah's latter-days vision establishes the mountain of YHWH's house as highest among mountains, a spatial counterpart to the commentary's raised houses for divine remembrance.

row.basis: come; go up to YHWH's house
row.note: Nations say “Come, let us go up” to YHWH's house for instruction, combining the commentary's upward invitation with a worshiping community.

row.basis: place for God's name to dwell
row.note: The chosen worship site is where YHWH makes his name dwell, providing a Torah antecedent for the commentary's raised houses where the name is remembered.

row.basis: house where God's name is; prayer
row.note: Solomon asks God to attend to the house of which he said “My name shall be there” and to the prayer toward it, closely pairing house, name, and prayer.
The people called by God's name must humble themselves, pray, and seek his face; this joins named belonging, prayer, and the reversal of proud elevation.
The prayer names God alone as maker of heavens and the highest heavens, whose host worships him, a direct counterpart to high heavens and praise of their Creator.

row.basis: lift eyes on high; Creator of stars
row.note: Isaiah commands hearers to lift their eyes on high and see the creator who brings out the starry host, furnishing a biblical celestial counterpart to the high-horizon imagery.
After deliverance from the furnace, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of the servants; the fire becomes a scene of divine praise rather than the final fate of the wicked.
Topheth is prepared deep and wide for the king, with abundant wood kindled by YHWH; it gives the commentary's great fire a royal-judgment analogue.
The final vision's fire is not quenched against rebels, supplying a prophetic comparison for the lasting punitive fire adjacent to 87:12–13.
Pharaoh calls wise men, sorcerers, and Egyptian magicians, the biblical counterpart to the commentary's Moses-and-magicians scene.
Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, a narrative precedent for the claim that Moses will be superior in a contest with magic.
Moses hides his face because he fears to look at God, giving a biblical fear scene for the commentary's frightened Moses before divine reassurance.
The Kaddish opens by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified, an enduring Jewish liturgical interpretation of praise as elevation of the Name.
The talmudic saying that God and the haughty person cannot dwell together sharpens the commentary's contrast between divine highness and possessed, corrupt greatness.
Rabbi Yohanan finds divine humility wherever Scripture speaks of divine greatness, a Jewish reading that prevents “Most High” from licensing human domination.

row.basis: pride begins by leaving the Lord
row.note: Sirach defines human pride as departure from the Lord, directly interpreting the commentary's self-raised ruler as a theological, not merely social, failure.

row.basis: profit of arrogance and boastful wealth
row.note: The wicked ask what arrogance and vaunted riches profited them, an explicit retrospective judgment on preferring a lower, present life.
Mattathias warns that the sinner's glory ends in worms and shame; it makes worldly exaltation transient and degradable.
The stricken king who had thought himself superhuman recognizes that he is mortal, a close royal counter-story to Pharaoh-like claims of supreme height.
Jesus teaches prayer beginning with the sanctification of the Father's name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to glorifying the Lord's name.

row.basis: ask in Jesus' name; Father glorified
row.note: Prayer in Jesus' name is ordered to the Father's glorification, explicitly joining name, prayer, and divine honor as 87:15 does.

row.basis: God highly exalts and grants the name
row.note: After Christ's self-humbling, God highly exalts him and gives the name above every name, setting bestowed elevation against self-claimed greatness.

row.basis: confession brings glory to the Father
row.note: The confession of Jesus as Lord is “to the glory of God the Father,” giving an explicitly verbal act of honoring God beside the commentary's name-praise.
The Son proclaims God's name among brothers and sings praise in the assembly, a communal form of naming and glorifying God.
Believers continually offer praise to God as lips confess his name, closely paralleling the commentary's remembered name expressed in worship.

row.basis: glorify God's name because he is holy
row.note: The heavenly song asks who will not glorify God's name, for he alone is holy; it fuses name-praise with the holiness content of tasbih.
The living creatures' continual “holy, holy, holy” before the enthroned Almighty offers a Christian heavenly analogue to transcendent praise.

row.basis: Son of the Most High; royal throne
row.note: Gabriel calls Jesus Son of the Most High and promises David's throne, setting a divinely granted royal title beside Pharaoh's falsely appropriated highest lordship.
Mary's song brings down the mighty from thrones and exalts the lowly, making the commentary's high/low axis a narrative reversal.

row.basis: Herod takes glory and is struck
row.note: Herod accepts a divine acclamation instead of giving God glory and is struck down, a concrete Christian royal warning against usurped greatness.

row.basis: self-exalting claimant who declares himself God
row.note: The lawless figure exalts himself against every god and declares himself God, a focused Christian counter-picture to Pharaoh's “most high lord” claim.
Jesus contrasts loving one's life in this world with keeping it for eternal life, directly matching the commentary's choice between the near life and what endures.
Jesus forbids storing treasure on earth because it decays and is stolen, concretizing why a life preferred as “lower” cannot be the final good.

row.basis: treasure in heaven does not decay
row.note: The complementary command locates uncorruptible treasure in heaven, supplying the durable upward alternative to present-world preference.
The question of gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life gives a sharp ethical measure for the commentary's preference of worldly life.
Paul commands a mind set on things above rather than earthly things, an unusually direct verbalized high/low orientation.
Those whose end is destruction set their minds on earthly things, a New Testament diagnosis of the orientation the commentary calls preference for the lower life.
The following verse supplies the opposing allegiance, citizenship in heaven, so the spatial axis becomes a communal identity rather than an abstraction.
The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, closely matching the commentary's present-life versus enduring-good contrast.
Believers have no lasting city here but seek the one to come, a concise Christian analogue to rejecting the nearer life for what abides.
The judgment scene sends the cursed to eternal fire, a direct eschatological counterpart to the commentary's greatest fire.
Jesus' Gehenna citation describes an unquenched fire and an undying worm, a close comparison for the continuing punitive condition surrounding 87:12–13.
The Lord's revelation in flaming fire brings retribution on those who do not know or obey God, making divine judgment rather than mere physical flame the point of the fire.

row.basis: lake of fire called second death
row.note: Revelation calls the lake of fire the second death, a Christian way of naming final fiery loss beside 87:12–13's paradoxical life/death condition.
The letter names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses, preserving a Christian interpretive identification for the Egyptian-magician contest developed in the commentary.

row.basis: God's face and name on servants
row.note: The final servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads, a concentrated Christian pairing of the commentary's sought divine face and remembered name.
The angelic hymn places glory “in the highest,” a concise heavenly response to the commentary's opening Most High and its account of a revelation-bearer.

row.basis: Melchizedek priest of God Most High
row.note: Hebrews receives Genesis 14's priest of God Most High into a Christian priestly argument, making the older high-title tradition an explicit interpretive resource.
The Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily, preserving “hallowed be your name” as a repeated discipline of name-sanctification.

row.basis: two loves; earthly and heavenly cities
row.note: Augustine's two cities arise from love of self to contempt of God or love of God to contempt of self, an interpretive framework for the commentary's proud earthly height and Godward orientation.
Ignatius rejects corruptible food and the pleasures of this life in favor of God, a concrete early Christian appropriation of preferring what is lasting.
Even while Solomon prays about the name-bearing house, he says the highest heaven cannot contain God; this qualifies a merely spatial reading of raised worship-houses.
The Mishnah distinguishes the Temple's pronunciation of the Name from its substitute outside, giving ritual precision to the commentary's house, name, and worship nexus.
The moon-testimony procedures ask witnesses about the new crescent's position, height, direction, and form, a concrete Jewish reading-world for the commentary's discerned crescent above the horizon.
The talmudic account of layered heavens locates the sun and moon within a structured upper cosmos, expanding the commentary's high-heavens and lunar imagery.
Josephus interprets the tower builders as seeking security and defiance rather than gratitude to God; this intensifies Gen 11's self-raised name in the commentary's terms.

row.basis: Most High not in handmade houses
row.note: Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in handmade houses, an interpretive tension with the commentary's raised houses: the Name may be worshiped there without containing the Most High.

row.basis: worship not bound to mountain or Jerusalem
row.note: Jesus anticipates worship no longer bound to a particular mountain or Jerusalem, offering a Christian reframing of elevation and sacred place.
Tertullian explains the opening prayer petition as asking that God's name be held holy in us, interpreting name-sanctification as lived conduct as well as speech.
Psalm 8 addresses YHWH by a majestic name throughout the earth and sets his glory above the heavens, bringing name-praise and cosmic height into one line.

row.basis: Most High; great king over earth
row.note: The psalm names YHWH Most High and a great king over all the earth, a royal title whose legitimate bearer contrasts with the commentary's self-exalting Pharaoh.
YHWH is Most High over all the earth and greatly exalted above all gods, extending the commentary's high divine title into a polemic against rival powers.
Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah parallel to name-praise and takbir.

row.basis: Moses sings YHWH's exaltation over Pharaoh
row.note: Moses' victory song calls YHWH highly exalted after horse and rider are thrown into the sea, directly joining the Moses-Pharaoh setting with rightful divine height.
The song asks who is like YHWH, majestic in holiness and awesome in praises, giving concrete Mosaic language for the commentary's tasbih as transcendence and majesty.
YHWH says that this is his name and that he gives his glory to no other; it directly answers the commentary's creaturely seizure of divine-high status.

row.basis: glory to God's Name, not ourselves
row.note: The prayer explicitly redirects glory from “us” to YHWH's name, a concise liturgical reversal of self-made name and self-glorification.
David ascribes greatness, glory, and all that is in heaven and earth to YHWH, who is exalted as head above all; it is a comprehensive scriptural form of the commentary's vertical praise.

row.basis: go up; build house; God glorified
row.note: The command to go up the mountain, bring wood, and build God's house joins the commentary's upward summons to a house whose purpose is divine glorification.
Even if Edom soars like an eagle and sets its nest among stars, God says he will bring it down, a sharp image of corrupted height reversed by God.
The wealthy person carries nothing away at death and personal glory does not go down with him, giving the lower present life a concrete terminal limit.
The priestly blessing places God's name upon Israel and God blesses them, a ritual use of the Name that complements the commentary's name, remembrance, and prayer.
The warning against saying “my power” gained wealth isolates the self-crediting impulse that accompanies the commentary's preference for worldly life and corrupt greatness.

row.basis: God brings low and lifts up
row.note: Hannah's hymn says that YHWH makes poor and rich, brings low and also lifts up; it gives the commentary's vertical axis a divine reversal in human status.
Rabbi Levitas' injunction to be very, very humble supplies a terse Jewish ethical counterweight to the commentary's ruler who turns height into pride.
Mary calls the Mighty One's deeds great and his name holy, continuing the name-and-greatness language beside the later reversal of the mighty and lowly in the same song.
Paul makes calling on the Lord's name the saving response, a direct Christian use of divine naming as invocation rather than self-honor.
The exalted Christ is above every rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name named, using height and naming together to deny final status to worldly powers.
The beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God and his name, the explicit opposite of the commentary's command to sanctify and glorify the divine name.
Babylon glorifies herself, lives luxuriously, and claims secure queenship; this is a concentrated apocalyptic portrait of proud height joined to worldly preference.
Paul contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal, closely framing the commentary's choice between the near life and what endures.
The present form of this world is passing away, a concise counterpart to the commentary's judgment that the selected worldly life is lower and nonlasting.

row.basis: rich not haughty or hopeful in wealth
row.note: The rich are not to be haughty or set hope on uncertain wealth, explicitly connecting worldly possession with the pride that the commentary treats as fallen height.
The faithful desire a better, heavenly country, an exact directional alternative to giving preference to the nearer worldly life.

row.basis: human glory versus glory from God
row.note: Jesus contrasts receiving glory from one another with seeking glory from the only God, making human honor a rival to true divine recognition.
Jesus says he manifested the Father's name to those given him, a New Testament development of the commentary's claim that a name discloses the one named.
The Son sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high after making purification, a concentrated heavenly-height image that joins exaltation to cleansing rather than arrogance.

row.basis: servants of the Most High amid divination
row.note: A divining slave calls Paul and companions servants of the Most High God; its setting makes a Christian comparison for the commentary's contest between revelation and magical power.

row.basis: Creator not dwelling in handmade shrines
row.note: Paul calls God maker of world and heaven and says he does not dwell in hand-made sanctuaries, a distinct Christian qualification of elevated worship-houses.

The letter describes Christians as passing their days on earth while holding citizenship in heaven, an early Christian interpretation of the vertical choice between present life and a higher homeland.
Origen treats “hallowed be your name” as a petition about God's name being sanctified in those who pray, extending the commentary's verbal glorification into moral practice.

row.basis: خلق فسوّى; dust formed and breath
row.note: The commentary reads خلق فسوّى as a body completed before breath is given. Genesis 2:7 likewise has God form the human from dust and then breathe life into that formed body.

row.basis: خلق فسوّى; fashioned body and reversal
row.note: Job says God's hands fashioned and made the speaker, then asks whether that same maker will destroy him. It gives a personal biblical counterpart both to ordered formation and to the commentary's later reversal of formed life.

Job grounds equal treatment of servant and master in one maker who fashioned both in the womb. This sharpens the commentary's claim that orderly human embodiment includes the hearer, not an abstract creature.
The commentary opens the womb as a place where an incomplete body is gathered and ordered. Psalm 139:14 says God formed the inward parts and wove the speaker in the mother's womb.
Isaiah identifies YHWH by making and forming Israel from the womb. Its action-based divine identification closely matches the relative clause that identifies the Lord through خلق and سوّى.

row.basis: stretching heaven, founding earth, forming spirit
row.note: Zechariah joins the stretching of heaven, founding of earth, and formation of the human spirit. That threefold formula places the commentary's sky, embodied person, and breathed interior in one creator's work.

row.basis: measured earth and stretched a line
row.note: The commentary hears in خلق the measured work that precedes an irreversible cut. Job's creation speech asks who fixed the earth's measures and stretched a measuring line over it, making cosmic order explicitly artisan-like.

row.basis: waters measured; hills weighed in balance
row.note: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in a hollow hand, marking off heaven, and weighing hills in scales. It supplies a concrete biblical analogue for the commentary's measured creation, balance, water, and completed fitting.

row.basis: formed earth, made it, established it
row.note: Isaiah says the creator formed, made, and established the earth rather than making it empty. Its sequence closely illuminates the commentary's insistence that خلق followed by سوّى is completed ordered creation, not a bare first act.

Moses names God by making and establishing Israel rather than by a detached title. This is a close biblical counterpart to the commentary's point that the Lord is known through the actions in a relative clause.
The commentary contrasts a craftsman's material work with creation effected by command. Genesis 1:3 gives the compact pattern of divine speech followed immediately by the existence of light.

row.basis: spoke, commanded, and it stood firm
row.note: Psalm 33 says God spoke and it came to be, commanded and it stood firm. The verbal creation and resulting stability parallel the commentary's reading of creation and completion as one uninterrupted divine work.
The surah's praise command is grounded in the Lord's creating action. Psalm 95 calls worshippers to bow and kneel specifically before YHWH their maker, providing the same liturgical logic.
Nehemiah calls YHWH alone the maker of all the heavens, earth, seas, and their contents, and says the heavenly host worships him. It joins exclusive creation to praise as the commentary does.

row.basis: praise because he commanded and created
row.note: Psalm 148 explicitly orders heavenly creatures to praise because God commanded and they were created. This is an unusually close parallel to praise attached to a creator-relative clause.

row.basis: creator gives breath and spirit to walkers
row.note: Isaiah identifies God as creator and stretcher of the heavens who gives breath to people and spirit to those walking on earth. It links cosmic ordering, formed life, breath, and the commentary's transition from made body toward guided walking.

row.basis: made earth and established world by wisdom
row.note: Jeremiah says God made the earth, established the world by wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by understanding. It supplies a biblical sequence of making, stabilizing, and cosmic proportion.

row.basis: all things made by the divine word
row.note: Wisdom addresses God as the one who made all things by his word. It gives a Jewish formulation for the commentary's contrast between a human cutter's materials and creation by a command.

Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. Its threefold account of cosmic proportion directly accompanies the commentary's extended claim that خلق already bears measured fitting.

Sirach says that when the Lord created his works he determined their boundaries. The verse offers a precise Jewish formulation of measured creation before the later guidance and provision developed in the commentary.
Sirach describes creation as paired in opposites and says nothing was made incomplete. That is a particularly close parallel to the commentary's سوّى as removing excess and supplying what is lacking.

row.basis: Creator formed humankind and restores breath
row.note: The mother tells her son that the Creator shaped human origins and will give life and breath back. It directly joins the commentary's womb formation, breathed life, and re-creation of a body after death.

row.basis: morning prayer: created, formed, breathed soul
row.note: The daily soul prayer says God created, formed, and breathed the soul into the worshipper. Its ordered verbs make a Jewish liturgical counterpart to the commentary's formed body, breath, and praise of the maker.

row.basis: formed dust and breathed a speaking spirit
row.note: This Targum expands Genesis 2:7's dust-and-breath scene into a living, speaking human. It is a Jewish interpretive elaboration of the commentary's completed bodily form awaiting the imparted spirit.

The commentary says the creator's measure needs no pre-existing model, unlike a leather worker's pattern. Genesis Rabbah compares creation to an architect using a blueprint and says God looked into Torah, a deliberately different craftsman-image that lets the contrast be assessed.

The commentary places Abraham's creator-and-guide confession against crafted idols. Genesis Rabbah's tale of Abraham smashing Terah's idols supplies the major Jewish expansion of that same anti-idol setting.

row.basis: craftsman measures and shapes a human-like idol
row.note: Isaiah's carpenter stretches a line, marks out, and shapes an image for worship. The human measuring and cutting scene mirrors the commentary's artisan imagery while exposing its opposite: an object fabricated as a god.

Isaiah identifies YHWH as maker of all things, stretching the heavens and spreading the earth alone. It closely supports the commentary's conclusion that the one who sets the measure needs neither model nor partner.

row.basis: carved image as teacher of lies
row.note: Habakkuk calls a crafted idol and its maker's trust a teacher of lies. This gives a precise biblical analogue for the commentary's secondary sense of خلق as fabricated false speech opposed to the true creator.

row.basis: gods that made neither heaven nor earth perish
row.note: This Aramaic verse declares that gods which did not make heaven and earth will perish from them. It makes the commentary's test between the creator and made idols, including the destructive end of false works, explicit.

row.basis: heavens and earth wear out like a garment
row.note: The commentary traces smoothness into the wearing of a garment and the reversal of formed creation. Isaiah says the earth will wear out like a garment while God's salvation remains, giving the image a cosmic scope.

row.basis: uneven ground made level for the way
row.note: The commentary preserves the destructive edge of سوّى, which can level a settlement, and joins bodily uprightness to a straight path. Isaiah's preparation scene raises valleys, lowers mountains, and makes rough ground level for a way.

Jeremiah's potter reworks a spoiled vessel into another as he sees fit. It renders the commentary's maker-and-material image concrete and shows that the one who forms can also re-form what has failed.

row.basis: bones in the womb and God's work
row.note: Ecclesiastes pairs the hidden formation of bones in a pregnant woman with the unknowable work of God who makes everything. It gives a close biblical analogue to the commentary's womb-stage meditation without reducing it to a mechanical account.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human service
row.note: The commentary follows ordered heaven toward water, pasture, and livelihood for people and animals. Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and vegetation for human use, matching that provision sequence.

row.basis: rain makes grass sprout in desolate land
row.note: In Job's creation speech, rain satisfies the waste land and causes grass to sprout. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's movement from ordered creation through water to pasture.

row.basis: rain waters earth and makes it sprout
row.note: Isaiah's rain descends, waters the earth, and brings sprouting, seed, and bread. It closely parallels the commentary's water-to-pasture-to-sustenance chain after creation is set in order.

row.basis: humankind made upright; humans devise schemes
row.note: Ecclesiastes says God made humankind upright but humans sought many devices. The contrast gives a biblical analogue to the commentary's formed balance versus self-devised, false construction.
The commentary extends ordered formation to the self, guidance, and purification. Psalm 51 asks God to create a clean heart, making inner restoration a fresh creative act.
Ezekiel promises a new heart and spirit in place of a stony heart. It gives a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's movement from shaped self to moral direction and purification.

row.basis: formed and made for divine glory
row.note: Isaiah calls those created, formed, and made for God's glory. It binds human formation to glorification of God's name, the relation that frames the commentary's opening command to praise.

row.basis: creation grounds a recurring act of worship
row.note: The Sabbath command is grounded in God's making heaven, earth, sea, and all within them. It provides a Torah instance where liturgical obedience is explicitly reasoned from complete creation.
Avot says the world was created through ten sayings. This rabbinic formulation develops the commentary's command-and-creation contrast while giving creation a moral and covenantal purpose.

row.basis: all things came to be through the Word
row.note: John says all things came to be through the Word and nothing came to be apart from it. It is a Christian formulation of the commentary's word-like, non-artisanal creation.

Hebrews says the worlds were prepared by God's word so that what is seen did not arise from visible things. This closely illuminates the commentary's claim that divine creation is not dependent on a prior material pattern.

In its Abraham-and-resurrection argument, Romans describes God as giving life to the dead and calling non-existent things into existence. It joins the commentary's unprecedented creation to its later resurrection horizon.

row.basis: all visible and invisible things created
row.note: Colossians gathers heaven, earth, visible, and invisible things under creation. It gives a Christian cosmic counterpart to the commentary's deliberately objectless خلق فسوّى, which embraces body and heaven together.

After speaking of creation, Colossians says all things hold together in Christ. This supplies a Christian idiom for the commentary's سوّى as coherence, fitting, and completed order rather than mere origination.

row.basis: maker of world not housed by human hands
row.note: Paul identifies the God who made world and all within it as Lord of heaven and earth, not confined to hand-made temples. It directly accompanies the commentary's creator-versus-human-maker contrast.

row.basis: giver of life, breath, and all things
row.note: Acts says God gives everyone life, breath, and all things. It closely parallels the commentary's formed body followed by imparted breath, while retaining the creator's independence from human service.

row.basis: divinity unlike art made by human design
row.note: Paul rejects likening the divine to gold, silver, or stone shaped by human craft and imagination. The verse provides a direct Christian counter-scene to the commentary's measuring artisan and fabricated deity.

Romans says people exchanged God's truth for the lie and served a creature rather than the Creator. It precisely matches the commentary's juxtaposition of true creating, fabricated speech, and idolatry.

row.basis: worship because all things were created
row.note: Heavenly worship names God worthy because by his will all things existed and were created. It gives the same rationale as the surah's praise: creation itself warrants liturgical glorification.

row.basis: worship maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs
row.note: Revelation commands worship of the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and water springs. It combines the commentary's praise command, cosmic maker, and life-giving water imagery.

row.basis: God gives each seed its own body
row.note: Paul says God gives a seed a body as he wills, each with its proper body. This is a focused analogy to the commentary's created thing made fit for its particular task and to resurrection re-embodiment.
Paul invokes the God who commanded light from darkness and applies it to illumination of hearts. It moves the commentary's spoken creation into inward knowing without confusing the two contexts.

row.basis: new self created for righteousness and holiness
row.note: Ephesians calls believers to put on the new self, created according to God in righteousness and holiness. It offers a Christian ethical counterpart to the commentary's formed self, guidance, and purification.

row.basis: Jesus fashions clay sparrows that fly
row.note: The commentary discusses Jesus shaping a bird from clay and insists that life comes by God's permission. The Infancy Gospel of Thomas recounts the closely related clay-sparrow scene, but presents the child Jesus commanding the birds to fly without the Qur'anic permission formula; the difference is interpretively central.
Hebrews says the heavens and earth will wear out like a garment. It gives a New Testament counterpart to the commentary's worn garment and the decline of what was once smoothly formed.

Romans describes creation's bondage to decay and hoped-for liberation. It gives theological depth to the commentary's secondary movement from ordered creation into deterioration and hoped-for renewal.

row.basis: valleys filled and rough ways made smooth
row.note: Luke applies a preparation-for-the-Lord prophecy in which valleys are filled, mountains lowered, and rough ways made smooth. It closely joins the commentary's leveling sense of سوّى to its straight-path and guidance imagery.

row.basis: not one letter passes from the Law
row.note: The commentary contrasts making complete with dropping a letter and connects it to the promise of unfailing recitation. Matthew's saying that not one iota or stroke will pass gives a specific Christian scriptural parallel for that preservation image.

row.basis: rain, fruitful seasons, food, and joy
row.note: Paul describes the living creator's witness through rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness. It is a close Christian analogue to the commentary's route from ordered sky and water to pasture and sustenance.

row.basis: God as builder of all things
row.note: Hebrews uses house-building to say that the builder of all things is God. This directly complements the commentary's artisan analogy while reserving universal creative agency for God.
The enthroned speaker says, 'I make all things new.' This provides a Christian eschatological counterpart to the commentary's claim that the maker can reverse decay and bring another creation.

row.basis: Creator established and ordered all things
row.note: 1 Clement praises the Creator who established the heavens and arranged creation by incomprehensible understanding. Its early Christian interpretation closely echoes the commentary's sequence from creating to setting in order.

Genesis says God blessed the seventh day because he rested from all the creating work he had made. It gives a biblical completion formula beside the commentary's reading of فَسَوّى as the finishing of creation.
Moses calls God's work perfect and all his ways just. It gives an ethical-theological counterpart to the commentary's سوّى as a making free of deficiency and imbalance.
Psalm 33 calls God the one who forms all hearts and attends to all deeds. It extends the commentary's formed body and soul into an account of inward moral life.

row.basis: all made for its fitting purpose
row.note: Proverbs says YHWH made everything for its purpose. Its purposive language helps articulate the commentary's secondary claim that what is created and measured is made apt for an end.

row.basis: Spirit makes and divine breath gives life
row.note: Elihu says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a compact Joban restatement of the commentary's ordered formation followed by enlivening breath.

row.basis: dust returns; spirit returns to giver
row.note: Ecclesiastes says dust returns to earth and spirit returns to the God who gave it. This gives the commentary's formed body and later reversal a mortality-and-return frame.

row.basis: God leads and makes crooked ground level
row.note: Isaiah promises to lead the blind on an unknown way and make crooked places level. It makes the commentary's passage from fashioned uprightness to divinely guided straight way concrete.

row.basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The commentary connects complete ordering to the assurance that no recited letter will be dropped. Deuteronomy says the covenant song will not be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a close Torah memory analogue.
The commentary's pasture finally becomes dark chaff and its water image distinguishes what remains from what passes away. Psalm 1 contrasts rooted fruitfulness with chaff driven off by wind.
Isaiah juxtaposes withering grass with the enduring divine word. It gives a biblical parallel both to the commentary's pasture-to-waste reversal and to its later concern for preserved recitation.
Job asks who can count clouds in wisdom and tip the waterskins of heaven. The image belongs beside the commentary's measured leather water-container and rain retained or released from the sky.

The commentary's Arabic خ ل ق B011 image is a hollow in smooth rock that retains water. Exodus reverses the direction: divine action brings water out of the struck rock, making a specific biblical counter-image for rock and life-giving water.

row.basis: image and likeness in human creation
row.note: The commentary emphasizes an unprecedented act that needs no prior model. Genesis frames human creation with the language of divine image and likeness, a different conceptual grammar that matters when comparing formed humanity.

row.basis: no form seen, therefore no image made
row.note: Moses warns that Israel saw no form at Horeb and must not make an image. It gives a Torah anti-idol frame for the commentary's separation of the creator from every fabricated likeness.

row.basis: source Arabic خ ل ق B008/B006; Hebrew חלק
row.note: The commentary's source labels give Arabic خ ل ق the secondary senses of smoothness and allotted share. Isaiah 57:6 plays on Hebrew חלק for the smooth stones of a valley and for one's portion amid offerings to them; the apparent cognacy and its phonology need verification, but the concrete semantic meeting is unusually rich.

row.basis: source Arabic خ ل ق B006; Hebrew חלק
row.note: The commentary uses the source label خ ل ق B006 for a measured share and contrasts worldly and otherworldly portion. Psalm 17:15 speaks of those whose Hebrew חלק is in this life, a likely cognate-based parallel that makes the worldly-share contrast explicit.

row.basis: source Arabic س و ي; Hebrew שוה
row.note: The commentary's Arabic س و ي explores equality, balance, and the maker without equal. Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה in the Holy One's question, 'to whom shall I be equal?'; the proposed Arabic-Hebrew cognacy should be checked, but the source context supplies the same divine incomparability.

row.basis: God's workmanship created for good works
row.note: Ephesians calls believers God's workmanship, created for prepared good works. It offers a Christian ethical development of the commentary's claim that formed things are made suitable for a directed task.
Paul calls the person in Christ a new creation. This is an interpretive Christian extension of the commentary's creation-and-recreation language rather than a parallel embryology scene.

row.basis: Jesus breathes and gives the Holy Spirit
row.note: The commentary repeatedly places breath after completed form. In John, the risen Jesus breathes on disciples and gives the Holy Spirit, reusing the breath-of-life pattern in a new-creation setting.

row.basis: Jesus makes mud and restores sight
row.note: The commentary's Jesus scene involves shaping clay and life by divine permission. John has Jesus make mud from earth and apply it to a blind man's eyes for healing, a canonical but differently purposed clay action.

The commentary's clay-bird account repeatedly qualifies Jesus' action by God's permission. Acts presents Jesus as attested by miracles that God did through him, a useful New Testament agency formula without claiming the same miracle.

row.basis: flesh and glory as grass that withers
row.note: First Peter compares all flesh and its glory to grass and a flower that wither and fall. It gives a Christian application of the commentary's pasture-to-chaff and formed-life-to-decline imagery.

row.basis: new self renewed after Creator's image
row.note: Colossians describes the new self as renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator. It brings Christian image language into the commentary's themes of formed self, knowledge, and renewed moral direction.

row.basis: outer person decays, inner person renewed
row.note: Paul contrasts the wasting outer person with the daily renewal of the inner person. It offers a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's aging reversal of created form and its inward renewal.

row.basis: creation seen as wholly very good
row.note: The commentary takes فسوّى as creation brought to a complete, balanced condition. Genesis 1:31's judgment that all God made was very good gives a whole-creation counterpart to that completed goodness.

row.basis: formed in womb and appointed for a task
row.note: Jeremiah is formed in the womb before birth and appointed for prophetic work. This joins the commentary's womb formation to its claim that what is measured and made is fitted toward a directed calling.

row.basis: father, potter, clay, work of divine hands
row.note: Isaiah calls God father and potter and the people clay, all the work of his hands. It offers the most explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's maker-and-material imagery without treating the maker as a merely human artisan.

row.basis: craftsman skillfully shapes a piece of wood
row.note: The commentary uses measured cutting and shaping as an analogy that must not be mistaken for divine dependence on a template. Wisdom describes a craftsman's skilled shaping of wood, supplying the human workmanship side of that comparison.

row.basis: mortal potter fashions a futile god from clay
row.note: Wisdom contrasts the mortal, earth-formed potter with the futile god he fashions from clay. This is a direct Jewish counter-scene to the commentary's creator versus fabricated deity and its clay-bird discussion.

row.basis: potter's control of clay in maker's hand
row.note: Sirach compares clay in a potter's hand with human beings in their maker's hand. It gives a Jewish wisdom analogue to the commentary's workmanship image and divine freedom to order or rework what is made.

row.basis: image is false and has no breath
row.note: Jeremiah says the image is false and that there is no breath in it. It exactly joins the commentary's false fabricated speech to its distinction between shaped material and the divine giving of life.

row.basis: idols are the work of human hands
row.note: The commentary contrasts the creator with objects made by craftsmen. Psalm 115 calls idols silver and gold, the work of human hands, giving the classic biblical formulation of that distinction.

row.basis: a craftsman made the calf, so it is not God
row.note: Hosea says the calf came from Israel and a craftsman made it, therefore it is not God. This makes the commentary's test of genuine creating against manufactured worship concrete.

row.basis: earth returned to waste and lightless disorder
row.note: Jeremiah sees the land as waste and void with no heavenly light in a judgment vision. It is a powerful biblical reversal of ordered creation beside the commentary's destructive edge of سوّى.

row.basis: fruitful land becomes wilderness and cities ruins
row.note: Jeremiah's judgment turns fruitful land into wilderness and ruins its cities. It directly parallels the commentary's movement from pasture and formed settlement toward blackened waste and leveling.

Isaiah promises new heavens and a new earth, with the former no longer remembered. It provides a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's claim that the creator can replace a decayed order with another creation.

row.basis: Spirit creates and renews the face of ground
row.note: Psalm 104 says that God sends forth Spirit, creatures are created, and the face of the ground is renewed. It closely combines the commentary's breath, creation, and renewal of earth after decline.

row.basis: breath enters dead bones and they live
row.note: Ezekiel's vision has God promise breath to dead bones so that they live. It is a direct prophetic counterpart to the commentary's formed body, imparted breath, and capacity for re-creation.

row.basis: maker of hearing ear and seeing eye
row.note: The commentary's bodily sequence includes hearing and sight as gifts after ordered formation. Proverbs explicitly names YHWH as maker of both ear and eye, extending the bodily detail into biblical wisdom.

row.basis: breath withdrawn, creatures die and return to dust
row.note: The commentary pairs a once-completed creation with aging and reversal. Psalm 104 says that when God withdraws breath, creatures die and return to dust, giving that reversal an elemental form.

The commentary makes measured limits part of creation before pasture and provision. Proverbs portrays God assigning the sea its boundary and setting earth's foundations, a distinct water-and-measure image.

row.basis: water wears away stone and washes soil
row.note: The commentary's Arabic root imagery moves from smooth rock and retained water to wearing and leveling. Job's waters wear down stones and wash away soil, giving a concrete biblical erosion image for that secondary development.

row.basis: three partners in human generation and God-given spirit
row.note: The commentary treats creation and enlivening as the one creator's action. Niddah 31a distributes parental bodily contributions and God's gift of soul and spirit, a Jewish anthropological counter-model that directly bears on formed body and breath.

row.basis: source Arabic س و ي; Hebrew שוה amid idol comparison
row.note: The commentary's source Arabic س و ي includes equality and the creator's lack of an equal. Isaiah 46:5 uses Hebrew שוה in its challenge about making God equal while its following context concerns goldsmith-made gods; the proposed cognacy requires lexical verification.

Deuteronomy depicts service to gods made by human hands that neither see, hear, eat, nor smell. It gives an expanded Torah counterpoint to the commentary's claim that crafted things lack the life and agency of their creator.

The commentary says the highest Lord is recognized in what he does rather than moved away from the world. Romans says God's power and divinity are perceived in the things made, a close New Testament formulation of that logic.

row.basis: all things sustained by a powerful word
row.note: Hebrews describes the Son as bearing all things by the word of his power. It offers a Christian development of the commentary's creation-by-command and its reading of ordered creation as ongoing coherence.

row.basis: things made by hands are not gods
row.note: Paul's Ephesian opponents are said to have heard that gods made by hands are not gods. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's rejection of an artifact as a true creator.

row.basis: all things from the Father and through one Lord
row.note: First Corinthians confesses one God, the Father, from whom all things are, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things are. Its twofold Christian creation formula is a significant theological counter-narrative to the commentary's unqualified single-agent formulation.
Paul contrasts a body sown perishable with one raised imperishable. It makes the commentary's formed body, decay, and anticipated re-creation into an explicit resurrection contrast.

row.basis: earth formed through water by God's word
row.note: Second Peter recalls heavens of old and earth formed out of and through water by God's word. It supplies a Christian water-and-word creation image beside the commentary's sky, measured water, and earthly provision.

row.basis: water from the rock given a Christological reading
row.note: The commentary develops smooth rock, retained water, and the provision that remains. First Corinthians rereads Israel's wilderness water from the rock as spiritual drink from Christ, a distinct Christian interpretive extension of the rock-and-water image.

The commentary's ordered pasture ends as dark chaff in its destructive horizon. Matthew's harvest image separates grain from chaff and burns the chaff, adding an eschatological use of the same agricultural remainder.

The commentary says the addressee will recite because God teaches him; Isaiah's speaker receives a trained tongue and a morning-awakened ear to hear like a disciple, joining divine instruction to receptive listening.

row.basis: words placed in the prophet's mouth
row.note: God touches Jeremiah's mouth and says he has put his words there; this gives a direct prophetic scene for the commentary's promise that God will make the addressee recite.

row.basis: prophet speaks words placed in his mouth
row.note: God promises to put his words in a prophet's mouth, who must speak all he is commanded; this frames recitation as received speech and accountable transmission.

row.basis: God teaches Moses what to say
row.note: Moses protests that he is not eloquent, and God answers that he will be with his mouth and teach him what to speak; the promise locates successful speech in divine enabling.

row.basis: Spirit and word on the tongue
row.note: David says the Lord's spirit speaks through him and God's word is on his tongue; this joins divine source and human utterance as the commentary does.

row.basis: spirit and words remain in mouths
row.note: God's covenant promises that his spirit and words placed in the addressee's mouth will remain with him and his descendants; this adds enduring communal transmission to the promise of retained recitation.
Jeremiah says he found and ate God's words, which became joy to him; this gives an image of divine speech taken inward before it is carried outward.
God tells Ezekiel to eat a scroll and then go speak to Israel; the sequence concretely joins receiving words inside with later public transmission, like the commentary's holding-then-releasing image.

row.basis: scroll enters the mouth and tastes sweet
row.note: The scroll fills Ezekiel's stomach and tastes like honey in his mouth; it portrays the prophetic message as fully received rather than merely heard.

row.basis: take the words to heart and listen
row.note: God tells Ezekiel to take all the words into his heart and hear them with his ears before speaking; this closely matches the commentary's inward retention of a received recitation.
Moses must write and teach a song so it can be put into Israel's mouths; the text makes memorized utterance a divinely arranged witness, extending the commentary's promise beyond one listener.
Moses says the song will not be forgotten from the mouths of Israel's descendants; unlike the individual prophetic promise, this makes preservation a multigenerational result.

The Hebrew qaraʾ verb here means reading the Torah before all Israel; it is a cognate of the Arabic q-r-ʾ label in the commentary and places the shared reading-family word in public scriptural recitation.

row.basis: public Torah reading to all Israel
row.note: Moses is instructed to read the law before the assembled people so they hear and learn; this gives the commentary's divinely enabled recitation a communal counterpart.
Moses reads the covenant book aloud and Israel answers that they will do and heed it; the sequence shows listening to a recitation issuing in following it.
The Hebrew qaraʾ reading verb occurs as the Torah is read; the cognate sense is specifically public scriptural reading, while the verse's explanation of the text adds interpretation to recitation.
The Levites read God's law and give its sense so the people understand; this illuminates the commentary's distinction between reciting words and having their meaning made clear.

row.basis: Hebrew qara, Baruch reads the scroll
row.note: The Hebrew qaraʾ verb describes Baruch reading Jeremiah's written words aloud; this is a cognate reading use, concretely tied to a message received from God and relayed by another voice.
Baruch reads the scroll before the people on a fast day; the mediated reading complements the commentary's image of a hearer following the reciter.

row.basis: scroll burned but its words answered
row.note: After the king burns the scroll, the Lord's word comes to Jeremiah again; the episode gives a concrete case of human rejection failing to make the divine message disappear.

row.basis: scroll ordered to be written again
row.note: God commands Jeremiah to take another scroll and write the former words again after Jehoiakim's burning; the repeated inscription supplies a narrative of preservation through renewed dictation.
Baruch writes the words again from Jeremiah's dictation, with many similar words added; this shows transmission surviving destruction and growing through a new recitation.

row.basis: word from God's mouth fulfills its purpose
row.note: God's word goes out from his mouth and accomplishes what he intends; beside the commentary's promise that recitation will not be lost, this emphasizes the efficacy of the source, not the hearer's memory alone.

Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's word standing forever; this meets the commentary's immediate move from pasture turned to refuse to the promise of a word that will not be dropped.
Israel must keep the commanded words on the heart; this offers a covenantal form of inward retention alongside the commentary's prophetic guarantee.

row.basis: teach and speak the words continually
row.note: The words are to be taught to children and spoken at home and on the road; this turns inwardly retained teaching into repeated speech across generations.
The command is very near, in the mouth and heart to be done; this links internal possession, spoken words, and action, rather than treating recitation as sound alone.

row.basis: law remains in the mouth and is meditated on
row.note: The book of the law is not to depart from Joshua's mouth, and he is to meditate on it day and night; this describes sustained recitation and practice, while the surah makes retention a divine promise.
The psalmist says he has treasured God's word in his heart; this is a clear image of gathered words kept inwardly, though here the speaker describes his own devotional practice.
The psalmist resolves not to forget God's word while delighting in the statutes; it concretizes the same result that the commentary attributes to God's recitation.
The speaker says God's precepts preserve his life and he will never forget them; this adds a received-word testimony in which memory sustains life.
God promises a covenant with the law placed within and written on the people's hearts; this communal inward inscription develops the commentary's image of a word held inside before it is spoken.

row.basis: forgetting God means failing to keep commands
row.note: Israel is warned not to forget the Lord by failing to keep his commandments; this clarifies the commentary's secondary sense of forgetting as abandonment, not only a lapse of memory.

row.basis: God will not forget Zion even if a mother might
row.note: The passage imagines a mother forgetting her nursing child, then denies that God will forget Zion; it adds a maternal image to the commentary's claim that the giver of memory does not abandon what is entrusted.

row.basis: God does not forget the covenant
row.note: God is merciful and will not abandon Israel or forget the covenant with the ancestors; this anchors retained revelation in divine fidelity to an earlier promise.

God hears Israel's groaning, remembers the covenant with the ancestors, and turns toward the enslaved people; this shows remembrance as active fidelity, the ground the commentary gives for a preserved message.

row.basis: God chooses not to remember sins
row.note: God says he blots out transgressions and will not remember sins; beside the surah's exception reserving memory to God's will, this shows divine non-remembrance as an act of mercy toward a different object.
The human being flourishes like field grass and disappears when the wind passes; this gives a scriptural form to the commentary's adjacent image of vegetation becoming refuse.

row.basis: steadfast love lasts beyond human life
row.note: After describing human life as grass, the psalm says the Lord's steadfast love is everlasting; this places divine permanence beside the commentary's contrast between withered pasture and enduring word.

row.basis: the forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
row.note: If a reaper forgets a sheaf, it must remain for the immigrant, orphan, and widow; unlike the commentary's abandoned camp refuse, the forgotten object becomes provision for the vulnerable, adding an ethical reversal.

row.basis: wishing to be an unregarded stillbirth
row.note: Job wishes he had been like a hidden stillbirth that never saw light; this shares the birth-lament behind Mary's wish to have been forgotten, while Job's own suffering rather than childbirth frames the speech.

row.basis: Jeremiah curses the day of his birth
row.note: Jeremiah wishes the day of his birth had not been blessed; this is a prophetic birth lament beside Mary's wish to die and become forgotten, but the two speakers and settings remain distinct.

row.basis: why was I born to see toil?
row.note: Jeremiah asks why he came from the womb only to see sorrow; the question shares Mary's acute labor-time wish for erasure without making her scene the same story.

Isaiah says grass withers and flower fades; beside the surah's pasture becoming dark refuse before the promise of retention, it sharpens the contrast between transient vegetation and lasting divine speech.

The Paraclete will teach the disciples and remind them of everything Jesus said; this is the closest Christian formulation of received words retained by divine agency, while its addressees are the disciples collectively.
The Holy Spirit will teach the disciples what they ought to say when brought before authorities; this parallels the future promise of divinely enabled speech in a specific trial setting.

Jesus says the Spirit of the Father speaks in the disciples when they testify; the saying locates their words' source in God, like the commentary's account of recitation received rather than self-generated.
Paul contrasts Spirit-taught words with human wisdom; this makes the content and manner of speech dependent on divine teaching, adding an apostolic setting to the commentary's promise.

row.basis: prophets carried by the Holy Spirit
row.note: Prophecy did not come by human will, but people spoke from God as they were carried by the Spirit; this gives a concise account of divine source and human utterance.
Paul calls the community a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God on hearts; this joins the commentary's inwardly held word to a Christian image of divine inscription.
The risen Jesus opens the disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures; this adds divine enabling of comprehension to the commentary's promise to make the addressee recite.

row.basis: Deuteronomy's word read as preached faith
row.note: Paul quotes the word near mouth and heart from Deuteronomy and identifies it as the word of faith he proclaims; this Christian interpretation turns Torah's inward and spoken command into a preached confession.

row.basis: law written on minds and hearts
row.note: The new-covenant quotation promises God's laws in minds and written on hearts; this develops inward retention as a covenantal gift, not merely a reader's discipline.

row.basis: doing rather than forgetting the heard word
row.note: The person who looks into the law and perseveres is a doer, not a forgetful hearer; this gives a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that true reading becomes a life of obedience.

row.basis: word held fast and bearing fruit
row.note: The good soil hears the word, holds it fast in an honest heart, and bears fruit with perseverance; it meets the commentary's agricultural setting with a distinct image of received speech retained until it yields action.

The seer is told to eat the scroll, sweet in the mouth but bitter in the stomach; like Ezekiel and the commentary's inward-retention metaphor, the message is taken inside, while Revelation adds the cost of its contents.

After eating the scroll, John is told to prophesy again about many peoples; the sequence makes inward reception the preparation for outward warning, close to the commentary's movement from not forgetting to reminding others.
Philip asks the Ethiopian whether he understands Isaiah's reading, and the man says he needs a guide; this gives a specific scene of recitation joined to teaching and interpretation.
Philip begins from the passage the Ethiopian is reading and tells him the good news about Jesus; this shows a received text being opened and transmitted to another listener.
Timothy is charged to attend to public reading alongside exhortation and teaching; the Syriac reading tradition also gives a cognate form for the commentary's reading word.
Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him by grace; this joins the commentary's womb image to prophetic vocation, though Paul is describing his own apostolic call.
God reveals his Son in Paul so that Paul may preach among the nations; this offers a distinct Christian sequence of inward reception and outward delivery.
The opening says all things came to be through the Word; this complements the commentary's pairing of creation and divine teaching by locating creation in the one who is God's Word.

row.basis: Word makes the unseen God known
row.note: The prologue says the only Son has made God known; read alongside its claim that creation came through the Word, it offers a Christian pairing of creator and revealer like the commentary's creator-teacher sequence.

row.basis: God speaks through prophets across times
row.note: God spoke to the ancestors in many ways through the prophets; this places the surah's direct divine address within a wider scriptural pattern of mediated revelation.

row.basis: Mary's birth narrated without the lament
row.note: Luke narrates Mary giving birth in Bethlehem, swaddling Jesus, and laying him in a manger, whereas the Qur'anic scene foregrounds her wish to be forgotten and God's consolation; the different framing matters without making a shared scene identical.

row.basis: king reads the law throughout life
row.note: The king must read the law all his days, learn reverence, and keep its words; this supplies a sustained practice of reading beyond the single prophetic promise.
Ezra sets his heart to study the law, do it, and teach it; this matches the commentary's reading-as-devotion and links inward learning to public instruction.

The midrash pictures God consulting Torah as a builder consults a plan before making the world; it gives a Jewish interpretive link between creation and revealed teaching like the commentary's creator-teacher pairing.

row.basis: scribe studies prophecy and speaks wisdom
row.note: The scribe studies the law and prophets, seeks hidden meanings, and is filled with a spirit of understanding to pour out wise words; this adds a learned Jewish model of received instruction becoming speech.
The speaker asks God to grant fitting speech and says both people and their words are in God's hand; this extends divine agency from recitation to the speaker's very words.

row.basis: wisdom and spirit sent from above
row.note: The passage asks who could know God's counsel unless God gave wisdom and sent a holy spirit from above; this frames understanding as a gift, beside the commentary's promise of divine teaching.

row.basis: Ezra dictates books by divine enablement
row.note: After Jerusalem's destruction Ezra is commanded to write, and the books are dictated through him; this gives a Jewish apocalyptic scene of preserved revelation being restored through an enabled human speaker.

row.basis: forgetting one word of Torah as culpable
row.note: The Mishnah treats negligent loss of a learned word as grave; beside the surah's promise that the prophet will not forget, it makes the contrast between human obligation and divinely secured retention explicit.
The rabbinic account has Moses repeat Torah teaching through Aaron, the elders, and Israel; it explains communal retention through rehearsed transmission rather than a single prophetic promise.

row.ref: John Chrysostom, Homilies on John, on John 14:25-26
row.basis: Spirit's reminder as Christ's teaching retained
row.note: Chrysostom reads Jesus' promise that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples in its immediate setting; this Christian interpretation stresses preservation of Jesus' words rather than an unrelated new message.

row.basis: eating the scroll as inward appropriation
row.note: Jerome's discussion of Ezekiel's eaten scroll treats reception of prophetic words as something to take within before teaching; it supplies a Christian interpretive bridge for the commentary's held-then-released word.

The Syriac Peshitta uses a verb from the nšy family for the sparrow not being forgotten before God; that is a cognate of the Arabic n-s-y label, while the Greek New Testament has a different root, and the context makes divine remembering concrete.
The Peshitta's Syriac reading term qeryānā belongs to the same Semitic reading-word family as Arabic q-r-ʾ; here it names public reading joined to teaching, while the SBL Greek word is not a cognate.

Isaiah commands that the testimony be bound up and the teaching sealed among his disciples; this gives a concrete preservation practice beside the commentary's promise that recited words will not be lost.
God tells Isaiah to inscribe the message in a book for future days as an enduring witness; this connects the commentary's assurance of retained speech with written preservation across time.

row.basis: Moses' promised prophet identified with Jesus
row.note: Peter quotes Moses' promise of a prophet like him and applies it to Jesus; this gives a Christian reading of the very Mosaic pattern in which God places words in a prophet's mouth.

Paul says he handed on what he had received about Jesus' death and resurrection; this makes the source-to-recipient-to-listener chain explicit, adding a communal transmission formula to the commentary's carrier-of-words image.

row.basis: vision written plainly for a reader
row.note: The prophet must write the vision on tablets so a reader can run with it; this joins inscription, legibility, and transmission to the commentary's account of a received message following a recitation.
Moses finishes writing the words of the law in a book; this adds a textual witness to the surah's claim that revelation continues in earlier pages.

row.basis: book placed beside the ark as witness
row.note: The book of the law is placed beside the covenant ark to remain a witness; this gives the commentary's preserved word an archival setting and a continuing role beyond its first hearers.

row.basis: sealed book preserved for the end
row.note: Daniel is told to shut and seal the book until the time of the end; this gives a specific apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's references to a hidden book and protected revelation.

row.basis: God forms the inward parts in the womb
row.note: The psalmist says God formed him and knit him together in his mother's womb; the passage's own creation scene gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's explicitly metaphorical womb image.

row.basis: womb formation and days written in a book
row.note: The psalm joins God's sight of the unformed body with days written in a book; this uniquely meets the commentary's conjunction of womb-held life and a word securely kept by God.

row.basis: book of remembrance for those who fear God
row.note: A book of remembrance is written before God for those who fear him and remember his name; this makes the commentary's divine knowledge and retained remembrance a recorded communal witness.

row.basis: books opened before the heavenly court
row.note: Daniel sees books opened for judgment; this adds a scene of deeds preserved in divine records beside the commentary's claim that what is public and hidden remains within God's knowledge.
The prophet asks whether a bride can forget her ornaments, then says Israel has forgotten God; this gives the commentary's secondary sense of forgetting as abandonment a concrete relational image.

row.basis: Moses, prophets, and psalms read as fulfilled in Jesus
row.note: Jesus says that what is written in the Law of Moses, Prophets, and Psalms must be fulfilled; this Christian account of continuity with earlier scriptures belongs beside the commentary's claim that the recited message is also present in the earlier pages.

row.basis: entrust what was heard to future teachers
row.note: Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others; this makes the retained message a deliberate chain of transmission, extending the commentary's inward reception and outward reminder.

The dead are judged from what is written in opened books; this gives a Christian apocalyptic instance of divine knowledge preserved as a record, like the commentary's connection between hidden deeds and God's book.

The Mishnah traces Torah from Moses through Joshua, elders, prophets, and later teachers; it presents revelation as a handed-on chain, adding a Jewish communal model beside the commentary's direct divine address to one recipient.

Sirach identifies personified Wisdom with the book of the covenant and the law commanded by Moses; this gives a Jewish interpretive bridge between divine teaching and the earlier Mosaic pages named in the surah.

row.basis: Enoch reads heavenly tablets and records them
row.note: Enoch reads the heavenly tablets, understands them, and records what they contain; this adds a Jewish apocalyptic image of revelation preserved in a celestial book and passed on in writing.

row.basis: prophets and apostolic memoirs read in assembly
row.note: Justin describes public reading of prophetic and apostolic writings followed by an exhortation to imitate them; this connects the commentary's recitation, listening, and lived devotion with early Christian worship.

row.basis: Mary's birth in the cave with a midwife
row.note: The apocryphal narrative places Jesus' birth in a cave and has Joseph summon a midwife, whereas the Qur'anic Mary scene foregrounds solitary labor, distress, and a wish to be forgotten; the distinct birth framing adds an early Christian account beside the Qur'anic one.
Exodus places shepherd Moses at Horeb, the mountain of God; it anchors the commentary's Moses seeing fire from the side of al-Ṭūr in the same mountain-call setting.
An angel appears to Moses in a flame from within a bush that burns without being consumed. It is the closest Hebrew-Bible fire-theophany to the commentary's fire at which Moses is addressed.

row.basis: great sight, not a practical beacon
row.note: Moses turns aside to investigate the great sight of a bush that does not burn up; the commentary's Moses first treats the distant fire as a possible ember, warmth, or guide. The different reason for approach is itself illuminating.
After Moses turns aside, God calls “Moses, Moses” from the bush. This supplies the same sequence of approaching visible fire and then receiving divine speech.
God stops Moses from coming nearer and names the place holy ground; it gives a biblical counterpart for the commentary's blessing and glorification around the fire.
At the bush God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out. This makes Exodus's commissioning the counterpart to “I have chosen you; listen to revelation” in the commentary.
God says Israel will serve God on this mountain after liberation. The mountain fire-call is thus ordered toward worship, as the commentary joins Moses's fire journey to remembrance and prayer.
God gives Moses the enduring Name and calls it his memorial through generations; this places name-remembrance within the same bush commission that the commentary ends in prayer.

The commentary's وَذَكَرَ / dhikr is matched by Hebrew זִכְרִי, “my memorial,” for the Name. The regular Semitic d/z correspondence supports a word-level link without identifying the Arabic roots for prayer and burning.

row.basis: voice from the midst of fire
row.note: Moses tells Israel that YHWH spoke from the midst of fire while they saw no form, only a voice. It sharpens the commentary's voiced fire while keeping the speaker distinct from the visible flame.

Moses says God showed Israel his great fire on earth and they heard words from the midst of fire. Its explicit great-fire/voice pairing reframes the commentary's opposition of the greatest fire and Moses's greatest signs.
The pillar of fire gives Israel light so they can travel by night; it is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's distant fire lit as a route-marker and to its huda/guidance link.

The three Judeans say the God they serve can rescue them from the blazing furnace. This reverses the commentary's fire/prayer polarity: service of God is voiced at the edge of fire as confidence of rescue.

Those who kindle their own fire and walk by its flame are told that they will lie down in pain. It reverses the commentary's small human fire as useful provision and its warning that an ignored reminder ends in greater fire.

At the end of Isaiah, those who rebelled against God are an abhorrence, with a fire that is not quenched. It closely matches the commentary's punitive, inescapable great fire rather than a warming or guiding flame.

row.basis: flame of fire in a bush
row.note: Stephen retells that an angel appeared to Moses in wilderness Sinai in a flame of fire in a bush; it is the New Testament's direct recollection of the fire scene.
Moses sees the sight, approaches to inspect it, and then the Lord's voice comes. The sequence matches the commentary's visible fire leading to a divine address.

The speaking Lord announces that he has seen Israel's affliction and sends Moses to Egypt. This Christian retelling preserves the commissioned response to the fire-theophany that the commentary calls divine choosing.
In the judgment scene, those at the left are told to depart into fire prepared for the devil and angels. It is a direct Christian counterpart to the wretched person entering the great fire.

John names worship of the beast and receipt of its mark as the opposed cultic act. It supplies a concrete alternative to the commentary's person who remembers the Lord's name and prays; its fire consequence is named in the next verse.

row.basis: fire and sulfur for the worshiper
row.note: That worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur before holy angels and the Lamb. This explicitly makes corrupt worship, rather than prayer to God, lead to punitive fire.
The smoke of that torment rises forever and its worshipers have no rest day or night. It adds an enduring experiential dimension to the commentary's account of entering and bearing the great fire.
Jesus's Gehenna saying retains the undying worm and unquenched fire. It supplies a concrete Christian form of the commentary's fire that neither releases nor spares its victim.

The Lord is revealed in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel. This joins rejection of a divine message to fiery judgment, as the commentary joins turning from reminder to the great fire.

Passover flesh must be eaten roasted with fire (צְלִי־אֵשׁ). Hebrew צלי/צלה is a likely cognate of the commentary's Arabic ص ل ي cooking sense, giving a concrete domestic-ritual use beside its suffering-in-fire sense.

Biblical Aramaic calls the blazing furnace נוּר. Its nūr “fire” is a controlled Semitic beside-word for the commentary's Arabic النار/nūr discussion, while the furnace context prevents importing its road-light sense.

Daniel kneels toward Jerusalem, prays, and gives thanks; the Aramaic verb צְלָא is the prayer-side cognate beside the commentary's فَصَلَّى. It reinforces the stated sound-echo with fire vocabulary without collapsing Arabic ص ل و and ص ل ي.

The verse calls God's word a נֵר, “lamp,” for the feet and light for the path. Hebrew nēr is a probable cognate of the commentary's nūr label, and the verse supplies the very path-guidance that its distant fire performs.

row.basis: fire followed by thin quiet sound
row.note: At Horeb the sequence is earthquake, fire, then qôl demamah daqqah, a thin quiet sound. That order contrasts with the commentary's Moses, whose call is located at the fire.

row.basis: warmth and danger of sages' coals
row.note: Rabbi Eliezer tells disciples to warm themselves by sages' fire yet beware their coals lest they be burned. It preserves the commentary's exact contrast between approaching fire for warmth and suffering it on entering too far.

Exodus Rabbah reads the burning, unconsumed thornbush as God's presence with Israel in affliction. That reading makes the Sinai fire a sign of solidarity rather than merely route, fuel, or punishment.

When Israel walks through fire, God promises that the flame will not consume it. This covenantal counter-scene reverses the commentary's entry into fire as endurance of its heat while leaving room for its sacred Moses-fire.

Azariah stands in the furnace and begins a spoken prayer blessing the God of the ancestors. The Greek-Jewish addition counterposes prayer inside a human furnace to the commentary's division of the prayerful person from the fire-bound one.

Jesus calls himself the light of the world and says a follower will not walk in darkness. Though not a fire scene, it is a precise Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire seen from afar as a guide toward the way.

On Malta the islanders kindle a fire and welcome the shipwrecked group because of cold and rain. Its human fire supplies warmth and shelter, the non-punitive use the commentary sets beside entry into the great fire.
Sodom and Gomorrah undergo a penalty of eternal fire and stand as an example. It joins the commentary's two functions of fire: judgment made into a warning or reminder for readers.
Hebrews recalls Sinai as a mountain with blazing fire, gloom, and tempest. It receives the Moses/Sinai fire tradition that frames the commentary's Mount Ṭūr address.

Because believers receive an unshakable kingdom, they are urged to offer God acceptable worship with reverence and awe. It places worship as response within Hebrews' immediately fire-marked Sinai discourse.

Hebrews calls God a consuming fire. Together with its preceding exhortation to worship, it provides a Christian configuration in which reverent worship and divine fire belong together, not only as opposites.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses 2.20–21
row.note: Gregory reads the unconsumed burning bush as a figure of the virgin conception: divine fire is present without consuming. This Christian interpretation expands the commentary's sacred, non-hell fire beyond navigation and judgment.

row.basis: pillar of fire turns on Egypt
row.note: During the night, YHWH looks down on Egypt's army through the pillar of fire and cloud and throws it into panic. This gives the commentary's route-guiding fire a second biblical role: the same wilderness fire also separates and judges those opposing God's deliverance.

Sinai smokes because YHWH descends upon it in fire, and the mountain trembles. Its mountain-scale fire is a close Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's fire seen at the side of al-Ṭūr, distinct from the contained bush.

row.basis: call the Name; answer by fire
