row.note: Elijah frames the Carmel test as calling on a god's name, with the god who answers by fire shown to be God. It gives a concrete biblical conjunction of divine Name, prayer, and fire beside the commentary's remembrance of the Name and prayer at Moses's fire.

David builds an altar, offers sacrifice, calls to YHWH, and receives an answer in fire from heaven. It provides another single-verse scene in which worshipful invocation, rather than entry into punishment, is answered by fire.

Fire goes out from before YHWH and consumes Nadab and Abihu. Alongside their unauthorized fire in the preceding verse, it complicates the commentary's blessed fire by making uncommanded cultic approach a site of lethal judgment.

Judith's judgment hymn says that God sends fire and worms into the flesh of hostile nations, with pain without end. Its bodily punitive fire is a close Jewish parallel to the commentary's skin-burning account of the great fire.

row.basis: agony and heat in the flame
row.note: The rich man in Hades asks for water to cool his tongue because he is in agony in the flame. It supplies the specific embodied heat and suffering that the commentary draws from the Arabic sense of entering and bearing fire.

At the end of the bush commission, Moses is told to take the staff with which he will perform signs. It gives the Exodus continuation for the commentary's shift from the greatest fire of judgment to the greatest signs shown to Moses.

Nadab and Abihu place fire and incense before YHWH that he had not commanded. The episode requires a distinction between sacred encounter and humanly initiated ritual fire, sharpening the commentary's several ways of approaching fire.

The commandment is called a lamp, Torah a light, and corrective reproofs the way of life. Its joined guidance and admonition supplies a Hebrew formulation for the commentary's road-marker fire, huda, and reminder.

Wisdom recasts the wilderness pillar as a flaming guide for an unknown journey and a harmless sun for Israel's wandering. That retelling directly develops the commentary's contrast between a helpful distant fire and a destructive one.

row.basis: ordinary fire as a foretaste of Gehenna
row.note: The rabbinic maxim calls ordinary fire one-sixtieth of Gehenna. It supplies a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the commentary's claim that a small human fire is a reminder of the great punitive fire.

Tongues as of fire appear, divide, and rest on each person at Pentecost. This non-punitive communal fire offers a Christian counterpart to the commentary's blessed fire around which divine speech and glorification occur.

Those victorious over the beast stand at the sea of glass mingled with fire, holding God's harps. It reverses the commentary's fire-bound wretch by placing victorious worshipers beside fire rather than as its sufferers.

row.basis: song of Moses at the fire scene
row.note: The victors sing the song of Moses and the Lamb, praising God's great and marvelous works. This adds Moses and praise to the preceding fire-mingled scene, echoing the commentary's Moses-fire journey toward worship.

The song asks who will not fear the Lord, glorify his Name, and worship him. Its Name-and-worship formula completes the fire-and-Moses sequence with a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's remembering the Lord's Name and praying.

Justin identifies the one who appeared and spoke to Moses in the bush's flame with the pre-existent Christ. This Christian reading changes the identity of the voice at the fire while preserving the fire-theophany shared with the commentary.
Jesus answers concern with cleansing by telling his hearers to give alms and declaring all clean; this directly parallels the commentary's given share that purifies what remains.

row.basis: giving to poor; righteousness remains forever
row.note: Paul joins scattering gifts to the poor with righteousness remaining forever; it combines the commentary's paid crop-share with its falāḥ and bāqī permanence.
God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, multiplies seed, and increases a harvest of righteousness; its gift context maps the commentary's blessed crop-growth to ethical fruit.
Paul's firstfruits analogy makes the whole dough holy from its consecrated portion; it gives a precise cultic counterpart to the commentary's share whose giving cleanses the remainder.
Sirach compares water quenching fire with almsgiving atoning for sin; it makes explicit the purificatory result assigned to tezekkā's charitable share.

row.basis: redeeming wrong by mercy to poor
row.note: Daniel's Aramaic counsel tells the king to break off sins through righteousness and wrongs through mercy to the poor; it joins relief of need to moral rescue like the commentary's gift and purification.

row.basis: seventh-year field; needy eat its remnant
row.note: The seventh-year field is left so needy people eat and animals take its remainder; it concretizes the commentary's harvested land as holding a claim beyond the owner's consumption.

row.basis: field corners and gleanings at harvest
row.note: At reaping, field corners and gleanings must remain; this is a direct legal form of the commentary's crop-right owed at harvest.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf for vulnerable people; blessing
row.note: A forgotten sheaf must remain for the alien, orphan, and widow so God blesses the work; it links surrendered harvest portion to blessing as the commentary links giving to purified productive remainder.
Israel must tithe all seed-yield of the field year by year; its stated annual crop measure closely meets the commentary's output-and-allotted-share facet.
After completing the third-year tithe of produce, it is given to Levite, alien, orphan, and widow; its distribution specifies whom a crop due supports.
Firstfruits and offerings given to priests make blessing rest on the household; it combines output-share and blessing in the commentary's z-k-w agricultural sequence.
Honoring the LORD from wealth and all first produce provides a concise biblical practice behind the commentary's payment from crop or wealth.
The verse pictures filled barns and overflowing vats after firstfruits; it supplies abundance as the outcome of offered produce, rather than generic prosperity.

row.basis: full tithe; heavens opened for blessing
row.note: The full tithe is brought to the storehouse and God opens heaven to pour out blessing; it makes a fixed due share and divinely granted increase mutually explicit.
Tobit carries firstfruits and tithes of produce to Jerusalem; the narrative embodies the commentary's zakāt-like harvest obligation in pious practice.

row.basis: third tenth for those in need
row.note: Tobit's third tenth goes to people for whom he has a duty of care; it supplies the vulnerable-recipient side of the commentary's harvest share.

row.basis: firstfruits of winepress and threshing floor
row.note: The Didache directs firstfruits from winepress, threshing floor, cattle, and sheep to prophets; it carries the commentary's harvest-due motif into early Christian community order.
If no prophet is present, the Didache directs firstfruits to the poor; it makes the crop share a relief obligation, not private purification alone.

row.ref: Basil of Caesarea, Homily 6 on Luke 12:18
row.note: Basil reads the rich man's larger barns as hoarding surplus that belongs with the needy; this Christian interpretation makes explicit the commentary's alternative between a harvest shared and one retained for self.

row.basis: larger barns for all grain and goods
row.note: The rich man demolishes barns to store all his grain and goods; against the commentary's harvest-day due, it stages productive output withheld for self.
Jesus commands almsgiving and calls the resulting heavenly treasury unfailing; it directly associates relinquished share with the commentary's better and more-lasting outcome.
Land that has drunk repeated rain produces a crop useful to its cultivators and receives God's blessing; it closely matches the commentary's worked, growing field rather than mere pasture.

row.basis: thorns and thistles; curse and burning
row.note: The contrasting land bears thorns and thistles and approaches curse and burning; it gives an ethical version of the commentary's same-ground contrast between productive cultivation and vegetation headed for ruin.
The vineyard-owner digs, clears stones, plants, and expects good grapes; divine care of a cultivated plot renders concrete the commentary's agricultural sense assigned to Rabb.

row.basis: no pruning or hoeing; briers; no rain
row.note: The ruined vineyard will neither be pruned nor hoed, so briers arise and rain is withheld; it is the inverse of the commentary's ploughed, watered, yielding field.
Isaiah identifies the LORD's vineyard with Israel and its expected fruit with justice and righteousness; it makes the commentary's agricultural success an explicitly moral outcome.

row.basis: LORD as vineyard keeper watering and guarding
row.note: The LORD calls himself the vineyard's keeper, watering it continually and guarding it night and day; this closely clarifies the commentary's farm-steward sense of Rabb.

row.basis: sow righteousness; reap loyal love; break fallow ground
row.note: Hosea commands sowing righteousness, reaping loyal love, and breaking fallow ground while seeking the LORD; agricultural labor becomes the ethical transformation that the commentary casts as purification and lasting success.

row.basis: rain waters earth; sprouting; seed and bread
row.note: Rain and snow water the earth, make it sprout, and provide seed and bread; this gives a precise biblical water-to-growth-to-food field scene beside the commentary's expanded field imagery.

row.basis: rain in season; land produce and tree fruit
row.note: God's timely rain makes land yield produce and trees fruit; it places the commentary's crop growth under divine blessing.
Jesus's seed parable narrates the ordered growth of blade, head, and full grain; it gives a kingdom reading of the commentary's field-process.
When the grain permits, the sickle is sent because harvest has arrived; it supplies the harvest-stage after the commentary's growth and cultivation.

row.basis: good soil bears fruit with endurance
row.note: Good soil is an honest, good heart that holds the word and bears fruit with endurance; it joins the commentary's cultivated crop to falāḥ as lasting in good.

row.basis: worldly care and wealth choke fruit
row.note: Worldly care and wealth are thorns that choke the word and make it unfruitful; this concretely meets the commentary's contrast between a worldly field and a fruitful, enduring one.
Jesus calls the Father the vinedresser; this is a direct Christian agricultural analogue for the commentary's Rabb who maintains and restores a farm.

row.basis: pruning cleans fruitful branches for more fruit
row.note: The vinedresser removes barren branches and prunes fruit-bearing ones so they bear more; it puts cleansing and maintenance directly inside a growth-to-fruit process.

row.basis: unabiding branch withers and is burned
row.note: A branch that does not remain withers and is gathered for fire; it supplies a pointed vegetal reverse to the commentary's crop that remains in good rather than becoming ruined growth.

row.basis: sowing to flesh or Spirit; corruption or eternal life
row.note: The two sowings culminate in corruption or eternal life; it gives direct field language to the commentary's contrast between a worldly crop and an afterlife-directed one.

row.basis: do good; reap in due season; do not give up
row.note: Doing good is to continue because one will reap in due season without giving up; it closely supplies the commentary's success as remaining in good.
The reaper gathers fruit for eternal life, so sower and reaper rejoice together; it makes harvest an image of the enduring good emphasized at 87:17.

row.basis: farmer waits for precious fruit and rains
row.note: The farmer waits patiently for the earth's precious fruit and its rains while believers await the Lord; this connects crop maturation to the commentary's enduring, eschatological good.

row.basis: fruitful tree; leaf does not wither; prospers
row.note: The righteous person is a watered tree yielding fruit whose leaf does not wither and whose work prospers; it is a close vegetal counterpart to cultivated success and permanence.

row.basis: watered tree does not cease bearing fruit
row.note: The tree by water stays green through heat and drought and does not cease producing fruit; it directly contrasts durable blessed growth with the commentary's perishing pasture.

row.basis: break fallow ground; do not sow among thorns
row.note: Jeremiah's call to break fallow ground and avoid sowing among thorns applies ploughing to repentance; it strengthens the commentary's ethical reading of broken soil and fruitful cultivation.

row.basis: God teaches the farmer right practice
row.note: In Isaiah's farming instruction, the farmer's God teaches him the right practice; it offers an indirect biblical counterpart to the commentary's Lord who tends and orders a farm.

row.basis: seed dies in order to live
row.note: The commentary uses a seed smothered under soil as purification's opposite, whereas Paul makes a sown seed's death the necessary image of resurrection; the opposed agricultural valuation is the link.

row.basis: earth's ripe harvest and final reaping
row.note: The angel announces that the earth's harvest is ripe and must be reaped; it supplies an explicitly final-harvest horizon for the commentary's crop and afterlife contrast.

row.basis: Arabic ف ل ح; Hebrew פלח; cleaving ground
row.note: The commentary's Arabic ف ل ح is developed as splitting and ploughing soil; Hebrew פֹּלֵחַ depicts cleaving the ground in the psalm's simile, retaining the same concrete root-scene in a different setting.

row.basis: pe'ah as an unfixed harvest obligation
row.note: The Mishnah lists pe'ah, the field-edge left from harvest, among obligations with no fixed measure; this legal reception sharpens the commentary's claim that produce bears a due share.
Rabbi Akiva's defense of supporting the poor makes charity a means by which the giver is saved from Gehenna; it develops the commentary's charitable purification into a salvation claim.

row.basis: deeds as roots that withstand the wind
row.note: Avot compares deeds exceeding wisdom to a deeply rooted tree that wind cannot uproot; its moral agriculture gives a Jewish image for the commentary's remaining in good.

row.basis: vine and elm; rich support poor
row.note: Hermas makes the fruitful vine depend on the otherwise fruitless elm, then reads their mutual support as rich and poor aiding one another; it turns agricultural fruit into a specific charity relation.

row.basis: hardworking farmer's first share of crops
row.note: The hard-working farmer ought first to receive a share of the crops; this provides a distinct New Testament use of cultivation, labor, and a rightful portion beside the commentary's farmer and yield.

row.basis: Arabic ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; cleansing hands
row.note: If Hebrew זכה is accepted as cognate with the commentary's Arabic ز ك و label, Job's cleansing of the hands supplies a physical-purity use; the cognacy and semantic scope need verification.

row.basis: sowing six years and gathering field yield
row.note: Six years of sowing and gathering a field's yield supply the ordinary cultivated stage that the next verse interrupts for the needy; this completes the commentary's soil-to-yield process.

row.basis: vineyard gleanings left to poor and alien
row.note: Vineyard gleanings are explicitly left to the poor and resident alien; this supplies the recipient of the harvest-right developed in the commentary.
After the tithe promise, God rebukes the devourer so it cannot destroy land-fruit or make the vine fail; it continues the commentary's due share with protected growth.

row.basis: hoarded goods fail to secure life
row.note: God demands the rich man's life that night and asks whose stored goods will be; it supplies the failed impermanence that turns the hoarded grain of Luke 12 into the commentary's worldly rather than lasting harvest.

row.basis: clean because of the spoken word
row.note: Within the vine and vinedresser discourse, Jesus calls the disciples clean because of his word; it gives a distinct purification claim beside the commentary's z-k-w cleansing within cultivated growth.
Isaiah asks whether a ploughman keeps opening and breaking his ground all day; it names the physical soil-splitting scene beneath the commentary's Arabic falāḥ.
After leveling the soil, the farmer sows differentiated seed in appointed places; it supplies the ordered planting stage after the commentary's split earth.
Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the growth; this is an unusually exact divine growth sequence for the commentary's cultivated crop.
Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who gives growth; it identifies divine agency in the increase the commentary connects with blessing.
Paul calls the community God's field; it converts the commentary's cared-for farm into a communal ethical image.
When fruit season approaches, the vineyard owner sends servants to receive the fruit due him; it is a direct narrative counterpart to the commentary's harvest carrying a rightful claim.
The kingdom is given to people producing its fruits; the vineyard's fruit-duty becomes a moral criterion, like the commentary's link of field yield with successful purification.

row.basis: digging and fertilizing a fruitless tree
row.note: The vinedresser proposes digging around a fruitless fig tree and applying manure; it gives a close farm-repair image for the commentary's Rabb who tends and restores a plot.
Fruit in the coming year prevents cutting, while continued barrenness ends the tree; it makes growth versus ruin the condition of the cultivated plant.

row.basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
row.note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food enduring to eternal life; it maps the commentary's food-and-field imagery onto its world-life and lasting-afterlife contrast.

row.basis: grass of the field is transient
row.note: Grass alive in the field today is thrown into an oven tomorrow; it gives a direct Gospel reverse to the commentary's durable good over perishing pasture.

row.basis: wheat gathered and weeds destroyed at harvest
row.note: At harvest the weeds are gathered for burning and the wheat stored in the barn; the same field distinguishes productive crop from destructive vegetation.

row.basis: grass dries and its flower falls
row.note: All flesh is grass whose flower falls when the grass dries; the formula closely matches the commentary's passing pasture image.
The Lord's word remains forever after the grass-and-flower contrast; it supplies an explicit enduring term beside the commentary's abqā.
The tree of life bears fruit every month and its leaves heal nations; watered, recurring produce gives an eschatological image of durable blessed yield.

row.basis: earth sprouts seed-bearing plants and fruit trees
row.note: God commands the earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees; it gives a creation-level counterpart to the commentary's God-brought pasture and growing crop.

row.basis: seedtime and harvest do not cease
row.note: Seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth remains; this directly supplies a crop-cycle formulation for the permanence sought in the commentary.

row.basis: sowing, hundredfold yield, and divine blessing
row.note: Isaac sows the land, finds a hundredfold that year, and is blessed by the LORD; it closely combines cultivation, increase, and divine blessing.
All fruit of a newly planted tree's fourth year is holy praise for the LORD; it gives a concrete sacred setting-aside of harvest before later enjoyment.
In the fifth year people may eat the fruit so that the tree's yield increases; it explicitly joins a prior consecrated portion with continuing growth.

row.basis: barley firstfruits given for the people
row.note: A man brings barley firstfruits to the man of God, who orders that the people receive them to eat; it is a narrative enactment of harvest share becoming communal provision.
After the shared firstfruits are set before the people, all eat and some remains by the LORD's word; it gives a concrete counterpart to the commentary's baqī as what is left from yield.
Job denies eating his land's yield without payment or causing its owners to suffer; it makes a field's produce ethically answerable to those with a claim on it.

row.basis: thorns instead of wheat for unjust use
row.note: For such unjust use of land, Job accepts thorns instead of wheat and weeds instead of barley; it gives a juridical reverse to the commentary's worked field that yields good.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human cultivation
row.note: God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human cultivation, bringing food from earth; it closely parallels the commentary's divine bringing-forth of pasture and crop.

row.basis: giving to poor and enduring righteousness
row.note: The righteous scatter gifts to the poor and their righteousness stands forever; it joins the commentary's charitable share to its enduring-good result in the Hebrew source behind 2 Corinthians 9.

row.basis: scattering increases; withholding due brings want
row.note: One person scatters and yet increases, while another withholds what is due and comes to want; this is a compact wisdom analogue to the commentary's share-and-growth logic.
The generous person is enriched, and the one who waters is watered; it links giving, water, and renewed plenty beside the commentary's blessed agricultural increase.

row.basis: rain for seed, abundant bread, and broad pasture
row.note: God gives rain for seed, rich bread from land, and broad pasture for livestock; this closely fills out the commentary's rain, crop, food, and pasture sequence.
With spirit poured from on high, wilderness becomes a fruitful field and the field a forest; it turns divine outpouring into the commentary's increase-and-growth imagery.

row.basis: justice in wilderness and righteousness in fruitful field
row.note: Justice dwells in wilderness and righteousness abides in the fruitful field; it makes the commentary's agricultural success explicitly ethical.

row.basis: righteousness produces lasting peace and security
row.note: The work of righteousness yields peace, quietness, and security forever; it supplies the durable-good outcome to the fruitful-field image just developed.

row.basis: grass withers, but God's word stands forever
row.note: Grass withers and flowers fade, but God's word stands forever; it directly pairs the commentary's dying pasture with an enduring reality.
As earth brings sprouts and a garden causes seed to spring up, the LORD causes righteousness and praise to spring forth; this exactly translates crop growth into moral flourishing.

row.basis: grain, wine, oil, watered garden, never languishing
row.note: Restored people receive grain, wine, oil, and become like a watered garden that never languishes; it joins harvested goods to enduring blessed vitality.

row.basis: multiplied fruit trees and field produce
row.note: God promises to multiply fruit of trees and produce of fields so Israel no longer bears famine's reproach; it provides a restoration form of the commentary's blessed increase.

row.basis: fruit trees fed by holy water
row.note: Trees beside the life-giving water bear fruit monthly and healing leaves; their unfailing yield provides a vivid scriptural image of lasting, beneficial produce.

row.basis: prosperous seed, vine fruit, ground produce, dew
row.note: The promised seed prospers as vine yields fruit, ground gives produce, and heaven dew; it is a compact restoration sequence of growth and divine blessing.

row.basis: full threshing floors and overflowing vats
row.note: Threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow with wine and oil; it gives a concrete harvest-abundance scene beside the commentary's output and yield.

row.basis: almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin
row.note: Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and purges every sin; it is an exceptionally close Jewish formulation of the commentary's gift, purification, and salvation sequence.

row.basis: almsgiving rescues from death and darkness
row.note: Tobit's instruction says almsgiving delivers from death and keeps one from darkness; it supplies a second narrative exhortation linking charitable giving to lasting rescue.

row.basis: tithe so that one may become rich
row.note: The rabbinic reading of the tithe command derives, "tithe so that you may become rich"; it explicitly interprets a crop share as the path to increase, sharpening the commentary's z-k-w sequence.
God places the human in Eden to work and keep the garden; the human stewardship role is an indirect counterpart to the commentary's farm-maintaining Rabb.

row.basis: one-fifth harvest share and four parts retained
row.note: Joseph's harvest rule gives one fifth to Pharaoh and retains four parts for seed and food; in a fiscal rather than charitable setting, it closely mirrors the commentary's measured output-share and remainder.

row.basis: planters enjoy their own crop for enduring days
row.note: God's restored people will not plant for another to eat, but enjoy their work for days like a tree; it offers a secondary vision of rightful yield and durable enjoyment.

row.basis: a planted vine withers under the east wind
row.note: Though planted, the vine withers when struck by the east wind in its growing bed; it supplies a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's warning that a field can lose its crop.
The judged people sow but do not reap, tread olives without oil, and grapes without wine; it reverses the commentary's expected process from cultivation to usable yield.
Haggai's audience sows much but brings in little and finds no satisfaction; it gives an economic and moral version of crop growth failing to become lasting good.

row.basis: gathering leftovers so nothing is lost
row.note: After all have eaten, Jesus orders the remaining fragments gathered so nothing is lost; this is a secondary food analogue for the commentary's baqī, the yield that remains.
Paul asks who plants a vineyard without eating its fruit; it offers a distinct New Testament use of farm labor and a rightful portion beside the commentary's farmer and yield.

row.basis: fruit of righteousness sown in peace
row.note: A fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace; it gives a concise ethical sowing-and-yield image for the commentary's field of purified good.

row.basis: training yields peaceful fruit of righteousness
row.note: Discipline is painful at first but later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained; it gives a secondary purification-to-fruit sequence.
The wealthy are commanded to be generous and ready to share; it directly develops the commentary's wealth-share aspect outside the harvest image.

row.basis: foundation for the future and true life
row.note: The result is a stored foundation for the future and grasping true life; it supplies a durable-life outcome for the generosity enjoined in the preceding verse.

row.basis: produce growing from earth liable to tithe
row.note: The Mishnah defines tithe-liable produce as food that is guarded and grows from the earth; this legal reception marks the crop-to-due boundary assumed by the commentary.

3 Makkabiler 2:29, kurban etmeyen Yahudilerin bedenine Dionysos’un sarmaşık yaprağı damgası vurulmasını ve köle statüsünü emreder; yorumdaki dağlama ile sahibin tanınması düşüncesine zorla dayatılmış, insan üzerindeki somut bir karşılık verir.
Yaratılış 17:11 sünneti et üzerindeki antlaşma işareti yapar; yorumun deriye basılan ve aidiyeti bildiren damgasına gerçek bir beden işareti çerçevesi ekler, ancak ateşle dağlama değildir.
Çıkış 21:6’da efendi kölenin kulağını deler ve hizmet ömür boyu sürer; yorumdaki kesilmiş kulakla tanınan hayvan ve rabbin mülkiyeti yanında, insan bedenindeki kalıcı bağlılık işaretini gösterir.
Çıkış 28:36’da başkâhinin altın levhasına mühür oymasıyla “YHWH’ye kutsal” yazılır; Rabbin adını kusurdan arındırma ve görünür işaretle ayırma yorumuna somut bir alın işareti getirir.
Çıkış 28:38 levhayı Harun’un alnında tutar ve kutsal sunularla ilgili sorumluluğa bağlar; yorumdaki yüzde okunan ibadet izi için sıradan bir yara değil, hizmete ait kamusal bir işaret sunar.

Yeşaya 44:5’te biri “YHWH’nindir” der ve eline YHWH’ye aitlik yazar; bunun dövme olup olmadığı ayetin kendisinden kesin değildir, fakat yorumdaki adın sahibini bildiren görünür aidiyet işaretine doğrudan yaklaşır.

Yeşaya 43:1, Tanrı’nın Yakup’u adıyla çağırıp “benimsin” demesini birleştirir; yorumdaki Rabbin adının eşyanın kime ait olduğunu göstermesi, bedensel damga olmaksızın kişi-isim-aidiyet ilişkisiyle açıklanır.
Hezekiel 9:4, kentteki kötülük için inleyenlerin alınlarına tav işareti konmasını emreder; işaret onları yaklaşan öldürmeden ayırır ve yorumun tanınan damgasına yargı içindeki koruyucu bir yön ekler.

Tesniye 6:8, Tanrı sözlerinin el üzerinde işaret ve gözler arasında bağ olarak taşınmasını ister; yorumdaki namazın iz bırakmasıyla birlikte ibadetin beden yakınında görünür bir hatırlatıcı oluşturmasını gösterir.

Sayılar 15:39’da İsrailli püskülü görerek emirleri hatırlar ve kendi kalbiyle gözlerinin peşinden gitmez; yorumun tercih edilen şeyin kişide iz bırakması savına, görünür ibadet işaretinin arzuyu yönlendiren örneğini ekler.
Levililer 22:32, “kutsal adımı kirletmeyin” ve “kutsallaştırılacağım” buyruğunu verir; 87:1’de Rabbin adını tesbih etme emrinin yorumdaki kusurdan arındırma yönüyle aynı ad-kutsallık formülünü kurar.
Hezekiel 36:23, uluslar arasında kirletilmiş büyük adın Tanrı tarafından kutsanacağını söyler; yorumun adın taşıdığı ilahî sahipliği lekeden koruma okumasına kamusal bir ilahî karşılık verir.

row.basis: baba-efendi onuru ve hor görülen ad
row.note: Malaki 1:6, Tanrı’yı hem baba hem efendi diye anar ve adının hor görülmesini suçlar; yorumdaki rabbin malik oluşu ile onun adını yüceltme buyruğunu tek bir hitapta birleştirir.

Sayılar 6:27’de rahipler Tanrı’nın adını İsraillilerin üzerine koyar ve Tanrı onları bereketler; yorumun adın kime aitliği ayırdığı düşüncesine, fiziksel dağlama iddia etmeyen ritüel bir ad-verme örneği ekler.
Mezmur 24:1 yeryüzü ve doluluğunun YHWH’ye ait olduğunu ilan eder; yorumdaki “her şeyin rabbi onun malikidir” tanımının kozmik mülkiyet iddiasıyla karşılaşır, fakat bir damgadan söz etmez.
Matta 6:9’daki “adın kutsansın” duası, 87:1’in Rabbin adını tesbih etmesiyle aynı litürjik yönelimi taşır; yorumun adı her kusurdan uzak tutma açıklamasını Hristiyan dua formunda görünür kılar.

1 Korintliler 6:20, inanlıların bir bedelle satın alındığını ve bedende Tanrı’yı yüceltmesini söyler; yorumdaki Rab sahip, ad ise aidiyet damgasıdır önermesine bedensel ama damgasız bir mülkiyet dili ekler.

Galatyalılar 6:17’de Pavlus bedeninde İsa’nın stigmalarını taşıdığını söyler; bunlar ayetin kendisinde dağlama diye tanımlanmaz, fakat yorumun kişinin kendisini tanıtan bedensel iz ve sahibine bağlılık temasına en yakın Hristiyan ifadedir.
Vahiy 7:3, Tanrı kullarının alınları mühürlenene dek yıkımın bekletilmesini buyurur; yorumdaki ayırıcı damganın bir kişiyi tanınır kılması burada yargıdan koruyan ilahî mühür olur.

Vahiy 13:16, canavarın herkese sağ el ya da alın üzerine damga koydurduğunu anlatır; yorumdaki Rabbin işareti karşısında rakip bir efendinin zorlayıcı beden işareti olarak iki aidiyet anlatısını karşı karşıya getirir.

row.basis: damga, ad ve sayı ile tanınma
row.note: Vahiy 13:17, damgayı canavarın adı ya da adının sayısıyla eşler ve onsuz alışverişi engeller; yorumdaki adın ayırıp sahibini göstermesi, damga-ad-kimlik bağının toplumsal sonucuyla keskinleşir.
Vahiy 14:1, Kuzu’yla duranların alınlarında onun Babasının adı yazılı olduğunu söyler; yorumun Rabbin adı ile ayırıcı işareti aynı sahnede duymasına doğrudan bir ad-alın birleşimi verir.
Vahiy 14:9’da canavara tapınanların alın ya da el damgası alması ilan edilir; yorumdaki Rabbin adıyla tanınma ile ateşe yönelen damga arasındaki iki yönlü yolu rakip ibadet biçiminde kurar.
Vahiy 14:10, önceki ayette damgayı alan kişinin Tanrı gazabını içip ateş ve kükürtle işkence göreceğini söyler; yorumdaki damganın iki sonucundan ateş olanını, işaretin sonucu olarak açıkça bağlar.
Vahiy 14:11, damgayı alanların azap dumanının yükseldiğini ve gece gündüz rahat bulmadığını söyler; 87:12–13’teki büyük ateş ve sonu gelmeyen olumsuz hâl için damga bağlamında ayrı bir katkıdır.
Vahiy 20:4, canavara tapmayan ve damgayı almayanların dirilip hüküm sürdüğünü söyler; yorumdaki izden tanınan iki yolun ateşe değil hayat ve hükümranlığa çıkan karşı tarafını belirginleştirir.
Vahiy 22:4’te kullar Tanrı’nın yüzünü görür ve adı alınlarındadır; yorumun yüzde okunan ibadet izi ile Rabbin adı arasındaki bağı eskatolojik yüz-alın sahnesinde birleştirir.

row.basis: Tanrı ile konuşmadan sonra ışıldayan yüz
row.note: Çıkış 34:29’da Musa’nın yüz derisi Tanrı ile konuşmasından sonra ışıldar; yorumdaki secdenin yüzde bıraktığı iz için, ibadî karşılaşmanın bedende görünür hâle geldiği fakat dağlama olmayan bir örnektir.

Yeşaya 3:9, insanların yüz görünümünün kendilerine karşı tanıklık ettiğini ve günahlarını Sodom gibi ilan ettiklerini söyler; yorumdaki yüzde iyilik ya da kötülük izini okuma iddiasına yüzün ahlâkî kanıt oluşunu ekler.

Süleyman’ın Özdeyişleri 20:11, çocuğun bile işlerinden tanındığını, davranışının temiz ve doğru olup olmadığının görüldüğünü söyler; yorumdaki tercih kişinin üzerinde tanınır bir iz bırakır düşüncesini beden yerine eylemler üzerinden taşır.
Matta 7:20, kişilerin meyvelerinden tanınacağını söyler; yorumdaki bir insanın seçtiği şeyin iziyle tanınması, fiziksel damga yerine görünür ahlâkî sonuçla açıklanır.
Yuhanna 20:25’te Tomas, İsa’yı tanımak için ellerindeki çivi izini görmek ister; yorumun izden tanıma sahnesine, geçmişteki acının beden üzerinde bıraktığı ayırt edici kimlik kanıtını verir.
Daniel 2:22, Tanrı’nın derin ve gizli şeyleri açtığını, karanlıkta olanı bildiğini söyler; 87:7’de onun açık olanı ve gizliyi bilmesi için doğrudan bir ilahî bilme karşılığıdır.

Mezmur 139:2, Tanrı’nın oturmayı kalkmayı bildiğini ve düşünceyi uzaktan anladığını söyler; yorumdaki görünür olmayan ilişkinin de iz sayılmasıyla 87:7’nin gizli bilgisi arasında yakın bir paraleldir.

row.basis: kalbi araştırıp yola göre karşılık verme
row.note: Yeremya 17:10, YHWH’nin kalbi araştırdığını ve herkese yolunun meyvesine göre verdiğini bildirir; yorumdaki tercihin kişide iz bırakması, gizli yönelim ile görünen sonucunun birlikte değerlendirilmesiyle karşılaşır.
Vaiz 12:14, Tanrı’nın iyi ya da kötü bütün işleri, gizli olanlar dahil, yargıya getireceğini söyler; 87:7’de gizliyi bilen Tanrı ile yorumdaki görünmeyen kalıntının hesap verebilirliği birleşir.
Sirak 42:20, hiçbir düşüncenin Tanrı’dan kaçmadığını ve hiçbir sözün gizli kalmadığını söyler; 87:7’nin açık-gizli bilgisine, İkinci Tapınak dönemi bilgelik dilinde yakın bir açıklama sağlar.

İbraniler 4:13, hiçbir yaratığın Tanrı’nın görüşünden gizli olmadığını, her şeyin onun gözleri önünde açık bulunduğunu söyler; yorumun görünür ya da görünmez izin bilindiği okumasını doğrudan destekler.
Luka 12:2, örtülmüş hiçbir şeyin açığa çıkmayacağı ve gizli hiçbir şeyin bilinmeyeceği söyler; 87:7’deki açık ile gizlinin ilahî bilgisi için eskatolojik ifşa yönünü ekler.
Vahiy 2:23, Mesih’in zihinleri ve kalpleri araştırdığını ve herkese işlerine göre vereceğini bildirir; yorumdaki tercih izi, iç niyet ve sonuç arasındaki bağla 87:7’ye bağlanır.
Eyüp 31:4, Tanrı’nın insanın yollarını gördüğünü ve bütün adımlarını saydığını sorar; yorumdaki devenin tabanına basılan ve yerde okunan iz, burada ilahî olarak sayılan insan adımlarına dönüşür.

1 Petrus 2:21, Mesih’in örnek bıraktığını ve inanlıların onun izlerini takip etmesi gerektiğini söyler; yorumdaki أثرün geride kalan iz ve tercih edilen yol oluşuna açık bir etik ayak izi anlamı ekler.
Malaki 3:16, YHWH’den korkan ve onun adını düşünenler için anı kitabı yazıldığını anlatır; yorumdaki Rabbin adını anma ile kişinin görünmeyen kalıcı izi, ilahî kayıt üzerinden birleşir.
Yaratılış 19:24, YHWH’nin Sodom ve Gomora üzerine gökten kükürt ve ateş yağdırmasını anlatır; yorumun Lut kavmini yıkan ateşli sabah sahnesi için ortak anlatı çekirdeğini verir.
Yaratılış 19:25, Tanrı’nın kentleri, ovayı ve oradaki bütün sakinleri altüst ettiğini söyler; yorumdaki Lut kentlerinin altının üstüne gelmesi ayrıntısının doğrudan Tevrat paralelidir.
Yaratılış 19:28’de İbrahim yıkım yerinden fırın dumanı gibi yükselen dumanı görür; yorumun yıkılmış mekândan iz okuma fikrine, olaydan sonra görülen maddi kalıntıyı ekler.

Bilgelik 10:7, Sodom’un kötülüğünün kanıtları olarak sürekli dumanlı çoraklığı ve duran tuz direğini sayar; yorumdaki yıkım izlerini okuyana işaret oluşunu Yahudi bilgelik geleneği kalıcı kanıtlara dönüştürür.

Josephus, Antiquities 1.203, Lut’un karısının tuz direği olduğunu ve bunu kendisinin gördüğünü söyler; yorumdaki felaket sonrasında kalan izin okunması, tarihçinin görülebilir kalıntı iddiasıyla somutlaşır.
Luka 17:29, Lut’un Sodom’dan çıktığı gün gökten ateş ve kükürt yağarak herkesi yok ettiğini anlatır; yorumdaki Lut bağlamında ateşin yargı oluşunu Yeni Ahit anlatısında yeniden kurar.
Luka 17:32, “Lut’un karısını hatırlayın” diyerek Sodom anlatısındaki kalan bedeni uyarı işaretine çevirir; yorumun yıkımdan kalan izi okuyana ders olmasıyla doğrudan kesişir.

2 Petrus 2:6, Sodom ve Gomora’yı yakıp yıkarak gelecek tanrısızlar için örnek kıldığını söyler; yorumdaki Lut yıkımının mutavassımîn için âyet oluşuna Hristiyan yorumunda açık bir “örnek” işlevi verir.
Yahuda 1:7, Sodom ve Gomora’yı ebedî ateş cezasına uğrayan bir örnek diye sunar; yorumun Lut sahnesi ile 87:12’deki büyük ateşi sonraki bir Hristiyan ibret okumasında bağlar.
Yeşaya 66:24, isyancıların kurdunun ölmeyeceğini ve ateşinin sönmeyeceğini söyler; yorumun büyük ateş ve ne ölüm ne hayat ufku için İbrani Kitabındaki en yakın sürekli ceza tasviridir.
Markos 9:48, ölmez kurt ve sönmez ateş sözünü cehennem bağlamında kullanır; 87:12–13’ün ateş içinde bitmeyen olumsuz durumuna Yeni Ahit paraleli verir.
Markos 8:36, bütün dünyayı kazanmanın canı kaybetmeye değmeyeceğini sorar; yorumun dünya hayatını tercih etmenin kişiyi ateş yolunda tanınır kılmasıyla, seçimin kalıcı kaybı arasındaki etik köprüdür.

1 Yuhanna 2:17, dünyanın ve arzularının geçip Tanrı iradesini yapanın kalacağını söyler; 87:16–17’de dünya hayatının karşısındaki daha hayırlı ve daha kalıcı olan için doğrudan bir süreklilik karşılaştırmasıdır.

Yaratılış 30:32, alacalı ve benekli hayvanları Yakup’un ücretini ayıran işaretler yapar; yorumdaki damgalı devenin ötekilerden ayırt edilmesi ve sahipliği göstermesiyle hayvan işaretinin ekonomik işlevi kesişir, fakat bunlar dağlanmış değildir.
Levililer 19:28, ölü için bedeni kesmeyi ve üzerine dövme işareti koymayı yasaklar; yorumun deriye basılan damgasına bedensel işaretin bizzat sınırlandırıldığı bir Tevrat karşı anlatısı verir.

Yaratılış 4:15’te YHWH Kayin’e onu öldürmek isteyenden koruyan bir işaret koyar; işaretin biçimi belirtilmez, fakat yorumdaki tehdit damgasına karşı ilahî işaretin koruma amacı taşıdığı ters işlevi gösterir.
Ezgiler Ezgisi 8:6, sevilenin kalp ve kol üzerinde mühür gibi konmasını ister; yorumun iz bırakıp kişiyi ayıran damgasına dış deriden iç bağlılığa uzanan sevgi ve mühür imgesi ekler.

Yeşaya 37:29’da YHWH Asur kralının burnuna kanca, ağzına gem vuracağını söyler; yorumdaki burna damga tehdidine aynı yüz bölgesinde gerçekleşen fakat işaret değil zorlayıcı yargı aracı olan bir karşılık verir.

row.basis: yüz görünüşü ile kalp arasındaki fark
row.note: 1 Samuel 16:7, insanın göz önündekine baktığını ama YHWH’nin kalbe baktığını söyler; yorumdaki yüzde iyilik ya da kötülük izini okuma düşüncesine, dış görünüşün tek başına güvenilir hüküm olmadığını belirten gerekli bir denge getirir.

Matta 6:16, ikiyüzlülerin oruç tuttuklarını göstermek için yüzlerini asıklaştırdığını eleştirir; yorumdaki secdeden geldiği söylenen yüz işareti yanında, görünen dindarlık belirtisinin yapay biçimde üretilebileceği uyarısını koyar.
Elçilerin İşleri 6:15, meclisin Ştefan’ın yüzünü melek yüzü gibi gördüğünü anlatır; yorumun yüzde okunan iyilik izine, yargı ve tanıklık sahnesinde algılanan kutsal görünüm örneği ekler.

row.basis: dövme için yazı ve delme ölçütü
row.note: Mişna Makkot 3:6, dövme yasağında yazma ile deriyi delmenin birlikte gerçekleşmesi gerektiğini tartışır; Levililer’deki beden işaretini kalıcı teknik bir işlem olarak ayırarak yorumun “deriye basılan iz”ini hukuki olarak keskinleştirir.

Mişna Bava Metsia 2:2, ayırt edici işareti bulunan kayıp eşyayı ilan edilmesi gereken sınıfa koyar; yorumdaki bir şeyin damgasıyla ötekilerden ayrılıp sahibine bağlanması düşüncesine hukukî bir tanınma ölçüsü ekler.

Mişna Avot 2:1, yukarıda gören bir göz, işiten bir kulak ve kitaba yazılan bütün işler bulunduğunu söyler; yorumun görünmeyen bağın bile eser kalması ve 87:7’de gizlinin bilinmesi düşüncesini rabbanî hesap diliyle açıklar.

Yeremya 2:23, putpereste vadideki yoluna bakıp yaptığını bilmesini söyler ve onu dolaşıp duran genç deveye benzetir; metin damgalı bir deve ayağını anlatmaz, ama yorumun deve iziyle davranışın okunması temasına özgül bir hayvan-yol köprüsü kurar.

Mezmur 77:20, Tanrı’nın yolunun denizde olduğunu ve ayak izlerinin bilinmediğini söyler; yorumdaki yerde tanınmak üzere basılan devenin izi karşısında, ilahî eylemin iz bıraktığı hâlde insan tarafından izlenemeyebileceğini gösterir.

Tesniye 30:19, hayatla ölümü halkın önüne koyar ve hayatı seçmesini ister; yorumun dünya hayatını tercih etmenin iki sonuçlu damga sahnesine, tercih ile nihai kader arasındaki Tevrat çerçevesini ekler.
Matta 6:19, güve ve pasın bozduğu yeryüzünde hazine biriktirmemeyi buyurur; yorumdaki dünya hayatını tercih etmenin kalıcı olmayan bir yöneliş oluşuyla örtüşür.
Matta 6:20, bozulmayan göksel hazine biriktirmeyi buyurur; 87:17’de âhiretin daha hayırlı ve daha kalıcı oluşuna, seçimin hedefi üzerinden tamamlayıcı bir karşılık verir.
1 Yuhanna 2:15, dünyayı ve dünyadakileri sevmemeyi buyurur; yorumun 87:16’daki dünya hayatını tercih etme fiilini sadece eğilim değil kişiyi biçimleyen bağlılık saymasıyla açık bir etik paraleldir.
Filipililer 3:19, sonu yıkım olan ve düşünceleri yeryüzündeki şeylerde bulunan kişileri tasvir eder; yorumun dünyevî tercihin ateş tarafında tanınır iz bırakmasıyla sonuç odaklı bir bağlantı kurar.

1 Korintliler 10:11, atalara gelen olayların örnek olarak gerçekleşip sonraki kuşakların öğretimi için yazıldığını söyler; yorumdaki önceki sayfalara “eskilerin masalları” deme sahnesine, eski anlatının ibret gücünü savunan bir karşı anlatı verir.

2 Petrus 1:16, elçilerin Mesih’in kudretini anlatırken ustaca uydurulmuş masallara uymadığını söyler; yorumun vahiy ve önceki anlatıları “öncekilerin masalları” diye küçümseme ayrıntısıyla aynı polemik söz dağarcığında, farklı bir hakikat iddiası kurar.

İbraniler 1:1, Tanrı’nın eski zamanda atalara peygamberler aracılığıyla birçok kez konuştuğunu bildirir; yorumdaki ilk sayfaları geçersiz masal sayan kişiye karşı önceki kuşaklara gelen sözün vahiy niteliğini vurgular.

row.basis: gizlide dua ve gizliyi gören Baba
row.note: Matta 6:6, kişinin gizli yerde dua etmesini ve gizlide gören Babanın karşılık vereceğini söyler; yorumdaki yüzdeki secde izi yanında ibadetin asıl tanığının görünür damga değil gizliyi bilen Tanrı olabileceğini gösterir.
Romalılar 2:16, Tanrı’nın insanların gizlerini Mesih aracılığıyla yargılayacağı günü bildirir; 87:7’de gizliyi bilen Tanrı ve yorumdaki görünmeyen tercihin iz bırakması için yargı boyutunu ekler.

Eyüp 38:14, şafağın yeryüzünü mühür altındaki kil gibi değiştirdiğini söyler; yorumdaki devenin tabanına demirle basılıp yerde okunacak iz için, toprağın üstünde beliren mühür iziyle çok yakın bir fiziksel imge sunar.

Çıkış 12:13, kapılardaki kanı evler üzerinde işaret yapar; Tanrı işareti görünce yıkıcı belanın o evden geçmesini sağlar. Yorumdaki ayırıcı damganın yargı içindeki tanınma işlevi burada bedenden eve taşınır.
Yeşu 2:18, Rahav’ın penceresine kızıl ip bağlamasını ve ailesini o evde toplamasını ister; yorumdaki işaretin sahibini ötekilerden ayırması, yaklaşan yıkımda bir haneyi tanıtan görünür işaret olur.

Yeşu 4:6, taşların çocuklar ileride anlamını sorabilsin diye işaret olacağını söyler; yorumdaki yıkılmış yerden iz ve âyet okuma sahnesine, geçmiş olayı sonraki okuyucuya açan maddi bir kalıntı ekler.

Çıkış 3:15 Tanrı’nın adını, İbranice šēm, kuşaklara anılacak ad olarak verir; šēm Arapça ism ile soydaştır. Bu yalnız 87:1’deki ism için gerçek bir Semitik karşılıktır; kaynak yorumdaki tartışmalı وسم türetimini doğrulamaz.

row.basis: mühür, kordon ve asa ile kişisel tanınma
row.note: Yaratılış 38:18’de Yahuda mührünü, kordonunu ve asasını rehin bırakır; sonradan sahibini belirleyen kişisel eşyalar yorumdaki sahibini gösteren damga ve ayırt edici işaret işlevini hukukî bir sahnede taşır.
Yeremya 32:10’da Yeremya satın alma belgesini yazar, mühürler ve tanık çağırır; yorumdaki damganın malikliği belirtmesi, arazi sahipliğini taşıyan resmî mühürle somutlaşır.
Yeşaya 49:16’da Tanrı Siyon’u avuçlarına kazıdığını söyler; yorumdaki görünen ya da görünmeyen kalıcı eser, ilahî bellekte beden imgesiyle silinmez bir iz olarak tasarlanır.

Yeremya 17:1, Yahuda’nın günahını demir kalem ve elmas uçla kalp levhasına ve sunak boynuzlarına kazınmış betimler; yorumdaki tercih kişinin içinde ve dışında iz bırakır iddiasına olumsuz, kalıcı bir yazı karşılığı verir.

Yeremya 31:33, Torah’ın içe konup kalbe yazılacağını, Tanrı’nın onların Tanrısı ve onların halkı olacağını söyler; yorumun adı, sahibini ve kişiyi ayıran işaret diye duyması burada içsel yazı ile aidiyete bağlanır.

row.basis: ateşle arıtma, adla çağırma, halk olma
row.note: Zekeriya 13:9 halkın üçte birini ateşten geçirip arıtmayı, onların Tanrı’nın adını çağırmasını ve Tanrı’nın “onlar benim halkım” demesini birleştirir; yorumdaki ateş, Rabbin adı ve malikiyet damgası aynı ayette birleşir.

Yeşaya 8:16 tanıklığın bağlanmasını ve öğretimin öğrenciler arasında mühürlenmesini buyurur; yorumdaki ilk sayfalar, tanınan iz ve gizli-açık bilgi arasında yazılı öğretinin korunan işaret oluşunu gösterir.

row.basis: herkesçe bilinen ve okunan insan mektubu
row.note: 2 Korintliler 3:2, Korintlileri herkes tarafından bilinen ve okunan bir mektup diye adlandırır; yorumdaki kişinin seçiminin izinden tanınması, insanın okunabilir bir yazı olmasıyla güçlü bir karşılık bulur.

row.basis: mürekkeple değil kalbin et levhasına yazılan mektup
row.note: 2 Korintliler 3:3, Mesih’in mektubunun mürekkeple değil diri Tanrı’nın Ruhu ile taş levhalara değil etten kalp levhalarına yazıldığını söyler; yorumdaki deriye basılan damgayı görünmeyen fakat kişide kalan ilahî yazıyla karşılaştırır.

row.basis: mühürde bilinen aidiyet ve adla ahlâk
row.note: 2 Timoteos 2:19, Tanrı’nın sağlam temelinin mühründe “Rab kendisininkileri bilir” ve Rabbin adını ananın kötülükten uzak durması bulunduğunu söyler; 87:1 ve 87:7’deki ad, tanınma ve bilme ayrıntılarını tek mühür formülünde toplar.

Vahiy 2:17, galip gelene beyaz taş ve yalnız alanın bildiği yeni bir ad vaat eder; yorumdaki adın ayırt edici işaret olması, herkese açık yüz damgasından farklı ama kişiye özgü kimlik armağanında görünür.
Yuhanna 12:28’de İsa “Baba, adını yücelt” der ve gökten adın yüceltildiği yanıtı gelir; 87:1’in Rabbin adını tesbih etmesiyle aynı ad-yüceltme eylemini ilahî yanıtla birlikte sunar.

Romalılar 2:24, Tanrı adının uluslar arasında muhatapların davranışı yüzünden kötülenmesini söyler; yorumdaki Rabbin işaretini kusurdan arınmış tutma okumasına, insan eyleminin ilahî adı lekeleyebilmesi yönünü ekler.

1 Korintliler 3:13, herkesin işinin gün tarafından görünür kılınacağını ve ateşin niteliğini sınayacağını söyler; yorumdaki tercih iz bırakır ve ateş iki yoldan biridir düşüncesine, işin ateşle teşhir edildiği bir değerlendirme sahnesi ekler.
2 Korintliler 3:18, açık yüzle Rabbin yüceliğine bakarken aynı imgeye dönüştürülmeyi anlatır; yorumdaki ibadetin yüzde okunur iz bırakması için yara ya da damga değil, dönüşen yüz imgesi sağlar.

row.basis: eylemden belli olan Tanrı ve şeytan çocukları
row.note: 1 Yuhanna 3:10, Tanrı’nın çocukları ile şeytanın çocuklarının doğruluk ve sevgi pratiğinden belli olduğunu söyler; yorumdaki iki aidiyet ve kişinin bıraktığı izden tanınması, bedensel olmayan aile işaretiyle açıklanır.

row.basis: elde işaret, gözler arasında anı ve ağızda Torah
row.note: Çıkış 13:9, Mısır’dan çıkışı ele işaret ve gözler arasına anı yapar ki YHWH’nin Torah’ı ağızda olsun; yorumdaki işaret, adın anılması ve ibadetin hafızada bıraktığı iz için Tesniye 6:8’den ayrı bir kurtuluş bağlamı verir.

row.basis: YHWH’nin çocukları için yas kesikleri yasağı
row.note: Tesniye 14:1, YHWH’nin çocuklarına ölü için kendilerini kesmeyi ve gözler arasında saç kazımayı yasaklar; yorumdaki beden-yüz işaretinin yanında, ilahî aidiyetin bazı ritüel beden izlerini özellikle dışladığı karşı anlatıyı verir.

Yeşaya 29:13, halkın Tanrı’yı dudaklarıyla onurlandırırken kalplerinin uzak olduğunu söyler; yorumdaki adı tesbih etme ve yüzde görünen ibadet izi yanında, dış söz ve görünüşün iç bağlılığı garanti etmediği uyarısını koyar.

Matta 6:18, orucun insanlara görünmemesi, gizlide olanı gören Babanın bilmesi gerektiğini söyler; yorumdaki secde izinin yüzde görülmesi yanında, Tanrı bilgisinin görünür işaret gerektirmeyen ibadet anlayışını verir.

row.basis: efendi onuru ile Tanrı adının korunması
row.note: 1 Timoteos 6:1, kölelerin efendilerine saygı göstermesini Tanrı adı ve öğretinin kötülenmemesine bağlar; yorumdaki rabbin malik oluşu ile onun adını kusurdan koruma düşüncesi toplumsal davranış üzerinden birleşir.

Habakkuk 2:2, görümün levhalara açıkça yazılmasını ister ki okuyucu okuyabilsin; yorumdaki izleri ve ilk sayfaları okuma imgesine, metnin kendi anlamını ilerideki okuyucuya taşıyan yazılı işaret işlevini ekler.

row.basis: tefillin, püskül ve mezuzanın günaha karşı işareti
row.note: Babil Talmudu Menahot 43b, baş ve kol tefillini, giyside püskülü ve kapıda mezuzası olan kişinin günah işlemeyeceğini söyler; yorumdaki görünür ibadet işaretinin seçimi ve izi biçimlendirmesi rabbanî bir uygulama sonucu kazanır.

row.ref: Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh 8
row.note: Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh 8, bedenin işaretlenmesini ruhun güçlenmesine bağlar; yorumdaki deriye basılı dinî işaret için Hristiyan vaftiz geleneğinde beden-ruh aidiyetini birlikte düşünen bir yorum sunar.

Kudüslü Kiril, Catechetical Lecture 13:36’da haçın alın üzerinde parmakla yapılacak mühür olduğunu öğretir; yorumdaki yüzde ve alın çevresinde tanınan ibadet işareti Hristiyan pratiğinde ritüel bir karşılık bulur.

4 Ezra 14:45 (verse division should be checked) distinguishes books to be made public from books reserved for the wise. It offers a concrete Jewish parallel for the commentary’s open/hidden knowledge and “first sheets,” without identifying those books with Abraham’s or Moses’ sheets.
The commentary makes the front place in a running file a warning that the first arrival need not win; Qohelet explicitly says the race is not won by the swift in its reflection on time and chance.
Hebrew אַחֲרִית, “end/latter,” is a close cognate of the commentary's ء خ ر/آخرة label; Qohelet says a thing's end is better than its beginning, giving the positional sequence a wisdom analogue.

Paul's athletic image has all runners race and tells hearers to run so as to obtain the prize; it gives the commentary's animal race an ethical and eschatological goal without identifying the two scenes.
Paul joins an athlete's self-control to a perishable versus imperishable crown, closely pairing the commentary's run held in reserve with its contrast between what passes and what endures.
Paul forgets what is behind and stretches toward what is ahead while pursuing Christ's prize; this makes the commentary's rear/front positions a deliberate spiritual movement.
In the next step of Paul's race image, he presses toward a goal and an upward prize, supplying an explicit finish-point for the commentary's running sequence.
After teaching about reward, Jesus says that many first will be last and last first; this is a direct eschatological reversal of the commentary's claim that the first to arrive does not thereby win.
Paul's resurrection argument explicitly orders the natural before the spiritual; its later, heavenly mode gives a precise Christian form to the commentary's first/later contrast.

In the sea-escape scene, the divine messenger and cloud move from before Israel's camp to stand behind it, a concrete fore-and-rear file that gives the commentary's spatial sequence theological action.
Isaiah's restoration procession has YHWH go before the people and Israel's God gather their rear; it supplies a second, non-racing use of the commentary's leader-and-tail arrangement.
Against a false prophet, Deuteronomy commands Israel to walk after God; its bodily following turns the commentary's secondary “follow a trace” motion into covenantal allegiance.
Christ's suffering is presented as an example so believers may follow in his steps; the explicit step/track image closely meets the commentary's أثر sense of coming in another's trace.
The heavenly group follows the Lamb wherever he goes and is called firstfruits; its leader, followers, and first portion make it a particularly close eschatological counterpart to the running file.
The wisdom teacher says he has guided the pupil in paths of uprightness, directly joining S87:3's divine guidance with the commentary's image of well-directed movement.
Proverbs promises that the taught person's steps will not be cramped and that running will not cause stumbling; it is a direct ethical counterpart to the animal with a smooth, well-placed gait.
Isaiah says God makes level the path of the righteous; the verse turns the commentary's ease and orderly footfall into a divine smoothing of a human way.
The psalm pictures the sun as a bridegroom and a strong man running his course across the sky, a specific biblical meeting of celestial motion and the commentary's running image.
At creation the morning stars sing together; this gives the commentary's moving stars a scriptural role of cosmic praise rather than merely astronomical motion.
Psalm 148 summons sun, moon, and all shining stars to praise, directly bringing S87:1's praise and the commentary's celestial swimmers into one liturgical scene.
The same psalm calls creatures to praise YHWH's Name because it alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely matching “the Name of your Lord, the Most High.”
In a royal plea, some invoke chariots and horses while the faithful remember the Name of YHWH; it links the commentary's horse imagery to S87:15's remembrance of the divine Name.
God's questions about the fixed ordinances and rule of the heavens supply a biblical frame for S87:3's measuring and guiding and for the commentary's ordered stellar courses.

1 Clement depicts heaven, day and night, sun, moon, and stars completing their prescribed courses without deviation; it is an unusually close Christian expansion of the commentary's orbital movement under divine determination.
Psalm 47 calls YHWH “Most High” and a great king over all the earth, providing the Hebrew Bible's direct divine title beside S87:1.

The commentary insists that the second-horse resonance of ص ل و does not replace prayer; Biblical Aramaic מְצַלֵּא in Daniel's thrice-daily kneeling is a close cognate and preserves that primary prayer sense.
Jesus' model prayer begins by hallowing the Father's Name, a close liturgical counterpart to remembering the Lord's Name and then praying in S87:15.
In thanksgiving worship the psalmist offers sacrifice and calls on YHWH's Name, a Hebrew Bible pairing of invocation of the Name with prayerful worship.
Isaiah contrasts grass and flower that wither with God's word that stands forever, giving an exact durable-versus-vanishing form to S87:16-17's worldly and abiding contrast.
Daniel's awakening of the dead includes everlasting life and everlasting abhorrence, placing the commentary's “more enduring” latter state in an explicit Jewish eschatological scene.

row.basis: vestibule before the World to Come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the World to Come and tells hearers to prepare in it for the banquet hall, making the commentary's near/after sequence into a spatial ethical preparation.

row.basis: this world and World to Come
row.note: Avot says an hour of bliss in the World to Come exceeds all life here, but also that present repentance and good deeds exceed the whole World to Come; it both parallels S87:17 and guards against treating present life as valueless.

row.basis: today for doing, tomorrow for reward
row.note: The rabbinic interpretation, “today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward,” gives the commentary's first/later sequence a disciplined present-work and later-reward reading.

row.basis: life in this world and eternal life
row.note: Jesus says that loving one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it here keeps it for eternal life; this is one of the closest New Testament formulations of S87:16-17's contrast.
Paul contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal, directly articulating the commentary's “near” present and more abiding latter reality.
First John says the world and its desire pass away, while the doer of God's will remains forever; its passing/remain contrast closely tracks the commentary's dunya and أبقى contrast.

row.basis: no abiding city, city to come
row.note: Hebrews says believers have no enduring city here but seek the one to come, using an explicit spatial and durable/future contrast for the commentary's near shore and later destination.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people rather than temporary enjoyment of sin, supplying a concrete counterchoice to the preference for immediate worldly life.
Moses treats reproach as greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it gives the commentary's better latter outcome a stated reason for reordering present preference.

row.basis: treasure where it is not destroyed
row.note: Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where moth, corrosion, and thieves do not destroy it; the storing image clarifies what “more enduring” means without making the horse's reserve literal wealth.

In the rich man and Lazarus story, Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things in life with Lazarus's present comfort and the rich man's distress; it narrates the temporal reversal developed in the commentary.

row.basis: storing for the future and true life
row.note: Those rich in this age are told to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of true life, a direct ethical alternative to preferring the immediately available life.
Paul says he has finished the race and kept the faith; this gives the commentary's animal that holds strength toward the end a human image of faithful completion.

The verse's מֵאַחֲרֵיהֶם, “behind them,” is a close Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ء خ ر family; its use is spatial in the cloud scene, so it supports the rear-of-a-file sense without importing an afterlife meaning.
Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light; it offers a Christian ethical use of ease beside S87:8, though it is a yoke rather than the commentary's animal's smooth gait.

row.basis: swift as a deer to do God's will
row.note: Avot tells the reader to be swift as a deer in doing the heavenly Father's will, a Jewish ethical transformation of animal speed that helps frame the commentary's running animals.
Deborah's song portrays stars fighting Sisera from their courses; it offers a biblical use of moving celestial tracks, although it does not describe orbital swimming.

1 Enoch invites attention to the heavenly luminaries that do not depart from their ordered paths, an early Jewish development of measured celestial motion relevant to the commentary's stars and divine guidance.
Daniel thanks and praises God for wisdom and power with מְשַׁבַּח, likely cognate with the commentary's س ب ح label; it supports the praise sense, not the commentary's horse or swimming associations.

row.basis: tyrant aspiring to the Most High
row.note: The Babylonian king says he will make himself like the Most High and is answered by descent in the surrounding oracle; beside the commentary's Pharaoh allusion, it contrasts a false highest lord with praise of the true one.
Esau eats the immediate meal and despises his birthright; while it is not an afterlife text, the narrative supplies a concrete Jewish pattern of preferring what is now over a lasting inheritance.
Those who hope in YHWH run and do not grow weary; it supplies a biblical endurance image beside the commentary's horse that reserves part of its running power.
Avot tells readers to run toward even a light commandment and flee transgression; it makes running a moral direction, though it does not itself contain the worldly/afterlife comparison.

Psalm 147 says that God takes no pleasure in a horse's strength or in human legs; it gives the commentary's running-horse figure a theological counterweight by refusing to make speed or power the ground of success.

row.basis: God delights in fear and hope
row.note: The verse supplies the positive counterpart to the preceding horse image: YHWH delights in those who fear him and hope for his steadfast love, redirecting the running sequence toward trust rather than athletic advantage.
The psalmist says he will run in the way of God's commandments because God enlarges his heart; it makes the commentary's running movement an obedient, enabled course.
Proverbs promises that acknowledging God brings straight paths; its straightened route supplies a concise biblical analogue to S87:3's guidance and the commentary's smooth gait.

row.basis: led in right paths for the Name
row.note: The shepherd restores and leads in paths of righteousness for the sake of his Name, combining the commentary's leader/follower motion with the Name named in S87:15.
YHWH identifies himself as the one who teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go; it is a particularly close covenantal formulation of “measured, then guided.”
The preparation of YHWH's way levels uneven ground and makes rough places a plain, giving the commentary's easy, well-placed footfall a concrete highway image.
In Isaiah's call to justice, the people's righteousness goes before them and YHWH's glory guards from behind; this ethical procession develops both ends of the commentary's moving line.

row.basis: stars brought out by number and called by name
row.note: Isaiah asks who brings out the heavenly host by number and calls every star by name; it joins the commentary's stars in their courses to divine measuring, ordering, and command.

row.basis: Mazzaroth in season and Ayish guided
row.note: God asks whether a human can bring Mazzaroth out in its season or guide Ayish with its children; this supplies a precise scriptural image of divine guidance of celestial bodies.

row.basis: statutes of moon and stars, stirred sea
row.note: Jeremiah calls the regularity of moon and stars their fixed statutes while also naming the God who stirs the sea; its juxtaposition is a close biblical frame for the commentary's ordered stars and swimming-water imagery.

row.basis: Most High, Aramaic praise, lives forever
row.note: In WLC's Aramaic numbering (often English Dan.4.34), the humbled king blesses the Most High, uses שַׁבְּחֵת for praise, and confesses the one who lives forever; it gathers the commentary's س ب ح, “Most High,” and enduring themes in a reversal of false sovereignty.

The commentary warns that preferring “the life of this world” misorders desire, whereas Deuteronomy commands Israel to choose life as covenant blessing; the contrast matters because the two texts give “life” different ethical functions.

row.basis: righteous live forever and have reward
row.note: Wisdom's final vindication says that the righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord, a Second Temple Jewish expression of the more abiding latter good.

The martyred brother expects the King of the universe to raise those dying for the law to an eternal renewal of life; its costly present action and enduring future outcome sharpen S87:16-17's comparison.

row.basis: World to Come without bodily consumption
row.note: The rabbinic description of the World to Come removes eating, drinking, and ordinary worldly competition and has the righteous delight in divine radiance; it gives a concrete Jewish interpretation of a superior, lasting future state.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: The Benedictus says that the dawn from on high will guide human feet into the way of peace, directly meeting S87:3's guidance and the commentary's attention to ordered footfall.

row.basis: run with endurance the race set before
row.note: Hebrews urges believers to run with endurance the race set before them; the explicit need to last through a course closely complements the commentary's horse that preserves running power for the end.

row.basis: make straight paths for your feet
row.note: Hebrews instructs readers to make straight paths for their feet so that the disabled may be healed rather than turned aside, a Christian ethical use of the commentary's smooth, guided gait.
Jesus says that the one who endures to the end will be saved; it gives the commentary's emphasis on what lasts at the end a direct eschatological criterion.
Hebrews says dispossessed believers know they have a better and abiding possession; its paired comparative is exceptionally close to S87:17's “better and more enduring.”
The patriarchs seek a better country, explicitly identified as heavenly; the verse gives the commentary's distant/later destination a pilgrim-country image.

Jesus tells hearers not to work for food that perishes but for food that endures to eternal life, closely matching the commentary's warning against priority for the immediately available and perishable.
Jesus asks what profits someone who gains the whole world but forfeits life; its whole-world versus life calculation is a sharp Gospel counterpart to preference for dunya.

After comparing bodily training with godliness, the verse says godliness promises both the present life and the coming life; it qualifies the commentary's contrast by valuing present life within a future-oriented discipline.
First Peter describes an inheritance as imperishable, undefiled, unfading, and kept in heaven; its safeguarded future good gives a Christian image for S87:17's abiding outcome.

row.basis: momentary affliction, eternal weight of glory
row.note: Paul says momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison; its time-scale makes the commentary's near/later reversal explicit.

row.basis: feet like a hind and high places
row.note: Habakkuk says the Lord makes his feet like a hind's and lets him tread high places; it is a divine-strength reading of animal footwork, though not a race or file.
The wicked speakers urge one another to enjoy present good things before they pass; their voice gives a specific Jewish portrayal of the immediate-life preference criticized in the commentary.

row.basis: two spirits in which to walk
row.note: The Community Rule says God assigned humanity spirits of truth and perversity in which to walk until visitation; it develops divine ordering, directed walking, and divergent outcomes without the animal imagery.

row.basis: works prepared beforehand to walk in
row.note: Believers are created for good works that God prepared beforehand so they might walk in them; it offers a Christian formulation of a divinely prepared and guided way.
Hebrews rereads Esau's sale of his birthright for one meal as a warning against irreverence, giving the immediate-versus-lasting choice in Gen.25 a Christian moral interpretation.

Jude calls false teachers wandering stars reserved for deepest darkness; as a moral inversion of the commentary's stars moving in ordered courses, it is image-based rather than an astronomical parallel.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The Didache's opening formula distinguishes a way of life from a way of death; it is a Christian two-way framework beside S87:3, 8, and 16-17, though it does not share the running-file scene.

Those who lose property under pressure accept it joyfully because they know they have a better, abiding possession; this gives the commentary's better-and-more-lasting contrast a concrete setting of threatened choice.
Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food remaining into eternal life, directly framing worldly provision against what abides.
The world and its desire pass away, while the doer of God's will remains forever; it closely matches the rejected worldly preference and abiding good.
Paul distinguishes temporary visible things from eternal unseen things, supplying the same evaluative contrast that governs the two sides of the commentary's scale.
The maxim calls one hour of bliss in the world to come better than all life in this world, an explicit analogue to 87:17's comparison.
A tortured brother tells the king that the King of the universe will raise them to everlasting renewed life; it is a choice under a human tyrant for an enduring divine future.
Those awakening from the dust receive either everlasting life or everlasting abhorrence, furnishing both the enduring good and the enduring adverse fate developed in the commentary.
The final separation explicitly pairs eternal punishment with eternal life, the same warning that permanence can belong to punishment as well as blessedness.
The youngest brother contrasts his brothers' short suffering and God's everlasting-life covenant with the king's coming punishment, sharpening the commentary's temporal-versus-lasting judgment.
Tortured faithful people refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection, a direct instance of choosing costly fidelity for a superior future.

row.basis: life in this world / eternal life
row.note: Loving one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it keeps it for eternal life; the verse makes the commentary's preference an existential choice.
The question about gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life concentrates worldly acquisition and ultimate loss into the commentary's two-sided valuation.
Believers have no abiding city here but seek the coming one, an especially close counterpart to the claim that the other life is what remains.
This world is a vestibule before the world to come, where one must prepare to enter the banquet hall; it turns present life into a passage rather than the preferred destination.
The righteous may appear punished to observers, yet their hope is full of immortality, making present appearance a poor measure of lasting worth.

row.basis: rich man's good things / Lazarus's comfort
row.note: Abraham recalls that the rich man received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but their postmortem conditions are reversed; it tests what worldly “good” is worth.
Treasure on earth is subject to moth, corrosion, and theft, concretizing the commentary's claim that the worldly side is not what lasts.
Treasure in heaven escapes moth, corrosion, and theft, giving a durable alternative to the perishable possessions of the preceding verse.
The rich fool's life is demanded on the night he relies on accumulated goods, so his planned abundance cannot secure a remaining possession.
The parable's conclusion contrasts laying up treasure for oneself with being rich toward God, a moral qualification of what counts as valuable wealth.
Generosity stores a good foundation for the future and takes hold of true life, connecting cleanly directed wealth, self-giving, and an enduring good.
The mishnah names deeds whose fruits are enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come, a precise Jewish account of good that remains.
Sirach calls kindness a blessed garden and says almsgiving endures forever, joining the commentary's remaining goodness to generosity rather than accumulation.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over temporary enjoyment of sin, a direct scriptural action of preferring a costly better good.
Moses judges reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; Pharaoh's sphere becomes the setting for a valuation unlike the fleeting ruler's power.
The Judean officials refuse the king's gods and image even if God does not rescue them; like the commentary's magicians before Pharaoh, they choose fidelity under royal threat.
The Hebrew midwives fear God and disobey Pharaoh's order to kill boys, another Mosaic-world instance in which divine fear defeats a ruler's temporary command.
The apostles state that they must obey God rather than humans, a concise Christian formulation of the threatened preference enacted in the commentary's Pharaoh scene.
Grass withers and flower fades under the LORD's breath; its pasture-to-fading image is a close companion to 87:5 and the commentary's worldly flower.
Against fading grass and flower, God's word stands forever, supplying the lasting side needed by the commentary's vegetation-and-abiding contrast.

Peter reapplies Isaiah's grass image to all flesh and human glory: grass withers and its flower falls. This makes transient human status explicit beside the commentary's grass and lowly-human imagery.
Peter's continuation says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the preached good news, interpreting the fading-grass contrast as a durable divine message.
The rich person's humiliation is likened to a flower of grass that passes away, directly tying social wealth to the commentary's flowerlike worldly life.
Sun and heat wither grass, drop its flower, and destroy its beauty; James applies that process to the rich person's pursuits, closely matching the meadow's discarded end.
Human days are grass and a person's flourishing is a field flower, a direct parallel for the commentary's flower image of worldly life.
After the wind passes, the flower is gone and its place knows it no more; this adds a specific fading-and-forgetting counterpart to the commentary's forgotten residue.
The LORD's steadfast love is from everlasting to everlasting, giving the psalm's answer to its prior grass-and-flower transience.
The wicked are chaff that the wind drives away, a pointed ethical use of plant refuse beside the commentary's discarded ghutha' and lower-human comparison.

row.basis: poor raised from dust and ash heap
row.note: Rather than leaving the lowly among refuse, the psalm says God raises the poor from dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap; it reverses the commentary's social application of debris.
God chooses what the world calls low and despised to nullify what is; this directly counters an inference that social lowliness marks what should be discarded.
God chooses the poor in the world as rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, reversing worldly rank while preserving the commentary's horizon of enduring inheritance.
The high and exalted God also dwells with the crushed and lowly to revive them, challenging any simple equation of low status with refuse.
God leaves a humble, lowly people who seek refuge in his name, joining low status to the positive remnant rather than to discard.
Israel's remnant does no wrong and speaks no lies; it gives the commentary's “remaining ones” a concrete moral profile.
God leaves seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal, a surviving moral remnant that resists corruption as the commentary's baqiyya image does.
The remnant no longer relies on its oppressor but relies faithfully on the LORD, specifying the faithful orientation of a remaining group.
After prosperity lifts the heart, Israel may forget the LORD; this supplies a concrete biblical form of the commentary's worldly preference joined to forgetting.
Agur fears that being full will lead him to deny God, giving the commentary's question of worldly wealth a particular spiritual danger.

row.basis: life and good / death and evil
row.note: Moses sets life and good against death and evil, an explicit scriptural scale for the commentary's claim that choice seeks what is better.
The command to choose life turns evaluation into an accountable act, as the commentary turns preferring the lower worldly side into blameworthy choice.
Esau eats, drinks, and despises his birthright; the narrative makes a one-meal preference over an inheritance a concrete warning about choosing the immediate.
Hebrews interprets Esau's sale of the birthright for one meal as profane conduct, making the Genesis choice an ethical reading relevant to the commentary's sorting of choices.
Hebrews adds that Esau later seeks the blessing with tears but cannot reverse the result, stressing the lasting cost of his short-term exchange.
Solomon does not ask for long life, riches, or enemies' lives, but discernment for justice; his choice gives a narrative instance of seeking a higher good.

row.basis: money for what does not satisfy
row.note: Isaiah asks why money and labor are spent on what does not satisfy, then calls listeners to eat what is good; it closely fits the commentary's scrutiny of valuable provision.
The proverb judges a little with righteousness better than large income with injustice, qualifying the commentary's abundance criterion by making moral source decisive.
The small portion of the righteous is better than the abundance of many wicked, another direct reversal of an amount-based account of good wealth.

row.basis: little with fear / treasure with turmoil
row.note: A little with fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with turmoil, comparing material plenty with the quality of the life that holds it.
A good name is chosen over great riches and favor over silver and gold, directly depicting selection by worth rather than mere material quantity.
The worry of the age and deceitfulness of wealth choke the word and make it fruitless, a specific New Testament account of worldly preference producing spiritual waste.
The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God, turning the commentary's hierarchy of goods into an instruction about trust.

row.basis: feast for those unable to repay
row.note: Jesus tells a host to invite poor, crippled, lame, and blind people rather than reciprocal guests, a practical enactment of preferring another's need over self-advantage.
Because such guests cannot repay, God repays the host at the resurrection of the righteous; generosity is explicitly joined to the lasting future.
Humility requires regarding others as surpassing oneself, directly corresponding to the commentary's explanation of preferring another over oneself.
Each person is told to attend to others' interests as well as personal interests, supplying a concrete ethical form for right-directed preference.
The instruction not to seek one's own interest but that of the other gives a compact analogue to the commentary's positive sense of ithar.

row.basis: repentance and deeds in this world
row.note: The first half of the same maxim says an hour of repentance and good deeds here is better than all the coming world; it complicates the commentary by valuing this life as the place of moral action.
