Israel is chosen not for numerical abundance but despite being the fewest people, offering a counterpoint to reading selectness through quantity or social rank.
God rejects human sight of outward appearance and looks at the heart; it reframes the commentary's language of low value and selection around hidden moral reality.
Paul's remembered saying of Jesus calls giving more blessed than receiving, a concise valuation of self-giving alongside the commentary's positive preference of others.

row.basis: foreign city and one's future city
row.note: Hermas treats believers as residents of a foreign city who should not build their hopes there because their proper city lies elsewhere; it develops the present-world versus lasting-destination image.
The homily calls the flesh's stay in this world brief and transient and sets it beside Christ's promised coming kingdom and eternal life, closely echoing the commentary's contrast.

row.basis: things to use and things to enjoy
row.note: Augustine distinguishes temporary things used on the way from God, who is to be enjoyed as beatitude; this interpretive hierarchy clarifies what a rightly ordered preference can mean.

Genesis explains Manasseh's name with Hebrew nashani, “has made me forget,” about Joseph's hardship. It is a likely Semitic cognate of the commentary's nasiya label, though the Genesis scene contains no debris image.

Joseph says God sent him ahead to preserve a remnant and keep his family alive; this is the Hebrew Joseph scene behind the commentary's Qur'anic notice of Joseph's being preferred, joined here to baqiyya.

A forgotten sheaf must be left for the alien, orphan, and widow, so that God blesses the owner. It reverses the commentary's negative “forgotten residue” by making an overlooked remainder provision for vulnerable people.

row.basis: fallen grapes left for poor and alien
row.note: Israel may not strip the vineyard or gather its fallen grapes, but must leave them for poor people and resident aliens; discarded produce becomes deliberate generosity.
Boaz orders workers to pull grain from bundles and leave it for Ruth to glean without rebuke, a narrative instance of turning surplus and leftovers toward a migrant widow's need.
Judah's surviving remnant will take root below and bear fruit above, merging the commentary's positive remnant with its pasture-and-lasting-fruit imagery.
Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation is forever and righteousness is not shattered; it makes the temporal/enduring comparison cosmic.
A human comes forth like a flower and withers, fleeing like a shadow that does not remain, a close poetic companion to the commentary's flower and non-abiding world.
Treasures of wickedness do not profit, whereas righteousness delivers from death; the proverb makes source and moral quality decisive for what counts as beneficial wealth.
Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death, pressing the commentary's contrast between present possession and ultimate outcome.
When one fixes one's eyes on wealth, it is gone and flies heavenward like an eagle; it is a concrete warning against treating visible wealth as what remains.
Jeshurun grows fat, abandons the God who made him, and despises the Rock of salvation; it gives worldly abundance the same spiritual danger as the commentary's preference for dunya.

row.basis: what accompanies a person at death
row.note: The teaching says silver, gold, and precious stones do not accompany a person at death, while Torah and good deeds do; it sharply distinguishes temporary possession from what remains.

row.basis: today for doing, tomorrow for reward
row.note: The talmudic reading of the commandment says this day is for performing them and the next for receiving reward, making present moral action and future recompense distinct without making present life the final good.
God alone possesses immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, closely corresponding to the commentary's statement that enduring being belongs uniquely to God.
The coming judge gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff with unquenchable fire, combining selected produce, discarded plant matter, and lasting adverse judgment.

row.basis: good fish collected, bad thrown out
row.note: In the net parable, fish are sorted: the good are collected into containers and the bad thrown outside. It is a precise sorting image for selected good and rejected refuse.
Jesus explains the net as a final separation of the evil from the righteous, giving the preceding culling image an explicitly eschatological value judgment.

row.basis: the least identified with the king
row.note: Care given to the least of the king's brothers is counted as care given to the king himself, reversing any association of socially low people with discardable material.

row.basis: God and wealth as rival masters
row.note: No one can serve God and wealth because divided service produces love for one and contempt for the other; this is an explicit account of preference as allegiance.
Jesus tells the rich man to give his possessions to the poor and have treasure in heaven, turning a costly redistribution into an enduring treasure.
Those who persevere in good work and seek glory, honor, and incorruptibility receive eternal life, articulating a pursuit of lasting good through action.
Paul reads Israel's survival through the Elijah narrative as a remnant according to gracious election, giving a Christian interpretation of the morally preserved remainder.
When the earthly tent is destroyed, believers have an eternal, God-made house in heaven; the image makes earthly dissolution and lasting dwelling a direct pair.
The generous person scatters gifts to the poor and his righteousness remains forever, directly uniting self-giving with the commentary's positive language of what remains.
Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; the agricultural metaphor turns the commentary's two-sided choice into two opposed harvests.
Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end, with appetite as god and shame as glory; it supplies a concrete New Testament diagnosis of worldly preference.
Believers' citizenship is in heaven and they await a savior from there, providing the positive location corresponding to the rejection of merely earthly-mindedness.
Those raised with Christ are instructed to seek the things above, where Christ is, making selection of an upper and lasting good an explicit practice.
The command to set the mind on things above rather than things on earth is a concise counterpart to refusing to privilege dunya.
Land that produces a useful crop for those who cultivate it receives blessing from God, setting fruitful vegetation on the accepted side of a moral agricultural image.
Land producing thorns and thistles is rejected, near a curse, and ends in burning; it supplies a fully developed counterpart to pasture becoming useless refuse.
God is not unjust so as to forget the work and love shown in serving the saints, turning 87:6's not-forgetting into the preservation of acts of care.
What can be shaken is removed so that what cannot be shaken may remain, a close conceptual formulation of sifting away what does not endure.
The person who continues in the perfect law is not a forgetful hearer but an active doer and is blessed, a specific ethical contrast for the commentary's forgetting motif.
A branch that does not remain in Christ is thrown outside, withers, and is gathered for fire; it joins abiding, vegetable waste, and adverse finality.
Builders use either gold, silver, and precious stones or wood, hay, and straw, a material hierarchy that gives the commentary's selected-versus-dross image a concrete test case.
The day exposes each person's work and fire tests its quality, so apparent building material is sorted by what endures testing.

row.basis: self-styled rich who are truly poor
row.note: The wealthy self-assessment is exposed as wretched, poor, blind, and naked; it overturns worldly measures of value in the commentary's register of high and low.
Those who die in the Lord rest from labor and their deeds follow them, specifying a form of good that survives the end of earthly life.

row.basis: sharing perishable goods because of imperishable goods
row.note: The Two Ways instruction requires sharing with a needy brother and argues that participants in imperishable things should share perishable things all the more; it unites other-preference with a hierarchy of goods.
At death dust returns to earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it; it offers a restrained biblical account of bodily transience beside a Godward remainder.
Wealth gained hastily dwindles, while gradual gathering increases it, adding a concrete temporal test to the commentary's concern for rightly qualified wealth.
The person who gets riches unjustly leaves them in midlife and ends as a fool, combining unclean source with wealth's failure to remain.

row.basis: giving to poor as loan to God
row.note: The one gracious to the poor lends to the LORD, who repays the deed; it makes voluntary preference for a needy other an act with divine return.
Tobit's father says almsgiving lays up a good treasure for the day of need, a Jewish exhortation to turn possessions into a durable good through giving.

row.basis: possessions and worry / Torah and life to come
row.note: Hillel contrasts increased possessions and worry with acquiring Torah and life in the world to come, giving an interpretive hierarchy for worldly accumulation.
God clothes field grass that exists today and is put into an oven tomorrow; the image closely accompanies the commentary's grass, flower, and rapidly discarded vegetation.

row.basis: Moses before Pharaoh; refusal to heed
row.note: In the Bible’s Moses–Pharaoh scene, Pharaoh asks who YHWH is and says he will not obey YHWH’s voice or release Israel; this gives the commentary’s rejected summons to Pharaoh a concrete counterpart, while making Pharaoh’s claimed ignorance explicit.

The commentary says the one who fears takes the reminder; during the hail warning, Pharaoh’s servants who feared YHWH’s word hurried their servants and livestock to shelter, showing fear as heedful response.

row.basis: Failure to set the heart on the warning
row.note: The next verse says those who did not set their heart on YHWH’s word left their servants and livestock in the field; it gives a precise refusal alongside the fear-led response in the preceding verse.

Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH and demand Israel’s release; this is the same ruler’s rejection of a divine summons, in the biblical narrative’s own terms.

row.basis: Hearing in order to learn fear
row.note: Moses recalls the assembly at Horeb so Israel would hear God’s words and learn to fear him throughout life, then teach their children; hearing instruction is explicitly the path to the reverent fear the commentary associates with receiving the reminder.

row.basis: Warning and reward in keeping instruction
row.note: The psalm says God’s rules warn the servant and that keeping them brings great reward; this joins an admonition’s warning function to a concrete benefit, as the commentary asks whether the reminder benefits.
Personified Wisdom says she called and was refused and stretched out her hand without being heeded; this gives the bedbaht’s avoidance of offered admonition a specific scriptural scene.

Proverbs says rebuking a scoffer brings hatred but rebuking a wise person brings love; like the commentary’s contrast between the one who takes the reminder and the one who avoids it, the response depends on the hearer.

row.basis: Instruction increases the wise hearer’s learning
row.note: The verse says instruction makes the wise wiser and teaching increases the righteous person’s learning; it supplies a concrete account of how admonition benefits the receptive hearer.
The one whose ear listens to life-giving reproof dwells among the wise; this closely matches the commentary’s hearer who receives admonition through an inwardly responsive disposition.

Proverbs contrasts the person who ignores instruction and harms himself with the one who heeds reproof and gains understanding, spelling out both sides of the commentary’s reception/avoidance contrast.

row.basis: Fear, wisdom, and turning from evil
row.note: Job’s poem identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding; this brings together the commentary’s knowledge-inflected fear and the distance from wrongdoing suggested by its avoidance language.
Isaiah says the Lord looks toward the lowly and contrite person who trembles at his word; this gives a scriptural profile for the commentary’s inwardly trembling hearer who receives admonition.

row.basis: A warning intended to turn its hearers
row.note: Jeremiah’s scroll is to recount coming disaster so Judah may hear, turn from evil, and be forgiven; the passage makes the intended benefit of a reminder explicit.

row.basis: Officials fear after hearing the scroll
row.note: After Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words, the officials look at one another in fear and say they must report them to the king; the warning produces the kind of fear-led attention that the commentary associates with receiving counsel.
As the scroll is read, Jehoiakim cuts off its columns and burns them; the act gives a stark, material form to the commentary’s image of the wretched keeping the reminder at a distance.

row.basis: The king and his servants feel no fear
row.note: The verse says the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments after hearing the words; it contrasts their response with the officials’ fear in 36:16 and shows refusal despite access to the warning.

row.basis: Whether the rebellious hear or refuse
row.note: God tells Ezekiel that whether the rebellious house hears or refuses, its members will know a prophet has been among them; the message’s delivery is distinguished from its acceptance, as in the commentary’s divided audience.

row.basis: Speak the words whether heard or refused
row.note: Ezekiel is told to speak God’s words whether the rebellious hear or refuse; this clarifies the admonisher’s task even where the reminder may not benefit its audience.

row.basis: The warned wicked person who will not turn
row.note: The watchman is to warn the wicked; if the warned person does not turn, he dies in his iniquity while the watchman has delivered himself. This links offered warning, refusal, and consequence without making the messenger responsible for the hearer’s response.

The people come to Ezekiel, sit before him, and hear his words, yet do not do them; their mouths show love while their hearts pursue gain. This complicates a simple hear/refuse split by showing outward attendance without inward reception.

row.basis: Turning away and stopping the ears
row.note: Zechariah says the ancestors refused to pay attention, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears; the bodily gestures make the commentary’s language of passing by an admonition concrete.

row.basis: A hardened heart that will not hear
row.note: The people made their hearts hard lest they hear the Torah and the words sent through earlier prophets, bringing great wrath; the verse ties refusal of warning to a chosen incapacity to receive it.
After Jonah announces Nineveh’s overthrow, its people believe God, fast, and put on sackcloth; their response gives a narrative instance of warning being received and changing its hearers.

row.basis: God relents after seeing Nineveh’s response
row.note: The narrative says God saw that the Ninevites turned from their evil way and did not bring the announced disaster; this completes the warning’s benefit in the story with a changed outcome.

row.basis: Josiah hears the book and tears his clothes
row.note: When the king hears the words of the book of the law, he tears his clothes; the scene offers a concrete example of a hearer registering a warning rather than passing it by.

row.basis: A humbled response to heard words
row.note: Huldah says Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself when he heard the words against Jerusalem, so God heard him; this makes inward responsiveness and its consequence explicit.

The chronicler says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets until wrath came; it is a concentrated account of rejecting repeated admonition and its outcome.

row.basis: Those who fear speak to one another
row.note: Malachi describes those who fear YHWH speaking with one another while YHWH listens and records them; this turns the commentary’s fear-led reception into a communal exchange whose hearers are remembered by God.

row.basis: Hearing and doing the sayings of Jesus
row.note: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does them to a house built on rock; it gives a concrete outcome for receiving instruction rather than merely encountering it.
Jesus contrasts the person who hears his words but does not do them with the wise builder; the foolish house’s collapse makes the consequence of non-reception concrete.

row.basis: Closed ears and an unhealed hearer
row.note: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah describes a people whose heart has grown dull and ears are hard, so they do not hear, understand, turn, and receive healing; it gives a scriptural account of refusal as blocked reception.
In the sower parable, good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this supplies a specific picture of a reminder that benefits its hearer.

row.basis: Refusal of Moses and the Prophets
row.note: In the rich man’s story, Abraham says that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead; the warning cannot be made effective by a more spectacular sign when prior admonition is refused.
Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing but God’s power to those being saved; one proclamation divides hearers by reception and outcome, like the commentary’s two responses.

row.basis: The message among those saved and perishing
row.note: Paul calls the apostolic mission Christ’s fragrance among both those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation reaches audiences whose outcomes differ, adding a Christian account of divided reception.

row.basis: A fragrance from death or from life
row.note: Paul specifies that the same fragrance is for one person from death to death and for another from life to life; this sharpens the commentary’s contrast between the person who receives the reminder and the one who avoids it.

row.basis: Daily exhortation against a hardened heart
row.note: Hebrews tells the community to exhort one another every day so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit; admonition is a mutual practice meant to keep hearers receptive.
Hebrews repeats, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”; this directly joins hearing a divine summons to the choice between receiving it and resisting it.

row.basis: The message that did not benefit its hearers
row.note: Hebrews says the good news heard by the wilderness generation did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this closely parallels the commentary’s question of whether the reminder benefits and makes faith the interpretive bridge.
James warns readers not to be hearers only who deceive themselves, but to do the word; this distinguishes exposure to instruction from receiving it in practice.

row.basis: The preacher’s duty to reprove and exhort
row.note: Timothy is charged to proclaim the word and to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with patience; this gives a concrete Christian formulation of the admonisher’s task even when response varies.

row.basis: A hearer who will not endure sound teaching
row.note: Paul says people will not endure sound teaching and will gather teachers to suit their desires; this describes avoidance as actively selecting away from admonition.
Paul says they will turn their ears away from truth and toward myths; the bodily image of turning away closely specifies the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance.

row.basis: Mockery and postponement after Paul’s announcement
row.note: In Athens, some mock when Paul speaks of resurrection, while others say they will hear him again; the scene records distinct responses to a public religious summons.
The following verse names people who join Paul and believe; it completes the same scene with the response of hearers who accept the proclamation.

row.basis: Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels the Arabic source root ذ ك ر and frames dhikrā as admonition; Hebrew זכר (zakar, “remember”) is cognate, and Moses uses it to command Israel to remember the wilderness road as a lesson in humility and keeping the commandments. The connection is the remembered lesson, not an equation of memory with admonition.

Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life; this gives a specific choice-and-consequence frame alongside the commentary’s contrast between the wretched and the opposite of happiness.

row.basis: A blessed person refuses wicked counsel
row.note: The psalm calls blessed the person who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked; unlike the bedbaht who avoids divine admonition, this person’s distance is good because of what is refused, making the object of avoidance decisive.

row.basis: Fear as the beginning of wisdom
row.note: The psalm says fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom and that those who practice the commands have good understanding; it links fear and knowledge in the reverse direction from the commentary’s claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge.

row.basis: Eliphaz calls the reproved person happy
row.note: Eliphaz says the person whom God reproves is happy and should not despise divine discipline; this touches the commentary’s contrast between the bedbaht and happiness, while remaining Eliphaz’s counsel within Job’s debate rather than an unqualified narrator verdict.

Wisdom’s opponents are said to hate knowledge and not choose fear of YHWH; alongside the commentary’s Arabic source note linking خشية to “I knew” and its claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge, Proverbs gives the relation in the opposite pedagogical direction.

Wisdom says whoever listens will dwell securely and be at ease without dread of disaster; this adds safety as the outcome of attending to counsel, while the commentary emphasizes the receiver’s fear as the disposition that makes listening possible.

Isaiah compares God’s word to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth, saying the word accomplishes God’s purpose; beside the commentary’s “if the reminder benefits,” this presents divine speech as effective, though not necessarily beneficial to every hearer.

row.basis: Those who tremble at the word amid hostility
row.note: Isaiah addresses hearers who tremble at YHWH’s word and then describes brothers who hate and expel them; this places reverent reception amid social hostility, a sharper conflict than the commentary’s brief contrast of receiver and avoider.

row.basis: An offered way rejected by its hearers
row.note: Jeremiah urges people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not; the scene makes rejection of offered guidance explicit.

row.basis: A prophet heard as a pleasant song
row.note: Ezekiel says his hearers treat his words like a beautiful song and listen without doing them; the image adds a form of non-reception in which people enjoy the sound of admonition while its claim passes them by.

Hosea says the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because they rejected knowledge and forgot God’s teaching; it connects the commentary’s knowledge-and-fear discussion to the consequence of refusing instruction.

The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر as its source root and uses dhikrā for admonition; Malachi’s זכרון (zikaron, “remembrance”) uses the cognate Hebrew root for the record of those who fear YHWH and speak together, where the sense is memorial rather than instruction.

row.basis: Fearers reinterpreted as paired Torah learners
row.note: The Mishnah reads Malachi’s people who fear God and speak together as two who sit with words of Torah between them, with the divine presence among them; this rabbinic interpretation turns fearful reception into shared study, echoing the commentary’s description of admonition as passing to another.

Ben Sira says fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; alongside the commentary’s account of fear as reverent and associated with knowledge, this Jewish wisdom text makes fear the entry into wisdom rather than its result.
Ben Sira says the one who loves listening gains knowledge and the attentive person becomes wise; this gives a concise account of instruction benefiting a receptive hearer.

row.basis: Disciples blessed with seeing and hearing
row.note: Jesus tells his disciples their eyes and ears are blessed because they see and hear; this supplies the positive counterpart to the dull hearing in the preceding verse and to the commentary’s fear-led recipient.

row.basis: Joyful reception that does not last
row.note: In the sower parable, rocky-ground hearers receive the word at once with joy but fall away when trouble comes; this preserves a secondary case beyond simple acceptance or avoidance, where initial reception fails to endure.

row.basis: Failure to see as imposed blindness
row.note: Paul says the god of this age has blinded unbelievers’ minds so they cannot see the gospel’s light; this gives a different account of failed reception from the commentary’s active image of the wretched person avoiding the reminder.

row.basis: Doing the heard word brings blessing
row.note: James describes the person who looks into the law and perseveres as a doer who will be blessed in doing; it specifies the benefit of receiving instruction as practice, not mere hearing.

row.basis: God’s outstretched hands to a disobedient people
row.note: Paul quotes God’s all-day outstretched hands toward a disobedient and contrary people; the image pairs persistent invitation with refusal and gives a Christian rereading of Israel’s resistance to divine speech.
The risen Christ says he reproves and disciplines those he loves, then urges repentance; this Christian text interprets correction as care and gives the admonition a restorative purpose.

row.basis: Noah’s preaching and the hearers saved
row.note: Clement presents Noah as preaching repentance and says those who heeded were saved; this early Christian retelling makes the outcome of a received admonition explicit.

row.basis: The soils as different kinds of hearers
row.note: Chrysostom’s homily on the sower reads the soils as differing hearers of the word; this Christian interpretation develops why one proclamation bears fruit in some and not in others, much like the commentary’s two responses to reminder.

row.basis: Nocturnal emission and exclusion from camp
row.note: The commentary’s Arabic source note links junub with distance from prayer and the mosque; Deuteronomy orders a man with a nocturnal emission outside the camp until evening, a specific ritual-distance comparison, though its setting is the military camp and it says nothing about prayer.

Deuteronomy continues that the man washes and returns to camp at sunset; this clarifies the temporary boundary behind the commentary’s junub association while differing from its prayer-and-mosque framing.

After Israel hears God’s voice at Horeb, YHWH wishes they would keep a heart to fear him and his commands always, so it would go well with them and their children; this directly joins heard instruction, reverent fear, and benefit.

row.basis: The God-fearer is taught the way
row.note: The psalm asks who fears YHWH and answers that God will instruct that person in the way to choose; it reverses the commentary’s order in a useful way, making fear the disposition that receives instruction.

In God’s indictment of people who recite his statutes, the wicked are said to hate discipline and cast God’s words behind them; this makes rejection of instruction a deliberate act, close to the bedbaht’s avoidance.

row.basis: Refusal followed by one’s own counsel
row.note: After Israel would not listen to God’s voice, the psalm says he gave them over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsel; this connects refusal of a divine reminder with self-directed wandering.
God says that if Israel would listen and walk in his ways, he would quickly subdue its enemies; the verse gives a concrete benefit that refusal has forfeited.

row.basis: The flock summoned to hear God’s voice
row.note: The psalm calls Israel the people of God’s pasture and the sheep of his hand, then says “today, if you hear his voice”; it frames reception of divine speech as the present duty of the addressed community.

row.basis: Do not harden the heart when hearing
row.note: The psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as at Meribah; it makes the inner refusal that counters a receptive, trembling hearer explicit.

row.basis: Fear expressed by hearing and serving
row.note: Samuel tells Israel that if they fear YHWH, serve him, and listen to his voice rather than rebel, they and their king will fare well; it directly links fear to taking divine instruction.

row.basis: Refusal brings the Lord’s hand against them
row.note: Samuel warns that if Israel will not listen to YHWH’s voice and rebels against his command, the Lord’s hand will be against them; this gives the non-hearing side its consequence.
Samuel tells Saul that listening to YHWH’s voice is better than sacrifice; the rebuke makes heedful response itself the required offering, not a religious substitute for it.
Samuel says Saul rejected YHWH’s word, so YHWH rejected him as king; this states the consequence of a ruler who hears the divine command but will not receive it.

row.basis: Instruction as a path of life
row.note: Proverbs says the one who heeds instruction is on a path of life, while the one who rejects reproof leads others astray; it gives both the benefit of receiving counsel and the danger of refusing it.

row.basis: The son who hears versus the scoffer
row.note: A wise son hears his father’s instruction, while a scoffer does not listen to rebuke; this is another precise contrast between a teachable recipient and one who avoids admonition.

row.basis: A stiff neck after repeated reproof
row.note: The person often reproved who stiffens his neck will suddenly be broken beyond healing; this develops the fate of persistent refusal beyond the single act of avoiding a reminder.
Isaiah says that if the people are willing and obedient they will eat the good of the land; it specifies a benefit for taking the prophetic demand to heart.
The paired warning says that if the people refuse and rebel, they will be devoured by the sword; it makes refusal of the same summons a concrete opposite outcome.

row.basis: Hearing without understanding in Isaiah’s commission
row.note: Isaiah is told to tell the people to hear without understanding and see without perceiving; in its own setting this is a prophetic commission to an unreceptive audience, offering a stark counter-scene to the commentary’s hearer who takes admonition.

row.basis: A people unwilling to hear instruction
row.note: Isaiah calls them rebellious children who will not hear the instruction of YHWH; this directly names refusal of the teaching the commentary calls a reminder.

row.basis: Demanding smooth words from the prophets
row.note: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, but to prophesy smooth things; this gives a specific way of avoiding correction by trying to control what the admonisher may say.

row.basis: Asking the Holy One to leave
row.note: They demand that the prophet turn aside from the way and that Israel’s Holy One cease from before them; this sharpens the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance into rejection of its divine source.

row.basis: The God-fearer listens to the servant’s voice
row.note: Isaiah asks who fears YHWH and obeys the voice of his servant, then tells that person to trust in YHWH while walking in darkness; this joins fear and listening while adding trust in a difficult circumstance.

row.basis: The wicked are urged to turn and receive pardon
row.note: Isaiah tells the wicked to forsake their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon; this shows prophetic admonition offered for a hearer’s benefit, not only to announce judgment.

row.basis: Turn so wrongdoing will not become ruin
row.note: Ezekiel urges Israel to repent and turn from its transgressions lest iniquity become its downfall; this makes the warning’s practical benefit explicit.

row.basis: Turn and live rather than die
row.note: YHWH says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death and commands Israel to turn and live; this places a life-giving invitation beside the commentary’s contrast of the one who receives counsel and the wretched one who avoids it.

row.basis: God calls the wicked to turn from death
row.note: YHWH swears he takes no pleasure in the wicked person’s death but wants that person to turn and live, repeating “turn back”; it makes the offered warning’s life-preserving purpose unmistakable.

row.basis: Those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words
row.note: Ben Sira says those who fear the Lord will not disobey his words and those who love him keep his ways; this directly links reverent fear with receiving and following instruction.

row.basis: Jerusalem is unwilling to be gathered
row.note: Jesus says he often wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood, but they were unwilling; the image makes refusal of a protective summons concrete.

row.basis: The word held fast and made fruitful
row.note: Jesus says good-soil hearers hold the word fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience; this specifies an enduring form of the beneficial reception described in the commentary.

Jesus warns his hearers to consider how they hear, since the one who has will receive more and the one who lacks will lose even what he thinks he has; this makes the consequences of response explicit.

row.basis: Blessing belongs to those who keep the word
row.note: Jesus says blessed are those who hear God’s word and keep it; this pairs reception with obedience and the blessed outcome that contrasts with the commentary’s unhappy avoider.

row.basis: Hearing and believing lead from death to life
row.note: Jesus says the one who hears his word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life; the verse links reception to a changed fate.
Jesus tells his interlocutors that they are unwilling to come to him to have life; this is a direct instance of refusing the offered source of life.
Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge: the word he spoke will judge on the last day; it connects non-reception to the judgment that follows.

row.basis: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
row.note: Stephen accuses his hearers of always resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did; this gives rejection of divine speech a repeated communal history.

row.basis: Paul says his hearers thrust aside the word
row.note: Paul and Barnabas say their audience judged itself unworthy of eternal life by thrusting aside God’s word, so they turn to the Gentiles; this concretely depicts a hearer’s active rejection of the announcement.
The Gentiles rejoice when they hear Paul’s message and believe; this supplies the receptive counterpart in the same proclamation scene.
After Paul explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the prophets, some are persuaded and others disbelieve; this is a clear scene of one teaching meeting divided responses.

row.basis: Pay closer attention lest hearers drift away
row.note: Hebrews urges readers to pay closer attention to what they heard so they do not drift away from it; this makes avoidance a gradual slipping from an already heard warning.
Hebrews asks how anyone can escape if they neglect such a great salvation; this adds the consequence of letting a saving announcement pass by.

row.basis: Do not refuse the one speaking
row.note: Hebrews warns its readers not to refuse the one speaking from heaven and recalls that those who refused the earthly warning did not escape; it explicitly joins refusal of admonition with judgment.

row.basis: Receive the implanted word that can save
row.note: James tells readers to put away wickedness and receive meekly the implanted word, which can save their souls; this makes admonition a saving gift that must be welcomed.

row.basis: Bringing a wanderer back from error
row.note: James says whoever brings a person wandering from truth back saves that person from death and covers many sins; this gives the reminder a neighbor-directed, restorative action.

row.basis: Knowing God and hearing his messengers
row.note: John says whoever knows God listens to the apostolic witnesses, while one not from God does not listen; this directly ties knowledge to receptivity, complementing the commentary’s discussion of knowledge and fear.

Isaiah’s commission continues by telling him to make the people’s heart dull and ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed; unlike the commentary’s account of the wretched person avoiding a reminder, this passage portrays non-reception within a judgment commission.

row.basis: Discipline understood as a father’s instruction
row.note: Moses tells Israel to know in its heart that YHWH disciplines it as a father disciplines a son; this offers a Jewish scriptural frame in which correction itself is instruction, though it does not describe the audience’s response to a spoken reminder.

row.basis: Sinai’s acceptance under threat and later reaffirmation
row.note: The Talmud imagines the mountain held over Israel as a barrel, with acceptance of Torah demanded under threat of burial, then says Israel reaffirmed acceptance in Ahasuerus’s days; this complicates a simple equation of reception with inward reverent fear by distinguishing coerced and later willing acceptance.

row.basis: Isaiah’s hard-hearing prophecy applied to Paul’s audience
row.note: Paul quotes Isaiah’s dull ears and closed eyes to explain why some hearers will not understand, turn, and be healed; this Christian continuation shows an interpretive tradition applying Isaiah’s account of failed reception to a new audience.

row.basis: Clement’s Jonah as a model of heeded warning
row.note: Clement recalls that Jonah preached destruction to Nineveh and that the city repented and obtained pardon; this early Christian retelling reads the scriptural warning as a summons whose reception changes the announced outcome.

row.basis: praise of the name; its exaltation
row.note: The commentary makes the name itself the object of praise and hears al-aʿlā with the name; this verse commands all creation to praise YHWH’s name because it alone is exalted.
The commentary stresses that 87:1 acts directly on the name; this psalm tells YHWH’s servants to praise the name itself, not merely to act by it.

row.basis: proclaiming the name and ascribing greatness
row.note: The commentary joins the divine name to height and praise; Moses says he will proclaim YHWH’s name and ascribe greatness to God, a close liturgical formulation.

row.basis: sanctifying rather than profaning the name
row.note: The commentary reads the command as guarding the name from false or unworthy attribution; Leviticus forbids profaning God’s holy name and calls Israel to sanctify it.

The commentary says the name must not be filled with an unsuitable meaning; here YHWH proclaims the name while describing mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love, showing the character the name bears.

row.basis: the high and lofty one whose name is Holy
row.note: The commentary preserves both readings of al-aʿlā, highest Lord and highest name; Isaiah calls God high and lofty and says his name is Holy.

row.basis: God’s name and glory not given to another
row.note: The commentary warns against transferring the Lord’s name to rivals; Isaiah identifies YHWH by name and says his glory and praise are not given to idols.

row.basis: the divine name for all generations
row.note: The commentary treats the name as a uniquely guarded designation; God gives Moses the name YHWH as the enduring name remembered through generations.
The commentary treats tasbih as declaring God’s name free of defect; Jesus’ prayer asks that the Father’s name be hallowed, making sanctification of the name the prayer’s opening petition.
The commentary makes the name itself the focus of the imperative; Luke preserves the same petition in a shorter prayer addressed to the Father, a second early Christian form of the formula.

The commentary says praise must become speech, action, and intention; Yoma 86a says Torah-shaped conduct can cause observers to praise God, making sanctification of the Name an ethical public practice.

row.basis: hallowed name as sanctified in the worshiper
row.note: The commentary says God is not made more perfect by tasbih, while the worshiper must speak and act rightly; Tertullian reads “hallowed be thy name” as a request that the already holy name be sanctified in believers.

row.basis: bowing, kneeling, and worship before the Maker
row.note: The commentary brings tasbih together with bodily prayer and prostration; this verse joins worship, bowing, and kneeling before YHWH the Maker in one embodied act.

row.basis: continual praise as lips confess the name
row.note: The commentary says tasbih is both a judgment and a practice carried by speech and body; Hebrews calls for continual praise, the fruit of lips confessing God’s name.

row.basis: creatures praising without rest, day and night
row.note: The commentary distinguishes human tasbih from the praise of creatures people cannot comprehend; Revelation’s four living creatures never stop proclaiming God’s holiness day or night.

The commentary connects divine glory with the bodily place of prostration; Revelation’s elders fall before the enthroned one and cast their crowns down, enacting worship without keeping honor for themselves.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars called to praise
row.note: The commentary places stars moving in their courses beside created praise; this psalm directly summons sun, moon, and shining stars to praise YHWH.

row.basis: the name praised from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary sets daytime activity beside extended worship; this verse gives the name of YHWH praise from the rising of the sun to its setting.
The commentary labels Arabic al-aʿlā with the ʿ-l-w root; Melchizedek blesses Abram by El Elyon, “God Most High,” creator of heaven and earth, a Hebrew cognate title for the height claim.

row.basis: Hebrew ʿElyon over all the earth
row.note: The commentary joins “highest” to the Lord’s unrivaled rule; the psalm calls YHWH Most High over all the earth and exalted far above all gods, using the Hebrew cognate title in that claim.

row.basis: no one can be made God’s equal
row.note: The commentary hears “namesake” as a rival who could bear God’s name or compete with him; Isaiah asks whom God can be likened or made equal to, directly denying such a counterpart.
The commentary rejects distributing lordship among separate claimants; Israel’s confession names YHWH as one, the foundational Jewish formulation of undivided allegiance.
The commentary connects praise with the claim that God has no namesake; after the sea victory, Moses’ song asks who among the gods is like YHWH and praises his holiness and wonders.

row.basis: no God beside Israel’s King and Redeemer
row.note: The commentary calls rival divine names unsupported names; Isaiah has YHWH declare himself first and last and say there is no God besides him.

The commentary describes lordship being distributed among many names; Paul acknowledges many so-called gods and lords in heaven and earth, then sets that language beside the community’s confession in the next verse.

The commentary’s warning against separate competing lords meets Paul’s formulation of one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ; the verse also gives Christian readers a distinctive two-part confession.

row.basis: keeping disciples in the Father’s name
row.note: The commentary says the name is to be kept from rival claims; Jesus asks the Father to keep his followers in the name given to him, making the name a sphere of protection and unity.

row.basis: Jesus makes the Father’s name known
row.note: The commentary links a singular messenger, revelation, and the divine name; Jesus says he has made the Father’s name known and will continue to do so, with the result that divine love may dwell in the disciples.

The commentary’s Adam scene says God teaches all names and the angels cannot supply them; Genesis instead has God bring animals to Adam to see what he will call them, giving Adam the naming act and a different emphasis on human knowledge.

row.basis: Hebrew šēm, name sought as renown
row.note: The commentary discusses Arabic ism as a name that raises its bearer; Hebrew šēm is its cognate, and Babel’s builders seek to make a šēm for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven, where name and self-exalting ascent meet.

row.basis: self-made name and tower reaching heaven
row.note: The commentary contrasts the true highest Lord with a creature claiming height for itself; Babel’s builders try to make their own name and a tower whose top reaches heaven, an earlier collective version of self-exaltation.

row.basis: God, rather than the person, makes Abram’s name great
row.note: The commentary says a name is raised but its bearer must not seize divine honor; God promises to make Abram’s name great, locating honor in divine gift rather than self-claim.

row.basis: Aramaic šēm, the name blessed forever
row.note: The commentary’s Arabic ism is a Semitic cognate of Aramaic šēm; Daniel blesses the name of God forever and immediately attributes wisdom and might to God, joining name, praise, and divine sovereignty.
The commentary’s Arabic tasbih is cognate with Biblical Aramaic š-b-ḥ; after God reveals the hidden dream, Daniel says he thanks and praises God, showing praise as acknowledgment of received wisdom.

The commentary hears ownership and care in Arabic rabbika; Mary addresses Jesus with the Aramaic rabbouni, which John glosses as teacher, preserving a related personal master-title in a human address.

row.basis: YHWH’s name and its proclaimed meaning
row.note: The commentary insists that a name must not be filled with a false quality; Exodus has God proclaim the name YHWH together with mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love, a concrete scriptural account of the name’s character.

row.basis: sanctifying a profaned name among the nations
row.note: The commentary says God’s name must be kept from misrepresentation; Ezekiel says Israel profaned it among nations and God will sanctify his great name before them, adding public reputation and restoration.

row.basis: prohibition against carrying the name in vain
row.note: The commentary’s command protects the divine name from misuse; Exodus forbids bearing YHWH’s name falsely or emptily, a legal boundary around speech about God.

row.basis: God shepherded Jacob throughout his life
row.note: The commentary hears owner, guide, and caregiver together in “your Lord”; Jacob calls God the one who shepherded him all his life, making the relation sustained care rather than bare possession.

row.basis: YHWH seeks his scattered sheep himself
row.note: The commentary develops the Lord as one who keeps together what might disperse; Ezekiel has YHWH personally search for and rescue his sheep, a close shepherding image of active guardianship.

row.basis: binding the injured and strengthening the weak
row.note: The commentary connects lordship with bringing what is cared for toward completion; YHWH’s shepherd promises to heal, strengthen, and seek the lost, specifying repair as part of divine rule.
The commentary develops the sequence from sky and first rain to pasture; the psalm says God prepares rain and makes grass grow on the mountains, a direct biblical counterpart to the provision scene.

row.basis: food given to animals that cry out
row.note: The commentary relates the Lord to a shepherd and provider; this verse says God gives food to beasts and young ravens, extending pasture’s growth into care for dependent creatures.
The commentary’s pasture turns from green growth to dark, spent residue; Isaiah compares all flesh to grass, framing the vegetation cycle as a picture of human transience.

The commentary stresses that the Lord’s ordering includes the pasture’s decline; Isaiah says grass withers when the breath of YHWH blows, making the same growth-to-loss movement a sign of human frailty.

row.basis: God’s word endures when grass withers
row.note: The commentary sets the high name against fading worldly life; Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the enduring word of God, adding permanence to the transient pasture image.

row.basis: the lot’s outcome belongs to YHWH
row.note: The commentary develops the image of arrows gathered in a bag and lots cast to assign a share; Proverbs says the lot is cast but its decision comes from YHWH, connecting chance-like allocation to divine governance.

The commentary mentions lots and measured shares among the Arabic root’s developed images; Leviticus assigns one goat to YHWH and one to Azazel by lot, a ritual use of lots to distribute distinct roles.

row.basis: Moses as God to Pharaoh, Aaron as his mouth
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses’ mission and his request for his brother’s help; Exodus appoints Aaron to speak for Moses and calls Moses God to Pharaoh, giving a close but differently framed account of delegated authority.

row.basis: Aaron’s staff swallows the magicians’ staffs
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses’ fear before Pharaoh’s sign-makers and God’s reassurance; Exodus tells the same contest through staffs becoming serpents and Aaron’s staff swallowing theirs, locating the outcome in a public sign.

The commentary presents Pharaoh as claiming “I am your highest lord”; Exodus instead has Pharaoh challenge Moses by asking who YHWH is and refusing obedience, a related confrontation expressed as denial rather than self-deification.

row.basis: Pharaoh raised so God’s name may be proclaimed
row.note: The commentary opposes Pharaoh’s appropriation of the highest lordship to the true Lord; Exodus says Pharaoh was raised so God’s power and name would be proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the direction of glory.

row.basis: the king of Tyre says, “I am a god”
row.note: The commentary sets Pharaoh’s self-declared highest lordship against the command to keep God’s name for God; Ezekiel’s king makes the explicit divine claim, and the oracle answers that he is mortal, sharpening the usurpation motif.

row.basis: a king’s resolve to be like the Most High
row.note: The commentary says Pharaoh takes the name and height for himself; Isaiah’s king of Babylon vows to make himself like the Most High, an explicit self-exalting counterpart.
The commentary contrasts true height with rulers who rise by tyranny; Isaiah follows the king’s ascent boast by placing him in Sheol, giving the reversal that the boast itself invites.

row.basis: Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the city he built
row.note: The commentary links a ruler’s claim to supreme status with the taking of glory; Nebuchadnezzar credits his power and majesty for Babylon, a concrete royal boast before his humbling.

row.basis: the humbled king blesses the Most High
row.note: The commentary’s central contrast is false self-exaltation versus praise of the true Highest; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses and honors the Most High, whose dominion is everlasting.

row.basis: the lot identifies Jonah on the ship
row.note: The commentary recounts Jonah’s flight on a loaded ship and the lot that marks him among the losing group; Jonah’s sailors cast lots to discover whose account brought the storm, a close shared episode with a different stated purpose.

row.basis: Jonah is thrown into the sea
row.note: The commentary says Jonah is swallowed after the ship’s lot; Jonah’s sailors throw him into the sea and the storm ceases, giving the sea episode and its immediate outcome in the biblical telling.
The commentary recounts Jonah swallowed while blameworthy; the Hebrew book says YHWH appoints a great fish to swallow him, sharing the rescue scene while identifying divine agency explicitly.

row.basis: Jonah cries from inside the fish and is heard
row.note: The commentary quotes Jonah’s confession in darkness and says God answers him; Jonah’s prayer from the fish says his cry reached YHWH, while its surrounding prayer does not use the same confession formula.

row.basis: thanksgiving and vowed sacrifice precede release
row.note: The commentary says prior tasbih keeps Jonah from remaining in the fish until resurrection; Jonah’s prayer promises thanksgiving and sacrifice, after which release follows, sharing piety and rescue but giving a different causal frame.

row.basis: the fish releases Jonah onto dry land
row.note: The commentary’s fish episode ends with rescue from the belly; Jonah’s book says the fish vomits him onto dry land at God’s command, a direct narrative parallel.

row.basis: Jonah’s three days become a sign of resurrection
row.note: The commentary contrasts Jonah’s deliverance from the fish with remaining there until the day of resurrection; Jesus interprets Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign for the Son of Man’s time in the earth, adding a Christian resurrection reading.

row.basis: alms given secretly and repaid by the Father
row.note: The commentary cites giving wealth to seek the highest Lord’s face without repaying a favor; Jesus says hidden almsgiving is seen and repaid by the Father, a concrete ethical parallel with divine rather than human recompense.

row.basis: treasure stored in heaven rather than on earth
row.note: The commentary contrasts the low, passing worldly life with what is higher and lasting; Jesus tells disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it is not lost, giving the ethical form of that vertical contrast.

row.basis: Jesus is called Son of the Most High
row.note: The commentary rejects rivals taking the highest Lord’s name; the annunciation names Jesus Son of the Most High and promises him David’s throne, presenting a Christian claim that joins filial language to the highest title.
The commentary’s tasbih verses reject the claim that God has a child; John says God gave his only Son, a central Christian assertion that makes the theological difference explicit.

row.basis: Thomas calls the risen Jesus “my Lord and my God”
row.note: The commentary cites Jesus’ denial of a rightful claim to divinity; Thomas addresses the risen Jesus with divine titles, an explicit Christian narrative counterclaim about Jesus’ status.

row.basis: the name above every name bestowed on Jesus
row.note: The commentary says the highest name belongs to God and must not be seized by a creature; Philippians says God highly exalts Jesus and grants him the name above every name, the central Christian reapplication of the exalted-name language.

row.basis: every knee bows at Jesus’ name
row.note: The commentary joins praise to bodily prostration; Philippians says every knee bows at Jesus’ name, extending worship to the Christian confession of Jesus.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord
row.note: The commentary resists transferring divine lordship to others; Philippians makes universal confession of Jesus as Lord the outcome of God’s exaltation, a distinctive Christian reading of the title.

row.basis: a mark distinguishes those spared judgment
row.note: The commentary presents the alternate Arabic root for name as a bodily brand identifying an owner; Ezekiel marks the foreheads of those who grieve over injustice so they are distinguished during judgment, a motif parallel without claiming Hebrew cognacy.

row.basis: the Lamb’s and Father’s names on foreheads
row.note: The commentary describes a mark as an identifying trace that separates one bearer from others; Revelation’s redeemed bear the Lamb’s name and the Father’s name on their foreheads, making identity and allegiance bodily visible.

row.basis: the beast’s name linked to its mark and economic allegiance
row.note: The commentary warns against a name being assigned to a false claimant; Revelation connects the beast’s name or number with its mark and the ability to buy or sell, a contrary mark of allegiance.

row.ref: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men 35
row.basis: all the works bless and exalt the Lord
row.note: The commentary distinguishes human praise from the praise of the heavens and creatures; the Three Young Men summon all the Lord’s works to bless and exalt him forever, a liturgical expansion of creation-wide tasbih.

row.basis: name exalted above all blessing and praise
row.note: The commentary keeps the name itself as the object to be raised; Nehemiah’s public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above blessing and praise, an unusually close liturgical formulation.

row.basis: no one like YHWH, whose name is great in might
row.note: The commentary joins the highest title to the absence of any namesake or rival; Jeremiah says there is none like YHWH and that his name is great in might, joining uniqueness, name, and power.
The commentary distinguishes praising the name itself from acting by means of it; this psalm tells worshipers to ascribe to YHWH the glory due his name and to bring an offering.
The commentary makes tasbih an enacted practice as well as a judgment; the next line of the psalm calls the earth to bow before YHWH in holy splendor, joining name-praise to bodily worship.

row.basis: praising the great and awesome name
row.note: The commentary says the name is to be guarded and held high; this psalm commands praise of YHWH’s great and awesome name and immediately calls him holy.

row.basis: the name great among nations with pure offerings
row.note: The commentary asks that the name be kept from false attribution; Malachi says YHWH’s name is great among the nations and associates it with pure offerings from sunrise to sunset, extending the name’s honor beyond one people.

row.basis: the Lord enthroned high and lifted up
row.note: The commentary preserves the reading of al-aʿlā as the Lord himself being highest; Isaiah’s vision places the Lord on a high and lofty throne as a prophet receives a commission.

The commentary presents tasbih as declaring God free of defect; the seraphim call one to another “Holy, holy, holy” and fill the scene with God’s glory, a foundational Jewish liturgical formula of divine holiness.
The commentary notes stars moving in their courses alongside the praise of creation; Job’s creation scene pictures morning stars singing together, making celestial praise explicit.

row.basis: do not invoke the names of other gods
row.note: The commentary warns against assigning divine naming to rivals; Exodus tells Israel not even to mention the names of other gods, a concrete discipline of exclusive worship.

row.basis: Moses says he is slow of speech
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses asking God to open his chest and make his mission easy; Exodus has Moses object that he is not eloquent and is slow of speech, a shared commissioning problem stated differently.

row.basis: Aaron is appointed to meet Moses
row.note: The commentary says Moses asks that his brother share the task so they can praise God; Exodus has God appoint Aaron, already on his way to meet Moses, as the brother who will speak with him.

row.basis: Aaron speaks while Moses is as God
row.note: The commentary links a single messenger, his brother’s aid, and a divine mission; Exodus says Aaron will be Moses’ mouth and Moses will be as God to him, clarifying delegated speech without the Qur’anic stated purpose of praise.

row.basis: the name that answers is declared God
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one true Lord with names humans assign to rivals; Elijah proposes a public test in which each side calls its god by name and the one who answers by fire is God.

row.basis: Baal’s name is called without an answer
row.note: The commentary calls idolatrous names unsupported names; the prophets of Baal invoke their god from morning until noon, but no voice answers, giving that critique a concrete narrative scene.

row.basis: Elijah invokes YHWH’s name before Israel
row.note: The commentary links praise of the name with a messenger’s public task; Elijah prays that the people will know YHWH is God and that he acted at YHWH’s word, making the name known through the sign.

row.basis: Israel confesses YHWH alone is God
row.note: The commentary says divine lordship must not be distributed among rivals; after the fire, the people fall down and confess that YHWH is God, the scene’s explicit verdict on the competing names.

The commentary develops a possible Arabic name-as-brand image but does not claim a Hebrew cognate; God marks Cain so others will recognize and spare him, adding protection to the mark’s identifying function.

row.basis: God gives Abram the name Abraham
row.note: The commentary says a name raises and distinguishes its bearer; God renames Abram Abraham and explains the name by his future role as father of many nations, showing identity conferred by God.

row.basis: knowledge of YHWH compared with dawn and rain
row.note: The commentary brings the first rain, green pasture, and the knowledge of God into one hearing; Hosea says let us know YHWH, whose coming is like dawn and like rain watering the land, a particularly close meeting of knowledge and agricultural renewal.

row.basis: YHWH is righteous, while the speaker rebelled
row.note: The commentary says Jonah’s tasbih assigns perfection to God and wrongdoing to himself; Lamentations says YHWH is in the right while the speaker has rebelled, a direct ethical form of that reversal.

row.basis: stars and natural powers mistaken for gods
row.note: The commentary distinguishes celestial motion from the Creator and rejects names placed on created things; Wisdom lists sun, moon, stars, and other natural powers as things people mistakenly treated as gods.

row.basis: creation’s greatness points to its Maker
row.note: The commentary places the sky, stars, rain, and pasture under one sustaining Lord; Wisdom argues that the greatness and beauty of created things allow their Maker to be perceived, sharpening the distinction between sign and source.

row.basis: a good name rises above other crowns
row.note: The commentary develops name as elevation and public distinction; this saying places the crown of a good name above kingship, priesthood, and Torah, giving Jewish ethical use to the image of a name raised above.

row.basis: the Lord’s Prayer recited three times each day
row.note: The commentary joins tasbih to repeated prayer and embodied practice; the Didache instructs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily, turning its hallowing of the name into a regular liturgical act.

The commentary rejects divine offspring; Hebrews quotes the royal son formula from Psalm 2 as speech about the Son, showing how Christian interpretation makes that Hebrew royal language christological.

The commentary rejects God having a child; Exodus calls Israel God’s firstborn in a covenant demand to Pharaoh, showing that biblical son language can name a people’s relation to God rather than biological offspring.

row.basis: the lawless one exalts himself as God
row.note: The commentary sets Pharaoh’s “I am your highest lord” against rightful divine sovereignty; Paul describes an end-time figure who exalts himself above every object of worship and proclaims himself God, a close later counter-image.
The commentary says tasbih separates God from false claims about him; Revelation’s beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God’s name, giving a Christian apocalyptic image of the name’s profanation.

row.basis: seeing God’s face with his name on foreheads
row.note: The commentary brings the divine face and a bodily name-mark into its reading; Revelation joins the two directly: the servants see God’s face and bear his name on their foreheads.

row.basis: one baptismal name over Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
row.note: The commentary says different names belong to one possessor; Matthew gives baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian formula that keeps unity while adding a distinct triune account.

row.basis: one king and one name over all the earth
row.note: The commentary holds the highest Lord’s name apart from competing claims; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, joining universal rule to exclusive naming.

row.basis: YHWH’s name and renown endure through generations
row.note: The commentary contrasts the enduring highest name with fading life; this psalm says YHWH’s name and renown endure through all generations, extending the name’s permanence beyond an individual lifetime.

row.basis: YHWH’s name as a strong tower of refuge
row.note: The commentary describes a name as a raised sign that protects and identifies its bearer; Proverbs says the name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe, making refuge part of the name’s force.

The commentary says qaddara assigns each thing its measure and limit; Wisdom says the Creator ordered all things by measure, number and weight, making proportion explicit as the structure of creation.
The commentary glosses qaddara as setting the amount of every thing; Job asks who determined earth's measurements and stretched its line, giving that claim a concrete creation image.
The commentary reads God's measure as extending across all creation; Isaiah pictures God measuring waters and marking off the heavens, a direct image of cosmic ordering.
The commentary says measure includes where a thing reaches and when it ends; Acts says God fixed nations' times and habitation boundaries, extending that ordering to human history and geography.
The commentary joins God's universal measure to guidance; Paul says the bounded times and places are so people will seek God and perhaps find him, giving human purpose to the allotted setting.
The commentary explicitly includes lifespan and endpoint in measure; Job says a person's days are determined and bounds set that cannot be passed, making temporal limit part of created measure.

row.basis: an appointed season for every matter
row.note: The commentary reads grass's greening and withering as one measured course; Ecclesiastes says every matter under heaven has its season, framing change as timed rather than contradictory.

row.basis: time to plant and uproot, be born and die
row.note: The commentary connects pasture's growth and decay with a thing's endpoint; Ecclesiastes sets planting beside uprooting and birth beside death, extending the cycle from vegetation to human life.
The commentary says every thing has an amount and term; the psalmist says his times are in God's hand, turning the measure of lifespan into personal trust.

row.basis: moon marks seasons; sun knows its setting
row.note: The commentary links measure to cycles that reach an end; the psalm assigns the moon to appointed seasons and the sun to its setting, showing timekeeping within creation.

row.basis: creatures wait for food in due season
row.note: The commentary leaves the object of measuring and guiding unstated so it can cover every being; the psalm says all creatures look to God for food in its season, giving that scope a concrete ecological form.

row.basis: God opens his hand and satisfies creatures
row.note: The commentary leaves the object of measuring and guiding unstated so it can cover every being; the psalm says God gives food, creatures gather it and are satisfied when he opens his hand, specifying how that provision arrives.
The commentary reads growth and withering as two ends of one measured course; the psalm says God takes away creatures' breath and they die and return to dust, making the endpoint explicit.
The commentary reads pasture's withering as one end of a measured course; the psalm says God sends breath and creatures are created and the earth renewed, joining an endpoint to renewed life.

The commentary presents the course of pasture and its end as part of one ordered work; the psalm closes its creation survey with God's rejoicing in his works, adding affirmation to their measured variety.
The commentary says measure reaches every created thing; the psalm says God counts the stars and calls each by name, combining number with individual address.

row.basis: rain prepares the earth and grass
row.note: The commentary connects measured rain with pasture's emergence; the psalm says God prepares rain and makes grass grow on the hills, directly joining ordered water to vegetation.
The commentary insists that guidance and measure are not limited to humans; the psalm says God gives food even to young ravens that cry, extending providence to vulnerable animals.

row.basis: starry host brought out by number and name
row.note: The commentary says God's measure covers everything; Isaiah says the Creator brings out the host by number and calls each one by name, making universal order both numerical and particular.

row.basis: sand set as the sea's boundary
row.note: The commentary defines measure as also setting a limit; Jeremiah says God set sand as a boundary the sea cannot cross, an image of a created force held within its assigned reach.
The commentary says the objectless verbs include all beings, not only people; Job asks who sends rain on land where no human lives, placing divine provision beyond human use.
The commentary links measured rain to pasture's growth; Job says rain makes the desolate ground sprout with grass, showing water, land and vegetation in a specific sequence.

row.basis: food for ravens and their young
row.note: The commentary extends God's guidance beyond humanity; Job asks who provides food for ravens when their young cry to God, making animal dependence part of the Creator's ordering.

The commentary says a created being receives a way suited to its nature; God asks Job whether the hawk flies south by Job's wisdom, presenting animal movement as beyond human control and within divine wisdom.

The commentary reads pasture's green growth and dark decay as stages in one measured course; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will continue, adding covenant assurance to natural cycles.
The commentary says rain descends by a measure that supports pasture; the psalm depicts God watering the land and preparing grain, joining measured provision to harvest.

row.basis: tree bearing fruit in its season
row.note: The commentary reads vegetation's growth and withering as a bounded course; the psalm's tree yields fruit in season and keeps its leaf, turning the seasonal image toward the life shaped by Torah.

row.basis: moon appointed for seasons and signs
row.note: The commentary connects the moon's measured phases with time and return; Sirach says the moon serves as a sign of times and seasons, presenting the calendar as part of creation's order.

row.basis: fixed courses and gates of the sun
row.note: The commentary says celestial bodies follow measured courses and mark time; Enoch describes the sun's assigned course through gates, expanding the same motif into an apocalyptic calendar.

row.basis: heavenly constellation makes each herb grow
row.note: The commentary says God's measure and guidance extend to pasture and every creature; Genesis Rabbah interprets creation by saying each herb has a heavenly constellation that prompts its growth, making divine ordering intimate at the level of a plant.

The commentary presents hidaya as a guide going ahead on the route; Exodus says the Lord went before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to lead them, giving the image a national journey.

row.basis: Israel travels when the cloud lifts
row.note: The commentary says guidance determines both direction and the course's timing; Numbers says Israel camped or set out according to the cloud's movement, making rest and travel part of the guidance.

row.basis: ark goes ahead to seek a resting place
row.note: The commentary describes a guide who leads toward a destination or home; Numbers says the ark traveled ahead for three days to find a resting place, pairing leading with the place sought.

row.basis: God goes ahead to find a camp
row.note: The commentary says the guide moves in front and identifies where the journey should end; Moses recalls God going ahead of Israel to search out a place to camp, by fire at night and cloud by day.

row.basis: God finds and guards Israel in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary develops the image of a guide responsible for a flock; Moses's song recalls God finding Israel in a desert waste, guarding and caring for him, giving the guidance motif a wilderness history.

row.basis: eagle stirs and carries its young
row.note: The commentary links leading with a creature moving ahead and carrying others along; the song compares God's care for Israel to an eagle hovering over its young and bearing them on its pinions.

The commentary says the guide brings the follower along rather than merely pointing from afar; Moses says YHWH alone led Israel and no foreign god was with him, specifying the source and exclusivity of that guidance.

row.basis: Abram goes to a land God will show
row.note: The commentary connects Abraham's confession that his Creator will guide him with a personal journey; Genesis has God tell Abram to go toward a land God will show, making trust in guidance an enacted departure.

row.basis: servant led by God to the bride
row.note: The commentary notes that h-d-y can mean leading a bride to her husband; Abraham's servant blesses God for leading him on the right path to Rebekah for Isaac, combining guidance and the bride's destination in one scene.

row.basis: YHWH named as the speaker's shepherd
row.note: The commentary's flock image presents the guide as caretaker; the psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, making the leader's relation to the follower personal.

row.basis: shepherd leads to pasture and water
row.note: The commentary's flock-and-pasture image presents the guide as caretaker; the psalm's shepherd makes the speaker lie in green pastures and leads him beside waters, joining direction to sustenance.
The commentary distinguishes showing a path from the traveler's following it; the psalm says the shepherd leads the speaker on right paths, supplying the route and the ethical quality of the way.

row.basis: staff and presence in a dark valley
row.note: The commentary connects a guide with a staff that reaches the ground before the walker and with shared travel; the psalm says the shepherd remains with the speaker through a dark valley, with rod and staff as comfort.

row.basis: light and truth lead to God's dwelling
row.note: The commentary says a guide shows both the path and the home it reaches; the psalm asks God's light and truth to lead the speaker to the holy mountain and dwelling, joining illumination to destination.

row.basis: Moses and Aaron lead Israel like a flock
row.note: The commentary places a flock's leader between God's sovereignty and pasture; the psalm retells the Exodus as God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, making human guides agents of divine guidance.

row.basis: lost travelers led to an inhabited city
row.note: The commentary says a guide reveals the way and the home at its end; the psalm describes wanderers in a desert waste whom God leads by a straight way to an inhabited city, closely joining route and arrival.

row.basis: word as lamp for feet and path
row.note: The commentary connects a distant light and a guide with a traveler's way; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and a light on the path, making instruction something that illuminates the next steps.

row.basis: voice says which way to walk
row.note: The commentary says guidance is more than pointing at a distant destination and includes a direction for the walk; Isaiah describes a voice behind the people telling them, “This is the way; walk in it,” when they turn aside.

row.basis: God leads the blind on unknown roads
row.note: The commentary says the objectless guidance applies broadly and can bring someone to a way not yet known; Isaiah says God will lead the blind by a way they do not know, turn darkness to light and rough places level.

row.basis: God teaches and leads in the way to go
row.note: The commentary joins the same Lord's act of measuring with his act of guidance; Isaiah calls God Israel's teacher and the one who leads it in the way it should go, an especially close prophetic formulation.

row.basis: shepherd leads to springs of water
row.note: The commentary joins a guide, pasture and provision; Isaiah's restored people are led by the one who has compassion on them and guided beside springs, giving the shepherd-like journey a restoration setting.

The commentary relates measured rain and pasture to the path of life; Isaiah says the Lord will guide continually and make the people like a watered garden, bringing guidance and sustained provision together.

row.basis: God leads Israel beside streams on a straight path
row.note: The commentary says guidance reveals both route and destination; Jeremiah depicts Israel returning with weeping and supplication as God leads them beside streams on a straight path, as a father leads Ephraim.

The commentary uses a flock's leading to connect care with pasture; Ezekiel says God will bring scattered sheep out from the peoples and gather them from the countries, giving the shepherd image a restoration scene.

row.basis: God feeds the flock in good pasture
row.note: The commentary names pasture as the concrete provision following guidance; Ezekiel says the flock will feed on rich pasture on Israel's mountains, pairing the shepherd's direction with nourishment.
The commentary treats a measured course as including where a creature settles; Ezekiel says God will feed his sheep and make them lie down, adding rest as part of the shepherd's care.

row.basis: lost, injured and weak sheep restored
row.note: The commentary's guide image includes leading and care for the flock; Ezekiel's shepherd seeks the lost, binds the injured and strengthens the weak, specifying what the divine shepherd does for those who cannot proceed unaided.
The commentary develops a form of walking while leaning on another; Hosea says God taught Ephraim to walk and took him up by the arms, making guidance bodily and accompanied.

The commentary says hidaya can be gentle guidance rather than forceful dragging; Hosea describes God drawing Israel with human cords and bands of love, giving that noncoercive relation a specific image.

row.basis: shepherd with staff among pasture lands
row.note: The commentary connects the guide's staff with a flock and its pasture; Micah asks God to shepherd his people with his staff in Bashan and Gilead, making the same image a prayer for restored care.

row.basis: shepherd calls sheep and leads them out
