row.note: The commentary says the guide goes ahead and knows the way of the flock; Jesus's shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, making personal recognition part of guidance.

The commentary distinguishes God's showing from the traveler's following; John says the shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow because they know his voice, directly separating leader's act from follower's response.

The commentary places the leader of a flock between the guide and pasture; Jesus says other sheep will be brought in so there will be one flock and one shepherd, extending the image to gathered people.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to living springs
row.note: The commentary joins shepherding, guidance and the arrival at provision; Revelation says the Lamb will shepherd the redeemed and guide them to springs of living water, carrying the pastoral image into final restoration.

row.basis: angel directs Philip to the Gaza road
row.note: The commentary says guidance can set a person on an actual route; an angel tells Philip to go south to the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, making divine direction concrete in a journey.

row.basis: Spirit directs Philip toward the chariot
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the guide's act from the traveler's response; the Spirit tells Philip to approach the chariot, and Philip runs to it, showing guidance received and acted upon.
The commentary says hidaya is wider than conversion and means guiding a way; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth, extending guidance to understanding and witness.

row.basis: Moses turns toward a flame in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses seeing a distant fire while seeking help on the road; Exodus says a flame in the bush catches Moses's attention, where the traveler encounters the God who will commission him.

row.basis: Moses sent to lead Israel out
row.note: The commentary says Moses moves from a traveler looking for guidance to a guide sent before Pharaoh; Exodus says God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out, making that change of role a liberation commission.

row.basis: Wisdom guides Israel on a marvelous way
row.note: The commentary presents Moses's account as creation followed by guidance and provision; Wisdom retells the Exodus by saying Wisdom guided the righteous on a marvelous way and sheltered them by day and night, interpreting the journey as Wisdom's work.

row.basis: Wisdom brings Israel through the sea
row.note: The commentary says a guide leads followers toward their destination; Wisdom's Exodus retelling says Wisdom brought Israel through the sea, adding the rescue at the route's decisive obstacle.

The commentary says qaddara can mean preparing an amount suited to its recipient; Proverbs asks for the food that is one's portion, making measured provision an ethical request for neither excess nor want.

row.basis: manna gathered by each person's need
row.note: The commentary says the measure of a thing prepares it for its use; Moses tells Israel to gather manna according to what each can eat and an omer per person, giving divine provision an explicit daily quantity.

row.basis: much gathered and little gathered both suffice
row.note: The commentary says measured provision is not humiliation but a fit amount; Exodus says the one who gathered much had no excess and the one who gathered little had no lack, showing the provision's measure by its result.

row.basis: life and death placed before Israel to choose
row.note: The commentary says the same shown path may be followed or avoided, without forced movement; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life, giving the human response an explicit covenant form.

row.basis: human choice between life and death
row.note: The commentary says guidance does not drag the traveler and that people may choose the path; Sirach says God made humans and left them to their own choice, then sets fire and water and life and death before them.

row.basis: all is foreseen, choice is granted
row.note: The commentary holds divine guidance together with the person's decision to follow or turn aside; Avot's maxim says all is foreseen yet freedom of choice is given, preserving both claims in a Jewish ethical formulation.

row.basis: fear of Heaven left to human response
row.note: The commentary says showing the road is God's act while taking it is the traveler's; the Talmud says everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven, marking the human response as the point not compelled.

The commentary says the shown way divides into people who heed instruction and those who avoid it; the Didache opens with the way of life and the way of death, then gives their different conduct, making the moral fork concrete.

The commentary warns that a person's own measuring can replace the path God shows; Proverbs says the heart plans its way but the Lord establishes a person's steps, distinguishing intention from the course taken.

The commentary calls it a misjudgment to measure God by human assumptions about revelation; Isaiah asks who directed the Spirit of the Lord or taught him the path of justice, refusing to make human judgment the standard.

row.basis: God apportions a measure of faith
row.note: The commentary warns that people should not replace God's measure with their own; Paul tells each person to think soberly according to the measure of faith God apportioned, applying measure to humility and communal life.

row.basis: grace given according to Christ's measure
row.note: The commentary says measure fits each thing for its purpose; Paul says grace was given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, making differentiated vocation a Christian application of measured provision.

row.basis: created for works prepared to walk in
row.note: The commentary links creation to the way that follows immediately after it; Ephesians says believers are created for good works God prepared beforehand for them to walk in, closely joining making and a prepared path.

The commentary says the objectless measure and guidance encompass every creature; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor reap yet are fed by the heavenly Father, making nonhuman provision a sign of God's care.

The commentary links the measured life of pasture to its growth and decay; Jesus asks disciples to consider how the field's grass grows and is clothed by God, making vegetation an example of provision beyond human effort.

row.basis: sparrows fall under the Father's care
row.note: The commentary says God's measure extends to every being; Jesus says not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father, making even a small creature's fate part of that scope.
The commentary says measure includes particulars rather than only broad cosmic totals; Jesus says the disciples' hairs are all numbered, turning divine measure into individual knowledge.
The commentary connects measured rain to pasture and sustenance; Paul says God gives rain and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness, joining cosmic provision to human experience.

row.basis: God as shepherd of Israel's flock
row.note: The commentary places the shepherd and flock between guidance and pasture; the psalm calls God Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph like a flock, making national deliverance a pastoral relation.

row.basis: rain as a key held by God
row.note: The commentary says rain descends in a measured amount and sustains pasture; the Talmud treats rain as a divine key, placing this ecological process among God's reserved acts and communal petitions.

row.basis: Pharaoh asks who the Lord is
row.note: The commentary highlights Qur'anic Moses answering Pharaoh's “Who is your Lord?” with the Lord who gives each thing its form and guidance; Exodus has Pharaoh ask who YHWH is and refuse obedience, so the Qur'anic scene answers a biblical challenge with a positive account of creation and guidance.

The commentary says a sacrificial animal is led until it reaches its appointed sanctuary; Deuteronomy tells Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and go there, supplying the Torah's destination for pilgrimage.

row.basis: offerings brought to the chosen place
row.note: The commentary describes an animal whose journey ends at a sacred destination; Deuteronomy lists offerings Israel is to bring there, giving a specific ritual setting for destination-bound worship.

row.basis: God leads Israel through the wilderness for forty years
row.note: The commentary says a measured path includes its duration and what the traveler learns along it; Moses recalls God leading Israel through the wilderness for forty years to humble and test them, making the journey's time purposeful.

The commentary distinguishes God's act of guidance from the person's choice to follow or avoid the way; the Community Rule describes two spirits and their lots shaping opposing ways, making the tension between divine ordering and human conduct explicit in a sectarian frame.

row.basis: human cannot direct his own steps
row.note: The commentary says a person cannot substitute private judgment for God's guidance; Jeremiah says a person's way is not in his own power and he cannot direct his steps, giving that limit a prayerful formulation.

row.basis: life as the Lord assigned and called
row.note: The commentary says every being receives a measure and a way suited to it; Paul tells each person to live in the condition the Lord assigned and God called him to, applying that principle to vocation.

row.basis: star leads the travelers to the child
row.note: The commentary says a celestial light may guide a traveler but is not itself the ultimate guide; Matthew's star goes before the Magi and stops over the child's place, treating the star as a sign that serves a destination.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 45
row.note: The commentary reads the guide as one who goes ahead and whose followers choose to follow; Augustine's exposition of John 10 interprets the shepherd's voice and sheep as Christ's authority recognized by the faithful, turning pastoral leading into ecclesial interpretation.
The commentary says every thing has a measure and term; Moses asks God to teach people to number their days so they may gain a wise heart, turning the allotted lifespan into a discipline of judgment.

The commentary says a creature's endpoint and lifespan belong to its measure; the psalm says the speaker's days were written before one of them existed, giving that claim a personal image of foreknown duration.
The commentary says qaddara includes the amount and timing assigned to each thing; Genesis gives the sun and moon their signs, seasons, days and years, making timekeeping part of creation's order.

The commentary says its objectless measure and guidance extend to every being; Genesis has the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds, showing the varied forms within that universal scope.

The commentary says qaddara determines how far each thing reaches; in WLC's wording, Moses says the Most High apportioned nations and fixed their boundaries according to the number of Israel's children, extending measured allotment to peoples.
The commentary connects measured celestial paths with time and travel; the psalm compares the sun to a runner that rejoices to complete its course, giving the solar route a vivid motion.

row.basis: sun's circuit reaches the ends of heaven
row.note: The commentary says a measured thing has a course with an endpoint; the psalm says the sun rises at one end of heaven and its circuit reaches the other, adding the full extent of its route.

The commentary says measure establishes the reach and limit of created things; Habakkuk portrays God standing and measuring the earth before nations tremble, making measurement an act of sovereign judgment over the land.

The commentary says a thing's measure includes its term and timing; Daniel blesses God as the one who changes times and seasons and raises or removes kings, extending providential ordering to political history.

row.basis: God declares the end from the beginning
row.note: The commentary defines a thing's measure by its reach, essence and end; Isaiah says God declares the end from the beginning and accomplishes his purpose, making the endpoint part of divine intention.

row.basis: each thing made for its purpose and day
row.note: The commentary says measure gives each thing where it will arrive and end; Proverbs says the Lord made everything for its purpose, including the wicked for a day of trouble, specifying purpose and endpoint.

row.basis: just scales belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary says human weighing must follow the measure God gives; Proverbs says honest scales and weights are the Lord's work, grounding fair human measurement in divine order.

row.basis: no injustice in measures and weights
row.note: The commentary connects divine measure to the human use of a scale; Leviticus forbids injustice in length, weight or capacity, turning measure into a concrete command for commerce.
The commentary says people may measure but must honor a measure they did not invent; Leviticus requires honest balances, weights, ephah and hin, giving that limit a practical legal form.
The commentary says the guide both shows a route and leads toward its destination; Proverbs tells the hearer to acknowledge God in all ways so that God will make the paths straight.

row.basis: God weighs the spirit behind human ways
row.note: The commentary says a person's self-measure may be mistaken; Proverbs says people may see their own ways as pure while the Lord weighs their spirits, placing judgment of inward motives with God.

row.basis: nations learn God's ways and walk in them
row.note: The commentary describes a guide who shows a way that followers then take; Isaiah pictures nations going to God's mountain to be taught his ways and walk in his paths, joining instruction to following.

row.basis: God teaches the way with his eye upon the learner
row.note: The commentary says a guide accompanies and identifies the route, not merely pointing from afar; the psalm promises instruction in the way to go and counsel with God's eye upon the person.

The commentary distinguishes the guide's action from the walker's progress; the psalm says a person's steps are established by the Lord and that the Lord upholds him when he falls, joining direction to support.

row.basis: steps made firm by God's word
row.note: The commentary says the path shown by God must be followed by the traveler; the psalm asks God to make the speaker's steps firm by his word and not let iniquity rule him, making guidance practical and ethical.
The commentary says the same road is taken by some and avoided by others; Proverbs compares the righteous path to dawn growing brighter, depicting one response as progress toward full light.

row.basis: wicked path is darkness and stumbling
row.note: The commentary says another person turns aside from the shown way; Proverbs describes the wicked person's path as darkness in which he cannot see what makes him stumble, giving the rejected way its own consequence.

row.basis: snow and frost given by God
row.note: The commentary presents weather and vegetation as parts of a measured natural course; the psalm says God gives snow like wool and scatters frost like ashes, adding cold season to the ordering of rain and grass.

row.basis: God's word melts ice and releases water
row.note: The commentary reads growth and decay as stages in one course; the psalm says God sends his word, melts the ice and makes waters flow, showing the natural transition from cold to movement.

row.basis: the farmer places different seeds in order
row.note: The commentary says qaddara can mean preparing something to fit its use; Isaiah's farmer sows different grains in their proper places, showing practical measure in cultivation.

row.basis: God teaches the farmer his craft
row.note: The commentary says preparation and measure are first God's work and then human work under a given measure; Isaiah says God instructs the farmer in the right way to proceed, presenting ordinary skill as taught by God.

row.basis: Rebekah follows the servant toward Isaac
row.note: The commentary notes the concrete sense of escorting a bride to her husband; Genesis says Rebekah and her attendants follow Abraham's servant on the journey, making the bride's movement toward her marriage an enacted image of being led.

row.basis: Isaac receives Rebekah as his wife
row.note: The commentary says the bride's guidance has a destination in the husband's home; Genesis ends the journey with Isaac taking Rebekah as his wife, naming the arrival that completes the escort.

row.basis: ark leads on a way Israel has not traveled
row.note: The commentary says a guide goes ahead and makes an unknown route knowable; Joshua tells Israel to follow the ark at a distance so they will know the way, because they have not passed that way before.

row.basis: light guides feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary connects light, a traveler's feet and the path to a destination; Zechariah says the dawn from on high will shine on those in darkness and guide their feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: Abraham departs without knowing the destination
row.note: The commentary presents Abraham's trust that God will guide him on the road ahead; Hebrews says Abraham obeyed the call and went out without knowing where he was going, making that trust a journey into an unknown future.

row.basis: a messenger sent ahead to prepare the way
row.note: The commentary says a guide is named for going in front of the traveler; Mark introduces the messenger sent ahead to prepare the Lord's way, giving that image a prophetic and communal role.

row.basis: voice prepares a straight road in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary links the way shown with the route the traveler must take; Mark's wilderness voice calls for the Lord's road to be prepared and made straight, turning guidance into communal preparation.

row.basis: Wisdom will guide and guard the speaker
row.note: The commentary says God's guidance can become a personal, continuing relationship; Solomon asks for Wisdom to accompany him, guide his actions and guard him, turning universal guidance into a prayer for daily direction.

row.basis: the king weighed and found wanting
row.note: The commentary depicts a man measuring revelation by his own judgment and reaching a false verdict; Daniel interprets the writing against Belshazzar as God having weighed him and found him wanting, reversing who sets the measure.

row.basis: do not require bit and bridle
row.note: The commentary says hidaya is gentle leading rather than forced dragging; the psalm warns the hearer not to be like a horse or mule that must be restrained with bit and bridle, making the contrast with coerced movement explicit.

row.basis: seasons judged for produce and water
row.note: The commentary says rain, pasture and time are measured parts of one natural course; the Mishnah assigns judgments for produce, tree fruit and water to their appointed festivals, giving seasonal provision a Jewish calendar and liturgical frame.

row.basis: birth, life and death beyond one's control
row.note: The commentary says each thing has an allotted term and endpoint; Avot says a person is born, lives and dies against his will and will give account, turning the measure of lifespan into a rabbinic reflection on agency.

row.basis: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
row.note: The commentary says guidance joins a route to the home it reaches; Jesus says he is the way and that no one comes to the Father except through him, making the destination personal in John's account.

row.basis: those led by God's Spirit are God's children
row.note: The commentary says guidance is God's act while taking the way identifies the follower; Paul calls those led by God's Spirit children of God, making the response a mark of belonging.

row.basis: wind weight and waters by measure
row.note: The commentary defines qaddara as making quantity manifest and extends it to rain and the created order; Job says God gives the wind a weight and apportions the waters by measure, matching both material elements.

row.basis: all things by measure, number, and weight
row.note: The commentary makes the verbs objectless so that measure reaches every created thing; Wisdom describes the Creator's ordering of all things by measure, number, and weight, an unusually exact cosmological counterpart.

row.basis: decree for rain and path for lightning
row.note: The page says rain descends in a specified measure and that divine measure governs a creature's course; Job joins God's decree for rain to a path for the thunderbolt in its account of creation's ordering.
The commentary insists that qadar includes a thing's term and endpoint; Job speaks of a human whose days and months are numbered by God and whose boundary cannot be passed.

The commentary applies measure to a creature's allotted duration; Sirach gives human beings a fixed number of days while granting them earthly authority, a close formulation of duration within creaturely limits.

The commentary universalizes divine measuring as a limit and destination for every being; Paul's Areopagus speech says God determined nations' allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling places.

row.basis: luminaries for seasons, days, and years
row.note: The commentary treats sun and moon as measured bodies whose courses disclose time; Genesis assigns the lights signs, appointed seasons, days, and years in the ordered creation account.

row.basis: moon for seasons and sun's setting
row.note: The commentary reads the moon's stations and return as a measured life-cycle; this psalm gives the moon its role in marking seasons and says the sun knows its setting.

row.basis: heavenly host brought out by number
row.note: The commentary uses calculated stars to display a measured cosmos; Isaiah portrays God bringing out the heavenly host by number and calling each one by name, with none missing.
The commentary joins the pasture's emergence to its eventual blackening and decay; Isaiah's grass withers and flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it.

row.basis: all flesh as grass that withers
row.note: The page makes vegetation's end a figure for creaturely limits; 1 Peter takes up the grass-and-fading-flower image for mortal flesh, extending the same movement from growth to transience.

row.basis: migrating birds know their appointed times
row.note: The commentary contrasts the bee's divinely fitted path with people who refuse shown guidance; Jeremiah's stork, dove, swift, and crane keep their appointed migrations while the people do not know the LORD's ordinance.

row.basis: continual guidance and provision in dry places
row.note: The commentary binds guidance to measured provision rather than humiliation; Isaiah promises that the LORD will guide continually, satisfy need in parched places, and make the recipient like a watered garden.

row.basis: God teaches benefit and leads the proper way
row.note: The commentary says guidance is the Creator's purposive leading, not mere direction at a distance; Isaiah names the LORD as the one who teaches for benefit and leads people in the way they should go.

The commentary places divine guidance beside the pasture that follows in 87:4 and develops a flock image; the psalm's shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them beside waters of rest.
The commentary distinguishes being shown the way from the traveler's following it; Psalm 23 has the shepherd restore the life of the sheep and guide it in right paths for his name's sake.

The commentary's guide goes before a flock toward grazing; Ezekiel's divine shepherd brings the scattered sheep into their land and feeds them on Israel's mountains, watercourses, and inhabited places.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
row.note: The commentary explains hidayet through the guide's physical precedence over the herd; Jesus' shepherd leads his own sheep out, goes ahead of them, and they follow because they know his voice.

row.basis: shepherd guiding to springs of water
row.note: The commentary moves from a leading shepherd to the pasture's nourishment; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherding and guiding the faithful to springs of the water of life.

row.basis: pillar of fire going before Israel
row.note: The commentary's guide is an ahead-going presence and Musa finds guidance at fire; Exodus says the LORD goes before Israel in cloud by day and fire by night in order to lead them on the way.
The commentary lingers over staff, flock, wilderness journey, and the fire-scene of Moses; Exodus introduces him while leading Jethro's flock beyond the wilderness to Horeb.

row.basis: fire in the bush at Moses' call
row.note: The commentary has the lost traveler see a distant fire and receive a different, divine guidance there; Exodus likewise makes flame in a bush the immediate setting of Moses' divine encounter.
Musa says at the sea that his Lord is with him and will guide him; at the bush God answers Moses' reluctance with the promise, in its commissioning context, that God will be with him.

The commentary pairs Musa's expectation of imminent guidance with the command to strike the sea using his staff; Exodus directs Moses to lift his staff so the sea will divide and Israel can pass through.
The commentary recounts Musa's fearful departure from the city and journey toward Midian while asking for the straight way; Exodus has Pharaoh seek his life and Moses flee to dwell in Midian.

row.basis: Pharaoh's question becomes refusal to obey
row.note: The commentary makes Pharaoh's question about the Lord elicit Musa's account of the creator who gives form and guidance; Exodus frames Pharaoh's question as a refusal to know the LORD, obey his voice, or release Israel.

row.basis: Wisdom leads through the Red Sea
row.note: The commentary reads the divided sea as the answer to Musa's trust that God will guide; Wisdom of Solomon retells the crossing as Wisdom leading the people through deep water, a Jewish interpretive recasting of the route.

row.basis: Red Sea crossing interpreted as faith
row.note: The commentary stresses a divinely opened way at the sea; Hebrews says the people passed through the Red Sea by faith while the Egyptians were overwhelmed, adding a Christian account of the travelers' response.
The commentary sets Ibrahim's claim that the Creator guides him beside a journey whose destination lies ahead; Genesis calls Abram to leave his country for a land that God will show him.

The commentary turns Abraham's creation-and-guidance confession into an ongoing personal journey; Hebrews interprets his departure as obedient travel toward an inheritance, even though he did not know where he was going.

row.basis: Moses asks to know God's ways
row.note: The commentary ends in the worshiper's request to be guided on a straight path and ties it to Musa; Moses asks God to make God's ways known so that he may know God and find favor.

row.basis: formed body and divinely given life
row.note: The commentary reads qaddara alongside creation and the fitted human body; Genesis forms the human from ground and gives life by divine breath, a foundational formation scene beside that claim.

row.basis: formed in the womb and appointed
row.note: The commentary develops measurement as a body's formation and a life's destined direction; Jeremiah is known, consecrated, and appointed before God forms him in the womb.

row.basis: body formed from seed over ten months
row.note: The commentary fills the unspoken object with the human made from a drop and held for an appointed term; Wisdom of Solomon describes its speaker as molded in the womb from human seed over a stated period.

The commentary separates a creature's given measure from the traveler's responsibility to follow guidance; this rabbinic passage assigns strength, wealth, and similar traits before birth but explicitly does not decree righteousness or wickedness.

row.basis: measured manna leaves neither surplus nor lack
row.note: The commentary says restricted provision is a fitting measure rather than disgrace; at the manna gathering, whoever gathered much had no surplus and whoever gathered little had no lack.
The commentary rejects reading constrained provision as divine contempt and calls it a measure; the prayer in Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches but for the food apportioned to the speaker.

row.basis: gift accepted according to what one has
row.note: The commentary cites the command to spend from what God has given and not be loaded beyond it; Paul makes a contribution acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what is absent.

The commentary contrasts human calculation with the God-given balance by which it should be judged; Leviticus commands just balances, weights, ephah, and hin under the authority of the liberating LORD.

The commentary says people may think and measure but wrongly replace the shown way with their own; Proverbs permits a person to plan a path while assigning the establishment of actual steps to the LORD.

row.basis: a walker's steps are not self-directed
row.note: The commentary makes human calculation answerable to the guidance that belongs to God; Jeremiah confesses that a person's way is not self-owned and that a walker cannot direct his own steps.

row.basis: voice saying this is the way
row.note: The commentary defines guidance as concretely showing a road while leaving the traveler to take it; Isaiah imagines a voice behind the people saying, This is the way, walk in it.

The commentary says the same shown way divides those who accept the reminder from those who pass by it; Jeremiah calls for the ancient good path and records the people's answer, We will not walk in it.

row.basis: life and death set before human choice
row.note: The commentary pairs complete divine guidance with the traveler's non-coerced choice; Deuteronomy places life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and commands them to choose life.
The commentary insists that hidayet is not forced dragging; Sirach says God created human beings and left them in the power of their own free choice.

row.basis: life or death given according to choice
row.note: The commentary's two ways issue in divergent outcomes while remaining a choice; Sirach puts life and death before each person and says whichever is chosen will be given.
The commentary holds divine measure and guidance together with real human following or refusal; Avot's compact maxim says that everything is foreseen while freedom of choice is granted.

row.basis: all in Heaven's hands except fear
row.note: The commentary assigns guidance to the Lord but response to the traveler who fears or turns away; the Talmud's maxim reserves fear of Heaven as the stated exception to what lies in Heaven's hands.

row.basis: the two ways of life and death
row.note: The commentary explicitly frames the shown road as two possible courses whose outcome depends on walking them; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.
The commentary says one person follows the shown way while another moves aside from it; Jesus' warning identifies a broad gate and way whose many travelers reach destruction.
The commentary's alternative to passing by guidance is a way actually taken toward a good end; Jesus names the narrow gate and constricted way that leads to life and is found by few.

row.basis: divine gathering refused by its hearers
row.note: The commentary rejects an account of guidance as coercion and describes people who decline its reminder; Jesus says he wished to gather Jerusalem's children but they were unwilling.
The commentary defines hidayet as gentle leading and links it to nourishment rather than force; Hosea pictures God drawing Israel with human cords and bands of love, then bending down to feed them.
The commentary's guide is both a flock's leader and a companion attentive to weakness; Isaiah's shepherd gathers lambs, carries them close, and gently leads those with young.

row.basis: star going before travelers to a destination
row.note: The commentary says measured heavenly bodies guide land and sea travelers, though they themselves set; Matthew's star goes before the Magi and stops over the place they are seeking.

row.basis: light guiding feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary develops guidance through fire, light, and a travelled way; Zechariah's song says the dawn from on high gives light in darkness and guides feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: need for a guide to understand the way
row.note: The commentary calls a guide one who makes a road and destination known and then shows the guided person becoming a leader; the Ethiopian asks Philip how he can understand Scripture unless someone guides him.

row.basis: courses, dominions, and seasons of luminaries
row.note: The commentary works through the measured movements of sun, moon, and stars; the opening of the Astronomical Book introduces the luminaries by their courses, dominions, seasons, names, and origins.

row.basis: moon marking festivals and completing its course
row.note: The commentary's moon reaches measured stations and wanes at its limit; Sirach makes the moon a sign for festal times and describes its light waning when its course is complete.

row.basis: each blade of grass commanded to grow
row.note: The commentary moves from God measuring and guiding all things to the pasture's emergence; this midrash imagines every blade of grass as receiving a heavenly directive to grow, a Jewish reading of creaturely guidance.

row.basis: angel sent ahead for the bride journey
row.note: The commentary explains hidayet through an ahead-going guide and through bringing a bride to her husband; Abraham says God will send an angel before his servant so a wife can be brought for Isaac.

row.basis: sacrifice taken to a divinely shown place
row.note: The commentary's sacrificial animal is defined by reaching its appointed sacred destination; Genesis sends Abraham with an offering to a mountain God will show, a related destination-bound sacrifice without equating the rites.

row.basis: rain, childbirth, and resurrection as divine keys
row.note: The commentary joins measured rain, formation in the womb, and the end that reaches resurrection; this Talmudic triad treats rain, childbirth, and revival of the dead as keys retained by God.

row.basis: testing bounded by ability and an escape way
row.note: The commentary says divine measure bounds a person's burden and opens a way after hardship; Paul says testing will not exceed ability and that God provides the way out so it can be endured.

row.basis: traveler's prayer for steps directed in peace
row.note: The commentary turns the general report that God guides into the worshiper's own request for a path; the Talmud's travel prayer asks God to lead the traveler and direct the steps in peace.

The commentary reads Adam's descent as followed by a promised guidance that can be followed without error or misery; Genesis ends its expulsion scene by guarding the way to the tree of life with cherubim and a flaming sword.

row.basis: prenatal Torah followed by forgetting at birth
row.note: The commentary joins womb-formation to the surah's promise that the Prophet will be made to recite and not forget; this Talmudic birth tradition has the embryo taught Torah and then made to forget it at birth.

row.basis: Spirit teaches and brings words to remembrance
row.note: The commentary makes non-forgetting the sequel to the creator's guidance and ties it to revelation; John says the Paraclete will teach the disciples all things and bring Jesus' words to their remembrance.

The commentary connects measured provision and guided travel with the promise of ease after hardship; Jesus characterizes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, a focused Christian counterpart to that eased way.

The commentary reads the difference between guidance and following as a protection against coercion; Irenaeus uses Christ's lament over unwilling Jerusalem to argue that God made human beings free to obey or refuse.

The commentary makes David's well-measured armor a divinely taught craft whose parts must fit; in the biblical David-and-armor scene, David removes Saul's untested gear because he cannot walk in it, giving a pointedly different emphasis.

row.basis: forty years before the flame at Sinai
row.note: The commentary calls Musa's arrival after years in Midian a coming at an appointed measure and places the call at fire; Stephen's speech similarly puts the flame in the Sinai wilderness after forty years, supplying a Christian chronological framing.

row.basis: waters measured, heavens spanned, mountains weighed
row.note: The commentary describes qaddara as fixing quantity and fitting the whole creation; Isaiah asks who has measured the waters, marked off the heavens, and weighed mountains, a concrete creator-and-measure formulation.
The commentary makes the calculated heavens part of the measure placed in creation; God's interrogation asks whether Job knows the ordinances of heaven or can establish their rule on earth.

row.basis: declaring the end from the beginning
row.note: The commentary defines divine measure by a thing's arrival, essence, and end; Isaiah's God declares the end from the beginning and says the divine purpose will stand.

row.basis: rain given in its appointed season
row.note: The commentary treats rain as descending by measure so that life can emerge; Deuteronomy makes the early and latter rains gifts given to Israel's land in their proper season.
The commentary's sequence moves from the God who measures and guides to the pasture brought forth for grazing; Deuteronomy has God give grass in the fields for livestock and food for the people.

row.basis: rain watering earth and making it sprout
row.note: The commentary connects measured rain to vegetation's renewal; Isaiah's rain-and-snow image waters the earth and makes it bring forth and sprout, giving seed and bread.

row.basis: rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness
row.note: The commentary reads provision and pasture as the result of a measured created order; Paul names rains from heaven and fruitful seasons as God's witness, filling human hearts with food and gladness.

row.basis: body clothed with flesh and knit with bones
row.note: The commentary gives qaddara the concrete sense of an ordered body gathered in the womb; Job addresses God as the one who clothes him with skin and flesh and knits him with bones and sinews.

row.basis: formed in the womb for a restoring mission
row.note: The commentary joins bodily formation to an assigned direction; Isaiah's servant is formed from the womb in order to bring Jacob back and gather Israel.

row.basis: just balance and weights as the LORD's work
row.note: The commentary says the human-held scale was itself placed by God; Proverbs calls a just balance and scales the LORD's and makes all the weights in the bag God's work.

row.basis: the servant led in the right way to the bride
row.note: The commentary's hidayet imagery includes showing the way to a house and bringing a bride to her husband; Abraham's servant blesses God for leading him in the right way to obtain Rebekah for Isaac.

row.basis: redeemed people led to a holy habitation
row.note: The commentary makes guidance an arrival at the place for which a thing is prepared; the Song of the Sea says God led the redeemed people in steadfast love and guided them to the holy abode.

row.basis: divine presence going with Moses and giving rest
row.note: The commentary stresses that the guide may be beside the traveler, as in Musa's confidence that his Lord is with him; God promises Moses that the divine presence will go with him and give rest.

row.basis: forty-year wilderness way led by God
row.note: The commentary reads Musa's years in Midian and later arrival as a measured journey; Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember the whole wilderness way by which God led them for forty years, testing their response.

row.basis: teaching wisdom's way and straight paths
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a guide's act of showing a road from the traveler's act of walking it; Wisdom says it has taught the way of wisdom and led its pupil in straight paths.

row.basis: blind led on unknown paths into light
row.note: The commentary's guidance is more than a distant sign: it makes a way, levels it, and is associated with light; Isaiah promises to lead the blind by unknown paths, turn darkness to light, and level rough places.

row.basis: highway where travelers do not go astray
row.note: The commentary says one who follows God's guidance does not lose the way; Isaiah's holy highway is described as a way on which travelers, even fools, will not go astray.

row.basis: straight path by streams without stumbling
row.note: The commentary joins guidance, water, and a destination to the image of a gentle leading presence; Jeremiah has God lead the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble.

row.basis: a person is led along the chosen way
row.note: The commentary says God shows the two ways but the traveler takes or declines one; the Talmud formulates the same relation as the principle that a person is led on the path the person wishes to go.

row.basis: opening for defilement and help toward purity
row.note: The commentary gives a guide's act and the traveler's response distinct roles; this rabbinic maxim says one who comes to defile is given an opening, while one who comes to purify is assisted.

row.basis: following the light rather than walking in darkness
row.note: The commentary unfolds hidayet through fire, light, and the way a traveler actually follows; Jesus identifies himself as the world's light and promises that the follower will not walk in darkness.

The commentary connects the Creator's guidance with revealed instruction and the Prophet's recitation; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth and disclose what is to come.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to shepherd and overseer
row.note: The commentary sets the person who takes the path against the one who turns aside and repeatedly uses flock imagery; 1 Peter calls its hearers sheep who were straying but have returned to their shepherd and overseer.
The commentary treats measure as a creature's set endpoint rather than only spatial quantity; Hebrews says human beings are appointed to die once and then face judgment.

row.basis: life and action conditioned by the Lord's will
row.note: The commentary contrasts God's measure with the human who thinks and calculates a course independently; James corrects plans for living and acting tomorrow with the formula, If the Lord wills.

row.basis: set apart from the womb and called by grace
row.note: The commentary makes pre-birth formation part of a life placed on a path; Paul describes his own calling as God's setting him apart from his mother's womb and then calling him through grace.

row.basis: grass clothed today and cast into oven tomorrow
row.note: The commentary reads pasture's present flourishing and imminent decay alongside God's provision; Jesus uses grass clothed by God today and thrown into the oven tomorrow to argue for divine care.

row.basis: blind guides who fall into a pit
row.note: The commentary says a would-be guide who still needs guidance cannot rightly lead another; Jesus' warning makes a blind person leading another blind person end with both falling into a pit.

row.basis: works prepared beforehand as a path to walk
row.note: The commentary presents divine preparation as preceding the direction in which a creature moves; Ephesians calls believers God's workmanship, created for good works prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them.

The commentary gives hidayet its travel sense and says a guide can direct a mission's route; Acts narrates Paul and companions being prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking in Asia, a concrete redirection on the road.

row.basis: command not to forget what has been seen
row.note: The commentary links Musa's creator-and-guide answer with the surah's following promise of unforgotten recitation; Deuteronomy commands Israel to guard itself, not forget what its eyes have seen, and teach it to descendants.

row.basis: weighed in balances and found wanting
row.note: The commentary contrasts human measuring with the God-given balance that judges it; Daniel's judgment scene weighs Belshazzar in the balances and finds him wanting.

row.basis: Moses completes a written Torah book
row.note: The commentary invokes earlier pages belonging to both Abraham and Moses; Deuteronomy's own closing scene gives a canonical account of Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, a different scriptural framing of Mosaic writing.
The commentary assigns the pasture’s drying to the same Lord who brought it out; Isaiah says the LORD’s breath dries grass and wilts its flower, making the agency explicit.
After grass and flower wither, Isaiah says God’s word stands forever; this sharpens the commentary’s sequence from vanishing pasture to the recitation promised not to be forgotten in 87:6.
The commentary hears guthā as debris carried off and later as what is discarded; Psalm 1 calls the wicked chaff that wind drives away, making the residue an image of judgment.

row.basis: grass grows then dries in a day
row.note: The commentary compresses pasture’s emergence and drying into one turn; this verse pictures morning growth and evening fading and drying, giving that short life a human-scale temporal image.
The commentary connects withered pasture to people who deny resurrection and become debris; this verse compares human days to grass and its flower, extending the plant’s transience to human life.
The commentary describes guthā as carried away and no longer counted; here wind passes over the flower, it is gone, and its place no longer knows it, closely specifying disappearance.

row.basis: green tree dried, dry tree made green
row.note: The commentary says the same divine hand brings out pasture and turns it to withered debris; Ezekiel says the LORD can dry a green tree and make a dry tree flourish, explicitly reversing both directions.

row.basis: a plant appointed to grow over Jonah
row.note: The commentary treats vegetation’s course as one of the Lord’s successive acts; in Jonah the LORD appoints a plant and makes it grow over Jonah, setting up a divinely governed plant life-cycle.
The commentary’s pasture is changed by its original giver; Jonah’s plant is struck by a divinely appointed worm and withers, so the same narrative names the giver’s action in a plant’s loss.
The commentary hears drying as the next act after growth; Jonah adds scorching east wind and the sun, and the plant’s death makes the change bodily and immediate for Jonah.

The commentary develops guthā as floating plant debris, pot foam, and something that disappears without being counted; Hosea places chaff blown from a threshing floor beside morning dew and smoke that vanishes.
The commentary links debris to the rejected side of choosing and sorting; Proverbs pictures a king winnowing the wicked and passing the wheel over them, making separation an enacted judgment.

row.basis: chaff swept away with no trace
row.note: The commentary says the debris is carried off and leaves nothing anyone counts; Daniel’s image has chaff swept away by wind until no place is found for it, adding total erasure.
The commentary joins floating debris, foam, dispersal, and forgottenness; Wisdom compares the ungodly’s hope to storm-driven froth and smoke, then to a guest’s unremembered stay.
The commentary’s guthā can be the rejected residue in a sorting scene; John’s image has a winnower gather wheat into the barn and burn the chaff, making the distinction eschatological.
The commentary reads the dark debris as pasture’s transient end; Peter quotes Isaiah’s grass and flower as the image of mortal glory, applying plant withering to human life.

Peter follows the withering grass quotation with the Lord’s enduring word; this closely meets the commentary’s juxtaposition of carried-off vegetation and the recitation that will not be forgotten in 87:6.
The commentary describes pasture changing into dry debris; James says a hot wind withers grass and its flower falls, using the plant’s sudden collapse to portray the rich person’s fading glory.

The commentary holds drying and pasture’s prior green life in one plant; Jesus uses a grain that falls into earth and dies before bearing much fruit, giving plant death a generative reading alongside the withering one.

row.basis: sown seed must die to live
row.note: The commentary connects plant emergence and decay with human return from earth; Paul answers a question about resurrection by saying what is sown must die before it comes to life, making the plant cycle an analogy for bodily resurrection.

The commentary develops dried vegetation as loose, useless matter carried away; Jesus pictures a branch that does not remain in the vine drying, being gathered, and burned, adding a relational and judgment reading.

row.basis: tree by water with unwithered leaf
row.note: The commentary imagines water held in hollows while surface debris goes; Psalm 1 contrasts wind-blown chaff with a tree planted beside water whose leaf does not wither, making rooted retention the other side of the image.

The commentary connects plant drying and renewal with the claim that humans too can be brought out of earth; Job says a tree may bud again at the scent of water, supplying a concrete plant-renewal image.

row.basis: human does not rise like a tree
row.note: The commentary uses the plant’s emergence from earth as a sign for human resurrection; Job’s lament says a human lies down and does not rise, preserving the contrary distinction between plant renewal and human fate.

The commentary holds darkened pasture’s former green within its final color and contrasts debris with retained water; Jeremiah’s tree by water keeps a green leaf despite heat, offering the enduring green counterpart.

row.basis: earth brings forth vegetation by command
row.note: The commentary treats pasture’s emergence as the Lord’s act before its transformation; Genesis begins plant life with God’s command that earth bring forth seed-bearing vegetation, locating growth within divine creation.
The commentary insists that mer'ā is pasture because animals eat it; Moses promises grass in the fields for livestock, making the pasture’s use and its giver explicit.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for people
row.note: The commentary identifies the emerging pasture as provision for grazing animals; the psalm says God causes grass to grow for cattle and plants for human use, linking vegetation to divine sustenance.
The commentary’s guthā is uprooted and swept along by water; the psalm says God sweeps people away like a flood before comparing life to grass, joining water’s force to transience.
The commentary contrasts debris carried on the surface with water caught and retained; Isaiah promises water on thirsty land and streams on dry ground, framing water as the source of restored growth.
The commentary remembers green pasture beneath the darkened debris; Isaiah pictures descendants sprouting among grass like willows by streams, giving the green stage a renewal and abundance reading.

The commentary sets what a flood carries away against hollows that hold its water; the psalm says God turns wilderness into pools and dry land into springs, a direct reversal from barren to water-filled.

The commentary describes pasture as food-bearing growth before its decline; after dry country becomes springs, this psalm has people sow fields and plant vineyards that yield fruit, showing renewal leading to provision.

The commentary contrasts floating residue with what remains held and green; Ezekiel’s river nourishes trees whose leaves do not wither and whose fruit continues, an image of lasting life sustained by water.

row.basis: God makes grass sprout in wasteland
row.note: The commentary treats emergence from dry earth as divine work; God asks whether he brings rain to desolate land and makes grass sprout there, extending agency to uncultivated ground.

The commentary says ahwā’s dark hue need not be ugly and recalls its use for beauty; the speaker calls herself dark yet lovely, giving a concrete literary instance where dark coloration and beauty coexist.

row.basis: straw distinguished from grain and true word
row.note: The commentary places worthless residue beside the enduring recited word; Jeremiah contrasts straw with grain while discussing what a prophet should do with God’s word, joining refuse-sorting to faithful speech.

The commentary links a plant’s withering to the denial of human return; Sirach explicitly maps falling and growing leaves onto generations that end and are born, making the plant-human analogy concrete.

row.basis: field grass alive today, burned tomorrow
row.note: The commentary treats drying pasture as part of the creator’s work; Jesus says God clothes field grass that lives briefly before being thrown into the oven, placing transience inside divine care.

row.basis: weeds gathered and burned, wheat stored
row.note: The commentary links the residue to what is rejected when the lasting is chosen; this parable has weeds gathered for burning while wheat is stored, giving the sorting image a final-judgment setting.
The commentary stresses pasture as useful feed before it becomes debris; Hebrews pictures land drinking rain and producing a useful crop, linking the land’s growth to blessing.
The commentary preserves the contrast between useful pasture and discarded residue; Hebrews sets thorn-bearing land against useful crop and says it is near a curse and ends in burning.

row.basis: rich person fades like a flower
row.note: The commentary extends withered pasture to people who prefer worldly life; James compares the rich person’s passing glory to a flower of the field, making the plant image a warning about status.

row.basis: seed differs from the body that grows
row.note: The commentary says the grass is changed in state rather than replaced by another object; Paul notes that what is sown is not the body that will be, preserving transformation and discontinuity in the seed image.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body
row.note: The commentary emphasizes the same creator’s successive acts over vegetation; Paul says God gives each seed the body he chooses, connecting plant transformation and divine agency.

The commentary sets withered pasture beside the next ayah’s recitation; Moses asks that his teaching fall as rain and his speech as dew on grass, joining authoritative speech to the plant’s source of life.
The commentary compares the pasture’s brief cycle with a preserved recitation; Isaiah says rain waters earth and makes it sprout before comparing that action to God’s effective word.

The commentary places the withering pasture beside a word that will not be forgotten; Isaiah says the word from God’s mouth will not return empty, completing its rain-and-growth analogy with durable efficacy.

row.basis: seed sprouts through night and day
row.note: The commentary says this ayah compresses a season into one immediate step, while Mark’s farmer sleeps and rises night and day as seed sprouts and grows by a process he does not know.

row.basis: stages from blade to ripe grain
row.note: The commentary contrasts its single fe with a longer sequence of growth and drying; Mark names successive stages from stalk to full grain before harvest, supplying a precise gradual counter-image.

The commentary turns the plant’s withering into an image for people who choose the transient world; this verse says evildoers soon wither like grass and fade like green herbs, making the moral application explicit.

The commentary’s guthā is plant matter swept away and no longer counted; Isaiah says all wither like a leaf and their iniquities carry them away like wind, adding a moral account of that disappearance.
The commentary sets floating debris against hollows that retain floodwater; Job asks whether papyrus or reeds can grow without marsh and water, making water retention a condition for plant life.
The commentary holds the green pasture within the darkened debris; Job says a plant can wither while still green and uncut, giving the color change a specific image of premature loss.

row.basis: root rots and blossom becomes dust
row.note: The commentary develops pasture turning into useless debris and being carried off; Isaiah likens judgment to fire consuming stubble, with a rotten root and blossom rising as dust, adding a moral cause and both plant parts.

row.basis: celestial agent makes each blade grow
row.note: The commentary assigns pasture’s emergence and drying to the same Lord; this midrash says each blade of grass has a heavenly constellation that strikes it and tells it to grow, adding an intermediary account of growth without denying divine rule.
The commentary describes guthā as uprooted vegetation that no longer holds to soil; in the sower parable a plant springs up, is scorched by the sun, and withers because it has no root.

row.basis: fruitless fig tree withers at Jesus’ word
row.note: The commentary frames pasture’s drying as a stage in the creator’s care; Jesus’ curse makes a leafy but fruitless fig tree wither, using plant death as a judgment sign rather than a seasonal passage.

row.basis: green wood contrasted with dry wood
row.note: The commentary traces green pasture into dry debris; Jesus uses the difference between green and dry wood to measure the severity of coming judgment, extending the plant contrast into a warning about human fate.

row.basis: God gives growth after planting and watering
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the same Lord brings out pasture and transforms it; Paul distinguishes planting and watering by human workers from God giving the growth, adding a division of agency within cultivation.

row.basis: hay and straw among building materials
row.note: The commentary links guthā to the rejected, uncounted side of selection; Paul includes hay and straw among works built on a foundation, materials that cannot endure the coming test.

row.basis: fire tests and burns perishable work
row.note: The commentary compares transient vegetation with what lasts; Paul says each person’s work is disclosed and tested by fire, adding a judgment in which the work, rather than the person, is what burns.

row.basis: builder survives loss of burned work
row.note: The commentary’s ğuŝâ imagery can turn people themselves into debris; Paul distinguishes the person from combustible work, saying the builder may suffer loss yet be saved, a useful limit on the analogy.

row.basis: patient waiting for rain and harvest
row.note: The commentary contrasts the compressed fe with longer stages of plant growth; James pictures a farmer waiting patiently for the crop until the early and late rains, giving the growing season its slow human rhythm.

The commentary says withered pasture remains the same plant in a changed, useless state; Ezekiel’s vine wood is worthless for craft and is cast into fire as fuel, giving the loss of usefulness a judgment image.

row.basis: sealed spring in an enclosed garden
row.note: The commentary explicitly treats water-holding hollows as a secondary image beside floating debris; the Song’s enclosed garden and sealed spring offer a specific image of protected water, though its setting is erotic rather than a flood basin.

row.basis: well of living water and flowing streams
row.note: The commentary contrasts what a flood carries away with water retained in hollows; the Song names a well of living water and streams, a related water-source image without the commentary’s debris or flood scene.
The commentary makes pasture's blackening an act of the One who produced it; Isaiah makes the grass wither when YHWH's breath blows on it, so decay remains within divine agency.
After the carried-away pasture the commentary places an unforgotten recitation; Isaiah sets the divine word that stands forever against grass that withers.
Peter reapplies Isaiah's grass to all mortal flesh, extending the commentary's grass image from pasture to human transience.
Peter identifies the enduring word as the preached gospel, a Christian reading of the contrast the commentary makes between passing debris and a recited word not forgotten.

row.basis: YHWH dries green tree and makes dry tree flourish
row.note: Ezekiel explicitly gives YHWH both directions of change, drying a green tree and making a dry one flourish; it closely meets the commentary's one hand that produces pasture and alters it.

row.basis: God causes grass to grow for cattle
row.note: The psalm's praise names God as the one who grows grass for animals, supplying the same pasture-as-deliberate-provision setting before the commentary follows it into decline.

row.basis: God takes breath and creatures return to dust
row.note: Within the same hymn, creatures die and return to dust when God takes their breath, supporting the commentary's rejection of an impersonal agent for life's ending.

row.basis: God sends breath and renews ground
row.note: God's sending of breath creates and renews the face of the ground, giving the reverse movement to the commentary's dry-ground-to-new-pasture horizon.

row.basis: one God kills and makes alive
row.note: The divine speaker says that he kills and makes alive and wounds and heals, a compact biblical analogue to the commentary's claim that the producer and changer are the same agent.

row.basis: YHWH kills, makes alive, brings down and raises
row.note: Hannah's praise assigns descent into death and raising up to YHWH together, framing opposite turns of life as praise-worthy divine acts.

row.basis: God sweeps mortals away like a flood
row.note: The commentary's flood carries loose vegetation away; Psalm 90 gives God the active verb of sweeping mortals away like a flood.
Psalm 90 makes grass flourish in the morning and fade and wither by evening, a sharply compressed season like the commentary's fa-linked pasture-to-waste movement.

row.basis: water-rooted tree that does not wither
row.note: The water-retaining side of the commentary's flood scene finds a close counterpart in the tree planted by streams that keeps its leaf and bears fruit.
Psalm 1 contrasts that rooted tree with wicked people as chaff driven away, joining useful rooted life to refuse that cannot remain.

row.basis: turbulent sea throws up mire and dirt
row.note: Isaiah's restless sea casts mire and dirt to its surface; it is a direct scriptural water-and-refuse image for the commentary's floating guthāʾ.
Jude turns water foam into an image for condemned people, closely matching the commentary's move from flood debris to humans who become uncounted waste.

row.basis: chaff carried away with no trace
row.note: The empires become threshing-floor chaff which the wind carries away until no place is found for it, sharpening the commentary's claim that dispersed debris leaves no reckonable remainder.

row.basis: ungodly hope as wind-driven chaff, frost, and smoke
row.note: Wisdom layers chaff, storm-driven frost, and dispersed smoke to describe the ungodly's vanished hope, a Jewish analogue for guthāʾ as humanly worthless and gone.
Jeremiah has God scatter a people like chaff before the desert wind, an exact judgmental transfer from vegetation debris to people.
The winnower gathers wheat but burns chaff, providing the explicit selection scene behind the commentary's contrast of what is retained with what is discarded.

row.basis: straw and grain in a dispute about true word
row.note: Jeremiah's question about straw and wheat occurs amid the true prophetic word, joining the commentary's refuse-versus-choice image to its nearby contrast between lost matter and preserved speech.

row.basis: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
row.note: Isaiah describes water descending to make the earth germinate and supply food, the generative half of the pasture cycle that the commentary sets beside drying and loss.
The rain-and-growth comparison culminates in God's word not returning empty; this closely parallels the commentary's placement of an enduring spoken word after transient vegetation.

row.basis: teaching as rain and dew on grass
row.note: Moses compares teaching and speech to rain and dew falling on grass, a precise meeting of the commentary's pasture and its immediately following recitation.

row.basis: passing heaven and earth, imperishable words
row.note: Jesus contrasts the passing of heaven and earth with words that will not pass, making the commentary's grass-that-goes and word-that-remains contrast cosmic.

row.basis: cut tree still has hope of sprouting
row.note: The commentary uses vegetation's emergence to open a resurrection horizon; Job grants that hope to a cut tree, setting up his deliberately darker comparison with a dead human.

row.basis: stump buds again at the scent of water
row.note: Job's water-revived stump supplies the same rain, ground, and renewed growth image, but serves his contrast with the apparent finality of human death.

row.basis: a human dies and is gone
row.note: Job immediately asks where the dead human is, the counter-voice to the commentary's use of plant return and re-emergence as a sign of being brought out again.

row.basis: dust-dwellers awake and earth gives up the dead
row.note: Isaiah joins sleepers in dust to the earth's giving birth to the dead, directly meeting the commentary's move from soil-born pasture to human re-emergence.

row.basis: God opens graves and brings people up
row.note: God himself promises to open graves and bring the people up, making resurrection an act of the same sovereign agent rather than a cycle without a hand.

row.basis: seed must die before it comes to life
row.note: Paul's seed image makes apparent death a condition of new life, a focused Christian development of the commentary's vegetation-and-resurrection connection.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body
row.note: Paul attributes the seed's embodied outcome to God as he wills, echoing the commentary's emphasis on divine agency across changes of state.
The sown-and-raised contrast applies plant language to the resurrection body, clarifying how a decaying earthly image can become an eschatological argument.

row.basis: all in tombs hear the voice
row.note: Jesus locates the dead in tombs yet under a summons, a close Christian answer to the commentary's focus on those brought out after returning to earth.

row.basis: those in tombs come out to divergent outcomes
row.note: The coming-out follows the summons and divides into life and judgment, adding explicit human accountability to the commentary's pasture and refuse contrast.

row.basis: earth and dust give back their sleepers
row.note: 4 Ezra depicts earth and dust yielding the dead entrusted to them, an especially direct Jewish formulation of return from the ground.

row.basis: the earth restores the dead it received
row.note: 2 Baruch treats the earth as preserving and then returning its dead, a useful counterpart to the commentary's contrast between what is carried away and what is held for return.

row.basis: ungodly claim birth by chance and nonexistence after death
row.note: The book places an impersonal, no-afterlife account in the mouth of the ungodly, furnishing a Jewish counter-narrative to the commentary's rejection of time or chance as the final explanation.

row.basis: God clothes grass today and it is burned tomorrow
row.note: Jesus explicitly makes God the dresser of grass while stressing its one-day transience, a close parallel to pasture under divine care and then rapid loss.

row.basis: rich person passes like a grass flower
row.note: James applies grass's passing flower to a wealthy human, matching the commentary's shift from fading pasture to a judgment on those who privilege worldly life.

row.basis: scorched grass, fallen flower, perishing wealth
row.note: The sun scorches grass and beauty falls as the rich person fades in pursuits, giving a detailed Christian worldly-life analogue to green darkening into useless remains.

row.basis: land drinks rain and yields useful vegetation
row.note: Hebrews makes rain-soaked ground blessed when it produces useful vegetation, closely reflecting the commentary's water that stays with what benefits people.

row.basis: thorn-bearing land is worthless and burned
row.note: The adjoining land becomes worthless when it bears thorns and ends in burning, supplying a judicial contrast to useful growth and retained water.

row.basis: grain falls into earth, dies, and bears fruit
row.note: Jesus' grain moves through burial and apparent death into abundant fruit, a Christian reversal that makes explicit the regenerative possibility the commentary finds beyond dry ground.

row.basis: people as field grass and roof grass blighted before growth
row.note: Isaiah renders defeated inhabitants as field grass and roof grass scorched before maturity, a specific human-to-vegetation judgment image beside the commentary's people made like debris.

row.basis: morning cloud, dew, chaff, and smoke that vanish
row.note: Hosea's chain of vanishing vapour, chaff, and smoke makes Israel's idolatrous instability legible through the same dispersed-material imagery developed for guthāʾ.

row.basis: human days like grass and its flower
row.note: Psalm 103 calls a human life grass and a field flower, a nonjudgmental mortality counterpart to the commentary's vegetal picture of the world's passing life.

row.basis: wind passes and the grass's place knows it no more
row.note: The vanished plant leaves even its place without recognition of it, closely serving the commentary's secondary sense of refuse that no one counts.

row.basis: water-rooted tree remains green in heat and drought
row.note: Jeremiah's tree sends roots to water and keeps green leaves during drought, giving the positive, held-water counterimage to floating and dried debris.

row.basis: parched ground becomes pool and grassland
row.note: Isaiah reverses parched land into springs and grass, directly complementing the commentary's observation that barren ground can become the site of another emergence.

row.basis: rain satisfies wasteland and makes grass sprout
row.note: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to sprout, a creation-speech counterpart to the commentary's pasture emerging from earth.

row.basis: God's keys of rain and resurrection
row.note: The rabbinic saying keeps the keys of rain and resurrection in God's own hand, linking the commentary's water, pasture, and return-from-death motifs under one divine agency.

row.basis: each blade of grass receives a heavenly command to grow
row.note: This midrash reads grass's growth as ordered rather than self-explanatory, an interpretive counterpart to the commentary's insistence that pasture belongs among the Creator's works.

row.basis: seed buried in earth as resurrection sign
row.note: Aphrahat's Syriac resurrection argument uses a seed's burial and renewal as a sign for bodily rising; it is a later explicit version of the commentary's vegetation-to-resurrection bridge, though the precise wording should be checked.

row.basis: God removes a vineyard's protection and makes it waste
row.note: Isaiah's vineyard owner actively turns a cultivated planting into trampling and consumption, a close parallel to the commentary's claim that the producer also brings the pasture to its ruined state.

row.basis: God commands no rain on the abandoned vineyard
row.note: The vineyard's briars and desolation include God's command to the clouds, making environmental decline a deliberate divine action rather than an impersonal season.

row.basis: God turns rivers and springs into desert and thirsty ground
row.note: Psalm 107 gives God the reverse movement from water-bearing land to barrenness, directly extending the commentary's one-agent account of life-giving and drying change.

row.basis: God turns wilderness and parched ground into water sources
row.note: The psalm immediately states the opposite turn, so its paired reversals illuminate the commentary's observation that dry ground may become the place of new growth.

row.basis: crop, vine, olive, field, flock, and herd all fail
row.note: Habakkuk lists a total failure of edible vegetation and livestock, giving a particularly close pastoral scene for the commentary's loss of pasture and food.

row.basis: rejoicing in God after ecological failure
row.note: The prophet's resolve to rejoice follows the failed pasture scene, making a biblical counterpart to the commentary's placement of vegetal ending within praise.

row.basis: green marsh plant withers before other vegetation
row.note: Bildad's plant remains green yet dries without sustaining water, a precise counterpart to the commentary's attention to green still visible beneath darkening and to water's role in what remains.

row.basis: forgotten God compared with a perishing plant's hope
row.note: Job applies the waterless plant's end to those who forget God, joining vegetal failure to the commentary's moral turn from pasture to human fate.

row.basis: chaff before wind driven by YHWH's angel
row.note: The psalm combines chaff, wind, and an explicitly divine pursuer, sharpening the commentary's account of debris being carried away under a responsible agent.

row.basis: roof grass withers before it grows
row.note: The enemies of Zion are likened to grass that fails before maturity, another human-to-vegetation judgment image beside the commentary's degraded pasture.

row.basis: unharvestable grass fills neither reaper nor binder
row.note: The next verse emphasizes that the failed grass supplies no one, closely matching the commentary's secondary sense of residue that is not counted or retained.

row.basis: unabiding branch dries, is discarded, gathered, and burned
row.note: Jesus makes a fruitless human likeness follow the full sequence of branch, drying, disposal, and fire, an unusually close New Testament transfer of withered vegetation to moral judgment.

row.basis: sleepers in earth's dust awake to divergent destinies
row.note: Daniel directly answers the commentary's question of people being brought out after death and adds the same final division between contrary outcomes.

row.basis: God gives spirit, makes dry-bone hearers live, and sets them on land
row.note: This continuation of the dry-bones vision joins divine breath, renewed life, and placement on land, completing the vegetation-and-resurrection horizon developed in the commentary.

row.basis: God revives and raises after deathlike judgment
row.note: Hosea's compact revival and raising formula offers a prophetic human counterpart to the commentary's movement from an ended earthly state toward being brought forth again.

row.basis: world and desire pass, while God's doer remains
row.note: The letter explicitly contrasts the passing world with the one who remains, closely matching the commentary's worldly-life versus enduring-reality contrast.

row.basis: water on dry ground paired with Spirit on descendants
row.note: Isaiah fuses water for parched soil with God's Spirit for descendants, a particularly clear biblical bridge between renewed land and renewed human life.

row.basis: descendants sprout like grass by watercourses
row.note: The human recipients of the promise sprout like grass beside water, making explicit the commentary's latent passage from pasture imagery to people.

row.basis: Creator gives breath and life again
row.note: The mother grounds hope after bodily death in the Creator who first made all things and can give breath and life back, supporting the commentary's same-agent theology of ending and renewal.

row.basis: hearing Jesus' words and building on rock
row.note: The commentary follows carried-away matter with a word that is not lost; Jesus similarly makes enduring stability depend on hearing and doing his words.

row.basis: rain, floods, and winds test the rock-founded house
row.note: The flood cannot carry away the house founded on rock, a concrete Christian counterimage to the commentary's unrooted debris swept along by water.

row.basis: hearing without doing builds on sand
row.note: Jesus contrasts retained, enacted speech with an unstable foundation, extending the commentary's proximity of remembered word and vanishing matter.

row.basis: flood and wind bring a sand-founded house to great fall
row.note: The destructive water scene supplies the negative counterpart: what lacks a lasting foundation is swept into collapse.

row.basis: creation subjected to futility in hope
row.note: Paul gives creation's transience a theological frame rather than treating it as mere accident, resonating with the commentary's attribution of vegetal decline to divine ordering.
The promised release of creation from decay gives a Christian eschatological completion to the commentary's reversible cycle of dry ground and renewed life.

row.basis: wicked sprout like grass only to be destroyed forever
row.note: The psalm treats lush grasslike flourishing as the prelude to the wicked's final loss, a direct moralization of the commentary's green-to-dark transition.
Psalm 37 supplies a concise ethical application of withering grass to people whose apparent worldly flourishing does not last.

row.basis: God gives field grass for cattle
row.note: The covenantal promise names God as giver of grass to livestock, another direct pasture-and-animal provisioning context for the commentary's merʿā image.

row.basis: God sends rain and makes grass grow in a hymn of praise
row.note: This praise psalm joins rain and grass growth to God's care, supporting the commentary's framing of pasture among the divine acts that call forth praise.

row.basis: dust returns to earth and spirit returns to God
row.note: Qohelet names both the body's return to earth and the spirit's return to God, an adjacent Jewish framing for the commentary's death, soil, and agency themes.

row.basis: denial of resurrection as a decisive theological error
row.note: The Mishnah opening this discussion excludes one who says resurrection is not from Torah, offering a rabbinic counterpart to the commentary's attention to people who reject being raised after death.
Paul's image of work exposed and tested by fire provides a Christian counterpart to the commentary's secondary claim that human works can be reduced to unretained matter.

row.basis: burned work brings loss despite the worker's rescue
row.note: The distinction between a disappearing work and a person still saved sharpens the commentary's distinction between what is discarded and what ultimately remains.

row.basis: sea, death, and Hades give up their dead
row.note: Revelation imagines even apparently holding realms returning their dead for judgment, an apocalyptic counterpart to soil or water no longer keeping what must be brought out.
The commentary stresses that ahwā's dark hue is not intrinsically ugly; the Song separately places blackness beside beauty, a tonal comparison rather than a direct botanical parallel.

row.basis: God's Spirit and words placed in a mouth, never departing
row.note: The commentary takes 87:6 as God's promise to make the recipient recite and retain the given word.
