Isaiah's covenant places God's Spirit and words in a recipient's mouth and promises that they will not leave that mouth or its descendants, extending secure recitation into a line of transmission.

row.basis: a song written, taught, and put in Israel's mouth
row.note: The commentary's instructor first gives the recitation and the recipient then carries it. God tells Moses to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths; the verse combines written preservation, teaching, and voiced reception.

row.basis: the covenant song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The promised “you will not forget” is a result of divine action in the commentary. Deuteronomy makes the song a witness precisely because it will not be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a communal analogue to retained recitation.

row.basis: the Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: The commentary insists that unforgetting is granted rather than commanded. Jesus promises that the Paraclete will teach the disciples and bring all his sayings to their remembrance, a direct Christian promise of divinely caused recall.

row.basis: YHWH with Moses' mouth, teaching what to speak
row.note: The direct divine “we” and enabled human speech are central to the commentary. At Moses' reluctance, YHWH promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, making speech possible without making Moses its independent source.

row.basis: YHWH puts words into a prophet's mouth
row.note: The commentary pictures the word moving from its source into the recipient's tongue. In Jeremiah's call, YHWH touches the prophet's mouth and says that the divine words have been put there, a particularly close prophetic counterpart.

row.basis: taught tongue and repeatedly awakened ear
row.note: The commentary's causative reading has the recipient hear the teacher before speaking for others. Isaiah's servant receives a taught tongue and an ear awakened morning by morning to hear as a learner, joining receptive hearing to fitting speech.

row.basis: the Holy Spirit teaches what must be said
row.note: The commentary treats 87:6 as a future assurance that God enables the addressee's utterance. Jesus tells disciples that the Holy Spirit will teach them, at the needed moment, what they ought to say; the setting is different, but the divine provision of speech is equally explicit.

row.basis: word in mouth and heart for enactment
row.note: The commentary describes the given word as held within the recipient and then given outwardly. Deuteronomy says the command is very near, in mouth and heart, in order to do it; it joins inner retention, oral expression, and lived obedience.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's B001/B002 labels develop ق ر ء as recitation that carries joined words to hearers. Moses reads the covenant book aloud to Israel in this verse; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ) is the clear cognate and its covenant setting shows reading as received, binding speech.

row.basis: a scroll eaten before the prophet speaks
row.note: The commentary's womb-and-heart image has revelation taken inside before it is released as public speech. Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then go speak to Israel, making ingestion the concrete bridge between receiving written words and proclaiming them.

row.basis: words received from God spoken to Israel
row.note: After the scroll scene, Ezekiel is sent to Israel with God's own words. This supplies the outward half of the commentary's sequence: a word retained in the prophet becomes warning addressed to others.

row.basis: the little scroll eaten, sweet in mouth and bitter within
row.note: The commentary compares a word held in the body to a pregnancy before its outward delivery. Revelation recasts Ezekiel's act: John takes and eats a scroll, experiencing it in mouth and stomach, an embodied reception of prophecy rather than mere reading.

row.basis: prophecy required after eating the scroll
row.note: The commentary moves from retained recitation to the task of reminding others. After the scroll is eaten, John is told that he must prophesy again about peoples and kings; this supplies the public-release side of the same received-word image.

row.basis: Torah placed within and written on hearts
row.note: The commentary says that the word is gathered and held in the recipient rather than merely external to him. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise has God put Torah within the people and write it on their hearts, a scriptural inner-inscription analogue.

row.basis: the word dwelling richly, teaching, admonishing, and singing
row.note: The commentary links unforgotten recitation to later reminder, worship, and a life shaped by the word. Colossians asks that Christ's word dwell richly in the community so that it teaches and admonishes through sung praise, joining inward residence to communal utterance.

row.basis: the good deposit guarded through the indwelling Spirit
row.note: The commentary calls the received word an entrusted deposit whose retention depends on the giver. Timothy is told to guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers, a Christian account of preserved teaching with divine, not merely human, custody.

row.basis: Arabic ن س ي B001/B002/B003 and Hebrew נשה (nāšâ)
row.note: The commentary's ن س ي material makes forgetting both failure to retain an entrusted word and, through the womb image, a falling-away from what was held. Deuteronomy says Israel is unmindful of the Rock that begot it and forgets the God who gave it birth; Hebrew נשה (nāšâ) is cognate with Arabic ن س ي, and the verse uniquely joins forgetting to birthing.

row.basis: a nursing mother who might forget, but God does not
row.note: The commentary contrasts human forgetfulness with the God who does not forget, while using maternal containment as a secondary image. Isaiah invokes a nursing mother and her child only to insist that even if she forgets, God will not forget Zion, binding maternal care and unfailing divine memory.

row.basis: do not forget what was received; make it known to children
row.note: The commentary's recipient is preserved from forgetting so that he can later remind others. Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget what it has witnessed and immediately turns that memory into teaching children and grandchildren, giving a covenantal counterpart to retention becoming reminder.

row.basis: withered grass and the word that stands forever
row.note: The commentary places the promise that the recited word will not fall away beside pasture turned into dark refuse. Isaiah's one verse contrasts grass and flower fading with God's word standing forever, making the vegetation-to-enduring-word relationship unusually close.

row.basis: the enduring word identified as announced good news
row.note: The commentary joins an unfailing word to its passage from the recipient to other hearers. Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it as the good news announced to the audience, coupling permanence with oral proclamation.

row.basis: a burned scroll recreated and expanded by dictation
row.note: The commentary grounds preservation in the divine source rather than the recipient's unaided memory. After Jehoiakim burns the first scroll, Jeremiah dictates its former words to another scroll and additional words are added; the scene tests the durability of revealed wording against material loss.

row.basis: God's word goes from the divine mouth and accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary presents the recited speech as originating with God and reaching its assigned result. Isaiah's word goes out from God's mouth, does not return empty, and accomplishes the sender's purpose, a source-to-effect account of effective revelation.

row.basis: the book kept in the mouth, meditated on, and enacted
row.note: The commentary rejects a reading that remains only on the tongue and ends with recitation joined to worshipful practice. Joshua is told that the book of Torah must not depart from his mouth, but be meditated on day and night so that he does what is written; it makes durable recitation a form of life.

row.basis: prophets speaking from God while carried by the Spirit
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the human reader from the God who supplies the word. Second Peter says prophetic speech did not arise by human will but that people spoke from God while borne by the Holy Spirit, expressing a comparable account of sourced prophetic utterance.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary treats recitation as joined words whose meaning is also opened for hearers. Nehemiah's assembly reads from the Torah and gives its sense so the people understand the reading; Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ), cognate with the commentary's ق ر ء, appears in a communal reading-and-explanation setting.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's recitation is held so that it governs the recipient's way of life. The king must keep a Torah scroll with him and read it all his days in order to learn reverence and keep its words; the Hebrew cognate קרא makes daily reading an antidote to abandonment.

row.basis: God's word stored in the heart
row.note: The commentary says the word is gathered within so it will not be lost. The psalmist stores God's saying in the heart in order not to sin, a devotional response that makes inner retention ethically consequential.

row.basis: one reader, hearers, and keepers of prophecy
row.note: The commentary traces a word from its divine source through a reader to those reminded by it. Revelation blesses the one who reads its prophecy aloud and those who hear and keep it, a liturgical community shaped by public recitation and retention.

row.basis: Christ's letter written by the Spirit on human hearts
row.note: The commentary's pages are not opposed to interior retention: words are gathered in the recipient before they are uttered. Paul calls the Corinthian community Christ's letter, written by the living God's Spirit on hearts rather than stone, a Christian transformation of scroll imagery into inward inscription.

row.basis: Deuteronomy's mouth-and-heart word read as proclaimed faith
row.note: The commentary brings a word into the mouth and heart before it goes out to others. Paul quotes the mouth-and-heart formulation of Deuteronomy and explicitly identifies it as the word of faith that he proclaims, a Christian interpretive reuse of the Torah's language of near, speakable instruction.

row.basis: heard teaching entrusted for further teaching
row.note: The commentary's protected path carries a received message onward instead of leaving it with one recipient. Timothy is to entrust what he heard before witnesses to reliable people who can teach others, giving a four-stage chain of retained and retransmitted instruction.

row.basis: tradition held in oral word and letter
row.note: The commentary repeatedly holds oral recitation beside pages and written preservation. Paul tells the Thessalonians to stand firm and hold the traditions taught either by spoken word or letter, a compact Christian pairing of memorized and written transmission.

row.basis: the doer rather than the forgetful hearer
row.note: The commentary defines forgetting as leaving an entrusted word and contrasts a merely vocal reading with a life of worship and understanding. James contrasts a forgetful hearer with one who continues in the perfect law and acts on it, making retention visible in conduct.

row.basis: God remembers sin no more as covenantal action
row.note: The commentary stresses that forgetting can mean abandoning rather than a simple failure of mental recall. Jeremiah's promise that God will no longer remember sin uses memory as a covenantal act of judgment or forgiveness, helping a reader hear the commentary's stronger relational sense of forgetting.

row.basis: forgetting even one word of Torah study
row.note: The commentary says 87:6 is assurance rather than a command imposed on the recipient. Avot treats forgetting a word of one's study as grave while qualifying unavoidable loss, placing rabbinic discipline of Torah memory beside the Qur'anic promise that the messenger will not forget.

row.basis: “write this song” read as preserving Torah in writing
row.note: The commentary ends by bringing retained recitation beside earlier pages associated with Moses. Sifre reads Deuteronomy's command to write the song as an injunction to write the Torah, a rabbinic expansion of oral teaching into durable manuscript practice.

row.basis: the enduring book of commandments held fast
row.note: The commentary contrasts gathered, retained revelation with a word discarded as debris. Baruch calls Torah the book of God's commandments that endures forever and sets holding it fast over against death, a Jewish formulation of preservation as life-giving fidelity.

row.basis: the Law burned and people left without its light
row.note: The commentary considers both God's power over revealed speech and the danger of a word being lost. Ezra's lament that the Law has been burned makes the loss of written revelation a concrete crisis rather than merely a lapse of personal memory.

row.basis: Ezra asks for the Spirit so he can write what was lost
row.note: The commentary makes the giver responsible for collecting and securing revelation. In response to the loss of the Law, Ezra asks for the Holy Spirit so that he can write what is needed for later people; the scene is a Jewish restoration analogue to divinely sustained transmission.

row.basis: instruction neither too difficult nor too distant
row.note: The augment links the promise to recite with God's making the way easy. Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or beyond reach, a Torah-side claim that accessible instruction can actually be received and enacted.

row.basis: an easy yoke and light burden
row.note: The commentary places the promised unforgotten word beside the later assurance of ease, while also noting a “weighty word.” Jesus' easy yoke and light burden provide a Christian image for divine teaching that does not finally crush the recipient.

row.basis: mortal life compared to grass and a fading flower
row.note: The commentary has the pasture become dark chaff immediately before the promise of retained recitation. Peter's verse compares all flesh and glory to grass and a flower that withers, supplying the perishable side of the contrast developed explicitly in the next verse.

row.basis: the passing cosmos and imperishable words
row.note: The commentary sets a word that will not be dropped against perishing vegetation. Jesus contrasts heaven and earth passing away with his words not passing away, a Christian saying of verbal permanence that sharpens the commentary's preservation claim.

row.basis: Mary's conception and birth announced by divine speech
row.note: The commentary's secondary image follows Mary as she carries a child and withdraws to give birth. Luke's annunciation likewise joins divine speech to Mary's conception and bearing of a son; the shared Marian scene gives a canonical Christian setting for the commentary's pregnancy image.

row.basis: Mary keeps and ponders words in her heart
row.note: The commentary lets Mary's bodily carrying illuminate a word held within rather than lost. Luke depicts Mary retaining and pondering the reported words in her heart, a Christian maternal image of memory that complements the commentary's contrast between carrying and being forgotten.

row.basis: Adam's transgression narrated as seeing, taking, eating, and giving
row.note: The commentary invokes the Qur'anic Adam who “forgot” an entrusted command as the negative foil to 87:6. Genesis narrates the corresponding fall through the woman's seeing, taking, eating, and giving the fruit, rather than naming Adam's act forgetfulness; the difference changes how disobedience is framed.

row.basis: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws without pages
row.note: The commentary's final page-image attributes earlier sheets to Abraham and Moses. Genesis retrospectively credits Abraham with obeying divine commands and laws but mentions no Abrahamic scroll; that absence is a cautious textual contrast to the Qur'anic “pages of Abraham.”

row.basis: no prophetic word allowed to fall to the ground
row.note: The commentary makes “you will not forget” the result of God-held recitation and contrasts it with a word dropped like worthless debris. Samuel grows with YHWH, who lets none of his words fall to the ground; this prophetic formula gives a close Hebrew Bible image for divinely sustained speech that does not fall away.

The commentary has the given word gathered within the recipient before it is voiced. Deuteronomy places these words upon Israel's heart, an early covenant formulation of interior retention that stands behind later oral teaching.

row.basis: words repeatedly taught and spoken in daily life
row.note: The commentary moves from retained recitation to passing the word outwardly. Deuteronomy requires parents to teach the words diligently and speak of them through the ordinary rhythms of day and night, making memory a recurrent oral practice.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary's ق ر ء material treats reading as voiced words received by listeners. At the pilgrimage assembly Moses is commanded to read the Torah in all Israel's hearing so that they hear, learn, and fear; the Hebrew קרא is the cognate in a public instructional setting.

row.basis: God's Torah kept in the mouth as a memorial
row.note: The commentary joins unforgotten recitation to memory of the divine giver. Exodus calls the festival sign a memorial so that YHWH's Torah may be in Israel's mouth, making oral retention a ritualized response to deliverance.

row.basis: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
row.note: The commentary brings oral recitation beside the earlier pages of Moses. Before the public reading of the covenant book, Moses writes all YHWH's words; this supplies the written half of the oral-and-page sequence developed in the commentary.

row.basis: testimony bound up and teaching sealed among disciples
row.note: The commentary describes a message whose path to the messenger is guarded and whose retention is secured by its giver. Isaiah orders the testimony bound and the teaching sealed among disciples, a compact image of protected instruction held within a defined receiving community.

row.basis: prophecy inscribed on tablet and book for future time
row.note: The commentary's final pages carry words beyond the first recipient. Isaiah is told to write the message before the people on a tablet and in a book so it remains for a future day, a direct preservation scene for revelation meant to outlast its first utterance.

row.basis: Arabic ق ر ء B001/B002 and Hebrew קרא (qārāʾ)
row.note: The commentary pairs gathering with a recited word that is not lost. Isaiah tells hearers to seek and read from YHWH's book, says none will be missing, and grounds the gathering in YHWH's mouth and Spirit; Hebrew קרא supplies the cognate reading verb within an unusually close no-omission context.

row.basis: divine words put in a mouth and protected by God's hand
row.note: The commentary's addressee speaks a word he did not originate and is kept by the speaker who gave it. Isaiah says God has put words in the servant's mouth and covered him with the shadow of the divine hand, joining enabled speech to protection.

row.basis: a word shut up inside that cannot be held back
row.note: The commentary's womb image gives the retained word a later outward release. Jeremiah tries not to mention or speak in God's name, but the word becomes a fire shut in his bones which he cannot contain; it offers a bodily image of inward revelation pressing toward proclamation.

row.basis: God's true word spoken faithfully over against straw
row.note: The commentary puts its undropped word immediately after pasture becomes refuse. Jeremiah distinguishes a dreamer's report from one who has God's word and must speak it faithfully, then contrasts straw with wheat; it joins trustworthy utterance to the commentary's vegetation-and-chaff contrast.

The commentary's language of gathering inside the recipient is not limited to intellectual recall. Jeremiah finds and eats God's words, which become joy and delight, a prophetic ingestion image that complements the scroll-eating scenes without merely repeating them.

row.basis: all divine words received in heart and heard with ears
row.note: The commentary insists that the recipient follows a word first supplied by its teacher. Ezekiel is told to receive in his heart all the words God speaks and to hear them with his ears, explicitly joining inward reception and attentive listening before his mission.

row.basis: God opens the prophet's mouth when speaking to him
row.note: The commentary reads the causative form as God making the addressee able to recite. After controlling Ezekiel's silence, God says that when he speaks with him he will open the prophet's mouth; the verse makes the possibility of prophetic utterance depend on divine initiative.

row.basis: vision written plainly so a reader can run with it
row.note: The commentary holds recitation together with ordered pages and a message carried onward. Habakkuk is told to write the vision clearly on tablets so that its reader may run, a scene where a fixed written revelation enables its bearer to transmit or act on it.

row.basis: Torah read, then confessed and worshipped
row.note: The commentary ends by joining reading to prayer and worship rather than treating it as bare sound. Nehemiah's community spends part of the day reading the Torah and another part confessing and worshipping, a liturgical realization of received words becoming devotion.

row.basis: God-written tablets given to Moses for teaching
row.note: The commentary's “pages of Moses” are words received from God and then given onward. Jubilees has God promise Moses tablets of law and commandment that God has written so Moses may teach them, a Jewish retelling that makes both divine authorship and transmission explicit.

row.basis: the heard word held fast in a good heart and bearing fruit
row.note: The commentary's word is retained in the recipient and subsequently released in beneficial reminder. In Luke's good-soil explanation, hearers hold the word fast in an honest heart and bear fruit with endurance, making fruitful outward consequence depend on inward retention.

row.basis: words received from the Father, given by Jesus, and received by disciples
row.note: The commentary follows revelation from its source through a messenger to those addressed. Jesus says he gave disciples the words the Father gave him and that they received them; this is a three-stage Johannine account of sourced and accepted speech.

row.basis: the Father commands what Jesus must say and speak
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the one who recites from the one who causes the recitation. Jesus says he has not spoken from himself because the Father who sent him commanded what he should say and speak, a closely related claim of divinely determined utterance.

row.basis: the Spirit speaks what it hears and guides into truth
row.note: The commentary has the recipient follow the giver's recitation rather than create an independent message. Jesus describes the Spirit of truth as not speaking from itself but speaking what it hears while guiding disciples, a Christian messenger model of received speech.

The commentary's “we will cause you to recite” attributes enabled proclamation to God. After prayer, the gathered believers are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak God's word with boldness, a communal narrative of divinely empowered speech.

row.basis: words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom
row.note: The commentary frames the recipient's reading as teaching received from a transcendent source. Paul says that he and his colleagues speak in words taught by the Spirit rather than human wisdom, a Christian articulation of divinely instructed expression.

row.basis: gospel received through revelation rather than human teaching
row.note: The commentary denies that the addressee independently produces the recitation. Paul says he neither received nor was taught his gospel by a human being but received it through revelation of Jesus Christ, a direct source-of-message parallel.

row.basis: God's word received as divine and active within believers
row.note: The commentary says the given word is held within the recipient, not merely heard as an external sound. The Thessalonians receive the preached word as God's word rather than a human one, and Paul says it is at work within believers; this connects reception to inward efficacy.

row.basis: the implanted word received with meekness
row.note: The commentary's pregnancy analogy presents the word as held within a body before outward consequence. James calls the saving word “implanted” and commands its reception, a concise Christian image of a word placed within and able to generate life.

row.basis: new birth through the living and enduring word
row.note: The commentary pairs womb, retention, and release with the word's not being discarded. First Peter attributes new birth to the living and abiding word of God, a Christian use of birth imagery that makes the enduring word generative.

row.basis: Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness
row.note: The commentary's old pages are preserved so their word is not lost. Moses orders the completed Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness; this is a material practice of keeping a received text available beyond immediate oral memory.

row.basis: a sealed book offered to one who says he cannot read it
row.note: The commentary's promise is that God will enable the addressee to recite and will preserve the word, while it also reflects on hidden and manifest speech. Isaiah's vision becomes a sealed book that even a reader cannot read; the contrast makes divine enablement, rather than literacy alone, the issue.

row.basis: instruction written on the tablet of the heart
row.note: The commentary joins pages to a word held in the recipient. Proverbs tells the pupil to bind the commands and write them on the tablet of the heart, a wisdom-text counterpart to inward inscription and memorized guidance.

row.basis: not forgetting God's works while keeping commandments
row.note: The commentary uses forgetting as leaving what has been entrusted and links memory to a later reminder. The psalm's educational purpose is that later generations not forget God's works but keep the commandments, an explicit memory-obedience relation.

row.basis: a book of remembrance for those who fear God and esteem the name
row.note: The commentary connects unforgetting, divine knowledge, and a lasting written record. Malachi describes God attending to those who speak together in reverence and a book of remembrance being written before him, a reciprocal scene of human remembrance and divine record.

row.basis: Moses receives Torah and transmits it through successive teachers
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that a sourced word reaches a recipient and then others. Avot begins its chain with Moses receiving Torah at Sinai and handing it to Joshua, elders, prophets, and the assembly, a rabbinic model of guarded transmission across generations.

row.basis: repeated teaching from Moses through Israel
row.note: The commentary describes the instructor reading first and the recipient following so the word remains. The Talmud's account of Moses teaching Aaron, his sons, elders, and all Israel in repeated cycles makes repetition the concrete practice by which revelation is retained and shared.

row.basis: twenty-four restored books made public for reading
row.note: The commentary sets preserved recitation beside enduring pages and asks how a word reaches later hearers. After Ezra's inspired restoration of books, the Most High orders the first twenty-four made public for worthy and unworthy readers, a Jewish account of recovered revelation opened for communal use.

row.basis: seventy restored books reserved for the wise
row.note: The commentary distinguishes what is openly uttered from what remains hidden under God's control. The next instruction reserves the remaining books for the wise, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpoint in which preservation does not imply unrestricted disclosure.

row.basis: Jewish refusal to add, remove, or alter sacred books
row.note: The commentary claims that the divine source protects the given word from loss and change. Josephus describes a Jewish conviction that no one has dared add to, take from, or alter the ancestral books, a later Jewish articulation of scriptural preservation.

row.basis: apostolic preaching handed on in written Gospels
row.note: The commentary moves from a word received by a messenger to a durable body of pages for later readers. Irenaeus describes the apostles first preaching and then handing down the Gospel in writings, a patristic account of oral revelation becoming preserved Scripture.

row.basis: Spirit gives utterance to the gathered speakers
row.note: The commentary's causative verb makes speech possible through God's action. At Pentecost the gathered disciples begin speaking as the Spirit gives them utterance; the speech is multilingual rather than a recited book, so the link is an enabled-utterance motif.

row.basis: faith comes through hearing the proclaimed word
row.note: The commentary presents recitation as a word carried from its source into the hearer's life. Paul grounds faith in hearing, and hearing in Christ's word, offering a Christian account of oral proclamation as the means by which a message reaches and changes its audience.

The commentary treats reading as more than isolated sound: retained words become reminder and instruction. Timothy is charged with public reading, exhortation, and teaching, a church practice that joins recitation to its communal effect.

row.basis: holding fast the taught word in order to exhort others
row.note: The commentary says the recipient must retain the word so that others may be reminded. Titus' overseer holds firmly to the trustworthy word according to teaching in order to exhort and answer opponents, an office-specific parallel to retention becoming instruction.

row.basis: close attention to what was heard lest it drift away
row.note: The commentary's promise removes the danger that the given word will be dropped or forgotten. Hebrews warns hearers to pay closer attention to what they have heard so that they do not drift away, the ordinary human vulnerability against which the Qur'anic assurance stands out.

row.basis: what was heard from the beginning remaining within
row.note: The commentary's gathered word remains in the recipient rather than becoming discarded residue. First John tells believers to let what they heard from the beginning remain in them, making continuance in the received message the condition of continuing communion.

row.basis: Moses receives words for his mission
row.note: The commentary connects Moses' prayer for a loosened tongue with the prophet's preparation to speak. In Exodus God answers Moses' speech fear by promising to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, making divine ease a concrete aid to prophetic speech.

The commentary recalls Moses asking for his chest and tongue to be prepared before addressing Pharaoh. In Exodus Moses says he is slow of mouth and tongue during his call, giving the same figure a speech impediment that frames the later promise of help.

row.basis: God claims the making of the mouth
row.note: The commentary says the one who prepares the messenger also knows and equips the person within. In Exodus God answers Moses' limitation by asking who made the human mouth, grounding the messenger's capacity in the sender.

row.basis: The word near the mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says revelation is made easy as the prophet's tongue becomes ready for the word. Moses says the command is near, in mouth and heart, so it can be done; both locate readiness in the person who receives and carries the word.

row.basis: The command is not too hard or far away
row.note: The commentary hears the unnamed easiest destination as a divine easing of the person. Deuteronomy describes its command as not too difficult or remote, an Israelite counterpart in which God's instruction is accessible for action.

row.basis: An enlarged heart makes the runner able
row.note: The commentary distinguishes smoothing a road from preparing its traveler. The psalmist says that when God enlarges his heart, he will run in the way of God's commandments; inner preparation enables swift movement along the way.

row.basis: A taught tongue sustains the weary
row.note: The commentary links an eased prophet to a tongue made ready for reminder. Isaiah's servant receives a trained tongue to sustain the weary and an awakened ear each morning, showing prophetic readiness as both listening and speech for others.

row.basis: God places words in the prophet's mouth
row.note: The commentary presents the reciting God as the source of a messenger's prepared speech. In Moses' promise of a prophet like him, God puts divine words in that prophet's mouth, specifying what being made ready to speak entails.

row.basis: A touched mouth receives God's words
row.note: The commentary describes the prophet himself as prepared for the work of reminder. At Jeremiah's call God touches his mouth and puts words there before appointing him to speak, a concrete scene of the messenger being readied rather than the task being simplified.

row.basis: The prophet must speak what God commands
row.note: The commentary says the prepared messenger is then sent to remind others. Deuteronomy makes the prophet responsible to speak God's commanded words, joining divine preparation to the work that follows.

row.basis: Words remain in the messenger's mouth
row.note: The commentary places ease between recitation and not forgetting. Isaiah's covenant promise says God's words placed in the mouth will not depart from the servant and descendants, adding lasting retention to the image of prepared speech.

row.basis: The prophet eats the scroll, then speaks
row.note: The commentary joins receiving recitation to becoming ready to remind others. Ezekiel is told to take the scroll into himself and then go speak God's words to Israel, presenting preparation as inwardly receiving the message before carrying it outward.

row.basis: A coal prepares Isaiah's lips for service
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses' wish for his tongue to be loosened and Muhammad's opened chest before a mission. Isaiah's lips are touched and his guilt removed before he is sent, making bodily preparation for prophetic speech visible.

row.basis: The prepared prophet answers the call
row.note: The commentary says easing does not end in rest but enables the messenger's work. After Isaiah's lips are cleansed, he volunteers to be sent when God asks who will go, linking preparation directly to renewed service.

row.basis: God guides the addressee with counsel
row.note: The commentary pairs a leader going ahead with a follower prepared to move easily. The psalm promises instruction and guidance with God's eye on the addressee, giving the leader-follower relation a personal form.

row.basis: A horse needs bit and bridle to be guided
row.note: The commentary's horse image is easy to direct with a light touch. The psalm warns that horse or mule without understanding must be restrained by bit and bridle, a pointed difference about whether the follower is already docile.

row.basis: Running and walking continue without fainting
row.note: The commentary says divine ease does not cancel the journey or let the messenger stop working. Isaiah promises that those who wait for the Lord will run without weariness and walk without fainting, sustaining movement through exertion.

row.basis: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow his voice
row.note: The commentary develops a leader in front of a compliant follower who takes the road by its own steps. Jesus' shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow because they know his voice, an especially close image of guided following.

row.basis: The Father's Spirit speaks through the messenger
row.note: The commentary says the prophet's tongue is prepared for the word rather than speaking ahead of it. Jesus tells disciples that the Spirit of their Father speaks through them under trial, locating their speech in divine aid.

row.basis: Words are given at the hour of testimony
row.note: The commentary reads ease as preparation of the person who must speak. Jesus tells disciples not to worry beforehand about what to say when handed over, because the words will be given then; readiness replaces anxious self-provision.

row.basis: The Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to memory
row.note: The commentary places the promise beside recitation, not forgetting, and later reminding. Jesus says the Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of what he said, joining preparation of understanding to remembered speech.

row.basis: Paul reads Deuteronomy's near word as proclaimed faith
row.note: The commentary makes a prepared tongue the place where the received word becomes ready speech. Paul quotes Moses' word near the mouth and heart as the word of faith he proclaims, giving Deuteronomy's accessibility a Christian preaching interpretation.

row.basis: An easy yoke and light burden
row.note: The commentary says the load need not disappear for the walk to become easier. Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, giving a direct Christian image of carrying an obligation under eased conditions.

The commentary notes that easing another can mean treating that person gently, alongside preparing the traveler. Jesus calls himself gentle and humble in heart and invites disciples to learn from him under a yoke, linking gentleness with instruction.

row.basis: Jesus offers rest to the burdened
row.note: The commentary insists that ease for the messenger is not a rest: after the work, he is told to take up the next task. Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come for rest, making the contrast in what ease promises explicit.

row.basis: Wisdom's yoke is taken up for instruction
row.note: The commentary portrays the prophet as prepared to bear a continuing task. Ben Sira urges the learner to put the neck under Wisdom's yoke and receive instruction, a Jewish wisdom picture of accepting disciplined service.

row.basis: Labor leads to much rest in Wisdom
row.note: The commentary says ease does not mean rest but makes renewed work possible. Ben Sira says he labored little and found much rest in Wisdom, setting a wisdom-seeking outcome beside the commentary's continuing prophetic labor.

row.basis: The Torah's yoke displaces worldly burdens
row.note: The commentary says the messenger's work remains, though he is made able to carry it. The Mishnah teaches that taking Torah's yoke removes the yoke of worldly concerns, a Jewish account of religious obligation changing how other burdens are borne.

row.basis: Run the appointed race after laying aside weight
row.note: The commentary's light-footed traveler still keeps moving and takes up the next task. Hebrews tells runners to lay aside every weight and run with endurance the race set before them, joining bodily lightness to sustained service.

row.basis: Straight paths are made for weakened feet
row.note: The commentary stresses that the ayah prepares the traveler while leaving the road as it is. Hebrews tells the community to make straight paths for its feet so the lame may be healed, a complementary reversal in which the path is adjusted for the weak.

row.basis: The easy road leads to destruction
row.note: The commentary associates the easiest destination with God's favor and contrasts it with the hardest way. Jesus says the broad, easy road leads to destruction, directly reversing the moral value attached to ease.

row.basis: The hard way leads to life
row.note: The commentary reads divine preparation toward the easiest as a good gift. Jesus says the narrow, difficult way leads to life and few find it, making difficulty rather than ease the mark of the saving route.

The commentary presents the person as made ready for a task rather than freed from it. First John says God's commandments are not burdensome for those who love God, a Christian ethical formulation of obedience made bearable.

row.basis: Open the hand to the poor despite scarcity
row.note: The commentary says material ease is not itself the promised good and points instead to the person who gives. Deuteronomy commands an open hand and a loan to the needy, placing generosity rather than retained wealth at the center of faithful action.
The commentary describes the person made easy for the good path as one who gives wealth away. Deuteronomy says to give freely and not resent it, connecting inward readiness with concrete generosity.

row.basis: The rich man promises himself ease and rest
row.note: The commentary separates spiritual ease from wealth and from resting after labor. In Jesus' parable the rich man tells himself to take ease, eat, drink, and be merry because of his stores, showing the false security of material abundance.

row.basis: Stored wealth cannot protect the rich fool from death
row.note: The commentary says a person's money will not help when he falls and that worldly ease can prepare one for hardship. In the parable God demands the rich man's life that night, exposing the failure of his possessions to secure his future.

row.basis: Being rich toward God differs from storing for oneself
row.note: The commentary contrasts the giver with the person who counts himself self-sufficient. Jesus concludes that one who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God has misunderstood prosperity, sharpening the same ethical contrast.

row.basis: The lot's decision belongs to the Lord
row.note: The commentary contrasts meysir's chance allocation with the divine speaker who measures and prepares a person. Proverbs says a lot is cast but its decision is from the Lord, a direct counter-reading of lots as mere chance.

row.basis: Lots assign the two goats for the atonement rite
row.note: The commentary treats the camel-share game as condemned chance-taking. Leviticus uses lots to distinguish the goat for the Lord from the goat for Azazel, showing an Israelite ritual use of lots with sacred, ordered ends.

row.basis: Land is apportioned by lot before the Lord
row.note: The commentary contrasts shares left to drawn arrows with a divinely measured portion. Joshua casts lots at Shiloh before the Lord to distribute the land among Israel's clans, making allotment a public sacred act rather than gambling.

row.basis: The high priest draws lots for the goats
row.note: The commentary's meysir scene has arrows determine shares of a slaughtered animal. The Mishnah describes the high priest drawing lots between the goats for the Temple rite, a Jewish ritual counterpart that distinguishes sacred selection from a game of gain.

row.basis: A lot selects Matthias for apostolic service
row.note: The commentary contrasts arbitrary shares with a person prepared by God's agency. Acts reports that the community casts a lot to select Matthias for the apostolic office, a Christian use of lot to assign a vocation rather than divide winnings.

row.basis: Jesus' easy yoke is joined to gentle lordship
row.note: The commentary hears ease as both preparation and gentle treatment. This apocryphal Jesus saying joins an easy yoke to a gentle lordship, giving the gentleness implicit in the commentary's Arabic usage a distinct Christian witness; it also promises rest, which the commentary withholds.

row.basis: Rabbinic reading of Deuteronomy's accessible Torah
row.note: The commentary interprets ease as the messenger being made ready for the work. The Talmud reads Deuteronomy's word as neither in heaven nor across the sea but accessible to the learner, shifting the parallel from prophetic aptitude to the effort of Torah study.

row.basis: The Torah is no longer adjudicated in heaven
row.note: The commentary stresses that the divine "we" supplies and prepares the prophetic word. In the Oven of Akhnai story, rabbis invoke Deuteronomy's "not in heaven" to place legal interpretation with human sages, a contrasting Jewish account of who governs revealed speech.

row.basis: Affliction is light while apostolic work continues
row.note: The commentary says hardship is not erased, but the burden is made carryable and the messenger keeps working. Paul calls present affliction light in view of eternal glory, placing enduring labor and a changed measure of weight together.

row.basis: God knows a word before it reaches the tongue
row.note: The commentary says the one who eases the prophet knows what is hidden within him. The psalm says God knows the speaker's word before it is on his tongue, joining inward knowledge to speech before utterance.

row.basis: God's Spirit causes the people to walk in the statutes
row.note: The commentary's central distinction is that the traveler is made ready, not merely given a smoother road. Ezekiel promises God's Spirit within the people will cause them to walk in God's statutes, directly locating readiness in the walkers.

row.basis: A voice commands that the Lord's way be prepared
row.note: The commentary stresses that the ayah makes the person easy while the road remains. Isaiah instead commands preparation of the Lord's way in the wilderness, a precise contrast in what is readied.

row.basis: Valleys are raised and rough ground made level
row.note: The commentary says ease can be placed in the traveler's gait even when the route is difficult. Isaiah pictures the route itself being leveled, so the shared journey image makes the different means of easing clear.

row.basis: Luke applies Isaiah's prepared-way voice to John
row.note: The commentary contrasts preparing the traveler with smoothing the path. Luke quotes Isaiah's command to prepare the Lord's way as the setting for John the Baptist's preaching, making the voice of a prophet the means of preparing a route.

row.basis: Wisdom's instruction keeps the walk and run unhindered
row.note: The commentary says the messenger is made light-footed and ready for the way. Proverbs says the instructed person's step will not be hampered when walking or stumbling when running, linking guidance with unhindered movement.

row.basis: God gives the speaker a deer's feet for the heights
row.note: The commentary develops the image of a responsive mount with light legs that carries its rider over a route. The psalm says God makes the speaker's feet like a deer's and sets him on the heights, a close image of divinely enabled movement.

row.basis: God widens the space beneath the speaker's steps
row.note: The commentary says the road stays as it is while the traveler is made ready. The psalm credits God with widening the speaker's steps so his feet do not slip, bringing the contrasting image of the route itself made spacious.

row.basis: God gives deer-like feet on high places amid scarcity
row.note: The commentary's light-footed traveler can keep moving even when the route is steep. Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and enables him to tread on heights, in a passage that names famine and crop failure immediately before this trust.

row.basis: The messenger's feet carry news of peace and salvation
row.note: The commentary brings together the prophet's reminder and the image of light steps on a route. Isaiah praises the feet of the messenger who announces peace and salvation, joining movement to the work of proclamation.

row.basis: Paul applies Isaiah's beautiful feet to gospel proclamation
row.note: The commentary's prepared messenger is enabled to carry a reminder. Paul quotes Isaiah's messenger with beautiful feet to explain the sending of Christian preachers, giving the older restoration image an apostolic preaching interpretation.

row.basis: God equips the community to do God's will
row.note: The commentary reads ease as preparation of the person for continuing work. Hebrews asks God to equip the community with everything good for doing God's will and to work within them, a direct Christian formulation of inwardly enabled service.

row.basis: A cleansed vessel is prepared for every good work
row.note: The commentary hears “we will make you easy” as “we will prepare you” for the assigned task. Second Timothy describes a person as a vessel prepared for every good work, giving that secondary sense a concrete Christian counterpart.

row.basis: The good works are prepared for the believer to walk in
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the prophet himself is the direct object of preparation. Ephesians says God prepared the good works beforehand for believers to walk in, shifting preparation from the person to the course of action.

row.basis: The Lord who knows hearts is asked to choose a messenger
row.note: The commentary connects the promise of ease with the speaker's knowledge of what is hidden in a person. Before a lot selects an apostle, Acts addresses the Lord as the one who knows everyone's heart and asks him to show whom he has chosen.

row.basis: The Spirit gives the utterance that the disciples speak
row.note: The commentary says the messenger receives and follows a recitation supplied by God. At Pentecost the disciples speak as the Spirit gives them utterance, extending divinely enabled speech from one prophet to a gathered community.

row.basis: Soldiers cast lots to divide Jesus' garment
row.note: The commentary describes meysir as a game in which arrows assign portions of a slaughtered camel. John depicts soldiers using lots to divide Jesus' clothing, a concrete scene of chance allocation presented as an act of humiliation.

row.basis: The lot identifies Jonathan in a crisis
row.note: The commentary distinguishes gambling for shares from an outcome assigned by divine measure. Saul's lot falls on Jonathan while the people seek the cause of a military crisis, showing lots used to identify responsibility rather than to win a game.
The commentary makes inward reverent fear the condition for receiving the reminder; Isaiah says God regards the humble, contrite person who trembles at his word.

row.basis: hearing the Torah to learn fear
row.note: After the command to remind listeners, this assembly is told to hear and learn to fear YHWH, making reception of instruction a cultivated inner response.
Josiah's heart is tender and he humbles himself when he hears the judgment read; the response depends on the hearer's disposition, as the commentary says the reminder works in the one who fears.

row.basis: those fearing YHWH and a book of remembrance
row.note: Those who fear YHWH speak together, are heard, and have a memorial written before God; this joins the commentary's inward fear to its account of remembering and preserving what might otherwise be lost.
The stones recall Israel's crossing so peoples know YHWH's strong hand and Israel fears him always, concretely linking retained memory with reverent fear.

row.basis: remembering the wilderness and testing the heart
row.note: Israel is told to remember the wilderness way because the testing disclosed what was in its heart and whether it would keep the command; recollection and inward orientation meet as in the commentary.

row.basis: children hear and learn to fear
row.note: The children who have not known the Torah are to hear and learn fear of YHWH, showing that the decisive response is acquired by the hearer rather than inherited as a group label.

row.basis: Noah fears concerning what is not yet seen
row.note: Warned about events still unseen, Noah acts in reverent fear and saves his household; this gives a concrete instance of fear before sight prompting a timely response.

row.basis: word held fast in a good heart
row.note: The hearers with an honest, good heart hold the word fast and bear fruit with endurance, closely matching the commentary's claim that the listener, not the messenger, must take the reminder inwardly.

row.basis: the hearer who forgets versus the doer
row.note: James contrasts a hearer who forgets with one who perseveres in the law and acts; it makes explicit the commentary's movement from recovering what slipped away to a changed response.

row.basis: fear of God and doing righteousness in every nation
row.note: Peter says that in every nation the person who fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him, concretely shifting the criterion from ancestry to the inward posture and conduct emphasized in the commentary.

row.basis: fear, glory, judgment, and worship of the Creator
row.note: The angel commands fear of God and giving him glory because judgment has arrived, then calls for worship of the Creator; this joins reverence to creation and worship as the commentary's surah does.

The community is to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe; the next verse grounds this in God as consuming fire, giving the commentary's fear-to-prayer movement a concrete Christian formulation.

row.basis: fear of the one with authority after death
row.note: Jesus redirects fear from human killers to the one who has authority after death, specifying a future, unseen consequence where the Qur'anic verse leaves the object of fear unstated.

row.basis: the Spirit bringing Jesus' words to remembrance
row.note: Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of what he said; this parallels the commentary's concern with future recollection while locating its source in divine aid.

row.basis: remembering after the judgment has begun
row.note: Abraham tells the rich man to remember his former life after the chasm is fixed; the memory is real but cannot repair the missed opportunity, like the commentary's late remembrance after Gehenna is brought.
Peter makes provision for his readers to recall his teaching after his death, a specific case of a messenger's reminder becoming the hearer's future act of memory.

row.basis: remembering the prior saying after a reminder
row.note: At the tomb the women remember Jesus' earlier words after the messengers call them to remember; the scene distinguishes the spoken reminder from the hearers' act of recollection.

The disciples first fail to understand the events, then remember Jesus' words after his glorification; this supplies a delayed, retrospective counterpart to the commentary's expected near-future remembrance.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels the Arabic root ذ ك ر; Deuteronomy uses its Hebrew cognate זכר for remembering YHWH as the giver of Israel's power, recalling dependence rather than crediting oneself.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכרון
row.note: The commentary labels ذ ك ر for remembering; Joshua calls the stones a זכרון, a memorial of the crossing, so a retained sign carries the past forward and leads in verse 24 to fear.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary's Arabic root label is ذ ك ر; the psalm uses Hebrew זכר for remembering God's precepts and doing them, joining memory to enacted obedience.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Exodus uses Hebrew זכר of God remembering his covenant and responding to Israel's groaning, a divine answer that contrasts with the hearer's own work of recollection.

row.basis: fear of YHWH as the beginning of knowledge
row.note: Proverbs makes fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge and contrasts it with despising instruction; this links the commentary's knowledge-laden fear to readiness to receive a reminder.

row.basis: fear and turning from evil as wisdom
row.note: Job identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding, connecting reverence to both knowing and a changed course.

row.basis: fear placed before Israel to restrain sin
row.note: At Sinai Moses says the divine testing is meant to put fear before Israel so they do not sin; fear is an apprehension of divine presence that shapes what the hearer does.

row.basis: steadfast mercy toward those who fear YHWH
row.note: The psalm describes enduring mercy as belonging to those who fear YHWH, then the next verse describes covenant-keepers who remember his commands; the two verses join inward reverence to active remembrance.
The rulers are told to serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling, a concrete route from reverence to worship that complements the commentary's later movement toward prayer.
The psalm says forgiveness is with God so that he may be feared, reversing the commentary's main order of fear leading to remembrance and showing a distinct scriptural sequence.

row.basis: fear placed in hearts so they will not turn away
row.note: God promises to put fear in the people's hearts to keep them from turning away; this gives the disposition a divine source, sharpening the commentary's account of listener agency within God's will.

row.basis: lips honor while the heart is far away
row.note: Isaiah condemns a fear of God taught as human precept when the heart remains distant, a precise warning against treating outward religious speech as the inward fear that receives the reminder.

row.basis: fear and belief after Israel sees the deliverance
row.note: Israel sees YHWH's great power, then fears and believes; unlike the commentary's person who fears before seeing, this places fear after visible deliverance and makes the difference in timing clear.
The psalm warns those who forget God to consider their end before there is no rescuer; it concretizes the commentary's contrast between pursuing what has slipped away and suffering the loss of it.

row.basis: counsel and covenant knowledge for those who fear
row.note: The psalm says YHWH shares his counsel with those who fear him and makes his covenant known to them, linking reverence with knowledge rather than treating fear as uncomprehending panic.

row.basis: conduct in fear before the impartial judge
row.note: Peter tells believers to conduct themselves in fear during their exile because God judges each person's work impartially; the fear is tied to knowledge of a real future reckoning.

row.basis: holiness brought to completion in fear of God
row.note: Paul urges cleansing from defilement and completion of holiness in fear of God, connecting reverence to the purification that the commentary places after remembrance.

row.basis: working out salvation with fear and trembling
row.note: Paul calls the community to act with fear and trembling, then says God is at work in them; this holds human response together with divine action as the commentary does for the listener's open door.

row.basis: fear as the opposite of prideful self-assurance
row.note: Paul says branches were broken off through unbelief and warns the standing branch not to become proud but to fear; this gives a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no need to recover anything.

row.basis: fear of punishment cast out by perfected love
row.note: John says fear has to do with punishment and is cast out by perfected love; this distinguishes punitive dread from the commentary's reverential fear instead of making the two senses identical.

row.basis: remembering generations while fearing the Lord
row.note: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to look at generations past and asks who trusted him and was forsaken; remembered precedent supports trust, joining memory and reverence in one argument.
The Mishnah says wisdom endures when fear of sin precedes it; this directly parallels the commentary's ordering of an inward fear before the act of remembering and receiving instruction.

row.basis: wisdom and fear as reciprocal conditions
row.note: The Mishnah says that without wisdom there is no fear and without fear there is no wisdom, preserving both directions of the relationship that the commentary illustrates with fear leading to remembrance and remembrance sometimes awakening fear.

row.basis: what is in Heaven's hand and fear of Heaven
row.note: The Talmud says all is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven; the commentary, citing the Qur'anic qualification that remembrance depends on God's will, keeps the listener's response inside divine willing, making their accounts of agency diverge.

row.basis: fear of God distinguished from fear of the devil
row.note: Hermas urges fear of God and says this displaces fear of the devil, distinguishing reverent accountability from panic and giving a concrete early Christian account of fear directing conduct.

row.basis: forgetting the God who brought Israel out
row.note: After warning Israel to beware when full and settled, Moses says not to forget YHWH who brought them from Egypt; remembered rescue corrects self-sufficiency and grounds response to instruction.
Israel is warned not to forget YHWH by failing to keep his commands when prosperous, a concrete case where a hearer's inner memory determines whether the received teaching governs life.
The imagined heart says its own power made its wealth; this is a specific counterpart to the commentary's self-sufficient hearer who sees no lack and therefore has no reason to seek what was lost.

row.basis: fear expressed in walking, love, and service
row.note: Moses asks what YHWH requires and lists fearing him, walking his ways, loving and serving him, and keeping his commands; fear is an inward posture that issues in a whole course of action.
The angel says Abraham's fear of God is now known because he did not withhold his son; fear is disclosed by a concrete response, not a group identity or mere claim.

row.basis: fearing YHWH while walking without light
row.note: Isaiah describes the person who fears YHWH, obeys the servant's voice, and walks in darkness without light yet trusts God's name; this concretely joins fear, hearing, and trust before visible resolution.

row.basis: YHWH himself as the one to fear
row.note: Isaiah redirects fear toward the holy Lord of hosts; it supplies an explicit object for the commentary's deliberately uncompleted “whoever fears” and frames awe as response to the transcendent.

row.basis: the Creator's boundary for the sea
row.note: The sea's fixed limit is given as evidence of YHWH's power, followed by the question whether people will fear him; the created order grounds the reverence that the surah's opening creation signs also invite.

row.basis: failure to say in the heart, “let us fear”
row.note: Despite seasonal rain and harvest, the people do not say in their hearts that they should fear YHWH; this locates the missing response inwardly even when signs are present.
The purpose of teaching the next generation is that they set hope in God, do not forget his works, and keep his commands; this joins transmitted reminder, recovered memory, and action.

row.basis: source-commentary Arabic root label ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر; Psalm 78 uses Hebrew זכר when it says Israel did not remember God's hand or the day he redeemed them, a concrete use of the cognate for lost rescue-history.
Israel fails to remember a deliverance it experienced and therefore repeats distrust; this adds the commentary's point that forgetting can be a failure to pursue what was once known.
The speaker calls children to listen and promises to teach them the fear of YHWH, making reverence a learned response to instruction rather than an inherited label.

row.basis: hearers who tremble at the word under pressure
row.note: Isaiah addresses those who tremble at YHWH's word even as their own brothers cast them out; the verse shows reception of the word persisting when the surrounding community rejects them.

row.basis: seeking YHWH with trembling in the latter days
row.note: In the latter days Israel will seek YHWH and David their king and come trembling to YHWH and his goodness; fear is a movement toward seeking, not mere flight.

row.basis: hearing today without hardening the heart
row.note: The quotation warns its hearers that when they hear God's voice they must not harden their hearts; the immediate, personal response to a reminder is the point.

row.basis: the heard message failing to benefit
row.note: The wilderness generation heard good news but it did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this makes the commentary's distinction between a reminder passing across and being taken in explicit.

row.basis: reminder of rescue followed by destruction
row.note: Jude says he wants to remind readers who already know that the Lord saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed the unbelieving; memory of rescue becomes a warning about the response that follows.

row.basis: remember, repent, and do the first works
row.note: The church is told to remember its former state, repent, and do its first works, with removal of its lampstand threatened if it does not; recollection must become action while there is time.

row.basis: remembering what was received and heard
row.note: The church is told to remember what it received and heard, keep it, and repent, or the coming will be unexpected; this directly joins received speech, memory, vigilance, and a deadline.
Readers are told to remember earlier days after they were enlightened, when they endured public suffering; recollection strengthens present fidelity rather than serving as passive recall.
After Peter denies Jesus, the Lord's look makes him remember the prediction, and he weeps bitterly; this gives a precise, painful case of a warning remembered only after failure.

row.basis: mercy to those who fear God through generations
row.note: Mary says God's mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation, carrying the commentary's individual inner quality across time without making it an ethnic class.

row.basis: past events written as warnings for readers
row.note: Paul says Israel's events were written as warnings for those at the end of the ages; this makes scriptural memory a present admonition with consequences, like the commentary's reminder before judgment.

row.basis: command to remember the risen Christ
row.note: Paul directly commands Timothy to remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead; the verse gives a concrete Christian instance of remembered proclamation as the hearer's continuing task.

row.basis: remembering Jesus' words after the resurrection
row.note: After Jesus is raised, the disciples remember his saying about the temple and believe; the delay shows how an event can restore the meaning of a word previously heard.

Hebrews recalls that even Moses said he trembled with fear at the terrifying manifestation; it supplies a concrete bodily response to divine presence alongside the later call to worship with reverent awe.

Peter tells believers not to fear what their opponents fear or be troubled; this distinguishes reverence toward God from social intimidation, a useful limit on the commentary's broad language of fear.

row.basis: honoring Christ as holy in the heart
row.note: The next verse directs believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts; with 1 Peter 3:14, it specifies where fear and reverence are directed when human pressure is present.
After Ananias and Sapphira die, great fear comes upon the church and all who hear; this is a counter-sequence to fear before sight, showing fear arising after a judgment has become visible.

row.basis: heart closed against hearing and turning
row.note: Jesus cites people whose heart is dull and whose ears and eyes are closed lest they understand, turn, and be healed; this gives a specific account of refusal at the level of perception that blocks a reminder's effect.

Zechariah speaks of being rescued from enemies so that God's people may serve him without fear; the context makes this freedom from human threat, not the reverent fear of God in the commentary, a meaningful distinction.

row.basis: fear of the Lord as wisdom's beginning
row.note: Ben Sira calls fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom and associates it with the faithful; this places reverence at the start of understanding, complementing the commentary's link between knowing and fear.

row.basis: those fearing the Lord wait for mercy
row.note: Ben Sira tells those who fear the Lord to wait for his mercy and not turn aside; fear sustains a listener through delay rather than being only an immediate fright.

row.basis: fear of God taught as communal conduct
row.note: Clement urges the community to fear the Lord and to teach the young fear of God; this concretely extends the commentary's personal reception of reminder into instruction and conduct across a community.

row.note: Exodus opens with Moses seeing a bush aflame yet unconsumed, a fire that draws him toward revelation; the Qur'anic Moses likewise sees a fire while traveling, but the scene's signal leads into a different account of his call.

God calls Moses from within the burning bush after he approaches it; this makes nearness to fire the threshold of a divine summons, unlike the condemned person's inescapable entry into the great fire.
A pillar of fire leads Israel by night; it supplies the concrete scriptural counterpart to the commentary's distant fire as a route-finding sign, while its fire guides rather than consumes.
Joshua is called a brand snatched from fire amid Satan's accusation; the image sharply contrasts the commentary's person fixed in fire with one taken out of it by divine rebuke.

Isaiah shows the corpses of rebels where worm and fire do not cease; the next Qur'anic verse says the entrant neither dies nor lives, and Isaiah's corpses make the difference between the images worth keeping visible.

row.basis: Worm does not die; fire is not quenched
row.note: Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire for Gehenna; alongside the Qur'anic entrant who neither dies nor lives, this gives an explicit neighboring-scripture formulation of punishment beyond ordinary death.
The day burns arrogant evildoers like stubble and leaves neither root nor branch; this joins the commentary's great fire to pride and final judgment, not simply to a larger physical flame.

row.basis: Who can dwell with devouring fire?
row.note: Isaiah's sinners ask who can live with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; the question directly frames the commentary's defining issue of what kind of person can abide in fire.

The following verse answers Isaiah's question with the one who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, then promises secure dwelling; it contrasts the Qur'anic wicked person's entry with an upright person able to dwell near divine fire.
John's winnowing separates wheat into the barn and burns chaff with unquenchable fire; it makes the commentary's two groups after admonition concrete as a sorting whose result is different fates.

row.basis: Eternal fire assigned to the condemned
row.note: The king sends the cursed to eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; fire is the assigned end of a class identified in judgment, matching the commentary's person defined by his destination.
Jesus pairs eternal punishment with eternal life as the two outcomes of judgment; this sharpens the Qur'anic contrast between the fire-bound person and the other person who prospers and prays.

row.basis: A dead rich man suffers in flame
row.note: In the parable the rich man is dead yet conscious, tormented in flame and begging for water; it gives a specific image for enduring fiery suffering, while the Qur'anic following verse describes the state as neither death nor life.

row.basis: No crossing out of the place of torment
row.note: Abraham says a fixed chasm prevents passage between the places of comfort and torment; this supplies a concrete account of the fire-bound person's inability to leave, like the commentary's gloss that yaslâ entails remaining with the fire.

row.basis: Sodom as an example of eternal fire
row.note: Jude recalls Sodom and neighboring cities undergoing punishment of eternal fire; the shared judgment-by-fire story adds a scriptural precedent while the Qur'anic verse applies the fate to an unnamed individual.

An angel warns that anyone worshipping the beast and receiving its mark will drink God's wrath in fire and sulfur; the commentary's fire-as-identifying brand thus meets a text where allegiance-mark and fiery fate are explicitly joined.

row.basis: Smoke rises and the condemned have no rest
row.note: The smoke of torment rises forever and the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night; this makes the commentary's abiding in fire a specific unending condition.

row.basis: The lake of fire is called the second death
row.note: Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas the Qur'anic next verse says its entrant neither dies nor lives; the difference is a direct theological contrast in how fiery punishment is described.
Moses' song says divine anger kindles a fire that burns to Sheol below and consumes the land; its downward and encompassing reach gives a concrete cosmic scale to the commentary's great fire.
Moses calls Israel's God a consuming fire and a jealous God; this locates fire also in divine presence and judgment, not only in the condemned person's destination.

Hebrew צְלִי־אֵשׁ (roasted by fire), likely cognate with the source commentary's Arabic ص ل ي label, names Passover meat eaten at the meal; it preserves the cooking sense of the source's fire-verb family apart from punishment.
The proverb asks whether one can carry fire in the bosom without burning clothes; it gives a concrete counterpoint to controlled warming, showing that close contact with fire carries consequences.

row.basis: Walking on coals burns the feet
row.note: The proverb asks whether one can walk on hot coals without scorching the feet; it makes bodily exposure to fire the issue, rather than merely seeing or approaching a distant flame.

The priestly law commands that fire remain continually lit on the altar; this is a persistent sacred fire maintained in worship, distinct from the punitive fire in which the commentary's person remains.

row.basis: Refiner's fire tests who can stand
row.note: The messenger's coming is compared to a refiner's fire, with the question who can endure the day; it connects fire's severity to a test of the person rather than only to destruction.
The refiner sits to purify silver and the sons of Levi so they may offer rightly; this gives the commentary's metalworking fire a scriptural use that corrects and restores rather than merely burns.

row.basis: A fourth figure walks in the furnace
row.note: Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking unbound in the furnace, with a divine-looking fourth; fire becomes the setting of protected presence, contrary to the bound person's suffering in the great fire.

row.basis: The furnace does not burn the faithful
row.note: Onlookers find that the men's bodies were unharmed and not a hair singed; this particular deliverance shows fire's force can be withheld, complementing the commentary's distinct fire of blessing and warmth.

row.basis: Passing through fire without being burned
row.note: God promises Israel that when they walk through fire they will not be scorched; the image reverses the commentary's entrant who must bear the fire's full heat and cannot leave.

The Aramaic verse says Daniel kneels and prays three times daily; its צלי prayer verb is a cognate of the source commentary's prayer-form صَلَّى, while the commentary carefully distinguishes that prayer root from the fire-verb ص ل ي.

row.basis: Tested through fire and brought out
row.note: The psalm says the people passed through fire and water before God brought them into abundance; fire names an ordeal one can survive, matching the commentary's secondary sense of suffering a hard trial.
Paul says the Day will disclose each person's work because fire tests what sort it is; like the commentary's fire that makes a person's identity legible, this fire exposes what the person has made.
Paul says a person's work may burn and he suffer loss, though he himself is saved as through fire; this provides a sharply contrary outcome to the one who remains inside punitive fire.

row.basis: Faith tested as gold by fire
row.note: Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire; the metaphor supplies a specific trial-and-refinement sense for the commentary's claim that the fire-verb can name undergoing hardship.
Hebrews applies Moses' consuming-fire image to God; alongside the Qur'anic great fire, it keeps divine holiness and danger in view rather than treating fire only as a place.

row.basis: Sodom reduced to ashes as warning
row.note: Peter says God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and made them an example of what comes to the ungodly; this joins remembered fire judgment to present warning, as the commentary calls the fire itself an admonition.

Genesis Rabbah expands Abraham's story with Nimrod throwing him into a furnace and God rescuing him; the tradition makes fire a test that reveals fidelity and grants rescue, not simply an identity assigned by punishment.

row.basis: Gehenna's punishment has a stated limit
row.note: The Talmud describes some sinners as judged in Gehenna for twelve months, after which bodies are consumed and souls burned; this later Jewish account contrasts with the Qur'anic description of a state in which the entrant neither dies nor lives.

row.basis: Abraham's and Balaam's disciples inherit different ends
row.note: The Mishnah classifies disciples by their traits and assigns Abraham's disciples the world to come but Balaam's disciples Gehinnom; it gives a Jewish interpretive example of a person's defining way of life determining the destination.

row.basis: Furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest
row.note: 4 Ezra reveals the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest and delight; it concretely pairs fiery punishment with the other destiny, as the commentary's surrounding verses divide people into two outcomes.
Genesis narrates YHWH raining fire and sulfur on Sodom; Jude later calls the cities an example of eternal-fire punishment, while this passage supplies the Hebrew Bible's own concrete judgment scene.

Israel sees the divine glory on Sinai as a devouring fire; this makes fire a visible form of divine presence, complementing the commentary's contrast between punitive fire and the blessed fire at Moses' call.

row.basis: A sign on the houses protects from judgment
row.note: The blood is a sign on Israelite houses, which God sees and passes over; this gives the commentary's fire-as-mark/recognition image a scriptural case where a visible sign identifies whose house is spared.

row.basis: A mark distinguishes mourners from the doomed
row.note: The man in linen marks the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations before the others are struck; like the commentary's identifying brand, a mark makes a person's allegiance or conduct legible before judgment.

row.basis: A burning coal touches the prophet
row.note: A seraph takes a live coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's mouth; this gives fire a precise contact-and-marking image, but the contact initiates purification rather than punishment.

row.basis: Fire removes guilt rather than destroying
