Hebrews says the promised new covenant makes the first obsolete and near disappearance; this is a Christian example of revelation's covenantal form changing, adjacent to the commentary's discussion of replacing verses.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.162–164
row.note: Gregory reads Moses' ascent into cloud and darkness as a deeper knowledge of the God who cannot be seen; this Christian interpretation changes the commentary's sight-limit scene into a path of knowing through unseeing.

row.basis: Jacob says he saw God and lived
row.note: Jacob names Peniel because he saw God face to face and his life was spared, a specific counterpoint to the commentary's Moses scene; the opponent's identity and the meaning of seeing God remain ambiguous in Genesis.

Moses recalls Israel standing before a mountain of fire, cloud, and thick darkness; this is a specific Sinai setting beside the commentary's account of Moses and Israel confronting the limits of divine sight.
At Horeb Israel hears God's voice from the fire but sees no form; this makes the commentary's pairing of recited sound and restricted vision an explicit feature of the same revelation scene.
Moses repeats that Israel saw no form and therefore must not make an image; beside Q 7:143, this gives a distinct scriptural consequence of a theophany without visible form.

While the people stand at a distance, Moses approaches the thick darkness where God is; this makes hiddenness the setting of direct encounter, complementing the commentary's open/hidden knowledge pair.
The people hide their counsel in darkness and ask who sees them; this is a direct prophetic example of the concealment the commentary says cannot remove anything from divine knowledge.
The psalm asks whether the one who planted the ear cannot hear and the one who formed the eye cannot see; this joins the commentary's audible and visual forms of cehr to their divine source.
The psalm says YHWH knows human thoughts; this gives a concise counterpart to the commentary's hidden contents remaining known even when not voiced.
Hannah's song says YHWH is a God of knowledge who weighs actions; after her silent prayer, this connects the commentary's prayer scene to divine knowledge and judgment.

row.basis: elders think God does not see
row.note: In Ezekiel's vision, elders worship in hidden rooms and say YHWH does not see them; the scene supplies a concrete false belief that the commentary's open/hidden knowledge claim overturns.

row.basis: God knows what comes to mind
row.note: YHWH says He knows what comes into the people's minds; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's unspoken contents of the heart being within divine knowledge.
Ecclesiastes says God brings every work, including every hidden thing, into judgment; this extends the commentary's claim that hidden matters remain known to a concrete judgment scene.
A book of remembrance is written before YHWH for those who fear His name; this joins the commentary's linked themes of divine memory, recorded words, and the name invoked in worship.

row.basis: no one can hide from God
row.note: Sirach challenges the person who thinks they can be hidden from the Lord among the crowd; this gives a distinct wisdom-text setting for the commentary's claim that no concealed thing escapes divine awareness.

row.basis: secret almsgiving seen by the Father
row.note: Jesus says the Father sees charitable giving done in secret; this extends the commentary's open/hidden pair from prayer and recitation to a specific concealed ethical action.
Jesus says what is covered will be revealed and what is hidden will be known; this is a direct continuation of the commentary's claim that hiddenness does not mean disappearance from knowledge.
Jesus says people will answer for every careless word; this applies the commentary's claim about God's knowledge of speech to words that speakers might treat as unimportant.

row.basis: Spirit supplies the persecuted speaker's words
row.note: Jesus tells disciples not to prepare their defense because the Holy Spirit will give them what to say; this is a Christian counterpart to the commentary's insistence that prophetic speech is given rather than owned.

Peter says prophecy did not arise from human will, but people spoke from God as carried by the Holy Spirit; this directly parallels the commentary's claim that the messenger does not possess the source of recitation.

row.basis: God judges human secrets through Christ
row.note: Paul says God judges people's secrets through Christ; this gives a Christian judgment formulation for the hidden contents that the commentary says God knows.
Christ says He searches minds and hearts and repays each according to deeds; this joins inward knowledge to judgment, as the commentary's account of hidden matters does.
John sees the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds; this gives an apocalyptic record-and-disclosure counterpart to the commentary's claim that God counts what people forget.

At the temple dedication Solomon says YHWH has chosen to dwell in thick darkness; this supplies a distinct biblical way to pair God's presence with concealment beside the commentary's manifest/hidden knowledge.

Isaiah calls YHWH the God who hides Himself and Israel's Savior; this adds a biblical theme of divine hiddenness to the commentary's distinction between God being hidden from human sight and knowing what is hidden.
God gives Moses His name as a memorial through generations; this complements the commentary's claim that the divine name at the ayah's hinge belongs to worship and remembrance, not impersonal fate.

row.basis: Israel's confession of the one YHWH
row.note: The Shema names YHWH as Israel's one God; beside the commentary's emphasis on Allah's name at the exception clause, this gives a central Jewish liturgical confession to read alongside al-Fatiha.

row.basis: love YHWH with the whole heart
row.note: The Shema immediately commands love of YHWH with all heart, soul, and strength; this concretely joins the divine name to worshipful devotion as the commentary does.

row.basis: stones as a sign for future questions
row.note: Joshua sets stones as a sign so children will ask what they mean; this gives a concrete human use of visible markers beside the commentary's claim that God's knowledge does not need a sign.
The stones are to be a memorial for Israel; this shows a community using a visible sign to preserve memory, contrasting with the commentary's divine knowledge that needs no landmark.

The Mishnah says all is foreseen while freedom is granted; this is a specific Jewish formulation of the tension between divine knowing and human willing that the commentary resolves through God's will.

row.basis: all is in Heaven's hands except awe of Heaven
row.note: The Talmud places everything in Heaven's hands except reverence of Heaven; this gives a rabbinic boundary to divine sovereignty beside the commentary's claim that human plans and memory remain dependent on God's will.

row.basis: God works both willing and doing
row.note: Paul says God is at work in believers both to will and to act; this closely parallels the commentary's claim that even human willing depends on God.

row.basis: Peter remembers after Jesus looks at him
row.note: After the rooster, Jesus looks at Peter and Peter remembers Jesus' prediction; this gives a narrative instance of a forgotten word returning when the commentary says remembering follows forgetting.

row.basis: Moses, fire, and not being consumed
row.note: Exodus makes the burning bush blaze without being consumed; it supplies the same Moses-and-fire encounter against which the commentary distinguishes Moses receiving guidance near fire from the wretched person entering fire in 87:12–13.
Moses turns aside to inspect the blazing bush, giving a narrative counterpart to the commentary's distant fire that draws him into a way of guidance.
God calls Moses from the bush when he comes near; this is the fire-side encounter behind the commentary's sequence of fire, choice, and address.

row.basis: Moses chosen and sent against Pharaoh
row.note: At the bush God sends Moses to bring Israel from Egypt, a direct counterpart to the commentary's election at the fire and its later Pharaoh scene.
God's sign to the commissioned Moses is that Israel will worship God at the mountain, supplying a biblical fire-to-worship movement beside the commentary's prayer after election.
At the bush the revealed name is God's perpetual memorial, Hebrew zikhri; its Semitic cognate relation to the commentary's li-dhikri joins divine name and remembrance at the same Moses encounter.

row.basis: Fire that leads by the way
row.note: The night pillar of fire gives Israel light in order to travel, a concrete biblical meeting of fire, path, and divine guidance rather than fire as punishment.
Acts explicitly retells an angel appearing to Moses in a flame of a bush in the wilderness, preserving the scene around which the commentary gathers call and guidance.

row.basis: The bush appearance and Moses's sending
row.note: Stephen calls Moses the man sent by God as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared in the bush; it joins election at the fire to opposition from Egypt.

row.basis: The book of Moses at the bush
row.note: Jesus identifies the bush episode as a passage in the book of Moses, directly joining the commentary's final Moses pages to its opening fire encounter.
Pharaoh summons wise men and sorcerers to meet Moses, the Torah's direct setting for the commentary's later gathering of Moses, Pharaoh, and magicians.
The magicians' staffs become serpents but Aaron's staff swallows them; this supplies the contest which the commentary reads through the magicians' eventual refusal of Pharaoh.
When their art fails, the Egyptian magicians tell Pharaoh that the plague is God's finger; their recognition is a biblical counterpart to the commentary's magicians breaking with Pharaoh's claim.
Wisdom presents the Egyptian magic arts as shamed during the plague darkness, a Jewish expansion of the Moses-versus-magicians setting that makes magical competence fail before God's act.
The letter gives traditional names to men who opposed Moses, a Christian reception of the Egyptian-magician conflict that the commentary brings into the Pharaoh scene.

row.basis: Refusal to worship under a king's fire threat
row.note: The Judeans refuse the king's gods even when a furnace is threatened; the scene closely meets the commentary's prostrating magicians who reject a tyrant's finite authority.

row.basis: Entrants into fire who are unharmed
row.note: The king sees the furnace's entrants walking unhurt; its outcome stands in deliberate tension with the commentary's person who enters the great fire and neither dies nor lives.

row.basis: A ruler's limited power over life
row.note: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill only the body from God who judges finally; this clarifies the commentary's assertion that Pharaoh rules only this worldly life while God is more enduring.
Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son, a specific Christian reading of the choice the commentary places beside Pharaoh's transient rule.
Moses chooses ill-treatment with God's people rather than sin's temporary enjoyment, closely matching the commentary's preference between the near worldly life and what lasts.

row.basis: Egyptian treasure weighed against a future reward
row.note: Moses values reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looks to recompense; the verse gives the commentary's choice and permanence an explicitly Mosaic Christian form.

row.basis: A tyrant ends present life, God raises to lasting life
row.note: A tortured brother tells the king that he may dismiss them from present life but the King of the world will raise them to everlasting life, closely meeting Pharaoh's threat and the better enduring life.

row.basis: Mortal death and resurrection unto life
row.note: Another brother contrasts death at human hands with hope of resurrection and tells the tyrant he has no resurrection to life; it is a pointed counter-formulation to neither dying nor living in the fire.

row.basis: A governor's brief fire and future judgment
row.note: Polycarp answers a ruler's fire threat by contrasting a short-lived flame with future judgment; the martyr tradition sharpens the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's claimed lasting punishment and divine permanence.

row.basis: The Most High gives kingdoms to whom he wills
row.note: Daniel says the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them as he chooses, directly contesting Pharaoh's self-exalting authority and joining highness to election.

row.basis: A humbled king praises the Most High
row.note: After his humiliation, the king blesses and honors the Most High whose dominion endures; it reverses the commentary's tyrannical high claim with praise and lasting rule.
Isaiah's final spectacle of the unquenched fire and worm that does not die is a close Hebrew-Bible horizon for the commentary's great fire and suspended death-life.

row.basis: Christian citation of undying worm and unquenched fire
row.note: Mark preserves Isaiah's image for Gehenna, making an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire in which ordinary death does not bring release.

row.basis: People seek death but death flees
row.note: In Revelation's torment people long to die yet cannot find death; this is a particularly close formulation beside the commentary's neither-dying-nor-living fire.

row.basis: Furnace as testing rather than annihilation
row.note: The furnace tests silver and gold while God tests hearts, supplying the corrective operation of fire that the commentary sets beside fire as punishment.
The divine messenger sits as a refiner and purifier of silver; this gives a biblical analogue for the commentary's distinction between a fire that sets something right and a fire endured as ruin.

row.basis: Dross removed so silver becomes usable
row.note: Removing dross from silver leaves material for the smith, a precise counterpart to the commentary's furnace foam: what is waste departs while what is useful remains.

row.basis: Gold tested in fire and the righteous in humiliation
row.note: Sirach's fire-testing of gold supplies a Jewish wisdom formulation for the commentary's corrective fire, without making it identical to the punitive fire.

row.basis: Fire tests the quality of each work
row.note: Paul's fire reveals whether work endures, directly extending the commentary's fire, useful remainder, and lasting good into a Christian assessment of works.
Paul can describe a person whose work burns yet who is saved through fire; that different result makes a useful counterpoint to the commentary's condemned person inside the great fire.
Job says God established weight for wind and measured the waters, closely meeting the commentary's flood running in valleys according to measure.

row.basis: God measures the waters and creation
row.note: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in his hand and the cosmos by span, expanding the commentary's measuring scene from floodwater to ordered creation.

row.basis: All things arranged by measure, number, and weight
row.note: This Jewish wisdom formula directly parallels the commentary's repeated movement from measured water to a created order apportioned by God.

row.basis: Rain makes earth sprout and yield
row.note: Rain descends, waters the earth, and makes it bear seed and bread; it is the biblical side of the commentary's rain, pasture, cultivated field, and beneficial yield.

row.basis: Rain makes grass sprout in waste ground
row.note: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to spring up, a precise meeting of the commentary's rain-shaken earth and brought-forth pasture.

row.basis: God causes grass and cultivated vegetation to grow
row.note: The psalm distinguishes grass for animals and vegetation for human cultivation, furnishing a close biblical landscape for the commentary's pasture and worked soil.

row.basis: Fruitful tree by streams that does not wither
row.note: The water-planted tree bears fruit and does not wither, concretely supplies the commentary's useful, enduring side of water and vegetation.
The wicked are wind-driven chaff, a biblical residue image beside the commentary's flood-carried foam and dried pasture that do not remain.
Nations roar like waters but flee like chaff before wind; this joins rushing flood imagery to transient residue as the commentary does.
Water wears stone and sweeps away soil, a literal counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying off what has dried and become refuse.
Isaiah's grass and flower wither under divine breath, giving a close biblical form to the commentary's worldly life becoming dried pasture.

row.basis: God's word stands forever after grass withers
row.note: The word's permanence is set directly against withering grass, completing the commentary's contrast between transient vegetation and what remains.
First Peter reapplies the grass-and-fading-flower image to mortal human life, a Christian articulation of the commentary's worldly-life-as-grass scene.
The citation's next verse makes the Lord's word endure forever, matching the commentary's passage from drying life to an enduring word and future.

row.basis: Rain-drinking ground that yields a useful crop
row.note: Ground receives rain and produces a crop useful to its cultivators, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's worked field that grows and remains beneficial.
Ground producing thorns is rejected and ends in burning; it gives the commentary's neglected weed, field, and fire a sharply opposed agricultural outcome.

row.basis: Break fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
row.note: Jeremiah turns cultivation into moral exhortation, making a direct Jewish parallel for the commentary's ploughed field versus vegetation left to become waste.

row.basis: Sow righteousness and break fallow ground
row.note: Hosea links cultivated ground, righteousness, and a coming divine response, a close ethical field analogue to the commentary's falah-like salvation and lasting crop.
The carefully cultivated vineyard gives wild fruit instead of the expected crop; it adds a prophetic moral version of the commentary's contrast between worked land and uncontrolled growth.

row.basis: A harvested sheaf deliberately left for others
row.note: The forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow, concretely illuminating the commentary's claim that a field's produce has a due share left behind.

row.basis: Sowing for decay or eternal life
row.note: Sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to Spirit reaps eternal life, translating the commentary's worldly and afterlife fields into a moral agricultural choice.

row.basis: Doing good and reaping in due season
row.note: The promise that persistent good will reap at the proper time supplies a Christian counterpart to the commentary's lasting good that remains after the transient growth goes.
The parable preserves wheat while gathering weeds for burning, closely pairing the commentary's useful field, rejected vegetation, division, and fire.

row.basis: Unfruitful branch dries and is thrown into fire
row.note: A branch not abiding is dried, gathered, and burned, a concentrated Christian image for the commentary's dried vegetation and fire-bound outcome.
God forms the human from ground and breathes life into it, furnishing the body-and-earth side of the commentary's creating and fashioning pair.

row.basis: Skin, flesh, bones, and sinews fashioned
row.note: Job describes God clothing and knitting the body, a concrete biblical counterpart to the commentary's secondary sense of bodily and embryonic formation.

row.basis: Formed in the womb and appointed
row.note: Before forming Jeremiah in the womb God knows, consecrates, and appoints him; it joins formation, election, and a divine mission as the commentary does at Moses's fire.

row.basis: Maker from the womb who has chosen
row.note: Isaiah calls God the maker and former from the womb and names the chosen servant, an unusually close pairing for the commentary's crafted body and selection.

row.basis: A mortal shaped in a mother's womb
row.note: Wisdom describes ordinary human formation in the womb from earthly mortality, a Jewish literary counterpart to the commentary's womb-to-earth connection.

row.basis: The servant made a polished arrow
row.note: Isaiah's servant is made into a polished arrow and kept hidden; this supplies the crafted-arrow secondary sense which the commentary finds in the creation verb.

row.basis: Clay, potter, and work of God's hand
row.note: The potter-clay image gives the commentary's craft language a biblical body-and-maker analogy without reducing it to a lexical echo.

row.basis: Set apart from the womb and called
row.note: Paul describes being set apart from his mother's womb and called by grace, a Christian counterpart to formed life that is also chosen for a task.
Paul uses a potter making vessels for different purposes, joining divine fashioning to differentiated allotment in the way the commentary connects creation and choice.

row.basis: God guides the blind on an unknown path
row.note: God leads blind people on paths they do not know and turns darkness into light, a close biblical formulation for the commentary's measure-then-guidance and fire-path scene.
The proverb makes weights and measures God's work, supporting the commentary's secondary move from cosmic measuring to a just apportioned share.
God sprinkles clean water, cleanses Israel, and removes its idols, giving the commentary's purification and Abrahamic distance from idolatry a single biblical cleansing horizon.

row.basis: Proclaiming the divine name and ascribing greatness
row.note: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah counterpart to the commentary's praise of the exalted Lord and mention of the name.
The psalm calls for praise of YHWH's name because that name alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely meeting the commentary's name, praise, and highness.

row.basis: Abraham invokes El Elyon, God Most High
row.note: Abraham names YHWH El Elyon, God Most High; Hebrew elyon and the commentary's al-Ala share the highness root and join the title to Abraham named in 87:19.

row.basis: The high and lofty one revives the lowly
row.note: The high and lofty God dwells with the contrite in order to revive them, pairing the commentary's highness with its purified, responsive person rather than the arrogant ruler.
The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer hallows the Father's name, an explicit Christian prayer counterpart to the commentary's remembering the Lord's name and praying.
The secret belongs to God while what is revealed is for communal obedience, a precise Torah counterpart to the commentary's hidden divine matter and disclosed teaching.

row.basis: God knows and reveals hidden things
row.note: Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness, closely meeting the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

row.basis: Do not forget the revelation and teach it
row.note: Israel must guard itself from forgetting what it saw and make it known to children, directly paralleling the commentary's word gathered, not forgotten, and offered as reminder.

row.basis: Write and teach the song as a witness
row.note: God tells Moses to write a song, teach it, and put it in Israel's mouths; it supplies a Mosaic written-and-remembered form for the commentary's recitation and warning.

row.basis: A song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The divinely given song will not be forgotten from descendants, a particularly close biblical analogue to the commentary's not-forgetting and enduring instruction.

row.basis: Book in the mouth and continual meditation
row.note: Joshua is told not to let the Torah book depart from his mouth but to meditate on it day and night, matching the commentary's preserved speech, remembrance, and practice.
The Mishnah applies Deuteronomy's warning to the deliberate forgetting of a learned word; it is a Jewish interpretive intensification of the commentary's not-forgetting motif.

row.basis: Not a forgetful hearer but a doer
row.note: James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the persevering doer of the perfect law, directly pairing the commentary's reminder with its division between response and avoidance.

row.basis: Life and good set against death and evil
row.note: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil, a Torah form of the two human outcomes the commentary traces from reminder through fire and purification.
The call to choose life gives explicit Mosaic form to the commentary's language of preference and its contrast between the near life and what truly endures.
Daniel's awakening divides people between everlasting life and enduring disgrace, furnishing a biblical future horizon for the commentary's high ranks and great fire.

row.basis: This world as corridor before the world to come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come, a precise rabbinic frame for the commentary's worldly life versus the later, enduring life.

row.basis: Good deeds here and bliss in the world to come
row.note: The saying weighs repentance and good deeds in this world together with the incomparable bliss of the world to come, closely mapping the commentary's earthly choice and better permanence.

row.basis: Seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary visible with the eternal unseen, giving the commentary's dunya-versus-lasting formulation a close Christian analogue.

row.basis: The world passes, the doer remains
row.note: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, directly matching the commentary's transient life and lasting good.
The final separation gives the two groups eternal punishment or eternal life, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's split between fire and the purified, praying person.
The righteous are in God's hand and no torment touches them, providing a Jewish wisdom contrast to the commentary's person destined for the great fire.

row.basis: Furnace of torment opposed to a place of rest
row.note: The apocalyptic vision displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest, a Jewish eschatological pairing for the commentary's fire and enduring differentiated outcome.

row.basis: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
row.note: Moses writes the divine words after Sinai, a direct Torah antecedent for the commentary's closing appeal to Moses's early pages.

row.basis: The written book of the covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses reads the book of the covenant to the people, bringing written pages together with recitation and hearing as in the commentary's preserved reminder.

row.basis: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
row.note: The verse explicitly depicts Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, the clearest canonical textual counterpart to Moses's pages in 87:19.
The Talmud's statement that Moses wrote his book is a Jewish reception of Mosaic textual authority relevant to the commentary's named pages of Moses.

row.basis: A restored corpus of revealed books
row.note: Ezra's scribes complete ninety-four books after the law's loss, a Jewish apocalyptic meditation on preserving and differentiating former sacred writings.

row.basis: Abraham keeps charge, commandments, statutes, and laws
row.note: Genesis attributes comprehensive obedience to Abraham, giving canonical footing for the commentary's Abrahamic former-scripture claim without assuming a canonical Abraham book.

row.basis: Abraham observed Torah before its giving
row.note: The Talmud reads Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's fulfillment of the whole Torah before Sinai, a major Jewish interpretation beside the commentary's Abrahamic pages.

row.basis: Jesus says Moses wrote of him
row.note: Jesus grounds his appeal in Moses's writing, a Christian interpretation of Mosaic pages that belongs beside the commentary's appeal to Moses as an earlier written authority.
Paul personifies Scripture as announcing blessing beforehand to Abraham, a Christian rereading that makes Abraham a recipient of prior scriptural proclamation.
Joshua locates Abraham's family beyond the river among worshippers of other gods, supplying canonical background for the commentary's Abrahamic plea to be kept from idols.
God takes Abraham from beyond the river and leads him through Canaan, matching the commentary's Abrahamic selection and its wider path-and-guidance movement.

row.basis: Put away foreign gods and serve YHWH
row.note: In the Abrahamic ancestral context Joshua calls Israel to remove foreign gods and serve YHWH, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's avoidance of idols.
Joshua's demand to choose service of YHWH or other gods makes the commentary's preference theme concrete at the point of idolatry.

row.basis: Abraham's idol challenge and the furnace
row.note: The midrash has Abraham reject idols and be cast into Nimrod's furnace, a Jewish expansion that tightly joins the commentary's Abrahamic anti-idolatry with its repeated fire scenes.

row.basis: Abraham obeys a call into an unknown destination
row.note: Abraham obeys and goes out without knowing his destination, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic trust, calling, and path imagery.

row.basis: A voice heard from the middle of fire
row.note: Israel hears God's voice from fire but sees no form; this provides a wider Sinai form of the commentary's fire as a place of speech and revelation.

row.basis: The day and hour known only to the Father
row.note: Jesus says the decisive day and hour are known to the Father alone, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's divinely concealed hour.

row.basis: Times and seasons fixed by the Father's authority
row.note: Jesus withholds the times and seasons as the Father's own domain, complementing the commentary's hidden temporal decree without claiming the same formulation.
Jesus commands the meal to be done in his remembrance; its explicit liturgical remembering is a Christian parallel to the commentary's fire-side prayer for remembrance.
Former practitioners publicly burn their magical books after confession, a later Christian scene of renouncing magic that complements the commentary's converted magicians without repeating its plot.

row.basis: A ruler aspiring to be like the Most High
row.note: The arrogant ruler seeks equality with the Most High, a non-Pharaoh biblical analogue for the commentary's additional Pharaoh claim to supreme height.

row.basis: Lake of fire called the second death
row.note: Revelation names the fiery lake the second death; its wording supplies a deliberate Christian contrast to the commentary's fire in which death and life are both denied.

row.basis: Faith tested as gold by fire
row.note: The letter compares tested faith to gold proved by fire, a Christian refinement image for the commentary's corrective fire and enduring value.

row.basis: The rich person fading like grass's flower
row.note: James uses scorched grass and fallen flower for the rich person's passing career, a specific Christian application of the commentary's worldly-life-as-drying-vegetation image.
The wicked are like a turbulent sea that throws up mire, a related prophetic water-and-waste image beside the commentary's flood-borne scum; the material correspondence is indirect.

row.basis: Following the light on the way to life
row.note: Jesus promises that followers of the world's light will not walk in darkness but have life's light; it is a Christian path-and-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought for guidance.

row.basis: Cleansed bodies and drawing near in worship
row.note: The faithful draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed, joining purification and worship as the commentary joins tazkiya, name-remembrance, and prayer.
Grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, a Christian individual-allotment image relevant to the commentary's move from measuring to portioning.

row.basis: A measure of faith allotted by God
row.note: God assigns each person a measure of faith, supplying another specific Christian use of divinely apportioned measure beside the commentary's qadar imagery.

row.basis: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath
row.note: Acts describes Moses as publicly read in every city from ancient generations, a Christian witness to the continuing recitation of the Mosaic writings invoked by the commentary.

row.basis: The song of Moses as praise
row.note: The heavenly worshippers sing the song of Moses in praise of God's great works, a Christian liturgical meeting of Moses, praise, and enduring divine rule.

row.basis: Receiving an unshakable kingdom and offering worship
row.note: The community receives an unshakable kingdom and offers acceptable worship with awe, a Christian framing for the commentary's worship and permanence after transient life.

row.basis: Abraham and the priest of God Most High
row.note: Hebrews names Melchizedek priest of God Most High in his encounter with Abraham, a Christian reuse of the highness title alongside Abraham; it is a title-and-scene meeting rather than a shared story.

row.basis: Abraham named God's friend and chosen lineage
row.note: Isaiah calls Israel the offspring of Abraham God's friend and the chosen servant, supporting the commentary's pairing of Abraham, election, and earlier divine promise.

row.basis: Abraham's early confrontation with household idols
row.note: The opening idol episodes are commonly cited for Abraham's testing and rejection of Terah's idols and fire-associated separation; the exact internal sequence should be verified, but it is a specific expansion of the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.

row.ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.20–21
row.basis: The unconsumed bush in Christian typology
row.note: In the burning-bush interpretation commonly placed in these sections, Gregory reads the bush's non-consumption through later Christian typology; the section numbering should be checked, but it is a concrete reception of the fire detail central to the commentary.
At the same fire God identifies himself by name before Moses's mission; it directly accompanies the source context of Q20:14, where prayer and remembrance follow God's self-declaration.
Moses may not approach casually and must remove his sandals because the fire-side ground is holy, adding a concrete bodily response to the commentary's fire that becomes election and worship.
Moses receives the staff with which he will perform signs, supplying the Torah's concrete bridge from the bush commission to the commentary's staff-and-magicians scene.

row.basis: Elijah's prayer to the God of Abraham at a fire contest
row.note: Elijah invokes the God of Abraham before the altar fire and asks that Israel know God and his servant; it joins fire, Abraham, divine name, and a public contest of allegiance.
The fire of YHWH falls on Elijah's offering, furnishing a Hebrew-Bible fire scene whose purpose is revelation and correction rather than the destruction of a condemned person.

row.basis: People fall on their faces and confess God
row.note: After the fire the people prostrate themselves and confess YHWH as God, a close narrative meeting of fire, praise, and bowing with the commentary's magicians' prostration.
At the temple dedication fire descends and God's glory fills the house, a further biblical scene in which fire marks divine presence rather than entry into punitive fire.

row.basis: Bowing and praise after the fire
row.note: Seeing the fire and glory, Israel bows and gives thanks for God's enduring steadfast love; it closely combines the commentary's fire, praise, prostration, and permanence.

row.basis: Write a memorial in a book and rehearse it
row.note: God tells Moses to write the event as a memorial in a book and place it in Joshua's hearing, directly joining Mosaic pages with remembrance and spoken teaching.

row.basis: Moses commanded to write covenant words
row.note: Moses is told to write the covenant words, another explicit Torah source for the commentary's final appeal to earlier Mosaic pages.

row.basis: A written Torah copy read throughout life
row.note: The king must write a Torah copy and keep it for continual reading and fear of God, a precise model of page, remembrance, obedience, and durable instruction.

row.basis: The Torah book kept as witness
row.note: The written Torah is placed beside the ark as a witness, giving the commentary's named Mosaic pages a preserved and judicial function.

row.basis: Moses records the stages of the journey
row.note: Moses writes Israel's journey-stages at God's command, meeting the commentary's scrolls with its fire-and-path movement.

row.basis: Book of remembrance for those who fear and esteem the name
row.note: A book of remembrance is written for God-fearers who honor the divine name, tightly joining the commentary's reminder, fearer, name, and earlier pages.

row.basis: Words shut up and book sealed until the end
row.note: Daniel is told to close the words and seal the book until the time of the end, a direct biblical combination of hidden end-time knowledge and written pages.

row.basis: Many purified and refined, while the wicked do not understand
row.note: The end-time division has many made pure and refined while the wicked continue blindly; it closely meets the commentary's tazkiya, reminder, and divided response.

row.basis: Those guiding many to righteousness shine forever
row.note: The wise shine and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars forever, a biblical counterpart to guidance, high degrees, and lasting reward.

row.basis: Write the vision so a reader may run
row.note: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader in motion, a specific meeting of the commentary's pages, public reminder, and path imagery.

row.basis: A vision for an appointed end that must be awaited
row.note: The vision has an appointed time and may seem slow but will come, a close prophetic analogue to the commentary's concealed decisive hour.

row.basis: Word as lamp for foot and light for path
row.note: The word gives a lamp and path-light, supplying a biblical verbal-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought as guidance.

row.basis: Command as lamp and teaching as light on life's way
row.note: The commandment is a lamp, teaching a light, and reproofs a way of life; it joins reminder, guidance, and life in terms specific to the commentary's movement.

row.basis: Walking through darkness by God's lamp
row.note: Job recalls walking through darkness by God's shining lamp, a concrete light-and-way image alongside the commentary's fire sought for a guide.

row.basis: Prayer to the Father who sees in secret
row.note: Jesus places prayer in the hidden room before the Father who sees in secret, directly combining the commentary's prayer-for-remembrance with its hidden divine knowledge.
All creatures are exposed before the God to whom account is given, a direct Christian formulation for the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

row.basis: Hidden things brought to light at judgment
row.note: God will disclose hidden things of darkness and heart-motives, giving a judgmental sequel to the commentary's hidden matter and differentiated outcomes.

row.basis: No one can hide beyond God's sight
row.note: The prophet asks whether anyone can hide in secret places from the God who fills heaven and earth, closely matching the commentary's claim of divine knowledge of the hidden.

row.basis: Hearing and doing words builds on rock
row.note: The person who hears Jesus's words and does them is likened to a wise builder, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's beneficial admonition.

row.basis: Rain and floods fail to overthrow the founded house
row.note: Rain, flood, and wind strike the rock-founded house but it remains, directly meeting the commentary's flood and the contrast between what goes away and what remains.

row.basis: Hearing without doing builds on sand
row.note: The hearer who does not act on the words builds on sand, providing a counterpart to the commentary's person who avoids the reminder.

row.basis: Flood destroys the house with no foundation
row.note: Rain and floods bring a great fall to the sand-founded house, completing the commentary's water-borne testing and opposed human outcomes.

row.basis: Refined in the furnace of affliction
row.note: God refines Israel in an affliction-furnace, an explicit prophetic development of the commentary's fire as corrective work rather than only punishment.

row.basis: A remnant refined by fire and calling God's name
row.note: God brings a remnant through fire, refines it, and answers when it calls the divine name, closely coupling fire, purification, name, and responsive relationship.

row.basis: Fire consumes stubble because teaching is rejected
row.note: Fire devours stubble and dry grass because people reject God's teaching, a very close prophetic fusion of dried vegetation, fire, and refusal of reminder.
The divine word is likened to fire and a hammer, supporting the commentary's movement from recited reminder to a fire that actively corrects.
Hebrews names God a consuming fire in a worship context, a concise Christian meeting of the commentary's divine fire, awe, and praise.

row.basis: Saving someone by snatching them from fire
row.note: Jude distinguishes rescuing people from fire from sharing their defilement, a concrete Christian complement to the commentary's concern with approaching versus entering fire.

row.basis: Wheat gathered and chaff burned with unquenchable fire
row.note: The coming judge stores wheat but burns chaff, tightly combining the commentary's useful remainder, agricultural waste, human division, and great fire.

row.basis: Fruit-bearing branches pruned for greater fruit
row.note: The grower prunes fruitful branches so they bear more fruit, supplying the corrective cultivation missing from the dried-and-burned branch image already developed by the commentary.

row.basis: Earth commanded to bring forth vegetation
row.note: Creation begins with the earth bringing forth seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees, an immediate Torah counterpart to the commentary's Creator bringing forth pasture.

row.basis: Rain, field growth, and a worker for the ground
row.note: Before cultivated plants appear, the text notes both the absence of rain and of a human to work the soil, closely joining the commentary's rain, earth, body, and cultivated field.

row.basis: Seasonal rain producing land-yield and field fruit
row.note: God's rain gives land its yield and trees their fruit, a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's rain-fed field and lasting useful produce.

row.basis: Teaching falling like rain on grass
row.note: Moses compares teaching to rain, dew, and showers on tender grass, directly connecting the commentary's reminder to its water-and-pasture landscape.
The renewed descendants spring up among grass like trees by water, a close prophetic image for the commentary's watered growth instead of dried refuse.

row.basis: Earth and garden making righteousness and praise sprout
row.note: As earth makes sprouts grow, God makes righteousness and praise grow, joining the commentary's cultivated field to purification and praise.

row.basis: Created things wear out but salvation lasts forever
row.note: Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation and righteousness endure; this closely matches the commentary's temporary worldly life and better permanence.

row.basis: Arabic mar'a and Hebrew mir'eh for pasture
row.note: Ezekiel depicts God feeding Israel in good pasture, Hebrew mir'eh, cognate with the commentary's Arabic mar'a; it turns the shared pasture image toward sustained divine shepherding.

row.basis: Arabic tazakka and Hebrew yizkeh around purity
row.note: Job asks how a human, including one born of woman, can be pure, using Hebrew yizkeh from the z-k-y root cognate with the commentary's tazakka; its setting adds bodily finitude to purification.

row.basis: Arabic hayat and Hebrew hayyim in the command to choose life
row.note: Beyond the existing choice motif, the Hebrew command choose hayyim and the commentary's hayat are cognate life terms; the verse grounds its life-choice in an explicit Semitic formulation.

row.basis: Praise offered with lips confessing God's name
row.note: The community continually offers praise to God as the fruit of lips acknowledging the name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to the commentary's name, praise, and prayer.

row.basis: Prayers ascending as a memorial before God
row.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, a specific Christian use of prayer and remembrance that complements the commentary's li-dhikri.
Those who hold the eschatological hope purify themselves, a compact Christian parallel to the commentary's purified person oriented toward the enduring future.

row.basis: Draw near, cleanse hands, and purify hearts
row.note: James pairs drawing near to God with cleansing and a divided heart's purification, directly meeting the commentary's tazkiya and worshipful response.

row.basis: Holy ones of the Most High possess an everlasting kingdom
row.note: The holy ones of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom forever, a direct biblical meeting of highestness, elevated status, and permanence.

row.basis: Everlasting kingdom given to the people of the Most High
row.note: All dominions serve the holy people whose kingdom endures, answering the commentary's tyrant's temporary rule with lasting high rule under God.

row.basis: A ruler claims divinity and is answered that he is mortal
row.note: The ruler of Tyre claims to sit as a god but is told he is human, a close prophetic counter-scene for the commentary's Pharaoh claiming supreme status.

row.basis: Hearing the word passes from death into life
row.note: The one who hears and believes has eternal life and has crossed from death to life, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's fire-bound non-life and purified alternative.

row.basis: Present goods reversed into future comfort and anguish
row.note: Abraham contrasts the rich man's received good things in life with his later anguish and Lazarus's comfort, closely framing the commentary's worldly preference and later permanence.
The broad gate and way end in destruction, providing a Christian path-and-outcome counterpart to the commentary's guidance, choice, and fire.
The difficult way leads to life and few find it, sharpening the commentary's sought guidance and its contrast between life-oriented response and loss.
Revelation's renewed world abolishes death, mourning, and pain; its eschatological endpoint gives a Christian counter-horizon to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life occurs.

row.basis: Righteous enjoying divine radiance in the world to come
row.note: The Talmud's world-to-come scene gives the righteous crowns and enjoyment of divine radiance, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to enduring high degrees rather than temporary worldly life.

row.basis: God reveals a secret to prophetic servants
row.note: Amos says God discloses the divine secret to prophets, a specific prophetic counterpart to the commentary's hidden matter becoming disclosed guidance.

row.basis: Melchizedek as priest of God Most High blessing Abraham
row.note: The priestly blessing names God Most High in an Abraham scene, supplying the canonical context for the highness title already central to the commentary's first and last images.

row.basis: A name highly exalted above every name
row.note: God highly exalts a name above every name, a Christian reapplication of name-and-highness that is relevant to the commentary's praise of the highest Lord but does not share its speaker.

row.basis: Every knee bends at the exalted name
row.note: The universal bending of knees at the name gives a Christian liturgical analogue to the commentary's prostration and exalted name, with a different christological setting.

row.basis: Green marsh plant withering before other growth
row.note: A water-dependent plant withers while still green, a specific wisdom image for the commentary's pasture turning into waste; the water setting differs from its valley flood.

row.basis: Floodwaters sweep away a false refuge
row.note: Hail and overflowing waters expose a refuge made of falsehood, a prophetic water judgment that complements the commentary's flood separating what vanishes from what remains.

row.basis: Weeds gathered and burned at the age's end
row.note: Jesus explains the weed-and-fire image as an end-time sorting, a necessary interpretive continuation of the field scene and the commentary's future fire.

row.basis: Righteous shining in their Father's kingdom
row.note: The righteous shine in the kingdom after the furnace judgment, a Christian continuation that meets the commentary's high degrees and lasting reward.

row.basis: Abraham chosen to command his household in righteousness
row.note: God says Abraham is known so that he will direct his household in God's way of righteousness and justice, adding a canonical Abrahamic election-and-teaching counterpart to the former-pages claim.

These verses are commonly associated with young Abram's recognition of the earth's error in following carved images and his prayer for deliverance; exact wording and division should be verified, but the link is a specific Jewish precursor to the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.

row.note: The commentary treats "glorify the Name" as keeping it from misuse; Leviticus directly forbids profaning YHWH's holy Name and requires that it be sanctified among Israel.
Ezekiel's restoration turns on God vindicating and sanctifying the great Name Israel profaned among the nations, a concrete public counterpart to guarding the Name.
The psalm calls all creatures to praise YHWH's Name because that Name alone is exalted and its majesty is above earth and heaven, joining the commentary's Name and height.
Isaiah names God the high and lofty one whose Name is Holy, supplying a compact Hebrew Bible counterpart to "the Most High" and the purified Name.

row.basis: Name praised from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary distributes praise across the day; this verse makes the praise of YHWH's Name run from sunrise to sunset.

row.basis: YHWH high above, glory above heavens
row.note: The psalm's high YHWH and glory above the heavens give a specific biblical pairing for the Lord's incomparable height.
The commentary distinguishes protecting the divine Name from merely uttering it; the commandment forbids bearing YHWH's Name for emptiness.
The Arabic ism in 87:1 is cognate with Hebrew šēm; at Moses' call God gives the enduring divine Name to be remembered through generations.
The commentary excludes rival claimants from the Name; YHWH says "this is my Name" and refuses to give his glory or praise to idols.
The commentary's no-rival reading of the Name meets Zechariah's eschatological formula that YHWH will be one and his Name one.
Isaiah asks whom God can be likened or made equal to, giving a direct biblical analogue to the commentary's no namesake, peer, or competitor.
The Arabic height root in al-a'la corresponds to Hebrew Elyon; Abraham invokes YHWH as God Most High, maker of heaven and earth.

row.basis: claim to be like the Most High
row.note: The boast to ascend above the clouds and resemble Elyon is the self-exalting reversal of the commentary's insistence that the highest lordship cannot be seized.

row.basis: tower to heaven, make a name
row.note: The builders seek a tower reaching heaven and a name for themselves, a concrete negative counterpart to a Name exalted by God rather than self-appropriated.
God promises to make Abraham's name great, sharpening the commentary's contrast between bestowed elevation and a ruler's self-exaltation.
The commentary's Moses is sent to Pharaoh; the call narrative likewise commissions Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt through Pharaoh.
Moses protests that he is slow of speech, the biblical narrative behind the commentary's request for an eased mission and opened speech.
God answers Moses by promising to be with his mouth and teach him what to speak, closely matching a messenger enabled before addressing others.
Aaron is made Moses' speaking partner and God promises instruction for both, paralleling the commentary's emphasis on Moses asking that his brother share the work.
Pharaoh's "Who is YHWH?" and refusal to obey make a biblical counterpart to the commentary's Pharaoh who rejects the lordship offered to him.

row.basis: Pharaoh exalts himself against the people
row.note: The plague narrative explicitly charges Pharaoh with exalting himself against God's people, matching the commentary's analysis of oppressive elevation.
The later oracle has Pharaoh claim the Nile as his own creation, another biblical portrait of pharaonic self-appropriation of divine prerogative.
Herod receives the crowd's cry that his voice is a god's, supplying a precise Christian example of a ruler being placed in the divine position.
The immediate judgment of Herod for not giving glory to God gives the consequence that the preceding divine acclamation lacks.
The commentary treats tasbih as excluding child-attribution to God; John places God's giving of the only Son at the center of its proclamation.

row.basis: Mary, Jesus, and Son of God
row.note: Luke calls the child born of Mary the Son of God, providing the New Testament's own coordinate for the Jesus-and-Mary issue raised in the commentary.

row.basis: the one Name and Father, Son, Spirit
row.note: The baptismal command uses the singular Name for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian Name formula that differs from the commentary's non-distribution of divine appellation.
Against the commentary's self-seizing Pharaoh, Christ does not treat equality with God as something to grasp, making humility integral to the later exaltation.
God highly exalts Jesus and grants the Name above every name; this closely meets the commentary's Name-and-height language while assigning it christologically.

row.basis: Jesus confessed Lord to God's glory
row.note: The universal confession of Jesus Christ as Lord is explicitly for the glory of God the Father, a Christian allocation of lordship beside the commentary's rejection of rival lords.
Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as Lord and God, the clearest New Testament counterpoint to the commentary's treatment of creaturely claims to divinity.
Luke gives Mary a prayer that magnifies the Lord, rather than a self-exaltation, which is essential context for the commentary's Mary-and-divinity scene.
Mary rejoices in God her Savior; this neighboring claim makes her own orientation to God explicit in contrast with her being imagined as a deity.
The commentary calls rival divine names empty claims; Paul says an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God except one.
Paul acknowledges the vocabulary of many so-called gods and lords, the exact plural field against which the commentary sets one true Lord.
Paul's one-God/one-Lord confession assigns "one Lord" to Jesus Christ, a sharply relevant Christian reconfiguration of the commentary's exclusive lordship.
The angel rejects John's prostration and commands worship of God, concretely enacting the commentary's return of worship from a creature to God.
The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer asks that the Father's Name be hallowed, a direct liturgical analogue to treating the Name as the object of sanctification.
Jesus' petition makes glorifying God's Name an explicit address to the Father, closely matching the commentary's imperative toward the Name.

row.basis: glorifying the Name, God alone holy
row.note: The heavenly song asks who will not glorify God's Name and calls him alone holy, bringing together purity, worship, and unmatched divinity.
This eucharistic thanksgiving thanks the holy Father for his holy Name made to dwell in believers' hearts, an early Christian liturgical development of the Name motif.
The priestly blessing ends with God placing his Name on Israel; it gives a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's Name as a marking claim of belonging.
Isaiah imagines persons writing "YHWH's" on the hand and taking Israel's name, a close textual meeting of name, inscription, and owned identity.

row.basis: Lamb's and Father's Names on foreheads
row.note: Revelation makes the brand image explicit: the redeemed bear both the Lamb's Name and the Father's Name on their foreheads.
The beast's mark and name control allegiance and commerce, a deliberate inverse to the commentary's claim that the divine Name must not be transferred to a false claimant.
The final vision joins seeing God's face with his Name written on servants' foreheads, a striking counterpart to the commentary's linked discussions of face, Name, and mark.
God brings living creatures to Adam so that Adam names them, the biblical scene most directly beside the commentary's Adam, names, and creaturely knowledge.
This midrash turns Genesis' animal naming into a test before angels: they cannot supply the names, while Adam can, making the commentary's angelic limitation an explicit Jewish interpretation.
The commentary's Yunus boards a ship while fleeing; the Hebrew story gives the same departure to Tarshish by sea.
The sailors cast lots to identify the cause of the storm, directly paralleling the commentary's shipboard lot that falls against Yunus.
In Hebrew WLC numbering this verse has the fish swallow Jonah, the direct counterpart to the commentary's prophet being engulfed rather than swimming free.

row.basis: prayer from the belly of Sheol
row.note: Jonah cries to YHWH from the belly of Sheol; it is the biblical fish-belly prayer beside the commentary's self-accusing tasbih.
The fish expels Jonah onto dry land, giving the narrative rescue that the commentary says prevents permanent confinement in the depths.

row.basis: Jonah interpreted as the Son of Man's sign
row.note: Jesus rereads Jonah's three days in the sea creature as the Son of Man's three days in the heart of the earth, changing the story's later Christian meaning.

row.basis: bowing and kneeling before the Maker
row.note: The psalm commands bodily bowing and kneeling before YHWH the Maker, a direct analogue to the commentary's tesbih joined to prostration and createdness.

row.basis: inner self blesses the holy Name
row.note: The whole inner self blesses YHWH and his holy Name, matching the commentary's claim that praise is carried through inward disposition as well as speech.
The seraphim proclaim God's holiness and filling glory, a biblical heavenly liturgy for the commentary's purification and universal praise.
The living creatures offer unceasing holy praise to the Lord God, a Christian visionary counterpart to continuous heavenly tesbih.
The psalm summons sun, moon, and stars to praise YHWH, placing the commentary's moving heavenly bodies within a scriptural cosmic praise.
Flying birds join beasts and other creatures in praise, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's birds spread in the air within their own praise and prayer.

row.basis: every creature praises God and the Lamb
row.note: Every creature in heaven, earth, under earth, and sea gives blessing to the enthroned God and the Lamb, extending the commentary's cosmic praise in a distinctively Christian direction.
The psalmist rises before dawn to cry out and hope in God's word, a specific biblical rhythm beside the commentary's daytime labor and night or dawn remembrance.
The psalmist's eyes anticipate the night watches to meditate on God's word, directly pairing night wakefulness with received speech.
Isaiah joins high heaven, creation, and naming: God brings out the host by number and calls every star by name, so none is missing.
The creator measures waters and marks out the heavens, a close biblical parallel to the commentary's Lord who creates, proportions, and guides.

row.basis: creator who formed and established earth
row.note: Isaiah identifies YHWH as the creator who formed, fashioned, and established the earth, a specific analogue to the surah's ordered creation sequence developed under Rabb.
God's hand founded earth and spread heaven, and when he calls them they stand together, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's sustaining of what might otherwise slip away.

row.basis: all things hold together in Christ
row.note: The commentary assigns cosmic holding to the Lord; Colossians says all things hold together in Christ, a Christian christological allocation of that sustaining work.
The heavens are stretched out like a tent, providing a biblical image for the commentary's sky as elevated roof or covering.

row.basis: heavens spread as a dwelling tent
row.note: Isaiah describes God above the circle of earth stretching out heavens like a tent to dwell in, joining height, canopy, and divine transcendence.

row.basis: rain makes earth bud and yield
row.note: Rain and snow descend, water the earth, and make it bud with seed and bread; this closely matches the commentary's cloud-to-rain-to-vegetation sequence.
The promised rain yields grass in the field for cattle, directly meeting the commentary's pasture, herd, and divine care imagery.

row.basis: grass for livestock and plants for people
row.note: YHWH causes grass to grow for livestock and plants for human use, a precise biblical parallel to the commentary's pasture produced and sustained by the Lord.
"The Lord is my shepherd" gives the most direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's Rabb as owner, guide, and shepherd of a flock.

row.basis: God feeds and rests the flock
row.note: God himself promises to shepherd, feed, and give rest to his sheep, extending the commentary's care-and-guidance meaning of Rabb.
The Lord disciplines Israel as a parent disciplines a child, giving a biblical form to the commentary's non-biological nurturing and formation.

row.basis: the good shepherd lays down his life
row.note: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, a Christian deployment of the shepherd-lord image central to the commentary's Rabb discussion.
The psalm credits God with forming inward parts and knitting a person in the womb, a biblical counterpart to the commentary's creator who brings bodies into ordered form.
The lot is cast in the lap but its every decision is from YHWH, a focused biblical companion to the commentary's lots, measured shares, and divine direction.

row.basis: God's Name in the sent messenger
row.note: God tells Israel to heed the messenger because God's Name is in him; it is a striking biblical case where the Name accompanies a commissioned agent without becoming the agent's possession.
Jesus says he manifested the Father's Name to those given to him; it makes Name-bearing mission central to Christian theology in a way that invites comparison with the commissioned addressee of 87:1.

row.basis: God of gods and Lord of lords
row.note: Deuteronomy calls YHWH God of gods and Lord of lords, a biblical superlative for the commentary's unshared lordship.

row.basis: "King of kings and Lord of lords" on Jesus
row.note: Revelation places the title King of kings and Lord of lords on the returning Jesus, a further Christian assignment of supreme lordship beside the commentary's exclusivity claim.
Solomon asks that God's eyes remain on the house where God said his Name would be, making the Name a concentrated locus of prayer rather than a mere label.

row.basis: the place for God's Name to dwell
row.note: Israel is to seek the place YHWH chooses to put his Name, a concrete cultic form of the commentary's claim that the Name is guarded and invoked.

row.basis: writing and sealing in a king's name
row.note: A decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring bears binding authority, supplying the legal-letter analogue to the commentary's image of a name at a letter's head.

row.basis: "Come, let us go up" to YHWH
row.note: Isaiah's nations invite one another to go up to YHWH's mountain to receive instruction, a concrete Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's ascent-laden call to come.

row.basis: Joseph made lord over Pharaoh's house
row.note: The Joseph story describes a human lordship over Pharaoh's house and Egypt granted by God, clarifying the commentary's observation that lord-language can have a human courtly use.

row.basis: one teacher and all are brothers
row.note: Jesus forbids status-seeking religious titles by saying the disciples have one teacher and are brothers, a Christian warning adjacent to the commentary's refusal to elevate human religious figures into lords.

row.basis: statutes of heaven and rule on earth
row.note: God's question about the ordinances of heaven and their rule on earth gives a biblical form to the commentary's ordered, sustained movements of the sky.
Ezekiel's mark identifies those who grieve over Jerusalem's evil; although it is not called the Name, it sharpens the commentary's bodily brand and distinguishing-sign image.
This expanded Jewish retelling develops Jonah's confinement in the fish and his penitential turn, a later interpretive companion to the commentary's rescue-through-confession reading.
The opening mishnah fixes the evening and morning times for reciting the Shema, a Jewish liturgical counterpart to praise and remembrance ordered across the day.
The Didache instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily, a concrete early Christian counterpart to the commentary's recurrent remembrance.
The Father's discipline is for believers' good so that they share holiness, a specific Christian counterpart to Rabb as gradual formation toward completion.
Moses compares his teaching and speech to rain and dew on tender grass, a close meeting of the commentary's commissioned speech with its cloud-to-pasture imagery.
Moses declares that he will proclaim YHWH's Name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God, an exceptionally direct biblical formulation beside the imperative of 87:1.

row.basis: YHWH descends and proclaims the Name
row.note: In the cloud on Sinai, YHWH descends, stands with Moses, and proclaims the Name, joining the commentary's Moses mission, Name, and cloud imagery.

row.basis: the Name declared through divine attributes
row.note: The divine Name is proclaimed with merciful, gracious, patient, and faithful attributes, clarifying how a Name can be guarded by true predication rather than empty use.

row.basis: no one like YHWH, majestic in holiness
row.note: Moses' victory song asks who is like YHWH among gods and calls him majestic in holiness and praise, a direct counterpart to the commentary's no-peer tesbih.

row.basis: glory due the Name and worship
row.note: The psalm couples giving YHWH the glory due his Name with worship, concretely joining the commentary's Name-object with praise enacted bodily.

row.basis: glory of the Name and offering
row.note: Ascribing glory to YHWH's Name is followed by bringing an offering, a biblical instance of the commentary's claim that praise reaches beyond words into religious action.
The congregation is called to praise YHWH's great and awesome Name because he is holy, a compact Hebrew liturgical parallel to purity and exaltation of the Name.

row.basis: great Name and pure offering among nations
row.note: Malachi joins YHWH's great Name among the nations to a pure offering, giving a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's protected Name and worship.

row.basis: nations' god-names and walking in YHWH's Name
row.note: Micah contrasts peoples walking in their gods' names with Israel walking in YHWH's Name forever, closely matching the commentary's rejection of names distributed to rivals.

row.basis: El Shaddai and the Name YHWH
row.note: The differentiated disclosure of El Shaddai and YHWH is a concrete biblical case for considering several divine appellations and their one divine referent.

row.basis: human pride brought low, YHWH alone exalted
row.note: Isaiah contrasts lowered human loftiness with YHWH alone being exalted, directly sharpening the commentary's distinction between rightful height and arrogant self-elevation.
The prophetic voice calls human flesh grass, providing the opening term for the commentary's later pasture-and-fading sequence.
The grass withers and flower fades under God's breath, a precise textual companion to the surah's pasture that turns dark and perishes.

row.basis: grass fades but God's word stands
row.note: The contrast between fading grass and God's enduring word closely joins the commentary's perishing pasture to its recipient who is taught and does not forget.
Jeremiah asks whether the nations' false gods or the heavens can give rain, then confesses dependence on YHWH; it joins empty rival names to rain and fertility.

row.basis: sign on hand, remembrance in the mouth
row.note: The exodus memorial is a sign on hand and before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction remains in the mouth, a concrete parallel to the commentary's brand, remembrance, and spoken worship.
The psalm identifies YHWH as maker and owner, with worshipers his people and sheep of his pasture, gathering several of the commentary's Rabb images in one verse.
Hosea portrays God teaching Ephraim to walk and taking the child in his arms, a vivid Hebrew Bible form of the commentary's gradual nurturing and guidance.
Jonah's fish-belly prayer turns to thanksgiving and declares salvation belongs to YHWH, a distinct continuation beside the commentary's confession that clears God and locates fault in the prophet.
The Ninevites repent at Jonah's preaching, and Jesus calls himself greater than Jonah; this supplies the teaching-and-reminder outcome beyond the fish episode.

row.basis: Jonah as a sign to Nineveh
row.note: Luke's Jesus makes Jonah himself a sign to Nineveh and the Son of Man a sign to his generation, a distinct Christian rereading from Matthew's three-days comparison.

row.basis: salvation in the Name of Jesus
row.note: Acts locates salvation in the Name of Jesus given among humans, a Christian assignment of saving Name-language that stands beside the commentary's exclusive Name theology.
The Son inherits a Name more excellent than the angels, a Christian high-name claim especially relevant to the commentary's Name, height, and angelic knowledge discussion.

row.basis: an easy yoke and light burden
row.note: Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a close New Testament analogue to the commentary's repeated ease given to a commissioned servant.
Paul describes God as giving rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness, a Christian missionary statement beside the commentary's divine provision from sky to vegetation.

row.basis: grass clothed today and gone tomorrow
row.note: Jesus invokes field grass alive today and destined for the oven tomorrow, a direct New Testament use of the commentary's transitory-pasture image.

row.basis: all flesh like grass, grass withers
row.note: First Peter quotes the grass-and-flower fading formula, extending the commentary's fading-pasture image to mortal human life.

row.basis: the Lord our God is one
row.note: Jesus recites Israel's one-God confession, giving a direct New Testament affirmation of the unshared lordship that frames the commentary.

row.basis: God's Name and Christ's new Name written on the victor
row.note: The conqueror receives God's Name, the new Jerusalem's name, and Christ's new name; this extends the commentary's brand-and-name image in a distinctive Christian configuration.

God makes Moses elohim to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet; this representative use supplies a nuanced biblical counterpoint to the commentary's contrast between Moses' true Lord and Pharaoh's self-deification.

row.basis: the Father's Name given to Jesus
row.note: Jesus asks the Holy Father to keep his followers in the Father's Name "which you have given me," a specific continuation of the Christian Name-sharing claim.

row.basis: the good Name invoked over believers
row.note: James speaks of the good Name invoked over believers, a New Testament instance of a Name placed upon persons that complements the commentary's mark-and-belonging image.

row.basis: human masters and the Master in heaven
row.note: Ephesians distinguishes earthly masters from the shared Master in heaven, a Christian clarification of the commentary's human-master and divine-Lord semantic field.

row.basis: heaven and highest heaven cannot contain God
row.note: Solomon says not even heaven and the highest heaven can contain God, a specific biblical check on spatial height alongside the commentary's Most High and heavenly roof images.
Jesus states that self-exalters will be humbled and the humble exalted, a direct ethical articulation of the commentary's good and bad forms of elevation.
Jewish tradition treats pronouncing the Name by its letters as a grave matter, an interpretive extension of the commentary's concern to protect the Name from misuse.
This mishnah is remembered as distinguishing the Temple's written pronunciation of the Name from a substituted provincial form; verify the exact subsection and wording before relying on it.
The commentary grounds praise in the Creator's work rather than a remote epithet; Genesis has light come to be at God's spoken command, giving a concrete scriptural scene of creation by word.
The commentary reads 87:2 as including the listener's body and later discusses form before spirit; Genesis depicts YHWH forming the human from soil and breathing life into him.
The commentary hears خلق and سوى as making and completing a fitting whole; after the six days God sees all that he made as very good, an explicit judgment on completed form.

row.basis: praise the Name because he commanded creation
row.note: The commentary attaches praise of the Lord's Name to the deeds that identify him; this praise summons creation to praise that Name because he commanded and they came to be.
The commentary treats glorifying the Name as grounded in works; Nehemiah's prayer names the maker of heavens, earth and sea, says he gives life to all, and ends with heaven's host worshiping.

row.basis: measures of waters, sky and mountains
row.note: The commentary holds together creation, measured proportion and the ordered heavens; Isaiah asks who measured the waters, spanned the heavens and weighed the mountains, making cosmic order the Creator's work.
The commentary's artisan measures before cutting, while the Creator needs no model; Job's question about who set earth's measures and stretched its line makes cosmic measurement a divine act.
The commentary says the Most High is known inside his work, not moved beyond the sky; Isaiah says the maker formed the earth to be inhabited rather than leaving it empty.

row.basis: blessing the Lord in view of his works
row.note: The commentary's opening links praise of the Name to the deeds that reveal the Lord; this psalm blesses YHWH and immediately describes his majestic ordering of light and heavens.

row.basis: grass made for people and animals
row.note: The commentary connects creation's ordering with pasture as provision for people and livestock; the psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human use.
The commentary holds completed form beside aging and decay; the psalm says creatures die and return to dust when God hides his face and takes away their breath.

row.basis: breath creates and renews the earth
row.note: The commentary connects bodily formation, breath and the later reversal of creation; this verse says God sends his spirit, creatures are created, and the face of the ground is renewed.

row.basis: praise for a wonderfully made body
row.note: The commentary says the hearer can find the Creator's work in their own body; the psalmist praises God because he is wondrously formed, joining bodily making directly to praise.
The commentary's womb discussion treats the body as shaped before its life unfolds; the psalmist says God's eyes saw his unformed substance and his days were written before they came.
The commentary moves from the body as evidence of its Maker to the Maker's knowledge; in the same psalm, God's thoughts are too many to count, extending the creation scene into divine knowledge.

row.basis: hands fashioned and shaped the speaker
row.note: The commentary compares creation to measured craft while denying the Creator's dependence on a pattern; Job addresses God as the one whose hands fashioned and shaped him.

row.basis: embryonic shaping like milk and curd
row.note: The commentary develops the body collected and ordered in the womb; Job depicts conception through the concrete sequence of pouring him out like milk and curdling him like cheese.
The commentary's body image is one of parts brought into proportion; Job lists skin, flesh, bones and sinews as God's work in forming him.

row.basis: formed in the womb and appointed to a task
row.note: The commentary links measured making with an apt direction; Jeremiah says God knew, set apart and appointed him before birth, joining prenatal formation to a particular vocation.

row.basis: Creator forms the human spirit within
row.note: The commentary extends proportioning from the body to inward life; Zechariah names the one who forms the human spirit within as the maker of heavens and earth.

row.basis: one Maker forms master and servant in the womb
row.note: The commentary locates the Creator's trace in the listener's body; Job says the same maker formed both him and his servant in the womb, giving shared creation an explicit social consequence.

row.basis: unseen formation of bones in the womb
row.note: The commentary stresses that bodily formation exceeds human observation; Qoheleth compares the unknown development of bones in a pregnant woman's womb with God's work.
The commentary discusses a formed body awaiting the breath of life; Ezekiel's dry-bones vision orders sinews, flesh and skin before breath, making restoration follow a bodily sequence.

row.basis: breath makes the assembled bodies live
row.note: The commentary joins completed form to life-giving breath; in Ezekiel's vision the bodies stand alive only after breath enters them.

row.basis: formed senses imply the Maker hears and sees
row.note: The commentary uses the body as a trace of the Creator's work; the psalm asks whether the one who planted the ear cannot hear and formed the eye cannot see, drawing divine knowledge from bodily design.
The commentary develops proportioning beyond visible form to inward character; this verse says God fashions the hearts of all and attends to their deeds.

row.basis: the maker who made and established Israel
row.note: The commentary identifies the Lord by what he does; Moses asks whether YHWH is Israel's father and maker, the one who made and established them, making creation grounds for covenant loyalty.

row.basis: God rides the clouds as his chariot
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Most High with a being transported beyond the sky; the psalm pictures YHWH riding the clouds, a concrete image for comparison whose own setting celebrates his power over creation.

row.basis: God rides the heavens to aid Israel
row.note: The commentary says the Most High is known by works rather than carried beyond the sky; Moses' blessing pictures Israel's God riding the heavens to help them, a contrasting sky image framed as protective nearness.

row.basis: prepare a straight way for YHWH
