row.note: The commentary joins making complete to the straight road of guidance; Isaiah calls for a highway in the wilderness for God, turning a straightened path into preparation for his arrival.

row.basis: valleys raised and rough ground leveled
row.note: The commentary gives سوى both completion and straightening, then links it to a road; Isaiah's next verse levels valleys and mountains and makes rough country a plain.
The commentary defines the سوى family through balance between things and protection from excess or deficiency; Proverbs applies that measure to fair weights and says the scales belong to YHWH.

row.basis: YHWH sets the speaker's allotted portion
row.note: The commentary explicitly labels an Arabic branch of خ ل ق as a measured share; the psalm says the lines fell to the speaker in pleasant places and YHWH holds his lot, a concrete allotment image without importing it as the ayah's main sense.

row.basis: polished arrow hidden until its mission
row.note: The commentary describes an arrow measured, smoothed and aimed as the next ayah's guidance image; Isaiah's servant says God made him a polished arrow and hid him in a quiver until his word was needed.

row.basis: earth wears out like a garment
row.note: The commentary develops smoothness as the worn nap of a garment and the leveling of a ruined trace; Isaiah says earth wears out like clothing, while the heavens vanish like smoke.

row.basis: grass withers under the Lord's breath
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from emergence to darkened refuse; Isaiah says grass withers when YHWH's breath blows on it, making the created pasture's transience explicit.

The commentary's rock image is a hollow that catches and holds rainwater; the psalm recalls God splitting rocks in the wilderness and giving drink from the depths, a related but reversed movement of water from rock.
The commentary describes a hollow in stone retaining water that would otherwise run off; this verse says God brought streams from the rock and made waters flow down like rivers.

row.basis: water comes out of the struck rock
row.note: The commentary's rock-and-water image makes stone a place where water is retained; at Horeb God tells Moses to strike the rock, from which water comes for the people.

row.basis: blessing after God guides a journey
row.note: The commentary joins travel, a mount and remembering the Lord's favor; Abraham's servant blesses YHWH after recognizing that God led him on the way to his master's kin.

row.basis: horses contrasted with invoking God's Name
row.note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord on a rider's back; the psalm contrasts those who trust chariots and horses with those who invoke YHWH's Name.

row.basis: idols are made by human hands
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Creator's unmodeled work with human fabrication and false worship; this psalm names silver-and-gold idols as human handiwork.

row.basis: idols have mouths but cannot speak
row.note: The commentary rejects the creature's fabricated claim as a counterfeit of the Creator; the psalm's handmade images have mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see.
The commentary says a lie made by a creature imitates the Creator's act but has no reality; the psalm says idol-makers and trusters become like the speechless images they fashion.

row.basis: measured carving made into a human likeness
row.note: The commentary contrasts a human artisan who measures and cuts with the Creator who needs no prior model; Isaiah describes the woodworker measuring and carving an image in human form.

row.basis: one piece of wood becomes fuel and an idol
row.note: The commentary exposes created objects as poor substitutes for their Maker; Isaiah says the same wood supplies fire and is also made into a god for worship.

row.basis: the remnant of wood is called a god
row.note: The commentary's created-versus-counterfeit contrast turns on the maker's false claim; Isaiah's image-maker bows to the leftover wood and asks it to save him.
The commentary says the Lord is known by works and needs no model or partner; Isaiah names YHWH as maker of all things who stretches the heavens alone.

row.basis: earth established by wisdom and understanding
row.note: The commentary presents creation as measured and completed work; Jeremiah says God made earth by power and established the world by wisdom and understanding.

row.basis: idol-makers' images are false and breathless
row.note: The commentary contrasts true creation with fabricated claims; Jeremiah says the images made by craftsmen are a lie and have no breath.

row.basis: Maker of all versus worthless idols
row.note: The commentary grounds praise in the one who truly creates; Jeremiah contrasts the portion of Jacob, who made all things, with idols that are not like him.

row.basis: God bears Israel from the womb
row.note: The commentary's riding image places a human on an animal; Isaiah reverses the carrying relation by portraying God as the one who has carried Israel from birth.

row.basis: God carries Israel through old age
row.note: The commentary connects formed bodies with later aging and wear; Isaiah promises that the God who carried Israel from the womb will carry them even into old age.

row.basis: the humble king comes riding a donkey
row.note: The commentary describes a rider settling on an animal and remembering the Lord; Zechariah's king arrives humbly on a donkey, a royal riding scene whose Gospel reception adds public praise.

row.basis: Jesus enters as king on a donkey
row.note: Matthew applies Zechariah's donkey-riding king to Jesus; beside the commentary's rider who praises the Creator of the mount, the difference is that this crowd welcomes the rider as king.

row.basis: crowd blesses the one who comes in the Lord's Name
row.note: The commentary has the mounted worshiper say praise to the Creator who subjected the animal; Matthew's crowd blesses the arriving king in the Lord's Name, shifting the praised figure while retaining the liturgical formula.

row.basis: create a clean heart and renew the spirit
row.note: The commentary extends proportioning from the body to the soul's moral direction; this prayer asks God to create a clean heart and renew a steadfast spirit, making inner ordering a new creation.

row.basis: neither add to nor subtract from the command
row.note: The commentary mentions a separate Arabic form for omitting a letter and places it beside the promise of recitation without forgetting; Moses likewise forbids adding to or subtracting from God's command.

row.basis: the king cuts and burns the scroll
row.note: The commentary's secondary root sense is dropping a letter from scripture; Jeremiah depicts Jehoiakim cutting the divine scroll with a knife and burning it, a concrete opposite to preserving recitation.

row.basis: valleys filled and crooked roads straightened
row.note: Luke applies Isaiah's leveling image to preparation for God's salvation; it gives the commentary's link between completed form and a straight path an explicit prophetic and ethical setting.
The commentary says the Creator's work is witnessed in the hearer's body; Luke's next line says all flesh will see God's salvation, widening the prepared road to a universal audience.

row.basis: rain makes the earth bud and seed grow
row.note: The commentary connects ordered creation with water, pasture and provision; Isaiah says rain waters the earth, makes it bud and supplies seed and bread, giving a specific scriptural path from creation to food.

row.basis: birds fed without sowing or harvest
row.note: The commentary treats created life as provision for people and animals; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor reap yet are fed by the Father, a specific ethical inference from creation's ordering.

row.basis: grain grows through stages to full ear
row.note: The commentary describes a shoot strengthening, thickening and standing on its stalk; Mark's seed parable likewise names the ordered sequence of blade, ear and full grain.

row.basis: Creator is not contained in human temples
row.note: The commentary says the Most High is not carried beyond the sky and is known by his works; Paul says the Maker of the world does not dwell in temples built by human hands.

row.basis: God gives life and breath rather than receiving service
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Creator with creatures and formed objects; Paul says God is not served by human hands but gives all people life and breath.

row.basis: nations receive appointed times and boundaries
row.note: The commentary's creation includes measured portions and subsequent guidance; Paul says God made every nation and fixed its times and boundaries, then connects those limits to seeking God.

row.basis: humans are meant to seek God who is near
row.note: The commentary links a made and proportioned creature to guidance; Paul says the nations' appointed setting is so they might seek God, who is not far from each person.

row.basis: divinity is not gold, stone or human craft
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Creator with images that creatures fabricate; Paul says divine nature cannot be like gold, silver or stone shaped by human art and imagination.

row.basis: all things came to be through the Word
row.note: The commentary stresses that the Creator needs no prior mold; John says all things came to be through the Word and not one created thing came to be apart from him.

row.basis: all things created through and for Christ
row.note: The commentary's objectless verb is said to encompass all creation; Colossians names visible and invisible things and every rank as created through and for Christ.

row.basis: worship because God created all things
row.note: The commentary grounds the command to glorify the Name in God's creative deeds; Revelation's heavenly worship says all things exist because God willed and created them.

row.basis: visible things made from what is not visible
row.note: The commentary says خ ل ق can cover originating without a model as well as bringing forth from something; Hebrews says the visible order was not made from visible things, making the unseen-origin reading explicit.

row.basis: God made heaven and earth from what did not exist
row.note: The commentary preserves creation both without a prior mold and from something else; the mother in 2 Maccabees explicitly tells her son that God made heaven and earth not from existing things.

row.basis: all things ordered by measure, number and weight
row.note: The commentary's measuring artisan image develops creation as proportion rather than decoration; Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number and weight.
The commentary defines سوى as balance between things and protection from excess or deficiency; Ben Sira says all things are in pairs and God has made nothing incomplete.

row.basis: God made all things by his word
row.note: The commentary joins the Creator's work to a command that needs no tool or mold; Solomon's prayer names God as the one who made all things by his word.
The commentary's bodily formation becomes a human made in fitting relation to the world; this prayer says God formed humanity by wisdom.

row.basis: all humans from earth, then distinguished
row.note: The commentary moves from common creation to each creature's measured share; Ben Sira says all humans come from earth and then describes the Most High distinguishing their ways.

row.basis: humanity as clay in the Maker's hand
row.note: The commentary's artisan measures material before shaping it; Ben Sira directly compares the human being in the Maker's hand to clay in the potter's hand.

The commentary extends bodily making toward inner capacities and the danger of false speech; Onkelos renders the human's resulting life as a speaking spirit, making rational speech part of the creation scene.

row.basis: one first human, many distinct faces
row.note: The commentary's objectless creation includes every hearer's body; the Mishnah says one human was created first, yet no two people resemble each other, grounding shared origin and individual form in human dignity.

row.basis: God's spirit equips a human artisan
row.note: The commentary compares measured craft to divine creation without a model; Exodus says Bezalel is filled with God's spirit, wisdom and skill for craftsmanship, making human making a capacity received from the Creator.
The commentary's craft image distinguishes a maker's measured work from later wear and failure; Jeremiah shows a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand being remade into another form.

row.basis: we are clay and God our potter
row.note: The commentary uses human craft to illuminate divine forming; Isaiah turns the same relation into confession and plea, calling Israel clay and YHWH its potter.

row.basis: the formed thing questions its maker
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the Creator's measured work from a creature's false judgment; Paul asks whether what is formed can say to its molder, Why did you make me this way?

row.basis: God places each member in the body as he wills
row.note: The commentary describes سوى as parts brought into relation without excess or lack; Paul says God arranged each body member in its place, giving that proportioning a communal consequence.

row.basis: God composes the body and honors weaker parts
row.note: The commentary says a sound whole is made by relation among its parts; Paul says God composed the body and gave greater honor to the part that lacked it, turning proportion into care for the weak.

row.basis: created for good works prepared beforehand
row.note: The commentary connects measured making to guidance along a path; Paul calls believers God's workmanship, created in Christ for good works God prepared for them to walk in.
The commentary says the Creator is known in the works rather than beyond the sky; Paul says God's invisible power is perceived through what has been made.
The commentary opposes the one who creates to images made by human hands; Paul describes people exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal humans and animals.
The commentary says a fabricated lie imitates the Creator's act and misdirects worship; Paul says people exchanged truth for a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator.

row.basis: failure to know God from created works
row.note: The commentary says the Lord is identified by what he has made; Wisdom criticizes people who failed to recognize the artisan from the beauty of his works.
The commentary contrasts real creation with false objects of worship; Wisdom calls the nations' handmade idols worthless gods and condemns their makers' craft.
The commentary includes the ordered sky and earth in the Creator's objectless work; Hebrews applies the psalm's creation words to the Son, who laid earth's foundation and made the heavens.

row.basis: he heavens wear out like clothing
row.note: The commentary develops smoothness as wear that erases the nap of a garment; Hebrews says the heavens will perish and wear out like clothing.
The commentary connects completed creation with the later wearing-down of bodies and land; Paul says creation itself will be freed from its slavery to decay.

row.basis: Jesus breathes the Spirit onto the disciples
row.note: The commentary connects formed body and breath; after the resurrection Jesus breathes on the disciples and gives the Holy Spirit, reusing the creation gesture for a renewed community.

row.basis: first Adam lives, last Adam gives life
row.note: The commentary's formation-and-breath sequence is applied to human origin and resurrection; Paul quotes the first Adam as a living being and calls Christ the life-giving Spirit, giving the creation scene an eschatological reading.

row.basis: Jesus grows in wisdom and stature
row.note: The commentary says a person may reach completion of youth and then receive knowledge; Luke describes Jesus increasing in wisdom and stature, a concrete Christian account of growth toward maturity.

row.basis: Jesus forms clay sparrows on the Sabbath
row.note: The commentary compares Jesus shaping a clay bird, breathing into it and acting by God's permission; this infancy narrative has the child Jesus make twelve clay sparrows on the Sabbath and clap them alive, relocating the scene to childhood and omitting the Qur'anic repeated permission formula.

The commentary says the Most High is known in his works rather than displaced beyond the sky; the psalm's next verse describes God stretching out the heavens, making the sky itself an act of his ordering.

The commentary's surrounding creation citations include the making of pairs; Genesis states that God created humanity in his image as male and female, a specific paired form within the creation account.

row.basis: Jesus invokes creation of male and female
row.note: The commentary notes the created pairs in its wider account; Jesus cites the Creator making male and female and uses their joining to explain marriage, giving that creation formula a relational interpretation.
The commentary connects bodily form with the vulnerability of aging; the psalm says God knows our frame and remembers that we are dust, linking care to the material from which humans were made.

The commentary's wear and leveling imagery reaches bodily death and renewed creation; Paul says the body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, distinguishing the formed body from its resurrection condition.

row.basis: natural body raised as spiritual body
row.note: The commentary connects bodily form with breath and resurrection; Paul distinguishes the natural body from the spiritual body, giving the Adamic formation image an eschatological continuation.

row.basis: bones interpreted as the restored house of Israel
row.note: The commentary's womb-and-breath sequence can sound solely bodily; Ezekiel explicitly interprets the assembled bones as all Israel restored to its land, giving the same image a national rather than anatomical referent.
The commentary connects ordered bodily life with aging's reversal; Deuteronomy presents Moses at 120 with undimmed eye and undiminished vigor, a specific counterexample to simple physical decline.

The commentary allows both creation without an exemplar and making one thing from another; Wisdom describes God's hand forming the world from formless matter, a distinct ancient Jewish account of the latter possibility.

row.basis: one work confirms the good of another
row.note: The commentary says a proportioned thing is fitted in relation to other things; Ben Sira adds that one work confirms another's good and that this ordered whole displays divine glory.
The commentary links making to the apt direction that follows; Solomon asks for wisdom to govern the world and judge rightly, making the human creature's purpose explicit.
The commentary pairs creation with guidance without describing humans as inert; Ben Sira says God created humans and left them in the hand of their own counsel, making moral agency explicit.

row.basis: life and death set before human choice
row.note: The commentary develops measured creation and a way to be followed; Ben Sira says fire and water are set before the hearer to choose, clarifying that guidance still addresses an agent.

row.basis: life or death according to the choice
row.note: The commentary's creation-and-guidance sequence can be read alongside human response; Ben Sira says life and death are before each person and what they choose is given to them.

row.basis: opposite works set against one another
row.note: The commentary describes balance and its contrary, flattening and decay; Ben Sira says the works of the Most High stand in pairs, one opposite the other.

row.basis: human beloved as created in God's image
row.note: The commentary asks the hearer to find the Lord's work in their own body; Akiva's saying makes being created in God's image the reason humanity is beloved.

row.basis: creation debated by Truth, Peace and Righteousness
row.note: The commentary contrasts the true Creator with lies fabricated by creatures; the midrash places Truth, Peace and Righteousness in debate over humanity's creation, then depicts Truth cast to earth, complicating the ethical meaning of making humans.

The commentary presents the womb as a place where a body is formed for later direction; this rabbinic image says a fetus is taught Torah before birth and forgets it on entering the world, adding a tradition of prenatal moral capacity.

row.basis: two spirits and two human paths
row.note: The commentary links inner formation to the later distinction between uprightness and deviation; the Community Rule describes humanity as walking in two spirits, truth and injustice, giving a specific sectarian account of moral direction.

row.basis: Israel is clay in the potter's hand
row.note: The commentary portrays creation as exacting work without making it a fixed mold; Jeremiah applies potter and clay to Israel, where the image concerns a people God may reshape in response to their conduct.

row.basis: one potter makes vessels for different uses
row.note: The commentary says measured creation makes things fit their purpose; Paul asks whether a potter may use the same clay for different vessels, adding a question of divine choice and human limits.

row.basis: members care equally for one another
row.note: The commentary's balance is not mere leveling but relational fitness; Paul explains that the body is arranged so there is no division and members care for one another.

row.basis: joined body grows as each part works
row.note: The commentary's body image treats completion as a relation among parts; Ephesians describes the whole body joined and held together as each part works, producing growth.
The commentary's praise of the Creator rejects false speech and false worship; James says the same tongue blesses God and curses human beings made in God's likeness, making creation a test of speech.

row.basis: greatness of works points to their Maker
row.note: The commentary makes the Creator's works the basis of praise; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of created things let observers infer their Maker.

row.basis: the potter shapes vessels from the same clay
row.note: The commentary's artisan scene measures material into a useful form; Wisdom describes a potter shaping the same clay into vessels for different uses, adding a Jewish reflection on craft and purpose.

row.basis: the maker is mortal but the image has no breath
row.note: The commentary contrasts the living Creator with fabricated forms; Wisdom says the maker is mortal and the handmade image has no breath, sharpening the difference between life-giving creation and craft.

row.basis: he worn creation is changed while God remains
row.note: The commentary holds ordered creation beside its eventual leveling and decay; Hebrews says the heavens will be rolled up like a cloak and changed while the Lord remains the same.
The commentary traces formation through bodily development and later decay; Paul pictures the whole creation groaning together in labor pains, making decay part of a hoped-for new birth.
The commentary connects the completion of youth to Moses' later receiving wisdom and judgment; Exodus marks the point when Moses has grown up before he acts among his people.

The commentary extends سوى from a complete body to the completion of youth; Irenaeus reads human beings as created immature and brought gradually to perfection, making development a feature of the Creator's pedagogy.

row.basis: tree by water bears fruit and does not wither
row.note: The commentary contrasts water's useful remainder with foam that washes away; Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a tree by streams whose fruit endures, adding an ethical reading of what remains fruitful.

row.basis: chaff blown away by the wind
row.note: The commentary's flood image distinguishes useful matter from passing foam; Psalm 1 contrasts the enduring tree with wicked people as chaff driven away, applying the separation to conduct.

The commentary describes fabrication as a creature's internally measured falsehood set against the Creator's true word; the serpent tells the humans they will not die, directly contradicting God's instruction.

row.basis: human life like grass and a field flower
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from emergence to withering refuse; this psalm compares human days to grass and the flower of the field, applying the same transience to a life God remembers.

row.basis: wind passes and the flower is gone
row.note: The commentary treats smoothness from wear as a sign of ending; the psalm says the wind passes over the flower and its place knows it no more, a concrete image of disappearance.

row.basis: dust returns to earth and spirit to God
row.note: The commentary links formed bodies with aging and death; Qoheleth closes the aging sequence by saying dust returns to earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

row.basis: grass fades but God's word stands
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes fading pasture with the promise that recitation will be preserved; Isaiah says grass withers and flowers fade while God's word stands forever.
The commentary joins proportioning to guidance along a straight road; Proverbs says to acknowledge God in every way and he will make the paths straight.
The commentary pairs a made creature with the Creator's guidance; the psalm asks YHWH to lead and teach the speaker in his paths, making direction an explicit response to dependence.
The commentary connects being made fit with being guided; the psalm asks God to lead the speaker in truth and teach him, a prayer for a path rather than a claim about bodily form.

row.basis: human crowned and given rule over creation
row.note: The commentary says creation's unnamed object includes the hearer; this psalm places humanity within the created order as crowned with glory and given responsibility over God's works.

row.basis: intelligible paradigm behind the visible world
row.note: The commentary presents the Creator as measuring without consulting a prior mold; Philo reads Genesis through an intelligible paradigm for the cosmos, giving a Jewish interpretation that makes the model question explicit.

The source commentary explicitly labels the سوى root as straightness and balance; Hebrew שוה here means making equal in a challenge about God's incomparability, a likely cognate connection whose lexeme does not by itself establish the Qur'anic verb's meaning.

row.basis: Hebrew חלק and the source's smoothness branch
row.note: The source commentary explicitly labels خ ل ق B008 as smoothness; Hebrew חלק describes Jacob's smooth skin here, a possible cognate with Arabic خ ل ق in that secondary branch, though the etymology is uncertain and does not define 87:2.

row.basis: created and formed Israel, called by name
row.note: The commentary says the Lord is identified by deeds rather than a remote epithet; Isaiah names YHWH as the one who created and formed Jacob, redeemed him and called him by name.

row.basis: created and formed for God's glory
row.note: The commentary ties glorifying the Lord's Name to the works that identify him; Isaiah says the people called by God's name were created and formed for his glory.
The commentary develops bodily formation in the womb as a secondary sense alongside creation; Isaiah names YHWH as the one who made and formed Jacob from the womb and will help him.

row.basis: Hebrew שוה, leveling a field before sowing
row.note: The source commentary explicitly labels سوى with straightening and balance; Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה for leveling a field's surface before seed is sown, a close cognate use in an agricultural setting that does not determine the Qur'anic verb's full sense.

row.basis: hands make and fashion, then grant understanding
row.note: The commentary joins being made to the guidance that follows; the psalmist says God's hands made and fashioned him, then asks for understanding to learn God's commands.

row.basis: Spirit leads the speaker on level ground
row.note: The commentary connects proportioning, guidance and the straight path; the psalm asks God to teach his will and let his good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground.

row.basis: life and breath of every creature in God's hand
row.note: The commentary treats each body as evidence of its Maker and develops breath as the completion of form; Job says the life of every creature and breath of humankind are in God's hand.

row.basis: God's Spirit makes and breath gives life
row.note: The commentary connects bodily formation to life-giving breath; Job says the Spirit of God made him and the breath of the Almighty gives him life.

row.basis: life, care and steadfast love preserve the spirit
row.note: The commentary says the formed body bears the trace of the Lord's work; Job adds that the same God who formed him granted life and care that preserved his spirit.

row.basis: created humans receive a task and blessing
row.note: The commentary links creation to the suitable direction that follows; after creating male and female, Genesis blesses them and gives them a role toward the other creatures.

row.basis: idols are nothing, YHWH made the heavens
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Creator with things fabricated for worship; the psalm calls the nations' gods idols and says YHWH made the heavens.
The commentary ties glorification to the Creator's acts; the psalm calls the congregation to bow before YHWH because he is their Maker.

row.basis: blessing for the body's openings and functions
row.note: The commentary asks the hearer to recognize the Creator in the body's fitted parts; this rabbinic blessing thanks God for forming the human body with its openings and cavities, whose obstruction would prevent life.

row.basis: the Maker forms, inspires soul and breathes life
row.note: The commentary contrasts the living Creator with lifeless images made by artisans; Wisdom says the idol-maker failed to know the one who formed him, inspired an active soul and breathed a living spirit into him.

row.basis: Solomon molded in the womb like every human
row.note: The commentary develops bodily formation before birth and the common human process; Solomon says he too was molded in flesh in his mother's womb and received breath like all people.
The commentary reads creation as including the listener's own body; Ben Sira says God endowed humans with strength and made them in his image.

row.basis: eyes, ears and a thinking heart
row.note: The commentary extends proportioned creation to inward and sensory capacities; Ben Sira says God gave humans discernment, eyes, ears and a heart for thinking.
The commentary links making with subsequent moral direction; Ben Sira says God filled humanity with knowledge and understanding and showed them good and evil.

row.basis: rewritten scroll includes all former words and more
row.note: The commentary sets the secondary image of omitting a letter beside the promise of preserved recitation; after the king burns the scroll, Jeremiah dictates it again with all its former words and many more.

row.basis: water wears stone and washes soil away
row.note: The commentary describes smoothness as wear that flattens a surface; Job says waters wear stones and torrents wash away the soil, giving a direct image of erosion.

row.basis: Tyre's walls reduced to bare rock
row.note: The commentary connects the smooth rock with a settlement leveled to the ground; Ezekiel's oracle says Tyre's walls and towers will be broken, its dust scraped away and the site left like bare rock.

row.basis: Zion plowed like a field and Jerusalem made ruins
row.note: The commentary links سوى's leveling sense to the end of a created settlement; Micah warns that Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become a heap of ruins because of its rulers' injustice.

row.basis: woman from man, man through woman, all from God
row.note: The commentary describes parts as fitted in relation and notes created pairs; Paul recalls the creation relation between man and woman but concludes that all things are from God.

row.basis: all things hold together in Christ
row.note: The commentary's سوى emphasizes that a whole is made complete through relations among its parts; Colossians says all things hold together in Christ, extending that order to the cosmos.

row.basis: every hair on the disciples' heads is numbered
row.note: The commentary says the listener can find the Creator's work in the body; in a teaching about the Father's care, Jesus says even the hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered.

row.basis: rain, fruitful seasons and food as witness
row.note: The commentary follows creation into pasture and provision for people and animals; Paul says God gives rain, fruitful seasons and food, leaving a witness of his goodness.

row.basis: man and woman are not independent in the Lord
row.note: The commentary describes proportion as relation rather than mere leveling; Paul says woman and man are not independent of one another in the Lord, giving paired creation a mutual reading.

row.basis: outer person decays while inner person renews
row.note: The commentary develops the worn garment and the reversal of bodily order with age; Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed day by day.

row.basis: spirit, soul and body kept complete
row.note: The commentary treats fitting form as extending through body and inward life; Paul prays that the whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless, an explicit Christian formula of integrated completeness.

row.basis: moon and sun assigned their times
row.note: The commentary treats the moon's gradual fullness as completion and cites its phases as measured; the psalm says God appointed the moon for seasons and the sun knows its setting.
The commentary presents the created world as measured and complete; the psalm marvels at the many works of YHWH and says they were all made in wisdom.

row.basis: creatures wait for food from God
row.note: The commentary describes pasture and crop as provision for living creatures; the psalm says all creatures look to God for their food in its season.

row.basis: God opens his hand and satisfies creatures
row.note: The commentary says the created order is fitted to sustain people and animals; the psalm says God gives food when he opens his hand and satisfies every living thing.

row.basis: humanity made for incorruption in God's image
row.note: The commentary connects created form with later bodily wearing and death; Wisdom says God made humans for incorruption and in the image of his own eternity, offering a Jewish account in which death is not the intended completion.
The commentary says the ayah's objectless creation can encompass all things; Jubilees' creation account includes the heavens and their host, expanding the creation scene beyond the human body.

row.basis: The word near at mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says the feminine “it” is the reminder offered in 87:9 and that the worst person keeps it beside him yet at a remove; Deuteronomy says the command is not far away but very near, in mouth and heart, to be done.

The commentary makes the ashqa actively turn away from the reminder; Job quotes the wicked saying to God to depart and that they do not desire knowledge of his ways, a direct speech of refusal, while Job’s context complicates any claim that such rejection is always punished immediately.
The commentary says the same reminder is offered and the difference begins in the hearer; Wisdom says she called and was refused, making rejection rather than the offer the decisive act.
The commentary’s “most wretched” turns aside from admonition; Wisdom says her counsel was rejected and her reproof ignored, then describes the consequence of that response.
The commentary treats turning from reminder as choosing wrongly what to keep at one’s side; Proverbs says the person who turns an ear away from hearing Torah makes even prayer abhorrent.
The commentary distinguishes the unchanged reminder from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the people did not listen or incline their ear, but followed their own counsel and went backward.

row.basis: Stopping the ear against prophetic words
row.note: The commentary’s ashqa keeps the reminder at hand but declines it; Zechariah says the people refused to hear, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears against the law and the words sent through prophets.

row.basis: A hardened heart and unanswered warning
row.note: The commentary connects rejection of the reminder with the person’s own chosen posture; Zechariah says they made their hearts hard so they would not hear the law or prophetic words, followed by the Lord’s anger.

The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people respond differently; Ezekiel’s hearers come, sit before the prophet, and hear his words, but do not do them because their hearts pursue gain.

row.basis: The prophet as a pleasing song
row.note: The commentary’s image of keeping admonition nearby yet treating it as alien fits Ezekiel’s hearers, who enjoy the prophet’s voice like a lovely song while not carrying out what he says.

row.basis: “Today” as an open moment to hear
row.note: The commentary presents one reminder offered to all, with the response still open; the psalm addresses its hearers as God’s people and says that today they hear his voice.
The commentary contrasts the one who takes warning with the one who avoids it; the psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as in the wilderness rebellion.

row.basis: The Rechabites obey while Judah will not hear
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder reaches different hearers; Jeremiah contrasts Rechabites who kept their father’s command with Judah, which did not listen when God spoke persistently through prophets.

row.basis: A messenger must speak whether hearers heed or refuse
row.note: The commentary separates the act of offering reminder from its reception; Ezekiel is told that the rebellious may hear or refuse, but will know a prophet has been among them.

row.basis: Responsibility after a warning is given
row.note: The commentary says the messenger offers admonition without controlling the hearer; Ezekiel’s watchman is delivered from guilt after warning, while the warned wicked person remains accountable if he does not turn.
The commentary emphasizes a single shared call and differing reception; Chronicles says God repeatedly sent messengers because he had compassion on his people and dwelling place.
The commentary’s worst person avoids the reminder and faces its consequence; Chronicles says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at the prophets until judgment came.
The commentary links the wretched condition to turning away from reminder; Hosea names the people’s rejection of knowledge and forgetting of God’s law as the cause of their ruin.
The commentary says the offered reminder is the same while its hearers divide by response; in Jonah, the people of Nineveh believe the warning and undertake repentance rather than dismiss it.

row.basis: Turning from evil changes the outcome
row.note: The commentary contrasts turning away from reminder with self-correction; Jonah says God saw that Nineveh turned from its evil way and relented from the announced disaster.

The commentary reads the response verbs as acts a person does upon oneself; Sirach says God left human beings in the hand of their own inclination, giving a Jewish wisdom parallel for accountable response.

row.basis: Fire and water set before the hearer
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but people choose their response; Sirach pictures fire and water before the person, who stretches out a hand to whichever he chooses.
The commentary places the wretched person at the far end of a chosen response; Sirach explicitly sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what he chooses.

The commentary recalls Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s ancestors, including Terah, served other gods, supplying the biblical background to the Qur’anic break with idolatry.

row.basis: The word received and made fruitful
row.note: The commentary contrasts one who takes reminder with the one who avoids it; Mark’s good soil hears the word, accepts it, and bears fruit, a concrete positive reception.

row.basis: Hearing and doing as the wise response
row.note: The commentary reads taking reminder and purifying oneself as actions a person undertakes; Jesus calls the hearer who does his words wise and compares him to a house built on rock.

row.basis: Hearing without doing as the ruinous response
row.note: The commentary’s ashqa hears the reminder’s availability yet turns aside; Jesus describes the hearer who does not do his words, whose house falls when the same storm comes.

row.basis: Moses and the Prophets are already available
row.note: The commentary says the reminder has been delivered and the hearer is responsible for receiving it; Abraham in the parable tells the rich man’s brothers that they have Moses and the Prophets to hear.

row.basis: A further sign will not cure refusal to hear
row.note: The commentary says those avoiding reminder cannot blame its absence; the parable answers that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

row.basis: Felix fears, then sends Paul away
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and receives warning with the worst person who turns from it; as Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and tells him to go away.

row.basis: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
row.note: The commentary portrays turning away from reminder as a repeated response to divine messengers; Stephen accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and doing as their ancestors did when they rejected the prophets.

row.basis: Turning away from the living God
row.note: The commentary’s verb makes withdrawal the person’s own act; Hebrews warns against an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.

row.basis: Do not harden the heart when the voice is heard
row.note: The commentary links the reminder to a present chance to respond; Hebrews repeats the psalm’s “Today” warning not to harden the heart upon hearing God’s voice.

row.basis: The message heard but not beneficial
row.note: The commentary says one unchanged reminder benefits one hearer while another avoids it; Hebrews says the good news came to its hearers but did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith.

row.basis: One proclamation among both saved and perishing
row.note: The commentary stresses one reminder offered to all with different reception; Paul calls the apostolic proclamation an aroma of Christ among both those being saved and those perishing.

row.basis: The same word as life or death
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder yields benefit to one and loss to another; Paul describes the proclamation as an aroma from death to death for one group and from life to life for another.

row.basis: The word of the cross divides hearers
row.note: The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people receive it differently; Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing and God’s power to those being saved.
The commentary emphasizes that the person does something to himself by taking or avoiding reminder; James tells hearers to become doers of the word and not deceive themselves by hearing alone.

row.basis: The hearer who sees and forgets
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Prophet’s preserved recitation with the person who lets reminder pass; James likens the hearer who does not act to someone who looks at his face in a mirror.

row.basis: The hearer turns away and forgets
row.note: The commentary’s image is of one who moves the reminder aside; James says the inactive hearer goes away and immediately forgets what he was like.

row.basis: Persevering in the word and doing it
row.note: The commentary links self-directed purification to sustained action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the one who looks into the law, perseveres, and acts.

row.basis: One sermon meets mockery and postponement
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is offered but response divides hearers; after Paul speaks of resurrection, some mock and others postpone hearing him again.
The commentary contrasts the worst person with one who takes the reminder; Acts adds that some listeners join Paul and believe after the same speech that others mocked.

row.basis: Not all obey the good news they hear
row.note: The commentary makes reception rather than delivery the point of division; Paul says not all obeyed the good news and cites the question of who believed the report.

row.basis: Jesus’ words are offered for salvation
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is given for benefit, even though its hearers may turn away; Jesus says he came to save the world rather than judge the one who hears his words.

row.basis: The rejected word judges its hearer
row.note: The commentary connects avoiding reminder with the coming fire and consequence; Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge, and the word will judge him on the last day.

row.basis: Seeking death but unable to die
row.note: The commentary reads the condemned state as neither dying nor living; Revelation says those tormented in the vision seek death but cannot find it, a striking parallel with the refusal of death as release.

row.basis: Abraham taken from beyond the River
row.note: The commentary says Abraham asks God to keep him away from idols rather than trusting his own power; Joshua recalls God taking Abraham from beyond the River and leading him, a related account of Abraham’s separation under divine guidance.

The commentary describes Moses inviting Pharaoh to purify himself and then Pharaoh denying and turning away; Exodus has Pharaoh answer Moses and Aaron by asking who the Lord is and refusing to obey his voice, a shared confrontation whose wording and demand differ.
The commentary develops the division between the one who remembers and the one who avoids reminder; Deuteronomy sets life and good against death and evil before Israel as a covenant decision.
The commentary says the response, not the offered reminder, divides people; Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and urges Israel to choose life, making the decision explicit.

row.basis: Wisdom speaks publicly in the streets
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is not delivered privately to only one favored hearer; Proverbs portrays Wisdom crying aloud in public places, where the invitation can be heard before some reject it.

row.basis: Eating the fruit of one’s own way
row.note: The commentary describes the response as what a person does to himself by moving the reminder aside; Wisdom says the refusers will eat the fruit of their own way, making consequence follow chosen conduct.

row.basis: Safety for the one who listens
row.note: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with the one who takes reminder; Wisdom promises that the one who listens will dwell securely, giving the positive outcome beside the warning of refusal.

row.basis: A people unwilling to hear instruction
row.note: The commentary describes people who choose to turn from reminder; Isaiah calls the people rebellious children unwilling to hear the Lord’s instruction.

row.basis: Requesting smooth words instead of warning
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person treats beneficial reminder as something to avoid; Isaiah’s hearers tell seers not to see and ask for smooth, agreeable things rather than truth.

row.basis: Prophets sent repeatedly, but no listening
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the universal offer from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the Lord persistently sent prophets, yet the people did not listen or incline their ear.

row.basis: A call to turn from evil is ignored
row.note: The commentary links rejecting reminder with refusing the offered chance to change; Jeremiah recounts repeated calls to turn from evil and serve God, which Judah did not heed.

row.basis: Neighbors invite one another to hear the prophet
row.note: The commentary’s side image says the reminder is beside the person, not far away; Ezekiel describes people speaking to one another and inviting one another to hear the Lord’s word from the prophet.
The commentary says the rejected reminder has reached the hearer and remains within reach; Isaiah urges seeking the Lord while he may be found and calling while he is near.
The commentary contrasts the person who takes the reminder with the person who avoids it; Isaiah calls the wicked to forsake his way and return to the Lord for mercy.

row.basis: The resident alien is to be loved as oneself
row.note: The commentary develops “foreign neighbor” as an image for someone kept beside but treated as unrelated; Leviticus commands Israel to love the resident alien as oneself, an ethical counterpoint to treating the nearby reminder as foreign.

row.basis: A famine of hearing the Lord’s words
row.note: The commentary stresses that the reminder is offered now and can be put aside; Amos announces a later famine of hearing the Lord’s words, a reversal in which people will lack what the commentary’s hearers still have.

row.basis: Searching for a word that cannot be found
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person lets a present reminder pass by; Amos portrays people wandering in search of the Lord’s word and not finding it, sharpening the cost of refusing it while available.

The commentary connects the worst person’s refusal with the great fire and the condition of neither dying nor living; Isaiah pictures the corpses of rebels under an unquenched fire and undying worm, sharing persistent judgment imagery but describing corpses rather than the same paradox of living punishment.

row.basis: The wicked later see the righteous vindicated
row.note: The commentary says the one who avoids reminder discovers too late what he has lost; Wisdom depicts the wicked seeing the righteous honored and confessing that they once misjudged him.

row.basis: A belated confession of straying from truth
row.note: The commentary connects refusal of reminder to a path whose loss becomes clear after judgment; Wisdom’s wicked confess that they strayed from the way of truth and did not know the path of righteousness.

row.basis: Two spirits and two paths to opposed outcomes
row.note: The commentary develops a person’s response as the dividing choice between outcomes; the Community Rule organizes human conduct under spirits and paths of truth/light or perversity/darkness, giving a Second Temple Jewish version of moral division.

The commentary says the one reminder is offered while reception differs; Jesus identifies the seed as the word, so the parable makes the hearer’s response determine whether the same sowing bears fruit.

row.basis: Initial reception can fail under pressure
row.note: The commentary’s “remembering” is not merely hearing once; Mark describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tribulation or persecution comes.
The commentary connects rejection of reminder to preferring worldly life; Mark says cares, wealth’s deceit, and other desires enter and choke the word so it becomes fruitless.

The commentary distinguishes a person who receives reminder from one who turns away; Jesus cites Isaiah about people who hear without understanding and have closed their eyes lest they turn and be healed.

row.basis: Jerusalem was unwilling to be gathered
row.note: The commentary says the reminder can be offered while its audience chooses distance; Jesus laments that he wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children but they were unwilling.
The commentary says response to the reminder, not its delivery, distinguishes hearers; Jesus warns listeners to take care how they hear, since what one has can be taken away or increased.

row.basis: The rich man turns away from a life-giving invitation
row.note: The commentary connects avoidance of reminder with preferring worldly life; Mark says the man who was invited to sell his possessions and follow Jesus went away grieving because he had great wealth.
The commentary reads purification as work a person does upon himself; James calls double-minded people to cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, and draw near to God.
The commentary groups remembering, avoiding, and purifying as self-directed actions; John says the one who hopes in Christ purifies himself as Christ is pure.
The commentary treats reminder as presently available and response as decisive; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and repeats the warning not to harden the heart.

The commentary’s condemned person neither dies nor lives and endures prolonged hardship; Revelation says the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night, a related but differently framed image of unending punishment.

The commentary develops the nearby reminder as treated like a foreign neighbor; Jesus identifies himself with the stranger who is welcomed, making reception of the socially distant one a test of response.

The commentary connects the worst person with the great fire and an unending state; Jesus invokes Gehenna where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, sharing persistence imagery without equating the scenes.

The commentary develops a sharp division between the one who takes reminder and the one who avoids it; the Didache opens by setting out a way of life and a way of death and stressing the great difference between them.

The commentary names a worst person by the path he chooses; the Didache’s catalogue of the way of death includes people who hate truth and love falsehood, giving an early Christian moral portrait of that path.

row.basis: Way of light and way of darkness
row.note: The commentary’s paired outcomes turn on a person’s response; Barnabas opens its “Two Ways” teaching with the way of light and the way of darkness, adding an early Christian moral framework for opposed paths.

The commentary emphasizes a reminder whose hearers may take it or turn away; Isaiah says the word sent by God will accomplish what he desires, a different emphasis on the efficacy of the divine word rather than a claim that every hearer responds alike.

row.basis: Fear of the Lord and despising instruction
row.note: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and remembers with the ashqa who avoids reminder; Proverbs makes fear of the Lord the beginning of knowledge and says fools despise wisdom and instruction.
The commentary sets the one who receives reminder against the one who turns aside; Wisdom says finding her brings life and favor from the Lord.
The commentary says the wretched person makes his own condition by putting the reminder aside; Wisdom says the one who misses her harms himself and those who hate her love death.
The commentary links avoiding the offered reminder to the ashqa’s ruin; Proverbs says the person who despises a word will be destroyed, while reverence for the command brings reward.

row.basis: Israel would not hear the Lord
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but some turn from it; the psalm says God’s people would not listen to his voice or submit to him.

row.basis: Handed over to one’s own counsel
row.note: The commentary treats turning away as the hearer’s own choice; the psalm says God gave the unheeding people over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsels.
The commentary says one person takes the reminder while another rejects it; Isaiah places willingness and obedience opposite rebellion, with the former receiving the land’s good.
The commentary links the ashqa’s avoidance with the consequence of his chosen response; Isaiah says those who refuse and rebel will be devoured by the sword.
The commentary emphasizes that the reminder has already come to the hearer; Isaiah says God called and spoke but the people did not answer or hear, instead choosing what displeased him.

The commentary contrasts receiving reminder with turning aside; Jeremiah invites the people to stand at the crossroads and ask for the good ancient path, but they answer that they will not walk in it.

row.basis: The watchmen’s warning is not heard
row.note: The commentary separates the messenger’s act of warning from the audience’s response; Jeremiah says watchmen sounded the trumpet, but the people replied that they would not listen.

row.basis: Rejecting the word of the Lord
row.note: The commentary identifies the ashqa by his refusal of reminder; Jeremiah says the wise have rejected the word of the Lord, so their claim to wisdom is exposed.
The commentary reads remembering, avoiding, and purifying as acts done upon oneself; Moses calls Israel to circumcise the heart and stop being stiff-necked, a concrete demand for inward change.

row.basis: Do not postpone good when it is at hand
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is beside the hearer yet treated as a foreign neighbor; Proverbs says not to tell a neighbor to return tomorrow when the needed good is already with you, an ethical parallel to leaving available good within reach unused.

row.basis: Delighting in Torah day and night
row.note: The commentary pictures the reminder as something one may take near and work into oneself; Psalm 1 describes the blessed person delighting in the Lord’s Torah and meditating on it continually.
The commentary develops a split between the one who receives reminder and the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 says the Lord knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes.

The commentary’s lexical aside links the south wind and its clouds with the pasture scene in 87:4; Psalm 65 describes God watering the earth and blessing its growth, a specific rain-provision image beside that reading.
The commentary links its wind-and-cloud aside to the surah’s pasture; Psalm 65 closes with pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, a related scene of rain’s result.

row.basis: A nearby neighbor can be closer than distant kin
row.note: The commentary develops the “side” as the place of either companion or stranger and says the reminder remains beside the person; Proverbs values the neighbor who is near over a brother who is far away, giving relational weight to nearness.
The commentary’s triad includes purifying oneself as a deliberate act; Isaiah commands people to wash, make themselves clean, and cease doing evil, a direct ethical image of self-correction.

row.basis: Clean hands and a pure heart
row.note: The commentary says purification is one of the hearer’s own responses; the psalm describes the person fit to approach God as one with clean hands and a pure heart.

row.basis: Make a new heart and turn from transgression
row.note: The commentary links avoiding reminder with a self-made ruin and purification with a chosen response; Ezekiel calls Israel to cast away transgressions and make a new heart and spirit so they may live.

row.basis: Moses asks Pharaoh to humble himself
row.note: The commentary’s Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, followed by Pharaoh’s rejection; Exodus has Moses and Aaron ask how long Pharaoh will refuse to humble himself before the Lord, making the refusal to heed a direct point of contact.

row.basis: Abraham and Balaam as opposed moral types
row.note: The commentary presents Abraham as entrusting himself to God and seeking distance from idolatry; Avot contrasts disciples of Abraham, marked by humility and a good eye, with Balaam’s pride and acquisitiveness, giving a Jewish ethical interpretation of the Abrahamic posture.

row.basis: Prophetic speech that is heard but not understood
row.note: The commentary stresses one reminder offered while hearers differ in response; Isaiah’s commission says the people will hear without understanding, framing prophetic speech as a judicial hardening, a different emphasis from the commentary’s open invitation.

row.basis: Hearing that does not lead to turning
row.note: The commentary contrasts the person who receives admonition with the one who avoids it; Isaiah’s commission describes closed eyes and dull hearts so the people do not turn and be healed, a contrary account of how the warning functions.

row.basis: The broad road leads to destruction
row.note: The commentary develops two opposed responses and their outcomes; Jesus describes a broad gate and road leading to destruction, entered by many, as a concrete image of the destructive path.

row.basis: The narrow way leads to life
row.note: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with one who receives reminder; Jesus says the narrow way leads to life and is found by few, giving the other side of the two-path image.
The commentary says the messenger offers reminder but does not control its reception; Jesus says whoever hears his messengers hears him and whoever rejects them rejects him.

row.basis: Do not refuse the one who speaks
row.note: The commentary ties turning away from reminder to judgment; Hebrews warns its hearers not to refuse the one speaking, recalling that those who rejected the earthly warning did not escape.

row.basis: People will not endure sound teaching
row.note: The commentary says some turn away from reminder because of their chosen response; Paul warns that people will reject sound teaching and gather teachers to suit their desires.
The commentary makes turning away the decisive act of the ashqa; Paul says people will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths.
The commentary says reminder is already present and offered; Jesus says the hearers search the Scriptures, which testify about him.
The commentary says the wretched one keeps the reminder nearby but will not receive it; Jesus tells his hearers they are unwilling to come to him to have life.

row.basis: People love darkness rather than light
row.note: The commentary describes the person who chooses distance from beneficial reminder; John says people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.
The commentary’s avoider moves away from the reminder; John says the one who does evil hates the light and does not come to it, lest his deeds be exposed.

row.basis: Doing truth and coming into the light
row.note: The commentary contrasts turning away with inward moral change; John says the one who does what is true comes to the light so his deeds may be seen as done in God.

row.basis: Love of this life risks losing it
row.note: The commentary links avoiding reminder to preferring the present worldly life; Jesus says the one who loves his life loses it, while the one who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life.

row.basis: The rejected stone is precious to believers
row.note: The commentary says the same reminder is differently received; Peter says the stone rejected by builders is precious to those who believe, giving a Christian image of one message/object valued by some and refused by others.

row.basis: A stumbling stone for the disobedient
row.note: The commentary portrays the ashqa as turning aside from what is offered; Peter says others stumble because they disobey the word, a specific outcome of rejection.

row.basis: The word rejected by some hearers
row.note: The commentary says the reminder’s offer is unchanged but its hearers divide; Paul and Barnabas say their hearers have rejected the word and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life.
The commentary contrasts the person who turns away with the one who receives reminder; Acts says Gentile hearers rejoice and believe after the same proclamation that some rejected.

row.basis: Jesus makes Nineveh’s repentance a witness
row.note: The commentary treats taking warning as the positive alternative to turning away; Jesus says Nineveh repented at Jonah’s proclamation and will condemn the generation that refuses a greater warning, a Christian rereading of Jonah’s response.

row.basis: The crowd silences a blind petitioner
row.note: The commentary recounts a blind man who comes seeking help while another turns away from him; Mark’s crowd rebukes blind Bartimaeus and tells him to be silent, but he cries out all the more.

row.basis: The blind petitioner follows the way
row.note: The commentary pairs the blind man’s humble approach with the person who avoids admonition; Jesus restores Bartimaeus and he follows Jesus on the road, a distinct reversal in which the blind petitioner responds and follows.
The commentary says the same reminder is offered but its recipients choose whether to respond; in Jesus’ banquet parable, the invited guests begin making excuses and refuse the invitation.

row.basis: The blind and poor are brought to the feast
row.note: The commentary’s Abasa scene gives attention to a blind seeker whom a prominent person neglects; after the invited guests refuse, the servant brings the poor, crippled, blind, and lame to the banquet.

row.basis: The blind see and the seeing are judged
row.note: The commentary uses the blind visitor to expose the failure of a sighted, socially prominent person to recognize who may benefit; Jesus says he came so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.
The commentary opposes the humble blind seeker to the one who turns away; Jesus tells the Pharisees that their claim to see leaves their sin, unlike the blind man whose encounter leads to sight.

row.basis: A messenger leaves when a household refuses to hear
row.note: The commentary limits the messenger to offering reminder and leaves response with the audience; Jesus tells messengers to leave and shake the dust off when a house or town will not receive or hear them.

row.basis: Pay attention lest one drift away
row.note: The commentary describes the ashqa as moving away from the reminder; Hebrews urges close attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away from it.
The commentary presents refusal as a response that can suppress what is offered; Paul warns the community not to quench the Spirit.
The commentary says the reminder is offered but may be put aside; Paul tells the community not to despise prophetic utterances, a direct instruction against rejecting admonition.

row.basis: Work out salvation with fear and trembling
row.note: The commentary reads self-purification and receiving reminder as deliberate action, and distinguishes it from the messenger’s work; Paul tells believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling.

row.basis: God works in the willing hearer
row.note: The commentary says human response remains dependent on God’s willing; Paul immediately says God is at work in believers both to will and to work, adding divine agency to the self-directed effort.

row.basis: Hearing the voice and opening the door
row.note: The commentary says the reminder is beside a person yet may be kept outside; Revelation pictures Christ standing at a door and knocking, with fellowship following if someone hears and opens.

row.basis: The burdened are invited to rest
row.note: The commentary contrasts the easy path prepared for the messenger with the hardship of the one who rejects guidance; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest.

row.basis: The yoke is easy and the burden light
row.note: The commentary connects wretchedness with hardship opposite the easy path; Jesus describes his yoke as easy and his burden as light, offering a contrasting response to a divine invitation.

row.basis: Torment continues day and night forever
row.note: The commentary reads the condemned condition as prolonged, with neither death nor life; Revelation portrays the devil and the beast’s followers as tormented day and night forever, a related image of unending punishment.

The commentary says one admonition becomes beneficial only in its receiver; Hebrews says the good news reached the wilderness generation too, but the heard word did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith.
The fearful recipient of the reminder is set against the one who shuns it; Proverbs makes fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge and says fools despise wisdom and discipline.
The page pictures deliberate sidelining rather than panic flight; Zechariah's ancestors refuse to heed, turn a stubborn shoulder, and stop their ears against prophetic correction.
Zechariah says they made their heart hard lest they hear Torah and the former prophetic words sent by the Spirit, identifying the offence as rejecting a word that has actually arrived.
God sets out ancient paths in which rest could be found, but the people answer that they will not walk there; this closely matches the offered guidance and chosen refusal in the commentary.
Instead of inclining their ear, people walk after their own counsel and stubborn heart and go backward; it makes self-directed turning from the reminder an alternative course, not a lack of access.

Ezekiel warns the wicked to turn; if the listener does not turn, he dies in iniquity while the watchman has discharged his task. This closely frames the commentary's non-coercive admonisher and responsible hearer.
The audience hears Ezekiel's words as a pleasant song but does not do them; this is a concrete counterpart to advice kept beside oneself rather than taken inward.
Wisdom's call and extended hand are refused, providing a particular scene of one offered instruction being rejected.
Those addressed neglect all counsel and refuse reproof, an exact ethical reversal of taking a beneficial reminder.
The liturgical call to hear God's voice today makes hearing a present response to divine address, closely framing the split between receiving and avoiding the reminder.
After the call to hear, the worshiper is told not to harden the heart as at Meribah; it gives the commentary's inward resistance a concrete historical and liturgical form.
Hebrews tells hearers to pay much closer attention to what they heard lest they drift away, capturing the page's quiet, continuing movement of putting admonition to one side.
Paul says opponents thrust the word of God aside and thereby judge themselves unworthy of eternal life; the self-directed rejection and outcome closely match the ashqa's active avoidance.
James calls those who hear the word without doing it self-deceived, sharpening the commentary's claim that the issue is what a person does with unchanged counsel.
James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the doer who remains at the perfect law and is blessed, directly accompanying the commentary's identification of turning from signs with forgetting them.
Paul's one ministry is an aroma among those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation yielding divided hearers mirrors the commentary's single reminder.

row.basis: death to death, life to life
row.note: The one aroma becomes death to death for some and life to life for others, supplying a compact Christian form of the page's same word and opposed destiny pattern.
The word of the cross is folly to those perishing but God's power to those being saved, another specific instance of one preached message differently received.
Jesus addresses people who search Scripture yet are unwilling to come to him for life; it connects proximity to revealed words with an active refusal of their life-giving offer.
People turn their hearing away from truth and turn toward myths; this gives the page's turning from remembrance a particular alternative object.
Ezekiel's rebellious house has eyes to see and ears to hear yet does neither, directly illuminating the page's post-refusal blindness as a moral response to signs rather than lack of organs.
YHWH's servant sees much but does not observe and has open ears but does not hear, adding a prophetic image for instruction available yet spiritually unreceived.

The self-satisfied speaker claims to need nothing but is called wretched, poor, blind, and naked. These terms concentrate the page's self-sufficiency, wretchedness, judgmental blindness, and Edenic exposure.

row.basis: do not forget what was seen
row.note: Moses tells Israel to guard itself lest it forget what it has seen and to transmit it, a direct Torah counterpart to the commentary's moral reading of forgotten signs.
Moses warns Israel not to forget YHWH by failing to keep commandments, making forgetting an enacted refusal as the page does.
Israel quickly turns aside from the commanded way to make and worship a calf; it is a concrete biblical inversion of the commentary's contrast between shunning idols and shunning God's reminder.

row.basis: do not turn aside after non-profit
row.note: Samuel forbids turning aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver; the page reverses this relation when the wretched treats beneficial admonition as the thing to avoid.
Israel is warned lest the heart be deceived so that it turns aside to serve other gods, supplying the inward deception behind the inversion of proper avoidance.
Paul asks believers to cleanse themselves from every defilement and complete holiness in fear of God, closely joining self-work, purification, and fear as the commentary joins them.
Everyone whose hope is fixed on him purifies himself; the active reflexive act is a direct Christian analogue for the commentary's account of tazakka as work done on oneself.

In Genesis the ground is cursed and eating becomes toil because the command was disobeyed. The page's post-garden hunger and hardship belongs beside this account, while its differently specified privations remain meaningful.
Genesis defines post-garden hardship as bread by sweat until return to dust; the page sets this mortal toil-and-death frame beside its later fire in which one neither dies nor lives.
Joshua says Terah and Abraham's ancestors served other gods beyond the River; the page turns that family background into Abraham's explicit anti-idol admonition and withdrawal.

Genesis Rabbah has Abraham expose the powerlessness of Terah's idols, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the page's Abraham asking his father why he worships things that cannot hear, see, or help before separating from them.
Pharaoh's refusal to obey YHWH in response to Moses supplies the Hebrew Bible scene behind the page's Moses invitation to purification and Pharaoh's denial and turning away.

Isaiah's rebels are displayed where the worm does not die and fire is not quenched, giving a Hebrew Bible image of enduring punitive fire beside the great fire and non-ending condition developed on the page.
Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire, closely paralleling the page's fate of entering great fire without death or life.
Jesus's final separation sends some to eternal punishment and the righteous to eternal life, supplying the page's polarized ultimate consequences in a judgment scene.
The smoke of idol-worshipers' torment rises for ages and they have no rest day or night, a specifically relentless Christian image for the commentary's prolonged, unrelieved fire.
Jesus asks what profit lies in gaining the whole world while forfeiting life; it mirrors the page's claim that the shunner substitutes worldly life for a beneficial reminder and loses lasting good.
The world and its desire pass away whereas the one doing God's will remains forever, directly accompanying the commentary's contrast of preferred worldly life with a better, more lasting hereafter.
God's kindness is meant to lead a person to repentance even when it is despised; this illuminates Moses's gentle invitation to Pharaoh to purify himself and the subsequent refusal.
Hebrews reads the Psalm's today as a mandate for daily mutual exhortation so none is hardened by sin's deceit, making sustained reminder a guard against the refusal described on the page.

The page calls final blindness a response to signs forgotten; Avot treats forgetting even one learned word as spiritually grave while distinguishing involuntary difficulty, sharpening the moral rather than merely mnemonic sense of forgetting.
God promises to cleanse Israel from uncleanness and idols; beside Abraham's plea to be kept from idols and the purified person in the page, it foregrounds divine protection as well as human response.
Draw near to God, cleanse hands, and purify hearts joins nearness and self-purification, helping the page's spatial language of the side and its call to purification read together.

row.basis: rising before dawn, hope in word
row.note: The psalmist rises before dawn, cries for help, and hopes in God's word; it gives a particular biblical night posture joining departure from bed, prayer, and receptive hope rather than avoidance.
Walking with the wise makes one wise while companionship with fools brings harm, lending moral force to the page's companion and alien-neighbor reading of what stands at a person's side.

row.basis: good or evil friend and neighbor
row.note: Rabbi Yohanan's disciples name good friend and good neighbor as ways of good, and evil friend or neighbor as ways to avoid; this gives a rabbinic companion reading for the page's side as either guide or estranged neighbor.

row.basis: life and good, death and evil
row.note: Moses sets before Israel life and good versus death and evil, giving the page's extremes of ease and wretchedness a covenantal two-way framework.
Jesus's broad way leads to destruction and many enter it; the page's road image creates a specific comparison with an easy-seeming route terminating in ruin.
Jesus calls the way leading to life narrow and hard and says few find it, creating an illuminating tension with the commentary's easy way and hard ascent.
Baruch calls Israel to hear commandments of life and learn wisdom, a deliberate address to the hearing recipient that fits the page's reminder received by one person and avoided by another.

row.basis: walking God's way and enduring peace
row.note: Baruch says that walking in God's way would mean living in peace forever, closely paralleling the page's Adam passage where following divine guidance prevents wandering and wretchedness.

Genesis says the garden pair are naked yet unashamed, whereas the page's Qur'anic Adam passage defines Eden by absence of nakedness. The difference matters because the commentary treats nakedness as a concrete index of hardship.
Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he does not listen to Moses and Aaron; set beside the page's emphasis on self-initiated avoidance, this biblical hardening language makes a relevant agency difference.

row.basis: lake of fire as second death
row.note: Revelation calls the lake of fire the second death, while the page insists its fire's inhabitant neither dies nor lives; the different death language creates a careful counter-reading of final punishment.
Abraham tells the rich man's brothers to hear Moses and the prophets; the page invokes Abraham and Moses around a warning that proximity to revelation does not compel reception.

Against the page's offered reminder and non-coercive teacher, Hebrews warns hearers not to refuse the one speaking; its contrast between an earthly warning and a heavenly address makes rejection of a delivered warning liable to judgment.
The commentary calls the reminder beneficial and contrasts guidance with self-directed avoidance; Isaiah has YHWH teach his people for their profit and lead them in the way they should go.
Isaiah says attention to the commandments would have made peace like a river; this adds the foregone good to the commentary's claim that the wretched person treats benefit as harm.
