Hebrews reproves readers for forgetting the exhortation that addresses them as children, making a prior scriptural warning itself the object that must be recalled.

row.basis: word choked by cares, riches, and pleasures
row.note: In the thorny soil the heard word is choked by cares, riches, and pleasures and reaches no maturity; this directly supplies a Christian picture of why benefit may fail where the commentary contrasts lasting good with worldly preference.

row.basis: creation known but not honored or thanked
row.note: Although people knew God, they neither honored nor thanked him and became futile in thought; this is the negative continuation of creation as a reminder that the commentary says can be seen yet not retained.

row.basis: deliberate overlooking of creation and water
row.note: The opponents deliberately overlook the creation of earth through and by water through God's word, a striking Christian counterpart to the commentary's water-and-creation reminders that can be ignored.

row.basis: Noah warned of unseen things, reverent, building an ark
row.note: Noah acts in reverent fear after a warning about unseen things and prepares an ark; it joins the commentary's fearful receiver, warning, and flood-water scene in one Christian retelling.

row.basis: heard words put into practice on rock
row.note: The wise builder hears Jesus' words and does them, building on rock; this provides a vivid Christian counterpart to the commentary's demand that retained reminder issue in stable, beneficial action.

row.basis: Timothy sent to remind communities of apostolic ways
row.note: Timothy is sent to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways as taught everywhere, an unusually exact New Testament instance of a messenger being delegated to perform remembrance for others.

row.basis: learned, received, heard, seen, then practiced
row.note: The Philippians are to practice what they learned, received, heard, and saw; its ordered reception-to-practice sequence closely reflects the commentary's account of reminder becoming the hearer's own deed.

row.basis: sacred writings able to make wise for salvation
row.note: Sacred writings are able to make Timothy wise for salvation, a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's prior sheets as a word whose benefit lies in the good to which it leads.
The sacrifices contain an annual remembrance of sins, a distinct Christian liturgical use of memory that bears on the commentary's discussion of dhikr's ritual as well as mental forms.

row.basis: honor with lips while heart remains distant
row.note: Jesus contrasts lip-honor with a heart far from God; this sharpens the commentary's warning that spoken remembrance is only a later branch if the inward holding of the word is absent.

row.basis: land drinks rain and yields crop, receiving blessing
row.note: Land that drinks repeated rain and bears a useful crop receives blessing; it gives a Christian agrarian analogue to the commentary's water, pasture, and beneficial remainder imagery.

row.basis: thorns after rain are rejected and burned
row.note: Land yielding thorns after the same rain is rejected and ends in burning, a specific contrary image for the commentary's one reminder producing different outcomes in its hearers.

row.basis: remember the one who speaks God's word and honor that speaker
row.note: The Didache tells its hearer to remember day and night the person who speaks God's word and to honor that person; it is an early Christian reception of the teacher-reminder relation developed in the commentary.
The commentary joins a received text, reverent fear, and active response; the king reads the written Torah daily precisely to learn fear of YHWH and keep its words.
The commentary's unnamed listener is defined by an inward reverence rather than a social label; Isaiah likewise singles out the humble and contrite person who trembles at YHWH's word.
Like the commentary's limit on the messenger's task, Ezekiel has warned the wicked; if the hearer does not turn, he dies for his own wrong while the watchman is delivered.

row.basis: hear words but heart pursues gain
row.note: The people sit before Ezekiel and hear his words but do not do them because their hearts pursue gain, a direct scene of speech reaching listeners without becoming received instruction.

The announced word did not benefit its hearers because it was not joined with faith, closely matching the commentary's distinction between an offered reminder and one that benefits a receptive person.
Jesus's good soil hears the word, holds it fast in an honest and good heart, and bears fruit in perseverance; this gives the commentary's inward taking-up of admonition a concrete narrative figure.
James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the doer who perseveres, directly joining the commentary's memory-versus-forgetting image to the listener's own enacted response.
The blessing falls on reader, hearers, and keepers together, a close Christian chain from spoken written warning through reception to practice.

row.basis: tender heart when book is heard
row.note: Josiah's tender, humbled heart responds when he hears the words of judgment from the book, supplying a biblical portrait of the inward disposition through which admonition takes effect.
The psalm's urgent today makes hearing a timely act, closely paralleling the commentary's near-future remembrance before the moment for response has passed.
The command not to harden the heart names the inward contrary to the commentary's reverent listener who can receive a reminder.
The Torah requires its words to be upon the heart, a precise counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the listener must carry the reminder within rather than merely hear it pass by.
After the words are placed on the heart, they are repeated and spoken through daily life; this illuminates the commentary's path from inward remembrance back to voiced practice.
Joshua is told to keep the book on his mouth, meditate on it continually, and do it, a compact analogue for the commentary's movement from transmitted speech through inner recollection to action.
The psalmist stores YHWH's word in the heart in order not to sin, giving the commentary's retained rather than lost reminder a moral consequence.
The explicit resolve not to forget the divine word directly accompanies the commentary's ذ ك ر B003 contrast between holding what one has received and letting it escape.

row.basis: ذ ك ر B003 and Hebrew זכר
row.note: The source label ذ ك ر B003 concerns remembering and holding; the Hebrew cognate זכר commands active Sabbath remembrance that takes ritual form in sanctifying the day.
Those who fear YHWH speak with one another, and a book of remembrance is written before him; the Hebrew זכר family brings together fear, voiced attention, and memorial record.

row.basis: remember what was received and heard
row.note: The church is told to remember how it received and heard, then keep it and repent, directly framing remembrance as recovery of a previously received word that still demands action.
The command to remember the height from which one has fallen and return to first works closely matches the commentary's tezekkür as seeking and recovering what has slipped away.

The person lacking virtue is blind and has forgotten cleansing from former sins, an unusually close counterpart to the commentary's pairing of remembered truth with opened sight and later purification.
Jesus joins unseeing eyes, unhearing ears, and failure to remember in one rebuke, closely matching the commentary's contrast between a reminder that opens sight and refusal that does not truly hear.
Isaiah's hardened heart, heavy ears, and shut eyes prevent hearing, seeing, understanding, and turning; it is the negative counterpart to the commentary's inward alertness becoming sight.
Hebrews requires closer attention to what was heard lest it drift away, giving a specific image for the commentary's concern that a received thing can escape unless the listener holds it.
After Jesus's resurrection the disciples remember his saying and believe Scripture and his word, a narrative in which recall of a prior utterance becomes renewed understanding and trust.
Job identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding, directly supporting the commentary's claim that reverent fear is bound to knowledge rather than mere fright.
The psalm makes fear of YHWH the beginning of wisdom, a concise biblical formulation for the commentary's knowledgeable, reality-responsive fear.

YHWH promises to place his fear in the people's hearts so that they will not turn away, paralleling the commentary's presentation of fear as an enduring inward condition that yields faithful response.
YHWH's intimate counsel and covenant are made known to those who fear him, linking fear with the knowing and receiving of divine instruction developed in the commentary.
Moses distinguishes immediate panic from fear of God set before Israel so that they do not sin, clarifying the commentary's distinction between ordinary fright and reverent, morally active fear.

row.basis: warning about unseen things and reverence
row.note: Noah is warned about things not yet seen and, acting in reverent fear, prepares the ark; this is a close figure for remembering and fearing before judgment becomes visible.

row.basis: gentle correction toward repentance and knowledge
row.note: Gentle instruction is offered in hope that God may grant repentance leading to knowledge of truth, closely echoing the commentary's soft speech to Pharaoh as a possible door into recollection or fear.

row.basis: coming to one's senses from the devil's snare
row.note: The corrected opponents may come to their senses and escape the devil's snare, a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's temptation-triggered remembering, renewed sight, and recovery.

row.basis: Moses and Aaron before hardened Pharaoh
row.note: Against the commentary's Qur'anic scene of gentle speech offered in hope that Pharaoh may remember or fear, Exodus's shared mission reports Pharaoh's hardened heart and refusal to listen; the differing outcome is the point of the comparison.
Habakkuk hears YHWH's report and responds with awe, supplying the inverse sequence explicitly considered in the commentary: revelation remembered or heard can awaken fear.
Personified Wisdom calls and stretches out a hand but is refused, a pointed counterpart to the commentary's reminder that can be offered by a speaker yet passed by by its audience.
After calamity those who rejected Wisdom call and seek, but receive no answer; it closely parallels the commentary's warning that remembrance after the decisive moment no longer benefits.
The refusal of Wisdom is explained as hatred of knowledge and refusal to choose fear of YHWH, tightly combining the commentary's two central inward conditions.

row.basis: refused call and unanswered later call
row.note: Because the people did not hear when YHWH called, he would not hear when they later called, giving the commentary's timely-warning and too-late-response structure a prophetic counterpart.

row.basis: remember the Creator before evil days
row.note: Qohelet commands remembrance of the Creator while life still affords response, directly matching the commentary's contrast between present remembrance and regret after the time has passed.
Esau seeks the blessing afterward but finds no place for repentance despite tears, a specific New Testament image for the commentary's ineffectual late turning.
Israel's claim that its own power produced wealth gives the commentary's self-sufficient figure a close Torah counterpart: perceived sufficiency obscures dependence and remembrance.
The command to remember YHWH as giver of power directly answers the self-credit of the preceding verse, like the commentary's call to recover what self-sufficiency refuses to see.

Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing, while not knowing it is poor and blind; this is an exceptionally close counterpart to the commentary's self-satisfied person who sees no lack and so does not seek what was lost.

row.basis: eye salve so that you may see
row.note: The counsel to anoint blind eyes so that they may see continues the Laodicean contrast and concretizes the commentary's image of recollection opening the eye.

row.basis: remembering the Name and keeping Torah
row.note: The psalmist remembers YHWH's name in the night and keeps Torah, a direct analogue for the commentary's final movement from inward recollection to voiced divine name and obedient practice.

row.basis: praise joined to not forgetting benefits
row.note: The soul blesses YHWH by not forgetting his benefits, making praise itself an answer to retained memory as in the commentary's zikir moving back into speech.

The word dwelling richly in the community produces teaching, admonition, and sung gratitude, closely paralleling the commentary's arc from spoken reminder through inward retention to worshipful speech.
The command to perform the meal in remembrance of Christ gives the commentary's move from recall to a repeated act of worship a specific Christian liturgical form.
The Messiah sanctifies and cleanses through the word, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's sequence in which a received reminder leads on toward purification.
The individual who sins bears his own iniquity, directly illuminating the commentary's insistence that the unresponsive hearer, rather than the warning messenger, carries the consequence.
Paul's maxim that each person carries his own load supplies a New Testament ethical analogue for the commentary's refusal to shift the listener's response or burden onto another.

The grass withers while God's word stands forever, a close counterpart to the surah's meadow turning to refuse and the commentary's contrast between perishing natural forms and a retained divine word.

row.basis: active salvation with fear and trembling
row.note: Believers are told to work out salvation with fear and trembling, bringing together the commentary's inward reverence and the listener's personal, active response.
Receiving the unshakable kingdom issues in acceptable worship with reverence and awe, closely corresponding to the commentary's movement from fear and remembrance into prayerful praise.

row.basis: fear God, give glory, judgment near
row.note: The angelic proclamation calls people to fear God and give him glory because judgment has come, an explicit fusion of warning, reverent response, and imminent eschatological time.
The psalmist's flesh trembles from fear of YHWH and his judgments, giving the commentary's bodily shudder of reverent hearers a direct biblical analogue.
Habakkuk's body and lips tremble when he hears, a concrete parallel to the commentary's account of hearing that first causes bodily trembling before a later inward response.

row.basis: Spirit teaching and bringing words to memory
row.note: Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach the disciples and bring his sayings to their remembrance; this places divine agency alongside the commentary's distinction between transmitted speech and the hearer's remembering.
The women remember Jesus's earlier words at the empty tomb, a narrative recovery of a prior utterance that changes how they understand the present event.
In the temptation scene Jesus answers Satan by voicing Scripture and commanding worship of God alone, a specific image of retained divine words resisting a satanic prompt.

Abraham tells the rich man to remember his former life after he is in torment, making explicit the commentary's contrast between useful present recollection and a painful, irreversible memory after judgment.

row.basis: refusal to hear Moses and the prophets
row.note: The claim that one who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection speaks to the commentary's image of people passing by an offered reminder while desiring a more exceptional sign.

row.basis: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: YHWH's song is promised not to be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a Torah image for preserving a divinely given utterance across forgetting and recitation.
The fading grass image recalls the commentary's meadow becoming refuse; Peter uses it to frame the transience of human life before the enduring proclaimed word in the following verse.

row.basis: abiding word proclaimed as good news
row.note: The word of the Lord remains forever and is identified as the good news preached to the hearers, a Christian counterpart to the enduring, transmitted reminder set against perishing grass.
The text argues that the greatness and beauty of creatures lead to perception of their Maker, closely serving the commentary's claim that attentive knowledge of creation can ground reverent fear.
Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa says that wisdom endures when fear of sin precedes it, a later Jewish ethical formulation that sharpens the commentary's ordering of inward fear before receptive understanding.
The mishnah extends remembrance of the exodus into nighttime recitation, a Jewish liturgical interpretation that helps illuminate the commentary's passage from memory into spoken devotion.

row.basis: fear of Heaven and human responsibility
row.note: The rabbinic maxim that all is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven gives a pointed later formulation for the commentary's tension between the listener's responsibility and divine sovereignty.

Augustine describes finding God in memory after learning him, a Christian theological reflection that enriches the commentary's claim that remembrance is an active return toward what one has received and lost.

row.basis: heart to know, eyes to see, ears to hear
row.note: Moses says that Israel has not been given a heart to know, eyes to see, or ears to hear; this complicates and deepens the commentary's discussion of listenerly response as occurring within divine willing.

row.basis: lips near, heart distant, learned fear
row.note: Isaiah contrasts lip service and a distant heart with a fear learned as human command, a counter-image to the commentary's knowledge-born, inwardly real reverence.
Because forgiveness is with YHWH, he is feared; this supplies another of the commentary's possible sequences, where awareness of God's act awakens reverence rather than merely following it.

row.basis: rejected word judging on the last day
row.note: Jesus says the word he has spoken will judge the one who rejects it on the last day, linking the commentary's non-coercive warning to its theme of a final moment when response is no longer open.

Moses warns Israel not to forget what its eyes have seen or let it depart from the heart, then commands transmission to children; this closely joins the commentary's retained memory, opened perception, and outward reminder.

row.basis: ذ ك ر B003 and Hebrew זכר
row.note: The source's ذ ك ر B003 label concerns active remembering; Israel is commanded to remember the wilderness way, whose testing disclosed what was in the heart and whether the people would keep command.

row.basis: ذ ك ر B003 and Hebrew זכר
row.note: The tassel is seen so that Israel remembers all YHWH's commandments and does them, giving the commentary's reminder-and-response dynamic a concrete visual and bodily form.

row.basis: ذ ك ر B003, Moses's Torah
row.note: The Hebrew command זכרו calls Israel to remember Moses's Torah; beside the surah's final scrolls of Moses, it makes remembrance an explicit return to a received written instruction.

row.basis: word near in mouth and heart
row.note: The word is very near, in mouth and heart, in order to do it; this compactly mirrors the commentary's path from speech received inwardly to personal enactment.

row.basis: write, teach, put the song in mouths
row.note: YHWH commands Moses to write a song, teach it, and put it in Israel's mouths, a close Torah continuation of the commentary's concern that a transmitted word must be retained and voiced by its hearers.

The new covenant places Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, an especially close counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the reminder must become an inner possession of the listener.

row.basis: receive words in heart and hear with ears
row.note: Before Ezekiel speaks to others, he is commanded to receive all God's words in his heart and hear with his ears, directly distinguishing the inward receiver's work from the speaker's delivery.

row.basis: words treated as a pleasant song
row.note: The audience treats Ezekiel's message like a beautiful song and hears its words without doing them, a distinct continuation of the commentary's distinction between an utterance arriving and a listener actually taking it up.
Wisdom begins when the addressee receives sayings and treasures commandments within, a precise sapiential analogue to the commentary's active holding of what the reminder offers.

The result of Wisdom's sought instruction is understanding the fear of YHWH and finding knowledge of God, closely matching the commentary's interrelation of remembered instruction, knowing, and reverent fear.
The one who fears continually is blessed, while the one who hardens the heart falls into calamity; this directly pairs the commentary's sustaining fear with its contrary inward closure.
The psalmist asks for opened eyes to behold wonders from Torah, a focused biblical image for the commentary's claim that recollection can make a person see again.
The opening of YHWH's words gives light and understanding to the simple, closely connecting transmitted speech to the commentary's light-bearing recovery of sight.

row.basis: not forgetting God's works and keeping commands
row.note: The next generation is to set hope in God, not forget his deeds, and keep his commands, tying memory of divine acts to obedient response as the commentary does.
YHWH gives the exiles a heart to know him, and they return with their whole heart; this supplies a positive prophetic counterpart to the commentary's inward capacity for recognition and response.

row.basis: seeking while God may be found
row.note: The command to seek YHWH while he may be found gives the commentary's contrast between timely recollection and uselessly late regret a sharp prophetic formulation.

Isaiah's final vision of the rebels' worm not dying and fire not being quenched directly accompanies the commentary's extension from rejected reminder to a fire in which escape from consequence is no longer possible.

row.basis: hearing Jesus's words and doing them
row.note: The wise builder is defined by hearing Jesus's sayings and doing them, a direct Gospel analogue to the commentary's contrast between a reminder merely spoken and one taken up by its listener.

When a house or town will not receive or hear the disciples, they depart and shake off its dust; this illustrates the commentary's non-coercive messenger whose warning does not remove the hearer's responsibility.
Jesus calls blessed those who hear God's word and keep it, a concise direct counterpart to the commentary's listener who receives an admonition into an active life.

row.basis: heart burning as Scripture is opened
row.note: The disciples' hearts burn while Jesus speaks and opens the Scriptures, a narrative analogue to the commentary's heard word producing a bodily and inward change before renewed understanding.

row.basis: seeking a lost coin until it is found
row.note: The woman's careful search for a lost coin supplies a concrete parabolic counterpart to the commentary's secondary image of tezekkür as pursuing what has escaped rather than passively recalling it.
The prodigal comes to himself, recalls the abundance of his father's house, and begins a return; this narrates the commentary's inward recovery of a lost truth becoming a change of course.
Paul tells the elders to stay awake by remembering his three years of unceasing warning, an unusually close apostolic instance of admonition deliberately becoming hearers' recollection.
Israel's earlier events happened as examples and were written for warning later readers, giving the commentary's preserved scenes and admonition a concrete scriptural rationale.

row.basis: one proclamation among saved and perishing
row.note: Paul describes the apostolic proclamation as Christ's aroma among both those being saved and those perishing, closely paralleling the commentary's one reminder encountering opposed inward responses.

The same aroma is death leading to death for some and life leading to life for others, a precise Christian formulation for the divergent effects of the single offered word developed in the commentary.

row.basis: obedience remembered with fear and trembling
row.note: Titus's affection grows as he remembers the community's obedience and how they received him with fear and trembling, uniquely joining reception, memory, reverence, and conduct.

The Thessalonians receive the preached message as God's word rather than merely human speech, and it works in believers; this closely complements the commentary's distinction between speech crossing over and the listener's effective reception.
The sacred writings are able to make Timothy wise for salvation through faith, a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's book as a reminder for those who become knowing and responsive.
Hearers who cannot endure sound teaching gather teachers to suit their own desires, a specific New Testament figure for turning away from offered reminder through a disordered inner preference.
Mutual daily exhortation guards against hardening through sin's deceitfulness, closely uniting the commentary's repeated reminder with its contrast between reverent openness and hardening.
The letter deliberately arouses the readers' sincere mind by reminder, making explicit the commentary's model in which an external reminder activates inward discernment.
The Gehenna saying's undying worm and unquenched fire closely accompanies the commentary's broader contrast between the timely hearer and the one who reaches enduring fire after rejecting warning.

row.basis: knowledge of God through created things
row.note: God's invisible power and divinity are perceived through created things, furnishing a New Testament counterpart to the commentary's claim that attention to creation can yield the knowledge from which reverent fear arises.

row.basis: known God not glorified, heart darkened
row.note: Though they know God, the ungodly neither glorify nor thank him and their heart is darkened; this sharply counterpoints the commentary's path from knowing and remembering to naming and worship.

row.basis: wisdom and fear of sin as reciprocal
row.note: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah's reciprocal sayings deny both wisdom without fear of sin and fear of sin without wisdom, a later Jewish formulation for the commentary's claim that fear and recollection or knowledge can lead into one another.

row.basis: fear of the Lord and obedience to words
row.note: Sirach says those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words and those who love him keep his ways, a compact Jewish counterpart to the commentary's fearful person who receives reminder in action.

row.basis: remembering the one who speaks God's word
row.note: The Didache directs the disciple to remember day and night the one who speaks God's word, an early Christian expansion of the commentary's relation between a messenger's spoken reminder and a hearer's continuing remembrance.

The worshipers of the beast have no rest day or night amid enduring torment, a Christian image that complements the commentary's secondary treatment of irreversible fire after the time for fruitful recollection.
Everyone who sets this hope purifies himself, furnishing a Christian analogue to the commentary's secondary sequence in which inward reception and fear move on toward personal purification.
Israel hears the living God's voice from the midst of fire and lives; this gives Moses' fire a life-giving hearing that reverses the reminder refused before 87:12 and 87:13's no-life.

row.basis: great fire as discipline and speech
row.note: The verse joins God's great fire to the voice that disciplines Israel and words heard from fire, closely matching the commentary's fire as warning before it becomes the great punitive fire.
Moses' bush burns without being consumed, the biblical scene behind the commentary's Moses-fire encounter and a concrete counterimage to a fire whose entrant undergoes irreversible burning.

row.basis: turning aside toward the great sight
row.note: Moses turns aside toward a burning bush he calls a great sight; the movement toward revelatory fire sharply illuminates the commentary's person who turns away from admonition and enters the great fire.
When Moses turns toward the fire, God calls him by name from it; this supplies the named, summoned counterpart to 87:12's unnamed person known through the fire he enters.

row.basis: pillar of fire guiding at night
row.note: YHWH's night fire gives light and leads a travelling people, directly alongside the commentary's distant fire that guides a traveller rather than enclosing a condemned person.

row.basis: fire without warmth or a place to sit
row.note: Isaiah's doomed diviners become stubble and find no coal for warming or fire before which to sit, an unusually exact counterpart to the commentary's contrast between warming oneself at a fire and enduring its punishment inside.
Those who kindle their own fire walk by its light but receive torment; it parallels the commentary's self-closing action, where what a person chooses becomes the fire that defines his fate.

Those who reject YHWH's instruction become like stubble before fire; its explicit sequence of refused teaching, vegetal residue, and burning meets the commentary's reminder, pasture-to-chaff, and great-fire sequence.
Topheth is prepared with an abundant, divinely kindled fire and wood; its deliberately immense pyre is a close biblical image for the commentary's great fire awaiting the refuser.
The rebels' fire is not quenched and their worm does not die, a direct scriptural comparator for the commentary's fire whose suffering does not resolve into death or restored life.

row.basis: arrogant people as stubble in an oven
row.note: Using Hebrew WLC numbering, this verse makes every arrogant evildoer stubble before the coming furnace, directly joining the commentary's misdirected greatness with a consuming great fire.

God promises his own that they may pass through fire without being burned; this makes a precise counterpart to the commentary's distinction between a bounded, saving relation to fire and entry into its punitive interior.
The three men walk free inside a furnace, unharmed and accompanied by a heavenly figure; this makes their fire a site of divine presence rather than the lasting affliction described for 87:12.

row.basis: fire leaves neither smell nor bodily mark
row.note: The survivors' hair, garments, and even smell are untouched by the furnace, a pointed counterimage to the commentary's hot brand and fire as a permanent identifying mark.

The coming one is like a refiner's fire and raises the question who can endure it, giving a biblical comparison for the commentary's claim that entering fire means bearing its heat rather than merely touching it.
The refiner sits to purify silver and Levi's descendants; this is the productive artisan-fire that the commentary explicitly distinguishes from the great fire that yields neither death nor life.

row.basis: fire, refinement, and calling God's name
row.note: The remnant passes through fire, is refined, then calls God's name and is claimed as God's people; it joins the commentary's fire-as-test, name, belonging, and prayer motifs in one sharply different outcome.

row.basis: person and own work burn together
row.note: The strong person becomes tinder and his own work a spark, so both burn with none to quench them; it closely parallels the commentary's claim that the person's doing folds back upon him in fire.

A person writes 'YHWH's' on his hand and takes Israel's name; this positive sign of ownership and naming stands beside the commentary's animal-brand image and its unnamed person identified instead by fire.

row.basis: awakening to everlasting life or contempt
row.note: Daniel divides those raised from the dust into everlasting life and everlasting contempt, a direct eschatological counterpart to the commentary's blessed/wretched division and its reflection on life and death in the fire.

row.basis: furnace of Gehenna opposite place of rest
row.note: 4 Ezra sets the displayed furnace of Gehenna opposite the place of rest and paradise, giving Jewish apocalyptic form to the commentary's two opposed destinations after admonition.

row.basis: entering life or Gehenna's unquenchable fire
row.note: Jesus contrasts entering life with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire, an especially close New Testament comparison for 87:12–13's fire and its refusal of ordinary life.

row.basis: Isaiah's undying worm received in Gehenna
row.note: Mark applies the undying worm and unquenched fire to Gehenna, making explicit the Christian reception of Isaiah 66 alongside the commentary's enduring great fire.
The judge gathers wheat but burns chaff with unquenchable fire; it brings the commentary's pasture-residue imagery into a final separation of people before fire.
The lawless are thrown into the fiery furnace with weeping and gnashing; its entry, furnace, and sustained misery closely match the commentary's yasla as entering and bearing the fire.
At the final division, those on the rejected side depart into eternal fire; this gives a direct Gospel comparator to the commentary's two responses to warning and their divergent destinations.

row.basis: unnamed rich man tormented in flame
row.note: In the rich-man story, the unnamed wealthy man pleads from anguish in flame; his wealth, namelessness, and fiery postmortem identity make a close companion to the commentary's fire-branded person.

row.basis: fire consuming adversaries after known truth
row.note: After deliberate sin against received truth, the prospect is judgment and a fiery zeal consuming adversaries; it directly links rejected instruction to the expected punitive fire.

row.basis: flaming fire on those who do not obey
row.note: Flaming fire is inflicted on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel, matching the commentary's person defined by turning from the summons and meeting the great punishment.

row.basis: unbelief, life withheld, wrath already remaining
row.note: The disobedient person will not see life while God's wrath remains on him already; this is a close grammatical and theological analogue to the commentary's present designation of a person by a future fiery fate.

row.basis: hoarded gold and silver eating flesh like fire
row.note: The corrosion of hoarded wealth bears witness and eats flesh like fire, directly alongside the commentary's heated hoard that brands the body and reveals what its owner did.
The Lamb's people bear his and the Father's names on their foreheads, the saving alternative to the commentary's person whose identity is read from his fire rather than named.

row.basis: beast's mark on forehead or hand
row.note: The beast's worshiper receives a visible mark on forehead or hand; this gives a precise apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's discussion of a bodily brand identifying a person's allegiance.
The marked beast-worshiper is tormented with fire and sulfur, directly joining bodily identification to the fire that follows it, as in the commentary's branding-and-fate image.

row.basis: no rest in the fire's lasting smoke
row.note: The torment's smoke rises forever and the marked worshipers have no rest day or night, a close New Testament formulation for the commentary's ongoing fire from which one does not depart.

row.basis: name absent from book, person thrown into fire
row.note: The lack of a recorded name determines being thrown into the lake of fire, a pointed counterpart to the commentary's unnamed individual whose fate is disclosed by fire.

The prophet offers salvation in returning and rest, but says the hearers were unwilling; read with the chapter's pyre, it specifies the prior refusal that the commentary places before entry into fire.
Wisdom says 'I called and you refused,' giving a compact biblical formulation of the commentary's person who withdraws from a spoken reminder.
Those who rejected counsel seek Wisdom only when calamity arrives and receive no answer; it parallels the commentary's delayed remembrance when the great fire has already come.

row.basis: one's own sin captures its maker
row.note: The wicked is caught in his own iniquities and held by sin's cords, a concrete biblical analogue for the commentary's action that closes over its own agent before the fire follows.

Jeremiah calls the prophetic word fire that shatters rock; it clarifies the commentary's paradox that a rejected admonition can itself be spoken of through fire imagery before punitive fire is entered.

row.basis: God alone exalted, human height brought low
row.note: Human haughtiness is lowered while YHWH alone is exalted, directly accompanying the commentary's distinction between greatness rightly given to God and greatness wrongly claimed by a person.

row.basis: forehead mark for those grieved by evil
row.note: Ezekiel's forehead mark identifies those who mourn wrongdoing before judgment; this provides a specific positive counterimage to the commentary's permanent fire-brand as a sign of a person's stance.
Biblical Aramaic נוּרָא (nura, 'fire') names the furnace threatened here, a close Semitic comparator for the commentary's n-w-r fire/light word family and its great fire.
Hebrew צְלִי (tsli, 'roasted') belongs to the ṣ-l-y word family developed in the commentary; Passover's deliberate roasting supplies the finite cooking-fire contrast to yasla's punitive endurance.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr, remembrance, fear, and name
row.note: Hebrew זכר (zkr, 'remember') is cognate with Arabic dhikr; the verse records fearers, their speech, and a book of remembrance for those who esteem God's name, the positive side of 87:9–15.
Hebrew כַּבִּיר (kabbir, 'mighty') is a likely cognate of Arabic kabir; Job's attribution of might to God gives the proper recipient of the greatness the commentary contrasts with human arrogance.

row.basis: ordinary fire as one-sixtieth of Gehenna
row.note: The Bavli calls fire one-sixtieth of Gehenna, a Jewish interpretive bridge for the commentary's small, useful worldly fire as a reminder beside the great fire.

row.basis: gold tested in fire, people in humiliation
row.note: Sirach compares the testing of acceptable people to gold in fire, directly engaging the commentary's extension of yasla to ordeal and its contrast between testing fire and final punishment.

row.basis: righteous tried as gold in furnace
row.note: Wisdom presents the righteous as gold tried in a furnace and accepted by God; it supplies a Jewish eschatological counterpoint to a fire that does not refine its entrant.

row.basis: Isaiah's unquenched fire read as Gehinnam
row.note: The Targum's Aramaic rendering associates Isaiah's undying punishment with Gehinnam; this reception gives the commentary's great fire a specifically Jewish interpretive setting, though its exact expansion should be verified.

row.basis: refusing the one who speaks and not escaping
row.note: Hebrews warns against refusing the speaker, because those who refused did not escape; it is a close exhortational counterpart to 87:11's withdrawal from the reminder before 87:12.
Following the warning not to refuse God's voice, Hebrews calls God a consuming fire; it places exhortation and fire together without reducing fire to the same function as punishment.

row.basis: fire reveals and tests each work
row.note: The last day reveals each person's work by fire and tests its quality, giving a Christian analogue to the commentary's artisan fire that assesses and separates rather than merely destroys.
A person whose work burns suffers loss yet is saved as through fire; this precise limited passage through fire contrasts with the commentary's permanent yasla.

row.basis: faith tested by fire for a final result
row.note: Faith tested like gold by fire is said to result in praise, glory, and honor, another deliberate contrast to the commentary's fire with no productive end.
Sodom and Gomorrah undergo the penalty of eternal fire and serve as an example, matching the commentary's insistence that fire is first narrated as a warning or reminder.

row.basis: evil person avoids light lest deeds be exposed
row.note: The evildoer hates and avoids the light because it exposes works; this clarifies the commentary's light/fire and turning-away imagery as an avoidance of disclosure, not merely a generic darkness trope.
By an unrepentant heart a person stores up wrath for himself for judgment day, a close moral analogue to the commentary's claim that a person's own action becomes his returning fate.
Abraham tells the rich man to remember his lifetime goods while he is in torment; it gives a Gospel form to the commentary's late remembering after choosing the near life.

row.basis: lake of fire called the second death
row.note: Revelation calls the lake burning with fire and sulfur the second death; its deliberate death-language is a useful comparison with 87:13's paradox of neither dying nor living in fire.

row.basis: enduring bodily punishment in infernal fire
row.note: Augustine argues that resurrected bodies can endure infernal fire without being annihilated, a Christian interpretive attempt to articulate the prolonged fiery condition developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Hebrew ner as lamp and light for a path
row.note: Hebrew נֵר (ner, 'lamp') may be related to Arabic nur; the verse's lamp and light guiding a path specifically fits the commentary's distant fire as a guide, but the etymological link should be checked.

The Peshitta's Syriac prayer root ܨܠܝ (sly) is a cognate of Arabic salla's prayer sense, helping keep the commentary's prayer sound-pattern distinct from Arabic yasla 'enter fire'; the exact inflected form should be checked.

row.basis: who can dwell with devouring fire
row.note: Zion's sinners ask who can dwell with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; this is an unusually direct biblical formulation for the commentary's person entering and remaining in the great fire.
Joshua is called a brand plucked from fire, a sharp inverse to the commentary's fire-brand that permanently identifies its subject: here divine rebuke rescues the burning brand.
Jeremiah warns that failure to heed a concrete command will kindle a fire that devours Jerusalem's gates and is not quenched, closely joining refused admonition to irreversible fire.

row.basis: passing through fire and being brought out
row.note: The community says God brought it through fire and water and then out into abundance; this bounded passage and rescue supply the opposite of yasla's fire from which the entrant does not depart.
The live coal touches the prophet's mouth and removes guilt, making fire the means of purification for a messenger rather than the final affliction of one who shuns the message.

row.basis: death followed by authority to cast into Gehenna
row.note: Jesus distinguishes ordinary killing from God's authority to cast after death into Gehenna, a precise New Testament comparison for the commentary's meditation on fire, death, and life.

Jesus calls the converted follower a child of Gehenna, a familial identity assigned by a fiery destination that closely meets the commentary's imagery of origin, belonging, and a person read through fire.

row.basis: scorched people refuse repentance and glory
row.note: After being scorched by fierce heat, people curse God rather than repent or give glory; this directly combines punitive fire with the continued refusal that defines 87:11–12.
The city that glorified itself and lived in luxury receives plagues and is burned with fire, closely matching the commentary's false greatness, preference for the near life, and ensuing fire.

row.basis: cast alive into lake of fire
row.note: The beast and false prophet are thrown alive into the lake burning with sulfur, a specific apocalyptic comparator for the commentary's paradoxical fiery state beyond ordinary death and life.
The devil is tormented in the lake of fire day and night forever, directly alongside the commentary's emphasis on ongoing fiery suffering with no release.
Deuteronomy names YHWH a consuming fire; as the source behind Hebrews 12:29, it sets the commentary's great fire beside the distinct biblical image of divine holiness and jealousy.
The proverb asks whether someone can carry fire against the chest without burned clothes, concretely sharpening the commentary's distinction between merely approaching fire and undergoing its heat.

row.basis: metals gathered and melted in a furnace
row.note: God gathers people as a smith gathers metals into a furnace to melt them in wrath; this is a punitive metallurgical fire alongside the commentary's productive craft-fire and its failure in the great fire.
A seraph carries a live coal from the altar toward Isaiah, supplying the liturgical fire that precedes the commentary's contrast between named prayer and the unnamed fire-bound person.

row.basis: Israel's light becoming fire and flame
row.note: Israel's Light becomes a fire and its Holy One a flame that consumes thorns; it gives a biblical meeting of light and fire beside the commentary's nar/nur meditation and its divergent paths.

row.basis: chosen in the furnace of affliction
row.note: God says Israel has been chosen in the furnace of affliction, a direct biblical use of furnace-heat as ordeal that clarifies the commentary's secondary sense of yasla as suffering a hard trial.

row.basis: thorns, curse, and an end in burning
row.note: Land bearing thorns and thistles is near a curse and ends in burning, carrying the commentary's pasture and useless residue imagery into a warning about receiving and failing to bear fruit from God's word.
The sun is permitted to scorch people with fire; paired with the following verse's refusal to repent, it adds an apocalyptic scene in which fire does not itself produce the response to warning.
Babylon glorifies herself, lives in luxury, and claims security; its self-assigned greatness and preferred present life provide the antecedent reversed by the fire in the following verse.

row.basis: rejected words judging on the last day
row.note: The one who rejects Jesus and does not receive his words is judged by that very word on the last day, a close Christian form of the commentary's reminder refused now and fate disclosed later.

row.basis: rejecting the word and judging oneself unworthy of life
row.note: Those who thrust aside God's word judge themselves unworthy of eternal life; it directly develops the commentary's self-enclosing logic in which the refuser's own motion defines the outcome.

row.basis: refined gold offered to the self-called rich
row.note: The self-satisfied rich are counselled to receive gold refined by fire so that they may truly be rich, a targeted counterpoint to the commentary's hoarded metal, branding fire, and false self-sufficiency.

row.basis: sinners' spirits in a furnace of fire
row.note: 1 Enoch describes sinners' spirits being cast into a furnace of fire and flame, a Jewish apocalyptic elaboration of the enduring fiery fate; wording and verse division should be verified.

row.basis: three classes in judgment and Gehinnom
row.note: The Bavli's three-class judgment tradition sends the intermediate through Gehinnom while invoking Zechariah's refining fire, a rabbinic reading of divided destinies and fire as testing rather than simply finality.

The Peshitta's Syriac nura ('fire') occurs in the eternal-fire saying, providing a Syriac member of the fire/light word family discussed in the commentary; the exact form and edition should be verified.

Isaiah leaves the rebels as corpses while their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched; 87:13 makes the sufferer himself unable to die, so the bodily condition is the pointed difference within the shared enduring-fire scene.

row.basis: Gehenna gloss, soul not dying, unquenched fire
row.note: Targum Jonathan's Gehenna paraphrase turns Isaiah's displayed corpses into sinners whose soul does not die while their fire is unquenched; that Jewish interpretation comes unusually close to the commentary's conscious, unending state in the fire.

row.basis: Gehinnom consumed but certain sinners remain
row.note: In its reading of Isaiah 66:24, the Bavli says certain apostates descend to Gehinnom for generations and that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not; it explicitly develops the asymmetry of lasting punishment without the punished passing away.

row.basis: enter life or Gehenna's unquenchable fire
row.note: Jesus contrasts entering life with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; that direct life/fire antithesis sharpens the commentary's claim that the fire of 87:13 is a place where the condemned does not live.

row.basis: worm does not die, fire not quenched
row.note: Mark retains Isaiah's imperishable worm and unquenched fire; it is a close Christian formula for punishment that never runs down, alongside the commentary's renewed torment and never-arriving death.

row.basis: people seek death but cannot find it
row.note: In an apocalyptic plague people long to die, but death flees them; this is a direct, though temporary, counterpart to the commentary's picture of agony in which death is wanted or approaches yet never arrives.

row.basis: fire, everlasting smoke, no rest day or night
row.note: The worshippers of the beast are tormented and have no rest day or night; its denial of repose closely meets the commentary's expansion of not dying into no easing, sleep, or stillness.

The rich man remains conscious and cries out that he is in anguish in flame; this supplies a narrated Christian analogue for the commentary's insistence that fire's occupant is not extinguished by suffering.
Abraham describes an impassable chasm that prevents passage from the place of torment; it specifically parallels the commentary's repeatedly frustrated desire to leave the fire.

Matthew's final judgment places eternal punishment and eternal life in one antithetical sentence, a close frame for the commentary's contrast between enduring torment and the real, lasting life denied to it.

row.basis: lake of fire called the second death
row.note: Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas 87:13 carefully says that its inhabitant does not die there; the contrast shows two different theological ways of naming fire's finality.

Augustine argues that the damned can suffer bodily fire without their bodies being destroyed; this patristic explanation directly addresses the commentary's problem of pain persisting while death never completes.

row.basis: longing for death that does not come
row.note: Job describes sufferers who dig for death but do not find it; although it is not a hell scene, the denied release provides a concrete analogue for the commentary's death withheld amid affliction.
Jesus calls Lazarus's death sleep before explaining that Lazarus has died; it closely supports the commentary's secondary sense of death as sleep and rest, which is unavailable in the fire.

row.basis: the dead in the Lord rest from their labors
row.note: The blessed dead are said to rest from their labors, furnishing the positive counterpart to the commentary's claim that the one who cannot die in the fire is also denied rest.

row.basis: dead do not live, shades do not rise
row.note: Isaiah says of hostile rulers that they are dead and will not live or rise; the negative Hebrew life verb closely matches the life/death language, but punishment here is exclusion from resurrection rather than 87:13's deathless suffering.

row.basis: your dead shall live and arise
row.note: Isaiah's answer to the preceding no-life statement is that God's dead will live and arise; it supplies the positive resurrection horizon against which the commentary distinguishes a fire that grants neither death nor life.

row.basis: awakening to everlasting life or contempt
row.note: Daniel's sleepers awake either to everlasting life or everlasting contempt; this gives a biblical two-outcome resurrection frame for the commentary's opposition between full afterlife and enduring punitive condition.

row.basis: martyr's resurrection to life and tyrant's exclusion
row.note: The martyred brother expects resurrection to life from God but tells the persecuting king that he has no resurrection to life; its death-to-life contrast illuminates the commentary's peaceful death-and-rising figures over against the doomed state.

row.basis: the living one became dead and lives forever
row.note: The risen Jesus names himself the living one who became dead and is alive forever; this compact death-life-resurrection sequence is the positive inverse of 87:13's suspended condition.

Paul says that the risen Christ dies no more and death no longer rules him; it provides a Christian account of deathlessness joined to actual life, precisely the conjunction the commentary says hell lacks.

row.basis: in Adam all die, in Christ all made alive
row.note: Paul binds Adam to universal death and Christ to being made alive; this directly meets the commentary's Adam-to-earth sequence of death and eventual resurrection, rather than an ultimate state without either.

row.basis: no more death in the renewed creation
row.note: In the new creation death, mourning, crying, and pain are removed together; it supplies the positive destination in which no death means healed life, contrasting with the fire's deathlessness without life.

row.basis: Arabic h-y-y and m-w-t, Hebrew hayyim and mavet
row.note: Moses sets life and death before Israel and commands them to choose life; the Hebrew life/death pair is cognate with the Arabic roots named in the commentary and makes ethical response determine which side is inhabited.

row.basis: turn from the wicked way and live
row.note: God calls the wicked to turn from their way and live; this closely parallels the commentary's moral reading in which turning from the reminder yields a final state without life.
Wisdom's hearers refuse her call and later call out without answer; it gives a specific biblical form to the commentary's warning that remembrance and a request for release come too late.
Proverbs calls disciplined instruction life itself; this makes a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's claim that accepting the admonition is a response to what gives life.

row.basis: hearing the word, passing from death to life
row.note: The one who hears and believes Jesus' word has eternal life and has passed from death to life; it directly parallels the commentary's spiritual use of life for a person who receives the warning.

row.basis: dead in transgressions, made alive with Christ
row.note: Ephesians says those dead through transgressions are made alive with Christ; it offers a concrete Christian use of death and life as present moral-spiritual conditions beneath the commentary's final outcome.

The self-indulgent person is said to be dead while living, a Christian moral metaphor that resembles an in-between state; the commentary instead stresses that 87:13 negates both exits without calling its victim merely half-dead.

The rich man's requested warning is refused on the ground that those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection; it joins refused warning to an irreversible postmortem setting as the commentary does.

row.basis: teaching as rain and speech as dew on grass
row.note: Moses compares teaching to rain and speech to dew upon grass; this directly links the commentary's rain-and-living-pasture imagery with admonition that nourishes rather than the fire that consumes.

row.basis: rejected Torah, stubble consumed by fire
row.note: Isaiah joins rejection of YHWH's Torah to roots rotting and stubble consumed by fire; its warning, vegetation, and fire form a particularly close triad beside the commentary's avoidance of reminder and grass-to-fire imagery.

row.basis: Spirit placed in the dead so they live
row.note: God promises to put his spirit in Israel's dry bones so that they live; it is the positive prophetic counterpart to the commentary's layered account of life as more than continued sensation.

row.basis: Torah-hearer as a watered fruitful tree
row.note: The person who meditates on Torah is like a tree by streams that bears fruit; this gives the commentary's admonition, flourishing vegetation, and living-versus-barren moral contrast a biblical form.

row.basis: grass withers but God's word stands forever
row.note: Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the enduring divine word; it clarifies the commentary's movement from short worldly life and fading pasture toward what is lasting.

row.basis: life of this world and bliss of the world to come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob compares the whole life of this world with the superior bliss of the world to come; this is a close rabbinic counterpart to the commentary's contrast between preferred near life and the more abiding life.

row.basis: gaining the world and forfeiting one's life
row.note: Jesus asks what profit comes from gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; it gives a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's claim that preferring the near life forfeits the true one.

row.basis: the life that is truly life
row.note: Paul urges storing treasure for the future in order to seize the life that is truly life; its explicit distinction between apparent present possession and real life closely matches the commentary's account of the enduring afterlife.

row.basis: earth, dust, and return to dust
row.note: Adam is told that he came from dust and will return to it; this grounds the commentary's contrast between earth as the place of ordinary life and death and fire as the place where neither transition occurs.

row.basis: aged couple and an improbable promised child
row.note: Abraham and Sarah are old and Sarah's fertility has ceased when a child is promised; this ancestral annunciation pattern stands beside the commentary's aged Zechariah and barren wife receiving Yahya.

row.basis: Zechariah's prayer, son, and name John
row.note: Gabriel answers Zechariah's prayer with a son who must be named John; it is the direct New Testament scene corresponding to the commentary's Yahya annunciation.

row.basis: Yahya wordplay and the Greek name Ioannes
row.note: Luke gives the child the Greek name Ioannes, representing Hebrew Yohanan, rather than a form meaning he lives; the shared prophet therefore preserves the narrative but not the commentary's specifically Arabic Yahya/yahya wordplay.

row.basis: John grows and becomes strong in spirit
row.note: Luke describes John as growing and becoming strong in spirit; this is a focused New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Yahya commanded to take the Book with strength.

row.basis: be strong in keeping the Torah
row.note: Joshua is told to be strong and courageous in observing all the Torah; this biblical command supplies a close scriptural pattern for the commentary's phrase about Yahya taking the Book with strength.
Herod recognizes John as a righteous and holy man; this bears on the commentary's portrayal of Yahya as given purity and set against the tyrannical, rebellious figure bound to the fire.

row.basis: fire and worms felt forever in the flesh
row.note: Judith's final hymn says that God will put fire and worms into the flesh of hostile nations and that they will feel them forever; its enduring bodily sensation is a particularly close Jewish counterpart to the commentary's pain that does not end in death.

row.basis: fire not quenched night or day, smoke forever
row.note: Isaiah's judgment-fire is not quenched by night or day and its smoke ascends forever; this gives the commentary's continually maintained fire a close Hebrew Bible formulation, even though Isaiah describes a devastated land.

row.basis: pit of torment and furnace of Gehenna opposite rest
row.note: 4 Ezra reveals the pit of torment and furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest and paradise; this Jewish apocalyptic pairing illuminates the commentary's opposition between fire without relief and the full life of the other destination.

row.basis: prisoners gathered in pit and shut up
row.note: Isaiah pictures rebels gathered like prisoners in a pit, shut in prison, and punished after many days; its sequence of capture, confinement, and delayed punishment parallels the commentary's entry into fire followed by an enduring state within it.

row.basis: book of life and lake of fire
row.note: Revelation sends anyone absent from the book of life into the lake of fire; it joins exclusion from life to fiery judgment in the same way the commentary sets the denied life of 87:13 inside the fire.
John's own warning culminates in chaff burned with unquenchable fire; it brings the commentary's Yahya section into direct contact with its earlier fire and fading-vegetation imagery.
John warns that every tree without good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this binds warning, failed living growth, root imagery, and fire more tightly than a merely verbal parallel.

row.basis: disobeying the Son, not seeing life, wrath remaining
row.note: John contrasts present eternal life for belief with not seeing life and wrath remaining for disobedience; it closely matches the commentary's refusal of the life-giving call issuing in an abiding punitive condition.

row.basis: resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment
row.note: Jesus distinguishes a resurrection of life from a resurrection of judgment; this gives a precise New Testament two-outcome horizon for the commentary's contrast between true postmortem life and the fire's condition.

row.basis: keeping the word and never seeing death
row.note: Jesus promises that one who keeps his word will never see death; it is a positive inverse to 87:13, where absence of death is not blessed because it is detached from life and reception of the word.
Jesus joins living and believing with never dying; this makes explicit the conjunction of deathlessness and life that the commentary says is present for the saved but denied in the fire.

Those counted worthy of the resurrection cannot die anymore and are called children of God; this is a close positive counterpart to the commentary's distinction between immortal resurrection life and deathless punishment.

Hebrews urges diligence to enter God's rest so that no one falls through the same disobedience; it links heeding versus refusal to rest, directly complementing the commentary's denial of rest in the fire.

Hebrews describes deliberate rejection after knowledge as facing judgment and fire that consumes adversaries; it shares the warning-to-fire movement but contrasts with the commentary's fire that does not consume its victim into death.

row.basis: God's call refused, later cry unheard
row.note: Zechariah states the exact reversal that people would not hear when God called, so God would not hear when they called; this strongly parallels the commentary's warning that rejected remembrance cannot later secure release.

row.basis: hear and the soul may live
row.note: Isaiah calls hearers to incline the ear and hear so that their soul may live; it is a close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's claim that answering the admonition is answering what gives life.

row.basis: life by every word from God's mouth
row.note: Deuteronomy says a human lives by every word from YHWH's mouth rather than bread alone; it gives the commentary's life-giving reminder a concrete scriptural form beyond bodily nourishment.

row.basis: God kills and makes alive, none can deliver
row.note: Moses attributes both killing and making alive to God and says none can deliver from his hand; it parallels the commentary's ordered death-life sequence while underscoring the impossibility of self-escape from final divine judgment.

row.basis: death swallowed forever and tears wiped
row.note: Isaiah's promised victory swallows death forever and wipes tears away; it supplies the positive destination where death's removal means healed life, heightening the commentary's claim that the fire has no such life.

row.basis: loving present life loses it, preserving life eternal
row.note: Jesus says that clinging to one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it preserves it for eternal life; this is a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's preferred near life versus the lasting life.

row.basis: perishing food and food abiding to eternal life
row.note: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that remains for eternal life; it specifically supports the commentary's contrast of a short chosen worldly provision with a durable, real life.

row.basis: passing from death to life, remaining in death
row.note: Love is said to mark passage from death to life, while lack of love leaves one in death; this offers another concrete Christian use of life and death as moral-spiritual states before final judgment.

row.basis: dwelling with devouring fire and everlasting burnings
row.note: Isaiah's frightened sinners ask who can dwell with devouring fire and everlasting burnings; although its immediate setting is Zion's judgment, its language of inhabiting enduring fire closely meets the commentary's focus on remaining inside it.

row.basis: righteous dead enter peace and rest
row.note: The upright person who dies enters peace and rests; this offers a prophetic positive counterpart to the commentary's secondary reading of death as stillness and rest, both withheld from the fire's inhabitant.

row.basis: seeking YHWH's word but not finding it
row.note: Amos foresees people wandering in search of YHWH's word and not finding it; it gives a concrete prophetic form to the commentary's too-late remembrance after the time for hearing has passed.

row.basis: the living give thanks, unlike the dead
row.note: Hezekiah says that the living, not the dead, give thanks to God; it clarifies the commentary's association of life with responsive remembrance and worship rather than bare continued sensation.

row.basis: the righteous dead are in peace
row.note: Wisdom says that those who seemed to die are in peace; this Jewish reflection makes death a secure state for the righteous, a deliberate opposite to the fire where the sufferer receives neither death nor peace.

row.basis: no share in the world to come for denial of resurrection
row.note: The Mishnah excludes from the world to come those who deny resurrection from the Torah and related fundamentals; this rabbinic rule concretely links rejection of revealed truth with loss of future life, as the commentary's warning logic does.

row.basis: John's moral exhortation and execution by Herod
row.note: Josephus portrays John as exhorting justice and piety before Herod has him killed; this Jewish witness supplies historical narrative context for the commentary's righteous Yahya and distinguishes ordinary mortal death from the fire's deathless condition.

row.ref: Arabic Infancy Gospel, opening cradle-speech (chapter numbering varies)
row.basis: newborn Jesus speaks from the cradle
row.note: The opening scene of the Arabic Infancy Gospel has the newborn Jesus speak from the cradle; its setting differs from the Qur'anic defense of Mary, but it is a specific Christian infancy parallel to the extraordinary cradle-speech invoked in the commentary.

row.basis: refusal to hear the prophet brings destruction
row.note: Acts says that every person refusing to hear the promised prophet will be destroyed from the people; it shares the commentary's warning-and-refusal logic but uses destruction where 87:13 depicts an unended condition without death.
Hebrews asks how people can escape after neglecting such a great salvation; this concise warning formula parallels the commentary's closed possibility of escape after the reminder has been evaded.

row.basis: dead and alive again, lost and found
row.note: The returning son is declared dead and alive again, lost and found; this recovery scene is a narrative positive counterpart to the commentary's moral death-life language and its final absence of a way back.

YHWH descends in the Sinai encounter and proclaims the Name. It gives a concrete scriptural setting in which the Name is voiced as an event demanding response, rather than treated as a bare designation.
Moses hastens to bow to the earth and worship in the Name-proclamation scene. The sequence closely illuminates the commentary's movement from a named Lord to an immediate bodily act of worship.

row.basis: blessing the great Lord, lifted hands, prostration
row.note: After Ezra blesses the great YHWH, the assembly answers Amen, raises its hands, and bows with faces to the ground. Its spoken blessing and coordinated bodily response are a particularly close counterpart to remembrance becoming prayer.

row.basis: place where the Name is remembered and an altar is served
row.note: YHWH promises to come and bless wherever he causes his Name to be remembered, in the verse's altar setting. It joins remembered Name, worshipful action, and divine blessing in one tightly bounded instruction.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr and the Name as memorial
row.note: God calls the revealed Name his zēker, his enduring memorial. Hebrew zkr is a genuine cognate of the commentary's Arabic ذ ك ر, and the verse itself pairs that memorial with the divine Name.

row.basis: Name and zēker desired by the soul
row.note: The speaker says that YHWH's Name and zēker are the soul's desire. The Hebrew zkr cognate makes this more than a general devotion parallel: it supplies a direct Name-and-remembrance formula.

Against confidence in chariots and horses, the worshippers use the Hebrew zkr verb for YHWH their God's Name. This is a specific lexical and theological counterpart to remembering the Lord's Name rather than relying on worldly power.

row.basis: fearers of YHWH, his Name, and a book of remembrance
row.note: Those who fear YHWH speak together and esteem his Name; a book of remembrance is written before him for them. It brings together the commentary's remembrance, reverent recipient, and scripture-like preservation of remembrance.

row.basis: Abraham's altar and calling on YHWH's Name
row.note: Abraham builds an altar and calls on YHWH's Name. Since the commentary explicitly locates prayer in the pages of Abraham, this is a direct ancestral instance of Name-invocation becoming cultic action.

row.basis: refining fire, calling the Name, and God's answer
row.note: The remnant is refined like silver and tested like gold; it then calls on God's Name and receives an answer. It is an unusually close biblical conjunction of purification, fire, invocation, and a reciprocal divine response.

row.basis: washing sins while calling on Jesus' Name
row.note: Ananias tells Paul to rise, be baptized, wash away his sins, and call on Jesus' Name. The verse tightly joins purification, embodied rite, and invocation, while its baptismal and Christological specification offers a substantive Christian configuration of the triad.

row.basis: fruit of lips confessing the Name as sacrifice of praise
row.note: The exhortation calls continual praise the fruit of lips that confess God's Name. It gives a precise Christian account of oral Name-confession becoming a sacrificial act of worship.

row.basis: hallowing the Father's Name in prayer
row.note: Jesus' model prayer begins by addressing the Father and hallowing his Name. It provides a direct liturgical analogue for the commentary's claim that the Name is uttered before the prayerful act.

row.basis: sanctified people who call on the Lord's Name
row.note: Paul addresses people made holy in Christ together with all who call on the Lord's Name. Its combination of sanctification and common Name-invocation closely maps the commentary's purification-and-remembrance portrait, in a distinct Christian frame.

row.basis: calling on the Lord's Name for salvation
row.note: The verse states that everyone calling on the Lord's Name will be saved, extending the Name-to-salvation link developed around 87:14-15. In Romans' surrounding argument that Lord is Jesus, the shared formula carries a theological specification the Qur'anic portrait does not make.

row.basis: God's Name placed on people and divine blessing
row.note: The priests place YHWH's Name on Israel, and YHWH promises to bless them. This is a biblical reciprocal counterpart to the commentary's turn from a human's remembrance and prayer toward God's beneficent action.

The Day of Atonement verse says that atonement cleanses Israel so that they are clean before YHWH. It supplies a concentrated priestly form of the purification that precedes the successful worshipper in the commentary.

YHWH refuses the many prayers offered with spread hands because those hands are full of blood. This qualifying counter-image tests the commentary's quick transition from voiced remembrance to bodily worship by making ethical cleansing decisive for accepted prayer.
Immediately after the rejected-prayer scene, the prophet commands washing and cleansing. Its placement makes purification the required repair to the failed worship in the preceding verse.

row.basis: kneeling plea to be made clean
row.note: A leper comes kneeling and asks Jesus to make him clean. The scene fuses a bodily posture of supplication with an explicit request for purification.

row.basis: drawing near, clean hands, and pure hearts
row.note: James commands people to draw near to God, cleanse their hands, and purify their hearts. It closely matches the commentary's bodily and inward dimensions of purification-oriented approach to the Lord.

row.basis: drawing near with cleansed heart and washed body
row.note: The exhortation to draw near to God specifies both hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water. Its paired interior and bodily cleansing gives a strong interpretive bridge to the commentary's purified person who proceeds into worship.

The instruction to pray everywhere while lifting holy hands makes moral purity and a visible bodily posture conditions of prayer. It directly complements the commentary's mouth-to-body account of salāt.

row.basis: heart, moving lips, and unheard voice
row.note: Hannah speaks in her heart; her lips move but her voice is not heard. This concrete prayer scene illuminates the commentary's insistence that remembrance can belong simultaneously to inner life and to speech without being loud.

row.basis: prayer to the Father in secret
row.note: Jesus directs the disciple to pray in an inner room to the Father who sees in secret. It is a precise Christian comparison for the commentary's open-and-hidden register of remembrance, not merely a general command to pray.

Jesus applies the accusation that people honor God with their lips while their heart remains far away. It supplies the inverse of the commentary's integrated oral and inward remembrance, warning that voiced devotion can be severed from its inner reality.
The covenant words are to be upon Israel's heart. This gives a biblical form for the commentary's claim that remembrance is preservation and non-forgetting within a person.

row.basis: repeating the words in ordinary speech
row.note: Israel is to repeat the covenant words to children and speak them at home, on the road, at night, and in the morning. It turns inwardly held words into continual voiced practice, as the commentary traces remembrance from heart and tongue into life.

row.basis: book in the mouth, meditation, and doing
row.note: The book of Torah is not to depart from Joshua's mouth; he is to meditate on it and do what it contains. The verse is a close scriptural sequence from preserved/recited word to enacted obedience.

row.basis: remember, repent, and do the first works
row.note: The risen Christ tells Ephesus to remember its former position, repent, and do its earlier works. This creates a particularly exact New Testament movement from remembrance to concrete action.

row.basis: the house bearing the Name and prayer toward it
row.note: Solomon asks that God's eyes attend the house called by his Name and the prayer his servant makes toward it. It grounds the commentary's sanctuary discussion in a named place where prayer is directed to God.

row.basis: God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples
row.note: The restored worship site is called a house of prayer for all peoples. It is a direct biblical partner for the commentary's expansion from one worshipper to communities and their worship spaces.

God identifies Abraham as a prophet whose prayer for Abimelech will preserve life. This supplies an Abrahamic instance of prayer as intercession for another, relevant to the commentary's secondary sense of salāt as benevolent petition.

row.basis: God accepts the righteous sufferer's prayer for others
row.note: God tells Job's friends that Job will pray for them and that he will accept Job's prayer. The verse gives a specific Hebrew Bible model for prayer whose benefit moves outward to other people.

When the people cry out, Moses prays to YHWH and the fire dies down. Instead of assigning fire and prayer to opposed human portraits, this narrative makes prayer the means by which destructive fire is stopped.

row.basis: fiery-furnace threat for refusal to worship an image
row.note: Nebuchadnezzar makes the furnace the penalty for refusing worship of the image. This reverses the commentary's fire-and-prayer contrast in a specific way: fidelity is shown by refusing a false bodily worship under threat of fire.

row.basis: refusal to serve or worship another god
row.note: The three Judeans declare that they will neither serve the king's gods nor worship his image. Read with the furnace challenge, their refusal makes correct worship the very reason they enter the fire trial.

The youths walk in the flames singing hymns and blessing God. It is a pointed alternative arrangement to the commentary's opposed fire and prayer images: worship is enacted from within the fire rather than as its opposite.

The refiner purifies the Levites so that they may present offerings in righteousness. This gives a textual biblical fire image for purification ordered toward acceptable worship, while remaining distinct from the commentary's lexical fire imagery.

row.basis: God's exaltation and the Name above every name
row.note: God highly exalts Jesus and grants him the Name above every name. The verse is a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's secondary image of the Name as what raises and makes its bearer conspicuous, though it is Christologically specific.
At Jesus' Name every knee bends in heaven, on earth, and below the earth. It joins the elevated Name to a bodily act with unusual precision.
Every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to God's glory. The oral naming of the Lord completes the bodily bowing of the prior verse and offers a distinct Christian configuration of praise.

row.basis: fear, glorify the Lord's Name, and worship
row.note: The heavenly hymn asks who would not fear the Lord and glorify his Name, then says all nations will come and worship. It is an explicit Name-to-worship sequence with the commentary's reverence motif.

row.basis: angel presenting the prayers of the saints
