row.note: An angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints at the heavenly altar. This supplies a concrete Christian liturgical image for the commentary's discussion of prayer's upward direction and angelic participation.

row.basis: Jeremiah praying much for people and holy city
row.note: In Judas's vision, Jeremiah is identified as one who loves the community and prays much for the people and holy city. This is a specific Jewish counterpart to prayer acting beneficently on behalf of others.

The letter calls believers to approach God in holiness while lifting pure and undefiled hands. It combines moral cleansing, approach, and bodily prayer in almost the same compact pattern as the commentary.

row.basis: the passing world and the enduring doer of God's will
row.note: The world and its desire pass away, whereas the one doing God's will remains forever. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's contrast between preferring worldly life and the better, lasting end.

row.basis: treasure in heaven rather than perishable treasure
row.note: Jesus commands storing treasure in heaven, where it is not destroyed or stolen. It gives a specific ethical redirection from present material preference toward an enduring future.

Daniel's resurrection vision contrasts those waking to everlasting life with those waking to shame and everlasting contempt. It offers the Hebrew Bible's sharpest eschatological counterpart to the commentary's surrounding contrast of the lasting hereafter and destructive fire.

God promises Abraham that his shem will be made great. Hebrew shem and Arabic ism are cognate name words, and the verse concretely supports the commentary's secondary picture of a name as raised or magnified.

The creator and former of Israel says, "I have called you by name; you are mine." It provides a particular biblical comparison for the commentary's unpacking of rabb as creator, owner, and personal Lord.

row.basis: clean hands and a pure heart before holy ascent
row.note: The person allowed to ascend YHWH's holy place is defined by clean hands and a pure heart. It frames purification as fitness to stand before God, an interpretive bridge to the purified worshipper of 87:14-15.

Israel is commanded to walk after, fear, serve, and cling to YHWH. This gives a scriptural analogue for the commentary's carefully limited secondary image of the praying person as one who follows what rightly goes before.

row.basis: forgetting YHWH through failure to keep his commands
row.note: The warning is not to forget YHWH by failing to keep his commands. It makes remembered Lordship covenantally practical and supplies the negative counterpart to the commentary's person who does not forget and whose remembrance becomes action.

Moses places life and death before Israel and commands the choice of life. The covenantal alternative is not identical to the commentary's worldly-life/afterlife contrast, but it gives a specific scriptural pattern in which allegiance is expressed as a life-or-death choice.

row.basis: Hannah's silent prayer as the norm for prayer
row.note: The Bavli derives requirements for prayer from Hannah's heart, moving lips, and unheard voice. That interpretation is especially useful beside the commentary's distinction between inward remembrance, voiced speech, and restrained sound.

row.basis: preparing and directing the heart before standing prayer
row.note: The Mishnah says that one should stand for prayer only in gravity and recalls early pietists who prepared in order to direct the heart to their Father in heaven. It develops the interior intention that the commentary places alongside bodily prayer.

row.basis: service of the heart interpreted as prayer
row.note: On the command to serve God with all the heart, the midrash asks what service occurs in the heart and answers: prayer. It offers a Jewish interpretive bridge between the commentary's inward dhikr and outward salāt.

row.basis: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as founders of set prayers
row.note: The Bavli links the three daily prayer times to the patriarchs. It amplifies the commentary's Abrahamic horizon by reading regular prayer as a patriarchal inheritance rather than merely a later ritual.

row.basis: blessing God's Name at the turns of light and darkness
row.note: The Rule of the Community orders blessing God's Name at the appointed changes of light and darkness. Its regulated time-pattern gives a sectarian Jewish analogue to continual remembrance enacted through prayer.

row.basis: prayers brought as a memorial before the Holy One
row.note: Raphael says that he brought the memorial of Tobit's prayer before the Holy One. The scene makes prayer itself a memorial, closely resonating with the commentary's treatment of dhikr as preserved remembrance.

row.basis: remembering the end in every action
row.note: Sirach tells the reader to remember the end in all deeds so as not to sin. This gives a Jewish wisdom parallel for remembrance that governs conduct in view of the final outcome.

row.basis: the Lord's Prayer three times each day
row.note: The Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily. It supplies an early Christian ritualization of recurring Name-centered prayer, rather than a vague appeal to private devotion.

row.basis: do this in remembrance of me
row.note: Jesus commands the bread rite to be done in remembrance of him. The verse supplies a distinct Christian liturgical meaning of remembrance: a repeated communal action that makes remembered speech bodily and enacted.

row.basis: remember Jesus Christ raised from the dead
row.note: The imperative to remember Jesus Christ gives the New Testament a direct remembrance command whose content is proclamation of resurrection. It is relevant to the commentary's dhikr chain while preserving its specifically Christian object.

row.basis: hearing the word and doing it
row.note: James tells hearers to become doers of the word rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone. This is a precise ethical bridge to the commentary's passage from a received reminder to a person's completed deeds.

row.basis: running the race set before the community
row.note: Hebrews exhorts its hearers to run with endurance the race set before them. It offers a specific Christian race image alongside the commentary's explicitly non-etymological runner-behind image for salāt, without claiming a lexical relationship.

row.basis: faith tested by fire and resulting praise
row.note: Faith tested by fire is compared to refined gold and is said to result in praise, glory, and honor. It provides a Christian refinement-and-praise development beside the commentary's carefully qualified fire imagery.

row.basis: setting the mind above rather than on earth
row.note: Paul commands believers to set their minds on what is above and not on earthly things. It makes the commentary's adjacent criticism of preferring worldly life into a concrete Christian ascetical instruction.

Peter declares that salvation is found in no other name under heaven given among human beings. It deliberately narrows the Name-salvation relationship to Jesus, so its difference from the Qur'anic Lord-name formulation is a substantive comparison rather than a loose parallel.

row.basis: ongoing intercession for those approaching God
row.note: Christ is said to live continually to intercede for those who approach God through him. It gives a Christian account of heavenly beneficent prayer that can be compared with, but not merged into, the commentary's account of divine and angelic salāt.

row.basis: remembering YHWH as prayer reaches the holy temple
row.note: At the point of inner collapse, Jonah says that he remembered YHWH and that his prayer came to God in the holy temple. It is one of the Hebrew Bible's most exact remembered-Lord-to-prayer sequences.

row.basis: thanksgiving sacrifice, vowed act, and YHWH's salvation
row.note: Jonah promises sacrifice with a voice of thanksgiving and fulfillment of his vow, then declares that salvation belongs to YHWH. This gives a distinctive prayerful completion to the commentary's purification, Name, worship, and salvation pattern.

row.basis: sign, zikkaron, and Torah in the mouth
row.note: The exodus rite is to be a sign and zikkaron so that YHWH's Torah will be in Israel's mouth. Hebrew zikkaron belongs to the zkr cognate family of the commentary's ذ ك ر, and the verse explicitly joins memorial, embodied sign, and spoken teaching.

row.basis: write the memorial in a book and recite it
row.note: YHWH orders Moses to write the event as a zikkaron in a book and place it in Joshua's ears. The zkr cognate supplies a concrete biblical precedent for the commentary's secondary sense of dhikr as a preserved, spoken scriptural record.

row.basis: seeing a sign, remembering commands, and doing them
row.note: The tassel is to prompt Israel to remember all YHWH's commands and do them rather than follow heart and eyes astray. It provides a direct sequence from material reminder through remembrance to completed action.

row.basis: written song taught and put in Israel's mouth
row.note: Moses is commanded to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths so it can remain a witness. The verse makes preserved words, oral repetition, and durable communal memory one practice.

row.basis: kneeling three times daily in prayer and thanksgiving
row.note: Daniel kneels on his knees three times each day, prays, and gives thanks before God as was his custom. It is a sharply drawn biblical portrait of habitual bodily prayer joined to thankful remembrance.

row.basis: penitence, kneeling, and outspread hands to YHWH
row.note: At the evening offering Ezra rises from fasting, falls on his knees, and spreads his hands to YHWH. The bodily action is expressly penitential, providing a close counterpart to purification culminating in prayer.

row.basis: fire and glory answered by prostration and thanks
row.note: When Israel sees the fire and YHWH's glory, the people bow face-down and worship with thanksgiving. Unlike the commentary's opposed fire and prayer portraits, this temple scene makes divine fire the immediate occasion of worship.

row.basis: bowing and kneeling before the maker
row.note: The summons is to worship, bow down, and kneel before YHWH the maker. Its Creator-language and successive bodily verbs make it a close poetic counterpart to the commentary's rabb as creator and prayer as embodied service.

row.basis: cup of salvation and calling YHWH's Name
row.note: The psalmist lifts the cup of salvation and calls on YHWH's Name. It connects the salvation language surrounding 87:14 with a named, physical act of thanksgiving in 87:15.

row.basis: giving thanks and calling on YHWH's Name
row.note: The liturgical charge joins thanksgiving, calling on YHWH's Name, and making his deeds known among peoples. It supplies a public vocal form of the Name-remembrance developed in the commentary.

row.basis: glory due the Name, offering, and worship
row.note: The assembly is told to give YHWH the glory due his Name, bring an offering, and worship in holy splendor. It traces an explicit movement from the Name's honor to embodied cultic action.

row.basis: commanded praise becoming song and bowed worship
row.note: Hezekiah directs Levites to praise YHWH with David's and Asaph's words; they praise with joy and bow to worship. The scene closely resembles the commentary's interest in an inherited command or text reaching fulfillment in human action.

row.basis: standing to bless the exalted glorious Name
row.note: The Levites command the people to stand and bless YHWH, whose glorious Name is exalted above every blessing and praise. It directly supports the commentary's Name-as-elevated image while retaining a communal liturgical posture.

row.basis: prayer toward the house and confessing God's Name
row.note: In drought, Israel prays toward the temple, confesses God's Name, and turns from sin. The verse brings together sanctuary, Name, prayer, repentance, and ethical correction more specifically than a general temple parallel.

Elijah contrasts calling on the name of a god with calling on YHWH, and identifies the God who answers by fire as God. The contest makes fire an authentication of correct Name-invocation, a distinct narrative arrangement beside the commentary's fire contrast.

row.basis: God sanctifies the great Name among nations
row.note: God promises to vindicate the holiness of his great Name before the nations. It supplies a restoration-oracle counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the Name is exalted and not a neutral verbal label.

row.basis: clean water cleansing impurity and idols
row.note: God promises to sprinkle clean water so that Israel will be clean from impurities and idols. It is a direct prophetic form of purification that prepares a people for restored relation to their Lord.
God gives a new heart and spirit in place of the hardened one. This intensifies the commentary's inner dimension of remembrance by making transformed inward life part of restoration.

row.basis: Spirit causing God's statutes to be done
row.note: God puts his Spirit within the restored people and causes them to walk in his statutes and do his judgments. It gives a strong biblical analogue for remembered or received divine speech becoming enacted human work.

The seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with a coal and declares his guilt removed and sin atoned for. It gives a specific prophetic image of speech-organs purified before their subsequent service to the holy Lord.

row.basis: lips that honor while the heart is distant
row.note: The people draw near with mouth and honor God with lips while their heart is far away. This is the Hebrew Bible's direct inverse of the commentary's united tongue-and-heart remembrance.

row.basis: purified lips calling the Name and serving together
row.note: God gives peoples a purified lip so that all may call on YHWH's Name and serve him shoulder to shoulder. The verse unusually combines purified speech, Name-invocation, and communal embodied service.

row.basis: great Name among nations with incense and pure offering
row.note: From sunrise to sunset YHWH's Name is great among nations, and incense and a pure offering are brought to it. This creates a global liturgical counterpart to the commentary's elevated Name and its movement from one worshipper to many places.

row.basis: not profaning and sanctifying the holy Name
row.note: Israel must not profane YHWH's holy Name, for he is to be sanctified among them. It is a priestly biblical ground for treating the Name as an object of reverent, morally disciplined worship.

row.basis: continuing to pray for the people
row.note: Samuel says that ceasing to pray for Israel would itself be sin, and pairs prayer with teaching the good and right way. It adds a continuing communal-intercession dimension to the commentary's secondary understanding of salāt as petition for another's good.

row.basis: saying Lord, Lord versus doing the Father's will
row.note: Jesus denies that everyone who says Lord, Lord enters the kingdom, limiting it to the one who does the Father's will. This directly tests any reading in which naming the Lord is sufficient without the embodied, ethical action the commentary itself emphasizes.
The tax collector stands at a distance, will not raise his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy as a sinner. The scene makes inward humility, body, and penitential prayer a single act.
Jesus' spoken petition asks the Father to glorify the divine Name, and a heavenly voice answers it. It is a concentrated Johannine Name-prayer formula with the commentary's elevation motif.

row.basis: asking in Jesus' Name for the Father's glory
row.note: Jesus promises to do what is asked in his Name so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. The verse creates a specifically Christian linkage of named petition, divine response, and glorification.

row.basis: making the Father's Name known and keeping his word
row.note: Jesus says he has made the Father's Name known to those given him, and that they have kept the word. It closely connects disclosed Name, preserved teaching, and obedient human response.
The Spirit intercedes in human weakness with groanings that cannot be spoken. It offers a precise Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that remembrance and prayer exceed audible language.

row.basis: bodies presented as living sacrifice and rational worship
row.note: Believers are urged to present their bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice, called their worship. This makes the body itself the offered form of worship, a strong companion to the commentary's mouth-to-body movement.
Those bought at a price are told to glorify God in their body. It gives an unusually compact New Testament statement that bodily life can enact the praise owed to God.

row.basis: praying and singing with spirit and mind
row.note: Paul resolves to pray and sing both with spirit and with mind. The deliberately paired faculties make it a close comparison for the commentary's outward and inward registers of remembrance.

row.basis: spoken psalms and heart-song to the Lord
row.note: Believers address one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs while singing and making melody in their hearts to the Lord. It joins communal voiced praise to interior devotion without collapsing either into the other.

row.basis: thanksgiving to the Father in Jesus' Name
row.note: The community gives thanks always to God the Father in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. It provides a clear Christian formula in which named Lordship governs verbal worship.

row.basis: word dwelling within and gratitude sung to God
row.note: The word of Christ is to dwell richly among believers through teaching, admonition, and grateful singing to God. It gives a churchly analogue to the commentary's dhikr as a preserved word active in heart, mouth, and communal practice.

row.basis: word and deed done in the Lord's Name
row.note: Whatever believers do in word or deed is to be done in the Name of the Lord Jesus with thanksgiving to God. It makes the named Lord the bridge between speech and embodied action.

row.basis: remembering a person in petitions night and day
row.note: Paul says he remembers Timothy unceasingly in his petitions night and day. The verse supplies a concrete Christian instance in which remembrance is itself maintained through ongoing prayer for another.

row.basis: loud cries, tears, reverence, and being heard
row.note: Jesus offers prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one able to save from death, and is heard because of reverence. This is a vivid counterweight to hidden prayer, showing the commentary's voice-and-body theme in an explicitly audible form.

row.basis: confession, prayer for one another, and healing
row.note: Believers are told to confess sins and pray for each other so that they may be healed; the righteous person's prayer is powerful. It links purification, reciprocal petition, and beneficial effect in a single communal instruction.

row.basis: confession followed by forgiveness and cleansing
row.note: Confession brings God's forgiveness and cleansing from all unrighteousness. The verse offers a tightly connected Christian account of voiced acknowledgement and divine purification.

row.basis: white garments and confession of the victor's name
row.note: The victor is clothed in white, and Christ confesses that person's name before the Father and angels. It combines purification imagery, a personal name, and a reciprocal heavenly acknowledgement.

row.basis: fear God, give glory, and worship the creator
row.note: The angelic proclamation calls all to fear God, give him glory, and worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs. Its Creator-centered worship and reverent fear echo major details developed around rabb and prayer.

row.basis: confession before the communal offering is made pure
row.note: The Didache directs the assembly to confess transgressions before giving thanks and breaking bread, so that its sacrifice may be pure. It is an early Christian liturgical sequence of purification into worship.

row.basis: God no longer remembers forgiven sin
row.note: In the new-covenant promise, God forgives iniquity and says he will remember sin no more. The negated Hebrew zkr verb gives a precise counter-form of remembrance: human dhikr preserves the Lord's Name, whereas divine mercy refuses to preserve forgiven guilt.

row.basis: atonement requires reconciliation with the injured person
row.note: The Mishnah says that the Day of Atonement atones offenses against God but not offenses against another person until reconciliation is made. It sharpens the commentary's purification-and-prayer motif by making ethical repair indispensable.

row.basis: worship tied to neither mountain nor Jerusalem
row.note: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that worship of the Father will be tied neither to that mountain nor to Jerusalem. This is a specific Christian counter-reading beside the commentary's discussion of named worship houses and sacred places.

row.basis: true worship in spirit and truth
row.note: The Father seeks worshippers who worship in spirit and truth. This develops the preceding relocation of worship into an inwardly truthful mode, useful beside the commentary's simultaneous concern for hidden remembrance and bodily rite.

row.basis: the appointed hour of prayer at the temple
row.note: Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer. It offers an early Christian scene of continuing scheduled prayer within a named sacred space.

row.basis: fasting and prayer night and day in the temple
row.note: Anna remains at the temple, worshipping through fasting and petitions night and day. This is a specific New Testament portrait of recurrent, bodily disciplined worship.

row.basis: communal worship and fasting followed by divine direction
row.note: While the Antiochene community worships the Lord and fasts, the Holy Spirit gives a directive. The scene offers a concrete continuation of the commentary's reminder-to-action pattern within communal liturgy.

row.basis: things sanctified through God's word and prayer
row.note: A created thing is said to be sanctified through God's word and prayer. It provides a distinct Christian use of prayer as a consecrating act, rather than simply as petition or praise.

row.basis: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
row.note: Recipients of the unshakable kingdom are urged to offer worship pleasing to God with reverence and awe. It closely matches the commentary's fearful recipient of reminder and its account of worship as the proper response.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr; name in the night
row.note: The commentary names ẕakara as keeping the Lord's name alive; the psalmist remembers YHWH's name in the night and keeps Torah, joining recollection to sustained practice.
The commentary's Arabic remembrance of the Lord's name has a close Hebrew counterpart: after revealing the name YHWH, God calls it a memorial for every generation.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr and honoring the name
row.note: Those who fear YHWH speak together and esteem his name; he attends and a book of remembrance is written for them, joining remembered name, reverence, and a recorded outcome.

row.basis: Hebrew zkr; invoking the name in danger
row.note: Against those relying on chariots and horses, the community remembers the name of YHWH; this makes the commentary's remembered name a ground of trust in its own crisis setting.
The psalm pairs YHWH's enduring name with his remembrance through generations, giving the commentary's name-and-remembrance relation a communal, lasting form.
The righteous rejoice in YHWH and give thanks to his holy remembrance; the Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ẕikr is used in praise.
In a prayer about waiting for YHWH, the speaker says that his name and memorial are the soul's desire; remembrance is a continuing orientation, not merely spoken repetition.
At the altar God says he will come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this joins invoked name, worship place, and blessing as the commentary does in its temple reading.
From the fish, Jonah remembers YHWH and says his prayer reaches the holy temple; the crisis prayer makes remembrance lead directly into bodily and verbal appeal.

row.basis: Wholehearted praise and the feared name
row.note: The psalmist asks for an undivided heart to fear God's name; this gives a concrete inward counterpart to the commentary's account of remembrance held in heart as well as tongue.
The speaker thanks God with the whole heart and glorifies his name forever, bringing inward recollection and voiced praise together.

row.basis: Blessing and lifted hands in the name
row.note: After seeking God in the sanctuary, the speaker blesses him while alive and lifts his hands in his name; remembrance becomes an embodied act of praise.
The worshippers bow, kneel, and fall before the one who made them; the verse supplies a direct bodily scene for the commentary's transition from remembered name to prayer.

row.basis: Clean hands and a pure heart
row.note: The person who approaches God's holy place has clean hands and a pure heart and does not lift the soul to falsehood; this makes the commentary's purification-before-prayer sequence concrete.
The verse names those who seek God's face as Jacob, following the clean-handed worshipper of the prior verse; purification is framed as entrance into a praying community.
The speaker tells the people to call on YHWH's name and make his deeds known among nations; the name remembered in 87:15 becomes publicly voiced testimony.

row.basis: Calling on the name and recounting deeds
row.note: The psalm joins thanksgiving, calling on YHWH's name, and making his deeds known; its own sequence links remembrance to public praise.
The servants are told to bless YHWH's name from now and forever, extending the commentary's single remembered name into enduring communal praise.
YHWH's name is praised from the rising to the setting of the sun; this gives a daily rhythm to the commentary's remembered name and prayer.

row.basis: The name placed on the people as blessing
row.note: The priests place YHWH's name on Israel and God blesses them; this supplies the communal and reciprocal side of the commentary's name-and-prayer relation.

row.basis: The temple as the place of God's name
row.note: Solomon asks that God's eyes attend the house where he said his name would dwell, and that he hear prayer directed there; the text links name, place, and prayer.
Solomon asks God to hear the supplication of king and people from heaven and forgive; the temple name in the preceding verse frames the communal prayer.

row.basis: Abram builds an altar and calls on YHWH
row.note: Abram's worship at Bethel combines an altar with calling on YHWH's name, a patriarchal instance of the prayerful life that the commentary says reaches back to Abraham.

row.basis: Abraham calls on the eternal God's name
row.note: After planting a tamarisk at Beersheba, Abraham calls on the name of YHWH, the everlasting God; the scene joins a living planted object and invocation in Abraham's own setting.

row.basis: Isaac builds an altar and calls on YHWH
row.note: Isaac builds an altar and invokes YHWH's name at Beersheba, showing the prayer practice associated with Abraham continuing in his son.

row.basis: Rabbinic derivation of daily prayer from the patriarchs
row.note: The Talmud reads Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as instituting the daily prayers from their biblical encounters; it develops the commentary's Abrahamic prayer lineage into a regular liturgical schedule.
Israel is told to keep the commandment's words on the heart; this matches the commentary's secondary account of ẕikr as guarding the Lord's name inwardly.
The words are to be recited sitting, walking, lying down, and rising; this places remembrance throughout daily embodied life, as the commentary's name moves from speech into prayer.
Israel is warned not to forget the God who brought them from Egypt; the explicit negative makes the memory-versus-forgetting contrast developed around 87:15 concrete.

row.basis: Serving and swearing by God's name
row.note: The next verse commands service of YHWH and oath by his name, so the remembered name issues in bodily allegiance rather than remaining an idea.

row.basis: Named people humble themselves, pray, and turn
row.note: God's people called by his name are to humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from evil; the response closely joins purification, name, and prayer.

row.basis: The Lord proclaims his name to Moses
row.note: YHWH descends and proclaims his name to Moses, making the name a revealed address before Moses responds in worship in verse 8.

row.basis: Moses bows after hearing the name
row.note: After YHWH proclaims his name and character, Moses hastens to bow to the earth and worship; this gives the commentary's word-to-body movement a specific scene.

row.basis: Calling on the name while receiving salvation
row.note: The worshipper lifts the cup of salvation and calls on YHWH's name; the prayerful name is set within a response to deliverance.

row.basis: Thanksgiving sacrifice and calling on the name
row.note: The speaker offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name, joining prayer, praise, and embodied offering.

row.basis: Blessing the name and announcing salvation
row.note: The psalm orders blessing YHWH's name and announcing his salvation day by day, a direct public form of remembering the name.

row.basis: The name, offering, and entry to worship
row.note: Worshippers ascribe glory due God's name, bring an offering, and enter his courts; this gives the commentary's remembered name a concrete liturgical destination.

row.basis: Prayer as incense and hands as offering
row.note: The psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and lifted hands be accepted as an evening offering; this directly joins verbal prayer to bodily worship.

row.basis: Entering worship with thanks and blessing the name
row.note: The people enter God's gates with thanksgiving and bless his name in the courts, showing the communal form of the individual prayer in the commentary.

row.basis: The Lord's name alone is exalted
row.note: The psalm says God's name alone is exalted above earth and heaven; this concretely meets the commentary's secondary image of the name as what rises above obscurity.

row.basis: One Lord and one name over the earth
row.note: The prophet's final vision says YHWH will be one and his name one; this gives a textual counterpart to the commentary's claim that the worshipper remembers a name belonging to no rival.

row.basis: The Lord's Prayer begins by hallowing the name
row.note: Jesus teaches disciples to address the Father and hallow his name before asking for daily provision; this directly joins remembered divine name and prayer.

row.basis: Prayer in secret before the Father
row.note: Jesus contrasts the public performance of hypocrites with a disciple praying unseen, where the Father sees what is hidden; this sharpens the commentary's contrast between voiced and inward remembrance.
The Peshitta uses the Syriac cognate ṣlōṯā for prayer in Jesus' warning about hypocritical synagogue and street prayer; it shows the shared Semitic prayer term in a concrete liturgical context.

row.basis: Wash away sins and call on the name
row.note: Ananias tells Saul to be baptized, wash away sins, and call on Jesus' name; this tightly combines purification, invocation, and embodied religious action.

row.basis: Calling on the Lord's name and being saved
row.note: Paul cites the promise that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, directly joining invocation of the name with the commentary's affirmed salvation.

row.basis: The name bestowed above every name
row.note: God highly exalts Jesus and gives him the name above every name; this is a direct textual counterpart to the commentary's secondary image of a name being raised.

row.basis: Every knee bows at the name
row.note: The next verse says every knee bows at Jesus' name, meeting the commentary's movement from named word to bodily prayer while retaining its different scene.

row.basis: Every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
row.note: The following verse makes every tongue confess Jesus as Lord; voiced confession completes the name-and-body sequence in the hymn.

row.basis: Syriac ṣlōṯā and hallowing the Name
row.note: In the Peshitta's Lord's Prayer the cognate ṣlōṯā introduces a prayer whose first petition hallows the Father's name, uniting the commentary's two key actions in one Semitic-language witness.

row.basis: Praise as sacrifice and confession of the name
row.note: The community is urged to offer a continual sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips confessing Jesus' name; this joins verbal remembrance with worship as an enacted offering.
Paul asks believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, their rational worship; this gives a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's name moving immediately into bodily prayer.

row.basis: A community calling on Jesus' name
row.note: Paul identifies the church with all who call on the name of Jesus as Lord; the ayah's single person's remembrance is here a shared communal practice.

row.basis: Naming the Lord entails turning from evil
row.note: The saying joins everyone who names the Lord's name with departure from unrighteousness; it makes the commentary's purification and invocation a linked ethical identity.

row.basis: Cornelius prays continually and gives alms
row.note: Cornelius is described as devout, God-fearing, generous to the poor, and constant in prayer; this is a specific portrait in which ethical giving and prayer mark one person.

row.basis: Prayers and alms as a memorial before God
row.note: The angel says Cornelius' prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial before God; the scene joins prayer, ethical action, and remembrance with a reversal in which God receives the remembrance.

row.basis: Prostration and prayers rising as incense
row.note: The elders fall before the Lamb, holding incense bowls identified as the prayers of the saints; this combines bodily bowing and prayer in one scene.
Paul's short instruction to pray continually makes prayer a sustained orientation rather than an isolated utterance, matching the commentary's completed life portrait.

row.basis: The Shema as the first confession
row.note: Jesus begins his answer with Israel's confession that the Lord is one; this provides the remembered monotheistic formula that frames the ensuing command to love and serve God.

row.basis: Love God with the whole person
row.note: The next verse commands love with heart, soul, mind, and strength; this supplies an embodied, inward allegiance behind the commentary's prayerful remembrance.
Hannah prays at Shiloh and vows her son to YHWH; the scene gives a particular Hebrew Bible portrait of a person defined by a prayerful response.

row.basis: YHWH remembers Hannah after her prayer
row.note: The narrative says YHWH remembers Hannah and she conceives; unlike 87:15's person remembering God, this reverses the direction of remembrance and makes prayer's answer the point.

row.basis: Aramaic cognate ṣlōṯā in the house of prayer
row.note: The Targum's Aramaic rendering calls the temple a house of prayer for all peoples; its ṣlōṯā cognate to Arabic ṣalāt meets the commentary's movement from a single worshipper to shared sacred spaces.

row.basis: Aramaic ṣlōṯā for prayer as incense
row.note: The Targum uses the Aramaic prayer word cognate with ṣalāt in a verse likening prayer to incense; its context also associates raised hands with an evening offering.

row.basis: Priestly praise followed by the people's prostration
row.note: In Simon's temple service, instruments and praise accompany the sacrifice and the assembly bows; this gives a communal liturgical scene for the commentary's bodily prayer.

row.basis: The first calling on YHWH's name
row.note: The verse says people began to call on YHWH's name, an early counterpart to the commentary's remembered name; the wider genealogy makes this an origin of public worship.

row.basis: Solomon's prayer toward the house bearing God's name
row.note: Solomon asks that God's eyes remain open toward the house where his name dwells and that he hear prayer; this expands the temple-name relation into a royal prayer.

row.basis: Hallowing the name in a repeated daily prayer
row.note: The Didache transmits the Lord's Prayer with its hallowed-name petition and instructs its repeated daily recitation; it shows early Christian liturgy making the name-and-prayer connection habitual.

row.basis: The tax collector's humble bodily prayer
row.note: The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, and asks for mercy; his prayer's posture and humility give a specific counterpoint to a merely external religious act.

row.basis: The humble worshipper goes home justified
row.note: Jesus says the tax collector, rather than the self-exalting Pharisee, goes home justified; this connects a person's enacted humility and prayer with the commentary's portrait of the one who prospers through purification.

row.basis: Prayer rises with incense before God
row.note: An angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the altar; this provides a heavenly liturgical image for the commentary's pairing of prayer and praise.

row.basis: Praise offered from within a fiery furnace
row.note: Azariah opens his mouth to pray amid the furnace and bless God; the commentary explicitly treats its second, corrective fire only as a lexical echo, so this is a limited comparison where fire becomes the setting for prayer rather than its punishment.

row.basis: Purified lips call the name and serve
row.note: YHWH says he will purify the peoples' lips so they call his name and serve him shoulder to shoulder; this tightly joins purification, voiced remembrance, and worship as in the ayah's sequence.

row.basis: Refining fire followed by calling the name
row.note: The remnant is refined like silver and gold, then calls on YHWH's name and receives his answer; this links the commentary's purification-to-prayer chain with its expressly secondary fire image.
YHWH refuses many prayers and hides his eyes because the worshippers' hands are full of blood; this warns that the commentary's prayerful portrait cannot be reduced to outward ritual.
The prophet commands washing and cleansing immediately after rejected prayer; the text makes ethical purification a necessary preparation for accepted worship.
The next verse defines cleansing through concrete justice and care for the vulnerable, supplying an ethical dimension to the commentary's person identified by deeds.

row.basis: Lips honor God while the heart is distant
row.note: Isaiah says the people honor God with lips while their hearts are far away and their worship is learned formula; this counters a merely vocal reading of remembering the name.

row.basis: The whole self blesses the holy name
row.note: The psalmist commands the inner self to bless YHWH and all within to bless his holy name; this directly joins the commentary's remembrance in tongue and heart.

row.basis: Do not forget the Lord's benefits
row.note: The next verse warns the soul not to forget God's benefits; the Hebrew forget/memory contrast reinforces the commentary's account of ẕikr against oblivion.

row.basis: Bowing in the temple and thanking God's name
row.note: The psalmist bows toward the holy temple, thanks God's name, and says God has exalted his word; this joins the commentary's name, bodily prayer, worship place, and elevation image.

row.basis: The great and holy name praised
row.note: The nations are told to praise God's great and awesome name because it is holy; this makes the name's exalted status a liturgical confession.
The worshippers are told to exalt YHWH and bow at his footstool; the verse pairs a raised divine name with a body lowered in worship.

row.basis: Glory due the name and bodily worship
row.note: The psalm asks worshippers to ascribe glory due YHWH's name and bow in holy splendor; it puts name-praise and bodily prostration together.

row.basis: The Lord's name majestic over all earth
row.note: The psalm opens by calling YHWH's name majestic throughout the earth; this gives a direct scriptural counterpart to the commentary's image of the name rising above obscurity.

row.basis: David asks that God's name be magnified forever
row.note: In David's prayer, the desired result is that YHWH's name be magnified forever; this is a direct prayer-context for the commentary's elevated-name image.

row.basis: The assembly blesses God's exalted name
row.note: The Levites call the people to bless YHWH's glorious name, exalted above blessing and praise; a gathered community performs the name-praise that 87:15 gives one person.

row.basis: Proclaiming the name and ascribing greatness
row.note: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God; this links the named Lord with voiced praise and elevation.

row.basis: Remembering God's wonders in a name-praising psalm
row.note: After calling on YHWH's name and recounting his deeds, the psalm tells Israel to remember his wonders; Hebrew zkr is used for the preserving remembrance developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Kneeling and thanking God three times a day
row.note: Daniel kneels toward Jerusalem three times daily and prays with thanks as he had done before; this is a concrete portrait of remembered allegiance enacted through the body.

row.basis: A plea for mercy because of God's name
row.note: Daniel asks God to hear and see the city's desolation, explicitly appealing to mercy rather than human righteousness; the prayer gives a counterweight to any idea that purification earns rescue.

row.basis: Hear for your sake and for the city called by your name
row.note: Daniel asks the Lord to hear, forgive, and act for his own sake because the city and people bear his name; it joins prayer, name, and communal identity.

row.basis: Foreigners pray toward the house because of God's name
row.note: Solomon includes the foreigner who comes because of God's great name and prays toward the temple, asking that God hear so all peoples know the name; this expands the commentary's house-of-prayer image beyond one community.

row.basis: The foreigner comes because of God's name
row.note: Solomon's dedication prayer explicitly imagines a foreigner coming from far away because of YHWH's name; the name draws worshippers to the house.

row.basis: Hearing a foreigner's prayer makes the name known
row.note: Solomon asks God to hear the foreigner's prayer so all peoples may know and fear his name; prayer at the named house becomes public witness.

row.basis: The temple called a house of prayer for all peoples
row.note: The prophet promises foreigners access to God's holy mountain and calls the house a house of prayer for all peoples; this directly grounds the commentary's move from an individual's prayer to worship spaces.

row.basis: The name honored among nations with incense and offering
row.note: YHWH's name is great among the nations, where pure offerings and incense are presented from sunrise to sunset; the text joins name-praise, prayer-like worship, and the daily horizon.

row.basis: A clean heart requested from God
row.note: In David's penitential prayer, he asks God to create a clean heart; purification is petitioned as a divine act before the speaker's later praise.
The psalmist asks God to open his lips so his mouth will declare praise; this gives a direct purification-to-verbal-worship sequence.

row.basis: Meditating on Torah day and night
row.note: The righteous person's delight and meditation in Torah provide a specific scriptural form of continual remembrance, related to the commentary's name held alive through ordinary life.

row.basis: The righteous person as a fruitful tree
row.note: The meditator is like a tree planted by streams, bearing fruit and prospering; this meets the commentary's explicit crop-growth image for purification without claiming a shared story or cognate.

row.basis: God's name and greatness have no equal
row.note: Jeremiah says none is like YHWH and that his name is great in might; this concretizes the commentary's exclusive, exalted divine name.

row.basis: Thanksgiving and an ordered way lead to salvation
row.note: God says the one offering thanksgiving honors him and the one ordering his way rightly will see salvation; this joins praise to enacted conduct rather than speech alone.

row.basis: The community magnifies YHWH's name together
row.note: After the psalmist blesses YHWH, he invites others to magnify the Lord and exalt the name together; the individual remembrance becomes communal praise.

row.basis: Seeking YHWH and receiving an answer
row.note: The speaker says he sought YHWH and was answered and delivered; this provides a prayer-and-response sequence alongside the commentary's person who remembers and prays.

row.basis: Rabbinic reading of the first invocation as profanation
row.note: A remembered rabbinic interpretation of Genesis 4:26 construes the early calling on YHWH's name as profaning or redirecting it toward idols; it warns that naming God can be corrupted rather than honored, though the precise gloss wording should be checked.

row.basis: Abram prays to the Creator after rejecting idols
row.note: After Abram rejects his father's idols, Jubilees gives him a prayer to the Creator; this expands the commentary's Abrahamic prayer lineage into an explicit repudiation of false worship.

row.basis: The faithful bless God's name from the furnace
row.note: In the Greek addition to Daniel, the prayer in the furnace blesses the God of the ancestors and praises his name; unlike the condemned fire in the commentary's neighboring portrait, this fire becomes a setting for faithful prayer.

Jesus cites Isaiah's contrast between honoring God with lips and having a distant heart; this Christian reuse makes the commentary's inward remembrance versus merely audible devotion an explicit worship test.

row.basis: Jesus invokes the house of prayer while cleansing the temple
row.note: Jesus calls the temple a house of prayer for all nations while driving out sellers; this reception of Isaiah 56:7 makes the worship place's name and purpose a critique of corrupted practice.

row.basis: Jesus says he made the Father's name known
row.note: In a prayer for his disciples, Jesus says he revealed the Father's name to them and that they kept his word; this joins the commentary's remembered name to reception and faithful action.

row.basis: The name made known so love may dwell in disciples
row.note: Jesus says he has made the Father's name known and will continue doing so, so divine love may be in the disciples; the prayer gives remembrance a continuing communal result.

row.basis: Every word and deed done in the Lord's name
row.note: Paul tells the community to do every word and deed in Jesus' name, giving thanks to the Father; this closely joins voiced remembrance, bodily action, and gratitude.

row.basis: Prayer with lifted holy hands and clean relations
row.note: Paul wants men to pray everywhere, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute; this is a specific embodied prayer whose moral posture matters.

row.basis: Draw near with cleansed hearts and washed bodies
row.note: The community is invited to draw near with sincere hearts, hearts cleansed from an evil conscience, and bodies washed; this closely joins purification to embodied approach in prayer.

row.basis: Psalms and songs voiced from the heart
row.note: The community is told to address one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing from the heart; this connects audible and inward praise as in the commentary's account of remembrance.

row.basis: Thanksgiving to God in Jesus' name
row.note: The next verse commands continual thanks to God the Father in Jesus' name, explicitly binding remembrance of the name to prayerful gratitude.

row.basis: A community devoted to prayers and shared worship
row.note: The first believers persist in teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers; this gives a communal form to the commentary's individual portrait without making prayer an isolated act.

row.basis: The Most High is not contained in handmade houses
row.note: Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands; this qualifies the commentary's extension from one person's prayer to named worship buildings by placing God's presence beyond their walls.

row.basis: Worship is not confined to a sacred location
row.note: Jesus says true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth, not by privileging either Jerusalem or the mountain; this offers a distinct Christian reading alongside the commentary's temple-and-prayer-place image.

row.basis: A people formed as a spiritual house and priesthood
row.note: Believers are built into a spiritual house to offer spiritual sacrifices; this recasts the commentary's many worship houses as a worshipping community.

row.basis: The Father's name marks the worshippers
row.note: The Lamb's followers have the Lamb's and Father's name written on their foreheads; this concretely meets the commentary's secondary image of a name as an identifying mark, without implying that the ayah uses that etymology.

row.basis: The redeemed sing a new song before the throne
row.note: The marked group sings a song that only the redeemed can learn; this gives voiced praise as a communal consequence of bearing the name.

row.basis: Abram's prayer contrasts the Creator with idols
row.note: The passage continues Abram's prayer against the worship of created things; the connection to the commentary's remembrance of the Lord's unique name is specific but depends on the remembered continuation of Jubilees' wording.

row.basis: The runner's race as disciplined religious effort
row.note: The commentary records a secondary Arabic use of ṣallā for a horse immediately following the leader; Paul uses a footrace to describe striving for an imperishable prize, a plausible race image parallel that does not define the ayah's prayer verb.

row.basis: The body disciplined in the race
row.note: Paul says he disciplines his body and makes it his servant; this is a limited counterpart to the commentary's bodily and race-following secondary imagery, not a claim that prayer means athletic training.

Israel, just freed from Egypt, says it would have been better to die by Egypt's meat pots; this gives the commentary's repeated preference for immediate sustenance over a promised future a concrete wilderness scene.

The Israelites recall fish, cucumbers and other foods of Egypt while craving them in the wilderness; the particular menu recalls the commentary's reading of Qur'an 2:61 as choosing familiar food over a better provision.
Esau sells and then despises his birthright for Jacob's lentil stew; the scene makes the commentary's warning about giving the first place to immediate appetite concrete.
Moses sets life and death before Israel and says to choose life; the commentary likewise treats the charge as a continuing choice of what to put first, not as lack of information.
The source commentary labels 87:16's word as Arabic ḥayāh; Hebrew ḥayyîm in Moses' command to choose life is its Semitic cognate, and the covenantal context makes this more than a bare word match.
Moses says to love, heed and cling to YHWH, “for he is your life”; this places the commentary's “near life” against a life defined by lasting attachment to God.

Moses warns Israel not to forget YHWH after prosperity; the commentary's preference is a repeated ordering of life, and this passage shows abundance displacing remembrance without making ignorance the diagnosis.
Moses pictures Israel eating its fill and living in good houses before warning of forgetting YHWH; this gives the commentary's repeated preference for near goods a concrete setting.
Isaiah's voice compares human flesh to grass; this supplies the commentary's specific green-life image with a biblical account of its short duration.
The grass withers when YHWH's breath blows on it; beside the commentary's fresh pasture that becomes dry refuse, the verse stresses how little the visible life can keep itself alive.
Isaiah contrasts withering grass with God's word standing forever; this concretely joins the commentary's transient near life to its claim that the old transmitted message endures.
Isaiah says the dead will live and those in the dust awake; the commentary's contrast between near life and life beyond it gains an explicit resurrection counterpart.
Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life; this names the durable life against which the commentary says the near life is wrongly preferred.

row.basis: labor spent on what does not satisfy
row.note: The prophet asks why people spend their labor on what is not bread, then calls them to listen and live; this makes the commentary's ordering of desire a choice between immediate consumption and life-giving attention.
Haggai rebukes people for living in paneled homes while YHWH's house lies in ruins; like the commentary's “head place” image, the verse identifies what their priorities serve.

The affluent recline with wine and oil yet are not grieved over Joseph's ruin; the scene shows near pleasure crowding out moral attention, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's diagnosis of a wrong ranking.
Those who take first place in feasting are first to go into exile; the reversal adds a consequence to the commentary's claim that being first with the near life does not mean lasting success.

row.basis: let us enjoy present good things
row.note: The speakers urge one another to enjoy the good things that exist now; this is an unusually direct Jewish articulation of the preference for present life that the commentary criticizes.
They propose crowning themselves with rosebuds before they fade; this adds the commentary's flower-and-withering image to a deliberate choice of present pleasure.
The speakers refuse to let any pleasure pass them by before their revel ends; the verse makes the commentary's repeated, daily prioritizing a program of hedonism rather than an isolated decision.
The souls of the righteous are in God's hand though their deaths seem like destruction; this challenges the near-life assumption by locating life beyond visible survival.
The righteous may appear punished before people, but their hope is full of immortality; this gives the commentary's “more enduring” life a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart.
A tortured brother says the King of the universe will raise those who die for his laws to everlasting life; his choice under threat dramatizes preferring God's promise to present survival.

Another brother says it is better to die at human hands while hoping for resurrection than to be raised to life without it; the scene makes the commentary's unstated comparison with the hereafter explicit.
The midrash expands the sale in Genesis 25 by treating Esau's act as contempt for the birthright; it sharpens why the meal is a misvaluation, not simply an exchange of food.
The Mishnah calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation there; its spatial image clarifies the commentary's “near” as a relation to what follows.

The Mishnah says one hour of repentance and good deeds here is better than the whole life of the world to come, yet one hour's bliss there is better than all this world's life; this preserves the commentary's hierarchy while showing why present deeds still matter.
Jesus says the heart follows the treasure one stores; this makes the commentary's account of “preference” as a practiced direction of love more precise than a single cold calculation.
Jesus says no one can serve both God and Mammon; the divided allegiance directly frames the commentary's question of which claimant receives first place.
Jesus tells hearers to seek God's kingdom first, with food and clothing discussed around it; the verse turns the commentary's critique of daily ordering into a positive order of priorities.

row.basis: sell all for the hidden treasure
row.note: The finder joyfully sells everything to obtain the field with its treasure; this reverses 87:16's direction by treating the coming kingdom as worth preferring to present holdings.
Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will find it; this counters the commentary's assumption that keeping present life is the sure measure of life.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world and forfeiting one's life; the explicit trade-off supplies the comparison left unstated in the commentary's ayah 87:16.
The rich man leaves grieving because he has many possessions after Jesus tells him to sell and follow; this is a narrative instance of preferring present wealth to the offered lasting life.

Jesus explains that life's anxieties, riches and pleasures choke the heard word so it bears no mature fruit; this links the commentary's avoidance of reminder to worldly attachments that take its place.
Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions; this directly separates the commentary's “near life” from the accumulation people may mistake for life itself.
The rich fool plans to store his goods and tell his soul to relax, eat, drink and be merry; this gives the commentary's daily preference for the near life a concrete voice.
God tells the rich fool that his life is demanded that night; the scene answers his present-focused plan with the limit of the life he tried to secure.
Jesus concludes that this is the fate of one who stores for himself but is not rich toward God; the contrast specifies what the commentary's wrong ordering costs.

Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things during his life while Lazarus received bad, but now their situations are reversed; the parable makes the commentary's present/future comparison a scene of changed fortunes.
Jesus tells the crowd to work for food that endures to eternal life, not perishable food; this answers the commentary's image of near life as the readily consumed pasture.

row.basis: life in this world and eternal life
row.note: Jesus says that the one who loves life in this world loses it, while the one who hates it keeps it for eternal life; this is the closest direct formulation of the commentary's ranking, with the important qualification that it is Jesus' saying.

row.basis: mind set on flesh or Spirit
row.note: Paul says the mindset of the flesh is death while the Spirit's mindset is life and peace; the verse joins inner orientation to the outcome, like the commentary's preference and its consequence.
Paul says those using the world should not be absorbed by it because its present form is passing; this gives a concrete reason not to enthrone what the commentary calls near.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; the distinction states why the commentary's near life is not the final measure.

Paul tells each person to look to the interests of others, not only their own; this gives a direct ethical counterpoint to the source commentary's explanation of īthār as preferring another over oneself.

Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people rather than the fleeting pleasure of sin; as the same Moses named in the commentary's final pages, he embodies preference for a lasting good over immediate pleasure.

Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward; the same figure named by the commentary models the opposite ordering of near wealth and future good.

The patriarchs, including Abraham, desire a better heavenly country rather than return to the one they left; this connects the commentary's mention of Abraham's pages with a concrete orientation beyond the near homeland.
Hebrews recalls Esau selling his birthright for one meal; its reuse of Genesis makes the commentary's preference-for-the-near pattern an explicit warning against trading away a lasting inheritance.
Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here but seek the one to come; this spells out the temporal contrast carried by the commentary's “near” life.
John warns against loving the world and its desires; the commentary likewise locates the failure in where love and priority are given, not in lack of information.
John says the world and its desire pass away, while the one doing God's will abides forever; this closely joins the commentary's near life, continuing action and lasting alternative.
Paul says Demas deserted him because he loved the present age; this concrete abandonment of costly work for current life gives the commentary's diagnosis a personal example.
Paul tells the rich to store a good foundation for the future so they may take hold of real life; this redirects possessions toward what the commentary calls more enduring.
Peter applies Isaiah's grass-and-flower image to mortal life; this brings the commentary's pasture and withering motif into the Christian proclamation of the enduring word.

Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the gospel preached to the readers; this connects the commentary's passing life with the old, transmitted message of its final verses.
Paul says what was written beforehand was written for instruction and hope; this supplies a Christian account of how the commentary's ancient pages can still address current hearers.
Timothy has known sacred writings from childhood, which can make him wise for salvation; this makes the commentary's inherited pages an active guide rather than merely an old report.
Paul says the wilderness events happened as examples and were written for later generations; this turns ancestral tracks into a record that later hearers can either heed or repeat.
Paul contrasts sowing to the flesh, which reaps corruption, with sowing to the Spirit, which reaps eternal life; this links repeated present conduct to what follows it.
The dead are judged from books according to their deeds; this gives the commentary's secondary image of traces left by one's steps a concrete judgment scene.
The proverb pictures wealth sprouting wings and flying away; it offers a specific image for the commentary's warning that what is given first place in near life cannot be kept.

Israel abandons the fountain of living water for cracked cisterns that hold none; unlike the commentary's focus on misranking rather than ignorance, this sharper indictment shows the biblical contrast between a lasting source and chosen substitutes.

row.basis: high and lofty, with the lowly
row.note: The One who is high and inhabits eternity also dwells with the contrite and lowly; this adds a biblical counterpoint to the commentary's vertical contrast between the Most High and the “low” near life.
Qoheleth says God brings every deed, including the hidden, into judgment; this concretizes the commentary's image of choices leaving a trace that later identifies the walker.

Ben Sira urges the reader not to deprive himself of a happy day; read with his surrounding reminders of death, this is a Jewish countervoice that treats present goods as gifts to use rather than a life to enthrone.
Ben Sira compares human life to a garment that wears out; the image adds mortality to his counsel to enjoy a present day without mistaking it for permanence.

Ezra's angel says the Most High made not one world but two; this gives the commentary's near/after contrast an apocalyptic Jewish frame, though the verse itself does not rank every present good as evil.

Paul says people knew God yet failed to honor or thank him; unlike the commentary's explicit restraint from accusing its hearers of ignorance or denial, Paul makes culpable knowledge part of his diagnosis.

Paul describes an exchange of the Creator's truth for a lie and worship of the creature; this gives a sharper idolatry account of misdirected allegiance than the commentary's narrower charge of preferring near life.
Paul urges humility that counts others more significant than oneself; this carries the self-giving side of the source commentary's Arabic-root discussion into a Christian ethical instruction.
James compares human life to a mist that appears briefly and vanishes; this gives the commentary's “near life” a concrete limit while its next verse makes plans conditional on the Lord's will.

The risen Jesus names the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms as written witnesses; this is a Christian interpretive claim about older scriptures that adds context to the commentary's appeal to Abraham's and Moses' pages.

Augustine explains the earthly and heavenly cities through opposed loves, self-love and love of God; this reads the commentary's repeated “preference” as the allegiance that forms a person's community, not merely a choice of possessions.

Paul says he bears the marks of Jesus on his body; beside the source commentary's secondary link from preference to bodily trace and its reference to the mark of prostration, this makes allegiance visible in a person's scars, though the marks have different causes.

The Lamb's followers bear his and his Father's name on their foreheads; this is a concrete Christian mark of allegiance that can be set beside the commentary's face-mark from prostration, while keeping their distinct settings clear.
Israel is commanded to repeat the words to children in ordinary daily settings; this gives a concrete Hebrew Bible practice for the commentary's image of a saying transmitted across generations.

Paul says everyone appears before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what was done through the body; the bodily actions that the commentary figures as unseen traces thus have an explicit accounting counterpart.
After the first humans disobey, they are told they will return to dust; this gives the commentary's “near life” a concrete mortal boundary that makes the later-life comparison meaningful.

God bars the humans from taking the tree of life and living forever; the narrative distinguishes present human life from life without end, sharpening the commentary's contrast between near and enduring life.

Moses says the commandments are to be bound as a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes; this joins transmitted divine words to a visible bodily marker, beside the commentary's secondary mark-and-remembrance imagery.

Moses tells Israel to remember former days and ask fathers and elders to recount them; this supplies a concrete practice of transmitted memory beside the commentary's image of a saying handed down from Abraham and Moses.

Ezekiel says God takes no pleasure in anyone's death and calls Israel to turn and live; this adds repentance as a still-open alternative to the commentary's repeated, changeable preference for the near life.

row.basis: feasting without regard for God's work
row.note: Isaiah depicts music and wine while people do not regard YHWH's work; this is a specific scene of present enjoyment displacing attention to divine action, close to the commentary's claim that worldly attachments crowd out reminder.

The person who trusts YHWH is like a tree by water whose leaves stay green and which does not cease bearing fruit; this reverses the commentary's withering pasture image by showing what enduring life rooted in God looks like.

Those who fear YHWH speak together, and a book of remembrance is written before him; this makes the commentary's secondary image of choices leaving a trace a specific written record tied to reverence.

Jeremiah says the nations inherited lies from their fathers; beside the commentary's account of people following ancestral footprints, this is a counterexample where the inherited trail must be rejected.

The man in linen marks the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations so they are distinguished in the coming judgment; this gives the commentary's mark-on-body motif a concrete biblical scene, though its mark signifies grief rather than prayer.

Jesus tells a host to invite the poor, disabled and blind rather than guests who can return the favor; this concretizes the self-preference reversal that the source commentary explains through īthār and its positive use for giving others priority.

Jesus says the host who gives without repayment will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous; this joins the commentary's self-giving preference to the future life that outweighs present return.

The Jerusalem believers sell property so no one among them is needy; this is a concrete communal counterpart to the commentary's account of the Helpers preferring the newcomers over themselves despite scarcity.

Paul's Greek says believers should take the lead in honoring one another; beside the source commentary's gloss of īthār as putting something first and its positive case of preferring others, this is a close ethical parallel without a claim of shared roots.

Paul says one community's present abundance should supply another's need, with the possibility of reciprocal help later; this gives a practical form to the commentary's positive choice to give the other person priority.
In response to disciples seeking rank, Jesus says the great one among them must be their servant; this reverses the commentary's image of giving the preferred object the head place.
Jesus says the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many; this extends the commentary's positive “prefer another” ethic to the giving of one's own life.

Paul describes opponents whose god is their belly and whose minds are set on earthly things; this concretely identifies appetites and earthly orientation as a rival allegiance to the one valued in the commentary.
Paul contrasts that earthly orientation with believers' citizenship in heaven; this gives the commentary's near-life/afterlife distinction a communal identity and destination.
Paul commands hearers to set their minds on things above rather than things on earth; this directly addresses the commentary's claim that the issue is the repeated direction of preference.
Paul says that when Christ, the believers' life, appears, they too will appear with him in glory; this names a future life hidden from present view, beyond the commentary's near life.
The addressees accept the plundering of their property because they know they have a better and abiding possession; this is a direct case of relinquishing near goods for what lasts.

Paul compares disciplined faithfulness to runners in a race who run to obtain a prize; this gives a concrete race image for the commentary's surah-wide sequence in which simply being first does not settle the outcome.
Paul contrasts a perishable athletic crown with the imperishable one sought by believers; this adds an explicit durable prize to the commentary's image of the later good as more lasting.

Jesus cites the place where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; this is a distinct punishment formula beside the commentary's reference to the one who neither dies nor lives in the great fire.

Jesus ends the judgment scene with eternal punishment for some and eternal life for the righteous; this makes the two enduring outcomes explicit beside the commentary's ranking of near life and the hereafter.

Jesus tells Martha that he is the resurrection and the life, and that the believer will live even after dying; this answers the commentary's contrast between merely present life and life beyond death.

row.basis: death ends in the new creation
row.note: The new Jerusalem vision says death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more; it gives a concrete positive horizon to the commentary's contrast with a life that does not truly live.

Wisdom says the one who finds her finds life and receives favor from YHWH; this presents life as the result of choosing a path of instruction, matching the commentary's choice-versus-ignorance distinction.
Wisdom says the one who misses her harms himself and loves death; this makes a person's preference itself the source of the outcome, as the commentary says the hearers know the way but rank wrongly.

row.basis: the command is not far away
row.note: Moses says the command is not too difficult or far away; with verse 14's word near in mouth and heart, this offers a spatial counter-image to the commentary's explanation that “near life” is named by its distance from what follows.
Qoheleth says a person leaves life as naked as at birth and cannot carry away labor's gain; this specifies why the commentary's near possessions cannot be the more enduring good.

Isaiah's final vision shows the corpses of rebels with worm and fire that do not cease; this supplies a Hebrew Bible punishment image related to, but distinct from, the commentary's “neither die nor live” formula.

The passage describes the world to come without eating, drinking or commerce, with the righteous enjoying the radiance of the Divine Presence; it gives rabbinic content to the commentary's enduring alternative while distinguishing it from present bodily life.
The treatise argues that reason can govern the passions; this gives a Jewish philosophical account of the self-ordering behind the commentary's repeated choice of what receives precedence.

Jesus tells his hearers not to be anxious about life and what they will eat or drink, since life is more than food; this qualifies the commentary's criticism by treating present needs as real but not life's highest measure.

Jesus says Mary chose the good portion while Martha is distracted by service; this makes preference for hearing the teacher's word a domestic scene, adding a specific example to the commentary's contrast between reminder and competing attention.

row.basis: not shaped by the present age
row.note: Paul tells the community not to be conformed to this age but to be transformed in mind; this connects present-age pressure to an ongoing reordering of judgment.

Peter says believers were redeemed from the futile ways handed down by their ancestors; this is a Christian counterexample to the ancestral footprints in the commentary, showing inheritance can also be abandoned.

Hebrews tells its hearers to lay aside every weight and run the race set before them with endurance; the shared race image adds disciplined persistence to the commentary's surah-wide sequence, though the passage focuses on faithfulness rather than worldly preference.

The saying calls the world a corpse and says it is unworthy of the one who has understood it; this is a deliberately harsher counter-reading than the source commentary, which locates the fault in preferring near life rather than declaring that life itself is dead.

Augustine says the heavenly city's pilgrims use the earthly city's peace during their journey while desiring the peace above; this interprets present life as a provisional good, qualifying any reading of the commentary as requiring escape from all earthly life.

For the commentary's Moses scene in which a people ask to exchange a superior provision for near food, the wilderness generation remembers fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic from Egypt; it gives the closest Hebrew narrative of appetite displacing manna.

The complainers say that they see nothing except manna. Alongside the commentary's claim that people can know a provision yet keep devaluing it, the verse makes the recurrent preference itself audible.

row.basis: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
row.note: Jesus redirects a crowd seeking bread from food that perishes to food that endures for eternal life. His reading of the manna setting makes the commentary's near life versus better and abiding life comparison explicit.

Jesus says that the ancestors ate manna in the wilderness and died. This Christian use of the Moses tradition makes immediate sustenance deliberately nonfinal beside the commentary's food-and-durability contrast.

The Egyptian magicians identify the plague as God's finger, while Pharaoh remains unpersuaded. Against the commentary's Qur'anic sorcerers who act on received signs against Pharaoh, the verse separates recognizing a sign from choosing what it demands.

Later Christian memory names Jannes and Jambres as Moses' opponents. Its lasting portrayal of Pharaoh's magicians as resisting truth is a pointed counter-narrative to the commentary's Qur'anic convert-sorcerers.

row.basis: royal threat and refusal of idolatry
row.note: The three Judeans refuse the king's command even if God does not rescue them from the furnace. It supplies a Hebrew scene for the commentary's choice against a ruler whose threat reaches only the present life.

row.basis: tyrant's torture and resurrection to eternal life
row.note: A condemned brother answers a king's torture with confidence that the King of the world will raise the faithful to enduring life. It closely parallels the commentary's contrast between temporal coercion and a lasting divine outcome.

row.basis: short-lived human fire and coming judgment
row.note: Polycarp contrasts a proconsul's briefly burning fire with the coming judgment. This early Christian martyr text crystallizes the commentary's claim that an earthly ruler's threat is not the final measure of life.

row.basis: those who kill the body and final judgment
row.note: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill the body from God, who holds final judgment. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's account of Pharaoh's authority as bounded by worldly life.

row.basis: not loving life even to death
row.note: The witnesses conquer through testimony and do not love their lives even to death. It turns the commentary's ordering of life into a concrete allegiance under lethal pressure.

Esau eats and drinks, then despises his birthright. The scene gives narrative form to the commentary's warning about accepting an immediate food or benefit while relinquishing a more durable inheritance.

row.basis: Esau exchanging birthright for one meal
row.note: Hebrews identifies Esau's sale of his birthright for a meal as profane. This Christian reading makes the commentary's wrong ordering of the immediate and the enduring an ethical warning.

Moses chooses suffering with God's people instead of the temporary enjoyment of sin. Its explicit language of choosing and temporariness closely matches the commentary's sustained preference for the near life.

row.basis: Moses valuing reproach above Egyptian treasure
row.note: Moses regards reproach as greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward. It gives the commentary's language of honor, love, and what receives first place a Moses-specific counterpart.

The addressees accept the plundering of possessions because they know they have a better and abiding possession. Its paired valuation is unusually close to the commentary's better and more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: no abiding city and a city to come
row.note: The community has no enduring city here and seeks the one to come. This spatial contrast helps read the commentary's worldly life as the near, nonsettled life rather than an ultimate home.

row.basis: gaining the world and forfeiting life
row.note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life. It gives the commentary's preference for worldly life its sharpest personal cost.

row.basis: the passing world and the abiding doer
