row.note: The world and its desire pass away, while the one doing God's will abides forever. This is a direct Christian formulation of the commentary's contrast between desired near life and what remains.

row.basis: seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
row.note: Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal. It gives a precise temporal grammar for the commentary's recurrent ranking of what is near against what abides.

row.basis: future foundation and the life that is truly life
row.note: The wealthy are told to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life. This closely illuminates the commentary's distinction between the named life now and the more lasting life beyond it.

Sowing to flesh ends in corruption, while sowing to Spirit ends in eternal life. Its continuing agricultural calculus parallels the commentary's present-tense preference as a repeated ordering with a future result.
Jesus forbids storing treasure on earth, where it is destroyed or stolen. It supplies the material side of the commentary's claim that the coveted near-life goods cannot be made enduring.

row.basis: treasure in heaven that is not destroyed
row.note: Jesus directs disciples to treasure in heaven, where loss does not reach it. This is the positive reordering that the commentary sets against giving worldly life the place of honor.

row.basis: the rich fool's stored goods and sudden death
row.note: The rich fool plans future ease from accumulated goods, but death immediately makes those preparations someone else's. It concretizes the commentary's warning that longed-for worldly permanence does not survive the appointed end.

Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things during life with his later anguish and Lazarus's later comfort. The scene directly stages the commentary's reversal between present advantage and the life to come.

The care of the age and deceitfulness of wealth choke the word and make it fruitless. It closely matches the commentary's claim that admonition is avoided because another object has moved in front of it.
Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. It directly questions the commentary's false equation of the favored near life with what gives life its value.
The saying that one cannot serve both God and Mammon makes love and service a matter of ordered allegiance. It closely fits the commentary's account of preference as giving something the chief seat.

row.basis: luxury now and the day of slaughter
row.note: The rich have lived in luxury and self-indulgence while preparing their hearts for a day of slaughter. It joins the commentary's augment about wealth's social misuse to its future reckoning.

Isaiah defines acceptable devotion through feeding the hungry, housing the poor, and clothing the naked. It supplies a concrete alternative to the commentary's linked critique of loving wealth while failing the orphan and needy.

row.basis: riches and the day of wrath
row.note: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. This compressed proverb gives the commentary's wealth-versus-lasting-outcome contrast a sapiential form.

row.basis: awakening to everlasting life or contempt
row.note: Those sleeping in dust awake either to everlasting life or to everlasting contempt. It gives a direct Hebrew Bible horizon for the commentary's contrast between present life and an enduring final state.
God brings every deed, including hidden ones, into judgment. This gives the commentary's call to prepare rather than merely prefer the present a concrete accounting horizon.
The dead are judged from opened books according to their deeds. It closely meets the commentary's image of acts and traces recorded, then evaluated beyond the near life.

row.basis: grass withering and God's word standing
row.note: Grass withers and flowers fade, but God's word stands forever. The verse joins the commentary's temporary pasture and flower imagery to its final concern with enduring, transmitted speech.
First Peter applies the grass image to mortal flesh and its fading glory. It is a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's near life as fresh vegetation that becomes dark chaff.

row.basis: the enduring word proclaimed as gospel
row.note: First Peter identifies the enduring word as the message proclaimed to its hearers. Its use of Isaiah connects the commentary's preserved recitation and first pages with a word that outlasts human life.

row.basis: the rich fading in their pursuits
row.note: The rich person fades in the midst of pursuits as sun and heat wither grass and its flower. The verse supplies a particularly close image for the commentary's attractive, short-lived worldly vegetation.

row.basis: this world as vestibule before the world to come
row.note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation before entering the banquet hall. It makes the commentary's daily present choice and later fixed outcome into a Jewish interpretive image.

row.basis: repentance now and delight in the world to come
row.note: The mishnah values present repentance and deeds while also valuing a moment of future bliss above all present life. Its two-sided formulation keeps the commentary's preference for the hereafter from becoming contempt for the time in which one prepares.

row.basis: today for doing and tomorrow for reward
row.note: The talmudic reading distinguishes today as the time for doing commandments and tomorrow as the time for reward. It illuminates the commentary's contrast between a continuing present action and a settled future judgment.
Abraham awaits the city with foundations whose architect and builder is God. It gives the commentary's Abraham-and-Moses pages an Abrahamic example of refusing to treat the current dwelling as final.

The patriarchs desire a better, heavenly country, and God prepares a city for them. Its explicit betterness and future homeland closely parallel the commentary's more excellent and enduring hereafter.

A mother says that the Creator who fashioned human birth will give breath and life again to sons who surrender themselves for the law. It brings the commentary's womb-and-emergence analogy into direct contact with resurrection.

Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord by failing to keep the command when abundance arrives. It gives the commentary's claim that the hearers are not simply ignorant a covenantal setting: fullness can reorder what they remember.

row.basis: knowing God through justice for poor and needy
row.note: Jeremiah says that judging the cause of poor and needy is what it means to know God. It sharpens the commentary's augment that misplaced love of wealth shows itself in withheld honor and care, not merely in a mistaken idea.

row.basis: Moses and the prophets as warning
row.note: In the rich-man narrative Abraham says that the living have Moses and the prophets to hear. It joins the commentary's final appeal to Musa's pages with the need for a warning before the irreversible reversal.

Abraham says that one who does not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by a resurrection. It closely develops the commentary's distinction between possessing or hearing a warning and choosing to follow it.
The mishnah's seeing eye, hearing ear, and book in which deeds are written give a Jewish analogue to the commentary's claim that what is sent ahead and the traces left behind are recorded.

row.basis: book of remembrance for those who fear God
row.note: A book of remembrance is written before the Lord for those who fear him and esteem his name. It links the commentary's remembrance of the divine name to an enduring record rather than a passing worldly trace.
The dead who die in the Lord rest, yet their deeds follow them. This supplies a concise Christian image for the commentary's claim that a person's choices leave a trail beyond bodily life.

row.basis: a mark on the foreheads of the faithful
row.note: A mark is placed on the foreheads of people grieving over Jerusalem's abominations before judgment falls. It is a specific analogue to the commentary's developed image of allegiance becoming a visible sign that identifies a person.

Paul calls the marks borne in his body the marks of Jesus. Beside the commentary's branding, bodily trace, and face-mark imagery, it gives a Christian case in which a visible mark declares enduring allegiance.

row.basis: futile ways handed down from ancestors
row.note: Believers are ransomed from futile ways inherited from their fathers. It directly illuminates the commentary's claim that one generation's preferences can leave a path that later generations keep walking.

Jeremiah calls the people to ask for the ancient paths and walk the good way, but they refuse. It gives a concrete Hebrew instance of the commentary's distinction between a transmitted path that can guide and a preference that turns away from it.

The mishnah traces Torah from Moses through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the men of the Great Assembly. It gives the commentary's transmitted sheets a Jewish model in which a received word leaves a living, accountable trail.

row.basis: Moses writing all the Lord's words
row.note: Moses writes all the Lord's words after receiving them at Sinai. It provides a concrete biblical textual counterpart to the commentary's concern with Musa's pages, preservation, and received speech.

Moses finishes writing the words of Torah in a book. The verse helps distinguish the commentary's claim about Musa's sheets from the Hebrew Bible's own portrayal of Moses as the writer of a preserved covenantal text.

row.basis: sacred writings and wisdom for salvation
row.note: The sacred writings known from childhood are said to make Timothy wise for salvation. It gives a Christian account of inherited scripture functioning as the warning that the commentary says listeners may hear yet set behind nearer aims.

Arabic al-hayat and Hebrew ha-hayyim are Semitic cognates, and Deuteronomy sets life and death before Israel as a covenantal choice. Its own horizon is life under Torah in the land, which usefully distinguishes the commentary's explicitly eschatological ranking.

row.basis: Arabic hayah and Hebrew hayye olam
row.note: The commentary's al-hayat has a Semitic cognate in Daniel's hayye olam, everlasting life. Daniel gives that cognate an explicit postmortem sense, making its life-and-continuance contrast especially relevant.

Rabbi Eliezer's instruction to repent one day before death is explained as making every day a day of repentance. It closely matches the commentary's present-tense preference as a condition repeatedly renewed before the appointed end.

row.basis: human loftiness brought low and the Lord exalted
row.note: Human haughtiness is brought low while the Lord alone is exalted in that day. It gives a prophetic high-and-low axis for the commentary's contrast between the Most High and the lower, near life.
The saying that many first will be last and last first gives a concise reversal to the commentary's wordplay on first, later, and the error of giving what comes first the highest value.

Paul rejects self-seeking and calls believers to regard others as surpassing themselves. It provides a Christian ethical inverse to the commentary's developed contrast between self-preference and giving another the first place.
Paul commands that no one seek his own advantage but the other's. This gives the commentary's discussion of preference as a directionally neutral act a concrete communal reversal.

row.basis: two cities formed by two loves
row.note: Augustine explains the earthly and heavenly cities through rival loves of self and of God. His account clarifies the commentary's insistence that preference is not cold calculation but a love that makes an enduring social order.
Proverbs pictures wealth as suddenly making wings and flying away. It supplies a vivid sapiential counterpart to the commentary's claim that people try to reserve permanence for what cannot stay.
The ungodly urge one another to enjoy present goods vigorously while youth lasts. It offers a Jewish Hellenistic portrait of the near-life preference that the commentary sets under later judgment.

row.basis: mind set above rather than on earth
row.note: Paul tells believers to set their mind on things above rather than earthly things. It gives the commentary's spatial language of near and beyond a disciplined form of attention.
Those whose end is destruction have their minds set on earthly things. This is a close Christian diagnosis of the commentary's present preference as a direction of attention with a final consequence.
The community's citizenship is in heaven, from which it awaits a savior. It supplies the positive counterpart to the commentary's refusal to treat the near life as the final place of belonging.

Discipleship requires self-denial and taking up the cross daily. Its daily discipline corresponds to the commentary's insistence that preference for the near life is not one choice but a habit that must be reordered again and again.

Joshua asks Israel to choose whom it will serve, naming the gods served by their ancestors as one option. It brings the commentary's inherited tracks and active present ordering together in a concrete covenantal choice.

row.basis: not walking in the fathers' statutes
row.note: Ezekiel tells the next generation not to walk in their fathers' statutes or keep their idols. It gives a direct corrective to the commentary's image of later people stepping into the traces of earlier preferences.

The commanded words are to be upon Israel's heart. It provides a Torah counterpart to the commentary's concern that preserved, recited words must become an inward ordering rather than merely an inherited text.

Israel is to write the words on doorposts and gates. Beside the commentary's pages and enduring traces, the verse shows remembered instruction becoming a visible mark at the boundary of ordinary life.

The psalm praises God for forming inward parts and weaving a body in the womb. The commentary uses its birth-and-nearness sense only analogically, so this is an indirect aid for its image of present life as moving toward an emergence.

row.basis: loving life in this world and eternal life
row.note: Jesus says that loving one's life loses it, while giving up one's life in this world keeps it for eternal life. It is an unusually direct Christian formulation of the commentary's preference for near life versus enduring life.

row.basis: possessions, the poor, and treasure in heaven
row.note: When the ruler asks about eternal life, Jesus tells him to give possessions to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and follow. It joins the commentary's chief-place language to its augment about wealth withheld from the needy.

row.basis: almsgiving and an unfailing heavenly treasure
row.note: Jesus connects giving alms with purses that do not wear out and treasure in heaven. It supplies a concrete reversal of the commentary's worldly self-allocation: what is given away becomes the enduring possession.
Jesus locates the heart where treasure is. This directly illuminates the commentary's claim that preference is a love that gives its object the place of honor, not a detached calculation.
God alone possesses immortality in this doxology. It gives a direct Christian formulation to the commentary's claim that permanence cannot finally be reserved by creatures for themselves.

row.basis: uncertain riches and hope in God
row.note: The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God. As the immediate context of the already relevant future foundation, it identifies the false object of confidence in the commentary's preference scene.

Laodicea claims to be rich and in need of nothing while not recognizing its wretched, poor, blind, and naked state. Its diagnosis of wealth's self-deception gives a counterpoint to the commentary's claim that wrong ordering may survive apparent knowledge.
Momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison. It supplies a precise temporal reversal for the commentary's contrast between a present cost and what endures.

row.basis: using the world as its form passes away
row.note: Those who use the world are instructed not to use it as though it were final, because its present form passes away. This closely fits the commentary's distinction between having a share in the near life and enthroning it.
James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and then vanishes. It directly sharpens the commentary's discussion of long life, the appointed end, and the inability to make near life remain.

row.basis: neglect of the least and final judgment
row.note: Failure to serve the hungry, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned is treated as failure to serve the Son of Man. It gives the commentary's orphan-and-poor augment an explicitly eschatological test of what one has put first.

The final separation ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other. It gives the lasting consequence that frames the commentary's contrast of the near life with the life beyond.
Moses refuses to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. This distinct first step in Hebrews' Moses sequence gives the commentary's choice of honor and chief place a direct courtly setting.

row.basis: Moses not fearing the king's anger
row.note: Moses leaves Egypt without fearing the king's anger and perseveres as though seeing the unseen. It closely accompanies the commentary's Pharaoh scene, contrasting a visible ruler's force with an unseen but decisive reality.

row.basis: spending for what does not satisfy and listening for good food
row.note: Isaiah asks why people spend and labor for what does not satisfy, then calls them to listen and eat what is good. It binds the commentary's food-preference scene to its larger issue of whether received divine speech displaces lesser appetites.

row.basis: hearing, life, and an everlasting covenant
row.note: Isaiah calls hearers to incline the ear so that they may live and receive an everlasting covenant. It gives the commentary's warning-and-remembrance sequence a direct alternative in which hearing becomes enduring life.

In a prophetic crisis, people answer with eating and drinking because tomorrow they die. This is a concentrated Hebrew version of the present-pleasure orientation that the commentary contrasts with a future reckoning.

row.basis: a rich person's false expectation of rest
row.note: A rich person says that there is rest and time to enjoy accumulated goods, without knowing that death will leave them to others. This Jewish wisdom scene closely mirrors the commentary's long-hope and appointed-end contrast.

row.basis: Torah and deeds accompany a person after death
row.note: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma refuses a place rich in gold and jewels because, at death, neither accompanies a person except Torah and good deeds. It makes the commentary's transmission and preparation motifs a direct critique of retained wealth.

row.basis: Abraham's disciples, Balaam's disciples, and the world to come
row.note: The mishnah contrasts Abraham's good eye, humility, and restrained desire with Balaam's opposite traits, assigning their disciples different ultimate destinies. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages, self-preference, high-and-low language, and final outcome a single Jewish interpretive frame.

row.basis: written song taught and placed in Israel's mouths
row.note: Moses is told to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths as a witness. It closely parallels the commentary's linked scenes of written pages, recitation, remembrance, and warning.

row.basis: a song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
row.note: The song will not be forgotten from the mouths of Israel's descendants. This gives an especially close Torah counterpart to the commentary's preserved recitation and its concern that an inherited word remain available to admonish later hearers.

row.basis: little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure
row.note: Proverbs explicitly calls little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure with turmoil. Its comparative formula closely matches the commentary's claim that value, not mere temporal priority, determines what should come first.

Jesus tells his hearers that they are unwilling to come to him in order to have life. It directly develops the commentary's distinction between access to a warning and the choice that actually turns toward life.

row.basis: hearts weighed down by the cares of life
row.note: Jesus warns that dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of life can weigh down the heart so the day arrives suddenly. It is a close counterpart to the commentary's present-tense pattern in which near-life concerns obstruct heedfulness.

row.basis: short fleshly sojourn and the coming age
row.note: This early homily contrasts the short residence of flesh in the present world with rest and eternal life in the coming kingdom, treating the two ages as opposed claims. It is a direct postapostolic formulation of the commentary's two-life ordering.

row.basis: foreign residence and the true city
row.note: The parable treats present residence as a foreign city where possessions must be left behind when one is summoned home. It concretizes the commentary's near-life language and its refusal to mistake temporary lodging for enduring belonging.

row.basis: life and good set against death and evil
row.note: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil. In its covenantal, land-centered setting it is not the same afterlife contrast, but it supplies the foundational choice-of-life formula behind the commentary's valuation of life.

row.basis: loving, obeying, and cleaving to the one who is life
row.note: Israel is to love, obey, and cleave to the Lord because he is its life and length of days. It shows that choosing life is an attachment of love and loyalty, as the commentary says preference is more than a calculation.

row.basis: hearers and doers of the word
row.note: James commands hearers to become doers rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone. It offers a compact Christian formulation for the commentary's concern that the listener may know the admonition yet arrange life against it.

row.basis: daily exhortation against a hardened heart
row.note: The community must exhort one another each day so that sin's deceit does not harden anyone. It matches the commentary's present-tense preference as a continually renewed condition rather than a single past decision.

row.basis: feasting without regard for the Lord's work
row.note: In Isaiah's woe, music and wine fill the feast while people do not regard the Lord's work. It gives a prophetic scene for the commentary's claim that near-life enjoyment can put divine reminder out of view.

row.basis: a deceived heart turning to other service
row.note: Israel is warned that its heart may be deceived and turn aside to serve other gods. It provides a covenantal analogue to the commentary's account of a foreground object displacing the right allegiance.

row.basis: instruction and knowledge above silver and gold
row.note: Wisdom tells hearers to receive instruction rather than silver and knowledge rather than fine gold. It gives the commentary's transmitted speech a concrete priority over the material goods of the near life.

row.basis: earning wages into a bag with holes
row.note: Haggai describes eating without satisfaction, clothing without warmth, and wages placed in a bag with holes. It supplies a vivid prophetic image for the commentary's claim that people try to hold what cannot be retained.

row.basis: labor and striving with no enduring gain
row.note: After surveying works, labor, and achievement, Qohelet finds them vapor and striving after wind with no lasting gain under the sun. It is a sapiential counterpart to the commentary's transience of what is pursued in the near life.

row.basis: Abraham's commanded legacy of righteousness and justice
row.note: Abraham is chosen so that he will command his descendants to keep the Lord's way through righteousness and justice. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages an ethical, generational content rather than merely a named ancient authority.

row.basis: Solomon choosing discernment over wealth and honor
row.note: Solomon asks for discernment instead of long life, riches, or the death of enemies. The scene gives a concrete royal counterexample to the commentary's ordering of honor, goods, and what should receive first place.

row.basis: wealth that leaves its owner before the end
row.note: Jeremiah says that wealth acquired unjustly leaves its owner in the middle of life and exposes folly at the end. It closely supports the commentary's claim that a retained worldly gain does not accompany its owner past the appointed limit.

row.basis: commerce restricted by a bodily mark
row.note: Buying and selling are restricted to those bearing the beast's mark. Beside the commentary's branded-foot, visible-trace, and worldly-priority imagery, the verse makes material access a pressure to display an allegiance.

row.basis: Egypt's food remembered before the gift of manna
row.note: Israel remembers Egypt's flesh pots and full bread, calls death there preferable, and then receives manna. Alongside the commentary's Quranic vegetables-for-superior-provision scene, this is a related but differently framed wilderness complaint about preferring familiar food to divine provision.
The commentary names Moses as recipient of the first pages; after Sinai, Moses writes the LORD's words in a book, locating the written witness in Moses' own scriptural story.

row.basis: Book of the Covenant read aloud
row.note: The commentary links old pages to a recited teaching; here Moses reads the written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer by undertaking to obey it.
The commentary says the current warning is already in ancient pages; this verse explicitly says Moses completed writing the words of the Torah in a book.

The commentary calls the first pages a witness against the charge of novelty; Moses orders the completed book placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel, giving the text a future-testimony role.
The commentary connects scripture with a message heard rather than a page handed to the Prophet; Moses orders the Torah read aloud before all Israel at the appointed gathering.
The commentary's pages preserve instruction for later hearers; this assembly includes men, women, children, and resident aliens so they hear, learn, and fear the LORD.
The commentary says the word reaches a later generation without the Prophet consulting a page; Moses specifically includes children who have not known the Torah, so they hear and learn it.
The commentary presents recitation as the means by which written teaching becomes present to hearers; in Nehemiah, Levites read from the Torah and explain its sense so the assembly understands.

The commentary contrasts old written pages with the Prophet's received recitation; Jeremiah dictates the LORD's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll, making the prophet's speech a written document.
The commentary joins ancient pages to audible proclamation; Baruch reads Jeremiah's scroll in the temple before the gathered people and officials.

The commentary says the teaching endured from the first pages to its present recitation; after Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah is told to write the same words again, showing the message surviving destruction of its copy.

The commentary pictures old writing as an open, legible surface; Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly on tablets so a reader can run with it, explicitly joining a written revelation to its public transmission.
The commentary says the pages' message reaches the Prophet as recitation and is retained; Moses commands Israel to keep these words in the heart, joining scripture with inward memory.
The commentary treats the old teaching as a living word heard by later people; Deuteronomy requires parents to teach and speak it at home, on the road, at bedtime, and at rising.

row.basis: What fathers heard is told onward
row.note: The commentary answers the claim that the message is new by locating it among earlier generations; the psalm says its teaching was heard and known from the fathers who told it.

row.basis: The next generation is not left ignorant
row.note: The commentary says an ancient warning remains present rather than forgotten; the psalm refuses to hide the fathers' praise-worthy acts from their children and pledges to tell the next generation.

row.basis: Remembering leads to trust and obedience
row.note: The commentary links recited remembrance to fear of God and the surah's counsel; Psalm 78 says the next generation should hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.

row.basis: Ask the elders about days of old
row.note: The commentary answers “we never heard this from our ancestors” by asserting ancient continuity; Moses tells the audience to remember former days and ask their fathers and elders.

row.basis: The word is near, in mouth and heart
row.note: The commentary says the Prophet receives the pages' content by recitation rather than by handling them; Deuteronomy describes the commandment as near, in the hearer's mouth and heart, ready to be done.
The commentary says the world passes but the statement about the lasting hereafter has itself endured; Isaiah contrasts withering grass and flowers with God's word standing forever.
The commentary treats the first pages as a durable witness across generations; the psalm says God's word is established in heaven forever, supplying a concrete scriptural image of permanence.

row.basis: A book of remembrance for the God-fearing
row.note: The commentary connects fear of God, remembrance, and preserved pages; Malachi describes those who fear the LORD speaking together while a book of remembrance is written before him for them.

row.basis: Prophetic words sealed for the end
row.note: The commentary says the first writing bears witness to the final outcome; Daniel is told to shut up and seal the words until the time of the end, a different but concrete model of an ancient text preserved for a later age.

row.basis: Each person answers for their own sin
row.note: The commentary joins self-purification to the saying that no bearer carries another's burden; Deuteronomy's legal rule says parent and child are not executed for one another's sin, but each for their own.

row.basis: A child does not bear a parent's iniquity
row.note: The commentary reads purification as one's own act and cites the rule that none bears another's load; Ezekiel explicitly assigns guilt to the person who sins, not to that person's father or son.
The commentary's “one who purifies himself” is an individual turning toward good; Ezekiel says the person who turns from transgression, keeps the statutes, and does right shall live.

row.basis: Each dies for their own iniquity
row.note: The commentary's cited page teaching denies transferred burdens; Jeremiah answers the sour-grapes proverb by saying each person dies for their own iniquity, sharpening the move from inherited blame to individual responsibility.

row.basis: Fear God and keep the commandments
row.note: The commentary's nearby verses join fearing God, purification, and prayer to the choice of the hereafter; Ecclesiastes closes by making fear of God and keeping his commandments the whole human duty.
The commentary places the more enduring hereafter against present preference; Ecclesiastes grounds that contrast in God's judgment of every deed, including what is hidden.
The commentary says the hereafter is better and more enduring than present life; Daniel's sleepers awake, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, giving that future a resurrection setting.
The commentary challenges preferring the near life to the lasting one; Psalm 49 says a person takes nothing from wealth at death and that splendor does not descend after him.

The commentary rejects preferring the present life because the hereafter is more enduring; Wisdom 2 puts the opposite case in the mouths of the wicked, who urge one another to enjoy present goods and youth.

row.basis: The righteous are safe beyond apparent death
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is the better, abiding outcome; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and seem only to have died, directly overturning a worldly judgment of their fate.

row.basis: A martyr chooses resurrection over survival
row.note: The commentary says the later life is better than the near one; the second brother accepts death under torture while confessing that the King of the world will raise the faithful to renewed life.
The commentary makes the enduring hereafter the reason not to privilege present life; the fourth brother says he hopes to be raised by God, while his persecutor has no share in resurrection to life.

row.basis: The world passes; God's will remains
row.note: The commentary contrasts the passing world with what is more enduring; John says the world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

row.basis: Moses values the future reward above Egypt
row.note: The commentary names Moses' pages as a source for rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews depicts Moses refusing Egypt's treasures and choosing reproach because he was looking to the reward.

row.basis: The whole world cannot outweigh life
row.note: The commentary asks why one would prefer the near world over the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life.
The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than worldly life; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy it.
The commentary says the world passes while the message about the hereafter lasts; Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal.

row.basis: Earlier writings teach and sustain hope
row.note: The commentary says 87:18 answers novelty by locating its teaching in first pages; Paul says what was written in former times was written for present instruction and endurance, to give hope.

row.basis: Ancient events written for later admonition
row.note: The commentary treats old pages as a warning to present hearers who prefer the world; Paul says the earlier events occurred as examples and were written down for admonition of later generations.
The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the first pages; Paul reads Genesis as scripture foreseeing the Gentiles' justification and announcing the gospel beforehand to Abraham.

row.basis: Moses' writing witnesses to a later message
row.note: The commentary answers that the present teaching is not a new invention by naming Moses' pages; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, making the older Torah a witness to a later proclamation and criticizing hearers who reject both.

row.basis: Paul claims continuity with Moses and the prophets
row.note: The commentary's central claim is that the current warning was already in ancient pages; Paul tells Agrippa that he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen.

row.basis: Scripture known from childhood guides salvation
row.note: The commentary describes an old text whose recited teaching still instructs its hearers; Timothy's sacred writings, known from childhood, are said to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ.
The commentary's adjacent claim is that worldly life passes while its message endures; Peter compares all flesh to grass and its glory to a flower that falls.
The commentary says the ancient pages' statement has survived to the Prophet's recitation; Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the gospel preached to his readers.

row.basis: The dead judged from opened books
row.note: The commentary links pages, deeds, and the eventual outcome; Revelation depicts books opened at judgment and the dead judged according to what was written in them and what they had done.
The commentary's reading of purification is personal and is paired with “no bearer bears another's burden”; Paul says each person will carry their own load.

row.basis: Each gives an account to God
row.note: The commentary connects the old pages' warning with each person's own conduct; Paul says each of us will give an account of himself to God.

row.basis: Each receives for deeds done in the body
row.note: The commentary links personal purification and the enduring hereafter; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat so each may receive for what was done in the body.
The commentary pairs individual action with the coming outcome; Paul says God will repay each person according to their deeds, explicitly connecting conduct and judgment.

row.basis: Eternal life for those seeking what lasts
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is better and more enduring; Paul specifies eternal life for those who persevere in good work while seeking glory, honor, and immortality.
The commentary says the successful person “purifies himself”; John uses the same reflexive moral pattern, saying everyone with this hope purifies himself as Christ is pure.
The commentary joins purification to remembrance of God and prayer; James calls those drawing near to God to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts.

row.basis: Prayer with unclean hands is rejected
row.note: The commentary places purification beside remembering God's name and prayer; Isaiah depicts worshippers spreading hands in prayer, but God refuses to hear because their hands are full of blood.
The commentary says the person who purifies himself succeeds; Isaiah's answer to corrupt worship is a concrete command to wash and cleanse, then cease doing evil.
The commentary links purification and prayer, not mere ritual display; Isaiah specifies learning good, seeking justice, and defending the vulnerable as the ethical turn that follows cleansing.

row.basis: God brings grass up for cattle
row.note: The commentary links the surah's opening pasture to Moses' description of God sending rain and bringing out plants; the psalm says God makes grass grow for livestock and plants for human use.

row.basis: Moses and the prophets already speak
row.note: The commentary says people asking for new sheets lack fear, since the old pages already give warning; in Jesus' story Abraham answers a dead rich man's request by pointing to Moses and the prophets, which his brothers should hear.

row.basis: A new sign cannot replace hearing scripture
row.note: The commentary says another page would not cure refusal to heed the existing warning; Abraham's reply is that those who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by someone rising from the dead.
The commentary joins fear of God to purification and prayer; Moses asks Israel to fear the LORD, walk in his ways, love and serve him with all the heart and soul.

The commentary describes a person purifying himself, while Ezekiel and other texts personalize responsibility; Deuteronomy adds that God circumcises the heart so Israel may love him, making divine aid part of inner renewal.
The commentary says hearers prefer the near life despite the better hereafter; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life by loving and clinging to God.

row.basis: The righteous meditate on Torah continually
row.note: The commentary says the old word is recited, remembered, and acted on; Psalm 1 locates the righteous person's delight in the LORD's instruction, meditated on day and night.
The commentary's world/hereafter contrast culminates in different outcomes; Psalm 1 says the LORD knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes.

The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Psalm 49 tells the hearer not to fear when another grows rich and his household's glory increases, setting up the death-boundary made explicit in v.17.

row.basis: God weighs the heart and repays deeds
row.note: The commentary says each person's choice matters and cites the rule that no one bears another's burden; Proverbs answers the excuse “we did not know” by saying the heart-weigher sees and repays each according to work.
The commentary's purification is a person's own turning, not a transferred act; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel to repent and turn from transgressions so iniquity will not be a stumbling block.

row.basis: Remember Moses' Torah before the coming day
row.note: The commentary names Moses' pages and says their teaching addresses the final outcome; Malachi closes by telling Israel to remember the Torah commanded to Moses at Horeb before the coming day of the LORD.

row.basis: The end announced from the beginning
row.note: The commentary says the first pages already tell where all things will end; Isaiah portrays God as declaring the end from the beginning and bringing his purpose to completion.

The commentary pictures the first writings as going ahead and later speech following their path; Joshua, Moses' successor, is told to keep the Torah book in his mouth, meditate on it, and act according to it.

The commentary names Abraham as recipient of ancient pages; Genesis says Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept his charge, commandments, statutes, and instructions, giving a concrete ancestral precedent for the teaching.
The commentary names Abraham among the first recipients; Genesis presents Abraham believing God and being counted righteous, the verse Paul later treats as an early scriptural witness to faith.

row.basis: Abraham keeps the law and covenant
row.note: The commentary's final verse names Abraham and Moses together; Ben Sira remembers Abraham as keeping the law of the Most High and entering a covenant, showing a Jewish retelling that makes him a model of ancient fidelity.
The commentary names Moses as bearer of the old pages; Ben Sira's praise of the ancestors turns to Moses as beloved by God and honored, adding a Jewish wisdom portrait of the named lawgiver.

The commentary's “first pages” include Abraham as well as Moses; this midrash reads Genesis 26:5 to say Abraham kept the Torah before it was given, extending the antiquity of revealed practice to the patriarch.

row.basis: Abraham's obedience rendered as Torah observance
row.note: The commentary names Abraham's pages but leaves their contents open; Onqelos renders the Genesis account in terms of Abraham keeping God's commandments and teachings, giving an Aramaic interpretive bridge from the patriarch to Torah.

The commentary connects enduring pages with personal accountability; Avot pictures an open book and a recording hand alongside judgment, making written record a rabbinic image for the moral accounting implied by the pages.

The commentary says a divine book preserves what happened to the first generations; Enoch is shown heavenly tablets and reads what is written there, an apocalyptic expansion of memory and record beyond earthly pages.

row.basis: The righteous are remembered in books
row.note: The commentary links fearers and a preserved record; Enoch depicts the books of the righteous and their prayers brought before the Lord of Spirits, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to a heavenly book of remembrance.

The commentary answers that the message is not a new invention by locating it in first pages; Josephus defends the antiquity and counted extent of Jewish sacred books, showing how a Jewish author argued for a stable inherited corpus.

The commentary answers novelty by saying the teaching was present in the first pages; Augustine argues that what is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients from the beginning, a patristic reading of present faith as recovery rather than late invention.
The commentary joins self-purification to the recited old teaching; Psalm 119 asks how a young person's way can be kept pure and answers by guarding it according to God's word.

row.basis: The word stored in the heart
row.note: The commentary says revelation reaches the Prophet by recitation and is not forgotten; the psalmist stores God's word in the heart to avoid sin, linking remembered scripture with moral purification.

row.basis: Clean hands and a pure heart in worship
row.note: The commentary joins purification to prayer; the psalm describes the one who may ascend God's holy place as having clean hands and a pure heart, tying inward and outward purity to worship.

row.basis: A prayer for a clean heart
row.note: The commentary describes the person who purifies himself; David asks God to create a clean heart in him, adding a distinct emphasis on purification received from God rather than self-congratulation.

row.basis: A lost Torah scroll is rediscovered
row.note: The commentary says first-page teaching endured into the present; in Kings, Hilkiah finds a Torah book in the temple after it had been absent from the king's practice, and its recovery prompts reform, complicating any simple picture of uninterrupted access.

The commentary says the old word has lasted; Jeremiah's scroll is cut and burned by Jehoiakim, a concrete counter-image of the vulnerability of the physical page before the message is rewritten in v.28.

row.basis: The righteous' hope is full of immortality
row.note: The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than this life; Wisdom says the righteous may seem punished at death, yet their hope is full of immortality, correcting the worldly reading of their fate.

row.basis: Those who trust God abide with him
row.note: The commentary calls the later life more enduring; Wisdom says those who trust God will understand truth and abide with him in love, specifying the lasting communion behind its reversal of worldly judgment.

The commentary pairs purification and prayer and its refs mention prayer with almsgiving; Tobit says prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, giving a Jewish ethical-worship combination rather than treating prayer as an isolated rite.

row.basis: Treasure laid up for the future life
row.note: The commentary contrasts present worldly preference with the lasting hereafter; Paul tells the rich to store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life.

row.basis: Riches gathered only for oneself do not last
row.note: The commentary warns against preferring the near life; Jesus' rich fool stores goods for himself but dies that night, and the story calls him poor toward God.

row.basis: The patriarchs seek a better country
row.note: The commentary names Abraham among the first pages and says the hereafter is better; Hebrews reads the patriarchs as desiring a better, heavenly country and a city prepared by God.

row.basis: The gospel promised beforehand in scripture
row.note: The commentary's claim is that the present word is already in the earliest writings; Paul introduces the gospel as promised beforehand through God's prophets in holy scriptures.

row.basis: Moses and the prophets interpreted as witnesses
row.note: The commentary says the recent teaching is contained in earlier pages; Luke depicts Jesus interpreting what the scriptures say about him, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, a Christian rereading of the old texts as testimony to the present.

row.basis: A written prophecy declared fulfilled in hearing
row.note: The commentary joins pages to a word heard in the present; after reading Isaiah in the synagogue, Jesus says the scripture has been fulfilled in the hearers' hearing.

row.basis: Earlier prophets searched the promised grace
row.note: The commentary says the first pages already contain the later warning; Peter describes prophets who searched and inquired about the grace now announced, connecting prior revelation with a later proclamation.
The commentary says the old word has reached the Prophet's audience; Peter says the prophets were serving not themselves but later readers, to whom the gospel is now announced.

row.basis: A letter read in human hearts
row.note: The commentary says the pages' content can be present without a page in the Prophet's hand; Paul calls the Corinthians a letter known and read by all, a human community serving as written testimony.

row.basis: Writing by the Spirit on hearts
row.note: The commentary contrasts a physical page with a message recited and retained; Paul says the Spirit writes on tablets of human hearts rather than stone, developing a Christian image of inwardly carried scripture.

The commentary says the same enduring warning was present in older pages; Hebrews describes God speaking to ancestors through prophets in many times and ways, then frames the present as a further stage of that speech.

row.basis: Self-cleansing perfected in fear of God
row.note: The commentary joins purification with fear and prayer; Paul urges believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and perfect holiness in fear of God, an explicit ethical counterpart to the surah's purifier who fears.

row.basis: The repentant prayer is accepted over self-display
row.note: The commentary warns that self-purification is not self-praise; Jesus' parable ends with the tax collector, not the self-congratulating Pharisee, going home justified, clarifying the difference between turning toward God and claiming one's own merit.

The commentary cites opponents of Moses calling his clear signs fabricated magic and unheard by their ancestors; Exodus stages a Moses-and-Pharaoh sign contest in which Pharaoh's magicians answer with their arts, a related scene framed as rival performance rather than ancestral novelty.

row.basis: The recovered book is read to the king
row.note: The commentary presents the ancient pages as a witness to the present; the king's secretary reads the rediscovered Torah book to Josiah, but the episode concerns recovery after neglect, so the link is about renewed hearing rather than uninterrupted preservation.

The commentary joins preserved pages to a word received and recited; God tells Moses both to write the Amalek remembrance in a book and to recite it in Joshua's hearing, combining writing, memory, and oral succession.

row.basis: The king makes a copy of the Torah
row.note: The commentary says the old pages guide present conduct; Deuteronomy requires a king to write a copy of the Torah, making the text a concrete guide for a later ruler.

row.basis: The king reads the Torah throughout life
row.note: The commentary warns against preferring the near world's status; the king must read his copy all his life to learn fear of God and avoid exalting himself over his kin.

row.basis: A written song taught by heart as witness
row.note: The commentary links ancient pages with recitation and remembrance; Moses is told to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths as a witness for later generations.

row.basis: The song witnesses when Israel forgets
row.note: The commentary says a lasting divine record stands against neglect of the warning; Deuteronomy anticipates Israel's later turning away and says the taught song will testify because it will not be forgotten by their descendants.

row.basis: Teach the remembered revelation to descendants
row.note: The commentary answers “we did not hear this from our ancestors” by asserting an ancient message; Moses warns Israel not to forget what it saw at Horeb and to make it known to children and grandchildren.

row.basis: Words of prophecy written in a book
row.note: The commentary says the current recitation is already in ancient pages; Jeremiah is specifically commanded to write all the words spoken to him in a book, preserving a prophetic message for later hearers.

row.basis: A book as a witness for future time
row.note: The commentary describes old pages as a public witness to a present warning; Isaiah is told to write the message on a tablet and in a book so it may stand for a future day as a witness forever.

row.basis: Words remain in mouths across generations
row.note: The commentary says the first-pages message has endured to the Prophet's recitation; Isaiah promises that God's words placed in the speaker's mouth will not depart from him, his children, or descendants.

The commentary says the page's teaching is heard and retained inwardly; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise places God's Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, an inward counterpart to external pages.

row.basis: A record written for a future generation
row.note: The commentary says the message survives from the first pages to present readers; the psalm explicitly says a future generation will praise the LORD and that this should be written down for a people yet to be created.

row.basis: A scroll written on both sides
row.note: The commentary asks the reader to picture a separate written sheet rather than a bound codex; Ezekiel sees an opened scroll written on its front and back, a striking prophetic image of a densely inscribed surface.

row.basis: The prophet eats the scroll and speaks its words
row.note: The commentary says pages reach the Prophet as an inwardly retained recitation rather than as a page in his hand; Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then speak its words to Israel, a bodily enactment of internalized prophecy.

row.basis: Books opened at the court of judgment
row.note: The commentary links ancient pages with the final accounting of deeds; Daniel's heavenly court sits and books are opened, a Jewish apocalyptic scene of written records at judgment.

row.basis: The delivered are found written in the book
row.note: The commentary says the first generations are not lost because their knowledge is kept in a book with God; Daniel speaks of those found written in the book being delivered at the final crisis.

row.basis: The world fades while salvation lasts
row.note: The commentary contrasts the passing world with a teaching that endures; Isaiah says heaven and earth will wear away like clothing while God's salvation and righteousness remain forever.

row.basis: Guided now and received to glory afterward
row.note: The commentary joins divine guidance in the surah's opening to the claim that the final destination is with the Lord; the psalmist says God guides him by counsel and afterward receives him to glory.
The commentary says the hereafter is more enduring than worldly life; the psalmist's flesh and heart may fail, but God is his portion forever, a personal formulation of lasting hope.

row.basis: God receives the speaker from Sheol
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is better and more enduring than the present; Psalm 49 contrasts the rich man's death with the speaker's confidence that God will ransom and receive him from Sheol.
The commentary's “more enduring” hereafter entails a future beyond death; the psalmist trusts not to be abandoned to Sheol or left to see the Pit, giving that hope a resurrection-shaped expression.

row.basis: The path of life ends in lasting joy
row.note: The commentary says the final arrival is with the Lord; Psalm 16 speaks of the path of life and fullness of joy in God's presence forever.
The commentary sets present worldly preference against the enduring hereafter; Psalm 37 says the days of the blameless are known to God and their inheritance endures forever.

row.basis: Purification expressed as freeing the oppressed
row.note: The commentary pairs purification with prayer and cites almsgiving alongside it; Isaiah's chosen fast is to loosen injustice and free the oppressed, giving purification an ethical and social form.

row.basis: Share bread and shelter the poor
row.note: The commentary's nearby purification and prayer are also associated with giving; Isaiah continues by naming bread shared with the hungry, shelter for the homeless, and clothing for the naked as the fast God desires.

row.basis: Pure religion keeps unstained from the world
row.note: The commentary joins purification to worship and warns against preferring worldly life; James defines pure and undefiled religion by care for vulnerable people and keeping oneself unstained by the world.

row.basis: Alms become treasure that does not fail
row.note: The commentary's references connect purification with giving and the hereafter with lasting reward; Jesus tells disciples to sell possessions, give alms, and make a heavenly purse that does not wear out.
The commentary contrasts a passing worldly life with what endures; Paul calls present affliction momentary and light in comparison with the eternal weight of glory it produces.

row.basis: Present suffering is outweighed by future glory
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is better than the near life; Paul says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed, giving the contrast an explicit scale.

row.basis: Hope limited to this life is inadequate
row.note: The commentary challenges those who prefer worldly life and dismiss the hereafter; Paul argues that if hope in Christ were only for this life, believers would be most pitiable, directly rejecting a this-world-only horizon.

row.basis: “Eat and drink” is the rival response to death
row.note: The commentary's opponents prefer the near life over the lasting one; in an argument for resurrection Paul cites the maxim to eat and drink because tomorrow one dies, presenting it as the consequence of denying resurrection.

row.basis: Scoffers appeal to what has always been
row.note: The commentary answers novelty and skepticism by saying the final warning was already in the first pages; Peter's scoffers ask where the promised coming is and claim everything has continued as from the beginning of creation.
The commentary says the oldest pages already announce the final outcome; Peter says the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, carrying the passage's answer to scoffers into its own conclusion.

row.basis: A prophetic charge of scribal distortion
row.note: The commentary cites the concealment of parts of earlier books but says this teaching is truly in the first pages; Jeremiah's own context accuses scribes of making the LORD's Torah into a lie, a sharp counter-witness about the handling of scripture.

row.basis: Joshua reads Moses' law to the assembly
row.note: The commentary pictures the first writing leading later generations; after Moses, Joshua reads the Torah's blessings and curses before all Israel, a distinct public scene of a successor carrying the earlier book forward.

row.basis: No word is omitted from the public reading
row.note: The commentary says the pages' teaching is available in the recited message; Joshua leaves out no word of Moses' command before the whole assembly, including women, children, and resident aliens.

row.basis: The people attend to a long public reading
row.note: The commentary makes the heard word central to access to old pages; Ezra reads the Torah aloud from morning until midday before the gathered people, whose ears are attentive.

row.basis: The word from God's mouth accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary says the old-page statement has endured into present recitation; Isaiah adds that God's word does not return empty but accomplishes what God intends, explaining the active effect of a message that is heard.

row.basis: Peter reads a psalm as prophecy of resurrection
row.note: The commentary says the first pages already tell of the final destination with God; Peter interprets David's words about not being abandoned to Hades as a prophecy of the Messiah's resurrection.

row.basis: Torah passes through a named chain
row.note: The commentary pictures the earliest pages leading the later word; Avot opens by tracing Torah from Moses at Sinai through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly, a rabbinic account of transmission across generations.

row.basis: Self-responsibility balanced by obligations to others
row.note: The commentary stresses that a person purifies himself and no one bears another's burden; Hillel asks who will act for a person if he does not act for himself, then warns against living only for oneself.

row.basis: This world as a vestibule to the world to come
row.note: The commentary says the later life is better and more enduring than the present; Avot compares this world to a vestibule and the world to come to the banquet hall, urging preparation in the former.

row.basis: Books of judgment opened at the year's beginning
row.note: The commentary links preserved pages and personal deeds; the Talmud describes books opened for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate, developing a Jewish tradition of recorded moral standing and judgment.

row.basis: A father hands written books to descendants
row.note: The commentary says what was written for the first generations reaches a later reciter; Enoch tells Methuselah to preserve the books received from his father's hand and pass them to generations of the world.

The commentary says an ancient message is still present in the recited Qur'an; Ezra's apocalyptic account says the twenty-four books he has written are to be made public for worthy and unworthy readers, a tradition of textual restoration and access.

row.basis: Law, prophets, and psalms all bear witness
row.note: The commentary says the present teaching is in the earliest pages; Jesus identifies what is written about him in Moses' law, prophets, and psalms as needing fulfillment, an explicit Christian claim that the old corpus anticipates later events.

row.basis: Deuteronomy's near word becomes proclaimed faith
row.note: The commentary says the Prophet receives the message orally and that the pages' content is present in recitation; Paul quotes Deuteronomy's word near the mouth and heart as the word of faith he proclaims, giving the old verse a new Christian referent.

row.basis: Hearers test a new proclamation against scripture
row.note: The commentary answers the charge that the current word is novel by pointing to older pages; the Bereans receive Paul's message eagerly but examine the scriptures daily to see whether his claims hold.

row.basis: A promise made to the fathers is now announced
row.note: The commentary says the old pages contain the current warning; Paul tells the synagogue that he is bringing good news of what God promised to the fathers.

row.basis: The fathers' promise interpreted as fulfilled now
row.note: The commentary argues that the present word confirms an earlier one; Paul says God fulfilled the promise to their descendants by raising Jesus and supports the claim with a psalm.

row.basis: Paul interprets Abraham's belief as counted righteousness
row.note: The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the first pages; Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 to make Abraham's belief a scriptural example of righteousness by faith, a distinct reading from Galatians' “gospel preached beforehand.”

row.basis: Jesus claims fulfillment rather than abolition
row.note: The commentary answers that its teaching is not new by locating it in the first pages; Jesus says he came not to abolish the law or prophets but to fulfill them, making continuity an explicit claim.

row.basis: The scriptures testify, yet hearers refuse to come
row.note: The commentary says the old pages already contain the warning and lack of response is the problem; Jesus says the searched scriptures testify about him, while his hearers will not come to him for life.

row.basis: The same God speaks in the last days through the Son
row.note: The commentary's “first” pages carry a message about the final outcome; Hebrews contrasts God's former speech through prophets with his speech in these last days through the Son, holding continuity and changed mode together.

row.basis: Abraham obeys and leaves without knowing the destination
row.note: The commentary names Abraham among the ancient recipients; Hebrews recalls his obedient departure by faith, showing the patriarch's own response to a divine word as part of the scriptural precedent.

row.basis: The end speaks of first, last, beginning, and end
row.note: The commentary says the first pages already disclose where all things finally arrive; Revelation names the speaker as Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end, a Christian formula joining origin to final outcome.

row.basis: Salvation is gift, not grounds for boasting
row.note: The commentary stresses personal purification and responsibility; Paul says salvation is by grace through faith, not from works, adding a Christian boundary against reading moral self-purification as earning rescue.

row.basis: Grace issues in a life of good works
row.note: The commentary does not equate personal action with boasting; Paul continues that those saved by grace are created in Christ for good works, preserving ethical action while denying that it is self-earned salvation.

row.basis: One person's act has consequences for many
row.note: The commentary's cited rule says no one bears another's burden; Paul says one man's disobedience made many sinners and one man's obedience makes many righteous, a distinct corporate account of consequence rather than a simple transfer of personal guilt.

row.basis: Letter and Spirit set in interpretive contrast
row.note: The commentary holds together physical pages and a word received inwardly; Paul contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit that gives life in a discussion of the new covenant, adding a Christian interpretive tension without making him reject scripture.

row.basis: writing and recitation of Moses' memorial
row.note: God tells Moses to write the Amalek memory in a book and rehearse it to Joshua. It concretely joins the commentary's Mosaic sheets to revealed words preserved by oral recitation.

row.basis: Book of the Covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses takes a written covenant book and reads it to Israel; it supplies the page-to-hearing movement developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Moses finishes writing Torah in a book
row.note: Within Deuteronomy Moses completes a written law-book. It is the closest Hebrew Bible anchor for the commentary's naming of Mosaic sheets, without equating their contents.
The book is deposited beside the ark as a witness against a resistant people; this sharpens 87:18's appeal to old writing against present objection.

row.basis: tablet and scroll for future days
row.note: Isaiah's contested warning is deliberately written on tablet and scroll for future time. Its context explains why an insistently spoken warning can invoke an enduring document.
Habakkuk requires a vision to be legible to a reader on tablets, a material counterpart to the commentary's spread-out, visible sheets.
The written vision awaits an appointed end and will prove true; it supplies a Jewish-scriptural analogue for the commentary's ta'wil as a word's eventual arrival.

row.basis: fading grass and enduring divine word
row.note: Isaiah contrasts perishing vegetation with God's word standing forever, matching the commentary's inference that an enduring word outlasts the near world.
Hilkiah's recovery of a long-neglected law book makes an old written word newly heard in Judah, a concrete alternative to calling its demand a novelty.
After the king burns Jeremiah's roll, a new scroll is ordered with all former words. It makes textual survival amid rejection a precise counterpart to old pages still speaking.
Torah is said to be near in mouth and heart for doing, not merely on an external object; this parallels the commentary's move from pages to memorized recitation.
Jeremiah relocates Torah from document to inward writing, a close Jewish analogue to the commentary's pages reappearing in a hearer's chest and voice.

row.basis: Ezekiel eats a scroll then speaks
row.note: Ezekiel receives and consumes a physical scroll before speaking. Against the commentary's claim that the Qur'anic messenger is given recitation rather than a sheet, the contrast marks two modes of prophetic embodiment.

row.basis: book of remembrance, fear, and name
row.note: The book records those who fear the Lord and esteem his name. It combines the commentary's unforgetting divine book with fear, name-remembrance, and worship.
God says the individual sinner will be blotted from his book, combining the commentary's divine record with its former-scroll rule of non-transferable guilt.
Mosaic law forbids executing children or parents for one another's sin. It is a direct legal antecedent to the commentary's 'no bearer bears another burden.'

row.basis: neither son nor father bears guilt
row.note: Ezekiel states the same rule as a theological axiom, making the commentary's individual purification and accountability legible within a later Jewish prophetic debate.
Job's speaker says God returns a person's work to them; it corresponds precisely to the former-sheet sequence of effort seen and recompensed.
Daniel's throne vision opens books in the final court. It pairs the commentary's preserved book with an eschatological disclosure of human history.
Daniel raises the dead to everlasting life or abhorrence, giving explicit Hebrew Bible form to the commentary's insistence that the later life is the decisive enduring horizon.
Ecclesiastes describes dust returning to earth and spirit returning to God, a concise counterpart to the commentary's 'the destination is to the Lord.'
Jesus opposes gaining the whole world to losing one's life; this specifies the commentary's warning about preferring the near life over the better future.
Jesus tells hearers to work for food that endures into eternal life, a close formal parallel to near, perishing provision versus a lasting destination.
1 John explicitly contrasts the passing world and desire with the one doing God's will abiding forever, directly mirroring the temporal and enduring antithesis.
Paul says each person will bear their own load, an especially close Christian parallel to the commentary's no-vicarious-burden formulation.
Each worker receives a reward according to their own labor; this matches the commentary's link between personal striving and its later recompense.

row.basis: judgment according to deeds in body
row.note: Each person appears before Christ's tribunal to receive what was done in the body, joining individual agency to the final outcome stressed by the commentary.

row.basis: opened books and judgment by deeds
row.note: Revelation's dead are judged from opened books according to deeds. It makes the commentary's pages, personal effort, and final accounting one scene.

row.basis: wash yourselves and make yourselves clean
row.note: Isaiah uses reflexive cleansing commands before ethical reform. That makes a concrete Hebrew parallel to 87:14's self-purification rather than a generic purity theme.
1 John links self-purification to hope in the appearing to come, closely joining the commentary's tazakka and its future horizon.
Raphael commends prayer together with fasting, almsgiving, and righteousness. It gives a Jewish late-antique counterpart to the commentary's prayer-and-purification pair.

row.basis: almsgiving purges sin and saves from death
row.note: Tobit gives almsgiving an explicitly purgative and life-preserving effect, a precise Jewish comparison for purification expressed through giving.
Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, directly pairing worship and giving like the commentary's surrounding prayer and purification.

row.basis: calling on the divine name and deliverance
row.note: Hebrew Joel says everyone calling on YHWH's name will escape. It provides a direct older-scriptural counterpart to remembering the Lord's name and praying.
Pharaoh refuses Moses after asking who YHWH is. This is the closest Hebrew Bible scene to the commentary's Pharaoh asking Moses about his Lord.
Paul expressly says earlier writings were written for current instruction and hope, a Christian account of how an ancient corpus can address present hearers.
Jesus frames his mission as fulfillment rather than abolition of Law and Prophets. It is a Christian model of a later proclamation claiming continuity with earlier writings.
Jesus appeals to Moses's writing as testimony about him. The verse is a focused Christian rereading of Mosaic text as witness to a later message.
Luke groups Moses, Prophets, and Psalms as writings whose contents must be fulfilled. It gives a canonical Christian version of old scripture carrying a later realization.
Paul calls God's promise to Abraham a prior proclamation of the gospel. This is a particularly direct Christian expansion of the commentary's appeal to Abraham's earlier sheets.

row.basis: better heavenly country of the patriarchs
row.note: Hebrews identifies the patriarchs' desired country as better and heavenly, placing Abraham's line inside the commentary's better, enduring-afterlife contrast.

row.basis: Moses rejects Egypt's treasure for reward
row.note: Hebrews interprets Moses as valuing God's reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked to reward. It supplies a Christian Mosaic reading of worldly preference versus future recompense.

row.basis: Moses and Prophets versus a demanded sign
row.note: Abraham says those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection. It closely matches the commentary's claim that a further visible sign or sheet would not cure refusal.

row.basis: examining Scripture to test a spoken message
row.note: The Bereans test a newly preached word against the Scriptures daily. It gives a concrete reception practice for the commentary's assertion that a current utterance belongs with old writings.
Moses is publicly read in synagogues every Sabbath, showing how an ancient Mosaic text remains a voiced communal teaching rather than a mute archive.
Jesus receives, unrolls, and reads Isaiah's scroll in synagogue. The scene materializes the commentary's sheet, voice, and present hearer in one act.
Paul contrasts ink and stone with a Spirit-written letter on human hearts. This develops the same page-to-interior movement that the commentary draws from recitation.

row.basis: in the scroll of the book it is written of me
row.note: Hebrews places its Christological claim in a book-scroll formula, a deliberate Christian claim that a later vocation is already inscribed in earlier Scripture.

row.basis: Moses offers blotting from the book for Israel
row.note: Moses offers his own erasure from God's book for Israel's sin. In contrast to the commentary's non-transferable burden, it foregrounds intercession; the next verse returns judgment to each sinner.

Paul commands bearing one another's burdens. Against Galatians 6:5's individual load and the commentary's judicial rule, this preserves a social-ethical sense of shared burden rather than transferred guilt.
Ezekiel promises God will sprinkle clean water and cleanse Israel. This is a deliberate counterweight to the commentary's reflexive tazakka, locating cleansing chiefly in divine action.

row.basis: new covenant with Israel and Judah
row.note: Jeremiah explicitly announces a new covenant with Israel and Judah. Alongside 87:18's denial that teaching is a mere novelty, it offers a different scriptural account in which newness and continuity coexist.

row.basis: a prophet charged with speaking falsehood
row.note: Judean leaders tell Jeremiah he is speaking falsely. The concrete charge against a prophet's command parallels the commentary's anticipated claim that a revelation is the speaker's invention.
Jesus's hearers ask how he has learning without formal study. It gives a Christian analogue to the commentary's attention to a messenger who has not learned ancient pages by ordinary reading.

Hebrew aḥarit, 'end' or 'latter outcome,' is a cognate of the commentary's Arabic akhira. Isaiah's God declares the aḥarit from the beginning, a lexical and structural companion to first pages carrying their end.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for human use
row.note: God causes grass for cattle and vegetation for human use. It closely matches the Taha–A'la comparison in the commentary: rain-grown plants, grazing animals, and provision after creation.
Jesus says all in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a Christian answer to the commentary's question about the first generations: they too are gathered for a future day.

The Talmud debates whether Torah was given scroll by scroll or as a completed whole. That reception history directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that suhuf are discrete sheets rather than a bound codex.

Mishnah Avot presents Moses handing Torah through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly. It makes the commentary's image of first writing leading later hearers into an explicit Jewish chain.

Rabbinic tradition says Abraham kept the whole Torah, even an eruv tavshilin. It offers a Jewish interpretive way to imagine Abraham as bearer of pre-Mosaic teaching, without positing extant Abrahamic pages.
Ezra says the law has been burned so no one knows what God has done or will do. It gives a Jewish counter-history to the commentary's confidence that former pages remain available.
After dictation restores books, Ezra is told to publish the first twenty-four for all readers. This furnishes a Jewish analogue to old written teaching made public again.

row.basis: seventy books reserved for the wise
row.note: Ezra is told to reserve seventy books for the wise. This contrasts with the commentary's rhetorical picture of an openly sufficient earlier warning, while concretely extending its concern with pages hidden or disclosed.

row.basis: Old and New Testaments mutually disclose
row.note: Augustine's formula that the New lies hidden in the Old and the Old becomes manifest in the New formalizes a Christian reading of the continuity claim, without making the Qur'anic text its premise.
Wisdom gives the righteous, though punished in human sight, a hope full of immortality. It is a Hellenistic Jewish articulation of the enduring future that the commentary sets over the near life.

row.basis: write the song, teach it, put it in mouths
row.note: God commands Moses to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths. It is a particularly exact Mosaic pairing of written witness, recitation, memory, and a resistant audience.

row.basis: king writes a Torah copy in a book
row.note: The king must write his own Torah copy from the priestly exemplar. This develops the commentary's concern with sheets as authoritative, transmissible written objects rather than an abstract antiquity.

row.basis: daily reading of the written Torah
row.note: The king reads the written Torah all his life in order to fear God and obey. It supplies an older scriptural account of a page becoming enduring ethical formation.

row.basis: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
row.note: Joshua's law-book must not leave his mouth but be meditated on and done. It closely joins the commentary's page, oral recitation, internal remembering, and conduct.

row.basis: prophetic words dictated onto a scroll
row.note: Baruch writes on a scroll all the words Jeremiah has spoken from the prophet's mouth. It gives a precise Hebrew Bible instance of oral revelation becoming separate written pages.

row.basis: seek and read the book of YHWH
row.note: Isaiah orders hearers to seek and read YHWH's book, whose announced creatures are not missing. It makes a preserved prior writing an available public check on a present claim.
The word sent from God's mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose. It supplies a close biblical analogue to the commentary's ta'wil: a spoken word reaches the end it declares.
