row.basis: Renewing the face of the ground
row.note: The commentary follows green growth into decay and sees the Lord as the source of emergence; the psalm says God sends forth spirit and renews the ground, giving the vegetation cycle a creation-and-renewal frame.

The commentary begins with a command to glorify the Lord and identifies him through creation and pasture; the psalmist vows to sing to the Lord while alive, placing praise directly in response to the created order.

row.basis: Clouds, rain, and grass on hills
row.note: The commentary hears the unmentioned rain behind the pasture that God brings forth; the psalm explicitly connects God’s cloud-cover and rain with grass growing on the mountains.

row.basis: Food for beasts from the same giver
row.note: The commentary says pasture names vegetation as the herd’s food; the psalm says God gives food to animals and young ravens, extending the provision claim beyond the flock.

row.basis: Teaching descending like rain and dew
row.note: The commentary links the grass passage to the later recitation and instruction; Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech distill like dew, joining divine teaching to the water that makes growth possible.

The commentary reads pasture as growth produced by water and later contrasts it with the recited word; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, making it yield seed for sowing and bread for eating, a precise provision chain.

row.basis: The spoken word accomplishes its purpose
row.note: The commentary connects the Lord who brings out pasture with the word later recited and retained; Isaiah’s next verse says the word from God’s mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, explicitly setting word beside the rain-and-seed image.

row.basis: Grass fades while God’s word stands
row.note: The commentary contrasts the pasture that becomes dark debris with the recitation that remains; Isaiah says grass withers but God’s word stands forever, giving the same concrete contrast between perishable vegetation and enduring speech.

row.basis: The earth gives birth to the dead
row.note: The commentary treats recurring growth from dead ground as a sign that the dead can be brought out; Isaiah calls the earth to give birth to its dead, making the earth’s production image explicitly serve resurrection hope.

row.basis: A heavenly command over each blade of grass
row.note: The commentary presents each emergence of pasture as a gift whose hidden growth belongs to God; this midrash says no blade of grass lacks a heavenly constellation that strikes it and commands it to grow, interpreting ordinary growth as supervised providence.

row.basis: Seed grows while the sower does not know how
row.note: The commentary describes growth from an unseen seed and root as an act whose source is the Lord; Jesus’ parable says the seed sprouts and grows while the person who scattered it does not know how, making hidden growth the point of the image.
The commentary follows pasture from concealed seed to visible green; the parable says the earth produces first a blade, then an ear, then full grain, a direct sequence of emergence and maturation.
The commentary calls pasture the land’s yield and follows it to its later end; Jesus’ parable ends when the grain is ripe and the sickle is put in, tying emergence to the harvest that follows.

The commentary insists that the Lord, rather than the human observer, is the one who brings pasture out; Paul says neither planter nor waterer counts, but God who gives the growth, an explicit account of divine agency in cultivation.

row.basis: A seed dies before it comes to life
row.note: The commentary reads pasture’s greening and subsequent decay as an analogy that makes resurrection imaginable; Paul says what is sown does not come to life unless it dies, using the plant cycle as his argument for resurrection.
The commentary contrasts grass that ends as debris with the human future that is raised into what lasts; Paul explicitly contrasts what is sown perishable with what is raised imperishable.
The commentary follows pasture from green growth to its end; Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh is grass and its glory like a flower, applying vegetation’s short life to human life.

row.basis: The Lord’s word endures as gospel proclamation
row.note: The commentary contrasts the grass that withers with the recitation that remains; Peter says the Lord’s word endures and identifies it with the good news preached to the readers, making the word/grass contrast an apostolic proclamation claim.

The commentary’s praise call is followed by claims about the Lord creating and sustaining pasture; Revelation’s elders praise the Lord as worthy because he created all things, a compact Christian doxology grounded in creation.

The commentary joins the Lord’s creative provision of pasture to glorification; the Didache’s meal thanksgiving says the Almighty created all things and gave food and drink so people might thank him, making the provision-to-praise relation liturgical.

row.basis: Field growth before rain or cultivation
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that 87:4 leaves soil and rain unnamed and foregrounds the one who brings pasture out; Genesis describes the field before rain and before a human works the ground, clarifying the conditions whose absence the short Qur’anic clause leaves unstated.

row.basis: God makes trees grow from the ground
row.note: The commentary describes grass rising from hidden seed and soil; Genesis says God makes trees grow from the ground, a related but broader account of vegetation’s emergence.

row.basis: Moses leads a flock to Horeb
row.note: The commentary recalls Moses’ years as a shepherd and links that work to his later encounter at the fire; Exodus places Moses at Horeb while leading his father-in-law’s flock, grounding the shepherd-to-revelation sequence in another scripture.

row.basis: Theophany while Moses is tending sheep
row.note: The commentary moves from Moses’ staff for tending sheep to the fire where revelation begins; Exodus has the bush blaze before Moses in the same scene, preserving the concrete meeting of pastoral work and divine appearance.

The commentary presents Abraham’s Lord as the one who feeds and sustains him; at the binding of Isaac, Abraham tells his son that God will provide the offering, giving divine provision a specific Abrahamic scene.

row.basis: Abraham receives Isaac back from death
row.note: The commentary’s Abrahamic sequence names the Lord as the one who kills and gives life; Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac and so received him back figuratively from death, interpreting the binding story through resurrection.

row.basis: Blessing after eating one is full
row.note: The commentary presents grass and food as a free gift that ends in glorifying the giver; Moses commands Israel to bless the Lord after eating and becoming full, making gratitude the human response to provision.

row.basis: Harvest left for the poor and sojourner
row.note: The commentary says a yield received without payment still carries a duty to give others their share; Leviticus forbids harvesting a field to its edge and leaves gleanings for the poor and the sojourner, specifying the social obligation attached to produce.

row.basis: A forgotten sheaf belongs to the vulnerable
row.note: The commentary connects free yield with giving a due from the harvest; Deuteronomy leaves a forgotten sheaf for the sojourner, orphan, and widow, turning that connection into a concrete harvest law.

row.basis: A cut tree can sprout again
row.note: The commentary takes recurring green growth as evidence that life can emerge after apparent death; Job says a felled tree can sprout again when it smells water, then contrasts that hope with human mortality, making the plant-to-human analogy vivid but unsettled.

row.basis: Job leaves human resurrection as a question
row.note: The commentary uses grass renewed from the earth to make the dead’s return plausible; after describing a tree’s regrowth, Job asks whether a dead human can live again, so the same natural analogy ends in an open question rather than an asserted answer.

The commentary says growth follows from water and that the visible green is a gift; the righteous person in the psalm is like a tree planted by streams that yields fruit in season, giving water-fed vegetation an ethical image.

The commentary’s pasture becomes dark debris and illustrates the passing life of this world; the psalm calls the wicked chaff driven by wind, using light plant remains for a moral image rather than a botanical cycle.

row.basis: Grass that flourishes and withers in a day
row.note: The commentary follows the pasture’s green life into decay; the psalm compares human life to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, applying the same daily plant arc to mortality.

The commentary sets pasture’s brief green phase against what lasts beyond this life; the psalm says a human’s days are like grass and flourish like a field flower, making the plant’s brevity a figure for human transience.
The commentary says the plant is turned into debris and disappears; the psalm says wind passes over the field flower and it is gone so its place knows it no more, sharpening the disappearance image.

The commentary turns from pasture’s short life to the Hereafter as better and more enduring; the psalm contrasts grass-like human days with the Lord’s everlasting steadfast love, supplying a close theological contrast of mortal vegetation and lasting divine good.

The commentary gives the shepherd’s work a sense of watching over the herd and its future; Proverbs tells the keeper to know the state of his flock and attend to the herds, making that practical oversight explicit in its own pastoral setting.

row.basis: The divine shepherd settles the flock in good pasture
row.note: The commentary says the Qur’anic clause names the one who brings pasture but does not call God a shepherd; Ezekiel explicitly depicts God feeding his flock and settling it in good pasture, showing how another scripture makes the shepherd-pasture connection explicit.

row.basis: God’s word runs through the earth
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes the Lord’s pasture-making with the Prophet’s recitation; elsewhere in the same psalm God sends his command through the earth before the cloud, grass, and animal-food lines, placing word and created provision within one hymn.

row.basis: A green tree endures drought by water
row.note: The commentary’s plant grows and then withers, while its creator sustains life; Jeremiah pictures a tree planted by water whose leaf stays green and which does not cease bearing fruit in drought, a counter-image of sustained rather than seasonal growth.

The commentary says the Lord provides pasture without demanding a fee; the rabbis teach that one may not enjoy the world before blessing God, because the earth belongs to God, adding human acknowledgment to apparently free provision.

row.basis: A blessing for produce of the ground
row.note: The commentary begins with glorification and then names vegetation as the Lord’s provision; the Mishnah assigns a blessing to fruit of the ground, showing how ordinary produce becomes a spoken act of praise.

row.basis: Field grass is temporary yet clothed by God
row.note: The commentary describes pasture becoming dark debris and treats vegetation as provision from its maker; Jesus says grass is in the field today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, yet God clothes it, joining transience to divine care.

The commentary notes that merʿā carries pasture and grazing while the root also names a shepherd’s work; Jesus says those entering through him will be saved and find pasture, placing the pasture image in a Christian shepherd-and-access teaching.

row.basis: Human planting and watering depend on God
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the Lord, not the human observer, brings pasture out; Paul describes himself planting and Apollos watering before saying God caused growth, distinguishing human labor from the source of life.

row.basis: The rich person fades like a field flower
row.note: The commentary uses the plant’s short life to frame the contrast between this world and what endures; James says the rich person passes away like grass and its flower, applying the same fading image to worldly status.

The commentary treats pasture as the land’s recurring annual yield; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will continue while the earth remains, giving that cycle a covenant frame.

The commentary notes that the pasture clause itself omits rain; the immediately preceding verse promises rain in its seasons so Israel can gather grain, wine, and oil, supplying the source and agricultural continuation beside the grass-for-livestock verse.

row.basis: Hebrew מַרְעִיתוֹ, flock of his pasture
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic merʿā with root r-ʿ-y and says it can name pasture as well as grazing; this psalm uses a cognate Hebrew pasture noun for God’s flock, joining the grazing ground to the creatures that depend on it.

row.basis: Wilderness changed to pools and springs
row.note: The commentary describes pasture appearing in dry, uneven ground as a distinct gift; the psalm says God turns wilderness into pools and parched land into springs, a direct reversal from barrenness to life-sustaining water.

The commentary calls pasture the earth’s yield and connects it to the survival of households; the psalm’s hungry settlers sow fields and plant vineyards that produce fruit, extending divine restoration into human cultivation and livelihood.

row.basis: God dries the green tree and makes the dry flourish
row.note: The commentary follows pasture from green growth into dark debris; Ezekiel puts both reversals under God’s hand, who can dry a green tree and make a dry tree flourish, making divine control of both sides of the cycle explicit.

row.basis: Water on dry land and spirit on descendants
row.note: The commentary reads pasture as new life brought out of hidden ground and points to resurrection; Isaiah promises water on thirsty land and God’s spirit on descendants, joining soil’s renewal to the renewal of a people.

row.basis: Descendants sprout among grass by streams
row.note: The commentary connects pasture’s emergence with a later spiritual and human emergence; Isaiah pictures descendants sprouting among grass like willows beside flowing water, giving the same water-fed growth an explicit communal meaning.

row.basis: Righteousness and praise spring up like a garden
row.note: The commentary makes the Lord’s pasture-making the ground for praise and connects plant emergence with moral instruction; Isaiah says God makes righteousness and praise spring up before the nations like earth’s growth and a garden’s seed, joining vegetation to public praise.

The commentary presents the green pasture as a gift that may later wither; Joel addresses the animals and says the wilderness pastures become green and the trees bear fruit after devastation, making restored pasture a concrete sign of recovery.

The commentary develops pasture’s yield into a lesson about what sustains life and what endures; Hosea commands the people to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, break fallow ground, and seek God until he rains righteousness upon them, turning cultivation into an ethical summons.

row.basis: A tithe of the land’s yield belongs to God
row.note: The commentary says the pasture arrives without a fee yet connects produce with a due given at harvest; Leviticus declares the tithe of seed and tree fruit holy to the Lord, adding a distinct claim of divine ownership over the yield.

row.basis: God’s word sustains beyond crop production
row.note: The commentary places the Lord’s pasture provision beside the recited word; Wisdom says the manna teaches that crops themselves do not sustain people apart from God’s word, a precise Jewish reflection on food and divine speech.

The commentary moves from visible new growth to glorifying its giver; the Talmud prescribes a blessing when one sees trees budding in Nisan, thanking God for a world that lacks nothing and for good trees made for human enjoyment.

row.basis: Field flowers grow without human toil
row.note: The commentary says that grass emerges by the Lord’s action and is received without payment; Jesus points to lilies growing without labor or spinning as evidence of God’s care, making unworked growth a concrete sign of provision.

row.basis: Rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness
row.note: The commentary identifies the Lord through pasture and says its yield is freely given; Paul tells his hearers that God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness, a compact Christian witness to the same provision chain.

row.basis: Seed, bread, and a harvest of righteousness
row.note: The commentary connects annual yield with a duty to give from what the land produces; Paul says God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, then multiplies seed and the harvest of righteousness, joining provision to generosity.

row.basis: Called out of darkness into light
row.note: The commentary reads vegetation’s emergence from hidden soil as an image for people brought from ignorance into light through scripture; Peter describes God calling a people out of darkness into marvelous light, giving that extraction image a communal and instructional form.

row.basis: Light shines from darkness into hearts
row.note: The commentary compares a shoot emerging from dark soil with people brought from darkness to light by teaching; Paul invokes the Creator’s command that light shine from darkness and applies it to knowledge shining in human hearts, connecting creation speech with inward illumination.

row.basis: Grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary treats the pasture’s passage from life to decay as a sign that death need not be the final state; Jesus says a grain falling into the earth must die to bear much fruit, using the plant’s death as a distinct Christian account of life emerging through death.

row.basis: Seed decays and rises to bear fruit
row.note: The commentary uses the pasture’s emergence and later decay to make resurrection imaginable; Clement describes dry seed falling into the earth and decaying before the Lord’s providence raises it into many fruitful plants, an explicit early Christian reading of vegetation as resurrection evidence.

The commentary pictures green pasture appearing patchily, with bare earth beside it; in Jesus’ sower parable the seed falls on good soil and yields at different rates, a specific agricultural image of uneven ground and growth.

row.basis: The flock’s milk supports its keeper
row.note: The commentary traces pasture from grass to the herd and then to human livelihood through milk, wool, and work; Paul asks whether a shepherd tends a flock without sharing its milk, making the animal-to-human support chain explicit in an argument about labor.

row.basis: The farmer waits for fruit and seasonal rains
row.note: The commentary links the plant’s temporary cycle with the later judgment and what endures; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth’s precious fruit until the early and late rains, turning the crop cycle into a picture of eschatological patience.

row.basis: The earth’s ripe harvest at judgment
row.note: The commentary places pasture’s short-lived growth before the surah’s final warnings; Revelation depicts the earth’s harvest as ripe and ready for reaping, giving agricultural growth an explicit end-time judgment image.

row.basis: Different measures of fruit from good soil
row.note: The commentary stresses that vegetation appears in patches rather than as a uniform carpet; Jesus interprets the good soil as yielding thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold, making variation in the fruit of receptive ground explicit.

The commentary follows pasture’s brief green phase into decay and relates that passing life to the Hereafter; Isaiah calls all flesh grass and its glory a field flower, explicitly extending the vegetation image to human transience.

row.basis: New birth from imperishable seed through the word
row.note: The commentary links plant emergence to human learning and then contrasts fading grass with retained recitation; Peter says believers are born again from imperishable seed through the living word, directly joining agricultural generation to enduring proclamation.

The commentary says pasture comes from an unseen place and connects emergence with God’s knowledge of what is hidden; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the heart’s purposes, giving that hidden-to-manifest relation an ethical and eschatological use.

row.basis: name exalted above earth and heaven
row.note: The commentary joins “exalt the Lord’s name” to al-aʿla; this psalm says the Lord’s name alone is exalted and his majesty is above earth and heaven, an unusually close praise formula.

row.basis: call on and proclaim the exalted name
row.note: The commentary’s command to praise the high name is matched by Isaiah’s thanksgiving instruction to call on the Lord’s name and proclaim among the nations that it is exalted.
The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with the elevation root ʿ-l-w; here YHWH is called ʿelyon, “Most High,” over all the earth, a related Semitic elevation title in a declaration of divine supremacy.

The commentary’s “Most High” language has a Hebrew counterpart in Melchizedek’s blessing of God as ʿelyon; the verse blesses that God for delivering Abram’s enemies, joining the title to praise and sovereignty.

The commentary sets the Lord’s highness against the low, near life and a ruler’s vaunted height; Isaiah calls God the High and Lofty One who also dwells with the contrite and lowly, redefining true elevation.

row.basis: majestic name and glory above the heavens
row.note: The commentary says the named one is lifted by the name; this prayer calls YHWH’s name majestic throughout the earth and places his glory above the heavens.
The commentary contrasts the truly exalted Lord with a creature claiming the highest rank; this hymn places YHWH above all nations and his glory above the heavens.
The commentary’s al-aʿla denotes real divine elevation, unlike Pharaoh’s self-assertion; this praise asks who is like the Lord, enthroned on high.
The commentary’s command to glorify the Lord’s name is matched by Moses’ song, which calls the Lord “my God” and says he will praise and exalt him after the sea deliverance.

row.basis: exaltation and praise of the name
row.note: The commentary links tasbih with raising the Lord’s name; Isaiah says “I will exalt you” and praise the Lord’s name for faithful wonders, giving that pairing a worship context.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every fault; this psalm calls for praise of the Lord’s great, awesome name and declares him holy.
The commentary’s ذَكَرَ is “remembered/mentioned”; the psalmist says he remembered the Lord’s name at night and kept the law, a direct Hebrew cognate in a devotional setting.

The commentary links remembrance to the Lord’s name; God identifies himself to Moses and says this name is his memorial through all generations, using the Hebrew z-k-r family for enduring remembrance.

row.basis: remembering the Lord’s name against worldly reliance
row.note: The commentary’s remembered name marks the worshipper’s orientation toward the Lord; this verse contrasts those who trust chariots and horses with those who remember the name of YHWH their God.

row.basis: remembrance and reverence for the name
row.note: The commentary’s dhikr links remembrance with the Lord’s honor; Malachi says those who fear the Lord and esteem his name speak together, and a book of remembrance is written for them.

row.basis: remembered royal name and enduring praise
row.note: The commentary says naming raises the named one’s remembrance; in this royal wedding poem the speaker promises the king’s name will be remembered through generations and peoples will praise him, though the addressee is the king, not explicitly YHWH.
The commentary cites houses raised for worship where the Lord’s name is mentioned; Solomon calls the temple the place where God said his name would be, tying a worship house to the indwelling name.

row.basis: a tower reaching heaven and a self-made name
row.note: The commentary contrasts the Lord’s high name with a ruler’s false elevation; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves while building a tower toward heaven, joining self-exaltation and name-making in one scene.

The commentary’s high/low axis includes a creature’s attempt to rise; after Babel’s tower project, God scatters the builders and the city is left unfinished, a narrative reversal of their ascent and self-made name.

row.basis: “I will make myself like the Most High”
row.note: The commentary cites Pharaoh claiming “I am your Lord Most High”; the taunting king in Isaiah explicitly resolves to make himself like the Most High, exposing the same creaturely seizure of divine height.
The commentary says a king’s rising can mean tyranny and arrogance; Isaiah’s self-exalting figure is brought down to Sheol, supplying the reversal implicit in the Qur’anic judgment on Pharaoh.

The commentary’s Pharaoh appropriates the Lord’s highest title; Ezekiel addresses Tyre’s ruler as a man who says “I am a god” while sitting in a godlike seat, another ruler’s false claim to divine rank.

row.basis: king boasts of his own majesty
row.note: The commentary identifies Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as arrogant self-exaltation; Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon was built by his own power for the glory of his majesty, making the ruler’s boast explicit.

row.basis: Aramaic title for the Most High
row.note: The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with an elevation root; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses the Aramaic “Most High” and praises his everlasting dominion, coupling a related Semitic title with worship.
The commentary opposes God’s true highness to a creature’s arrogance; Nebuchadnezzar honors the King of heaven and concludes that those who walk in pride God is able to humble.

row.basis: human pride lowered, Lord alone exalted
row.note: The commentary makes height reversible when a ruler exalts himself; Isaiah says the proud eyes of humanity will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted.

The commentary quotes Pharaoh’s direct claim to be the highest lord; Exodus instead has Pharaoh deny knowing YHWH and refuse obedience, preserving a distinct biblical portrayal of the same ruler’s resistance.

The commentary’s Pharaoh claims the highest rank for himself; God tells the biblical Pharaoh he has been kept standing so divine power may be shown and God’s name proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the claim.

row.basis: magicians recognize God’s act but are not converted
row.note: The commentary notes that Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Exodus has Pharaoh’s magicians admit “the finger of God” but remain in the confrontation, without the conversion and reward narrated in the Qur’anic scene.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of evil and cites divine majesty; Moses’ song asks who is like the Lord, majestic in holiness and awesome in deeds.

The commentary treats Pharaoh’s self-ascribed height as arrogance; Moses warns Israel against saying “my power and the might of my hand” made its wealth, a specific warning against taking divine provision as one’s own greatness.

row.basis: worship under threat of the furnace
row.note: The commentary joins praise of the Lord’s high name to the great fire; after the three Judeans survive Nebuchadnezzar’s blazing furnace, the king blesses their God because they refused to worship any god but him.
The commentary names the great fire awaiting the wretched; Isaiah’s closing vision shows the corpses of rebels with an unquenched fire, a related scriptural image of divine judgment by fire.

The commentary labels سَبِّحِ as tasbih, glorifying God; Daniel thanks and praises the God of his fathers for revealing the king’s secret, using the Aramaic praise cognate in a prayer that credits divine wisdom.

row.basis: this world as a vestibule to the world to come
row.note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the lower and nearer life that people choose; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for entry into the latter.

row.basis: relative worth of the two worlds
row.note: The commentary’s choice of the nearer life is a value judgment; Avot says one hour of good deeds in this world is better than the whole world to come, yet one hour of serenity in the world to come is better than all this world, preserving both sides of the contrast.

row.basis: magnifying and sanctifying the great name
row.note: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; the Qaddish opens with a prayer that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified in the world he created.

row.basis: Babel’s tower as rebellion against God
row.note: The commentary treats a creature’s claim to height as arrogant usurpation; Genesis Rabbah reads the tower builders’ ascent as rebellion against heaven, making the biblical tower more than an architectural project.

row.basis: worship and glorification of the Lord of Spirits’ name
row.note: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise and highness; 1 Enoch pictures earth’s inhabitants falling down to worship and bless, glorify, and celebrate the name of the Lord of Spirits.

row.basis: prayer that the Father’s name be hallowed
row.note: The commentary’s opening command is praise of the Lord’s name; Jesus’ prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, placing sanctification of the name inside communal prayer.
The commentary links the Lord’s name and remembered honor to elevation; Mary’s prayer begins by magnifying the Lord, a direct worship formula from a lowly speaker.
The commentary’s tasbih declares God free of defect and exalts his name; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and holy is his name.
The commentary pairs a self-exalting ruler with the low/near life; Mary’s hymn says God brings rulers down from thrones and exalts the lowly, a direct reversal of claimed human height.
The commentary’s command to raise the Lord’s name is echoed when Jesus prays that the Father glorify his name; the heavenly voice answers that it has been glorified and will be glorified again.

row.basis: exalted and given the name above every name
row.note: The commentary says the Lord’s name is raised and honored; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, locating exaltation in the Christ hymn.

row.basis: every knee bows at the name
row.note: The commentary’s name-and-prayer pairing becomes embodied worship here: at Jesus’ name every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is to bow.
The commentary joins remembering the Lord’s name to prayer; Paul says every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of God the Father.

row.basis: praise and confession of the name
row.note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord’s name before prayer; Hebrews describes continual praise as a sacrifice of lips that confess God’s name.
The commentary links tasbih, majesty, and the Lord’s name; Revelation asks who will not fear and glorify God’s name, then says he alone is holy and nations will worship.

row.basis: thanksgiving for the holy name in prayer
row.note: The commentary’s remembered and praised name is a liturgical act; the post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for his holy name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
The commentary calls Pharaoh’s highest-lord claim arrogance; Jesus says the one who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

row.basis: humility before the Lord brings exaltation
row.note: The commentary makes height and lowliness an axis; James commands readers to humble themselves before the Lord, who will exalt them.
The commentary contrasts the proud ruler with the lowly life; Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God’s mighty hand so he may exalt them at the proper time.
The commentary places Moses’ story beside the warning against choosing the near life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God’s people over the temporary pleasure of sin.

row.basis: Moses values reward above Egypt’s wealth
row.note: The commentary’s low-life choice is a question of value; Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looked to the reward.

row.basis: the world passes, God’s will abides
row.note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life; John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and abides forever.

row.basis: gaining the world and losing one’s life
row.note: The commentary criticizes preferring the low, near life; Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life, making the choice’s cost explicit.

The commentary says Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Paul names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses who resist the truth, preserving a contrary Christian memory of the magicians.
The commentary links divine majesty and light with the great fire; Paul describes God as dwelling in unapproachable light and as the one to whom honor and eternal dominion belong.
The commentary names the great fire as the wretched person’s end; Jesus’ judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
The commentary says people prefer the near, lower life; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy, giving the choice a concrete object and cost.
Against the commentary’s preference for the near life, Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it cannot be destroyed, supplying the alternative value.
The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; in David’s psalm the worshippers are told to magnify YHWH together and exalt his name together, a direct communal formulation.

row.basis: name praised from sunrise to sunset
row.note: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise; this hymn says the Lord’s name is to be praised from the rising of the sun to its setting, extending the act across the whole day.

row.basis: glory due the name and offerings in the courts
row.note: The commentary links raised houses, the Lord’s name, and worship; the psalm tells worshippers to ascribe glory to the Lord’s name and bring an offering into his courts.

row.basis: chosen sanctuary where God places his name
row.note: The commentary cites houses authorized for worship with the Lord’s name in them; Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and dwelling, supplying the covenant sanctuary background.
The commentary links remembering the Lord’s name with prayer; God says he will come and bless at every altar where he causes his name to be remembered, joining invocation to sacrifice.

row.basis: great name among nations and pure offering
row.note: The commentary ties praise of the Lord’s name to worship in houses; Malachi says the Lord’s name is great among the nations and that offerings are made to it across the earth.

row.basis: glorious name exalted above blessing and praise
row.note: The commentary commands exaltation of the Lord’s name; the Levites’ public prayer blesses God’s glorious name, exalted above all blessing and praise.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of every evil; after losing his children and possessions Job blesses the Lord’s name, showing praise under calamity rather than only in prosperity.

row.basis: blessed name, kings raised and removed
row.note: The commentary contrasts God’s true height with a ruler’s claim; Daniel blesses God’s name forever because wisdom and might belong to him and he removes and sets up kings.

The commentary’s Pharaoh claims supreme rule for himself; the heavenly decree in Daniel says the Most High rules the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whom he wills, framing Nebuchadnezzar’s later boast and humbling.

row.basis: kingdom taken during the king’s boast
row.note: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “I am the highest lord” as a creature’s false claim; Daniel’s heavenly voice interrupts Nebuchadnezzar’s boast and announces that his kingship has departed from him.

row.basis: the Lord descends and proclaims his name
row.note: The commentary calls for praise of the Lord’s name; at Sinai the Lord descends in a cloud and proclaims the divine name before Moses, giving the naming formula a theophanic setting.
The commentary defines tasbih as denying every evil of God; the proclamation following the name calls the Lord merciful, gracious, patient, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.
The commentary’s cited expression about the radiance, majesty, and light of the Lord’s face has a close benediction parallel: the priest asks that the Lord make his face shine upon Israel.

row.basis: prayer for the light of God’s face
row.note: The commentary connects the Lord’s face with glory and light; the psalmist prays for the light of God’s face to shine upon the worshippers, making the image explicitly devotional.

row.basis: seeing God’s face and the limit of mortal life
row.note: The commentary cites language about the Lord’s face as overwhelming glory and light; when Moses asks to see God’s glory, Exodus says no human can see God’s face and live, setting a distinct boundary around that face imagery.

row.basis: glory appearing as devouring fire on the mountain
row.note: The commentary connects divine majesty and light with the great fire; at Sinai the Lord’s glory appears to Israel like a devouring fire on the mountain’s summit, joining height, glory, and fire.
The commentary names the great fire in the judgment scene; Moses warns Israel that the Lord their God is a consuming fire, so the fire image also expresses divine holiness and judgment.

The commentary pairs the Lord’s exaltation with a worshipper’s prayer; Hannah says her strength is exalted in the Lord and rejoices in his salvation, placing elevation in grateful devotion rather than self-claim.

row.basis: God brings low and raises up
row.note: The commentary makes highness and lowliness opposite ends of one axis; Hannah’s prayer says the Lord makes poor and rich and brings low and raises up.

row.basis: the needy raised from dust to sit with princes
row.note: The commentary describes the chosen life as low and lesser; Hannah says God lifts the needy from the dust and seats them with princes, a concrete reversal of low status.

row.basis: God raises the humble and casts down the wicked
row.note: The commentary contrasts true divine elevation with a ruler’s arrogance; the psalm says the Lord raises the humble and casts the wicked down, assigning the upward and downward movement to God.

row.basis: God puts one down and lifts another
row.note: The commentary treats elevation as the Lord’s rightful attribute and worldly self-exaltation as false; the psalm calls God the judge who brings one down and raises another.

The commentary labels ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ with k-b-r and explains tekbir as declaring God great; Job calls God kabbir, “mighty,” attesting a related Semitic greatness word, though the Hebrew verse emphasizes might.

row.basis: one king over earth and one name
row.note: The commentary praises the Lord as highest and links the name to worship; Zechariah says YHWH will be king over all the earth and his name one, uniting universal rule with the divine name.

row.basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in the self-made name
row.note: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as a name whose mention is raised; Babel’s builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven. Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, though the Hebrew verse does not derive it from height.

row.basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in praise
row.note: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as the name that raises the named one’s remembrance; the psalm calls YHWH’s shem majestic throughout the earth. The cognate appears in a praise formula, without importing the commentary’s proposed etymology.

The commentary develops a silhouette rising above the horizon and a ruler’s claimed height; Isaiah addresses a fallen morning star before recounting the speaker’s ascent and boast, adding a celestial image to the self-exaltation scene.

row.basis: throne glory, streams of fire, and unapproachable face
row.note: The commentary’s gloss connects the Lord’s facial radiance and majesty with light and fire; Enoch’s heavenly throne vision joins fiery streams to overwhelming glory and a face no flesh can behold.
The commentary treats Pharaoh’s claim to highest rank as arrogance; Mary’s hymn says God scatters the proud in the intention of their hearts, adding the divine reversal of self-exaltation.
The commentary says people choose the low and near life; Jesus says the heart follows its treasure, making the preference for earthly life an inward allegiance rather than a mere circumstance.
The commentary names a choice of the lower, nearer life; Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon, making that preference a direct choice of master.

row.basis: Paul reads Pharaoh’s role as serving God’s name
row.note: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as false human elevation; Paul quotes Exodus to say Pharaoh was raised up so God’s power and name would be proclaimed, interpreting the same ruler as an instrument of divine sovereignty.

row.basis: God’s glory shines in Christ’s face
row.note: The commentary’s gloss joins radiance and light to the Lord’s face; Paul describes the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, with light shining in human hearts.

row.basis: visible transient things and unseen eternal things
row.note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life and the surah contrasts it with what lasts; Paul says visible things are temporary while unseen things are eternal.

row.basis: trying to save life and losing it
row.note: The commentary warns that people prefer the low, near life; Jesus says whoever seeks to save life will lose it, while whoever loses life for his sake will save it.

row.basis: set the mind above, not on earth
row.note: The commentary sets the high against the near earthly life; Paul commands believers to seek the things above rather than things on earth, stating that orientation directly.

row.basis: earthly-mindedness as the road to destruction
row.note: The commentary calls the chosen earthly life low and nearer; Paul describes people whose minds are set on earthly things and whose end is destruction, supplying a concrete moral consequence.
The commentary’s axis contrasts the near life with a higher enduring orientation; Paul says believers’ citizenship is in heaven, naming the alternative to earthly-mindedness.

row.basis: God as consuming fire in a call to worship
row.note: The commentary links divine majesty and the great fire; Hebrews urges reverent worship because God is a consuming fire, bringing the image into a Christian liturgical warning.

The commentary sets true divine height against a creature’s arrogant claim; Jesus says he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, a specific heavenly fall that resonates with the descent of Isaiah’s self-exalting figure.

row.basis: Mary’s “magnifying” as the soul’s reception of God
row.note: The commentary says the name raises the named one’s remembrance; Origen’s homily on Mary’s Magnificat explains her soul’s magnifying of the Lord as a change in the human recipient’s capacity to perceive and receive God, not an increase in God’s greatness.

row.note: The commentary reads 87:2's creating and proportioning bodily; Genesis narrates God forming the first human from ground and breathing life into him, adding the dust-to-living-body sequence.
Job addresses God as the maker who fashioned and made him, a personal bodily counterpart to the commentary's account of creation and arrangement.
Job pictures his own formation in the womb as milk becoming cheese; this gives concrete gestational process to the commentary's fetal-forming life-stage reading.
Job says God clothed and knit these body parts together, closely specifying the bodily ordering that the commentary hears in 87:2–3.
The psalmist credits God with forming inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, making explicit the prenatal bodily scene behind the commentary's life-stage reading.
The psalm's hidden, intricately woven formation in the body's depths adds a concealed-making image to the commentary's womb and shaping sequence.
The psalm joins an embryo not yet formed to days written beforehand; it brings prenatal formation together with the measured lifespan heard in the commentary's qaḍara and life-cycle reading.

row.basis: formed in womb before prophetic commission
row.note: Jeremiah is known and set apart before being formed in the womb; this shares the commentary's divine prenatal formation while adding vocation before birth.
Solomon presents himself as mortal and descended from the first human formed from earth; this places the commentary's bodily ordering within a Jewish reflection on universal human origin.
Solomon describes being molded in flesh in his mother's womb over ten months, a direct gestational counterpart to the commentary's fetal formation.
Solomon says he was swaddled and cared for, giving a concrete childhood instance of the commentary's branch of Rabb as raising a child.

row.basis: from leaving the womb to returning to the mother of all living
row.note: Sirach describes human toil as spanning birth from the womb to return to earth, an unusually explicit lifespan parallel to the commentary's womb-to-aging sequence.

row.basis: all things ordered by measure, number, and weight
row.note: Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight; this closely specifies the commentary's reading of 87:3 as putting each thing in its particular measure and form.
God says he has borne and carried Israel from the womb; this makes the commentary's Rabb-as-raising image a lifelong divine-care metaphor, though Isaiah speaks collectively of Israel.
The same oracle promises to carry Israel into old age and gray hairs, bringing the commentary's womb-to-senescence life arc under one image of divine care.

row.basis: God relied on from the womb
row.note: The speaker says God has been his hope from birth and benefactor from the womb, an individual prayer counterpart to the commentary's nurturing life-cycle sense of Rabb.
The psalmist asks not to be abandoned in old age; this makes the commentary's senescence sense concrete as a prayer about divine care at life's late stage.

row.basis: fruitful and green in old age
row.note: The righteous remain fruitful, fresh, and green in old age; the verse uniquely joins the commentary's aging body with its surah's pasture and vegetation imagery.

row.basis: remember the Creator before aging days
row.note: Ecclesiastes urges remembrance of the Creator before difficult years and old age arrive, joining the commentary's Creator-centered bodily life course to its age-related reading.
The poem pictures trembling hands, bent strength, failing teeth, and dim eyes; it gives physical detail to the commentary's otherwise brief old-age sense.
Isaiah identifies all flesh with grass and its glory with a field flower; this makes the commentary's pairing of human body and drying pasture an explicit image of mortality.

Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's enduring word; beside the surah's dried pasture and its enduring-afterlife contrast, it adds a biblical word-versus-mortal-life formulation.

row.basis: human days like grass and field flower
row.note: The psalm compares human days and flourishing to grass and a flower, directly joining bodily lifespan to vegetation as the commentary does in its life-stage and pasture reading.
The flower disappears when wind passes; this adds the disappearance of mortal life to the commentary's warning carried by drying pasture.

row.basis: fetus taught Torah, then made to forget
row.note: The Talmud says an angel teaches the fetus Torah in the womb and strikes it at birth so it forgets; this meets the commentary's womb association for the root of 87:6 with that verse's recitation and not-forgetting, while the Talmud's fetus and Qur'anic addressee differ.

row.basis: living soul rendered as speaking spirit
row.note: Onqelos interprets the formed human's life-breath as a speaking spirit; this Jewish reading connects the bodily formation discussed for 87:2 with the surah's adjacent gift of recitation in 87:6.
Luke describes Jesus growing as a child, becoming strong and filled with wisdom; it supplies a concrete growth-to-maturity scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-child-rearing branch.

row.basis: Jesus advances in age and stature
row.note: Jesus increases in wisdom, stature, and favor; this is a direct bodily-growth counterpart to the commentary's reading of maturation through a human life.

row.basis: seed must die to be made alive
row.note: Paul's seed analogy makes death the condition for new life; beside the commentary's embryo-to-resurrection argument and its formed-body/drying-plant pairing, it joins plant and bodily renewal.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body as willed
row.note: Paul says God gives each seed its own body as he wills, a close specific counterpart to the commentary's measured and specially formed body under 87:3.
Paul's contrast between a perishable body sown and an imperishable body raised directly answers the commentary's link between bodily creation and resurrection.
Paul distinguishes the body sown as natural from the body raised as spiritual, extending the commentary's formed body and resurrection connection into a claim about transformation.
Paul pictures all creation groaning in labor pains; this brings the commentary's womb-centered bodily life cycle into a cosmic creation image.
Believers groan while awaiting bodily redemption; this connects the commentary's formed human body and resurrection argument with Paul's future transformation of the body.

row.basis: new birth through imperishable seed and word
row.note: Peter says his readers have been born anew through imperishable seed by God's living word; this meets the commentary's womb-and-recitation cluster and introduces a Christian new-birth image.
Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh and its glory are like grass and flower; this directly joins the commentary's mortal body and withering pasture.
Peter contrasts withering flesh with the Lord's enduring word, applied to the proclaimed gospel; it develops the commentary's pasture and lasting-life contrast through Christian proclamation.
John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will abides forever; this closely matches the surah's worldly-life versus better, enduring hereafter contrast.
Jesus contrasts earthly treasure vulnerable to decay with treasure secured in heaven; this gives a concrete image to the surah's preference for worldly life over what is better and enduring.
Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal, giving a Christian formulation of the surah's worldly-life and enduring-afterlife contrast.
The infant receives breath and cries at birth; it extends the commentary's prenatal-to-lifespan sequence across the body's emergence from the womb.
Even a king's birth has no different beginning; this Jewish reflection makes the commentary's bodily life stages universal rather than a lexical claim about one person.
All people share one way into life and one way out; it frames the commentary's womb-to-old-age arc with mortality and a common human course.

row.basis: fear of heights and journey to the eternal home
row.note: The old-age poem moves from bodily frailty to the human going to an eternal home, adding the life's endpoint to the commentary's aging stage.

At death, dust returns to earth and spirit to God; this reverses the dust-and-breath formation of Genesis 2:7 and supplies an endpoint to the commentary's bodily lifespan, without itself arguing for resurrection.
The psalm assigns human life seventy or, at strength, eighty years, then says it passes swiftly; this makes the commentary's measured-body and old-age senses an explicit lifespan measure.
Proverbs contrasts young men's strength with gray hair as elders' splendor, giving a compact scriptural life-stage pair beside the commentary's maturity and senescence readings.

The earth yields first a stalk, then an ear, then full grain; this plant-growth sequence meets the commentary's child-raised-in-stages and pasture imagery while remaining an agrarian, not human, account.
The ripe crop is harvested, completing Mark's growth sequence; beside the commentary's vegetation growth and drying, it adds the endpoint of maturity and harvest.

row.basis: birth brings a child into the world and ends remembered anguish
row.note: Jesus compares the disciples' sorrow to labor pain that gives way to joy when a child is born into the world; this meets the commentary's delivery-nearness sense for al-dunya and its womb-related reading of qaraʾ, without claiming either Arabic branch as the verse's literal meaning.
Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and lose one's life; this states explicitly the danger implicit in the commentary's identification of preferring worldly life.

The Syriac Peshitta uses the cognate q-r-ʾ verb when Jesus stands to read Isaiah; this is a specific scriptural reading use beside 87:6's recitation, while the commentary's separate womb-related branch should not be transferred to this verse.

row.basis: newborn with cord uncut, unwashed, and unswaddled
row.note: The commentary's camel idiom mentions fetal membranes not gathered; Ezekiel's allegory depicts a newborn left with its cord uncut and without birth care. The objects differ, but both make perinatal handling concrete.

row.basis: bones formed in a pregnant woman's womb
row.note: Ecclesiastes contrasts the unknown formation of bones in the womb with God's work as maker of all; this directly joins the commentary's fetal body-shaping and divine ordering, while stressing that the process is hidden.

row.basis: one maker fashioned both people in the womb
row.note: Job grounds equality between himself and his servant in the same maker forming them in the womb; this adds an ethical consequence to the commentary's account of shared human bodily formation.

row.basis: taught Ephraim to walk and lifted him by the arms
row.note: God recalls teaching Israel as a child to walk and carrying him; this is a concrete child-rearing scene for the commentary's Rabb-as-raising-a-child sense.

row.basis: lifted infant and bent down to feed
row.note: God describes lifting Israel like an infant and bending down to feed him; this extends the commentary's nurturing life-stage image into hands-on parental care.

row.basis: Creator says he formed Israel from the womb
row.note: Isaiah joins forming the addressee in the womb to the Lord's making of all things; this ties the commentary's prenatal formation directly to universal creation.

row.basis: Sarah and Abraham advanced in age; her monthly cycle had ceased
row.note: The narrative names the aged body's reproductive limit before Isaac's promised birth, bringing the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth stages together in one concrete case.

row.basis: Sarah conceives and bears Isaac in old age
row.note: Isaac is born to Sarah at the time God promised, when Abraham is old; this gives a narrative reversal in which the commentary's late-life stage becomes the setting for birth.

row.basis: Sarah nurses a son in Abraham's old age
row.note: Sarah marvels that she has borne and nursed a son in Abraham's old age; this uniquely combines the commentary's child-rearing and senescence stages.
Job says a person's days are determined, months numbered, and limit set; this closely meets the commentary's reading of 87:3 as assigning each thing its measure, here applied to human lifespan.

row.basis: sinews, flesh, skin, and breath restore a body
row.note: In a vision interpreted as Israel's restoration (37:11), God reassembles the dry bones with bodily tissues and breath; this supplies a detailed scriptural image of the ordered body and renewed life discussed in the commentary.

row.basis: body assembled but still without breath
row.note: The bones have sinews, flesh, and skin, yet no breath; this makes bodily formation and animation distinct stages, sharpening the commentary's creation-and-order sequence.

row.basis: breath summoned from the four winds to the slain
row.note: The prophet is told to call breath into the slain so they may live; this joins the commentary's formed body with divine breath and revival, in a vision whose stated referent is exiled Israel.

row.basis: the breath enters and the slain live
row.note: The bodies stand alive after the breath enters them; this is a vivid resurrection-like image beside the commentary's argument from bodily formation to God's power to raise the dead, though Ezekiel interprets the vision corporately.

row.basis: dead awaken and earth gives birth to shades
row.note: Isaiah calls the dead to live and the earth to give birth to its dead; this joins bodily resurrection to birth imagery, meeting the commentary's fetal formation and resurrection argument.

row.basis: sleepers in dust awake to opposed destinies
row.note: Daniel says many sleeping in the dust awake to everlasting life or shame; this gives a Hebrew Bible resurrection counterpart to the commentary's creation-to-resurrection argument and places judgment after bodily renewal.

Rabbi Meir answers a question about resurrection by pointing to grain buried bare that emerges clothed; this Jewish argument uses plant transformation to make renewed embodiment imaginable, meeting the commentary's pairing of bodily creation, resurrection, and vegetation.
The angel says Elizabeth, called barren, is now six months pregnant in her old age; this precisely brings the commentary's old-age and approaching-birth senses into one Christian narrative.

row.basis: first Adam living soul, last Adam life-giving spirit
row.note: Paul interprets Genesis 2:7 by contrasting the first Adam as living soul with the last Adam as life-giving spirit; this links the commentary's formed human and breathed life to resurrection through a Christian reading of Adam.

row.basis: Gehenna's worm does not die and fire is not quenched
row.note: Jesus uses Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire image as a warning about Gehenna; beside the surah's great fire and its continuation that the condemned neither die nor live, it gives a Christian judgment image with a different formulation.

After the human is taken from the ground, God says he will return to it; this completes the earth-to-body sequence cited in the commentary with its bodily endpoint before the Qur'anic resurrection argument.

row.basis: martyr expects to receive his limbs again
row.note: A tortured brother says he received his limbs from heaven and hopes to receive them again; this Jewish witness makes resurrection bodily and specific, beside the commentary's inference from bodily creation to raising the dead.

row.basis: king has no resurrection to life
row.note: The youngest brother expects God to raise him to life, while the king has no resurrection to life; this adds the commentary's bodily revival theme together with opposed postmortem destinies.

Paul says Christ will transform the body of humiliation to conform to his glorious body; this is a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's ordered body and resurrection, with transformation rather than mere return.

row.basis: Israel forgets the God who gave it birth
row.note: Moses accuses Israel of forgetting the God who gave it birth; this meets the commentary's womb and child-raising senses beside 87:6's promise not to forget, but reverses the roles: Israel forgets its divine parent.
Isaiah asks whether a mother can forget the son of her womb, then says God will not forget Zion; this meets the commentary's womb, nurture, and not-forgetting cluster through a maternal-memory image.

row.basis: human born of woman, brief as a fading flower
row.note: Job joins birth from a woman to a short life that flowers and withers; this connects the commentary's lifespan arc to its body-and-drying-vegetation warning.

row.basis: Job asks whether a dead person will live again
row.note: Job asks whether a human who dies will live again and says he would wait for release; this places the commentary's confident move from bodily formation to resurrection beside a Hebrew lament that frames renewed life as a question and hope.

row.basis: time to be born and time to die
row.note: Ecclesiastes frames human life with a time for birth and a time for death, a concise lifespan formula beside the commentary's womb-to-old-age reading.

row.basis: measure of days and life's end
row.note: The psalm asks God to make known the measure of its days and its end; this makes the commentary's measured-life reading of 87:3 a prayer about human limits.
The psalm asks God to teach people to number their days; it joins the commentary's measured lifespan to the guidance of 87:3, with numbering leading to wise living.
At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb; this adds a concrete action of the fetus within the womb to the commentary's prenatal life-stage imagery.

row.basis: Sarah conceives beyond the age for childbearing
row.note: Hebrews interprets Sarah's conception as faith in the promise despite her age; beside the commentary's old-age and birth stages, it adds a Christian reading of the Genesis reversal.

row.basis: childhood put away on becoming an adult
row.note: Paul contrasts speaking and thinking as a child with becoming an adult; this gives the commentary's child-to-maturity sequence a distinct ethical and interpretive use.

row.basis: milk-fed child unskilled in the word
row.note: Hebrews likens the inexperienced hearer to an infant needing milk; this meets the commentary's child-rearing and maturation image while applying it to learning, not bodily formation.
Hebrews contrasts infants with mature people whose faculties are trained; this develops the commentary's growth-to-maturity sequence as discernment acquired over time.

row.basis: no one can add a cubit to stature or lifespan
row.note: Jesus asks whether anxiety can add a cubit to a person's ἡλικία, read as stature or lifespan; this specific ambiguity meets the commentary's measured body and measured human course.

row.basis: field grass clothed today, burned tomorrow
row.note: Jesus says God clothes grass that is thrown into the oven the next day; the image joins the commentary's pasture that withers to bodily care and fire, while Matthew's point is trust rather than judgment.

row.basis: people seek death, but death flees
row.note: During the locust torment, people desire death without finding it; this concretely meets the surah's adjacent statement that those in the fire neither die nor live, although Revelation's torment scene is not itself the final lake of fire.

row.basis: resurrected people can no longer die
row.note: In Jesus' reply about the resurrection, those deemed worthy of that age can no longer die; this gives a Christian contrast to the surah's condemned who neither die nor live.

Isaiah's closing vision has worshipers view the corpses of rebels with undying worms and unquenched fire; beside 87:12–13, it shares fire and undying imagery but depicts corpses rather than living people unable to die.

Yorum surenin yağmur, bulut ve kararan ot sahnesini okuma ve bilmeyle bağlar; İşaya gökten inen yağmurun toprağı sulayıp filiz, tohum ve ekmek verdiğini anlatır. İlahî söz benzetmesinin zeminindeki su-ot döngüsünü sağlar.

Yorum, göğüste duran söz için çamur altındaki kuyu ve tükenmeyen su imgesi kurar; İsa'nın verdiği su içende sonsuz yaşama fışkıran bir kaynak olur. İçte saklı duran ve dışarı taşan su imgesi belirli bir Hıristiyan karşılığıdır.

Yorum, insanın kendisine bile gizli kalan şeyi Tanrı'nın bildiğini vurgular; tohum benzetmesinde ekinci uyurken tohum filizlenip büyür, nasıl olduğunu kendisi bilmez. Gizli süreç ile sınırlı insan bilgisi arasında somut köprü kurar.

Yorum, istisnanın bazı şeyi ilahî isteme altında unutturabilmesini tartışır; İşaya Tanrı'nın günahları kendi uğruna silip onları anmayacağını söyler. Unutmanın vahiy değil suç bağlamındaki seçici ilahî biçimini ayırt etmeyi sağlar.

Yorum, unutmanın rahmetle ve kayıpla farklı sonuçlar doğurabileceğini işler; İbraniler Yeremya'nın günahları ve yasasızlıkları artık anmama sözünü Mesih'in tek kurbanı bağlamında aktarır. İlâhî hatırlamamanın Hıristiyan yorumdaki işlevini gösterir.
Yorumda hatırda kalmak insan hakkı değil ilahî iradeye bağlıdır; Vahiy galibin adını hayat kitabından asla silmeyeceğini vaat eder. İlahî kayıt ve korunmuş ad imgesini eskatolojik biçimde sunar.

Yorum Allah adını kulluk edilen özel ad olarak öne çıkarır; bu ayetteki İbranice Eloah, Arapça Allah ile aynı Sami ad ailesindendir ve yaratıcı Tanrı'nın terk edilmesini anlatır. Yakın dilsel adı somut bir Tora kullanımında gösterir.

Yorum, gizliyi bilenin bazı bilgiyi elçisine açmasını vurgular; Pavlus Tanrı'nın daha önce gizli olan bilgeliği Ruh aracılığıyla açtığını ve Ruh'un Tanrı'nın derinliklerini araştırdığını söyler. Gizli bilginin seçilmiş açıklanması için Hıristiyan karşılıktır.

Yorumdaki gizli kalan ile yeniden görünür olma yönüne karşılık Pavlus çağlar ve kuşaklar boyunca gizlenmiş gizemin şimdi kutsallara açıklandığını söyler. Gizliliğin tarih içinde vahiy yoluyla kaldırılmasını anlatır.

Yorum, ortaya çıkma gününde gizli hiçbir şeyin saklı kalmadığını söyler; Pavlus Tanrı'nın insanların gizli şeylerini Mesih aracılığıyla yargılayacağı günü bildirir. Gizli içeriği son hesapta görünür ve sorumlu kılar.

Yorumda okutulan ve unutmayışı vaat edilen söz verende kalır; Tesniye'de Rab, peygamber için kendi sözlerini onun ağzına koyacağını bildirir. Vahyin konuşanın kişisel mülkü olmadığını aynı ağız imgesiyle kurar.

row.basis: ağızla birlikte olan ve söylemeyi öğreten Tanrı
row.note: Yorum, Peygambere okumanın emredilmiş bir görevden çok verilmiş bir vaat olduğunu söyler; Musa'ya Rab ağzıyla birlikte olacağını ve ne söyleyeceğini öğreteceğini vaat eder. Konuşma yetisinin ilahî öğretime bağlılığı doğrudandır.

Yorumun göğüste tutulan ama dileyenin elinde kalan vahiy tasvirine karşılık Rab, Yeremya'nın ağzına dokunarak sözlerini onun ağzına koyduğunu söyler. İlâhî sözün peygamberin söyleyişine verilmesini somut bir çağrı sahnesiyle gösterir.
Yorumdaki unutmayış vaadine karşılık İşaya, Rabbin koyduğu sözlerin peygamberin, soyunun ve soyunun soyunun ağzından ayrılmayacağını bildirir. Sözün kuşaklar boyunca muhafazası özellikle yakındır.

row.basis: ağızda ve yürekte çok yakın söz
row.note: Yorum, açık ses ile göğüste korunan sözü ayırır; Tesniye sözü yapmak için insanın ağzına ve yüreğine çok yakın sayar. Aynı vahyi iç hafıza ve söylenen söz olarak iki yerde tutar.

Yorum, gaybı yalnız Rabbin bildiğini ve elçilerinden dilediğine bildirdiğini vurgular; Amos Rabbin işini kulları peygamberlere sırrını açmadan yapmayacağını söyler. Seçilmiş elçiye sınırlı açıklama motifi doğrudandır.

Yorumda gizliyi bilen Rab dilerse onu açığa çıkarır; Sodom bağlamında Rab yapacağı şeyi İbrahim'den gizleyip gizlemeyeceğini sorar. Gizli ilahî kararın seçilmiş bir muhataba bildirilmesi için anlatısal bir eşliktir.

Yorum, insanın ulaşamadığı bilgiyi bilen Rabbe bağlar; Yeremya'ya Rabbe seslenmesi ve bilmediği büyük, erişilmez şeylerin kendisine bildirilmesi söylenir. Gizli bilginin dua üzerine açılması belirgindir.

row.basis: tanıklığı bağlamak, Tora'yı öğrenciler arasında mühürlemek
row.note: Yorum, vahyin korunması ile dileyenin onu saklı tutabilmesi arasındaki sınırı işler; İşaya tanıklığın bağlanmasını ve Tora'nın öğrenciler arasında mühürlenmesini buyurur. Açıklanmış sözün belli bir çevrede saklanması ayrı bir metinsel sahnedir.

Yorumdaki istisna, verilmiş vahyin ilahî denetim altında kalmasını anlatır; Daniel'e sözleri kapatması ve kitabı son vakte dek mühürlemesi emredilir. İşitilmiş-yazılmış şeyin geçici olarak gizlenmesi bakımından güçlü bir karşılıktır.

Yorumun okutma, sözün kalması ve açık olma eksenine karşılık Rab, Habakkuk'a görümü yazıp levhalara açıkça kazımasını, okuyanın koşabilmesini buyurur. Görümün saklı tecrübeden kamusal ve kalıcı yazıya geçişini verir.

Yorum, okutulan sözün göğüste bir kuyu suyu gibi durması imgesini kurar; Hezekiel tomarı yiyip karnını doldurur ve söz ona bal gibi tatlı gelir. Vahyin dış nesneden içte tutulan şeye dönüşmesi somuttur.

Yorum, gizli kalanın yeniden çıkarılmasını ve unutulan sözün içte kalmasını birlikte düşünür; Yeremya Tanrı'nın sözlerini bulup yediğini, onların yüreğine sevinç olduğunu söyler. Bulunma, içselleştirme ve peygamberlik kimliği aynı ayette birleşir.

Yorum, gizlilik kökünün örtüyü kaldırıp toprak altındakini çıkarma yüzünü açıkça işler; Eyüp'te madenci saklı olanı ışığa çıkarır. Yorumdaki kuyu ve yer altı imgesine belirli bir İbranice sahne ekler.

row.basis: hikmetin yolunu ve yerini bilen Tanrı
row.note: Yorum, insanın gizli süreçleri bilmemesine karşı Rabbin bilgisine dayanır; Eyüp hikmetin yolunu ve yerini Tanrı'nın anladığını söyler. Yer altından çıkarılan şeylerin ardından yalnız Tanrı'nın bilmesi temasını tamamlar.

Yorum, göğüste duran unutulmuş sözü çamur altındaki kuyuyla karşılaştırır; Özdeyişler insan yüreğindeki tasarıyı derin suya, anlayış sahibinin onu dışarı çekmesini de kuyudan su almaya benzetir. İç sır, kuyu ve açığa çıkarma aynı formülde birleşir.

row.basis: karanlık hazineler, gizli servet ve çağıran ad
row.note: Yorum, gizli olanın bilinebilmesini özel ilahî adla bağlar; İşaya karanlığın hazinelerini ve gizli yerlerin servetini verirken çağıranın Rab olduğunu bilmeyi amaçlar. Gizli-çıkarma-bilme-ad dizisini birleştirir.

Yorumun sessiz dua ile Rabbin unutmaması arasındaki bağ için Hanna'nın kocasıyla birlikte ibadetinden sonra Rabbin onu hatırladığı söylenir. Daha önceki sessiz dua sahnesine ilahî hatırlama ile verilen cevap eklenir.

Yorum, çamurun örttüğü kuyudan suyun yeniden görünmesini hatırlama imgesine dönüştürür; Yakup anlatısında sürüler toplanınca kuyu ağzındaki taş yuvarlanır ve hayvanlar sulanır. Örtülü suya erişme sahnesi ayrı bir somut karşılıktır.

Yorum, Peygamberin bilgisi ve hafızasının kendine ait bağımsız güç olmadığını söyler; İsa, kendiliğinden konuşmadığını, Baba'nın ne söyleyeceğini buyurduğunu bildirir. Söylenen vahyin kaynağını konuşandan ayırır.

Yorum, ilahî isteme ile elçiye verilen söz arasındaki bağı kurar; bu ayet peygamberliğin insan istemiyle gelmediğini, insanların Kutsal Ruh tarafından taşınarak Tanrı'dan konuştuklarını söyler. İstem, söz ve peygamberlik aynı formülde buluşur.

Yorum, Peygamberin gaybı bilmediği, bilenin Rab olduğu ayrımını özellikle geliştirir; İsa son günün saatini meleklerin ve Oğul'un değil yalnız Baba'nın bildiğini söyler. Elçinin bilgi sınırını ilahî bilgiyle karşılaştırır.

Yorum, yüksek ses, gizli kalan söz ve vahyin ilahî denetimi üzerine durur; Yuhanna yedi gök gürültüsünün söylediklerini yazmak üzereyken onları mühürlemesi ve yazmaması emredilir. İşitilmiş sözün bilerek kapalı tutulmasına somut örnektir.

row.basis: yüksek sesle okuyan, işiten ve tutan topluluk
row.note: Yorumun okuma, hatırda tutma ve sesli ibadet hattına karşılık Vahiy okuyan, işiten ve onda yazılanı tutanları kutlar. Bir metnin kamusal ses, dinleme ve koruma yoluyla yaşamasını gösterir.

Yorum, gizli olanın her zaman insan sesiyle açığa çıkmadığını ve bilgi sınırını işler; Pavlus cennette duyduğu, insanın söylemesine izin verilmeyen sözleri anlatır. İşitilen vahyin dahi insan söyleyişine verilmeyebileceği sınırı ekler.

Yorum, Rabbin gaybı dilediği elçiye açtığını söyler; İsa krallığın sırlarını bilmenin öğrencilerine verildiğini, başkalarına ise benzetmelerle konuşulduğunu açıklar. Bilginin seçilmiş muhataplara verilmesi için yakın bir Hıristiyan formülüdür.

Yorum, açık söz ile göğüste gizlenen şeyin Rab tarafından bilinmesini işler; İbraniler Tanrı sözünün yüreğin düşünce ve niyetlerini ayırt ettiğini söyler. Bilinen gizliyi ilahî sözün etkinliğiyle birleştirir.

row.basis: Kutsal Yazıları anlamak için açılan zihin
row.note: Yorum, okunmuş sözün anlaşılması ve tutulmasının ilahî bağış olduğunu vurgular; dirilmiş İsa öğrencilerin zihinlerini Yazıları anlamaları için açar. Bilginin yalnız dinleyenin sahipliği olmadığını anlatır.

Yorum, sesli okuma ile insanın içinde kalmış söz arasında bir derecelenme kurar; Pavlus Ruh'un zayıflıkta söze dökülmeyen iniltilerle aracılık ettiğini söyler. İç dua, işitilebilir sözün ötesinde ama Tanrı'ya yönelmiş olur.

row.basis: Tora'nın unutulup unutulmayacağı üzerine rabbanî tartışma
row.note: Yorumun 87:6–7'deki unutmayış vaadi için bu sugyada Tora'nın İsrail'den unutulacağı iddiası, Tesniye 31:21'deki “unutulmayacak” sözüyle tartışılır. Rabbanî gelenek aynı metin üzerinde bellek kaybı ile ilahî koruma gerilimini işler.

row.basis: Musa ile yüz yüze konuşma formülü
row.note: Yorum Musa'nın Tanrı'yı görme isteğini insan gözünün sınırıyla anlatır; Çıkış başka bir bağlamda Rabbin Musa'yla bir dostla konuşur gibi yüz yüze konuştuğunu söyler. Görme yasağı ile yakın konuşma formülünün ayrımını incelemeyi gerektirir.

row.basis: ağız ağıza konuşma ve Rabbin biçimi
row.note: Yorum, Musa sahnesini görülemezlik sınırıyla okur; Sayılar'da Musa ile ağız ağıza, açıkça konuşulduğu ve onun Rabbin biçimini gördüğü söylenir. Musa geleneğindeki görme ve konuşma iddialarının gerilimini görünür kılar.
Yorumda yüz yüze görme talebi yıldırım ve bayılma sınırına varır; Yakup Peniel adını Tanrı'yı yüz yüze görüp canının kurtulmasına bağlar. Farklı anlatıdaki hayatta kalma sonucu karşı okuma sağlar.

Yorum vahiyde kaldırma ve unutturma ihtimalini ilahî isteme bağlamında tartışır; Vahiy, kitabın peygamberlik sözlerinden eksiltene karşı ilahî yaptırım ilan eder. İnsan müdahalesiyle metni azaltmaya ilişkin keskin bir karşı anlatıdır.

Yorum gizliyi bilen Rab ile işaret arayan insan arasında ayrım yapar; Özdeyişler bir işi gizlemeyi Tanrı'nın, araştırmayı kralların yüceliği sayar. Gizlilik ile insan araştırmasının farklı yetkilerini karşılaştırmaya açar.

row.basis: daha önce bilinmeyen gizli şeylerin duyurulması
row.note: Yorumun gizliyi bilenin gerektiğinde açması yönü için İşaya, şimdiye dek bilinmeyen yeni ve gizli şeylerin duyurulduğunu söyler. Vahyin zamanlı ve seçici açılışını somutlaştırır.

row.basis: kitabın ağızdan ayrılmaması ve gece gündüz düşünülmesi
row.note: Yorumun sesli okuma ile göğüste saklanan söz çiftine karşılık Yeşu'ya yasa kitabının ağzından ayrılmaması, gece gündüz üzerinde düşünmesi buyurulur. Sürekli ses ve iç düşünme, insan görevine dönüştürülür.

Yorum verilen bilginin ve okunmuş vahyin insan muhatabın elinde sınırsız olmadığını söyler; İsa öğrencilerine söyleyecek daha çok şeyi bulunduğunu ama onların şimdilik taşıyamayacağını bildirir. Açıklamanın muhatabın kapasitesine göre sınırlandığını ekler.

Yorum, cehrin yüksek sesini gizli ve kısık sesle karşılaştırır; İlyas anlatısında rüzgâr, deprem ve ateşten sonra ince bir sessizlik sesi gelir. İlâhî karşılaşmanın gürültü yerine zayıf sesle gelmesi ses motifini derinleştirir.

row.basis: Tesniye'nin ağız-yürek sözünü iman sözü olarak alma
row.note: Yorum, sözün hem ağızda hem göğüste bulunduğunu işler; Pavlus Tesniye'nin yakın sözünü ağız ve yürekle iman edilen Mesih mesajı diye aktarır. Aynı Tora formülünün Hıristiyan alımlamasını verir.
