row.note: The commentary supplies an unnamed rain between 87:4's pasture and 87:5's residue; this verse says God covers heaven with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on hills, giving that whole vertical sequence in one scene.
The commentary says God brings pasture out without naming water; Job describes rain reaching desolate land and causing tender grass to sprout, specifying the same life-giving result.
The commentary traces a line from the Most High through rain to pasture; Isaiah says rain descends from heaven, waters earth, and makes it sprout, then compares that efficacy to God's word.

The commentary reconstructs rain as the missing cause of pasture; Zechariah joins a request for seasonal rain to storm clouds, showers, and plants in the field, making the same weather-to-growth link explicit.

The commentary closes by recalling Moses and links divine guidance with pasture; Moses' song pictures teaching as rain and words as dew falling on grass, joining revelation to the scene's weather and growth.

The commentary treats rain as the unnamed link between pasture emerging and its later decay; Rashi reads Genesis' pre-rain plants as waiting for Adam to pray, after which rain falls and vegetation grows.

The commentary glosses 87:1's اسم as “name”; the Hebrew cognate שֵׁם appears in a call to praise God's name, which the verse says is exalted above earth and heaven, closely joining name-praise with height.

The commentary describes 87:4 as God concretely bringing pasture out; Genesis has God command the earth to bring forth vegetation and seed-bearing plants, adding the creation scene in which the ground yields plant life.

The commentary says المرعى carries grass, grazing, and pasture-place together; this verse says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human use, setting pasture in its provision-for-creatures context.

The commentary contrasts the pasture's decay with a source-labeled plant family whose plants do not dry in summer; Jeremiah's water-fed tree has green leaves and does not stop bearing fruit when heat comes.

The commentary explains غثاء as dried vegetation gathered and carried off by a flood; Psalm 1 likens the wicked to chaff driven away by wind, applying field residue to human moral fate while changing the force that carries it.
The commentary follows pasture from green life to dry debris; Isaiah says grass withers and the field flower fades, then uses that plant cycle to describe mortal human glory.

The commentary calls rain life for earth and later treats the plant's life and death alongside the hereafter; Hosea promises Israel revival and likens the Lord's coming to seasonal rains that water the land, joining renewal to rain.

The commentary sets pasture that dries against source-labeled plants said not to dry in summer; Psalm 1's person rooted beside streams remains fruitful with an unwithered leaf, an ethical image of sustained greenness.

The commentary contrasts the pasture's short life with plants said not to dry in summer; this verse says the righteous still bear fruit in old age and remain green, extending that counter-image into a portrait of enduring life.

The commentary notes that Qur'anic غثاء can describe people swept away after a cry; Wisdom has the wicked confess that their life and hope vanish like wind-driven chaff, carrying the plant-debris image into judgment.

The commentary traces plant life into dry residue and then places a person in fire; Hebrews says thorn-bearing land is rejected and ends in burning, joining failed growth and fire in an ethical warning.

row.basis: farmer awaits early and late rain
row.note: The commentary reconstructs rain as what brings pasture from earth and notes the first rain's seasonal mark; James tells farmers to wait patiently for precious fruit through the early and late rains, adding the human labor and timing of the crop cycle.

The commentary moves from dead soil through living grass to decay and also discusses life and death; Paul uses a seed that must die before it comes to life to explain resurrection, making the plant cycle an explicit model for bodily renewal.

The commentary says the plant's journey includes both life and death; Jesus compares his own death and resulting many lives to a grain falling into earth and dying, giving the botanical sequence a distinct christological reading.

The commentary explains غثاء as dried plant matter swept together and also describes the person in fire; John the Baptist's image separates grain from chaff and burns the chaff in unquenchable fire, bringing crop residue into judgment.
The commentary's grass dries after greenness and its next image concerns fire; Jesus says branches outside the vine wither, are gathered, and are burned, linking plant desiccation to judgment.

row.basis: lake of fire called second death
row.note: The commentary stresses that the one in the fire neither dies nor lives; Revelation names the lake of fire “the second death,” a direct difference in how the fiery afterlife is framed.

row.basis: Isaiah's enduring word applied to the gospel
row.note: The commentary joins 87:5's fading plant to 87:17's more-lasting hereafter; Peter follows the grass image with the word that endures and identifies it with the proclaimed good news, giving Isaiah's contrast a Christian interpretive application.

The commentary connects the plant's life, death, and reappearance from earth with resurrection; Clement reads a seed buried and decaying in soil as evidence of resurrection, making the botanical sequence an explicit Christian proof-image.

The commentary stresses that rain is absent from 87:4 even as it supplies the missing link; Genesis says shrubs had not yet appeared because there was no rain and no person to work the ground, making the absent conditions explicit.

The commentary reconstructs rain behind pasture emerging but notes that 87:4 does not name it; the next Genesis verse instead has water rise from earth and water its surface, offering a distinct mechanism for the ground's fertility.

The commentary's pasture is a plant-life scene; this royal prayer compares the king's life-giving justice to rain on mown grass and showers on earth, adding a political use for the same agricultural image.

The commentary identifies the first year's rain as the wasmi because it marks earth with growth; Joel's restoration oracle promises former and latter rains, placing seasonal rainfall within a renewed agricultural cycle.

The commentary describes the cloud's first appearance before rain brings life; Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea as the first sign of rain after drought, a concrete cloud-to-rain scene.

The commentary links a persistent cloud and wind with the rain that brings pasture; this verse describes the sky darkening with cloud and wind before heavy rain, presenting the same weather sequence in Elijah's drought story.

The commentary labels the Arabic root ر ع ي for المرعى and says the word spans grazing, grass, and place; Ezekiel uses the cognate Hebrew shepherding verb while describing a flock fed in good pasture, grounding the lexical link in a pastoral scene.

The commentary labels يَحْيَىٰ with Arabic root ح ي ي and calls rain ḥayā because it gives earth life; Ezekiel uses cognate Hebrew חיה when God promises life to dry bones, shifting the shared life verb from vegetation to bodily restoration.
The commentary's plant begins in barren earth and receives life through rain; Job says a cut tree can bud again at the scent of water, adding a specific image of renewed growth after apparent loss.

The commentary connects the pasture's brief cycle to 87:17's claim that the hereafter is more lasting; following Isaiah's grass-withers image in the preceding verse, this verse names God's word as what stands forever, a distinct enduring counterpart.

The commentary links 87:7's hiddenness to weak lightning at cloud edges; Job asks whether a human knows how God commands the clouds and flashes lightning, joining storm signs to limits on human knowledge.

The commentary treats rain as the source of earthly life and links plant life and death to resurrection imagery; the Talmud places the divine keys of rain and resurrection together, making their shared dependence on God's power explicit without equating them.

The commentary follows rain-fed pasture from emergence toward decay; Hebrews describes land drinking repeated rain and yielding a useful crop, using the agricultural response as a moral image of what a received gift produces.

The commentary compresses a plant's entire life into emergence and dry residue; Mark's seed grows through blade, head, and ripe grain before harvest, expanding the same field process into successive stages.

row.note: The commentary hears asr as late working time with a day's pay; Rabbi Tarfon says the day is short, work abundant, workers sluggish, wage great, and master pressing, gathering its work and time images in a single teaching.
The commentary makes the last available time a chance for good action; Rabbi Tarfon adds that one need not finish the work but is not free to desist, qualifying how urgency should be heard.
The commentary makes time and deeds resemble capital and transaction; Akiva's shop parable describes extended credit, an open ledger, daily collectors, and an eventual reckoning.

The commentary treats the prison years as a bounded delay before rescue; this midrash applies Job's phrase about setting an end to darkness to Joseph's confinement, interpreting his release as arriving at its allotted time.

row.ref: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 94
row.basis: Ephesus sleepers' cave and long sleep
row.note: The commentary's youths find refuge in a cave and wake after centuries thinking little time has passed; Gregory retells the Christian Ephesus sleepers who are enclosed through a long sleep and later awakened, the close story behind this time-and-shelter meeting.

row.basis: Mary at puberty moved from sanctuary
row.note: The commentary's protected maiden is held at first maturity because of a boundary around her; the priests in this story worry that twelve-year-old Mary is reaching an age at which her presence may defile the sanctuary and arrange her departure, another threshold managed by enclosure.

The commentary turns a long period into a fleeting instant when viewed late; Job compares his days to a shuttle that moves quickly and ends without hope, though its textile image differs from afternoon light.
The commentary's fiery storm makes accumulated provision disappear suddenly; Proverbs says the wicked is no more when a whirlwind passes, a compact moral use of a destructive gust without a garden.

The commentary stresses that Joseph is imprisoned after his innocence becomes clear; Joseph tells the cupbearer he was taken from his land and has done nothing deserving the dungeon, making the imposed wait an injustice in his own account.
The commentary follows the dreamer whose pressed grapes precede release; Joseph gives the other prisoner a three-day prediction of execution, so the shared prison interval leads to opposite ends.

row.basis: Joseph brought out of the pit
row.note: The commentary's delayed prison years finally end in rescue; Pharaoh summons Joseph and he is hurried out of the dungeon, marking the actual release after the forgotten request.

The commentary makes the sheltered harvest available after the hard years begin and hears asr as gain; people from all lands come to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph because famine spreads, making storage a wider rescue and transaction.

The commentary lays Joseph's release and stored crop across a measured calendar; Joseph tells his brothers that two famine years have passed and five remain without plowing or harvest, specifying the continuing span that stored grain must cover.

row.basis: wages placed in a bag with holes
row.note: The commentary's time is capital and pressing separates valuable flow from residue; Haggai says people sow much but harvest little and earn wages only to put them in a pierced bag, an exact image of labor's yield leaking away.

The commentary reads the ruined garden as a picture of moral loss after withheld good; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice but found bloodshed, giving the garden's failed crop its ethical referent.

row.basis: blessing remains inside a grape cluster
row.note: The commentary separates extracted good from dry remainder and makes rescue an exception to loss; Isaiah says not to destroy a cluster because new wine is found in it and uses that reason to spare some servants.

The commentary's generous hand, guarded harvest, and endangered garden meet here; after the tithe promise, God says he will rebuke the devourer so crops are not destroyed and the vine does not fail to bear.

The commentary makes rain or its restraint determine whether stored effort yields food; God says he withheld rain three months before harvest and sent it on one city but not another, joining timed scarcity and uneven release.
The commentary's pressed cloud behaves like a container whose water is released; God's question about who can tip the water jars of the heavens supplies another concrete vessel image for rainfall.

The commentary contrasts released water with compressed dry residue; Job's next question describes dust hardening into a mass and clods sticking together, the arid earth after the heavenly jars image.

The commentary traces squeezed cloud to grain, plant, and provision; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, make it sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, a full agricultural sequence.

The commentary contrasts withholding with a pressured hand that gives; Elijah tells the widow with a final meal in view to first make him a small cake, making her scarce provision the test of release.

row.basis: flour and oil survive the drought
row.note: The commentary's protected contents last through lean time after a gift; the widow's flour jar does not empty and her oil jug does not run dry, just as Elijah had promised.

The commentary joins enclosure to a beneficial outflow rather than mere retention; Elisha tells the widow to close the door behind her and her sons and pour her small supply of oil into gathered vessels.

row.basis: sell oil, pay debt, live on remainder
row.note: The commentary hears squeezing and stored yield as income that can rescue a household; Elisha tells the widow to sell the multiplied oil, discharge her debt, and live with her sons on what remains.

row.basis: winepress yield given to freed servant
row.note: The commentary's press product becomes a gift when the hand releases it; Deuteronomy commands an owner freeing a servant to provide generously from flock, threshing floor, and winepress.

row.basis: cloak returned by sunset as shelter
row.note: The commentary pairs the day's closing edge with whether one holds back another's protection; the creditor must return a poor person's pledged cloak by sunset so that person can sleep in it.

row.basis: heaven and earth hear before verdict
row.note: The commentary's opening oath suspends its judgment until the next line; Moses first summons heaven and earth to hear his speech before his song states God's ways and Israel's response, another cosmic opening that makes the following verdict weighty.

row.basis: persecuted people seek wilderness hiding places
row.note: The commentary's youths withdraw from hostile worship to a hidden refuge; royal officers learn that Jewish families who rejected the king's command have fled to wilderness hiding places, giving flight and shelter a similar social cause.

The commentary's hidden refuge protects faithful youths across a long interval; the fugitives in 1 Maccabees die with their families when attacked on the Sabbath, a pointed reversal of safety after flight.

row.basis: open to receive, shut to repay
row.note: The commentary's grasp can receive while refusing to release; Sirach warns against stretching the hand out to take and closing it when repayment is due, exactly distinguishing the two directions of a hand.

row.basis: alms stored for a day of need
row.note: The commentary's productive gift and future shelter meet when Tobit says almsgiving stores a good treasure against a day of necessity, making generosity a reserve rather than depletion.

row.basis: hands open to receive, closed to give
row.note: The commentary's asr images make grasping ethically double; the Didache forbids extending the hands to receive while drawing them back when it is time to give, making the hand's direction the whole contrast.
The commentary names taking back a previous gift as a form of squeezing; the Didache tells hearers to give to those who ask and not demand it back, an exact ethical opposite to reclaimed donation.

The commentary reads a barren or lost garden against the time left to work; the vineyard owner has sought fruit from his fig tree for three years and orders it cut down, measuring unproductive time before loss.

The commentary's late afternoon may still allow a final productive interval; the gardener asks to leave the fig tree one more year while he digs and manures around it, making delay a chance for fruit.
The commentary's pressure yields either benefit or dry loss; the gardener says future fruit will spare the tree, otherwise it can be cut down, completing the time-limited exception.

The commentary's garden owners plan to keep all produce; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner sends servants to receive his fruit when harvest time arrives, setting up a precise conflict over what must be handed over.
The commentary's withheld crop brings the holders' loss; the hearers say the owner will destroy the violent tenants and lease the vineyard to others who will deliver fruit in season.

The commentary makes constriction either draw out good fruit or leave a dry loss; Jesus says the vinedresser removes branches without fruit and prunes fruiting ones for more yield, distinguishing two outcomes of cutting.
The commentary's garden is ruined while its keepers sleep and appears lost at daybreak; the disciples see Jesus' fig tree withered to its roots as they pass it in the morning.

row.basis: farmer waits for early and late rain
row.note: The commentary's crop survives a long interval before the year of pressing; James tells readers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit and early and late rains, tying endurance to delayed yield.

row.basis: rain makes land useful and blessed
row.note: The commentary's pressed cloud starts a chain from water to benefit; Hebrews says land that drinks repeated rain and produces a useful crop receives blessing, then uses that field to describe the hearers' response.
The commentary's destroyed garden is the loss side of a moral agricultural image; Hebrews contrasts land bearing thorns, near a curse and ending in fire, with the rain-fed useful crop just described.
The commentary's late-coming hour can turn protected waiting into missed opportunity; in the bridesmaids' parable the bridegroom is delayed and all fall asleep, setting up the later closed door.
The commentary's shelter can preserve those inside through a span while others lose entry; prepared bridesmaids enter the wedding and the door is shut when the bridegroom comes.

row.basis: unknown day and hour require watchfulness
row.note: The commentary's unnamed asr leaves its exact temporal extent open while the coming judgment matters; Jesus concludes the bridesmaids' scene by telling hearers to watch because they do not know the day or hour.

The commentary's cave shelters believers from hostility across centuries; Revelation shows rulers and others hiding in caves and rocks when judgment arrives, making a cave a place of fear rather than assured rescue.

row.basis: cave dwellers ask rocks to hide them
row.note: The commentary's protected sleepers can leave their cave in mercy; Revelation's terrified people instead ask mountains and rocks to conceal them from the enthroned one, so earthly enclosure cannot promise safety.
The commentary's believers leave their people and find refuge in a cave; Hebrews recalls faithful sufferers wandering deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of earth because of persecution.
The commentary contrasts a hand that retains wealth with one that lets benefit flow; the wealthy are instructed to do good, be rich in works, and be generous and ready to share.
The commentary lets a gift function as lasting provision after ordinary stores fail; the next verse calls sharing a good foundation stored for the future so the givers may take hold of real life.
The commentary's accumulated yield can disappear at the wrong hour; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth, corrosion, and thieves destroy or take it.
The commentary's guarded grain and refuge suggest a store that endures; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where the stated destroyers and thieves cannot reach it.

row.basis: spend wealth to gain lasting welcome
row.note: The commentary asks whether today's capital yields generosity and shelter later; Jesus says to make friends through worldly wealth so that when it fails they may welcome the giver into enduring dwellings.
The commentary lets the day and a whole life contract toward their end; Paul says the remaining time has been shortened and immediately revises how ordinary attachments are to be held.
The commentary's oath gives force to a later verdict about human loss; the angel proclaims that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls people to fear and worship him.

row.basis: heavens withhold dew after failed harvest
row.note: The commentary's cloud release or closure governs agricultural gain; Haggai says the heavens withheld dew and the earth withheld its produce, supplying the weather side of the pierced-wages lament.
The commentary joins raised storm cloud, rain, and vegetation; Zechariah urges asking the LORD for spring rain and says he makes storm clouds and showers that give plants to every field.
The commentary's stored grain and patience can turn present hardship into eventual yield; the psalm says those sowing in tears will reap with joy, joining time, grain, and reversed loss.

row.basis: fugitive prophet shelters in a cave
row.note: The commentary's youths flee their community into a cave; Elijah reaches a cave and lodges there before hearing the LORD's question, a briefer prophetic refuge without a centuries-long sleep.

row.basis: caves from fear of divine rising
row.note: The commentary's cave opens room for mercy to endangered believers; Isaiah's people enter rock caves and ground holes from the LORD's terror, giving enclosure a contrary meaning at judgment.
The commentary makes the difference between grasping and giving depend on what leaves the hand; Tobit instructs his son to give alms from his property and not turn his face away from the poor.

The commentary's shrinking time remains a place to prepare for what follows; Avot compares this world to a vestibule before the world to come and tells the hearer to prepare there before entering the hall.

The commentary holds a lifetime and a brief final interval together; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world exceeds the whole life of the coming world in that respect, placing moral weight on a small unit of time.

The commentary's same grasp can make a giver or a miser; Avot's four property dispositions include treating one's own as another's and another's as another's for the generous case, versus taking both for oneself in the wicked case.

row.basis: master shuts door to late arrivals
row.note: The commentary's time-bound refuge suggests a threshold that can close; Jesus describes a householder shutting the door while people stand outside and ask to be admitted too late.

The commentary's late-day work depends on a finite span of light; Jesus asks whether there are twelve hours in the day and says walking in daylight keeps one from stumbling, elaborating the same time-to-act image as his later saying.

The commentary's delayed relief in Joseph's story and the sleeper's long interval can be heard as purposive waiting; 2 Peter says the Lord is not slow about the promise but patient, giving a specific interpretive bridge for delay.

row.note: The commentary imagines haqq as a blow that reaches inside; God's word here is sharper than a two edged sword and penetrates to the division of soul and spirit, making inward reach the point of the image.
The commentary's worked spear and unswerving thrust make accuracy central; Paul says he boxes without beating the air, turning directed effort into a test of disciplined action.
The commentary's secondary sense of sabr makes a human the fixed target; Job says God set him up as a target after breaking him, shifting the blow onto a suffering person.
The commentary's thrust reaches the belly; Job says archers surround him and God pierces his kidneys, a contrary scene in which the inward wound belongs to the human target.
The commentary's human target and directed weapon meet the speaker's claim that God bent his bow and made him the target of an arrow; here the person receives the attack.
The commentary's blow penetrates to the interior; the lament says arrows from God's quiver entered the speaker's kidneys, developing the bodily result of being made a target.
The commentary associates the human being with a target set up for a strike; Job asks God why he has made Job his target, giving that secondary image a direct human voice.
The commentary treats truth as a directed penetrating force; the servant says God made his mouth a sharp sword and made him a polished arrow, joining speech to a prepared projectile.

The commentary reads haqq as a blow against what deviates; the ideal ruler strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth and kills the wicked with the breath of his lips, making just speech effective force.
The commentary's truth is hurled to strike falsehood; a sharp sword comes from the rider's mouth to strike the nations, similarly giving utterance a weapon's impact.
The commentary's directed work and penetrating truth meet the instruction to take the sword of the Spirit, identified as God's word, as a weapon in a struggle.
The commentary presents truth as an impact that breaks falsehood; Paul's weapons have divine power to demolish strongholds in an argument over knowledge and obedience.

The commentary says haqq reaches and overcomes its opposing target; Paul describes demolishing arguments raised against knowledge of God and bringing thoughts captive, specifying the intellectual target of the preceding weapons.

The commentary cites truth being thrown upon falsehood; Wisdom depicts God's all powerful word leaping from the royal throne like a stern warrior into the doomed land, joining divine utterance to forceful arrival.

The commentary's truth penetrates and destroys its opponent; Wisdom's personified divine word bears the sharp sword of God's command and fills the land with death, making the weapon an enacted judgment.
The commentary stresses a blow without deviation; Wisdom describes lightning bolts launched like arrows from a drawn bow against the ungodly, adding explicit aim to the divine attack image.

The commentary's haqq is a penetrating blow that serves truth; Proverbs says rash speech cuts like sword thrusts while wise speech heals, distinguishing destructive penetration from beneficial speech.
The commentary makes truth the directed weapon against falsehood; Proverbs makes the false witness against a neighbor a hammer, sword and sharp arrow, reversing which side wields the projectile.
The commentary's truth blow reaches within; after Peter's address the hearers are pierced in the heart and ask what to do, making inward impact lead to action.

row.basis: walk in truth on taught way
row.note: The commentary joins haqq to a course that avoids deviation; the psalmist asks to be taught God's way so that he may walk in God's truth, putting truth and directed travel in one prayer.
The commentary opposes haqq to leaving the line; the psalmist chooses the way of faithfulness and sets God's judgments before him, making the right course an intentional choice.
The commentary's loss is a move off the line; this instruction forbids turning either right or left and directs the foot away from evil, giving moral deviation a literal path image.
The commentary's mutual counsel of truth keeps action on course; a guiding voice says this is the way to walk when the hearers would turn right or left.
The commentary's claim that after truth comes deviation has a precise alternative here: receptivity to apostolic testimony distinguishes the spirit of truth from the spirit of error.
The commentary sets haqq against the false that it destroys; the letter tells its addressees that no lie comes from truth, making their opposition categorical.
The commentary interprets loss as leaving the line; the false teachers have abandoned the straight way and gone astray, tying moral error to misdirected travel.
The exception to human loss names faith, right action and sabr; Revelation identifies the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus under pressure.
The exception combines belief, deeds and patience; the address to Thyatira names works, faith and endurance together and commends later works greater than earlier ones.
The commentary turns amal into exertion with effect; James says faith by itself is dead if it has no works, giving the verse's faith and righteous action an explicit relation.
The exception joins believing and doing; James says Abraham's faith was active together with his works and completed by them, making the pairing operative rather than merely adjacent.
The exception names those who believe and do good deeds; Titus urges those who have believed God to devote themselves to good works, matching that sequence as practical instruction.
The verse's mutual counsel in truth prevents loss by deviation; Hebrews commands daily reciprocal exhortation so that sin's deceit does not harden anyone.

row.basis: spur one another to good works
row.note: The verse combines good deeds with mutual urging; Hebrews asks its audience to consider how to stimulate one another to love and good works.
The verse pairs right action and sabr; Paul urges hearers not to grow weary in doing good because a harvest comes if they do not give up.

The verse's sabr belongs to the exception from loss; James says steadfastness must complete its work so the believers are complete and lacking nothing, joining endurance to the opposite of deficiency.
The commentary juxtaposes universal loss with directed good work; Paul urges steadfast abundance in the Lord's work because such labor is not in vain, specifying the exception to futility.

row.basis: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary reads Arabic amal as effort put to work; Ecclesiastes asks what profit a human has from all his Hebrew amal under the sun, testing whether strenuous effort yields gain.

row.basis: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's worked force is aimed at a result; Qoheleth reviews his handiwork and toil, calls it vapor and finds no gain, giving the same root's Hebrew toil a counterpoint of frustrated outcome.

The commentary makes loss a deviation from the line; Qoheleth places what cannot be straightened beside what is lacking and cannot be counted, joining crookedness and deficiency without equating them.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's khusr is a loss connected with the wrong course; Proverbs contrasts the satisfied righteous eater with the wicked person's stomach that lacks, making deprivation follow an ethical contrast.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary exempts good action from loss; Proverbs says the one who gives to the poor will not lack, relating an enacted good deed to the absence of Hebrew deficiency.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's human loss has a faithful exception; the psalm says seekers of the Lord lack no good thing even while young lions hunger, giving Hebrew lack a specific exception.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary treats loss as leaving the right course; the shepherded speaker says he shall not lack, and the psalm's guidance setting makes security from deficiency the effect of being led.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's haqq is what holds the deed to its true line; the psalmist wishes his ways established for keeping God's statutes, using the Hebrew root for prescribed bounds in a prayer about directed conduct.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary makes haqq the guiding line for action; the psalmist asks to learn the way of God's statutes and keep it to the end, where Hebrew prescribed ordinances organize the path.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש; table sound correspondence, BDB note
row.note: The commentary's insan can be the human set in the path of a blow; the psalm uses Hebrew enosh for a person whose days are like grass, emphasizing the mortal vulnerability of that target.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש; table sound correspondence, BDB note
row.note: The commentary's insan is exposed to loss except under right conduct; Eliphaz asks whether Hebrew enosh, mortal man, can be just before God, making human frailty a question about righteousness.
The commentary defines loss as straying; God calls his people lost sheep whom shepherds led astray on mountains, giving loss an agent and a wandering route.

row.basis: all turn to their own way
row.note: The commentary says the human is in loss understood as deviation; the servant poem says all have wandered like sheep and each has turned to his own way, then places their iniquity on the servant.
The commentary makes loss a move off the line; Peter tells his addressees they had been straying like sheep but have now returned to the shepherd of their souls.
The commentary's khusr is deviation; Jesus describes a sheep that has strayed and the owner leaving the ninety nine to seek it, making recovery the response to lost direction.
The commentary equates loss with going astray; the shepherd in Jesus' question goes after the one lost sheep until he finds it, giving the lost state an active remedy.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's haqq is a line from which the thrust does not swerve; Wisdom recalls God assigning the sea its prescribed boundary so its waters would not transgress, a spatial use of Hebrew ḥoq rather than a claim that the words mean the same thing.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary gives the successful blow a fixed line; God says he prescribed the sea's bounds and set its bars and doors, a Hebrew enactment of a limit that controls movement.
The commentary makes loss departure from truth; the psalmist seeks God with his whole heart and asks not to wander from God's commandments, making deviation a danger within devotion.
The commentary understands khusr as straying; the psalmist confesses wandering like a lost sheep and asks to be sought, while still remembering God's commandments.
The commentary's right action proceeds without deviating; Moses orders Israel to act as commanded and not turn right or left, a law shaped version of the unswerving course.

row.basis: seeming right way ends in death
row.note: The commentary distinguishes truth from the deviation that produces loss; Proverbs warns that a way can seem right to a person yet end in death, testing apparent aim against its outcome.

The commentary's target image asks whether a course really hits the right end; this repeated proverb says a way may seem right to a person yet lead to death, reinforcing that appearance of direction is insufficient.
The commentary joins haqq with the path that avoids deviation; Jesus calls himself the way and the truth and the life, locating true direction in a person in this passage.
The commentary's amal is exertion aimed at a target; Paul presses on toward the goal for the prize of God's call, making directed effort explicit without a striking weapon.
The commentary ties directed action to sabr; Hebrews calls for endurance in the race set before the community, a sustained course rather than a single unswerving thrust.
The commentary's faithful workers must keep from swerving into loss; Colossians conditions its hope on continuing in faith, established and steadfast, without moving away from the gospel's hope.
The verse's believers recommend patience; Paul boasts of the community's steadfastness and faith amid persecutions and afflictions, giving sabr a social setting of pressure.
The verse pairs action and patient persistence; Hebrews says the audience needs endurance so that, after doing God's will, they may receive the promise.
The commentary's thrust penetrates inward; Simeon tells Mary a sword will pierce her own soul and thoughts of many hearts will be revealed, making interior wounding disclose what is hidden.

row.basis: truth cast down in dispute over humanity
row.note: The commentary cites God hurling truth against falsehood while the human stands in loss; the midrash has Truth object to humanity's creation because humans lie, then God casts Truth to the ground, changing the direction and target of the cast.
The commentary's truth is thrown as an effective force; the psalm says truth springs from the earth while righteousness looks from heaven, the verse Genesis Rabbah 8:5 uses after Truth is cast down.

row.basis: straight path chosen by a person
row.note: The commentary makes human action an aimed course that can deviate; the mishnah asks which straight path a person should choose and evaluates the path by honor to the doer and from others.
The commentary makes amal effective exertion and contrasts it with loss; Proverbs says all toil has profit while mere lip talk leads to want, testing whether effort results in gain.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's exception from loss requires sustained right direction; Nehemiah recalls God sustaining Israel for forty wilderness years so they lacked nothing, giving Hebrew lack a historical case of provision on a journey.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's loss is linked to error; Proverbs contrasts righteous lips that feed many with fools dying for lack of sense, a concrete moral and verbal setting for Hebrew deficiency.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש; table sound correspondence, BDB note
row.note: The commentary places insan in a vulnerable human position; the psalm asks what Hebrew enosh is that God remembers him, emphasizing how small a mortal is within the larger creation.
The commentary cites God hurling truth against falsehood; Daniel's hostile horn casts truth to the ground while acting successfully, reversing the agent, direction and immediate outcome of the cast.
The commentary's penetrating projectile carries haqq; Jeremiah calls the deceitful tongue a deadly arrow even as the speaker offers a neighbor peace, assigning the weapon to false speech.
The commentary's truth is launched at falsehood; the plotters sharpen their tongues like swords and aim bitter words like arrows, making malicious speech the projectile instead.
The commentary's unswerving strike serves haqq; the conspirators shoot suddenly at the blameless without fear, giving the preceding verbal arrows an innocent human target.
The commentary presents a directed blow against falsehood; after addressing a deceitful tongue, the psalm answers it with a warrior's sharp arrows and burning coals.
The commentary says truth thrown upon falsehood breaks its target; God compares his word to fire and to a hammer that breaks rock, making authoritative speech a destroying force.
The commentary's truth becomes an effective weapon; God tells Jeremiah he will make the words in the prophet's mouth fire and this people wood for it to consume.
The commentary's haqq is a blow that reaches its object; God says he has hewn the people by prophets and killed them with the words of his mouth, linking speech to a bodily strike.

The commentary's worked blow does not swerve or miss; God's outgoing word will not return empty but will accomplish the purpose for which he sent it, making successful arrival central without a weapon image.
The commentary's projectile carries truth toward falsehood; Proverbs pictures a reckless person throwing firebrands, arrows and death before identifying deceptive treatment of a neighbor.
The commentary's directed action is answerable to haqq; the comparison's target is a person who deceives a neighbor and says he was only joking, exposing a false excuse for the preceding projectiles.

row.basis: word lodged like arrow in flesh
row.note: The commentary brings together a penetrating weapon, an inward bodily destination and speech; Sirach likens a word lodged inside a fool to an arrow stuck in a person's thigh, though its point is the fool's urge to let the word out.
The commentary hears an inward striking force in haqq; Sirach says a tongue's blow can break bones, treating speech as bodily violence in a warning about harmful talk.
The commentary's verbal truth has a weapon's effect; Sirach compares deaths by sword with still more falls caused by the tongue, emphasizing the dangerous reach of words.

row.basis: worker handles word of truth rightly
row.note: The commentary joins amal as directed effort to haqq as an unswerving result; Timothy is told to be an approved worker who handles the word of truth rightly and need not be ashamed.

row.basis: word of truth and righteous weapons
row.note: The commentary lets truth function as a directed weapon; Paul places the word of truth and God's power beside weapons of righteousness in his account of ministry.
The commentary's truth strikes what has deviated; the speaker commands repentance and threatens to fight the offenders with the sword of his mouth, giving verbal judgment a stated target.
The commentary reads haqq as a penetrating projectile; John's vision gives the exalted figure a sharp two edged sword issuing from his mouth, a recurring image of forceful utterance.
The commentary's blow reaches the inside; the continuation of the piercing word says no creature is hidden and all are exposed before God, identifying what the inward reach discloses.
The commentary's directed work and haqq meet in combat imagery; the exhortation has believers fasten truth around the waist as part of their equipment before naming the word as a sword.
The exception names righteous action and sabr in response to loss; Paul describes people seeking eternal life through patient persistence in good work.
The commentary treats right action as force aimed on a line; Timothy is told to pursue righteousness, faith and endurance, putting the verse's qualities into directed motion.
The exception combines deeds and patience; the address to Ephesus names its works, toil and endurance and says it cannot bear evil people.
The commentary's right effort must keep its course; the same address says the community has endured for the speaker's name and has not grown weary.
The exception joins faith with sabr; this call amid captivity and death names the endurance and faith of the saints, an earlier formulation of the combination.
The commentary pairs truth counsel with patience; the address says its hearers have kept the speaker's word of endurance, joining faithful response to utterance with perseverance.
The verse says believers mutually commend truth; Colossians asks that Christ's word dwell in them as they teach and admonish one another in wisdom, supplying an explicit communal verbal act.
The verse's tawasaw bil haqq is mutual; Ephesians tells each person to put off falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor because they belong to one another.
The verse joins reciprocal counsel and sabr; Paul asks the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with everyone.
The verse couples recommending truth with patience; Timothy is instructed to proclaim the word, correct and exhort with complete patience and teaching.

row.basis: word held through labor without vain result
row.note: The commentary contrasts lost effort with a true directed word; Paul asks the community to hold fast the word of life so he can say he neither ran nor labored in vain.
The commentary's weapon image meets its mutual exhortation; Proverbs says iron sharpens iron as one person sharpens another, giving reciprocal correction the action of preparing a blade.
The commentary combines an operated weapon with mutual guidance toward truth; Proverbs says battle is waged by wise guidance and victory comes through many counselors.
The commentary's exhortation prevents departure from the true line; Proverbs puts heeding instruction on a path to life and says rejecting reproof leads astray.

row.basis: foolish way versus listening to counsel
row.note: The commentary's loss is a missed course that mutual truth can correct; Proverbs contrasts a fool whose way is right in his own eyes with a wise person who listens to advice.

row.basis: false way rejected by right precepts
row.note: The commentary places haqq opposite deviation; the psalmist regards all God's precepts as right and hates every false way, stating both sides of that choice together.

row.basis: false way put away by teaching
row.note: The commentary's counsel of truth wards off a wrong line; the psalmist asks for the false way to be removed and for God's law to be graciously taught.
The commentary's good action follows an unswerving course; the psalmist holds his feet back from every evil way in order to keep God's word.
The commentary cites God sending truth as a force; the psalmist asks God to send light and truth to lead him to the holy hill, turning the sent truth into guidance along a route.
The commentary makes haqq the line that prevents loss; the psalmist asks God to guide him in truth and teach him, joining truthful instruction to a directed path.
The commentary contrasts the accurate course with loss by deviation; Proverbs says integrity guides the upright while the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them.

row.basis: evil devisers stray, good devisers gain fidelity
row.note: The commentary opposes wrong direction to effective good action; Proverbs asks whether devisers of evil go astray and promises steadfast love and faithfulness to devisers of good.
The commentary makes loss a wrong course; the psalm contrasts the Lord's knowledge of the righteous way with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving each path its outcome.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's haqq directs action without deviation; Wisdom says rulers decree justice by her, using Hebrew ḥqq for an authoritative prescription joined to right judgment.

row.basis: ح ق ق / חקק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's haqq is the true course; Isaiah condemns rulers who enact unjust decrees, showing that a Hebrew ḥqq prescription can itself be crooked rather than true.

row.basis: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary gives human work an intended outcome yet places humanity in loss; the psalm says builders labor in vain unless the Lord builds the house, making Hebrew toil's success conditional.

row.basis: ع م ل / עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary couples effective work to mutual counsel; Qoheleth says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their Hebrew toil, supplying a concrete benefit to shared effort.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary calls loss a moral deviation; Qoheleth describes a wealthy person lacking nothing desired yet unable to enjoy it, showing that absence of Hebrew material lack can still coexist with frustrated gain.

row.basis: خ س ر / חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's loss follows a wrong course; a covenant curse says Israel will serve enemies in hunger, thirst and lack of everything, making Hebrew deficiency an outcome of disobedience in its context.

row.basis: unjust decree turns needy from justice
row.note: The commentary's haqq is a blow that does not deviate; the continuation of Isaiah's unjust decrees says they turn the needy aside from justice, spelling out the harmful deviation enacted by such rules.

The commentary gives truth an effective strike against falsehood; Isaiah instead portrays truth stumbling in the public square while justice is turned back, a specific reversal of truth's immediate success.

row.basis: truth absent and upright person prey
row.note: The commentary says the faithful escape loss by truth and right conduct; Isaiah says truth is missing and the one who turns from evil becomes prey, exposing a contrary outcome for the upright.
The commentary's haqq functions through a forceful utterance; Jesus asks that his disciples be sanctified in truth and identifies God's word as truth, giving the verbal and moral terms a direct link.
The commentary opposes truth to falsehood as a forceful conflict; Jesus calls the devil a murderer and the father of lies, giving false speech a destructive agent rather than a neutral wrong turn.

The commentary's effective truth is cast against its opponent; James calls the tongue a fire that stains the body and sets a life's course ablaze, a contrary example of speech as uncontrolled destructive force.
The verse's exception combines righteous deeds and patience; Peter asks those who suffer in accordance with God's will to entrust themselves to the faithful Creator while continuing to do good.

cost_basis: API-equivalent at codexrun.RATES (Codex subscription; usage counts)
