row.note: Daniel explains the writing against Belshazzar as a weighing that finds him deficient; the commentary likewise reads loss as an account coming up light at judgment, though Daniel addresses a king's immediate downfall.

The Aramaic verdict says Belshazzar was found lacking after weighing; this gives the commentary's خسر as deficit at the scales a precise semantic analogue, while the proposed root correspondence remains unverified.
Daniel first says Belshazzar's kingdom has been numbered and brought to an end; this joins the commentary's allotted time to the closing of a judicial account.
At the heavenly court books are opened before judgment; this corresponds to the commentary's deeds present as a record when each person's account closes.
Daniel's people whose names are found written in the book are delivered at the time of distress; the commentary likewise makes a recorded status matter at the decisive day.
Daniel distinguishes the awakened dead by everlasting life or disgrace; this corresponds to the commentary's final division of good and bad, with a bodily resurrection in Daniel's setting.

row.basis: time for every work and judgment
row.note: Qoheleth says God will judge righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work; this directly joins the commentary's allotted time, work, and judgment.

row.basis: every deed and hidden thing judged
row.note: Qoheleth says God will bring every deed, including hidden good or evil, to judgment; the commentary similarly makes even tiny acts present at the final account.

Qoheleth asks what gain a person gets from all his toil under the sun; the commentary hears human loss beside work and passing time, though this verse questions earthly gain rather than announcing final punishment.
Qoheleth surveys his works and toil and finds no lasting gain; this sharpens the commentary's accounting sense of human loss, while its exception for good deeds gives another outcome.
Qoheleth urges doing whatever work one's hand finds because the grave has no work; the commentary likewise treats time as a deadline for deeds that later face accounting.

row.basis: let God weigh in just scales
row.note: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity; the commentary likewise pictures scales settling a person's case by what he has done.

row.basis: Hebrew חקק in fixed bounds; table sound correspondence
row.note: Job says human days and their limits have been prescribed and cannot be crossed; this makes concrete the commentary's appointed term within its reading of حَقّ and the day of reckoning, without equating Hebrew statute with Arabic truth.
Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows excuses and repays each person according to work; this combines the commentary's scales, personal deeds, and binding recompense.

row.basis: apparently pure ways weighed by God
row.note: A person sees his ways as pure, but the Lord weighs the spirits; this probes the commentary's case of people confident their work is good before divine measurement.
Proverbs attributes just scales and weights to the Lord; this anchors the commentary's judgment-day balance in a concrete image of divine fairness.
The Lord searches the heart and repays each person according to ways and fruit of deeds; the commentary's day likewise brings each person to the consequence of his work.

God says he will judge each Israelite according to that person's ways and calls for repentance; this gives the commentary's individual work-based account a setting where conduct can still change before judgment.
The psalm says the Lord repays a person according to work; this is the same work-to-recompense relation used to explain the commentary's appointed day.

The psalm places human ranks in balances and finds them lighter than breath; the commentary likewise visualizes human loss as insufficient weight, though the psalm weighs human frailty and pretension.

row.basis: speak together and book of remembrance
row.note: Those who fear the Lord speak to one another and a book of remembrance is written before him; this joins the surah's mutual counsel to the commentary's record of deeds.

At God's coming action people will again distinguish the righteous from the wicked and the one who serves God from one who does not; the commentary likewise ends with good and bad separated by their conduct.
The Lord names the day on which he acts and spares those he calls his own; this supplies a concrete appointed-day counterpart to the commentary's exception from loss.
Judah's sin is written with an iron stylus on the tablet of the heart; this gives a bodily image of deeds as an enduring record beside the commentary's account attached to each person.
God says the offense is written before him and that he will repay; this pairs the commentary's present record of acts with inescapable recompense.
The psalm says God sets iniquities and secret sins before him; the commentary likewise says what people did will be present rather than lost from the account.
God says he will set the wrongdoer's acts before his eyes when rebuking him; this closely matches the commentary's claim that one's own deeds confront one at judgment.
The Amorites' iniquity has not yet reached its full measure, delaying judgment; this provides an appointed accumulation of evil beside the commentary's heap of bad deeds.

The person rooted in the Lord's instruction prospers in what he does; this gives the commentary's righteous works an outcome opposed to loss, although Hebrew prosperity is not identical to Arabic صالح deeds.
Joshua is told to observe and do the law so his way will prosper; the link to the commentary is the joined action and favorable result, with only a proposed sound correspondence between roots.
Jeremiah asks why the way of the wicked prospers even though God is just; that apparent present success complicates the commentary's final separation of good works from loss.
The psalm urges waiting before the Lord while a person carrying out wicked schemes prospers; its temporary success reverses the commentary's judgment-day valuation of works.

Daniel prospers after his deliverance from the lions; this gives a narrative setting for good outcome after steadfastness beside the commentary's good work and patience, without making the roots proven cognates.
The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's belly lacks; this maps the commentary's good/bad division onto a concrete lack, though Proverbs speaks of present provision.
The psalm says seekers of the Lord lack no good thing; that absence of lack is a pointed counterpart to the commentary's exception from human loss.

Proverbs calls the adulterer lacking in sense and says he destroys himself; the commentary's loss through sinful deeds gains a specific self-destructive example, though the Hebrew lack first denotes understanding.
Deuteronomy reserves vengeance and repayment for the time when the wrongdoers' foot slips; the commentary likewise lets a fixed time mature into binding recompense.
Proverbs tells the hearer to bind loyalty and truth around the neck; the commentary's record bound to each person's neck meets a contrasting image in which truth is what one chooses to carry.

row.basis: speak truth to neighbor and judge justly
row.note: Zechariah joins truthful speech to one's neighbor with judgments of truth and peace at the gates; this gives the surah's mutual counsel in truth a communal judicial setting.
Paul says God has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness; this directly corresponds to the commentary's named day on which the claim of justice becomes binding.
The Son of Man comes in glory and repays each person according to conduct; the commentary likewise brings everyone to an appointed day and settles the account by works.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the world while forfeiting one's life; this gives the commentary's human loss a pointed accounting comparison.
Paul says God repays each person according to works; this precisely matches the commentary's explanation that the day assigns each human a consequence by work.
Paul assigns eternal life to those who persist in doing good; this combines the commentary's good deeds, patient endurance, and exception from loss.
Paul contrasts those who reject truth and follow wrongdoing with the patient doers of good, assigning wrath; this connects the commentary's communicated truth and bad works to its final division.
All must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive what is due for deeds, good or bad; this is a close counterpart to the commentary's two classes of work and inescapable accounting.
The dead stand before the throne while books are opened and are judged by what their works record; this joins the commentary's present deeds to its individual ledger and final tribunal.
Death and Hades yield the dead, who are judged individually according to deeds; the commentary likewise insists each person meets the consequence of his own work.
The coming speaker brings recompense to repay everyone for what each has done; this links the commentary's approaching appointed day to personal reward.
The Son of Man gathers the nations and separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; this supplies a scene for the commentary's final sorting of good from bad.
The welcomed people fed the hungry and gave drink to the thirsty; the commentary's righteous deeds gain small, tangible instances used in the final verdict.

row.basis: act for the least counted for the king
row.note: The king says deeds done for one of the least of his family were done for him; this makes the commentary's minute good deed unexpectedly weighty at final judgment.
The rejected are sent to eternal fire after the separation; this connects the commentary's inverted patience, doing the works of fire's people, to a final destination.
The passage concludes with punishment for one group and life for the righteous; this matches the commentary's decisive division after the accounting.
Jesus describes angels separating evil people from righteous at the end of the age; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's end-time distinction between bad and good.
Anyone absent from the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire; this joins the commentary's record and the fire-bound consequence of evil work.

row.basis: spur one another to good works
row.note: The community is to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works; this parallels the surah's mutual counsel and righteous action as a collective practice.
Believers are to encourage one another increasingly as they see the Day approaching; this meets both the surah's reciprocal exhortation and the commentary's deadline.

row.basis: exhort one another while today lasts
row.note: The community is told to exhort one another daily while it is called Today, lest sin harden them; this makes mutual counsel a time-limited defense against losing one's way.
The saints' endurance is described as keeping God's commands and faith in Jesus; this places patience, faith, and action together beside the surah's exception.
God is just and will not forget the work and love shown in service; this complements the commentary's claim that deeds remain present for a just account.
The community is urged to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this gives the surah's faith and endurance an explicit outcome.
Paul says a person reaps what he sows; this is another precise work-to-consequence formula for the commentary's day of settlement.
Paul separates sowing to flesh from sowing to Spirit, with corruption or eternal life as outcomes; this parallels the commentary's good/bad work distinction and loss.

row.basis: do good patiently until due season
row.note: Paul urges not wearying in doing good because harvest comes at the right time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's good deeds, patience, and appointed term.
The faithful are urged to abound in the Lord's work because their labor is not vain; this directly reverses the surah's general human loss through faithful action.
Paul says a burned work brings loss while its worker may still be saved through fire; this complicates the commentary's alignment of deficient works, personal loss, and fire.
The Day exposes each person's work and fire tests its quality; this is a concrete counterpart to deeds becoming present and differentiated at judgment.
Many appeal to prophecy, exorcism, and mighty works done in Jesus' name on that day; this mirrors the commentary's people who think their efforts good before judgment.
Jesus rejects those claimants as workers of lawlessness; the commentary likewise says apparent good effort can prove valueless when the actual work is judged.
Jesus says people will give account on judgment day even for careless speech; this gives the commentary's tiny measured deed a speech-sized counterpart.
Jesus says a cup of water given to his people will not lose its reward; this answers the commentary's claim that even the smallest good is seen in the account.

row.basis: hidden matters disclosed and praise allotted
row.note: At the Lord's coming, hidden things and heart motives are brought to light before praise is assigned; this parallels the commentary's deeds made present, while adding intent to visible work.
Paul says a hard heart stores up wrath for the day of righteous judgment; this meets the commentary's accumulated evil and appointed day.
Jesus tells his opponents to fill up the measure of their ancestors; this makes moral evil accumulate toward judgment like the commentary's bad things piled one on another.
The corrosion of hoarded riches testifies against the rich, who have stored treasure in the last days; the commentary's bad accumulation likewise becomes evidence at the final reckoning.
God tells the rich planner that his life is required that night and asks who will own his stores; this makes the commentary's deadline and lost balance concrete in an unexpected accounting.
Peter distinguishes endurance under punishment for sin from endurance when one does good and suffers; this clarifies the commentary's reversal of patience into work meriting fire.
The Lord's revelation in fire brings punishment upon those who disobey the gospel; this connects the commentary's fire-bound work to a judicial rather than merely physical fire.
The psalm asks to number our days so that wisdom may follow; this supports the commentary's allotted-time reading, though it teaches present wisdom rather than describing final scales.
Job imagines his transgression sealed in a bag before God; this offers another personal record of wrong beside the commentary's deeds kept for later confrontation.
God says the one who sins against him will be erased from his book; this reverses the commentary's image of acts attached to the person while keeping the same individual-account logic.

row.basis: remember deeds and do not blot them
row.note: Nehemiah asks God not to wipe out his deeds done for the temple; the commentary's good works present at judgment have a concrete prayer for preserved memory.

Isaiah condemns those who decree unjust decrees; this sets an unjust human use of prescribed law against the commentary's binding just recompense on the day, without treating Hebrew lawmaking as Arabic truth.
Proverbs tells the hearer to tie parental teaching around the neck; beside the commentary's deed record attached there, this shows a life-guiding text voluntarily carried before judgment.
The one who gives to the poor will not lack, while ignoring them brings curses; this gives the commentary's good-deed exception from loss a material example.

The psalmist understands the prosperous wicked only after entering God's sanctuary and considering their end; this interprets the commentary's loss as an eventual outcome beyond apparent present success.
Job says humans are born to trouble; this shares the commentary's universal human condition but locates it in earthly toil rather than necessarily in punishment for misdeeds.
The Mishnah says all inhabitants of the world pass before God for judgment at the new year; this interprets the commentary's every-person account through a recurring Jewish liturgical day.
The Talmud speaks of books opened for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate at the new year; this gives the commentary's present deeds and good/bad division a specific Jewish record tradition.

The discussion urges a person to imagine oneself and the world balanced between merit and liability so one deed can tip the outcome; this interprets the commentary's minute weighed acts as morally consequential.
Avot describes an open ledger, a writing hand, collectors, and a true judgment of all actions; this supplies a detailed account metaphor for the commentary's closing of each person's record.
Avot says one commandment gains an advocate and one transgression an accuser; this personifies the commentary's good and bad acts standing ready when judged.

row.basis: give an account to the King
row.note: Avot says a person will eventually give a reckoning before the King of kings; this parallels the commentary's inevitable personal settlement after one's allotted life.
Avot urges calculating a commandment's loss against its reward and a sin's gain against its loss; this gives the commentary's profit-and-deficit language an explicit moral ledger tradition.
Hebrews says human death is appointed once, followed by judgment; this gives the commentary's allotted time and settling day a succinct sequence.

row.basis: world kept for judgment by fire
row.note: The present world is kept for the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly by fire; this connects the commentary's deadline to the fire-bound result of bad works.

row.basis: patience until coming as farmer waits
row.note: James tells believers to wait patiently for the Lord's coming like a farmer awaiting the crop; this gives the surah's patience and the commentary's appointed end a seasonal image.
The warning against grumbling says the Judge is standing at the doors; this ties communal conduct while waiting to an imminent accounting.
Believers are instructed to speak truth with neighbors because they belong to one another; this gives the surah's reciprocal counsel in truth a communal relation.

row.basis: impressive charity without love gains nothing
row.note: Even giving away all possessions gains nothing without love; this illuminates the commentary's apparently good efforts that prove valueless when judged by their real character.
Jesus says the humble tax collector, rather than the self-assured Pharisee, goes home justified; this offers a concrete reversal of people who suppose their own work good.
Jesus warns that righteousness performed to be seen by others receives no reward from the Father; this specifies why work that looks good might fail the commentary's account.

row.basis: work of faith and patient hope
row.note: Paul remembers the community's work of faith and endurance of hope; this places action, faith, and patience together as the surah's exception does.
God considers it just to repay affliction to those who afflict believers; this concretizes the commentary's binding recompense as reversal for injurious work.

row.basis: Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence; piled wealth
row.note: Job says a wicked person may heap up silver; the next verse transfers what he prepared to the righteous, making material accumulation and final loss an indirect counterpart to the commentary's piled evil. The Hebrew heaping sense is distinct from Arabic patience.

row.basis: wicked's stores enjoyed by just people
row.note: Job says the just will wear what the wicked prepared; this indirectly reverses the commentary's piled bad deeds into an earthly redistribution rather than an end-time scale.

row.basis: Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence; heaped goods
row.note: The psalm says a person heaps things without knowing who will gather them; this provides a time-limited loss for amassed goods, only an indirect parallel to the commentary's heap of bad works. The Hebrew heaping sense is distinct from Arabic patience.
Isaiah tells the righteous they will eat the fruit of their deeds; this is a direct good-work counterpart to the commentary's final division and recompense.
The next verse says the wicked will receive what their own hands have done; it supplies the adverse half of the commentary's work-by-work settlement.
Hosea says the people forget that God remembers their evil, while their deeds now surround them and stand before him; this closely matches the commentary's deeds found present at the account.
Elihu says God repays a person for work and causes each to find the consequence of a way; this states the commentary's personal work-to-recompense formula in another setting.

row.basis: eyes on all ways and deeds
row.note: Jeremiah praises God's eyes upon all human ways so as to give each according to conduct and the fruit of deeds; this joins the commentary's complete record to individual repayment.

Ezekiel denies that child or parent bears the other's guilt and assigns each one's righteousness or wickedness to that person; this specifies the commentary's every-person account as individually owned.

Ezekiel says a turning sinner's former transgressions will not be remembered when he lives by righteousness; this qualifies the commentary's image of every past deed remaining present in the final record.

The psalm's qualified guest walks blamelessly, does righteousness, and speaks truth in the heart; this combines good action and truth as the surah's exception does, with access to God's dwelling as its outcome.

row.basis: books of sins and stored righteousness
row.note: The apocalypse places written sins beside treasuries of righteous deeds when judgment arrives; this develops the commentary's present records and divided good and bad acts into two kinds of stored evidence.

The apocalyptic description says works follow, reward appears, good deeds awaken, and wicked deeds do not sleep; this gives the commentary's acts found present at judgment a vivid independent formulation.

row.basis: recompense at death according to conduct
row.note: Sirach says it is easy for the Lord to repay a person at death according to that person's ways; this joins the commentary's allotted term and binding individual recompense.
A voice says those who die in the Lord rest from labors and their works follow them; this closely meets the commentary's time limit, enduring good works, and deeds present afterward.

row.basis: doers of good and evil rise differently
row.note: Jesus says those who have done good rise to life and those who have done evil to judgment; this makes the commentary's good and bad deeds decisive at the final separation.
James says faith by itself is dead if it has no works; this gives the surah's pairing of belief and righteous deeds a specific consequence when action is absent.
Jesus tells threatened disciples they will gain their lives through endurance; this sets patient perseverance directly opposite the commentary's human loss.

row.basis: endure to end and be saved
row.note: The hated disciple who endures to the end will be saved; this joins the surah's patience to the commentary's deadline and exception from loss.
The risen speaker tells Sardis that its works have not been found complete before God; this is a precise counterpart to the commentary's apparently good work that fails the final assessment.

row.basis: impartial judgment of each one's work
row.note: Peter says the Father judges impartially according to each person's work and tells believers to conduct themselves in reverent fear during their time away; this joins personal deeds, just measurement, and a limited present term.
Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, the hearers may receive the promise; this links good action and patience to a future recompense.
Jesus adds that one's own words will justify or condemn; this gives the commentary's exact accounting an explicit verdict for the small speech acts named in the preceding verse.
Jesus says entry into the kingdom belongs to one doing his Father's will, which explains why the impressive acts claimed in the following verse can still fail the commentary's good-work test.
The rejected did not feed the hungry or give drink to the thirsty; this supplies the negative half of the commentary's smallest deed carrying weight at the division.
The speaker says he searches mind and heart and will give each person according to works; this adds the inward quality of deeds to the commentary's personal final account.
Daniel's third explanation says Belshazzar's kingdom is divided and given away; it specifies what is lost when the weighed account in the preceding verse proves deficient.

Proverbs contrasts gain from labor with need arising from mere talk, using the table's Hebrew lack root; this is a present-life analogue to the commentary's work and loss account, not an end-time verdict.

row.basis: Hebrew חקק in decree; table sound correspondence
row.note: Zephaniah urges action before the decree takes effect and before the Lord's angry day arrives; this places a prescribed term beside the commentary's appointed judgment day, while the root link remains unverified.

After the fruitful righteous person, the psalm depicts wicked people as chaff driven away by wind; this supplies a contrasting failure of substance beside the commentary's separated losers, without asserting a literal scale.

The apocalyptic court opens books of the living before the divine presence; this develops the commentary's record-and-day scene, though the books concern those counted as living rather than a list of every act.
Ephesians explicitly denies that salvation arises from works, complicating a reading of the commentary's good deeds as the basis of rescue from loss.
The next verse says believers are made for good works prepared for them to walk in; this preserves good action alongside the preceding grace claim and the surah's believing doers.
Paul says faith works through love; this gives the surah's paired belief and action a concrete communal form rather than treating faith as mere assent.
Peter says the Lord's apparent delay expresses patience so people may repent; this gives the commentary's appointed day a different role for patience, allowing change before the account closes.
The rejected ask when they failed to serve the king in his needs; their surprise is a concrete instance of the commentary's people who misjudge the worth of their own conduct.
The Laodiceans claim to need nothing but are called poor and exposed; this supplies the commentary's self-mistaken assessment with a striking deficit image.
Jesus says greater trust brings a greater demand; this is a specific proportional-account rule beside the commentary's precise weighing of each person's acts.
Paul promises relief to the afflicted when the Lord is revealed; this completes the reversal of affliction and repayment in the surrounding judgment passage and the commentary's righteous exception.

Augustine discusses the books opened at the last judgment as a disclosure of what people have done, possibly through divine recall rather than physical ledgers; this changes how the commentary's visible account can be imagined.

row.basis: qere לו; deeds measured by God
row.note: In Hannah's song the traditional qere makes God the one by whom deeds are measured, closely matching the commentary's scales for human action; WLC's written ketiv ולא differs, so this connection depends on the named reading.

row.basis: WLC ketiv ולא versus qere לו
row.note: The written ketiv can be read as denying that deeds are measured, unlike the commentary's scales; the familiar qere gives the opposite sense, so the reversal is textually uncertain and should be checked against the WLC stream.

A scene in this recension appears to bring a soul's merits and sins into a heavenly weighing, close to the commentary's personal balance; the chapter placement and the roles of the heavenly figures are uncertain from memory.

cost_basis: API-equivalent at codexrun.RATES (Codex subscription; usage counts)

row.basis: gain the world, forfeit the life
row.note: The commentary makes the trader's final capital his own self; Jesus asks what profit the whole world brings if a person forfeits his life, making the apparent gain a net personal loss.
The commentary reads loss of one's self as the last entry in the account; this verse explicitly asks what benefit remains when a person gains the world but loses or forfeits himself.
The commentary distinguishes apparent accumulation from the true balance; Paul says things once counted as gains became loss for Christ, reversing his own ledger.
The commentary's trade between perishing capital and lasting gain has a close counterpart in Paul's reckoning of everything as loss compared with gaining Christ.

row.basis: profit from toil under the sun
row.note: The commentary joins time, work and the merchant's question about real gain; Ecclesiastes asks what profit a human has from all the toil he toils under the sun.

row.basis: root table ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary puts a lifetime's work in the loss account; the speaker surveys works done by his hands and the עמל spent on them, finding no lasting profit under the sun.
The commentary treats passing time as spent capital; the psalm asks God to teach humans to number their days so that they gain a wise heart.
The commentary's late day and dwindling lifetime meet this psalm's seventy or eighty years, their toil and trouble, and their swift passing.

row.basis: riches fail on day of wrath
row.note: The commentary contrasts counted money with the final moral account; the proverb says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death.
The commentary's profitable trade through right action meets the proverb's claim that wicked treasure yields no profit but righteousness rescues from death.
The commentary sets money counted as increase against the loss of the owner himself; God asks the rich fool whose stored goods will be his when his life is demanded that night.
The commentary describes a hidden deficit while possessions grow; Jesus concludes that one who stores treasure for himself can fail to be rich toward God.
The commentary stresses a loss one does not feel; Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing while failing to know its poverty and blindness.

row.basis: Moses notices fire in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary follows Moses noticing fire on a journey and seeking guidance; Exodus places the divine fire in a bush that burns without being consumed, specifying the sight he is drawn to investigate.

row.basis: Moses turns to inspect unconsumed bush
row.note: In the commentary's Qur'anic scene Moses hopes for an ember or guide for his family; in Exodus he turns aside to inspect why the burning bush is not consumed, a different immediate purpose for approaching the fire.
The commentary's seller secretly reduces the buyer's portion; Leviticus forbids injustice in measures of length, weight and quantity, grounding the market image in a concrete legal rule.

row.basis: two different weights in one bag
row.note: The commentary describes one trader using different scales depending on whether he takes or gives; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small weight together in one's bag.

row.basis: small measure, great price, false balances
row.note: The commentary's two-directional fraud matches merchants in Amos who shrink the ephah, enlarge the shekel and falsify balances while selling grain.
The commentary joins fair weighing to moral truth; the proverb calls a false balance abominable to the Lord and a just weight his delight.

row.basis: God weighs the person on a just balance
row.note: The commentary moves from market scales to the weighing of a person's own worth; Job asks that God weigh him in a just balance and know his integrity.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary joins a deficient balance to personal loss; Daniel interprets TEKEL as the king weighed in the balances and found חַסִּיר, lacking.
The commentary's final scale finds the person himself light rather than a short measure of goods; Daniel pronounces that the king has been weighed and found deficient.

row.basis: way seeming right ends in death
row.note: The commentary's gravest loser believes his work is good while straying; this proverb says a way can seem right to a person yet end in the ways of death.
The commentary says its judgment first includes the whole human kind and describes loss as going astray; Isaiah says all like sheep have strayed, each turning to his own way.

row.basis: all turned aside, none doing good
row.note: The commentary's generic human is under a negative verdict before an exception is named; the psalm says all have turned aside and none does good, giving a parallel universal diagnosis.
The commentary emphasizes a judgment on humanity as a class; Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, a comparably universal shortfall.
The commentary contrasts the human's good created condition with a later loss; Ecclesiastes says God made humanity upright but people sought many schemes.

row.basis: return to dust after mortal labor
row.note: The commentary treats time and the self as capital that finally runs out; the judgment on Adam makes his eating by sweat end in a return to dust.

row.basis: work tested by fire on the day
row.note: The commentary joins work, judgment and a fire storm that can erase a lifetime's produce; Paul says the Day and its fire disclose the quality of each person's work.
The commentary's ultimate deficit can be loss of the self; Paul describes a person's work burning and that person suffering loss yet being saved through fire, a narrower outcome for loss.

row.basis: fruit dried by east wind and burned
row.note: The commentary imagines a life's crop ruined by a destructive wind with fire; Ezekiel's vine is uprooted, its fruit dried by the east wind and its branches consumed by fire.

row.basis: storm destroys house without secure foundation
row.note: The commentary opposes a refuge to exposure when destructive weather arrives; Jesus' rain, floods and winds strike the house built on sand, which falls greatly.

row.basis: face reflected in water, heart answered by another
row.note: The commentary's small image of a person seen in another's eye bridges solitary self-knowledge and mutual counsel; the proverb makes a reflected face the analogy for one human heart answering another.

row.basis: reprove neighbor to prevent shared sin
row.note: The commentary's escape from loss includes people recommending truth to one another; Leviticus requires frank correction of a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin because of him.

row.basis: exhort one another every day called Today
row.note: The commentary unites expiring time with reciprocal advice against unnoticed ruin; Hebrews tells believers to exhort one another each day lest sin's deceit harden anyone.

row.basis: mutual stirring toward love and good deeds
row.note: The commentary's exception joins good action to mutual counsel; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to stir love and good works.
The commentary's generic human remains in an ongoing condition of loss; this psalm addresses God as returning mortals to dust, putting humanity inside a bounded mortal state.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary names the generic visible human and asks what loss takes from such a being; the psalm calls the person אֱנוֹשׁ while asking why God remembers him, emphasizing mortal smallness beside divine regard.

row.basis: root table ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary links truth, the appointed day and a life's spent time; Job says a human's days and months are fixed and God has set his limits, using a form of חק for the allotted boundary.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary calls loss an unmeasured deficit in an account; Ecclesiastes says what is lacking, חֶסְרוֹן, cannot be counted, joining deficiency with reckoning while leaving the shortfall unresolved.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's alternative to losing one's capital is right use of it; this proverb says the one who gives to the poor will not lack, using חסר for lack and making generosity the decisive transaction.

row.basis: appointed time to judge every work
row.note: The commentary relates the passing hour to a day that brings each deed to account; Ecclesiastes says God will judge righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.
The commentary joins failing perception with losing oneself; Proverbs says the adulterer lacks sense and destroys his own life, making a hidden deficit in judgment lead to self-loss.

row.basis: claim to see leaves sin remaining
row.note: The commentary's seeing human may fail to perceive his own loss; Jesus tells his hearers that because they say they see, their sin remains.

row.basis: entrusted money traded to gain more
row.note: The commentary reads the lifetime as trading capital placed in human hands; the first servant immediately trades his master's five talents and gains five more.
The commentary distinguishes merely retaining possessions from making a profitable moral return; the fearful servant hides the entrusted talent in the ground and returns only the original sum.
The commentary says loss can consume the principal itself; Jesus' conclusion to the talents story says the one who has not will lose even what he has.

row.basis: short day, much work, great wage
row.note: The commentary imagines time as the trader's expiring capital and good deeds as work for gain; R. Tarfon's saying turns the short day, plentiful work and great wage into an urgent moral account.
The commentary's exceptions are counted by belief and deeds rather than by ancestry; Avot says one need not finish the work yet may not cease from it, and a faithful employer pays the wage.

row.basis: open shop, ledger, collectors and true judgment
row.note: The commentary's market account and final balance meet Avot's shop on credit, open ledger recording actions, daily collectors and judgment declared true.

row.basis: this world as antechamber, preparation beyond
row.note: The commentary places the human inside a temporal condition whose use determines later gain; Avot calls this world an antechamber and urges preparation there before entering the banquet hall.
The commentary notes that the exception from human loss names faith together with good works; James makes the link pointed by declaring faith dead when it has no works.
The commentary puts right action against an otherwise diminishing life's work; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in due season if one does not give up.

row.basis: wealth flies away when gazed at
row.note: The commentary's rich counter can grow while true capital melts away; Proverbs asks whether one fixes eyes on wealth that vanishes and flies toward heaven.

row.basis: toiler departs with nothing in hand
row.note: The commentary's trader can spend the principal of life and end empty; Ecclesiastes says a person departs naked as he came and takes nothing from his toil in his hand.

row.basis: great wealth destroyed in one hour
row.note: The commentary connects the late hour to a lifetime's accumulated goods lost suddenly; the lament over Babylon says its great wealth has been laid waste in one hour.
The commentary says worldly profit can conceal loss of the person; Mark's version of Jesus' question uses the same economic comparison between gaining the world and forfeiting life.

row.basis: all appear for recompense of deeds
row.note: The commentary's universal human category and final scale lead to deeds being reckoned; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they have done in the body.
The commentary spends the mortal's time toward an appointed day of reckoning; Hebrews places judgment after each human's one death.

row.basis: nothing brought in or taken out
row.note: The commentary contrasts counted goods with the person's last balance; Paul says people brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out.
The commentary uses the orphan's property to connect discerned maturity with entrusted capital; Jesus says reliability in a small matter shows reliability in a great one.
The commentary's guardian sees whether a ward is ready to receive property; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with unrighteous wealth.

row.basis: minor heir under guardians until set time
row.note: The commentary cites testing an orphan's maturity before releasing property; Paul describes an heir who, while a child, remains under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time.

row.basis: warning not to afflict widow or orphan
row.note: The commentary treats an orphan's property as a trust needing care; Exodus forbids afflicting the vulnerable widow or orphan, supplying the ethical duty behind such guardianship.
The commentary contrasts humanity's given good beginning with its later place inside loss; Genesis records God's judgment that all he made was very good.
The commentary places the human kind, not one individual, under an enveloping negative condition; Paul says death passed to all people after sin entered the world.

The commentary names an exception after its universal verdict; immediately after Paul's statement that all fall short, he says people are justified by grace through Christ, an alternate account of escape.
The commentary's exception explicitly joins faith with righteous deeds; Paul denies that salvation comes from works, sharpening a difference in how the saving relation of deeds is stated.
The commentary extends loss to losing one's way and finally perishing; the psalm contrasts God's knowledge of the righteous way with the way of the wicked that perishes.
The commentary's traveler eats through provisions after losing direction and faces ruin; Jesus describes a spacious road on which many travel toward destruction.
The commentary calls the last loss a loss of oneself and also stresses failure to perceive it; the son in the parable comes to himself after dissipating his property and falling into hunger.
The commentary juxtaposes loss of property, self and companionship; the father describes the returning son as lost and found and celebrates restored family relation.

row.basis: apparently right road ends in death
row.note: The commentary says the worst loss is the laborer who thinks his route sound; a second proverb states that a seemingly right human way ends in death.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary says the human who can notice things may miss his own deficit; Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful and אנש, desperately sick, then asks who can know it.

row.basis: God searches heart and repays deeds
row.note: The commentary opposes self-deception to an objective account of actions; Jeremiah's next verse says the Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to his ways and deeds.
The commentary's named seeing being fails to see the situation he is in; Paul says the minds of unbelievers are blinded so they do not see the gospel's light.
The commentary's reflected self in another's eye leads to reciprocal truth telling; Jesus says first to remove one's own obstruction so one can see clearly to help a brother with his.

row.basis: indirect reflection and eventual face-to-face sight
row.note: The commentary uses a tiny reflected face to describe limited self-knowledge through another person; Paul describes present seeing through a mirror dimly and later face-to-face knowing.
The commentary says the solitary human emerges from loss through others' counsel; Proverbs makes one person sharpen another as iron sharpens iron.
The commentary moves from the isolated human to someone who receives truth from another; Avot tells a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, naming relationships as part of moral formation.
The commentary treats companionship and mutual counsel as an exit from solitary loss; this maxim explicitly warns against separating oneself from the community.
The commentary's third verse replaces the isolated figure with mutual exhortation; Paul directs believers to encourage one another and build one another up.
The commentary develops a beast carrying a load and then humans helping each other on the way; Paul converts burden bearing into a reciprocal command among people.

row.basis: root table ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary hears refuge against destruction in the first verse's secondary sense; the plague is עָצַר, stopped, after Phinehas intervenes, offering a concrete image of destruction held back rather than a claim that the Arabic and Hebrew senses are identical.

The commentary exposes the illusion that ever more counted wealth is safety; Job pictures the wicked heaping silver like dust before describing how another will wear it. Hebrew צבר in the root table is only a sound correspondence to Arabic صبر, not evidence of a shared meaning here.

row.basis: use wealth to make friends and find dwelling
row.note: The commentary makes reciprocal companionship an alternative to loss in the market; Jesus urges using temporary wealth to make friends who will welcome one into lasting dwellings.

row.basis: remember origin, end and final accounting
row.note: The commentary's human has an unseen deficit that an appointed day reveals; Avot asks a person to remember his beginning, his end and before whom he must give account.

row.basis: life and death lead to an account
row.note: The commentary speaks of each human brought to his due day with his deeds; Avot insists that birth, life, death and the eventual account before the divine king are inescapable.

row.basis: hearing and doing make a secure house
row.note: The commentary's refuge against a ruinous storm depends on faith and good action; Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a house built on rock.
The commentary's business account distinguishes growing sums from preserving principal; the proverb says wealth gained hastily diminishes while gathered wealth grows steadily.
The commentary's dishonest measure makes another person's principal short; James says wages withheld from harvest laborers cry out, turning economic theft into a charge before God.
The commentary joins accurate scales to one's own final condition; Deuteronomy commands a full and just weight so that the people's days may be long in the land.
The commentary's lost cultivated produce connects present deeds to a later account; Paul says people reap what they sow, making the harvest an ethical measure.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's generic insan is initially lost but its exception allows another outcome; Daniel sees one like a son of אֱנָשׁ brought before the Ancient of Days, an exalted humanlike figure. The link is limited because Daniel presents a vision figure, not a verdict on humanity as a whole.

The commentary imagines loss outside a shelter under destructive weather; David's rescue song pictures God surrounded by gathered water and thick clouds. The root table's Hebrew חשר has a possible sound relation to Arabic خ س ر but the cloud word does not mean loss; this is only an atmospheric image meeting.

row.basis: companionship or death in Honi's return
row.note: The commentary says the human needs others to escape solitary loss; the Honi story ends with his isolation when others do not recognize him and the maxim that one needs companionship or death. This extends the commentary's social image rather than interpreting its verse directly.
The commentary's worst loser thinks his own work good and cannot see his deficit; this proverb says all a person's ways look pure in his own eyes while the Lord weighs the spirits.
The commentary combines undetected wandering with a final true balance; here every human way seems right to its owner, but the Lord weighs hearts.

row.basis: rich and poor alike light on scales
row.note: The commentary's scale finds the person, not goods, deficient and disregards rank; the psalm calls people of low and high estate alike a breath, rising together on the balance as lighter than breath.

row.basis: just scales belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary joins the marketplace balance to God's true balance; Proverbs says honest scales and balances are the Lord's, and the weights in a merchant's bag are his work.
The commentary's trader accumulates money by reducing another's measure; Micah places ill-gotten treasures beside a scant measure under divine accusation.

row.basis: wicked scales and deceptive weight bag
row.note: The commentary's manipulated weights can appear balanced while cheating the buyer; Micah asks whether one can be acquitted with wicked scales and a bag of deceitful weights.

row.basis: honest weights and measures as covenant duty
row.note: The commentary's two kinds of market fraud involve weighing and measuring; Leviticus commands honest balances, weights, ephah and hin together.

row.basis: large and small measures in one house
row.note: The commentary describes a seller taking full measure but giving short measure; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small measure at home, extending its adjacent ban on unequal weights to volume.

row.basis: fraud enriches seller by taking the poor
row.note: The commentary says the fraudulent seller reduces another person's capital while growing his own; Amos continues the false-balance scene with merchants buying the poor for silver and selling even grain sweepings.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's loss account can reverse apparent financial gain; Proverbs says one gives freely and increases, while another withholds what is due and comes to מַחְסוֹר, want.
The commentary separates a cheerful or prosperous appearance from the actual account; Proverbs describes one who pretends to be rich yet has nothing, and another who seems poor yet has great wealth.

row.basis: little with righteousness better than unjust revenues
row.note: The commentary measures profit by righteous action rather than growing receipts; the proverb values a little with righteousness above large revenues gained by injustice.

row.basis: wind passes, bloom and place disappear
row.note: The commentary's storm can erase a lifetime's cultivated produce and the person who owned it; the psalm's wind passes over the mortal's flower so it is gone and its place knows it no more.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's generic insan spends a mortal lifetime as capital; this psalm calls the human אֱנוֹשׁ and compares his days to grass and his brief flourishing to a field flower.

row.basis: truthful measure sweeps false refuge away
row.note: The commentary connects a true scale with shelter from destructive weather; Isaiah makes justice a measuring line, then says hail will sweep away a refuge of lies and water flood its hiding place.

row.basis: rooted tree bears fruit and prospers in season
row.note: The commentary's alternative to losing a lifetime's crop is good work that survives its allotted time; the righteous person in the psalm is a watered tree yielding fruit in season and prospering in what he does.

row.basis: wicked driven by wind like chaff
row.note: The commentary's lost traveler and ruined crop meet the psalm's contrast: unlike the fruitful rooted tree, the wicked are chaff carried away by the wind.

row.basis: fire at night guides people on their way
row.note: The commentary joins Moses' noticed fire, a night journey and hoped-for guidance; Exodus tells of the Lord leading travelers by a pillar of fire at night so they can travel.

row.basis: human sees surface, God sees heart
row.note: The commentary says a being equipped to see can remain blind to his own real state; Samuel is told humans look at outward appearance while the Lord looks at the heart.

row.basis: fool trusts own way, wise hears advice
row.note: The commentary's mistaken confidence in one's path meets its remedy of counsel from another; the proverb says the fool's way is right in his own eyes but the wise listens to advice.

row.basis: many counselors protect against a fall
row.note: The commentary moves from one human lost alone to people helping one another find a way; the proverb says a people falls without guidance and finds safety in many counselors.

row.basis: two workers gain a better reward
row.note: The commentary joins labor and its wage to companionship as an escape from loss; Ecclesiastes says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their toil.

row.basis: companion lifts the one who falls
row.note: The commentary's lost solitary human needs another's help; Ecclesiastes blesses the one whose companion lifts him after a fall and laments the one alone with no one to lift him.
The commentary's true counsel is also likened to an accurate blow that does not miss its mark; the proverb makes even a friend's wounds faithful, giving correction a concrete and costly social form.

row.basis: rich man takes poor man's only lamb
row.note: The commentary's dishonest seller secretly consumes another's principal; Nathan's parable has a rich man spare his own livestock and take the poor man's single cherished lamb instead.

row.basis: another's story exposes one's hidden guilt
row.note: The commentary's seeing human needs another person's truthful address to see himself; after David condemns the parable's rich man, Nathan tells David that he is that man.

row.basis: all deeds including hidden ones judged
row.note: The commentary says loss can grow unseen until a final account reveals it; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed and every hidden thing, good or evil, into judgment.

row.basis: days of kingdom numbered and ended
row.note: The commentary treats passing time as capital spent toward an appointed reckoning; immediately before Daniel's verdict of deficient weight, he explains that God has numbered the king's days and ended his reign.
The commentary says the deficient person can lose far more than goods; immediately after Daniel finds the king lacking on the balance, he declares the kingdom divided and given away.

row.basis: weigh a commandment's loss against reward
row.note: The commentary reads loss and gain as a moral account rather than an emotion; Avot tells a person to reckon the loss of a commandment against its reward and a transgression's reward against its loss.

row.basis: final judgment asks about honest business
row.note: The commentary's market fraud is answered by a later scale for the trader himself; the Talmud says that when one is brought to judgment, one is asked whether one conducted business faithfully.

row.basis: buy true gold and salve for blind eyes
row.note: The commentary joins false wealth to a seeing being who misses his own loss; the speaker follows Laodicea's unrecognized poverty by urging it to buy refined gold and eye salve so it may see.

row.basis: great and small judged from books of deeds
row.note: The commentary's verdict includes every rank and opens a ledger of deeds; Revelation has the dead, great and small, stand before a throne as books are opened and they are judged by recorded works.

row.basis: fool enlarges barns for surplus crops
row.note: The commentary says counted accumulation can mask the loss of life's principal; in the rich fool's own plan, larger barns will hold his abundant grain and goods just before his life is required.

row.basis: stored goods mistaken for years of life
row.note: The commentary's trader mistakes growing assets for safety while time is vanishing; the rich fool tells his soul that goods stored for many years let him rest, eat and drink, an error exposed by the next verse.

row.basis: unseen tomorrow, life as brief vapor
row.note: The commentary's expiring time is capital people cannot safely count in advance; James says they do not know tomorrow and their life appears briefly like vapor before vanishing.
The commentary's apparently accumulating store is exposed to real depletion; Jesus warns that earthly treasure is destroyed by moth and rust and broken into by thieves.
The commentary sets profitable righteous action against perishing capital; Jesus directs hearers to store treasure in heaven, where the losses named in the preceding verse do not consume it.

row.basis: rich in good deeds and generous sharing
row.note: The commentary's exception names good work while money can be lost; Paul tells the wealthy to be rich in good works and ready to share, turning abundance into action for others.

row.basis: good deeds lay up future treasure and life
row.note: The commentary's true balance measures what endures beyond a lifetime; Paul says generous people store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life.

row.basis: give everything yet gain nothing without love
row.note: The commentary links good deeds to reciprocal human relations as the route out of loss; Paul says even giving away all possessions yields no gain if love is absent.
The commentary's rescue from loss joins righteous works with patience; Paul promises eternal life to those who persist in doing good while seeking glory, honor and immortality.
The commentary's third verse combines good action and mutual counsel in patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, people receive what was promised.

The commentary sets moral action rather than inherited status as the decisive separation from universal loss; John the Baptist calls for fruit worthy of repentance before confronting reliance on ancestry.

The commentary says noble or low origin does not determine who escapes loss; John warns hearers not to presume that having Abraham as father suffices, since God can raise children for him from stones.

The commentary makes action rather than lineage the visible difference among humans; Jesus answers an appeal to Abrahamic descent by demanding the works of Abraham from those claiming to be his children.

row.basis: man sees his own face in a mirror
row.note: The commentary's reflected little human in another's eye is tied to truthful counsel and action; James compares a hearer who fails to act to a man looking at his own face in a mirror.

row.basis: forgets own face immediately after seeing
row.note: The commentary says a seeing being can miss his own deficit; James' mirror-gazer walks away and at once forgets what he looked like, making self-sight ineffective without lasting response.

row.basis: another turns a wanderer from truth
row.note: The commentary unites truth, a lost path and mutual counsel; James addresses believers whose companion wanders from truth and whom another person turns back.

row.basis: returning wanderer saves life from death
row.note: The commentary says straying can progress from depleted provisions to self-loss; James says one who brings a sinner back from wandering saves a soul from death.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel must repair a lost person without forgetting one's own vulnerability; Paul tells the spiritual to restore someone caught in a trespass while watching themselves.

row.basis: younger son receives his estate early
row.note: The commentary cites guardians withholding an orphan's property until maturity is discerned; in Jesus' parable the father gives the younger son his share on request, setting up a different narrative treatment of entrusted capital rather than a competing legal rule.

row.basis: son squanders entrusted property far from home
row.note: The commentary moves from handed-over capital to lost direction and finally self-loss; the younger son leaves home and dissipates his estate in reckless living before he comes to himself.

row.basis: storm cannot ruin house on rock
row.note: The commentary's shelter contrasts with exposure to destructive weather; Jesus' rain, flood and wind strike the house built on rock, but it does not fall because of its foundation.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's generic insan is a vulnerable being under a sweeping verdict; Job asks what אֱנוֹשׁ is that God magnifies him and attends to him. Job's question concerns oppressive divine attention in its context, making the emotional direction different from the psalmic praise of human regard.
The commentary pictures the person's condition as continuous rather than one past loss; Job complains that God visits and tests him every morning and every moment, a darker continuous scrutiny.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's universal human verdict meets Eliphaz's question whether mortal אֱנוֹשׁ can be righteous before God or pure before his maker; the connection is qualified because the claim is made within Eliphaz's disputable speech.

row.basis: high-status human perishes like a beast
row.note: The commentary refuses to separate noble from low human beings in its loss verdict and develops tame and wild animal imagery; the psalm says a human in honor cannot remain and becomes like beasts that perish.

row.basis: rich and poor share one maker
row.note: The commentary's human includes both high and low status before any exception is counted; Proverbs says rich and poor meet together because the Lord is maker of them all.

row.basis: companions resist attack like a strong cord
row.note: The commentary makes connection with others a refuge on the exposed road; Ecclesiastes says two can withstand an attacker and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

row.basis: free choice and judgment by weight of deeds
row.note: The commentary holds a universal condition beside action that distinguishes an exception; R. Akiva's saying in Avot places human choice beside judgment according to the preponderance of deeds.
The commentary turns the solitary named human toward reciprocal truth telling; Avot calls wise the person who learns from every person, making another human a source of self-correction.

row.basis: true richness as contentment with share
row.note: The commentary warns that counting more possessions can conceal actual loss; the same Avot saying calls rich the person content with his portion, redefining wealth without an expanding hoard.

The commentary's Qur'anic account sets Moses on a journey with his family when he notices fire; Exodus introduces him tending Jethro's flock at Horeb, a specific change in the scene surrounding the same fire encounter.

row.basis: breath or wind withers the flower
row.note: The commentary's destructive wind erases growth that seemed secure; Isaiah says grass withers and flowers fade when the Lord's breath blows on them, making human flourishing fragile.

The commentary's way out of loss includes action and patience after seeing truth; James contrasts the forgetful mirror-gazer with one who looks into the law, perseveres and acts, receiving blessing in the doing.
The commentary imagines the passing hour as capital available for good work; Ephesians urges readers to make the most of time because the days are evil.

row.basis: desire for riches leads to ruin
row.note: The commentary says financial increase can carry a person toward destruction rather than profit; Paul says those determined to be rich fall into desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.
The commentary's profitable trade exchanges perishable capital for righteous action; Jesus tells the wealthy man to sell what he has, give to the poor, and gain treasure in heaven.
The commentary contrasts the consumed lifetime crop with enduring good work; Paul completes the fire-testing image by saying the builder whose work remains will receive a reward.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The commentary treats loss as a misdirected path that ends in destruction and truth as another way; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, rather than treating the error as a mere feeling.

The commentary says the named seeing human may not perceive his own deficit; Thomas has Jesus say those who fail to know themselves dwell in poverty and are poverty, making an internal condition invisible to its bearer.

The commentary develops losing one's way as a moral loss answered by truthful direction; Barnabas introduces opposing ways of light and darkness. The overlap is the two-path framework, since its particular signs differ from the commentary's trade and scale imagery.
