row.basis: Evening and morning form one day
row.note: The commentary joins night to day as parts of time; Genesis names light day and darkness night, then closes the first day with evening and morning, giving the pair an ordered whole.

The commentary links successive days with winter's appointed interval; the promise that seedtime, harvest, cold, heat, summer, winter, day, and night will not cease makes those alternating parts a stable covenantal rhythm.

row.basis: Day speaks to day, night to night
row.note: The commentary pictures adjoining periods as a chain; the psalm has each day pour speech into the next and each night disclose knowledge to the next, making succession itself communicative.

row.basis: Day and night belong to God
row.note: The commentary treats the paired periods as more than an undifferentiated flow; the psalm addresses God as owner of both day and night and maker of the luminaries that mark them.

row.basis: Summer and winter formed by God
row.note: The commentary moves from daily pairs to winter's middle and cold; this verse attributes the formation of summer and winter, as well as earth's bounds, to God.

row.basis: An appointed time for every affair
row.note: The commentary calls time a sequence of distinct intervals; Ecclesiastes introduces its paired occasions by assigning each affair its own time under heaven.

row.basis: Birth and death have their times
row.note: The commentary develops youth, age, and the end of life; this pair places birth and death at separate appointed moments rather than treating a life as a single span.
The commentary says a long lifetime shrinks to an evening or a daytime hour when viewed at the end; the psalm compares a thousand years before God to yesterday once passed and to a night watch.
The commentary puts human life inside a vast time before one existed; Bildad says humans are only of yesterday and know little because their earthly days are a shadow.
The commentary makes the countable stages of a life matter for righteous action; the psalm asks God to teach humans to count their days so that they acquire a wise heart.

row.basis: My times are in your hand
row.note: The commentary places the pieces and limits of a person's life under God's ordering; the psalmist entrusts his own times to God's hand while asking deliverance from enemies.

The commentary juxtaposes a long time before human existence with life's later stages; the psalm says the speaker's days were recorded when none of them had yet come, placing the life course in divine foreknowledge.
The commentary names youth as one interval of a finite life; Ecclesiastes commands remembrance specifically in youthful days before difficult later years arrive.

row.basis: Old age and the next generation
row.note: The commentary joins successive life stages to people sustaining one another; the aged speaker asks not to be forsaken until he tells the next generation of God's power.

row.basis: Even a century is a small life span
row.note: The commentary counts human ages and then reduces a whole life to a brief interval; Sirach calls a hundred years a large number of human days before measuring them against eternity.
The commentary says lengthy human residence looks like only a small daytime fraction; Sirach likens human years against eternity to a drop of sea water or a grain of sand.

row.basis: The impious claim death returns them to nonexistence
row.note: The commentary recalls the claim that time alone destroys and counters it with final reckoning; Wisdom puts in the impious speakers' mouths the claim that chance brought them into being and afterward they will be as though they had never existed.

The commentary says the long stay contracts to an evening or an hour; the impious speakers in Wisdom compare life to a passing shadow, though the book presents their conclusion about death as mistaken.

row.basis: Truth taught while waiting all day
row.note: The commentary places counsel in truth and patience inside the day's span; the psalmist asks to be taught God's truth and says he waits for God all day.
The commentary binds patience to a true promise whose fulfillment has its own time; the vision points to its appointed end and the hearer must wait even if it seems delayed.

row.basis: Blessed one who waits through counted days
row.note: The commentary makes endurance stretch over a measured interval; Daniel blesses the person who waits to the specified day count, joining a finite duration to perseverance.
The commentary sets truth-oriented persistence across the two periods; the righteous person's meditation on the Torah fills both day and night.
The commentary joins right deeds to a time-spanning attachment to truth; Joshua must meditate on the book of Torah day and night so that he acts according to it.

row.basis: Teach others at lying down and rising
row.note: The commentary says people become linked through repeated counsel while time passes; Israel is to teach the words to children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising.
The commentary has people uphold one another through truth across successive mornings; the servant receives an awakened ear morning by morning so he can sustain the weary with a word.

row.basis: The God-fearing speak to one another
row.note: The commentary depicts the surviving group as people bound by reciprocal exhortation; those who fear God speak together, and God attends to them and records their remembrance.
The commentary's mutual counsel is specifically counsel in truth; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and to render truthful, peace-making judgments.

row.basis: One group urges another to seek God
row.note: The commentary's people attach themselves to one another through counsel; the city's inhabitants invite others to go entreat God and add that they themselves will go.

row.basis: Accumulation and ignorance of its heir
row.note: The commentary recalls the preceding surah's race to multiply possessions until death; the psalm says a person heaps wealth without knowing who will gather it after him. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, but this row rests on the developed accumulation motif, not a claimed shared meaning with patience.

The commentary gives winter's cold a place in patient seasonal time; the sluggard refuses to plow in winter and therefore seeks food at harvest without finding it, showing how one interval governs the next.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: fixed life limit
row.note: The table offers a sound correspondence only, not proven cognacy; Job says a human's days and months are determined and God set a חק, a limit he cannot pass, a specific counterpart to the commentary's allotted life stages and due times.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: prescribed light cycles
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah calls the sun for daylight and the moon and stars for night divinely established ordinances, connecting the commentary's linked periods to a prescribed cosmic order.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring ordinances
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; the continued existence of Israel is made contingent on those day-night ordinances departing, linking regular time to the survival of a people.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: inscribed light-dark boundary
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Job describes a marked circle on the waters at the boundary of light and darkness, giving the commentary's adjoining night and day a sharply marked boundary.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: eighth-day assembly
row.note: The table gives a sound correspondence, not a proven cognate of time; after seven days of offerings this verse prescribes an eighth-day עצרת, where successive counted days culminate in people assembling.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: seventh-day assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence alone does not establish cognacy; after six days of unleavened bread the seventh is an עצרת, joining a counted sequence to communal gathering as in the commentary's meeting of time and people.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: daily reading, eighth-day assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Ezra reads the Torah day by day through the festival, then the people hold an eighth-day עצרת, making repeated instruction and a final joined assembly one timed practice.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: call an assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; the command to blow the trumpet, sanctify a fast, and call an עצרה gives the commentary's people joined through urgent exhortation a concrete communal form.
The commentary names stages of life before showing people joined; Joel's summoned gathering explicitly includes elders, children, nursing infants, bridegroom, and bride.

row.basis: Assembly joined to injustice is rejected
row.note: The commentary makes righteous deeds and truth conditions of collective survival; Isaiah refuses an assembly held together with wrongdoing, testing the value of a gathered religious community by its conduct. Hebrew עצרה is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r, without proof of cognacy.
The commentary says those who endure remain through the chain of time; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making persistence across the whole interval decisive.

row.basis: Stored years collapse into one night
row.note: The commentary contrasts a lifetime of numerical accumulation with its abrupt end; the rich man's planned many years are cut short that very night, and he is asked who will have his stored goods.

row.basis: Possessions imagined to guarantee many years
row.note: The commentary links the competition to increase possessions with failure to notice time passing; the rich man addresses his soul as though stored goods secured many years of rest.
The commentary recalls multiplying wealth until the grave; the rich man decides to build larger barns to store all his grain and goods before his mortality is exposed in the story.
The commentary reduces a seeming long residence to a small interval; James calls human life a vapor that appears a little while and disappears, addressing people who plan future years.

row.basis: One day and a thousand years
row.note: The commentary contrasts long duration with its apparent contraction; this verse reversibly compares one day and a thousand years before the Lord, relativizing ordinary measures of waiting.
The commentary connects patience to the true promise through a shrinking lifetime; this verse says the promised coming is not slow as some reckon but delayed in divine patience to allow repentance.
The commentary divides time into assigned intervals while people remain joined; Paul says God made every nation from one and determined their appointed times and dwelling boundaries.

The commentary says a long life is seen as compressed when its end approaches; Paul tells believers the appointed time has grown short and therefore their ordinary life relations must be held lightly.
The commentary tracks bodily life through aging while patience persists across days; Paul says the outer person wastes away but the inner person is renewed day by day.
The commentary's people remain joined through reciprocal counsel across linked days; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation while it is called Today, to prevent hardening through sin.

row.basis: Stir one another to good works
row.note: The commentary makes shared righteous action part of how people remain connected; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to provoke love and good deeds.

row.basis: Gather and encourage as the Day approaches
row.note: The commentary connects communal exhortation to passing time; Hebrews opposes abandoning assembly and urges increasingly mutual encouragement as the approaching Day is seen.
The commentary ties mutual counsel to morning/evening and a lasting interval; Paul recalls three years in which he warned each person night and day with tears.

row.basis: Exhort at every season with patience
row.note: The commentary's counsel and patience fill successive times; the charge to proclaim the word in season and out of season includes correction and exhortation with complete patience and teaching.

row.basis: Good action sustained until its season
row.note: The commentary joins righteous deeds and patience across time; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good because a harvest will come at its proper time if people do not give up.

row.basis: Night is advanced, day draws near
row.note: The commentary makes night-to-day transition a call to moral action; Paul says the passing night and approaching day demand casting off dark works and taking up the armor of light.
The commentary links right deeds to the short allotted interval; Jesus says the works of the sender must be done while it is day, since night comes when no one can work.

row.basis: Use the time because days are evil
row.note: The commentary makes limited time the setting for righteous action; Ephesians asks its hearers to make the most of the time because the days are evil.

row.basis: Elect cry day and night for justice
row.note: The commentary places truth and patient appeal across daily cycles; Jesus describes God's chosen crying to him day and night for justice in a parable about persistent prayer.

row.basis: The slain ask how long until judgment
row.note: The commentary connects waiting with a true final reckoning; the slain ask the sovereign Lord how long before he judges and vindicates their blood.

row.basis: Rest a little longer until number complete
row.note: The commentary gives patient waiting a finite interval and links the fates of people; the martyrs are told to rest a little longer until their fellow servants are complete.
The commentary's surviving group combines belief, deeds, and patience; Revelation characterizes the saints' endurance by keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.
The commentary makes counsel in truth a way people are joined; speaking truth in love is the means by which members grow toward their common head, Christ.

row.basis: The body joined by every working part
row.note: The commentary says the people who remain are added to one another; the body is joined and held together as each part works, building itself up in love.
The commentary's repeated reciprocal counsel makes a durable community; Paul explicitly tells believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

row.basis: Admonish, help, and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary couples mutual counsel with patience; this instruction names admonishing the idle, helping the weak, and being patient with everyone as communal practices.

The commentary names winter's hard cold as one temporal condition for patience; Jesus tells hearers to pray that their flight does not occur in winter, when that season will worsen their urgent journey.
The commentary pairs morning and evening as recurring occasions for patient devotion; the sabbath psalm assigns proclamation of God's kindness to morning and his faithfulness to nights.

row.basis: Remember God at night and keep law
row.note: The commentary has enduring adherence to truth through the nighttime portion; the psalmist remembers God's name at night and keeps his law.

row.basis: Wake through night watches for instruction
row.note: The commentary makes patient fidelity stretch across night and morning; the psalmist's eyes anticipate the watches of the night to meditate on God's saying.
The commentary explicitly pairs morning with late day; the psalmist names evening, morning, and noon as repeated times of appeal to God, dividing the day into acts of persistence.
The commentary makes night and day adjoining parts of a lived religious interval; the psalmist expects God's kindness by day and a song-prayer with him at night.

row.basis: Human cannot grasp time's whole work
row.note: The commentary says the connected pieces are more than a flat flow; Ecclesiastes says God made each thing fitting in its time while humans cannot discover the work from beginning to end.

row.basis: Old age approaches the lasting home
row.note: The commentary takes youth through decline to the grave; Ecclesiastes' portrait of the aging person's fears ends with going to the lasting home while mourners walk outside.

row.basis: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
row.note: The commentary catalogs life stages but says all that time can contract at the end; the psalm gives a human span of seventy or eighty years and says it quickly passes.
The commentary counts childhood and old age among life's parts; Isaiah's promised city reverses premature death, saying infants will not live only a few days and elders will complete their days.

row.basis: As though never existing, womb to grave
row.note: The commentary recalls a time when a human was not yet a mentioned thing and a later journey to death; Job wishes he had been as though he had not existed, carried directly from womb to grave.
The commentary compresses lifetime into a brief seeming stay; the psalm says human days resemble a shadow that passes away.
The commentary's phases of life culminate in disappearance; the psalm compares mortal days to grass flourishing briefly as a flower of the field.

row.basis: A passing wind erases its place
row.note: The commentary asks how much of a long life remains at its end; when wind passes over the flower it is gone and its place knows it no more, the next part of the mortal image.
The commentary calls winter a particular hard interval and ties waiting to its end; the lover announces that winter and its rain are over, so the harsh season has a bounded duration.

row.basis: Ant stores food in summer and harvest
row.note: The commentary connects accumulation to passing time; the ant gathers provisions in summer and at harvest, supplying a purposeful seasonal counterpart to accumulation that distracts humans until death.

The commentary recalls competitive increase of possessions before mortality; Job's wicked figure heaps silver like dust and clothing like clay, preparing the reversal in the next verse. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, not a demonstrated shared sense with patience.
The commentary's hoarder cannot carry accumulated time or goods beyond life's end; Job says the righteous will wear the wicked person's prepared clothes and the innocent will divide his silver.

row.basis: Joseph heaps grain across good years
row.note: The commentary recalls multiplying material stores before a later interval; Joseph piles grain beyond counting ahead of famine, giving accumulation a collective preserving purpose. Hebrew צבר is only the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r; the connection is the concrete stored-grain scene.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night statutes
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God's fixed ordinances of heaven and earth accompany his covenant with day and night, tying the commentary's alternating periods to continuing communal existence.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: heaven's ordinances
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God asks Job whether he knows the ordinances of heaven or can establish their rule on earth, an interpretive bridge from the commentary's due times to cosmic prescription.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: assigned sea boundary
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Wisdom recalls God setting the sea its prescribed limit, a spatial analogue to the commentary's precisely bounded intervals and seasonal middles.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: communal crisis assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence does not prove cognacy; Joel calls a fast and an עצרה in which elders and all inhabitants gather at God's house and cry out, linking group survival to shared action in a hard time.

row.basis: Be still and wait despite evildoer success
row.note: The commentary says patience must be sustained while truth is not yet manifest; the psalm tells its hearer to wait patiently for God rather than fret over a person succeeding in an evil course.
The commentary treats patience as what lets people keep standing through a long interval; Isaiah says those waiting for God renew strength and continue without fainting.
The commentary connects a difficult period with patient endurance; Lamentations calls quiet waiting for God's salvation good amid its account of suffering.

row.basis: Three daily prayers despite hostile decree
row.note: The commentary stretches the act of patience between recurring times of day; Daniel continues praying three times daily even after the written decree against that practice.

row.basis: People hold onto another to go together
row.note: The commentary says people are added to one another through a shared orientation to God; Zechariah imagines people of many languages grasping a Jew's garment and asking to go with him because God is with the group.
The commentary's reciprocal exhortation makes persons sustain one another; the proverb compares one person's effect on a friend to iron sharpening iron, giving counsel a mutual formative action.

row.basis: Named ages of a human life
row.note: The commentary explicitly parses youth, maturity, and decline as time's pieces; Avot gives a sequence of ages with different pursuits and capacities, including forty for understanding and seventy for old age. Section numbering varies by edition.

row.basis: Acquire a friend and a teacher
row.note: The commentary makes people remain linked by guidance; Avot directs a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, turning endurance into a sustained interpersonal practice.

row.basis: If not now, when; if only for self, what am I
row.note: The commentary binds short time to the need for others; Hillel's paired questions reject delay and self-enclosure in the same ethical saying.

row.basis: Do not defer study until free time
row.note: The commentary says time is spent in successive limited pieces; Avot warns that a hoped-for leisure interval may never come, making present instruction urgent.

The commentary says a long life can shrink suddenly to its last fraction; the rabbinic explanation of repentance one day before death is to repent each day because no one knows which day will be last.

row.basis: Evening before morning in prayer order
row.note: The commentary puts night and day into a deliberate sequence; the discussion explains beginning the daily Shema with evening by appealing to creation's evening followed by morning, turning Genesis' order into a repeated act.

row.basis: Prayer and fasting night and day
row.note: The commentary places steadfast worship across the paired periods; the aged Anna serves in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, joining old age with continuous devotion.

row.basis: Hope for unseen end requires patience
row.note: The commentary asks people to wait through an interval for a promised resolution; Paul says those hoping for what they do not yet see wait for it with endurance.
The commentary joins patience to the true promise; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will so that hearers may receive what was promised.
The commentary joins the waiting interval to the chance to remain among the saved; Peter explicitly asks readers to regard the Lord's patience as salvation, supplying the purpose of the delay.

The commentary names winter's severity and the waiting that spans seasons; James asks believers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit through early and late rain until the Lord's coming.

row.basis: Prophets as examples of patient speech
row.note: The commentary couples truth-telling with endurance; James names prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.

row.basis: Present opportunity used for good to all
row.note: The commentary says righteous deeds and mutual support occupy limited time; Paul says that while opportunity remains believers should do good to everyone, especially fellow believers.
The commentary defines the surviving group through mutual counsel; Colossians asks believers to let Christ's word dwell among them as they teach and admonish one another wisely.

row.basis: Speak truth as members of one another
row.note: The commentary brings truth and people being joined into one image; Ephesians gives membership in one body as the reason for each person to speak truth to a neighbor.
The commentary stretches patience between repeated times of worship; Paul joins patience in tribulation to constancy in prayer as the group's practice.

row.basis: Day of the Lord arrives during night
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes the day-night pair with the sudden end of a seeming long stay; Paul says the Lord's day comes like a thief in the night, challenging complacency about the remaining time.

row.basis: Believers belong to day, not night
row.note: The commentary makes remaining people a distinct group amid the alternation of night and day; Paul calls believers children of light and day, assigning the temporal images an ethical identity.
The commentary develops short sleep and patient alertness across time; Paul tells the community not to sleep as others do but to keep awake and sober in view of the approaching day.

row.basis: Rich are to become rich in good works
row.note: The commentary contrasts accumulating possessions with righteous action that endures; Paul instructs the rich to be rich in good works and generous to others.

row.basis: Store a foundation for the future life
row.note: The commentary's accumulation motif ends at the grave unless joined to right deeds; Paul pictures generosity as storing a firm foundation for the future so that people may grasp true life.

row.basis: The rich fade in the midst of pursuits
row.note: The commentary says acquisitive effort can consume the person's unnoticed time; James likens a rich person's fading during pursuits to a flower withered by the rising sun.

row.basis: Twelve hours mark the usable day
row.note: The commentary treats the day as a bounded segment in which one's way matters; Jesus asks whether the day has twelve hours and connects walking without stumbling to its light.
The commentary puts patience across segmented night; Jesus calls servants blessed if found alert when their master comes in the second or third watch.

row.basis: Pray flight will not be in winter
row.note: The commentary treats winter's cold as a concrete trial inside the calendar; Jesus tells hearers to pray that the expected flight not happen in winter, making season alter the hardship of endurance.
The commentary links winter's coming with people maintaining one another through time; Paul urges his addressee to come before winter, making the seasonal deadline matter for their meeting.
The commentary makes daily alternation part of continuing allegiance; the rescued multitude stands before God's throne and serves him day and night, extending joined devotion beyond mortal time.

row.basis: Separate times for scattering and gathering
row.note: The commentary makes successive pieces of time carry opposing actions and later joins people; Ecclesiastes assigns separate times to scattering stones and gathering them, a concrete temporal analogy rather than an explicit claim about people.

row.basis: Known before formation in the womb
row.note: The commentary recalls a span when the human was not yet a mentioned thing; Jeremiah's prophetic commission says God knew him before forming him in the womb, complicating any inference that pre-birth absence means divine unawareness.

The commentary makes endurance in truth span harsh conditions; the psalmist describes himself as a wineskin in smoke yet says he has not forgotten God's statutes, though the image is not explicitly winter cold.

row.basis: Tyre piles silver before its fall
row.note: The commentary recalls abundance amassed before a terminal reversal; Tyre heaps silver like dust in this verse before its wealth is stripped in the next. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, with no asserted patience cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: withholding birth
row.note: The table gives only a sound correspondence; God asks whether he would bring to birth and then restrain delivery, an indirect counterpart to the commentary's movement through appointed life stages and resistance to time stopping.

row.basis: One not yet born has not seen evil
row.note: The commentary recalls a pre-existence interval in human life; Ecclesiastes calls the unborn person better off because that person has not witnessed oppression, though its judgment about nonexistence has a different purpose.

row.basis: Fathers and young people addressed separately
row.note: The commentary names distinct stages of a life; the letter addresses fathers and young people with different spiritual descriptions, an analogy through communal age categories rather than a literal lifespan sequence.

row.basis: Lights mark days, years, and appointed seasons
row.note: The commentary joins night and day to longer seasonal and lifetime intervals; Genesis assigns the lights the work of marking days, years, and appointed times, making several scales of time depend on the same cycle.
The commentary treats morning and late day as recurring joined pieces; Ecclesiastes has the sun rise, set, and hurry back to the place of its rising.

row.basis: Moon marks appointed times and sun its setting
row.note: The commentary places seasonal middles alongside daily transitions; the psalm says the moon was made for appointed times while the sun knows its setting.

row.basis: Human years swept away like sleep
row.note: The commentary names a short sleep and says a long human span is later perceived as brief; the psalm says God sweeps humans away like sleep before its morning-grass comparison.
The commentary compresses a life into the morning-to-evening interval; the psalm's grass flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, completing the time image begun in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Long night spent waiting for dawn
row.note: The commentary develops broken sleep, morning and evening, and patience stretched between them; Job describes lying down, waiting to rise, and tossing through a seemingly prolonged night until dawn.

row.basis: Waiting more than watchmen for morning
row.note: The commentary turns patience into a posture held across night toward morning; the psalmist repeats that his soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for morning.

row.basis: Accumulated wealth cannot go through death
row.note: The commentary recalls multiplying possessions until the grave; the psalm says a wealthy person carries none of it away when dying, specifying the limit that accumulation cannot cross.

row.basis: Riches fail at reckoning, righteousness delivers
row.note: The commentary puts accumulated goods beside righteous deeds and final loss; the proverb says wealth is useless on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers from death.

row.basis: Dust returns but spirit returns to God
row.note: The commentary reports the denial that passing time alone destroys humans and recalls final accountability; Ecclesiastes instead says the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to the God who gave it.

row.basis: The long dead awaken for judgment
row.note: The commentary's brief-seeming stay ends at a gathering where deniers lose; Daniel says many who sleep in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame, supplying a direct alternative to death as time's final word.
The commentary names youth as one stage and ends with reckoning of a whole life; Ecclesiastes tells the young person to rejoice while young but to know God will bring these acts into judgment.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: decreeing justice
row.note: The package's root table offers an unverified sound correspondence; Wisdom says rulers decree justice by her, linking the commentary's counsel in haqq to enacted right order rather than merely to a seasonal due date.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: annual perpetual ordinance
row.note: The table offers an unverified sound correspondence; the exodus day is to be remembered as a festival through generations by perpetual חקה, making a fixed calendar date bind successive people.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night covenant at its time
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah says the covenant with day and night would have to be broken for either to fail to come at its appointed time, tying the commentary's sequence to reliable recurrence.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: unjust decrees
row.note: The table offers only a sound correspondence; Isaiah denounces those who inscribe unjust decrees, showing that a prescribed order can oppose the commentary's haqq and righteous action when its content is corrupt.

The commentary says a community persists through righteous conduct, truth, and patience; Amos has God reject its festivals and solemn assemblies, complicating the assumption that recurring gatherings alone preserve a people.

The commentary joins truthful counsel to the group's endurance; after rejecting festivals Amos calls for justice to roll like water and righteousness like an enduring stream, identifying the needed practice beyond assembly.

row.basis: One hour of repentance and good deeds
row.note: The commentary says long earthly time contracts to an hour and makes righteous action decisive; Avot values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world while separately valuing an hour of the coming world's peace.

row.basis: If the dead do not rise, eat and drink
row.note: The commentary reports deniers who treat mortal time as final; Paul voices the practical conclusion of denying resurrection, eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death, then challenges that premise in his resurrection argument.

row.basis: The dead rise according to deeds
row.note: The commentary's final compressed stay ends in loss for deniers and survival through right action; Jesus says those in the tombs come out to resurrection of life or judgment according to what they have done.

row.basis: The dead judged from records of deeds
row.note: The commentary reports that time itself is said to destroy and recalls an accounting after a brief-seeming stay; Revelation has the dead stand before the throne as books are opened and each is judged by deeds.

The commentary recalls competitive accumulation that hides life's shortness; James addresses people planning a year of travel and trade for gain, the precise plan exposed as uncertain in the next verse.

row.basis: Self-stored goods versus wealth toward God
row.note: The commentary opposes multiplication of possessions to deeds that endure; Jesus closes the rich fool's story by contrasting storing up for oneself with being rich toward God.

row.basis: Delay produces sleep in a waiting group
row.note: The commentary gives broken sleep a place between periods of waiting; in Jesus' bridegroom story the delay makes all the attendants drowsy and asleep before the decisive arrival.

row.basis: Prepared attendants enter before the door closes
row.note: The commentary asks who remains when an apparently long wait abruptly ends; in the bridegroom story those prepared enter the feast on his arrival and the door is shut.

row.basis: Times and seasons introduce the final Day
row.note: The commentary moves from named periods to a sudden terminal hour; Paul explicitly invokes times and seasons before describing the Lord's Day as unexpectedly arriving in the following verse.

The commentary's remaining group combines persistence with righteous deeds; Paul concludes his resurrection argument by telling believers to be steadfast and always active in the Lord's work because that labor is not futile.
The commentary reduces a human lifetime to a passing interval; Peter applies Isaiah's fading-grass image to all flesh, making mortal brevity part of his appeal to a community born through the gospel.

The commentary joins short human life to truth that can hold people together; Peter completes the Isaiah citation by contrasting fading humanity with the Lord's enduring word and identifies that word with what was proclaimed to his hearers.

row.basis: A new Today after a long time
row.note: The commentary describes time as linked parts in which an appeal remains open; Hebrews says God appoints another day called Today after a long time, using David's warning to demand a present response.

row.basis: Now is the accepted time and day of rescue
row.note: The commentary's finite interval calls for righteous response before the end; Paul applies a promise about the favorable time and salvation day to his hearers' present now.

row.basis: Keep watch because the hour is unknown
row.note: The commentary stretches patience through uncertain time before the final contraction; the Didache tells believers to watch their lives and keep lamps ready since they do not know the Lord's hour.

row.basis: Meet often; faith must endure to the end
row.note: The commentary connects repeated meetings among people with the need to remain through time; the Didache urges frequent gathering for the soul and says a lifetime of faith is of no benefit unless completed at the end.

row.basis: Lights govern day and night and distinguish them
row.note: The commentary holds night and day together without dissolving their distinction; Genesis says the lights govern the two periods and separate light from darkness, adding ordered difference to their succession.
The commentary's two daily periods are each assigned a place; the litany names the sun as ruler of the day, with its companion night assignment in the next verse.

row.basis: Moon and stars govern the night
row.note: The commentary pairs night with day as adjacent ordered parts; the litany gives the night to moon and stars after naming the sun's daily rule in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Horn blown at recurring lunar feast
row.note: The commentary extends morning-evening segments to prescribed seasonal observance; the psalm orders the horn at new moon and full moon for the festival day, whose status as statute is given in the next verse.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: festival statute
row.note: The root table supplies an unverified sound correspondence; the festival marked in the preceding verse is called a חק for Israel, connecting a recurring appointed day to a shared obligation.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring cosmic decree
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God establishes the heavenly bodies permanently and gives them a decree that will not pass, an ordinance behind the commentary's dependable recurring periods.

row.basis: Mortal grass fades while divine word stands
row.note: The commentary joins a vanishing human lifespan to the truth that sustains the community; Isaiah says the grass withers and flower fades but God's word remains forever.

The commentary ties calendrical practice to righteous action; Isaiah defines God's chosen fast as releasing unjust bonds and freeing the oppressed, giving a concrete ethical test for a designated day.

row.basis: Humans do not know their fatal time
row.note: The commentary says a long life can suddenly end in a fraction of a day; Ecclesiastes says people do not know their time and compares their capture by disaster to fish and birds trapped unexpectedly.

row.basis: Nighttime recitation has a bounded interval
row.note: The commentary makes night a distinct period filled with a sustained religious act; the Mishnah asks when the evening Shema is read and sets competing limits within the night's watches.

row.basis: Morning recitation begins with visible dawn
row.note: The commentary joins morning to the night before it as a new part of disciplined time; the Mishnah asks when morning Shema begins and uses the ability to distinguish colors to mark the transition.

The commentary couples counsel in truth with righteous works; Shammai says to make Torah study regular, speak little, and do much, specifying how words and acts should be ordered across ordinary time.

row.basis: sharpened tongue as sword; bitter word as arrow

row.basis: God's word sharper than a two-edged sword, reaching joints and marrow

row.basis: sword from the rider's mouth strikes nations

row.basis: do not turn right or left; turn the foot from evil

row.basis: seduction ends bitter and sharp as a two-edged sword

row.basis: ways wander from the path of life

row.basis: righteous tree planted by streams bears fruit in season

row.basis: wicked are chaff driven by wind

row.basis: crooked ground made straight for the Lord's road

row.basis: iron sharpens iron; one person sharpens another

row.basis: run the set race with endurance

row.basis: God's word as fire and a hammer breaking rock
row.note: Jeremiah compares God's word to fire and a hammer that shatters rock; this gives the commentary's haqq-as-projectile a second image of forceful impact and adds the destruction of hard resistance.

row.basis: sent word accomplishes its purpose and does not return empty

row.basis: saints' endurance with God's commandments and faith

row.basis: preach the word, correct and exhort with patience

row.basis: daily mutual exhortation guards against sin's deception
row.note: Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation so no one hardens through sin's deceit; this links the commentary's counsel in truth to preventing a person's deviation and adds a daily communal practice.
James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this describes sabr as formed under pressure, giving the commentary's human target image a process of remaining steadfast through impact.

row.basis: endurance completes its work so one lacks nothing
row.note: James says endurance should complete its work so a person becomes complete and lacks nothing; this joins the commentary's sabr and amal to an explicit overcoming of lack.
Paul says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth; this gives the commentary's haqq a communal ethical setting, where truth marks the difference between right and wrong action.

row.basis: make straight paths for the feet so the lame may heal
row.note: Hebrews commands straight paths for feet so the lame limb may be healed rather than dislocated; this combines the commentary's straight trajectory with its bodily penetration image, and turns straightness toward restoration.

row.note: Jacob calls his sons to hear what will happen to them; the commentary reads mutual counsel as a word handed on at the edge of death, while its cited Qur'anic Jacob asks specifically whom they will worship.
As death approaches Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers; it joins a dying instruction, an heir and a binding oath in one scene.
Dying Joseph makes Israel's sons swear to carry his bones away when God visits them; an obligation is entrusted to a later generation.
God chooses Abraham so he will command his children and household after him to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice; faith and right conduct are transmitted together.

Jacob orders his household to put away foreign gods and purify themselves; this supplies an earlier concrete worship instruction beside the commentary's deathbed question about what his sons will worship.
Israel is told to repeat the commanded words to its children in daily settings; counsel becomes a continuing intergenerational duty like the commentary's inherited recommendation.
God establishes testimony in Jacob and commands fathers to make it known to their children; the commentary's passed-on faith has a precise communal analogue.

row.basis: children yet unborn tell their children
row.note: The next generation is to arise and tell its own children; this explicitly extends the chain beyond the first recipients of the bequest.
When David's death draws near he gives Solomon a charge; this is a royal deathbed instance of instruction left to someone who must act after the speaker.
David tells Solomon to keep God's charge and walk in his ways; the inherited instruction has religious practice, rather than property alone, as its subject.

row.basis: Moses warns what follows his death
row.note: Moses says Israel will turn aside after his death, making the survival of a transmitted charge after the speaker's absence the explicit issue.
A person gives a neighbor silver or goods for safekeeping and the goods are stolen; this is the concrete entrusted property behind the commentary's emanet image. This is WLC verse 22:6.
If the thief is not found, the householder must come before God about the neighbor's property; custody creates accountable testimony, as in the commentary's deathbed trust.
An oath of the Lord settles whether the keeper has touched the owner's animal, and the owner accepts it; entrusted goods and an oath share a single legal scene. This is WLC verse 22:10.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: A single witness cannot establish a charge, whereas two or three can; it gives legal weight to the commentary's pair of witnesses at a bequest.
Judges must examine testimony carefully and determine whether a witness lied; this matches the commentary's concern that a first bequest testimony may prove deceptive.
The false witness receives the consequence intended for the accused; the commentary's replacement oath likewise treats corrupt testimony as a wrong requiring correction.
A person who hears an adjuration and can testify but fails to tell what was seen or known bears guilt; oath and the duty to disclose meet in the commentary's witness scene.
A person accused by a neighbor comes to swear before God's altar; the commentary likewise places a disputed oath after communal worship.
Solomon asks God to judge the sworn dispute and vindicate the righteous; this specifies the concern for a truer testimony when a first oath is suspect.
God declares Zelophehad's daughters' claim right and commands their father's inheritance be transferred to them; the commentary treats heirs' portions as enforceable rights.

The inheritance sequence ends by making its order a fixed statute of judgment; Hebrew חֻקַּת from the table's חקק correspondence links prescribed law to the commentary's binding haqq, without equating the two senses.

row.basis: father may not redirect firstborn status
row.note: A father with loved and unloved wives cannot favor the loved wife's son when allocating his estate; the bequest must respect a preexisting heir's right.
The father must recognize the unloved wife's firstborn with a double share; this concretizes a binding inheritance portion despite personal preference.

row.basis: prince's gift to son becomes inheritance
row.note: When the prince gives from his property to a son, it belongs to his sons as inherited possession; this tests the commentary's image of a father's gift and heirs' rights.

row.basis: gift to servant reverts at release
row.note: A prince's gift to a servant reverts to the prince at the year of liberty, while the son's inheritance in the preceding verse persists; it sharply qualifies the commentary's father who takes back a gift.
Judah personally stands surety for Benjamin and offers to bear blame if he fails to return him; the Genesis Joseph story supplies a guarantor with a specific obligation.
Before Joseph, Judah says he became surety for the boy to his father; the guarantor's earlier word remains binding in a later crisis.

row.basis: Judah offers himself in the boy's place
row.note: Judah asks to remain a slave instead of Benjamin, putting his own body behind the guarantee; this makes the commentary's image of a surety standing behind another concrete.
The psalmist asks God to be surety for the servant's good against oppressors; the commentary's kefil image extends here from a human promisor to divine protection.

row.basis: Jesus guarantor of a better covenant
row.note: Jesus is called the guarantor of a better covenant; the commentary's kefil and binding inherited obligation meet in a person who stands behind a covenant.
The speaker recalls that his father taught him to hold fast to words and keep commandments; advice is received and passed on, the commentary's generational chain in miniature.
The address to a child instructs acceptance and patience through humiliation; it joins parental admonition with the precise adversity borne in the commentary's Luqman scene.

row.basis: admonish, support and be patient with all
row.note: Paul asks the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient with everyone; mutual counsel and patience operate together.

row.basis: provoke one another to good works
row.note: The assembly must consider how to stir one another to love and good works; the commentary's mutual charge has an enacted ethical goal.

row.basis: keep assembling and encourage one another
row.note: Believers are told to encourage one another as the day approaches; counsel is repeated communally under awareness of limited time.

row.basis: entrust teaching to teachers of others
row.note: What Timothy heard before witnesses is to be entrusted to faithful people able to teach others; testimony, faithful custody and another generation of speakers coincide.
Timothy is told to guard an entrusted good deposit through the Holy Spirit; the commentary's bequeathed instruction is explicitly treated as something in custody.

row.basis: Paul's farewell entrusts elders to God
row.note: In his farewell Paul commends the elders to God and the word able to give inheritance; the departing speaker hands over care and names a future inheritance.
Expecting his departure, the writer promises to enable continued remembrance afterward; instruction deliberately survives the speaker's death.
The argument says a testament requires the death of its maker; it places the commentary's deathbed transfer of binding words beside an explicit death and inheritance analogy.
The next verse says a testament becomes effective on death; it specifies the moment at which a speaker's word binds the living.
Christ mediates a new covenant so the called receive the promised eternal inheritance; the bequest image is used for a religious promise rather than divided property.

row.basis: farewell command to love one another
row.note: At the farewell meal Jesus gives a new command to love one another; a departing teacher leaves a reciprocal obligation to his community.
Abraham trusts the Lord and it is reckoned to him as righteousness; the table's אמנ correspondence links the commentary's faith to a patriarchal act with ethical standing.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; trust and firmness
row.note: Isaiah warns that if the addressed king and house do not trust, they will not stand firm; the verse plays on אמנ twice, making steadfastness the practical stake of belief.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; fidelity through crisis
row.note: The righteous lives by faithfulness while facing the proud oppressor; Hebrew אֱמוּנָה from the table connects the commentary's belief with endurance under strain.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; child asks about statutes
row.note: A child asks what the Lord's decrees mean, prompting parental explanation; חֻקִּים from the table's חקק correspondence turns prescribed right into transmitted teaching.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; decree to Jacob
row.note: God confirms the promise to Jacob as a statute and enduring covenant; Hebrew חֹק from the table's חקק correspondence joins fixed obligation to the patriarchal chain.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; enduring inscribed words
row.note: Job wishes his words written and inscribed in a book; the table's חקק verb gives a concrete form to the commentary's word left behind, though Job seeks a record of his protest rather than an heir's instruction.

The rabbinic account has the dying Jacob fear a fault in his sons, who answer with the Shema; it turns the patriarch's final exchange into the very question of inherited worship developed from Qur'an 2:133.

row.basis: Jacob's final blessings interpreted as faith
row.note: Hebrews describes Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons as an act of faith at death; it interprets the deathbed transfer as trust in a future he will not see.

row.basis: Joseph's dying charge interpreted as faith
row.note: Hebrews interprets Joseph's instruction about his bones and Israel's exodus at death as an act of faith; it makes the generational obligation depend on confidence in a future event.

row.basis: faith inherited from grandmother and mother
row.note: Timothy's sincere faith is remembered as having lived first in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice; this is a named household chain for the commentary's bequeathed belief.

row.basis: death interrupts plans for stored goods
row.note: God tells a man his life is required that night and asks who will own what he prepared; the commentary's warning that one may lose the chance to leave a bequest becomes an explicit question about successors.
With Moses' death near, he is told to summon Joshua for a charge; it gives the commentary's instruction across a departing generation a named successor.

row.basis: Joshua told to be strong and courageous
row.note: Joshua receives a charge to lead Israel into the land and not lose courage; fortitude accompanies a transferred task, close to the commentary's counsel joined with sabr.

row.basis: choose whom your household will serve
row.note: Joshua sets before Israel a choice of whom to serve and declares his household's allegiance; this is a public answer to the commentary's question of worship after a leader departs.

row.basis: covenant oath not limited to hearers
row.note: Moses explicitly says he makes the covenant and oath with more than the immediate audience; this frames the inherited religious obligation as publicly sworn.
Moses names both those standing there and those not present; the commentary's charge passing beyond its immediate hearers has a precise covenantal counterpart.
A child is told to keep a father's command and not forsake a mother's teaching; this supports the commentary's practical definition of advice as instruction to act.
A good person leaves an inheritance to grandchildren; the commentary's tangible shares and generational gift are joined in one maxim.
Abraham gives all he has to Isaac; the patriarchal transmission of faith in the commentary also has an explicit material inheritance in Genesis.

row.basis: gifts to other sons during life
row.note: Abraham gives gifts to concubines' sons during his life and sends them away from Isaac; the verse shows how a living father distinguishes gifts from the main inheritance.
Reuben offers his sons as a guarantee for Benjamin's return; before Judah's surety, the Genesis Joseph story offers a stark alternate form of standing behind another.
A parent warns a son against pledging himself for a neighbor or stranger; it makes the guarantor's moral exposure explicit where the commentary names the kefil.
The proverb warns that one who guarantees a stranger suffers, while refusal is secure; it supplies the risk implicit in the commentary's surety image.
The Spirit is called a pledge of believers' inheritance until redemption; an assurance stands behind a promised future possession, connecting guarantor and bequest.
God gives the Spirit in hearts as a pledge; the promise is secured before fulfillment, analogous to the commentary's guarantor standing behind a future delivery.

The younger son asks for his share and the father divides his property between them; it supplies a narrative test case for the commentary's distinction between a living father's gift and inherited portions.
The father tells the elder son that all he has is his; even after the younger son has spent his portion, the remaining heir's claim is explicitly preserved.
The sage advises assigning the inheritance at the end of life; this specifies the commentary's moment when a living person's control becomes a charge to heirs.

Amid reflection on life's brevity, a person heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; this sharpens the commentary's concern to assign goods before death. Hebrew צבר here means heap, not Arabic sabr's patience.
A wicked person heaps silver and stores clothing, but the following verse assigns them to others; the commentary's estate can outlast the owner without preserving the owner's intended control.
The righteous will wear the stored clothing and the innocent divide the silver; this reverses the accumulator's claim to determine who receives his goods.
Jesus instructs his hearers not to swear at all; the commentary's bequest witnesses are required to swear, so the texts put a different weight on compelled truth telling.
James forbids oaths and requires an unambiguous yes or no; the commentary's oath secures disputed bequest testimony by a legal act that James tells his audience to avoid.
The high priest adjures the detained Jesus by the living God to answer, and Jesus has been silent; a compelled religious oath appears in an interrogation, unlike the commentary's estate witnesses.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: Jesus cites the two or three witness rule when a private rebuke fails; the commentary's disputed testimony likewise requires a claim to be publicly established.
An accusation against an elder is not received without two or three witnesses; the procedure shows why an initial claim needs independently accountable testimony.
A person asks Jesus to tell a brother to divide an inheritance; the commentary's regulated heirs' shares are here voiced as a contested family demand.
Jesus warns the disputants against greed and says life does not consist in possessions; the estate scene adds a moral check on the commentary's concern for rightful shares.
Paul asks believers to encourage and build each other up, and the next exhortation specifies patience with all; this is a communal pattern of mutual counsel.
The community is to let Christ's word dwell richly and teach and admonish one another; a received word is actively passed among peers.
Humility and patience are expressed by bearing with one another in love; the commentary's mutual recommendation of sabr is lived as responsibility for others.
The community is to speak truth in love so the body grows; truth becomes a reciprocal act rather than a private possession.
Timothy is charged to reprove, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching; the commentary's linked counsel and endurance are applied to instruction.
Paul describes himself as being poured out and his departure near; the surrounding charge to Timothy becomes a deliberate word handed on before death.

row.basis: writer expects to lay aside his body
row.note: The writer says his bodily dwelling will soon be put off, immediately before promising enduring remembrance; the bequest of teaching is motivated by expected death.
Believers are told to stand firm and hold traditions taught orally or by letter; the commentary's inherited charge is preserved in two concrete channels.

row.basis: faith handed over once for all
row.note: Jude urges a community to contend for the faith entrusted to the saints; a received deposit calls for continued action by those who inherit it.
At the final meal Jesus calls the cup the new covenant in his blood; a departing speaker leaves a binding religious relation to his followers.
Jesus says when giving alms, do not display it for praise; beside the commentary's Qur'anic Jesus commanded to give alms, the Gospel describes how his hearers should give.
Jesus says when praying, do not perform it for spectators; beside the commentary's Qur'anic Jesus commanded to pray, the Gospel passes prayer instruction to hearers.
Cornelius is told his prayers and alms have ascended before God; the two practices paired in the commentary's speech of Jesus are joined in a remembered disciple's life.
Jesus answers a disciple's request by giving words to pray; the Qur'anic command laid on Jesus becomes a practice he hands to his followers in this scene.
God warns Israel and Judah through every prophet and seer to turn back and keep his commandments; it gives concrete precedent for the commentary's one charge passing through messengers.

row.basis: God speaks through prophets across generations
row.note: God formerly spoke to the ancestors by prophets in many ways; it parallels the commentary's continuous chain of divine instruction to successive messengers.

row.basis: God speaks in the Son in last days
row.note: The following verse presents speech through the Son in the last days; it marks a specifically Christian culmination beside the commentary's sequence from Noah to Jesus.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; supported hands stay steady
row.note: Others support Moses' hands until sunset, and they remain אֱמוּנָה, steady; the table's אמנ family makes firmness a supported communal action beside the commentary's faith and patience.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; faithful covenant keeper
row.note: God is called faithful and keeps covenant and loyalty with those who love and obey him to a thousand generations; the table's אמנ family joins trustworthiness to a long inherited obligation.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; faithful covenant promise
row.note: God says his steadfast love will not be removed or his faithfulness made false; אֱמוּנָה from the table's אמנ field marks the reliability of a promise continuing to descendants.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; statutes and descendants
row.note: Israel must keep God's statutes so that it goes well with them and their children after them; the table's חקק correspondence joins prescribed duty to the commentary's bequest across generations.
The Passover day is to be kept as a statute through generations; Hebrew חֻקָּה from the table's חקק correspondence makes a binding inherited instruction into a recurring act.

row.basis: hope in God and keep commandments
row.note: The purpose of telling children is that they set hope in God, remember his works and keep his commands; transmitted faith and action are both named.

row.basis: Jacob promises God will accompany sons
row.note: As death nears Jacob says God will be with his sons and bring them back to their fathers' land; the parting word carries a future promise beyond the father's life.
A person who vows to the Lord or binds himself by oath must not break his word but do what he said; the commentary's binding testament and weighty oath meet in the force of an utterance.

row.basis: parental teaching addressed to a son
row.note: A son is instructed to hear his father's discipline and not abandon his mother's teaching; the form of address matches the commentary's Luqman instructing his son.

row.basis: wait patiently and keep the way
row.note: The psalm calls its hearer to wait for the Lord and keep his way amid the wicked's apparent success; obedience and endurance are joined as in the commentary's final counsel.
James points to prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience; it unites the commentary's messenger chain with the sabr expected of those who inherit their charge.
The community is told it has heard of Job's endurance and seen the Lord's outcome; endurance is transmitted as a remembered example to later hearers.

row.basis: people do not know their time
row.note: Like fish in a net and birds in a snare, people are caught by sudden calamity; it makes concrete the commentary's warning that death may arrive before a bequest can be made.

Jesus tells disciples to be ready because the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour; this is an indirect analogue to the commentary's people overtaken before they can leave an instruction, although the verse concerns the Son of Man's coming.

row.basis: plea for someone to be surety
row.note: Job asks God for a pledge and who will give surety for him; the legal image resembles the commentary's kefil, though Job's disputed standing before God differs from Joseph's announced reward.

row.basis: Monica's final request to her sons
row.note: Near death Monica asks her sons to remember her at the Lord's altar; this is a Christian example of a dying parent's religious charge, though it concerns memorial prayer rather than inheritance or a sworn witness.
Joshua is told to be strong and carefully do all the law Moses commanded him; a successor receives both an actionable charge and the endurance needed to carry it out.

row.basis: command children to obey all the words
row.note: Moses tells Israel to set its heart on his warning and command its children to observe the law; the dying generation actively passes an obligation to the next.

row.basis: David charges Solomon to know his father's God
row.note: David tells his son Solomon to know the God of his father and serve him wholeheartedly; the commentary's inherited worship and practical instruction meet in a father's direct charge.

row.basis: aged speaker tells the next generation
row.note: The aged psalmist asks not to be forsaken until he has declared God's power to the next generation; an approaching end makes transmission of testimony urgent.
The Rechabites refuse wine because their ancestor Jonadab commanded them and their children never to drink it; a concrete instruction continues after its speaker's death.

row.basis: Jonadab's words observed to this day
row.note: God cites the Rechabites' continuing obedience to their ancestor's instruction as a rebuke to Judah's failure to heed repeated divine speech; inherited counsel becomes a measure of faithfulness.
The law treats deception over a neighbor's deposited goods as a breach against the Lord; it gives moral and legal weight to the commentary's emanet left in another's keeping. This uses WLC numbering.

The same law names finding lost property, denying it and swearing falsely; the commentary's suspicion of corrupt sworn testimony concerns an equally concrete property dispute. This uses WLC numbering.
Laban tells Jacob that if he mistreats Laban's daughters, God is witness even with no human observer; a father's concern for descendants is secured by testimony beyond his presence.

row.basis: oath honored even at personal cost
row.note: The person fit to dwell with God swears to his own hurt and does not change his word; it clarifies the weight of the commentary's binding oath when keeping it becomes burdensome.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; believer does not hurry
row.note: The one who trusts the tested cornerstone will not hurry in panic; Hebrew אמנ from the table joins believing with a concrete form of patient steadiness.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; trust and be established
row.note: Jehoshaphat tells Judah to trust the Lord and be established, then trust his prophets and prosper; the verse repeats אמנ and links firm faith to heeding a transmitted prophetic word.
Isaiah condemns those who decree oppressive decrees; Hebrew חקק from the table shows that a binding rule can itself be unjust, sharpening the commentary's concern about an unfair will.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; forgetting decree harms rights
row.note: A king who drinks may forget what is decreed and distort the poor person's legal claim; Hebrew חקק from the table puts prescribed law and vulnerable claimants in the same maternal admonition.
The rabbinic chain has Moses receive Torah and hand it to Joshua, then elders, prophets and the Great Assembly; it interprets religious instruction as an inherited trust across successive speakers.

row.basis: dying father's instructions to his son
row.note: Believing he may die, Tobit calls Tobias and charges him to bury him and care for his mother; a dying speaker gives a son concrete duties to perform afterward.
Paul asks Philemon to charge to him anything Onesimus owes or any wrong he has done; he personally stands behind another's liability like the commentary's kefil.

row.basis: Paul writes his promise to repay
row.note: Paul writes with his own hand that he will repay Onesimus's debt; the guarantor's undertaking becomes an explicit, durable promise.

row.basis: continue in learning received from others
row.note: Timothy is told to continue in what he learned, knowing the people from whom he learned it; the received charge depends on identifiable transmitters and continued practice.
Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy, and they can make him wise for salvation; the inherited word is a specific text learned before adulthood.

row.basis: what Paul received he handed on
row.note: Paul explicitly says he handed to the Corinthians what he received about the Lord's final meal; a departing speaker's act becomes a repeated communal instruction.
Paul says he handed on as first importance what he received, beginning with Christ's death for sins; belief is carried by a deliberate chain of testimony.
Jesus prays at his farewell for people who will believe through his disciples' word; his instruction moves beyond those present to a future generation.
Readers are to remember the words spoken by holy prophets and the Lord's command through apostles; the charge crosses a chain of messengers and remains active in its hearers.

row.basis: teach children fear of God from youth
row.note: The community's instruction tells parents to teach sons and daughters reverence for God from childhood; the inherited religious charge is made a household duty.

row.basis: Joshua speaks as his death nears
row.note: Joshua says he is going the way of all the earth and reminds Israel that God's promises have not failed; a leader's last speech preserves a standard for successors.
David tells Solomon he will prosper if he observes the statutes given through Moses and urges him to be strong, courageous and unafraid; inherited law is paired with fortitude.
Moses says the commanded word is no empty thing but Israel's life, by which their days in the land will be prolonged; the inherited counsel has an explicitly future consequence.

A dispute over an animal, garment or lost article is brought by both parties before God for judgment; this supplies a procedure when a custodian's claim about entrusted property is contested. This uses WLC numbering.

The wrongdoer must restore the property in full and add a fifth when guilt is acknowledged; the commentary's correction of an unjust transfer has a concrete restitution analogue. This uses WLC numbering.

row.basis: speak truth and judge for peace
row.note: People are told to speak truth to one another and render truthful judgments that make for peace; mutual truth telling has the restorative legal effect sought when a bequest is disputed.

row.basis: false oath rejected with harmful intent
row.note: The next instruction rejects plotting harm against a neighbor and loving a false oath; the commentary's contested witnesses unite the same dangers of malice and sworn deception.
Israel is forbidden to spread a false report or join a wicked person as a malicious witness; the rule addresses collusion behind the commentary's suspect testimony.
The proverb forbids becoming a witness against a neighbor without cause and deceiving with one's lips; it spells out the ethical fault when legal testimony is manufactured.
The sage praises becoming surety for a neighbor while contrasting it with a shameless person's failure to do so; it supplies a Jewish ethical valuation of the commentary's kefil.
The beneficiary is warned not to forget a guarantor who has exposed himself for another; the commentary's surety carries a personal cost beyond merely announcing a pledge.
The sage says it is better for children to seek from a living parent than for that parent to depend on them; this qualifies the commentary's image of a father trying to retrieve a gift already made.

row.basis: Joseph stores grain for future need
row.note: Joseph directs grain to be collected under Pharaoh for the coming famine; this supplies the food administration behind the Joseph story's promised load of grain, independently of Hebrew צבר, whose heaping sense is unrelated to Arabic sabr.

row.basis: prophet entrusts his words to a scribe
row.note: Baruch writes the words Jeremiah dictates on a scroll; the commentary's advice passed to another to act becomes a specific transfer of a prophet's speech.

row.basis: restrained speaker must use a delegate
row.note: Jeremiah says he is barred from entering the Lord's house, so Baruch must carry and read the message; a speaker's inability to act makes a successor's faithful performance necessary.

row.basis: חקק sound correspondence; decree given to a son
row.note: The king recites the Lord's decree declaring him a son; Hebrew חֹק from the table connects a prescribed word to a father-son relation, though it is a royal oracle rather than an inheritance allotment.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; unfaithful covenant hearers
row.note: The generation instructed about God's deeds is said to be unfaithful to his covenant; Hebrew אמנ from the table supplies the contrary case to the commentary's inherited faithfulness.

row.basis: אמנ sound correspondence; Abraham's faithful heart
row.note: The prayer says God found Abraham's heart faithful and made covenant with him; the table's אמנ family joins the patriarch's trust to a promise carried to descendants.

row.basis: unjust decrees dispossess widows and orphans
row.note: The continuation says the decrees deprive the needy of justice and make widows and orphans prey; it specifies whose rights are injured when prescribed allocations are corrupted.
Paul says he writes to admonish the Corinthians as beloved children; spiritual parenthood supplies the commentary's personal relation between adviser and heir.
Paul sends Timothy to remind the Corinthians of his ways in Christ, as he teaches in every church; a recipient of instruction becomes its bearer to another group.

row.basis: practice what was learned and received
row.note: Paul asks believers to put into practice what they learned, received, heard and saw in him; the inherited word includes conduct for its recipients to enact.

row.basis: parents bring children up in admonition
row.note: Fathers are told to raise children in the Lord's discipline and instruction; household advice is a sustained responsibility, as in the commentary's father-to-child counsel.
Paul says destructive wolves will enter after he leaves; the farewell charge anticipates dangers the recipients must meet when the original speaker is gone.
Paul tells elders to stay alert and remember that he admonished each with tears for three years; the departing teacher leaves a remembered practice of warning.
The writer intends to keep reminding hearers even though they know and are established in the truth; repeated counsel protects what will remain after his departure.

row.basis: two or three witnesses in apostolic dispute
row.note: Paul invokes the rule that a matter is established by two or three witnesses before his next visit; the commentary's bequest dispute likewise requires accountable plurality in testimony.
Jesus cites the legal rule that the testimony of two people is true while defending his own witness; the estate-witness formula is reused in a different dispute over credibility.
Jesus says he bears witness and the Father who sent him also bears witness; the preceding two-witness rule is given an unusual father-son application.
