row.note: The commentary makes care for an overdriven mount part of righteous action; this law requires helping even an enemy's donkey lying under its load, giving that care a concrete ethical demand.

row.basis: fallen donkey or ox on the road
row.note: The commentary joins the road, the working animal, and its rider's treatment; this command requires raising a fallen beast encountered on the road.
The commentary glosses doing good as treating a beast well; the proverb makes the righteous person's concern for an animal's needs a test of righteousness.
The commentary pictures a person through a laboring mount; the blessing likens Issachar to a sturdy donkey, making the animal a figure for human capacity.
The commentary asks what a bearer can rightly carry; Issachar sees a desirable resting place yet bends his shoulder to a burden and becomes a laborer.

row.basis: riders and walkers on a road
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a rider from travelers called walkers; Deborah addresses those riding donkeys and those walking the road in one summons.
The commentary's pack animal carries loads through a difficult way; the oracle sends treasure on young donkeys and camels across a dangerous land, toward an unprofitable ally.
The commentary places a rider, a load, and a route together; Ziba meets David in flight with saddled donkeys carrying food and wine.

row.basis: donkeys to ride and wine for the faint
row.note: The commentary distinguishes humane travel from exhausting a mount; Ziba assigns donkeys to the royal household's riders and wine to those faint in the wilderness.

row.basis: God carried Israel all the way
row.note: The commentary calls the human a bearer and traveler; Moses reverses the direction of carrying by saying God bore Israel like a father bearing his son throughout the wilderness way.

row.basis: burden too heavy to carry alone
row.note: The commentary describes a load beyond the carrier's strength; Moses says he cannot carry the people alone because the burden is too heavy for him.
The commentary asks whether loads are borne rightly by animals; the oracle depicts idols as cargo on tired beasts, a pointed image of a burdensome false trust.
The commentary links correct bearing with loss or rescue at journey's end; these gods cannot deliver the load and themselves go into captivity.
The commentary's human shoulders an entrusted load; this oracle reverses the burden image by calling Israel a people carried by God from the womb.
The commentary worries about a carrier weakening under load; God promises to carry his people even into old age and to save them.
The commentary's losers carry weights on their backs; Aaron places Israel's confessed sins on the live goat's head, turning guilt into a visible animal load.
The commentary's load and wilderness journey meet in the goat that bears the people's iniquities away to an uninhabited land.
The commentary links loss to burdens borne at the journey's end; the psalmist's iniquities rise over his head like a weight too heavy for him.
The commentary joins human labor, right action, and burdens; the servant sees the fruit of his toil and bears others' iniquities, changing who bears the load.
The commentary sets the limit at what a carrier can endure; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to him for rest.
The commentary imagines a human traveler under a load; Jesus offers his yoke and learning from him as the way to rest.
The commentary contrasts a fit burden with exhausting a beast; Jesus calls his own yoke easy and his burden light.
The commentary condemns driving an animal beyond its capacity; Jesus condemns teachers who bind heavy loads on human shoulders yet will not move them with a finger.

row.basis: injured traveler placed on own beast
row.note: The commentary calls care for the mount good action; the Samaritan uses his own animal to carry a wounded road traveler and takes him for care.

row.basis: man carries found sheep on shoulders
row.note: The commentary depicts the human using an animal to carry a load; the shepherd joyfully carries the recovered animal himself, reversing that relation.
The commentary presents humans as bearers whose loads determine the journey; Paul makes mutual burden bearing a fulfillment of Christ's law.
The commentary asks what load a person can properly carry; Paul also says each person will carry his own load, alongside his command to share burdens.
The commentary's excessive driver imposes what a beast cannot bear; Paul says God will not allow a test beyond capacity and will supply a way to endure it.
The commentary questions a load too hard for its bearer; Peter calls imposed observance a yoke that neither the ancestors nor his hearers could bear.
The commentary distinguishes fitting loads from overloading; the council's letter explicitly limits the burden laid on Gentile believers.
The commentary imagines a traveler weakened by the way; Elijah is fed because the coming journey is too much for him without provision.
The commentary's road climbs a mountain; strengthened by food, Elijah walks forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God.

row.basis: run without weariness, walk without fainting
row.note: The commentary praises a dependable mount that does not tire or stumble; those waiting for the Lord receive renewed strength to run and walk without exhaustion.
The commentary's beaten way becomes a moral journey; Jeremiah calls people to ask for the good way, walk in it, and find rest.
The commentary's opened road carries a moral consequence; Isaiah describes a highway defined by holiness, with access distinguished by the traveler's conduct.
The commentary turns patience into a mountain on the route; the psalm asks who can ascend the Lord's hill and stand there.
The commentary ties the difficult ascent to good action and truth; the next verse admits the person with clean hands, pure heart, and no false oath.
The commentary pictures legs doing the work of a steep route; Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and enables him to tread high places.
The commentary's reliable camel does not stumble on its route; the pilgrim's keeper will not let his foot slip.
The commentary dwells on tiring travel and dependable legs; Moses says Israel's foot did not swell during forty years in the wilderness.

row.basis: carried on eagle wings to God
row.note: The commentary treats people as travelers under a burden; God says he carried Israel on eagles' wings and brought them to himself.
The commentary's trustworthy carrier bears vulnerable travelers; Moses compares God's care to an eagle carrying its young on its pinions.
The commentary glosses right action as care for a beast; the divine shepherd carries lambs close and gently leads those with young.

row.basis: carried the redeemed through former days
row.note: The commentary's human load and journey are reversed when God lifts and carries the people in compassion through their days.
The commentary makes the human a laboring traveler facing loss; Adam must eat by the sweat of his face until he returns to the ground.

row.basis: burdens for donkey and work for servant

The commentary praises a mount that will not stumble; the wisdom traveler is promised a secure way and an unslipping foot.
The commentary connects right treatment to a traversable way; the shepherd restores and leads the speaker in paths of righteousness.

row.basis: walk blameless, do right, speak truth

row.basis: Arabic ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק; table sound correspondence

row.basis: Arabic ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק; table sound correspondence

row.note: The commentary casts mortal life as a tiring road; the psalm calls even its longer span toil and trouble before it quickly passes.

row.basis: human rule over works under his feet

The commentary turns good action into a route; the letter says love consists in walking according to God's commandments.
The commentary values care for the one making a journey; the letter asks its hearer to send itinerant brothers onward in a manner worthy of God.
The commentary praises safe travel without stumbling; the letter says one who loves a brother abides in light and has no cause for stumbling.
The commentary joins good treatment with an unwearied journey; Paul urges persistence in doing good and promises a harvest if people do not give up.
The commentary's right work and patience matter at the end of the journey; Paul speaks of eternal life for those persisting in good work.
The commentary's steep route requires patience until arrival; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will to receive the promise.

row.basis: endure to end and be saved

The commentary connects a human burden to travel; Jesus tells followers to take up their cross daily and follow him.

row.basis: Jesus bears cross to execution place

The commentary condemns driving a beast beyond its strength; Jacob warns Esau that nursing flocks and herds would all die if driven hard for even one day.

row.basis: pace matched to livestock and children

row.basis: Moses asked to carry people like infant

row.basis: God seeks camp and shows the way

row.basis: shouldered idol cannot move or answer

The commentary joins inner trust to a traversable way; this blessing gives strength to the pilgrim whose heart holds the highways to Zion.

row.basis: hard valley becomes a place of springs

row.basis: pilgrims go from strength to strength

row.basis: wanderers find no road to city

The commentary's rider or walker can be exhausted by the route; the same wanderers grow hungry and thirsty until their lives faint within them.
The commentary's beaten road points toward an end; God leads the lost wanderers by a straight way until they reach an inhabited city.
The commentary praises a mount that does not stumble and an opened path; God leads the returning people beside water on a straight road where they will not stumble.
The commentary's dependable carrier does not trip despite continued travel; wisdom promises that a walker's steps will not be cramped and that a runner will not stumble.
The commentary makes legs and endurance part of the steep way; the prophet tells the community to strengthen weak hands and make feeble knees firm before the promised return.

row.basis: up the mountain to learn ways
row.note: The commentary joins a mountain ascent to righteous travel; the nations invite one another up the Lord's mountain so they may learn his ways and walk in his paths.

row.basis: who may dwell on holy hill

row.basis: good works prepared as a way to walk
row.note: The commentary places good action on the human journey; the letter says people are created for good works prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them.

row.basis: worthy walk bearing good work's fruit
row.note: The commentary joins a right road to effective work; the letter asks believers to walk worthily while bearing fruit in every good work.

row.basis: Jesus endures cross for joy ahead
row.note: The commentary's bearer must endure a difficult route to its outcome; the runner is directed to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him.
The commentary praises a carrier who does not grow weary; Hebrews asks readers to consider Jesus' endurance of hostility so they themselves do not tire or lose heart.

row.basis: work and labor not in vain
row.note: The commentary asks whether human labor ends in loss; Paul urges steadfast work for the Lord on the ground that such labor is not in vain.

row.basis: running and laboring not in vain
row.note: The commentary combines the road, human work, and the danger of loss; Paul hopes at Christ's day to find that he neither ran nor labored in vain.
The commentary's trusted mount and good treatment put confidence beside action; Paul describes effective faith as working through love.

row.basis: Moses and people wear out under heavy task
row.note: The commentary warns that even a willing bearer has a limit; Jethro tells Moses that he and the people will wear out because the judging burden is too heavy for one person.
The commentary's overloading image calls for a changed distribution; Jethro proposes other judges handle smaller cases and share Moses' burden.
The commentary makes a beast both load bearer and support for travelers; Joseph sends loaded male and female donkeys with goods and food for his father's journey.
The commentary explicitly attends to the human side used for mounting; Rebekah gets down from her camel on seeing Isaac, though this verse does not name a side.
The commentary notices the physical relation between rider and mount; Abigail quickly gets down from her donkey when she meets David, though the side is unspecified.
The commentary turns a repeatedly trodden path into moral action; the psalmist proposes to run the way of God's commandments when his heart is enlarged.
The commentary's traveler and reliable animal must resist exhaustion; God gives power to the faint and increases strength for those without it before the running and walking of Isaiah 40:31.
The commentary considers the rider's character through his mount; following the humble king's donkey, the prophecy removes warhorses and announces peace.

row.basis: mountain ascent to learn walking paths
row.note: The commentary joins a steep destination to the way of right action; Micah's parallel oracle has nations ascend God's mountain to learn his ways and walk his paths.
The commentary joins a beast and a steep road in the endurance image; Habakkuk names the failure of flocks and herds before speaking of feet fitted for the heights.
The commentary's journey is evaluated by response to loss; after listing failed crops and absent animals, Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in God before describing his strengthened feet.
The commentary calls kindness to a strained beast good action; the rabbinic discussion permits placing cushions to help an animal fallen into a pit because of its suffering.

row.basis: first aid even for enemy's beast
row.note: The commentary tests a rider's goodness by the animal's welfare; the discussion gives priority to helping an enemy's animal in order to subdue hostility, a reason distinct from relieving animal suffering.
The commentary's human carries a moral load along a path; after urging the pupil to shoulder wisdom, Sirach says to follow her ways with all one's strength.
The commentary asks which burden is fitting for a person; the teacher invites pupils to put their necks under wisdom's yoke and receive instruction.
The commentary links exertion on a hard route to its result; the teacher says he labored a little and found much rest in wisdom.
The commentary distinguishes a reliable animal from a human traveler; Jesus himself is wearied by his journey and sits beside a well.
The commentary's burden image implies attention to what another can carry; Paul asks the strong to bear the weaknesses of those without strength.
The commentary opposes driving a creature under an intolerable load; this letter says God's commands are not burdensome for the loving believer.

row.basis: light affliction and weight of glory
row.note: The commentary weighs a journey's burden against its final outcome; Paul sets momentary light affliction beside the immense lasting weight of glory it produces.
The commentary makes the human a burden bearer facing mortality; Paul describes people in an earthly tent as groaning while burdened and awaiting life beyond mortality.

row.basis: lawyers impose burdens they will not touch
row.note: The commentary condemns forcing another beyond capacity; Jesus says legal experts load people with hard burdens while refusing to touch the loads themselves.
The commentary makes good treatment of a traveler concrete; the letter commends faithful work for visiting brothers, including strangers, before urging their onward journey.
The commentary contrasts an exhausting load with one that can be carried; this saying invites people under an easy yoke and promises rest, a second Christian form of the burden image.
The commentary makes kindness to an animal a good act; after the sheep-in-a-pit example, Jesus says doing good on the Sabbath is lawful and compares human worth with the sheep's.
The commentary distinguishes a fitting load from excessive demands; the speaker says he lays no other burden on the faithful hearers at Thyatira.
The commentary's bearer needs patience through the whole way; the next verse tells those hearers to hold fast what they have until the speaker comes.
The commentary's human road can lead to loss; after the claim that Christ bore sins, Peter calls his readers wandering sheep now returned to their shepherd.

row.note: The commentary says parts are joined into a firm whole; Psalm 122 calls Jerusalem a city built and compactly joined together, giving that construction image a communal form.

row.basis: joined wall; people minded to work
row.note: The commentary makes work lay bricks and counsel join pieces; Nehemiah says the wall was joined together while the whole people had a mind to work, uniting labor and assembly in one scene.

row.basis: frame tenons received by silver sockets
row.note: The commentary’s door foot fitting its socket has a precise joinery counterpart in the tabernacle frames, whose tenons sit over paired silver sockets; the image is exact fitting rather than a loose attachment.
The commentary glosses counsel as connecting one thing to another; Exodus describes woven curtains fastened by clasps so they become one tabernacle, making joining a concrete act of assembly.

row.basis: bones came together bone to bone
row.note: The commentary calls the meeting place of bones haqq; in Ezekiel’s vision the dry bones come together bone to bone before sinews and flesh return, turning that junction into the first step of bodily restoration.

row.basis: body held together by joints; each part works
row.note: The commentary joins work, repair, and fitted parts in one structure; Ephesians describes a body joined through its joints, with each part working as it should so the whole builds itself up.

row.basis: speak truth to neighbor; members of one another
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect people; Ephesians tells each person to speak truth with a neighbor because they are members of one another, joining truthful speech to communal interdependence.

row.basis: does righteousness and speaks truth in the heart
row.note: The commentary places righteous action beside truthful counsel; Psalm 15 describes the person who does righteousness and speaks truth inwardly, joining ethical conduct and truth in one portrait.

row.basis: truthful lips endure; lying tongue is momentary
row.note: The commentary calls haqq a weighty, sound word; Proverbs says truthful lips stand forever while a lying tongue lasts only a moment, making durability an effect of truthful speech.
The commentary develops tightly woven thread and pieces made secure by joining; Ecclesiastes says a threefold cord is not quickly snapped, a direct image of strength through strands joined together.

row.basis: stir one another to love and good works
row.note: The commentary’s mutual counsel connects people in constructive action; Hebrews asks readers to consider one another and stir each other toward love and good works, making that reciprocity explicitly ethical.

row.basis: encourage and build one another up
row.note: The commentary says counsel joins parts into a sound structure; Paul tells the community both to encourage one another and to build one another up, transferring the construction image to mutual support.
The commentary puts work and haqq together in a constructive account; 1 John says love must be shown in deed and truth, pairing action with truth while warning against speech alone.

row.basis: house on rock; hears and does the words
row.note: The commentary sets sound construction against a weak house; Jesus’ wise builder hears and does his words and builds on rock, making practiced teaching the secure foundation.

row.basis: neighbors help and urge one another
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect and strengthen parts; Isaiah depicts people helping a neighbor and telling a brother to be strong, a concrete scene of reciprocal strengthening.

row.basis: spider webs cannot serve as clothing or cover

row.basis: justice as line; righteousness as plumb line

row.basis: house built by wisdom and established by understanding
row.note: The commentary’s builder’s work produces a structure made sound; Proverbs says wisdom builds a house and understanding establishes it, an explicit pairing of construction with stability.

row.basis: one lifts the companion who falls
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect separate parts; Ecclesiastes says one companion can lift the other after a fall, giving that connection a practical form of repair and support.

row.basis: reprove neighbor rather than bear sin
row.note: The commentary’s repeated counsel concerns people correcting and joining one another; Leviticus commands frank reproof of a neighbor to prevent sin, a specific ethical form of corrective counsel.

row.basis: exhort one another daily against deception
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel part of a sound communal structure; Hebrews calls for daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit, showing counsel as protection against moral failure.
The commentary’s joining image treats connection as constructive; Paul tells the community to pursue peace and what builds one another up, making the goal of connection communal edification.

row.basis: house built by injustice and unpaid labor
row.note: The commentary’s work and repair make a sound structure; Jeremiah condemns a ruler who builds his house through unrighteousness and unpaid labor, exposing a building that embodies injustice rather than repair.

row.basis: building to make a name and avoid scattering

row.basis: wall coated over a claim of peace

The commentary juxtaposes firm weaving with the spider’s weak dwelling; Isaiah says wrongdoers weave spider webs, linking the spider image to destructive rather than protective work.
The commentary contrasts firm, fitted construction with a fragile shelter; Jesus’ foolish builder puts his house on sand, specifying the unstable foundation behind failure.

row.basis: house collapses with a great fall
row.note: The commentary contrasts a sound structure with a weak house; Jesus says the sand-built house falls when storm waters and winds strike, making collapse the consequence of a bad foundation.

row.basis: builder lays a foundation and must take care how he builds
row.note: The commentary makes construction an image for coordinated action; Paul describes himself as a skilled builder who laid a foundation and warns each builder to take care, making workmanship and responsibility explicit.

row.basis: gold, stone, wood, hay, straw as building materials
row.note: The commentary distinguishes sound construction from the spider’s weak house; Paul lists materials of sharply different durability for what people build, making the quality of the work consequential.

row.basis: each person’s work is tested by fire
row.note: The commentary links work to a structure that can hold or fail; Paul says fire will disclose and test each builder’s work, adding an explicit test of what construction can endure.

row.basis: living stones built into a spiritual house
row.note: The commentary turns building and joined pieces into a moral image; 1 Peter calls its readers living stones being built into a spiritual house, giving communal construction a religious interpretation.

row.basis: hears words but does not do them
row.note: The commentary contrasts constructive deeds with a weak house; Jesus’ foolish builder hears but does not do the words, and so builds on sand, making the missing practice the moral fault behind the unstable structure.

row.basis: heals broken hearts and binds wounds

The commentary makes mutual counsel join and strengthen separate parts; Proverbs says one person sharpens another as iron sharpens iron, a direct image of reciprocal strengthening.

The commentary says mutual advice connects pieces and haqq makes the weave firm; Colossians speaks of hearts knit together in love and reaching full assurance, linking cohesion with shared understanding.

row.basis: whole structure joined and growing into a temple
row.note: The commentary fits parts into a secure structure; Ephesians describes the whole building being joined together and growing into a holy temple, an architectural image for a community.

The commentary says one piece is joined to another; in the Shepherd’s vision, stones fit together in the tower identified with the Church, giving that connection an early Christian communal interpretation.
The commentary stresses soundness and exact fit; Isaiah describes a tested cornerstone laid as a firm foundation, connecting reliable construction with trust.
The commentary’s fitted door and joined structure depend on a sound meeting point; the Psalm’s rejected stone becomes the head of the corner, making a once-discarded piece structurally decisive.

Jesus applies the rejected-stone saying to the builders’ judgment of him; this Christian reading of Psalm 118 makes the building image a reversal in which the rejected one becomes structurally central.

row.basis: Isaiah’s chosen cornerstone applied to Christ
row.note: The commentary’s firm fit and foundation imagery meets Peter’s citation of Isaiah’s tested cornerstone as Christ, adding a Christian interpretation in which trust in the chosen stone prevents shame.

The commentary makes work place bricks and repair what is broken; James insists that faith without works is dead, directly pairing belief with enacted conduct while adding a distinct argument about their necessity.

row.basis: wise woman builds; folly tears down
row.note: The commentary’s good work repairs and constructs; Proverbs contrasts a wise woman building her house with folly tearing it down, making the same household image express constructive and destructive conduct.
The commentary makes counsel join parts into a stable structure; Jesus says a house divided against itself cannot stand, giving disunity the opposite structural consequence.

The commentary’s builder and repairer produce a sound moral structure; Isaiah’s owner clears stones, plants a vineyard, and builds its tower, yet receives wild grapes, a crafted project whose result fails its purpose.

The commentary joins constructive action with haqq; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice and righteousness but found bloodshed and a cry, making failed ethical fruit the reversal of sound building.

row.basis: members care for one another without division
row.note: The commentary makes counsel connect parts; Paul says the body should have no division and its members should have the same care for one another, giving bodily cohesion a reciprocal ethical consequence.

row.basis: חקק ~ ح ق ق; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Isaiah says Zion is engraved on God’s palms and her walls are continually before him; this possible root correspondence extends the commentary’s firm word and bodily-junction imagery to an enduring inscription, without establishing cognacy.

The commentary’s mutual counsel in truth resembles the command to reprove one’s neighbor; Arakhin discusses how difficult it is both to give and receive rebuke, making reciprocal correction a demanding practice rather than a simple formula.

row.basis: firm foundation paired with turning from iniquity
row.note: The commentary opposes sound construction to a weak house and corruption; 2 Timothy says God’s firm foundation stands, then pairs its seal with the command to depart from iniquity, joining structural security to ethical conduct.

row.basis: Source root خ س ر; Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary labels khusr as loss and describes the person found deficient on the scales; Daniel's Aramaic חסר says Belshazzar was found deficient after weighing. The package table marks خ→ח, س→ס, ر→ר as an unverified regular correspondence, so this is a lexical echo in a matching context, not a proven etymology.

The commentary's deficient account at judgment is closely matched by Daniel's weighing of Belshazzar and finding him lacking, which ends his kingdom. Daniel applies the measure to a ruler's historical sentence; the commentary extends the image to every person's recompense.
Hannah's song says the Lord is a God of knowledge and actions are weighed by him; this gives a direct biblical image for the commentary's scales measuring each person's work.
The commentary says every deed is present for judgment and good is distinguished from evil; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including hidden things, to judgment, whether good or evil.

The commentary makes the day bring each human being face to face with his work; Jeremiah's searching God repays each according to conduct and the fruit of deeds, making the individual accounting explicit.
The commentary's scales miss no deed; Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each person according to work, joining scrutiny with recompense.
The commentary describes a universal accounting by deeds; Ezekiel makes the verdict personal, with God judging the house of Israel each according to his ways and calling them to turn.

The commentary identifies the Hāqqa with resurrection and judgment; Daniel's sleepers awaken from the dust, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, supplying an early Jewish scriptural scene of divided destinies.
The commentary's final sorting of good from evil is echoed by Malachi's promised renewed distinction between the righteous and wicked, specifically between serving God and not serving him.

The commentary makes truth something people mutually urge on one another; Leviticus commands a person to rebuke a neighbor rather than bear sin with him, giving mutual moral correction a concrete communal form.
Job says a person's days are determined and God sets a limit that cannot be passed; this concretizes the commentary's reading of time as a term that brings each person to reckoning.
Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity; the commentary's scales test deeds, while Job turns the same image into a plea for an honest verdict on a life.
The commentary's judgment uses scales of justice; Proverbs condemns a deceptive balance and delights in a just weight, linking accurate weighing with moral justice in ordinary dealings.

The commentary joins a fixed term with patience; Habakkuk says the vision awaits its appointed time and, even if delayed, is to be awaited. Its context is a promised vision, not a final judgment, but it makes waiting an active response to a fixed divine term.

The commentary's mutual urging of truth has a close communal counterpart in Zechariah's command to speak truth to one another and judge with truth and peace in the gates; Zechariah locates this ethic in civic restoration.

row.basis: Source root ع م ل; Hebrew עמל; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary labels the deeds with ع م ل and presents work within a profit-and-loss account. Ecclesiastes 1:3 asks what gain a person has from all the toil under the sun; עמל is the package table's unverified regular correspondence, and its sense is toil rather than morally good deed.

row.basis: Source root ص ل ح; Hebrew צלח; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary labels the exception's righteous deeds with ص ل ح. In Psalm 1:3 the righteous person's activity prospers; צלח is the package table's unverified regular correspondence, adding a prosperity outcome to the commentary's moral sense of righteous action.

The commentary makes work a moral account of gain and loss; Avot tells a person to weigh a commandment's loss against its reward and a transgression's reward against its loss, then says deeds are recorded in a book.

The commentary's account ends by sorting people according to their work; Avot says the world is judged with goodness and everything depends on the preponderance of deeds, a rabbinic formulation that makes action's cumulative weight explicit.

The commentary says not even a small deed escapes the balance; Kiddushin teaches that a person should see himself and the world as balanced, since one commandment can tip both toward merit and one transgression toward guilt.
The commentary's scales weigh human deeds; 1 Enoch's heavenly vision explicitly includes the actions of people being weighed in a balance, extending the image into an apocalyptic tour of heaven.

row.basis: souls; good and evil deeds on scales
row.note: The commentary's balance tests work and separates outcomes; Abraham's vision of judgment has a soul's good and evil deeds weighed, with the result determining its fate, giving a close Jewish apocalyptic scene.

The commentary says humanity is in loss except for the faithful who do good; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and appear untouched by torment, challenging the inference that visible death means final loss.

row.basis: coming judge repays each by deeds
row.note: The commentary's appointed day brings every person to recompense for work; Jesus says the Son of Man comes in glory and repays each according to what that person has done.
The commentary describes the final distinction between good and evil; Matthew gathers all nations before the Son of Man, who separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.

row.basis: deeds to the least count as deeds to the king
row.note: The commentary says deeds determine the account; Matthew makes acts of care toward the least of the king's siblings count as acts done to the king, giving the judgment criterion a concrete social face.
The commentary's sorting ends in reward or punishment; Matthew closes the sheep-and-goats judgment with eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other.
The commentary says the day brings every person to account by deeds; Paul states that God repays each according to works, applying the rule without a named exception.
The commentary's exception combines righteous work with patience; Paul describes those who persist in good work while seeking glory and honor as receiving eternal life.

The commentary warns that persistence can be directed toward deeds of fire; Paul contrasts the good-work endurance with self-seeking disobedience to truth, which meets wrath, preserving the moral direction of perseverance.
The commentary makes every person's work present at judgment; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat so each receives for what was done in the body, whether good or bad.

row.basis: day reveals work; fire tests it
row.note: The commentary's deeds are brought into view and judged; Paul says the Day discloses each person's work and fire tests what sort it is, giving the image of examination a material test.
The commentary says what people did is present at judgment; Revelation shows the dead before the throne, books opened, and judgment according to what is written of their deeds.
The commentary joins the appointed end to recompense for each person's work; the returning Christ says he brings reward to repay each according to work.
The commentary says every human faces an account by deeds; Peter calls God the impartial judge of each person's work and makes that expectation shape conduct during exile.
The commentary's exception names both belief and righteous action; James argues that faith without works is dead, pressing the same conjunction by insisting that belief must take embodied form.
The commentary says tiny deeds are seen and every work is present; Jesus says people answer on judgment day for every careless word, extending accountability to speech.
The commentary's truth is mutually urged; Ephesians commands each person to speak truth with a neighbor because believers are members of one another, explicitly tying truthful speech to community.
The commentary pictures mutual counsel as a protection against loss; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by sin's deceit, giving the practice a preventive purpose.

row.basis: stir one another to love and good works
row.note: The commentary's people mutually urge one another toward truth and righteous work; Hebrews makes mutual provocation toward love and good works a communal duty.
The commentary places communal exhortation within an approaching accounting; Hebrews tells the community to encourage one another all the more as the Day draws near.
The commentary joins patience to the work that reaches its term; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will in order to receive the promise.

The commentary's mutual exhortation makes the community responsible for one another; Paul tells the Thessalonians to encourage and build one another up in the immediate context of the Day of the Lord.
The commentary pairs mutual counsel with patience; Paul tells the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone.

The commentary's exception joins belief and good action with patience; Revelation identifies the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments, and faith in Jesus in an apocalyptic judgment setting.
The commentary makes patience a qualification before the term arrives; James urges patience until the Lord's coming and compares it to a farmer waiting for the harvest.

row.basis: Source root ح ق ق; Hebrew חֹק; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary labels Hāqqa with ح ق ق and explains the day as the due, appointed end of each person's account. Job says human days and months are fixed and their limit is set by God; חֹק is from the package table's unverified חקק correspondence, so the shared prescribed-limit sense is specific but etymology remains unproven.

The commentary's scales distinguish those whose account is deficient; Psalm 62 says people together are lighter than breath when set on scales. The shared image sharpens a difference: the psalm weighs human worth as vanishing, while the commentary weighs deeds and preserves an exception.
The commentary treats time as a finite term before accounting; the prayer asks God to teach people to number their days so they gain a wise heart, making mortality a prompt to live rightly.

The commentary's exception separates the righteous from those in loss; Psalm 1 ends by contrasting the way known by the Lord with the way of the wicked that perishes, framing the division as two paths.

The commentary distinguishes the people who escape loss from those condemned; the rabbinic New Year judgment tradition pictures the righteous, wicked, and intermediate as entered in three books, giving a developed Jewish account of classification at judgment.

The commentary's exception joins belief, righteous action, and truth; Wisdom says those who trust God understand truth and the faithful remain with him in love, grounding the righteous group's future in trust and divine mercy.

row.basis: work lost; person saved through fire
row.note: The commentary's gloss turns patience toward deeds of fire and punishment; Paul distinguishes the builder from work burned in the fire, saying the person may suffer loss yet be saved through fire. The image assigns loss to failed work rather than necessarily to the worker.
The commentary's patience belongs to the people who escape loss; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, placing perseverance within an apocalyptic warning.

row.basis: community perfected at the last time
row.note: The commentary makes mutual exhortation and patience part of readiness for the end; the Didache tells believers to gather and seek what benefits their souls because faith will not profit them unless they are found perfected at the last time.

The commentary presents patience as part of the way out of loss; Jesus' apocalyptic warning says that by endurance the disciples gain their lives, linking steadfastness to survival through the coming crisis.

The commentary makes people urge one another toward truth and patience; Shavuot says all Israel are guarantors for one another, adding a covenantal account of why a person's conduct concerns the whole community.

row.basis: repayment according to work and way
row.note: The commentary makes each person answer for work at the appointed reckoning; Job says God repays a person according to his work and makes each find according to his way, a direct formulation of individual moral accounting.
The commentary's scales test deeds; Proverbs adds that God weighs the spirits behind a person's apparently pure ways, bringing motive as well as outward action under scrutiny.

row.basis: repaid according to each one's work
row.note: The commentary's deficient account rests on work; this verse says God repays each person according to his work, supplying a distinct recompense formula in the psalm whose earlier verse weighs humanity on scales.
The commentary connects time with the due day and says good and bad works are separated; Ecclesiastes explicitly says there is a time for every matter and work when God judges righteous and wicked.

The commentary says deeds are present at judgment; Daniel's heavenly court takes its seat and opens books, adding a courtroom and record-book scene distinct from Daniel's weighed king and resurrection.

The commentary separates those whose work preserves them from the lost; after the beasts' oppression Daniel says judgment is given in favor of the holy ones and their time comes to possess the kingdom, adding vindication for the righteous.

The commentary distinguishes those who escape loss; Daniel says those found written in the book are delivered during unparalleled trouble, adding a register of the spared immediately before the resurrection division.
The commentary's exception is marked by righteous work; Isaiah tells the righteous it will be well because they will eat the fruit of their deeds, tying outcome to the person's own conduct.
The commentary's loss and punishment follow bad work; Isaiah gives the converse verdict that it will go badly for the wicked because what their hands have done is repaid to them.
The commentary's accounting concerns every person; the psalm pictures the Lord coming to judge the world and peoples with righteousness and equity, extending judgment to the whole inhabited world.

The commentary says each person's work is present at judgment; Malachi describes a record written before God for those who fear him and esteem his name, preserving the words and deeds of a faithful group.

row.basis: life ends in an account before the King
row.note: The commentary brings each human to the term of an account; Avot says every person is born, lives, dies, and must give account before the King of kings, compressing life's whole course into an unavoidable reckoning.

The commentary makes faith and work answerable at the end; the Talmud imagines the court asking whether one dealt faithfully, fixed time for Torah, hoped for salvation, and pursued wisdom, turning judgment into concrete questions about a lived life.

The commentary joins truth, work, and final recompense; 4 Ezra's end-time vision says judgment remains, truth stands, reward is shown, and good and evil deeds awaken, making the moral record explicit at the end.
The commentary links resurrection and division by work; Jesus describes those who did good rising to life and those who did evil rising to judgment, joining conduct directly to the two outcomes.

The commentary's exception includes belief and righteous deeds; Jesus says entry into the kingdom belongs to the one who does the Father's will, distinguishing verbal confession from enacted obedience.
The commentary says good and evil are distinguished at the end; Jesus' net parable has angels separate the wicked from the righteous at the close of the age.

row.basis: evil cast into the fiery furnace
row.note: The commentary associates evil work with punishment by fire; the net parable ends with the wicked thrown into a fiery furnace, giving separation a specific punitive outcome.

row.basis: word kept; fruit borne with endurance
row.note: The commentary combines truth, good work, and patience; in the seed parable the good soil holds the word in an honest heart and bears fruit with endurance, bringing those elements together in one image.

The commentary says each person's work is brought before the judge; in the minas parable the returning nobleman summons servants to learn what each gained in trade, a concrete audit of entrusted work.
The commentary ties work to recompense; the servant praised for faithfulness in a small matter receives authority over cities, making reward proportionate to performed work.
The commentary says work is found present at judgment; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the intentions of hearts, adding inward motive to the public accounting.
The commentary frames work as a loss-and-recompense account; Paul says a person reaps what is sown and that God is not mocked, giving moral consequence the image of harvest.

row.basis: flesh or Spirit; corruption or life
row.note: The commentary divides bad and good work by their end; Paul contrasts sowing to the flesh, which reaps corruption, with sowing to the Spirit, which reaps eternal life.
The commentary joins patience to good work before the term arrives; Paul tells the community not to grow weary in doing good because there will be a harvest at the proper time.

row.basis: God does not forget work and love
row.note: The commentary says deeds remain present at judgment; Hebrews says God is not unjust to forget the community's work and love shown in service to the saints, making faithful labor remembered.
The commentary's exception joins belief, righteous work, and patience; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit the promises through faith and patience.

row.basis: work of faith; labor of love; steadfast hope
row.note: The commentary's exception gathers faith, work, and patience in community; Paul remembers the Thessalonians' work produced by faith, labor prompted by love, and endurance grounded in hope.

The commentary says the day binds recompense to deeds; Paul calls it just for God to repay affliction to those who afflict the community, a reversal in which the persecutor receives the measure imposed.
The commentary makes the appointed day the end of a period of loss; Paul promises relief to the afflicted when Jesus is revealed from heaven, pairing the same event with vindication for sufferers.

row.basis: account to the judge of living and dead
row.note: The commentary says every person meets the account; Peter says wrongdoers will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead, explicitly universalizing the reckoning.
The commentary says what people have done is present at judgment; Revelation blesses those who die in the Lord and says their deeds follow them, making work accompany a person beyond death.

The commentary's accounting divides people by what they do; Justin says people go to everlasting punishment or salvation according to the merit of their actions, an early Christian defense of judgment by conduct.

row.basis: judge of all earth; righteous not swept with wicked
row.note: The commentary says humanity is in loss but preserves an exception; Abraham asks whether the Judge of all earth will destroy the righteous with the wicked, making the justice of a collective sentence depend on distinguishing the righteous.
The commentary says deeds are found present at reckoning; the psalm says God sets iniquities and hidden sins before his face, adding the exposure of what a person conceals.

The commentary treats time as a term ending in reckoning; Ecclesiastes permits the young to follow heart and eyes but warns that God will bring them into judgment for all this, joining present action to future accounting.

The commentary makes the present term the span in which work counts; Ecclesiastes urges doing what one's hand finds with strength because there is no work or knowledge in Sheol, making life's limit a reason for action.

The commentary's mutual counsel in truth recalls Leviticus' command to rebuke a neighbor; the rabbis debate whether people know how to give or receive rebuke, showing how the duty can fail in practice.
The commentary describes a due day that closes the account; 4 Ezra says the Most High appears at the seat of judgment as compassion and long-suffering pass away, giving the end a sharper finality.
The commentary's exception is the group not lost; Wisdom pictures the righteous standing with great confidence before those who oppressed them, adding vindication after apparent defeat.
The commentary uses an account image for loss and recompense; Jesus begins a kingdom parable with a king settling accounts with servants, then develops how debt and mercy affect the verdict.

row.basis: forgiven debtor punished for withholding mercy
row.note: The commentary sorts deeds toward punishment or reward; in the parable a servant whose debt was forgiven is handed over after refusing mercy to another, making the treatment of one's neighbor decisive.

row.basis: the spoken word judges at the last day
row.note: The commentary makes truth something mutually upheld and deeds answerable at the end; Jesus says the word he has spoken will judge the hearer on the last day, specifying the received message as a standard.

The commentary brings each person to a personal reckoning; Paul says each of us will give an account of himself to God, stressing individual answerability within a dispute about judging fellow believers.

The commentary warns of persistence in deeds that lead to fire; James describes desire giving birth to sin and fully grown sin bringing forth death, a specific account of how evil action reaches its outcome.

row.basis: holy conduct while awaiting the Day
row.note: The commentary pairs the approaching term with work and patience; Peter asks what sort of people believers should be in holy conduct and godliness while awaiting the Day of the Lord.

row.basis: patience as a practice of righteousness
row.note: The commentary makes patience part of the work that marks the exception; Hermas contrasts patience with short temper and connects endurance to right conduct, treating patience as morally active rather than passive delay.

row.basis: watering furrows; soil softened for grain
row.note: The commentary begins with rain squeezed from clouds and later with crops; this psalm has God water the furrows and prepare grain, joining rainfall directly to yield.
The commentary links rain to plants that grow after it; Joel's restoration promise names seasonal rains as the setting for renewed agricultural abundance.
After Joel's rain promise, this verse says the threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow, giving the same rain-to-harvest sequence the commentary draws from cloud to crop.

row.basis: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
row.note: The commentary moves from rain to plant growth and harvest; Isaiah's rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts, supplying seed for sowing and bread for food, a closely matched growth sequence.

row.basis: grass for cattle; plants for people
row.note: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and describes grain as human yield; this verse pairs God-grown grass for cattle with plants for human use.

row.basis: pastures with flocks; valleys with grain
row.note: The commentary connects rain-fed pasture and harvested grain; this verse places flocks in pasture and grain in valleys in one picture of a fruitful landscape.

row.basis: fat cows grazing beside lean cows
row.note: The commentary's camel fattens on spring growth; Pharaoh's dream makes fat, grazing cows the sign of abundant years, with their lean counterparts marking the coming reversal.
The commentary describes pasture nourishing a herd; the shepherd here leads the speaker to green pasture and water, adding a personal image of provision that prevents want.

row.basis: tree beside water; fruit in season
row.note: The commentary pictures the exception to loss as plants joined in unbroken greenery; Psalm 1's planted tree bears fruit at its time and its leaf does not wither, giving that flourishing a righteous figure.
The commentary's whirlwind lifts dust and its crop image ends in disappearance; Psalm 1 contrasts its fruiting tree with the wicked as wind-scattered chaff.

row.basis: watered tree endures heat and drought
row.note: The commentary's connected greenery stands against the lost harvest; Jeremiah's tree by water stays green in heat and continues bearing fruit even in drought, a specific image of endurance.

row.basis: fruit in old age; fresh and green
row.note: The commentary says a life's accumulated crop can be lost in its late years; this psalm instead says the righteous still bear fruit in old age, explicitly reversing that late-life outcome.

row.basis: עצר; rain restrained (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary's ع ص ر image releases rain from a pressed cloud; the package's table gives Hebrew עצר as a sound correspondence, and this verse uses it for heaven being restrained so rain and land-yield cease.

row.basis: חשר; collection of watery clouds (table notes BDB's Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary develops rain-bearing and layered clouds, while the package's חשר entry describes a gathering of watery clouds and notes an Arabic cognate; Job's context concerns the spread of clouds, so the lexical link is suggestive but uncertain.

The commentary labels خسر as the loss of a harvest; the package lists חסר as a corresponding Hebrew root, and the shepherd-speaker says he will not lack, giving a concrete opposite outcome under care.

row.basis: מחסור; lack of everything (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary glosses خسر as a crop's disappearance; the package's חסר correspondence appears here in a covenant curse of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and total lack, making the loss material and collective.

row.basis: צבר; grain heaped up (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary gives صبرة as food piled upon food; the package lists צבר as a sound correspondence, and Genesis uses it for Joseph's immense heaping of grain, matching the concrete heap sense.

row.basis: חק; a prescribed share of produce (table sound correspondence only)
row.note: The commentary calls the crop's due on harvest day its حق; the package's חקק correspondence means something prescribed, and Genesis fixes a fifth of the land's yield as a statute, making the crop's allotted share concrete.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
row.note: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; this law leaves a forgotten sheaf for the immigrant, orphan, and widow, showing harvested produce as a social obligation.

row.basis: sowing much, gathering little to locusts
row.note: The commentary's central loss image is a vanished harvest; this curse has abundant sowing yield little because locusts consume it, specifying one way the crop is lost.

row.basis: produce worked for but not enjoyed
row.note: The commentary says a lifetime's yield can disappear; Micah names sowing without reaping, olives without oil, and grapes without wine, turning that loss into denied agricultural labor.

row.basis: sow righteousness; reap steadfast love; rain righteousness
row.note: The commentary joins good deeds and mutual counsel to its green-growth image; Hosea commands sowing righteousness and seeking God until rain comes, linking ethical action to a promised harvest.

row.basis: sowing in tears, reaping in joy
row.note: The commentary pairs steadfastness with the crop's rise and loss; this psalm makes a painful sowing issue in joyful reaping, adding a hope-filled harvest after hardship.

row.basis: sow morning and evening without slackening
row.note: The commentary's exception holds to patient good work; Ecclesiastes tells the sower not to rest because the successful yield is unknown, giving patience an agricultural practice.

row.basis: grass and flower wither when wind blows
row.note: The commentary's cyclone lifts dust and destroys the crop; Isaiah says grass withers when the divine breath blows and identifies people with grass, bringing human transience into the weather image.
The commentary describes a whirlwind lifting dust into a column; this verse makes enemies like rolling dust and wind-driven chaff, using airborne scattering as an image of defeat.
The commentary's fiery cyclone burns a garden; this verse compares judgment on enemies to fire consuming a forest, extending the storm image to vegetation destroyed by flame.
The commentary's إعصار is a destructive wind column; this verse calls for enemies to be pursued by storm and tempest, using violent weather as an image of reversal and judgment.

row.basis: continue the work without needing to finish it
row.note: The commentary's righteous community keeps urging patience while doing good; this maxim says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence when a lifetime may not see the yield.

The commentary says the grain is named عصر when its husk appears and then describes its yield; Mark's seed parable traces growth through stalk, head, and full grain, closely matching that crop-stage sequence.

row.basis: sickle when the harvest is ready
row.note: The commentary moves from grain's formation to its yield; Mark ends the growing sequence with the sickle at harvest, supplying the moment when the crop becomes gathered produce.
The commentary joins good deeds and patience to its crop imagery; Luke's good-soil hearers hold fast and bear fruit with endurance, directly linking ethical reception to patient yield.

row.basis: farmer waits for fruit and early and late rain
row.note: The commentary connects rain-fed growth with patience; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth's precious fruit through the rains, adding patient expectation to the crop image.

row.basis: community told to be patient and strengthen hearts
row.note: The commentary says the righteous mutually urge one another to patience; James addresses the community and tells them to be patient and steady-hearted as the Lord's coming draws near.

row.basis: doing good reaped in due season
row.note: The commentary links righteous action and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because the harvest comes at its season if they do not give up, making the ethical crop analogy explicit.

The commentary's cloud gives rain and the exception is a green, productive community; Hebrews compares hearers to land that drinks frequent rain and produces useful vegetation, interpreting response as fruitful growth.
The commentary's storm can burn an entire garden; Hebrews contrasts productive land with ground bearing thorns and thistles, near a curse and destined for burning.

row.basis: vine and branches bear fruit by remaining joined
row.note: The commentary says those excepted from loss interconnect like continuous greenery; Jesus depicts branches joined to a vine and bearing much fruit by abiding, giving the joined-plant image a communal source of fruitfulness.

row.basis: severed branch withers and is burned
row.note: The commentary's crop can be destroyed by a fiery whirlwind; Jesus says the branch that does not abide withers, is gathered, and burned, joining disconnection, loss, and fire.

row.basis: truth spoken as the body grows
row.note: The commentary's people mutually counsel one another to truth; Ephesians joins speaking truth with growing into Christ, adding growth as the outcome of truthful communal practice.

row.basis: joined body grows as each part works
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel into plants connected as one green pasture; Ephesians describes a body joined together with every part working so it grows and builds itself up, a specific social counterpart to interconnected growth.

row.basis: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary's exception consists of people who urge one another to truth and patience; Paul specifies communal admonition, encouragement of the fainthearted, help for the weak, and patience toward all.

row.basis: rain and wind strike a house founded on rock, but it stands
row.note: The commentary pairs a destructive storm with hard stone; Jesus' house withstands rain, flood, and wind because it is founded on rock, making stability the opposite outcome of the ruined garden.

row.basis: grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary's late-life storm destroys a life's yield; Jesus says a grain of wheat that dies produces much fruit, turning the death of a seed into multiplication rather than loss.

row.basis: work burned and its maker suffers loss, yet is saved
row.note: The commentary likens failed works to ash blown away; Paul says a person's work may be burned and suffer loss while the person is saved, distinguishing lost product from lost person.

row.basis: abundant crops stored in larger barns
row.note: The commentary's harvest can represent a life's accumulated product; the rich man plans larger barns for his abundant produce, making stored yield the object later put at risk.

row.basis: life required before stored goods can be used
row.note: The commentary says the storm may destroy the whole accumulation late in life; the rich man is told that his life is required that night and is asked who will own his stored goods, making the harvest's futility personal.

row.basis: water bound in clouds; cloud holds its burden
row.note: The commentary's cloud is compressed with rain before releasing it; Job depicts God binding water in clouds without their bursting, adding a precise image of cloud containment.

row.basis: small cloud rising from the sea
row.note: The commentary develops rain-bearing clouds; Elijah's servant sees a cloud rising from the sea, a specific cloud sign that precedes the rain.

row.basis: sky blackens and heavy rain begins

row.basis: storm clouds, showers, and field grass

row.basis: first produce placed in a basket

The commentary makes fruitful life a shared community image; the firstfruits rite culminates in rejoicing with the Levite and immigrant, extending the crop's benefit beyond its grower.

row.basis: threshing ox allowed to eat grain

The commentary calls lineage and rank a human status measure; Paul lists circumcision, Israelite identity, and Benjaminite descent among his credentials, supplying a concrete pedigree catalogue.

row.basis: boast in knowing the God who does justice

Hebrews says a death is necessary for a testament to take effect; this makes explicit the legal logic behind the commentary's dying speaker leaving a binding word to survivors.
A testament is said to take effect only after the maker dies; this sharpens the commentary's metaphor of advice as a last bequest by explaining when such a bequest binds.
Paul writes in his own hand that he will repay what Onesimus owes; this is a direct Christian instance of the commentary's guarantor personally standing behind another's debt.
Hebrews recalls that Joseph, near death, gave instructions about his bones; it interprets the Genesis deathbed oath as an act of faith transmitted beyond the testator's life.

Proverbs warns that one who guarantees a stranger will suffer; beside the commentary's approving image of the guarantor standing behind another, it exposes the personal risk carried by that role.

Tobit tells his son, as his own death approaches, to bury him and not neglect his mother; this Jewish deathbed charge gives the commentary's image of a father's bequest to the living a concrete family setting.

The Mishnah opens with Moses receiving Torah and transmitting it through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the assembly; this Jewish tradition makes the commentary's successive handoff of counsel into an explicit chain of teachers.

The discussion of a sick person's oral gift asks when it takes effect and whether recovery permits retraction; it supplies a rabbinic legal lens on the commentary's binding testament and its source lexicon's contrasting image of a gift withdrawn.

In the closing testament scene, Job gathers his children and distributes his possessions, with a special inheritance for his daughters; this Jewish pseudepigraphic expansion makes the commentary's link between last counsel and heirs' shares unusually concrete.

A mother urges her youngest son not to fear execution but to accept death with his brothers; this Jewish martyr story makes counsel in faith under coercion a concrete analogue to the commentary's paired truth and ṣabr.

Jesus tells Peter that, once he turns back, he must strengthen his brothers; the instruction turns personal faith through a coming test into support passed to others, like the commentary's mutual counsel.
The writer tells Timothy to endure hardship and fulfill his ministry; read with the letter's imminent-death statement, it is a concrete last charge that carries steadfast service forward.
The writer says he is already being poured out and that the time of departure has come; this supplies an explicit deathbed frame for the succession and deposit language elsewhere in the letter.
The speaker says he knows that putting off his tent is imminent; like the commentary's dying testator, he frames his teaching as words left before death.
The speaker will ensure that his addressees can recall his teaching after his departure; this is a direct Christian formulation of advice preserved as a legacy.
Jesus is named guarantor of a better covenant; this supplies a distinct Christian use of surety for the commentary's figure who stands behind another's obligation.

row.basis: faith and endurance of the saints
row.note: The verse identifies the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments, and faith in Jesus; it brings faith and steadfastness together as a communal witness, though without the commentary's reciprocal advising.

The commentary's cited will procedure requires witnesses to swear, whereas James says not to swear and to let yes mean yes and no mean no; the contrast makes truthful speech without an oath an alternative account of reliable testimony.
Paul tells believers to bear one another's burdens; this gives a concrete communal form to the commentary's image of a guarantor standing behind another and carrying an obligation with them.

row.basis: law deposited beside ark as witness
row.note: Moses tells Israel to place the written law beside the ark as a witness; this unites the commentary's inherited instruction, entrusted object, and witness in one testament-like act.
Jeremiah signs, seals, and has witnesses attest a purchase deed; the legal transfer gives the commentary's rights of heirs and witness scene a concrete documentary analogue.
The deed is placed in an earthen vessel so it may last many days; this closely matches the commentary's entrusted legacy preserved for successors.
Boaz calls the elders and people as witnesses that he has acquired Elimelech's property; this joins property succession to public testimony as the commentary does.
Jacob blesses each of his twelve sons according to his blessing; this is a distinct patriarchal testament in which the father's last words are distributed among successors.
Jacob grants Joseph one portion more than his brothers; this concretely develops the commentary's claim that an inheritance consists of apportioned shares.
The good person leaves an inheritance to children's children; this states directly the intergenerational transfer that the commentary uses to illuminate mutual counsel as a legacy.

row.basis: old age and testimony to generations
row.note: The aging speaker asks to remain until he has told the coming generation of God's strength; this gives the commentary's deathbed image a living elder's explicit concern to pass testimony onward.
The psalm says its words are written for a generation yet to come; this makes the commentary's spoken bequest into a preserved written testimony for later believers.

row.basis: Jacob asks his sons about their faith
row.note: The Talmud reads Jacob's deathbed gathering as his asking whether his sons remain faithful, to which they affirm Israel's God; this is a close Jewish interpretation of the commentary's Jacob asking what his sons will worship after him.
A man asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him; this directly stages the claim over heirs' shares that the commentary treats as rights.

Jesus refuses the role of judge or divider in the inheritance dispute and warns against greed; this contrasts a legal allocation of heirs' rights with a warning that the claim itself can be spiritually misdirected.
In the rich fool parable, God asks who will receive the goods the man prepared after his death; this counters confidence in a self-managed estate with the uncertainty of who inherits it.
The Spirit is called the pledge of the believers' inheritance until its redemption; this closely joins the commentary's guarantor standing behind a claim with heirs awaiting their due.

Paul says he handed on what he first received about the Lord's Supper; this is a Christian formula for preserving a teaching and ritual across generations, matching the commentary's word passed from one believer to another.
The cup is identified with the new covenant and the rite is to be repeated in remembrance; this gives the commentary's transmitted counsel a specific liturgical form of communal remembrance.

Timothy is told to continue in what he learned and believed, knowing from whom he learned it; this explicitly links faith to a trustworthy chain of teachers, as the commentary links faith to counsel passed onward.

In the final charge before the writer speaks of his approaching death, Timothy is told to correct, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching; this directly pairs the commentary's mutual counsel with ṣabr.
The community is told to encourage one another and build one another up; this is a direct formulaic counterpart to the commentary's reciprocal act of enjoining one another.

row.basis: stirring one another to good works
row.note: The readers are to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works; this directly joins reciprocal exhortation to the commentary's faithful people's good action.
The readers are told to keep assembling and encourage one another; this makes mutual counsel an ongoing communal practice rather than a solitary last instruction.
God confirms the promise to its heirs with an oath; this directly combines the commentary's heirs and sworn testimony, showing an oath used to assure rather than test a claimant.

row.basis: attempt to seize the heir's inheritance
row.note: The tenants identify the owner's son as heir and kill him in hopes of taking his inheritance; this counter-scene makes the commentary's concern with heirs' rights vivid through their violent denial.
Moses publicly tells Joshua to be strong and lead the people into the land; this is a succession charge from a departing leader to the person who will carry the community forward.
Moses completes writing the law in a book before the farewell scene ends; together with its deposit by the ark, this makes the instruction a durable object for later generations.
Jacob declares Joseph's two sons to be his own sons for inheritance; this extends the commentary's discussion of who receives a share beyond the obvious line of sons.

Jacob predicts that the younger Ephraim will become greater than Manasseh, reversing birth order in a blessing; this complicates any reading of inherited portions as an unalterable firstborn entitlement.

Boaz explains that redeeming the property also preserves the dead man's name; this adds the continuation of a deceased person's household identity to the commentary's material inheritance and testament.
Jeremiah's witnessed deed is interpreted by the promise that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in the land; this frames the preserved document as a promise to future inheritors.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew ḥ-q-q; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary labels بِٱلْحَقّ with Arabic root ḥ-q-q and describes a binding right; the Hebrew king announces a חֹק, a decree, from the candidate root חקק, so the psalm shows a related legal sense without proving cognacy.
The royal son is promised the nations as his inheritance; this develops the commentary's image of a binding grant passing from a father to an heir.

row.basis: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary labels ءَامَنُوا۟ with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Deuteronomy joins Hebrew אֱמוּנָה, faithfulness, with God's justice and uprightness, bringing the commentary's adjacent faith and al-ḥaqq together while leaving the sound-based cognacy unverified.

row.basis: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Aramaic ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary labels faith with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Aramaic describes Daniel as מְהֵימַן, faithful, in a court where officials can find no fault except by attacking his observance of God's law, joining the root candidate to testimony and legal pressure.
The Mishnah defines the legal scope of an oath of testimony and the witnesses bound by it; it adds a rabbinic procedure for the compulsory witness oath that the commentary develops.

A midrash on Jacob gathering his sons reads the scene as his attempt to reveal the end of days, interrupted when the Divine Presence departs; this shifts the deathbed words from a family bequest toward an eschatological disclosure. Section numbering can vary by edition.
Believers are sealed with the promised Spirit after hearing and believing the message; this adds a seal of authentication to the commentary's pairing of entrusted faith and a guarantor.
Paul calls believers heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided they suffer with him; this links inheritance with endurance, a combination central to the commentary's reading of faith and ṣabr.
Jesus promises the land to the meek; this gives the commentary's patience and inheritance motifs an explicit Christian pairing, though in an eschatological rather than legal estate setting.

row.basis: farewell command to love one another
row.note: Jesus gives his disciples a command to love one another on the eve of his death; this is a concrete last instruction entrusted to a community, though its content differs from the commentary's truth and patience.
Jesus says he leaves and gives his peace to the disciples; the farewell gift formula gives a distinct Christian example of a legacy passed to survivors.

Clement says the apostles appointed approved successors so that others could succeed them after their deaths; this early Christian account makes the commentary's chain of counsel an explicit succession of entrusted responsibility.

The sound correspondence is unverified.
