row.note: The commentary recalls the prisoner's dream of squeezing grapes; in Joseph's prison the cupbearer presses the grapes into Pharaoh's cup, joining confinement, extracted drink and service in one scene.

The commentary reads pressing after hardship as a sign of relief; Joseph interprets the cupbearer's pressing dream as restoration to his former office in three days, while the cupbearer rather than Joseph receives this immediate relief.
The commentary joins post-famine pressing to preserving the extracted good; Joseph orders grain stored under Pharaoh during the good years so that produce can outlast the scarcity ahead.

row.basis: ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's sabr root names the bitter extract and the stopper that keeps it; Genesis says Joseph heaped up grain beyond counting before famine, using צבר for a different act of gathering and preserving what pressure will make valuable.

row.basis: خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary calls human khusr a diminution; Daniel's verdict says the king has been weighed and found lacking, making deficiency a judgment on a person rather than only a reduced quantity.

The commentary makes the juice pressed from grapes an image of good that should be kept; Isaiah says a cluster containing new wine must not be destroyed because a blessing is in it, then applies that preservation to God's servants.
The commentary expects a useful extract after pressing; Micah's judgment reverses that expectation, as people tread grapes yet will not drink their wine because their labor yields them no enjoyment.
The commentary's post-scarcity year is marked by pressing again; Amos pictures restored abundance so great that the mountains drip wine and the hills flow with it.

The commentary names the tongue dried by thirst alongside a person unable to pass food; Lamentations depicts nursing infants whose tongues stick to their palates for thirst while children ask for bread and receive none.
The commentary's pressed, dry tongue needs liquid relief; Isaiah describes needy people seeking water with none available and tongues parched with thirst, before God's promise to answer them.

The commentary links pressure on a person with a tongue dried by thirst; the suffering speaker's strength dries like a potsherd and his tongue sticks to his jaws. This is WLC verse 16, including the Hebrew superscription in the numbering.

The commentary calls the expressed sabr an unpleasant medicine; after thirst in the wilderness Israel finds water at Marah but cannot drink it because it is bitter, so the desired liquid initially fails to relieve need.
The commentary moves from an acrid extract to healing relief; Moses is shown a tree to put into Marah's bitter water, and the water becomes drinkable through an intervention within the liquid itself.
The commentary calls the bitter extract a medicine; after making Marah's water drinkable, God names himself Israel's healer, making the preceding unpleasant-water episode a setting for healing.
The commentary's stopper and vessel preserve a valuable liquid; the beloved is called an enclosed garden and sealed fountain, so closure marks the guarded worth of what can flow from within.

row.basis: give water to a thirsty enemy
row.note: The commentary connects flowing essence with generosity and relief of thirst; Proverbs directs a person to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy water, turning an ordinary drink into a costly good act.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's loss stands opposite goodness given away; Proverbs says a person who gives to the poor will not lack, using חסר to make generosity a way through deficiency rather than a cause of it.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's pressure and dry tongue are tied to withholding liquid; Deuteronomy warns that God may shut the heavens so no rain falls, using עצר for held-back water that brings loss of the land's produce.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's dry mouth asks how pressure can end in liquid relief; Solomon's prayer envisages the heavens being restrained from rain and the people seeking forgiveness so water may return.

row.basis: ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary puts the losing human between pressed produce and what is stored; the psalm says a person heaps up wealth yet does not know who will gather it, using צבר for accumulation that cannot secure its owner.

The commentary's pressure produces a useful, bitter essence; the rabbinic reading of Israel as an olive tree says the olive gives oil only when beaten and Israel turns toward the good through affliction, making the extraction a moral process.

The commentary's stopper and vessel keep the pressed essence from loss; Jesus' wineskin saying says old skins burst under new wine so the wine spills, whereas suitable skins preserve both wine and vessel.

The commentary joins a valuable extract, its vessel and generous outflow; the woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly nard and pours its contents on Jesus, making the opened container the condition of the gift.
The commentary names a thirst-dried tongue and liquid that could relieve distress; the rich man in torment asks for a fingertip of water to cool his tongue, but the relief he requests is withheld.

The commentary places diminished humanity between valuable contents and a holding vessel; Paul describes treasure carried in clay jars so the extraordinary power belongs to God rather than to the fragile holders.

The commentary develops pressure on the human as a possible route to saving essence; Paul says the afflicted are pressed on every side but are not crushed, making the difference between pressure and final loss explicit.
The commentary's bitter remedy comes out of pressure and heals; Hebrews calls discipline painful in the present but says it later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
The commentary places sabr after the human's pressured loss; James says testing faith produces endurance, stating the productive sequence behind the commentary's pressed remedy.

The commentary connects sabr to overcoming khusr as diminution; James asks that endurance complete its work so the faithful become complete and lack nothing, joining endurance to the reversal of lack.
The commentary's pressure can issue in sabr rather than mere loss; Paul says tribulation produces endurance, making affliction the occasion for the saving quality named at the surah's end.

The commentary develops sabr as something poured over threatened people; in Paul's sequence after tribulation and endurance, God's love is poured into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit, giving a distinct beneficial liquid image to what follows pressure.
The commentary's middle human is in loss and its close calls for sabr; Jesus tells persecuted hearers they will gain their lives through endurance, directly reversing threatened loss.
The commentary's final sabr answers the human's peril of loss; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved in a discourse about affliction and betrayal.
The commentary treats the hard-won essence as goodness given to others; Paul says his affliction serves the community's comfort and salvation, effective as they patiently endure the same sufferings.
The commentary's dried tongue belongs to one under pressure; at the cross Jesus says he is thirsty, bringing bodily thirst into an account of sustained suffering.
The commentary's liquid can be bitter rather than simply refreshing; at the cross sour wine is lifted to the thirsty Jesus on a sponge, coupling distress with an acrid drink rather than plain water.

row.basis: life poured out as drink offering
row.note: The commentary's extracted liquid represents the value produced under pressure; Paul, nearing death, describes himself as already being poured out as a drink offering, turning personal loss into an offered gift.

The commentary couples good action and patience under pressure; Peter distinguishes punishment for wrongdoing from enduring suffering while doing good, so moral value depends on what the pressured person does.

The commentary expects good essence from pressing; Isaiah's vineyard owner prepares a winepress but gets bad grapes from carefully tended vines, reversing the hoped-for product before the vineyard's judgment.

The commentary gives the pressed extract a moral sense of goodness; Isaiah explains his vineyard's failed fruit as Israel's failure to yield justice and righteousness, clarifying why a harvest image can judge a human community.

The commentary's full press can signify recovered abundance; Joel instead calls for the winepress to be trodden because wickedness is great, making the overflowing vats an image of judgment. This is WLC's Hebrew Joel 4:13.
The commentary's pressing produces a potentially healing good; Isaiah's solitary winepress treader makes red garments an image of wrath against peoples, a specific contrary use of the same action.
The commentary recalls renewed pressing after scarcity; Joel promises threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing with wine and oil as the land recovers from devastation.

The commentary's stopper and vessel keep something valuable for later; Jeremiah orders purchase documents put in an earthenware jar so they survive many days during Jerusalem's siege, preserving a sign of future restoration.
The commentary's human stands in diminishment between pressure and relief; Job says a person born of woman has few days and is full of trouble, sharpening the vulnerability of the one being pressed.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary defines khusr as lack or decrease; the speaker whose shepherd is the Lord says he lacks nothing, using חסר to picture the opposite of human deficiency through care received.

row.basis: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary places loss against good preserved; the psalm contrasts hungry young lions with seekers of the Lord who lack no good thing, using חסר to make need and its relief concrete.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's opening root evokes pressure and its close calls people to counsel one another; Joel calls a solemn assembly, using עצרה, and gathers elders and inhabitants to cry to God amid a ruined harvest, turning held-together people toward a shared answer to scarcity.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB cognate note
row.note: The commentary puts al-insan under pressure and loss; the psalm asks what frail man is that God remembers him, using אנוש for humanity whose smallness receives unexpected divine attention. This is WLC verse 5 after the superscription.

row.basis: gall for food and vinegar for thirst
row.note: The commentary's food obstruction, thirst and bitter remedy converge in one sufferer's plea; the psalm says enemies give gall for food and vinegar for thirst, turning what should nourish and refresh into affliction. This is WLC verse 22.

The commentary turns expressed essence into generosity; Isaiah asks a person to give of himself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted, after which light rises from darkness, connecting costly giving to relief.

The commentary's dried tongue and beneficial outflow invite a restoration image; Isaiah promises guidance and satisfaction in parched places until the person is like a watered garden and unfailing spring.

The commentary recalls patience poured on people facing danger; Lamentations tells Jerusalem to pour out her heart like water before the Lord for children fainting from hunger, joining a liquid prayer to communal deprivation.

The commentary treats a saving quality as poured onto the pressured person; Hannah explains that she has poured out her soul before the Lord amid deep distress, an inward liquid image for responding to affliction.

The commentary describes a bitter medicine produced by pressure; the rabbinic teaching says Torah, the land of Israel and the world to come are granted through suffering, interpreting pain as a passage to valuable goods.

The commentary proposes a healing value in painful pressure; a sage in the discussion of afflictions says he wants neither the sufferings nor their reward, preserving a dissenting response to the claim that pain is worth its yield.

The commentary values the held essence and the vessel that protects it; the rabbinic exchange about fine wine in earthen jars uses the vessel to explain why wisdom is preserved with humility, transferring storage to a human quality.

The commentary distinguishes valuable contents from the container and diminished exterior; Avot says to inspect what a jar holds, since a new jar may contain old wine and an old jar may contain none, making contents the measure of worth.
The commentary's dry tongue requires a life-giving drink; Jesus calls anyone thirsty to come to him and drink, offering spiritual relief through the bodily action named in the scene.

The commentary's beneficial extract becomes an outflow to others; Jesus says living water will flow from the believer's inner being, turning received drink into a source rather than a private possession.
The commentary makes liquid relief an act of goodness; the king identifies himself with a thirsty person to whom the righteous gave drink, tying a small bodily gift to the judgment of good action.

row.basis: cup of water given to a disciple
row.note: The commentary says expressed goodness can take the form of a gift; Jesus promises a reward for giving even a cup of water because the recipient belongs to Christ, measuring charity by a concrete drink.

The commentary places patience after pressed produce and scarcity; James asks the community to wait like a farmer for the precious fruit of the earth through its early and late rains, joining endurance, water and eventual yield.

The commentary calls sabr a bitter but healing result of pressure; James recalls Job's endurance and the Lord's compassionate outcome, locating patience within a particular sufferer's eventual relief.
The commentary joins righteous deeds to mutual counsel in patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will to receive what was promised, linking conduct and sustained waiting.
The commentary's valuable result of pressure is shared goodness; Paul says comfort received from God in affliction equips sufferers to comfort others, making the product of distress transferable.

The commentary describes pressure drawing out an essence of worth; Peter says tested faith is more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, using another physical ordeal to explain enduring value.
The commentary links a treasured liquid with giving and thirst; Revelation invites the thirsty to take the water of life without payment, making the valuable drink an unrestricted gift.

The commentary's container matters because it keeps something useful; Paul says a cleansed vessel is set apart and ready for every good work, moving from a vessel's condition to the person's capacity for beneficial action.

row.ref: Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Romans 4:1
row.note: The commentary imagines a person under pressure yielding something precious; Ignatius asks that beasts grind him like God's wheat so he may become Christ's pure bread, giving martyrdom the shape of painful production.

The commentary's bitter extract is a medicine; Elisha adds flour to the pot after the prophets fear death in the stew, and the food becomes harmless. The bridge is a healing substance in a vessel, though the passage does not call the flour bitter or describe squeezing it.

row.basis: poured offering joined to others' faith
row.note: The commentary's pressured essence is given away; Paul depicts himself as poured out upon the community's sacrificial service of faith, though the passage supplies neither a pressed plant nor a sealed container.

row.basis: stored food prevents death in famine
row.note: The commentary connects the return of pressing after lean years with keeping valuable produce; Joseph says the stored food will sustain Egypt through seven famine years so the land will not perish, stating the life-saving purpose of the storage ordered in the preceding verse.

The commentary's pressed and stored good becomes relief when want arrives; as famine spreads, Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to Egyptians, bringing the preserved supply into use rather than leaving it sealed away.

row.basis: evil converted into preservation of life
row.note: The commentary imagines pressure on a person yielding a good that others receive; Joseph tells his brothers that the evil they intended against him was turned toward preserving many lives, interpreting the outcome of his imprisonment and food administration.

The commentary locates pressing beside confinement and scarcity; Gideon beats out wheat inside a winepress to keep it from Midian, using the grape vessel as a hiding place for food under oppression rather than as a source of drink.

row.basis: broken cisterns unable to hold water
row.note: The commentary's vessel keeps its valuable liquid from loss; Jeremiah contrasts the living-water source with cracked cisterns that cannot hold water, making a failed container an image of a people's self-inflicted deprivation.

The commentary makes renewed pressing a sign that scarcity has ended; Isaiah's judgment removes joy from the vineyards and silences the treader in the winepress, so the same action's absence signals loss.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB cognate note
row.note: The commentary places the human being under pressure; Job asks what frail human is that God magnifies him and sets his attention on him, using אנוש to turn divine notice into an anguished question amid suffering.

row.basis: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's al-insan is exposed to loss; Daniel sees one like a human being coming with heaven's clouds before the Ancient of Days, using the Aramaic cognate for a humanlike figure poised for a different outcome.

The surah's close calls believers to counsel one another in truth; Zechariah tells the restored community to speak truth each to the other and to render true judgments, making truthful speech a shared public practice.

row.basis: drink that ends thirst and becomes a spring
row.note: The commentary links a dry tongue, a relieving drink and a valuable liquid kept within; Jesus says the water he gives ends thirst and becomes a spring within the recipient, turning received relief into a continuing source.

row.basis: outer person wastes, inner person renews
row.note: The commentary places the diminished human beside a preserved inner good; Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed daily, specifying what can endure inside the fragile vessel of 4:7.

The commentary says pressure may yield a valuable result beyond the loss it inflicts; Paul says momentary affliction produces an eternal weight of glory, continuing the account of pressed but uncrushed people in 4:8.

row.basis: wine mixed with gall offered and refused
row.note: The commentary's drink can be a bitter product amid suffering; before crucifixion Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting, so an acrid cup accompanies pressure without becoming the healing drink the commentary imagines.
The commentary calls the bitter extract a medicine; Revelation says waters made bitter by Wormwood kill many drinkers, a concrete reversal in which bitter liquid is harmful rather than curative.

The commentary's press can yield goodness for people; Revelation has an angel gather the earth's grape harvest into the great winepress of divine wrath, giving the same extraction scene a punitive end.

row.basis: blood flows from the trodden press
row.note: The commentary treats the outflow from pressing as a possible valuable essence; Revelation's next verse says blood flows from the winepress after it is trodden, specifying a violent extract rather than a remedy.

The commentary imagines something removed under pressure so that good can emerge; Jesus says the Father prunes a fruit-bearing branch to make it bear more fruit, joining painful subtraction to a larger yield.
The surah names good deeds and reciprocal counsel; Hebrews calls hearers to consider how to stir one another to love and good works, supplying a concrete communal form for the surah's linked actions.

row.basis: encouraging one another as the day nears
row.note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel is urgent under human loss; Hebrews asks the assembly not to abandon meeting and to encourage one another increasingly as the day approaches, adding persistence in a gathered community to the preceding call to good works.

The surah closes with believers counseling one another in patience; Paul directs the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient toward all, putting counsel and endurance in the same set of relations.

row.basis: food and drink given to an enemy
row.note: The commentary interprets beneficial liquid as generosity under pressure; Paul repeats the instruction to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy drink, carrying the concrete act from Proverbs into counsel to a Christian community.

The commentary's bitter liquid is a healing medicine; in the ordeal of jealousy the woman must drink water of bitterness that carries a curse, giving an ingested bitter fluid a punitive effect instead.

The commentary's al-insan is liable to diminution; after asking what frail humanity is, the psalm says God crowns the human with glory and honor, continuing the human scene with elevation rather than loss.

The commentary's human undergoes pressure; Job continues his question about the אנוש of 7:17 by saying God tests him every moment, making divine attention feel like sustained examination. The root itself is in the preceding verse.

The commentary's human stands under the sentence of loss; the figure described as humanlike in 7:13 receives lasting dominion and a kingdom here, completing that scene with an opposite destiny. The Aramaic אנש occurs in the preceding verse.
The commentary's vessel preserves and dispenses good under pressure; the psalmist's cup overflows at a table prepared in the presence of enemies, so contained abundance appears while threat remains.

row.basis: thirsty and hungry filled with good
row.note: The commentary links obstructed food, thirst and a good that relieves need; the psalm says God satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry soul with good things, bringing the two bodily lacks into one act of provision.

The surah's reciprocal counsel follows the image of pressure yielding value; Proverbs says iron sharpens iron and one person sharpens another, a specific abrasive image for mutual improvement rather than solitary patience.

row.basis: reward according to effort and pain
row.note: The commentary proposes that a painful process can produce a valuable good; the maxim associates reward with the labor or pain expended, providing a Jewish ethical reading of effort's yield without claiming literal grape pressing.

The commentary calls patience a bitter but beneficial outcome of pressure; Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him, giving a particular sufferer's ordeal and later good beside the discipline image in 12:11.

row.basis: cup of suffering and yielded will
row.note: The commentary makes a cup and its difficult contents part of the pressured person's response; Jesus asks that the cup pass from him but submits to the Father's will, using the vessel for an ordeal faced with endurance.
The surah makes patience and counsel reciprocal under human loss; Paul tells believers to carry one another's burdens, giving shared weight a practical communal answer.

The surah joins giving counsel and sabr; Timothy is instructed to correct, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching, making endurance a quality of the counsel itself, though the instruction is addressed to one teacher.

row.basis: good overcomes evil after water gift
row.note: The commentary says a squeezed essence can become goodness given away; after directing food and drink to an enemy in 12:20, Paul says to overcome evil with good, naming the moral effect of that costly gift.

row.basis: fruit of vine deferred until kingdom
row.note: The commentary recalls renewed pressing after a time of deprivation; Jesus says he will not drink the fruit of the vine again until drinking it new with the disciples in his Father's kingdom, setting present abstention beside future shared wine.

The commentary calls the sap named sabr a bitter medicine; this mandate presents patience as sweet and valuable in moral struggle, offering a contrary taste for the virtue. The precise subsection within Mandate 5.1 needs verification.

row.basis: Commentary's 12:36 prison dream; grapes pressed into a cup
row.note: The imprisoned cupbearer dreams of taking grapes and pressing them into Pharaoh's cup, giving the commentary's prison grape-press scene in its own narrative setting.

row.basis: Wine with no vent; new wineskins ready to burst
row.note: The commentary's cork holds squeezed liquid in a bottle; Elihu instead likens unspoken words to fermenting wine with no vent, so the same containment intensifies pressure toward rupture.
The commentary's stopper keeps the bitter extract inside its vessel; the poem's sealed spring likewise contains a source, but presents closure as erotic exclusivity rather than medicine.
The commentary ends with a sealed bottle that retains its medicinal essence, whereas Jeremiah's chosen cisterns are cracked and cannot hold water, making failed containment a charge against Judah.

row.basis: Marah's bitter water and the wood
row.note: At Marah the people cannot drink bitter water until Moses throws a tree into it and it becomes sweet; this reverses the commentary's bitter tree extract, which remains bitter yet is named medicine.

After the bitter-water episode, YHWH identifies himself as Israel's healer; this makes explicit the healing frame that the commentary gives to bitter sabr, though the remedy and bitterness work differently.

row.basis: Judah trodden as grapes in a winepress
row.note: The lament says the Lord has trodden Judah like grapes in a press; the commentary's human squeezed into loss becomes a crushed people here, and the press yields devastation rather than a useful essence.

row.basis: Winepress trodden in wrath; blood on garments
row.note: The divine speaker treads the press in anger and blood stains his clothing, a direct counter-image to the commentary's extracted juice as good and generous giving.

row.basis: Ripe harvest; vats overflowing with wickedness
row.note: The harvest press overflows because the nations' wickedness is great; the shared pressing and yield imagery makes the commentary's beneficial extract read against a judgment harvest.

row.basis: Fig cake applied to a boil; recovery
row.note: Isaiah orders a fig cake laid on Hezekiah's boil and Hezekiah recovers; this gives a concrete plant-based remedy alongside the commentary's bitter tree extract called medicine.

Sirach says the Lord made medicines from the earth and a sensible person does not reject them; it supplies a Jewish wisdom frame for the commentary's medicinal plant exudate as a beneficial natural substance.

row.basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The Hebrew verb עצר closes the heavens so rain and yield cease; this restraint is the agricultural inverse of the commentary's squeezing that releases juice and, in its Yusuf comparison, marks relief after scarcity.

row.basis: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Moses says Israel lacked nothing during the wilderness years; the cognate sense of lack gives a direct counter-reading to the commentary's human placed in decrease and loss.

row.basis: Commentary label root ء ن س; Hebrew אנש, regular sound correspondence and BDB Arabic-cognate note
row.note: Job asks what אנוש, a mortal human, is that God gives him such attention; it lends the commentary's generic human between pressure and loss a specific mortal and vulnerable register.

Paul places treasure in fragile earthen vessels; this gives a close vessel image for the commentary's bottled essence, while locating the value in the vessel's contents rather than in a bitter remedy.
Paul says the community is pressed yet not crushed; this directly answers the commentary's image of the human as squeezed matter that decreases, with pressure failing to exhaust the people.
Paul distinguishes being struck down from being destroyed; this counters the commentary's equation of human pressure with decrease by describing survival after blows.
Paul says affliction produces endurance, which gives the commentary's squeezed, bitter sabr a developmental reading: pressure can generate the quality that sustains a person.

Paul says God's love has been poured into believers' hearts; the commentary specifically notes Qur'anic patience poured over people, and this supplies a Christian liquid metaphor for an inward virtue, while naming love rather than patience.

row.basis: Painful discipline later yields peaceful fruit
row.note: Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit; this gives a precise interpretive bridge to the commentary's bitter medicine, whose discomfort is paired with healing benefit.

row.basis: Saints' endurance, God's commands, and faith in Jesus
row.note: The verse defines the saints by endurance, keeping God's commands, and faith in Jesus; this closely gathers patience, faithful action, and belief in the kind of people the commentary exempts from loss.

row.basis: Persistence in doing good and harvest in due season
row.note: Paul urges doing good without weariness because a harvest comes in due time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's righteous action and patience to an agricultural yield.

row.basis: Stirring one another to love and good works
row.note: The addressees are told to provoke one another toward love and good works; this closely matches the commentary's reciprocal counsel and righteous deeds, though it specifies love rather than truth.
The assembly is to encourage one another as the day approaches; this supplies the reciprocal communal action behind the commentary's repeated mutual exhortation.

row.basis: Turning a wanderer back from truth
row.note: James addresses fellow believers and says that whoever turns a brother back from wandering from the truth performs a communal corrective act like the commentary's mutual counsel in truth.
James adds that bringing the wanderer back saves that person's soul from death; this makes the truth-directed mutual correction a rescue from loss, not merely instruction.

row.basis: Speak truth each with the neighbor
row.note: Paul commands each person to put away falsehood and speak truth with the neighbor because they belong to one another; this is a direct communal truth-speaking analogue to the commentary's mutual counsel.

row.basis: Perseverance in doing good leads to eternal life
row.note: Paul describes those who persist in doing good and seek glory and immortality as receiving eternal life; this combines the commentary's good action and patience in a salvific outcome.

row.basis: Salvation as a gift through faith
row.note: Paul says salvation is by grace through faith and is God's gift; set beside the commentary's list of belief and righteous deeds, this frames the ground of rescue differently.

row.basis: Not from works, so no one may boast
row.note: Paul explicitly denies that salvation is from works, while the commentary includes righteous deeds in the description of those outside loss; the contrast concerns how deeds relate to rescue.
Paul immediately says believers are created in Christ for good works; this keeps the contrast from erasing action and offers a distinct account of deeds as the intended result of salvation.

row.basis: Faith and patience inherit the promises
row.note: The author urges imitation of those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this directly pairs two qualities named in the commentary's saved group.

row.basis: Steadfast work is not in vain
row.note: Paul calls the community steadfast and abundant in the Lord's work, assuring them that their labor is not empty; this counters the commentary's language of human loss with enduring good action.
James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's bitter, pressed sabr an explicit formation process under trial.
James says endurance must have its full effect so people become complete; this interprets patience as a formed quality with a beneficial end, like the commentary's medicine metaphor.
The community must exhort one another daily so no one is hardened by sin's deceit; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel a concrete protective purpose against moral loss.
Peter asks what credit there is in enduring punishment for wrongdoing, then calls it grace to endure suffering while doing good; this tightly joins patient endurance to righteous action.

row.basis: The farmer patiently waits for precious fruit
row.note: James tells the community to wait patiently like a farmer for the earth's precious crop; it links patience to delayed yield, though the image is cultivation rather than extraction.

Ignatius calls the shared Eucharist medicine of immortality and an antidote to death; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's medicinal image toward communal nourishment and rescue from death.
The verse commands honoring YHWH with one's wealth and first produce; beside the commentary's claim that extracted juice figures good and generosity, it makes abundance an act of giving.
The next verse promises vats brimming with new wine; the commentary's juice as beneficial abundance finds a concrete biblical image of overflowing produce.
The psalm names wine as what gladdens the human heart; it gives a biblical instance of the commentary's extracted juice as goodness for people.
In Jotham's fable the vine says its wine gladdens God and people; this concretely parallels the commentary's report that Arabs make expressed juice a figure for good and generosity.

row.basis: A winepress prepared for grapes but wild grapes produced
row.note: The vineyard owner builds a winepress expecting good grapes but finds wild grapes; the image makes the commentary's generous essence contingent on a yield that can instead disappoint.

row.basis: Seven years of famine after seven years of plenty
row.note: Joseph's dream interpretation predicts seven lean years after abundance; it parallels the commentary's sequence of scarcity and eventual relief while preserving a different order from its pressing year.
When famine covers the land, Joseph opens the storehouses; this connects the commentary's retained essence in a closed bottle with stored provision later released to sustain people.

row.basis: Wine left on its lees and not poured between vessels
row.note: Moab's undisturbed wine retains its flavor because it has not been poured from vessel to vessel; the commentary's cork likewise preserves a liquid, but Jeremiah makes stillness a figure for complacency.

row.basis: The cup of divine wrath and its dregs
row.note: The psalm's cup contains foaming wine and dregs that the wicked must drink; it turns contained liquid toward judgment rather than the commentary's medicinal extract.

row.basis: Maror eaten to recall Egyptian oppression
row.note: At the Passover meal bitter herbs are part of the narrated memory of bondage; this makes bitterness a communal ritual of remembered suffering, unlike the commentary's bitter remedy.
Tobit's father regains sight after fish gall is applied; this is a concrete natural-substance cure alongside the commentary's medicinal tree exudate, though its source is animal rather than plant.

row.basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The Hebrew form עצר says YHWH had closed every womb in Abimelech's house; this related closure gives a bodily analogue to the commentary's stopper sealing a vessel, with withheld fertility instead of preserved medicine.

row.basis: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Abraham asks whether five righteous people might be lacking from fifty; the Hebrew cognate makes decrease numerical and ties the missing count to whether a city is spared.

row.basis: Colleagues sharpen one another in Torah
row.note: The Talmud applies iron sharpening iron to scholars who sharpen one another in Torah; this interprets mutual counsel as reciprocal learning and correction, a specific Jewish account of the commentary's tawāṣī relation.
The proverb says one person sharpens another as iron sharpens iron; this gives mutual exhortation a concrete image of improvement through another's words.

row.basis: Accept what comes and be patient in humiliation
row.note: Sirach tells the reader to accept what comes and be patient in humiliation; it links patience to receiving painful experience, an explicit bridge to the commentary's bitter remedy.

row.basis: Gold tested in fire; acceptable people in humiliation
row.note: Sirach compares tested people to gold in a furnace; it supplies a refining image in which affliction tests and qualifies, alongside the commentary's pressure that produces bitter sabr.

row.basis: Correct, rebuke, and exhort with patience and teaching
row.note: Paul charges Timothy to preach, correct, and exhort with patience and teaching; unlike the commentary's mutual practice, this is a ministerial instruction, but it joins truth-directed correction to patience.

row.basis: Endurance produces tested character and hope
row.note: Paul says endurance produces tested character and hope; this continues the commentary's image of a beneficial quality formed through pressure.

row.basis: Commentary label root ص ب ر; Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The Hebrew verb צבר describes Joseph piling up grain beyond measure; beside the commentary's corked bottle retaining squeezed essence, the narrow connection is accumulation and storage, not a shared sense of patience.

row.basis: Commentary label root ء ن س; Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence only and unverified
row.note: Daniel sees one like a bar enash, a humanlike figure who receives dominion; this contrasts the commentary's collective humanity with a singular exalted use of the related Aramaic word.

row.basis: Tongue of the infant clings from thirst
row.note: The commentary names a thirst-dried tongue as maʿṣūr; in Jerusalem's siege the infant's tongue clings to the palate for thirst, making the bodily image concrete in a scene of deprivation.

row.basis: Tongue fails for thirst; water is promised
row.note: The needy have no water and their tongue fails from thirst; this closely matches the commentary's dried tongue, while Isaiah's promised springs reverse depletion with relief.

row.basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The proverb names the closed womb with עצר; this table correspondence links the commentary's root to bodily closure, while the proverb's unsatisfied earth and water add a distinct thirst setting.

row.basis: Closed womb and earth unsatisfied with water
row.note: The proverb places a closed womb beside earth that is never satisfied with water; this meets the commentary's closure and thirst images together, but as unsated lack rather than a bottle retaining medicine.

row.basis: Bitter water that brings a curse
row.note: The suspected woman is made to drink water of bitterness that brings a curse; this is a concrete counter-use of bitter liquid beside the commentary's bitter plant extract called medicine.
The ritual's consequence is that the water becomes bitter within the woman and brings a curse; bitterness here exposes and punishes rather than healing as in the commentary's medicinal sabr.
The speaker says he has been filled with bitterness and wormwood; the plant bitterness is imposed misery, a counter-reading to the commentary's painful but beneficial remedy.

row.basis: Wormwood makes waters bitter and kills many
row.note: The star named Wormwood makes the waters bitter and many die from them; this directly reverses the commentary's bitter plant extract as medicine by making bitter liquid lethal.

row.basis: Scroll sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
row.note: John is told to eat the scroll, which will be sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach; the two-stage taste gives the commentary's swallowed bitter medicine a distinct prophetic counterpart.

row.basis: Sweet taste turns bitter after eating
row.note: John reports that the scroll tasted sweet and then made his stomach bitter; this locates bitterness after ingestion, unlike the commentary's bitter extract whose bitterness is already the medicinal quality.

row.basis: Wine mixed with gall is offered and refused
row.note: Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall and refuses it after tasting; this gives a specific bitter drink in a suffering scene, but the text presents no healing benefit like the commentary's medicine.

row.basis: Wine mixed with myrrh is refused
row.note: Mark says wine mixed with myrrh is offered to Jesus and he does not take it; the plant resin in a wine drink recalls the commentary's plant-derived bitter essence, though Mark does not call it bitter or medicinal.
At the crucifixion Jesus says he thirsts; this is a specific bodily thirst scene beside the commentary's dried tongue, with the speaker's impending death making the need unresolved.

row.basis: Sour wine lifted to the thirsty Jesus
row.note: The bystanders raise sour wine to Jesus after he says he thirsts; the drink is acidic relief in a death scene, not the beneficial bitter remedy described in the commentary.

Jesus says new wine put into old wineskins bursts them and both wine and skins are lost; unlike the commentary's corked bottle retaining a medicinal essence, this vessel fails under pressure and causes loss.

row.basis: Earth's grapes thrown into the winepress of wrath
row.note: The angel gathers the earth's grapes and throws them into God's great winepress; this directly turns the commentary's pressing that yields good essence into an apocalyptic harvest of wrath.
The press is trodden outside the city and blood flows from it; this specifies the destructive yield of the preceding winepress, in contrast to the commentary's useful extracted juice.

row.basis: Jar of meal and jug of oil do not fail during drought
row.note: Elijah promises that the widow's jar and jug will not be emptied until rain returns; the contained provision in scarcity parallels the commentary's stored essence and its Yusuf scene of relief after famine.

row.basis: The jar and jug remain supplied
row.note: The narrative says the widow's jar and jug did not fail as promised; this continuation shows stored liquid and food sustaining life through drought, unlike a one-time extracted dose.

row.basis: Oil fills every borrowed vessel and then stops
row.note: The widow's oil keeps filling containers until there is no vessel left, when the flow stops; it gives a precise parallel to liquid collected and held by a vessel, with provision released rather than a corked medicine.

row.basis: Treader of grapes overtaken by the sower; hills drip wine
row.note: Amos pictures restoration so abundant that grape-treading overlaps sowing and mountains drip sweet wine; this makes pressing the sign of relief and plenty, as in the commentary's post-scarcity year.

row.basis: Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress to hide it
row.note: Gideon works grain in a winepress while hiding from Midianite raiders; the press belongs to threatened subsistence here, unlike the commentary's press as the sign that scarcity has ended.

row.basis: Commentary label root خ س ر; Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The verse says young lions lack and hunger while those who seek YHWH lack no good thing; Hebrew חסר gives the commentary's decrease a direct cognate contrast between want and provision.

row.basis: Put on patience with other virtues
row.note: Paul tells the community to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience; this places patience among shared ethical dispositions, extending the commentary's community defined by sabr.

row.basis: Bear with and forgive one another
row.note: The addressees are told to bear with and forgive one another; this gives the commentary's mutual counsel in patience a concrete practice of forbearance.

row.basis: Teach and admonish one another with the word
row.note: Paul tells the community to teach and admonish one another with wisdom as Christ's word dwells among them; this is a close communal counterpart to mutual counsel in truth.

row.basis: Admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
row.note: Paul urges the church to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this combines mutual moral care with patience in concrete cases.

row.basis: Seek the good of one another and everyone
row.note: The church must not repay evil for evil but always pursue good for one another and all; this connects reciprocal ethical counsel to doing good.

row.basis: The Lord's servant must be patient and able to teach
row.note: Paul describes the Lord's servant as not quarrelsome but patient and able to teach; this joins patient conduct to truthful instruction, though it is pastoral rather than reciprocal.

row.basis: Correct opponents gently toward knowledge of truth
row.note: The servant is to correct opponents gently in hope that God grants them knowledge of truth; this directly joins correction and truth, adding a one-directional teaching scene to the commentary's mutual counsel.
James asks whether a person who claims faith but has no works can be saved; this directly tests the commentary's pairing of belief and righteous action, making their relation explicit.
James says faith without works is dead; this gives a specific Christian account of why belief and deeds belong together in the commentary's exception from loss.

Paul contrasts those who obey truth with those who disobey truth and pursue unrighteousness, who receive wrath; this counters the commentary's mutual truth-counsel by depicting refusal of truth as a path to judgment.

row.basis: Losing life for Jesus saves it
row.note: Jesus says the one who loses life for his sake will save it; this reverses the commentary's general human loss into a paradoxical self-loss that leads to rescue.

row.basis: Enduring trial leads to the crown of life
row.note: James calls blessed the person who endures trial and promises the crown of life; this connects patience under pressure to a salvific outcome.

row.basis: Tested faith compared with refined gold
row.note: Peter says tested faith, more precious than perishable gold refined by fire, will result in praise and honor; this gives pressure a refining yield, though by fire rather than squeezing.

row.basis: Pruning a fruitful branch for more fruit
row.note: Jesus says the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so it bears more fruit; this gives the commentary's grape and pressure images a contrasting cultivation model where cutting increases future yield.

row.basis: Jesus asks that the cup pass, then submits
row.note: Jesus asks whether the cup can pass but submits to the Father's will; the cup makes suffering a drink-like burden, while the scene adds willing endurance rather than the commentary's extracted medicine.

row.basis: Jesus accepts the cup he must drink
row.note: Jesus says that if the cup cannot pass unless he drinks it, the Father's will be done; this continuation turns the cup from a requested escape into accepted suffering.

row.basis: God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness
row.note: Paul uses seed, bread, and an increased harvest of righteousness; this connects agricultural yield to the commentary's good essence and gives generosity an ethical harvest image.
Paul says the community is enriched in every way for generosity; this closely matches the commentary's report that expressed juice serves as a figure for goodness and giving.

row.basis: Commentary label root ع ص ر; Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The proverb's closed womb uses the Hebrew root the table matches to Arabic ع ص ر; it supplies a bodily use of closure distinct from pressing and from the bottle-stopper sense in the commentary.

row.note: The commentary treats night/day and dawn/evening as joined units of time; Genesis marks the first day by evening followed by morning, giving that paired rhythm a creation formula.
The commentary joins day to night, names seasonal time and winter cold, and treats survival as continuity; this verse puts those cycles together and says they will not cease while the earth remains.

The commentary says time is made of attached parts rather than a single flow; Qohelet opens its sequence by assigning a time to every matter under heaven, making time itself the frame for distinct phases.

The commentary moves from human life stages to a life compressed at its end; this verse places birth and death and planting and uprooting in their appointed times, making human life one of the paired cycles.
The commentary traces a person's life through ages and then reduces its span to an evening or hour; Job calls the human being short-lived and troubled, a direct wisdom parallel on life's brevity.
The commentary says an entire lifetime contracts to a brief interval; Job pictures a person as a flower that withers and a shadow that does not remain, giving that contraction a natural image.
The commentary names morning/evening as a time pair and says life's long span shrinks to a short part of a day; the psalm's grass sprouts in the morning and withers by evening.

row.basis: seventy or eighty years; toil; swift passing
row.note: The commentary follows human life through its stages and says its accumulated years look like only an hour at judgment; this verse measures the ordinary lifespan in decades, then says it passes quickly.

row.basis: a thousand years; a watch in the night
row.note: The commentary contrasts long duration with a short sleep interval and a brief end-of-life span; this verse compares a thousand years to yesterday and to a night watch, explicitly collapsing time scales.
The commentary names dawn/evening and night/day as linked pairs and develops haqq as truth; this liturgical verse assigns lovingkindness to morning praise and faithfulness to night praise.
The commentary says sabr can express waiting and holds it between day parts; the psalmist waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for morning, joining endurance to the passage from night into day.
The commentary presents night and day as attached parts; this verse makes the transition morally meaningful, with weeping lodged in the night and joy arriving in the morning.
The commentary makes night and day a recurring pair and sabr a patient wait; the watchman's question places a listener inside a night watch, giving waiting a concrete scene.

The commentary presents time as linked intervals rather than a one-way account; the watchman's answer says morning comes and night comes again, then invites the questioner to return and ask, joining recurring time to continued inquiry.

row.basis: waiting and hope in the Lord's word
row.note: The commentary glosses sabr as waiting; this verse has the speaker wait for the Lord and hope in his word, adding trust to the act of waiting.

row.basis: heat by day; cold by night
row.note: The commentary's sabr branch names winter's severe cold, while its asr discussion pairs day and night; Jacob recounts heat consuming him by day and cold at night during years of service, combining both images in an endured labor.
The commentary names paired times and seasonal terms; this verse assigns the moon to appointed seasons and the sun to its setting, linking calendar time to daily time.

row.basis: sun by day; moon and stars by night
row.note: The commentary treats day/night as a joined order; Jeremiah names the lights that govern each side of that order and calls it a fixed ordinance.

row.basis: Israel's continuity tied to day/night order
row.note: The commentary says those who endure remain joined through time; Jeremiah says Israel would cease to be a nation only if the fixed order of day and night departed, making communal continuity depend on temporal continuity.

row.basis: true judgment and compassion toward one another
row.note: The commentary's final verse has people exhort one another in haqq; Zechariah commands true judgment and compassion each toward a fellow, joining right judgment to reciprocal ethical treatment.

row.basis: speak truth to one another; judgments in the gates
row.note: The commentary's tawasaw bil-haqq is mutual counsel in truth; Zechariah explicitly commands people to speak truth to one another and render true, peaceable judgments, adding a public civic setting.

row.basis: source root وصي; package table lists no regular Hebrew/Aramaic correspondence; neighbor rebuke
row.note: The commentary makes advice reciprocal; Leviticus requires a person to reprove a neighbor rather than leave wrongdoing unaddressed, giving mutual ethical counsel a concrete corrective act. The table lists no regular Hebrew or Aramaic correspondence for the source root وصي.

The commentary says the human beings at the surah's end are joined and thereby remain standing; Qohelet says one companion can lift another who falls, making support the practical result of being joined.
The commentary links sabr with severe winter cold and people with mutual support; Qohelet says two lying together keep warm, an exact social answer to cold.

row.basis: wise lead many to righteousness and shine forever
row.note: The commentary says people attach to one another through exhortation and remain within a chain; Daniel describes the wise who make many righteous shining like stars forever, a transmission of right conduct with enduring outcome.

row.basis: commentary root ح ق ق; table's sound correspondence חקק is unverified; Hebrew חֹק, fixed limit
row.note: The commentary labels haqq and develops appointed seasons and human life stages; Job says a person's days and bounds are set so the person cannot pass them, using חֹק for an allotted limit. This is a specific semantic bridge for the table's candidate sound correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

The commentary names night/day and dawn/evening as paired time units; this Mishnah defines when the evening and morning recitations of Shema begin and end, showing those same boundaries structuring Jewish daily liturgy.

row.basis: the day is short; work is abundant
row.note: The commentary says the human span contracts to an hour while good action remains its answer; Avot explicitly pairs a short day with abundant work and a pressing master, making ethical urgency the point of the time limit.

row.basis: one hour of repentance and good deeds
row.note: The commentary contrasts long life with a compressed hour and names righteous deeds as a way through loss; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the world to come, giving that hour explicit moral weight.

row.basis: human lifespan capped at a hundred years
row.note: The commentary follows age stages and says a lifetime shrinks to a short interval; Sirach measures human days at most a hundred years, adding a wisdom-text reckoning of the finite span.
The commentary reduces the whole lifespan to an evening or day-hour; Sirach compares a few years to a drop of water and a grain of sand beside eternity, making the disparity explicit.

row.basis: short and sorrowful life; no return from Hades
row.note: The commentary quotes deniers who say time alone destroys them; Wisdom gives the ungodly a speech that life is short and death final, then its larger argument contests their conclusion, adding a Jewish wisdom debate over the denial.

row.basis: work while it is day; night comes
row.note: The commentary pairs day and night and treats human action as a response to finite time; Jesus says the sender's work must be done while it is day because night is coming, giving the daily boundary an explicit urgency for action.

row.basis: sleeping and rising; growth night and day
row.note: The commentary's asr discussion includes night/day and sleep in portions, while sabr is waiting; the seed in Jesus' parable sprouts as the farmer sleeps and rises, night and day, joining bodily rest to unobserved duration.

row.basis: first blade, then ear, then full grain
row.note: The commentary names stages of a human lifespan and appointed seasons; the parable makes growth a sequence of stages before harvest, a specific image of time unfolding toward ripeness.

row.basis: harvest when the grain is ripe
row.note: The commentary connects sabr with waiting; the farmer sends the sickle when the crop is ready, making patient waiting end at its appointed season.

row.basis: doing good; harvest at the proper time; do not give up
row.note: The commentary joins righteous deeds to mutual exhortation and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not give up, joining all three actions in one claim.

row.basis: consider one another; provoke love and good works
row.note: The commentary says people join through reciprocal exhortation and righteous action; Hebrews makes the relation active by telling readers to consider one another and stir up love and good works.

row.basis: encourage one another as the Day approaches
row.note: The commentary joins human exhortation to long time and the final gathering; Hebrews commands mutual encouragement as the Day draws near, making the approaching end a reason to remain connected.
The commentary's tawasaw is reciprocal counsel within a chain; Hebrews says to exhort one another every day so none is hardened, adding a daily rhythm and a reason for the practice.

row.basis: speak truth to neighbor; members of one another
row.note: The commentary pairs mutual counsel with haqq; Paul commands truthful speech to a neighbor because the speakers are members of one another, making truth-telling the practice that sustains their shared body.

row.basis: goodness, knowledge, and ability to admonish one another
row.note: The commentary joins good action to reciprocal counsel; Paul says the community is filled with goodness and knowledge and able to admonish one another, specifying the qualities that make mutual advice possible.

row.basis: admonish, encourage, support; be patient with all
row.note: The commentary distinguishes counsel in truth from counsel in patience; Paul assigns different kinds of mutual care and closes with patience toward all, a close ethical configuration of the paired exhortations.
The commentary says those joined by patience remain standing through time; Jesus says life is gained through endurance, making perseverance the means of survival.

row.basis: work of faith; labor of love; endurance of hope
row.note: The commentary names faith, good works, and patience as the actions of those who escape loss; Paul recalls this community's work, labor, and endurance in faith, love, and hope, preserving the same linked ethical pattern.
The commentary pairs faith and righteous acts with sabr; Revelation defines the endurance of the saints through keeping God's commands and faith, making patience a lived obedience.

The commentary reduces a lifetime to the gathering day and asks what survives it; Revelation says the dead rest from their labors and their deeds follow them, giving action an after-death persistence.
The commentary couples mutual counsel with haqq; Paul makes truth the object of love's rejoicing, locating truth inside a durable ethical relation.
The commentary couples haqq with sabr; Paul describes love as enduring all things, placing endurance inside the same ethical frame as truth in the preceding verse.

row.basis: one day like a thousand years; a thousand years like one day
row.note: The commentary says the entire lifespan becomes an evening or a day-hour; Peter cites the Lord's different scale of time, explicitly comparing a day with a millennium.

row.basis: steadfast work is not in vain
row.note: The commentary says human beings lose time except through faith and good deeds; in a chapter about resurrection, Paul urges steadfast work because labor in the Lord is not in vain, answering the fear that time erases action.

row.basis: farmer waits patiently for the earth's crop
row.note: The commentary explains sabr as waiting and names winter/seasonal time; James tells readers to be patient like a farmer waiting for the earth's precious crop and its early and late rains.

row.basis: establish hearts; the Lord's coming is near
row.note: The commentary stretches patience across the day and compresses life at its end; James commands steadfast hearts because the Lord's coming is near, joining endurance to an approaching end.

The commentary names youth as one stage of a human life; Qohelet urges remembrance of the Creator in youth before the evil days and years without pleasure arrive, making conduct responsive to life's stages.

row.basis: desire fails; the eternal home approaches
row.note: The commentary follows life toward its final shortening; Qohelet describes the failing desires of old age and movement toward the eternal home, giving the end-of-life image a concrete bodily setting.

row.basis: dust returns to earth; spirit returns to God
row.note: The commentary says human life runs through stages and contracts at its end; Qohelet states what happens at death, distinguishing the body's return to earth from the spirit's return to God.

row.basis: morning prayer, afternoon prayer, evening prayer
row.note: The commentary names dawn and evening as paired times; this Mishnah assigns prayer to morning, afternoon, and evening limits, showing daily divisions shaping Jewish worship.

row.basis: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning watches
row.note: The commentary names night/day and dawn/evening pairs and links sabr to waiting; Jesus lists four night watches and tells servants to stay awake for the master's return, making the divided night a scene of patient readiness.

row.basis: second or third watch; servants found awake
row.note: The commentary glosses sabr as waiting across time; Jesus blesses servants whom the returning master finds awake in the second or third watch, giving waiting a specific night-time interval.

row.basis: seasonal birth of mountain goats and deer
row.note: The commentary says a haqq branch names the camel's annual mating time; Job asks whether anyone knows when mountain goats give birth and deer calve, extending the same concern with animals' appointed reproductive seasons.

row.basis: teach children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising
row.note: The commentary joins night/day and develops reciprocal exhortation; Deuteronomy distributes teaching across ordinary daily activities, showing instruction woven through time, though its speaker assigns it parent-to-child rather than mutual counsel.
The commentary's camel example is an annual reproductive season; Job asks whether the months of wild animals' gestation can be counted, specifying the duration within an animal cycle.
The commentary pairs morning with evening and extends patience across the day; this verse says people go out to work until evening, placing human action within that finite daily span.

The commentary says people join one another through reciprocal exhortation; Proverbs pictures one person sharpening another as iron sharpens iron, giving that relation a formative rather than merely verbal effect.

row.basis: a threefold cord not quickly broken
row.note: The commentary describes those who survive as linked in a chain; Qohelet's threefold cord is a specific image of joined strength that is not quickly broken.

The commentary says life's duration contracts and that the righteous should remain through it; this prayer asks to be taught to number days so the heart may gain wisdom, turning limited time into ethical instruction.

row.basis: wealth piled up beside shadow-like life
row.note: The commentary says the race to accumulate numbers consumes time until the graves; this verse places צבר, piling up wealth, beside human life passing like a shadow and not knowing who will gather the pile. The table's ص ب ر / צבר sound correspondence is unverified, and Hebrew means heap rather than the commentary's patience, so the link is the surrounding accumulation-and-mortality motif, not a shared sense.

row.basis: commentary root ح ق ق; table's sound correspondence חקק is unverified; statutes beside righteousness
row.note: The commentary labels haqq and uses it for right guidance; Deuteronomy places חֻקִּים, prescribed statutes, beside the claim that Israel's instruction is righteous, giving a legal-order use of the table's candidate correspondence without equating prescription with truth.

row.basis: work cannot be finished, but one must not desist
row.note: The commentary links sabr with waiting and persistence across time; Avot says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, distinguishing perseverance from control over the whole lifespan.

row.basis: acquire a friend; appoint a teacher; judge favorably
row.note: The commentary says people are linked by reciprocal counsel; Avot turns that into practices of friendship, learning, and favorable judgment, giving the social chain an ethical form.

row.basis: life passes like a cloud; name and works forgotten
row.note: The commentary says time consumes people and their lifespan contracts; the ungodly in Wisdom say their name and works will be forgotten and life passes like a cloud, dramatizing the same fear of erasure.

row.basis: make the most of the time
row.note: The commentary says number-chasing consumes time unnoticed and that good action matters within a short life; Paul tells readers to make the most of the time because the days are evil, turning the finite span into an ethical opportunity.

row.basis: works, love, faith, service, and endurance
row.note: The commentary's exception to loss joins faith, good works, and patience; the risen Christ names a church's works, love, faith, service, and endurance together, adding a concrete communal evaluation.
The commentary's tawasaw makes counsel reciprocal; Paul describes a community teaching and admonishing one another through wisdom and song, a communal practice parallel to that reciprocal relation.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel is tied to haqq; the Didache directs members to reprove each other without anger and in peace, specifying both correction and its manner.

row.basis: pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day
row.note: The commentary sets dawn/evening and night/day as named units; the Didache schedules a repeated Christian prayer three times through the day, giving temporal divisions a liturgical practice.

row.basis: patient in affliction; constant in prayer
row.note: The commentary stretches patience across daily prayer times and ties sabr to waiting; Paul joins patience in affliction to constancy in prayer, giving that waiting a devotional form.

row.basis: present pain; later fruit of righteousness
row.note: The commentary links sabr with cold and waiting and gives righteous action as the survivor's practice; Hebrews says discipline later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it, explicitly making endurance fruitful over time.

row.basis: sun, light, moon, and stars darkened
row.note: The commentary's paired day/night image and its account of late life contracting toward evening meet in Qohelet's image of the lights darkening as old age approaches.

row.basis: silver cord snapped; bowl and wheel broken
row.note: The commentary pictures time and people as linked, enduring parts; Qohelet pictures the silver cord snapping and the water wheel breaking at life's end, a specific image of the link finally failing.

row.basis: commentary root ح ق ق; table's sound correspondence חקק is unverified; חֹק as boundary
row.note: The commentary's haqq branches include fixed seasonal points; Jeremiah says God set a lasting חֹק for the sea at the sand boundary that it cannot cross. This is a concrete boundary sense of the unverified root correspondence.

row.basis: commentary root ع ص ر; table's sound correspondence עצר is unverified; festival assembly
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic العصر for paired periods; Deuteronomy closes six days of unleavened bread with an עֲצֶרֶת, an assembly on the seventh day. The link is a bounded festival time culminating in assembly, while the Hebrew word's assembly sense does not establish cognacy with the Arabic time word.

row.basis: luminaries mark seasons, days, and years
row.note: The commentary joins night/day and dawn/evening and develops seasonal time; Genesis assigns the lights to mark seasons, days, and years, giving the daily pair a wider calendar frame.

row.basis: meditate day and night; do what is written
row.note: The commentary links day/night with the people who act rightly; Joshua makes uninterrupted day-and-night meditation the preparation for doing the law, joining the temporal formula to ethical action.

row.basis: meditation on Torah day and night
row.note: The commentary treats night/day as linked units and says the ones who endure are those who act rightly; Psalm 1 describes the righteous person meditating on Torah day and night, tying the same cycle to a life of fidelity.

row.basis: fruit in season; leaf does not wither
row.note: The commentary connects seasonal time to those who remain standing; Psalm 1's righteous tree bears fruit in its season and does not wither, making endurance a seasonal image.

The commentary names night/day and morning/evening pairs and describes patience across the day; this psalm's speaker prays and is heard at evening, morning, and noon, extending the paired hours into a recurring daily practice.

row.basis: day and night belong to God; lights established
row.note: The commentary presents day and night as a joined order; this verse says both belong to God and that God established the lights, grounding the temporal pair in divine ordering.

The commentary names seasons and treats time as a sequence of joined portions; the next verse says God fixed the earth's boundaries and made summer and winter, connecting cosmic order to seasonal division.

row.basis: human days like grass; flourishing like a field flower
row.note: The commentary follows life's stages and says its full span contracts to a brief interval; the psalm compares a person's days to grass and a flower, giving the short lifespan a natural image.

row.basis: wind passes; the place is known no more
row.note: The commentary says the long duration of human life collapses and ends in loss; this verse says the wind passes over the flower and it disappears, sharpening the image of erasure.

row.basis: human life contrasted with enduring divine love
row.note: The commentary sets human transience against those who remain through faith and right action; the next verse contrasts the fleeting flower with the Lord's steadfast love from everlasting to everlasting.

row.basis: sun by day; moon by night
row.note: The commentary joins day and night and says the faithful remain through time; this verse assigns danger by day and night and locates protection across both periods.

row.basis: human life as hard service; days like a hired worker
row.note: The commentary describes a life passing through stages and ending in a short span; Job's lament asks whether human life is hard service and whether its days are like a hired worker's, adding labor and longing for release to the image of time.

row.basis: days swifter than a weaver's shuttle
row.note: The commentary says the whole lifetime shrinks to an evening or hour; Job says his days are faster than a weaver's shuttle and end without hope, a specific image of time slipping away.

row.basis: sow in the morning and keep working at evening
row.note: The commentary joins morning to evening and speaks of patience while time passes; Qohelet tells the worker to sow in the morning and not hold back at evening, while admitting the outcome is unknown, joining action to uncertain time.

The commentary names morning/evening as paired spans and counsels patience; Lamentations says divine mercies are new each morning, making the daily return of morning a ground for hope amid affliction.
The commentary explicitly explains sabr as waiting; Lamentations says the Lord is good to those who wait for him and seek him, joining patience to seeking.

row.basis: wait quietly for the Lord's salvation
row.note: The commentary links patient waiting to survival through time; Lamentations calls it good to wait quietly for the Lord's salvation, specifying the hoped-for outcome of that waiting.

row.basis: appointed time; wait if the vision seems delayed
row.note: The commentary develops fixed seasonal time and glosses sabr as waiting; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and instructs the hearer to wait if it seems delayed, joining a set time to patient expectation.

row.basis: sleepers awake; everlasting life or disgrace
row.note: The commentary compresses human time toward the gathering day and speaks of loss; Daniel describes those sleeping in the dust awakening to divergent everlasting outcomes, adding an explicit resurrection horizon.

row.basis: blessing for waiting through a counted span
row.note: The commentary says sabr is waiting and the life span contracts to a short interval; Daniel blesses the one who waits and reaches the end of a specified number of days.

row.basis: rest, then stand at the end of days
row.note: The commentary joins death, the gathering day, and the fate of those who endure; Daniel is told to go his way, rest, and rise to his allotted place at the end of days, adding a personal resurrection promise.

row.basis: the dead live; dwellers in dust awake
row.note: The commentary mentions graves, the gathering day, and the human lifetime ending; Isaiah calls the dead to live and those dwelling in dust to awake, making resurrection an explicit answer to the grave.

row.basis: word is truth; righteous rules endure forever
row.note: The commentary pairs haqq with sabr; this verse calls God's word truth and says the righteous ordinances endure forever, directly joining truth with permanence.

row.basis: acts whose fruits are enjoyed now and whose principal remains for the world to come
row.note: The commentary names righteous deeds as the answer to loss and describes people helping one another; the Talmud lists concrete acts such as honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, and peacemaking whose reward extends beyond this life.

row.basis: endure to the end and be saved
row.note: The commentary says those who attach to one another through patience remain standing; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, giving patience a clear terminal horizon.

row.basis: inherit promises through faith and patience
row.note: The commentary's exception to loss joins faith, righteous action, and sabr; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit the promises through faith and patience, aligning endurance with promised outcome.

row.basis: endurance after doing God's will; receive the promise
row.note: The commentary couples patience with right action; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will in order to receive what was promised, making persistence the bridge between action and outcome.
The commentary names faith and sabr together; James says the testing of faith produces endurance, giving patience a process rather than treating it as a static trait.
The commentary says patient persistence carries people through time; James tells endurance to complete its work so that the person may be mature and whole, linking duration to ethical formation.

row.basis: wait patiently for what is not seen
row.note: The commentary describes sabr as waiting and directs it toward survival; Paul says hope for what is not seen requires waiting with patience, adding the unseen promise as the object of endurance.

row.basis: faithful to death; crown of life
row.note: The commentary traces a human span to its end and says the faithful endure; Revelation calls the community to faithfulness even to death and promises the crown of life, linking lifetime's limit to reward.

row.basis: lamps burning; be ready because the hour is unknown
row.note: The commentary joins night/day divisions to patience and waiting; the Didache tells its readers to watch their lives, keep lamps lit, and be ready because the Lord's hour is unknown, giving the temporal image an early Christian practice of vigilance.

row.basis: cloud vanishes; descent to Sheol does not return
row.note: The commentary quotes people who say time destroys them and describes life shrinking toward death; Job's lament says the one who descends to Sheol does not come back, a voice of temporal despair whose placement within Job's complaint keeps it from being a simple doctrinal statement.

row.basis: grain heaped like sea sand across years of plenty
row.note: The commentary links accumulated time to survival and recalls the destructive race to amass numbers; Joseph heaps grain during the seven years of plenty to preserve life through famine. The table's ص ب ر / צבר sound correspondence is unverified, and Hebrew means heap rather than the commentary's patience, so this is a contrastive accumulation motif, not a shared sense.
The commentary develops haqq as right/truth; this verse calls God's Torah truth and its righteousness everlasting, joining truth to enduring right order.

The commentary contrasts transient human time with the survival of the faithful; Lamentations grounds hope in the Lord's unfailing compassion, the reason given in the surrounding morning and waiting lines.

row.basis: Abraham waited patiently and received the promise
row.note: The commentary ties sabr to waiting for an outcome; Hebrews says Abraham patiently endured and obtained the promise, giving a narrative example of long waiting rewarded.

row.basis: patient endurance; an approaching hour of testing
row.note: The commentary stretches patience across time and reduces the final span to an hour; Revelation connects keeping the word of endurance with preservation from an hour of testing that is coming on the world.

row.basis: seek the Living One while alive
row.note: The commentary emphasizes the shortness of life and its closing encounter; this saying urges seeking the Living One before death, turning limited lifetime into an immediate obligation. English wording varies by translation.
