row.note: The commentary treats the person himself as the final lost capital; Jesus asks what gain there is in winning the whole world while losing oneself.
The rich man counts years of stored goods as security, but his life is required that night; the scene makes the commentary's hidden loss of principal concrete.
This parallel rich-fool saying has a man plan to fill his stores and lack nothing, then die that night; it sharpens the gap between expected profit and the actual account.
Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing yet does not know it is poor and wretched; this enacts the commentary's loss that can grow unseen beneath apparent success.
After a long interval the master returns and settles accounts with servants entrusted with capital; the parable joins time, work and final reckoning as in the commentary's market image.
The speakers plan to travel, trade and make a profit for a year; James places the commentary's merchant's forecast inside the uncertainty of human life.
James says people do not know tomorrow and their life is a brief vapor; this supplies the finite lifetime that the commentary calls the capital being spent.

row.basis: riches kept to their owner's hurt
row.note: Qohelet says wealth can be kept to the owner's harm, directly matching the commentary's principal that diminishes even while a person appears to possess it.

row.basis: wealth lost in a bad venture
row.note: A failed venture makes the rich man lose his property and leave nothing to his son; this gives the commentary's unprofitable trade a concrete household consequence.

row.basis: wealth amassed without knowing its heir
row.note: The fleeting human heaps up riches without knowing who will gather them; this joins the commentary's passing lifetime to its image of capital that cannot be kept.

row.basis: wages in a bag with holes
row.note: Haggai says people earn wages only to put them into a pierced bag; the image makes the commentary's principal loss visible in an apparently completed day's work.
The rich man says he can now enjoy his goods but does not know how soon he will die and leave them; this is a Jewish parallel to the commentary's false confidence in accumulated capital.
The speaker asks what wealth and pride profited the wicked, then says it passed like a shadow; the text explicitly judges apparent gain by what remains.

row.basis: labor spent on what cannot satisfy
row.note: Isaiah asks why people spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy; this directly tests the commentary's unprofitable trade and wasted life-capital.

row.basis: short day, much work, great reward
row.note: Rabbi Tarfon's saying makes the day short, the work much and the reward great; it turns the commentary's time-as-capital image into an explicit account of finite time and labor.

row.basis: an hour of deeds and repentance
row.note: The Mishnah values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world above the whole life of the world to come; it makes each unit of time consequential as in the commentary's account.
The teaching to repent one day before death is answered by the uncertainty of that day, so one should repent today; it gives the commentary's passing time an urgent, practical consequence.
Paul says a person's work may burn and he will suffer loss; this gives the commentary's final accounting a specific test of what a lifetime's work actually yielded.
All things are exposed before God, to whom people must give account; this complements the commentary's contrast between visible success and an unseen loss.
Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory; the wording gives the commentary's comprehensive human deficit a specific moral and theological measure.
God repays each according to deeds; this connects the commentary's person-in-loss to its neighboring ayah's faith and action as the basis of the final account.
Paul says God shows no partiality; with the preceding verse's judgment by deeds, this matches the commentary's refusal to distinguish people by lineage or rank.

row.basis: no preference for rich or prince
row.note: Elihu says God does not favor princes or the rich over the poor, since all are his handiwork; this closely matches the commentary's human class that cuts across social rank.
The merchants shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel and falsify the scales; this is the commentary's specific image of making another person's purchase come up short.

row.basis: buying the needy and selling sweepings
row.note: The merchants exploit the poor and sell the grain's sweepings; this shows the human cost of the under-measure that the commentary describes as taking another's principal.
Proverbs calls a false balance abhorrent and a just weight pleasing to God, joining the commentary's market scale to moral judgment.
Israel is commanded to use just balances, weights and measures; this supplies the positive counterpart to the commentary's trader who secretly gives less than was paid for.

row.basis: Job asks to be weighed fairly
row.note: Job asks to be weighed in just balances so God may know his integrity; the speaker's appeal makes the market scale an image for testing a person's standing.

row.basis: God weighs what people cannot see
row.note: A person's ways seem pure in their own eyes, but the Lord weighs the spirit; this directly answers the commentary's unaware loser who thinks his account is sound.
The solitary worker has no heir, never stops laboring and deprives himself of good; this joins the commentary's isolated human, depleted capital and loss of self.
Qohelet says two are better than one because they have a good return for their toil; this counters the commentary's solitary person in loss with benefit made possible by companionship.
If one falls, the other can lift him; this gives concrete form to the commentary's claim that people leave isolation through mutual relation.

row.basis: speak truth as members of one another
row.note: Paul commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor because they are members of one another; this closely meets the commentary's transition from an isolated human to reciprocal counsel in truth.
The community must exhort one another daily so none is hardened by sin; this links reciprocal counsel to the commentary's time-limited escape from loss.
Paul says what a person sows is what that person will reap; the harvest image makes the commentary's labor-and-account metaphor a concrete rule of consequence.
Sowing to the flesh yields corruption, while sowing to the Spirit yields eternal life; this distinguishes loss from lasting gain by the kind of life invested.
Paul urges persistence in doing good because the harvest comes in due time; this connects the commentary's finite time and good work to patient endurance.
Job calls human life on earth hard service and its days those of a hired worker; this is an unusually close image for the commentary's human spending time as capital and receiving a day's wage.

row.basis: short human life full of trouble
row.note: Job says a human born of woman has few days and much trouble; this gives the commentary's universal human condition a concrete account of brief, burdened life.
Adam must eat from cursed ground through painful toil all the days of his life; this connects the commentary's account of human loss with labor that consumes a finite life.

row.basis: sweat, bread and return to dust
row.note: The human eats bread by sweat until returning to the dust; this places work and death together as the commentary does when it calls time the principal spent.

row.basis: fixed days and an impassable limit
row.note: Job says a person's days are determined and their boundary cannot be crossed; this makes explicit the due term that the commentary associates with each person's final account.
The house built by one who hears and does Jesus' words withstands rain, flood and wind; this brings together the commentary's shelter, storm and distinction by action.
The house of the one who hears but does not do collapses under rain, flood and wind; this is a concrete image of loss tied to the deed that the commentary says changes one's outcome.

Jesus concludes the rich fool story with the person who stores up for himself but is not rich toward God; this states the commentary's distinction between visible accumulation and a sound final account.
The vineyard owner gives the last workers the same denarius as the first; this revises a strict market ledger by making the kingdom's reward rest on the giver's generosity, not hours worked.

Paul contrasts visible things, which are temporary, with unseen things, which are eternal; this illuminates the commentary's tension between the visible human and a loss or value that sight alone misses.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's source word is ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ; Job calls the wage-bound mortal אֱנוֹשׁ. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while Job's hired-worker image adds the short, allotted human day.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity in loss; Psalm 8 calls the mortal אֱנוֹשׁ and asks why God remembers him, keeping the source's mortality term within a text of divine regard.

The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Daniel's Aramaic humanlike figure appears with the clouds before the Ancient of Days among beastly kingdoms. The table's sound match is unverified; this is a distinct apocalyptic human image, not an identity.

row.basis: Daniel's humanlike figure applied to Jesus
row.note: Jesus applies Daniel's cloud-coming human figure to himself before the council and speaks of vindication and authority; this Christian reading makes the humanlike figure's dominion a reply to defeat and loss.

The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; Qohelet uses מְחַסֵּר for depriving one's own self of good amid fruitless solitary labor. This is a candidate root correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

The source word خُسْرٍ names loss; Daniel says the king was weighed and found חַסִּיר, deficient. The table's unverified Aramaic sound match is reinforced by the passage's exact image of judgment by measure.

The commentary's neighboring exception says وَعَمِلُوا۟, righteous action as labor in the profitable trade; Qohelet asks what gain a person gets from עָמָל beneath the sun, exposing toil without surplus.

The commentary links its neighboring بِٱلْحَقِّ to the day that brings each person to a term; Job uses חֻקָּיו for the fixed bounds of human days. The sound correspondence is unverified, but the allotted-limit motif is specific.

row.basis: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary says the human named by ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ can fail to see his own loss; Jeremiah calls the heart אָנֻשׁ, desperately sick, and asks who can understand it, joining the table's weak/ill form to self-ignorance.

The source commentary's خُسْرٍ is an account of loss; Proverbs warns that one rushing after wealth will not know that חֶסֶר, want, will come. This joins hidden deficit to pursuit of gain without claiming cognacy.

The source commentary places the human in indefinite loss; Moses describes the promised land as one in which Israel will lack nothing. The table correspondence is unverified, and the verse offers a concrete counter-image of sufficiency.

The commentary's separate source image under عَصْر includes pressing and storm; Job says God can withhold waters until drought or release them until the land is overwhelmed. The table's עָצַר means restrain, a related but unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: seeing another's eye, missing one's own
row.note: Jesus pictures a person noticing a speck in a brother's eye while ignoring a beam in his own; this echoes the commentary's eye imagery and its warning that the person may not see his own condition.
The hearer who looks in a mirror goes away and forgets what he looks like; this gives a specific image for the commentary's claim that a person may fail to see himself without another's reflection.

row.basis: treasure vulnerable to decay and theft
row.note: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is eaten by moth and rust or stolen; this gives physical form to the commentary's principal that can diminish while a person thinks he is accumulating.

The commentary's separate B008 image records a closed-mouthed vessel under عَصْر; Genesis says God had shut Abimelech's women's wombs, using עָצַר, restrain/close. This is only a shared closure image, not evidence that the Arabic word means loss by closure.

row.basis: finite lifespan, toil and swift passing
row.note: The psalm numbers a human life at seventy or eighty years, marked by toil, then says it passes quickly; this develops the commentary's time-as-principal image into a lifespan.

The commentary's neighboring وَعَمِلُوا۟ names good action; this verse says human years are עָמָל and trouble before they fly away. The table's Arabic ع م ل–Hebrew עמל correspondence is unverified, while the shared labor context is explicit.

row.basis: wealth cannot follow its owner in death
row.note: The rich person takes nothing when he dies and his glory does not descend after him; this matches the commentary's claim that accumulated capital cannot save the person who spent it.

row.basis: nothing carried from birth or toil
row.note: A person leaves as naked as he came and cannot take the fruit of his labor; this supplies a direct account of worldly gain failing at death.
Proverbs warns against wearing oneself out to get rich; this directly questions the commentary's merchant-like pursuit of gain as a use of finite human time.
The wealth a person fixes his eyes on suddenly makes wings and flies away; the image makes visible the commentary's principal that disappears despite apparent accumulation.
One who gains wealth unjustly is likened to a bird hatching what it did not lay and will leave it in midlife; this joins fraudulent gain to the loss of the person who thought it secure.

row.basis: riches fail on the day of wrath
row.note: Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; this contrasts market capital with what can answer at final judgment.
Hannah says the Lord is a God of knowledge and actions are weighed by him; this links the commentary's unseen human account to divine assessment.
The verse says just balances and weights are the Lord's work; this joins the commentary's fair market scale to divine order and judgment.
Micah asks whether wicked treasure remains in a house with a scant measure; the prophet links stored wealth to the short measure that the commentary describes as stealing another's principal.
The Lord asks whether he can acquit someone with wicked scales and deceptive weights; this makes the dishonest trader's reduced measure answerable to judgment.

row.basis: worker longs for shade and wages
row.note: Job compares the sufferer to a slave longing for shade and a hired worker waiting for wages; this continues the commentary's connection between human time, labor and its due.
Job says months of emptiness and nights of misery have been allotted to him; the verse gives a concrete example of living inside loss as an extended condition.

row.basis: a person's allotted day as a hireling's
row.note: Job asks God to turn away until a person's day, like that of a hired worker, is complete; this links the commentary's due term to the end of labor and life.

row.basis: righteous and wicked share one fate
row.note: Qohelet says the same event happens to righteous and wicked alike; this counters the commentary's exception group at the level of earthly outcomes, without directly addressing its afterlife account.

row.basis: fruitful tree that does not wither
row.note: The righteous person is a tree bearing fruit in season whose leaf does not wither; this contrasts the commentary's crop lost to a destructive wind with a life that remains productive.
The wicked are like chaff driven away by wind; this gives a scriptural contrast between the fruitful life and the commentary's image of a life's produce swept away.

row.basis: fruitless tree cut down and burned
row.note: Jesus says a tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this joins the commentary's produce imagery to judgment based on what a life yields.
Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this makes the commentary's comprehensive human reckoning concrete down to speech.

row.basis: dead judged from books by their works
row.note: At the great throne, the dead are judged from opened books according to their works; this is a direct image of the final account that the commentary hears behind loss and deeds.
The verse says humans die once and afterward face judgment; it fits the commentary's image of each person reaching a fixed term and being assessed.

row.basis: postmortem reversal of rich and poor
row.note: Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, and now their conditions are reversed; this shows status and present comfort do not settle the final account.

row.basis: steward reduces a debt by half
row.note: The steward changes an oil debtor's bill from one hundred measures to fifty; unlike the commentary's condemned short measure, the parable places debt reduction inside a crisis strategy for future welcome.

The master praises the dishonest steward's foresight, not his dishonesty; this complicates the commentary's pairing of financial manipulation and loss by distinguishing prudent use of wealth from moral accounting.

row.basis: preserving life leads to losing it
row.note: Jesus says whoever seeks to preserve life will lose it, while whoever loses it will keep it; this gives a distinct saying in which self-protection reverses into the commentary's loss of self.
Paul says the things that were gain to him he counted as loss for Christ; the accounting language directly meets the commentary's distinction between apparent assets and true profit.

row.basis: all things loss for the greater gain
row.note: Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him; this adds a deliberate revaluation in which relinquishing worldly capital is itself gain.

row.basis: nothing brought in or carried out
row.note: Paul says people bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out; this directly undercuts the assumption that accumulated wealth can secure the self.

row.basis: desire for riches plunges people into ruin
row.note: Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and destructive desires; this connects pursuit of wealth to the commentary's loss of health, faith and self.
James says the rich person's wealth has rotted and garments have been eaten by moths; this gives physical form to the commentary's claim that capital can diminish while held.
Gold and silver rust becomes evidence against their owners and consumes them like fire; the verse links hoarding to a coming reckoning and adds a fire image to the commentary's crop-loss scene.

row.basis: joyful sale for a greater treasure
row.note: The finder sells everything to buy the field with hidden treasure; this reverses the commentary's loss account by showing a total expenditure that is profitable because the acquired good is greater.

row.basis: work of faith and steadfast hope
row.note: Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; this is a specific Christian formulation of faith joined to action and endurance.
James says faith by itself, without works, is dead; this closely matches the commentary's neighboring exception, where belief is joined to righteous action.
In the vision's contrast between the proud and the upright, the righteous live by faith; this gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's group whose faith keeps them from loss.

row.basis: Paul rereads Habakkuk as gospel principle
row.note: Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous-by-faith line as the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel; this Christian reading emphasizes faith as the principle of life alongside the commentary's fuller faith-and-deeds description.
The Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death; this gives a concrete early Christian form to the commentary's secondary sense of loss as leaving the right path.

row.basis: self, community and the urgency of now
row.note: Hillel asks who one is if wholly for oneself and, if not now, when; the saying joins the commentary's isolated human, mutual counsel and finite time.

row.basis: do not separate from the community
row.note: The Mishnah warns against separating from the community, trusting oneself until death, or postponing study until free; this connects collective support and urgency to the commentary's path out of isolation and loss.

Akavya ben Mahalalel tells a person to know where he came from and where he goes, and before whom he will give account; this is a direct Jewish formulation of the commentary's human life reaching its reckoning.
Ben Zoma asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this challenges the commentary's market image by defining wealth through sufficiency rather than accumulation.

row.basis: one deed tips the moral scales
row.note: The Talmud asks each person to see himself as balanced between merit and guilt, so one deed can tip himself and the world; this is a close rabbinic meeting of human action, scales and final consequence.

row.basis: people inscribed by their deeds at the New Year
row.note: The Talmud describes books opened on the New Year and distinguishes the righteous, wicked and intermediate by their inscription for life or death; this gives the commentary's universal verdict and exception group a Jewish judgment-day framework.

The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; the Hebrew speaker says לֹא אֶחְסָר, “I lack nothing,” within the shepherd's provision. The table's sound correspondence is unverified, and the verse supplies a precise counter-image of sufficiency.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Isaiah asks why anyone fears אֱנוֹשׁ, a mortal who dies and is like grass. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while the verse adds human mortality and fear.

row.basis: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The source's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ is linked in the table to Hebrew אנש; Jeremiah calls his wound אָנֻשָׁה, incurable. This is the root's illness/weakness usage, not a claim that the Arabic noun means illness.

row.basis: Joseph in prison; grapes pressed into Pharaoh’s cup
row.note: The commentary joins Joseph’s confinement to pressing; in Joseph’s prison story the cupbearer dreams of squeezing grapes into Pharaoh’s cup, while the dream belongs to the cupbearer.
The commentary’s Yusuf year makes relief follow scarcity; Genesis has Joseph gather the abundant years’ produce into storehouses so the later famine can be survived.
The commentary pairs Joseph’s imprisonment with patience; the psalm retelling puts his feet in fetters and his neck in iron, making confinement part of the Joseph story.

row.basis: Joseph tested while awaiting the promise
row.note: The commentary makes patience meet detention; the next line of the psalm says the Lord’s word tested Joseph until its fulfillment, giving his confinement a waiting-for-release dimension.
The commentary’s aged gardener loses the yield before enjoying it; Jesus’ rich farmer plans many years around his abundant stores, then is told that his life ends that night.

row.basis: Merchants’ wealth lost in one hour
row.note: The commentary compresses accumulated produce and capital into sudden loss; Revelation says Babylon’s great wealth is laid waste in one hour, as merchants watch their trade collapse.
The commentary joins rain, fruit, and sabr; James tells the farmer to wait patiently for the precious crop until it receives the early and late rains, making delay before yield the point.

row.basis: Life flourishes, then withers at evening
row.note: The commentary reads asr as the evening of a life; the psalm compares human flourishing to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening.
The commentary makes a lifetime’s yield vulnerable at its late hour; the psalm counts human years as short and full of toil, then quickly gone.

row.basis: Light and rain clouds dim before old age
row.note: The commentary layers life’s late afternoon with rain and its destructive turn; Ecclesiastes pictures sun, moon, and stars darkening and clouds returning after rain in its approach to death.

row.basis: Fruit still borne in old age
row.note: The commentary’s old owner loses his garden as age advances; the psalm instead pictures the righteous still bearing fruit in old age, a concrete counter-image of fruitful late life.

row.basis: Short day, much work, pressing master
row.note: The commentary treats time as expiring capital and deeds as urgent; Tarfon says the day is short, the work abundant, and the Master of the House presses, joining time, labor, and accountability.

row.basis: Do not desist from unfinished work
row.note: The commentary’s closing community keeps transmitting good action within limited time; Tarfon says one need not finish the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence without claiming control of the outcome.

row.basis: Good deeds as fruit and principal
row.note: The commentary makes good works the lasting yield of time; Peah says certain deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come, an explicit investment image.

row.basis: Release the bound and break the yoke
row.note: The commentary defines the steep ascent through freeing a captive; Isaiah’s fast is to loose wicked bonds, undo the yoke, and let the oppressed go free.
The commentary names feeding on a day of hunger as part of the ascent; Isaiah places sharing bread with the hungry in the same account of true fasting.
The commentary moves from struggle toward companionship and mentions a beast of burden; Torah commands helping even an enemy’s donkey rise under its load, making cooperation concrete.

row.basis: A wounded traveler carried on an animal
row.note: The commentary’s road and burden imagery turns toward care; the Samaritan binds the robbed traveler’s wounds and places him on his own animal, converting a dangerous road encounter into help.
The commentary makes feeding the hungry part of the difficult ascent; in Jesus’ judgment scene, feeding the hungry is named as a deed by which people answer the king.
The commentary pairs release from captivity with feeding; Jesus’ judgment scene separately names visiting a person in prison, connecting practical care to final reckoning.
The commentary’s movement from enmity to fellowship has a concrete ethic in Paul’s instruction to feed a hungry enemy, answering hostility with care.
The commentary turns from the isolated person to mutual counsel; Paul tells the community to carry one another’s burdens, making shared endurance an enacted duty.
The commentary’s steep path and transition into togetherness meet Ecclesiastes’ image of one companion raising another who falls on the road of life.
The commentary reads holding together as rescue from danger; Ecclesiastes says a three-strand cord is not quickly broken, giving the communal bond a material image.

row.basis: Two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: The commentary’s deathbed bequest depends on witnesses; Deuteronomy likewise rejects a single witness and requires two or three for a charge.
The commentary gathers oath, testimony, and truth at the moment of a bequest; Leviticus treats hearing a public oath and withholding testimony as a legal offense.

row.basis: Death activates a will or covenant
row.note: The commentary’s death-triggered bequest meets Hebrews’ use of Greek diathēkē as a will: the writer uses the testator’s death to explain how the covenant takes effect.

row.basis: Signed deed, witnesses, and weighed silver
row.note: The commentary says the debt scene joins market and trust; Jeremiah records a land purchase with a signed deed, witnesses, and silver weighed out, a close transactional analogue.

row.basis: Sealed deeds kept in an earthen vessel
row.note: The commentary joins financial trust to preserved contents; Jeremiah orders sealed and open copies of the deed stored in a jar so they last, showing custody protecting a transaction.
The commentary brings debt together with trust; Sirach tells a lender to keep a promise and deal faithfully with the borrower, making reliability part of credit.
The commentary joins market trust to the day when deeds are faced; the Talmud’s first judgment question is whether one dealt faithfully in business.

row.basis: Faithfulness with wealth and entrusted riches
row.note: The commentary’s debt verse brings commerce and trust together; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with worldly wealth.
The commentary’s testament and debt scenes make obligation transferable; Paul tells Philemon to charge any debt or wrong by Onesimus to him.
The commentary joins a financial obligation to trust; Paul says he writes in his own hand that he will repay, turning personal assurance into a written pledge.

row.basis: A friend’s wounds can be faithful
row.note: The commentary lets truth be a straight, painful blow; Proverbs says a friend’s wounds may be trusted, presenting frank correction as a form of loyalty.
The commentary’s mutual counsel is centered on truth; Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and render judgments that make for peace.
The commentary turns truth into reciprocal counsel within a community; Paul says to speak truth with one’s neighbor because members belong to one another.

row.basis: Entrusted teaching passed to further teachers
row.note: The commentary ends with truth and patience changing hands; Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others, an explicit chain of transmission.

row.basis: Encourage the weak and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary’s community counsels patience; Paul joins encouraging the fainthearted and helping the weak to the instruction to be patient with everyone.

row.basis: Provoke one another to good works
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel issue in righteous action; Hebrews says to consider how to spur one another toward love and good works.

row.basis: The Day tests each person’s work
row.note: The commentary imagines deeds fitting like building material and truth as the day of reckoning; Paul says the Day reveals each builder’s work and fire tests it.

row.basis: People built together as living stones
row.note: The commentary pictures righteous action as bricks set in place; Peter calls believers living stones being built into a spiritual house, making the community itself constructed.

row.basis: Each part builds the whole body
row.note: The commentary’s believers add to one another; Paul’s body is joined through each supporting part and builds itself up in love.
The commentary’s mutual counsel makes the group interdependent; Paul says the body’s members should have the same care for one another.
The commentary reads sabr as self-restraint; Proverbs says ruling one’s spirit is greater than taking a city, making inner restraint the achievement.
The commentary treats patience as something retained through hardship; Sirach tells the faithful to accept what befalls them and be patient in humiliation.

row.basis: Faithfulness tested like gold in fire
row.note: The commentary’s patience has a bitter, fiery trial aspect; Sirach says the faithful are tested in the furnace of humiliation as gold is tested in fire.
The commentary calls condemned people’s readiness for fire a perverse patience; Daniel’s three youths accept the possibility of fire rather than worship another god, reversing what endurance serves.
The commentary says the day makes each person face their work; Ecclesiastes says every deed, including what is hidden, comes into judgment.
The commentary links severed kinship to scales that come up light; Daniel’s wall-writing scene weighs a king and finds him wanting, making weight a verdict on conduct.

row.basis: Righteousness cannot be transferred to a child
row.note: The commentary places severed kinship beside individual weighing; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves, not sons or daughters, so family ties do not transfer standing.
The commentary says the day confronts everyone with their work; Paul states that God repays each person according to deeds.

row.basis: The dead judged by recorded deeds
row.note: The commentary joins the loss of kinship with personal weighing; Revelation depicts the dead judged from books according to what they had done.

row.basis: A seemingly right road ends in death
row.note: The commentary describes the human as straying within time; Proverbs warns that a way can seem right yet end in death, specifying the danger of misjudgment.
The commentary describes human life as capital that can melt into loss; Jesus asks what is gained by acquiring the whole world if one forfeits oneself.

row.basis: A year of trade and expected profit
row.note: The commentary treats time as capital; James depicts merchants planning a year in a city to trade and make profit, exposing life’s plans to uncertainty.
The commentary reads the time of a human life as brief and vulnerable; James calls life a vapor that appears briefly and then vanishes.

row.basis: Patient good work bears a later harvest
row.note: The commentary closes with deeds and patience transmitted together; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in its season if people do not give up.
The commentary’s believers join faith to good action and sabr; Peter’s sequence adds self-control and endurance to faith-informed virtue.
The commentary gathers belief, right action, and patience in a community; Revelation names the saints’ endurance together with keeping God’s commands and faith in Jesus.

row.basis: The world’s form is passing away
row.note: The commentary treats time and worldly capital as expiring; Paul tells believers to use the world without clinging to it because its present form is passing.

row.basis: Earthly treasure can be destroyed or stolen
row.note: The commentary’s accumulated fruit and capital remain vulnerable; Jesus warns that earthly stores are exposed to moth, corrosion, and thieves.
The commentary’s garden contains grapes and fruit meant for pressing; Isaiah’s cultivated vineyard has a winepress prepared for its expected grapes, though its yield proves different.

row.basis: A vineyard ruined when rain is withheld
row.note: The commentary’s garden is destroyed by a sudden storm after fruitfulness; Isaiah instead makes a failed vineyard waste and withholds rain, a distinct judgment pattern.

row.basis: A violent wind destroys a house amid accumulated loss
row.note: The commentary makes a whirlwind erase what was gathered; Job’s children die when a great wind collapses the house during their feast, after earlier losses of property.

row.basis: Wages vanish into a bag with holes
row.note: The commentary says human capital melts away; Haggai pictures earned wages disappearing into a bag with holes, tying loss to futile labor.

row.basis: Wealth perishes in a bad venture
row.note: The commentary’s garden loses its accumulated yield at the moment of expectation; Ecclesiastes describes wealth kept to its owner’s hurt and lost through a disastrous venture.

row.basis: Wealth grows wings and flies away
row.note: The commentary makes stored capital vulnerable to sudden disappearance; Proverbs pictures riches sprouting wings and flying off, turning possession into impermanence.

row.basis: Riches fail on the day of wrath
row.note: The commentary contrasts loss with deeds that carry a person through judgment; Proverbs says riches cannot deliver on the day of wrath but righteousness delivers from death.
The commentary links debt to trust; the psalm contrasts a wicked borrower who does not repay with a righteous person who gives generously.
The commentary develops debt as one face of truth; Deuteronomy commands release of loans at the appointed remission, connecting obligation to mercy within the community.
The commentary brings market trust and truthful judgment together; Proverbs condemns false scales and approves accurate weights in commerce.
The commentary’s witness scene uses an oath to establish a bequest; Jesus’ sermon tells disciples not to swear, giving a contrasting ethic for truthful speech.

row.basis: A house stands through rain and wind
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes ruined gardens with refuge; Jesus’ house on rock survives rain, floods, and wind because its builder acts on his words.

row.basis: A house collapses in the storm
row.note: The commentary calls the spider’s house an inadequate refuge and describes a storm ruining a garden; Jesus’ house built on sand falls when rain, flood, and wind strike.
The commentary makes the spider house a refuge that fails; Job says the confidence of the godless is like a spider’s web, matching the fragile shelter image.
The commentary links the spider’s house to textile and failed protection; Isaiah says webs cannot serve as garments, making the woven product useless as covering.
The commentary contrasts a spider’s false shelter with real security; the psalm names God as refuge and fortress, supplying a contrasting image of protection.
The commentary layers refuge with rain and tempest; Isaiah pictures a just ruler as shelter from wind and storm, a safe counterpart to the fragile garden or web.

row.basis: Ropes pull Jeremiah out of a pit
row.note: The commentary says a community is pulled back from an edge; Jeremiah is physically drawn from a cistern by ropes, a concrete rescue image with a different meaning from the shared covenant rope.

row.basis: A message sweet in the mouth and bitter inside
row.note: The commentary calls patience a bitter essence kept and passed on; John eats a scroll that tastes sweet and turns bitter in his stomach, making internalized truth costly.

row.basis: A received message must be spoken onward
row.note: The commentary ends with truth and patience changing hands; after eating the scroll, John is told to prophesy again to peoples and nations, connecting inward reception to transmission.

row.basis: A person sells all to gain hidden treasure
row.note: The commentary names buying error as a ruinous bargain; Jesus’ parable reverses the valuation, as a man sells what he has to gain a treasure worth more.
The commentary imagines pressure and patience meeting; Paul says suffering produces endurance, interpreting hardship as a source of steadfastness rather than only loss.
The commentary’s final community joins belief and patience; Hebrews says faith and patience characterize those who inherit the promises.

row.basis: A yoke and burden made light
row.note: The commentary defines the ascent through a burden and a freed neck; Jesus describes his own yoke as easy and burden as light, recasting burden as sustaining discipleship.
The commentary makes freeing a captive the answer to the steep ascent; Paul says Christ set people free and warns them not to return to a yoke of slavery.
The commentary opens with pressure that can destroy accumulated yield; Paul describes believers as hard pressed but not crushed, distinguishing pressure from final loss.

row.basis: Light affliction and a weight of glory
row.note: The commentary joins time’s pressure to scales and loss; Paul contrasts brief affliction with an eternal weight of glory, reversing the apparent measure of value.

row.basis: Good works stored as future treasure
row.note: The commentary makes righteous deeds the secure yield of mortal time; Timothy tells the rich to be rich in good works and store treasure for the future.

row.basis: This life as a vestibule before the next world
row.note: The commentary treats time as a limited span whose use determines what follows; Avot compares this world to a vestibule in which one prepares before entering the banquet hall.

row.basis: A will takes effect after death
row.note: The commentary’s bequest is activated by impending death; Hebrews’ next legal step says a will takes effect only after death, sharpening the contrast between present custody and later transfer.
The commentary pairs Joseph’s prison with patience; after the cupbearer is restored, he forgets Joseph, adding the concrete delay of being left confined and unremembered.

row.basis: Two years pass before Joseph is recalled
row.note: The commentary makes detention and patience meet; Genesis marks two full years before Pharaoh’s dream brings the imprisoned Joseph back into view, specifying the length of the wait.

row.basis: A dying patriarch asks for an oath about burial
row.note: The commentary’s testament scene joins approaching death, trust, and obligation; Jacob, near death, asks Joseph to swear that he will not bury him in Egypt.

row.basis: The deathbed request is secured by an oath
row.note: The commentary places oath and bequest together at death; Joseph swears to Jacob’s burial request, turning a dying person’s instruction into an entrusted duty.

row.basis: A final oath entrusted to the next generation
row.note: The commentary joins death, custody, and what passes between people; Joseph makes Israel’s descendants swear to carry his bones when God visits them.

row.basis: Fire consumes accumulated flocks and servants
row.note: The commentary’s ruined garden includes a destructive fiery storm; in Job’s sequence of calamities, fire from heaven consumes sheep and servants, one part of the sudden loss of his holdings.
The commentary treats time as expiring capital; the psalm asks to be taught to number one’s days so the heart may gain wisdom, turning limited time into a prompt for action.

row.basis: Meditating on instruction day and night
row.note: The commentary says communal counsel joins like night and day; the psalmist meditates on Torah day and night, making ethical instruction a sustained practice across time.

row.basis: A righteous tree bears fruit in season and does not wither
row.note: The commentary’s fruitful garden is destroyed at the moment of expected yield; Psalm 1 pictures the righteous as a watered tree whose seasonal fruit remains, a counter-image of stability.
The commentary layers ripe produce with life’s late hour and the end of time; Amos’s basket of summer fruit signals that Israel’s end has arrived, making harvest itself an omen of ending.

row.basis: Human growth fades while the word endures
row.note: The commentary moves from mortal time to truth that is transmitted and kept; Isaiah contrasts fading grass and flowers with the enduring word of God.

row.basis: Truth bound at the neck and written on the heart
row.note: The commentary joins truth to holding and binding; Proverbs tells the reader to bind faithfulness and truth around the neck and write them on the heart, combining tethering with inward preservation.

row.basis: A person becomes surety for a neighbor
row.note: The commentary gives patience the secondary image of a guarantor and joins trust to debt; Proverbs depicts someone pledging security for a neighbor, making the guarantee a concrete accepted burden.

row.basis: A pledged garment returned before sunset
row.note: The commentary joins debt, holding, and release within passing time; Exodus requires a creditor to return a poor borrower’s garment by sunset, so the pledge cannot become lasting captivity.

row.basis: A freed servant sent away with produce
row.note: The commentary defines the ascent through freeing a captive and feeding the hungry; Deuteronomy says not to send a released servant away empty-handed but to provide from flock, threshing floor, and winepress.

row.basis: A creditor threatens to take a widow’s sons as slaves
row.note: The commentary brings debt and release from captivity together; the widow’s unpaid debt puts her sons at risk of enslavement, making the financial obligation a threat to family freedom.

row.basis: Oil sold to pay debt and preserve a livelihood
row.note: The commentary’s debt and release scenes meet in Elisha’s instruction: the widow sells the multiplied oil, pays the creditor, and lives on what remains.

row.basis: Remember the one who stood as guarantor
row.note: The commentary calls patience a guarantor; Sirach warns not to forget the kindness of one who guaranteed a neighbor’s debt and risked much on that person’s behalf.

row.basis: Jesus as guarantor of a better covenant
row.note: The commentary’s secondary guarantor image meets Hebrews’ explicit description of Jesus as guarantor, applying financial surety language to the covenant.
The commentary gathers belief, truth, and what is kept; Ephesians says its readers heard the word of truth, believed, and were sealed with the promised Spirit.
The commentary calls patience a guarantor and ends with what is preserved; Ephesians calls the Spirit the guarantee of inheritance until redemption.

row.basis: Patience expressed by bearing with one another
row.note: The commentary turns patience into reciprocal communal counsel; Paul joins humility, patience, and bearing with one another in love.

row.basis: Unity held by a bond of peace
row.note: The commentary pictures people holding together; Paul urges preservation of the Spirit’s unity through a bond of peace.
The commentary makes truth the content of mutual counsel; Paul says love rejoices with the truth, placing truthful conduct inside communal ethics.

row.basis: Love bears and endures all things
row.note: The commentary presents patience as a quality exchanged within the community; Paul describes love as bearing and enduring all things, a sustained communal form of sabr.
The commentary’s exception to loss joins belief, good deeds, and patience; Paul describes those who persist patiently in good work as seeking glory and eternal life.
The commentary’s community advises one another; Hebrews commands daily encouragement so that no one is hardened by sin’s deceit, specifying both the repeated action and its danger.
The commentary closes with good action and patience held together; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God’s will in order to receive what is promised.

row.basis: Lay aside weight and run with endurance
row.note: The commentary makes the steep ascent a road with a load; Hebrews tells runners to lay aside every weight and run the set race with endurance.

row.basis: Good deeds as advocates and a shield
row.note: The commentary says deeds distinguish those who escape loss; Avot pictures a commandment as an advocate and repentance with good deeds as a shield against punishment.

row.basis: The word stored in the heart
row.note: The commentary ends with truth received and preserved; the psalmist stores God’s word in the heart as a safeguard against sin, making inward keeping an ethical act.

row.basis: Time treated as something to redeem
row.note: The commentary calls time capital that can be spent or lost; Paul urges believers to make the most of the time because the days are evil, giving time an explicit economic value.

row.basis: Ripe grapes cast into the winepress of judgment
row.note: The commentary layers fruit, pressing, and the end; Revelation gathers ripe grapes and casts them into God’s great winepress, making the press a harvest image of judgment.

row.basis: Steadfast work is not in vain
row.note: The commentary says most human effort is loss but closes with faithful work and patience; Paul calls believers steadfast and abundant in the Lord’s work, assuring them that such labor is not empty.

row.basis: One more year for a fruitless tree
row.note: The commentary overlaps orchard, aging time, and the risk of losing fruit; the gardener asks for one more year to tend the barren fig tree, making patience a limited extension before judgment.

row.basis: Truth as a means of release
row.note: The commentary joins truth to freeing a captive; Jesus says knowing the truth will make his hearers free, recasting liberation as an effect of truth.

row.basis: The word as fire and a rock-breaking hammer
row.note: The commentary gives truth the image of a straight blow; Jeremiah compares God’s word to fire and a hammer that breaks rock, making truthful speech forceful rather than merely abstract.

row.basis: A dying Jesus entrusts his mother
row.note: The commentary’s testament scene gathers approaching death, entrusted care, and a transfer between people; Jesus from the cross gives his mother and the beloved disciple to one another.

row.basis: The entrusted person is received into a home
row.note: The commentary says trust and custody meet at death; the disciple takes Mary into his own home, carrying out the deathbed entrustment as practical care.

row.note: The commentary sets firm weaving against the spider's house; Isaiah says wrongdoers weave spider webs, turning the textile image into a judgment on their deeds.

row.basis: few of noble birth among the called
row.note: Paul says the called include few people of noble birth; this directly tests the commentary's noble lineage against the community formed by faith.

row.basis: God chooses the low and despised
row.note: Paul's low and despised are chosen to overturn what claims standing; this closely matches the commentary's lowest freedmen and its reversal of rank.

row.basis: no flesh may boast before God
row.note: Paul gives the aim of the preceding choice of low people: no human may boast before God; inherited rank cannot ground superiority.

James says God chose the poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom; faith overturns the low social rank assigned to the weak.
James reproaches believers for dishonoring the poor while the rich oppress them; this supplies the social action behind calling the lowly inferior.

The hungry receive good things while the rich leave empty; this gives material force to the commentary's pairing of the weak and low with a reversal of value.

row.basis: low and high, rich and poor together
row.note: The psalm addresses both low and high and both rich and poor before its teaching about mortality; it makes the commentary's universal insan cross rank boundaries.

row.basis: no favor to prince over poor
row.note: Elihu says God favors neither princes nor rich over poor because all are God's handiwork; noble and lowly share one standing before judgment.

row.basis: rich and poor share their maker
row.note: Proverbs says rich and poor meet under one Maker; this gives the commentary's whole human species a basis independent of social rank.

The verse gives male and female humanity the divine image without a noble lineage; it supplies an account of common human standing.

row.basis: great and small judged by deeds
row.note: The dead, great and small, stand before the throne and are judged by what they have done; rank disappears before the criterion of action.

row.basis: child does not bear parent's guilt
row.note: Ezekiel makes each person's righteousness or wickedness their own; ancestral status does not decide the loss or survival described in the commentary.
Even if Noah were present, Ezekiel says he would save neither son nor daughter but only himself by righteousness; this makes the end of kinship as protection concrete.
John warns hearers not to rely on Abraham as father, since God can raise children for Abraham from stones; a prized ancestry does not settle divine standing.
Those who receive the Word and believe are given the right to become God's children; faith supplies belonging beyond inherited family standing.
The new children of God are born neither from blood nor human will but from God; the verse explicitly displaces pedigree as decisive status.
Paul distinguishes merely physical children from children counted through promise; inherited lineage alone does not establish the standing at issue in the commentary.
Paul calls those of faith Abraham's children; the relationship to an ancestor is redefined by faith rather than birth.
Paul says God repays each person according to deeds; this closely matches the commentary's move from lineage to work.
Paul denies partiality in God's judgment after describing differing deeds; noble or low social identity cannot tilt the verdict.

row.basis: fear God and do right in every nation

row.basis: slave and free one in Christ

Paul calls the slave summoned by the Lord a freedperson of the Lord; the commentary's pairing of freed status with the lowest rank meets a spiritual reversal.
Paul names circumcision, Israelite descent, Benjamin, and Hebrew identity as status credentials; he then assesses that pedigree against faith.
Paul counts his preceding pedigree and religious advantages as loss for Christ; the same human claim to gain becomes loss when measured by faith.
Jesus says the expected sons of the kingdom are thrown into outer darkness; inherited proximity is no guarantee against final loss.
Lazarus, poor at the rich man's gate, is carried to Abraham's side while the rich man dies; low standing in life is reversed at death.
Abraham recalls the rich man's good things and Lazarus's bad things in life while their conditions now reverse; rank and fortune do not settle final worth.

row.basis: giving to poor as lending to God

row.note: The commentary warns against driving a camel beyond its capacity; Exodus says to help an enemy's donkey when it collapses under its load. The law makes relief of the working animal a duty even toward an enemy.

The commentary glosses aslahtu as treating the animal well; Proverbs says a righteous person knows the needs of a beast, while the wicked person's compassion is cruel.

row.basis: donkey beaten for leaving the road

Abraham saddles a donkey and prepares wood for the journey to Moriah; the animal carries the party's travel burden toward a mountain.

Rebekah draws water until the camels finish drinking; beside the commentary's reliable mount and care for an animal, hospitality includes the beasts' needs.
Rebekah and her attendants mount camels and follow Abraham's servant to Isaac, a close scene of human travel on the animal the commentary describes.
The oracle pictures Judah's envoys carrying wealth on young donkeys and camels through a dangerous land. It joins loaded beasts to a journey whose destination is trouble.

row.basis: God carries Israel like a parent

The next verse says believers are created in Christ for good works prepared for them; it reconnects faith and action while making works the result of grace.

row.basis: justified by works and not faith alone

The audience needs endurance after doing God's will to receive what is promised; this joins action, patience, and final outcome.
Jesus tells followers to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him; this makes a carried burden part of a sustained path of discipleship.
Sirach says the farmer's wisdom is in his fieldwork and labor; this gives the commentary's working animal and human labor a specific agricultural setting.

Those who wait for YHWH renew their strength, mount up with wings, run without weariness, and walk without fainting; this directly joins trust, animal-like movement, and endurance on the road.

The source glosses emûn as a dependable camel; God calls Moses faithful in the divine household. The Hebrew אמנ root is the table's sound-correspondence candidate, and this verse gives the human stewardship sense.

row.note: The commentary's haqq is a shared right rather than a weapon of contention; Isaiah condemns those who decree unjust decrees using the proposed Hebrew root, showing that enacted rules can contradict right.

row.basis: ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The source commentary uses sulh for removing mutual estrangement; the psalm's royal rider advances for truth, humility and righteousness with a verb from Hebrew צלח. The martial advance differs from interpersonal peace, so the semantic link remains uncertain.

row.basis: ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary pairs salihat with faith and relational right; Jeremiah asks why the wicked's way prospers, using Hebrew צלח. This contrast shows that prospering in the corresponding root's Hebrew use does not itself establish righteous deeds.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The source commentary gives asr a secondary sense of affection or kinship; Joel calls a solemn assembly during communal crisis with a noun from Hebrew עצר. The gathering gives a social point of contact, but the roots' meanings may be unrelated.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary's asr names a bond whose absence is felt; Isaiah says God cannot bear wrongdoing joined to a solemn assembly, using Hebrew עצר. An assembled group does not guarantee the just relation the commentary seeks.

row.basis: ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary joins good action with communal attachment; God rejects Israel's festal assemblies in Amos, with Hebrew עצר, making mere gathering insufficient for the commentary's ethical togetherness.

row.basis: ص ل ح / Aramaic צלח (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary's salihat are deeds performed by the believing group; Ezra's elders prosper as they build together under prophetic encouragement, using the proposed Aramaic root. Prosperous progress is a different sense from reconciliation.
The commentary begins with estrangement that peace must remove; Joseph's brothers hate him and cannot speak to him in peace, making the broken bond audible in their speech.

row.basis: comfort and kindly speech after fear
row.note: The commentary's frightened separation becomes close companionship; Joseph tells his brothers not to fear, promises provision for their children, and speaks to their hearts after their plea for forgiveness.

The commentary answers the solitary human's loss through responsibility for companions; Cain evades responsibility for his murdered brother with this question, giving the stark opposite of mutual care.

The commentary moves from quarrels among kin to repaired ties; the list of hated acts ends with a false witness and a person who spreads strife among brothers, connecting untruth to broken fellowship.

row.basis: hatred stirs strife; love covers offenses
row.note: The commentary reverses contention into affection; this proverb gives both movements in one line, with hatred stirring up disputes and love covering wrongs.
The commentary's close friend stands by a suffering group; this proverb says a friend loves at all times and a brother is born for adversity, joining affection to endurance.

The commentary's secondary senses include chosen intimacy and kinship; this proverb says a faithful friend may cling more closely than a brother, showing how a chosen bond can exceed inherited kinship.
The commentary asks that opposed people exchange good rather than contend over right; after Job's hard dispute with his friends, he prays for them and his fortunes are restored.
The commentary moves from contention to the truth and peace named later in Zechariah 8; this earlier verse recalls a time without peace, when every person was set against his neighbor.
The commentary's opening parties contest a right; Jesus urges agreement with an accuser while still on the way, providing a concrete settlement before judgment escalates the quarrel.
The commentary joins truthful counsel with repaired kinship; Jesus directs a disciple to rebuke a sinning brother and forgive him on repentance, giving both actions their place.
The commentary makes each believer responsible for another's progress; Paul calls them to pursue what makes for peace and builds one another up amid disputes over conduct.
The commentary stresses that each person both gives and receives counsel; Paul says the Romans are full of goodness and knowledge and able to admonish one another.
The commentary's claimed right can become injury to the other side; Paul says the litigating Corinthians themselves wrong and defraud their own brothers, reversing the ethic of mutual benefit.

row.basis: one hungry while another is full
row.note: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the needy; in the Corinthians' common meal, one goes hungry while another becomes drunk, exposing a failed shared table.

row.basis: wait for one another at the meal
row.note: The commentary's reciprocity must include material care; Paul tells the gathered Corinthians to wait for one another when they eat, answering the hungry member's exclusion in the same scene.
The commentary changes mutual action from dispute into affectionate service; Paul commands believers to use freedom to serve one another through love.
The commentary says contention weakens a community; Paul warns that biting and devouring one another can end with the disputants consumed by each other.
The commentary makes counsel a patient act for a companion's good; Paul directs spiritual members to restore someone caught in a transgression gently while watching their own vulnerability.
The commentary's separated people become a connected believing group; Paul says Christ's peace should rule in their hearts because they were called in one body.
The commentary's mutual action replaces retaliation; Paul forbids repaying evil for evil and directs believers always to seek good for one another and everyone.
The commentary transforms the opponent into a companion through counsel; Paul says the disobedient member is to be admonished as a brother rather than regarded as an enemy.

row.basis: brother or sister lacks food and clothes
row.note: The commentary cites failure to urge food for the poor as a breach of mutual obligation; James places a needy brother or sister without daily food before the speaking community.

row.basis: go in peace without giving food
row.note: The commentary insists on good deeds beside faith and on real care for the needy; James depicts someone wishing a needy person peace but withholding bodily necessities, exposing empty peaceful speech.

row.basis: confess and pray for one another
row.note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel includes receiving help; James commands mutual confession and prayer so members may be healed, joining truthful disclosure to reciprocal care.
The commentary's patience permits estranged companions to stay together; Peter urges sustained love for one another because love covers a multitude of sins.
The commentary's close friendship issues in righteous action; John says Christ's laying down his life teaches believers to lay down their lives for brothers.
The commentary's peace removes fearful estrangement; Paul urges the community to forgive and comfort a punished person so excessive sorrow does not overwhelm him.
The commentary turns disagreement toward an enduring bond; Paul asks the community to confirm its love for the person it disciplined, making affection an explicit act of restoration.

The commentary's two sides can transmit truth and still become companions; this interpretation pictures father and son or teacher and pupil contending fiercely in Torah study yet parting as loving friends.

The commentary's reciprocal truth requires a giver and receiver; Rabbi Yohanan mourns Resh Lakish's challenging objections because their exchange developed the teaching, unlike a companion who only confirms him.
The commentary contrasts the human alone in loss with the belonging of companions; the Honi story ends with a scholar unable to find companions and a saying that one needs fellowship or death.

row.basis: if only for myself, what am I
row.note: The commentary's solitary human cannot escape loss through self-concern; Hillel's question makes the inadequacy of living only for oneself explicit.
The commentary turns adversarial truth claims into mutual counsel; the Didache directs communal reproof without anger and in peace, joining correction to a nonhostile manner.

row.basis: share with a brother in need
row.note: The commentary's fellowship reaches the needy rather than merely speaking to them; the Didache tells its reader to share possessions with a brother and not claim them as exclusively one's own.
The commentary names affection and kinship as bonds among close friends; Jonathan's soul is knit to David's and he loves David as himself, giving narrative form to chosen attachment.
The commentary's close companions remain connected through difficulty; Jonathan sends David away in peace under a covenant binding them and their descendants.

row.basis: loyal care due to a suffering friend
row.note: The commentary's patient companion stands beside someone at risk of loss; Job complains that a suffering person should receive steadfast kindness from a friend rather than abandonment.
The commentary's lost affection leaves a human isolated; Job laments that intimate friends abhor him and those he loved have turned against him, an inverse of patient companionship.
The commentary's isolated sufferer is rejoined by people who stand with him; Job's brothers, sisters and former acquaintances eat with him and comfort him after his ordeal.
The commentary's sabr allows enmity to become intimacy; this proverb calls slowness to anger prudent and overlooking an offense a person's glory.
The commentary's secondary asr sense names affection and kinship by their absence; this proverb warns against forsaking one's friend or father's friend when trouble comes.
The commentary's reconciliation reverses fear and withdrawal; Micah says not to trust a neighbor or intimate friend, depicting social breakdown at the level of close ties.

row.basis: no longer teach neighbor and brother to know God
row.note: The commentary gives believers a continuing duty to urge one another in truth; Jeremiah imagines a new covenant in which neighbor and brother no longer teach each other to know God because all know him, a particular limit on mutual instruction.
The commentary's close friend gives security after frightened separation; Sirach calls a faithful friend a sturdy shelter and a treasure, making companionship protective.
The commentary's peace must heal the bond beneath formal settlement; Jesus closes the unforgiving servant story by requiring forgiveness of one's brother from the heart.
The commentary's reciprocal action draws separated members into concord; Jesus says two who agree on earth about a request will be heard by the Father, within his teaching on community disputes.
The commentary's intimate friend receives truth rather than being held at a distance; Jesus calls disciples friends because he has made known to them what he heard from his Father.
The commentary's estranged parties become companions; Paul commands mutual welcome as Christ has welcomed them, giving the bond a concrete reception practice.

row.basis: speech that builds the other up
row.note: The commentary's mutual exhortation gives another person what is needed; Paul asks for speech suited to building up hearers and giving them grace, rather than harmful talk.
The commentary starts with rival claims inside a group; Paul points to jealousy and strife among the Corinthians as evidence of immature, merely human behavior.
The commentary's failed urging to feed the poor has communal consequences; Paul rebukes the Corinthians for shaming members who have nothing at their shared meal.
The commentary's reciprocal care keeps others close; Peter asks members to show hospitality to one another without complaint, giving affectionate attachment a household practice.
The commentary's reciprocal counsel requires receiving the other's word and patient speech; James commands quick hearing, slow speaking and slow anger.

row.basis: warn then separate from divisive person
row.note: The commentary emphasizes holding a group together through counsel; Titus directs warning a divisive person twice and then having nothing further to do with him, marking a limit to maintained companionship.
The commentary contrasts the solitary human with a believing company; Hillel's instruction not to separate oneself from the community treats continued belonging as a deliberate duty.
The commentary treats reconciliation as work among opposed people; the rabbinic list of deeds whose benefits extend into the world to come includes making peace between one person and another.

row.basis: correct rather than hate a person
row.note: The commentary's counsel must be joined to affection; the Didache forbids hatred and distinguishes those one should correct, pray for, or love beyond oneself.

row.basis: ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary's haqq is a claim that must serve right relations; Wisdom says rulers decree what is just, using Hebrew חקק. The proposed consonantal correspondence links right to a public decree, though the Hebrew root's meaning is legal enactment.

row.basis: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary's insan is vulnerable to loss; the psalm says God returns mortal enosh to dust. The table proposes the root correspondence, while the psalm's concern is mortality rather than intimacy.

row.basis: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש (table sound correspondence)
row.note: The commentary begins with the human in loss; Daniel's vision presents a human-like figure coming with heaven's clouds, an exalted use of Aramaic enash. The roots may correspond, but the figure is not the commentary's ordinary solitary person.

row.basis: peaceful speech to someone who sinned
row.note: The commentary's counsel repairs a bond after wrongdoing; this testament urges love among brothers and peaceful speech to someone who sins against a companion. The exact verse division within chapter 6 is uncertain from memory.

cost_basis: API-equivalent at codexrun.RATES (Codex subscription; usage counts)
