row.basis: sow wind; reap whirlwind; grain without yield
row.note: Hosea makes wind sown into a whirlwind reaped, then says the stalk has no grain; it joins the commentary's storm, lost harvest, and failed human work in one agricultural judgment.

row.basis: rain drunk by earth; useful crop
row.note: The earth repeatedly drinks rain and grows useful vegetation for its cultivators; this matches the commentary's rain-to-productive-growth sequence and makes the crop's value depend on what it yields.
The same watered earth bears thorns and ends in burning; this supplies a direct reversal of the commentary's fruitful growth destroyed at the end.
Ezekiel pictures a mother as a fruitful vine beside abundant water with many branches, paralleling the commentary's watered, connected vegetation as an image of a living group.

row.basis: east wind dries fruit; vine burned
row.note: Ezekiel's once fruitful vine is uprooted, dried by the east wind, and consumed by fire; the reversal closely matches the commentary's lifetime yield destroyed by a fiery storm.
Fire emerging from the vine's own branch consumes its fruit and leaves no ruling branch; the commentary likewise reads the burned garden as a life's yield and vulnerable future lost together.
In Pharaoh's dream thin grain ears are scorched by the east wind; this gives the commentary's grain-ear stage a specific destructive counterpart before the harvest can feed anyone.
Seven thin ears consume the seven full ears in Pharaoh's dream; the image makes accumulated agricultural plenty disappear, as the commentary's late loss does.

row.basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; grain heaped
row.note: Joseph orders grain from the good years to be heaped and guarded against famine; Hebrew צבר matches the commentary's secondary صبر image of piled food, though the table's sound match does not establish etymology.

row.basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled grain
row.note: Joseph heaps grain in immense quantity before famine; the concrete stored-food heap corresponds to the commentary's صبرة of food stacked layer upon layer, without claiming proven cognacy.
Joseph says the collected food will preserve the land through seven famine years; this offers a deliberate preservation of yield against the harvest loss envisaged in the commentary.
The promised rains in their seasons allow Israel to gather grain, wine, and oil; this reproduces the commentary's move from rain cloud to usable produce.
God gives grass in the fields for livestock so that the people eat and are satisfied; it pairs the commentary's pasture feeding animals with the livelihood that follows.

row.basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; rain shut off
row.note: The divine closing of the heavens stops rain and thus the land's produce; Hebrew עצר expresses restraint, a pointed reversal of the commentary's rain-releasing cloud and ensuing harvest.
The beloved prepares a vineyard and expects grapes but receives bad fruit; the text tests the commentary's claim that productive growth can figure the moral result of human work.
The vineyard's hedge is removed so it can be devoured and trampled; its protection gives way to destruction, as the commentary's flourishing garden does at the end.
God commands the clouds to give no rain to the now desolate vineyard; this reverses the commentary's rain-to-greenery sequence through judgment on a failed crop.
Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and the expected crop as justice and righteousness, clarifying how the commentary's harvest imagery can evaluate human conduct rather than farming alone.

row.basis: fire consumes crop for rejected law
row.note: Fire consumes stubble and flame dries grass, while rotten roots and blown blossom picture those who rejected God's instruction; the commentary likewise lets a life crop end in fiery moral loss.
The people fail to acknowledge the giver of seasonal rain who preserves the appointed weeks of harvest; the verse makes rain and harvest an ordered provision with a moral obligation to recognize it.

row.basis: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; harvest ordinance
row.note: Jeremiah's fixed harvest weeks use חקות from the table's חקק family; the prescribed season provides a concrete counterpart to the commentary's conjunction of the crop and its due right, without equating the words.
Jeremiah says sins have kept those good gifts from the people; the commentary's disappearance of yield likewise turns agricultural loss into a judgment on conduct.
The field's owner must leave the edge and gleanings at harvest; this gives an exact social practice beside the commentary's claim that a crop's right is given on harvest day.
Grapes and fallen fruit must be left for the poor and resident alien; the harvest right extends to the commentary's vineyard and makes fruitfulness support others.
A sheaf forgotten in the field is to remain for the foreigner, orphan, and widow; it specifies who receives the harvest's due, linking produce to the weak dependents in the commentary's garden scene.

row.basis: farmer waits for fruit and rains
row.note: James urges patience by the farmer waiting for the precious crop and its early and late rains; the commentary's rain-grown yield is joined here to the explicit virtue of patient endurance.
Elijah prays again, heaven gives rain, and earth produces its fruit; this explicitly joins the commentary's rain cloud to its eventual productive crop in a communal prayer setting.
The withheld wages of harvest workers cry to the Lord in James's indictment of wealthy landowners; it gives the commentary's harvest due an economic and ethical edge.
Jesus describes good soil bearing fruit with perseverance after receiving the word; the commentary's patient, connected greenery becomes a specific figure for enduring faithful people.

row.basis: branch joined to vine bears fruit
row.note: Jesus says a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine; this directly illuminates the commentary's unusual image of plants joined together as the condition of living growth.
The vine and branches produce much fruit through remaining joined; it supplies a relational image for the commentary's exception of people who sustain one another like contiguous plants.
A branch that does not remain is cast out, dries, is gathered, and burns; it states the exact contrary fate of the commentary's joined vegetation and burning garden.
Paul says a person reaps what he sows; the commentary's crop as the product of a life receives an explicit ethical harvest formula.
Sowing to the flesh yields corruption while sowing to the Spirit yields life; the two outcomes sharpen the commentary's distinction between a ruined yield and enduring good action.

row.basis: persist in good; harvest in time
row.note: Paul urges against growing weary in doing good because a harvest will come if one does not give up; it ties the commentary's patient mutual goodness to sustained crop growth.
Jesus begins the rich fool's story with land yielding abundantly; this supplies the productive first stage of the commentary's lifetime crop lost near its end.
The man plans larger barns to store grain and goods; his amassed agricultural gain is the counterpart of the commentary's stacked food and accumulated life's produce.

row.basis: life ends before harvest can secure him
row.note: God demands the man's life that night and asks who will own his stores; the reversal mirrors the commentary's late catastrophe that makes an accumulated yield useless.
Paul's giving appeal says sparing and generous sowing have corresponding harvests; this adds the commentary's almsgiving setting to its agricultural account of human gain.
In Paul's quotation, one who distributes to the poor has righteousness that endures; it explains how the commentary's crop right at harvest becomes a lasting moral yield.

row.basis: seed and bread; harvest of righteousness
row.note: God supplies seed and food and multiplies the harvest of righteousness for givers; the commentary's rain-fed grain and obligation to share meet in this single farming image.
Bringing the tithe into God's storehouse is followed by promised abundance from heaven; it links the commentary's piled produce and due share with renewed provision.
God promises to restrain the devourer so field fruit is not destroyed and the vine does not fail; it reverses the commentary's loss of a ripened crop after its due has been given.
The righteous are a tree planted by channels of water that gives fruit in season; the commentary likewise sees the exceptional faithful as greenery sustained by water and productive time.
The wicked are chaff driven by wind, against the fruitful watered tree of the preceding verse; it precisely matches the commentary's contrast of lasting growth and works blown away.

row.basis: truth sprouts from earth beneath righteousness
row.note: The psalm pictures truth springing from the earth while righteousness looks down from heaven; it gives the commentary's joined greenery and call to truth a striking common image.
The next verse promises the Lord's good gift and the land's yield; it supplies the harvest stage after truth springs from the ground in the preceding verse.

row.basis: fruit and green growth in old age
row.note: The righteous still bear fruit in old age and remain fresh and green; this is an exact positive alternative to the commentary's aged owner losing a mature garden just when dependents need it.
Sowing in tears ends in reaping with joy; the agricultural sequence gives patient difficulty before harvest the positive ending preserved by the commentary's exception.

row.basis: sow without reaping; pressed crops lost
row.note: Micah threatens that the people will sow but not reap, tread olives yet lack oil, and crush grapes yet not drink wine; this is the commentary's lost harvest in a judgment on unjust gain.
Haggai lists much seed with little harvest and wages disappearing as if through a pierced purse; it connects the commentary's failed crop to the vanishing gain of human labor.
The people bring home little of what they expected and God blows it away; the image matches the commentary's wind-scattered works and abrupt removal of accumulated yield.
Because of the people's neglect, heaven withholds dew and earth withholds its produce; the commentary's rain, growth, and loss are compressed into one reversal.
The called drought reaches grain, wine, oil, people, animals, and all labor of hands; it relates a failed harvest to the whole community and its work, as the commentary does.
Joel's devastated land has ruined fields and grain, alongside dried wine and failing oil; it gives a specific prophetic instance of the commentary's harvest as loss.
The vine and fig tree dry up, as do the other fruit trees, while human joy withers; it joins vegetative loss to lived human loss as in the commentary's ruined garden.
Joel cries to God because fire has devoured the wilderness pastures and burned trees; it gives the commentary's animal-feeding meadow a destructive fiery counterpart.
Joel promises early and later rain in restored measure; after the destroyed crop, this supplies a recovery of the commentary's rain-to-growth sequence.
The restored rains are followed by threshing floors filled with grain and vats with wine and oil; it gives a concrete positive answer to the commentary's lost and heaped harvest.
A person boasting of a gift never given is likened to clouds and wind without rain; this applies the commentary's rain cloud to its nearby warning about showy giving whose benefit vanishes.
Jesus warns against giving alms publicly for praise, because such givers have received their reward already; it directly illuminates the commentary's showy spending that yields no lasting benefit.

row.basis: poor person's crop swept away by injustice
row.note: The poor person's field can provide much food, yet injustice destroys it; the verse makes the commentary's harvest right and lost yield a social issue rather than mere weather.

row.basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; withheld share causes lack
row.note: The proverb says one who withholds what ought to be given comes to lack; Hebrew מחסור from חסר connects the commentary's lost gain with its duty to give a crop's share, while cognacy remains unverified.

row.basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; giver has no lack
row.note: The one giving to the poor will have no lack, but ignoring them draws curses; Hebrew מחסור gives an explicit inverse to the commentary's loss and its harvest-day obligation.

row.basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no lack
row.note: The shepherd's speaker says he lacks nothing; Hebrew אחסר marks provision as the inverse of the commentary's ruined yield, and the following pasture image makes that inverse concrete.
The shepherd settles the speaker in green pastures beside quiet water; the commentary's meadow that gives itself to animals becomes a picture of sustained care.

row.basis: خسر / Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence only; found deficient
row.note: Daniel declares the king weighed and found lacking; the Aramaic חסיר gives the commentary's loss an explicitly evaluated human life, though the consonant match alone does not prove cognacy.

row.basis: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; rain prescribed
row.note: God sets a prescribed order for rain; the Hebrew חק in a rain passage meets the commentary's rain sequence and its mention of a crop's due, while preserving the difference between ordinance and right.

row.basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; sky restrained
row.note: Solomon describes heaven shut so there is no rain when Israel sins; עצר names the restraint, contrasting with the commentary's cloud releasing water onto a community.

row.basis: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; closed sky and eaten land
row.note: God says he can shut heaven against rain or send locusts to devour land; עצר makes a concrete opposite to the commentary's pressed rain cloud and fruitful harvest.
If God's people turn and pray, he promises to heal their land; this adds a communal ethical remedy to the preceding rain-and-crop destruction and the commentary's collective exception.

row.basis: mass of waters in thick clouds; חשר table sound match has different sense
row.note: David's hymn depicts God surrounded by dense water clouds; it supports the commentary's layered, water-filled cloud image on its own terms, while the table's חשר is semantically distinct from Arabic خسر 'loss'.
God binds water within thick clouds without their bursting; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's cloud filled with rain before releasing it.
Job says the skies pour their drops abundantly upon humanity; the rain-laden cloud's release corresponds to the commentary's cloud giving water to a community.

row.basis: full cloud empties rain on land
row.note: A cloud filled with water pours itself onto earth; this expresses the commentary's compressed rain cloud and its release without requiring a shared root.

row.basis: God gives rain and field plants
row.note: Those asking for spring rain receive showers and field plants; the verse carries the commentary's paired images of rain cloud and resulting greenery.
Before the garden's plants had appeared, God had not yet caused rain on the earth; the negation makes rain the missing beginning of the commentary's sequence of growth.

row.basis: vine fruit, land produce, heavenly dew
row.note: Zechariah's restored remnant receives a seed of peace, fruitful vine, productive ground, and heavenly dew; this unites the commentary's collective, watered garden, and tangible harvest.

row.basis: truth spoken to neighbors after restored harvest
row.note: After promising dew and yield to the remnant, Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and judge justly; this connects the commentary's green community to its mutual exhortation in truth.
God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on hills; this gives the commentary's cloud-to-pasture transition in one verse.
The next verse says God gives food to animals; it connects the commentary's pasture given to herds to divine provision rather than vegetation alone.

row.basis: whirlwind and storm; clouds as dust
row.note: Nahum joins a divine whirlwind and tempest with clouds described as dust beneath God's feet; this puts the commentary's rain cloud and dust-raising whirlwind into one memorable storm image.

row.basis: rain makes earth sprout, seed and bread
row.note: Rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts and gives seed and bread; the commentary's cloud, joined growth, grain, and food yield follow this same ordered sequence.

row.basis: water on dry land and descendants
row.note: God promises to pour water on thirsty ground and blessing on descendants; the commentary's rain-fed greenery and concern for weak offspring meet through this joined promise.
Those descendants sprout like grass among watercourses; the verse makes a living group into adjacent flourishing plants, as the commentary does for the mutually supporting faithful.
An outpouring from above transforms wilderness into a fruitful field; it gives the commentary's rain-to-garden movement a communal renewal sense.
Justice comes to dwell in the transformed fruitful field; the commentary likewise places truth and a crop's due amid flourishing vegetation.

row.basis: human generations swept away like grass
row.note: The psalm says God sweeps people away as grass renewing in the morning; it places the commentary's human loss inside the short life cycle of vegetation.
Grass blossoms in the morning and withers by evening; it closely parallels the commentary's quick turn from luxuriant growth to destroyed yield.
The psalm reckons a human span as seventy or eighty years, full of trouble and swiftly gone; it adds the late-life horizon of the commentary's elderly garden owner to the nearby grass image.
James compares the rich person's passing to a wild flower; it joins the commentary's accumulated material yield with the brief life of vegetation.
A rising sun with scorching heat dries the grass and drops its flower, as the wealthy fade amid their pursuits; this is another sudden destruction of apparent prosperity.
The letter quotes human flesh as grass whose flower falls; it transposes the commentary's withering harvest to the brevity of human life.

row.basis: blade then ear then full grain
row.note: Jesus describes the earth producing first a blade, then an ear, then full grain in the ear; the commentary's distinctive attention to visible grain husks and mature crop finds a staged analogue.
When the grain is ripe, the sower sends the sickle because harvest has come; it provides the decisive harvest moment beside the commentary's produce and harvest-day obligation.
In Jesus' explanation, wealth's deceit chokes the word so it becomes unfruitful; it offers an ethical counterpart to the commentary's showy spending and lost crop.
The receptive person is good soil that bears a multiplied crop; the commentary's exceptional believers likewise appear as productive ground after the warning of loss.

row.basis: seed on bare rock withers for lack of moisture
row.note: Seed on rock sprouts but dries because it has no moisture; the commentary's hard bare stone is a precise contrary surface to its watered, continuous greenery.

row.basis: rain and wind test true work
row.note: Rain, floods, and winds strike the house that survives because its builder acted on Jesus' words; this gives the commentary's storm a test of lived conduct rather than a mere weather event.

row.basis: rain and wind destroy failed work
row.note: The same storm makes the house of the hearer who does not act collapse; it parallels the commentary's image of a whole life's work lost in a violent final event.

row.basis: planting and watering; growth from God
row.note: Paul assigns planting and watering to different workers while God causes growth; the commentary's rain-fed community of mutually contributing lives receives a concrete division of work.

row.basis: fire reveals quality of each work
row.note: Paul says the day exposes each person's work as fire tests its quality; it links the commentary's burning at the end to an evaluation of accumulated human work.
If a person's work burns, that person suffers loss even though saved; the precise distinction between a life and its ruined product clarifies the commentary's garden consumed late in life.

row.basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled wealth
row.note: The wicked man may heap silver like dust, yet the following verse gives it to others; צבר matches the commentary's piled store while the context makes accumulation vulnerable to loss.

row.basis: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; life's hoard
row.note: The passing human heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; צבר joins the commentary's stacked gain to the old-age question of what a life's product finally secures.
The transplanted vine is set in good soil beside abundant water so it can bear branches and fruit; it parallels the commentary's rain-fed connected plants that grow into yield.
Even a planted vine will wither when the east wind touches it; the commentary's productive garden similarly remains vulnerable to a destructive wind.

row.basis: wind kills children at life's height
row.note: A great wind strikes the house where Job's children are together and kills them; it offers a family-loss counterpart to the commentary's storm scene with vulnerable offspring, though Job's loss is not a garden fire.

row.basis: east wind carries away accumulated wealth
row.note: The east wind drives away the wicked person after the account of his piled silver; the commentary likewise makes wind undo accumulated gain.
Job asks whether the wicked become chaff before wind and straw snatched by a whirlwind; the wording puts a human fate in the commentary's image of works scattered by a violent wind.
The nations' tumult is rebuked and chased like mountain chaff before wind and rolling dust before a storm; this shares the commentary's dust-raising whirlwind as an image of works unable to remain.
After the flood, God promises seedtime and harvest will continue while the earth remains; this stable cycle sets the ordinary expectation against which the commentary's ruined harvest is a reversal.
The generous person prospers and the one who gives water receives water; the commentary's rain-fed, mutually joined plants become an ethical pattern of reciprocal support.
Measured manna leaves neither surplus for the great gatherer nor lack for the small one; it offers an alternative to the commentary's stacked private food by meeting each person's need.

row.basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no food deficit
row.note: The smaller manna gatherer does not lack, using חסר; the negated deficiency connects the commentary's loss to a shared-food scene that prevents it.
Paul asks that one community's present abundance supply another's need; this makes the commentary's mutually joined believers and harvest due a concrete exchange of resources.

row.basis: consider one another for good works
row.note: The community is to attend to one another so as to stir love and good works; this gives a specific ethical action beside the commentary's joined plants representing believers who mutually urge what is right.
Those who fear the Lord speak with one another and are heard and remembered; their reciprocal speech provides a human counterpart to the commentary's plants joining in a faithful group.
Birds neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet God feeds them; the commentary's stores of grain and pasture for animals meet a different account of secure provision.
Grass now growing in the field is soon thrown into an oven; the commentary's green abundance suddenly consumed by fire gains a short-lived plant counterpart.

At harvest the weeds are bundled for burning while wheat is gathered into a barn; this places the commentary's stored grain and final fire at one decisive sorting, though its garden fire acts on an already productive plot.

row.basis: last season to make fig tree fruitful
row.note: The gardener asks for one more year to tend the fruitless fig tree; this creates a patient interval before the kind of final crop judgment the commentary describes.
If the tree bears after tending it may remain, otherwise it will be cut down; the commentary's survival of fruitful growth and loss of an unproductive garden meet in this conditional ending.

God withholds rain from one city while another receives it, leaving one field watered and another dry; the commentary's cloud releasing rain upon a group becomes an ethical question of who receives it.
God strikes gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees with blight and insects; this provides a more gradual counterpart to the commentary's storm destroying a developed crop.
Grass dries and flowers fall when God's breath blows on them; the commentary's wind-driven loss of lush vegetation likewise turns growth into impermanence.

Isaiah pairs whirlwind and tempest with the flame of a devouring fire in a judgment scene; it is a specific storm-and-fire analogue to the commentary's fiery whirlwind, though no crop is named in this verse.

Jeremiah calls prosperous people fat and sleek while they fail to defend an orphan's claim; it turns the commentary's image of fattening from abundant food toward the obligation to support vulnerable people.
Honi asks first for rain, then for rain of favor when the downpour is too violent; the story distinguishes life-giving rain from a damaging storm within the commentary's weather sequence.

A man brings firstfruits and fresh grain ears to Elisha, who orders them given to the people; the commentary's ears becoming food and a due share can be read beside this concrete communal distribution.

row.basis: field corner and firstfruits as obligations
row.note: The Mishnah lists the field corner and firstfruits among duties with no fixed measure; it gives a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's claim that a crop carries a right owed to others at harvest.

Job describes a thick cloud burdened with moisture while its luminous cloud disperses; the burdened cloud resembles the commentary's rain-filled layers, but its release into a community is not explicit here.
God promises rains in season and land yielding produce for obedience; the sequence is exact, though it does not include the commentary's mutual plant growth or later violent loss.
The coming figure gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff; it juxtaposes stored harvest with final fire, though the commentary's fire consumes a whole garden rather than separated chaff.
Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rising from the sea after repeated inspection; the commentary's rain-bearing cloud gains a narrative moment before its release onto the land.
The sky darkens with clouds and wind and then heavy rain falls; this joins the commentary's cloud, forceful wind, and needed rainfall in a single scene following drought.
The hoped-for king comes like rain on mown grass and showers watering earth; it places restorative rain precisely after cutting, the positive answer to the commentary's lost harvest.
Abundant grain covers the land while people flourish like field plants; the psalm turns the commentary's grain crop and joined green community into a linked vision of prosperity.
God waters mountains from above and earth is filled with the fruit of divine work; this supplies the commentary's downward rain and ensuing yield as one ordered provision.

row.basis: grass for animals; plants for human food
row.note: Grass grows for livestock and cultivated plants provide human food; it directly joins the commentary's meadow for herds to the crop that becomes a community's provision.

row.basis: rain, abundant grain, and broad pasture
row.note: God promises rain for seed, rich grain from the land, and spacious pasture for livestock; the verse contains the commentary's sequence from cloud-water to crop and fed animals.

row.basis: sown fields and planted vineyards yield fruit
row.note: People sow fields and plant vineyards that yield produce; the commentary's grain and vine garden likewise become the usable product of human labor on renewed land.
The following blessing multiplies both people and livestock; it links the commentary's productive pasture to the vulnerable descendants whose future depends on a preserved yield.

row.basis: feed the hungry from one's own resources
row.note: Isaiah calls for giving sustenance to the hungry and meeting the afflicted person's need; this specifies an ethical use for the commentary's grain and its due share.

After the command to feed the hungry, the Lord promises the giver will be like a watered garden whose spring does not fail; this makes generous action itself the opposite of the commentary's garden destroyed after showy giving.

The person who trusts God is a tree rooted by water, remaining green through heat and bearing fruit in drought; this supplies a direct durable counterpart to the commentary's fruitful garden lost to adverse weather.

row.basis: sow righteousness; reap mercy; awaited rain
row.note: Hosea calls the people to sow righteousness and reap loyal love until God comes and rains righteousness; it links the commentary's ethical injunction, patient waiting, rain, and harvest in one appeal.

God rebukes those who feed on good pasture but trample the rest and muddy water for others; the commentary's pasture giving itself to animals meets a precise demand that abundance remain available to the weak.

row.basis: weaker flock inherits spoiled food and water
row.note: The other sheep must consume the trampled pasture and muddied water; this gives the commentary's vulnerable dependents a concrete counterpart harmed when the first beneficiaries misuse a shared meadow.

row.basis: judgment between fat and lean sheep
row.note: God judges between fat and lean sheep; this puts the commentary's fattened animal beside its concern for weak dependents and assigns moral weight to their unequal access to pasture.

row.basis: showers of blessing at the right season
row.note: God promises showers in their season for the restored flock; the commentary's cloud releasing rain upon a community becomes an explicit collective blessing.

row.basis: trees and land yield fruit after rain
row.note: The trees and ground yield produce and the people live secure after the promised showers; this completes the commentary's rain-to-harvest sequence with protection from loss.
God promises to be like dew to Israel, who blossoms and puts down roots; the commentary similarly treats renewed vegetation as a living people sustained by water.
People return and flourish like grain and bloom like a vine; this gives the commentary's joined green community both its grain crop and vineyard forms.
In promised restoration, the plowman catches the reaper and grape-treader the seed-sower; this is a striking instance of the commentary's continuous growth and yield with no gap between crops.

row.basis: plant vineyards and eat their garden fruit
row.note: Restored people plant vineyards and gardens and enjoy their fruit; it reverses the commentary's late disaster by letting the makers retain the mature garden's benefit.

row.basis: plant vineyards and eat their fruit
row.note: The restored people plant vineyards and eat their own fruit; it is a direct positive inversion of the commentary's owner losing the garden that should have supported him.
No one else will eat what the people plant, and their days are compared to a tree's days; this answers the commentary's late-life fear that an aged cultivator will lose his accumulated crop.

row.basis: no futile labor or children born for calamity
row.note: The people will not labor in vain or bear children for sudden disaster; both claims specifically reverse the commentary's burning garden and elderly owner with vulnerable offspring.

row.basis: grain, herd, and watered garden together
row.note: The restored people stream toward grain, wine, oil, young flock, and herd, becoming like a watered garden; one verse brings together the commentary's crop, pasture animals, and living garden community.

As earth brings shoots forth and a garden grows what is sown, God makes righteousness and praise sprout before the nations; this makes the commentary's greenery a direct image of the good works expected from the saved group.

row.basis: wealth perishes and son receives nothing
row.note: Ecclesiastes describes wealth lost through a bad venture and a son left with nothing; the combination of vanished lifetime gain and unprovided child closely matches the commentary's aged gardener and weak offspring.

row.basis: watching wind and clouds delays sowing and reaping
row.note: One who watches wind never sows and one who studies clouds never reaps; the commentary's cloud, wind, and crop are joined here to the danger that anxious waiting itself can forfeit harvest.
The instruction to honor God from one's produce and firstfruits provides a concrete practice alongside the commentary's claim that a crop has a due share at harvest.
The ensuing promise of barns filled with plenty turns the commentary's stacked grain into a yield linked to giving rather than showy or withheld charity.

row.basis: fruitless branches removed; fruitful branches tended
row.note: Jesus distinguishes a branch removed for bearing no fruit from one pruned to bear more; this adds the maintenance of living, productive attachment to the commentary's plants joined together.

row.basis: fattened hearts on day of slaughter
row.note: James says unjust rich people have fattened their hearts in a day of slaughter, immediately after the unpaid harvesters' cry; it gives the commentary's spring fatness an ominous late reckoning tied to harvest injustice.

row.basis: fruit season brings a claim on vineyard yield
row.note: At harvest time the vineyard owner sends servants to receive its fruit; this is a narrative counterpart to the commentary's assertion that fruit carries a due claim when harvested.
Jesus says the kingdom will be given to a people producing its fruits; it parallels the commentary's exception of a faithful group pictured as an ongoing productive planting.

row.basis: mutual counsel and patience with the weak
row.note: Paul directs the community to admonish some, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this spells out the mutual exhortation and care for vulnerable members pictured by the commentary's connected plants.

row.basis: exhort one another each day before hardening
row.note: The addressees must encourage one another daily while it is called Today so no one hardens; the commentary's reciprocal exhortation and closing time horizon meet in a concrete repeated practice.

row.basis: elm supports vine; vine yields fruit
row.note: Hermas sees a vine that bears abundant fruit by clinging to an elm that supports it; this is a particularly close Christian image for the commentary's plants physically joining so that growth can continue.

row.basis: rich supply poor; poor pray for rich
row.note: Hermas explains the elm and vine as materially generous rich people and poor people who pray for them; the joined plants thus yield reciprocal benefit, much as the commentary connects mutual support to the crop's due share.

row.basis: watered fruit tree and enduring shoots
row.note: The rabbinic blessing tells of a traveler nourished by a tree's fruit, shade, and water, then wishes its shoots to resemble it; it makes the commentary's productive greenery a source of care and continuity for later generations.

row.basis: watered tree gives fruit every month
row.note: The tree of life stands by the river and yields fruit month after month, with leaves for the nations' healing; it offers the commentary's connected, uninterrupted greenery an enduring communal yield.

row.basis: large sowing yields little because devoured
row.note: The people carry much seed to the field yet gather little because locusts consume it; this gives the commentary's human loss a specific crop-failure form within a covenant curse.
They plant and tend vineyards but cannot drink the wine or gather grapes because worms consume them; it parallels the commentary's carefully built garden that fails to benefit its owner.

row.basis: spent labor yields neither crop nor fruit
row.note: The land will not give produce and the trees will not give fruit despite expended strength; the commentary's lost harvest is likewise the loss of a lifetime's labor, though this verse names no storm.

row.basis: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; cultivated land without lack
row.note: In a land of abundant food, Israel will lack nothing, using Hebrew חסר; it is the explicit inverse of the commentary's crop as loss, with cognacy still only the table's unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: rain falls where no person lives
row.note: God sends rain even onto uninhabited desert land; it gives a specific counterpoint to the commentary's cloud raining upon a community, showing that the same gift can precede any human receiver.
The rain satisfies waste ground and brings forth grass; this completes the preceding verse's empty-land rain with growth, extending the commentary's rain-to-pasture sequence beyond settled land.
Jesus says giving unseen by others is seen and repaid by the Father; it supplies the positive alternative to the commentary's showy donor whose apparent good is stripped away.

row.basis: stored crop seems to promise many years
row.note: The rich farmer addresses his soul as if stored goods guarantee years of ease; this expectation makes the next verse's sudden end a sharper counterpart to the commentary's late loss of a life's product.
Jesus says the seed crowded by cares, riches, and pleasures never reaches mature fruit; it gives the commentary's threatened crop a specific failure of ripening through worldly entanglement.

A wheat grain must fall and die to bear much fruit; it is an inverse agricultural path to the commentary's mature garden destroyed at the end, with the loss occurring before abundance rather than after it.

row.basis: truth spoken in love as growth
row.note: Speaking truth in love, believers grow toward Christ; this joins the commentary's charge to exhort in truth with its unusual image of shared living growth.

The whole body is joined and held together, each part working so it grows in love; though anatomical rather than botanical, it develops the commentary's claim that the faithful sustain one another by being connected.

row.basis: do good especially to fellow believers
row.note: Immediately after the promised harvest for persistent good work, Paul directs good to all, especially the household of faith; it identifies the mutual beneficiaries of the commentary's patient moral crop.
A tree without good fruit is cut down and cast into fire; this relates the commentary's garden consumed by fire to a moral test of what the planting produced.

row.basis: communal remembrance of rain at festival
row.note: The Mishnah debates when rain should first be invoked during the autumn festival; it places the commentary's rain-bearing cloud within a community's timed, recurring liturgical concern.

row.basis: strong wind strips unripe fig tree
row.note: Stars fall like unripe figs shaken from a fig tree by strong wind; the comparison gives the commentary's destructive wind a specific instance of fruit torn away before it can support anyone.
