tool_diagnostics.message: apply_patch verification failed: Failed to find expected lines in /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec1/sol/list.tsv:

row.note: The commentary's afternoon laborer reaches payday as the day ends; the vineyard owner calls the workers at evening to receive wages, making the daily deadline concrete.

row.basis: One hour versus full day's labor
row.note: The late workers have worked only one hour, while others bore the whole day's burden; the contrast sharpens the commentary's question of time spent and recompense.
The workers hired at the eleventh hour receive a denarius; payment after little remaining daylight complicates any simple equation of duration and wage.
Jesus says work must be done during daylight because night comes when no one can work; this gives the commentary's closing workday a direct moral deadline.
The hired poor worker's wage must be paid that day before the sun sets, providing a legal counterpart to the commentary's afternoon and due wage.

row.basis: Wages in a bag with holes
row.note: Workers earn wages only to put them in a pierced purse; the commentary's capital eaten away by passing time becomes an image of labor without retained gain.
Jesus asks what it profits a person to gain the whole world and forfeit life; the commentary's losing capital ultimately means losing the self.
The rich man's accumulated goods cannot extend the deadline when his life is required that night; this closely meets the commentary's hoarder who thinks property lengthens life.

row.basis: Stored wealth and poverty toward God
row.note: The parable concludes that storing for oneself leaves one poor toward God; it supplies the distinction between a full earthly account and lasting gain.

row.basis: Wealth cannot profit on judgment day
row.note: The proverb says riches do not profit in the day of wrath but righteousness rescues from death; it gives the commentary's failed trade a final accounting.
Jesus contrasts labor for perishing food with food enduring to eternal life; the commentary likewise asks which expenditure of finite work survives.

row.basis: Good work and harvest in due season
row.note: The community must not tire of doing good, because it will reap in due time if it does not give up; good action, patience, and deferred pay meet in one verse.
Paul says planter and waterer each receive wages according to their labor; this directly joins the commentary's intentional work and earned payment.
Paul says a builder whose work burns suffers loss though the person is saved; it distinguishes lost work from lost self in the commentary's final account.

row.basis: Lose work or receive full reward
row.note: The readers are warned to watch themselves so their labor is not lost and they receive a full reward; it binds vigilance, loss, and complete payment.
The dead in the Lord rest from labor and their deeds follow them; the wage scene acquires a precise boundary between ended labor and surviving deeds.
The coming speaker brings payment to repay each according to work; it matches the commentary's final rather than immediate settlement.

row.basis: Profit from toil under the sun
row.note: Ecclesiastes asks what gain people have from all the toil they perform under the sun; the same accounting question frames life as spent effort.
The speaker surveys all the work his hands made and finds no lasting profit under the sun; it is a concrete contrary ledger to profitable moral work.
Psalm 90 measures the human span and says its strength is toil and trouble that soon flies away; finite time and labor are the commentary's spent capital.
The prayer asks to be taught to number days so as to gain a wise heart; counting the finite resource of time answers the commentary's running loss.
Job compares himself to a hired worker longing for his wages; the commentary's wage at the end of the workday has a biblical sufferer's voice.
Job asks God to look away until the mortal finishes the day like a hired worker; the comparison joins life's fixed span to an end-of-day wage.
A deceptive scale is abominable and a just weight pleasing to God; the commentary's short-weighted customer becomes an explicit moral violation.

row.basis: Shrink measure, enlarge price, falsify scales
row.note: Merchants impatient for sacred time to end make the grain measure small and the price large; market hours and short measure meet exactly as in the commentary.
The law forbids wronging another in measuring length, weight, or quantity; the commentary's deficit on the scale is a named social wrong.
The command supplies just scales, just weights, and honest measures; these specify what the commentary's mutual right requires at a sale.
The demand for a complete and just weight is attached to prolonged days in the land; measured fairness and the duration of life intersect.
The prophet asks whether dishonest scales and a bag of false weights can be counted clean; short weighing becomes a judicial question of right.
The giver receives a good, pressed, overflowing measure, and the measure used is returned; it reworks the commentary's short measure into ample recompense.

row.basis: Lending to God by aiding the poor
row.note: The person who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the deed; God as counterparty and the other person's due converge.

row.basis: Use passing wealth for enduring welcome
row.note: Jesus says to make friends by means of unrighteous wealth so they receive one into eternal dwellings when it fails; finite capital can be spent for an enduring return.
Treasure kept in heaven is beyond moth, rust, and thieves; it answers the commentary's contrast between exhausted human holdings and what endures with God.
The wealthy are urged to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life; the commentary's altered investment of wealth has a close analogue.
Treasures gained wickedly profit nothing while righteousness delivers from death; moral action is the profitable alternative to a full but failing purse.
Paul counts what had been gains as loss for Christ; it gives the commentary's profit-and-loss vocabulary a deliberate reversal of value.
Paul accepts the loss of all things to gain Christ; the text distinguishes chosen material loss from the commentary's ruinous loss of self.
The merchant sells all he has to buy the uniquely valuable pearl; surrendering capital becomes a successful transaction, beside the commentary's saving trade.

row.basis: Buy refined gold from the speaker
row.note: The speaker counsels a materially self-satisfied church to buy gold from him so it becomes rich; true capital is defined against apparent wealth.
Paul says the Day reveals each builder's work and tests what sort it is; the commentary's payday includes judgment of the work itself.
Work that survives the test brings its worker a reward; it supplies the positive balance opposite the loss in the adjoining verse.
Sowing to flesh yields decay while sowing to Spirit yields eternal life; the commentary's competing trades have concrete divergent returns.

row.basis: Work remembered by a just payer
row.note: God is not unjust to forget work and love shown in service to the saints; the wage due for good work is backed by divine justice.
The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; two terms of the surah's exception become conditions of deferred receipt.

row.basis: Persistence in good work seeks immortality
row.note: People who persist in good action seek glory and immortality and receive eternal life; patient work answers the hoarder's false bid for immortality.
Paul urges steadfastness and abundance in the Lord's work, knowing that labor is not empty; the commentary's loss versus enduring wage is stated directly.

row.basis: Work of faith and endurance of hope
row.note: Paul remembers the congregation's work produced by faith and endurance sustained by hope; faith, deed, and patient continuation are inseparable.
The speaker knows this church's works, faith, service, and endurance, and says its later works exceed earlier ones; the surah's exception is matched in a timed communal assessment.
James says faith by itself is dead if it lacks works; it makes the commentary's paired believing and intentional good action a necessary conjunction.
The community is told to love in action and truth, rather than merely in words; it specifies how mutual commitment to truth becomes practiced good.
The addressees must exhort one another daily while it is called today, lest anyone harden through deceit; mutual counsel has the commentary's passing-time urgency.

row.basis: Provoke one another to good deeds
row.note: The congregation must consider how to stir one another to love and good works; it is a direct communal form of the commentary's reciprocal exhortation.

row.basis: Patiently admonish and help one another
row.note: The congregation is urged to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all; the counsel to patience takes concrete social form.
Each should speak truth with a neighbor because they belong to one another; the commentary's truth as an obligation owed across the community has a textual counterpart.

row.basis: Work honestly to share with the needy
row.note: The former thief must work with his hands at what is good so he has something to share with one in need; intentional labor becomes another person's due.
The wages kept from harvest workers cry out to the Lord of hosts; it specifies the wrong of failing to pay when work is done.
The addressees are told to be patient until the Lord's coming as a farmer waits for precious fruit; deferred yield and endurance meet in a work scene.
The audience must also be patient and firm because the Lord's coming is near; it makes the promised settlement, rather than waiting alone, the point.
The prophet condemns building a house by injustice while making a neighbor work for nothing and not giving wages; labor, rights, and payment join explicitly.

row.basis: Hired worker's pay not held overnight
row.note: The law forbids retaining a hired worker's wages until morning; it sets an enforceable due time for the commentary's worker.
Jesus instructs envoys to accept a host's provision because the worker deserves wages; the commentary's wage is treated as a right, not a gift.
The letter cites the maxim that the laborer deserves wages in a discussion of support for elders; earned pay is an obligation of the beneficiary.
The plans of the diligent lead to profit, while haste leads to poverty; this specifies how intention and duration change the trade's result.
Wealth gained rapidly shrinks, but gathering little by little increases it; the passage counters the commentary's image of a balance steadily diminishing.

row.basis: Do not exhaust oneself for riches
row.note: The proverb warns against toiling to acquire wealth; it challenges the worker who gives finite strength to a capital that cannot secure life.
When one looks at riches they are gone, flying away like an eagle; it gives the commentary's vanishing earthly capital a sudden image.

row.basis: Wealth lost in a bad venture
row.note: Ecclesiastes describes riches lost through a bad business affair, leaving nothing for a child; the loss of principal and family consequence are both present.

row.basis: No earnings carried out of life
row.note: A person leaves this life as naked as at birth and carries nothing gained by toil; the commentary's trader cannot take the day's proceeds past death.
One must do with strength whatever the hand finds because no work or planning is done in Sheol; it makes a finite work period ethically urgent.
God will bring every deed, even hidden ones, to judgment; the commentary's final pay is based on a complete account of work.
The psalm depicts rising early and sitting late to eat bread of painful toil while God gives sleep; it tests whether long hours alone secure gain.
The speakers say service to God is vain and ask what gain comes from keeping his charge; the market question is raised within moral work itself.

row.basis: People speak together, remembered by God
row.note: Those who fear the Lord speak with one another and a book of remembrance is written for them; mutual counsel is entered into a lasting account.

row.basis: Serving God shown apart from not serving
row.note: God promises a visible distinction between the righteous and wicked, one serving him and one not; it answers the preceding dispute over the profit of service.
The psalm joins trust in the Lord with doing good and dwelling securely; belief and beneficial action occupy one instruction.
Abram believes the Lord, who counts it to him as righteousness; faith is entered as a positive item in a divine account.
The divine word tells Abram not to fear and promises great reward; a promised recompense precedes Abram's believing response later in the scene.
The passage requires one approaching God to believe he exists and rewards seekers; trust and eventual payment are deliberately linked.
The righteous are told that things will go well because they will eat the fruit of their own actions; it puts moral labor and due return together.
The wicked are told they will receive what their hands have done; this is the negative entry in the commentary's wage account.
After a long time, the master returns to reckon with servants entrusted with talents; passing time and entrusted capital end in an account.
The first servant trades the master's five talents and makes five more; the commentary's believer as faithful trader has a concrete scene.
The master calls the profitable servant good and faithful and sets him over more; profitable dealing is judged as trustworthiness.
A nobleman gives money to servants and orders them to do business until he comes back; the commentary's market stays open for a limited absence.
At his return the owner summons the servants to learn what they gained by trading; it is a direct closing of the ledger after elapsed time.
Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to those unfaithful with worldly wealth; handling temporary capital becomes a test of entrusted responsibility.
The requirement for a steward is to be found faithful; it supplies a concrete office for the commentary's trust opposed to betrayal.
The rich are told not to hope in uncertain riches but in God; it corrects the illusion that one's holdings can secure a future.
The wealthy are directed to be rich in good works and ready to share; it defines the alternate capital that the next verse stores for the future.
The outer person wastes away while the inner is renewed daily; the commentary's continual expenditure of mortal capital need not entail loss of the person.
The visible things are temporary and the unseen eternal; this supplies a specific axis for finite holdings versus enduring return.
In the morning one sows, and at evening one must not let the hand rest, since one cannot know which work succeeds; action continues up to the day's boundary.
The proverb asks whether riches or a crown persist through generations; it rebukes confidence that stored money outlasts mortal time.
Peter and John go to the temple at the ninth hour, explicitly an hour of prayer; this is a concrete afternoon prayer beside the commentary's asr prayer.
Cornelius recalls praying in his house at the ninth hour; it shows the afternoon prayer time in another early Christian setting.
Cornelius is told his prayers and alms have come before God as a memorial; the afternoon prayer scene's charity is kept in a divine account.
The mishnah assigns a latest time to the afternoon prayer, with a reported disagreement over its extent; it contextualizes the commentary's named afternoon prayer as timed practice.

row.basis: Day short, work great, wage great
row.note: Rabbi Tarfon's saying calls the day short, work great, workers sluggish, and reward abundant; the commentary's entire daily labor image is compressed here.
The continuation says the employer is trustworthy to pay for labor and places the righteous person's reward in the future; it joins amanah, wage, and delayed payment.
The parable's shop extends credit while a written ledger and collectors bring every debt to account; it mirrors the commentary's open market and mutual obligations.
The present life is a vestibule where one prepares for the coming hall; finite preparatory time precedes the lasting result of work.

row.basis: One hour of deeds before the next world
row.note: The saying values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this life above the whole coming life, giving a sharp reason to use remaining time now.
The thirsty are invited to buy food and wine without money or price; the commentary's rescue from a losing trade likewise moves value beyond ordinary payment.

row.basis: Spend wages on what does not satisfy
row.note: The speaker asks why people spend money for nonbread and labor for what does not satisfy; this diagnoses a failed exchange of finite work for an empty return.

row.basis: Silver cannot rescue on the day
row.note: Neither silver nor gold can deliver people on the day of the Lord's wrath; monetary capital loses all purchasing power at the final deadline.

row.basis: Door closes while buyers are away
row.note: While the unprepared bridesmaids go to buy oil, the bridegroom arrives and the door shuts; the commentary's market closure becomes a concrete missed final opportunity.

row.basis: Sell goods for an unfailing purse
row.note: Jesus directs hearers to sell possessions and give alms, making a purse that does not grow old; diminishing earthly goods can yield lasting treasure.
The condemned ask what their arrogance profited and what wealth brought them; the commentary's profit-and-loss question is spoken by those who have already lost.
The condemned say all their apparent gains have gone like a shadow; the line makes the trader's disappearing capital a matter of elapsed time.
Tobit tells his son that almsgiving stores up good treasure for a day of need; the commentary's finite possessions can become a lasting credit through another's right.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The tree bears fruit in its season and prospers in all it does; the table's Hebrew root means prospering, a suggestive but unverified sound link to the commentary's salih deeds and timed reward.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Keeping and meditating on the law day and night makes one's way prosper; the sound-corresponding Hebrew verb links success to sustained obedient conduct, though Arabic salih here means good deeds.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Potiphar sees the Lord prosper all that Joseph does; the Hebrew success verb gives the commentary's evaluated work a narrative example without proving cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Joseph's prison keeper need not inspect what is entrusted to him, and the Lord prospers his work; trust, labor, and successful outcome converge with the source's secondary marketplace scene.

row.basis: Arabic ص ل ح / Aramaic צלח, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus after surviving a trial of fidelity; the Aramaic prosperity verb is a cautious sound link to the commentary's salih outcome.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Moses' hands remain steady until sunset because Aaron and Hur support them; the Hebrew faithfulness root physically joins supported endurance to an evening boundary.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The righteous lives by faithfulness while the proud one is not upright; the table's Hebrew firmness root adds fidelity over time to the commentary's believing exception.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Works of God's hands are truth and justice and his precepts are trustworthy; the Hebrew root ties reliability to deeds and right order rather than assent alone.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The precepts are established forever and done in truth and uprightness; the table's firmness family gives a lasting counterpart to transient human accounts.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only
row.note: God delights in people who act faithfully while lying lips offend; the shared consonants connect the commentary's trust opposed to betrayal with actual conduct.

row.basis: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Even young lions lack and hunger, but seekers of the Lord lack no good thing; the Hebrew deficiency root offers a cautious lexical link to the commentary's depleted balance.

row.basis: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The person giving to the poor will not lack, while one hiding the eyes gets curses; the table's deficit root connects loss avoided with an obligation to another.

row.basis: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: What is lacking cannot be counted, the speaker says; the Hebrew deficiency noun makes the commentary's arithmetic of loss explicit, though the proposed root relation remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Joseph heaps up grain beyond counting until counting stops; Hebrew piling resembles the source commentary's secondary heap bought without weighing, while neither text makes it patience.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Joseph proposes collecting grain during seven good years for the future; the Hebrew heaping root supplies a timed economic setting for the source's measured or unmeasured heap.

row.basis: Arabic ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The psalm calls the brief human span toil and trouble; Hebrew toil shares the table's consonants with the commentary's work but foregrounds its burden.

row.basis: Arabic ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, table sound correspondence only
row.note: One who toils with wisdom and skill may leave the result to someone who has not toiled; the Hebrew labor root asks who ultimately gets the worker's earned portion.

row.basis: Arabic ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Builders labor in vain if the Lord does not build; the Hebrew toil root adds dependence on God to the commentary's contrast of productive and lost work.

row.basis: Arabic ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Job says human days and months have appointed bounds not to be passed; the Hebrew prescription root gives a fixed due boundary to the commentary's time and payable right.

row.basis: Arabic ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The prophet condemns those who decree unjust decrees; the Hebrew prescribed-law root puts formal obligation under moral scrutiny beside the commentary's due right.

row.basis: Unjust decree deprives needy of right
row.note: The unjust decrees in the adjoining verse deprive the needy of justice and rob the poor of their right; this specifies whose due is lost when legal form becomes corrupt.

row.basis: Arabic ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, table sound correspondence only
row.note: Rulers decree justice through Wisdom; the Hebrew enactment verb links the commentary's obligatory right with an enacted, just order.
The command is to open the hand and lend a needy brother enough for his need; the commentary's mutual debt becomes a specified financial duty.

row.basis: Give without grief, blessing on work
row.note: The giver is told to give freely, with God's blessing promised on work; another's material due and the worker's return are joined.
The proverb warns against becoming security for debts; it is a contrasting practical judgment on the source commentary's secondary sabir as guarantor behind a payment.
The addressee is pictured as having guaranteed a neighbor's debt; it supplies the specific debt relation behind the commentary's lexically named guarantor.
Jesus asks who by anxiety can add to life's span; the hoarder's attempt to outlast time faces an explicit limit on extending life.
Paul says momentary suffering produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison; patient endurance yields a return not commensurable with the spent time.
The person who remains steadfast under trial receives the promised crown of life; patience is tied to a deferred and nonmonetary wage.
The audience must not discard confidence because it has great recompense; the commentary's entrusted faith is sustained in view of pay.
The audience needs endurance to do God's will and receive the promise; the time between work and due reward is filled by patience.
Paul describes finishing his course and keeping faith; the commentary's worker must carry purposeful effort through to its endpoint.
A crown of righteousness is laid up for Paul, to be awarded by the righteous judge on that day; payment comes after finishing the course.

row.basis: Deeds toward least count toward king
row.note: The king treats care for the least of his brothers as done to himself; another person's due becomes part of the worker's final assessment.
James imagines a sibling without clothing and daily food; the commentary's claims about good deeds and others' rights gain a concrete beneficiary.
Saying warm words without supplying a sibling's bodily needs is useless; mutual counsel must involve effective work rather than advice alone.
Someone with worldly resources sees a needy sibling and shuts compassion; it tests whether capital is used to meet the other's claim.

row.basis: Encourage more as day draws near
row.note: The community must keep meeting and encourage one another increasingly as the Day approaches; reciprocal counsel intensifies toward a fixed deadline.

row.basis: Do good while there is opportunity
row.note: As opportunity remains, the community should do good to everyone, especially the household of faith; the moral task has a limited open period.
The speaker urges sending bread on the waters because it will be found after many days; it images an expenditure whose return waits beyond the present.

row.basis: Establish the work of our hands
row.note: The prayer asks God twice to establish human handiwork; in a psalm of short lives, this seeks durability for labor that would otherwise vanish.

row.basis: Agreed wage owed to the worker
row.note: The owner tells the complaining worker he has fulfilled the agreed denarius; this specifies the commentary's wage as a settled contractual right.
The owner appeals to his right to use his own money generously; the text complicates the commentary's strict wage ledger with unmeasured gift.

row.basis: Nothing brought in, nothing carried out
row.note: Paul observes that people enter the world with nothing and can take nothing away; the commentary's goods expire at the human boundary.
The prohibition on large and small weights describes the exact equipment for the commentary's cheating scale.
The cheating merchants then buy the needy for silver; the crooked market's loss reaches a human person, not merely a measure of grain.
A person coming to a grain heap for twenty measures finds ten; the deficit is shown as a concrete count beside the commentary's diminished capital.
Jesus asks what a person gains by winning the whole world but losing or forfeiting oneself; it is especially close to the commentary's gloss that the ultimate loss is the person.

row.basis: Leaving family and property for life
row.note: Jesus promises a manifold return and eternal life to followers who leave family or fields for his name; it turns loss of family and holdings, disastrous in the commentary's quoted warning, into a chosen cost with promised return.
Jesus calls believing in the one God sent the work of God; it ties the commentary's belief and work more tightly than a mere sequence of two acts.
The person admitted to God's tent walks blamelessly, does righteousness, and speaks truth in the heart; deed and truth function together as criteria.
God repays every person according to deeds; the commentary's final wage uses an individual account of actual work.

row.basis: Recompense according to ways and deeds
row.note: God searches the heart and gives each person according to conduct and the fruit of deeds; intention and work both matter at settlement.

row.basis: One who watches souls repays works
row.note: The proverb asks whether the one who weighs hearts and watches lives will not repay each according to work; divine weighing includes motives as well as output.

row.basis: Do not delay aid near debt release
row.note: The lender is warned not to refuse a needy brother merely because the seventh year is near; the debt deadline must not cancel the other's immediate due.
The prepared bridesmaids tell the unprepared to buy oil from dealers; the concrete market action immediately before closure clarifies why the opportunity cannot be recovered.
The late bridesmaids return and call to be let in; their failed return from the market echoes the commentary's plea for a brief extension once the term has ended.
The speaker urges placing one's treasure according to the Most High's commandments and promises more profit than gold; moral expenditure is a safer investment than hoarding.
The instruction praises giving security for a neighbor; it supplies a Jewish debt scene for the source commentary's secondary sense of sabir as a guarantor.
The community is told to gather often and seek what benefits souls because even the whole time of faith will not profit if one is not complete at the end; time, gain, and final perseverance converge.

row.ref: Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels 19
row.basis: Vineyard hours as ages of life
row.note: Gregory reads the vineyard's laboring hours as stages of human life and the evening payment as final recompense; this makes explicit the commentary's move from a day's wage to an expiring lifetime.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The final festival day is called a solemn assembly and ordinary work stops; the table's Hebrew root may suggest a bounded communal time beside the commentary's afternoon prayer and ended work, though its restraint sense is different from the developed Arabic time sense.

row.basis: Arabic خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The king is weighed in the balances and found deficient; the table's Aramaic lacking root joins a literal scale to the commentary's moral shortfall, though cognacy remains unverified.

row.basis: Numbered kingdom brought to an end
row.note: Daniel explains that God has numbered the king's days and ended his rule; the counted time immediately precedes the short weight in the next verse.

row.basis: Silver weighers and traders cut off
row.note: The inhabitants are told to wail because traders are destroyed and those weighing out silver are cut off; market, balance, and final closure meet in one announcement.

row.basis: Buyer and seller at the approaching day
row.note: When the time and day arrive, neither buyer should rejoice nor seller mourn because judgment falls on all; the ordinary logic of a profitable transaction is suspended.
Silver is thrown into the streets and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath or satisfy hunger; the commentary's capital has no use when its trading day ends.
God comes as a witness against those who defraud hired workers of wages and wrong vulnerable people; the commentary's due wage is a matter for final judgment.

row.basis: Integrity weighed on an honest scale
row.note: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity; the commentary's market scale becomes a test of the person rather than the goods.

row.basis: Do not withhold good that is due
row.note: The addressee must not withhold good from those to whom it is due when able to act; it states the commentary's mutual right as an immediate obligation.

row.basis: Do not defer payment until tomorrow
row.note: One must not tell a neighbor to return tomorrow when the goods are in hand today; the owed portion has a deadline before time runs out.

row.basis: Do not exploit a needy hired worker
row.note: The rule forbids oppression of poor hired workers, including resident foreigners; it identifies who is vulnerable before the same-day wage rule in the next verse.
The mortal heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; this precisely unsettles the commentary's hoarder who expects his capital to outlast his own time.
The speaker says God has made his days a few handbreadths and his lifetime nothing by comparison; time itself is a small measured holding.

row.basis: Workers enjoy the work of their hands
row.note: People will build and inhabit and plant and eat, with days like a tree's; this reverses labor lost to another and gives the commentary's wage a durable setting.
The promised people will not labor in vain or bear children for calamity; enduring work and preserved family answer both forms of loss developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Reaper receives wage for eternal harvest
row.note: The reaper already receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life; the commentary's daily worker and final, lasting payment are joined explicitly.
The master says the idle servant should have placed his money with bankers so it returned with interest; merely preserving the principal fails the investment test.

row.basis: Stored goods imagined to buy many years
row.note: The rich man addresses his soul as having goods stored for many years and plans to rest; it states the precise illusion about wealth and lengthened life corrected in the following verse.
The earth's merchants mourn because no one buys their cargo anymore; the commentary's open market ends without another buyer.
The lament says great wealth is laid waste in a single hour; it compresses the commentary's continuing capital loss into a final moment.

Paul distinguishes a worker's pay credited as an obligation from a gift credited by grace; this tests the commentary's moral wage metaphor against an explicit refusal to make divine credit ordinary wages.
Paul says the one who does not work but trusts God is credited with righteousness; the passage presses against reading belief and good work as jointly earning the payment.

row.basis: Gift produces credit in the giver's account
row.note: Paul says he seeks fruit increasing to the donors' account rather than the gift itself; generosity becomes an accumulating return in the commentary's moral ledger.

row.basis: Lost property and better lasting possession
row.note: The audience accepted the plunder of its goods because it knew it had a better and enduring possession; material principal can be lost without final loss.
Paul says his work showed the need to help the weak and recalls that giving is more blessed than receiving; earned goods become another's benefit.

row.basis: Worldly gain cannot compensate a soul
row.note: Jesus asks what profit gaining the world has if one forfeits life and what could be given in exchange; it repeats the commentary's ultimate calculation of self-loss in another Gospel setting.
The Son of Man will come in glory and repay each person according to what each has done; the self-loss question in the preceding verse is followed by the work account.

row.basis: Agreed denarius for a day's work
row.note: The vineyard owner agrees with laborers on a denarius for the day before sending them out; it sets the contracted amount whose evening distribution drives the story.
The owner still finds idle workers at the eleventh hour and asks why they stand there; meaningful work remains possible just before the daily deadline.
Jesus asks who will give the stewards their own if they have not been faithful with someone else's; entrusted capital is the test for lasting possession.
The person faithful in very little is faithful in much; the commentary's trust in dealings applies to small transactions before a greater settlement.

row.basis: Calculate loss of a good deed against reward
row.note: The saying instructs a person to reckon a commandment's apparent loss against its reward and a transgression's apparent gain against its loss; it articulates the commentary's moral profit calculation.
The borrower is told not to forget a guarantor who has given his life for him; the source's secondary sabir as guarantor becomes a concrete and costly interpersonal obligation.
Jacob has Esau swear and Esau sells his birthright; a lasting share is exchanged for immediate consumption, making a disastrous trade of one's due portion.
Esau eats and drinks, leaves, and is said to have despised the birthright; the scene shows the short appetite behind the preceding loss of a lasting right.

row.basis: Esau's bargain read as moral warning
row.note: Hebrews recalls Esau selling his birthright for a single meal to warn against an unholy choice; it interprets Genesis's market exchange as sacrificing a durable inheritance.
Hebrews says Esau later wanted the blessing but was rejected despite seeking it with tears; its reading of the birthright story meets the commentary's too-late plea for an extension.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ and Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondences only
row.note: Jehoshaphat tells the people to believe the Lord and be established, and believe his prophets and succeed; the verse puts two table roots in sequence, linking trust to a prospering outcome without proving either cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, table sound correspondence only
row.note: The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's stomach lacks; the Hebrew deficiency verb marks a concrete moral shortfall rather than a mere sad feeling.

row.basis: Life as a hired worker's term
row.note: Job compares human days on earth to the days of a hired worker; it frames the wage longing in the next verse as a figure for mortal duration.
The wicked borrow and do not repay, while the righteous are generous and give; the commentary's mutual right is tested at the point of an outstanding debt.
The speaker commands rescue of people being taken to death; the next verse's divine weighing and repayment rests on this concrete neglected duty.
The prophet recalls a period with no wages for human or beast and no peace for travel; the absence of pay makes the coming restoration more than abstract prosperity.
The speaker's flesh and heart may fail, yet God remains his portion forever; the lasting share is opposed to the exhausted mortal self and goods.
The people are promised light if they pour themselves out for the hungry and satisfy the afflicted; the commentary's expiring personal capital is put to another's need.
The proverb calls a just balance and scales the Lord's and treats the weights as his work; fair commercial measurement belongs within divine order.
The prophet identifies wicked wealth and a deficient grain measure in the house; hoarded capital and short measure share one household.
The instruction says to remember that death will not delay; it counters the commentary's hope that a short extension will remain available.

row.basis: Give to a friend before death
row.note: The speaker urges doing good to a friend and giving while still alive; possession can meet another's claim only before the human deadline.
Tobit tells his son almsgiving delivers from death and prevents descent into darkness; the stored treasure in the prior instruction has a concrete life-saving return.

row.basis: Little with righteousness exceeds unjust wealth
row.note: Raphael ranks prayer and almsgiving with righteousness above riches with injustice; the scale of moral value differs from the amount in a purse.

row.basis: The grave does not cancel accounting
row.note: The saying warns that death cannot serve as a refuge because one must give an account before the divine king; the commentary's closing day still leaves an audit.
The addressees must not store treasure where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in; this specifies how the commentary's earthly capital can disappear.

row.basis: Sell holdings and give poor for heavenly treasure
row.note: Jesus tells a wealthy man to sell his possessions and give to the poor to have treasure in heaven; another person's need converts current capital into enduring value.

row.basis: Salvation described as grace through faith
row.note: The letter says salvation comes by grace through faith as God's gift; it puts a gift frame beside the commentary's wage frame for believing.

row.basis: Not from works, so no boasting
row.note: The writer explicitly excludes works as the source of salvation; this differs from any reading of the commentary's good-work wage as earned entitlement.

row.basis: Good works still prepared for believers
row.note: The saved are described as created for good works in which to walk; it qualifies the previous gift language with a continuing place for intentional deeds.
James says Abraham's faith was active with his works and brought to completion through them; it develops the conjunction of believing and acting beyond the bare formula.
James concludes that a person is justified by works and not faith alone; it places the commentary's joined belief and work within a specific interpretive dispute.

row.basis: Sparing or generous sowing and reaping
row.note: The measure of what one sows determines the harvest in Paul's appeal for a collection; charity is treated as an investment whose return follows its measure.
Paul says current abundance should supply others' lack and later the relationship may reverse, creating equality; the commentary's mutual rights are an exchange across time.
Paul asks what his wage is and answers that he preaches without charge rather than using his right in the gospel; refusing immediate pay itself becomes his chosen return.
The speaker says he searches minds and hearts and will give each according to works; intentional acts and the final payout are assessed together.
The one who conquers and keeps the speaker's works until the end receives authority; the reward requires continuing good action across the remaining time.
The scorching sun withers a flower, and the rich person similarly fades while pursuing business; time erodes both the trader and the expected gain.

row.basis: Unknown day and hour require watch
row.note: The parable closes by telling hearers to watch because the day and hour are unknown; the closed door has an unknowable rather than negotiable deadline.
The teaching asks believers who share in immortal things to share even more in mortal goods and not claim these as solely their own; the commentary's passing capital carries a mutual obligation.

row.note: The endangered person in the commentary clings to a refuge; here the righteous run into the LORD's name and are set safely beyond reach, making safety a destination.
The commentary locates a refuge before human loss; this communal confession calls God an available refuge and strength precisely in trouble.
The commentary joins shelter to faith as security from fear; the psalmist names God both fortress and the one in whom he trusts.
The commentary joins protective armor to truth that must be guarded; this verse makes divine faithfulness a shield under sheltering wings.
The commentary moves from refuge to holding to truth; the speaker calls God hiding place and shield while hoping in God's word.
The commentary associates safety with a secure city; this song pictures salvation itself as that city's walls and ramparts.
The commentary connects entering safety with faith and right conduct; this verse opens the protected city's gates to a righteous nation that keeps faithfulness.
The commentary calls faith an entry into security against fear; this verse says the trusting mind is kept in peace.
The commentary's safe home stands against inescapable calamity; God here tells his people to enter their rooms and close the doors until wrath passes.
The commentary makes a dwelling the place of security; Israel must remain inside its marked houses through the dangerous night.
The commentary's refuge saves from destruction; here the LORD bars the destroyer from entering the blood-marked home.
The commentary links a cordlike hold, safe house, and ancestral shelter; Rahab must display a scarlet cord and gather her parents, brothers, and household inside.
The commentary imagines an exception from destruction as arrival in safety; Rahab's rescuers make the house boundary decisive for her relatives' survival.
The commentary's asylum scene involves shelter for a person in immediate danger; the law establishes a city of refuge where a killer escapes the avenger pending judgment.
The commentary's communal guarantor stands with the endangered; the congregation rescues the killer from the avenger and returns him to his refuge city.
The commentary makes loss of shelter perilous; this verse specifies the killer's departure beyond the refuge city's boundary.
The commentary opposes fear with faith and protection; God tells the endangered, childless Abram not to fear because God is his shield.

row.basis: אמנ / ء م ن; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary calls believers people entering security; Abram believes God's promise of descendants, and the Hebrew אמנ root makes trust the response to a threatened lineage.

row.basis: אמנ / ء م ن; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary connects faith with standing safe under threat; amid a threatened kingdom the Hebrew verse plays on trusting and being established with forms of אמנ.

row.basis: אמונה / ء م ن; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary places believers outside the general loss; the righteous one lives by faithfulness amid the vision of judgment, a specific survival claim using אמנ.

row.basis: אמנ / ء م ن; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary makes faith the answer to peril; this verse says Israel did not believe God or trust his salvation despite wilderness provision.

row.basis: חסר / خ س ر; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary describes human loss as ruin; the shepherd's speaker says he lacks nothing, a Hebrew חסר counterimage of safety under care rather than identical Arabic meaning.
The commentary pairs danger with graspable protection and freedom from fear; the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the speaker through the death-dark valley.
The commentary calls a safe home the place to which one comes; the shepherd's speaker expects to dwell in the LORD's house after danger.
The commentary names refuge as the endangered person's destination; the psalmist expects God to hide him in a shelter on the day of trouble.
The commentary considers ancestry a refuge; this verse tests that refuge by saying even if parents abandon the speaker, the LORD receives him.
The commentary's clinging person needs support against destruction; Israel's blessing puts everlasting arms underneath and calls God its dwelling refuge.
The commentary connects communal safety and armor; this blessing calls Israel a people saved by the LORD, its helping shield.
The commentary invokes the Qur'anic son who trusts a mountain and is lost; Genesis instead has Noah's sons enter the flood shelter with him.
The commentary's false mountain fails to save Noah's son; Genesis describes Noah and those with him in the ark as the survivors, making the family outcome different.
The commentary quotes the son's claim that a mountain will protect him from water; Genesis makes mountains the ark's eventual landing place, after the vessel has preserved its occupants.
The commentary describes a refuge that truly protects from water; the LORD himself shuts Noah inside the ark as the flood begins.
The commentary combines asylum and family as a root of safety; God calls Noah and all his household into the ark before judgment.
The commentary contrasts real asylum with a false mountain or spider shelter; God asks where the gods are whom Israel treated as its rock.
The commentary says a refuge can prove unable to save; this taunt challenges the rival gods to rise and become a shelter to their worshippers.
The commentary contrasts true security and false shelter; Jerusalem's leaders claim a pact with death and explicitly make lies their refuge against an overwhelming scourge.

row.basis: false refuge swept by hail and water
row.note: The commentary puts truth beside a shelter endangered by destruction; divine justice here sweeps away the refuge of lies and floods its hiding place.
The commentary's right hold rescues at the brink; God lays a firm stone in Zion, and the one who trusts it need not panic in the announced disaster.
The commentary warns that a shelter may be false; immediately beside the LORD's strong tower, this proverb calls wealth a high wall only in its owner's imagination.
The commentary's person faces a calamity with no escape and can choose a false shelter; Amos pictures someone fleeing predators into a house only to be bitten there.
The commentary distinguishes a reliable asylum from wrong protection; Judah seeks Pharaoh's shelter and Egypt's shade without consulting God.
The commentary pairs faith with entry into safety; God offers salvation in returning and rest, strength in quiet trust, but the addressees refuse.
The commentary joins lineage as a refuge with the danger of false shelter; Jeremiah calls the LORD his refuge in distress while nations confess inherited lies.
The commentary links a safe city and protective presence; God hovers over Jerusalem, protects it, and delivers it.
The commentary's secure city holds a threatened community; in Hebrew Joel numbering the LORD roars from Zion amid cosmic shaking yet is refuge for his people.
The commentary's mountain is an unsafe alternative to real asylum; this psalm says people sheltered in God need not fear even when mountains collapse into the sea.
The commentary invokes a secure city; this psalm locates the city's stability in God's presence within it during surrounding upheaval.
The commentary contrasts the right hold with false protection; some trust military equipment, while the community invokes the LORD's name.

row.basis: horse as false hope of escape

row.note: The commentary makes loss a market account and names underweighing; Hosea condemns a merchant who keeps deceitful scales and loves to oppress. It joins commercial fraud to character.

Where the commentary contrasts a short measure with a full one, Leviticus specifies the correct balance and standard measures. The detail grounds just trade in a public rule.
The commentary's underweight scale is condemned directly: Proverbs calls a false balance an abomination and contrasts it with a full weight. The text adds the moral status of the market device.

The commentary treats work as labor that earns a right; Deuteronomy forbids oppressing a needy hired worker, whether Israelite or resident foreigner. It extends wage justice beyond one's own kin.

The commentary's day laborer reaches the wage deadline at day's end; Deuteronomy requires payment before sunset because the worker depends on it, and says the worker may cry to God. It makes delay a matter of life and justice.

The commentary presents wage as a worker's due; Jacob tells his household that Laban deceived him and repeatedly changed his wages. The narrative gives a concrete case of an employer manipulating the account.

The commentary says the worker's wage is due; Jeremiah condemns a ruler who builds by making his neighbor work without pay. The unpaid labor is framed as injustice in the ruler's household and public power.

The commentary pictures the day laborer reaching the end of work and awaiting pay; Job compares human life to a hired worker longing for shade and waiting for wages. The image makes mortality itself feel like exhausting labor.

row.basis: wages in a purse with holes
row.note: The commentary describes principal steadily dwindling; Haggai pictures people earning wages only to put them into a pierced purse, alongside meager harvest and food. It turns economic loss into the felt result of wasted labor.

row.basis: gain from toil under the sun
row.note: The commentary makes time the capital spent in work; Ecclesiastes asks what a person gains from all toil and anxious effort under the sun. The question sharpens the uncertainty of labor's return.

The commentary says the market will close and the worker's day will end; Ecclesiastes urges doing with might what one's hand finds, because there is no work in Sheol. It makes finite time the condition for action.

The commentary warns that capital can be spent without profit; Isaiah asks why people spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy. The prophet turns failed exchange into a summons to seek what truly nourishes.

The commentary describes a trade that eats away at principal; Proverbs contrasts wealth that dwindles with wealth gathered little by little. It adds a scriptural contrast between erosion and patient accumulation.

The commentary makes each passing moment part of the capital being spent; Proverbs warns against boasting about tomorrow because one does not know what a day will bring. It grounds the deadline in uncertainty.

The commentary says people counsel one another to the truth and to each person's right; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and judge truthfully at the gates. It gives mutual truth-telling a civic setting.

The commentary's reciprocal counsel implies speaking when another is wrong; Leviticus commands rebuking a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin. It makes moral correction part of mutual responsibility.

The commentary calls haqq a person's due share; Deuteronomy requires a forgotten sheaf to remain for the foreigner, orphan, and widow. It makes the vulnerable person's claim visible in ordinary harvest work.

row.basis: do not muzzle the threshing ox
row.note: The commentary includes work done by hands and the wage due for labor; Deuteronomy forbids muzzling an ox while it threshes. The law recognizes a worker's right to benefit while producing.

row.basis: short day, abundant work, great reward
row.note: The commentary's human life is capital spent in work and paid at day's end; Rabbi Tarfon says the day is short, the work abundant, and the reward great. The saying compresses the commentary's time-and-wage image into one maxim.

The commentary imagines time as capital and a final account; Avot depicts the world as an open shop with credit, a ledger, and collectors making daily rounds. It turns daily life into a debt that will be collected.

row.basis: one hour for deeds in this world
row.note: The commentary insists that work must be done before the market closes; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world outweighs the whole life of the world to come. It makes present time the irreplaceable arena of action.

The commentary treats a laborer's wage as a right; in this story an employer takes porters' cloaks after they break barrels, and Rav orders him to return the cloaks and pay them. The case gives worker rights priority over the employer's loss.

The commentary ends with a person asking for a little more time to give and do right; Sirach warns not to delay turning to the Lord, since judgment can come suddenly. It makes postponement itself a danger.

row.basis: wealth cannot secure one's remaining time
row.note: The commentary rejects the belief that amassed wealth can outlast time; Sirach describes a rich person who plans to enjoy his goods but does not know how soon he will die and leave them. It directly joins capital to a life one cannot extend.
The commentary pictures righteous workers receiving their wage; Wisdom says the righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord. It gives the wage image an explicitly enduring outcome.

The commentary names al-ʿaṣr as the afternoon prayer; Acts says Peter and John went to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. The shared practice is an afternoon prayer rhythm, not an identical named rite.

The commentary sets the day worker's labor against the day's end; Jesus says his work must be done while it is day, since night is coming when no one can work. The saying makes the workday a figure for a closing opportunity.

The commentary's day laborer reaches the wage deadline at the day's end; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner orders the workers called and paid when evening comes. The scene directly joins a day's labor to its wage.

The commentary treats wages as the worker's due; Jesus tells the traveling disciples that the laborer deserves his wages while they stay in a household. It applies the wage-right formula to religious workers.

The commentary makes business an account whose capital can be lost; the rich man in Jesus' parable demands an account from a steward accused of squandering his property. It makes stewardship answerable before the owner.

The commentary glosses trust as the opposite of betrayal; Jesus says faithfulness in little predicts faithfulness in much, and dishonesty in little predicts dishonesty in much. The next verse applies this to money, making trust a test of stewardship.

row.basis: settling accounts after a long time
row.note: The commentary says capital is spent as time passes; in the talents parable the master returns after a long time and settles accounts with the servants entrusted with money. It links investment, delay, and reckoning.

The commentary makes the market open only for a limited time; the nobleman tells servants to conduct business with the entrusted money until he returns. The parable makes the interval before return a period of accountable investment.

The commentary imagines an account closing after a period of work; on returning, the nobleman summons the servants to learn what each gained in trade. The scene makes the yield of entrusted capital reviewable.

row.basis: treasure consumed by moth and rust
row.note: The commentary warns that what one owns is used up; Jesus says earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth, rust, and thieves. It supplies a concrete image of stored capital that cannot be secured.
Against the commentary's eroding principal, Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy. It redirects investment toward a durable return.

row.basis: rich man expects many years of ease
row.note: The commentary rejects the idea that wealth makes a person outlive time; the rich fool tells his soul to rest because he has goods stored for many years. The speech exposes the assumed conversion of capital into extra life.
The commentary says a market will close and a person may then ask for more time; God tells the rich fool his life is required that very night. It makes the deadline sudden and non-negotiable.

The commentary treats lifetime as capital spent in exchange; James addresses people planning to travel, trade, and make a profit for a year. The passage puts the trader's plan inside an uncertain lifespan.
The commentary says the human being remains inside loss as time passes; James calls life a mist that appears briefly and vanishes. It gives the dwindling capital of time an explicit image.

row.basis: now is the day of salvation
row.note: The commentary warns that the final day has no market or chance to transact; Paul quotes Isaiah to say now is the acceptable time and now the day of salvation. It makes the present the open window for action.
The commentary links work to the wage due; Paul says the planter and waterer are one and each will receive a wage according to labor. It directly connects effort to compensation.

row.basis: Paul's reading of the unmuzzled ox
row.note: The commentary says the worker has a right to the wage of the work; Paul reads Deuteronomy's rule against muzzling a threshing ox as written for human workers, so the plowman and thresher may share in the crop. This Christian interpretation extends the law's protection to laborers.

The commentary says the wage is owed when work is done; in instructions about elders, Paul cites the saying that the worker deserves his wages. It applies the laborer's due to support for community leaders.
The commentary makes wage a due share; James says the wages withheld from field workers cry out and have reached the Lord of hosts. It links labor injustice to divine hearing.
The commentary names belief and righteous deeds together; James says faith without works is dead. The passage makes action integral to a living faith, rather than a separate supplement.

row.basis: work of faith, labor of love, endurance of hope
row.note: The commentary's exception combines belief, righteous work, and patient endurance; Paul recalls the Thessalonians' work of faith, labor of love, and steadfastness of hope. The triad closely joins the same kinds of action.

The commentary says people urge one another toward what is right and toward patience; Paul tells the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all. It supplies concrete forms of reciprocal counsel.

row.basis: stir one another to love and good works
row.note: The commentary makes mutual urging toward truth and patience part of the exception; Hebrews tells hearers to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works. It gives mutual exhortation an explicitly ethical aim.

row.basis: encourage one another as the Day approaches
row.note: The commentary says the market closes on a coming day; Hebrews commands mutual encouragement all the more as the Day draws near. The approaching deadline intensifies communal action.
The commentary joins patient endurance to a wage still to be received; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will to receive the promise. It makes waiting part of completed work.

The commentary's patient worker receives a wage after labor; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good, for a harvest will come in due season if one does not give up. It joins patient action to delayed return.

The commentary calls haqq each person's share and mutual recognition of another's due; Paul says one community's abundance should supply another's need so there may be equality. It turns right share into reciprocal material care.

row.basis: reward according to each person's work
row.note: The commentary presents a wage arriving after a period of labor; the returning Christ says he brings recompense to repay each according to work. It makes the final wage explicit.

The commentary couples labor with patience and a later wage; Paul urges steadfast, abundant work, saying labor in the Lord is not in vain. It assures the worker that present effort has a future result.

The commentary includes manual labor and the wage earned by it; Paul tells the church that one unwilling to work should not eat. It expresses work as a condition of ordinary sustenance, though its context concerns idle members.
The commentary's lexical branch calls sabīr a guarantor standing behind a debt; Proverbs addresses someone who has become surety for a neighbor. It shows the personal risk carried by a guarantor.

row.basis: profit of the world, loss of the self
row.note: The commentary says the ultimate loss is the person and family; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life. The saying puts market gain directly against losing the self.

row.basis: merchant buys the pearl of great value
row.note: The commentary presents faith and righteous action as a better trade; Jesus' merchant sells all he has to buy one pearl of great value. The parable gives costly exchange a positive, kingdom-directed outcome.

The commentary says God buys the believers' selves and promises a return; Paul says the community was bought at a price and therefore should glorify God in the body. The purchase image makes belonging entail action.

row.basis: people purchased for God by blood
row.note: The commentary pictures God as buyer of believers' lives; the heavenly song says the slain one purchased people for God by his blood. The image parallels redemption as costly acquisition while naming a different purchaser's price.

row.basis: ransom not paid in silver or gold
row.note: The commentary's divine purchase turns a person's life into capital; Peter says believers were ransomed from inherited futile conduct not with perishable silver or gold. It keeps the purchase image while changing both price and emphasis.
The commentary makes patience the condition of receiving a later wage; James compares patient endurance to a farmer waiting for the precious crop. It gives patience a concrete work-and-harvest scene.

row.basis: patience because the Lord's coming is near
row.note: The commentary urges mutual patience as the end approaches; James tells hearers to be patient and establish their hearts because the Lord's coming is near. It binds endurance to a closing time.
The commentary pairs belief with patience and a future wage; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit promises through faith and patience. It makes endurance part of receiving what is promised.

row.basis: another person stands behind a debt
row.note: The commentary's lexical branch calls sabīr a guarantor; Paul tells Philemon to charge any debt or wrong by Onesimus to Paul's own account. It gives the guarantor image a concrete personal act of bearing another's liability.

The commentary's exception requires belief expressed through righteous deeds; Avot says action is the essential thing, not study alone. It gives Jewish ethical weight to the move from conviction to practice.

row.basis: what profit came from wealth and boasting
row.note: The commentary calls loss a failed account; at judgment Wisdom has the wicked ask what profit their wealth and boasting brought. It turns the market's profit question into a final moral reckoning.

The commentary presents work as earning a due wage, while also saying the patient receive reward beyond calculation; the vineyard owner gives the same denarius for one hour and a full day and defends his generosity. The parable presses gift beyond proportional labor.

The commentary asks whether capital is spent on a durable return; Jesus tells disciples to use worldly wealth in a way that may welcome them into eternal dwellings. The link is a deliberate investment whose payoff exceeds the market.

row.basis: wage counted as debt, not gift
row.note: The commentary says a worker's wage is due and uses the language of a right; Paul says a worker's wage is reckoned as debt rather than grace. His argument about justification makes the earned-wage analogy precise while distinguishing it from a gift.

The commentary makes belief a condition for escaping loss; Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous one living by faith in his account of the gospel's revealed righteousness. This Christian reading shifts the verse toward faith in the gospel from Habakkuk's faithful endurance under threat.

row.basis: workers protest equal pay for unequal hours
row.note: The commentary speaks of the due wage for labor; the first-hired workers protest that the one-hour workers were made equal to them after they bore the day's heat. The complaint exposes the tension between measured effort and equal payment.

row.basis: rich toward God rather than stored wealth
row.note: The commentary says amassed property cannot make its owner outlive time; Jesus concludes that the person who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God is a fool. It gives the alternative to temporal accumulation.

The commentary says the final day has no market in which to act or settle accounts; in the rich man and Lazarus story a fixed gulf prevents passage after death. It pictures the irreversibility of the closed opportunity.

The commentary distinguishes a losing trade from the profitable exchange of faith and deeds; Paul says what had been gain he now counts as loss because of Christ. The passage reverses the account's valuation, making apparent profit a loss.

row.basis: selling grain refuse as good grain
row.note: The commentary describes a market where the scale makes a short measure; Amos's sellers wait to sell even the refuse of grain. This adds deception about quality to the commentary's image of deception by weight.

row.basis: Arabic root ع م ل; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew עמל
row.note: The commentary labels ʿamal as intentional work, manual labor, and its wage; Ecclesiastes uses עמל for toil and asks its gain. The shared labor term links work to uncertain return, though the table does not verify cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
row.note: The commentary labels belief with the root ء م ن; Genesis says Abram trusted God and it was counted as righteousness. The Hebrew usage adds trust in a promise to the commentary's faith-and-action condition; cognacy remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
row.note: The commentary makes belief one condition for escaping loss; Habakkuk says the righteous live by faithfulness (emunah) amid arrogant violence. The Hebrew context adds steadfast fidelity to belief; the table's correspondence is unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew/Aramaic אמנ
row.note: The commentary glosses amānah as trust opposed to betrayal; at judgment the Talmud asks whether a person conducted business faithfully. This joins trust to commerce in the same concrete setting, though cognacy is unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר
row.note: The commentary's source lexical branch calls صبرة a heap sold without measure; Genesis uses צבר for Joseph's grain piled like sea sand beyond counting. The same heap image supports a possible cognate, but the Hebrew describes storage, not an unmeasured sale.

row.basis: Arabic root خ س ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חסר
row.note: The commentary labels loss by خ س ر, including a deficit; Proverbs says the wicked person's belly lacks, using חסר. The specific lack-image fits, but the package offers only an unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: Arabic root ص ل ح; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צלח
row.note: The commentary labels righteous deeds صالحات; Joshua uses צלח for prospering through attention to Torah. The sound and success-related usage may illuminate the label, but the meanings differ and cognacy is unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ح ق ق; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חקק
row.note: The commentary glosses haqq as a person's right or share; Proverbs calls daily bread the speaker's prescribed portion (חֹק). The shared allotment sense is specific, but the root connection remains unverified.

row.basis: just balances belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary treats a short measure as a concrete market loss; Proverbs says just balances and weights belong to the Lord. This adds divine ownership to the duty of accurate trade.

row.basis: God weighs the speaker in just scales
row.note: The commentary joins deficient scales to a final account; Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity. The verse brings commercial measurement into divine judgment.

row.basis: wealth lost in a bad venture
row.note: The commentary describes trade consuming its principal; Ecclesiastes says wealth can be lost in a bad venture, leaving a father with nothing to pass on. It gives the loss of capital a concrete household consequence.

The commentary says accumulated wealth cannot outlast a person's time; Ecclesiastes says a person leaves as naked as at birth and takes nothing from toil. It makes the final loss bodily and irreversible.

The commentary rejects the belief that wealth can secure a person's future; Proverbs says wealth can suddenly make wings and fly away. It adds an image of capital disappearing beyond its owner's control.

row.basis: riches fail on the day of wrath
row.note: The commentary contrasts a losing trade with the righteous path; Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. It directly contrasts wealth with the return of right conduct.

row.basis: remember the creator before difficult days
row.note: The commentary says a late plea for more time comes after the market has closed; Ecclesiastes urges remembering the creator in youth before the difficult days arrive. It makes the timing of good action urgent.

row.basis: faithfulness with money and true riches
row.note: The commentary sets trust against betrayal in a commercial setting; Jesus says that failure to be faithful with unrighteous wealth means no one will entrust true riches. It makes money management a test of trustworthiness.

row.basis: God and wealth as rival masters
row.note: The commentary frames the righteous trade as choosing the lasting good over a losing exchange; Jesus says a person cannot serve both God and mammon. It makes wealth a question of allegiance, not merely its amount.

row.basis: money placed with bankers for interest
row.note: The commentary describes capital invested for gain; in the talents parable the master says the servant should have placed the money with bankers so it could return with interest. It makes the expected return explicit.

The commentary connects faithful work to a wage; the master praises a servant faithful over a little, entrusts him with much, and invites him into joy. It adds increased responsibility as the reward for stewardship.

row.basis: agreed denarius as a worker's due
row.note: The commentary says a wage is an obligation once due; the vineyard owner answers a complaint by pointing to the agreed denarius. This gives the parable's wage a contractual basis alongside its generosity to later workers.

row.basis: faithful through death, crowned with life
row.note: The commentary couples patience with a wage at the end of the worker's time; Revelation tells Smyrna to remain faithful even to death and promises the crown of life. It makes endurance under threat part of the reward image.

row.basis: selling goods to give alms and store unfailing treasure
row.note: The commentary presents a trade whose return does not fail and recalls a plea for time to give charity; Jesus tells hearers to sell possessions, give to the poor, and provide an unfailing heavenly treasure. It makes generosity a deliberate transfer from perishable wealth.

row.basis: lending to the Lord by helping the poor
row.note: The commentary says God is the buyer and guarantor of a promised return; Proverbs says whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the giver. It casts care for the poor as a loan whose return comes from God.

The commentary links righteous deeds to a later wage; Jesus says a host who invites the poor, disabled, lame, and blind will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous. It specifies generosity that cannot be repaid in the present market.

row.basis: service to the least counted as service to the king
row.note: The commentary says mutual counsel must recognize another person's due; in the judgment scene the king identifies care for the least of his siblings as care for himself. It gives acts of service a direct relation to the final judge.

row.basis: alms stored as treasure for a future day
row.note: The commentary contrasts wealth that perishes with a trade that does not fail; Tobit says alms lay up a good treasure for the day of need. It makes generosity a future-oriented deposit.

row.basis: others receive the wealth the hoarder prepared
row.note: The commentary says wealth cannot outlast its owner; Job says the righteous will wear the garments the wicked prepared and the innocent will divide the silver. This neighboring verse makes the transfer of accumulated wealth explicit.

row.basis: God rewards those who seek him
row.note: The commentary makes belief one condition of escaping loss and describes a later wage; Hebrews says faith is necessary to approach God and that God rewards those who seek him. It joins faith to expected recompense.

row.basis: fixed times for Torah study at judgment
row.note: The commentary treats a person's time as capital that must be spent before the account closes; Shabbat 31a asks at judgment whether one fixed times for Torah study. This adds deliberate use of time to the passage's separate question about honest business.

row.basis: shared support keeps hands steady until sunset
row.note: The commentary joins mutual urging to patience with the end of the workday; Aaron and Hur support Moses' hands until sunset so they remain steady. The scene adds physical, shared endurance through the day's limit.

row.basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
row.note: The commentary glosses amānah as trust opposed to betrayal; Deuteronomy calls God faithful and without injustice. This Hebrew use joins fidelity to justice, though the root correspondence remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root خ س ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חסר
row.note: The commentary defines loss through diminution and deficiency; Deuteronomy commands opening a hand to a poor person for whatever he lacks (חסר). It connects lack to a neighbor's material need, though cognacy is unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר
row.note: The commentary's Arabic lexical branch calls a ṣubrah a heap sold without weighing; the psalm uses צבר for heaping up wealth and says the person does not know who will gather it. The heap becomes a warning about wealth outliving its owner; cognacy is unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר
row.note: The commentary's lexical branch connects ṣubrah with a heap; Job says the wicked may heap up silver like dust. The shared heap image is specific, while the sound correspondence remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ
row.note: The commentary's Arabic lexical gloss associates amānah with trust and firmness; Exodus describes Moses' hands as steady (emunah) until sunset. The Hebrew usage gives the root a bodily sense of sustained firmness, but the sound correspondence is unverified.
