row.basis: Abraham commands children to do justice
row.note: The commentary presents advice as a transmitted task to perform; Abraham is chosen to command his household after him to keep the LORD's way by doing righteousness and justice.
The commentary calls a will a word joined to the next generation; Israel is told to impress the words on children and speak them at home and on the road.

row.basis: children yet unborn learn and tell
row.note: The commentary's linked speech reaches beyond the speaker's life; the psalm intends the next generation, even unborn children, to learn and tell its children.
The commentary invokes Jacob's deathbed charge as a binding word left behind; Jacob commands his sons to bury him with his ancestors.
The commentary's inherited counsel attaches later generations to a duty; Joseph makes Israel's sons swear to carry his bones when God visits them.
The commentary recalls the brothers' false report and Jacob's withheld trust; Genesis likewise has the brothers dip Joseph's tunic in goat's blood as fabricated evidence.

The commentary explores giving or withholding belief from family testimony; Genesis later says Jacob's heart goes numb and he does not believe the brothers' news that Joseph lives.
The commentary develops sabır as a guarantor who bears another's obligation; Judah makes himself surety for Benjamin and accepts lifelong blame if he fails to return him.

row.basis: Judah offers himself in place of Benjamin
row.note: The commentary pictures community members holding another when he cannot bear the debt; Judah asks to remain as slave instead of Benjamin.
The commentary distinguishes a rightful load from crushing overload; Moses is instructed to appoint others to judge ordinary cases so they carry the burden with him.
The commentary's reciprocal patience shares what one cannot carry alone; God puts the spirit on elders so they bear the people with Moses.
The commentary's day closes with earned wages due; Deuteronomy requires a poor hired worker's wages on that day before the sun sets.
The commentary gives hak the sense of a payable share; Proverbs forbids withholding good from its rightful recipient when one can give it.

row.basis: reprove neighbor rather than bear sin
row.note: The commentary makes truth a word responsibly handed to another; Leviticus requires open reproof of a neighbor instead of silently sharing the neighbor's sin.

row.basis: speak truth and judge for peace
row.note: The commentary moves hak from litigation into communal counsel; Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and judges to make truthful judgments that yield peace.
The commentary distinguishes solitary belief from reciprocal speech; those fearing the LORD speak with one another, and a record is written before God for them.
The commentary's joined pasture lets one person feed another and tests goodness in practice; Isaiah's chosen fast requires sharing bread and bringing the homeless into one's house.
The commentary's rain-fed joined growth represents lives that sustain one another; after acts of justice, the LORD promises to guide and make the people like an unfailing watered garden.
The commentary's cloud must nourish connected vegetation; the person who boasts of a gift never given is likened to wind and clouds without rain.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence

The commentary's inherited advice should become a walked path; the elder rejoices that some of the addressee's children are walking in truth as commanded by the Father.

row.basis: love one another as inherited command
row.note: The commentary's will is a binding word passed onward; the elder asks the addressee to love one another, calling it a command held from the beginning.
The commentary says a recommended truth must be worked into conduct; the letter defines love by walking according to the commandments already heard.
The commentary's sound work does not disappear when the day's capital runs out; Hebrews says God will not overlook the work and love shown through service to fellow believers.
The commentary grounds endurance in a due promise; Hebrews tells the community to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience.

row.basis: flee to refuge and hold hope
row.note: The commentary hears both safety and active holding in iman and sabır; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge and grasp the hope set before them.
The commentary's vessel stopper and firm rock picture an inner good held against a storm; Hebrews calls hope a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul.
The commentary's reliable road and intentional work require persistence; Hebrews calls believers to lay aside encumbrance and run their appointed race with endurance.

row.basis: Jesus endures cross for future joy
row.note: The commentary says a trustworthy outcome makes painful patience meaningful; Hebrews presents Jesus enduring the cross for the joy set before him.
The commentary gives true counsel and patience their own places; Paul orders preaching, reproof, rebuke, and exhortation with all patience and teaching.
The commentary's believer pursues sound conduct and patience together; Paul commands pursuit of righteousness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness.
The commentary distinguishes believing from holding another through hardship; Titus is to teach older men to be sound in faith, love, and endurance.
The commentary binds taking refuge in trust to active good work under suffering; Peter tells those suffering according to God's will to entrust their souls to a faithful creator while doing good.

row.basis: do good and endure unjust suffering
row.note: The commentary's patient truth costs its speaker something; Peter says enduring suffering incurred for doing good is pleasing to God.
The commentary opposes quarrelling over truth to giving truthful counsel; Peter commands a ready account of hope to questioners, delivered with gentleness and respect.

row.basis: walk worthily and bear fruit in good work
row.note: The commentary joins road, useful vegetation, and sound action; Paul prays that believers walk worthy of the Lord while bearing fruit in every good work.
The commentary says the group must hold its place under pressure; Paul asks that believers receive power for all endurance and patience with joy.

row.basis: hope, endurance in trouble, steady prayer
row.note: The commentary's patient waiting is active and grounded in a promised good; Paul calls believers to rejoice in hope, endure affliction, and persevere in prayer.
The commentary's final day gives every person the due of their work; Paul states that God will repay each person according to works.

row.basis: all appear for deeds to be recompensed
row.note: The commentary's Hāqqa confronts each worker with what was done; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due for bodily deeds, good or bad.
The commentary specifically meets vegetation with intentional construction; Paul calls the community God's field and God's building in a single verse.

row.basis: work survives and worker receives wage
row.note: The commentary measures the soundness of a worker's deed by whether it lasts through the final day; Paul says the builder whose work survives the fire receives a reward.
The commentary relates escape from loss to good work that remains; Paul allows a different outcome in which a person's work burns and brings loss while the person is saved through fire.
The commentary's securely fitted work is proved by pressure rather than appearance; Jesus' rock-founded house survives rain, floods, and winds because its foundation holds.
The commentary's joined green growth needs patient holding after belief; Jesus says the rocky-ground hearers believe for a while but fall away in a time of testing because they lack root.
The commentary turns disputed hak into counsel that repairs and yields sound deeds; James calls heavenly wisdom peaceable, gentle, merciful, and full of good fruits.
The commentary's linked vegetation and reconciliation are carried by patience; James says a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those making peace.
The commentary says speaking truth may bring the hardship for which patient support is needed; James offers the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.
The commentary's reciprocal true advice reconnects a person who has broken from the path; James tells the community that someone can bring back a member wandering from the truth.
The commentary's saving exception is sustained by one person's intervention for another; James says turning a sinner from wandering saves a soul from death and covers sins.
The commentary's sabır must hold through the whole threatened period; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The commentary orders faith, sound obedience, and patience as traits of those rescued; Revelation calls for the saints' endurance, identifying them as command-keepers who hold faith in Jesus.
The commentary's threatened believers ask for patience up to death; the risen speaker tells the persecuted assembly to be faithful unto death and promises the crown of life.
The commentary makes inherited teaching and communal belonging mutually necessary; the first believers devote themselves to apostolic teaching and fellowship, shared meals, and prayer.
The commentary's right includes a share owed to someone lacking support; the believers distribute sale proceeds according to each person's need.

The commentary's individual believers become a connected group in which each can sustain another; Acts describes the multitude of believers as one heart and soul and not claiming possessions as purely private.
The commentary's joined pasture leaves no hungry gap between members; Acts says none of the believers was needy because owners sold property for distribution.

row.basis: do good and lend even to enemies
row.note: The commentary's hak includes a debt owed and sabır that can transform an enemy; Jesus commands doing good and lending without expecting return to enemies, and promises a great reward.

row.basis: bless, pray, and fast for persecutors
row.note: The commentary's patient answer turns hostility into a healing bond and includes fasting as restraint; the Didache urges blessing cursers, praying for enemies, and fasting for persecutors.

row.basis: strong support weak; rich help poor
row.note: The commentary's community takes another's weight when that person cannot stand; Clement says the strong should care for the weak and the rich provide for the poor.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's advice links generations to something enduring; the psalm joins God's faithfulness, אמונה, through all generations to the firm establishment of the earth.

row.basis: Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary combines trust and a walked right path; the psalmist chooses the way of faithfulness, אמונה, and sets God's judgments before himself.
The commentary contrasts capital that shrinks with good action that lasts; the righteous person distributes to the poor and his righteousness endures forever.
The commentary defines patience as keeping still without losing confidence; Isaiah says salvation lies in returning and rest, strength in quietness and trust, while the addressees refuse.

row.basis: right instruction in heart without fear
row.note: The commentary makes belief a refuge for bearers of true speech; God addresses people with his law in their hearts and tells them not to fear human reproach.
The commentary makes advice an act owed to another, not control over their response; the watchman who warns the wicked has saved his own life even if the wicked refuses to turn.

The commentary says completed actions characterize those excepted from loss; Ezekiel insists that someone once righteous can turn to injustice and die in it, preserving moral reversal beyond a fixed label.
The commentary connects paying another's due to an unmeasured return; Moses says to give a poor brother generously and without a begrudging heart, promising blessing in the giver's work.
The commentary's sabır can mean standing guarantor for another's debt; Proverbs warns that pledging oneself for a stranger brings suffering, providing a limit to that secondary image.
The commentary defines patience as restraining the inner cry under an inescapable blow; Job rebukes his wife for accepting good but rejecting adversity from God and does not sin with his lips.

row.basis: wait quietly for the day of trouble
row.note: The commentary's patience remains still before a promised day even with bodily alarm; Habakkuk trembles at the vision yet resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress.
The commentary's dependable load animal and mountain stand for not stumbling under pressure; Habakkuk calls God his strength and says he makes his feet like a deer's on the heights.
The commentary joins iman to a road that can be walked patiently; Sirach directs the son to trust God for help and make his ways straight.

row.basis: guarantor gives his life for another
row.note: The commentary develops sabır as a friend who underwrites someone else's debt; Sirach tells the debtor not to forget the guarantor's kindness because that person has put life at risk for him.
The commentary says belief and work can be individual but saving advice must pass between people; Hillel asks what a person is if only for himself.

row.basis: world stands on teaching and kindness
row.note: The commentary's sound community combines a true word with useful action; the mishnah names Torah, worship, and acts of lovingkindness as supports on which the world stands.

row.basis: legal right alone does not repair society
row.note: The commentary moves hak from winning a dispute toward mutually owed care; the Talmud says Jerusalem's downfall was connected to judging by strict law without going beyond its letter.
The commentary says speaking right may bring hostile blows and demand patience; the opponents in Wisdom propose insult and torture to test the righteous person's gentleness and endurance.
The commentary's bitter medicine and earned due meet in suffering that proves worth; Wisdom says the righteous, disciplined for a little while, receive great good after God tests them.
The commentary moves from believing to work of a specified quality; Peter asks believers to supplement faith with virtue rather than leave faith unworked.
The commentary defines sabır as first holding oneself, then remaining in place; Peter's sequence moves from knowledge to self-control and from self-control to endurance.
The commentary's self-restraint becomes a bond with the next person; Peter's sequence leads from endurance to godliness, sibling affection, and love.
The commentary's patient person remains held under a blow; Paul describes believers as persecuted yet not abandoned and struck down yet not destroyed.
The commentary joins the passing day with an inner good kept from loss; Paul says that even as the outer person wastes away the inner person is renewed day by day.

row.basis: brief suffering and weight of glory
row.note: The commentary's right load, labor, and reward meet in a paradox; Paul says momentary affliction prepares an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison.
The commentary contrasts passing worldly capital with something that remains; Paul directs attention from seen temporary things to unseen eternal ones.
The commentary says patient action must hold to the end of the day; Hebrews asks each hearer to show the same diligence for full assurance of hope until the end.

row.basis: faith as assurance of hoped reality
row.note: The commentary hears trust in the truth of a promise before it arrives; Hebrews defines faith by confidence concerning what is hoped for and conviction about what is not seen.
The commentary binds an advised truth to practiced action and endurance; Paul reminds Timothy that he observed Paul's teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, and steadfastness.
The commentary makes repeated work over time a defining completed act; Paul says he fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.

row.basis: righteous crown due on the day
row.note: The commentary's finished work and patient wait meet a day of due recompense; Paul says the righteous judge will award him the crown on that day.
The commentary's true word can become a defended standard under mortal threat; the faithful conquer by their testimony and do not cling to life even when facing death.
The commentary's patience keeps connected people from splitting apart; Jesus says increasing lawlessness makes the love of many grow cold before his call to endure.
The commentary tests whether a sound deed nourishes the next person; the king names feeding, giving drink, and welcoming as acts that mark those accepted at judgment.

row.basis: care for least counted as service
row.note: The commentary's mutual support gives a needy neighbor a concrete claim; the king identifies deeds done for the least of his brothers with deeds done for him.

row.basis: believers gather with things in common
row.note: The commentary's scattered patches become a joined group; Acts says believers stay together and hold their possessions in common before describing need-based distribution.
The commentary's shared hak is an actual material due; believers lay sale proceeds at the apostles' feet and distribution is made according to need.

row.basis: life lost for true message is saved
row.note: The commentary's rescue from loss can require holding fast under threat; Jesus says one who loses life for him and the gospel will save it.
The commentary contrasts handing on hak with pulling it into a dispute; Paul describes the self-seeking as disobedient to truth and obedient to injustice.
The commentary contrasts capital that distracts with useful fruit that lasts; Jesus says life's cares, riches, and pleasures choke the heard word so its hearers fail to mature fruit.

The commentary's guarantor carries another's weakness and its worker anticipates gain; Ignatius urges Polycarp to bear everyone's infirmities like a trained athlete and links harder labor to greater gain.
The commentary's hard stone and straight blow make patience a strength under impact; Ignatius compares the addressed leader to an anvil that receives strikes and stays firm.
The commentary's day of work comes to its wage; Clement contrasts the diligent worker who can receive bread from the employer with the idle one who cannot face him.

row.basis: shared funds sustain people in need
row.note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel must become practical provision; Justin describes a gathered Christian community collecting voluntary gifts for orphans, widows, the sick, strangers, and prisoners.
The commentary's linked pasture feeds people unable to sustain themselves; Tertullian describes voluntary community contributions used for the poor, bereaved, aged, shipwrecked, and imprisoned.

row.basis: world as antechamber for coming world
row.note: The commentary's brief working day prepares an enduring recompense; this saying makes the present world a vestibule in which a person prepares for the next, though its architectural image only indirectly meets the commentary's work-and-wage scene.

row.basis: patience rules anger and supports right acts
row.note: The commentary's sabır restrains the inner eruption before it harms others; Hermas contrasts patience with anger and connects patience with righteous conduct, though subsection numbering varies among editions.

row.note: The commentary's exception joins belief, righteous deeds, and mutual exhortation to patience; Revelation calls the endurance of the saints those who keep God's commands and faith in Jesus. It brings the same cluster of fidelity and perseverance into an apocalyptic community.

The commentary makes sabr something believers enjoin on one another; Paul tells the congregation to encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone. Its context makes patience a shared practice toward vulnerable people.

The commentary pairs righteous action with reciprocal counsel to patience; Paul joins not growing weary in doing good with the promise of harvest for those who do not give up. The link makes ethical work a practice sustained through waiting.

row.basis: mutual encouragement as the Day approaches
row.note: The commentary's repeated tawāṣaw is reciprocal counsel; Hebrews tells believers to encourage one another, increasingly as they see the Day approaching. It locates mutual support inside an expectation that calls for endurance.

The commentary glosses sabr as holding oneself back from panic; Proverbs ranks slowness to anger above military might and ruling one's spirit above capturing a city. It makes self-restraint a form of strength rather than domination.

The commentary contrasts the self-held person with the person held by others; Proverbs likens a person without self-control to a breached city without walls. The image makes restraint protection against becoming capturable.

The commentary's B001 gloss says sabr holds the self back from panic or outcry; Proverbs contrasts a fool who vents his whole spirit with a wise person who stills it. This is a direct wisdom parallel for keeping an impulse from spilling out.

The commentary presents sabr as self-restraint; Ben Zoma interprets Proverbs' ruler of his spirit as the truly mighty person who subdues his inclination. This Jewish reading turns the proverb's city-conquest comparison into inward mastery.

The commentary calls the withholding hand miserly and cites the human who holds back from spending; Proverbs says one who withholds what should be given comes to want. It makes retention itself a path into the loss the surah announces.

The commentary joins the withholding of wealth to the soul pledged for what it earns; in Jesus' parable the rich fool enlarges his barns, then has his life demanded that night. The verse makes material accumulation unable to retain life.

The commentary calls the human captive to death; Hebrews says people are held in lifelong slavery through fear of death, and its surrounding argument presents Christ as liberator. This supplies a Christian account of death as captivity rather than only an individual fate.

row.basis: held for slaughter, silent under oppression
row.note: The commentary's B002 gloss describes the one held for death; Isaiah's servant is oppressed and led like a lamb to slaughter, yet does not open his mouth. The verse brings external restraint and inward silence together in one figure.

The commentary sets the person held for killing beside the one who holds himself back; Peter says Christ did not retaliate or threaten when suffering, but entrusted himself to the just judge. It reads restraint under injustice as chosen trust rather than mere helplessness.

row.basis: bound and delivered to the governor
row.note: The commentary's B002 gloss is a person detained for death; Matthew says the leaders bound Jesus and delivered him to Pilate, leading into the execution narrative. This gives the passive, externally held figure a concrete Passion setting.

The commentary describes al-maṣbūra as one kept for death; in the Aqedah Abraham binds Isaac and places him on the altar before the killing is stopped. The scene gives a specific near-sacrifice example while preserving the difference that Isaac is spared.

The commentary's B002 image is a person bound for killing; Genesis Rabbah has Isaac ask to be bound securely so that he will not flinch and invalidate the offering. The midrash makes external restraint also an act of the victim's self-control.

The commentary cites Jonah as the prophet who called out while constricted and warns against his response; WLC Jonah records his prayer beginning with a call from distress in the fish, followed by God's answer. The shared scene exposes the difference between a distress-call and the commentary's demand to wait.

row.basis: receiving adversity without speech against God
row.note: The commentary glosses sabr as holding oneself back from panic or lament; after Job's losses he refuses his wife's counsel to curse God and does not sin with his lips. Job supplies a concrete response to calamity through restrained speech.

row.basis: the eye of God on those who wait
row.note: The commentary quotes the prophet told to be patient because he is in God's eyes; this psalm places the LORD's eye on those who hope in his steadfast love. It joins waiting with being watched, rather than leaving patience as an unseen private effort.
The commentary explains sabr as waiting for the Lord's decree; the psalmist waits for the LORD and hopes in his word. It gives the waiting stance a textual object and a first-person prayer form.

The commentary's waiting sabr looks toward the Lord's judgment; James compares it with a farmer patiently awaiting the precious crop through the early and late rains. The agrarian image makes delay a season that must be borne.

row.basis: communal fast before a risk of death
row.note: The commentary's B015 gloss calls fasting a form of self-restraint; Esther asks the Jews to fast for three days before she approaches the king despite the death penalty. The fast becomes communal preparation and solidarity before a lethal risk.

The commentary equates fasting with self-restraint; the Mishnah specifies Yom Kippur's abstentions, including eating and drinking. It gives the Torah's self-affliction a concrete ritual practice and limits what the word alone states.

The commentary calls fasting restraint of one's own self; Isaiah says the fast God chooses loosens wicked bonds and frees the oppressed. The prophetic text redirects attention from self-denial toward releasing people held by others.

The commentary describes the miserly hand withholding wealth and grain; Isaiah's fast includes sharing bread with the hungry and bringing the homeless poor into one's house. It turns restraint from consumption into generosity toward others.

The commentary's B015 gloss treats fasting as one form of self-restraint; Matthew says Jesus fasts forty days and nights and becomes hungry. This gives the restraint a sustained Christian practice in a wilderness testing scene.

The commentary's B013 gloss reads sabr as daring toward Fire, sarcastically of those choosing error; Daniel's three Judeans refuse the king's image even if God does not rescue them from the furnace. Their courage is fidelity under threat, a pointed contrast to defiant indifference toward punishment.

row.basis: bound and thrown into the furnace
row.note: The commentary describes the person held for death and also develops courage toward fire; Daniel says the youths are bound and cast into the furnace, but later appear unbound. The narrative combines captors' restraint and fiery danger while reversing the expected death.

The commentary's B013 gloss develops audacity toward Fire; Sirach says gold is tested by fire and acceptable people by the furnace of humiliation. It changes fire from final punishment to a trial that discloses steadfastness.

row.basis: the martyr's answer to a threat of fire
row.note: The commentary's B013 gloss hears boldness toward Fire; Polycarp tells the proconsul that a brief earthly fire is less than the coming judgment and invites him to proceed. The Christian martyr text makes that boldness a refusal to abandon Christ under execution.

The commentary makes mutual counsel to patience part of the exception from loss; the mother in 2 Maccabees encourages each son as they face execution for refusing forbidden food. Her words make steadfastness communal under coercion and orient it toward resurrection hope.

The commentary's B001 gloss is holding the self back from panic; 4 Maccabees opens by asking whether devout reason rules the passions. Its philosophical frame makes self-restraint the governing question for the martyr stories that follow.

The commentary's B002 gloss describes a person held for death; Wisdom says the ungodly plot to condemn the righteous person to a shameful death because his life differs from theirs. It makes the held victim's righteousness, rather than guilt, the occasion for the sentence.

row.basis: Job's endurance and the Lord's outcome
row.note: The commentary treats patience as waiting for God's judgment; James names Job's endurance and points readers to the Lord's compassionate purpose. This Christian reading makes Job's suffering a model of endurance whose outcome rests with God.

The commentary calls sabr waiting for the Lord's judgment; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will in order to receive what was promised. It connects patience to a delayed divine outcome, not passive time alone.

row.basis: Arabic ء ن س and Hebrew אנש; table correspondence, BDB notes Arabic
row.note: The commentary explicitly labels al-insān with Arabic root ء ن س and reads the human as death-bound; Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ in this verse is returned to dust. The table treats אנש as a regular sound correspondence and notes BDB's Arabic cognate, giving the human term a specifically mortal setting.

row.basis: Arabic ء ن س and Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary labels al-insān with root ء ن س as the human held for death; Aramaic bar ʾĕnāš in Daniel's vision is brought before the Ancient of Days and receives dominion. The table's sound candidate connects the human designation to an apocalyptic reversal, without proving cognacy.

The commentary's image joins a person held for slaughter to self-restraint; Acts quotes Isaiah's lamb led to slaughter and silent before its shearer. The quotation carries that double image into a Christian scene of scriptural reading; Philip's interpretation is stated separately in Acts 8:35.

row.basis: the servant interpreted as good news about Jesus
row.note: The commentary fuses being held with holding oneself back; Philip begins from the Isaiah passage and proclaims Jesus. This New Testament interpretation makes the silent, slaughtered servant a Passion reading, extending the connection beyond the quotation in Acts 8:32.

row.basis: compelling a prophet to swear truthfully
row.note: The commentary's B002 source gloss gives ṣabartu yamīnahu as making someone swear; Ahab asks how often he must adjure Micaiah to speak only truth in YHWH's name. This is a direct coercive-oath scene, unlike the surah's mutual counsel to truth.

The commentary's B002 gloss includes compelling someone by an oath; the high priest adjures detained Jesus by the living God to say whether he is the Messiah. Matthew's detail is an oath-bound demand for testimony, though Jesus is adjured to answer rather than made to swear an oath himself.

The commentary's B002 lexicographic example describes making another swear; Saul puts the troops under a curse-oath not to eat until evening. The scene makes restraint externally imposed and bodily costly rather than chosen self-discipline.

The commentary's B015 source identifies fasting as a type of sabr because the self abstains; Saul's oath forces the troops to refrain from food until evening. The shared abstention sharpens the difference between a chosen fast and another person's command.

The commentary's B015 source connects fasting with holding oneself back; Leviticus commands the community to afflict itself on the Day of Atonement and cease work. It places bodily restraint within a collective ritual; the verse itself says self-affliction rather than explicitly naming a fast.

row.basis: faith tested like gold in fire
row.note: The commentary cites the audacious patience of the condemned toward Fire; Peter compares tested faith to gold refined through fire. The shared fire image shifts from punishment to a process that proves faith under trial.

The commentary has believers mutually enjoin truth and patience; Sirach urges striving for truth even to death and says God will fight for the faithful. It makes the cost of holding to truth explicit and joins it to trust in divine vindication.

The commentary's B001 gloss explains sabr as holding the self back; Sirach tells the reader not to follow base desires but to restrain appetites. This gives the inward act a concrete ethical object beyond merely waiting.

row.basis: the father releases the son's property
row.note: The commentary's B006 source gives a father withholding his child's property; the younger son asks for his share and the father divides his property between the sons. The reversed transfer makes the parent-child relation a specific counterexample to retention, though the parable develops a different issue.

row.basis: the righteous held in God's hand
row.note: The commentary cites the soul as pledged for what it earns; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and no torment touches them. It turns being held from punitive custody into protection, qualifying a simple reading of captivity.

row.basis: stored grain cannot secure the soul
row.note: The commentary's B010 source describes grain guarded in its husk, and its B006 image is wealth held back; Jesus' rich fool stores abundant produce but is told his life is required that night. The parable contrasts preserved goods with a life that cannot be kept.

row.basis: grain must die to bear fruit
row.note: The commentary's B010 source presents grain kept safe in its husk; Jesus' grain of wheat remains alone unless it falls into the earth and dies, then bears much fruit. The image offers a contrary valuation of preservation: fruitful life requires surrender rather than enclosure.

row.basis: unquenched fire and the fate of rebels
row.note: The commentary cites the question of how daring people are toward Fire as a warning about punishment; Isaiah ends with observers seeing the corpses of rebels where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. It specifies the irreversible judgment behind the fire image.

row.basis: hope under threat, with a textual split
row.note: The commentary treats sabr as waiting for God's judgment; Job speaks under threat of being killed, but WLC's ketiv לֹא reads no hope while its qere לוֹ supports hoping in God. The verse holds protest and patient trust together without resolving the textual alternative.

The commentary's B009 source gloss calls a young woman held at home at first menses; Leviticus gives a menstruating woman seven days of impurity and rules for contact, but does not say she is confined indoors. It is a concrete ritual frame for bodily separation, not evidence of the same social practice.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر and Hebrew עצר; table sound candidate only
row.note: The commentary labels al-ʿaṣr B006 as restraint and al-muʿṣir B009 as a girl held indoors; Hebrew עצר here says God closed every womb in Abimelech's house. The table's sound correspondence supplies a bodily restraint comparison, but this is reproductive stoppage, not menstrual confinement.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر and Hebrew צבר; table sound candidate only
row.note: The commentary labels ṣabr B001 as self-restraint and separately describes grain kept in its husk as ʿaṣr B010; Hebrew צבר here is Joseph piling up grain for famine stores. Accumulation is a specific neighboring sense of retaining grain, though Joseph's public reserve differs from miserly withholding and cognacy is unverified.

row.basis: faith and patience inheriting the promise
row.note: The commentary's exception begins with belief and ends with mutual counsel to sabr; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. This gives the faith-patience pairing a concrete inheritance horizon.

The commentary pairs righteous deeds with patience; Paul describes those who seek glory and immortality through endurance in good work and receive eternal life. It joins ethical action and perseverance in a judgment setting.

row.basis: mutually spurring love and good works
row.note: The commentary says believers repeatedly counsel one another and do righteous deeds; Hebrews asks the community to consider how to stir one another to love and good works. This is a distinct reciprocal-action detail from the encouragement in Hebrews 10:25.

row.basis: Jeremiah lowered into a cistern to die
row.note: The commentary's B002 image is a person held for death; Ebed-Melech says Jeremiah was put in the cistern to die of hunger because no bread remained. The verse supplies an explicit instance of detention with death as its intended outcome.

row.basis: asking that a sin not be held against killers
row.note: The commentary says each soul is held to what it has earned; while being stoned, Stephen asks the Lord not to hold this sin against his killers. The dying victim's plea reverses the image of deeds holding a person liable.

row.basis: delayed judgment as patience for repentance
row.note: The commentary has the prophet wait for the Lord's judgment; Peter says the Lord's apparent delay is patience, allowing people time to reach repentance rather than perish. It makes waiting itself a merciful postponement of loss.

row.basis: the returning master finds servants watching
row.note: The commentary says the one who waits is under observation; Jesus blesses servants whom their returning master finds awake and watching. This gives the watched wait an eschatological household scene and a reward for readiness.

The commentary defines sabr as waiting for the Lord's decree; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and, even if it seems delayed, the hearer must wait for it. It makes delay part of the promise rather than evidence that it failed.

The commentary calls sabr a wait for the Lord's judgment; the psalmist says he waited patiently for the LORD, who inclined to hear his cry. This gives waiting an urgent prayer setting rather than making it a general disposition.

The commentary sets self-restraint beside being held by another; the next verse says the LORD draws the psalmist from a destructive pit and mud. This supplies a specific image of release from confinement, distinct from the preceding verse's patient wait.

The commentary opposes sabr to panic and describes waiting for the Lord's judgment; Lamentations says it is good to wait quietly for the LORD's salvation in the aftermath of Jerusalem's ruin. It gives restrained waiting a voice within communal catastrophe.

row.basis: God slow to anger after rebellion
row.note: The commentary makes patience restraint and waiting for judgment; after Israel's breach, God describes himself as slow to anger and abundant in steadfast love. It adds divine patience as the quality that makes judgment and renewed relationship coexist.

row.basis: the Lord waits to show grace and blesses those who wait
row.note: The commentary has the prophet wait for the Lord's decree and says the waiting person remains in God's sight; Isaiah says the LORD waits to show grace and blesses those who wait for him. The two-sided waiting makes delay a merciful encounter.

The commentary glosses sabr as holding oneself back from panic or outcry; the Talmud praises people who suffer insult without insulting back or replying. Its reading of the lovers of God in Judges 5:31 turns restraint under humiliation into a sign of devotion.

The commentary says humanity is in loss except for those who do righteous deeds; in Jesus' parable the owner reports three years of seeking fruit from a tree that bears none and orders it cut down. It gives fruitlessness a specific scene of impending loss.

row.basis: delaying the felling for another year
row.note: The commentary frames sabr as waiting for the Lord's judgment; in the same parable the gardener asks that the tree be left one more year to be dug around and fertilized. The delay gives the condemned tree time to bear fruit.

row.basis: reinterpreting apparent loss as hidden good
row.note: The commentary presents humanity as being in loss and patience as waiting for God's decree; Rabbi Akiva interprets a chain of setbacks as for the good after those very losses protect his life. This Jewish story preserves trust without pretending the setbacks initially look beneficial.

row.basis: refusing coerced food at the cost of death
row.note: The commentary distinguishes self-restraint from being restrained by another and calls fasting a kind of sabr; Eleazar is pressured to eat forbidden meat but accepts torture rather than violate the law. The martyr narrative makes bodily abstention an act of chosen fidelity under lethal coercion.

row.basis: waiting for grace rather than immediate judgment
row.note: The commentary's waiting sabr is directed toward God's ruling; Isaiah links the Lord's own waiting to grace. This adds the specific reading of divine delay as mercy, distinct from the verse's reciprocal pattern of the Lord and people waiting.

row.basis: Joseph's prison cupbearer dream; grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup
row.note: The commentary's imprisoned cupbearer dreams of pressing grapes and serving wine; Genesis gives the same prison dream in which the cupbearer squeezes grapes into Pharaoh's cup, a direct scene parallel.

The commentary says the cupbearer forgets Joseph after his release, leaving Joseph in prison; Genesis likewise says the restored cupbearer did not remember Joseph, making the delay part of the shared story.
The commentary makes delayed recollection lengthen Joseph's imprisonment; Genesis marks two full years before Pharaoh dreams and the cupbearer remembers, giving that wait a measured duration.

The commentary's freed cupbearer remembers Joseph only after a long interval; Genesis has him recall his failure before Pharaoh and recount Joseph's prison interpretation, ending the forgotten interval.

The commentary links Joseph's seven abundant years with preserving grain for scarcity; Genesis says Joseph gathers the produce of those years and stores food in the cities, the same plan of holding yield through time.

row.basis: End of the years of plenty
row.note: The commentary orders Joseph's story as abundance, hard years, then renewed yield; Genesis says the seven years of plenty end, marking the same turn in the agricultural calendar.
The commentary's stored grain is for the years of hardship; Genesis says famine begins and the land still has food in Egypt, showing the preserved yield surviving the time of loss.
The commentary's final Joseph year restores productive pressing after scarcity; Genesis has all lands come to Egypt to buy grain, showing stored abundance flowing outward when famine arrives.

row.basis: Oath and exclusion from the sworn land
row.note: The commentary places an oath just before a verdict of loss; Numbers says the rebellious generation will not see the land sworn to their ancestors, joining oath, missed inheritance, and a closed future.

After the generation is excluded, Numbers singles out Caleb, who followed fully and will enter the land; this gives a precise biblical instance of a general loss followed by an exception for the faithful.

row.basis: A thousand years as a day and night watch
row.note: The commentary holds a long era and a short day-part together; the psalm measures a thousand years as yesterday or a night watch, explicitly collapsing vast time into a brief interval.

The commentary hears the afternoon as a closing day with dwindling light and a life nearing its end; the psalm describes grass flourishing in the morning and fading by evening, making mortality visible in the daily cycle.

row.basis: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
row.note: The commentary says the same word can name an era and a person's age; the psalm measures human years at seventy or eighty and says they soon fly, linking a long life to a finite span.

row.basis: Oath that bars entry into rest
row.note: The commentary's opening oath stands at the threshold of a verdict; the psalm ends its warning with God's sworn denial of entry into rest, a close formal and thematic parallel of oath followed by loss.

row.basis: Merchants impatient for the sacred day to end
row.note: The commentary makes the day's closing edge a time when work and opportunity run short; Amos depicts grain sellers asking when the new moon and Sabbath will end so they can trade and falsify measures, turning sacred time into an obstacle to profit.

row.basis: An oath against those who exploit the poor
row.note: The commentary's garden owners swear to keep the poor from their harvest; Amos has the Lord swear not to forget merchants who trample the needy, joining oath, withheld food, and judgment.

The commentary's garden owners plan to exclude the poor from their crop; Deuteronomy commands leaving remaining grapes for the stranger, orphan, and widow, setting shared yield against total retention.

The commentary contrasts a hand that keeps produce with one that lets its extract become a gift; Proverbs says people curse the one who withholds grain and bless the seller, making the ethical difference between retention and release explicit.

The commentary hears afternoon as the closing part of the day, when undone work has little time left; Jesus says to do the work while it is day because night comes when no one can work, making the shrinking window explicit.

row.basis: Pressed measure overflowing as a gift
row.note: The commentary makes pressing yield an image of generosity when the extract flows out; Jesus describes a measure pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing into another's lap, a striking image of abundance given away.

row.basis: A thirsty tongue with no available sip
row.note: The commentary's dried tongue and failed rescue-sip image meets the rich man after death asking for a drop of water to cool his tongue; Luke makes relief unavailable after the decisive time has passed.

The commentary's withheld garden yield ends in deprivation; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but their conditions are now reversed, making the lost opportunity irreversible.

row.basis: Full wage for the eleventh-hour workers
row.note: The commentary's closing hour warns that little time remains to finish work; Jesus' parable pays those hired at the eleventh hour a full denarius, countering the assumption that a late start must mean a diminished share.

The commentary links refuge in a cave with sleep that seems brief to the sleepers but spans centuries; Honi sleeps within a rocky shelter for seventy years and wakes into a changed generation, a Jewish time-dislocation parallel.

row.ref: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 1.95
row.note: The commentary's cave youths sleep through centuries and wake in a changed age; Gregory recounts the Christian Seven Sleepers of Ephesus in their cave, a direct narrative parallel whose chronology varies among tellings.

row.basis: Hebrews repeats the oath of exclusion
row.note: The commentary frames the oath as the threshold to a verdict of loss; Hebrews quotes Psalm 95's oath that the wilderness generation will not enter God's rest, reading the oath as a warning about salvation and missed time.

The commentary moves from loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews interprets the wilderness oath by saying that those who believe enter the rest, giving faith the role of escape from the exclusion.

row.basis: Midrash explains Joseph's extra prison years
row.note: The commentary treats the cupbearer's forgetting as a long delay; Genesis Rabbah reads Joseph's doubled plea to be remembered as the reason for two more years in prison, turning the delay into a lesson about reliance and trust.

The commentary describes asr as the hour when work is nearly done and remaining time narrows; the psalm says people go out to work and labor until evening, giving that closing edge an ordinary workday scene.

row.basis: Prayer at evening, morning, and noon
row.note: The commentary pairs devotion at the day's two edges; the psalmist says he prays at evening, morning, and noon, extending the pattern into a full daily cycle.
The commentary hears the day's beginning and close together; the psalm appoints praise of steadfast love in the morning and faithfulness at night, a daily liturgical counterpart.
The commentary names the afternoon prayer and the day's closing edge; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense and raised hands like an evening offering, joining prayer to the late-day rite.

row.basis: Prayer times bounded by afternoon and evening
row.note: The commentary notes that asr can name the afternoon prayer; the Mishnah sets the afternoon prayer's time until evening, placing a daily prayer within the same shrinking daylight boundary.

row.basis: Isaac's evening meditation read as afternoon prayer
row.note: The commentary leaves open whether asr is the afternoon hour or a wider span of time; the Talmud derives the afternoon prayer from Isaac going out to meditate toward evening, giving that hour a Jewish interpretive tradition.

The commentary includes the afternoon prayer among possible senses of asr; Acts places Peter and John at the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer, showing a Christian practice at a named late-day hour.

The commentary describes the squeezed extract as generosity flowing outward; the angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and alms have risen as a memorial, linking devotional practice with concrete giving.

The commentary names a fixed afternoon prayer within the day; Tertullian recognizes third, sixth, and ninth hours as customary times for prayer, showing a Christian daily rhythm that includes the closing daylight hours.

row.basis: Daily offerings at morning and twilight
row.note: The commentary pairs the day's edges and names the afternoon prayer; Exodus assigns one lamb to morning and another to twilight, a daily ritual cycle ending as daylight closes.

row.basis: Rain waters furrows and blesses growth
row.note: The commentary traces rain from squeezed clouds to grain and plants; the psalm describes God watering furrows with showers and blessing their growth, a close rain-to-crop sequence.
The commentary lets asr name both a day-part and a long age, then links time to yield; the psalm says God crowns the year with goodness, joining a temporal cycle to its harvest.

row.basis: Rain fills threshing floors and vats
row.note: The commentary's squeezed-cloud image leads to grain, plants, and gardens; Joel describes threshing floors full of grain and vats overflowing after rain, a parallel chain from water to agricultural abundance.
The commentary's pressing can yield a gift or leave a dry remainder; Joel summons the sickle and treading of a full winepress as the nations' judgment, making the same harvest image destructive.

row.basis: The divine warrior treads the winepress alone
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the flowing extract from the dry residue; Isaiah pictures God treading the winepress until garments are stained with blood, a counter-image in which pressing signifies judgment rather than bounty.

row.basis: The earth's vintage cast into God's winepress
row.note: The commentary's grape pressing may stand for a good yield; Revelation gathers the earth's vintage and casts it into the winepress of divine wrath, giving the harvest image an apocalyptic judgment sense.
The commentary describes pressing as separating liquid from dry pulp; Revelation says blood flows from the trampled winepress, turning that flow into a measure of catastrophic judgment.

row.basis: A rich man counts on many years of stored goods
row.note: The commentary's garden owner has a final crop and an aging life; Luke's rich farmer stores abundant produce and assumes many years ahead, making stored yield a wager on future time.

The commentary's old orchard owner loses the one harvest on which he depends; God tells Luke's farmer his life is required that very night, making the end of time arrive before expected use of stored goods.

row.basis: A great wind kills the children in a collapsing house
row.note: The commentary's garden is destroyed by a whirlwind while its owner has weak descendants; Job reports a wind that collapses a house onto his children, a specific parallel of destructive wind and vulnerable offspring.

row.basis: A plant briefly shelters a distressed person
row.note: The commentary calls asr a refuge for the distressed; Jonah's plant grows to shade him from discomfort, giving shelter a temporary, living form that can soon be lost.
The commentary calls the refuge a haven for a person in distress; the psalm names God as refuge and strength, a help in trouble, matching the concrete relation of shelter to pressure.
The commentary says lineage can be a place of refuge; Proverbs says the children of one who fears the Lord have refuge, directly joining descent and protection.
The commentary links refuge to armor that wraps and protects the body; Paul describes the shield of faith extinguishing flaming arrows, giving the protective covering an ethical and spiritual use.

The commentary describes time's pressure as extracting an essence and connects the surah's final patience to a bitter extract; James says tested faith produces endurance, a specific ethical parallel between trial and patient strength.

row.basis: The delayed bridegroom and sleeping waiters
row.note: The commentary includes late arrival and a sleep that may last only a moment; Matthew's bridegroom is delayed and the waiting women all grow sleepy and sleep, placing delay and sleep inside a story about readiness.

row.basis: The door closes before the late arrivals
row.note: The commentary warns that work left undone near day's end may run out of time; Matthew's late bridesmaids arrive after the door is shut, making delay a lost opportunity.

row.basis: Menstruation as a timed ritual boundary
row.note: The commentary's lexicon describes the first menstruating girl as held at home for protection; Leviticus assigns menstrual bleeding a seven-day impurity and contact rules, offering a distinct ritual reading of that timed threshold rather than confirming the commentary's protective etymology.

row.note: The package table gives Hebrew עצר a festival-assembly sense; Leviticus marks the eighth day with a sacred assembly, a calendrical use alongside the commentary's afternoon prayer and day-boundary senses, without establishing cognacy.

row.basis: A day and a thousand years
row.note: The commentary holds the long age and short day-part together; Second Peter applies the psalm's thousand-years-as-a-day scale to the apparent delay of the Lord's coming, making divine and human time differ.

The commentary includes the sense of a late arrival and the dwindling time left to act; Second Peter interprets apparent delay as patience that gives people time to repent, turning lateness into mercy.

row.basis: Life as a mist that appears briefly
row.note: The commentary lets asr range from a long era to a fleeting instant; James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and vanishes, a precise but less developed image of life's short span.

row.basis: Arabic ص ب ر / Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary links its final word ṣabr, patience, to a bitter tree extract and to waiting through lean years while grain is saved; Genesis says Joseph heaped grain in extraordinary quantity. The table's ص ب ر / צבר match is only an unverified sound correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary gives the Arabic dictionary sense of al-ʿaṣr as holding or detaining; Manoah asks to detain his visitor while preparing food, using Hebrew עצר. The package table marks the sound match as a candidate only.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary includes late or slow arrival and the sense of being held back; the Shunammite tells her servant not to slow her journey to Elisha, using Hebrew עצר. This is a precise semantic echo but the table does not verify cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary connects holding tightly with refuge and protection; Aaron stands between the dead and living while the plague is stopped with Hebrew עצר, a protective restraint that echoes that image.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary links squeezed rain clouds to grain and plants; Deuteronomy uses Hebrew עצר for shutting the heavens so rain and crop fail, a relevant withholding sense, though the root match remains unverified.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary contrasts rain that flows from clouds with a dry, pressed remnant; Job says that when God holds back waters they dry up, and when he releases them they flood the land, a close semantic fit through the table's unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The commentary describes a young woman held at a reproductive threshold; Genesis says God had closed the wombs of Abimelech's household using Hebrew עצר, a specific withholding sense but not proof that the roots are cognate.

row.basis: Joseph asks the released cupbearer to remember him
row.note: The commentary notes Joseph's request to be remembered and the cupbearer's later forgetting; Genesis gives the request itself, asking the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh and bring him out of prison.
The commentary places Joseph's waiting in prison; the psalm retells his story as feet bound in fetters until the promised time, giving the confinement a bodily image.

row.basis: Joseph tested until his word comes true
row.note: The commentary arranges Joseph's prison years around delayed remembrance and eventual release; the psalm says the word of the Lord tested Joseph until what he had said came to pass, interpreting the delay as a trial.
The commentary follows Joseph's reading of Pharaoh's dream as a calendar of plenty and scarcity; Genesis predicts seven years of great abundance throughout Egypt, specifying the productive span.
The commentary's Joseph narrative turns from years of yield to years of hardship; Genesis forecasts seven years of famine after the abundance, making the saved grain's time horizon explicit.

row.basis: The plenty is forgotten in famine
row.note: The commentary says the hard years consume what was stored; Genesis adds that the famine is so severe that the former plenty is no longer remembered, a sharper account of yield erased by loss.

row.basis: The land produces abundantly during the good years
row.note: The commentary follows the movement from productive years to preserved grain; Genesis says the land yields abundantly through the seven years, the harvest that makes Joseph's storage possible.

row.basis: Joseph opens the storehouses in famine
row.note: The commentary ends Joseph's cycle with renewed access to produce after scarcity; Genesis says Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain during the famine, showing reserve released when need arrives.
The commentary's garden owners plan to keep the poor from their crop; Amos addresses people who trample the needy and bring the poor to an end, naming the injustice that the garden scene dramatizes.

row.basis: Poor people traded for silver while wheat is sold
row.note: The commentary contrasts hoarded produce with giving; Amos condemns buyers who acquire the poor for silver and sell even wheat refuse, making grain control an instrument of exploitation.

row.basis: Do not close the hand against the poor
row.note: The commentary describes holding a gift back and excluding the poor from a garden; Deuteronomy forbids hardening the heart or shutting the hand against a poor kinsman, a direct ethical counterpoint.

row.basis: Open the hand to meet another's need
row.note: The commentary says squeezing can let its extract flow as generosity; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need, making release the ethical response to scarcity.

row.basis: Give freely without a grudging heart
row.note: The commentary contrasts a generous person with one who withholds or reclaims a gift; Deuteronomy commands giving without regret and promises blessing for the work, joining openhandedness to fruitful outcome.

row.basis: A forgotten sheaf left for the poor
row.note: The commentary's owners plan to keep a garden's entire yield from the poor; Deuteronomy says a forgotten sheaf must remain for the stranger, orphan, and widow, applying release to grain harvest.

row.basis: Ruth allowed to glean among the sheaves
row.note: The commentary's garden owners bar the poor from entering; Boaz tells his workers to let Ruth glean even among the sheaves and not reproach her, reversing exclusion in a concrete harvest scene.

row.basis: Extra grain deliberately left for Ruth
row.note: The commentary treats a crop's extract as a gift that may either flow or be retained; Boaz orders handfuls pulled from the bundles and left for Ruth, making generosity exceed mere permission to glean.

row.basis: A close relative as guardian and redeemer
row.note: The commentary says ancestry and kinship can be a refuge; Naomi identifies Boaz as a near kinsman and redeemer, where family connection becomes practical protection and provision.

row.basis: The day is short, work is abundant, and the master presses
row.note: The commentary calls late afternoon the point when work is nearly done and time for unfinished tasks narrows; this saying makes the same pressure explicit through a short day, much work, and an urgent master.

row.basis: An oath measures the time until oppression ends
row.note: The commentary opens with an oath on time and leaves the promised verdict just beyond the verse; Daniel's angel swears by the living God and gives a measured period whose end coincides with the breaking of the holy people's power.

row.basis: Blessed is the one who waits to the appointed days
row.note: The commentary includes delayed arrival, a fleeting moment, and patience through hard years; Daniel blesses the person who waits and reaches the stated number of days, linking endurance to a measured end.

row.basis: An oath that there will be no more delay
row.note: The commentary hears both a broad age and a late, shortened interval in asr; Revelation's angel swears that there will be no more delay before the mystery is completed, joining oath, waiting, and time's end.

row.basis: The oath is directed at the disobedient
row.note: The commentary places an oath before a verdict of loss; Hebrews continues its reading of Psalm 95 by identifying those excluded from rest as the disobedient, specifying why the sworn exclusion occurs.

The commentary moves from a general human loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews says the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, giving the faith contrast a precise interpretive role.

row.basis: The present day is still called Today
row.note: The commentary treats a named time as a threshold before action becomes too late; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and warns against hardening the heart, reading the old oath as a present opportunity.

row.basis: Prayer when heaven is shut and rain withheld
row.note: The commentary connects prayer at a set time with clouds, rain, and crop yield; Solomon prays for the people when heaven is closed and there is no rain, linking drought, prayer, repentance, and renewed provision.

row.basis: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The package table marks Hebrew עצר as a possible sound correspondence to Arabic ع ص ر; Solomon's prayer describes heaven being shut so rain stops, a relevant restraint of the rain that the commentary links to yield, without proving cognacy.

row.basis: God is refuge in the cave prayer
row.note: The commentary treats a cave as refuge for people whose time is hidden from them; Psalm 142's superscription places David in a cave, and the cited verse calls God his refuge and portion while he is in distress.

row.basis: Fleeing for refuge and holding fast to hope
row.note: The commentary joins seeking shelter with clinging tightly to a person or place; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge to seize the hope set before them, bringing refuge and grasping together.

row.basis: Daniel prays three times each day under threat
row.note: The commentary describes believers praying at the day's edges; Daniel continues praying three times daily toward Jerusalem despite a decree that endangers his life, showing fixed prayer times maintained under pressure.

row.basis: The Lord's Prayer said three times daily
row.note: The commentary names the afternoon prayer and describes morning-evening devotion; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, evidence of a timed daily discipline.

row.basis: Cornelius prays at the ninth hour
row.note: The commentary leaves open the afternoon-prayer sense of asr; Acts places Cornelius in prayer at the ninth hour when he sees an angel, a distinct Christian scene of late-day devotion.

The commentary lets one unqualified time-name span an afternoon, an era, or a fleeting interval; Jesus lists the night watches and warns that the master may come at any one of them, making readiness depend on an unknown hour.

The commentary describes perfume swelling and rising behind a passing person; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense, a distinct connection to the commentary's scent image apart from this verse's evening-offering detail.

row.basis: Wind releases garden spices and fruit
row.note: The commentary brings together wind, garden produce, and fragrance carried after movement; the Song calls on the winds to blow through a garden so its spices flow and its fruits can be eaten, joining those images in one scene.

row.basis: Fragrance set beside the day of death
row.note: The commentary follows a woman's perfume trail into a reflection on what remains after someone passes and also makes asr a life's closing time; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than fragrant oil and the day of death better than birth.

row.basis: Sow in the morning and keep working in the evening
row.note: The commentary says the late day leaves little time for work still undone and connects time with uncertain yield; Ecclesiastes commands sowing in the morning and not letting the hand rest in the evening because the outcome is unknown.

row.basis: Light darkens as old age approaches
row.note: The commentary hears afternoon's fading light alongside the end of a human life; Ecclesiastes depicts sun, light, moon, and stars darkening as the days of aging arrive, giving that decline a bodily and cosmic image.

row.basis: A life poured out as departure nears
row.note: The commentary treats squeezing as extracting a life-giving essence and asr as the close of a lifespan; Paul says he is already being poured out as a libation and that the time of his departure has come.

row.basis: Transformation in a moment at the last trumpet
row.note: The commentary holds long ages beside the instant and says a whole lifetime can shrink to a small part of a day; Paul places the change of the dead in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.

row.basis: A grain dies and bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary describes grain protected in its husk through scarcity and later used for food; Jesus says a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, making fruitful release rather than protected storage the condition of abundance.

row.basis: Harvest comes in due time to those who do not give up
row.note: The commentary links the final patience-word to waiting through lean years for stored grain to yield; Paul urges continued good work because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not grow weary.

row.basis: The tested righteous are refined like gold
row.note: The commentary says time's pressure extracts an essence and connects patience with a bitter extract; Wisdom pictures the tested righteous as gold tried in a furnace and accepted like a burnt offering, interpreting pressure as refinement.

row.basis: A material gift is a fragrant offering
row.note: The commentary makes pressed yield an image of generosity and perfume a good trace left behind; Paul calls the Philippians' delivered gift a fragrant offering, joining concrete giving with lingering fragrance.

row.basis: The fragrance of knowledge spreads everywhere
row.note: The commentary describes a scent rising and trailing after movement; Paul says God spreads the fragrance of knowledge through the apostles everywhere, turning a passing procession into a lasting trail.

row.basis: Aroma received differently by the saved and perishing
row.note: The commentary contrasts a good trace left behind with destructive dust and loss; Paul says the same aroma is associated with those being saved and those perishing, adding opposed outcomes to the scent image.

The commentary's poem imagines water itself as the thing choking the speaker, with no rescuing sip left; at Marah, God shows Moses a tree and the bitter water becomes sweet, a contrasting scene where the obstructing water is made into relief.

row.basis: The gardener asks for one more year
row.note: The commentary's old garden owner loses his final yield when there is no time or strength to plant again; Jesus' gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize the barren tree, making time an opportunity for restoration.

row.basis: Rich toward God rather than oneself
row.note: The commentary contrasts generous outflow with stored yield kept from others; Jesus concludes that the farmer who stores goods for himself is not rich toward God, giving the accumulation scene its ethical verdict.

row.basis: A fixed chasm makes relief impossible
row.note: The commentary's thirsty speaker has no remaining rescue sip; Abraham says a great chasm is fixed between the two places and no one can cross, explaining why the rich man's requested relief cannot arrive.

The commentary's pressed yield can leave only a dry remainder, and its garden owners lose what they tried to retain; James says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten, showing stored wealth failing to preserve its owner.

row.basis: Corroded treasure testifies in the last days
row.note: The commentary joins accumulation and the closing time of a life; James says hoarded gold and silver corrode and become evidence against their owners in the last days, making stored wealth a witness to judgment.

row.basis: Withheld wages cry out to God
row.note: The commentary describes a father withholding a child's property and garden owners denying the poor their produce; James says wages kept back from workers cry out, giving retention a concrete social and judicial consequence.

row.basis: Luxury before the day of slaughter
row.note: The commentary's aging garden owner loses the yield on which his future depends; James depicts the rich living in pleasure and fattening their hearts for a day of slaughter, joining abundance to an approaching end.

row.basis: Yusuf brothers' bloodied robe; visual testimony
row.note: The commentary quotes the brothers anticipating that Yaqub will not believe them; Genesis has them present Joseph's bloodied robe and ask their father to identify it. Both stage a claim through an object offered for inspection.

In the commentary's Qur'anic scene Yaqub rejects the brothers' account as something their souls invented; Genesis has him infer from the robe that Joseph was devoured. The changed response to misleading evidence is the point.

The commentary quotes the brothers saying their father would not believe them even if truthful; in Genesis they report Joseph is alive and Jacob does not believe them. The shared family scene turns on whether a report is credible.

The commentary permits a reading in which seeing precedes confirmation; Genesis says Jacob's spirit revives when he sees the wagons Joseph sent. Here visible evidence changes his response to the report.

The commentary quotes Musa saying he saw a fire and may bring back a coal or find guidance; Exodus has Moses see the angel of the LORD in a flame within a bush. The shared encounter presents fire as a visible sign, while the Qur'anic gloss stresses wayfinding.
The commentary develops seeing as noticing and examining; Moses turns aside to see why the bush is not consumed. The biblical scene makes looking an inquiry rather than mere sight.

The commentary's Yusuf example makes credibility the issue; Moses tells the LORD that Israel will not believe him or listen to his voice. This is a distinct biblical scene where a messenger worries that his report will not be accepted.
